Jacob names the place Bethel to underline this connection, anticipating a time in the future when God's presence will fill the earth. Jacob's dream of a meeting place between heaven and earth also points forward to Jesus Christ, the God-man who reunites heaven and earth (John 1:51 and note). Through Christ, the only "mediator between God and men" (1 Tim. 2:5), we have access to the Father (Eph. 2:18).

**LORD** stood above it. Or, "the LORD stood beside him." If this second reading is preferred (note Jacob's response in v. 16: "Surely the LORD is in this place"), then God comes down the stairway in Jacob's dream. He does not stand above the stairway, but over a sleeping Jacob. I am the LORD. See note on 27:20. land on which you lie. God's promise is adapted to the immediate situation. offspring. The Hebrew term here may be translated "seed" or "descendants" (12:7 note). The language of vv. 13–15 vividly recalls God's promises to Abraham (cf. 12:3; 13:14–16).

See 26:3; Ex. 3:12; Pss. 23; 46; Heb. 13:5. The promises of this verse pertain to Jacob's lifetime. wherever you go. In contrast to pagan deities, whose powers were thought to be tied to particular localities. until I have done. The Hebrew here signifies only that the promise will be completed, not that it will be changed after its fulfillment.
Worshipful fear in God's presence is appropriate (Ex. 3:6; 19:16; Ps. 2:11).
A witness and monument drawing attention to the importance of the place (cf. 31:45–59). poured oil. An act of consecration (35:14; Ex. 40:9; 2 Sam. 1:21).

The longest vow recorded in the OT. 28:20 If God will be with me. Jacob's reaction contrasts strikingly with Abraham's (15:6). Though Jacob's journey of faith has begun, he still has far to go. Note that God's unconditional promises of vv. 13–15 are here transformed into a conditional bargain: if God does His part, then Jacob will acknowledge Him as God (v. 21). God had sovereignly chosen Jacob in the womb (25:23 and note), and now He graciously bestows the patriarchal promise quite apart from Jacob's faith; that, too, must be the gift of God (17:2 note; Eph. 2:8-9).
See note on 14:20.

Jacob experiences the blessings of divine providence in meeting Rachel (vv. 1–14), and in a bitter irony the deceiver becomes the deceived (vv. 15–29). Behind the two scenes, the gracious and just hand of the sovereign God, who works all things according to His own purpose and who promised to be with Jacob (28:15), can be discerned.

The similarity of this meeting at the well with the meeting in 24:11–33 suggests the benevolence of divine providence but also highlights the contrast between the prayerful servant and the prayerless patriarch.
The greeting is a gesture of goodwill.

The stone is large (v. 2). Earlier the gold jewelry of Abraham's servant had attracted Laban's attention (24:30); now Jacob's feat of strength impresses Laban with the kind of service Jacob could render.
A customary greeting among relatives (v. 14; 31:55).
The name Rachel means "ewe," while Leah perhaps means "wild cow" or "wild ox."

As Jacob took advantage of his father's blindness to deceive him, so Laban uses the cover of night to outwit Jacob. he took his daughter Leah. The custom of veiling the bride (24:64, 65 note) and of marrying off the elder daughter first (v. 26) serve Laban's selfish intentions. He shamelessly uses his unloved daughter and introduces a source of continuing discord into Jacob's family (30:1, 2; 31:15). Laban's daughters are not deceived by his unscrupulous behavior (31:14–16).

This statement underscores the irony of Jacob's situation. Jacob has stolen the blessing customarily reserved for the firstborn (ch. 27), and here Laban deceives Jacob in order to uphold a similar custom.
The week of bridal feasting. The extended feast (v. 22) celebrates Laban's cleverness and Jacob's humiliation, turning what should be a joyous occasion into a bad joke.

God blesses Jacob with twelve sons in spite of his prayerlessness and the rivalry of Rachel and Leah, who compete for his affections by bearing him sons (25:19–35:29 note). The names the mothers give these children reflect this struggle and also their recognition of God's assistance to them in their unloved or childless states. God will graciously build up Israel by championing the needy (e.g., Hannah in 1 Sam. 1), but the spiritual failures of Jacob's family will later result in rivalries among Israelite tribes. 29:31–35 God graciously gives Leah, the unloved wife, half of Jacob's sons, including the priestly line of Levi (v. 34) and the messianic line of Judah (v. 35; 49:10). The first and last of the children born in Paddan-aram are given by the Lord to compensate disgraced wives, first Leah (v. 32), then Rachel (30:23, 24). 29:31 opened. See 16:2; 20:17, 18. barren. See 11:30; 25:21.
The name means "praised," here of the Lord, and in 49:8 of Judah himself.
A hyperbolic expression of her extreme distress (25:32; 27:46). Ironically, she later dies in childbirth (35:16–18).
Jacob's angry retort contrasts sharply with the fervent prayer of Isaac for his childless wife (25:21).

See 16:1, 2 and notes. on my behalf. Literally, "on my knees." The knee was symbolic of parental care (48:12; 50:23; Job 3:12). According to ancient Near Eastern custom, the delivery of the concubine's child upon the knees of the wife symbolized the adoption of the child by the wife.
Sometimes called "love apples," the roots of the mandrake plant were considered an aphrodisiac by the ancients and used to promote sexual activity and conception (cf. Song 7:13).
A dowry.
Because Dinah figures prominently in ch. 34, she is the only daughter of Jacob whose name is given (cf. 46:7).
See note on 8:1. This verse is the climax of 29:31–30:24. Rachel credits the birth of Joseph not to the aphrodisiac (v. 14 note) but to God (v. 23).

God sovereignly blesses Jacob's flocks at Laban's expense in spite of the inexcusable cunning of both men. Jacob appears to outwit Laban, repaying Laban's trickery, but he obtains his family and wealth entirely by God's grace (29:31–30:24; 31:9).

A formula of courtesy in negotiations. learned by divination. Many ancient extrabiblical texts from Mesopotamia pertain to the practice of occult divination, something forbidden in Israel (Deut. 18:10, 14). Noting Jacob's good fortune, the pagan Laban has attempted to discover the reason through divination (31:19 and note). blessed me because of you. Once again, others are blessed through their association with the patriarchs (12:2, 3; 13:5, 6; 14:13 and note). This anticipates the greater blessing that will come through Jesus Christ.
The opportunistic Laban is reluctant to let Jacob go, for he hopes to receive God's blessing.

In the ancient Near East, many lambs were white and most goats black or dark brown. Thinking the agreement poses little risk to himself, Laban eagerly grants Jacob's request for the unusually colored animals (v. 34). Even though Jacob's scheming denies God His rightful praise, God's intention to bless Jacob is not thwarted (31:11, 12).
The unscrupulous Laban immediately resorts to cheating. According to the agreement, the unusually colored animals should be Jacob's starting flock (v. 32). Jacob begins with none of these.
Jacob's success is due to God's grace (31:9–12).
God does abundantly more than Jacob has asked (28:20).

In fulfillment of His promise in 28:15, the Lord leads a chastened Jacob back to the Promised Land with great wealth at Laban's expense, and over Laban's opposition (v. 42). God remains faithful to His promises despite Jacob's scheming and the pagan idolatry in his household (v. 19 and note; 28:20 note).

Having previously fled from Canaan to avoid being killed by Esau, Jacob is now divinely instructed to go back. God's call comes at a time in his life when he is unsettled by Laban's attitude toward him. I will be with you. See 28:15 and notes.
Jacob responds to God in prompt obedience (cf. 12:4; 17:23; 22:3).
Acknowledging the Lord's faithfulness, Jacob is ready to pay his vow (v. 13; 28:20–22 and notes).
See note on 29:10.
Jacob deplores the magnitude of Laban's dishonesty. God did not permit him. In spite of his own schemes, Jacob recognizes that the Lord has blessed him.
See note on 30:31–34.
Through his dishonest behavior toward Jacob, Laban no longer enjoys God's blessing (12:3; 27:29).
See note on 16:7.
In bitterness against their dishonest father (vv. 14–15) and in recognition of God's providence (v. 16), Leah and Rachel decide to follow Jacob.

They resent that their father has squandered the bride price that Jacob gave to him; Rachel and Leah cannot look to their father for financial security in the future. The price paid was Jacob's labor (29:18, 27). devoured our money. This phrase occurs in similar social contexts in Mesopotamian texts from Nuzi (c. 1500 B.C.). Legally, at least part of the bride price received by a father in return for giving his daughter in marriage was to be given to the daughter.
See note on 25:20.

Small household gods or teraphim were thought to provide protection and were used in divination (30:27 note; Ezek. 21:21; Zech. 10:2). Unlike Sarah and Rebekah, Rachel has not given up her pagan idols or ethics (vv. 34, 35; 35:2). Perhaps Rachel hid the idols before she left Laban so that he could not use them to harm Jacob through divination.
Laban has military superiority (v. 29).
God sovereignly protects Jacob as He did Abraham (12:17; 20:3) and Isaac (26:8 and note).
Again Laban appeals to custom (cf. 29:26), this time complaining that the conventional departure ritual had not been followed (cf. 24:60).
See v. 23 and note.

The narrative ridicules the false gods — here the powerless idols are sat on by a woman (v. 35 note; Lev. 15:19–24). felt all about. Trusting in their senses, neither Isaac nor Laban discover the truth (27:18–27 note).
The time of her menstrual period. As in ch. 27, the younger child deceives the father.
According to ancient laws specifying the responsibilities of shepherds, such as those in the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1750 B.C.), Jacob should not have been liable for the loss.

See 28:15, 20 and notes. the Fear of Isaac. Or, "the Awesome One of Isaac." See v. 53 and note. sent me away empty-handed. An allusion to one of Laban's more conspicuous faults — his failure to pay workers their just wages (29:25; 31:7, 41).
Laban's claim shows that Jacob's fears have been justified (v. 31).
This covenant, or "treaty," is like the nonaggression treaties Abraham and Isaac made with the Philistines (21:27; 26:28), but unlike the unconditional covenant God made with Abraham (15:8).

Laban is deeply concerned to ensure that the status and security of his daughters will not be undermined by Jacob taking other wives. This prohibition is found commonly in marriage contracts from the ancient Near East.

The pagan Laban apparently regards the God of Abraham as one of the gods of his family. Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor, had probably been a moon-worshiper in Ur (11:27 note; Josh. 24:14). Fear of his father Isaac. Not equating the God of Abraham with the God of Nahor, Jacob swears by the "Fear of his father Isaac" (v. 42 note), another name for the God of Abraham.
See 24:60; 27:7; 28:1 and notes.

Jacob again encounters the angels of God whom he had met earlier at Bethel (28:12). These angelic encounters upon leaving and returning to the Promised Land frame Jacob's experiences with Laban (28:10–22 note) and attest to God's promise to be with and protect Jacob wherever he goes (28:15). Faithful to His promise, God has been with Jacob — not only protecting him but also remaking his character. The formerly prayerless and ambitiously deceptive Jacob is now a humble man of prayer (vv. 9–12).

See text note. Jacob may have in mind both his camp and God's camp, a heavenly shield and escort. As Bethel was the house of God and the gate of heaven (28:17), Mahanaim was God's camp on earth. Mahanaim later served as a capital for Saul's son Ishbosheth (2 Sam. 2:8) and as a refuge for David during Absalom's rebellion (2 Sam. 17:24). Mahanaim was situated east of the Jordan River near the River Jabbok, but its precise location is uncertain.
See 25:25 and note.

Jacob's humble manner of address toward his brother and former rival suggests that his character change is real (v. 1 note). Like Abraham with Lot (13:8, 9), Jacob does not insist on his covenantal privileges but leaves the matter in God's hands.
Jacob has reason to fear (14:14; 27:40, 41), yet he has survived Laban's forces with God's help (31:29 and note).
Jacob's first recorded prayer (vv. 9–12) stands between the two presents to Esau (vv. 3–8, 13–21). This structure suggests that he trusts God to prosper his two gifts.

A spiritual transformation has taken place in Jacob: he submits to Esau and recognizes his unworthiness before God. steadfast love \... faithfulness. Words often used to describe God's loyalty to His covenant promises (24:27; Ex. 15:13 note; Pss. 40:11; 61:7). Jacob now identifies himself fully with God's covenant with Abraham and Isaac, and his faith rests firmly on God's covenant promises.
In faith Jacob applies to himself the language of the covenantal promise to Abraham (22:17; cf. 28:14).
The Hebrew here connotes tribute, a gift expressing loyalty to a superior. See notes on 33:3, 4 and 33:11.
Five-hundred-fifty animals was an extravagant gift.
Lit. "cover his face," an expression meaning the covering over of guilt. Jacob is painfully aware that he has sinned against his brother.
In wrestling with Jacob, God appears in human form and deprives Jacob of his natural strength, but Jacob tenaciously clings to God for blessing.
This mysterious man is a theophany, a visible (and in this case tangible) manifestation of God, the Angel of the Lord (16:7 note; Hos. 12:4). The Lord unexpectedly initiates the match.

Though Jacob is apparently a man of considerable strength (29:2, 10), the Angel of the Lord accommodates His strength to Jacob's. touched. God dislocates Jacob's hip, the wrestler's pivot of strength (v. 31). Having previously depended upon his wits and strength, Jacob's natural powers are now crippled. All his future steps will remind him of his dependence upon divine grace.
See note on 3:9.

See note on 17:6. Israel. See text note. The new name indicates that the patriarch is radically transformed through this encounter with God. striven with God. The "man" is implicitly identified as God Himself (v. 30).

In ancient times, a name was thought to express essential nature as well as identity. The divine name partakes of the sacredness of God's being (Judg. 13:18) and was to be reverenced (Ex. 20:7). The pagans believed that knowing the name of a god imparted ability to invoke that deity's power. Here, however, the divine name is withheld (cf. 28:13; Hos. 12:5), showing that the Lord's revelation of His name is a gracious act of divine initiative, not a response to human effort to invoke and control God.

See text note. Peniel was located on the River Jabbok near the modern Tulul edh-Dhahab. The town was destroyed by Gideon (Judg. 8:8) and later fortified by Jeroboam I (1 Kin. 12:25). delivered. Jacob's preservation during his "face-to-face" meeting with almighty God anticipates his preservation during his imminent encounter with Esau, a mere human being (cf. v. 11).
The restriction against eating the sciatic tendon, mentioned elsewhere only in extrabiblical Jewish literature, commemorates this significant event in the nation's history.
See note on 32:6.

Jacob greets Esau as a vassal greets his patron in the ceremony of a royal court, with the deference appropriate to a superior — note the sevenfold obeisance (common practice in ancient Near Eastern court protocol, v. 3), the submissive address of a "servant" (v. 5) to his "lord" (vv. 8, 13), and the presentation of gifts of homage (vv. 10, 11). In contrast, Esau greets Jacob as one brother greets another after a long separation (vv. 4, 9).
As Jacob remembers his troubled history, he confesses God's unmerited kindness in giving him children (29:31–30:24) and prosperity (30:25–31:55).

See 32:13 and note. like seeing the face of God. As at Peniel, when Jacob saw God's face by theophany and his life was graciously spared (32:30), so also here he sees the dreaded face of Esau and is graciously received.

Although this refers to Jacob's gift to Esau (v. 10), it recalls his earlier theft of the paternal blessing in ch. 27. Jacob here offers recompense out of the many blessings God has given him. urged \... took. The reconciliation is sealed by accepting the gift.

Given his intention to travel to Succoth (v. 17), Jacob may have been speaking deceptively, but more probably Esau knows that this was Jacob's polite way of not contradicting him (cf. 23:11 note). Though reconciled, the brothers will live apart.

This final section of "the account of Isaac" (see Introduction: Outline), like the closing section in "the account of Abraham" (22:20–25:11), records the transition of patriarchies. It is structured according to Jacob's itinerary back in the land, featuring deaths at various sites (which mark the passage of Isaac's generation), and important episodes in the "account" such as the sins of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi.
Jacob builds his altar at Shechem where Abraham built his first altar in the Promised Land (see 12:6, 7). See also 28:20–22.

The threat to the covenant community at Shechem was severe. Hamor's proposal would have meant the assimilation of Jacob's family into the surrounding peoples (vv. 8–10; Num. 25:1–3 note). The transition from Jacob's act of worship (33:20) to the depraved behavior of ch. 34 is striking. Instead of residing at Shechem (33:18, 19), perhaps Jacob should have fulfilled his vow at Bethel (28:22; 31:13; 35:1). There is no mention of God in this chapter and no separation from idolatry (35:1–5), a sad commentary on Jacob's spiritual leadership (35:4 note).

See 9:25; 10:15, 17 and notes. saw \... seized \... humiliated. The precise nature of what Shechem does is open to debate. He may have intercourse with Dinah prior to being betrothed, which would have be unacceptable. It is also likely that he rapes her, since the Hebrew word translated "humiliated" is rendered "violated" in 2 Sam. 13:12, 14, 22, 32. The sequence "saw \... seized" recalls 3:6 and 6:2.
The nation of Israel. This description assumes the later development of the nation from the sons of Israel (cf. 49:28).
See note on ch. 34.
This is not the dowry given by the bride's family to the groom, but rather a reciprocal gift given by the groom to the bride's father (24:53; 1 Sam. 18:25).
Jacob reaps the whirlwind; his sons copy his deception (27:35, 36).
Jacob's sons sacrilegiously empty the holy covenant sign of its religious significance (17:10, 11 and notes) and abuse it for the purpose of inflicting vengeance.
See note on 23:10.
The Shechemites probably neither know nor care about the religious significance of the rite; they agree only to advance their own interests (v. 23).

Under the Mosaic law, Shechem's sin against Dinah does not merit such excessive punishment (Deut. 22:28, 29). The action of Simeon and Levi is totally unjustified according to the doctrine of retribution. Furthermore, it endangers their households (v. 30). For an evaluation of just how distasteful this act is in their father's eyes, see Gen. 49:5–7.
By their unbridled, faithless, and rash revenge, Simeon and Levi lose leadership and land in Israel (49:5–7).
Jacob here displays fear, not obedient faith (cf. 35:5).

Jacob's journey through time, as indicated by births (vv. 16–18), deaths (vv. 8, 19, 20), and genealogies (vv. 23–26), and through space, as indicated by itineraries (vv. 6, 16, 21, 27), is brought to completion because God is with him (v. 3). He returns to pay his vow at Bethel (vv. 1–8), is confirmed as the successor to God's Abrahamic promises (vv. 9–15), sees his twelve sons safely settled in the Promised Land (vv. 16–26), and is reunited with his father and brother (vv. 27–29). 35:1 go up to Bethel. Jacob has a vow to fulfill (28:20–22; 34:1–31 note). God's revelation at Bethel (vv. 9–13) reiterates the covenant promises to Abraham, who himself had earlier worshiped at Bethel (12:8; 13:3, 4).

Repentance involves renouncing whatever hinders or tarnishes the worship and service of God. The covenant's primary requirement is exclusive allegiance to the Lord (Ex. 20:3–5; Josh. 24:14; Judg. 10:16). foreign gods. See notes on 31:19; Josh. 24:23.

Jacob recovers his spiritual leadership of the family (30:2 note; 34:1–31 note). rings \... ears. These are amulets associated with pagan worship (cf. v. 2). terebinth tree \... near Shechem. Probably the sacred tree associated with Abraham (12:6 and note).

God's protection of Jacob's family by divinely induced panic (cf. Ex. 23:27; Josh. 2:9) is necessary because their reputation has changed from that of peaceful shepherds (34:21) to rapacious warriors (34:30).

Jacob finally fulfills his vow to the Lord (28:20–22). By such altar building, the patriarchal family acknowledges the covenant promises and consecrates the Promised Land. Regular worship is crucial if they are to maintain their religious separation from the surrounding Canaanites (ch. 34; Num. 25:1–3 and notes). See 12:7 and note; 13:18; 22:9; 33:20.
She is briefly mentioned in 24:59. Scripture memorializes the death of the aged, faithful nurse of Rebekah rather than the matriarch herself, perhaps because of Rebekah's deception (ch. 27).

God's revelation to Jacob after his return from Paddan-aram to Bethel confirms the earlier promises of 28:13, 14. Using language that closely parallels the Abrahamic promises of nations, royalty, and land (17:5–8), God confirms His promises to Israel, the transformed Jacob (32:28), and indirectly to his twelve sons. 35:9 Paddan-aram. See note on 25:20.
God's gracious blessing on all humankind (1:28; 9:1, 7) is focused particularly on the covenant community (28:3; cf. 47:27; Ex. 1:7 note).
See notes on 12:7; 13:15.
This recalls Jacob's first meeting with the Lord at Bethel (28:13 note).
Near Ephrath, Rachel dies giving birth to Jacob's twelfth son (30:1 note). The birth of Benjamin completes the patriarchal roster of the twelve tribes of Israel.
Rachel's prayer is answered (30:24).

See text note. Rachel's weeping for her child portends an anguished future for the nation (Jer. 31:15–17; Matt. 2:17, 18). Benjamin. See text note. The Hebrew word yamin can refer both to the right hand and to the south (the Hebrews often described directions in terms of a person facing the east; the right hand thus pointed to the south). Jacob's other sons were born in Paddan-aram, northeast of Canaan.

To gratify his lusts and perhaps to certify his leadership as firstborn over the next generation (cf. 2 Sam. 16:15–23; 1 Kin. 2:22). For his sin Reuben is deprived of his status as firstborn (48:1 note) and of his leadership (49:3, 4; Deut. 22:30), which Joseph will assume instead (1 Chr. 5:1–2). Later, Joseph's leadership will pass to the tribe of Ephraim, although Ephraim is ultimately rejected by God as the leader of His people in favor of Judah (Gen. 49:8–10; Ps. 78:67–72).

Benjamin is not actually born in Paddan-aram, but after the return to Canaan (vv. 16–18). The statement must be taken as an informal review of the sons born to Jacob during this general period of his sojourn in Paddan-aram and the immediate aftermath (46:8–27 note).
Isaac again appears in the narrative (28:5). His journey ends with a full length of years.

With this genealogy, or account, of Esau, a new section of Genesis begins (2:4 note). Esau (that is, Edom). "Edom," derived from the Hebrew word for "red," was another name for Esau (25:25; 25:30 and note). The term was appropriate also for the land of Edom, with its red sandstone formations and soil.

This genealogy focuses on Esau's Canaanite wives and the children born in Canaan prior to his migration to Mount Seir. 36:2 took his wives. See 26:34; 27:46 and notes. Canaanites. See 9:25; 10:15–19. The word broadly covers the tribes in the land. Adah. The names of Esau's wives here differ from those in 26:34; 28:9. The use of alternate names for the same individuals may account for some of the variation.
Jacob's return to Mamre clinches Esau's decision to move permanently to Edom. Separated in spirit, Jacob and Esau will be separated by geography as well (cf. 33:14 note).
This genealogy focuses on Esau's twelve sons (vv. 2–8), not counting Amalek, the son of Eliphaz's concubine, Timna (v. 12).
This list shows the transition of Esau's descendants from a family to a tribal structure.
This genealogy presents the aboriginal inhabitants of Mount Seir whom the sons of Esau later destroy (Deut. 2:22) and, in other cases, marry (vv. 22, 25).

The list shows Edom's transition from tribal structure to designated kingship. 36:31 before any king reigned over the Israelites. This creates an expectation that in the subsequent narrative, kings will reign over Israel. Or perhaps v. 31 was later updated after the establishment of the monarchy. See Introduction: Date and Occasion.

The final section of Genesis, "the generations of Jacob," begins. It starts on a negative note with the shattering of the covenant family's peace (ch. 37) but concludes with the family's reconciliation and preservation in Egypt. Just as Jacob figured prominently in the "account of Isaac," so also does Joseph in the "generations of Jacob." God used Joseph, the rejected, godly brother, to save and reconcile the covenant family (45:5–8; 50:24). Though these parallels are not developed explicitly in the NT, the Christian church has traditionally recognized several parallels between the life of Joseph and the life of Christ. Godly Joseph, beloved by his father (37:3; cf. Mark 1:11), was sent to his brothers, was rejected by them, and was then sold for twenty pieces of silver (37:28; cf. Matt. 26:15). After suffering persecution and temptation (37:18–36; 39:7–20; cf. Matt. 4:1–11), righteous Joseph was exalted as lord over his brothers (37:5–11; 41:37–45; 42:6; cf. Phil. 2:9, 10). 37:2 the generations of Jacob. The material to follow will focus on Jacob's children. See note on 2:4. sons of Bilhah and Zilpah. Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher (30:4–13).

As in the case of Jacob, parental favoritism again promotes family discord, deception, and the disappearance of the preferred son, but God graciously uses it to achieve His good purpose (cf. 25:28). old age. See 30:22–24. robe of many colors. A sign of Joseph's preferential status, perhaps suggesting that he is a prince (cf. 2 Sam. 13:18), and a galling reminder to Joseph's brothers of their father's favoritism. The exact nature of the coat is uncertain. The rendering "of many colors" reflects the Septuagint (Greek OT) translation. Some suggest that the Hebrew means a "long coat with sleeves."

Or, "could not greet him with peace." The greeting, or salutation, was a crucial element of ancient etiquette (cf. 1 Sam. 25:6). Such a failure to extend the greeting indicates the depth of the brothers' animosity toward Joseph.

As in certain other Genesis narratives, the key to the Joseph story is given in an opening revelation (cf. 12:1–3; 25:22, 23). This prophetic dream shows that God's sovereign purpose lies behind all the events of the narrative (45:5–8). See note 20:3.

Their rhetorical question is later answered when Joseph comes to rule "over all the land of Egypt" (41:43) and then over the covenant family living in Egypt. Joseph's status as head of the covenant family is confirmed when he receives the birthright from his father Jacob (1 Chr. 5:2; cf. Deut. 33:16).

The reiteration of the theme in Joseph's second dream, like the similar repetition in Pharaoh's dreams (41:1–7), shows that the matter has been determined by God and will quickly come to pass (41:32).
Probably a reference to Joseph's stepmother, Leah; his mother Rachel is already dead at this point (35:16–20).
This statement perhaps anticipates Jacob's later decision to give Joseph the birthright and double portion (v. 8 note; 48:5, 6).
Because of this divinely ordained delay, the Ishmaelites arrive at just the right time (vv. 21–28).

As the eldest brother (29:32), Reuben assumes leadership in Jacob's absence and is responsible for the safety of his brothers (vv. 29, 30). In attempting to rescue Joseph, Reuben may wish to regain his father's favor after acting inappropriately with Bilhah (35:22).

The brothers later acknowledge the heartlessness of their behavior (42:21). Ishmaelites. These traders are also identified as Midianites (v. 28). Both groups are descended from Abraham and had no doubt intermarried by this point (25:2, 12).
Note the later prohibition in the Mosaic law against kidnapping (Ex. 21:16; Deut. 24:7).
See Lev. 27:5.
Under such circumstances, Reuben dreads returning to his father, to whom he must give an account (v. 21 note).
Note the irony of these verses. Having deceived his father Isaac with goat skins (27:9) and with Esau's clothing (27:27), Jacob here is deceived by goat's blood on his son's clothes.
This Egyptian name means "he whom \[the sun god\] Ra has given."

The report of Joseph's being sold into slavery is immediately followed by an episode involving Judah, the brother who proposed selling Joseph as a slave. Attention focuses on the continuation of Judah's family line, ending with a brief report on how twin boys are born to Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar. The report of Judah's dealing with Tamar suggests that his son Perez will have a role to play in continuing the unique family line that began with Adam. That the bizarre episode of Judah and Tamar should contribute to the genealogy of Jesus Christ is a vivid demonstration of God's grace (Matt. 1:3–16 note). A major reason this story interrupts the Joseph narrative is that it serves as a foil to chapter 39 of the Joseph story. Judah marries a Canaanite, and after his wife's death he has sexual relations with a woman he thinks is a prostitute. Joseph, on the contrary, does not succumb to sexual temptation. The events of the story also parallel Gen. 37. Judah is deceived by Tamar just as Jacob was earlier deceived by Judah and his brothers regarding Joseph's "death." Through Joseph's wisdom God preserves Israel in Goshen, both physically, by providing food and land (45:10 note), and spiritually, by providing for their isolation from the pagan Egyptians until the exodus (43:32; Num. 25:1–3 and notes). Under Jacob's blessing on Pharaoh (47:7, 10; cf. 12:2) and Pharaoh's honoring of Israel (45:17–20; 47:6; cf. 12:3) everyone prospers: Pharaoh gains control of all the property and people in Egypt (47:19–21), the Egyptians hail Joseph as a savior (47:25), and Israel prospers even more than the Egyptians (47:27; Ex. 1:7). This mutual blessing and prosperity contrasts with the situation four hundred years later when another pharaoh exploits Israel and suffers the consequences (Ex. 1:8–14).

Their identity as shepherds will assure Pharaoh that they entertain no social or political ambitions under their brother's auspices and will help insulate them from intermarriage with the pagan Egyptians (v. 34; 43:32 and notes). The blessings of the inspired patriarch prophesy the fate of the twelve tribes descended from his sons, mostly by means of wordplays on their names or comparisons to animals. Similarly, the priestly tribe of Levi is allotted cities.

Signifying strength, courage, and boldness (Judg. 14:18; Prov. 28:1), the lion is an apt symbol of the warrior kings of Judah's Davidic line — a royal line culminating in the conquering Messiah, Jesus Christ (Rev. 5:5).

The scepter symbolizes royal authority. This prophecy is further elaborated and confirmed by the Davidic covenant (2 Sam. 7:16). until tribute comes to him. Lit. "Until Shiloh comes." The precise meaning of this phrase is debated. Some understand "Shiloh" as a place name ("until Judah's leadership comes to Shiloh"; cf. Josh. 18:1) or as a reference to tribute ("until tribute is brought to Judah"). According to Ps. 78:67–72, the tribe of Judah, through David, assumes leadership of the nation of Israel after God rejects Shiloh as the location for His temple. Others see Shiloh as a reference to a coming Judahite ruler: "until he comes to whom it belongs" (cf. Ezek. 21:27) or "until Shiloh \[possibly a messianic term\] comes." The subsequent mention of dominion over "people" (or "peoples" — the Hebrew noun is plural) points to the final realization of this prophecy in the universal messianic reign of Christ (1 Cor. 15:24–28; Rev. 5:5). God's plan for humanity to rule and have dominion (1:26–28) is concentrated in Him.
The blessedness of the messianic ruler is represented by wine (a symbol of prosperity, 27:28) and by his beauty (Ps. 45:2–9).

Later failing to drive the Canaanites out of its territory, the tribe of Issachar is apparently willing to trade its liberty for forced labor (cf. Judg. 1:28, 30). Issachar throws off the Canaanite yoke under the leadership of Deborah and Barak (Judg. 5:15).
Or, provide justice for them. See 30:6.
Though small, Dan is dangerous and strikes unexpectedly to overthrow larger foes (Judg. 18). The Danite Samson single-handedly strikes the Philistines with great destruction (Judg. 13–16).
A brief prayer stands in the middle of the oracles.
This verse consists of a play on words (four of the six Hebrew words sound like "Gad") that points to the constant danger to Gad from its southern and eastern neighbors (Ammon and Moab).
A reference to its fertile land (Deut. 33:24; Josh. 19:24–31). See 30:13.
See 30:24; 48:15–20. fruitful. Barren Rachel will produce the most fruitful tribe (30:2, 22; 41:52). run over the wall. The children of Joseph later seek to increase their territory (Josh. 17:14–18).

Note the striking multiplication of divine names. 49:24 Stone. Israel's sure defense (Deut. 32:4 note). 49:25 Almighty. See note on 17:1. bless. The Hebrew root for "bless" is used six times in this verse. These blessings are fertility of land fed by water from heaven above and earth below (1:6–8 and note) and fertility of body (1:22; cf. Num. 24:5–7). Blessings given humankind at creation and later associated especially with Abraham are concentrated on Joseph. Through Joseph, the divine promise to bless the nations is continued (cf. 22:18).
See note on Deut. 33:16.
See 35:18. This tribe will later have a fierce reputation (Judg. 20:14–25; 1 Kin. 12:21; 2 Chr. 14:8; 17:17).

Believing in God's promises to Abraham and Isaac about the Promised Land (13:15 and note), Jacob arranges for his burial with them in Canaan (49:29–32; cf. 47:29–31). Joseph also instructs his family to bury him in the Promised Land after the exodus (50:24–26; cf. Josh. 24:32). The burial of Jacob in the ancestral cave and Joseph's determination to be buried in Canaan underscore the covenant family's solidarity and point forward to the exodus from Egypt. The unity of the family is further emphasized by Joseph's kind words and provisions for his offending brothers (50:15–21). 49:29 in the cave. See ch. 23; 25:9 and notes.

An Egyptian practice designed to preserve the body after death and so to maintain personal identity in the afterlife; embalming was not practiced in Israel. Here the embalming preserves the body for transport back to Canaan.
Having just mourned his father's death (Deut. 34:8 note), Joseph's appearance is probably unsuitable for an appearance before Pharaoh (cf. 41:14).
The Hebrew verb translated "hewed out" can also mean "purchased" (cf. ch. 23). If the text reading is followed, Joseph simply expresses Jacob's instructions in words Pharaoh will understand.
The protection given the burial party by Egyptian arms contrasts with the threat of Egyptian chariots during the Mosaic exodus (Ex. 14:9; 15:4, 5).
It is unclear whether Jacob has actually said this or the fearful brothers simply have invented it. In any case, they base their plea for forgiveness on their worship of the same God (v. 17).
Joseph recognizes that his captivity has been part of God's gracious plan to save the covenant family (45:5–8); it is not his place to question God's wisdom.

A classic statement of God's sovereign overruling of human history to accomplish His gracious purposes (24:27; 45:5, 7, 8 and notes). See "Providence" at Prov. 16:33. that many people should be kept alive. In Egypt, Canaan, and elsewhere (41:57). Viewed in the light of God's earlier promise to Abraham that all the nations will be blessed through one of his descendants (22:18), Joseph's actions prefigure those of Jesus Christ. The salvation provided by Christ, however, extends far beyond feeding people in a time of famine.

See notes on 30:3 and 48:12. Joseph apparently adopted these great-grandchildren. Machir is an important son of Manasseh who becomes the progenitor of the Gileadites (Num. 26:29; 32:39; Deut. 3:15; Josh. 13:31). His descendants later settle the areas of Gilead and Bashan on the eastern side of the Jordan River (Josh. 17:1).

Like his father, Jacob, on his deathbed (48:21), Joseph expresses firm confidence in God's covenant promises and His gracious visitation. The Hebrew verb translated "visit" denotes a divine encounter that will change one's fortunes for good or ill. For other instances of God's gracious "visitation," see 21:1 (Abraham and Sarah); Ex. 3:16 and 4:31 (the exodus); Luke 1:68, 78 (the birth of Jesus); and Acts 15:14 (the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles). Abraham \... Isaac \... Jacob. For the first time the three patriarchs are mentioned together; the patriarchal era has passed, but not its hope (Ex. 3:6; Deut. 30:20; 1 Kin. 18:36; 2 Chr. 30:6).

Joseph's bones will be taken from Egypt by Moses (Ex. 13:19) and later buried at Shechem (Josh. 24:32). Ultimately, he sees his time in Egypt as merely a sojourn. His true home is in God's blessed presence, which is prefigured in dwelling and burial in the Promised Land.

Exodus.note: Genesis and Exodus are linked by this introduction (Gen. 46:8–27). God's promise of nationhood to Abraham begins to be fulfilled by Israel's fruitfulness (Gen. 12:2).

The number going into Egypt is sometimes given as seventy-five (Acts 7:14), with the difference due to who is counted. The Septuagint text adds five of Joseph's further male descendants, yielding a total of seventy-five. See notes on Gen. 46:15–27.

The terms "fruitful," "multiplied," and "the land was filled" remind us of Gen. 1:26–28. Israel fulfills the mandate given to humankind in Gen. 1. By opposing the growth of the Israelites, Pharaoh sets himself against God's purposes for humanity.

God's multiplication of Israel leads to their oppression by the Egyptians. 1:8a new king. The beginning of a new era is marked off by the advent of a new pharaoh. This pharaoh may have been Ahmose I (1550–1525 B.C.) of the eighteenth dynasty, who expelled the Hyksos, the Semitic rulers of Egypt from about 1700–1550 B.C. (Introduction: Date and Occasion; Acts 7:18 note).

These cities for storing agricultural provisions and military supplies were located in the strategic Nile Delta region. Pithom was probably located at modern Tell er-Ratabah or at Tell Hisn, and Raamses is identified as modern Qantir. The city name Raamses was given to the location by Ramesses II (1279–1213 B.C.), who made the city his capital. Prior to this the city was known as Avaris during the period of the Hyksos, then possibly Peru-nefer before being renamed Raamses. Recent archaeological excavations at Qantir have revealed the remains of an impressive city from the second millennium, when a branch of the Nile flowed beside the city. When this branch silted up, Raamses was abandoned, with much of its valuable stonework being removed to Tanis.
The bitter oppression of Egypt is later commemorated by the bitter herbs of the Passover meal (12:8).

See note on Gen. 14:13. midwives. Two midwives to serve such a large population seems far too few; they may be guild leaders. Their names are Semitic, and v. 15 identifies them as Hebrews. While the Pharaoh remains anonymous, the names of the two midwives live on.
This consisted of two stones upon which women in labor squatted.
The fate of Israel hangs on one family member. Moses has an older sister (v. 4) and brother (7:7). His parents, Amram and Jochebed, are nephew and aunt (6:20).
Moses is a healthy child and likely to survive.
A box of woven papyrus reeds, daubed with tar to make it watertight (cf. Job 9:26; Is. 18:2). The Hebrew term translated "basket" here is used for Noah's craft in Gen. 7–9.
There is great irony in the fact that Pharaoh's daughter rescues Moses from the Nile; her father had commanded the Egyptians to throw all male children into the river (1:22).

This name is Semitic (text note), though perhaps it is compatible with the Egyptian word Mose meaning "born of" (e.g., Thutmose, meaning "born of Thut"). He is educated in the Egyptian court as a promising young noble (Acts 7:22).

Now forty years old (Acts 7:23), Moses identifies himself with God's people (Heb. 11:24–27). His effort to deliver an Israelite from oppression proves vain when he seeks to be a judge of Israel (v. 14). While the Israelite challenges Moses's role as judge, God later appoints Moses to fulfill this task.
This is a judicial term (Deut. 25:1; 1 Kin. 8:32).
Probably the name of an early tribal confederacy operating in the Arabian desert. The Midianites were descendants of Abraham and Keturah (Gen. 25:1–6; Num. 10:29–32; Judg. 6).
The women do the difficult task and then are driven off.
This is Moses's third intervention in defense of the weak. Strife over water rights was common in that region.
The name means "Friend of God." Moses's father-in-law is known by two names: Reuel and Jethro (3:1; 4:18). Jethro and Reuel may be variant names, or Reuel a clan name.
See text note. Moses is conscious that Midian is not his home. He will later lead Israel from Egypt to the homeland of the people of God.

Israel's anguished cry is balanced by a fourfold description of God's response. God "heard \... remembered \... saw \... knew" (vv. 24, 25). This summary prepares for the call of Moses and underscores the theme of divine faithfulness to the covenant promises.

An uncultivated area but capable of sustaining grazing livestock. According to 13:4 and Num. 10:11, the wilderness of Sinai later sustains Israel's flocks for a year. Horeb and Sinai are terms that possibly distinguish Horeb as a wider region from Mount Sinai. mountain of God. This term anticipates how the mountain will be closely associated with God. Moses is now eighty years old (7:7) and has been in Midian forty years.

**LORD** . This is a theophany, a visible manifestation of God (v. 4). See note on Gen. 16:7. fire. A frequent biblical symbol for God's presence (13:21; 19:18; cf. Gen. 3:24; 1 Kin. 18:24, 38); it particularly expresses His all-consuming holiness (Heb. 12:29).
A real bush is illumined with supernatural fire. God is transcendent, but reveals Himself as fire in the bush to call Moses.
The spot is made sacred by God's presence. See 19:23; 24:2. Only those who are holy can remain in God's presence. Israel must become a holy nation if God is to dwell among them.
God remembers His covenant promises to the patriarchs and identifies Himself as their God. See Gen. 26:24; 28:13; 31:42; 32:9.

The inhabitants of the Syro-Palestinian coastland. Hittites. See note on Gen. 10:15. Amorites. See note on Gen. 10:16. Perizzites. Possibly the peasantry located in central Palestine (Josh. 17:15). Hivites. See note on Gen. 10:17. Jebusites. The original occupants of Jerusalem, later dispossessed by David (Gen. 10:16 note; 2 Sam. 5:6–9).
Probably Thutmose III (1479–1425 B.C.). See Introduction: Date and Occasion.
Moses felt inadequate for the task, as did Gideon (Judg. 6:15) and Jeremiah (Jer. 1:6). This is the first of his four objections (cf. v. 13; 4:1, 10).

God's call will be confirmed by His future action. God will be with Moses to bring him back to worship ("serve God") on this same mountain. Having served the Egyptians under duress, the Israelites will become God's servants in response to His rescue of them.

Moses anticipates a question from the people regarding the identity of the God who has sent him back to Egypt. In Scripture, a personal name is not merely a form of address but a description of character and personality (Ps. 9:10; cf. 1 Sam. 25:25). In Genesis, God is known to the patriarchs by different names: e.g., God Most High; God Almighty; God Everlasting.

.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} This expression, which builds on God's promise to be with Moses (v. 12), repeats twice the word ehyeh ("I AM"). God will be who He is. He does not change in His perfections. What He is now, He will be in the future. Other designations of God usually draw attention to some particular aspect of His nature. This expression is all-inclusive.

**LORD** . The Hebrew is Yahweh, associated here by wordplay with the Hebrew verb for "to be" (thus meaning "he is" or "he will be"). The corresponding first person is ehyeh, that is, "I am." Note the parallels: "I AM has sent me" (v. 14) and "The Lord \[Yahweh\] \... has sent me" (v. 15). remembered throughout all generations. Yahweh, the divine name particularly associated with God's covenant relationship with Israel, is henceforth to be used in worship. English versions of the OT usually render the Hebrew name "Yahweh" as "the LORD." The Jews thought the name too holy to pronounce, and when reading the text substituted adonay ("my Lord"). The vowel signs for adonay were later added to the Hebrew consonants of Yahweh as a pronunciation reminder, and this hybrid form was rendered "Jehovah" by William Tyndale's English translation (A.D. 1530).
These are family heads who represent Israel. They will be assembled to hear of God's faithfulness (4:30, 31).
The usual biblical description of Canaan. The Hebrew term translated "honey" probably refers here to a sweet syrup derived from dates or grapes.
This mention of extraordinary deeds anticipates the miraculous events that will take place in Egypt (7:14–12:30).
As He promised, God will see that their years of bondage are recompensed (Gen. 15:14).

God gives Moses three miraculous signs to perform before the Israelites. Later, similar signs will be performed before the Pharaoh. Whereas the Israelites will believe, Pharaoh will disregard both these and subsequent signs warning of disaster. 4:1 But behold. Moses's third objection (3:11 note). Israel must be persuaded. This will be a difficult task, but God has purposed to see that Israel will believe (3:18). Nothing is said here about convincing Pharaoh (cf. 6:12).

The Hebrew word for "hand" often connotes power. Against the oppressing hand of Egypt (3:8; 14:30; 18:10), the mighty hand of God will be stretched out (3:19–20). God will use the hand of Moses to show His power. Moses's staff will become the staff of God (v. 20).
Not what is today called Hansen's Disease, but a common skin disease of the time. God shows His power to judge and to heal.
The Nile was revered as a god and was the source of Egypt's life.

The fourth objection. Moses claims not to be fluent, but God equips whom He calls (cf. Jer. 1:9). God is teaching Moses and his successors to depend on Him for their gifts. Since God made the mouth, He can enable a person to use it (v. 11).

Left without excuse, Moses still tries to decline his commission. But the Lord has already summoned his brother Aaron. The relation of Moses to Aaron sheds light on the nature of prophecy: Aaron will be a mouthpiece for Moses just as a prophet is for God (v. 16). See also 6:30; 7:1.
The supernatural events are again anticipated (3:20 note). These miraculous deeds will be performed with this same staff.
Including the Egyptian pharaoh (Introduction: Date and Occasion).
Gershom (2:22) and Eliezer (18:4).

Since in this context "heart" denotes "will," God states that He will strengthen Pharaoh's resolve not to release the Israelites. Strange as this may seem, God will give Pharaoh the courage to do what Pharaoh has chosen to do from the outset. God does not force Pharaoh to act contrary to his own will. God will display His power over the stubborn hostility of the king so that His people might know that He is the Lord, their deliverer (6:6–8).

The Lord puts His claim upon Israel as His firstborn son. God's claim is the reason for God's deliverance and the covenant to be sealed at Sinai ("that he may serve me," v. 23). This claim issues in God's threat against Pharaoh's firstborn (i.e., the firstborn of Egypt).

The Hebrew is slightly ambiguous. Most likely the attack is directed against Moses himself, perhaps because of his failure to circumcise his son. Alternatively, it may be against Moses's firstborn, Gershom.

Presumably a ceremonial instrument. Zipporah intervenes to circumcise her son. Moses' feet. Lit. "his feet"; the word "Moses' " is supplied (cf. v. 24 note). The connection of Zipporah's action with the "bridegroom of blood" is uncertain. The Lord, the God of the patriarchs, requires the sign of circumcision that He gave to Abraham (Gen. 17:10).
Aaron will now function as Moses's spokesman (vv. 13–16 note).
Israel now believes as God said they would (3:18). They worship, praising God for His care.
The confrontation with Pharaoh begins with God's demand. The people are His, not Pharaoh's. hold a feast. This is a pilgrimage to a shrine where a festival will be held (3:18).
**LORD** ? Pharaoh's question highlights an important theme within the book of Exodus. Subsequent events will make the Lord known.

After presenting God's demand, Moses and Aaron seek to reason with Pharaoh. The Lord is the God of the Hebrews; the distance will be only a three-day journey (3:18); and Israel's disobedience to God's command might seriously reduce Pharaoh's work force.
Later this term comes to mean the responsible landowners in Israel (2 Kin. 11:18–20; Jer. 34:19), but here it means peasant workers attached to the land.
The bricks of the time were much larger than modern bricks; they were molded of Nile mud with straw to increase their strength.
The slave masters and section leaders pass the order down through the ranks. During the events of vv. 6–19, Moses and Aaron do not intervene. This crushing reply of Pharaoh shows his human supremacy.
were urgent. The taskmasters continue to pressure the people to produce the same number of bricks as before.
Israel appeals to Pharaoh for relief and complains to Moses and Aaron about their plight.
**LORD** \... judge. Not for the last time, the leaders of Israel curse Moses for obeying the command of the Lord.

As a mediator, Moses speaks God's Word to the people, and he pleads the plight of the people to God. This pattern is repeated throughout Exodus. God's reply gives assurance that the hopeless situation will be the occasion for His mighty action (see ch. 6).
The Lord's power will more than prevail. Pharaoh will not only let them go, he will drive Israel out.

Note the repeated use of the revelation (authority) formula, "I am the LORD," in these verses (vv. 2, 6–8). The use of God's name underscores the surety of His covenant promises and faithfulness (3:15 and notes).

God had revealed Himself to the patriarchs as God Almighty (Hebrew El Shaddai; cf. Gen. 17:1; 28:3; 35:11). Throughout Genesis, however, the name Yahweh is much more commonly used, and it was clearly known by the patriarchs (e.g., Gen. 15:7). While some scholars suggest that the significance of the name Yahweh was not fully known by the patriarchs, it is more likely that the final part of v. 3 ought to be translated: "My name is Yahweh. Did I not make myself known to them?"
Yahweh is also El Shaddai, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. His covenant promises to these earlier patriarchs include the gift of the land of Canaan.
When used of God, "remembered" means that He is prepared to act on His promises, not simply recall them.

God's reply to Moses's complaint of 5:22–23. This is the central core of the section, a solemn assurance of redemption and of covenant reaffirmation. The concept of redemption points to the redemptive work of Christ for His people (Luke 4:16–21; Gal. 3:13; 4:5; Heb. 9:15). redeem. This term normally refers to the restoration of rights to a disadvantaged family member by the payment of a price or a ransom; such redemption was normally effected by the next of kin (Lev. 25:25; cf. Ruth 4). Israel, as Yahweh's son (4:22), is redeemed from Egypt to be God's own people. Redemption and covenant relation are the keys to the passage. The heart of the covenant is God's claim on His people and the reciprocal claim that He allows them to make on Him.
This anticipates 19:5–6.
In spite of God's renewed promise, the Israelites remain unconvinced, and even Moses has difficulty believing that his mission will be effective.

The genealogical material in vv.14–25 interrupts the flow of the story, which is picked up in vv. 26–30; these latter verses deliberately echo vv. 10–12. In this transitional section, Moses and Aaron are formally identified, and the story of their work is reviewed and resumed in preparation for the description of the signs and wonders. The formal identification is accomplished through a genealogy that begins with Reuben, Israel's oldest son, then proceeds to Simeon, the second son, and finally to Levi. Levi's genealogy establishes the link to Moses and Aaron. Among the Levites Amram is singled out, then Aaron and Moses. The subsequent names constitute the priestly line for Israel (Num. 25:10–13; 26:57–62). For Korah, see Num. 16:1–35.

The record of the marriage of Amram to his paternal aunt would be most unlikely if the genealogy were fictional. Such a marriage was later forbidden in the Mosaic Law (Lev. 18:12), so an author who was making up the genealogy to put Moses's family in the best light possible would certainly not have invented such a potentially scandalous relationship. The form of the genealogy changes between vv. 19 and 20, suggesting that the Amram of v. 20 was a different person than the Amram of v. 18. The genealogy deliberately omits a number of generations while still establishing that Aaron and Moses were descended from Levi. Three women are mentioned in tracing the line: Jochebed, Elisheba, and a daughter of Putiel.

No descendant of Moses is named, but those of Aaron continue for the next two generations to establish priestly succession from Aaron through his successor Eleazar. The genealogy spans only four generations for the sojourn in Egypt and is clearly selective (Gen. 5:3–32 note).
Those named appear later in the story of Israel's time in the wilderness.
Having told Moses what he should say to the Israelites (6:6–8), the Lord now instructs him regarding Pharaoh. His real demand now appears: not a temporary absence, but a definitive exodus from Egypt.
The function of Aaron in relation to Moses demonstrates the function of a true prophet in relation to God (4:13–16 note).

These verses provide an insight into God's purpose in sending a series of supernatural events against the Egyptians. As v. 5 highlights, these events are designed to make God known to the Egyptians, addressing Pharaoh's earlier question, "Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go?" (5:2). In order to fulfill this aim, God states that He will "harden Pharaoh's heart." This is a difficult concept to grasp, complicated by the fact that whereas in English the idiom "to be hard-hearted" implies that one lacks compassion, in Hebrew it implies that one is determined or resolved to do something, not necessarily with negative connotations. At no point does God cause Pharaoh to act contrary to his own desires. On the contrary, He actually gives Pharaoh the courage to remain stubbornly committed to his initial plan. Remarkably, God does not use force to manipulate other people to do His will. Pharaoh is allowed to resist — even when the signs and wonders clearly indicate that such resistance will ultimately be futile.

The Hebrew is a broad term describing the center of feeling, thinking, and willing. though I multiply. Or, "in order that I might multiply." my signs and wonders. The expression "signs and wonders" is the one used most regularly in the rest of the OT to denote the events that took place in Egypt (cf. Deut. 4:34; 6:22; 7:19; 26:8; 29:3; 34:11; Neh. 9:10; Pss. 105:27; 135:9; Jer. 32:20). Although it has become customary to speak of these as the "ten plagues," this designation is misleading. Whereas today the term "plague" is generally understood to denote some form of infectious disease, it previously meant in English a "blow" or "stroke" (based on the Latin term plaga). In the Hebrew text of Exodus, the signs and wonders are presented as a series of blows that God sends against the Egyptians, blows often symbolized by the use that Aaron and Moses make of the "staff of God" (4:20).
God's purpose in saving the Israelites from Egypt is not merely for their good but so that people will know that He is the Lord (cf. 18:10–12; see Introduction: Theology of Exodus).

The Hebrew word here (different from the word for "serpent" in 4:3) often refers to a reptile associated with water (Gen. 1:21; Ezek. 29:3; 32:2). A crocodile may be in view. Alternatively, it might be a cobra, which is a major symbol for the land of Egypt.
The Hebrew term refers to priests who were associated with the worship of Egyptian deities. Their power to perform miracles may be occultic. See note on 9:11.
**LORD** had said. As predicted in 4:21 (cf. 7:3).

A theory of natural causes for the signs and wonders does not do justice to the clear statements of the text (7:17; 9:5 notes). A particular order would be essential for an explanation of the plagues as normal events associated with the overflow of the Nile, but neither the narrative here, nor the lists in Ps. 78:44–51; 105:28–36, suggest such an order. The signs and wonders are arranged in three groups of three (7:14–8:19; 8:20–9:12; 9:13–10:29), preceded by the transformation of Moses's staff into a reptile (7:9–13) and climaxed by the death of the firstborn (12:29–32). In the first plague of each series, Moses contacts Pharaoh in the morning; no time indication is given for the other two. The first two plagues in each sequence are preceded by a divine warning, but the third comes unheralded. There is a progression in the severity of the signs, as gradually God persuades some of the Egyptians to take seriously Moses's request for the release of the Israelites. Pharaoh, however, remains resistant to letting them go. 7:14 hardened. Pharaoh's heart is strong; he possibly takes courage from the fact that his sorcerer-priests are able to duplicate what Moses and Aaron did.

Repeated references to the rod point to Yahweh as the source of power for all that occurs. I will strike. Aaron will strike, but the Lord will perform the miracle (vv. 14– 20). The striking is by God's hand, by His rod. The deed of Aaron is owned by God no less than the word that God gave him through Moses. blood. In Hebrew the word never denotes its red color, but always blood as a substance. The red clay that comes down at the time of flooding from the Ethiopian highlands (coloring the Nile water red) is not in view.

All the natural waters of Egypt are involved, including the natural arms of the Nile, the irrigation canals, and the pools formed by river flooding. The Nile River, the source of Egypt's agricultural life, was revered as a god by the Egyptians in Moses's day. Beginning with this plague, the Lord's superiority over the Egyptian pantheon of gods is demonstrated.
See note on 7:11.
Here the allegedly divine river and frogs bring misery on the Egyptians — another demonstration of the Lord's supremacy.
The sorcerer-priests can only add to the distress (9:11 note).
Pharaoh, personally affected, makes his first concession. However, he will renege on his promise once the frogs are removed.
God raises His rod against the dust, turning it into an outbreak of gnats or, perhaps more likely, lice.
The magicians now admit that a divine intervention is directly involved (cf. 31:18; Ps. 8:3), but Pharaoh is not persuaded.
This first plague of the second sequence again finds Pharaoh at the Nile (cf. 7:15).
See text note. In the second set of the three signs, God distinguishes between Goshen and the rest of Egypt. He shows His favor toward His own people. Pharaoh later investigates this (9:7).

During the swarms of flies, Pharaoh offers to let the people sacrifice, but he is not prepared to agree to all that the Lord demands. Moses regularly refuses to compromise: he will neither worship in the land nor go less than a three-day journey (v. 28); neither will he leave behind the women and children (10:9–11) nor the flocks and herds (10:24–26). At last, after Pharaoh repeatedly breaks faith, God's liberation is total. Israel not only goes out to worship at Sinai but leaves Egypt for Canaan.
The ancient Egyptians may have deified the animals customarily sacrificed by the Israelites, but some other reason, now unknown, may have caused the Egyptians to abhor Israelite sacrifices.

The horse was brought into Egypt by the Hyksos (c. 1700 B.C.). camels. Though sporadically used during this period (cf. Gen. 12:16), widespread use of the camel in Egypt only came much later. Perhaps camels of the merchant traders from Arabia and elsewhere are referred to here.
The wonder has not come by coincidence. The biblical account gives no room for a naturalistic explanation.
Since the next plague affects livestock also, this phrase must designate either "all kinds of livestock" or all the livestock in the field (cf. vv. 18–19).
See 8:23 and note.
This is done before Pharaoh to underscore that the event is supernatural.

The defeat of the sorcerer-priests has been clear from the start, when Aaron's staff-become-reptile swallowed up the reptiles they produced (7:12). They have been able to imitate turning water to blood and producing frogs, but they have been able only to add to, and not reverse, these wonders (7:22; 8:7). When they cannot imitate the production of lice (or gnats), they tell Pharaoh that this is of divine origin (8:18, 19). Finally, the magicians are struck with boils and retreat in discomfort and disgrace (9:11).

These plagues (lit. "blows" or "strokes") show the power of God's hand in striking Egypt (3:20; 7:25; 12:13). The last three wonders fall when the staff of the Lord is stretched out to heaven, earth, and heaven (9:22; 10:13, 21). Ex. 9:13–19 is one of the longest speeches in the plagues cycle, with God explaining His own actions.

God's actions are tempered by mercy. He withholds total destruction so that the Egyptians might know His power and repent (v. 15). Further, God's actions against Pharaoh will cause God's name to be proclaimed to the nations.
Some Egyptians learn to fear God's word (10:7).
See Ps. 29:5.

Pharaoh confesses his guilt for the first time, but the phrase "this time" points to the superficiality of his confession. Though not believing him, Moses nevertheless shows God's power over the earth by stopping the hail.

This information seems to set the time in January–February, a time when hailstorms are frequent in Egypt. Flax was in the bud in January. Barley was in the ear at that time; it would have been harvested in February.
Pharaoh's will is strengthened four times in this one narrative: vv. 8, 10–11, 16–17, 20.
A clear statement of the divine plan involving Pharaoh. The signs and wonders are designed to teach Israel and to leave an indelible impression on their posterity (Deut. 6:20–25).
Moses demands that Israel's permission to worship be unqualified and total. See note on 8:25.
Pharaoh is willing to let the men go, but not the rest of the Israelite population. Note the sarcasm of v. 10.
Goshen is presumably exempt.
The speed of Pharaoh's action and his confession of sin underscore Egypt's peril. Severe famine is threatened ("Not a green thing remained"; see v. 15).

This darkness is clearly more than a blinding sandstorm or an eclipse of the sun. It is an unnatural darkness, like that associated with the day of the Lord (Is. 8:22; 58:10; Joel 2:2; Amos 5:20; Zeph. 1:15; cf. Deut. 28:29). This supernatural darkness is further demonstration of the Lord's authority and power over nature and the false gods of Egypt. The ancient Egyptians regarded Amon-Ra, the personification of the sun, as their chief deity. In this plague, he is not allowed to shine and give life to his people.

A different Hebrew word for "plague" (9:14 note) is used to emphasize the climactic act of divine judgment — the death of the firstborn. The Hebrew word means "stroke" or "blow" and was translated into Latin by the term plaga, from which comes the English term "plague." Unfortunately, the term "plague" today is generally understood to be a synonym for "pestilence" rather than meaning a strike or blow, which is what it meant when the KJV was translated.
All four references to this event (3:21–22; 11:2–3; 12:35–36; Ps. 105:36–38) emphasize that Egypt gives gladly because of the Lord's intervention.
The grinding of corn was menial work done by slaves and prisoners of war.

The first month of the Hebrew year was Abib (March–April). This verse appears to report the institution of this new religious calendar, in commemoration of the exodus. In the later Babylonian calendar, the month of Abib is called Nisan (Neh. 2:1; Esth. 3:7).

Like the sacrifices of Israel (e.g., Lev. 1:3), the Passover lamb must be without flaw. The idea of substitution is evident — the lamb dies in place of the firstborn. Jesus, whose death is prefigured by the Passover sacrifice, is called "the Lamb of God" and "the firstborn" (John 1:29, 36; Rom. 8:29; Col. 1:15, 18; 1 Pet. 1:19; Heb. 1:6; Rev. 5:6).
The slaughter occurs at sunset (Deut. 16:6). The act marks the beginning of the Passover.
Blood symbolizes the life of a victim (Lev. 17:11).
The Passover meal must be eaten as if in haste — the lamb roasted whole and accompanied by unleavened bread. The bitter herbs recall the bitter suffering of slavery in Egypt (1:14).
The story has arrived at a climactic moment, and the Hebrews must be ready to flee immediately. Their garments, which resemble loose skirts, must be tied up in preparation for a hasty departure.
The impotence of Egypt's deities to protect the land's inhabitants is vividly demonstrated to all.
Due to the haste of their departure from Egypt, the Israelites are unable to bake bread leavened with yeast. Unleavened bread becomes a symbol of their swift departure.
See note on Lev. 7:20. Resident aliens and native-born non-Israelites were expected to observe this regulation.

Hyssop was a species of marjoram used for purification (Lev. 14:4–6; Num. 19:6, 18; Ps. 51:7). The richly textured branches and leaves held enough blood to perform the required act. Hyssop has many stalks, and its use prevents the blood of the animal from coagulating.
The precise identity of the "destroyer" is uncertain; the alternative translation "destruction" may be preferable.
See "The Sacraments" at Matt. 28:19.
See note on v. 11. In Jewish Passover celebrations today, the youngest child asks the ritual question, and the father then recites the story of the exodus (cf. 13:8).
The threefold command underscores Pharaoh's urgency. He admits defeat.
The blessing sought is presumably to countermand the dreadful curse that has gone through the land.
These actions confirm the statement in 11:3 (cf. 3:22).

See note 1:11. Succoth cannot be precisely located but must have been in the eastern Delta, possibly at Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat. The coastal routes to Canaan (13:17) were shorter but well guarded. six hundred thousand men on foot. Males of military age (v. 41 note; cf. Num. 11:21; 26:51). Against objections that this number is too large, it has been argued that four centuries might well produce such numbers (1:7). As is often suggested, the Hebrew word for "thousand" can also be taken as meaning "family" or some subsection of a tribe such as a clan (Judg. 6:15). Others have argued that certain numbers were inadvertently altered on account of scribal misreading, which may explain the differences evident between other portions of the biblical text as presently known (cf. 2 Sam. 10:18 and 1 Chr. 19:18; See Introduction to Numbers: Special Issues).

Perhaps persecuted minorities or other slaves come with them. Egyptians who had intermarried with the Hebrews, and even God-fearing Egyptians, are doubtless also included (cf. 9:19–20; 12:48; Is. 56:3).
See Gen. 15:13; note on Acts 7:6.
The Hebrew term denotes clans (cf. 6:19).

This added explanation of the Passover regulations, focusing on the restriction of the ceremony to the covenant community, is occasioned by the mention of non-Israelites leaving Egypt with Israel (v. 38). Only circumcised covenant members are eligible to participate.

None of the meat is to be taken outside of the house where non-covenant members can have access to it. bones. No bones of the animals are to be broken, perhaps as a symbol of covenant unity. As with the Passover lamb, no bones of Jesus were broken at His crucifixion (John 19:36; cf. 1 Cor. 5:7).

Due to the Passover, firstborn males of humans and cattle belong to the Lord (cf. vv. 11–16). The firstborn from the womb represents God's claim on all. The principle is enunciated here and the details are given at 13:12–16; 22:29, 30; 34:19, 20. In this way, Jesus is later presented as Mary's firstborn (Luke 2:22–23).
See note on 12:26.

Interpreting this figurative expression literally, Jews later put brief passages of the Law (13:1–10, 11–16; Deut. 6:4–9; 11:13–21) in small boxes and attached them to the left arm and forehead. These are the tephillim, the phylacteries (protections) of later Judaism, to which Jesus refers in criticizing the Pharisees' ostentatious displays of piety (Matt. 23:5).
An animal from the herd or flock can be given to the Lord as a whole burnt offering. The firstborn son is always to be redeemed (v. 13). firstborn \... males. See note on v. 2.
This does not involve the shedding of blood and is not a sacrifice.
Like the Passover ritual (12:26, 27; 13:8), the ransom of the firstborn is to remind the Israelites that their firstborn males had been ransomed from death.

Israel is not exempted from the death sentence on the firstborn in Egypt. The firstborn were spared only through the blood of the Passover lamb. Subsequent generations must be ransomed, either through the life consecration of the Levites, chosen by God in place of the firstborn (Num. 3:11–13), or through the redemption price of five shekels (Num. 3:46–51).

The strongly fortified caravan route that ran parallel to the Mediterranean coast (see Introduction: Special Issues). The Philistines were not in Palestine in considerable numbers until the twelfth century B.C., but there may have been coastal pockets of Philistine (Minoan) trading colonies there earlier.

The Hebrew term (yam suph) is used to designate the Gulf of Aqaba (23:31), the Gulf of Suez (10:19; Num. 33:10), as well as the body of water crossed in the Exodus. Scholars suggest that the term may mean "sea of reeds" or "sea of the end." The "Red Sea" of the exodus was probably one of the Bitter Lakes north of the Gulf of Suez. Perhaps it was the southern extension of the present Lake Menzaleh, or possibly it was Lake Ballah. Archaeological evidence suggests that the Bitter Lakes were at one time joined to the Gulf of Suez. equipped for battle. This expression translates a rare Hebrew word that may not necessarily have military connotations. "In an orderly fashion" might be a better translation, especially given what is said in v. 17.
Moses fulfills the request made by Joseph centuries earlier (cf. Gen. 50:25; Josh. 24:32).
Israel camps on the edge of the wilderness near what may have been an Egyptian fortress at Etham (since the name seems Egyptian), where they understandably turn back (14:2).
Customary symbols of the immediate presence of God (3:2 note; 33:9–10; 40:34–38; Num. 9:15–22; 11:25; Pss. 99:7; 105:39). God guides Israel day and night by His presence.

By divine command, Israel turns back and camps at Pi-hahiroth. This invites Pharaoh's pursuit (cf. vv. 3–4). Migdol. A general word for "fortification"; its location is presently unknown. Baal-zephon. This site ("Baal of the North") may have been a shrine dedicated to the worship of a god who was viewed as a protector of sailors. The precise location of Baal-zephon is unknown.

Pharaoh is in earnest since his elite chariot force is deployed. The horse and chariot seem to have been introduced into Egypt by the Hyksos (c. 1700 B.C.). The Egyptian chariot normally carried two men, although it may have been accompanied by another man who was a runner.
Israel's rebellious complaints against God's leading are a continuing theme in Exodus (5:21; 15:24; 16:3; 17:2; 32:1).

At the crucial point of Israel's deliverance they must see that their salvation is entirely God's work. His signs and wonders in Egypt, His leading Israel to this hopeless impasse, pinned between Pharaoh's chariots and the sea — all prepare for the climactic display of His saving power. The Lord will fight for them; they need only be still. He will gain the glory (14:18).

**LORD** will fight. This phrase indicates the origin of the theme of the Lord as "divine Warrior," celebrated in ch. 15. War in the ancient world was viewed as a sacred undertaking in which the honor of the deity was at stake. In Israel, God was the "God of the armies of Israel" (1 Sam. 17:45), but also the "Lord of Hosts" (i.e., the Lord of the armies of heaven, the architect of Israel's victories and the inflicter of Israel's defeats). An early account of Israel's conquests under the Lord's leadership was called "the Book of the Wars of the Lord" (Num. 21:14). The theology of Holy War, which arose as a result, finds expression throughout both the OT and NT.
A prayer of Moses is to be understood.
The rod of Moses, used in bringing God's signs and wonders on Egypt, will now bring salvation to His people.
The Angel of the Lord is identified with God's own presence in the cloud (23:20–22). See note on Gen. 16:7.
God sends the wind to accomplish His purpose.

The night was divided into three watches of four hours, the last of which (the morning watch) was from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m., often the time for surprise attacks (cf. 1 Sam. 11:11). The Lord Himself throws the Egyptian army into confusion.
**LORD** fights. Egypt recognizes the victory as God's (cf. v. 14).
The outstretched hand and staff of Moses are the instruments of destruction for the pursuing army, and they bring about Israel's deliverance.
**LORD** saved Israel. Verses 30, 31 summarize God's saving deed and its effect on Israel.

**LORD** and in his servant Moses. At this point, Israel is a community that professes faith. Later, in the wilderness, they will apostatize and come under God's wrath (Num. 14; Ps. 95). The church, as a professing community, must avoid this example (1 Cor. 10:6–12).

Moses and Israel sing of deliverance and hope. The poem of vv. 1–18, unique in the OT, is a victory song expressed in the first person singular, sung by Moses and all the people. It celebrates the Lord's majestic power in saving Israel at the sea (vv. 1–13) and claims His power in planting Israel in the land (vv. 14–18). The song's many archaic expressions point to its origin in the Mosaic period. 15:1 I will sing. The Lord has shown His glory as He promised, and it is the privilege of His people to praise the God of their salvation. The form of the Hebrew verb indicates that this song was sung regularly by the Israelites thereafter.
The theme of Yahweh as the Divine Warrior is emphasized. See Is. 59:16–18.

A symbol of power. In Canaanite art the god Baal was sometimes depicted with a mace upheld in his right hand. Here, the symbol of divine power is the outstretched hand of Moses holding the rod of the Lord.

Through the threatening waters of death God brings His people to Himself. The waters are an instrument of judgment for Egypt and a means of deliverance for Israel. Paul, with some support from Jewish tradition, understands the Red Sea crossing as Israel's "baptism" (1 Cor. 10:2; cf. 1 Pet. 3:21 note).
The staccato repetition of these first person claims reveals an arrogance that is soon silenced.
The comparison is rhetorical in this threefold presentation of God's nature and power.
An expression for their reception into the abode of the dead (Pss. 63:9; 71:20).

This translates the Hebrew word hesed, the precise sense of which is difficult to render in English. Here it refers to God's loyalty and devotion to His people, a loyalty created by the bond of God's covenant with them. Though we might expect it to be used for the devotion of God's people to Him, its overwhelming use in the OT is as a description of God's devotion to His people. There is no stronger term to express the free and faithful grace of His love (34:6, "abounding in steadfast love"; Ps. 136, "his steadfast love endures forever"). God's abiding covenant love and mercy find particular illustration in the book of Hosea (Hos. 2:19). your holy abode. The term used here denotes a temporary resting place, which shepherds might use. While Sinai represents the Lord's resting place at this moment in the exodus, Zion ultimately serves as the place where God gathers His people and dwells among them.

The extraordinary, divinely induced fear of the inhabitants of Canaan is here depicted (Deut. 2:25 note). The peoples are mentioned in the approximate order they will be encountered by the Israelites as they journey to the Promised Land.

An important summary of the aims of the exodus that gives prominence to the motif of God dwelling on the earth. The purpose is the settlement of Israel as God's special people in the Promised Land, the sanctuary of God's dwelling. your own mountain. The point of contact between heaven and earth will be here. The OT regularly associates God's earthly dwelling place with mountains. Here the whole of Palestine is viewed as the place of revelation (cf. Ps. 78:54; Is. 11:9). sanctuary. The land will become such by God's indwelling presence, reminding readers that the goal of the exodus is the worship of God in the land. Apart from God's gracious presence, there is no point in going to the land (33:15).

**LORD** will reign. Apart from two other explicit references to God's kingship in the Pentateuch (Num. 23:21; Deut. 33:5), the tabernacle is presented as a royal tent. The concept of divine covenant with Israel involved a recognition of God's kingship (1 Sam. 8:6–9).

As the Lord leads His people into the wilderness, He tests and delivers them in ways that reveal His purposes. He heals bitter water to show Himself as the Healer (15:22–27); gives manna and quail to show Himself as Provider and the one who establishes rest (Sabbath) for His people (16:1–26); and gives the water of life (17:1–7). Finally, in military victory, it is the Lord Himself who is the ensign of His people (17:15). 15:22 wilderness of Shur. Israel travels in the Sinai peninsula (about 260 miles \[418 km\] long and 150 miles \[240 km\] wide). The word "wilderness" refers here to grazing land as opposed to cultivated land. Shur was located northeast of the Sinai Peninsula, between Egypt and Palestine (Gen. 16:7; 20:1; 25:18).
