The word means "bitterness." The location is suggested to be modern Ain Hawarah, inland and 50 miles (80 km) south of the northern end of Suez. Apparently Israel went down the west coast of the peninsula until they turned east toward Sinai.

The first instance of Israel's wilderness complaint — behavior that typifies Israel's unbelief in the wilderness. The situation is critical. After nine days the water skins are empty, and death from dehydration is an immediate threat. Further, their hopes are dashed — they have located water, but have found it undrinkable (v. 23).

The complaint of the people directed to Moses is really against God. Since Moses leads at God's command (17:1), he appeals to the Lord. showed. God instructs Moses by showing him a tree. The general term for God's law (Hebrew torah) is a form of the verb "showed." God's revelation in this event is a "statute and a rule," preparing for the statutes and ordinances to be given at Sinai and then inscripturated as God's Word written. God's Word instructs Israel as He leads and tests them (cf. Jesus' use of Deut. 8:3 in Matt. 4:4). The tree is a sign of healing and sweetness (Gen. 2:9; Judg. 9:11; Jer. 8:22; Ezek. 47:7, 8).

See Deut. 28:26, 60–62; 7:15. Diseases mark the effects of the divine curse. I am the **LORD** , your healer. God has the power and the mercy to heal (Deut. 32:39; Ps. 103:3). He alone can heal in the peace of His salvation (2 Chr. 16:12; Is. 38:17). To the prayer of anguish (Jer. 17:14), God responds (Jer. 30:17; 33:6). Healing from the damage inflicted by sin and death will come through the Lord's Anointed, by whose wounds we are healed (Is. 53:5; 61:1,2; Matt. 8:17).

The precise location of this site is uncertain. The Lord, who healed the water of Marah (v. 23), leads His people to a place of rest and refreshment. Had the people trusted God fully, there would have been no need to grumble at Marah. Elim was only a short distance away.

The Israelites continue their journey toward Mt Sinai. A theophany occurs in response to the people's complaints (16:9–13). The chapter draws to a close with a rest on the following Sabbath (16:27–30). Israel's keeping of the Sabbath prior to the revelation at Sinai is highlighted, as is God's continued testing of Israel (v. 4; cf. 15:25; 17:2). 16:1 wilderness of Sin. Situated in the southwest of Sinai.

The people cry for bread and meat (v. 3), and God will give both (v. 8). Manna is called the "bread of the angels" (Ps. 78:25). In John 6:26–58, Jesus calls Himself the true manna ("bread of life") of which this provision in the wilderness was a symbol and type.
The word normally refers to the manifested presence of God. Here, the Lord's gracious provision of the manna is in view.

These small migratory game birds of the partridge family come from their winter habitat in Africa in the spring. They are miraculously provided by God to demonstrate His concern for the hunger of the Israelites (see Ps. 78:27). The gift of quail prepares for the sending of manna, which will become the daily food of the Israelites. Quail are given only on one other occasion (Num. 11).

An elevated term normally reserved for holy festivals. The implication is that the weekly Sabbath was normally kept by Israel before Sinai. The Sabbath ordinance in the Ten Commandments represents a codification of Sabbath observance, not its inauguration.
This seed is small, globular, grayish, and aromatic, tasting like honey cakes.
To commemorate the gift of manna, a daily portion is preserved in a special container, called "the golden urn" in Heb. 9:4. Normally, any manna kept overnight decomposed rapidly and became inedible.
The manna continues until they come to Canaan (Josh. 5:10–12). The nomadic lifestyle of the Israelites in the wilderness prevents them from growing crops.
This region, generally identified with the modern Wadi Refayid, about eight miles (13 km) south of Jebel Musa, is the last stop before Sinai.

This translates the Hebrew word rib, which appears in the name "Meribah" (v. 7). test the **LORD** . It is not Moses who is being put on trial, but God. God is being accused of abandoning Israel to die of thirst in the desert. Previously, God indicated that He would test the Israelites through their wilderness experience.
Moses, taking his rod in his hand and accompanied by elders of Israel who are summoned as representative witnesses of the nation, is to pass on before the people (cf. v. 6).

God stands on or beside the rock and is identified with it. God is called the "Rock" in the song of Moses (Deut. 32:4, 15, 18, 31) and in the psalms that speak of this event (Ps. 78:35; 95:1). strike the rock. Moses lifts the rod associated with God's power and strikes the rock. The fearful solemnity of Moses's blow appears when he later strikes the rock in disobedience, thereby dishonoring the holiness of God (Num. 20:9–12).
Only here and in Ps. 95:8 are Meribah and Massah used in combination with reference to these events. The shorter name Massah is used in place of Massah and Meribah in Deut. 6:16; 9:22; 33:8.

The Amalekites, a nomadic group based in southern Palestine, were possibly descendants of Esau (Gen. 36:12–16). The Amalekites attacked from the rear (Deut. 25:18). God has provided manna from heaven and water from the rock; now He provides deliverance from enemies.

Joshua, an Ephraimite previously known as Hoshea ("salvation"), is called Joshua ("Yahweh saves") at Kadesh, possibly as a result of this victory (Num. 13:8, 16). I will stand \... with the staff. Joshua will choose men to fight, but they will do so under the uplifted staff, the sign of the Lord's victory.

Joshua prevails in this battle only when Moses holds up to heaven the staff symbolizing the Lord's presence that brought the signs and wonders in Egypt (4:2; 9:23) and dried up the sea (14:16). Hur. Hur, attested in later tradition as the husband of Moses's sister Miriam, was possibly the grandfather of the famous artisan of the tabernacle, Bezalel (1 Chr. 2:19–20).
One of several references to writing in Exodus. The account was perhaps written in the Book of the Wars of the Lord that is mentioned in Num. 21:14.

**LORD** Is My Banner. The Hebrew word translated "banner" underlies "staff" in v. 9 and is used for the "pole" on which the bronze serpent will later be placed (Num. 21:8). Since "banner" suggests cloth to us, this connection is lost. A spear could serve as a standard in battle, with or without bits of cloth tied to it. Moses's staff is the ensign to which Joshua's army can look and that symbolizes God's saving power. Moses declares that God Himself is the standard, the ensign of His people.

**LORD** . The Hebrew is difficult to translate and interpret (cf. text note). The central message is nevertheless clear: God gives Israel the victory, and the continuing warfare between Israel and Amalek is the Lord's. On the historic enmity between Israel and Amalek, see Num. 24:20; Deut. 25:17; 1 Sam. 15:2–33; 27:8, 9; 30:1–20; 2 Sam. 8:11, 12; 1 Chr. 4:42, 43; Esth. 3:1 note.

The visit of Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses's father-in-law, provides an important hinge in the book of Exodus, linking what has already occurred with the covenant about to be ratified. The first half of ch. 18 records Jethro's reaction to the report of all that God has done for the Israelites in releasing them from Pharaoh's control. Jethro responds appropriately by worshipping God. The second half of ch. 18 anticipates how the covenant will impact the daily lives of the Israelites by setting out God's standards for holy living. Because of their sinful nature, the Israelites will need to be taught these standards and have disputes resolved using values derived from these divinely revealed regulations.
me. Moses apparently sent Zipporah and his family back to Jethro sometime after the incident of 4:24–26.

This formula could indicate either the beginning of Jethro's faith (2 Kin. 5:15) or its strengthening (1 Kin. 17:24). In any event, Jeth­ro offers sacrifices and shares the communion meal as a worshipper of the Lord of Israel, the one true God. By delivering the Israelites from Egypt, God has made Himself known to Jethro (cf. 7:5 and note).
"Statutes" perhaps suggests standing regulations, and "laws" suggests instructions or teachings.

Delegation is often difficult for an able leader. Men are chosen here on moral rather than intellectual grounds to deal with simple matters. Difficult cases, perhaps those without precedent, are brought to Moses. This is how Israel's legal system will later function. No difference is made between the sacred and the secular. The entire law was God's gift to Israel, and obedience to it amounted to obedience to God.

The Lord liberates His people from Egypt to bring them to Himself, to make them His special possession among all peoples. In order to enjoy this blessing, however, they must obey Him and keep His covenant. The revelation at Sinai manifests the holy character of the covenant God and defines the character and behavior appropriate for God's covenant people. The Sinai covenant also underscores the special role of the mediator. The Lord declares His intention to descend and speak directly so that the people might hear and trust Moses forever (19:9). However, the face-to-face revelation so terrifies the people that they plead with Moses to go up to God and receive the commands, then return and report to them (20:18–21). Another crucial lesson of the theophany and revelation at Sinai is the importance of recognizing the holiness of God. 19:1 came into \... Sinai. The wilderness of Sinai probably lay in the southeast region of the Sinai peninsula. Mount Sinai is traditionally identified as Jebel Musa, a mountain with a broad plain at its base that seems to fit the biblical evidence (v. 2; cf. Deut. 9:21 note). Arriving at Sinai possibly seventy days after the Passover, Israel will remain there for almost eleven months (Num. 10:11).

God's words begin (v. 3) and end (v. 6) with an instruction of God to Moses. What lies in between is a summary of God's covenant faithfulness and Israel's covenant responsibilities. God invites the Israelites to enter into this special covenant relationship. He does not compel them by force to accept His lordship over them.

God's deliverance from slavery was not just liberation, but also adoption. He has brought the Israelites out and carried them through the wilderness to bring them to Himself, to make them His (Gen. 17:7 note).

Terms summarizing the proper human response to God's gracious covenant (Gen. 17:2 note). treasured possession. As the following clause shows, God means that Israel will be His personal treasure within what is more generally owned (1 Chr. 29:3). Israel is separated by God's election from the world, which belongs in its entirety to Him.

Israel is to be a priestly royalty, that is, they are to have the status of both priests and kings. This is the status that Adam and Eve forfeited when they betrayed God in the garden of Eden. The Israelites will be a holy nation because God, the Holy One, will come to dwell among them. The emphasis here falls on Israel's relation to God rather than on any priestly ministry to the nations, yet Israel's relation to the Lord also bears witness to the world. What this passage prescribes for Israel, the new covenant makes a reality for believers (1 Pet. 2:9–10; Rev. 1:6; 5:10; 20:6).

Arrangements to ensure ritual purity (washing clothes, v. 10; abstention from sexual intercourse, v. 15; Lev. 15:18; 1 Sam. 21:4) and to safeguard the holiness of the mountain (vv. 12, 13) are commanded in preparation for the theophany, a special visual manifestation of divine presence. come down on Mount Sinai. The mountain is the Lord's place of meeting with His people, not His residence. The tabernacle is soon to be His earthly dwelling place.

God comes as promised on the morning of the third day. No natural explanation of vv. 16–19a (e.g., a volcanic eruption) is sufficient. This is a divine manifestation by storm and fire. a very loud trumpet blast. Later, special occasions of worship are signaled by the blast of the horn (Num. 10:10).
This may refer to those who discharged the duties of priesthood prior to the establishment of the Levitical priesthood.

The Ten Commandments, or "Ten Words" of the covenant. These are expressions of the eternal moral values of God that transcend the OT and the NT. The first four commandments describe how the people are to relate to God, while the remainder describe how God's people are to relate to each other (Deut. 4:13 note). See "The Threefold Use of the Law" at Deut. 13:10. 20:1 See theological note "The Law of God." God spoke all these words. God speaks only these commandments directly to the people (vv. 18–20 and notes; 19:9; Deut. 4:10–14; 5:22–27; 9:10; Neh. 9:13). What are called "words" here are elsewhere called "commandments" (34:28; Deut. 4:13; 10:4). The Hebrew for "word" (dabar) was the term for stipulations in the political treaties of the time. The Decalogue (from the Greek term meaning "ten words") itself possibly reflects the ancient treaty framework (see Introduction: Literary Features). First comes the treaty preamble ("I am the LORD your God," v. 2), then the historical prologue ("who brought you out of the land of Egypt"). The commandments themselves are the treaty stipulations. God is Israel's Suzerain-King, to whom the people owe complete allegiance. The absence of penalties indicates that the Decalogue is not a legal code but rather a foundational covenant document. The "ten words" are framed as broad principles and not as legislation intended for use in a law court. These covenant principles are then applied in the "Book of the Covenant," part of which is a set of sample case laws with penalties attached, which follows (20:22–23:19).
God's claim comes first. Israel is His by right of creation and redemption. The Lord's covenant commands are given to those whom He has already redeemed for Himself from enslavement to Egypt (19:4).
Lit. "before My face" or "in My presence." The Lord is a jealous God who already claims Israel as His (v. 5 note).

The term means something hewn from wood or stone. The prohibited image may be that of the Lord, since other deities have been excluded by v. 2, though the qualifying words "any likeness of anything" suggest that pagan idols may be in view. Israel is to be distinguished from the nations by worship that does not make use of images of God. Images are forbidden, not because there can be none, since God made mankind in His own image (Gen. 1:26, 27), but because God must reveal Himself. He is not subject to human imagination. In His own time, God did provide His own image — Jesus Christ is the true image of the Godhead in bodily form (Col. 1:15; 2:19). See "Syncretism" at Hos. 2:13.

When used of God, this word describes His passion for His holy name, a zeal that demands the exclusive devotion of His people. It is employed when that claim is threatened by other deities (Deut. 6:15; Josh. 24:19). third and the fourth generation. The long­est span of generations represented in a given household at any one time. The severity of God's judgment on subsequent generations warns those who love their children's children of the terrible consequences of their sin.
God's covenant mercy, or steadfast love (Hebrew hesed) is His devotion to His people (15:13 note).

God's name is a gift of grace to Israel. And it is in the name, not through an idol, that Israel has access to God in worship. God's name is therefore to be revered. This command forbids the use of God's name in false worship, for incantations or divination, as well as for attesting falsehood or speaking blasphemy (Deut. 28:58). Jesus teaches His disciples to pray that God will hallow His name, and Jesus hallows the Father's name on the cross (Matt. 6:9; John 12:27, 28).

The Hebrew word (shabbat) apparently derives from the verb meaning "to cease" — the Sabbath being the day that regular labor ceased. Exodus cites God's work of creation as the basis for the command (v. 11), while Deuteronomy bases the Sabbath ordinance on the deliverance from Egypt (Deut. 5:12 and note). The Sabbath ordinance is rooted in both creation and of redemption — it looks backward to God's good creation (Gen. 2:2, 3) and forward to the final redemptive Sabbath rest for God's people (Heb. 4:1–11). Just as circumcision is the sign of the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 17), so the Sabbath becomes the sign of the Sinai covenant (31:13), reminding God's people of their place within God's purposes for creation and of their salvation from physical bondage in Egypt. Ultimately, the Sabbath points to Christ, our Creator and Redeemer, who brings rest to the people of God (Matt. 11:28; Col. 2:16, 17).

The Sabbath is not designed as a burden, but as a blessed release from hard labor (Mark 2:27). The holiness of the day separates it to the Lord so that it is enjoyed by sharing His rest, celebrating His work of creation and redemption (Deut. 5:15).

With this fifth commandment, the Decalogue turns to human relations, beginning with the family. Honor toward parents anchors society, and it binds children to parents in the community of faith. The promise and implied warning of this commandment are unique in this series. Disrespect for parents is a serious matter, for it also dishonors the Lord.

The Hebrew term used here prohibits more than just murder, hence the KJV translation "Thou shalt not kill." It refers to the taking of any human life when this is not sanctioned by God, the giver of life. OT legislation distinguishes between manslaughter and premeditated murder, both of which are forbidden but incur different penalties (Num. 35:9–34). The verb here is never applied to Israel at war, and capital punishment was authorized before the revelation of this command (Gen. 9:6; cf. Lev. 24:17; Num. 35:30–34). Human life is sacred because man bears God's image (Gen. 9:5, 6 and notes).

The commandment emphasizes the importance of faithfulness in human relationships. When such faithfulness is absent from the most intimate of relationships, all relationships are undermined. If Israelites break a marriage covenant, they are very likely to break their covenant with God. See "Marriage" at Mal. 2:16; "Divorce" at Mark 10:2.
Property is placed below life and marriage in God's scheme of moral values.
See "Oaths, and Vows" at Neh. 5:12.
The awe that recognizes God's power and glory deters sin (v. 20).
Moses's authority as God's mediator is acknowledged. That God actually did speak distinguishes Him from false gods, who cannot speak (vv. 22, 23).

See notes on Lev. 1:3–17 and 3:1. Only two types of sacrifices are briefly mentioned here; the list of sacrifices will be expanded in Lev. 1–7 after the tabernacle is constructed and God comes to dwell among the people.

The reasons for this prohibition are no longer clear. Some suggest that this provision was designed to prevent the Israelites from using the altars of Canaanite holy places, which typically were constructed of cut stones. The altar of burnt offering for the tabernacle was made of wood, covered with bronze. The type of altar described here was used for sacrifices made away from the tabernacle. See note on Deut. 27:5.
See note on 28:42.

The Lord sets forth the obligations of His covenant. Civil and penal case laws are presented at 21:1–22:20; moral imperatives that go beyond what laws might enforce are listed in 22:21–29; instructions for sabbatical periods and the celebration of festivals come in 23:10–19; instructions relating to the occupation of the land of Canaan are given in 23:20–33. The purpose of these covenant obligations was to regulate Israelite life in the Promised Land. Interestingly, many of the laws are paralleled in the Code of Hammurabi. 21:1 rules. The Hebrew word here means "precedents," or guiding principles determined by case decisions. These sample laws, which apply the foundational Decalogue (20:1–17) to society, extend to 22:20.

The case law appropriately commences with laws regulating slavery, for that had been Israel's position in Egypt. A person could sell himself or his wife into slavery because of poverty or debt (2 Kin. 4:1; Neh. 5:1–5; Amos 2:6). Though the Mosaic law allowed the practice of indentured servitude, abuses were carefully limited (Deut. 15:12 note) — such servitude was limited to six years (v. 2) and the rights of slaves were underscored. See note on 1 Pet. 2:18.

The judges probably held court at God's sanctuary. Whether the door or doorpost was at the sanctuary or the home is not specified here, but Deut. 15:17 favors the latter. The piercing of the ear was a public indication of permanent slavery.
The sale of a woman as a slave-wife seems intended, hence the protection.
An instance of unintentional manslaughter is in view. See note on Deut. 19:4.
Such actions transgress the fifth commandment (20:12).
See note on Deut. 24:7.
A further transgression of the fifth commandment. The Hebrew word for "curses" may denote other forms of overt dishonor to parents in addition to spoken curses.
Evidence that he is recovering from his injury.
That the slave does not die immediately is taken as evidence that the master did not intend to kill.

While indentured slavery was accepted in the OT, the clear implications of the Christian gospel led to its abolition (1 Pet. 2:18 note). The laws governing Israel's life should be interpreted in light of their cultural and social setting. They restrained exploitation and oppression in recognition of man's "hardness of heart" (cf. Matt. 19:8).

The usual Hebrew word for "child" is used (as in v. 4 and 1:17, 18). The Hebrew verb describes the emergence of a child in Gen. 25:26; 38:28–30. There is no reason to limit the "harm" spoken of to the mother. If there is no lasting harm either to the mother or the child, compensation for the hurt inflicted is to be paid to the husband, fixed by a third party. Otherwise, the penalty is proportionate to the injury to the mother or child. Although the harm to the woman or child was not intentional, there was culpable negligence in disregarding the welfare of the pregnant woman.

The fundamental principle is that punishment should fit the crime (Lev. 24:19, 20; Deut. 19:21). Similar statements are found in the laws of Hammurabi (c. 1750 B.C.). It seems that "eye for eye" was idiomatic for the principle of proportional justice, and that such penalties were not literally imposed as the immediate context clearly shows (cf. vv. 18–21; 26–27).
Harm done by animals is the responsibility of the careless owner, and appropriate compensation must be paid. Since the ox had been involved in blood guilt, its flesh was not to be eaten.
The value of a slave's life and the price Judas was paid to betray Jesus (Matt. 26:15; cf. Zech. 11:12).

Thieves who compound their guilt by profiting from and disposing the stolen animals are to restore fourfold or fivefold (cf. v. 4). More compensation is required in the case of oxen, which take longer to raise.

The killing of an unknown nighttime burglar does not incur bloodguilt, since confronting the burglar might endanger the homeowner's life. The daytime thief is readily identifiable, and killing is not justified.
See note on v. 1.
Thorns were used as hedges to keep animals out of fields (Mic. 7:4); they were also flammable and used for fuel (Ps. 58:9).
If the thief is not found, the one entrusted with his neighbor's goods is brought to the sanctuary (21:6 note), where an oath of innocence is presumably sworn.
The man entrusted with his neighbor's animal is presumed to have been negligent.
In the owner's absence, the onus of proof falls on the borrower.
The cost of renting the animal is to cover the possibility of loss.
Laws on premarital intercourse require full responsibility from the male for its consequences. The exploited person must be protected. See note on Deut. 22:22–29.

Sorcery, the attempt to determine and influence the future through occult means, is strongly condemned (Deut. 18:9–13; 2 Kin. 21:6; Jer. 27:9–10; Mic. 5:12; Nah. 3:4). The future is in God's hands alone (Deut. 18:9 note).

Lit. "devoted to sacred use" or "put to the ban" (Deut. 20:17 note). If a sacred use is impossible, as here, the item is destroyed. In Israel's holy war — by which God's judgment was executed against the Canaanites — the spoils were under the ban, devoted to God (Num. 21:2, 3; Josh. 7:11).
This refers to a temporary dweller without family support, much as Israel had been in Egypt.
Widows and orphans, who might lack family defenders, are God's special concern. He will hear their cry and avenge them.
The poor must not be exploited because they are more vulnerable and lack the power or wealth to defend themselves. See note on Deut. 23:19.
See note on Deut. 24:6. A pledge must be returned before hardship is caused by its absence (Deut. 24:10, 11; Amos 2:8).

This text is cited by Paul at Acts 23:5. To question duly appointed authority amounts to questioning God's authority (Rom. 13:1, 2). Neither God nor the ruler whose authority comes from Him are to be reviled.
Because the firstfruits are symbolic of God's claim on everything, Israelites are not to hold back this offering (13:2 note).
Since the blood will not have been properly drained (Lev. 3:17; 7:22–27).
The covenant member is not to take advantage of an enemy's misfortune. See Matt. 5:43–48; Rom. 12:20, 21.
The substance of 22:21 is repeated, framing the moral obligations set out in 22:21–23:9. These obligations go beyond what courts can enforce and demand exemplary moral behavior.

Like the weekly Sabbath on which it was patterned, the sabbatical year is intended for the good of humanity and of creation (20:8–11 and notes). It reminds Israel that God, the true owner of the land, has entrusted it to them (Lev. 25:2). The land is to lie fallow, and what grew of itself is reserved for the poor, who will not have been able to save sufficient food resources. Leviticus 26:34–35 suggests that the sabbatical year was not always observed, but it is clearly in place at Neh. 10:31.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread occurred in March or April in celebration of the Israelites' divine rescue from slavery in Egypt. Seven weeks later came the Feast of Weeks, celebrating the harvest of cereal crops such as wheat. Finally, the Feast of Tabernacles celebrated the final harvest and the end of the agricultural season in autumn (September).

Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are closely associated — the Feast begins the day after Passover. Some have mistakenly argued that the Feast of Unleavened Bread is simply an agricultural festival, but its commemoration of the exodus is clear here. See note on Deut. 16:9–12.

See v. 14; Deut. 16:9–12 and notes. Also known as the Feast of Weeks or Pentecost. The Holy Spirit later came in great power at Pentecost (Acts 2:1–39; cf. Rom. 8:23). Feast of Ingathering. Also called the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths. See v. 14; Deut. 16:13–17 and notes. end of the year. This refers to the end of the agricultural, not calendar, year. See note on 12:2.
The details of this verse apply to the Passover celebration (cf. 12:10).
See notes on 13:2; 1 Cor. 15:20. You shall not boil. See note on Deut. 14:21.
Despite the reference to pardoning sin, this angel is probably not the Angel of the Lord who is associated with the burning bush (3:2) and the cloud (14:19). See note on Gen. 16:7.
These were stone pillars connected with Canaanite shrines.
For a longer list of blessings, see Deut. 28:1–14.
See note on 15:14.
See note on Deut. 7:20.
The coming conquest will be gradual. The Israelites will not assume responsibility for the whole land until they are able to defend and care for it.
See note on Gen. 13:15. Red Sea. See note on 13:18.
Israel is quick to disobey this command (Josh. 9). The collection of covenant obligations ends as it began — with an emphasis upon keeping the first two commandments (20:1–4, 22).

The terms of the covenant having been stipulated, the people ratify the covenant by agreeing to abide by its conditions (vv. 3, 7; cf. 19:8). 24:1 Then he said to Moses. Having set out the covenant obligations, God now gives further instructions to Moses and the leaders of Israel. The mention of Aaron and his two sons speaks for the authenticity of the narrative, for the sons were later killed for an offense against God (Lev. 10:1–2).
This may mark Moses's delivery of the Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33), since all Israel has heard the Decalogue (20:1 note). The "rules" are the material in 21:1–22:20.
For another reference to Moses writing, see note on Deut. 31:9.
There is no appointed priesthood as yet. The offerings seal the covenant, indicating that God's acceptance of Israel is on the basis of blood atonement for sin.
This phrase probably applies to 20:22–23:33, which Moses recorded (v. 4).

The people are sprinkled with "the blood of the covenant," the blood that puts the covenant into effect (Heb. 9:16–22 and notes). The blood signifies cleansing from sin so that the people might enter the covenant relation, and it underscores that the ultimate penalty for breaking the covenant is death. This ritual, like the Passover, resembles how the Aaronic priests are consecrated for service in the tabernacle. The people are sanctified to become a holy nation (cf. 19:6). Jesus proclaims the fulfillment of the symbolism at the Last Supper when He offers the cup: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt. 26:28).

They see a visible manifestation of the Lord, but not the fullness of His glory and power. Moses is later privileged to view the "goodness" and the "back" of God (33:19–23 and notes), though the limited character of the manifestation is emphasized. feet. The description concentrates only on God's feet, an indication of the partial character of the divine manifestation. pavement. Perhaps the vault of the sky under the throne (cf. Ezek. 1:26). sapphire. The area beneath God's feet is compared to a pavement of blue lapis lazuli. This semiprecious stone was available in a natural form from Cyprus and Scythia, and in artificial form from Egypt.
His power (4:2 note). Not only do they see God, they eat and drink before Him. Similar meals in celebration of the conclusion of a covenant are recorded at Gen. 31:46; Matt. 26:28.
Moses ascends Mount Sinai to receive the covenant tablets and further instructions regarding Israel's worship and the tabernacle.
Moses's absence sets the scene for the golden calf incident in ch. 32.
The term is used for a manifestation of the divine presence. The remainder of Exodus deals with the preparations necessary for God to dwell permanently with His people.

This section goes into great detail regarding the divine pattern for the place where the Lord Himself will dwell among His people. The tabernacle and its ministry are the two central features — details of the tabernacle construction, and the precise elements, manner, and persons to be employed in God's service are carefully specified. The inauguration of the covenant established God's kingship over Israel. That kingship is now to be appropriately recognized by the Israelites via the building of a portable residence for God as a symbol of His royal authority over Israel. 25:1 The materials are to be gathered as freewill offerings from the treasures of the people (12:35, 36). Ironically, while these instructions are being given, the people are contributing gold for an idol at the foot of the mountain (32:1–4).
The nearer the divine presence, the finer and more precious the material required. Metals and colored yarns are listed in descending order of value.

Or violet. Violet and purple dyes were obtained from shellfish; scarlet from insects. These colors were precious because of the cost of the dye. The blue of the tabernacle particularly came to be associated with the Lord (Num. 15:38). fine twined linen. The fine linen was probably Egyptian. goats' hair. The goat hair was undyed. It was to be used as a first covering for the tabernacle, and over it other skins would be placed (26:14).

The ram skin leather was tanned or dyed, perhaps both. goatskins. The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. Dolphin (text note) and sea cow skin are also possible. Such leather may have been cured only, in which case there may be a descending order of value in the skins selected. acacia wood. A hard, long-lasting wood suitable for carving and overlay.
The stones set in the two shoulder pieces of the ephod were of a substance that could be engraved, such as carnelian, onyx, or lapis lazuli (24:10 note; 28:9–12; 39:6–7).
This term underlines the holy nature of God's residence. It is holy because the Holy One is present there.

The pattern shown to Moses is a model or plan of the tabernacle to be built (cf. the plan of the temple revealed to David in 1 Chr. 28:19). At the same time, it reflects the heavenly residence which already existed (Heb. 9:24). See Ezek. 43:10, 11. tabernacle. The term means "dwelling place." With the construction of the tabernacle, God comes to dwell among the Israelites. This marks a radically new stage in the divine-human relationship, because God had no earthly residence prior to this. This tabernacle foreshadows the dwelling of God with humanity in the person of Jesus Christ (John 1:14 note).

The revelation of the pattern for the earthly sanctuary begins with the plans for the ark of the covenant, the most holy object in the tabernacle. This ornate chest later contains the Ten Commandments, the pot of manna, and Aaron's staff (16:33; 25:16; Num. 17:10; Deut. 10:1–5; Heb. 9:4). The ark is viewed as a footstool of the heavenly throne (vv. 18, 22 and notes). cubit. A cubit is roughly the distance from the tip of the middle finger to the elbow — about eighteen inches.
So that the ark can be moved without being touched (cf. 2 Sam. 6:6, 7). Its holiness and portability are stressed.
The stone tablets of the Sinai covenant. God's written Word is His witness to the terms of His covenant.

Lit. the "atonement covering," a place at which estranged parties are reconciled. "Atonement" is the normal English translation for the Hebrew root that means "to wipe away" or perhaps "to cover" the guilt of sin from God's eyes so that believers may be reconciled with God. Propitiation (i.e., turning away divine wrath and satisfying the claims of divine justice) is effected by blood sacrifice in the OT (Lev. 17:11). This shedding of blood dramatizes the cost of forgiveness, and it points forward to the sacrificial death of Christ on the Cross, where the symbolism of the Passover was fulfilled (1 Cor. 5:7). Paul declares that Jesus has been made the propitiation for our sins (Rom. 3:25; cf. 1 John 2:2). The "mercy seat" is the ark cover, which is sometimes mentioned in distinction from the ark as the place where God is propitiated. In the Septuagint, the Greek term for "mercy seat" (hilasterion) means lit. "place of propitiation" (also in Heb. 9:5).

In the OT, the cherubs are usually associated with the throne of the Lord as guardians or bearers of the throne (1 Sam. 4:4; Is. 37:16). In the pagan world, cherubs were minor deities protective of palaces and temples; here they symbolize angelic guardians (Gen. 3:24). They were perhaps depicted as winged sphinxes (winged lions with human heads).

The Lord is the One "who is enthroned on the cherubim" (1 Sam. 4:4; 2 Sam. 6:2; 2 Kin. 19:15; Ps. 80:1; 99:1; Is. 37:16). The mercy seat becomes the focal point for God's meeting with His people. The purpose of the exodus was the bridging of the chasm separating God and humanity (29:45, 46).

The revelation of the earthly sanctuary pattern continues with the plans for objects to be housed in the holy place — the table of the bread of the Presence, its dishes, and the golden lampstand. Instructions for the altar of incense, also housed in the Holy Place, are given in 30:1–10. 25:23 make a table. Called "table of the bread of the Presence" (Num. 4:7) and the "table of pure gold" (Lev. 24:6, 2 Chr. 13:11) on which the bread was arranged (1 Kin. 7:48). It stood on the north side of the holy place (40:22).

These dishes, all of pure gold, include a plate on which the bread of the Presence was placed, a small pan for the frankincense, a pitcher for the wine libation or drink offering, and a bowl into which this was poured (37:16; Lev. 24:7; Num. 4:7).

This bread can only be eaten by the priests (Lev. 24:8, 9). The careful placement of the twelve loaves (probably symbolizing the twelve tribes of Israel) before the Lord and the eating of the loaves by the people's religious representatives (the priests) remind Israel of its constant dependence on God's life-giving presence.

The lampstand, which stood opposite the table in the Holy Place, is constructed of a talent (about seventy-five pounds) of hammered gold and patterned to suggest a growing almond tree. Perhaps symbolic of new life, the almond tree blossomed in late January, before other trees.

The pedestal and main upright represent the trunk of the tree, out of which grew three branches on either side. The six branches probably rose to the height of the central shaft, with seven lamps (the number signifying completeness) resting on the topmost ornaments of the shaft and branches (v. 37).

God reveals the pattern for the tabernacle proper. The tabernacle, God's holy dwelling in the midst of His sinful people, serves a double function. On the one hand, it protects the people from the dangers of unauthorized intrusion into God's holy presence — the curtains of the Most Holy Place, of the Holy Place, and even of the courtyard stand between the people and the threat of God's consuming holy presence. On the other hand, the tabernacle provides a way of approach to the Lord. Worshipers enter the outer court to pray and offer sacrifices; the priests carry the people's petitions into the holy place; and once a year on the Day of Atonement, the high priest enters the Most Holy Place, the very throne-room of the Almighty, with a blood atonement to meet the Lord at the mercy seat. Nevertheless, the tabernacle was a provisional symbol of God's dwelling with humanity, rather than the full reality. It symbolized the heavenly temple of God (Heb. 8:1–6; 9:1–15) and pointed forward to the dwelling of God with humanity in Jesus Christ, God incarnate in human flesh (John 1:14 note). As the author of Hebrews makes clear, the tabernacle and its ministry were insufficient in themselves (Heb. 10:1–4). Rather, they foreshadowed the final and completely sufficient priestly work of Christ (Heb. 10:11–18). The tabernacle was also viewed as a model of the cosmos, anticipating a future time when God's presence would fill the whole earth. The vision of the New Jerusalem in Rev. 21–22 reveals the fulfillment of this expectation. 26:1 tabernacle. The tabernacle itself, which houses the Holy and Most Holy Places, is forty-five feet long, fifteen feet wide, and fifteen feet high. It is covered with ten curtains woven of expensive fabrics adorned with cherubim. Two sets of five curtains, forty-two feet long by six feet wide, each of fine linen, are connected so as to provide a continuous piece measuring forty-two feet by sixty feet. This is then draped over the wooden framework. This inner covering ends one cubit (18 inches) short of the ground on either side (vv. 1–6).

As protection for the inner curtain, two sets of curtains of goats' hair are to be joined by loops and clasps to make one curtain of forty-five feet from top to bottom and sixty-six feet from end to end.
The outer curtains are two cubits (three feet) longer than the inner ones and barely reach the ground (v. 1 note).
Two further covers of rams' skins and goatskins, apparently arranged in that sequence, are made to protect the two inner sets.

These provide the framework on which the curtains are draped. They are planks, or more likely open frames, that are set vertically to provide the sides and back of the structure. They are stabilized with cross bars and anchored in silver bases driven into the ground. There are twenty on each side and six at the back (west).
The frames are supported by fifteen cross members overlaid with gold, five for each of the enclosed sides. The entire structure can be dismantled or assembled in a minimum amount of time.

The interior of the tabernacle tent is to be divided by the "veil of the screen" (39:34; 40:21; Num. 4:5) that separates the inner Most Holy Place from the outer Holy Place. This veil is a tapestry that hangs thirty feet from the entrance to the tent, creating an inner cube fifteen feet square where the ark is kept. This is the Most Holy Place, the throne room where the Lord will meet with Israel's high priest on the Day of Atonement. The Holy Place, a royal antechamber, extends thirty feet from the veil to the tent entrance.

The gate at the east end is covered by a screen supported by acacia pillars set in bronze sockets. The screen is made of the same material as the inner curtains and the veil, but is of embroidery rather than tapestry since it was further from the Most Holy Place.

The altar of burnt offering is made of acacia wood overlaid with bronze. The horns at the four corners are important in the ritual and were smeared with blood at the consecration of priests (29:12), in the sin offering (Lev. 4:25, 30), and on the Day of the Atonement (Lev. 16:18). They give sanctuary to anyone who lays hold of them (1 Kin. 1:50). This altar differs from those made of earth or uncut stones (20:24–25).
Accessories, being outside of the tabernacle proper, are all of bronze.

The grate details and its function are obscure. It is placed halfway down the altar running from below the ledge of the altar to the ground. Perhaps it is for ventilation of the altar fire. The "ledge" of v. 5 is apparently for priests to stand on when offering sacrifice.
The court is a rectangle of 150 by 75 feet (46 by 23 m) enclosed by white linen hangings seven and one-half feet high that separate it from the surrounding camp of Israel (v. 18).

A thirty-foot opening on the east side was covered by a screen (v. 16). Fifty-six pillars (twenty on the north and south sides, ten on the west, and three on either side of the entrance on the east) in bronze sockets hold up the linen hangings. Another four pillars support the screen. Their arrangement is not specified, and neither is the placement of the tabernacle within the courtyard. The pillars may be held in place by pegs and guy ropes (35:18).

The court apparently consists of two equal seventy-five-foot squares containing the tabernacle proper and the open space before it. The ark and the altar of burnt offering are the respective central objects. The eastern, open half of the court provides public space for sacrifices and the gathering of worshipers.
Pure olive oil provides a virtually smoke-free light. The lamp is the golden lampstand that stands on the south side of the Holy Place (Lev. 24:1–4).

The tabernacle is so named because God and Israel's priestly representatives meet there as determined by liturgical regulation. It is not identical with the tabernacle of meeting outside the camp where God meets Moses (33:7 note; Num. 12:4).

Having revealed the pattern of the earthly sanctuary (25:1–27:21), God now reveals the regulations for the priestly ministry of the sanctuary. 28:1 serve me as priests. First and foremost, the priests are to serve as mediators between God and humanity. As priests and representatives of a holy God, Aaron and his sons participate in the holiness of the tabernacle and are held to strict standards of ritual purity (Lev. 21:1–22:16). In addition to their ceremonial duties, such as offering sacrifices and caring for the place of worship, they act as judges (Deut. 17:8–13), dispense blessings (Num. 6:22–27), give oracles (Num. 27:21), and teach God's rules and instructions to the people (Deut. 33:10). Nadab and Abihu. These two sons of Aaron are killed for unlawful activity (Lev. 10:1–2). Aaron is succeeded by Eleazar (Deut. 10:6).
The vestments of God's holy high priest are of paramount importance. They are designed for glory and for beauty, and they are made of the same expensive materials as the tabernacle.

This sleeveless linen garment decorated with colored thread is made from costly materials and reached from the breast down to the hips. It has shoulder straps with two onyx stones engraved with the names of the tribes, and a waistband (39:2–7). The breastpiece that contains the Urim and Thummim is fastened to the ephod (v. 27; 1 Sam. 23:9–10).
This is a single piece of fabric, folded double to form a square pouch with gemstones bearing the names of the twelve tribes on its front (v. 21) and the Urim and Thummim inside (v. 30).
Ropes of twisted gold thread connect the breastpiece to the shoulder straps of the ephod.
Aaron carries this reminder of the nation he represents when he enters the Holy Place.

Lit. "lights and perfections." They are used to receive oracles from God (Num. 27:21; Deut. 33:8; 1 Sam. 23:6–13; 28:6; Ezra 2:63). There is no hint of how they function or what they are — perhaps stones of different colors, or two small objects engraved with symbols or letters of the alphabet.
This blue robe with bells is worn under the breastpiece and ephod to identify and protect the priest when he enters an area of special sanctity.

**LORD** . On the turban of Aaron is fastened a plate or diadem. The same object is called a crown (29:6; 39:30; Lev. 8:9) and worn by kings (2 Sam. 1:10; 2 Kin. 11:12; Ps. 89:39). The engraved plate is of pure gold, and it identifies Aaron as set apart to the Lord and as Israel's representative.

The other priestly garments are only briefly described. The coat seems to have been a long shirt-like garment worn under the robe. These priestly garments are to be worn in God's presence (v. 43). Ordinary priests wear plain coats, a less ornate sash, and a headdress different from the high priest's.
The undergarment is worn so as not to violate the command of 20:26. Ritual nakedness, so common in other ancient religions, is forbidden in Israel.
Or "make them holy," set them apart from their fellow Israelites for God's service. To serve within the tabernacle, the priests have to be holy.
Three kinds of grain offering are to be presented (cf. Lev. 2:4–10).
Aaron and his sons cannot enter the tabernacle until they have been ceremonially cleansed by washing and sacrifice has been made for them (cf. Heb. 7:26–28).
Aaron and his sons are to be clothed with sacred garments symbolic of their office. Only Aaron is anointed and thereby authorized to act as chief priest.
Lit. "fill the hand." Possibly a Hebrew idiom for induction into office, but it may refer to how they will receive meat from the sacrifices offered by the Israelites in the future (cf. vv. 27–28).

Priests lay their hands on the bull calf to symbolize personal identification and substitution in this sin offering. Blood is to be smeared on the horns of the altar of burnt offering as it was for laymen, since Aaron and his sons are still unconsecrated (Lev. 4:25, 30). The remainder of the blood is poured at the bottom of the altar as in the sin offering (Lev. 4:7; 9:9). Certain parts are to be burned on the altar (v. 13), but the remainder is to be burned outside the camp as unclean (v. 14).
This ram will be offered as a dedicatory burnt offering (Lev. 1:3–17 note).
The other ram will be offered as a peace offering (Lev. 3:1 note).
The ear, hands, and feet of the priests (extremities as representative parts of the whole) are cleansed from impurities to consecrate for service.
Normally part of the priest's portion (Lev. 7:32), it is also burned in this sacrifice for the priests.
The ceremonial waving symbolizes their dedication as gifts to God.

Moses, since he is acting as priest, will receive the breast and the thigh of the ram from the consecration of Aaron and his sons as his portion; thereafter, the priests are to receive these (Lev. 7:31–32).

The requirements for the daily priestly offerings are reviewed (vv. 38–46). The author of Hebrews contrasts these daily sacrifices for sin (whose repetition pointed to their insufficiency) with the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ (Heb. 10:11–14).

This passage states the goal of the exodus (and of the book). God "brought them out of the land of Egypt" that He might "dwell among them" (v. 46; cf. 7:5; 18:10–12 and notes). The covenant relationship between God and His people is fundamentally one of communion between God and humanity (Gen. 17:7; Ex. 6:7).

The altar is to be placed in front of the veil at the entrance to the Most Holy Place (v. 6). It is lit by the high priest morning and evening. The smoke that then covers the mercy seat protects the high priest from the divine presence (Lev. 16:13).

The half-shekel atonement money that accompanies each census witnesses to Israel's dependence on the Lord's mercy. Their lives are forfeit because of sin and must be redeemed. The lesson of the Passover and the redemption of the firstborn is applied to all Israel (13:15; 22:29; Num. 3:40–51). ransom. Lit. "atonement." The payment serves as an act of individual atonement and is an assertion of God's rights over Israel.

The priests wash their hands and feet when they approach the altar or enter the tabernacle for ministry. No dimensions are given for the basin, though Solomon's temple basins are massive (1 Kin. 7:38). Neglecting to wash might cause death — the holy God is not to be approached casually (vv. 20, 21).

The tabernacle is to be constructed according to the divine design by gifted men who are supernaturally enabled by the Holy Spirit to oversee all the tasks required (vv. 3–6, 11). All the work is described to Moses by God and little room is left for creative variation (25:9).
The name is archaic and means "in El's \[God's\] shadow" (cf. 17:10 note).
Bezalel's assistant. His name means "the father is my tent."

The Sabbath commandment is reiterated and designated as the covenant sign of the Mosaic covenant (Gen. 9:12 note). To keep God's Sabbath is to keep the covenant since the Sabbath is a sign of the special relationship between God and Israel. To disregard God's Sabbath is to disregard God's purposes for creation through His redemption of Israel.

See note on Deut. 5:22. Some suggest that these were two identical copies. Consistent with ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaties, one copy belonged to each treaty partner and the copies were housed in the respective sanctuaries of the suzerain and the vassal. The ark was both the focal point of Israel's sanctuary and the special dwelling place of God. Hence, both copies were placed in the ark. finger of God. See 8:19a and note.

God's continued mercy shown to the people of Israel in these chapters is striking indeed. Even after His mighty exodus deliverance and miraculous provisions for them in the wilderness, they respond with complaints, recriminations, and the idolatrous worship of the golden calf (16:2, 3; 17:1–3; 32:1–6). We should note, however, that this section displays not only the treachery of Israel and the kindness of their God, but also the central role of Moses the mediator. Because the Lord is pleased with the mediator, He does not cast off the people and start anew to make a great nation out of Moses (32:10–14). We should not conclude that Israel's continuing in God's favor is due solely to the merit of Moses as God's mediator. Rather, the ground of Moses's plea for mercy is his concern for God's glory and his appeal to the gracious covenant promises God had made to the patriarchs (32:11–14). The crisis of Israel's disloyalty, and the Lord's threat to destroy them, is resolved in the faithfulness of God revealed through the successful appeal of the man Moses, who knows God and His intent to glorify Himself by keeping His promises. 32:1 gathered themselves together. The phrase is ominous (used of the rebellion of Korah at Num. 16:3; 20:2). The problem is not with Moses's past leadership, but with his absence.

The bull as a symbol of deity was common in the ancient world. Perhaps a symbol of Apis, the Egyptian fertility bull-god, was meant. Aaron himself may be presenting the calf as a symbol of the true God, and he apparently attempts to blunt the apostasy by building an altar and announcing a festival to the Lord (v. 5). Noting that the Hebrew term elohim, translated "gods" in vv. 1 and 4, can be rendered as singular or plural, some have argued that the people are worshiping the calf as a symbol of the Lord (if so, they are still guilty of idolatry; 20:4 note). But the shout of the people is reported here using the plural verb ("brought \... out") with 'elohim. The singular form is always used with this noun when it refers to the true God; thus, it is more likely that the people are turning to the bull-god to lead them, in gross violation of 20:2 (cf. Acts 7:39–41).
The first, second, third, and probably the seventh commandments are violated in this festival (v. 6 note; 20:2–7, 14).

They rise from their meal to engage in what is probably a fertility cult orgy (the bull-god Apis was the Egyptian god of fertility). That this festival involves sexual immorality is further indicated by the later reference to shameful lack of restraint (v. 25).
In righteous anger against their idolatry, God does not acknowledge the people as His own. Instead, He designates them to Moses as "your people."

Anticipating the intercession of Moses, God proposes to destroy the stiff-necked apostates and to make a new nation of Moses. If He were to do so, God would be setting aside His promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Gen. 12:2; 26:4; 28:14).

Moses rejects God's offer of v. 10. Instead, arguing on the basis of the honor of God's name (v. 12) and appealing to God's faithfulness to the covenant promises made to the patriarchs (v. 13), Moses pleads that God would continue to acknowledge Israel as His people.
Elsewhere the sequence is "Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (cf. 2:24; 3:6; Deut. 1:8), but the substitution is made by Moses to suit the occasion.

**LORD** relented. See note on Gen. 6:6. Moses's intercessory prayer itself is also part of God's will and purpose to show His grace. But the effectiveness of Moses's intercession can only be described by characterizing the Lord in human terms: He relents and withholds the total judgment He had threatened.
Attention is emphatically drawn to the divine origin of the tablets to be smashed. See theological note "Special Revelation and the Bible."

Moses replies in a short graphic poem with a threefold use of the word for "singing," which lit. reads: "Not the sound of singing victory, not the sound of singing defeat, but the sound of singing I hear."
The broken tablets of the Ten Commandments powerfully picture the broken covenant (20:1 note).

The calf seems to be wooden with a golden overlay. Israel was forced to drink this symbol of their sin to demonstrate that they would bear the responsibility for it (cf. the water of bitterness that an accused adulteress must drink, Num. 5:18–22).

In Aaron's pathetic defense he blames the people for his own unfaithfulness, and even suggests a miraculous origin for the calf (v. 24). Aaron's conduct throughout this episode suggests that the Levitical priesthood is destined for failure from its inception (Heb. 5:2, 3; 9:7). Divine judgment upon Aaron is averted only by Moses's intercession (Deut. 9:20; 10:6–9 and note on 10:6).

LORD'S side. Only the Levites, Moses's own tribe, answer his call to arms to put down the rebellion. They are prepared to use the sword of judgment against neighbors and even family members (v. 28; cf. Num. 25:1–9).
Lit. "filled the hand." See note on 29:9.
**LORD** . Although the rebellion has been put down, Israel's guilt before God still looms. Moses again must leave Israel and climb the mountain to meet the Lord.

As there is a register of Israel (cf. Num. 1–4), so God Himself has a register of His people (Ps. 56:8; Is. 4:3; Mal. 3:16). If God will not forgive His people, Moses asks to be disinherited with them (cf. vv. 10, 11). Note the similar attitude of Paul in Rom. 9:3.

Moses's intercession is partially successful: God does not finally reject His people, but the sinful individuals will be judged. The limitations of Moses's mediatorial office and ministry point to the need for a greater mediator who will present a full and efficacious atonement for sin (Heb. 3:1–6; 10:11–18). See "Jesus Christ as Mediator" on p. 2157.
Israel's punishment is presented as certain but undefined. Apparently, a plague was soon added as a temporary punishment (v. 35). According to 1 Cor. 10:8, twenty-three thousand people died.
"You" suggests that God absolves Himself of responsibility for Israel since the covenant has been broken (32:7 note).

This is possibly a different angel than the Angel of the Lord that appeared to Moses in the burning bush (3:2). The key to understanding God's proposal is found in v. 3 ("I will not go up among you"). At issue is God's gracious dwelling in the midst of the people (29:44–46). If God does not dwell in Israel's midst, then there is no point in building the tabernacle; indeed, Israel can "depart" immediately without constructing it (v. 1). Instead, another arrangement, already in operation (described in vv. 7–11), is continued. God will meet with Moses and with inquiring Israelites at a tent "outside the camp, far off from the camp" (v. 7). This new "tent of meeting" is not God's dwelling; Joshua accompanies Moses there (v. 11). God will come in the pillar of cloud from time to time to the entrance of the tent to speak with Moses (vv. 9, 10).

One might think that the Israelites should rejoice at the prospect of receiving their inheritance in the land without the threat of God's immediate presence. Instead, they mourn, for no longer will Israel be a nation of priests, enjoying immediate fellowship with God (19:3–6; 29:45, 46). This episode is one of the great crises of the Exodus story.

They strip off the festive dress associated with idolatry (cf. Gen. 35:4) and assume the posture of mourners. But this is remorse, not true repentance. They have been and will continue to be a stiff-necked people. Still, there is a note of hope in God's words, "that I may know what to do with you."

The Hebrew verbs used here indicate this was the customary practice during the period at Sinai. This "tent of meeting" was a temporary structure that served as a meeting place for God and Moses until the tabernacle proper could be built (v. 2 note). outside \... far off from. At this stage God is not present among the people in the camp.

**LORD** . Moses responds to the dismaying threat of vv. 1–3. He cannot argue that Israel is not stiff-necked, or that the golden calf is an uncharacteristic aberration. He can only plead God's grace and covenant mercy. He does so by repeatedly asking for precisely what the Lord threatened to withdraw: the revelation of His own Presence (vv. 13–18). Moses's faithful persistence in intercession is grounded in God's covenant promise of divine-human communion (6:7; 19:5, 6; Gen. 17:7 note), and reminds us of Jacob's persistent struggle with God in the quest for divine blessing (Gen. 32:24–30). whom you will send with me. Moses wants to know who will go with him, for he is not prepared to lead the people without God accompanying them. I know you by name. God eariler declared His knowledge of Moses, implying a personal relationship (32:10; 33:11), and will repeat that assurance expressly (v. 17). Because the Lord knows Moses by name personally and intimately, Moses will know the Lord (Num. 12:6–8).
Moses will know the Lord Himself and His purposes for Israel.
Lit. "face." God Himself will go with Moses. give you rest. Use of the singular pronoun "you" means that the promise of 3:13–15 for all Israel is now repeated for Moses alone.

Moses prays for God's presence to go with "us," linking Israel with himself. If God chooses not to go with His people by dwelling among them, it will be useless to go to the Promised Land. The goal is not just milk and honey in Canaan, but a holy land where God will dwell with His people.
Israel's distinctness is grounded in the gracious presence of God Himself.
God includes Israel for Moses's sake; Israel depends upon Moses as mediator. Moses's intercession is a type of Christ's work as the new covenant Mediator (cf. Heb. 3; 9:16–22).

The Lord sealed His covenant with Israel by revealing Himself (24:9–11), and Moses now seeks a further revelation of God in His glory. His only hope for God's continuing mercy to Israel lay in God Himself. Having tasted God's mercy, Moses yearns for a full disclosure.

Though the visible magnificence of this theophany is apparent from the text, the emphasis falls on a revelation to Moses of God's sovereign, gracious, and compassionate nature (cf. 34:5–7). In Jesus Christ, the glory of the gracious and compassionate God that was withheld even from Moses is displayed to believers through the Spirit (John 1:14; 2 Cor. 3:18). to whom \... on whom. The Lord is sovereign in His purposes of mercy (Rom. 9:14–16). See "Predestination" at Mal. 1:2.
The Lord's goodness withholds what Moses cannot bear and reveals all that he can.
The replacement of the tablets signals the renewal of the covenant (20:1 note).
The uniqueness of Moses's mediatorial office is emphasized. The encounter of ch. 19 is to be repeated, but this time with Moses only (cf. 19:24; 24:9).
**LORD** descended. This is the revelation promised in 33:19–23: Yahweh passed by and proclaimed His name. Moses receives an overwhelming answer to his prayer (33:19 note).

This description of God is foundational for later Israelite knowledge of God (Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jon. 4:2; Nah. 1:3). God's mercy is still proclaimed toward Israel despite her dismal failure (Hos. 11:8). Remarkably, in the light of the golden calf incident, these verses contain echoes of 20:4–6. While God forgives the Israelites, the original covenant obligations are not abandoned.

This is what the Lord said He would not do, because the people were too sinful, too "stiff-necked" (33:3, 5). Now Moses cites their sin as the very reason for the Presence of God. In effect, he is asking the compassionate and merciful Lord of grace to dwell in His tabernacle among His people and forgive their sin. Then comes the amazing request: "take us for your inheritance." Moses does not say "give us our inheritance in the land" (cf. 33:2, 3), but "take us for your special treasure in Your faithful love" (the thought contained in 19:5).

God warns against apostate practices. The selection of cultic laws points to the area where Israel has sinned or is weak. Singular pronouns are used almost totally throughout, for God is making His covenant with Moses and with Israel through him (v. 27).

These cultic objects were sacred trees or poles that stood beside the Baal altars in Canaan and represented the Canaanite goddess of fertility (Asherah; cf. Judg. 6:25). Israel must not be compromised by adopting the pagan practices of peoples in the land.
The theme continues with allusions to the first (vv. 14–16) and second commandments (v. 17). God begins at the point of Israel's sin and with the Decalogue that was violated.
This section parallels the cultic instructions in the Book of the Covenant (23:14–19).
The commands of vv. 12–26.
The Lord Himself writes the Ten Commandments on the tablets (v. 1; 20:1 note).

Lit. "sent out horns." Although the Hebrew root usually refers to horns, it seems that rays of light are in view here (cf. Hab. 3:4). Moses's leadership is confirmed by the reflected light of God's glory.
The reaction of fear recalls the events of chs. 19 and 20. Only when they draw near and converse without harm are they reassured.

The purpose of the veil is not to calm the anxiety of the people, for Moses puts on the veil only after the people come near and after he finishes declaring the covenant obligations to the people (vv. 31, 32). Rather, as Paul makes clear, the veil is to keep the Israelites from seeing that the glory is fading away (2 Cor. 3:13). According to Paul, this fading glory shows the temporary and inadequate character of the old Mosaic covenant and points to the need for a greater covenant Mediator — Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 3:12–4:6).
The work on the tabernacle starts with an admonition to keep the Sabbath, just as the instructions for the work had concluded with such a reminder (31:12–18).

This entire section is based on chs. 25–31 but follows a different order. While chs. 25–31 give the instructions for the tabernacle, this section describes its construction. Beginning with the reiteration of instructions for the gathering of offerings and artisans (35:4–19), the narrative then moves logically to the gathering of materials and the recognition of artisans (35:20–36:7), the construction of the tabernacle parts and contents (36:8–38:31), the preparation of sacred vestments (39:1–31), the erection of the tabernacle (39:32–40:33), and finally to the climactic arrival of the glory of the Lord in the tabernacle (40:34–38).

Women are mentioned for the first time. Their involvement both in the donation and preparation of the materials is significant (vv. 25, 26, 29). They, no less than the men, are to worship the Lord from their hearts. Their relationship to the Lord is personal and not subsumed under their husbands' relationship to God.
The work of Bezalel, Oholiab, and their crew of skilled laborers is recounted. The detail of the account underscores the attention paid by the builders to the word of the Lord (39:42–43).

At the recognized ratio of three thousand shekels to the talent (a talent was roughly 75 pounds \[34 kg\]), a total of 2,193 pounds (995 kg) of gold, 7,544 (3,422 kg) of silver, and 5,310 (2,409 kg) of copper is collected. The amount of silver, a total of 301,175 shekels, is linked to the head count of the Israelites: half a shekel from all males over the age of twenty (603,550 men of military age; Num. 1:46). See note on 30:12.
The finished components are brought to Moses for inspection. Moses received the instructions from the Lord (chs. 25–31), and only Moses can determine the fitness of what has been made.

The Lord's detailed instructions to Moses regarding the erection of the tabernacle and the consecration of tabernacle and priests (vv. 1–15), together with the subsequent narrative of Moses's obedience (vv. 16–33), emphasize that the tabernacle is completed and its ministry inaugurated in precise obedience to the divine commands.
The tabernacle is set up about nine months after the arrival at Sinai.
Following the placement of the basin, Moses and Aaron comply with the law of priestly washing (30:19–21).

The glory of the Lord filling the tabernacle brings the book of Exodus to a climax. God, who brought Israel out of Egypt, makes and renews His covenant with them and makes His dwelling in their midst. A careful recapitulation of the primary theme of the book — the reestablishment of God's dwelling with man — is given in vv. 34–38. This passage also indicates that Israel has begun corporate worship. The history of God's guidance to the Promised Land will follow in the remainder of the Pentateuch.
Israel's journeys are linked to the guiding Presence. The covenant God dwells among His people at last and will lead the nation to the land He promised them.

Leviticus.note: Leviticus continues the narrative that concludes in Exodus with God coming to dwell in the midst of the Israelite camp. Of necessity, special arrangements need to be put in place for the Holy One to reside among the Israelites. Priority is given to outlining a range of sacrifices that address the serious consequences of human sin. The regulations are subdivided into sections addressed to the laity (1:1–6:7) and to the priests (6:8–7:38). Sacrifice in Israel involved the offering of selected domestic animals, grain, oil, and wine. In every animal offering the worshiper placed his hand on the victim's head, thereby identifying himself with the animal, saying in effect, "This animal represents me." The animal sacrifices involved the animal's death, and so the sacrifices had atoning symbolism: the animal dying in the sinful worshiper's place represented redemption from the death he deserved. There is then a common core of meaning and significance shared by all the sacrifices. But each sacrifice also had its own distinctive ritual features and religious emphases. This is indicated by the different names of the sacrifices, which sometimes highlight the ritual distinctiveness ("burnt offering") and sometimes the theologically distinctive feature ("peace offering"). Although the Lord, in response to Moses's intercession (Ex. 32), had rescinded His verdict to judge the people for their idolatrous worship of the golden calf, their ongoing sin remained a problem. These sacrifices provided atonement for them. 1:1 tent of meeting. The tent shrine or tabernacle described in Ex. 26.

Israel must obey these divinely given instructions on how to be fit to live in the presence of God. God, not humans, prescribes the way His people must live with Him. of livestock. Only unblemished (v. 3) domesticated animals can be offered. Wild animals, which cost nothing to the worshiper, cannot be offered.

The burnt offering, which begins the list of sacrifices, is the most comprehensive sacrifice. Its distinctive feature is that the whole animal, except for the skin, is burned on the altar. This symbolizes the total consecration of the worshiper to God's service, and it serves to cover the sins of the worshiper (v. 4 and note). The regulations begin by specifying the most expensive kind of animal that could be offered, the bull (vv. 2–9), and end with the cheapest, the young pigeon (vv. 14–17). No Israelite is excluded from making a burnt offering because he is too poor. 1:3 he shall offer. The layman offering the sacrifice (vv. 4–6, 9) is to kill, skin, cut up, and wash the animal, whereas the priest brings it to God by putting the blood and flesh on the altar. entrance of the tent. The screened-off courtyard surrounding the tabernacle of meeting. The great altar and a laver for washing the sacrifices stand in the courtyard (v. 9).
Lit. "to cover over." The death of the animal in place of the sinner "covers over" or shields the worshiper from the holy wrath of God.

**LORD** . The meaning of this phrase is seen most clearly in Gen. 8:21. Sacrifices avert God's anger, causing Him to look benevolently on the worshiper. God is holy and cannot look at sin. The phrase is anthropomorphic, describing in human language how the sacrifice is satisfying to the Lord. The NT speaks of the death of Christ in similar language (Eph. 5:2).
Sheep and goats are sacrificed in the same way as bulls in vv. 3–9.
A simpler procedure is prescribed for doves or pigeons, the offering of the poor. Due to the smaller size of the offering, the priest carries out the whole ceremony.

Usually offered in conjunction with an animal sacrifice, it consists of wheat flour mixed with olive oil, incense, and salt. The mixture is baked, fried, or, in the case of a grain offering of firstfruits, roasted (vv. 4–7, 14). Like the other sacrifices, the grain offering symbolizes the worshiper's dedication of himself to God. The Hebrew name for this offering suggests that it was a gift, expressing the worshiper's gratitude to God. This name is also used to describe tribute, which underscores the subservience of the presenter to someone greater (Gen. 32:13; Judg. 3:15; 2 Kin. 8:8).
Only a handful of the grain offering is burned; the rest goes to the priest (v. 3). Such offerings constitute an important part of a priest's income.
Possibly omitted because they cause fermentation or decay, which suggests corruption.
Because salt is a preservative, it symbolizes the enduring covenant between God and Israel (Num. 18:19 note).
See 23:9–14; Deut. 26:1–11. The Israelite is expected to give the first of his harvest to God, and on this occasion the grain offering is prepared differently.

Also called the "fellowship offering." The Hebrew name for this offering is related to the word shalom, meaning "peace, well-being." This sacrifice is unique in that the worshiper and his family can eat much of the meat, as only part of the offering is given to the priests or burned on the altar. It is a sacrifice brought when someone is seeking God's blessing or celebrating blessings received. It is offered to underline a solemn prayer (such as a vow), when such a prayer is answered, or out of simple gratitude (7:16). Eating meat was a rare luxury in ancient times and was usually something of a celebration. Moses prescribes that every animal killed for food must be offered in sacrifice first (17:3 note), so at least during the wilderness period, every meal involving meat is preceded by a peace offering.
The choicest parts of the carcass are symbolically given to God by being burned.

The OT insists that God supplies man with food, not vice versa (Gen. 1:29; Ps. 50:12–14). Therefore, this comment must be understood figuratively — God is pleased with the sacrifice offered in faith (cf. Heb. 11:4), just as human beings enjoy food.

Fat from sacrificial animals belongs to God (v. 3). Eating blood means eating meat from which the blood has not been drained (1 Sam. 14:33). The theological reason for this ban is given in 17:11 (see Gen. 9:4 and note).

With the words "If anyone sins" (4:2), Moses introduces his instruction to the laity regarding the sin or purification offering. While most sacrifices make atonement for sin to some extent, purification is the dominant concern of the sin offering. Sin and uncleanness make a person unfit to be in God's presence and also pollute the sanctuary, making it impossible for God to dwell there. The sin offering is designed to cope with this aspect of sin by purifying the sanctuary. The distinctive feature of the sin offering is the use to which the sacrificial blood is put. In other sacrifices the animal's blood is splashed over the side of the altar, but in the case of the sin offering it can be applied to the horned corners of the altar, or sprinkled inside the tabernacle tent (on the incense altar or veil) or even inside the Most Holy Place. The greater the sin, the greater the defilement caused within the sanctuary. Because the tabernacle and its furniture were closely associated with the people who met God there (Heb. 9:22 note), the people's sin defiled the tabernacle. Such pollution required cleansing.

These verses deal with four cases where people of various ranks do something sinful "unintentionally" (v. 2 text note): the high priest (vv. 3–12), the congregation (vv. 13–21), a ruler (vv. 22–26), and a common person (vv. 27–35).

The high priest. His sin has the direct consequence of "bringing guilt on the people" and requires the most expensive atonement, a bull. he shall offer. The sin (or purification) and guilt (or reparation) offerings were compulsory after committing certain sins, whereas the other offerings could sometimes be offered voluntarily when the worshiper felt so inclined.
The serious effects of high priestly sin are shown by the need to purify "the veil of the sanctuary" (the veil separating the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place, Ex. 26:31–35).

This piece of sacred furniture stands in front of the curtain leading into the Most Holy Place. It is cleansed by sprinkling with blood, the holy cleansing agent, making it possible for God to dwell in the tent.

See Heb. 13:11–13 and notes. a clean place. Many places outside the camp contained impurity that would make the priest unfit to officiate in worship. He was to avoid these and put the ashes left from the burnt offering in a designated clean place, where the remainder of the sacrificial bull was burned.
For sin involving the congregation as a whole, a procedure like the one described in vv. 3–12 is prescribed, with the community elders representing the people at the altar (v. 15).

A sin by a leader of a tribe or clan is not as serious a threat to the tabernacle's holiness as the first two cases (vv. 3–21). This is reflected in that he is required to offer only a male goat (v. 23), whose blood is applied not within the tent, but outside to the altar of burnt offering (v. 25).
Unintentional sins by ordinary Israelites are treated similarly to those of leaders. However, they can offer a female goat instead of a male goat, and if they are poor, birds or grain (5:7–13).

It is debated whether this section belongs with what precedes (the sin offering, ch. 4) or with what follows (the guilt offering, 5:14–6:7). Because of the similarity of 4:1 and 5:14, as well as the occurrence of the Hebrew term for "sin offering" throughout 4:1–5:13, many argue that the description of the guilt offering begins at 5:14. Alternatively, the occurrence of the Hebrew word asham (meaning "guilt" or "guilt offering") in 5:6, 7 has led some to conclude that the discussion of the guilt offering begins in 5:1. 5:1–6 These verses treat sins of omission, inadvertence, or rashness. The cases in view are (a) the sin of withholding evidence (v. 1); (b) the sin of contact with anything unclean (vv. 2, 3); and (c) the sin of careless oath-taking (v. 4).
See notes regarding cleanness and uncleanness on chs. 11–16.
These sins require confession to God in the presence of a priest and a sin offering for the forgiveness of the sinner (cf. 1 John 1:7, 9).
The poor man's sin offering is like the humblest burnt offering (1:14–17), except for the sprinkling of the blood (5:9; cf. 1:15).
See "Atonement" at Rom. 3:25.
The items brought here as sin offerings resemble those of the grain offering of ch. 2, but no oil or incense is included.

Moses gives instructions to the laity regarding the guilt or reparation offering. While the focus of the sin offering is upon purification of the sanctuary, the guilt offering is concerned with restitution or reparation. Three types of sins requiring guilt offerings are mentioned: misuse of "the holy things of the LORD" (5:15, 16), supposed sin involving things that "ought not to be done" (5:17–19), and trespasses against a neighbor's rights and property (6:2–7).
