In these chapters, Moses explains the difference between the ceremonially clean and unclean. For the Israelites, people, objects, places, and even time could be placed along a spectrum with holiness on one side and uncleanness on the other. Holiness is associated with God, for He alone is inherently holy. At the other extreme is uncleanness, associated with forces opposed to God. To be in God's presence requires a person to be holy; sin causes him to be ritually unclean and means that he cannot come near God. Anyone who is unclean or who has come in contact with uncleanness is to abstain from public worship until he is cleansed. Because holiness is linked to God, it is associated with perfection and life. Uncleanness, in marked contrast, is linked to chaos and death. Normal, healthy creatures are clean, but abnormal or unhealthy creatures, and particularly corpses, are unclean. Abnormalities that suggest or that might lead to death are marks of uncleanness. Life and death are not to be mixed, so the unclean is never to enter God's presence. Ultimately, it is Christ, the great Mediator and High Priest, who triumphs over death and corruption in behalf of those who trust in Him (1 Cor. 15:20–28, 50–57). 11:1–47 Moses instructs the Israelites regarding the principles of cleanness, showing them that, though all corpses are unclean (vv. 24, 27, 31–40), some perfectly healthy creatures are also stated to be unclean in a milder sense and therefore must not be eaten. Although some of the forbidden animals posed a possible health threat (e.g., pigs as carriers of trichinosis), the classification of uncleanness is not based on health grounds. Rather, the principle teaches basic moral and spiritual truths. Carnivorous animals and birds of prey eat flesh with blood in it, something forbidden to human beings (7:26). Such animals also come into contact with carcasses, which are unclean. The clean creatures here symbolize Israelites, while unclean animals symbolize Gentiles. Only domesticated clean animals may be offered in sacrifice, for the sacrificial animal symbolizes the priest. In restricting his diet to clean animals, the Israelite was reminded that God had chosen Israel alone among the nations. Only when the new covenant admitted Gentiles to the community of God were the food laws abrogated (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15).
Cud-chewing, cloven-hoofed land animals are clean and so can be eaten. Other animals are unclean. Animals with claws are normally carnivorous.
Only ordinary fish with fins and scales are clean. Other water creatures are unclean and therefore inedible.
Birds of prey, associated with death, are unclean, but most other types of bird are clean.
Insects that hop may be eaten (v. 21), but not others.

The word "holy" is often taken to mean "separate" or "set apart," but it implies much more than simply being set apart. It is associated with wholeness and perfection. Only God is intrinsically holy. He is by nature majestic, awesome, pure, and perfect. He demonstrated His transcendent holiness by His creation of the world (see Gen. 1:1, 3 and notes), by His great acts in history such as redeeming His people from Egypt, and by His perfect laws. Israel's holiness is derived from her unique covenant relationship with the only true and living God. His covenant provides, among other things, moral and judicial laws that reflect God's own righteous standards, and the sacrificial system to atone for sin. The immediate background for this designation of Israel as a "holy nation" is the Lord's appearance on Mount Sinai: they washed their clothes, avoided contact with the mountain, and abstained from sexual intercourse in preparation for that unique event (Ex. 19:10–15, 21–24; Heb. 12:18–21). By dwelling among the people, God makes them holy and demands that they be holy as He is holy (cf. 1 Pet. 1:16). Jesus Christ, the Mediator of the new covenant (Heb. 8:6; 9:15; 12:24), also demands perfection (Matt. 5:48). But He provides the new Israel with holiness by His perfect sacrifice, which removed the sins of His people forever (Heb. 9; 10), and by His Holy Spirit, who inscribes God's moral law on their hearts (2 Cor. 3:3; cf. Jer. 31:31–34). Without holiness, no one will see God (Heb. 12:14).

The flow of blood after childbirth makes a mother unclean (vv. 4, 5, 7). Loss of blood could lead to death, thus illustrating the equation of uncleanness with death or the threat thereof (chs. 11–16 note).

The text does not explain why the birth of a daughter made a mother unclean for twice as long as the birth of a son. Perhaps a daughter, as a potential mother and subject eventually to the loss of blood in childbirth, was subject to uncleanness in a way a son was not (12:2 note).
These sacrifices for atonement and purification are offered after the birth of Jesus (Luke 2:24).

These chapters contain God's laws concerning unclean skin diseases referred to as "leprous disease" (13:2, 8). Modern physicians recognize here the symptoms of various modern complaints, but we should remember that the biblical classification is based primarily on spiritual rather than hygienic or medical considerations. The key principle in identifying a skin disease as "unclean" was whether the skin seemed to be rotting away, suggesting the spiritual principle of death. Patchy complaints amounted to uncleanness (vv. 9, 10), but a complaint affecting the whole body did not (vv. 12, 13). Stable conditions were clean, but deteriorating ones were unclean (vv. 5–8, 18–37). Similar principles applied to the diagnosis of uncleanness in clothing: progressive mildews were unclean (vv. 47–52), but stable ones were clean (vv. 53–58). The close association of uncleanness with death is shown in 13:45–46. The person afflicted with a serious skin disease behaved as a mourner ("let the hair of his head hang loose"). He was excluded from the camp, not to protect the health of Israel, but because God was in the camp and uncleanness (death) had to be separated from the presence of God (life). See Num. 5:1–4; 12:14, 15.

These ceremonies conducted by the priest do not cure skin disease. A diseased person comes to the priest after he has been healed (Luke 5:14). The task of the priest is to make ceremonially clean the person who, due to his uncleanness, has been excluded from the camp, from his people, and from God. Through these ceremonial cleansings, which take place in two stages a week apart, the diseased individual is restored to fellowship with God and with His people.

The first stage of cleansing takes place outside the camp. The man washes himself and his clothes, and he shaves. Two birds are taken. The blood of one is used to purify the man. The death of that bird portrays the end of the man's old life outside the camp, and the flight to freedom of the other pictures his liberation from the effects of the disease. Then, the man can enter the camp again.

In the second cleansing stage, the Israelite is brought back into full communion with God. The ceremonies here resemble the consecration of the priest (ch. 8). The Israelite is daubed with blood and anointed with oil, being linked to the altar, the symbol of God's presence. A variation on this restoration procedure is prescribed for the poor in vv. 21–31.

This passage adapts principles of diagnosis (13:47–58) and cleansing (14:1–7) to the problem of "disease" (mildew or dry rot) in houses. This problem would have arisen after the settlement in Canaan (v. 34).

This chapter deals with the uncleanness caused by discharges from the sexual organs: (a) long-term male discharge (e.g., gonorrhea; vv. 2–15); (b) short-term male discharges (vv. 16–18); (c) short-term female discharge (menstruation; vv. 19–24); and (d) long-term female discharges (vv. 25–30). That perfectly natural processes like sexual intercourse (v. 18) or menstruation should make someone unclean (i.e., unfit to worship) is surprising. But all these cases involve the loss of bodily fluids (blood or semen), and any loss of a "life fluid" suggested death and was incompatible with the presence of God, who is perfect life. The NT shows God, the giver of perfect life, incarnate in Jesus Christ, healing those who suffered exclusion from His presence under these OT rules (Matt. 9:20–22). The divine program of redemption was historically progressive. The old covenant arrangements that seem so strange to us were early object lessons, a "guardian" pointing forward to the full redemption accomplished in Jesus Christ (Gal. 3:24, 25).

The Day of Atonement, when annual atonement is made for the sins of the nation, is the holiest day in the OT calendar. It falls in the seventh month of the Hebrew calendar (September/October) and involves the offering of various sacrifices, the entry of the high priest into the Most Holy Place (in this chapter referred to simply as the "Holy Place" or "holy sanctuary"), and the dispatch of a goat into the wilderness carrying the people's sins. For a summary of the sacrifices, see notes on chs. 1; 4; and 5. A summary of the rites is given in vv. 6–10 and fuller details in vv. 11–28. The Day of Atonement proceeds according to the following steps: (a) The high priest washes and dresses (v. 4); (b) he sacrifices a bull as a sin offering for himself (v. 6; cf. v. 11); (c) he enters the Most Holy Place and sprinkles the ark with blood (vv. 12–14); (d) he takes two goats and by lot chooses one to be the scapegoat (Azazel) and the other to be a sin or purification offering (vv. 7, 8); (e) he sacrifices one goat as a sin or purification offering (vv. 9, 15); (f) he enters the Most Holy Place and sprinkles the ark with blood (v. 15); (g) he goes out to the outer part of the tabernacle of meeting and sprinkles the blood (v. 16); (h) he goes out into the courtyard of the tabernacle and sprinkles the main altar with blood (vv. 18, 19); (i) he confesses the sins of the Israelites as he lays his hands on the scapegoat's head (v. 21); (j) he sends the scapegoat into the wilderness (vv. 21, 22); (k) the scapegoat gone, the high priest changes into his regular garments and washes (vv. 23, 24); and (l) finally, he offers burnt offerings for himself and for the people (vv. 24, 25). For the high priest, the most important aspects of the ceremony are his entry into the Most Holy Place with the blood of the sin or purification offering and the dispatch of the scapegoat into the wilderness. These actions atone for the sins of repentant Israelites (vv. 16, 19, 21, 22). All sin offerings serve to cleanse both the earthly sanctuary and the worshipers, but on other occasions the high priest does not enter the (inner) Most Holy Place, but only the anteroom before the separating veil (usually called the "Holy Place"), the chamber containing the altar of incense, the gold lampstand, and the table of showbread. Because the ark of the covenant, the focal point of God's presence in the tabernacle (v. 2 note; Ex. 25:17–22 and notes), is housed in the Most Holy Place, entry to the Most Holy Place is rare and dangerous (v. 2). That the high priest enters the inner chamber only on this one day of the year indicates the depth of atonement being made. The scapegoat ceremony was also unique to this day. By placing his hands on the goat's head and confessing the nation's sins, the high priest transfers those sins to the goat. The goat then symbolically carries the people's sins away into the wilderness. Christians have long regarded the scapegoat as a type of Christ. That Christ was delivered to the Gentiles and killed outside the walls of Jerusalem indicates that He was sent "outside the camp" like the scapegoat of old (Heb. 9:6–28; 13:11–13). 16:1 death of the two sons of Aaron. See 10:1–3.

Lit. "atonement covering" or "place of atonement" (Ex. 25:17 note). This slab of pure gold serves as a lid for the ark and as a base for the two golden cherubim. The divine presence appears above the lid of the ark (Ex. 25:22; Ps. 99:1), and Aaron sprinkles the mercy seat with blood on the Day of Atonement. God symbolically reveals the gospel through this cover on the ark. The ark contains the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments inscribed by the finger of God Himself, representing the principal obligations of the Sinai covenant (Deut. 10:1–5). Since all humans have violated God's moral demands, the righteousness of God demands death (Ezek. 18:20; Rom. 6:23). God provides the only means of atonement for His chosen people and for their reconciliation to Him — the atoning blood on the ark's cover. That blood-drenched cover is the meeting point of the holy God with His unholy people. It resembles the heavenly sanctuary where Christ has entered with His own blood (Heb. 9:12), blood that is efficacious for all the sins — past, present, and future — of His people (Rom. 3:21–26; Heb. 9:15).

Before offering a goat for the people, Aaron is to offer a bull as a sin or purification offering and a ram as a burnt offering for himself and his family (v. 5). By contrast, Jesus Christ, the Mediator of the eternal new covenant, is without sin and therefore offered sacrifice for His people only (Heb. 7:26, 27).

In these chapters, the Lord's demands for holiness clearly reach into every aspect of Israel's life. In a discussion on topics as diverse as sexual behavior and the Year of Jubilee, capital crimes, and the tabernacle loaves, the Lord teaches that Israel must reflect His holiness in their behavior.

In the wilderness period, animals could be killed only at the tabernacle, even for ordinary meals. This was to prevent secret sacrifices to idols (v. 7). After entering Canaan, this rule was relaxed (Deut. 12:15–16).

One of the most important theological statements in Leviticus (see also Lev. 18:5). Life is sacred because it belongs to God. As a mark of respect for life and for its Creator, no Israelite may eat meat with blood in it "for the life of the flesh is in the blood" (cf. Gen. 9:4–6). A second reason is that it is the blood that makes "atonement for your souls." The animal's life, represented by its blood shed in sacrifice, takes the place of the life of the worshiper, symbolically redeeming him. Because animal blood is the sign of salvation, people may not consume it. These ideas are both assumed and transformed in the NT. Christ's shed blood actually atoned for sin (Heb. 9:14, 22; 1 John 1:7), and those who drink that blood spiritually — receiving the benefits of His death through faith in Him alone — have eternal life (John 6:54). have given it for you. The sacrificial system of the OT is God's gracious gift to His people to enable them to live in God's presence. In anticipation of the final and perfect blood sacrifice offered by Christ, God Himself ordains the procedures whereby His righteous wrath might be averted and His people reconciled to Him.

Moses instructs Israel concerning unlawful practices linked to sex and family, including incest (vv. 6–20), child sacrifice (v. 21), homosexuality (v. 22), and bestiality (v. 23). Israel's neighbors were much less restrained in their sexual attitudes and behavior (v. 3). They permitted closer intermarriage than allowed here; they allowed homosexuality (cf. v. 22), and even some types of bestiality (cf. v. 23). The regulations in this chapter presuppose that an Israelite would normally marry another Israelite. However, unions between blood relatives of the first degree (brother-sister, father-daughter) and the second degree (father-granddaughter, nephew-aunt) were prohibited. Marriage between close relatives by marriage was also banned.

You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules. The passage is one of only two passages from Leviticus that the apostle Paul quotes (cf. Gal 3:12ff. and Rom 10:5ff.). This command expresses in a single sentence the goal and rationale of the law, which requires perfect, personal, and perpetual obedience from all people.

Not one's own mother (cf. v. 7), but the father's second wife (cf. 1 Cor. 5:1). The phrase "it is your father's nakedness" recalls the teaching in Gen. 2:24 that the married couple "become one flesh."

The daughter of the woman would be the man's stepdaughter or step-granddaughter.

The custom of sacrificing children was practiced among the ancient Phoenicians and pagan inhabitants of Canaan (Deut. 12:31 note). The cult of Molech, a god of the Ammonites, was a temptation to the Israelites (cf. 1 Kin. 11:7; 2 Kin. 23:10).

Ritual uncleanness, caused by sin, was contagious — all and everything that came in contact with it was infected, including the sanctuary (16:16 note) and the land. The pollution of the land by impurity was seen as a grave danger and a major threat to Israel. Though the Israelites would be given the privilege of occupying the Promised Land, the land would "vomit" them out if they were to defile it as the previous inhabitants had. vomited. Ceremonial cleanliness regulations specific to the priests are recorded. These deal with priests in general (vv. 1–9), the high priest (vv. 10–15), and priests suffering from defects (vv. 16–24). All priests who serve within the tabernacle have to show God's holiness in their character and in their bodies. Because their duties bring them closer to God, it is essential that they be holy. Holiness in restored man ultimately involves his perfection and health (fullness of life; freedom from mortality and decay), so priests with certain handicaps are forbidden to offer sacrifice (vv. 17–21). Wholeness is closely associated with holiness. But handicapped priests still enjoy a full share of priestly provisions (v. 22). 21:1 Holiness (as a key attribute of God, who is Himself life) and death are incompatible; therefore, priests may not mourn for any save their closest relatives (vv. 2–3).
Mourning customs involving disfigurement of the body were also banned, for priests as holy men had to have whole bodies (Deut. 14:1 note).
The high priest, who has the privilege of entering into God's immediate presence, is obliged to avoid all contact with death (cf. 10:6, 7).
For any unclean person to eat holy food from a sacrifice is to risk death (7:20–21). Uncleanness (death) and holiness (life) are not to mix.

Designed to curb exaggerated revenge (cf. Gen. 4:24), this formula vividly expressed the principle that punishment should be proportionate to the offense. It seems not to have been enforced literally (see Ex. 21:26, 27; Deut. 19:21 note). Jesus' opposition to the use of this phrase in everyday relationships and not in court cases for which it was intended was not an abrogation of the principle of equivalence (cf. Matt. 5:38–42). God never intended the rule to be strictly enforced in the normal course of everyday problems and disagreements, but gave it as a legal principle of restitution. Jesus calls for viewing this principle in light of its original intent for use in a court setting, as well as in light of the love commandment (19:18; cf. Matt. 7:12), in the interests of the kingdom (Matt. 5:10–12), and in the knowledge of God's coming wrath (Rom. 12:17–21; cf. Deut. 32:35).

The Lord demonstrates His ownership of the Promised Land through laws preventing the exploitation of the land and its tenants (v. 23 note). 25:1–7 Just as humans need a day of rest, land without fertilizers needs to lie fallow for a time. See the similar regulations in Ex. 23:10, 11.

More than a fallow year, this was a year in which all the poor who had fallen into debt were given a fresh start. Loans were written off. Land that had been sold was returned to its original owner, and slaves were released (v. 40).

God protected His gift to each family within the covenant community. In this way He protected the family structure, provided life in perpetuity for them, and prevented unrestrained commercial exploitation of His gift.

Although God gave Israel the land as one of His good gifts to them to be enjoyed (Deut. 6:10–12; 8:10–13), He still retained final ownership and could terminate the lease should the people prove undesirable tenants. They did not possess the land as an inalienable right but within the structures of a covenantal relationship with God. The land was not property over which the Israelites had total and final control. It symbolized life with God.
All the sales described here took place because of hardship. Land was not to be permanently sold from one family to another.
It was hoped that a relative would buy a poor man's land and return it to him. In any event, he or his family would receive it back in the Year of Jubilee.
In contrast to agricultural land, houses within cities had to be redeemed within a year or the sale was permanent.
See note on Deut. 23:19 (Ps. 15:5).

If a man sold a son or a daughter into slavery because of debt, the slave was released after seven years (Ex. 21:2–11; Deut. 15:12–18). This text deals with an even worse debt where, presumably after selling his land for a sum insufficient to pay the debt, a man and his whole family were sold as slaves (v. 41). In such a case they were released in the Year of Jubilee.
The Lord's instruction to the Israelites culminates in promises of blessings for obedience (vv. 3–13) and of curses for disobedience (vv. 14–39).

Israel's obedience to the covenant requirements would be rewarded with blessing (Ex. 20:12; Deut. 28:1–14; cf. Matt. 6:4), culminating in the greatest of all blessings — the presence of God with His people (see Ex. 29:42–46 and note).

Disobedience to God brings suffering (Ex. 20:7; Deut. 28:15–68). Many prophetic passages echo Lev. 26 and Deut. 28, as the prophets argued that the people were suffering — or were about to suffer — God's anger over their sins.

Even in judgment there was always hope (Deut. 30:1–10). Punishment did not mean an end to the covenant (vv. 44, 45; Gen. 17:2 note; Rom. 11:1–29). God's judgments on His people proved He still cared about them (Heb. 12:5, 6).
A summary conclusion to the variety of instructional material in chs. 1–26. The Hebrew term "laws" refers to teaching or instruction and not legislation.

The final chapter of Leviticus deals with gifts promised to God, probably by Israelites in dire distress when they made a vow. Later, they might wish to take back the property vowed. The provisions of this chapter showed when and how this could be done.

It was possible to offer oneself or a member of one's family to the full-time service of God in the temple (1 Sam. 1:11). But only Levites could serve God as temple priests; other vowed persons had to be redeemed according to the tariff described in vv. 3–8.
Sacrificial animals could not be withdrawn once vowed.
Non-sacrificial animals had to be redeemed.

Property and persons devoted to God (i.e., placed under the ban) were irrevocably to be placed in the service of God (v. 28), or utterly destroyed (v. 29). This solemn vow was probably pronounced by national leaders, often in time of war (Num. 21:2; 1 Sam. 15), or against those practicing idolatry (Deut. 13:16; 20:17 note).
A tenth of agricultural produce was given to God (i.e., to the priestly tribe of Levi, see Num. 18:21–29; Deut. 12:6–18; 14:22–29 and notes).

Numbers.note: With the completion of the tabernacle (Ex. 35:4–40:38) and the giving of instructions for holy living (Lev. 1–27), the Lord continues to prepare His people to occupy the Promised Land. A census of fighting men is taken (ch. 1). Then, measures to ensure the order and purity of the camp are related — the organization of the camp, the commissioning of the Levites and their ministry, and various provisions for ceremonial purity and religious observance. Finally, provisions are made for direction and guidance of the community (9:15–10:10). 1:1 –46 In preparation for the conquest of the land, God commands that a census of the fighting men of Israel be taken. Another census, recorded near the end of the book, is taken some forty years later to establish military strength (26:2). In the ancient Near East, a census could be taken for military, forced labor, or taxation purposes. 1:1 The **LORD** spoke to Moses. Such statements occur dozens of times in Numbers. The OT views Moses as the preeminent prophet. God spoke to the prophets in visions and dreams, but with Moses He spoke face-to-face (12:8), giving him greater authority. the tent of meeting. The tent shrine or tabernacle where God speaks to Moses (Ex. 29:42; 40:34, 35). This term occurs frequently in the Pentateuch and occasionally in later books. in the second year. Numbers begins thirteen months after the exodus and relates events that occur during the next thirty-nine years.

The heads of all the tribes, except the Levites (who are set apart for the service of the tabernacle), are listed here and also in chs. 2; 7; and 10. Although the Levites are not counted as one of the twelve tribes of Israel (v. 49), the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh are listed under Joseph (v. 10), preserving the number of twelve tribes.

These verses list the number of fighting men in each tribe. Except for the differences in the numbers, these verses follow a strict formula. The tribes are listed in the same order as in vv. 1–15, except that the tribe of Gad is now mentioned third instead of eleventh (vv. 24, 25).
These two verses give a total for the census. Various view have been suggested as to how these census numbers should be interpreted. See Introduction: Special Issues.

The Levites are not counted with the others, since they are set apart to care for the tabernacle and are exempt from military service. Their inheritance is also set apart among the Israelites (ch. 3).

Regulations for the placing of the various tribes in the camp and for their order on the march are given. The people are divided into four groups of three tribes, with each group located some distance from the tabernacle on the north, south, east, and west. The Levites camp around the tabernacle (1:53). On the march, the tribes are to follow one another in the same order in which they are mentioned. Compare this arrangement with the four-square city of Rev. 21:16, the final dwelling place of God with man.
Some Hebrew manuscripts have "Deuel." The misspelling "Reuel" is due to the similarity of R and D in the Hebrew alphabet. It is traditional to note the correction rather than to alter the text.
Aaron, who is older than Moses, is mentioned first because his family is the subject of the chapter.
The anointing of Aaron and his sons as priests of the Lord is described in Lev. 8 (cf. Ex. 29 for instructions).

The serious misdeed and resulting death of Aaron's older sons is described in Lev. 10:1–3. Similar divine judgments occur at other important points in salvation history (Josh. 7:13–26; 2 Sam. 6:7; 2 Chr. 26:16–21; Acts 5:1–11).

The Levites are taken by God in place of the firstborn Israelite males (vv. 40–51; Ex. 13:15 note). The firstborn males belong to God in a special way because they were delivered from death at the Passover.

The Levite clans are identified and their various duties prescribed: the Gershonites are to care for the large structures of the tabernacle (vv. 21–26), the Kohathites for its interior furnishings (vv. 27–32), and the Merarites for the smaller parts of the structure (vv. 33–37).
Moses, Aaron, and Aaron's sons are to camp in front of the tent of meeting and to have exclusive approach to the sanctuary.
Firstborn Israelite males are to be redeemed by devoting the Levites to God's service. Money is given to redeem the excess number of firstborn males (vv. 46–49).

The work of the Levitical families — the Kohathites (vv. 1–15), the Gershonites (vv. 21–28), and the Merarites (vv. 29–33) — is further explained. In vv. 16–20 Aaron's son Eleazar is assigned supervision of the entire tabernacle. But all Kohathites, except the descendants of Aaron, are forbidden direct access to the holy things.
Persons ceremonially unclean are sent outside the camp. This action is taken because uncleanness is incompatible with the holiness of God. See note on Lev. 13:1–14:57.

When someone wrongs another, restitution must be made, plus an additional fifth (Lev. 5:14–6:7). If the wronged person is not available and has no relative to whom restitution can be made, it is to be given to the priest, as representing the Lord.

A procedure is described by which the priest can determine whether a woman accused of unfaithfulness by her husband is guilty or innocent. If she is guilty, God will make her sick and unable to bear children (v. 27); if innocent, she is able to bear children (v. 28). This is an example of the ancient legal practice of trial by ordeal.

The Nazirite vow was a special type of voluntary devotion to God in ancient Israel. People could take a special vow of separation for a limited period of time, during which they were not to eat or drink anything that came from the grapevine and were not to cut their hair or beard. The grapevine was a source of physical pleasure, and abstention from it represented a life given over to God. Allowing the hair to grow signified abstention from human adornment. During the period for which the vow was taken, the Nazirite was to be careful to avoid becoming ceremonially unclean for any reason (v. 7). If someone should die suddenly in the presence of one who had taken a Nazirite vow, it would be necessary to make certain prescribed offerings (vv. 9–12), shave one's head, and start the period of separation all over again (v. 12). A special ceremony ending the period of Nazirite separation is described (vv. 13–21).

This threefold, divinely inspired blessing was pronounced by the priest with uplifted hands (Lev. 9:22). It moves from a general blessing (v. 24), to an invocation of God's favor and presence (v. 25), and finally to a climactic mention of the peace that comes only with God's gracious presence (v. 26). The pronouncement of this blessing placed God's covenant name "LORD" (Yahweh) on the people (v. 27). This Aaronic benediction has been discovered on two small silver scrolls found at Ketef Hinnom that date to the seventh and sixth centuries B.C.
A vivid figure for God's looking favorably upon His worshipers. The closer one's access to the face of God, the greater the blessing.

Offerings made at the dedication of the tabernacle are listed. Each of the twelve tribal leaders has a day in which he brings a number of expensive gifts and specified offerings. These gifts and offerings are mentioned in precise detail in each case, even though all the lists are identical — a vivid reminder that God is interested in every part of the spiritual service rendered by His people. 7:1–9 The carts and the oxen are presented. The tribal leaders join together to provide carts, as well as oxen to pull them, for the use of two of the Levitical clans in carrying the parts of the tabernacle that have been assigned to their care (3:21–26, 33–37; 4:21–33). No cart is given to the Kohathites; they are expected to carry the holy things on their shoulders (v. 9).

This designation of the ornate cover of the ark represents one Hebrew word (lit. "atonement covering" or "place of atonement"). The mercy seat is mentioned twenty-five times in the Pentateuch but only once in later books (1 Chr. 28:11). See notes on Ex. 25:17 and Lev. 16:2.

This ceremony, which sets apart the Le­vites for service to the Lord, differs significantly from the consecration ceremony of the priests (Ex. 29:1–37; Lev. 8). Key terms in the ordination of Aaron and his sons as priests are "hallow" and "consecrate" (Ex. 29:1, 9 and notes); the Levites are "cleansed" (vv. 6, 15, 21). The priests receive new garments (Ex. 29:5–9); the Levites shave the hair on their bodies and wash their clothes. The rituals reflect the different degrees of holiness required in order to undertake the specific duties assigned to the priests and the Levites.
See note on 3:11–13.

In 4:3 the term of service is listed as from thirty to fifty years old. Rabbinic sources suggest that a five-year apprenticeship was served prior to full service. Alternatively, 4:3 may designate the time when complete responsibility for transporting the tabernacle is to undertaken, with lighter duties being assumed at age twenty-five. Later on, David lowers the age of Levitical service to twenty because transportation of the tabernacle was no longer necessary (1 Chr. 23:24–26).

A special problem is identified, and God's answer is given: a person who is unclean or on a journey at the regular time may celebrate Passover exactly one month later. No others may postpone its observance.

As a covenant rite, the Passover is to be celebrated only by members of the covenant community. Male strangers who want to participate must accept the terms of the covenant by being circumcised (Ex. 12:48).
Two kinds of guidance are arranged for the march: supernatural guidance by the cloud (9:15–23) and orders from Moses given by trumpet (10:1–6).

This section begins with the Lord's guidance of the people immediately to the area of Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran (10:12; 12:16; 13:3, 26), the camp from which they will begin the settlement of Canaan. Instead of the promised victory, the spies' gloomy report creates a rebellion that affects the entire nation except for Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and Caleb. The Lord pronounces judgment on the entire first generation of people who were counted in the census and tells them to leave Kadesh and turn back toward Sinai. In view of this judgment, the regulations and results of the meager history in chs. 15–19 are striking for two reasons: (1) after the judgment, the Lord immediately tells Israel how to serve Him in the Land of Promise (ch. 15), a clear indication that they will eventually go there as promised; and (2) for the whole period of the wilderness judgment we are given only two events (which are actually one connected incident): Korah's rebellion and the budding of Aaron's rod. The events in chs. 20 and 21 are clearly transitional, beginning with the return to Kadesh, a hint that the conquest is on again. The victory over the king of Arad also signals the change, as the place of victory is named "Hormah," "destruction" (21:3), in contrast to the tragic defeat in ch. 14. 10:11 year \... month \... day. Almost fourteen months after the exodus from Egypt and about eleven months after the arrival at Sinai (Ex. 19:1 note).
The order of the march follows the prescription of ch. 2, though more detail about the Levites is given here (vv. 17, 21).
Yet another element of guidance is found. Moses asks his Midianite brother-in-law, a man familiar with the wilderness, for assistance (Ex. 2:16–3:1; Judg. 1:16).

Moses is intensely conscious of God's mighty presence with His people. These prayers honor the Lord as the divine warrior who goes before the host of the people (v. 35) and as the source of divine protection for the camp (v. 36).
These are the non-Israelites who came out from Egypt with the Israelites (Ex. 12:38 note).
See note on Ex. 16:14.
An instance of divinely inspired ecstatic utterance by the elders (cf. 1 Sam. 10:10; 19:24). This apparently temporary phenomenon serves to authenticate the leadership of the elders.
The quail are not piled to this depth but are flying blindly at a level of about three feet, where they are easily seized or struck down. See note on Ex. 16:13.

Cush is the region south of Egypt. Although it is possible that Moses's wife Zipporah (Ex. 2:16–21) is in view here, the directness of the explanation that Moses "had married a Cushite woman" suggests Zipporah died before this episode and that Moses has married again.

The real reason for the criticism comes to view — jealousy of Moses. Miriam and Aaron have important places in God's plan for Israel (cf. Mic. 6:4). Miriam is a prophetess (Ex. 15:20), and Aaron, as the high priest, wears the Urim and Thummim (Ex. 28:30). However, their jealousy of Moses, if not corrected, might greatly injure the work of God.

Many suggest that this statement about Moses was added by someone other than Moses, though the Mosaic origin of this verse is not impossible. (A unique feature of Scripture is its accurate representation of both the good and bad qualities of its characters; cf. Neh. 13:14, 22; 1 Cor. 4:16, 17.) The statement establishes that Moses has done nothing to provoke the complaint of Miriam and Aaron and explains God's swift defense of His prophet.
This phrase is often used in Scripture to indicate a special act of God in dealing with earthly events (e.g., Is. 64:1).

The Lord summons Moses and his two accusers to the tent of meeting. There He rebukes Aaron and Miriam for their arrogance in opposing Moses. In light of the clarity and directness of God's self-revelation to Moses, they should accept their subordination to his unique status and support him. See theological note "The Prophets of God" on p. 279.

The NT contrasts the great honor of Moses referred to here with the even greater honor of Jesus Christ — Moses was a faithful servant in God's house, but Christ is "faithful over God's house as a son" (Heb. 3:6).

In contrast to the way God revealed His will even to Elijah (1 Kin. 19:9–18). No other OT figure had as intimate a relation to God as Moses, and this description in turn highlights the greater privilege of the Christian — in Jesus Christ, the glory of God's goodness and mercy that was withheld even from Moses is displayed to believers through the Spirit (Ex. 33:19, 20; John 1:14; 2 Cor. 3:18). But the believer also looks forward to a yet greater visio dei (vision of God) — seeing Christ "face to face" (1 Cor. 13:12; Rev. 22:4). clearly, and not in riddles. With respect to the clarity of divine revelation given to him, Moses stands apart from all other OT prophets (cf. v. 6).

The Hebrew word can refer to various skin diseases, not necessarily Hansen's disease. It is clear to anyone who sees Miriam that God has condemned her attitude. Aaron shares the humiliation, for it is evident to all that he, too, is being chastened for joining her in claiming that they are as great as Moses. God does not make Aaron leprous, however, since his position as high priest (second in importance only to that of Moses) needs to be safeguarded (cf. Num. 16:6–17:11). Later on, Uzziah, a beloved king of Judah, is stricken with leprosy when he tries to assume the prerogatives of the high priest (2 Chr. 26:16–21).
The region southwest of the Promised Land in the east-central portion of the Sinai Peninsula (Gen. 21:21).

**LORD** spoke to Moses. God tells Moses to send spies, apparently in response to an earlier petition of the people. (Deut. 1:22, 23 indicates that they asked for this, and God approved.) The response of the spies shows that the people as a whole are not yet ready to enter the Promised Land.

The names in vv. 4–15 are not found in the earlier lists of leaders and heads of houses (chs. 1; 2; 7; 10). The spies are a separate group of persons specially chosen for the dangerous task of reconnaissance.

The name "Hoshea" simply means "salvation"; "Joshua" means "the Lord saves." It is appropriate that the man succeeding Moses as leader should bear a name that points to the Lord as the one from whom the nation's salvation must come.

The city of Hebron has a long history and has been rebuilt on various occasions. Hebron is well known as the gravesite of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Gen. 23:19; 25:10b; 49:29–33; 50:13). Zoan, which was built seven years after Hebron, is the city of Tanis in Egypt founded in c. 1430 B.C. Another name for Hebron is Kiriath-arba, and it is associated with the Anakim or descendants of Anak, a clan of large and intimidating fighters (Josh. 14:15). In later history, David occupies Hebron and is anointed there, first as king of Judah and then as king of Israel and Judah (2 Sam. 2:1–3; 5:1–5).

See note on Gen. 6:4. The Hebrew term is used in Gen. 6:4 for a group of strong and wicked men who lived in the earth before the flood. The spies' exaggerated and cowardly report disheartens the people and brings God's judgment on the spies themselves (14:36, 37).
The exodus generation provides an example of apostasy that the psalmist (Ps. 95:7–11) and NT authors (1 Cor. 10:5; Heb. 3:12–4:13) use as a warning for later generations of God's people.
The Israelites make a futile attempt to conquer Canaan. Despite Moses's opposition, the disappointed people try to enter the Promised Land and are driven back.
A place of some importance in later history (21:1–3; Josh. 15:30; 19:4; Judg. 1:17; 1 Sam. 30:26–30).

The location of this chapter — between the disastrous defeat at the hands of the Amalek­ites and Canaanites (14:39–45) and Korah's rebellion (ch. 16) — is significant. Through ch. 15 and its instructions for Israel's behavior in the land (v. 2), God assures the Israelites that despite their failures and rebellions, He still plans to give Canaan to them.
This expectation is a key to the chapter.

Sacrifices of atonement for unintentional sins are prescribed. The whole community (vv. 24–26) or an individual alone (v. 27) might be responsible for such transgressions, e.g., of ritual commandments like those given in vv. 1–21.
The treatment of an individual who sins defiantly is laid down: first, the rule (vv. 30, 31), and then, the illustration of the Sabbath breaker (vv. 32–36). cut off. See note on Lev. 7:20.
Tassels with blue threads are to be affixed to garments as reminders to be holy and to keep God's commands (v. 40).

This chapter describes a complicated series of events in which two separate movements combine forces to oppose Moses and Aaron. One group, led by Dathan, Abiram, and On, from the tribe of Reuben, is jealous of the leadership that God has established and propagandizes against Moses and Aaron. The other disaffected group consists of Kohathites (Levites), the very group to which Moses and Aaron belong. The Kohathites are already privileged above others by having special duties associated with the tabernacle.
Moses deals first with the Kohathites, who have access to the tabernacle. Moses's proposal in vv. 6, 7 sets the stage for divine judgment in v. 35.
Moses next deals with Reubenites Dathan and Abiram. After refusing to leave their tents, they are destroyed with their families (vv. 31–33).
Again Moses acts as an intercessor together with Aaron for the assembly (11:2; 12:13; 14:13–19; and 16:45–48). See notes on Ex. 32–34 and 33:17.
Moses depends on God for his defense (cf. 12:3), relying on divine provision of an irrefutable sign ("something new").
The children of Korah appear to have survived (26:11; cf. 1 Chr. 9:19).
The metal censers are removed from the ashes and made into sheets to cover the altar as a permanent reminder that none but Aaron's descendants are to serve as priests.
–48 Moses and Aaron again act as intercessors for the sinful people (v. 22 note).

Further evidence of Aaron's unique priesthood is given by God. The blossoms of Aaron's rod teach the leaders of Israel that God has chosen Aaron and his descendants as priests. Aaron's rod is kept permanently in front of the ark as a witness (v. 10).
In front of the ark in the Most Holy Place (cf. vv. 8, 10).
This terror of approaching God's dwelling highlights the importance of the mediatorial ministry of the priests and Levites described in ch. 18.

The duties and support of the priests and Levites are detailed. Only Aaron and his family can go near the furnishings of the sanctuary or the altar; the other Levites answer to the priests and are to do all the work at the tent of meeting (vv. 1–7). The males of Aaron's family are to receive the parts of the most holy offerings that are kept from the fire (vv. 8–10). All members of this family who are ceremonially clean share the wave offerings (v. 11; cf. Ex. 29:24–27; Lev. 7:30–34) and the firstfruits (vv. 12, 13; cf. Ex. 23:16–19; 34:22–26; Lev. 23:20; Deut. 18:4; 26:10). Support for the Le­vites comes from the tithes offered by the people (Deut. 14:22–29 and notes). 18:1 bear iniquity. Aaron and his sons are responsible for offenses against the holiness of the sanctuary and for violations of the rules of the priesthood. The imperfection of their priesthood is indicated by their having to make sacrifices for their own sins as well as for the sins of others (Ex. 29:38; Heb. 9:7). This imperfection points forward to a greater, perfect priest who will not need to offer sacrifices for His own sin (Heb. 10:11–14).

Based on the apparent indestructibility of salt, which does not burn, the phrase "covenant of salt forever" indicates the permanent nature of God's promise. The priests have no inheritance in the land. Rather, through the tithes and offerings presented to the Lord by the people, the Lord Himself is to be the Levites' portion (vv. 20, 21).
From the tithes they receive from the people, the Levites, too, are to give a tenth to the priests. It must be taken from the best and holiest parts (vv. 29–32).

Arrangements for cleansing those ceremonially unclean are presented. Under the direction of Eleazar the priest, a red heifer without blemish (v. 2) is taken outside the camp and killed (v. 3). The priest performs a prescribed ceremony (v. 4), and the heifer is burned (v. 5, 6; cf. Heb. 9:11–13). Then the ashes are gathered and put in a clean place outside the camp to be kept for use in the water of cleansing (vv. 9, 10). Situations of uncleanness requiring ceremonial cleansing are discussed in vv. 11–16, followed by the procedures for use of the water for impurity (vv. 17–22).

Christ "suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood" (Heb. 13:12). The ceremonies for cleansing and purification provide an interpretive backdrop to Christ's ministry.

This exact phrase occurs nowhere else in the Bible. "Cut off from Israel" occurs twice (Ex. 12:15; Num. 19:13). Similar expressions occur in Lev. 17:10; 20:3, 5, 6; 23:29; Num. 9:13; 15:30; Ezek. 14:8. On the meaning of "cut off," see note on Lev. 7:20.

In his exasperation with Israel, Moses acts presumptuously and fails to honor the holiness of God (Ex. 17:6 notes). The seriousness of Moses's sin is evident from the resulting judgment — he is not allowed to enter the Promised Land (v. 12). 20:1 the first month. This will be at the end of the forty years of wandering decreed in 14:32–34. (Deut. 2:14 speaks of thirty-eight years.) The period of wandering in the wilderness is nearing its end. Everyone under sixty is, in effect, from a new generation about to begin the next part of God's plan — entrance into Canaan and conquest of the Promised Land. Miriam died. Moses's sister was a godly woman. When Moses was a baby, she helped preserve him from destruction (Ex. 2:4–10). After the deliverance at the Red Sea, she led the victory celebration (Ex. 15:20, 21). Yet 12:5–15 shows her serious sin and the resulting punishment.
Water is the greatest need in wilderness travel (cf. Gen. 21:14–19; Ex. 17:1–7). 20:2–5 The people complain again — an echo of previous complaints (Ex. 15:24; 16:2; 17:3; Num. 11:1; 14:2).

After years of constant service and unparalleled patience, Moses falls at his strongest point (12:3): (1) he speaks in anger; (2) he usurps the place of God, saying, "Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" and (3) he acts violently, striking the rock twice, when God has told him only to speak to it. On the symbolism of the rock, see notes on Ex. 17:6.
God's word of judgment is directed to both Moses and Aaron, for Aaron has accompanied Moses and is implicated in the rashness of his brother's action. Their ministry is coming to an end.
See text note. A similar name, "Massah and Meriabah," was used at the first incident of striking water from a rock (Ex. 17:7; Ps. 95:8 and text notes).

The Edomites, descendants of Jacob's brother Esau (Gen. 25:25–34; 27:1–42; 28:5–9; 32:3–33:16; 35:29; 36:1–43), show an unbrotherly attitude toward Israel. Moses makes a courteous request of the Edomites, asking permission to go peacefully through their territory and offering to pay the Edomites for anything the travelers might need on the way. Since Israel is denied permission and they do not want to fight their way through, they cannot reach the Promised Land without first making a long march through a particularly unpleasant part of the wilderness. 20:14 your brother Israel. Jacob (later called Israel, Gen. 32:28) and his brother Esau had quarreled in their youth, but they were reconciled in their later years (Gen. 33:9–16; 35:29).

Eleazar succeeds his father as high priest. Aaron has the joy of seeing his work carried on by a son; God establishes a priestly dynasty through Aaron. Moses, whose ministry as mediator of the Sinai covenant is unique (12:8 note; Ex. 18:1–24:18 note), is not succeeded by his son. Leadership of the nation passes to Joshua, who belongs to the tribe of Ephraim (27:12-23).
See note on Deut. 34:8.

The Israelites' first victory against the Canaanites is over Arad at Hormah, where Israel had suffered stinging defeat many years before (14:45). This victory marks a shift in focus from the exodus generation condemned to die in the wilderness (14:29–35) to the generation born in the wilderness.

This event typifies both the sacrifice of Christ and the faith of His people. Just as the bronze representation of the poisonous serpent is lifted up, so Christ, as one born "in the likeness of sinful flesh" (Rom. 8:3), will be lifted up (John 3:14). The afflicted Israelites have no other means of rescue than to look at the bronze snake, just as sinners have no hope for salvation except faith in the crucified Christ (John 3:15, 16). Unfortunately, this bronze serpent later becomes the object of idolatrous worship (2 Kin. 18:4).

**LORD** . This is the only biblical reference to a book of victory songs that was apparently current in the land of Israel at the time of David or before. A similar work, the Book of Jashar, is quoted in Josh. 10:12, 13 and 2 Sam. 1:17–27. Arnon. This perennial stream flowed into the Dead Sea from the east, through a deep ravine. It formed the border between the territory of Moab and the Amorite kingdom of Sihon (21:21–31). See Deut. 1:5 note.
Moses narrates Israel's conquest of Hesh­bon and Bashan. Both of these kingdoms were in eastern Palestine, across the Jordan from Canaan (the Transjordan).
See note on Deut. 3:1.

After the conquest of Heshbon in the southern Transjordan (21:21–26) and Bashan in the north (21:33–35), the Israelites return south to the area across the Jordan from Jericho and north of the territory of Moab.

Though the narrative itself has considerable literary charm (22:28 note), the Balaam incident must also be viewed within the context of God's covenant relationship with His people. The preceding narrative in Numbers focuses on God's punishment of the rebellious adult generation of Israelites, but Balaam unexpectedly pronounces a series of blessings that recall God's promises to the patriarchs. Despite their sinfulness, God has not abandoned the Israelites. God is faithful to the covenant promises made to Abraham (Gen. 12:3 and note). Ironically, the Lord also uses the pagan prophet Balaam, who has been hired by the Moabite king to curse the Israelites, to bless them instead and to prophesy the coming of a royal star out of Jacob — the Messiah Himself — who will triumph over Israel's enemies (24:17–19).
The Moabites are descendants of Lot's incestuous relationship with his daughter (Gen. 19:37, 38 note). The Moabites are asking the Midianites to help them resist the Israelite invaders.

The pagan prophet Balaam lives at Pethor, a city in northern Mesopotamia on the banks of the Euphrates River. That Balak sends emissaries such a great distance is evidence of Balaam's considerable reputation for supernatural powers. The nature and extent of Balaam's knowledge of the true God is uncertain. Though a famous sorcerer and false prophet, Balaam has some regard for the true God (22:8, 18), and the Lord uses Balaam to communicate His word (23:7–10, 18–24; 24:3–9, 15–24). Fundamentally, however, Balaam seems to be a syncretistic opportunist who seeks to manipulate the spirit world for his own gain. In the course of this narrative, Balaam establishes himself as a prime example of the false prophet and teacher (31:16; 2 Pet. 2:15; Jude 11).

In light of God's earlier permission to travel (v. 20), the Lord's response is perhaps surprising. The narrative as a whole indicates, however, that Balaam's trip is perversely motivated and that he certainly hopes to curse Israel (v. 32). God uses this confrontation between Balaam and the angel of the Lord to underscore His command to say nothing except what He might direct (v. 35). the angel of the **LORD** . See note on Gen. 16:7.
The story of Balaam abounds in comic irony. The donkey is able to see the path better than the diviner and tell him about it (2 Pet. 2:16).
Balaam is calling for a sword without knowing that he is about to see one pointed at him.
Because Balaam and the princes receive the meat, this is probably a sacrificial meal, though some suggest a reference to the pagan use of animal entrails for divination (cf. 24:1).

The number seven was of profound symbolic significance in the ancient Near East. The sum of the sacred numbers three and four, it often appears in a ritual context in the OT (Gen. 21:28; 33:3; Ex. 12:15; 29:35–37).

Balaam's second oracle reaffirms God's determination to bless Israel by giving them victory over the Moabites. Verse 21 is surprising in view of the sins described in the book of Numbers. Despite their failings, God regards His people as righteous for the sake of His covenant promises, and He provides the means of their forgiveness (Gen. 17:2 note).
Balak superstitiously decides to see whether another location or additional sacrifices can bring a more favorable result.
Balaam's third oracle pictures the blessings that God plans for Israel, ending with a curse from the Abrahamic promise against those who curse her (v. 9; Gen. 12:3).

The word translated "Almighty" (also in v. 16) is the Hebrew word shaddai, a divine name associated with the patriarchal narratives (Gen. 17:1; 28:3; 35:11; 43:14; 48:3; 49:25) that also occurs frequently in Job.

1 Samuel 15:32, 33 recounts the death of an Amalekite king who bore this name. Here Balaam may refer to an earlier prominent king of the Amalekites who bore the same personal name. It is also possible that "Agag" was a title, just as the title "Pharaoh" was used by many Egyptian rulers.
Balak refuses to pay the hired prophet his "wages of unrighteousness" — the "honor" he is expecting (22:7; 2 Pet. 2:15).

In his fourth oracle, Balaam predicts the future advent of a royal conqueror who will triumph over Moab and Edom. An initial fulfillment of these predictions is found in 2 Sam. 8:2–14, which describes David's victory over the Moabites and Edomites. But his accomplishments prefigure the greater conquests of Christ (cf., Col. 2:15; 1 Cor. 15:25, 26; Rev. 20:10, 14).
In his final oracles, Balaam predicts the downfall of the other nations in the area. 24:20 Amalek. See notes on Ex. 17:8, 16.

A nomadic tribe of metalworkers found in the ancient Near East from the Patriarchal period onward (Gen. 15:19). Moses's father-in-law is identified as both a Midianite and a Kenite (Ex. 2:16; Judg. 1:16). The Rechabites of Jer. 35 are thought to be descendants of the Kenites (1 Chr. 2:55; Neh. 3:14).
The Assyrians of northern Mesopotamia are already an important military power at this time, but their greatest conquests will be made centuries later (cf. Is. 36).
The Hebrew name for Cyprus came to represent the Mediterranean region to the west of Palestine. In Dan. 11:30 this word is used to predict the effects of Roman naval power.

Afraid to attack the vast throng of Israelites (22:3) and having failed to thwart them by means of Balaam, the Moabites and Midianites (at Balaam's instigation, 31:16) seek to subvert and assimilate Israel through idolatry and immorality. When the world cannot eliminate the witness of God's people through direct conflict, it often tries to neutralize that witness by absorbing them into the world. OT Israel must survive in physical separation from her neighbors (Lev. 18:24; Deut. 7:3; Josh. 23:12, 13), trusting in God's promises of land and the Messiah. This incident at Beth Peor is later seen as a prime example of the temptations that the surrounding peoples provide to the covenant people (Deut. 4:3; Josh. 22:17; Ps. 106:28; Hos. 9:10). 25:1 Shittim. This Hebrew word identifies the region across the Jordan from Jericho (cf. Josh. 2:1). Here worship of the local fertility god is joined with ritual prostitution (vv. 1–3, 6).
In gross defiance of the covenant between the Lord and Israel, the Israelites yoke themselves to the false god through their idolatrous worship.
See note on Deut. 21:22.

Note the stress on Phinehas as embodying God's own zeal for the purity of His people. Such zeal earns Phinehas divine commendation and the promise of a perpetual priesthood (v. 13). Later in Jewish history, Phinehas becomes a symbol of uncompromising loyalty to God's law (Ps. 106:30, 31).

The final major section of Numbers concerns preparations for entering the Promised Land, with particular attention paid to matters relevant to life in the land. 26:1–51 Like the census taken thirty-eight years earlier (ch. 1), this second census counts only males, aged twenty or older, able to serve in the army (v. 2). It records only the total number for each tribe, though in each case the names of the tribe's subdivisions are included. Overall, there has been a decline of nearly two thousand in the total number of fighting men. The census reveals that of all the men counted previously, only Joshua and Caleb remain alive to enter the land of Canaan.

The tribe of Jacob's eldest son, Reuben, is listed first. Although it suffered losses because of the rebellion of Dathan and Abiram (vv. 8–10), it has recovered sufficiently to be almost as numerous as at the first census. Korah (of the tribe of Levi) is mentioned here because of his association with Dathan and Abiram, and it is observed that his line has not died out (v. 11).

Simeon's numbers have declined far more than those of any other tribe (from nearly 60,000 to a little over 22,000), probably indicating that the Simeonite leader killed during the Midianite seduction shortly before this census was taken (25:14) was but one of thousands of Simeonites involved in the Midianite seduction (25:1–9). See note on Gen. 49:7.
See Gen. 38:1–10 and notes.
The Promised Land is to be divided in proportion to the size of each group, with locations decided by lot.

Rules for inheritance of land, which notably include women, are explained after the account of Zelophehad's daughters. These legal requirements are similar in form to those listed in Ex. 21:1–22:17. Zelophehad had died without leaving a male heir, and his daughters petition Moses and the leaders to allow the daughters to inherit their father's portion in the land and not to let his name be cut off. The names of all five daughters are recorded in v. 1. In ch. 36 a related question is raised by the tribal leaders: if the daughters of Zelophehad marry men of a different tribe, will their father's inheritance be transferred to that tribe? In response to both questions, the Lord answers that the family and tribal legacies should be protected (27:7; 36:6). These protections, as well as the prohibition against permanent transfer of land from one family to another, are rooted in God's ultimate ownership of the Promised Land (Lev. 25:23) and the fact that He has entrusted it to all His people as a good gift and permanent possession to be enjoyed (Lev. 25:34; Deut. 6:10–12; 8:10–13). The land is not simply private property to be transferred on the basis of human convention and agreement; rather, it symbolizes life with God.
Moses is not permitted to enter the Promised Land but only to see it from a distance. This is punishment for his failure at Meribah (20:9–13 and notes).
See note on Deut. 34:9.
Moses's office and ministry are unique (12:6–8; 20:22–29 note), but a portion of his honor and authority will be imparted to Joshua.

In preparation for entry into the land, the instructions for regular sacrifice and celebration presented earlier (see cross-references) are summarized. Beginning with daily (28:1–8), Sabbath (28:9, 10), and monthly offerings (28:11–15), and then with the celebration of annual feasts (28:16–29:40), the summary shows clearly how Israelite life in the land is to revolve around the worship and service of the Lord.

Ordinarily, people are obliged to fulfill any vow or obligation they make, including even a rash promise (v. 6). However, the vow of a subordinate member of a household can be cancelled by the head of the house (vv. 5, 8, 12–13, 15). Moses urges the people not to make rash vows but declares that if made, they must be fulfilled (Deut. 23:21–23; cf. Prov. 20:25). For a terrible instance of a rash vow, see Judg. 11:30–40 and notes.

Vengeance against the Midianites for their efforts to seduce the Israelites into idol worship and sexual immorality (ch. 25) is undertaken. This narrative deals particularly with details concerning the plunder taken from the Midianites. Because the plunder of war must be handled in a fashion that preserves the holiness of God and of the people, the principles stated here help prepare the Israelites for the coming conquest of the land.
See note on 25:11.
See note on 22:5.

Although the Israelite soldiers initially spare the Midianite women and children, Moses's command that all the women who are not virgins must be killed is due to their role in causing the Israelites to sin at Peor (see 25:1–18, esp. vv. 16–18). All males are killed, including children, probably to prevent any resurgence of the Midianite clans (cf. v. 7).

Israel divides the Midianite spoils: half to the soldiers and half to the community (vv. 25–27). As a tribute to the Lord, one out of every five hundred from the soldier's half, and one out of every fifty from the community's half is to be given to the Levites (vv. 28–31, 41). A detailed enumeration of the portions is given (vv. 32–47).

The tribes of Reuben and Gad, possessors of much livestock, request permission to settle in the Transjordan territory (the region east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea) already conquered (vv. 1–5; cf. 21:24–26, 31–35). Because all of Israel is to participate in the conquest and because their departure would dishearten the other tribes if it were to occur, Moses sternly warns them against the sin of the exodus generation (vv. 6–15). His admonition includes a classic recognition of God's sovereign dominion as judge: "be sure your sin will find you out" (v. 23).

Apparently, many from this tribe joined Reuben and Gad in wishing to live east of the Jordan. During the time in the wilderness, Manasseh has increased from 32,200 to 52,700 (cf. 1:35 and 26:34). Reuben and Gad settle territory already conquered (vv. 33–38), but the half-tribe of Manasseh goes further north and makes new conquests (vv. 39–42).
These verses give a vivid summary of the Israelites' departure from Egypt.
Many of the names in this list may represent wilderness camps that have since disappeared. For other mentions of some of these locations, see the cross-references.
See Deut. 10:6.

God orders the complete removal of the Canaanites and the destruction of all marks of idolatry, as was done to the Midianites (ch. 31). The command to drive out (cf. v. 55) suggests that the Israelites are to expel rather than exterminate all the inhabi­tants of Canaan. However, those who resist with force place their own lives in danger.
God sets forth rules for settlement, summarizing the directions in 26:52–56.
These boundaries of Canaan do not include the territory already assigned in Transjordan, east of the Jordan River (vv. 13–15). See ch. 32.

The Lord designates men to assign the portions of the land of Canaan: Eleazar the priest (Num. 20:25–26) and Joshua the commander (Num. 27:18–23) are to be in charge, together with a leader from each of the ten tribes that has not yet been given their inheritance. None of these ten names are included in earlier lists of leaders (Num. 1:5–15; 2:3–29; 7:12–78), nor is any one of them the son of a man included in those lists.
Because the Levites were not given a tribal land inheritance (18:20), they are instead assigned forty-eight towns with surrounding pastureland, including six "cities of refuge."
Six cities of refuge are to be established for those who accidentally kill another person. See note on Deut. 4:41–43.
In ancient Israel, a member of the victim's family was customarily designated to avenge the victim's death by seeking the death penalty in the case of murder.

See also v. 28. The death of the high priest brings a change in the legal status of a person guilty of manslaughter. The guilty one is no longer liable to the penalty for manslaughter — confinement within a city of refuge.
No one is to be put to death on the evidence of only one witness.
Accepting a ransom payment is forbidden in cases of murder and manslaughter. This provision emphasizes the value God places on human life.

Because the shedding of human blood defiles the land, it will become ritually unclean. Since God dwells among the Israelites, they must ensure that the land remains undefiled. Pollution of the land by bloodshed can be removed only by shedding the blood of the murderer (Gen. 9:5, 6 and notes).
See note on 27:1–11.

In the Jubilee year, all property will revert to its original (male) owner or (male) heir (Lev. 25:8–17). In the case of the daughters of Zelophehad, it has been established that women can inherit land (27:1–11). If a daughter inheriting property marries outside her tribe, it appears that the law of Jubilee will cause the land to be transferred to the tribe of the new husband. (In a society where tribal membership is reckoned according to one's father, a property-owning woman who marries outside her tribe and bears a son creates an heir for her husband's tribe, granting her son a claim to land that should belong to her own father's tribe, not her husband's.) To keep this from happening, Moses rules that a woman with property may not marry outside her tribe. In agreement with this, the daughters of Zelophehad marry relatives in Manasseh, thereby ensuring that all of their heirs will be from the tribe of Manasseh just like Zelophehad.

Deuteronomy.note: These introductory verses set the scene, identifying Moses and the circumstances of his addresses to the people just before he dies and the people cross the Jordan. 1:1 beyond the Jordan. See Introduction: Author. the Arabah opposite Suph. The exact location is uncertain, but taken as a whole, the description points to the region of Moab. This Arabah or "plain" extends along the eastern edge of Palestine from the Sea of Galilee south to the Gulf of Aqaba. Suph, meaning "reeds," may refer to a location in Moab near the Arnon River. The names Paran and Hazeroth are mentioned during Israel's travels in the Sinai Peninsula (Num. 10:12; 11:35; 12:16; 33:17), but it is unclear whether they are the same places as mentioned here. Tophel, Laban, and Dizahab are mentioned only here.

The distance between Horeb and Kadesh-barnea is about 150 miles (240 km). The Israelites went by way of the Mount Seir road, which probably means they traveled part of the time along the valley north of Ezion-geber, a journey of 175 miles (280 km) or more. They made good time if the whole nation arrived in eleven days. But the "eleven days' journey" could be a conventional expression for the distance involved rather than the time taken on this particular journey.

This date (forty years since the exodus from Egypt) serves to fix the time for the book as a whole. The years of divine judgment have ended (Num. 14:33, 34), and Israel prepares to enter the Promised Land. This forty-year period included thirty-eight years in the wilderness, followed by two years for the conquest of Transjordan (2:14).

The conquest of Transjordan is detailed in 2:24–3:11. Heshbon. The name has been preserved in the modern Tell Hesban, located in Transjordan some thirty-five miles (56 km) east of Jerusalem. Extensive excavations have discovered no remains at Hesban from Moses's time (i.e., from the fourteenth century B.C.). It is possible that a nearby mound that does contain fourteenth-century remains is the Heshbon of Moses's day. Edrei. The name is probably preserved in the town name of modern Der'a on the border between Syria and Jordan, which does have ruins of this period.

The Israelites are camped in the plains of Moab (e.g., Num. 22:1; 26:3, 63), otherwise called "the land of Moab" (e.g., Deut. 29:1; 32:49). This probably refers to the region north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan River. This territory was once part of Moab, but Sihon the Amorite drove the Moabites southward prior to Israel's arrival (Num. 21:26). Jephthah rehearses this history in Judg. 11:14–27. to explain this law. On the brink of entering into the land of promise, Moses, as their leader for the past forty years, explains to the Israelites the obligations that they need to fulfill as God's cov­enant people. The term "law" translates the Hebrew word torah, which has the connotation of teaching or instruction. The English term "law" is too narrow to be an exact translation, for much of the material expounded by Moses is not formulated as legislation. The covenant obligations are not restricted to laws. Because Moses explains to the people the obligations given at Mount Sinai, much of the book of Deuteronomy sounds like a sermon with exhortation to obey what is being taught.

Moses reviews the history of Israel prior to this covenant ratification occasion. He provides a travelogue of the nation's movements from the Sinai region to Hormah, on to the Arnon, and into the Transjordan area. This segment of the book concludes with an overview of the covenant now to be renewed with the generation born in the wilderness. 1:6 Horeb. The name for the area around and including Mount Sinai. The name Sinai nearly always has the designation "Mount" or "wilderness." Horeb only once has the designation "Mount" (Ex. 33:6), and probably denotes a region larger than that covered by the term Sinai.
These borders of the Promised Land were given to Abraham in Gen. 15:17–21. The promise to Abraham included driving out the Canaanites and the other nations (Gen. 15:14).

**LORD** swore. God's solemn oath to give the land to Abraham's descendants is mentioned at least six times in Genesis and is found at least twenty-five times in Deuteronomy (it is also mentioned in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers). Deuteronomy anticipates that the Israelites will very soon begin to take possession of the land of Canaan.

A reference to the episode in which Moses took the good advice of Jethro, his father-in-law (Ex. 18:24–26). During the year at Mount Sinai, Moses, under God, organized the nation's judicial system and worship. Regarding the judges, see 16:18; 17:8–13; 19:17.

The place was called simply "Kadesh" in Num. 13:26. Kadesh means "holy place," and the name was doubtless given by the original inhabitants to many supposedly sacred places. This place was called Kadesh-barnea to distinguish it from other such places (e.g., in Judah, Josh. 15:23; in Naphtali, Judg. 4:6).
This account of the people's failure at Kadesh parallels extensively the account in Num. 13.

The name "Anak" appears in Egyptian texts of the early second millennium as the name of a ruler in Palestine. It probably is related to the biblical Anak whose descendants lived in Hebron (Num. 13:22). They were taller than the Israelites and were feared for their military prowess. Joshua conquered them, and their remnants merged with the Philistines (Josh. 12:21, 22).

The mention of the pillar of fire and the cloud refers to Ex. 13:21, where the pillar guided them out of Egypt, and especially to Num. 9:15–23, which tells of the Lord's guidance through the whole wilderness journey.

**LORD** was angry. Mention of the doom of the lost generation recalls that God was also displeased with Moses and refused to allow him to enter Canaan (32:51; Num. 20:9–11 note; 27:14). Joshua, a faithful spy, would carry on as leader (Num. 27:12–23).

Little is said in Numbers or Deuteronomy about the forty years of lost time. Numbers gives examples of the people's rebellions against Moses (Num. 16; 17). It is likely that the list of the wanderings in Num. 33:18–49, after they left Hazeroth and the wilderness of Paran, indicates where the tabernacle was set up and the core of the people stayed. As for the rebellious majority, they may have fanned out over the peninsula of Sinai with their flocks in order to find forage.

Because the term "Red Sea" could include the Gulf of Aqaba (Ex. 13:18 note), this was likely the desert road to the gulf. traveled around Mount Seir. Or "we circled around Mount Seir." The Israelites lived a nomadic life in the wilderness.

As explained in v. 8 and in Num. 20:14–21, the Edomites refused peaceful passage, so Israel went around their territory. Deuteronomy adds to the Numbers account that this was the Lord's command. The Edomites were related to Israel in ancestry (Gen. 25:25, 26).

Stops at Punon, Oboth, and Iye-abarim are mentioned at Num. 33:43, 44. Punon is probably modern Feinan, in the valley south of the Dead Sea, where there is a good spring. Israel is bypassing Edom and Moab and will attack Canaan from the eastern gateway.

We know little about these former inhabitants of Transjordan, but their names occur in Gen. 14, the report of the raid of eastern kings throughout this area in the days of Abraham. The Emim, also called Rephaim (or "giants"), lived where Moab later lived; the Zam­zummim, also called Rephaim, lived where the Ammonites later lived; and the Horites preceded the Edomites (vv. 10–12, 20–23). This remark that the Emim and Zamzummim are tall like the Anakim (but had nevertheless been conquered) boosts the morale of Israel who has yet to conquer the Anakim (the -im ending of such names is the Hebrew plural suffix) at this point. The identity of the Horites is puzzling. An important early people in Mesopotamia were called Hurrians (an equivalent of the Hebrew term translated "Horite"). Some Horites in Canaan seem to have Hurrian names, but their relationship to the Hurrians is unclear.

**LORD** gave to them. This phrase seems to be a later insertion after Israel conquered Canaan, but Moses could have spoken it after the significant conquest of Transjordan and settlement of the two-and-a-half tribes there.
See note on 1:3. as the **LORD** had sworn. Another clear reference to Numbers, where God swore that the faithless generation would die in the wilderness (Num. 14:21–23).
The kinship with Ammon, as with Moab and Edom, has long been remembered up to this point (Gen. 19:37, 38).

We know nothing of these people. If the Gaza mentioned is the same as the Gaza in southeastern Canaan, then Moses mentions it here only as part of his survey of earlier dislocations of peoples. the Caphtorim. If Caphtor means Crete, as is usual, then the reference is to an early and probably local Philistine community (before the later, great Philistine invasion of c. 1200 B.C.), of which the Abimelech in Gen. 20 was perhaps a member (cf. Jer. 47:4).
Israel was to begin its conquest, but the people were to remember that it is God who goes before them. This was to be the emphasis of God's people ever after (cf. Ps. 44:3).

The same offer as was given to Edom and Moab. Here, however, it was God's will for Israel to conquer the territory. Sihon refused Moses's offer, but God was in sovereign control as He had been with Pharaoh (Ex. 4:21). Sihon's resistance became Israel's opportunity.

About seven miles (11 km) south of Heshbon, Sihon was beaten and his territory conquered. The cities were put under the ban (i.e., Israel left no survivors, v. 34; Lev. 27:28 note). The calculated effect of the ban in ancient times was to make the inhabitants of an area flee without putting up resistance. Israel was commanded not to use this procedure except in their conquest of Canaan and Transjordan (20:10–15), where the holy nation would be corrupted by the influence of the remaining pagan culture (Ps. 106:34–39). The name of the city of Jahaz is found on the Moabite Stone from the ninth century B.C. Mesha, king of Moab, relates how he captured the city from the Israelites.

Bashan was a fertile region located east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee, extending from the Yarmuk River in the south to Mount Hermon in the north. It is wheat country today, and in ancient time was famous for its cattle and flocks (Ps. 22:12; Deut. 32:14). The spoil of this area must have seemed a treasure to the nomadic Israelites.
The east side of the river. This territory was more than half as large as Canaan proper. From the Arnon River to Mount Hermon is about 150 miles (240 km).
Both terms for Mount Hermon are witnessed in ancient Canaanite and Mesopotamian texts.

Og's bed, thirteen feet and six inches long by six feet wide (4.1 x 1.8 m), suggests he was a giant and that his people, the Rephaim, were also giants (2:10–12 note). The word translated "bed" is rare and could here be a euphemism for a sarcophagus large enough to hold tomb objects. The reference to "iron" may mean only that it was joined or trimmed with iron, a new material at this date (before the beginning of the Iron Age c. 1200 B.C.). See note on 8:9.
These tribes received the southern part of the conquered Transjordan area. Sparsely populated in the modern period, it was more thickly settled in ancient times.
The north half of Gilead, beginning near Zarethan, and all of Bashan went to this half-tribe.

Manasseh had but one son, Machir, and he had one son, Gilead, who had many descendants (Num. 26:29–34). The conquest of Jair, who must have been one of the descendants of Gilead, is mentioned in Num. 32:41.
Note the required unity. None can settle until all the tribes have conquered their inheritance. Details are given in Num. 32. See the fulfillment of the pledge in Josh. 22.
**LORD** your God \... fights for you. When Moses passed the command to Joshua (Num. 27:12–23), he emphasized the promise: the Lord will give victory.

Moses's account of his prayer in the valley opposite Beth-peor is instructive (vv. 24, 25). It shows his knowledge of the Lord's anger because of his sin at Meribah (Num. 20:12), and his knowledge that God does not "keep his anger forever" (cf. Ps. 103:9). In his prayer, Moses recognized God's sovereign power and asked for mercy.
Means "House of Peor." See note on 4:3.
"Statutes" may include regulations concerning worship (e.g., Ex. 12:24, the Passover); "rules" denotes case laws (Ex. 21:1–22:20).
God's instructions to Moses must be treated as sacred and kept inviolate (12:32). See the similar certification in Rev. 22:18, 19, which is quite possibly modeled on this prohibition in Deuteronomy.
A dreadful warning. The reference is to Num. 25, which details the idolatry at Baal-peor that God judged by killing twenty-four thousand people.
Israel's fidelity will be a testimony to the world that God is near His people and that His moral demands are righteous.
Deuteronomy stresses the covenant responsibility of parents for their children (6:7; 11:19). This covenant concern for children continues in the NT (Matt. 19:14 note; Acts 2:39; Eph. 6:4).
A reference to the great theophany (visible self-revelation of God) at Mount Sinai recorded in Ex. 19:9–20:19. It was an unforgettable experience.
