This title is used also in 10:4 and Ex. 34:28. Most Protestants usually divide them into four commandments dealing with duty to God and six with duty to man. Roman Catholics unite the first and second and divide the tenth, resulting in a division of three and seven. The command regarding the Sabbath is pivotal: it has reference to God and is for the benefit of both people and animals as well (Mark 2:27). The first three commandments concern God exclusively; the last six deal with humans.
God is transcendent Spirit (John 4:24), which rules out any idolatrous representation of the divine nature in the form of animate objects (vv. 16–18) and any worship of the created order (v. 19).
A hot furnace used to smelt iron, making for a vivid metaphor for a place of great suffering (8:9 note).
**LORD** was angry with me. See 1:37; 3:26; Num. 20:12.
God's presence is often associated with fire (Gen. 15:17; Ex. 3:3–5; 13:21; Num. 11:1–3), and divine judgment comes occasionally through fire (Lev. 10:2). a jealous God. See note on Ex. 20:5.
Here in brief form is found the warning embodied in the curses of 28:15–68. But here also is a promise to the repentant.

**LORD** will scatter you. Such passages have been taken by some as proof that Deuteronomy was not written by Moses but by someone in the sixth century B.C. during the Jewish exile in Babylon. However, the warning is general, and there is no mention of captivity in Babylon or of conditions in that later period, which would be expected if the book was written then.
This phrase, repeated in 31:29, refers to any future time of apostasy and renewal (cf. Num. 24:14).

This description may allude to the name of God given in Ex. 34:6 ("the LORD, a God merciful"). The theme of God's love for His people is highlighted in Deuteronomy (7:7–9, 13; 10:15, 18; 23:5; 33:3), anticipating the more complete revelation of God's love in the NT (John 3:16; Rom. 5:8; Eph. 2:4, 5; 1 John 3:1). the covenant with your fathers. See 1:8.
Except for the creation account in the early chapters of Genesis, this is the only mention in the Pentateuch of the creation of human beings.
A reference to the deliverance from Egypt, a topic repeatedly mentioned in Deuteronomy.
See Ex. 33:14.

This parenthetical section, in narrative style, marks the close of the first great speech. Moses names the cities of refuge for Transjordan. The principle of having cities of refuge was given in Ex. 21:13; that there should be six was stated in Num. 35:6. This section names the three for Transjordan, while 19:1–13 specifies that three should be designated for Canaan itself. Finally, all six cities are named in Josh. 20:7, 8. This progressive unfolding is consistent with Mosaic authorship and an indication that Deuteronomy was not written after the conquest of Canaan.

In his second address (and in the section to follow, chs. 12–26), Moses expounds the way of life in the covenant. The exposition focuses on love for the Lord, love that issues in obedience and consecration, as exemplified among the Le­vites set apart for service to the Lord. The sermon closes with a preview of the solemn declaration of covenant obligations elaborated in chs. 27–30.

Note the use of covenantal language. This portion of Deuteronomy, with its listing of covenantal requirements, resembles the stipulation sections of ancient treaties, especially those of the second millennium B.C. (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).
See the similar area description in 3:17.

This solemn form of address to Israel is found only in Deuteronomy: first here, then in the great Shema of 6:4, and finally in the exhortation of 9:1–3. Here the foundational covenant at Mount Sinai in Horeb is recalled.

Moses is differentiating the Sinai covenant from the promise of the land made to the patriarchs — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not the patriarchs who stood before God at Sinai but the Israelites who left Egypt with Moses (11:2 note).
Directly, without a mediator. After God spoke the Ten Commandments to the people, out of fear they asked for Moses to be a mediator between them and God (Ex. 20:18–19).
See Ex. 20:2–17 and notes.
The exalted monotheism of this commandment and of the whole OT was unique in ancient times. There are no other gods (4:39), and the worship of anything other than God Himself is forbidden.
See 4:15–18; note on Ex. 20:4.

Whereas God's anger extends only to the third and fourth generation, His love extends to thousands. In light of 7:9, some interpret "thousands" to refer to generations. This may not necessarily be implied here.

Most of the commandments in Deuteronomy parallel almost verbatim those in Exodus. Although there are numerous subtle distinctions between the two passages when read in Hebrew, they nevertheless demonstrate an obvious interdependence. Deuteronomy bases these commands on the deliverance from the bondage of Egypt, whereas Exodus cites God's work of creation as a basis. The continuing sabbatical principle commands a weekly day of rest. The change from the seventh day to the first day or Lord's Day by the NT church (Rev. 1:10), in celebration of Christ's resurrection, points to the inauguration of the new creation (1 Cor. 15:45–49; 2 Cor. 5:17; cf. Ex. 20:11) and to the believer's redemption from bondage to sin through the death and resurrection of Christ.

Other passages suggest that this clause may primarily be a promise of settled conditions and long peace for the people in the land, which also includes freedom from early death in war and revolution (5:33; 30:18, 20; cf. 25:15).

Lit. "and He did not add," perhaps an idiom meaning that He spoke no more. This would fit the statement in Exodus that the people in their fear asked that God speak no more to them directly but to address them only through Moses (Ex. 20:19). two tablets of stone. The tablets are mentioned in Ex. 31:18, where they are called the "two tablets of the testimony \... written with the finger of God." In addition, the tablets were inscribed on both sides (Ex. 32:15). These tablets were broken (Ex. 32:19), but new ones were made (Ex. 34:1–4, 27). Called "the testimony," the tablets were placed in the ark of the testimony (Ex. 25:16; 40:20), also called the "ark of the covenant" (Num. 10:33). The "testimony" refers to the written record attesting the terms of the covenant (Ex. 25:16 note).
These words translate the same Hebrew phrase as in 5:33. Here also we may understand the meaning as "long life in the land."

Often called the Shema, from the initial Hebrew word meaning "hear," this verse is the great confession of Israel's monotheistic faith, and to this day it is recited morning and evening by Jews (cf. Mark 12:29). See note on 5:1. The **LORD** \... **LORD** is one. Though the Hebrew may be translated several ways (see text note), it is best to understand the verse as affirming both God's uniqueness and unity or singularity — the only God is "one" (Mark 12:29). As the OT implies and the NT explicitly teaches, however, there is differentiation of persons within the unity of the Godhead. See theological note "The Triunity of God" on p. 1204.

The Hebrew expresses totality. For this reason the NT sometimes renders it "mind and strength" (Mark 12:30). This is the language of devotion. God demands not mere outward obedience to His commands but the heartfelt love and commitment of the whole person (Prov. 23:26).

The phrases in this section are multiplied to emphasize the overall importance of God's demands. Jews since before the time of Christ have taken these verses literally and tie little boxes containing these verses on their arms and foreheads and fasten them on their doorposts (cf. Matt. 23:5).
See 5:3 and note. This is one of many references in Deuteronomy to God's solemn promise to the patriarchs.

The third commandment does not forbid the invocation of God's name in oaths and vows (cf. Judg. 8:19), but it forbids false oaths and vows. Because swearing by the name of a god implies the recognition and worship of that god, the Israelites are not to swear by other gods (cf. Jer. 5:7; Zeph. 1:5). This verse is quoted by Jesus when tempted by Satan (Matt. 4:10; Luke 4:8).
See note on Ex. 20:5.
This word means "testing" (Ex. 17:7). Later in OT history, King Ahaz of Judah cites this verse insincerely (Is. 7:12). This verse is quoted by Jesus when Satan tempts Him (Matt. 4:7; Luke 4:12).
See note on 4:9.
**LORD** . See John 14:23.

See note on 2:32. Here the Israelites are specifically promised that the Lord will drive out the inhabitants. seven nations. These seven nations are difficult to identify. In 20:17 only six nations are mentioned (as also in Ex. 3:8, 17; 13:5; 33:2; 34:11), and the Girgashites are omitted. The Jebusites inhabited Jebus, another name for Jerusalem, and there is some indication that they were Hurrians (2:10–12). Amorites are known from ancient Mesopotamia. The ancient lawgiver Hammurabi (1792–1750 B.C.) was an Amorite, as were Og and Sihon, kings of Transjordan. The word "Canaanite" seems to include them all.

See note 2:32. Some think that the God of the OT was harsh and vengeful to decree the destruction of the Canaanites, but this is to forget that God is just. The sins of the land's inhabitants were extreme, and the time for judgment had come (cf. Gen. 15:16). God used Israel to punish the Canaanites but warned that if Israel committed apostasy, leaving the God who had graciously revealed Himself to them, they too would perish (28:15–68). Centuries later, God used the Assyrians and the Babylonians to punish Israel.

Marriage is the closest of human ties, and its sacredness is guarded in OT law. The corollary is that marriage must not be contracted with unbelievers, a principle repeated in the NT (1 Cor. 7:39). Israel did not maintain her spiritual purity and suffered for it (Ps. 106:37–39).

Israel was chosen to be a holy people (v. 6), and God does not tolerate false religions. Although the means of separation have changed, believers today have been chosen for holiness (Eph. 1:4) and are called to separate from false worship (2 Cor. 6:15–18).

The election of Israel as a holy nation set apart for God (vv. 6, 7) was grounded not in any merit or intrinsic goodness in Israel but in God's love and in His faithfulness to the covenant promises made to the patriarchs (6:10). God's election of the church is based on His oath to Jesus, the son of Abraham, the Son of God (Ps. 110:4; John 17:6). See theological note "Covenant" on p. 37.
See 5:10 and note.

See 28:4, where a similar verse is included in a litany of blessings. grain \... wine \... oil. The three staples of the ancient agricultural economy, here symbolic of prosperity (11:14; 14:23; 18:4); the "oil" is the olive oil used in cooking and lamps.
The same promise of health is given in Ex. 15:26, and the converse is given as a curse in Deut. 28:60.

The Hb. word for "hornet" may mean "depression" or "discouragement." The figure of stinging insects chasing the enemy is used elsewhere (1:44; Is. 7:18), and the metaphor of a hornet is quite appropriate (Ex. 23:28 note). God promises to fight for His people with the same power He manifested in the exodus (v. 18).
See theological note "The Incomprehensibility of God" on p. 630.

Another call for Israel to utterly hate pagan idolatry. But the idols were often made of gold and were valuable. The precious metal was under the ban (Hb. herem); the idols were to be destroyed, and what could pass through the fire was to be given to the Lord (Josh. 6:18, 19).

The initial giving of manna is mentioned in Ex. 16:15, its cessation in Josh. 5:12. God chose to sustain His people in the wilderness by a means previously unknown to them. Through this miraculous provision God humbled the people (by challenging their self-sufficiency) and tested their obedience (v. 16; cf. Ex. 16:16–30). man does not live by bread alone. See Matt. 4:4; Luke 4:4. every word that comes from the mouth of the **LORD** . Even more basic to life than physical food is the sustaining Word of God (Heb. 1:3).
This miraculous preservation is mentioned also in 29:5 but not elsewhere.
God let them hunger that He might show them His supply (v. 3). Discipline usually includes initial difficulty followed by blessing (Prov. 3:11, 12; Heb. 12:5, 6).

The description is more extensive than the familiar "flowing with milk and honey" found in most of the rest of the Pentateuch. Palestine certainly had more variety and more rainfall than the flat land of Goshen, but today much of the land is arid. The climate may have been different then, for a small difference in rainfall can significantly affect productivity. The land today has suffered from years of mismanagement — modern hills that were forested within recent memory are now barren. In Assyrian reliefs from c. 800 B.C., Israel is depicted with lush vines and grapes, and there is no reason to deny the characterization of the land as pleasant (11:9–12).

The Iron Age (c. 1200–300 B.C.) came to Palestine after Moses died (c. 1406 B.C.), but iron was known before that. Inventories in ancient Ugarit (c. 1400 B.C.) mention two talents of iron. The copper mines of the Sinai Peninsula and the area of south Transjordan were a valuable resource in antiquity and probably were a source of Solomon's wealth.

Continuing fidelity is the requirement for blessing. Israel without God is no better than the pagans. But God will keep His covenant with the fathers and save a remnant chosen by grace (v. 18; Rom. 11:28, 29).
See note 5:1. In this long section of exhortation (9:1–11:32), Moses turns toward the future. In the forthcoming conquest of Canaan, God will go before them (v. 3).
See 1:28; 2:21. The Anakim frightened the faithless spies forty years earlier (Num. 13:22, 28).

Note the threefold emphasis in this section (vv. 4–6) that the victory was not because of Israel's goodness but was entirely the work of God's grace. Repetition was characteristic of Hebrew literature and aided learning and memori­zation.
Moses retells the story given in Exodus (Ex. 24:12, 18; 32:7–10, 15–20).

Today, no stream flows down from Jebel Musa, the peak often identified as Mount Sinai (Ex. 16:1 note). The ground has some moisture, and low bushes grow, but the mention of a stream implies that in Moses's time there was more rainfall than now (8:7–9 note).
See Num. 11:3. Massah. See 6:16 and Ex. 17:7. Kibroth-hattaavah. See Num. 11:34.

The sheer persistence in rebellion by the Israelites (v. 24) points to the importance of Moses's intercession (vv. 25–28; Ex. 32:11–13) and to the gracious power of God, who remains faithful to His covenant despite the failings of His people (v. 29).

Summarizing the material in Ex. 34:1–4 and 37:1–9, Moses here telescopes the receiving of the commandments and the building of the ark. The tablets were put in the ark when the tabernacle was set up, as mentioned in Ex. 40:20. 10:1 two tablets of stone. It has generally been assumed that the law was written once, the extent of the material requiring two tablets or a double tablet. More recently, some have suggested that there were two tablets, each a separate copy of the law. This reflects the ancient practice of providing each treaty partner with a copy of the agreement. Because the ark was both the place of God's presence with His people and the focal point of Israel's worship, it was appropriate for both copies of the covenantal terms to be housed in the ark. See note on Ex. 31:18.
See note on 4:13.

Some have suggested that this parenthetical section breaks the narrative and is, therefore, a later insertion. It is evident, however, that this section ties together a number of themes from the preceding context: Aaron's role in the golden calf incident, for which he was threatened with death that was averted only by Moses's intercession (9:20); the impending possession of the land (9:1–4), in which the Levites would not participate because the Lord was their inheritance (v. 9; cf. 9:29); and the ark (vv. 1–5), which the Levites were to tend (v. 8). The journeys in vv. 6, 7 appear to correspond to Num. 33:31–33. These movements are difficult to locate because we can identify only a few of the places mentioned. 10:6 Moserah \... Aaron died. This mention of Aaron's death underscores the effectiveness of Moses's intercession (9:20). Aaron was not killed at Sinai but lived until the fortieth year after the exodus (Num. 33:38).
This does not refer to the time of Aaron's death (v. 6) or to the events of v. 7 but to the time of the revelation at Sinai (Ex. 28; 29).
To the patriarchs (9:5; Ex. 33:1).

**LORD** your God require of you. This rhetorical question resembles the much-quoted Mic. 6:8, which calls us to justice, mercy, and humility in our walk with God (cf. Matt. 23:23). To walk with God requires that we love Him with all our being and keep His commandments — love and obedience go together (John 14:23). To love God with our whole being is the greatest commandment (Deut. 6:5; Mark 12:29–34).
The contrast is a noble one, between God's sovereignty over and common grace to all creation (v. 14) and His special electing love for the patriarchs and the nation (v. 15).

This verse (along with Deut. 30:6 and Jer. 4:4) is an effective answer to those who imagine that the OT teaches merely a religion of outward form. Circumcision was a sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Gen. 17:10–14). What really mattered was a life oriented toward what the covenant promised and demanded, not the physical act of circumcision itself. As Paul indicates, circumcision in itself has no saving significance. True circumcision is "of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (Rom. 2:29).

The Lord of surpassing greatness and sovereignty ("God of gods and Lord of lords," v. 17) is also revealed to be the supremely compassionate God who has deep concern for the least in human society: the fatherless, the widow, and the alien. In this He is our example (v. 19).
See note on Ex. 1:5. Mention of the number who went into Egypt emphasizes God's great love in increasing Israel's population.

Since the people have seen God's wonderful deliverance (v. 8), they should therefore obey God's commands all the more faithfully. In his mention of "children," it does not seem that Moses distinguishes the adults over age forty in his audience, who saw the exodus, from the youths who did not. The younger generation also has seen God's preserving care and discipline in the wilderness (vv. 5, 6). Probably, therefore, Moses is distinguishing the current generation to which he is speaking from their children yet to be born.

Moses distinguishes Dathan and Abiram from Korah. Likewise, Ps. 106:17 does not include Korah with those buried alive. This distinction is not because the information about Korah belongs to a later time of writing, as some have held; rather, this distinction by Moses is precise. Closer reading of the record in Num. 16:16–35 shows that Korah was at the tabernacle among the 250 men with censers. Dathan and Abiram, who were not Levites, were in front of their tents with their families when the earth swallowed them up and Korah's family with them. But Korah himself perished with the 250 in the fire from the Lord.
See note on 5:16.

The precise detail of this allusion is unclear. It may refer to the sluice gates of irrigation canals (which were often opened by the gardener's foot), or to the burdensome practice of carrying water by bucket. In contrast to the Promised Land, which had sufficient rainfall for agriculture (vv. 9, 11), arid Egypt depended heavily upon irrigation for farming.
The command to love the Lord "with all your heart" (6:5) is echoed in Deuteronomy nine times.
See note on 7:13.
See note on 4:9, and the similar exhortations and metaphors in 6:6–9.

The same expression and the same boundaries of Canaan are repeated in Josh. 1:3–5. Because the boundaries need to include a southern limit, "wilderness" probably means the Sinai Desert. The boundaries include all of modern Israel and Lebanon, together with part of Syria. This expression may refer to the practice of gaining formal title to a land by walking through it.

This introduction to the ceremony of blessing and cursing that is to take place at Ebal and Gerizim is reiterated in Deut. 30:19 at the end of Moses's speech. Under divine inspiration, Moses emphasizes the people's obligation to love God and obey His commands.

The details of this ceremony are provided in chs. 27; 28; the ceremony itself is performed according to Moses's direction by Joshua (Josh. 8:30–35). The phrase "beyond the Jordan \... toward the going down of the sun" (v. 30) point to a location in Canaan (i.e., west of the Jordan). According to Gen. 12:6, the "oak of Moreh" was near Shechem. The precise location of Gilgal is uncertain, but it seems to have been near Jericho (Josh. 4:19). The Canaanites inhabited this whole territory, and there is no reason to doubt the usual identification of these mountains as the two mountains near Shechem astride the main north-south road.

Moses continues to expound the covenant way of life, reiterating laws governing Israel's worship and conduct. The laws pertain to topics from idolatry to tithes, from priests to divorce, from nations to the individual. The section concludes with exhortations to obey the Lord, who is both redeemer and king. 12:1 statutes and rules. See 4:1 note. Moses explains in chs. 12–26 the covenant obligations.

**LORD** your God will choose. This passage has been used to argue that Deuteronomy was written in the sixth century B.C. so as to support Josiah's centralization of worship at Jerusalem in that period (Introduction: Date and Occasion). But that view, which presupposes an untenable evolutionary theory of the development of Israelite religion, misreads this verse. The reference here to "the place" certainly need not imply that the location of the temple in Jerusalem was known when this text was written. In the course of Israel's history, worship of the Lord was successively centered in several places: Shiloh (Josh. 18:1) and Gibeon (1 Chr. 16:39) as well as later in Jerusalem. The stress here is on the contrast between "the place \... the LORD your God will choose" and "the places where the nations \... served their gods" (v. 2). Purity of worship in obedience to divine command, rather than centralization, is primarily in view.

Some sacrifices are shared by priests and worshipers. The worship of Israel is meant to be holy, reverent, and joyful. The worship of the holy God involves repentance and cleansing, but the redeemed heart is full of joy and praise. Psalms frequently expresses such joyful devotion.
The gifts of the worshipers are, in part, to support the priests and Levites, who are allotted no farmland of their own (10:6–9).
The same rule is given in vv. 20, 21. They can slaughter for meat anywhere, but sacrificial meat and foodstuffs devoted to God can only be eaten at the central place of worship. See note Lev. 17:3.

The same principle is given in Gen. 9:4 and Lev. 17:10–14. The treatment of the blood in the sacrificial system shows that it stands for the life of the animal. When the blood is gone, the life is gone. When blood is sprinkled on the altar, innocent life is shed for a guilty sinner. The OT sacrifices show a theology of substitution of the innocent for the guilty. This concept anticipates something more important to come, because an animal, no matter how perfect, is by no means as valuable as a human being (Mic. 6:6, 7). For this reason, Is. 53:10 looks forward to the innocent Servant of the Lord dying as a sin offering (cf. John 1:29).

Child sacrifice was common in ancient times, especially in the Phoenician colony of Carthage in North Africa. In ancient pagan cultures, children were sometimes sacrificed in times of great need as an expression of devotion to a god (2 Kin. 3:27). Even some Israelites at times engaged in this detestable practice (Judg. 11:30–40; Ps. 106:34–39; Jer. 7:31).
See 4:2.

Moses issues warnings against apostasy in ch. 13. The first (vv. 1–5) concerns false prophets. The other sections warn against a near relative who tempts a family member to apostasy (vv. 6–11) and the apostasy of a whole town (vv. 12–18). In each case, the penalty is death. 13:1–5 The caution against a false prophet is given to emphasize that even though a prophet seems to carry impressive credentials, the theological test is still crucial. No true prophet can possibly advance a false religion, since Israel's God is the true and only God. All other gods are the creations of men. Those who follow them and worship them must be eliminated from Israel.

Attention turns to the second instance of seduction to apostasy. 13:6 your brother \... friend. The closest ties on earth do not dissolve the obligation to remain faithful to the true and only God (cf. 21:18–21).
See theological note "The Threefold Use of the Law."

In the third instance of apostasy, the case of a whole town is considered. First, investigation is undertaken (vv. 12–14). If the thing is true, the town must be destroyed (vv. 14–15). Note that the plunder of the town is not to be taken for private gain (vv. 16–18). The thought of gain might cloud the judgment of those who investigate the charges of apostasy. The Hebrew for "heap" is tel, the word now used by archaeologists for the mounds comprising the ruins of successive generations of the buried cities they excavate.

See Lev. 19:27, 28, where the same rules are given. Details of this custom are unclear, but it doubtless involves practices associated with ancestor worship and pagan ritual mourning. Because Israel has been chosen by God as His special possession (v. 2; 26:18), Israel is to be different and was to reject all pagan religion and associated rituals.

This section and Num. 5:1–4 are the main references to the legislation regarding cleanness and uncleanness outside of Lev. 11–15. The only ground given for the prohibitions is that Israel is to be holy to the Lord. Several reasons, ranging from religious to medical, have been suggested for these laws. While in some cases the prohibitions require what is good public health procedure, the distinction of clean and unclean is not a matter of health. Rather, it reflects an important way of viewing the world, a view in which holiness and cleanness are associated with life and uncleanness with death. To be holy is to be like God, the source of life; to be unclean is to be under the power of death. The food laws will distinguish Israel as a holy nation; other nations are considered to be unclean. At the coming of Jesus and the inauguration of a new era in God's redemptive purposes, the makeup of the holy nation changes with the incorporation of Gentiles (1 Pet. 2:9). See notes Lev. 11–15.

No easy formula is given to identify clean birds. In general the scavenger birds are unclean, probably because of their frequent contact with carrion. Such birds might pose a health risk as well. Some of the birds listed in vv. 12–18 can no longer be precisely identified.
But there are exceptions: Lev. 11:22 explicitly mentions the locust, destroying locust, cricket, and grasshopper as clean.

This prohibition is not fully explained. Appearing also in Ex. 23:19 and 34:26, it is the basis of the practice among orthodox Jews of not eating milk and meat products together. Some have also suggested that cooking a goat in milk may have been a Canaanite practice with pagan religious implications, but the evidence is not clear. More likely, the regulation is intended to avoid mixing life and death; milk is meant to nourish the kid and should not, therefore, be associated with its death.

A tenth. The custom of the tithe was known as early as the time of the patriarchs (Gen. 14:20; 28:22). Lev. 27:32 specifies that the tithe of animals must not be selected but must be "all that pass under the herdsman's staff."

**LORD** . The tithe is to be taken to the sanctuary (12:17), where the worshipers are to eat a portion in joyful fellowship with the priests, Levites, and the poor. Far from being a burdensome requirement, the giving of the tithe is to be an occasion of celebration and worship (12:7 note; cf. 2 Cor. 9:7).

Travel in the ancient world was not easy, and the transportation of agricultural products was harder still. Here, Moses gives practical solution for these ancient Israelites — they can convert the goods to money and carry the money (v. 25).

The third-year tithe is mentioned again only in 26:12, and the precise details are unclear. Because it is a special gift for the Levites and the poor, and because the Levitical cities will be scattered throughout Israel (Josh. 21), it will be impractical to take all the tithes at one time to the central place of worship. Thus, these tithe offerings are to be stored in the towns of Israel and used to provide for the needy.

The sabbatical year was established and described in Ex. 23:10, 11 and Lev. 25:1–7, which require that the land should lie fallow during the seventh year. This passage (15:1–11) adds the provision that debts should be forgiven in that year. Since a loan might be arranged shortly before the sabbatical year, and thus be almost immediately forgiven, it might amount to a gift. For this reason vv. 7–11 warn against refusing to lend to the poor under these circumstances.

The forgiveness of personal loans to the poor is apparently in view here. God desires to bless His people materially in the Land of Promise so that borrowing would be unnecessary (vv. 5, 6). Although full obedience will result in the eradication of poverty from Israel, Moses realistically recognizes that some poverty will remain (v. 11; cf. Matt. 26:11). The sabbatical year and the Jubilee provisions (Lev. 25:8–34) are God's gracious provisions to minimize the oppression of the poor in Israel.

Because this law of servitude is similar to the sabbatical year regulation, one might think that the sabbatical year freed all slaves. But that is not stated. Rather, the period of servitude is six years for every Hebrew slave, and in the seventh year he goes free. Recalling the nation's experience of servitude in Egypt (v. 15), Israel is to be merciful to its slaves. Slaves will have rights (Ex. 21:1–11, 20), and the redemption provisions here are generous — the freed slave must be given something with which to start fresh (v. 13, 14; cf. Ex. 12:35, 36). The law of servitude described does not contradict the provision for freedom in the Year of Jubilee (Lev. 25:39–43). That provision probably refers to the special case of an impoverished servant whose ancestral property is gone and who therefore has nowhere to go if freed. When the Year of Jubilee comes, his home is to be restored and he will go to it.
See 12:17; 15:19 text note. nor shear. The firstborn ox is not to be worked nor the firstborn sheep shorn, because they are to be given to the Lord while still young.

Most of ch. 16 deals with the three pilgrimage festivals, so called because they require all grown males to celebrate them at the sanctuary. These feasts are mentioned briefly in Ex. 23:14–17, ending with the same charge given in similar language at Deut. 16:16: every man must bring his offering. The feasts are listed again in Ex. 34:18–23, where the Passover is simply included with the closely associated Feast of Unleavened Bread (Ex. 23:15 note). All five major feasts are listed more fully in Lev. 23, and they are listed with their offerings in Num. 28; 29. 16:1 the month of Abib. In Exodus, the Passover (Ex. 12:1–14) and the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Ex. 12:15–20) were instituted in the "first month" (Ex. 12:2, 18), also called the month of Abib, one of the Canaanite month names (Ex. 13:4; 23:15). The Babylonian name of the first month is Nisan, and Babylonian month names appear in the OT of the exilic and postexilic periods (e.g., Esth. 3:7). keep the Passover. See notes on Ex. 12:1–26. The Passover clearly symbolizes substitution, since the lamb is slain in place of the firstborn. Although the blood of animals cannot, in itself, redeem human beings, the Passover lamb points forward to the effectual sacrifice of Christ (Heb. 10:1–14). So Paul is fully justified in saying, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor. 5:7; cf. John 19:31–36).
At the location of the sanctuary. See note 12:5.

The lamb or goat is to be slaughtered at the sanctuary at sundown, roasted in that area for several hours, and then eaten at midnight. Following the celebration, the people will return to their tents in the morning. After their settlement in Canaan, when they assemble at the central sanctuary, the majority will surely live in tents again. In modern times, the Samaritan Passover on Mount Gerizim is performed precisely in this way.

The Passover is always celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month (corresponding to modern March–April). The Israelites use the lunar month, so the Passover is always close to a full moon. Associated with Passover is the presentation of the first ripe sheaf of grain (Lev. 23:4–14). On the day following the seventh Sabbath after that presentation (Lev. 23:15, 16) is the one-day "Feast of Weeks" (v. 10), called "Pentecost" in the NT because of this fifty-day (and seven-week) calculation.

The "Feast of Booths" (v. 13) is so called because for a week the people are to gather at the sanctuary and live in temporary structures. It begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month (modern September–October), at the end of the agricultural season after the grain has been threshed and the grapes harvested. Naturally, the tithe of the harvest is to be brought at this feast, which is also to memorialize Israel's pilgrim experience in leaving Egypt (Lev. 23:43). In addition, at every seventh celebration of this feast, the covenant obligations recorded by Moses are to be read publicly (31:10–13; Neh. 8).
Moses appointed leaders at Sinai (1:13), and this section specifies that such an organization should continue. Moreover, the high ideal of justice is to guide their conduct (19:15–21 note).
This fact is often emphasized (Ex. 23:8; Prov. 17:23).

A reference to the wooden poles, images, or trees that represent the Canaanite goddess Asherah. There is to be no compromise with pagan idolatry (17:2–7). Despite such warnings, these pagan Asherah shrines later become a snare to the Israelites (Judg. 3:7, 8; 2 Kin. 13:6; 17:10).

It is repeatedly commanded that any flaw or defect makes an animal unsuitable for sacrifice (15:21; Lev. 22:19–25; Num. 19:2). Also, Lev. 21:16–23 specifies that any priest with a physical deformity cannot officiate. The symbolism is clear: God is holy (Lev. 21:23), and He demands perfection. To be fully holy is to be fully perfect, both physically and morally. As symbols of the coming perfect Savior and His worthy sacrifice, the sacrificial animals are to be without defect.

The sin of idolatry is in view, the seriousness of which is indicated by the consistently prescribed death penalty (v. 5; ch. 13). In such instances, the judicial goal is not rehabilitation or restitution but to purge Israel of the abomination of idolatry (vv. 4, 7). The covenant originally ratified at Mount Sinai demands exclusive allegiance to God from the Israelites. They are to have no other gods (Ex. 20:3).

Condemnation does not take place on the basis of hearsay. Two or three witnesses must agree (v. 6; 19:15–19; Num. 35:30), and must be sufficiently convinced and sincere to take part in the stoning, knowing that the penalty for false witness to a crime is the same as for the crime itself (19:19). There is no torture for confession or torture of witnesses.

We do not know the precise details of the ancient Israelite judicial system (19:15–21 note). There were graded courts to take care of difficult cases (Ex. 18:21–26), with priests who judged and also other judges, probably tribal elders or leaders drawn from the people. There were no professional judges in ancient Israel. This passage stresses that the judicial office is divinely ordained and that verdicts were to be accepted on pain of death (v. 12).

The reference to "a king" (v. 14) is conditional and need not imply that the text was written when a king ruled Israel, although critics have argued that with its reference to horses, wives, and wealth, the section refers to Solomon and was written long after him by one of his detractors. There was no king in Moses's time, but the future possibility of such a ruler was obvious since expectations of a king are central to the fulfillment of God's redemptive purposes as revealed in Genesis (Gen. 17:6; 27:29; 49:10). That Israel might have a king is never denied, although it is stated most emphatically that God is their king (33:5). In addition, v. 15 warns against choosing a foreign king, a stipulation that cannot be directed against Solomon and his successors, who were native Israelites.

The phrase "this law" may refer to a substantial part of the book of Deuteronomy (see 31:9–13; cf. 27:1–7), or it may signify the law given at Sinai (see 1:5). As a covenant nation, Israel is to be governed according to the covenant obligations.

Not only the priests but the whole tribe of Levi, numbering twenty-three thousand, is to receive no inheritance (Num. 18:20; 26:62; Deut. 10:9). This tribe will have no farms for livelihood but will depend on the tithes and offerings of the people (vv. 3–5). Moses specifically allots them forty-two cities, six of which will be cities of refuge (Num. 35:2–8). In due time these cities are allocated by Joshua (Josh. 21).

In place of a land inheritance and in recognition of their priestly duties, the priests have a right to specific portions of the animals offered for sacrifice. Later, this practice is sometimes abused by corrupt priests (1 Sam. 2:12–17).

Anticipating the instructions regarding true and false prophecy in vv. 19–22, Moses forbids all attempts to discern the future through occult, pagan means. All other forms of sorcery and witchcraft are also prohibited. The detestable character of these practices is underscored and cited as a reason for divine judgment upon the Canaanites (vv. 9, 12). All of these are illegitimate ways in which to receive divine knowledge. God will provide a different way by sending prophets to deliver His words to His people (v. 15).

Moses, the preeminent prophet of the OT period, introduces the topic of Israelite prophecy. God will communicate His word to Israel through a succession of prophets. As mediators of God's words to the people, the other OT prophets will function in ways similar to Moses (v. 16). But none will be the initial mediators of a covenant, and none will equal Moses's intimacy with God or receive divine revelations in the same manner that he does (Num. 12:6–8; Deut. 34:10). This passage, then, finds final fulfillment in the prophet who is equal to, indeed greater than, the prophet Moses — Jesus Christ (Acts 3:22–26; 7:37; cf. John 5:45–47; Heb. 3:2–6). Like Moses, Christ is the mediator of a covenant between God and His people (Luke 22:20; Heb. 8:7–13). Unlike Moses, Christ not only speaks God's words — He is the Word of God (John 1:1–18). See theological note "The Prophets of God."

Two means of discerning false prophets from true prophets are given in Deuteronomy. The first is theological integrity — a true prophet will not teach error or lead the people astray (v. 20; 13:1–5). The second is that his prophetic predictions of the future will come true (v. 22).
These cities of refuge are to be set aside in Canaan. The three cities of refuge for Transjordan have already been named and set aside. See 4:41–43 for the sequence of establishing these cities.

The law of manslaughter is given first in Ex. 21:13, then more fully in Num. 35:6–28. This passage repeats some matters given in Numbers. Other regulations are added, such as the provision for building access roads to the cities of refuge. Also, this passage specifies three extra cities in Canaan if the nation's territory is greatly enlarged. But it is plain in both Numbers and Deuteronomy that a man guilty of premeditated murder must die. The death penalty is grounded not in disrespect for life but in intense respect for the life of the innocent victim made in the image of God (Gen. 9:6).

Though this verse has sometimes been misinterpreted to urge respect for ancient customs and beliefs, the term "landmark" actually refers to stones that serve as boundary markers. This law is essential to prevent encroachment and theft of land (27:17; Prov. 22:28; 23:10, 11).

The general principle is that a conviction is not to be based on the testimony of a single witness (v. 15). When false testimony is detected, the false witness is to receive the same punishment that the person falsely accused and convicted of a crime receives (vv. 19–21). In the jurisprudence of the ancient Near East, much responsibility was given to judges. They did not simply compare an offense to a particular law and pronounce a verdict. Rather, they compared a case with the principles of the law and with typical cases, and then they gave a decision in accordance with justice and equity (1:13; 16:18; 17:8). 19:15 single witness. See 17:6.
See theological note "The Threefold Use of the Law" on p. 273.

The phrase "eye for eye" occurs twice more in the Pentateuch (Ex. 21:24; Lev. 24:20). In each case, the verse is in a legal context, so it is a principle of public justice — the penalty must fit the crime, being no more or no less than is deserved. The only physical penalty mentioned in the law is flogging, and that limited to forty strokes (Deut. 25:3). There is evidence that this principle is not intended to be taken literally in practice (Ex. 21:24 and Lev. 24:20 notes).

Morale in the army, particularly the importance of single-minded reliance upon God, is the subject of vv. 1–9. The exemptions cited illustrate the principle that anyone whose heart is not in the fight should not be enlisted (vv. 5–8). The power of God, rather than numerical superiority, will guarantee Israel's victory (v. 4; cf. 32:30 note; Judg. 7:1–8). One result of such an attitude will be high morale, which will itself contribute to victory.

Ancient walled cities could withstand attack for some time, and attackers wanted to avoid the trouble of a lengthy siege. An offer of peace in exchange for vassal tribute (v. 11), coupled with the threat of death for the defending soldiers, could be attractive to both sides. These warfare provisions (comparatively humane for that period) are applied to enemies outside the Promised Land (v. 15).

The Hebrew word for this practice is herem, which means "to put under the ban" (i.e., to devote everything to the Lord), as occurred at Jericho during the conquest (Josh. 6:17–19). See notes Lev. 27:28; Deut. 7:25.
The reference is clearly to fruit trees (v. 20). One of Israel's covenant blessings is to enjoy the fruit of the land God had given them (7:12, 13).

In the case of an unsolved murder, the elders from the nearest town are to take an oath of innocence and ignorance. The symbolism of the heifer, killed while the oath is taken, is clear: it dies as a symbol of the murderer who ought to die. The land, which has been defiled by the shedding of innocent blood, is to be purged of serious guilt. The vicarious death of the heifer is based on the same principle that underlies the death of Christ as a satisfaction for the sins, known and unknown, of His people.

The law preserves the sanctity of marriage. An Israelite man might take a captive woman, but he must wait a month. She is to be given a chance to adjust and to grieve for her lost family. She is a wife, not property, and if the husband later divorces her, he cannot sell her as a slave.

It may be that just as divorce was allowed "because of your hardness of heart" (Matt. 19:8), so polygamy was permitted, but its harsher evils were mitigated. Alternatively, the situation described here could involve a situation in which a man remarries after the death of his first wife. The unloved wife has her rights, and the firstborn son of an unloved wife cannot be dispossessed.

In view here is not the petty disobedience of children but a long-term pattern of rebellion and deep sin. Although "stubborn and rebellious" is not precisely defined, in v. 20 the son is called "a glutton and a drunkard" (cf. Prov. 23:21). In such cases, even the parents are not to shield their offspring (cf. Zech. 13:2, 3).

Hanging as a method of execution is not mentioned in the OT. The practice in view here is the exposure of the corpse of a criminal or an enemy (1 Sam. 31:10–13). Such gruesome exposure, symbolizing the divine curse (v. 23), is not to be continued more than a day. This verse motivated the Pharisees' request to have the body of Jesus taken off the cross before nightfall (John 19:31). The point of Gal. 3:13 is that Christ, though innocent, died a criminal's death, taking the curse that we deserved (cf. Acts 5:30).

The law concerning lost property requires that an effort be made to find the owner of strayed or lost property and return the property to him (cf. Ex. 23:4). If the owner cannot be found, the property is to be kept for him until he is found.

Again, accidental loss of private property is to be prevented if possible (cf. Ex. 23:5). Jesus quotes this verse to justify healing a man on the Sabbath. The Pharisees allowed the law of helping a fallen animal to supersede their rules for Sabbath keeping but had no pity on a man in serious need (Luke 14:5).

Women are not to adopt the accoutrements of the male (e.g., carrying weapons), and men are not to dress as women. The symbols of gender difference are to be respected, and while such symbols vary over time and from culture to culture, the principle of gender distinction remains (Gen. 1:27; cf. 1 Tim. 2:13). Violations of the creation order, such as homosexuality and bestiality (Lev. 18:22, 23; 20:13; 1 Cor. 6:9; 1 Tim. 1:10), are an "abomination."

This is a law against criminal negligence. Roofs in ancient Israel were flat and often reached by an outside stairway. The roof was used for work (Josh. 2:6) or leisure. To prevent accidental injury or death from falling, a parapet or fence is specified.

Similar prohibitions of mixtures are found in Lev. 19:19. Reasons for these regulations are no longer clear. Of the various suggestions that have been made, the most likely are that these verses teach the importance of creation-order distinctions or that they remind Israel of her call to purity and separation from the surrounding nations (v. 11 note).

The reason for this may be the impracticality both of making a donkey pull an ox's load and of making an ox go at the faster donkey's pace. Or, perhaps more likely, the contrast between clean animals (the ox) and unclean (the donkey, 14:1–8) may be intended to remind Israel of her call to purity. Paul cites this verse in 2 Cor. 6:14 to forbid the fellowship of believers and unbelievers in matters of faith and worship.

Some suggest that this prohibition is due to the fact that such material might shrink unevenly and therefore not wash well. Others argue that through eating pure food (14:3–21) and not mixing their seeds (Deut. 22:9), their draft animals (22:10), or the materials of their garments, Israel will be reminded that they are to be a pure people (7:2–5 and notes).
These tassels are to remind Israel of the Lord's commandments and the nation's responsibility to be holy before God (Num. 15:38–40).

These verses provide for judging a husband's complaint that his wife was not a virgin when they married. Such an accusation, when made by a man who wished to be rid of a wife who displeased him, can be disproved by the wife's parents presenting visible "evidence of \... virginity," presumably the stained bedclothes of the wedding night (v. 15).

The implications of the seventh commandment (5:18; Ex. 20:14) are developed with respect to instances of adultery and rape. Particular care is given to guarding the sanctity of the marriage covenant: adultery with a married or betrothed woman is punishable by the death of both consenting parties (vv. 22–24), while lesser penalties are prescribed for a sexual relationship with an unmarried woman (vv. 28, 29). Women depended on their marriage relationship for protection and status in ancient Near Eastern society, and the law provides important protections for women. The penalty for forcible rape of a married woman is the death of the offending man (vv. 25–27). The man who violates the honor of a virgin is compelled to marry her and cannot later divorce her (v. 29).
Sexual relations with a stepmother are probably in view (Lev. 18:7, 8; 20:11).

**LORD** . This phrase possibly refers to the worshiping community gathered before the presence of God rather than to Israel's population as a whole (Neh. 13:1–3). It may, however, have a much narrower connotation, since apart from the present context it appears only in Mic. 2:5. The similar expression "assembly of God" comes in Neh. 13:1 at the start of a passage that focuses on the inappropriate provision of accommodation within the temple courts for Tobiah the Ammonite. The Hebrew word for "assembly" (qahal) is usually rendered ekklesia in the Septuagint. This is also the term used in the Greek NT for "church."

As the word "forever" in this verse indicates, "tenth generation" is probably an idiom denoting permanent exclusion for all who reject the God of Israel. This special exclusion of Ammon­ites and Moabites is due not to their incestuous origin (Gen. 19:30–38) but to their stubborn opposition to Israel (v. 4; Neh. 13:2). The OT also looks forward to a new covenant in which the exclusions of this passage are transcended (Is. 56:3–8), though even under the old covenant, all those who trusted in the God of Israel could join the community of Israel. Ruth, the Moabitess who became the ancestor of David and of the Messiah, illustrates this (Ruth 1:4; 4:17; Matt. 1:5).
Note the clear reference to details in Num. 22–24.

Because the camp of Israelite soldiers is a place of God's presence as divine warrior (v. 14; 20:4), the camp is to be kept pure of unclean things. In view here are occurrences that are both unseemly and ceremonially unclean: instances of urination or perhaps nocturnal emission (v. 10; cf. Lev. 15:16), and defecation in the camp (v. 13). A sense of God's presence in the camp is meant to impact everything done by the Israelites.
Slavery in Israel was carefully regulated and its abuses limited (15:12 note). In view here is an escaped slave from another country who takes refuge in Israel.
Ritual prostitution, involving both male and female prostitutes, was characteristic of the Canaanite fertility religions.

God desires to bless an obedient Israel so that borrowing will be unnecessary (15:4 note), and those whom the Lord has blessed materi­ally are to assist fellow Israelites in distress by not charging interest. This regulation does not apply to those outside the covenant (the "foreigner," v. 20). The agricultural economy of ancient Israel was different from the commercial economy of today, and borrowing was usually due to poverty.
**LORD** . Such a vow is given voluntarily (v. 22). It is a serious matter and, if a valid vow, must be kept. The regulations for vows are given fully in Lev. 27 and Num. 30.

See "Marriage" at Mal. 2:16 and "Divorce" at Mark 10:2. The situation described (vv. 1–3) is followed by the legal prescription (v. 4). Divorce is permitted in the Mosaic law, as Jesus later says, because of "hardness of heart" (Matt. 19:8). The restriction on remarriage of a divorced couple after an intervening marriage (v. 4) discourages casual divorces. 24:1 some indecency. The Hebrew of this phrase is the same as "anything indecent" in 23:14, and is rather general. Adultery is apparently not in view, for adultery is punishable by death (22:22). The fact of divorce for a variety of reasons is recognized but not necessarily condoned (vv. 1–3 are descriptive, not prescriptive).

A one-year exemption for the newly married not only strengthens the marriage relationship and benefits the home but also prevents a man from being criticized for not joining the army just after being married.

Because loans in ancient Israel were typically given to relieve the economic hardship of the borrower (23:19 note), the material given in pledge was likely not collateral property of equal value to the amount of the loan but a personal possession given as a token of the promise to pay. In keeping with the purpose of the loan, the lender may not to cause further hardship to the borrower by confiscating essential items such as household millstones or outer garments (vv. 10–13, 17). Other references to OT borrowing practices include Ex. 22:26, 27; Job 22:6; 24:3, 9; Amos 2:8.

The chief purpose of kidnapping in the ancient world was the enslavement of others for profit. To sell fellow Israelites into slavery in other countries is forbidden on pain of death, probably because such slaves are cut off from the life of the covenant community (itself a form of "death"; cf. Ex. 12:19 and Lev. 7:20 notes). Indentured slavery is allowed within Israel but is tempered in several important ways (15:12 note). Paul condemns slave traders ("enslavers") together with other violators of the Ten Commandments (1 Tim. 1:10).
See note on Lev. 13; 14.
God's concern for the poor and oppressed is emphasized in this passage (Ps. 9:18 note).
This interesting and just law is quoted in 2 Kin. 14:6 and 2 Chr. 25:4, where it is cited as from the "Book of the Law of Moses" or the "Law in the Book of Moses."
The compassionate intention of this law is realized in Ruth 2:2–23 (cf. Lev. 19:9, 10; 23:22).
This is the back­ground of the Jewish practice of giving "forty lashes less one" (2 Cor. 11:24). The intent is to guard against any possible miscount by erring on the side of mercy.

According to Paul, this provision for oxen points to the more general principle that those who labor, particularly Christian ministers, deserve fair remuneration for their work (1 Cor. 9:9–12; 1 Tim. 5:18).

The law of levirate marriage (Lat. levir, meaning "husband's brother") is given only here. The limitation to brothers who "dwell together" may indicate that it applies only to an unmarried brother, but it is doubtful that this limitation held in practice. The obvious purpose of the arrangement is to maintain the property rights of the deceased's family line. The levirate custom dates to patriarchal times and is mentioned in Gen. 38:8–11; Ruth 3:1–4:12; Matt. 22:23–28; Mark 12:18–23; and Luke 20:27–33.
God's displeasure at dishonest business dealing is stressed (Lev. 19:35, 36; Prov. 11:1; 16:21; 20:10, 23; and Mic. 6:11).
On the historic conflict between Israel and Amalek, see Ex. 17:16 and note.

Many scholars suggest that vv. 1–11 refer to a special firstfruits offering that Israel was to bring when they took possession of the land (v. 4), although some relate the ceremony described in these verses to the perpetual firstfruits offering (Lev. 23:9–14). Either way, it is probable that the words of the ceremony reciting God's mighty acts on Israel's behalf (vv. 3–10) continued to be used in Israelite worship. place \... God will choose. See note on 12:5.

This verse may refer either to the advanced age of Jacob when he went down to Egypt (Gen. 47:9; cf. 46:30) or to Jacob's changing circumstances and travels to Aram, back to Canaan, throughout Canaan, and finally to Egypt (Gen. 28:2–5; 29:1; 31:20, 21; 33:18; 35:1, 16, 21; 46:1–28).
Regarding the tithe and third-year tithe, see notes on 14:22 and 14:28.
As holy things (belonging to God), the tithes are not to be put to any unclean or idolatrous use (v. 14). The phrase "offered \... to the dead" (v. 14) may refer to idolatrous practices (14:1 note).
This phrase is adapted by Solomon in his great prayer at the dedication of the temple (1 Kin. 8:30).

These verses conclude the covenant stipulations section that began at 12:1. Here the people accept the terms of God's covenant by their pledge of obedience to the covenant stipulations (v. 17; cf. Ex. 24:7), and the two parties of the covenant (God and the people) "declare" loyalty to the other (vv. 17, 18). 26:16 statutes and rules. See 12:1 note.

Moses continues his book of farewells with a third address devoted especially to the sanctions by which the covenant requirements will be enforced. After summoning the people to covenant oath in light of their rebelliousness and prophesying covenant renewal in the future, Moses calls for the people to "choose life" according to the promise given to their fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. 27:1 Moses \... commanded. Moses and the elders specify a ceremony of dedication to be held after the Israelites enter the land. The teaching of Moses will be published for everyone to see; the ceremony will be impressive; the people will add their "amen," and a liturgy of promised blessings and curses will follow.

Moses provides for the publication of his speech at the covenant renewal ceremony on Mount Ebal (vv. 3, 8). Large stones are to be whitewashed and the words of Moses written on them. This technique of writing upon a whitewashed surface was typically Egyptian (the Canaanite and Mesopotamian practice was to inscribe words into stone surfaces). Because Moses was intimately familiar with Egypt and its practices, these verses provide another indication that the text of Deuteronomy dates to the Mosaic era.

The stones are to be uncut (cf. Ex. 20:25). This may indicate that the altar is not to become a permanent feature. Because iron is later used in the building of Solomon's temple (1 Chr. 22:3, 14), we need not conclude that it is a taboo metal forbidden for religious worship. See note on 8:9.

There is no apparent reason for the precise tribal assignments. Here Levi is included among the regular tribes (even among the six that pronounce the blessings), although some of the Levites are to recite the curses that the people will answer. The tribe of Joseph unites Manasseh and Ephraim, so the enumeration follows the names of the twelve sons of Jacob rather than the later tribal divisions.

This list of offenses subject to curse is not exhaustive. These offenses may be chosen as representative of the sorts of sins that might escape detection and so remain secret (cf. vv. 15, 24). Even secret sins will affect Israel's covenant relationship with God (cf. Josh. 7:10–26). 27:15 the man who makes a carved \... image. The first curse concerns idolatry (5:7–9). Amen. The Hebrew word means "so be it."
The second curse concerns the fifth commandment (5:16).
See note on 19:14.
Leviticus 19:14 commands care for the disabled.
God upholds the cause of the helpless (10:18).
See note on 22:30.
The penalty for this perversion is death (Ex. 22:19; Lev. 18:23; 20:15).
This curse concerns both a full sister and a half-sister (having the same father but a different mother). See Lev. 18:11; 20:17.
The penalty is death (Lev. 18:17; 20:14).
Both the secret attacker and the hired assassin fall under the divine curse, even though both might be expected to avoid detection (vv. 15–26 note).

The final curse covers all the rest of God's commandments. Paul quotes this verse to underscore the stringency of the law's demands and the impossibility of meriting salvation by works (Gal. 3:10). Measured by God's standards, all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). But this does not remove the obligation of the believer to obey the moral demands of God by the enabling of the Holy Spirit. Yet, such obedience does not merit justification; rather, it is the evidence and fruit of justifying faith.

After recording the liturgy for the covenant ritual at Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim (ch. 27), Moses calls on the congregation at Moab to obey the commands of God, setting forth God's promised blessings for obedience and His curses for disobedience. The blessings are briefer and come first. The curses are, in some cases, the exact reverse of the blessings, and they continue with awesome emphasis before climaxing in a note of doom (v. 68). The relative lengths of the two lists possibly imply that in the future the Israelites, due to their disobedience, will be more likely to experience God's curses rather than His blessings. Based on Deut. 31:16–17 and 32:20–21, God indeed declares that the people will fail in their obedience to His commands (cf. Hos 1–3).
Their children, crops, and herds will be blessed. For an agricultural people, these are the crucial elements of physical life.
Household endeavors will be blessed.
This idiom referring to normal, everyday activities underscores the comprehensiveness of divine blessing (cf. 31:2). God will bless an obedient people in every way.
The blessings detailed above will be realized in the Land of Promise — itself a major part of the blessing.

This idiom expresses the conviction that the rainfall, so crucial to Israel's agricultural prosperity, is a gift of God (11:11–17; Ps. 104:13). Here is an implicit warning against the Canaanite fertility religions, which ascribed the rainfall to the pagan god Baal.
The curses here negatively mirror the blessings of vv. 3–6.
These metaphors of rainless sky and barren land are frightful to an agricultural people so dependent on rain and soil (cf. Lev. 26:19).
The expression is the reverse of the blessing in v. 7, with the added horror that their corpses will be exposed and not enjoy a proper burial (v. 26).

The various diseases mentioned here cannot be precisely identified. They may be included in the "diseases of Egypt" (v. 60), from which God has promised to deliver them (7:15; Ex. 15:26) if they will obey His laws. The ancient Egyptians suffered from a variety of tropical diseases and parasites (cf. 14:3–21 note).
A description of great torment also used to describe Job's boils (Job 2:7).

The covenantal curse of captivity and exile mentioned here becomes an important element of the prophetic covenant lawsuits against disobedient Israel later in the OT (e.g., Is. 5:13; Jer. 13:19; 29:17–19).
This curse, like several in this section, is the reverse of an earlier blessing (vv. 12, 13; 23:19 note).
This expression for extreme distance is based on how the eye perceives the earth to end where horizon and sky meet; it is equivalent to "far off from you" (cf. 13:7).

Cannibalism was a dreadful accompaniment of ancient sieges, when a city's food supply was cut off for lengthy periods. This curse finds frightful fulfillment during the sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem (2 Kin. 6:28, 29; Jer. 19:9; Lam. 2:20; 4:10).

The written record documenting the terms of a covenant had legal status and was a crucial part of the ancient Near Eastern treaty (Introduction: Date and Occasion). Much of Deuteronomy, probably 5:1–29:19 and perhaps also 28:1–68, preserves the record of God's covenant with His people (v. 58; 31:24–26). It is the written record of the terms of the covenant and was legally binding on Israel.

Some argue that these threats of exile indicate that portions of Deuteronomy were written during or after the Babylonian exile (sixth century B.C.). This argument is rooted in the view that supernatural predictive prophecy is impossible. But, in fact, this covenant curse is couched in more general terms than those that apply only to the Babylonian exile. It threatens a widespread dispersion "from one end of the earth to the other." It finds fulfillment in the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles, and perhaps also in the dispersion of the Jews after the fall of Jerusalem in A.D. 70.

This theme of abandonment echoes v. 29. The aggregation of curses here is overwhelming. This chapter should be compared with the similar but shorter Lev. 26, which ends with the possibility of confession, repentance, and restoration. Here, the theme of possible restoration is left for ch. 30.

Scholars debate whether v. 1 concludes what precedes or introduces what follows. The latter, as reflected in the ESV text division, is more likely. This "covenant \... in the land of Moab" is a renewal of the Sinai covenant ("the covenant \... at Horeb"). As usual, Moses recites the history of God's mighty acts on Israel's behalf in the exodus from Egypt and in the wilderness (cf. Moses's speech in 1:6–4:38). There follows a warning against departing from the Lord, a promise of restoration upon repentance, and a solemn charge to obey. Horeb. See note on 1:6.
The deliverance from Egypt, which occupies a third of the book of Exodus, is mentioned many times in Deuteronomy (e.g., 1:30; 4:20, 34; 5:6; 11:2–7).
**LORD** has not given \... eyes to see. Paul combines this verse with Is. 29:10 and applies both verses to the Jews of his day (Rom. 11:8).

The special preservation of clothes is mentioned in 8:4. The additional fact given here is that they have drunk no wine or other fermented drink, since there are no grapes in the desert. They have also had no bread, but God has supplied them with manna.

In terming this a renewal of the Sinai covenant, we should remember that the covenant is the same, but the people are not. All those over twenty years of age at Sinai have perished in the wilderness. Many of the people under twenty years of age at that point are now between the ages of forty and sixty, and they saw the great events at Sinai. Now they, too, are to affirm their personal commitment to God by renewing the covenant.

The Hebrew of this phrase (apparently an ancient proverb) is difficult to translate. The entire phrase as translated here means that the sinner will not escape judgment by hiding undetected in the company of the righteous (cf. v. 21). Another possibility is to render the phrase "so that the well-watered land is destroyed along with dry land" or "so that the drunkard is destroyed along with the thirsty," indicating that the sin of one brings disaster on many (cf. vv. 22–25). Another possible translation is "to add drunkenness to thirst," meaning that the sinful man compounds his guilt by sinking further into sin.
See note on 28:61 (cf. Josh. 1:7, 8).

The four cities of the plain that were destroyed in Abraham's day are named. In Gen. 14 five cities of the plain are mentioned but not their destruction. In Gen. 19 Sodom and Gomorrah are mentioned, and the whole area is said to be destroyed, but Zoar is spared. Deuteronomy puts the two records together and lists the four destroyed cities. The judgment of Sodom is a prophetic model of divine wrath. Like Moses, Isaiah compares the judgment of Israel to that of Sodom (Is. 1:10). Jesus also compares the judgment at His second coming to that of Sodom (Luke 17:28–35), as does Peter (2 Pet. 2:6).

The meaning of the latter part of this verse is apparent: God's revealed instruction is of vital importance, and the Israelites and their children must follow this teaching. The reference to "secret things" may suggest that Moses anticipates the uncertain future of the nation, remembering their waywardness and how they turned to the golden calf at Horeb (Ex. 32). In this uncertainty, Moses trusts the hidden future to his trustworthy God.

Anticipating the real possibility of judgment and exile for Israel, Moses looks beyond the time of judgment to Israel's future repentance, restoration, and divine blessing. Significantly, this future blessing will include deliverance from slavery to sin. Moses's reference to the circumcision of the "heart" (v. 6; cf. 10:16) is foundational for the later prophetic expectation (Jer. 31:31–34; Ezek. 36:25–27), and it finds fulfillment in the NT (Rom. 2:29).
Moses refers again to the great commandment of 6:5, holding out the hope of repentance even when there has been apostasy and judgment.
The measure of God's compassion in restoration will exceed the measure of His wrath in judgment and exile.

**LORD** \... will circumcise your heart. See notes on vv. 1–10 and 10:16. The promised restoration and renewal will result from a sovereign work of God in the hearts of His elect. By circumcising (transforming) their hearts, He will replace their total inability and stubbornness (5:29; 10:16; 29:4) with the humility and repentance they need (cf. vv. 1, 2), purifying for Himself a people who will love and obey Him. See "Legalism" at Matt. 23:4.

The future restoration will bring a fulfillment of the promise made to Abraham and his seed: "Him who dishonors you I will curse" (Gen. 12:3). Moses links the restoration pictured in vv. 3–10 to a future judgment by God against the enemies of His people.

The blessings of the renewed covenant will be inseparable from, but not based on, the obedience of the restored remnant of the people to their Lord's commandments (cf., e.g., Matt. 7:21). The obedience of Christ, which is the victory over sin in which the remnant by faith will share, is the only meritorious basis of such blessings (1 Cor. 1:30–31; 2 Cor. 5:21; Eph. 2:8–10).

Recalling his words in 6:6, Moses maintains that the covenant obligations God revealed through him and the righteousness required are readily accessible to and attainable by Israel (v. 11) — if they will seek such things properly, namely, by trusting only in the Lord and His mercy. He anticipates, however, that those with uncircumcised hearts and ears will raise questions denying these truths and will seek to establish a righteousness of their own (vv. 12, 13). Moses rebukes such stubbornness, insisting that the word of righteousness is found "in your mouth and in your heart" (v. 14) — in the mouth and heart that speak not in the unbelief and rebellion of their own imperfect righteousness but in the faith and humility of the Lord's perfect righteousness alone. This righteousness the Lord has demonstrated to Israel in the works of salvation and judgment by which He confirmed His oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (cf. 8:17, 18; 9:4–6; 30:1–7; esp. 1:29–33; 9:23). The commandment that Moses proclaims here is a word calling for trust in God and His promises alone, and the righteousness it reveals is a righteousness attained only by faith (cf. v. 10 note; Gen. 15:6 note). Paul later alludes to these verses in Rom. 10:6–8, updating Moses's admonition in view of the revelation of God's righteousness in the person and work of Christ. Paul preaches the word that calls for faith where Moses had to leave off, insisting that Israel (and the Gentiles) must now confess with their mouths that Jesus is Lord (Rom. 10:12, 13; cf. Deut. 6:4), and believe with their hearts that God raised Him from the dead (Rom. 10:9). God's work in Jesus Christ yet again reveals His righteousness (Rom. 3:21–26) and confirms His oath to the fathers (cf. Rom. 4:18–25; Gal. 3). See "Special Revelation and the Bible" at Ex. 32:16.

Moses calls for a decision. There are two ways: life or death, God's blessing or sure judgment. Joshua later presents the same alternatives (Josh. 24:15), and Jesus, who is greater than Moses or Joshua, calls His disciples to take the narrow path that leads to life (Matt. 7:13, 14).

The mention of witnesses recalls the form of ancient Near Eastern treaty documents, which have a list of witnesses at the end, often the names of pagan gods. In the biblical covenant, God's creation is called to witness against His people because He alone is the Lord and there are no gods beside Him.

In this final section of his work, Moses provides for a smooth transition in covenant administration after his death. Also included are the Song of Moses and Moses's blessing of the twelve tribes. The book concludes with an obituary for Moses. 31:1 Moses continued to speak. This brief exhortation (vv. 1–8) can hardly be called another address but is part of Moses's arrangement of his final affairs and the transfer of authority to his successor Joshua (Introduction: Outline).

Acts 7:30 tells us that Moses spent forty years in Midian tending sheep. This time was not wasted, as he learned the geography and climate of the Sinai Peninsula in preparation for leading the Israelites in that area for another forty years. The humiliation of being reduced from a prince in Egypt to a hired tender of sheep also accomplished the divine disciplinary purpose of preparing Moses for his greater role as shepherd of God's people. This leaves forty years for Moses's youth and training in Egypt. Thus, God ensured that Moses was well prepared for his great task. no longer able to go out and come in. Moses anticipates that he will soon die and no longer participate in the regular affairs of the community. Moses's many-faceted role as Israel's leader is coming to an end.

See notes on 1:37 and 3:23-28. Though the aged Moses is still active (34:7), the conquest of Canaan will require some years, and it is time for the younger man to take charge. Most importantly, the Lord Himself will lead Israel under Joshua as He has done with Moses (Ex. 33:14, 15).
These and the following words resemble the encouragement God gives Joshua after Moses died (Josh. 1:9).
The transfer of leadership is often a delicate matter. Moses wisely, and at God's command, elevates Joshua in the presence of the people.

The conclusion of Moses's covenant ministry is marked by the recording in writing of Moses's speech (vv. 24–26; 28:61 note). Repeatedly in Exodus and in Deuteronomy, Moses is said to have written down the regulations and instructions given by the Lord. In Leviticus most of the chapters begin with the words, "The Lord spoke to Moses." God used Moses preeminently to speak and write His word for Israel.

Moses provides for regular instruction of the people and their children in the covenant stipulations by the priests at a point in the year when the people have ample time to learn. The Feast of Booths comes in the fall and lasts a week (16:13–17 note). During the sabbatical year the land is to lie fallow, and the people will not be burdened with agricultural duties (15:1 note). This practice of reading the covenant stipulations at regular intervals was characteristic of the suzerainty treaties among nations of Moses's time, which typically provided for the regular publication of the covenantal terms of agreement (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

Joshua's legitimacy and authority as Moses's successor are underscored by his commission at the tent of meeting (that is, the tabernacle), accompanied by God's appearance in the pillar of cloud (cf. Num. 12:4–12).

Knowing the people's inclination to be unfaithful (v. 21), and realizing the power of song in worship and in memory, the Lord commands Moses to write a song that will serve as a testimony in future days. Other examples of poetry associated with Moses include Ex. 15:1–18; 32:18; Num. 10:35, 36; and Ps. 90.
Moses called heaven and earth as witnesses at the end of the covenant renewal in 30:19.
**LORD** . This song is to witness in future days to the Lord, His goodness, and His saving work for Israel (31:19).

This chapter provides the first instances in Scripture of "Rock" as a name for God (vv. 15, 18, 30; there is a similar image in Gen. 49:24 using a different Hebrew word). Suggesting God's steadfast faithfulness and permanence, the term is common in the Psalms and other poetic passages (Ps. 95:1; Is. 44:8).
Note the sharp contrast between the steadfast, righteous God (v. 4) and the corrupt nation (v. 5).

The meaning here is that God by decree gave the Promised Land to Israel. It was an ancient grant to the patriarchs (v. 7). according to \... the sons of God. Moses is recalling the ancient days (Gen. 10, the table of nations and the dividing of peoples) in order to make the point that Israel alone is selected in the midst of the dispersion of tribes and nations for the Lord's special vocation. God is sovereign over all of history, but history itself is ordered in the interests of God's plan of redemption for His chosen people Israel (Gen. 12:3).
A reference to the pupil of the eye. Just as the pupil of the eye is closely guarded against harm, so God protects Israel. God's people are thus at the very core and heart of God's vision.
The image is of an eagle teaching its young to fly. The poetic figures of the Song of Moses are powerful expressions of God's dealings with His people. See also Gen. 1:2 and note.
See note at 3:1.

From the Hebrew term for "upright" (yashar). Often used to represent Israel as the upright people of a holy and righteous God (33:5, 26; Is. 44:2), here the term is used ironically. grew fat, and kicked. Israel is described with the telling figure of a well-fed ox.
See theological note "Demons."

Just as Israel provoked God by worshiping that which was "no god," so God will provoke them by means of "those who are no people" (people outside the sphere of the Mosaic covenant). This prophecy is partly fulfilled in the OT as Israel is defeated by God's instruments of judgment, the Assyrians and Babylonians (Is. 10:5; Jer. 21:4–10). In the NT, Paul finds further fulfillment of this verse in the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles (Rom. 10:19; 11:11).

For the figure of God's anger as a consuming fire, see Ps. 21:9; Jer. 15:14; 17:4. The poetic figure here represents God's wrath as an all-devouring fire that burns to the deepest grave, consumes the surface of the earth, and reaches to the roots of the mountains. "Sheol" is often simply a term for the grave, but it may also refer to the location where the wicked go after death to await final judgment.

Though Israel deserves utter destruction because of her disobedience (v. 26), the Lord preserves a remnant of the people, lest the Gentiles take credit for their victory over Israel and fail to see God's hand in history. Assyria and Babylon are later judged for their arrogant misunderstanding (Is. 10:12–19; 47:6–8).

Numbers are of no consequence when the Lord intervenes. Israel with God's help will put to flight vast numbers of adversaries (Lev. 26:8), while a numerous but disobedient Israel will be defeated by a few, even fleeing when no one pursues (Lev. 26:17).
False gods bring evil deeds and poisonous fruit. Sodom symbolizes awful destruction (29:23 note).
The NT quotes this verse twice, using a slightly different wording (Rom. 12:19; Heb. 10:30).
Israel must see that they have no help apart from the one true God.

The Hebrew emphasizes by repetition. This whole stanza is a towering expression of the uniqueness of God in His being, power, providence, and justice. Because God is both infinitely just and all-powerful, we can be sure that evil will at last be destroyed (Rev. 19:1, 2).

The Septuagint and one of the Dead Sea Scrolls contain a longer version of this phrase (text note). This longer version is possibly quoted in Heb. 1:6. he avenges the blood of his children. This triumphal Song of Moses is echoed at the consummation of human history (Rev. 19:2).

Moses emphasizes again that obedience to God's commands, from the heart, is a matter of life — eternal life — and death (30:19, 20). Because sinners cannot render the perfect obedience that the Lord commands, the obedience that secures eternal life is ultimately the obedience of another — Jesus Christ, the perfect Lamb of God prefigured in the OT sacrifices (Rom. 3:21–26; 5:12–21; Heb. 9:1–10:18).

Usually identified as the modern Jebel Neba, a mountain twelve miles (19 km) east of the Jordan River's point of entry into the Dead Sea. Rising over four thousand feet (1,219 m) above the Dead Sea, Mount Nebo will provide Moses a vantage point from which to view the Promised Land.

In Gen. 49, Leah's children are listed first, followed by those of the handmaidens and Rachel. Here the order is different.
