Reuben, the firstborn, is mentioned first (v. 6), followed by the royal tribe of Judah (v. 7; cf. Gen. 49:10) and the priestly tribe of Levi (vv. 8–11). The tribes descending from Rachel's sons are next (vv. 12–17), followed by two remaining sons of Leah, Zebulun and Issachar (vv. 18, 19). Finally, the servants' children are listed (vv. 20–24). The tribe of Simeon is omitted, perhaps to retain the number twelve, although Jacob's blessing predicted that Simeon would be scattered throughout Israel (Gen. 49:7). 33:1 the man of God. This expression is used customarily for prophets (1 Sam. 9:6; 1 Kin. 13:1; 17:18; 2 Kin. 4:7) but is applied to Moses only here and in the title of Ps. 90.

**LORD** came from Sinai. The defining event of Moses's ministry, the revelation at Sinai, is recalled in terms describing the theophany on the mountain (Ex. 19:18; cf. Hab. 3:3). holy ones. This is likely a reference to the angels of the heavenly host surrounding God's throne (cf. 1 Kin. 22:19; Dan. 7:9, 10). The NT also mentions the role of angels in giving the Mosaic law (Acts 7:53; Gal. 3:19; Heb. 2:2 and note).
A reference to the Lord as king over His people (cf. 1 Sam. 12:12; Ps. 10:16). Moses is never called a king. On "Jeshurun," see note 32:15.
This reading could reflect the curse on Reuben in Gen. 49:3, 4.

This blessing hints at the warrior role of the Davidic kings, descendants of Judah, in leading Israel into battle. But the blessing on Judah is extremely brief in view of the promise of rulership to Judah in Gen. 49:8–12 and in view of Judah's large part in later history. Because a later writer might have wanted to give Judah more prominence, the brevity of this blessing points to a date of composition during Moses's lifetime.

The blessing on Levi reflects the tribe's fidelity at the time of the golden calf, when the Levites rallied to Moses's side and acted in judgment against their sinful brethren (Ex. 32:27–29). Thummim \... Urim. See note on Ex. 28:30.

Moses alludes to Ex. 3:4. prince among his brothers. The Hebrew word translated "prince among" is sometimes used for one who is set apart by the Nazirite vow (cf. Num. 6:1–21 note). See Gen. 49:26. This may be the basis for Jesus being called a Nazarene in Matt. 2:23.

During this period, Ephraim is smaller than Manasseh (Num. 26:34, 37), but Ephraim will become more numerous and important (cf. Gen. 48:17–20). Because of the tribe's importance, the name "Ephraim" is later applied to the ten tribes making up the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Chr. 25:7; Hos. 5:3, 11–14).

See note on 3:1. This blessing may refer to the northern settlement of Dan, located near Bashan (Judg. 18:27–29). More likely, a comparison of Dan to the strength and ferocity of the lions inhabiting the forests of Bashan may be in view.
Olive oil, valuable for food and also as fuel for lamps, is here symbolic of the tribe's material prosperity (Gen. 49:20; cf. Job 29:6).

This final stanza has blessed the hearts of God's people through the ages. He is the majestic God (v. 26), the eternal God (v. 27), the protecting and providing God (v. 28). The great blessing of Israel was that He was their God. The great blessing of the new covenant church is that this same God is our God. Such a splendid hymn of praise is perhaps only matched by passages in the NT such as "the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb" in Rev. 15:3, 4. 33:26 Jeshurun. See 32:15 and note.

This chapter is a supplement. Many suggest that it was added by the author of the book of Joshua in order to connect his work with the books of Moses, though it also could have been the addition of a later editor (Introduction: Author). 34:1 Gilead as far as Dan. The descriptions here and in v. 2 name the areas in terms of the tribal areas as designated in the book of Joshua (Josh. 13–19).
See note on 31:2.

The same period of mourning as for Aaron (Num. 20:29; cf. Gen. 50:3, 10; 2 Sam. 1:12). Ritual displays of mourning in the OT include weeping, fasting, tearing of clothing, wearing sackcloth, and throwing dust on the head (Gen. 37:34, 35; Ps. 35:13; Lam. 2:10). Certain mourning practices were forbidden to Israel (14:1 note).
Moses previously put his hand on Joshua to symbolize the transfer of divinely ordained leadership (Num. 27:18). God empowers those whom He chooses and ordains for service.

See theological note "The Prophets of God" on p. 279. 34:10 since. Because no length of time is specified, these words need not imply that many generations had passed since Moses's death. Joshua took Moses's place, but he realized that Moses's miracles and access to God had been unique (Num. 12:6–8).

The miraculous displays of God's power in Egypt at the time of the exodus. Jesus arose as a prophet like Moses yet superior to him. He did miracles, signs, and wonders before the kings and rulers of the people and in the sight of all Israel (Matt. 4:23–25; John 20:30–31; Acts 2:22; 3:22–26).

Joshua.note: The opening words indicate both the historical starting point of the book and the theological crisis with which it deals. Moses's death, recorded at the end of Deuteronomy, concludes the judgment of God on the generation that came out of Egypt (5:4–6; Deut. 1:35; 32:51). What is to be said now that Moses has died and the people of Israel have fallen under God's judgment? Ch. 1 introduces the answer to this question, namely, that even "after the death of Moses" the Lord is faithful to His promises. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes. This reality and its consequences are spelled out by God to Joshua (vv. 1–9), and then by Joshua to the people in general (vv. 10, 11) and the two-and-a-half tribes in particular (vv. 12–15). Finally, the people's response is recorded (vv. 16–18). 1:1 the servant of the **LORD** . This title of honor, first given to Moses in Deut. 34:5, recalls the special role of Moses in God's purposes (vv. 1, 2, 7, 13, 15; cf. Is. 42:1). It is later applied to Joshua at his death (24:29). Joshua. Joshua's name was changed from Hoshea ("salvation") to Joshua ("the Lord is salvation") by Moses (Num. 13:16). Joshua appears as Moses's assistant as early as Ex. 17. He was one of the men sent from Kadesh-barnea to explore the land (Num. 13:8), and he joined Caleb in calling on the Israelites to trust the Lord and not to rebel against Him (Num. 14:6–9). Like Caleb (Deut. 1:36), he escaped the judgment that fell on that generation because of its refusal to obey God at Kadesh-barnea. Joshua is here presented as the successor to Moses, as was anticipated before Moses's death (Num. 27:12–23; Deut. 3:28; 31:1–8). Joshua's role, however, continues to be subordinate to that of Moses. This is expressed in his submission to the "Book of the Law" (1:8 note) and his obedience to the commands of Moses, something repeatedly emphasized throughout the book (e.g., 1:7; 8:31; 11:12, 15; 14:2, 5; 20:2). Importantly, Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim and as a descendant of Joseph may well have been viewed by his contemporaries as belonging to the unique family line through which God would establish a monarchy in Israel. Only later, in the time of Samuel, would the tribe of Ephraim be rejected by God in favor of the tribe of Judah (cf. Ps. 78:67–72), though this development is anticipated as early as Joseph's lifetime (Gen. 49:8–10).

The people are east of the river (Deut. 1:1), which forms a boundary between them and the land God promised to the west. See also 3:15. into the land. The land is God's gift to the Israelites, in faithfulness to His promise to Abraham (see vv. 3, 6). This is the dominant theme of the book: note the elaboration of this idea in 24:13, echoing Deut. 6:10, 11. See note on 21:43.
"Your" and "you" are plural, indicating the promise is addressed to all Israel.

The extent of the land promised here exceeds what is actually received in the days of Joshua and corresponds to the dimensions of Solomon's kingdom (1 Kin. 4:21). Despite the emphasis on fulfillment in Joshua (21:45 note), the book sees the promise as still pointing to the future (13:1 note; 23:5, 12–13).

These promises are addressed to Joshua individually, as the successor to Moses. The section begins and ends with God's promise to be with him. Near the end is the exhortation to be strong and courageous. In the middle is the commandment to keep God's instructions, along with the promise of success if he does. In ch. 23 Joshua applies these ideas to the whole people of Israel in the light of the faithfulness of God, which the whole book proclaims. 1:5 I will be with you. See Gen. 26:3 and notes; Ex. 3:12. The divine presence is not a general concept or a mystical experience, but rather the presence of God to fulfill His promises. Cf. the promise of Jesus in Matt. 28:20.

Confidence based on the promises of God is the essence of biblical faith (vv. 9, 18; 8:1; 10:8, 25; 11:6). inherit. The land as an inheritance is important in this book. An inheritance is something handed down from the past, as the land was first given in the divine oath made to Abraham (Gen. 15:18–21) and subsequently restated to Isaac and Jacob (Gen 26:3–4; 28:13–15).

The essential relationship between faith and obedience is illustrated here. Faith is confidence based on God's promise (v. 6), and such faith bears the fruit of obedience (v. 7). the law. The Hebrew word is broader in meaning than the English word "law"; a better translation is "instruction" (see 1:8). See theological note "Special Revelation and the Bible" on p. 142. have good success. Success is understood in terms of what God has promised. Such success cannot be understood simply as a reward earned by obedience, because the promise is issued before any obedience. It is more accurate to understand the promised success as something that can be forfeited by disobedience. Ultimately, however, God preserves an inheritance for His elect (Rom. 8:28–30).

The material recorded by Moses after he spoke to the Israelites in the wilderness east of the Jordan. It probably refers to all that is now preserved in Deut. 5:1–26:19. According to Deut. 17:18–19, Israelite kings must make a copy of the Book of the Law and meditate upon it every day in order to know how to lead the people of Israel. The Israelites will be judged by God on the basis of their obedience to the Book of the Law. Deut. 31:24–26 records how Moses wrote this book and entrusted it to the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant. See 8:34–35; 23:6; 24:26. meditate. Cf. Ps. 1:2. From meditation on the Book of the Law flow all the consequences of the promise already seen in vv. 6, 7: obedience and success (v. 8); faith and the presence of God (v. 9).

While it is also possible that "three days" is not a precise expression and means "a few days," it seems best to understand it here as a precise length of time. to possess. The promise that God has given (v. 2) demands the human act of taking possession, an act of obedience that demonstrates true faith (vv. 6; 18:3; and notes).

Num. 32 shows how the Reubenites, Gad­ites, and half-tribe of Manasseh (13:8 note) have already received their portion of land east of the Jordan. It has been understood that they will join in Israel's conquest of the western portion of the Promised Land (Num. 32:16–32; Deut. 3:18–20). All Israel must participate in taking possession of the whole land. There is a dramatic sequel in ch. 22. See notes on 12:1; 13:8–33.

See also v. 15. The goal of God's gift of the land is often referred to as "rest" (11:23; 21:44; 22:4; 23:1), a condition or state that links the land with God's purposes in creation (Gen. 2:2, 3). For the NT extension of this idea, see Heb. 3:7–4:11.

The people's obedient response to Joshua, and therefore to God, will be echoed and elaborated at the end of the book (24:16–24). The essential connection between faith and obedience is implicit: the obedience of the people is not meritorious in any sense for salvation; nevertheless, it provides unambiguous evidence that they believe the Lord's promise (cf. James 2:14–26 and notes). The necessary qualities for Joshua's leadership are that God is with him (v. 5 note) and that he is a man of faith (v. 6 note).

The Israelites divide and conquer the land in a series of three campaigns. They start with a central campaign (chs. 2–8), then progress to a southern campaign (chs. 9–10), and finally march on the northern territory (ch. 11). The first major section of the book recounts the movement of the Israelites from Shittim (2:1), across the Jordan River (chs. 3; 4; cf. 1:2), and into the center of the land of Canaan. This movement marks the end of one era (5:9) and the beginning of the new life in the Land of Promise (5:12). It is the book's first main testimony to God's faithfulness to His promises. 2:1–24 Before the expected sequel to ch. 1 (see 3:1), there is the surprising story of the spies who return to Joshua proclaiming the promise of God (v. 24; cf. 1:2–5). Although the book of Joshua describes in graphic detail the defeat of the Canaanites (chs. 6–12), it gives a prominent place to Rahab, a Canaanite harlot (6:17). It is from her lips that the spies hear testimony to the promise and the power of God (vv. 9–11), wherein she seeks and finds His kindness (vv. 12–14). She will be spared from the coming judgment (6:22, 23) and find a place among the people of God (6:25). The chapter testifies to the grace of God in bringing such a woman to seek and find His mercy. The story of Rahab supplies an important perspective on the judgments of God that occupy much of this book. 2:1 Shittim. The site is a reminder of a time when Israel was guilty of harlotry (both physical and spiritual; Num. 25:1–3), a time not forgotten in this book (22:17). spies. The role of these spies is as unusual as the conquest to follow. Both their role and the conquest are shaped by the promise of God. See their report in v. 24; cf. Num. 13:17–20. prostitute \... Rahab. The narrative does not say why the spies choose Rahab's house. She is remembered in the NT as an ancestor of David and of Christ through her marriage to Salmon (Matt. 1:5) and as an example of faith (Heb. 11:31) and good works (James 2:25).
The Israelites invade a Canaan made up of city-states, each with its own king.
The skillfully narrated story creates a moment of tension before telling the reader that the men have been hidden (v. 4).

Undoubtedly Rahab did know (v. 9). The writer of Joshua does not justify or condemn Rahab's deception, although her actions clearly save the lives of the Israelite spies (vv. 9–11). In the NT, James approves Rahab's rescue of the spies because it was an act of faith based on the belief that God would give Jericho to the Israelites (James 2:25).
Note the narrative style in which information is given out of chronological sequence. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.
The suspense of the narrative increases, since the spies now seem to be trapped.

Rahab knows what God wants Israel to know (3:10), namely, that the promise of God is true. fear. This is the inevitable response to finding oneself on the wrong side of what God has promised to do (cf. 1:6). God's destruction of the Egyptian army is a warning to the people of Canaan, though few Canaanites besides Rahab heed it (5:1; 9:24; 10:2; cf. Ex. 15:14–16; Deut. 2:25).

The cause of Rahab's knowledge, and the Canaanites' terror, is the news of what God has already done for Israel in faithfulness to His promises. See note on 9:3. Amorites. The term is flexible, sometimes applying to all the peoples of Canaan (e.g., 24:15), sometimes more specifically to people in the hill country (e.g., 5:1), especially as distinct from the Jebusites, who also occupied the hill country (e.g., 3:10). Sihon and Og. See note on 12:2–5. destruction. See notes on 6:17, 18.
**LORD** your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath. The acknowledgment of God required in Israel (Deut. 4:39) is made by Rahab.

As the footstool to the heavenly throne (1 Chron. 28:2), it signifies not only the presence of the Lord (Num. 10:33–36) but specifically His covenant, which means His commitment to His promises as well as the consequent obligations of Israel. This circumcision is necessary because the generation that came out of Egypt had fallen under God's judgment. In His grace God is raising up a new generation for Himself (v. 7). Physical circumcision has its spiritual counterpart in circumcised hearts (Deut. 10:16; 30:6 and notes).
**LORD** . The simplest description of the behavior that brought judgment. The reference is to Num. 14 (Deut. 1:32, 43). the **LORD** swore. The promise of God can be negative.
These people are, in effect, a "new Israel."

These words indicate the great significance of this moment. The redemption from Egypt is complete only with the entry into the Promised Land. See the promise of the exodus and its goal in Ex. 3:8. Had that goal not been reached, the reproach or scorn of Egypt would have remained (Deut. 9:28). to this day. See note on 4:9.
Another indication that a new era has begun, and the first major section of the book is concluded; see Introduction: Outline. On manna and its significance, see Ex. 16; Deut. 8:3.

The second major section of the book describes how the Israelites subdue Canaan. It is commonly thought that the Israelite invasion was accompanied by widespread violence and destruction. Yet, the book of Joshua records only three cities being razed by the Israelites — Jericho (6:24), Ai (8:28), and Hazor (11:11) — and in each instance, the Israelites give their enemies an opportunity to avoid death by abandoning their territory or, as with Rahab, seeking refuge in Israel's God. While every opportunity is given for people to flee from the Israelites, those who resist forfeit their lives. As Gen. 15:16 reveals, the Israelites are to take possession of the land only when the sin of the Amorites has reached its full measure. In a similar fashion, Lev. 18:25 states that the expulsion of Canaan's descendants is due to their defiling of the land. Leviticus uses the image of the land vomiting out its inhabitants, a motif that associates possession of the land with righteous behavior and loss of land with immoral behavior. In light of this, Israel's seizure of Canaan is a vivid reminder of the reality of divine judgment upon those who by their unrighteous actions lose their land. These accounts of destruction, no less than anything else in the book, prefigure God's final judgment on those who reject His grace (Matt. 25:46; Heb. 9:27; 10:26–31). 5:13–15 The account of the conquest begins with the appearance of "the commander of the army of the LORD," which shows that God, not Joshua, controls the ensuing action. Joshua is the servant of the same God who appeared to Moses in the burning bush (Ex. 3:5).

The commander of the Lord's army encourages Joshua, but He is not under Joshua's command. God is bound neither to destroy all Canaanites nor to deliver all Israelites, as is powerfully illustrated in the subsequent chapters in the experiences of Rahab (6:25) and Achan (ch. 7). See notes on 6:17, 18. commander of the army of the **LORD** . Some scholars believe that the commander is an appearance of the preincarnate Son of God. As v. 15 reveals, the ground is made holy by God's presence. The divine warrior and His army are prepared for war, reassuring Joshua of victory.

This command is like that of Ex. 3:5, establishing a continuity between what began with Moses and what follows under Joshua. Joshua is the successor to Moses. Holiness is fundamentally a quality of God. People (3:5 note) or things are described as holy when they belong to God in some special way.

Its name means "moon," implying that the city is a center for astral worship in Joshua's time. 6:1–27 The essential elements for a theological understanding of the Israelite conquest of Canaan are indicated in this account of Jericho, the first city to be destroyed. The destruction of the Canaanites, no less than the crossing of the Jordan, is the powerful work of the sovereign God (note the role of the ark of the covenant in chs. 3, 4, and 6; see notes on 3:3, 11, 14, 17; 4:16). The fearful judgment of God working to bring about the promised deliverance of His people is an important biblical theme (e.g., Ex. 14:13–14; Rev. 19:1–2). Furthermore, that the grace of God is not restricted to Israel (Gen. 12:3) is evidenced by the experience of Rahab and her household (v. 25). Here we observe the principle that faith in God saves despite physical descent. God is not simply anti-Canaanite (see note 5:14). Moreover, the people of Jericho are given six days in which to escape from the city.

**LORD** . Probably refers to the "commander of the army of the LORD" (5:13–15), although these verses may be part of a separate episode introducing the whole of the conquest of Jericho. See, I have given. A striking paradox, since all that has been seen is Jericho's shut gates (v. 1). The promise of God creates possibilities not inherent in the present situation. The contrast between present circumstances and God's promises is found often in the Bible (Gen. 15:2–5; Is. 65:17; Rom. 8:18).

Suggests a parallel to the work of creation. Just as the work of creation reached its goal in the seventh day (Gen. 2:1–3), so the work of redemption from Egypt reaches its goal with possession of the Promised Land. Sabbath rest is related to both creation and redemption (Ex. 20:8–11; Deut. 5:12–15; Josh. 1:13 note). In Heb. 3:7–4:11 "rest" refers to the ultimate goal of God's people.
The collapse of the wall will allow access from every direction.

See note 3:3. The procession, with the ark at its center, applies the covenant promises of God symbolically to Jericho. For Jericho, the covenant promises will mean judgment as the city stands in opposition to God.
**LORD** . As in 3:11 (note), the presence of the ark is identified with the presence of the Lord Himself. See note on 1:5.
The whole procession can be summed up with reference only to the ark. in the camp. At Gilgal (5:10).

The description of the seventh day is expanded with a report of Joshua's speech. In accordance with the narrative style noted elsewhere (1:11; 2:6 and notes), the words of vv. 17–19 may have been spoken earlier but are recorded here for dramatic effect.

Holy war involves the awful reality of God's judgment on Jericho, as also on the whole of Canaan (11:11–12, 14, 20; Lev. 27:28–29; Deut. 13:16; 20:10–18). All that is captured in battle is to be given over to God, which involves the death of everyone — men, women, and children (e.g., Deut. 2:34; 3:6). While people and property are devoted to destruction frequently in Joshua (2:10; 6:17, 18, 21; 7:1, 11–15; 8:26; 10:1, 28, 35–40; 11:11–12, 20–21; 19:38; 22:20), earlier passages speak of the Israelites "dispossessing" or "expelling" the nations of Canaan. It is therefore noteworthy that the concept of total destruction in war was first introduced in the context of the Israelites being attacked by the Canaanite king of Arad (Num. 21:1–3). Later, Deut. 2:34 and 3:6 apply the same concept to Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, both of whom deliberately attack the Israelites. A survey of the book of Joshua also suggests that the concept of total destruction is applied only to those who are actively hostile toward the Israelites. Since such hostility is actually directed against God, all those involved forfeit their right to life. Only Rahab \... and all who are with her. Judgment on Canaan does not exclude grace. The mercy she sought in 2:12 will be extended to her.

Unbelief destroys, regardless of physical descent. Chapter 7 recounts the first instance of disobedience in the Promised Land, an ominous event in light of the history that follows (2 Kin. 17:7–20) and an occasion reminiscent of Gen. 3 (v. 21 note). The incident and its lesson for Israel are recalled in 22:18–20. 7:1 the people of Israel. Although the offense was committed by one man, all Israel is involved and affected (see v. 11; 22:18). The anger of God is His personal, righteous hostility to evil. Unlike ancient pagan conceptions of divine wrath, God's anger is never arbitrary or capricious. It is as much a part of the NT message as it is of the OT (Matt. 3:7; John 3:36; Rom. 1:18; Col. 3:6; 1 Thess. 1:10; Heb. 10:26–31; Rev. 6:16).

In contrast to the stories of the spies (ch. 2) and the conquest of Jericho (ch. 6), Israel is now under God's anger, and the outcome will be different. 7:2 from Jericho to Ai. This deception will bring a curse on the Gibeonites (v. 23) and is a contrast to Rahab's action toward the representatives of Israel in ch. 2.

The third major section of the book details the division of the land among the tribes. The significance of these chapters is made explicit in 21:43–45. The lists of boundaries and towns represent the objective content of God's promises. However, many of the places are no longer known, and their allotment here does not in all cases mean that the designated tribe actually occupies them at this point in Israel's history (23:13). Nevertheless, these allotments are an elaborate testimony to the faithfulness of the Lord. Note also the important contrast drawn between some of the tribes. Whereas Judah, Ephraim, and half of Manasseh have actively taken possession of territory in Joshua's lifetime, the tribes of Benjamin, Simeon, Zeb­ulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan have yet to settle in their allocated regions. The prominence given to Judah, in particular, anticipates how that tribe will provide leadership for the whole nation of Israel through the Davidic dynasty. Though the tribe of Ephraim enjoys the privilege of being the leading tribe in the time of Joshua, the book of Judges will chronicle the tribe's fall from divine favor, something already signaled by its reluctance to overthrow the Canaanites in the Valley of Jezreel and in Beth Shan (17:16–18). 13:1 Joshua was old. At the end of his life Joshua leads Israel in a reaffirmation of the covenant, much as Moses did before he died (Deut. 32:46). As with Deuteronomy, there may be an analogy between this covenant renewal and the kind of treaties that were typically used to formalize relations between powerful sovereign nations and weaker client states in the ancient Near East (see Deuteronomy: Introduction). Called "suzerainty treaties," they commonly included elements such as those found in Josh. 24: a historical prologue reviewing the care given by the powerful party to the client (vv. 2–13); a prohibition of any outside alliance (vv. 14, 23); and provision for a written document (vv. 25, 26). The promise of many descendants to Abraham is a preeminent concern in Genesis (Gen. 12:2; 15:5; 17:2 and notes) and is related to God's blessing on humanity in Gen. 1:26–28 (cf. Ex. 1:7 note).
Joshua's summary of the exodus reviews the actions that directly led up to the occupation of the Promised Land.
See note on Ex. 13:18.

The people of Joshua's day have participated in the redemptive events of the past. This emphasizes that they must see the goodness of God toward them not only in their personal experience but also in the larger history of their people. See note on 4:23, 24. in the wilderness a long time. A few words summarize everything from leaving Egypt to arriving at the land. See note on vv. 5–7.

Joshua's summary of Numbers does not mention the rebellions that took place in the wilderness (Num. 14; 25), probably because the emphasis of his review is on the deeds of God. 24:8 Amorites. See note on 2:10.
See Num. 22–24; note on Josh. 13:22.
Balaam illustrates God's complete power over those who would bring harm to His people.
See 3:10 and note.

This echoes what is said in Ex. 23:28 and Deut. 7:20. The precise meaning of the Hebrew term used here is unclear; it could possibly refer to a swarm of insects. not by your sword. The Israelites received the land as a gift, so the conquest must not be considered their own achievement (1:2 note; cf. Eph. 2:8).

**LORD** . See 4:24. This response is demanded by the history of God's faithfulness to His promises in vv. 2–13. The fear of God is associated with knowledge of His grace and is fully compatible with love for Him (Deut. 10:12, 13; Ps. 130:4). Cf. 2:9, where the Canaanites fear God because of His coming judgment; and 7:5, where the Israelites experience His anger. Put away the gods. This may refer literally to idols, or metaphorically to abandoning the gods they represent, or to both. The goodness of God to Israel (vv. 2–13) demands exclusive allegiance, summed up by the first commandment (Ex. 20:3). the River. The Euphrates; see note on v. 2. and in Egypt. Israel's idolatry in Egypt will be remembered by Ezekiel (20:7–10; 23:3–8, 19–21, 27).

With irony Joshua presents the alternatives that are available if the Israelites reject the Lord. The choice is between the gods Abraham left behind (vv. 2, 3) and the gods of the dispossessed Amorites (vv. 12; 2:10 note). me and my house. See 6:25; 7:24; Acts 16:15.
In response to the call of v. 14, the people repudiate other gods (v. 16), acknowledge the Lord's goodness from the exodus to the conquest, and conclude by promising obedience to the Lord.

**LORD** . This paradoxical statement will be proven true all too soon (v. 31 note; 7:1–26 note; 23:12, 13 note; Judg. 2:7, 10–13; 2 Kin. 17:7–23; Deut. 31:16). Joshua warns the people because he knows their rebellious nature from personal experience (22:17 and note). holy. Only a people separated from pagan ways (Lev. 18:3; 20:26) can serve the God who is holy, entirely separate from other gods (Lev. 19:2). jealous. See Ex. 20:5 and note. will not forgive. The transgressions in view here amount to the apostasy described in the following verse.
By forsaking the Lord for other gods, the people will experience God's righteous anger.
**LORD** . The people reject the possibility envisaged or predicted in v. 20.
When they are accused of forsaking the Lord, the case against them will be supported by their decision on this occasion.

Possibly the Book of the Law in 1:8; 8:31; 23:6, although it could be a book very similar to that produced by Moses (Deut. 31:24). terebinth. Cf. Gen. 12:6; 35:4; Judg. 9:6.
Cf. how the stones at Gilgal were to provide a testimony to what God had done (4:20–24 and note).

An appropriate concluding note to the book that tells of God's giving the promised inheritance to Israel. Similar words occur, after a considerably different period, at the end of Judges (Judg. 21:24). See note on 1:6.

The deaths of Joshua and Eleazar mark the end of the period that has been the subject of this book. Their burials, along with the burial of the bones of Joseph, in the land that is now Israel's possession symbolizes God's faithful fulfillment of His promises to the patriarchs. 24:29 servant of the **LORD** . See note on 1:1. 110. The same age as Joseph at his death (Gen. 50:22 and note). Such long lives signify God's blessing (cf. Deut. 34:7).
See 19:49–50. Unlike Abraham, who had to purchase land for a burial plot (Gen. 23:4; cf. Gen. 33:19), Joshua is buried in his own land.

**LORD** all the days of Joshua. The faithfulness of the generation of Joshua and the elders is a testimony to the Lord's power in everything He has done for Israel. That such faithfulness is so short-lived supports Joshua's assertion in vv. 19, 20 (notes; Judg. 2:7, 10–13).

The promise believed by Joseph (Gen. 50:24, 25 and notes) now comes to fulfillment. Jacob bought. See Gen. 33:19. The new situation of owning the land is again contrasted with the time of the patriarchs, who had only the promise of it.
See note on 14:1. Phinehas. See note on 22:13.

Judges.note: This section serves as the first part of an introduction to Judges, and in it the gradual shift from conquest to coexistence comes to expression. Additionally, the need for leaders who will fight against the Canaanites is expressed in the opening verse of the book. The covenant-keeping successes and failures of the various tribes, and God's judgment on Israel for the covenant failure of letting the Canaanites live in the land, are recounted (cf. Deut. 7:1–2; 20:16–20). The space and detail given to Judah's successes (vv. 3–20) contrast strongly with the brief accounts of the failures of the other tribes (vv. 21–36). The house of Joseph is treated positively (vv. 22–26), but Judah's prominence is evidence that Israel should look to that tribe for leadership. 1:1–8 This opening story demonstrates that the land was conquered in principle under Joshua, yet there remain both pockets of Canaanite resistance (cf. Josh. 13:1) and large areas that still need to be settled. The allotted territory generally belongs to Israel, but many of the original inhabitants need to be dislodged. 1:1 After the death of Joshua. The book of Joshua opens similarly: "After the death of Moses" (Josh. 1:1). Who. The Israelites ask an almost identical question at the end of the book: "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" (20:18). A question raised at the beginning of the book to initiate holy war against the Canaanites is raised near the end of the book to initiate holy war within Israel. Canaanites. The Canaanites are one of several groups inhabiting the land of Canaan. The Israelites have been commanded to dispossess and destroy them (Deut. 7:1–2; 20:16–20). Whether the Israelites can obey these terms of the covenant will be the issue for this entire introductory section.

God's choice is Judah. David and his heirs will come from this tribe, and this serves as evidence for God's choice of the house of David during the war between the house of David and the house of Saul.
The severing of the digits of Adoni-bezek is a form of ironic justice: he committed this act against seventy kings, and now it is done to him. It is a symbol of taking away one's power and authority.
Judah obeys the covenant by destroying the inhabitants without mercy (Deut. 7:1–2; 20:16–20). Judah does not occupy Jerusalem at this point (v. 21).
These verses, describing the victories of Caleb and Othniel, are essentially the same as Josh. 15:15–19.
Caleb, though of Kenizzite ancestry (Gen. 15:19; Num. 32:12), is counted as belonging to the tribe of Judah. He represented Judah when the spies were sent into Canaan (Num. 13:6).

He is the first judge whose judgeship is recounted in the book (3:7–11). Achsah. It is significant that Othniel, the first and best of the judges, is married to the daughter of the godly Caleb, one of two (Joshua being the other) from the wilderness generation to enter the Promised Land. The significance is seen in connection with the theme of intermarriage to pagan women as the problem that leads eventually to apostasy (3:5–6). Othniel represents the solution, not the problem; in contrast, Samson is the epitome of the problem (14:1; 16:1; 16:4).

**LORD** was with Judah. God keeps His covenant promise (v. 2). With the exception of the house of Joseph, the writer deals briefly with the rest of the tribes, describing the failures of their efforts at settlement (1:27–36 note). Although the Ephraimites considered themselves to be the leading tribe among the Israelites, the book of Judges points to the ever-increasing role played by Judah, as was promised in Jacob's blessing to Judah in Gen. 49:8. chariots of iron. Such chariots, with their wooden wheels overlaid with iron, were powerful weapons, especially on the level plains. According to archaeological site surveys of the land, the major concentration of Canaanite settlements was in the valleys and plains of Canaan. In Iron Age I (c. 1200 B.C..), settlement surveys have demonstrated a great increase of sites in the hill country.
Caleb, from the tribe of Judah, is an example of faithfulness to the covenant. In Deut. 1:36–37, Caleb is rewarded for his covenant obedience, which flows from faith in God's promise.

The writer specifies that Benjamin, Saul's tribe, does not make a final conquest of Jerusalem. This contrasts with the victories of Judah and provides an argument for Israel not to side with the house of Saul during the war between the house of David and the house of Saul.
**LORD** was with them. Besides Judah (v. 19), only with regard to the house of Joseph is it said that "the LORD was with them."
Judah, Benjamin, and Joseph have already been mentioned. The shortcomings of the remaining tribes are briefly presented in outline fashion.
See chs. 17, 18.

This passage reviews the preceding chapter and, like 2:20–3:6, provides the background for the narrative that follows. The covenant was made between God and "your fathers," and the covenant terms forbid treaties or mixed worship with the Canaanites. Failure to observe these requirements brings the judgment of the covenant on Israel (Deut. 28–31). 2:1 the angel of the **LORD**. Because the words of God's preeminent messenger are the words of the Lord Himself (6:11–24; cf. Ex. 3:1–17), this should likely be read as a theophany, that is, a visible revelation of God. See 6:11–24; 13:2–23. The angel of the Lord led Israel out of captivity in Egypt and fought for them (Ex. 14:19; 23:20–23; 33:2; Num. 20:16; Is. 63:9). Some commentators suggest that the angel of the Lord, at least in these cases, is a preincarnate appearance of the Messiah. Gilgal. At this time, the ark of the covenant is at Gilgal (Josh. 5:1–12). I brought you up from Egypt. The Ten Commandments begin with the same statement (Ex. 20:2; Deut. 5:6), a reminder that the history of what God has done is linked to His commands. The sovereign God who sets out the terms of the covenant identifies Himself as the benefactor of His people. and brought you into the land that I swore. God has kept His oath (Josh. 23:3–16). The chief difference here between God and His people is that God keeps His vow while the people break theirs. I will never break my covenant. See Deut. 7:9.

Idolatry is the leading, typical act of covenant breaking (v. 11; Ex. 34:13; Num. 33:52; Deut. 7:5; 12:3; Josh. 23:16). you have not obeyed. Israel has contracted marriages with the people of the land (3:5–6) and has not torn down their altars (6:25–32). The Canaanites cannot be driven out because of Israel's sin.

Intermarriage and all other relationships with the Canaanites have been forbidden because such contact will lead to idolatry (Ex. 23:33; 34:12; Num. 33:55; Deut. 7:16; Josh. 23:12–13). For disobeying the terms of the covenant, Israel will suffer what Canaan suffered: removal from the land (Num. 33:56; Josh. 23:13; 2 Kin. 17:5–8; 25:1–11).

This section serves as the second part of an introduction to Judges, and in it the gradual shift from Israel's mere coexistence alongside the Canaanites to Israel's apostate embrace of Canaanite religion comes to expression. 2:6–10 This section, except for v. 10, is similar to Josh. 24:28–31 and introduces the pattern for the cycle of the judges that follows.
**LORD**. Echoes Josh. 24:31. Covenant obedience led to blessing in the land for Joshua's generation.

**LORD** or the work that he had done for Israel. One generation is to declare God's wonders to the next (Deut. 4:9; 6:1–6). Later psalmists extol them (Pss. 44:1–3; 78:2–8). If God's people know Him personally and what He has done, they will obey the commands of His covenant. But after Joshua, the leaders — heads of families, priests, and judges — fail to keep the covenant or to tell the next generation about God's mighty deeds.

This passage presents the macrostructure or pattern of Israel's history during the period of the judges. The first part of the sketch is Israel's apostasy (vv. 11–13). It is followed by God's response of anger and judgment by giving Israel into the hands of her enemies (vv. 14, 15). Subsequently, the Lord raises up a judge to deliver the people (v. 16). Although the judge succeeds for a time, the nation quickly returns to its ways of apostasy (v. 17). The nation reverts to wickedness, and the people become more corrupt than the previous generation (vv. 18, 19). The period of the judges is a downward spiral. See Introduction. 2:11 did what was evil. Lit. "the evil"; the definite article refers specifically to the sin of apostasy. This refrain occurs at 2:11; 3:7, 12; 4:1; 6:1; 10:6; 13:1. served the Baals. Israel's evil is summed up in their worship of false gods (v. 2 note). They choose Baal, the Canaanite storm god, and reject the Lord, who brought them through the Red Sea and is the true Lord of the storm. "Baals" is plural because Baal is worshiped differently in various Canaanite localities. Thus, "Baal" contrasts with the Lord, who is one who has integrity of character and is the same wherever and whenever He is encountered (Deut. 6:4; Heb. 13:8).
These are the goddesses of fertility in the Canaanite pantheon.

See Deut. 28:48; 1 Sam. 12:9. Israel's enemies and oppressors have no power over God's people unless God allows it. Israel's conquest is now reversed, as people from outside Canaan (Arameans, Moabites, Midianites, Amalekites, and Philistines) oppress the Israelites, the new inhabitants of the land (3:8–12; 4:2; 6:1; 10:7; 13:1).

**LORD** was against them. The hand of the Lord is associated with the saving power of God (Ex. 3:20; 6:1; 13:3; Deut. 4:34). Now the same hand is turned against them in punishment. The Lord is faithful both to bless and to judge. When God rescues His people, He rescues them from their enemies as an act of grace. It is His own judgment that allows their enemies to prevail, and in rescuing them He must turn His own judgment aside.

The term for "judge" is not used in the sense of one who decides court cases but of one who delivers from injustice and oppression. The primary task of a judge is military in nature. The bulk of the material in the cycle of judges focuses on the military deliverance of the judges.
Since the covenant agreement can be compared to marriage, harlotry is a standard metaphor for faithlessness and disobedience (8:33; Deut. 31:16; Hosea).
The people's groaning moves their God (Ex. 2:24; 6:5).

Neither their judges (v. 17) nor the memory of how they have been delivered is enough to make the people keep the covenant (v. 10). stubborn. This is one of the words used in Exodus regarding Pharaoh's hard heart. He adamantly refused to allow Israel to leave Egypt; Israel now displays a similar obstinacy in her apostasy.

Explains why there are still Canaanites during a period when Israel was faithful (vv. 6–9; cf. Deut. 7:22–23; Josh. 13:1–7). Verses 20–22 and 3:1–4 provide a new reason for God's leaving the Canaanites: to test the hearts of the people.

See 2:10. Even God's judgment is not without grace. The testing is an opportunity for a generation who has not seen the Lord work on their behalf to exercise faith and see His might with their own eyes (v. 2).
The Canaanites and the Hivites are to be utterly destroyed (Deut. 7:1, 2).
All these are nations devoted to destruction (3:3 note). Israel violates the covenant by living among them and not destroying them.

This coexistence leads the Israelites into the apostasy of idolatry. The result of making covenants with the Canaanites rather than destroying that population is repeatedly explained in the following narrative cycles (2:2). It becomes clear that the people care more about covenants with their pagan neighbors than about their covenant with God.
See 2:11, 13 and notes. This is the apostasy that results from the coexistence mentioned in v. 6.

See notes on 1:13. Othniel is the epitome of a godly judge, being married to the godly Achsah. He forms a sharp contrast with Samson, seen in his relations with foreign women (14:1; 16:1; 16:4); see Introduction: Literary Features. In this account the prominence of Judah in Israel is highlighted, since the first judge is from Judah and is the only judge without an explicit failure in his covenant keeping. The success of Judah anticipates the future enthronement of David, who comes from that tribe.

**LORD**. The Spirit is also mentioned in connection with Gideon, Jeph­thah, and Samson. By the gift of the Spirit, the judge is empowered to deliver the people (6:34; 11:29; 13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14). This idiom does not necessarily reflect spiritual regeneration, but it signifies a special dispensation of the Lord's power and authority granted to the judge. The Spirit of God temporarily empowers the judge to perform extraordinary feats of deliverance. he judged Israel. This means he fights for Israel and delivers the nation. See Introduction: Title.
Though the pattern in 2:11–19 does not mention the time length of peace, the stories themselves end with a comment about peace or the lack of it (v. 30; 5:31; 8:28; 12:7; 15:20; 16:31).
The story of Ehud humiliates the oppressor of God's people. 3:12 See note on 2:11. Eglon the king of Moab. The Lord strengthens the pagan king to be used as His instrument of judgment.

Old enemies from the exodus period (Num. 14:45; 21:24). the city of palms. The city of Jericho in the Jordan Valley; it was the first site conquered by Israel during the period of the conquest (Josh. 6).

Lit. "with his right hand restricted." This is not the usual Hebrew word for "left-handed." It is used elsewhere only in 20:16, also for the men of Benjamin. "Benjamin" can be translated "son of the right hand," and the writer may be making a pun about a left-handed son of the right hand.
Lit. "two mouths." The sword of Ehud is double-edged.
The Hebrew term for "message" is "word" or "thing." Perhaps a double entendre in which Eglon believes Ehud had a secret word, when in fact Ehud has a secret thing, a sword, in his cloak.

The secret message of v. 19 becomes a divine message. It is not a false word but the true word of God working against the same rod raised up by God to punish His people (v. 12 note). Eglon has been useful as a tool of God's wrath against Israel, but now that wrath comes back upon him. Ehud does not invoke the covenantal name of Yahweh but rather employs the generic name Elohim.

**LORD** has given. Each major judge except for Othniel verbally acknowledges God's control in Israel's victory (4:14; 7:15; 11:21–30; 15:18; 16:28). the fords of the Jordan. This seizure results in the conquest of Canaanites, whereas the corresponding seizure in 12:5 results in the conquest of Israelites. See Introduction: Literary Features. Holy war against Canaan later gives way to civil war within Israel, owing to Israel's apostasy.
See note on v. 11.

Shamgar is mentioned only here and in the song of Deborah (5:6). Since Anath was a Canaanite goddess of war, perhaps "son of Anath" was a war hero's nickname. Alternatively, Anath could be a place name (see 1:33 for mention of Beth-anath). 600 \... with an oxgoad. Samson later slays one thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey (15:15–17).

Perhaps a descendant of the Jabin mentioned in Josh. 11:1–9. Hazor. During the northern campaign under Joshua, Israel had destroyed this city (Josh. 11:10–13). Apparently, the Canaanites recaptured and resettled the site, and it had become a royal center in Canaan.

The same verb is used of Israel's circumstances in Egypt (Ex. 22:21). twenty years. The first oppression lasted eight years (3:8) and the second for eighteen years (3:14), but this one under Jabin lasts two decades. There is an intensification in Israel's sin and its oppression.

Lit. "a woman, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth." This emphasizes that this woman is the leader in Israel, and this is because the men lack faith, courage, and leadership (vv. 8, 9 notes). Deborah, a prophetess, is introduced at the point where the narrator usually mentions the deliverer (6:8 note). The word "prophetess" occurs five times in the OT (Ex. 15:20; 2 Kin. 22:14; 2 Chron. 34:22; Neh. 6:14; Is. 8:3). Although there is a feminine ending on the word "prophet," the author adds the word "woman" in his description. He is underscoring the unique, special character of this judgeship.
That is, she is a magistrate, handing down legal decisions.
A rounded hillock standing isolated on the north side of the plain in the Jezreel Valley, approximately fourteen miles (22 km) southwest of the Sea of Galilee.
The River Kishon is near the base of Mount Tabor and is virtually dry for much of the year (v. 15 note).

Barak is asking Deborah to risk her life to verify the truth of her words, and he is also asking a woman to do what he had been assigned to do. From his point of view, the mission is suicidal, since the exposed Mount Tabor can easily be surrounded by the chariots of Sisera, cutting off any escape. Barak's faith is not equal to this danger.

Barak is punished for doubting (v. 8). Deborah has spoken the word of God to him (v. 6), yet he hesitates to obey. He refuses to go unless Deborah accompanies him. for the **LORD** will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. The enemy will not be delivered to Barak but to a woman. Jael (v. 17) will succeed where faithless Barak will fail (vv. 18–22). The male leaders in Israel are shamed for their lack of courage and leadership.
See 5:13–18. These are the two tribes located directly north of the Jezreel Valley and Mount Tabor.
See note on v. 7.
**LORD** has given Sisera. Deborah confirms her word from the Lord (v. 7). It is the Lord who fights for Israel.
**LORD** routed. From Deborah's song we learn that the Lord does this by sending rain that causes flash floods, trapping the chariots (5:4).
See 5:24–27 for the poetic account.

No motive is given for Jael's action. A woman kills Sisera by striking his head, and the Lord's word to Barak is fulfilled (v. 9). In this era, women are not normally warriors, and it is considered shameful to die at the hands of a woman (9:53–54). Jael drives the point home that Israel is saved by the hand of a woman. In the corresponding story about Abimelech, a woman crushes the head of Abimelech by dropping a millstone on him (9:53); see Introduction: Literary Features.

The song of Deborah and Barak is a victory song celebrating what has just taken place (cf. Ex. 15:1–18, the song of Moses). Scholars acknowledge that its structure, grammar, and vocabulary reflect an early date. The song is also recognized for its outstanding literary quality.
Leadership is a major theme in Judges.

Mount Seir is the main mountain ridge running through Edom, Israel's point of departure for the battles of conquest (Deut. 33:2). God is pictured as the mighty warrior going before His people. 5:4, 5 the earth trembled \... before the **LORD** . God is pictured as a warrior who fights by means of the created elements. earth \... heavens. A literary feature called a merism, which references two opposites that are all inclusive. In other words, all creation trembled at the movement of the Lord.

Israel's failed leadership prior to Deborah resulted in chaos and foreign domination. It was not like the days in which God was the warrior at the front of Israel (vv. 4–5). The roads were abandoned because they were not safe for travel on account of the foreign oppressors and robbers. No one provided protection.

This probably indicates that due to the dangerous times, most people were living in walled cities for protection. a mother in Israel. Since the princes would not lead (implied by v. 2), a woman was raised up to lead Israel. Cf. this "mother in Israel" with the despairing mother of Sisera (v. 28).
A poetic representation of the cycle of sin and punishment (2:11–19). Idolatry brings suffering to the city.
Later in the song, there is a pointed comparison of those who volunteered to fight and those who for some reason refused (vv. 13–23).

Donkeys were ridden by nobility in the era of the judges. you who walk. The mention of both the rich who ride and the lowly who walk reflects the point that all types of people are to retell the story of Deborah and Barak and, in particular, the work of the Lord.
**LORD**. The Lord's righteous acts are His intervention and defeat of His people's enemies. These are His judgments in the earth (cf. Rev. 15:4).
Six commands appear in this verse to emphasize what Deborah and Barak are to do.

–18 The following tribes and clans took part in the battle at Mount Tabor: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (Gen. 50:23), Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali. Not all Israel participated because it was a regional conflict.
The failure of Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher (v. 17) to participate shows that Israel was not united prior to the battle and remains disunited thereafter.
Obviously the migration of Dan to the north had not yet taken place.
The forces of nature fought on the side of the Lord. The participation of the heavens means that God was intervening, fighting as the divine warrior from heaven.
A city of uncertain location, although it probably lies just north of Mount Tabor.
This section of the song closely parallels the narrative of 4:18–22.
The scene changes from the tent of Jael to the house of Sisera's mother.
This standard conclusion ties Deborah's and Barak's song to ch. 4 (cf. 2:18; 3:11).

Gideon was one of the greatest judges, as evidenced by several facts: (1) his story is the longest in the book; (2) the Lord is more visibly active in his story than in any of the others; (3) the angel of the Lord appeared to him but to no other judge (vv. 11–24); (4) centuries later, Isaiah remembers Gideon's defeat of Midian as a significant victory (Is. 9:4; 10:26); (5) he is listed first in Samuel's list of deliverers ("Jerubbaal," 1 Sam. 12:11); (6) he is paralleled with Moses (6:11–24 note); (7) the people sought to make him king (8:22–23); and (8) he lived like a king (8:26–27, 30, 32). Yet for all this, Gideon was conflicted and failed badly at one point by making a gold ephod that drew him and others into sin (8:27). Gideon is thus the turning point in the downward spiral of the judges. In both his greatness and his deficiency, Gideon points to the need for a better deliverer, a king who will truly keep the covenant — Jesus Christ.

None of the other stories in Judges devotes such attention to the details of the Midianite oppression as this one. Homes, crops, and livestock were subject to the covenant curse (Deut. 28:30–33, 38–42).
Lit. "made small." The covenant curse is a reversal of God's promise to Abraham (Gen. 15:5; 22:17; Deut. 28:62; Ps. 107:38, 39). cried out. See 2:18; 3:9.

An anonymous prophet. The prophets constantly remind the people of their covenant obligations. The words of this unnamed prophet (vv. 8–10) are virtually identical to the words of the angel of the Lord in 2:1–3. 6:8, 9 brought \... delivered \... drove them \... gave you. In Israel, religious apostasy is always linked to forgetting God's saving acts and His law. Remembering these saving actions of God and His revelation is the first part of keeping the covenant.

This is the heart of the Gideon narrative. His call is similar to Moses's call (Ex. 3); he asks the question that is central to the book's message (v. 13); and his search for faith begins with signs (6:1–8:32 note). The need for a covenant-keeping deliverer like the prophet Moses and the resulting search for one is the focus of Judges. 6:11 angel of the **LORD** came. See 2:1; 13:3.

This question is central to Judges. The angel does not answer the question, since the prophet has already answered it (vv. 8–10; Deut. 28:47–52; 29:24–27; 31:17, 18). Some of the psalms ask a similar question (Pss. 44:20; 74:9–11).
**LORD**. The Hebrew text identifies the angel of the Lord with the covenant Lord Himself.
When asked about kingship, Saul uses similar words (1 Sam. 9:21). Gideon's response is reminiscent of Moses's question in regard to his call to deliver Israel from Egypt (Ex. 3:11).
See 13:22; Deut. 5:24; Is. 6:5; 1 Tim. 6:16. Again, this is reminiscent of Moses's relationship with God (Deut. 34:10).

This episode in Gideon's life reveals how he comes to be known as Jerubbaal. His father's idolatry is tragic in light of what Gideon says about "our fathers" in v. 13. 6:25, 26 pull down the altar. See Deut. 12:3. 6:26 due order. That is, according to the prescriptions of the Book of the Covenant (Ex. 20:24–25).
Gideon's struggle to believe is seen in his seeking of signs (v. 17), which the Lord does not refuse to give him (cf. Luke 1:18–20).
Even though the Spirit has come upon him, Gideon still struggles to trust the Lord.

The drastic reduction of troops demonstrates God's power to save Israel and brings Him glory. It also challenges Gideon and encourages Israel to trust him. 7:1 Harod. Gideon and his men are encamped near this spring, which lies south of the Midianites who are spread out in the Valley of Jezreel.

Israelite laws of warfare allow for certain exemptions from military service (Deut. 20:5–9). One exemption is for the cowardly person, because timidity is infectious and can easily spread to other troops. This is the first test to reduce the size of Gideon's force.
This second test probably reflects how ready and alert the soldiers are for battle. One who kneels down appears more vulnerable to attack than the one who brings the water to his mouth by his hand.
God provides Gideon with a preview of the victory that he will soon have over the Midianites.

The Hebrews in Gideon's day divide the night into three watches. Ex. 14:24 and 1 Sam. 11:11 mention the "morning watch." In the NT period, the Jews separate the night into four watches (see Matt. 14:25). The middle watch signifies the period after the Midianites had gone to sleep.

**LORD** and for Gideon. The Israelites send the Midianites into panic and flight by employing trumpets, jars, and torches, but no swords of Israel are mentioned. Ironically, the swords of Midianite destruction are their own (v. 22).
Israel's lack of unity is apparent in the difficulties between Gideon, Ephraim, Succoth, and Penuel.
See Is. 10:26.

The conflict here between Ephraim and Gideon is similar to the conflict between Ephraim and Jephthah (see 12:1–6). Gideon belongs to the tribe of Manasseh (6:15). The Ephraimites resent Gideon's victory because they see themselves as the tribe that should provide leadership for the Israelites.

Gideon has problems with the men of Succoth and Penuel and ultimately punishes both for failing to help him in his pursuit of the Midianite leaders. Many problems during the period of the judges occur because of the infighting among Israelite tribes, clans, and cities.
The text reveals that Gideon's attack on the Midianites is partly a personal feud because Zebah and Zalmuna, Midianite kings, destroyed his brothers some time earlier.

**LORD** will rule. These verses demonstrate a major antithesis in the book: the people desire a human king to rule over them, yet the Lord is their true king. This conflict finds its climax in 1 Sam. 8. These verses also show Gideon's inner conflict regarding whether he should be king (v. 31 note).
Though Gideon rejects kingship, he acts like a king (v. 30).

The genuine ephod of the high priest is employed for seeking the Lord's will (1 Sam. 23:9–11; 30:7, 8). whored after it. Gideon, the greatest of the judges until Samuel, gives the people occasion to sin (2:17 and notes). a snare to Gideon and to his family. Gideon's father was an idolater (6:25), and now Gideon falls into the same sin.
Gideon names the son of his concubine "Abimelech" ("my father is king") notwithstanding all Gideon's claims to the contrary. See vv. 23, 24.

Though not called a judge, Abim­elech is treated as a judge in the outline of the book because he is described in the concentric pattern of the stories about the judges (see Introduction: Literary Features). The Abimelech story demonstrates the disaster wrought by the wrong kind of king. Abimelech is an anti-deliverer, an oppressor of the people, and a breaker of the covenant. His story raises the question of who should be king (9:2, 8–20, 28, 29). In light of this question, it is significant that Abimelech and Saul resemble each other in important ways (9:23 note; 9:54 note). This implies that Saul and Abimelech are the same sort of king. 8:33 Baal-berith. Lit. "Baal (lord) of the covenant," a counterfeit of the God who truly is the Lord of the covenant. See note on 9:4.
Remembering God and His work of salvation is the first step in covenant obedience (2:10 note).
See note on 8:31.

See notes on v. 46; 8:33. The temple of Baal-berith paid the wages of those who oppressed Israel under Abimelech. Archaeologists have discovered a temple from the era of Joshua and the judges at Shechem that contained an altar and a huge standing stone (Josh. 24:26, 27). The excavators have identified this cultic structure with the temple of Baal-berith or El-berith in Judges 9.
The men were in effect sacrificed to Baal-berith (v. 53 note).
The mount of blessing (Deut. 27:12) was used for a curse. This highlights the reversal theme that permeates the Abimelech story (8:33–9:57 note).
As the product of idolatry (v. 4), Abim­elech's kingship will be a thorn to Israel (2:3 note).
Jotham's curse is fulfilled in vv. 45–52.
Both Abimelech and Saul experience an evil spirit come against them as they begin to lose their kingdoms (1 Sam. 16:14).

Lit. "god of the covenant." El was the father of the gods in the Canaanite pantheon. This is probably the same temple as the one mentioned at 9:4, which supplied Abimelech money. Now he returns to destroy it.

Towers are mentioned elsewhere in Judges (8:17; 9:46–49). At the site of Giloh the foundations of a square tower (124 sq. ft.; 11.5 sq. m.) have been found from this period. This discovery indicates that the tower was well built, having been constructed of large, roughly hewn stones; its interior was filled with rubble.

A stone figures prominently in Abimelech's death, as it did in the murder of all his brothers (9:5 note). This is part of a grinding stone used to reduce wheat into flour; such stones are frequently found in excavations of the period. Abimelech's death is an example of ironic justice (see v. 56).

Like Saul (1 Sam. 31:4), Abimelech seeks to die proudly. This incident, like the presence of an evil spirit from God (9:23 and note), is a strong point of resemblance between Saul and Abimelech. A woman killed him. He shares this indignity with Sisera (4:9).
God is not highly visible in this narrative (9:23 note), but He brings Abimelech to judgment.
Two judges, Tola and Jair, are introduced with few details. Four other minor judges are described in similar fashion (3:31; 12:8–15). 10:1 Tola. Tola is mentioned only here in Scripture.
Like Tola, Jair is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible.
Thirty sons, thirty donkeys, and the control of thirty towns indicate great wealth and power (5:10).

Cf. 1 Sam. 12:11. The list of idols that Israel is following grows, and the internal chaos of Israel becomes more pronounced (10:6; 12:1–7), indicating further decline. Jephthah brings only six years of peace (12:7) instead of peace for a generation (3:11, 30; 5:31; 8:28). Finally, Jephthah rashly and sinfully sacrifices his daughter (11:30–40 note). Many things about Jephthah are reminiscent of Gideon, Abimelech, and Saul. Jephthah, like Gideon, is a "mighty man of valor" (6:12; 11:1). Both men make the Ephraimites angry by not calling them to participate in battle (8:1–3; 12:1–6). Jephthah and Abimelech are both outcast sons, one born to a concubine and the other to a harlot. They gather to themselves bands of adventurers (9:4; 11:3). Both Jephthah and Saul are made leaders in Mizpah (11:11; 1 Sam. 10:17), and both men face Ammonites as their first adversaries (11:12–29; 1 Sam. 11:1–11). Jephthah and Saul each make an unwise vow that threatens their firstborn, and each offers an unlawful sacrifice (11:30–40; 1 Sam. 13:8–14; 14:24–25). 10:6 gods. In previous accounts, only the Baals and the Ashtaroth are mentioned (2:11, 13; 3:7). This longer list of gods indicates a downward spiral in Israel's violations of the covenant. See also vv. 11–12 and note. The peoples mentioned surround Israel on its borders during the era of the judges.

This is the only account in Judges where Israel not only cries out to God but also puts away idols. Elsewhere, they simply cry out to the Lord, and He delivers them (3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:6, 7). 10:10 forsaken our God and have served the Baals. The same language is used in their indictment in v. 6.

The list of gods in v. 6 coincides almost identically with the list of oppressing nations. Israel has rejected the God who had saved them and instead has followed the compassionless gods of their oppressors.
See Deut. 32:37, 38. The same taunt is made in Jer. 2:28; 11:12, 13.

**LORD** at Mizpah. The covenant is confirmed before the Lord in Mizpah. Years later, the people make Saul king, also before the Lord, at Mizpah (1 Sam. 10:17).

For the historical background to this conflict, see Num. 20:14–21; 21:10–35; Deut. 2:16–3:11. At the time of Jephthah, the Ammonites hope to extend their territory into what once was their land but has now been Israel's for three hundred years. Jephthah counters Ammonite demands by rehearsing this history and showing that the Israelites took no more than what the God of Israel gave them and, having been instructed by Him (Deut. 2:18, 19), the Israelites did not take anything from Ammon. 11:12 king of the Ammonites. Like Saul later, Jephthah's first adversaries are the Ammonites (1 Sam. 11:1–11). Gilead is the region threatened in Saul's story as well.

**LORD**, the God of Israel. Warfare in the ancient world was viewed as a battle between the gods of the opposing forces. Israel's victory over Ammon in the days of Moses was the work of the God of Israel, and no one could dispute the result (v. 24). See v. 21.

**LORD**, the Judge, decide this day. See vv. 21, 23. Jephthah declares that God is the judge over all peoples and gods. Here the word is used in a legal sense, as in handing down a decision, although God will ultimately be a deliverer as well (vv. 32, 33). Judges affirms that God is the true king (8:23) and judge who alone can solve Israel's woes.
**LORD**. See 3:10 and note. Because the king of Ammon rejected Jephthah's plea for peace, Jephthah is likely traveling through Gilead and Manasseh to raise an army (see v. 32).

Jephthah defeats the Ammonites, but in the process sins greatly when he makes a rash vow to the Lord and sacrifices his daughter as a burnt offering. God is not to be worshiped in the way the pagans worship their gods, namely, by human sacrifice (Deut. 12:31; 18:10; Ps. 106:37, 38). Although he is a deliverer who has given evidence of his faith, Jephthah does not show the people how to keep the covenant (vv. 10, 11, 21, 23, 27). Like Jephthah, Saul also makes a rash vow that turns out to be a threat to his child (1 Sam. 14:24–45).

A sacrifice that is totally consumed by fire (Lev. 1) or what the Septuagint calls a "holocaust." It may be that Jephthah expects an animal to come out of the house to meet him. At this time, animals roam freely in the courtyards of houses. Excavations at Megiddo from this period have revealed houses that were two-storied, three-sided complexes in which families probably lived in the second floor.

Human sacrifice is sin, an imitation of pagan practice (11:30–40 note; Deut. 12:31; Ps. 106:38). 11:39–40 This ritual is never mentioned again in the OT. Perhaps it was a mere regional activity that died out after the time of the judges.

Following immediately after the sacrifice of his daughter (11:30–40), this story implies that Jephthah's struggle with Ephraim and his abbreviated judgeship (v. 7) are God's judgment on him for making the sacrifice. Ps. 78 (esp. vv. 9–11, 67) reflects on Ephraim's failure to fight and explains God's rejection of Ephraim as the ruling tribe in Israel. David from the tribe of Judah is chosen by God to lead Israel (Ps. 78:68–72). 12:1 men of Ephraim. Like Gideon, Jephthah has trouble with Ephraim (8:1–5); unlike with Gideon, this trouble leads to civil war. Unity is sorely lacking in Israel, and the Ephraimites grumble against Jephthah because they view him as usurping their position as the leaders of Israel. On this occasion their failure to lead responsibly results in their punishment. Why. See 8:1 for an almost identical question put to Gideon.
The Gileadites are descended from Joseph, as are the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.
Gilead is on the east side of the Jordan, Ephraim on the west. This seizing contrasts with that in 3:28 (see Introduction: Literary Features).

The Ephraimites can be recognized by the way certain words are pronounced in their dialect. The word is fairly uncommon in the Hebrew Bible, and it likely means "a flowing stream," "an ear of grain," or "a bunch of twigs." Whatever the meaning, it is a rare word used to trap an Ephraimite, who has difficulty pronouncing it.

Previous judges led for forty or eighty years, and peace lasted a generation or two. Jephthah's abbreviated rule, the increased number of gods being worshiped, and the civil war with Ephraim contribute to a picture of Israel's downward spiral.

Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon are briefly mentioned (10:1–5 note). Nothing more is known about them. They bring the total of judges mentioned in the book to twelve. The descriptions of Ibzan and Abdon in particular demonstrate that they are men of means and power.

Samson's story is the last in the cycle of the judges. A Nazirite from the womb, his birth is a supernatural gift to barren parents. As happened with the great judge Gideon, the Angel of the Lord appears at his calling, but unlike any other judge, he is called from the womb. He also experiences the Spirit coming upon him more than any other judge (13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14). Of all the judges, Samson is perhaps the most complex. Having taken the Nazirite vow (13:4, 5, 7, 14; 16:17; cf. Num. 6:1–21), he exhibits through his conduct a growing disregard for God's covenant and his vow. His interest in delivering Israel seems at times to be overshadowed by his pursuit of pleasure and personal glory. The fanfare of his calling and the circumstances surrounding his birth only heighten the tragedy of his life and emphasize the depths to which Israel has descended. Nevertheless, God raises him up to deliver Israel from the Philistines (v. 5), and He uses even the sins of Samson as an occasion against them (14:4). Though the Spirit comes upon him repeatedly, this has no apparent impact on his character. Yet the account of the end of his life (16:25–31) reflects a renewal of his faith while a prisoner of his (and God's) enemies. In spite of his shortcomings, Samson demonstrates genuine faith in the Lord, as is evidenced by the fact that the author of Hebrews lists Samson on the honor roll of faith (Heb. 11:32). 13:1 the people of Israel again did what was evil. The usual introductory formula is especially abbreviated (cf. 2:11–19). gave them \... Philistines. See 2:14; 1 Sam. 12:9.

Like Gideon (6:11–24), Samson's parents do not recognize the Angel of the Lord. They see a miraculous fire and then fear the consequences of having seen the angel. These strong parallels pose the question as to whether Samson might not become as great a judge as Gideon (13:1–16:31 note). Three times the Nazirite requirements are spelled out even before Samson is born (vv. 4–5, 7, 14). This repetition heightens their importance. 13:2 barren. Like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Hannah, Samson's mother is barren (13:1–16:31 note; see Gen. 16:1; 25:21; 29:31; 1 Sam. 1:2, 5).
For background, see Num. 6:1–21. Normally, the Nazirite vow is taken for a set amount of time and not from birth (13:1–16:31 note).
She fails to recognize that it really is the Angel of the Lord (6:22; 13:16).
They repeat Gideon's hospitality (6:19).
Jacob asks the same question (Gen. 32:29).
The incidents here parallel episodes in Gideon's life (6:20–22).
**LORD** blessed him. Cf. God's blessing upon Samuel (1 Sam. 2:26; 3:19) and His blessing upon Jesus (Luke 2:52).
**LORD** . See note on 3:10.

Immediately after learning that the Lord is with Samson and that the Spirit has begun to stir in him (13:25), the reader is told that Samson seeks a wife from among the Philistines (14:1–2). In this section, Samson's prodigious strength, poetic abilities, and intense pride and temper are revealed. The narrative revolves around the pursuit and loss of the Philistine wife and the consequences for both Philistia and Samson. In the course of these events, it is possible that Samson breaks the Nazirite vow by touching a dead thing (14:8, 9) and by drinking wine (v. 10). If so, all that remains is for him to cut his hair. Three times the Spirit of the Lord comes on him, and he kills his enemies. He leads Israel for twenty years (15:20). Based on the accounts of the other judges, the reader expects the narrative to end at this point. However, Samson continues to be distracted by foreign women, and the story concludes with his consequent demise (ch. 16). 14:1–2 The verbs "went down" and "came up" reflect the geography of the story: the Israelites have settled mainly in the highland areas, and the Phil­istines live in the coastal plain. Thus, Samson goes down to Timnah, which is located at the site of Tel Batash. Excavations there have revealed a thriving Philistine city from the early Iron Age.
Israelites must not marry foreign wives (3:1–6; 14:3; cf. Deut. 7:3–4; 1 Kin. 11:1–6; Ezra 9–10).
she is right in my eyes. Samson's desire to take this woman as his wife illustrates a motif in Judges: "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 21:25).

**LORD**. This is one of only two times that Samson is mentioned as having spoken to the Lord (16:28). shall I now die of thirst. Like the Israelites who experienced miracle upon miracle in the wilderness, Samson complains to God. The parallel is marked by the cry for water and the miraculous manner in which God supplies it (v. 19; Ex. 17:1–7; Num. 20:1–13). Both Israel and Samson complain to God, but God in His mercy and compassion meets their need (cf. Ex. 16).

The typical signal for the end of the story, but not so here (14:1–15:20 note). Unlike all of the earlier judges except Jephthah (12:7), Samson does not lead Israel for a full generation (forty years).

This account contains two parallel stories showing Samson's desire for women, his prodigious strength, and the efforts the Philistines make to capture him. Samson's continual covenant breaking is judged by God when he is finally captured by the Philistines and blinded (vv. 21, 22). Delilah's attempts to snare Samson reveal Samson to be a fool for remaining with her. It is noteworthy that the Spirit of God leaves him only when his hair is cut, not at an earlier point of his covenant breaking. God is patient with Samson until the last sign of his vow is gone, and then God judges him. 16:1 Gaza \... a prostitute. A common prostitute, not a temple prostitute, from one of the Philistines' pentapolis cities. Samson once again breaks the covenant (14:2).
Indicates an incredible feat of strength and endurance because the distance from Gaza to Hebron is approximately forty miles (64 km) and uphill.

Lit. "drove the peg," the same expression used of Jael's thrusting a tent peg into Sisera's temple. The similarity is that both men, Sisera and Samson, are unaware of great danger from the hands of women.
