Samson is taken to serve in the city from which he earlier stole one of its gates (vv. 1–3).

A god of agriculture and the main deity of the Philistines. His name means "grain," a fitting name in that the Philistine plain was an excellent area for growing grain. Dagon was once thought to be the fish-god because the common Semitic word for fish is dag, but this reconstruction is unlikely. Our god has given. God is the judge who allows oppressors to mistreat His people on account of their sin (v. 20); it is not the power of the gods of the nations that enables them to overcome Israel (2:14, 15).

**GOD**. Samson's final plea is to avenge the loss of his sight. The writer does not comment on this motive. God in His grace answers the prayer and allows Samson to kill the enemies of Israel (10:10–16; 15:18, 19).

A Philistine temple from the time of the judges that was constructed with two pillars that support the roof of the whole building has been discovered at the site of Tell Qasile. This design and construction are unlike either Canaanite or Israelite temples of the Iron Age.
See note on 13:1–16:31.
See note on 15:20.

This section is a twofold conclusion that focuses on chaos in worship (17:1–18:31) and chaos in morality (19:1–21:25) rising from the apostasy recounted in the body of the book of Judges. The section is held together by a refrain highlighting the anarchy that has resulted from the lack of proper leadership: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). 17:1–18:31 This section, recounting the Danite idolatry, is part of the conclusion to Judges. The phrases "In those days there was no king in Israel" (17:6; 18:1) and "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6) are repeated in the last section of the narrative cycles (19:1; 21:25). Without a king, the people lack moral direction from a God-appointed leader.

The story starts abruptly with the return of stolen goods. The mother seems to be unsurprised. No reason is provided for why Micah absconded with the silver. His theft of the silver from his mother implies that he disregards two of the Ten Commandments.

**LORD** \... to make a carved image and a metal image. This statement is highly ironic. She uses the covenantal name for the God of Israel, Yahweh. However well intentioned, consecrating the silver in this way violates the second commandment (Ex. 20:4; Deut. 5:8), an indication of the spiritual ignorance of the period.
See 8:27 and note.

See 18:1; 19:1; 21:25. The refrain comments on the ignorance of Micah and his mother that is typical of the time. They make idols in the name of the Lord and appoint their own priest. Not only is there political anarchy in the land, but this story highlights the reality of spiritual anarchy as well.

The Levites have no allotment of land in Israel except for forty-eight Levitical cities distributed among the other tribes. Bethlehem is not a Levitical city, so this Levite is sojourning among the people of Judah. Levite. The Levites' inheritance is to serve the Lord at His dwelling place, the tabernacle (Deut. 18:1–8; Josh. 13:14, 33; 14:3, 4).
That is, in a religious sense.
That the Levite is "content" with the arrangement shows complete insensitivity to apostasy. An appointed officer of the tabernacle is serving an idol.
The religious corruption in this story is highlighted by Micah's ordination of a Le­vite to the office of priest.
A foolish statement (v. 3 note; 17:1–18:31 note) that further illustrates the darkened understanding of the time, descending to the level of superstition.

The repetition (see also 17:6) subtly indicates from the very outset of the narrative that the Danites are doing what is right in their own eyes. no king in Israel. See note on 17:6. no inheritance \... had fallen to them. The Danites have failed to conquer the portion assigned to them (1:34–36). They are in violation of the covenant.
They are imitating their forefathers (Num. 13:2, 12).
That is, the distinctive accent of the young man from the south of Israel (cf. 12:6).
Priests in ancient Israel apparently used an ephod to seek the will of the Lord (8:27 and note).
**LORD**. The tragic irony of this story — the Levite ministering to idols; Micah's absurd confidence (17:13) — cancels the validity of such a benediction uttered by unholy lips.

The region in which this city sits is frontier territory where the inhabitants dwell in unfortified towns and villages, making for great difficulty in trying to repel a Danite attack. This city is renamed Dan, and it becomes infamous when Jeroboam I sets up his golden calf at the site (1 Kin. 12:28–30). quiet and unsuspecting. This whole list (17:5) is repeated three times in the next six verses (vv. 17, 18, 20) and is twice referred to more generally (vv. 27, 30, 31).

The Danites' action is a kind of parody of the conquest of the land begun earlier under Joshua. They go in the strength of overwhelming numbers against a single household rather than in the strength of the Lord against a fierce enemy. The armed men are mentioned twice as standing outside the door.
See note on 17:10.
He is happy for advancement. He took the ephod \... carved image. The priest is going to lead Dan in false worship as he had Micah's household.
That is, to protect them from an attack from behind.
Micah is a pathetic figure, believing that God will bless so-called obedience in any way that he chooses to offer it (17:13).

See v. 14. a people quiet and unsuspecting. The Israelites were to destroy only the seven proscribed Canaanite nations (Deut. 7:1). To other peoples they were first to offer peace (Deut. 20:10–18). The tribe of Dan does not ask who these people are (Josh. 9:1–27) and may destroy an innocent population. Moreover, this is not the land God allotted them (Josh. 19:47).

An example of what it means for everyone to do what is right in his own eyes in the absence of a king (v. 14; 17:6). Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses. The Levite whom Micah hired (17:10, 13). That apostasy has infected even the lineage of Moses was too much to bear for some scribes. Scribal emendation of this text is commonly found in various manuscripts, and it reads "Jonathan the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh" (see text note). until the day. Since v. 31 specifies that Micah's idol is set up as long as "the house of God was at Shiloh," the captivity mentioned here is the time of oppression that will begin with the Philistine victory near Shiloh, when the ark is removed from there (1 Sam. 4:4, 11). The captivity in Babylon occurs much later.

That is, the tabernacle, which is at Shiloh up to the time of Samuel (Josh. 18:1; 1 Sam. 3:21; 4:3) before David's reign. The ark is taken by Eli's sons from Shiloh into battle and lost to the Philistines (1 Sam. 4:4–11). After that, the ark is never in Shiloh again.

The situation in Israel has deteriorated so much that some of God's people behave like the people of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:1–11). Civil war between the tribes is the result. This final story in the conclusion of Judges blames the misery of Israel on the lack of a king (19:1; 21:25; cf. 17:6; 18:1). Benjamin is the tribe that sins. Even more, it is the men of Gibeah, Saul's hometown, who behave like the people of Sodom. Saul's action in 1 Sam. 11:6–8 recalls the Levite's desecration of his concubine (19:29 note). Finally, Judah, the tribe of David, is the Lord's choice to be the leader against Benjamin (note the similarity of wording between 1:1, 2 and 20:18). The Benjaminites have practically become Canaanites. No one is without fault, however. Each tribe is doing as it sees fit (21:25). The conclusion to be drawn is that a king is needed — a king from Judah and not Benjamin. David, not Saul, will qualify. Yet even David, being only a man, proves unequal to the task, as later developments show (2 Sam. 12:10, 11). The Lord alone, whom the people have rejected (1 Sam. 8:7, 8), can be their true king (8:22, 23). 19:1 Levite. This man is from the tribe that serves the Lord as His priests. concubine. In this era, a concubine is usually a slave and has a lower legal status than a wife (8:31; 9:18).
The law demands the stoning of adulterers (Deut. 22:22), but the people are not following the law (17:6; 21:25).
See 1:21 and note.

Ironically, they refuse to lodge with foreigners, only to find that their fellow Israelites are no better than the residents of Sodom (19:1–21:25 note). Gibeah. When Judges was written, Gibeah was well known as the hometown of Saul (19:1–21:25 note).

The story of what happened to the Levite in Gibeah is similar to the story of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:1–13). Gibeah's sin is like that of the men of Sodom, and the Benjaminites are largely destroyed by the Lord's permission and assistance (20:18, 28, 35). Saul is from Benjamin, and these events foreshadow his own failure as Israel's leader.
In this manner, the travelers advertise their need for hospitality (vv. 16–20).
It takes another foreigner from another generation to show hospitality.
LORD. That is, to the tabernacle in Shiloh (18:31).
See Gen. 19:5.

Whatever else may be said, according to the customs of hospitality, the host cannot contemplate surrendering his guest to violence. In the law, the sexual act contemplated is described as "an abomination" (Lev. 18:22; 20:13).

As Lot offered his daughters to protect his guests (Gen. 19:8), the host offers his daughter to protect the Levite. The author does not comment on the morality of this offer, but the whole story is presented as a final illustration of the evil consequences of forsaking God's rule and doing what is right in one's own eyes.
The Levite gives his concubine to the men. There is no mention of the old man's daughter being given to them.
The Levite displays no concern for the well-being of his concubine. The narrator underlines his callous behavior.
She is dead.

It is often assumed that the Levite divides the concubine into twelve parts and then sends one piece to each tribe to draw attention to Benjamin's horrific deed in Gibeah. However, the text says that he sends "her" throughout all the land of Israel, that is, her whole body cut into twelve pieces. It is thus to be a symbol to anyone who sees it that Israel is not one entity but is acting as a divided body. The original audience of Judges was well aware of how Saul later cut up oxen into twelve parts in order to summon Israel to fight against the Ammonites (1 Sam. 11:6–8).
Refers to the grotesque use of the woman's body. The downward ethical and spiritual spiral of Israel is accentuated by this statement.

The attack upon the Levite and his concubine results in civil war between all Israel and Benjamin (ch. 19). Repeated references to Israel's oneness (vv. 1, 2, 8, 11) makes an important point: the Israelites are united for the first time in the book. Although their action is not unjust, it is sad that they finally unite only in order to punish one of their own number (v. 23). Judah is to lead against Benjamin as it had led against the Canaanites (v. 18; 1:1, 2 and notes). 20:1 from Dan to Beersheba. A biblical idiom to denote the entirety of Israel. assembled as one man. For the first time Israel is united, but the purpose is to wage war against her brothers. to the **LORD** at Mizpah. See note on 11:11. Saul is later made king at Mizpah.
After the repeated cycle of sin, judgment, and deliverance, it is an evidence of God's mercy that Israel is still called His people.
The Levite omits the details of how the concubine has been offered (19:23, 24).
See vv. 1, 11, and note on 20:1–48. The Israelites take an oath to see this through to the end.
The Israelites do not see the evil that pervaded their community.
See note on 3:15.

The ark of the Lord and the priest with the ephod are at Bethel at this time (v. 27). Who shall go up first. The same language that is used at the beginning of Judges, where the question to be decided is who should lead against the Canaanites (1:1). Judah. The Lord gives the same answer as in 1:2 in a different situation.
**LORD**. See vv. 18, 27, 28; cf. 1 Sam. 28:6. our brothers, the people of Benjamin. The Israelites now add the word "brothers" to their inquiry (v. 18).
The Israelites treat the Benjaminites like the Canaanites (1:8, 17). Moreover, the Benjamin­ites' end is like that of the inhabitants of Sodom (19:14–20:48 note).

The actions of Israel in this final episode should be interpreted in light of the concluding comment: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (v. 25). The Israelites wonder why this evil has come upon them (vv. 3, 15; 6:13 note). As with Gideon (6:13), no answer is given explicitly. Yet the book's larger context gives the clear answer: Israel has sinned and continues to sin in horrible ways.

This city is located on the east side of the Jordan River. The inhabitants obviously do not feel threatened by the situation in Benjamin, and thus they do not heed the call to arms. Saul's first act as king is to defend Jabesh-gilead. Since he was a Benjaminite from Gibeah, Saul may have descended from one of the women taken from Jabesh-gilead (v. 12).
**LORD** had made a breach in the tribes of Israel. God does this to punish the Benjaminites for their sin.

Israel's degeneracy is now so complete that they even propose and allow the kidnapping of their own women to avoid breaking a rash vow. The nation is indeed acting — unchecked — in accord with its own sinful inclinations (v. 25; cf. 17:6).

Israel's hope is directed toward a godly human king who will reflect the Lord's righteous kingship. This hope will be fulfilled temporarily by David, but it finds everlasting fulfillment in David's greater Son, Jesus Christ (Matt. 1:1–14; Rom. 1:1–4).

Ruth.note: The preface moves quickly through the necessary background (time, place, and source of conflict), setting the stage for the scenes that follow. 1:1 In the days when the judges ruled. The period of the judges in Israel was infamous as a time of instability and apostasy. The final verse of the book of Judges summarizes the moral quality of the time: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judg. 21:25). a famine. Famine in ancient Israel was a common calamity: Abraham fled to Egypt due to a famine (Gen. 12:10); Jacob led the Hebrews to Egypt because of a severe famine (Genesis 42–45). Famines were often understood as a sign of God's displeasure (Lev. 26:18–20; 1 Kin. 17:1). The occurrence of a famine at this time reflects Israel's overall disobedience and unfaithfulness during the period of the judges. Bethlehem in Judah. This city lies in the tribal region of Judah. This distinctive name first occurs in the final chapters of Judges (17:7–9; 19:1, 2, 18) and in the opening verses of Ruth (vv. 1, 2). Bethlehem means "house of food," but at this point the house of food is empty. to sojourn. A technical term in antiquity for someone living as an alien in a foreign land. It describes the social standing of one who works in a foreign country but has few of the rights and privileges of a native citizen. country of Moab. Lit. "fields of Moab." Moabites, who were related to Israel through Lot (Gen. 19:37), occupied parts of central Transjordan at various times. Although God protected them at first from the Israelite invaders (Deut. 2:9), the Moabites were subjugated by Saul (1 Sam. 14:47) and then by David (2 Sam. 8:2). See also Deut. 23:3. There were some periods of friendly relations, with considerable cultural and economic interchange, as shown by David's placement of his parents with the king of Moab while he was a fugitive (1 Sam. 22:3). During the period of the judges, in which the book of Ruth takes place, there were times of hostility between Israel and Moab (see Judg. 3:12–30).

Lit. "my God is king." There is irony in the fact that Elimelech's actions belie his name: he does not trust God, his king, to provide for him in the Promised Land, and so he moves to a pagan land where he dies. The ensuing drama emphasizes the role of the women in the family as they demonstrate the trust in the Lord that Elimelech lacked (4:14, 16). Naomi. Lit. "pleasant/sweet" (vv. 20, 21). Naomi's story is told first. Mahlon and Chilion. Like their father, Mahlon (lit. "illness") and Chilion (lit. "destruction") die outside the Promised Land.

These marriages are ill-advised. Biblical law demands that the Israelites not intermarry with pagan peoples (e.g., Deut. 7:1–4). The irony is that an heir, and an ancestor of the great king David, will come through one of these foreigners. God will take these questionable marriages and redeem them for His own glory and purposes. Orpah. The meaning of this name is not certain, but it may be related to "stubborn," which is consistent with Orpah's decision to stay in Moab. Ruth. This name sounds like the Hebrew word for "friend," and Ruth's actions epitomize covenant friendship.

Naomi is an elderly widow, a sojourner in a foreign land, with two Moabite daughters-in-law who are also widows and childless. She is completely empty at this point and seems an unlikely prospect for any role in the Lord's covenantal history of redemption.

These verses set the stage for vv. 8–18. The women must decide what factors will determine their paths: finding a husband and having children, living in one's own country, being close to one's family, or (finally, for Ruth) trusting in the sovereign Lord of Israel and the only true God. Naomi's love for her daughters-in-law and her reaction to bitter experiences at God's hand dominate this scene. Ruth's decision and her irrevocable vow of fidelity to Naomi's people and her God say much about the impact of Naomi's character and faith on her daughter-in-law. 1:6 the Lord had visited his people. A note of hope is sounded. Ruth's story never loses sight of God, whose faithful love determines history.
This initial declaration of both daughters heightens the dramatic tension.

Naomi's talk of raising up sons to replace the missing husbands only exaggerates her loss. The idea itself may refer to the law of levirate marriage. According to this law, if a man dies leaving a widow, his brother is obligated to marry the widow, taking his place and preserving the family line (Deut. 25:5, 6). The term "levirate" derives from the Latin levir, which means "husband's brother." There is also a custom that when someone dies, a close relative (or redeemer) is supposed to buy (or redeem) the deceased's estate (2:20 note).
**LORD** has gone out against me. Naomi understands that no matter what happens to her, good or ill, her circumstances are playing out according to the providence of God.

A new element is introduced. It becomes clear that the choice of homeland is a choice for or against the true God. Against the background of Orpah's choice, the courage and beauty of Ruth's declaration (vv. 16, 17) are all the more obvious.

This verse includes four constructions known as idem per idem, a literary device in which the same verb or noun is used of one person's actions and then of another person's actions. It is used to underscore the intensity of the action as well as the totality of commitment.

As noted in 1:2, Naomi's name means "sweet." She does not want to be called this anymore because this name does not reflect her current life situation. She now wants to be called "Mara," a Hebrew word meaning "bitter" (cf. 1:13).

She is not just any Ruth. For the story it is crucial that she be remembered as a foreigner (1:4; 2:2, 6, 21; 4:5, 10; esp. 2:10). Also, the reader is prompted to think of Ruth's ancestor, Lot's daughter, and the incestuous beginnings of the Moabite nation (Gen. 19:30–38). In both cases, the problem is childlessness or lack of a male heir. barley harvest. Early calendars, like the Gezer calendar from the tenth century B.C.., associated months with the agricultural cycle. Barley was the first of the cereals to be harvested, in April; wheat was the last. In later tradition the barley and wheat harvests came to be identified with the festivals of Passover and Pentecost. The season of harvest was a time of celebration, rejoicing together before God, and remembering the poor. The narrative development is tied to this scheme. The women return home at the barley harvest, a time of God's favor and the beginning of fruitful restoration for Naomi.

Ch. 2 introduces the last main character, Boaz, and the major theme, that of the close relative, or redeemer, who has certain responsibilities for the family and property of a relative who dies (2:20 note). The narrator, who already knows what is ahead, gives only a hint with the description of Boaz as "a relative" in v. 1. Only after the natural kindness of Boaz and the natural winsomeness of Ruth have taken their course does Naomi reveal the key to the entire story: Boaz is "a close relative" (2:20). Even then, no claims are made; there is no appeal to custom. Events must wait their time; while Naomi plans, Ruth serves quietly, and Boaz finishes the harvest. However, God had already provided an answer through the law (Leviticus 25). 2:1 relative. Or "acquaintance." The Hebrew text leaves the technical status of Boaz unclear, but the story unfolds as if he is the one described in Lev. 25:25 as the "nearest redeemer," whose responsibility relates primarily but not exclusively to the property of an impoverished relative (1:11; 2:20 and notes). Later (2:20; 3:9), Boaz will be identified as a "close relative," but at this point he is introduced to prepare the reader for the events that place Ruth in his field. worthy. This Hebrew word describes someone powerful and important in society. Boaz. Lit. "in him is strength," and Boaz shows himself to be a man of strong covenant character.

Ruth's initiative, on the surface, is simply to keep herself and Naomi alive, according to a custom codified in Leviticus (19:9, 10; 23:22) and Deuteronomy (24:19). As poor people, Ruth and Naomi will receive some help, but much more is about to come their way. A hint of this provision is given in Ruth's plaintive request that she might glean "after him in whose sight I shall find favor."
From Ruth's perspective, where she ends up working is mere happenstance. However, in reality, all is unfolding according to the mysterious providence of God.
Boaz's arrival satisfies the expectations raised in vv. 1–3.

The servant's answer establishes Ruth's character. She is faithful, having come while still in her youth to a foreign country for the sake of her mother-in-law. She is hardworking, having been busy since morning.

Events unfold quickly as Boaz accedes to the request and offers his protection and provision (vv. 8, 9). Ruth acknowledges his favor to her, an undeserving "foreigner" (v. 10). Only then does the narrative give some inkling of God's providential working (vv. 11, 12). Boaz already knows that Ruth is no ordinary foreigner. She has taken "refuge" under the "wings" of the Lord, and she will receive "a full reward" from Him (v. 12). Though a foreigner, Ruth's loyalty to God is a key element in God's great plan of redemption. The plan will be worked out through two of Ruth's descendants: David, the covenant king, and Christ, David's greatest son. The reward of Ruth's faith far transcends local time and circumstances.
There is a wordplay here, as the term "foreigner" is related to the verb "to take notice of."
A frequent image of safety and protection in the Psalms (17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 61:4; 63:7; 91:4).
Boaz's permission is clearly extraordinary. 2:14 wine. A sour but refreshing drink or dip (cf. Num. 6:3).

Beating out the grain, or threshing it, separates the kernels from the husks, chaff, and stalks. An ephah is a measure of dry capacity equal to three-fifths of a bushel, or about thirty pounds (13 kg) of barley.
What she set aside from her noon meal (v. 14).

God is faithful, and He will not forget the ones He loves. The blessings He promises will pass from Boaz to Ruth to Naomi, and eventually to all the elect. close relative of ours. The law of redemption now comes into view. According to this law, the nearest male blood relative has the duty of preserving the family name and property. This duty might entail avenging the death of a family member (Num. 35:19–21); buying back family property that was sold to pay debts (Lev. 25:25); buying back a relative who sold himself into slavery to pay debts (Lev. 25:47–49); and levirate marriage, marrying the widow of a deceased relative (Deut. 25:5–10). Apparently, these duties can be renounced or declined under certain circumstances (cf. Ruth 3:12; 4:1–8). Boaz is such a "close relative" (or "redeemer") to Ruth, and this fact now determines the course of action (1:11; 2:1 and notes). Ruth's destiny will proceed according to the law, unlike that of her ancestor, Lot's daughter, who committed incest (Gen. 19:30–38).
The time of Ruth's labor amounts to approximately three months in the fields.

Now the narrative moves toward resolution. In a late-night visit, Ruth carries out and expands Naomi's plan, putting her own reputation and all her expectations at risk. She claims the protection of Boaz as a "redeemer" (v. 9). Her trust in his character is vindicated, and she is unharmed. God's activity behind the scenes continues without a break. But even at this moment, the engagement must be delayed; there is a closer relative (3:12), and Boaz, a man of outstanding honor, will not rest until this obstacle is removed. 3:1 rest for you. This means that Ruth should be married, a need that Naomi has taken to heart (1:9).

A cleared area where grain is crushed or torn to separate the chaff, straw, and grains. The harvest is then winnowed, or thrown into the air for the wind to blow away the chaff as the grains fall directly to the ground. All this takes place in the spring at the time of the harvest festivals.

A highly symbolic act. By coming to the threshing floor and lying at Boaz's feet, Ruth is asking Boaz to marry her. She is, in effect, saying she wants to be redeemed, and she awaits Boaz's judgment in the matter. lie down. Ruth lies patiently at Boaz's feet until he awakens (vv. 8, 9); nothing unseemly happens between them during the night (v. 11).

Boaz has been drinking but is hardly drunk. He is content and fulfilled with his day's labor and his evening meal. After all the work of the day, Boaz goes to "the end of the heap of grain," a place where Ruth is able to meet him privately. God's providence is clearing a path for her.

Boaz has wished for protection for Ruth under God's wings (2:12); Ruth now gives Boaz the opportunity to be the answer to his own prayer. See text note. Ezek. 16:8 explains the idiom. Ruth asks directly for the favor of marriage, although Naomi's instructions were not quite so bold (v. 4). redeemer. The law does not specify marriage as the responsibility of such a person, though an extension of Leviticus 25 can readily be envisioned. Mahlon's name and property will be preserved (4:10), suggesting the levirate marriage, but it is difficult to see how Deut. 25:5, 6 can be strictly applied.

Lit. "covenant love." Throughout the book, God's own covenant love (1:8; 2:20) is mirrored by that of Ruth (1:8, 16, 17). Now her faithfulness is proved as she invokes the duties of a close relative and declines to follow any of the young men. The "kindness" Boaz refers to is evidently Ruth's proposal to follow the custom that will provide an heir for Naomi. the first. When she chose to accompany Naomi.

The feminine equivalent of the Hebrew phrase in 2:1. Ruth has risen from being a Moabite and servant to becoming attractive to Boaz as a possible marriage partner. In the Hebrew canon, the book of Ruth follows the book of Proverbs. In the last section of Proverbs, the author asks, "A worthy woman who can find?" one whose "works praise her in the gates?" (Prov. 31:30, 31). The answer is immediate in the Hebrew canon: Boaz has found a "worthy woman" who is praised in the gates, one who is known for her selflessness and her covenant love for Naomi (2:8–13).

Boaz suddenly mentions a complicating factor. Hebrew law appears to mandate an order of rank of kinsman-redeemers (Lev. 25:47–49), and there is a closer kinsman than Boaz who has the first right of acceptance or refusal. The custom of redemption seems to be leading to a solution, but now it creates a problem along the way. The engagement must be postponed.

This gift of barley shows Boaz's magnanimity toward Ruth (v. 17) and is a symbol of Naomi's changed estate (1:21). Ruth receives grain from Boaz as an emblem of her future fruitfulness. Then she went into the city. Lit. "Then he went into the city." The latter makes perfectly good sense: as soon as Boaz gives his word to Ruth, he goes directly into Bethlehem to fulfill his oath.
The same Hebrew words are translated "Who are you?" in v. 9.
The grain serves as a token and pledge not only to Ruth but also to Naomi. It is a visible sign of a promise.
This is an ironic touch, for the time to wait will be very short. Naomi does not expect a conclusion to be long in coming.

Ch. 4 brings out the divine purpose behind Ruth's original decision to follow Naomi and Naomi's God. The necessary arrangements seem to turn on a combination of levirate marriage regulations (Deut. 25:5–10) and the laws for a redeeming relative (Lev. 25). Ruth is taken as a wife, and ancient blessings for fruitfulness are invoked. Naomi's bitterness turns to joy, and her grandson is shown to be the grandfather of King David. In these events the Lord's hidden providence is revealed. 4:1 the gate. Excavations at Iron Age Israelite sites have revealed a number of gateways with built-in benches where the elders sat in judgment (e.g., Megiddo and Gezer). The city gates were an area of economic activity. friend. Boaz must know the man's name, but the narrator quotes Boaz as referring to the man with an indefinite phrase, something like the English expression "Mr. So-and-So." Because the other names in the book are related to one's character, it is likely that this man has no name because he has no character. For the purposes of the story, he is "Mr. No Name."

There is no recorded legal requirement for a particular number of men. The later Jewish tradition by which ten men make up a quorum for worship may derive from this incident. In a rural culture, where the use of writing was limited, it was important for a contract to be made with a number of official witnesses.

This sale is a surprising new element, no hint of which has been given up to now. Details about the sale are not necessary for the story and are omitted. A parallel example can be seen in Jer. 32:6–15.
Little is known about the symbolism of this custom. Its point clearly is to confirm the transaction legally. See Deut. 25:9, 10 (a different setting) and Amos 8:6.
The OT considers the disappearance of one's name an extreme misfortune (1 Sam. 24:21; 2 Sam. 14:7).

These are the two wives of Jacob (Israel), the mothers, either naturally or through their maids Zilpah and Bilhah, of all the sons of Israel, the heads of the twelve tribes. Ephrathah \... Bethlehem. As in 1:1, 2, these place names, associated with David, are given special prominence.

In a much earlier time, Judah became the father of Perez because Onan refused to carry out his obligation as a close relative (Gen. 38:29). Perez is a symbol of the fruitful offspring. In the same way, Boaz becomes the father of Obed (v. 21) because another person has refused to carry out the levirate obligation. Despite human failures, the messianic line is preserved (Matt. 1:3, 5, 16). Interestingly, strong parallels exist between Tamar and Ruth, both of whom are women and foreigners who play key roles in continuing the messianic line.
**LORD** gave her conception. This statement underscores the providence of God in the story.

The women's praises celebrate the fulfillment of God's covenant love to Naomi. Her daughter-in-law Ruth is more to her than seven sons would be (v. 15). Moreover, Naomi in effect has a son in her grandson Obed (v. 17). He will become the grandfather of David. Remarkably, the infant Obed is described by the women of Bethlehem as a redeemer. This implies that the line of Boaz is associated with the concept of redemption. Ultimately, Jesus Christ is the Redeemer of the world.

This is probably not a formal rite of adoption. Rather, it is a symbol that Naomi views the child as her own in a manner of speaking. He is the heir of Elimelech's estate and the continuation of her husband's lineage.
Lit. "servant," because he will serve Naomi in her old age.

The closing genealogy is almost exactly what is recorded in the genealogy of Jesus in Matt. 1:3–6. The book of Ruth finds its climax in the coming of the Messiah, Jesus Christ. The main characters, Boaz and Ruth, have faded from the story. The emphasis is now on the lineage that points to Christ. The coming of the Messiah is the end-all of the book of Ruth.

Here and in v. 17, the author mentions ancient Israel's greatest king explicitly. We are not to view the book of Ruth as merely a story of honorable people in a dishonorable era, but as the account of God's providence and grace in providing a king who gives rest to His people Israel (2 Sam. 7:1–17). Of course, David fails to give Israel permanent rest, but in providing a son for Naomi, the Lord also preserves a lineage that births David's greatest son, Jesus Christ, who gives rest to all who trust in Him (Matt. 11:28–30).

1 Samuel.note: God rules and delivers His people before the time of the monarchy. He does so by raising up Samuel (chs. 1–3), intervening directly against the Philistines (4:1–7:1), and giving Samuel victory over the Philistines (7:2–17). 1:1 a certain man. This expression and the accompanying genealogy suggest that Elkanah is a man of standing. The reference to a barren wife (v. 2) resembles the introduction to the birth of Samson (Judg. 13:2). Ramathaim-zophim. Possibly meaning "twin heights," the name occurs only here in the OT. It may be the same location as the NT Arimathea (northwest of Bethel). Samuel's hometown is usually called Ramah, about five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem (1:19; 2:11; 7:17; 8:4; 15:34; 19:18; 25:1). of Zuph. "Zuph" is both a personal name (1 Chr. 6:35) and a territory (9:5). Ephrathite. Ephraim is the place he is from, not necessarily the tribe of his ancestry (1 Chr. 6:16–30, 33–37).

Monogamy is God's design for humanity (Gen. 2:18–25). Polygamy is first mentioned in Gen. 4:19. It is possibly recognized and regulated, though not endorsed, in Deut. 21:15–17, although this passage may address a situation in which a man remarries after the death of his first wife. no children. Hannah is childless and is provoked by her fertile rival (vv. 6, 7). A barren but favored wife who receives a special offspring from Yahweh is not uncommon in the OT. See Gen. 18:1–15 (Sarah/Isaac); 25:21–26 (Rebekah/Esau and Jacob); 30:22–24 (Rachel/Joseph); and Judg. 13:2–5 (Manoah's wife/Samson). In the NT, see Luke 1:5–25 (Elizabeth/John).

Perhaps he observes "the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh" (Judg. 21:19), or perhaps he goes for a family ceremony (20:6). In the Pentateuch, reference is made to three annual pilgrim feasts (Ex. 23:14–17; 34:18–23; Deut. 16:1–17).

The Hebrew is difficult but has usually been interpreted as an especially honorable portion or perhaps a double portion. Elkanah's attempts to lessen Hannah's sorrow by expressing his love for her (v. 8) are ineffective. the **LORD** had closed her womb. Hannah's barrenness comes not by chance or as a form of punishment (2 Sam. 6:23) but is under the Lord's sovereign control.
See note on 1:2.

Hannah refuses to eat until the Lord answers her prayer; cf. David's actions in 2 Sam. 12:16–20 and Saul's in 1 Sam. 28:23–25. In the NT, fasting often accompanies serious dealings with the Lord (Acts 13:2, 3; 14:23).

The mention of a "doorpost" here and "doors" in 3:15, as well as sleeping quarters in 3:2, 3, may suggest a more permanent structure than the tent of Moses's time. Other designations for the structure in Samuel are "the house of the LORD" (v. 7; 3:15) and "the tent of meeting" (2:22). From 2 Sam. 7:6 it is clear that in the era before the time of David, the tabernacle or temple is a tent and not a permanent structure.

On the making of vows by married women and the husbands' responsibility to confirm or nullify, see Num. 30:6–15. remember me. Hannah asks not simply for the Lord to keep her in mind but for Him to do something special to help her. no razor. Hannah's vow reflects elements of the Nazirite vow (Num. 6:1–21), which includes abstaining from grapes or anything made from grapes, not cutting the hair, and avoiding all contact with dead bodies. While such vows are generally made for a limited period of time, Hannah's is for "all the days" of her son's life (cf. Judg. 13:5 note).

Eli's conclusion that Hannah is drunk is an unsettling element in the narrative because it suggests that he is unfamiliar with fervency in prayer. Drunkenness in the tabernacle precincts is a severe offense, particularly priests, who are to be executed for ministering in such a condition (Lev. 10:9).
Lit. a "daughter of Belial," which is an idiom for a worthless person. The word "Belial" is later used of Eli's own sons (2:12).
Hannah's actions in response to the benediction of v. 17 give evidence of her belief.

Various meanings of the name "Samuel" have been suggested, including "heard by God," "he who is from God," "name of God," and even "son of God" (as one "given" or "promised" by God). Regardless of the linguistic etymology, "heard of God" is the folk etymology: Hannah asked and her prayer was heard by God. "Saul" is also from the Hebrew verb "to ask" (8:10 note).
See Lev. 7:16 and note.
In the ancient Near East a child was weaned later than is customary today. Weaning may also have been celebrated with a feast (Gen. 21:8).
"Your word" is also a plausible translation here. Elkanah, as Hannah's husband (1:11 note), invokes the Lord's assistance in Hannah's fulfillment of her vow.
According to Num. 15:8–10, the fulfillment of a vow is to be accompanied by an offering of a young bull, fine flour, and wine. Hannah brings all three but in larger measure than required.

Her prayer for a son having been answered, Hannah offers a jubilant song of thanksgiving. Focusing on the Lord's sovereignty and the exaltation of the humble, Hannah anticipates the major themes of the books of Samuel. The same themes of sovereignty, grace, and deliverance are reiterated in David's song of thanksgiving near the end of 2 Samuel (ch. 22). The two songs provide a poetic frame for 1 and 2 Samuel. Mary's briefer song of praise (the Magnificat, Luke 1:46–55) seems to be modeled on Hannah's. The settings of the two stories are similar: a childless woman receives God's intervention in the birth of a son. Both descendants grow up to deliver their people. Both songs open with rejoicing in the Lord's deliverance (v. 1; Luke 1:46–48), extol the Lord's uniqueness and holiness (v. 2; Luke 1:49, 50), condemn proud boasting (v. 3; Luke 1:51), point to reversals of human fortune as the result of interventions by the sovereign Lord (vv. 4–8; Luke 1:52, 53), and express the Lord's faithful care for His own (v. 9; Luke 1:54, 55). Hannah's song concludes with the assertion that the Lord Himself will give strength to His king, His anointed (vv. 9–10). 2:1 horn. It is God who exalts the strength of the righteous but cuts off the strength of the wicked (Ps. 75:10).

As a metaphor for God, this term is concentrated in poetic passages such as the song of Moses in Deut. 32; the song of David in 2 Sam. 22; Psalms; and Isaiah. The metaphor suggests God's strength and sovereignty and the security of those who trust in Him. Here the focus is on the uniqueness of the one true God as opposed to false sources of security (cf. false gods, also called "rock," in Deut. 32:31, 37; Is. 44:8).
The number seven represents ideal completeness (see Ruth 4:15).

Hannah's acknowledgment of the actions of the Lord takes the form of four merisms. A merism is a figure of speech in which two opposite terms signify inclusiveness. As these words express, the Lord is sovereign over all things.

Hannah's reference to God's raising the poor to sit with princes highlights an important theme in the books of Samuel. Those who display humility are promoted to king. However, the reverse is also true. Arrogance and pride are important factors in the divine rejection of Saul.

The subsequent narratives confirm that it is not physical prowess but God's presence that brings success. In the ark narrative of chs. 4–6, the Lord makes His hand felt by the Philistines without the assistance of human agents (5:6). Other such examples are the Lord's victory through Samuel in ch. 7; the contrasting successes of Saul and Jonathan in chs. 13, 14; the choice of David, the youngest of Jesse's sons, in ch. 16; and David's victory over Goliath in ch. 17.

The reference to the Lord's king here points forward to the central event of the books of Samuel, namely, the institution of a monarchy, and implies that the idea of kingship, properly conceived, is not wrong. That Israel will have a king is anticipated in various places in the Pentateuch (Gen. 49:10; Num. 24:7, 17–19; Deut. 17:14–20). exalt the horn. The horn is a symbol of power that derives from the picture of the strength of a goring animal such as a bull (v. 1 and note). his anointed. Numerous objects and persons were subject to religious anointing in ancient Israel (Ex. 30:22–33), but it was the king ultimately who had the title of the "Lord's anointed" or simply "the anointed." Persons chosen for divine service were anointed to signify their calling and their authority to perform the service. Anointing also signified that God would give them the help they needed. References to the king as the Lord's anointed are prevalent in the books of Samuel (v. 35; 12:3, 5; 16:6; 24:6) and Psalms (2:2; 18:50). The present passage is the first reference to a king of Israel as God's anointed, though the idea of anointing a king is found in Jotham's fable (Judg. 9:8, 15). The English word "messiah" comes from the Hebrew word meaning "anointed." In the NT, "Christ" translates the Greek word Christos, also meaning "anointed."

This Hebrew phrase (lit. "sons of Belial") connotes vile persons. It is used of those who incite to idolatry (Deut. 13:13) or insurrection (10:27; 2 Sam. 16:7; 20:1); the sexually immoral (Judg. 19:22); and liars (1 Kin. 21:10, 13). Since the time of Abel's offering of the fat of the firstborn of his flock (Gen. 4:4), the fat portion was considered to be the best, and as such, to belong to the Lord. The priests had the duty of burning the fat on the altar as an offering to the Lord (Lev. 3:16; 7:31). Like blood, the fat was strictly forbidden for human consumption, and anyone who ate it would be expelled from the people (Lev. 3:17; 7:23–25).

Eli's point is that while there may be some mediation of disputes between people, when someone offends God there is no one who can intervene. Eli's sons have sinned first and foremost against the Lord (v. 17), and they seal their doom by refusing to hear Eli's warning. it was the will of the **LORD** to put them to death. This clear statement of God's sovereignty over the destiny of the wicked does not diminish people's responsibility for their own actions.

**LORD** . The gravity of Eli's sons' refusal to listen to their father or God is emphasized by the striking contrast to Samuel, who grows in favor with God and people. The emphasis on Samuel's growth as more than merely physical foreshadows a theme that is later developed in the contrasting portraits of Saul and David. The expression of v. 26 is used by Luke to describe the childhood of Jesus (Luke 2:52; see Prov. 3:4).

The words of the man of God to Eli exhibit features typical of prophetic judgment speeches. There is an accusation (expressed here through accusing questions that emphasize the contrast between the Lord's grace and Eli's disobedience) and an announcement of judgment confirmed by a sign. Other examples of prophetic speeches of this type are found in chs. 13; 15; and 2 Sam. 12:7–12. 2:27 man of God. Or perhaps "carry" an ephod. Both in the OT (Num. 18:8; Deut. 18:1) and in the NT (1 Cor. 9:13, 14; 1 Tim. 5:17, 18), God provides for the support of those who are called to full-time ministry.

The Hebrew is difficult, and parts of vv. 31, 32 are lacking in the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Prophetic utterances are often confirmed by signs in the OT (2:27–36 note; cf. 10:7, 9; 1 Kin. 13:3, 5; 2 Kin. 19:29; 20:8, 9).

The descendants of Zadok hold the high priesthood from the time of Solomon to the time of Antiochus Epiphanes and the Maccabees (for details see Introduction to the Intertestamental Period). my anointed. **LORD**. Let him do what seems good to him. Eli confesses God's right to rule in the affairs of people. His words establish a benchmark by which later characters in the narrative should be judged: Saul (20:30, 31) and David (2 Sam. 15:25, 26).

Dan is the northernmost city in the Promised Land and Beersheba the southernmost, so the phrase "Dan to Beersheba" is a colloquial way to refer to all Israel (cf. 2 Sam. 3:10; 17:11; 24:15; 1 Kin. 4:25). While Samuel's responsibilities as judge take him on a circuit of the central hill country (7:15–17), his reputation as a prophet spreads throughout "all Israel."
See note on 1:3.

Philistines. The Philistines are one of the "Sea Peoples" named in Egyptian texts from the time of Rameses III. By the time of the judges (Judg. 3:31; 13–16), the Philistines had settled along the coastlands of southern Canaan in a league of five cities: Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, Gath, and Gaza (6:17; Judg. 3:3). The Philistines often tried to expand their territory, and in the time of Samuel and the early monarchy they came in direct conflict with the Israelites to the north and east. During the rule of Samson, the last judge, the Philistines were a thorn in Israel's side (Judg. 15:20). Ebenezer. This may be an archaeological site about two miles (3 km) east of Aphek (cf. v. 6). They do not wait for an answer, however, but immediately take matters into their own hands. Let us bring the ark. The elders' apparent conviction that the ark is a magical guarantee of the Lord's presence is similar to that of the Philistines (vv. 7–9). This has caused considerable debate about whether the biblical Hebrews are the same as these people. The Habiru seem to have been a landless class of aliens or refugees who survived either by hiring themselves out as soldiers or farmers or by plundering. Although the names "Hebrew" and "Habiru" look similar, no linguistic connection exists between them.

See note on 4:1. Ashdod. One of the five main Philistine cities (6:17), Ashdod is about thirty miles (48 km) south of Ebenezer and three miles (5 km) inland from the Mediterranean. Philistine occupation of Ashdod during the twelfth and eleventh centuries B.C.. is attested archaeologically. In the NT period, the site is called Azotus (Acts 8:40).

A prominent deity among the Phil­istines as well as other peoples in Mesopotamia, Syria, and Phoenicia from the middle of the third millennium B.C.., Dagon was once thought to be a fish deity because of the similarity between the name Dagon and the Hebrew word for fish (dag). It now appears more likely that the name is associated with the Hebrew word for grain (dagan), making Dagon an agricultural or fertility god. Dagon seems to have headed the Philistine pantheon (Judg. 16:23; 1 Chr. 10:10), which included the goddess Ashtoreth (31:8–10) and the god Baal-zebul ("Baal the prince"). Baal-zebul was worshiped at Ekron, and his name was intentionally distorted by the Israelites to Baal-zebub ("lord of the flies," 2 Kin. 1:1–6, 16). The worship of Dagon is attested as late as the Maccabean period (second century B.C..). set it up beside Dagon. In the ancient Near East the victorious army would carry off the gods of the vanquished and deposit them in the temple of their own gods as a sign of the inferiority and subordination of the captured gods. Though not an idol, the ark of God is treated that way by the Philistines after it is captured.
The supposedly victorious deity falls on its face doing homage to the ostensibly vanquished one (v. 2 note).

The specific damage to the idol is to be understood in light of the common practice in antiquity of removing the head and hands of the enemy dead (Judg. 7:25; 8:6; 1 Sam. 17:54; 31:9; 2 Sam. 4:12). The same vocabulary is used of Goliath's death at the hands of David (1 Sam. 17:48–51). What happens to the Philistine god Dagon after the ark is captured later happens to his most infamous disciple, Goliath.

Thresholds are often invested with special significance, and the practice of not stepping on the threshold of a sacred place is known, if not approved, in Israel at this time (cf. Zeph. 1:9). Linking the custom of the priests of Dagon with this humiliating incident may be intended more to ridicule them than to convey information about their ritual practice. to this day. Samuel sets up a memorial stone with the name Ebenezer, "Stone of Help," not only to commemorate the victory but also as a reminder of the different results brought about by presumption on the one hand and by repentance on the other. Till now the **LORD** has helped us. The saying means that the Lord has been with them all the way "to this place," or "to this hour."

Throughout Samuel's lifetime God continues to give Israel victory, though the fighting at times is fierce (14:52). The defeat recounted in ch. 31 comes only after Samuel's death (25:1).
Ten miles (16 km) north of Jerusalem. Gilgal. Probably in the Jordan Valley near Jericho (Josh. 5:10). Mizpah. See note on 7:5.

See note on 1:1. Samuel travels a yearly circuit to perform his judgeship duties. His home is Ramah, and from there he travels to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. All four of these sites are located on the main north-south road in the central hill country called "the spine." In addition, the four towns are in a cluster, each within a twelve miles (19 km) from one another. This is one indication that the rule of the judges was more local than national.

Samuel's sons are judges in this city, which is located about fifty miles (80 km) south of Jerusalem at Tell es-Seba. It is considered the southern border of the land of Israel. Their wicked activity is far from the authority of their father.

The reasons given by the elders for wanting a king, though acceptable in themselves (as confirmed by the narrator in vv. 1–3), are really a pretext; what they really want is to become like "all the nations" (cf. v. 20).

Since the elders couch their request in terms of a "king to judge us" (v. 5 note), Samuel initially interprets their overture as an attack on his leadership (v. 6). But the Lord points out to him that the affront is far graver than that. they have rejected me. The offense of the elders' request lies not in the concept of human kingship in itself, for kingship in Israel has long been anticipated by this point (2:10 note), but in breaking their covenant relationship with God. Their sin is to reject God as their king and to take instead a human monarch (10:19; 12:12–20; cf. Gideon's refusal in Judg. 8:23).

For the second time in 1 Samuel, an individual is requested. The individual given in response to the first request is Samuel (1:20 note), and it is Saul (whose name is based on the Hebrew root meaning "ask for") who will be given in response to the second request.

Israel's Canaanite neighbors and many of the Israelite kings were guilty of harsh practices such as those described in vv. 11–17. run before. Cf. the actions of Absalom in 2 Sam. 15:1 with those of Adonijah in 1 Kin. 1:5. chariots. See 2 Sam. 8:4; 15:1; 1 Kin. 4:26; 10:26–29.
See note on 22:7.
The demands of the king will either take from what belongs to the Lord (Lev. 27:30–32; Deut. 14:22, 28) or create a tax burden for his subjects.

A common verb in the book of Judges when the people of God call for divine aid because of their oppression under a foreign monarch (Judg. 3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:7; 10:10). your king. See 12:13; cf. 16:1. the **LORD** will not answer you. Judging by the consequences, Israel's rejection of the Lord in favor of a human king is the moral and religious equivalent of forsaking the Lord to serve other gods (Judg. 10:10–14).
See note on v. 5. fight our battles. To be contrasted with "the LORD's battles" (18:17; 25:28).

The Lord's concession to the people's sinful request is, at this point in the account, perplexing. If their desire for a king is sinful, amounting to a rejection of God as king (vv. 7, 18 and notes), how can God grant it? One answer lies in the standards of acceptable kingship that the Lord will establish. God is graciously willing to give the people a king and even to bless him (see Deut. 17:14–20), although not the sort of king they envision (10:1, 7, 8 and notes). At the same time, because they adopt kingship in unbelief, they come to suffer under kings like those of the nations. Go every man to his city. Samuel's dismissal of the men of Israel implies that appointing a king will require some preparation. The course of that preparation will be related in the chapters that follow.

The opening verse of the account of Saul's adventures is formally similar to the beginning of the birth narrative of Samuel (1:1). In both instances the father of the principal character is introduced with sufficient genealogical references to suggest a man of standing. This description is employed elsewhere in the OT to picture one who is not only wealthy but of upright character (e.g., Boaz in Ruth 2:1). In Samuel's introduction we are also told of the father's faithful religious observance (1:3–5), whereas in this account we are introduced immediately to Saul (v. 2), and the focus remains exclusively on external qualities.
The emphasis of this description is Saul's physical stature and impressive appearance. Cf. the description of Absalom in 2 Sam. 14:25, 26.
Saul looks for his father's donkeys not only in his own tribal territory of Benjamin but also in the land of Ephraim. Ephraim lies directly north of Benjamin.

A "man of God" is a prophet. That Saul is unaware of the presence and reputation of the man of God or has not thought of consulting him reflects negatively on his judgment. all that he says comes true. The man of God is Samuel, of whom it is said in 3:19 that the Lord "let none of his words fall to the ground." This is a sign that Samuel is a true prophet of the Lord (Deut. 18:21, 22).

The first-century historian Josephus interprets Saul's words as a sign that he is ignorant that a true prophet will accept no reward. Israel's writing prophets express disdain for those who prophesy for money (Mic. 3:5, 11), although there are various references to goods being offered in return for prophetic favors (e.g., 1 Kin. 14:3; 2 Kin. 4:42; 8:8). In two instances payment is explicitly refused (1 Kin. 13:7–9; 2 Kin. 5:15, 16), and in one instance where goods are accepted, the payment does not benefit the prophet personally but is distributed among the people (2 Kin. 4:42).
The terms are synonymous.

In the Hebrew, vv. 12, 13 convey excitement and animation as the girls urge Saul to hurry up to the city, where he will arrive just in time to meet Samuel. high place. Although it was recognized that such high places (often sites of Canaanite worship) posed a clear danger to the purity of Israelite worship (e.g., Lev. 26:30; Num. 33:52; Deut. 12:2, 3; Jer. 2:20), it is apparent from passages such as this that worship of Yahweh was sometimes conducted there, especially during the early monarchy (10:5; 1 Kin. 3:2–4). After the division of the kingdom, worship at "high places" was a serious problem both in the north (1 Kin. 12:31, 32; 13:32–34) and in the south (1 Kin. 14:22–24). Removal of the high places was a major goal of reform movements under southern kings such as Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:4) and Josiah (2 Kin. 23:5).

See note on 2:10. prince. The word appears to be a title for "one designated to rule" (cf. its use with reference to Solomon as crown prince in 1 Kin. 1:35). Saul's assignment in the immediate context is to deliver Israel from the Philistines, and against the background of ch. 8, the logical assumption is that he will go on to become king. Philistines. See note on 4:1.
Saul's failure to recognize Samuel is a troubling hint of spiritual insensitivity and inattentiveness that will increasingly characterize Saul as the narrative progresses.
This expression may suggest that Saul is just the kind of king the people want.

The special treatment given Saul illustrates not only his newly elevated status but also Samuel's divinely enabled anticipation of his arrival (vv. 15, 16). This scene is perhaps a pre-coronation banquet (see 2 Sam. 15:10–12).

Perhaps a sign of loyalty to the new king (1 Kin. 19:18; Ps. 2:12). anointed you to be prince. See note on 9:16. his heritage. See 9:16 ("my people Israel"); 2 Sam. 20:19 and note; Deut. 32:9. The Lord's willingness to grant the people a human king does not mean that He forfeits His rule over Israel. The appointed king is always subordinate to God.
Samuel's words will be confirmed to Saul as the sequence of events comes to pass in the order foretold. Finally, Saul will come under the power of the Spirit (vv. 5, 6).

The mention of a Philistine garrison foreshadows the task ahead for the one designated to deliver the people of God from the Philistines (9:16). On the stationing of garrisons in subject territories, see David's practice in 2 Sam. 8:6. group of prophets. Samuel is associated with a group of prophets in 19:20, where he is described as their leader. Note the similar association of Elisha with the "sons of the prophets" in 2 Kin. 2; 6:1; 9:1; etc. These prophetic guilds appear to have been made up of defenders of true religion in times of widespread apostasy and spiritual indifference. prophesying. Prophecy in the OT is often, though not exclusively, associated with the giving of a message (see Aaron's role as Moses's "prophet" or spokesman in Ex. 7:1; cf. Ezek. 21:9; Amos 3:8). According to Scripture, God's prophets are His messengers (2 Sam. 7:1–5; 12:1; 24:11, 12). In some places, prophecy is associated with music (Ex. 15:20, 21; 1 Chr. 25:1). The prophesying in view here seems to be praising God and exhorting the people with musical accompaniment.

**LORD** will rush upon you. See v. 10; note on 11:6. The activity of the Spirit with Samson is expressed in identical terms (Judg. 14:6, 19; 15:14). Whereas the Spirit is ultimately withdrawn from Saul (cf. 16:14; 18:10), David's endowment with the Spirit is permanent (16:13). Frequently in the OT, the bestowal of the Spirit is an empowerment by God of an individual for a particular task. Conversely, God can send a lying spirit (1 Kin. 22:23) or an evil ("distressing") spirit (16:14–16, 23; 18:10; 19:9; Judg. 9:23).

In light of Saul's general commission to deliver Israel from the Philistines (9:16) and of Samuel's specific mention of a visible symbol of Philistine domination at the site of the third and final sign (v. 5), Samuel's words can be taken to imply that Saul should respond to his anointing by attacking the Philistine outpost. Samuel's words can also be interpreted as an encouragement for Saul to submit to the prophetic influence mentioned in v. 6.

Gilgal is one of the cities on Samuel's normal circuit (see 7:16). When Saul has done what his "hand finds to do," he is to meet Samuel in Gilgal so that the latter can offer sacrifices and give Saul further instructions. burnt offerings. A full description of the ritual of the burnt offering can be found in Lev. 1:3–17. Burnt offerings are also mentioned in 6:14, 15; 7:9, 10; 13:9, 12; 15:22; 2 Sam. 6:17, 18; 24:22–25. peace offerings. The peace offering is described in Lev. 3 and is first mentioned in Ex. 20:24. Other references in Samuel to peace offerings are 11:15; 13:9; 2 Sam. 6:17, 18; 24:25.
The language is similar to Ezek. 11:19; 36:26 (cf. Jer. 31:31–34; John 3:3). But it is difficult to define Saul's experience precisely.

Or, "Is even Saul among the prophets?" The proverb (v. 12) expresses surprise at something highly improbable. The onlookers who know Saul are surprised to find him associating with religious enthusiasts. This question becomes proverbial in Israel when someone acts out of character (19:24).

Since the leader of a prophetic guild is sometimes called "father" (2 Kin. 2:12; 6:21), this question might be asking for the leader of this particular guild. If, on the other hand, the onlookers are contemptuous of prophecy, their surprise might be that a man of good family and social standing such as Saul is associating with such "mad fellows" (cf. 2 Kin. 9:11), whose fathers were inferior to his. Still another possibility is that the question means that the "father" or origin of the prophetic band does not follow normal rules, and Saul, unlikely as it may seem, has found a place with them. See theological note "The Prophets of God" on p. 279.
The significance of this conversation has long puzzled commentators. Some have understood Saul's reluctance to mention the kingship (v. 16) as a sign of humility.
The Lord's choice of Saul is now made public at Mizpah, apparently through casting a lot or using the Urim and Thummim (v. 20 and note).
Casting lots is probably the method of selection (cf. Lev. 16:8–10; Num. 26:55), and it may involve the Urim and Thummim (2:28; cf. Ex. 28:30 note; Num. 27:21; Deut. 33:8).
The Lord singles out Saul even though he is not immediately present. Something similar occurs with David (16:11).

A similar expression in 8:9–11 refers to the negative consequences of having a king. Here it means the regulations that a king must follow (Deut. 17:14–20; 2 Kin. 11:12 note). laid it up before the **LORD** . See Deut. 31:26; Josh. 24:26.

Lit. "sons of Belial"; this term was previously used of the wicked sons of Eli (2:12). How can this man save us. Those who pose this question are rebels because they call into question the Lord's process of selection.

Descended from Lot, the Ammonites were a Semitic people (Gen. 19:38; Deut. 2:19) whose kingdom was on the east side of the Jordan, south of the Jabbok River. The capital of Ammon was Rabbah, located next to a spring that feeds the Jabbok River. While Ammon was sometimes on friendly terms with Israel (2 Sam. 10:2), the Ammonites often exerted pressure on Israel's eastern border (Judg. 3:13; 11:4–32), as the Philistines did on the west. According to the Dead Sea Scrolls and the first-century historian Josephus, the siege of Jabesh-gilead was part of a larger campaign by Nahash. Jabesh-gilead. A principal city in what was probably the territory of East Manasseh, Jabesh-gilead was east of the Jordan River, twenty-two miles (35 km) south of the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee).

While the stated reason for such treatment is to "bring disgrace on all Israel," Josephus remarks that the loss of the right eye would have made military service impossible, since the sight of the left eye would be hindered by the shield.

While the elders of Jabesh clearly intend Nahash to understand their words as a surrender, the Hebrew verb employed is often used in the sense of soldiers "going out" to battle (8:20; 18:30; 2 Sam. 18:2–4, 6). When in v. 10 the men of Jabesh again promise to give themselves up to the Ammonites, it is with some irony because the Ammonites are still thinking of "surrender," but the townspeople are planning to fight.
Similar language is used of the Lord's Spirit empowering some of the judges: Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson (Judg. 3:10; 6:34: 11:29; 13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14).

Saul's action roughly parallels that of the Levite in Judg. 19, and the city of Gibeah plays a central role in both episodes. The Levite's sin was notorious, and the comparison is not at all complimentary. and Samuel. See notes on 10:1, 7, 8.

Located at Khirbet Ibziq, twelve miles (19 km) west of the Jordan River, opposite of Jabesh-gilead. people of Israel \... men of Judah. Even before the division of the kingdom (1 Kin. 12), a distinction is often made between the northern and southern tribes (17:52; 18:16; cf. 2 Sam. 2:10; 3:10; 5:5; 11:11; 12:8; 19:11, 40–43; 20:2; 21:2; 24:1, 9).
See note on v. 3.
See 13:17; Judg. 7:16; 9:43; 2 Sam. 18:2. in the morning watch. Between 2 and 6 A.M., taking advantage of the cover of darkness.
The reference includes, but may not be limited to, the "worthless fellows" of 10:27.
**LORD** has worked salvation in Israel. Saul interrupts a question directed to Samuel with a confession that marks a high point in his own life.
The process of Saul's accession to the throne can now be resumed (v. 15 note), but on a deeper level it is the continued reign of the Lord that must be renewed (ch. 12). Gilgal. See note on 13:4.

The rise to leadership in ancient Israel can be seen as following a three-step process: (1) designation as the Lord's choice; (2) demonstration of valor and of having the Lord's power through performing a heroic feat; and (3) confirmation by the people. Saul is designated by Samuel, and he has a prophetic experience (ch. 10). Although he could have attacked the Philistine garrison at Gibeah immediately (10:5, 8), he gains an important victory by delivering Jabesh-gilead (v. 13). He is then crowned at Gilgal. peace offerings. See note on 10:8.
The process of accession to the throne has been completed, and Samuel's speech in ch. 12 marks the end of the period of the judges.

Samuel advances a three-pronged argument to compel the people to recognize their guilt for requesting a king. First, he invites agreement from the people that his leadership has been blameless (vv. 4, 5). Second, he points out that in the past it was always the Lord who appointed leaders (v. 6), and these proved fully adequate (vv. 7, 8). Third, he emphasizes that even when Israel "forgot the LORD their God," the Lord was gracious to them. Although the Lord subjected them to enemy oppression (v. 9), He heard their confessions of sin and cries for deliverance (v. 10) and raised up judges, among them Samuel himself (v. 11). Against this background of the sufficiency of the Lord's provision, the people's demand to have a human king, even though the Lord is their king (v. 12) can be seen for what it is (8:7). Nevertheless, kingship can succeed, if both king and people "fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice" (v. 14). 12:3 his anointed. See note on 2:10. Saul's anointing is ordered in 9:16 and performed in 10:1. Whose ox \... whose donkey have I taken. Valuable possessions in biblical times, the ox and the donkey are mentioned in the tenth commandment as typical objects of covetousness (Ex. 20:17; Deut. 5:21). Samuel declares he has never taken an ox or a donkey, and this contrasts with the ways of a king (see 8:11–17).

Samuel has taken the stand himself as a defendant and been acquitted (vv. 3–5); now he takes the role of prosecutor, and the people become the defendants. Their crime is having desired a king in total disregard of all the "righteous deeds of the LORD" throughout the time of the exodus and the judges (vv. 7–11).

Though it is not explicitly mentioned in ch. 8, it is possible that the Ammonite threat was already a concern at that time (11:1 note). Alternatively, Samuel may simply be citing the Ammonite episode as the most recent example of the people's faithless tendency to seek help from men rather than God. Saul himself gave the Lord credit for the victory (11:13).
See 8:18; cf. 16:1. for whom you have asked. See note on 8:10.

**LORD**. A fundamental prerequisite for covenant blessing in Moses's day (Deut. 6:2, 24; 10:12; 31:12, 13), in Joshua's (Josh. 4:24; 24:14), and now in the new era of the monarchy. To "fear the LORD" means standing in awe of Him and giving Him the honor and obedience that is His due as God and gracious Father.

Having made his case against the people in vv. 3–15, Samuel now invokes a dramatic sign to drive home the point of the people's guilt. The sign achieves the desired result, and the people repent for having "added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king" (v. 19). On signs accompanying prophetic utterances, see note on 2:34. 12:16 stand still and see. These two imperatives are the same commands that Moses gave to the people at the Red Sea when God divided the waters (Ex. 14:13).
The wheat harvest took place in late May and June, early in Israel's dry season.
In response to the people's repentance, Samuel comforts them, "Do not be afraid," and challenges them to renewed commitment (v. 20).
Samuel's responsibilities in the kingdom will include intercession and instruction (12:1 note; for other duties of Samuel, see 10:8).
**LORD**. See note on v. 14. with all your heart. See v. 20; 16:7.

Saul's reign officially begins. Cf. the chronological notice of 13:1 with similar formulas in 2 Sam. 2:10; 5:4; 1 Kin. 14:21; 22:42. The narrative turns to Saul's first encounters with the Philistines, who are a continuing threat to Israel. 13:1 Existing Hebrew manuscripts contain what is likely an inadvertent scribal departure from the original wording, since as it stands the Hebrew says that Saul was one year old when he began to rule. Saul probably reigned about twenty years, and if so, the number "forty" in Acts 13:21 is a round figure meaning "a long time." See the chronology in Introduction: Date and Occasion.

Some four miles (6 km) northeast of Gibeah in the tribal territory of Benjamin. Gibeah of Benjamin. It lies at modern Tell el-Ful in the central hill country three miles (5 km) due north of Jerusalem.
This could be the same garrison near where Saul prophesied. blew the trumpet. Trumpets were used in war as a signaling device (2 Sam. 2:28; 18:16; 20:1). Hebrews. See note on 4:6.

Saul responds to the crisis precipitated by Jonathan (v. 3), gathering the people at Gilgal in accordance with Samuel's instructions (10:8). Gilgal's situation in the Jordan Valley near Jericho placed it outside immediate Philistine control, making it a strategic site for a general muster of the troops. Already at this point, Gilgal has figured prominently in Israel's history (Josh. 4:19, 20; 5:10; 9:6; 10:6–15, 43; 1 Sam. 7:16; 11:14).
These are the people summoned in v. 4, not the troops already deployed in v. 2.
Samuel previously specified seven days (10:8).
See note on 10:8.

See note on 2:27–36. When I saw. From a purely human perspective, Saul's excuses seem to carry some weight. But they do not take into account the freedom of God to act on behalf of His people, as Jonathan's testimony in 14:6 confirms.

This Hebrew expression implies both intellectual and moral failure. For a similar confrontation between a prophet and a king, see 2 Chr. 16:7–9. You have not kept the command. In this context, Saul had transgressed by offering sacrifices on his own authority and usurping priestly sacrificial duties.

Saul's hopes of establishing a dynasty are dashed, though Saul himself will not yet be deposed (15:23). a man after his own heart. This phrase occurs only one other time in the OT, Deut. 20:8, which is translated "like his own heart." In the light of passages such as 2:35 and 16:7, the text appears to be saying that David was "after God's heart" in the sense of being committed to His will and purposes. Acts 13:22 seems to understand the text in this way when it says, "I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will."

Because of Saul's foolish action, Samuel apparently departs without giving Saul any further instructions (10:8). The longer reading of the Septuagint (see text note) suggests that after Samuel's departure, Saul rejoins Jonathan at Geba (v. 2 note; v. 16 note).
The two armies are mustered and positioned. These two sites are approximately one mile (1.6 km) apart, and they are separated by the Wadi es-Suwenit.

Raiding parties in this era plunder and terrorize, as well as keep up military pressure by reconnoitering and controlling important routes. The three bands raid in separate directions: Ophrah is north, Beth-horon is west, and the wilderness is east.

The Israelites are short of weapons and depend on the Philistines even for making their tools. Archaeological evidence confirms that the Philistines learned how to work iron earlier than their neighbors.
This notice pins the hopes of Israel on two people in particular, and the following chapter compares them to the disadvantage of Saul.

An armor bearer had an important military position in antiquity; he was not a mere servant (1 Sam. 16:21; 31:5–6). But he did not tell his father. Jonathan's decision not to tell his father of his daring plan may imply a lack of confidence in him (cf. Abigail's similar action in response to her husband, Nabal, in 25:19).

The presence of a member of the rejected priestly house of Eli (2:30) in Saul's camp is a reminder of the recent rejection of Saul's own royal house (13:14). wearing an ephod. The presence in Saul's camp of the ephod used for seeking God's will (2:28 note) encourages the expectation that he will use it to ask the Lord's guidance, as David does later (23:9–12; 30:7, 8). In this instance, however, Saul leaves it to Jonathan to discover the Lord's will (v. 10 note). In v. 19 (note) Saul shows a lack of respect for the ephod; later he savagely turns against those whose task it is to oversee its care and use (22:18; cf. 21:9). In the end, Saul's efforts to discover the Lord's will are met with silence (28:6 note).
These names possibly mean "slippery" and "thorny," and so dramatize the challenge facing Jonathan.

The uncircumcised are people like the Philistines, who stand outside God's covenant (Gen. 17:14; Ex. 12:48; Judg. 14:3; 15:18). nothing can hinder the **LORD** from saving. Cf. David's confidence in 17:47. Although the narrator does not offer a criticism of Saul's excuse in 13:11 (that "the people were scattering" and so forth), Jonathan's bold confession makes an indirect commentary on the inadequacy of that excuse.

Jonathan is not willing to move ahead without the Lord's approval. In this regard he is more faithful than his father, who seems to show a declining commitment to obtaining divine guidance (13:8–15; 14:18, 19, 36 and notes).
See note on 4:6.
The Septuagint reads "ephod." The ephod is clearly present in Gibeah (v. 3 note), where it is used to inquire of the Lord (2:28 note).
In ordering the priest to let go of the instrument by which the will of the Lord can be determined, Saul takes matters back into his own hands (cf. 13:9).

This is an account of something that took place earlier the same day, that is, after Jonathan left to make an attack on the Philistines (vv. 13, 14) but before Saul joined the battle (v. 20). laid an oath. This verb in Hebrew is related to another verb that means "to play the fool"; it is a wordplay that underscores that, in reality, Saul's vow is foolhardy.

Probably Jonathan has not heard because he left the camp before the oath was imposed (v. 24 note). his eyes became bright. An expression indicating that his physical energy has been renewed, owing to the sugar from the honey.

The lack of confidence implicit in Jonathan's exclusion of his father from his plans (v. 1) now rises to an outright condemnation of his father's foolish action in binding the people under an oath. As in the case of Achan (Josh. 7:16–18, 25), a lot will be cast to uncover the guilty party, the "troubler" of the land. The lot reveals Jonathan as the one who violated the oath (v. 42), but the real troubler of Israel is Saul.
About fifteen miles (24 km) west of Michmash in the Valley of Aijalon, the route the Philistines probably follow back to their homeland.

Prohibitions against eating blood are recorded often in the OT (Gen. 9:4; Lev. 3:17; 7:26, 27; 17:10, 12; 19:26; Deut. 15:23; Ezek. 33:25). You have dealt treacherously. The plural "you" indicates that Saul places the blame for the broken vow directly on the troops. He takes no responsibility for the affair.
This is also the only altar to be mentioned.
It is unusual that the priest, probably Ahijah (v. 3), should take the initiative. But this agrees with the pattern of Saul's declining commitment to obtain the Lord's guidance (v. 10 note).
The people protect Jonathan.

When forced by Saul's hardness (vv. 39, 44) to choose between Saul and Jonathan, the people choose Jonathan, whom they clearly recognize as the one the Lord used in the battle that day. Saul's foolish behavior has alienated him from everyone around him, even his own people. His isolation is not permanent, however, for Jonathan becomes his confidant again later (20:2), and the people show signs of renewed loyalty (23:19; 24:1). Even Samuel has further dealings with him (ch. 15).

This gives a summary of Saul's military accomplishments (vv. 47, 48) and details about his family and Abner's (vv. 49–51). A comparison of this section with the longer summary of David's victories and officers in 2 Sam. 8 reveals a number of similarities but also a telling difference: nowhere in the summation of Saul is there anything akin to the statement repeated about David, that "the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went" (2 Sam. 8:6, 14).

Saul had four sons and two daughters. One son, Abinadab, is not mentioned here but is listed in 1 Chr. 8:33; 9:39. Later, David is offered the hand of both daughters of Saul in marriage (18:17–27). Ishvi. He is probably to be identified with Ish-bosheth (2 Sam. 2:8–15; 3:7–15; 4:1–12) and Eshbaal (1 Chr. 8:33; 9:39).
See notes on 7:13.

**LORD** sent me to anoint you. Samuel mentions his role in anointing Saul to set the context for his continuing service as mediator of God's orders to Saul (10:1 note). listen to the words of the **LORD** . The Hebrew word translated "listen" is repeated several times in this chapter, underscoring the central theme of obedience ("listen," "hear," "obey," and "voice," "bleating," "lowing" in vv. 1, 14, 19, 20, 22, 24).
Descendants of Esau (according to Gen. 36:12, 16), the Amalekites were a nomadic desert people who lived in southern Judah and beyond, toward Egypt. They fought frequently with the Israelites.

Lit. "place them under the ban." This meant to devote persons or things completely to the Lord. In war it usually required the total destruction of properties and execution of people. The inclusion of animals in this verse is especially striking. The ban was an element of holy war and could not be decreed by anyone but God. The concept of the ban was not a uniquely Israelite practice. As seen in the Moabite inscription of the ninth-century B.C.. King Mesha, Moab devoted to destruction all the Israelites who were in his land, dedicating them to his god Chemosh. man and woman, child and infant. See 22:19 and note.
Probably the Telem listed in Josh. 15:24 as one of the cities of Judah. The Septuagint has Gilgal instead, which some have suggested was the site of Samuel's instructions to Saul (vv. 1–3).
Perhaps an allusion to the kindness of Moses's Kenite father-in-law (Judg. 1:16) recorded in Ex. 18.
