See Gen. 25:18. Shur is mentioned in 27:8 as lying at the frontiers of the territory of the Amalekites, near the eastern border of Egypt. The location of Havilah remains uncertain, but the general sense of the reference is that Saul's victory is extensive.

This is either a personal name or a title, such as in the use of "Pharaoh" (Num. 24:7; cf. "Agagite" in Esth. 3:1). all the people. That is, all who have fallen into Saul's hands (there are later references to Amalek­ites in 27:8; 30:1, 18). For this limited sense of "all," cf. 13:7; 31:6.

They go against the Lord's command (v. 3). A desire to profit from the victory may be the underlying reason for the unwillingness to destroy anything that is good. Achan kept back goods that were devoted to destruction, apparently because he was greedy (Josh. 7:1). The reader is not told Saul's motive for sparing Agag, whether political, like Ahab's mercy to Ben-hadad (1 Kin. 20:30–34), or a prideful desire to parade his captive as a trophy of war. Saul does set up a victory monument "for himself" (v. 12).

See note on v. 29. turned back. A serious indictment in view of 12:14, where obedience and following the Lord are named as the essential requirements for a successful reign. Samuel was angry. The same Hebrew expression is used in 18:8 and 2 Sam. 6:8. he cried to the **LORD** all night. Clearly, Samuel takes no pleasure in Saul's rejection (v. 35; 16:1).

About seven miles (11 km) south of Hebron (25:2; cf. Josh. 15:55). This is not the Mount Carmel on the northern coast. monument for himself. The closest parallel is in 2 Sam. 18:18, where Absalom erects a pillar "for himself" to commemorate his name. This act symbolizes the central focus of Saul's kingship. Whereas Saul was humble at the start of his reign, his increasing pride contributes to his downfall as king (cf. 1 Sam. 2:7, 8).
These verses display the standard features of a prophetic judgment speech to an individual (2:27–36 note), but in this instance the accused, Saul, vigorously contests the charges.
In response to Samuel's accusation, Saul offers two excuses: first, the people are responsible and not he; second, the animals will be killed as sacrifices. Samuel will answer these excuses.
Whatever ideas Saul has about his role as king, Samuel rejects his attempt to avoid personal responsibility for what has happened.
Samuel rejects Saul's claim that the animals were spared because they were needed for sacrifice. On the verb translated "pounce," see note on 25:14.
Ignoring Samuel's refusal to accept his excuses, Saul repeats them adamantly.

The poetic form of these two verses highlights their climactic importance in the episode. 15:22 burnt offerings. See note on 10:8. to obey is better than sacrifice. Although Samuel clearly disbelieves Saul's excuse (v. 19 note), he accepts it for the sake of argument and makes the point that ritual performance is worthless when not accompanied by a sincere and submissive spirit. For similar denunciations of empty ritual by Israel's later prophets, see Is. 1:10–17; Jer. 6:19, 20; 7:21–26; Hos. 6:6; Amos 5:21–24; Mic. 6:6–8; also Ps. 51:16, 17; Prov. 15:8; 21:3, 27.

At last Saul begins to accept responsibility ("I have sinned"), though he still blames the people for initiating the unfortunate events ("I feared the people and obeyed their voice"). On the surface, Saul's confession sounds adequate, but against the background of Samuel's warnings in 12:14, 15, his admissions lead not so much to a possibility that there will be reconciliation as to the certainty that he will be "swept away" (12:25). Saul will offer a second, more candid confession in v. 30.
Samuel's refusal to return with Saul suggests Samuel is not satisfied with the sincerity of the confession as a whole (v. 30 note).
Samuel seizes upon the tearing of the robe as a fitting symbol of the Lord's having "torn the kingdom" from Saul (cf. 24:4, 5; 1 Kin. 11:29–33).

Saul's rejection is final, and no attempt to mitigate its consequences will avail. There is no contradiction between this statement and the notices in vv. 11 and 35 that the Lord "regretted" having made Saul king. As in Num. 23:19, the point is that when the Lord makes a pronouncement intended to be final, He cannot be talked out of it.

Saul's real concern becomes clear in this, his second confession (cf. vv. 24, 25 and note). As Samuel seems already to suspect (v. 26 note), Saul is less concerned with being reconciled to the Lord than with finding honor before the elders of "my people." In return for this honor, Saul offers to do obeisance before the Lord "your" God. Samuel's God should be Saul's God as well, but Saul has been faithless and cannot rightly say, "my God."

Several reasons for Samuel's reversal of his earlier decision (v. 26) may be suggested: (1) Saul has at last issued a candid confession; (2) there is no danger after vv. 28, 29 that Saul might interpret Samuel's actions as a retraction of his judgment; (3) Samuel must still deal with Agag.
Samuel completes the task that Saul failed to do.
See note on v. 11.

These chapters narrate David's rise to power and Saul's fall from the throne to his death. David's rise is marked by his anointing by Samuel and his time in Saul's service (chs. 16–18), his flight from Saul (chs. 19–23), his avoidance of bloodguilt (chs. 24–26), and his escape to the Philistines (chs. 27–31). 16:1 Jesse the Bethlehemite. His genealogy is provided in Ruth 4:18–22. He is the grandson of Boaz and Ruth and the great-grandson of Rahab, the Gentile prostitute from Jericho (see Matt. 1:5–6). First mentioned in Gen. 35:19, Bethlehem is David's hometown (17:12, 15). On the significance of this site for the Messiah ("the anointed one"), see Mic. 5:2; Matt. 2:5, 6; John 7:42. I have provided for myself. The selection of a king for "myself" (the Lord), contrasts with the choice of a king for "them" (the people) in 8:22 (8:18; 12:13).

While true insofar as it goes, this statement does not disclose the real reason for Samuel's journey to Bethlehem (v. 1). There may well be an ironic tone in the Lord's instruction to Samuel, coming as it does on the heels of Saul's claim to have spared animals only "to sacrifice" them (15:15, 21). Cases of deception like this one must be weighed in their particular circumstances (20:6; 21:2; 27:10; 2 Sam. 16:17–19; Josh. 2:4 and notes).
See note on 2:10.

See the similar response of Ahimelech upon David's arrival alone in Nob (21:1). No reason is given for the elders' trembling. It probably has to do with Samuel's prophetic function as an instrument of God's judgment.

The reference to "stature" as a false measure of an individual's qualification to be king, along with the notice that this son of Jesse is "rejected," is reminiscent of Saul, who was notable for his height (9:2; 10:23) but was rejected (15:23, 26). Samuel is not acting as a seer, for he sees only the outward appearance of the brothers. the **LORD** looks on the heart. It is an axiom that God's standards are inward, not outward (13:14 note; Rom. 2:28, 29).

It is likely that the elders also witness David's being anointed (vv. 4, 5). The emphasis on the brothers being present at the event may shed light on Eliab's behavior in 17:28. Spirit of the **LORD** rushed upon David. See notes on 10:6; 11:6. David's endowment with the Spirit "from that day forward" sets him apart from Saul (and also Samson) upon whom the Spirit descends only temporarily.

**LORD** departed from Saul. The empowering and validating presence of God's Spirit must have been removed from Saul at his definitive rejection as king in ch. 15 (cf. also v. 1). harmful spirit. Cf. 1 Kin. 22:21–23. The Hebrew word may describe something that is troubling, annoying, or evil.

This speech may seem to conflict with Saul's statement in 17:33 that David, who is but a youth, will be no match for Goliath. In response one can say that the servant's recommendation of David may be exaggerated. Saul for his part is comparing David to Goliath and is reluctant to take the risk of sending anyone against the Philistine giant. the **LORD** is with him. This fact, more than any human quality, accounts for David's persistent, if circuitous, rise to power, while Saul's increasing recognition that David is preferred to him plays no small part in his own psychological disintegration (3:19; 17:37; 18:12, 28, 29; 20:13; 2 Sam. 7:9 and notes).
Saul unwittingly invites his eventual replacement to enter his court. David's rise to power is providentially directed and not the result of human effort or grasping for power.
Note Jonathan's response to David (18:1, 3; 20:17) as well as the responses of Michal (18:20, 28), the people (18:16), and possibly even Saul's other servants (18:22).

Socoh is located at modern Khirbet 'Abbad, fourteen miles (23 km) west of Bethlehem on the Philistine border. Azekah is identified with Tell Zakariyeh, which is three miles (5 km) northwest of Socoh, and five miles (8 km) east of the Philistine capital of Gath.
This valley runs east to west from Bethlehem to Gath through the "shephelah" or foothills, of Palestine.

Trial by single combat, where the outcome of a fight to the death between two champions is taken as the will of the gods, is rare in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 2:14–16). It is well attested, however, among some of Israel's neighbors. six cubits and a span. That is, nine feet, nine inches or approximately three meters. The Septuagint and other ancient sources all have four cubits instead of six, making Goliath six and a half feet tall (2 m), still a remarkable height by ancient standards.
The detailed description of Goliath's armor and weapons is striking. David does not have to trust in equipment (vv. 39, 50).
The Philistine challenge to the "servants of Saul" was to "choose a man" (v. 8). The logical choice is Saul (9:2; 10:23, 24), but he is terrified like everyone else.
David's time is split between duties to his king (16:21–23) and to his father. David's whole family is introduced with him (vv. 12–14).
The number forty in Hebrew often denotes a period of trial and testing (Gen. 7:4; Num. 14:33, 34). Goliath taunts Israel every morning and evening for forty days.
See notes on 18:17–19, 20–27.
See note on 14:6.

Eliab's sudden anger is the reaction of a man who is unable to meet a challenge and who resents being outdone by his little brother. David's anointing will certainly increase Eliab's jealousy. In Gen. 37, Joseph's older brothers react in the same way to the knowledge that he will one day be superior to them (vv. 2–19). with whom have you left those few sheep. Whatever his excitement about the battle, David has acted responsibly in regard to his more mundane duties (vv. 20, 22). your presumption. Or "your insolence." the evil of your heart. Cf. Eliab's judgment of David with God's evaluation, as indicated by statements such as "a man after his own heart" (13:14), and "the LORD looks on the heart" (16:7).

The conversation between Saul and David vividly illustrates the radical difference in their perspectives. Saul continues to think in terms of what is humanly possible ("You are not able," v. 33), while David is confident that "The LORD \... will deliver me" (v. 37).
See note on 14:6.

**LORD** be with you. David's rise to power continues to be furthered, if unwittingly, by Saul. Having brought him into his court (16:19 note), Saul now sends him out to fight his battle. Most ironic of all, Saul invokes over David the benediction that most clearly distinguishes them and will account for David's ultimate success — "the LORD be with you" (16:18 and note).

Saul attempts to equip David with weaponry similar to that of Goliath (17:5). David's rejection of Saul's armor and weapons supports the point of the narrative that "the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's" (v. 47).

**LORD** of hosts. See note on 1:3. David comes "in the name" of God, that is, by the authority and power of God. On the significance of God's name in relation to His character, see, e.g., Ex. 34:5–7.
David outdoes Goliath's threat (v. 44) by extending his counter-threat to encompass the entire Philistine army.
**LORD**'s. See notes on vv. 38, 39; 14:6.
The same thing previously happened to Goliath's god, Dagon (5:3, 4).

That is, deals him the mortal wound (v. 51 note). There was no sword. This verse marks the climax of the contest between Goliath, who physically speaking has all the advantages, and David, who has God on his side and is able to triumph even without a sword (cf. vv. 45–47).
A form of the Hebrew verb different from that used in v. 50; the sense is "dispatched," as in 14:13.
See notes on 4:1; 5:8, 10.

At this time, Jerusalem is still under the control of the Jebusites. It does not come under Israelite rule until later in David's reign (2 Sam. 5:6–9). Perhaps David is taunting the Jebusites by displaying Goliath's head to them (cf. 31:9, 10).

Saul's question and Abner's response appear to conflict with the events described in 16:18–22. At the same time, a chronological relationship between chs. 16 and 17 seems warranted (v. 15 and 18:2). Saul's question may be prompted by concerns about the social status of someone who might receive the position promised in 17:25, including marriage to his daughter. The intensity of Saul's interest may also reflect his knowledge that the kingdom will ultimately be given to "a neighbor of yours, who is better than you" (15:28). See 18:8 and note.
See 8:11 in which the king is described as one who forcibly takes young men into his service. would not let him return. See note on 17:15.
The nature of the covenant is not explicitly stated but see the note on v. 4. Further references to the covenant between Jonathan and David include 20:8, 13–17, 42; 22:8; 23:18.

As crown prince (20:31), Jonathan is the one ordinarily expected to succeed his father as king. In 13:22 Jonathan and Saul were distinguished from the rest of the people by their possession of swords and spears. Here Jonathan's gifts of his robe and weapons to David not only signifies his loyalty but also implies his recognition of David as God's choice for the next king. See Jonathan's explicit confession in 23:17; note on 2 Sam. 1:10.
Military success continues to be David's hallmark, and Saul gives David a rank in the army commensurate with his accomplishments.

See 21:11; 29:5. It is a common feature of Hebrew poetry for one or more terms in the first half of a verse to be increased or intensified in the second half. For the thousand-ten thousand parallelism, see Deut. 32:30; Pss. 91:7; 144:13; Mic. 6:7. Whether the women's song praises Saul and David as equals or implies that David is better than Saul, Saul certainly takes offense to it (v. 8).
Saul rightly senses that David may be the "neighbor" who will replace him (15:28; 17:55 note).
See note on 16:14. raved. Ecstatic experiences can be caused by God's Spirit (10:6, 15) but also by evil spirits or false prophets (1 Kin. 18:29).
**LORD** was with him. See 16:18 and note. had departed from Saul. See 16:14 and note.

Saul's removal of David from the court, with an accompanying demotion in military rank, may be intended to decrease David's visibility and popularity as well as to increase the risk of his dying in battle. The effect of Saul's scheming, however, is actually the reverse. David is brought into closer contact with the people, so that "all Israel and Judah loved David" (v. 16).

In view of David's great popularity, Saul cannot continue to delay fulfilling his promise (17:25). Nevertheless, he adds a further condition, that David "fight the LORD's battles," in the hope that the Philistines would kill David for him (vv. 17, 21, 25). David says that he lacks the social standing to marry the king's daughter, a conventional protest in such circumstances (cf. 9:21). At the last minute, Saul reneges on his promise and gives Merab to someone else.

When Saul's second daughter, Michal, falls in love with David, Saul offers David another chance to become his son-in-law (vv. 20, 21). He adds again to the conditions David must fulfill (v. 25). David wastes no time in meeting Saul's requirement twice over and becomes the king's son-in-law (vv. 26, 27).

**LORD** was with David. Saul's increasing fear of David is well founded, since the Lord is with David (vv. 12, 14). David's success would not distress Saul so much if, like Jonathan, Saul were able to accept his rejection with equanimity.
Saul's covert attempts on David's life having come to nothing (ch. 18), he decides to take a direct approach.

Jonathan's magnanimity toward David stands in stark contrast to Saul's malevolence, continuing the unfavorable comparison of father and son noted earlier (13:22; 14:1, 6, 10, 29 and notes). It seems likely that Jonathan's loyalty to David stems not from ignorance of David's destiny but from a willing acceptance of it (18:4; 23:17 notes).
See note on 16:14.
Perhaps again galled by David's military success (v. 8; 18:8), Saul resorts to one of his old tricks (18:10, 11).
As Saul's designs on David's life become increasingly intense and overt, David is warned first by Saul's son (v. 2) and then by Saul's daughter.
Henceforth, David will be on the run from Saul.
The same Hebrew term is translated "household gods" in Gen. 31:19, 34, 35; Judg. 18:14. The Genesis references imply small objects, while the present reference suggests something larger.
Michal's deception here has an element of self-preservation. In light of Saul's later behavior (20:32, 33), Michal has reason to be afraid of her father (cf. 16:2).

See note on 1:1. Naioth. This word, which occurs only in this section, is associated with the place name Ramah. It is quite possibly not a proper noun at all but a word meaning the "camps" in which the prophets at Ramah are active (cf. the prophets' lodge in 2 Kin. 6:1, 2).
See note on 10:5.

Secu is unknown, but it may be a site about two miles (3 km) north of Ramah. Some have suggested reconstructing the difficult Hebrew on the basis of the Septuagint to read "well of the threshing floor on the bare height." This may be a familiar landmark; such landmarks are mentioned more than once in Samuel (20:19; 2 Sam. 20:8).
Having set out to destroy David, Saul has been frustrated by Jonathan, Michal, Samuel, and now finally by God Himself.

Robes in the books of Samuel often seem to have a symbolic significance, frequently pertaining to the kingship (15:28; 18:4; 24:4–6 and notes). While Jonathan's gift of his robe to David in 18:4 was voluntary, Saul's action here is under the compulsion of God's Spirit. Is Saul also among the prophets? This question appeared first in 10:11, 12, and there it had a positive sense. The present case seems to be a negative evaluation of the king.
See note on 19:18.
Apparently Jonathan is unaware of the most recent attempts on David's life (19:9–24) and assumes that the oath of 19:6 still stands.

This festival was a time of rejoicing at the beginning of each month. It was marked by the sounding of trumpets (Num. 10:10; Ps. 81:3) and special sacrifices (Num. 28:11–15). The festival is often mentioned in conjunction with the Sabbath (2 Kin. 4:23; 1 Chr. 23:31; Neh. 10:33; Is. 66:23; Ezek. 46:3) and may have been subject to similar regulations (Amos 8:5). The new moon celebration is mentioned once in the NT (Col. 2:16).
Jonathan goes along with David's pretext in vv. 28, 29. Bethlehem. See note on 16:1. yearly sacrifice. See note on 1:3; cf. 1:21.
This address expresses humility and deference (1:11, 16; 3:10; 17:32; 22:15; 23:10; 25:24).
See 18:3, 4 and notes. Pledges of friendship and loyalty are reiterated in vv. 13–17, 42.

**LORD** be with you, as he has been with my father. Recognizing that David is now God's chosen king (18:4; 23:17 and notes), Jonathan gives him allegiance over and above allegiance to his own father (v. 16).
For the fulfillment of this request, see 2 Sam. 9:1–8; 21:7.

See note on v. 13. Since it is David himself who will be accountable to keep covenant with Jonathan, "enemies" is probably a euphemistic reference to Saul, Jonathan's father (cf. 25:22; 2 Sam. 12:14).
See note on v. 8.
See note on v. 5.

The site is otherwise unknown. The Hebrew may mean something like "departure stone." The stone is possibly a familiar landmark on the way out of town; for other such landmarks mentioned in Samuel, see 19:22; 2 Sam. 20:8 and notes.
**LORD** is between you and me. See Gen. 31:50, 53.
Saul's relative and military commander (14:50).

See esp. Lev. 7:19–21; 15:16–18; Deut. 23:10, 11. Laws of cleanliness are covered most fully in Lev. 11–15, though references to "clean" and "unclean" are frequent throughout the Pentateuch (e.g., Gen. 7:2; Lev. 5:2; Num. 5:2; Deut. 14:3–21). The point is not physical but ritual or religious uncleanness.
Saul is insulting David by refusing to call him by name.
See note on v. 6.
As in similar modern expressions, the insult is meant for Jonathan and not necessarily his mother.

Despite Samuel's words in 13:14, Saul still clings to hope for his dynasty (cf. 18:8 note). Cf. Jonathan's ready acceptance of the Lord's will (v. 13; 18:4; 23:17 and notes). It may be inferred from Saul's words that Jonathan is his firstborn and thus in line for the throne.
Saul's and Jonathan's opposite reactions to David have driven a wedge between them. Saul's attempt on Jonathan's life matches his earlier attempts on David's (18:11; 19:10).
The arrow travels farther than where the boy is standing, and this is a negative sign that David must run for his life (see v. 22).
See note on v. 8.

Probably located less than two miles (3.2 km) northeast of Jerusalem (Is. 10:32), Nob became "the city of the priests" (22:19) sometime after the disaster that came upon Shiloh (1:3; 2:32 and notes) at the hands of the Philistines (4:1–11). Ahimelech. Either Ahijah's brother or simply another name for Ahijah (14:3), Ahimelech occupies the position of high priest once held by his great-grandfather Eli (1:9). See also Mark 2:26 and note.
Having employed a pretext to good advantage not long before (20:6 note), David does so again, with disastrous results for Ahimelech and the priests at Nob (22:6–19).

That is, "the showbread" (v. 6; cf. Ex. 25:30; 35:13; Lev. 24:5–9; 1 Chr. 9:32). Twelve fresh loaves of bread were placed on the table in the holy place each Sabbath, and the priests were the only ones allowed to eat this bread (Lev. 24:5–9). See Jesus' reference to this episode in Matt. 12:3, 4; Mark 2:25, 26; Luke 6:3, 4. kept themselves from women. Ritual cleanliness was a part of consecration prior to battle or other important occasions (Ex. 19:15; Lev. 15:18; Deut. 23:9–14; Josh. 3:5; 2 Sam. 11:11–12).
See v. 4 and note.

The presence of Doeg at these transactions arouses apprehensions in the reader as it does in David (22:22). These apprehensions prove well founded as the narrative progresses (22:9, 10, 18, 19). Doeg is also mentioned in the title of Ps. 52.
See 17:51, 54. ephod. See note on 2:28.
See 27:2–12; 29:1–11; title to Ps. 34, where "Abimelech" may be a name for Philistine kings. Gath. See notes on 4:1; 5:8.

Outside as well as inside Israel, David's royal destiny seems to be recognized, even if the Philistines' statement is best understood as popular exaggeration. David his ten thousands. See note on 18:7.

Adullam, which may mean "refuge," is located in the foothills of Judah at the site of Khirbet ash-Sheikh about ten miles (16 km) east of Gath. See also 2 Sam. 23:13; cf. Josh. 12:15; titles to Ps. 57 and 142. his father's house \... went down there to him. The vehemence that has driven Saul to attack even his own family (20:33) leaves David's family with little reason to feel secure.

The specific location of this city is unknown. On the name Mizpeh ("watchtower"), see note on 7:5. king of Moab. Moab had a king already in Judg. 3:12. stay with you. David's decision to seek sanctuary in Moab may be based not only on the assumption that a nation at odds with Saul (14:47) might well wish to side with a rival but also on David's family ties to the Moabites (Ruth 4:13–17). what God will do for me. While taking whatever practical measures he can, David nevertheless sees God in sovereign control of his situation (2 Sam. 15:25, 26).
See note on 23:14.

Later to serve as King David's seer (2 Sam. 24:11; 2 Chr. 29:25; cf. 1 Chr. 29:29), Gad's presence at this point is a reminder that David's destiny is divinely appointed and that he is under the Lord's protection. David will later be joined by a priest (vv. 20–23).
The mention of Saul's spear here may be a reminder of Saul's violent temper (18:10, 11; 19:10; 20:33), which comes to full expression in this episode.

Having apparently surrounded himself with members of his own tribe (9:1, 2; 10:21), Saul seeks to reinforce their loyalty with an appeal to self-interest; he is becoming more like the kings of surrounding nations (8:12–14). fields and vineyards. The questions addressed by Saul to his officials suggest that he engaged in at least some of the abusive royal practices about which Samuel had warned (8:10–18).
See notes on 18:3, 4.
See 21:7 and note. Ahimelech the son of Ahitub. See 21:1 and notes.

Saul's assumption that Ahimelech has plotted with David against the king is baseless; Ahimelech was simply misled by David (21:2 note). Saul has accused the priests of Nob of conspiring against him as well (22:8). risen against me, to lie in wait. Saul's assumption of hostile motives on David's part is as ill founded as his assumption about Ahimelech.
Ahimelech may still think at this point that David was doing covert work for Saul when he came for help (21:2).

Saul's command that the priests of the Lord be slaughtered is so evil and irrational that his own men refuse to carry it out. At least once before, Saul's men found it necessary to go against him (14:45 and note).
See note on 2:31. linen ephod. See note on 2:18.

It is an irony extremely damaging to Saul's image that the description of the total slaughter of the inhabitants of Nob, "the city of the priests," matches almost verbatim the order Saul received to slaughter of the Amalekites (15:3), an order he failed to carry out.

Support for David continues to build, chiefly as a result of Saul's misguided attempts at self-preservation. David now has the support of both prophet (v. 5) and priest. Abiathar brings to David the ephod used for discerning the Lord's will (23:6; cf. 2:28; 14:3 and notes).

It would be easy for David to excuse himself for the massacre at Nob by simply condemning Saul. Instead, he readily admits his share of responsibility for the disaster (21:2 note). In this admission, the reader glimpses a major difference between David and his predecessor in the quality of their repentance, linked to humility (15:24–26, 30 and notes; 2 Sam. 12:13 note).

Located about three miles (5 km) south of Adullam (22:1) near Philistine territory, Keilah is also mentioned in Josh. 15:44. robbing the threshing floors. Cf. Judg. 6:3–6. The primary reason for the raid is to plunder foodstores.
Not the linen ephod traditionally worn by all priests (cf. 22:18), but the ephod associated with divine inquiry (2:28 note).
Saul's interpretation of events is without foundation, as the narrator's diametrically opposed assertion makes clear: "God did not give him into his hand" (v. 14).
In view of Saul's ruthless treatment of the city of Nob, the behavior of the Keilahites probably reflects fear rather than ingratitude to David.
The growth of David's company from four hundred (22:2) to six hundred is an indication of his increasing strength (22:20 note).

The term "strongholds" (plural) suggests a geographical area, not a single location (22:4; 2 Sam. 5:17; 23:14). wilderness of Ziph. The village of Ziph is thirteen miles (21 km) southeast of Keilah and five miles (8 km) southeast of Hebron. The wilderness is the desert area south of Hebron. Ziph is mentioned in Josh. 15:55, along with Maon (v. 24) and Carmel (15:12; 25:2). God did not give him into his hand. God is in sovereign control of David's destiny (v. 7; 22:20 and notes).

No longer ignorant of his father's malevolence toward David (cf. 20:2), Jonathan acts as a true friend by aiding David in finding strength where true strength can alone be found. See 30:6, where David once more "strengthened himself in the LORD his God."

Though Jonathan will not survive to serve David (31:2), his readiness to let go of personal ambition for the sake of God's chosen king (18:4; 20:13) is a foil to Saul's desperate efforts to hang on to a kingdom that is no longer his (15:23). Saul \... knows this. See 20:30, 31. Saul's refusal to accept his rejection (cf. Eli's response in 3:18) cannot be excused on the grounds that he does not know to whom the kingdom should go.
See notes on 18:3, 4.
See note on v. 14; 26:1. Ps. 54 is later penned by David in light of the Ziphites' betrayal. Gibeah. Saul's hometown (10:26).
About eight miles (13 km) south of Hebron, Maon is mentioned in 25:2 as the hometown of Nabal.
The providential timing of this Philistine incursion is obvious.
Engedi is a large spring on the steep western shore of the Dead Sea. Its vicinity affords David provisions and protection in his flight from Saul.
See note on 23:29.
Saul's elite troops.

**LORD** said to you. While it is providential that Saul should enter the very cave where David and his men are hidden, there has been no hint that God wants David to lift a hand against Saul (cf. v. 6). The suggestion by David's men that he do so is a mistaken conclusion. cut off a corner of Saul's robe. David restricts himself to a symbolic act (v. 5 note). The robe symbolizes Saul's authority as king.

Although David later displays the corner of Saul's robe as evidence of his goodwill toward Saul (v. 11), his pangs of conscience (cf. 2 Sam. 24:10) suggest that a desire to secure such proof may not have been his only reason for going so close to Saul. In view of the royal significance of robes (15:28; 18:4; 19:24 and notes), David may have felt guilty of an inappropriate grasping after the kingship and of an act of aggression against the Lord's anointed (v. 6).
**LORD**'s anointed. David recognizes and safeguards the sanctity of the Lord's anointed (26:9; cf. 2:10 note), leaving judgment and vengeance to the Lord (v. 12).
David's point seems to be like Jesus' teaching, "You will recognize them by their fruits" (Matt. 7:16, 20). David is known by his restraint, but Saul is known from his efforts to harm David.

David abases himself before Saul, as Mephibosheth will later do before David (2 Sam. 9:8). The expression "dead dog" occurs only one other time in the OT, in 2 Sam. 16:9. "Dog" is usually an insult (17:43; 2 Sam. 3:8; 2 Kin. 8:13). This comment by David underlines his humility (see 1 Sam. 2:7, 8).

Having just escaped with his life, Saul experiences a rare moment of remorse. His testimony to David's righteousness recognizes David's right to rule; even Saul acknowledges that David did not rise to power by illicit means.

Cf. Samuel's rebuke of Saul in 13:14: "But now your kingdom shall not continue." Yet in contrast to Jonathan's action in 18:4 (note), Saul gives no sign of being ready to give the throne to David (cf. 26:25 note).

The extent of mourning is a sign of Samuel's prominence as a leader. Cf. the mourning that accompanied the deaths of Jacob (Gen. 50:10), Aaron (Num. 20:29), and Moses (Deut. 34:8). Ramah. Samuel's hometown (1:1 note). Paran. A region located in the northeast Sinai Peninsula immediately to the northwest of the Gulf of Aqaba and southeast of Kadesh-barnea.

See 23:24. Carmel. The same Carmel where Saul erected a monument in his own honor (15:12 notes). The setting of this incident near Carmel is the first of many reminders of Saul in this chapter. Although Carmel is a Judahite site, it seems to have political leanings toward Saul.

In v. 25 Abigail explains the name as meaning "folly." It seems unlikely that parents would name a child "fool." The etymological meaning of the name is probably related to an Arabic word that means "noble." "Folly" is thus a disparaging play on a name that sounds like "fool." Calebite. Nabal is of the clan of Caleb, the trustworthy spy during the conquest who later settles in Hebron. Maon is merely eight miles (13 km) south of Hebron. On Caleb's tribal holdings, see Josh. 14:13; 15:13. The similarity of the name "Caleb" to the Hebrew word for "dog" (cf. 24:14 note) may account for the inclusion of this particular detail in the introduction of Nabal.
Cf. the attitude of respect and deference adopted by David in addressing Saul as "my father" in 24:11.

Nabal's attack on David's messengers is vicious. The Hebrew verb translated "railed" means "to shriek" or "to fly at" something and is closely related to the Hebrew noun for "birds of prey." The same verb is used of Saul in 15:19 to describe his unrestrained "pouncing" upon the Amalekite spoils (cf. 14:32).
Not only have David's men refrained from inflicting harm (v. 7); their presence has given protection to the shepherds of Nabal (v. 21).
The designation "worthless man" is lit. "a son of Belial" (cf. 1:16; 2:12; 10:26, 27). Nabal's plight springs from his wickedness. His lack of knowledge is a refusal to know.

In refusing to confide in her husband, Abigail shows her lack of confidence in him. In view of Abigail's insight into the Lord's choice of David (v. 28 and note), her decision to go against her husband's wishes seems to fall under the category of obeying God rather than men (Acts 5:29).
Unrestrained by any special status of the man Nabal (cf. 24:9–12), David is intent upon exacting personal revenge.
Abigail calls Nabal "a son of Belial" (see note on 25:17). as his name is, so is he. See note on v. 3.

Abigail's perception of David is as right as her husband's is wrong (vv. 10, 11; 2 Sam. 7:11–16). fighting the battles of the **LORD** . Abigail's words hint at the difference between David's proper military role and the personal vendetta he is now pursuing. Righteous engagement in conflict means standing boldly for God and leaving personal injuries to be dealt with by the Lord (24:12). evil shall not be found in you. To take his own revenge on an enemy will make David little better than Saul, and David later praises the Lord for sending Abigail to deter him from such a transgression (v. 32).
Note the poetic repetition in Abigail's speech.
This phrase invites the thought that Nabal is somehow like another king, Saul.

**LORD** . It would have been wrong for David to take matters into his own hands, but not because Nabal was innocent. Having heard of Nabal's death, David thanks the Lord for keeping him from personal wrongdoing while at the same time upholding his cause.
David now has three wives: Michal, Saul's daughter, who has been given to someone else; Ahinoam; and Abigail. See also 2 Sam. 2:2; 3:2, 3.
See note on 23:19; cf. 24:2.
See note on 2 Sam. 2:18.
See note on 24:4.
**L****OR**D's anointed. See note on 24:6.
**LORD** will strike him. David's words express an assurance gained, or at least reinforced, by the Lord's recent dealings with Nabal (25:38, 39).
**LORD** . David's survival and ultimate success are divinely overseen and directed (cf. 30:2, 19 and notes).
**LORD** . See note on 2 Sam. 20:19. Go, serve other gods. David means that he has been expelled to live among aliens, away from the people of God.
Cf. 24:14. a partridge. The partridge (Heb. "caller") is a cleverly chosen name for David, who stands on the crest of a mountain and "calls" (vv. 13, 14).
David's response to Saul's confession and invitation (v. 22) indicates he doubts Saul's sincerity; cf. Samuel's response to a similar invitation by Saul in 15:24–26.
Saul's behavior is erratic, and David trusts neither his confessions nor his blessings (27:1; 24:20 note).

Despite recently learned lessons of faith (26:10), David tires of being a fugitive in constant danger and gives in to the human fear that Saul will eventually succeed in destroying him. David's anxiety may be heightened since he and his men have their families with them (v. 3). For the second time (21:10), David seeks refuge among Israel's archenemies, the Philistines.

Now that the rift between David and Saul is conspicuous and indisputable, Achish readily accepts David's presence, doubtless hoping to benefit from David's allegiance in his own struggles against Saul (29:6). For the location of Gath, see 5:8.
See note on 25:40–44.

While David's request to be assigned to "one of the country towns" is ostensibly based on a desire not to burden the royal city, it promises him a greater freedom of action by removing him from the eyes of Achish (vv. 8–11).

Once an Israelite possession, Ziklag is under Philistine control at this time. Listed among the cities of Judah (Josh. 15:31; 19:5), ancient Ziklag may have been at Tel esh-Shariah, fifteen miles (24 km) northwest of Beersheba. kings of Judah. This expression is probably from the viewpoint of a time after the division of Israel into the northern and southern kingdoms (1 Kin. 12).

Neighbors of the Philistines (Josh. 13:2), these people are not the same as the Geshurites from east of the Jordan (Josh. 13:11; 2 Sam. 15:8; 1 Chr. 2:23). David's wife, Absalom's mother (2 Sam. 3:3), is from the Geshurites east of the Jordan. Girzites. Not identifiable; Gezer is quite distant. Amalekites. See note on 15:2. Shur. See note on 15:7.

David's practice will conceal his double-dealings from Achish (v. 11). Whether it was right is doubtful at best in the absence of any indication that the Lord has ordered his actions. This is was a partial ban in which David destroys all humans but takes other things for spoil.

This is not the first time David thinks it necessary to deceive (20:6; 21:2 and notes; cf. 16:2 note). the Negeb of Judah. See 2 Sam. 24:7; 2 Chr. 28:18. The large southern region of Israel, the Negeb, extends from Beersheba south to the Gulf of Aqaba. Jerahmeelites. 1 Chr. 2:9–15 mentions Jerahmeel as a descendant of Judah through Hezron and as a brother of Ram, an ancestor of David. Kenites. Kenites and Jerahmeelites are mentioned together in 30:29.
Achish is deceived by David's pretense of raiding villages in Judah and its environs.
Achish points out that his benevolence to David has certain strings attached. The same Hebrew phrase is used in Solomon's warning to Shimei in 1 Kin. 2:37, 42.

The irony of David's ambiguous answer (will David fight for or against him?) has a counterpoint in the perhaps unconscious irony of Achish's reply. my bodyguard for life. Presumably Achish's offer is contingent on David's performance in battle. The Hebrew term used by Achish for "bodyguard," lit. "keeper of my head," is an unfortunate choice of words in view of David's treatment of Goliath (17:49–54). This story will resume in 29:1.

The death of Samuel signals the passing of an era. the mediums and the necromancers. Although Saul's expulsion of mediums and necromancers is fully in keeping with Mosaic law (Lev. 19:31; 20:6, 27; Deut. 18:9–14), it does not prove his personal zeal for the religion of Israel. Saul's consultation of a medium is a clear indication of unfaithfulness and disobedience (1 Chr. 10:13); Lev. 20:6 says that such a person is to be "cut \... off from among his people."

Located at modern Sulem in the eastern part of the Jezreel Valley. Shunem is the site of the Philistine camp on the eve of the battle in which Saul died (ch. 31). Gilboa. This is probably the mountain range that begins five miles (8 km) south of Shunem and extends south along the eastern edge of the plain of Jezreel. It could also be a village located in the heart of the Gilboa range eleven miles (18 km) south of Shunem. See 29:1 and note.
See 17:11 and note.

**LORD** did not answer him. Saul's inquiry is prompted by anxiety (v. 5), not piety, and the Lord's refusal to answer is reminiscent of the threat of 8:18. by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets. Saul rejected the Lord and as a consequence was rejected by the Lord (15:23 and note). This has cut him off from the usual means of divine inquiry. Whereas David had the prophet Gad in his retinue (22:5), it is unlikely that a true prophet has accompanied Saul. Moreover, the authentic ephod containing the Urim and Thummim (2:28 note) has come into David's possession through Abiathar (23:6).

His purge of the land notwithstanding (v. 3 note), Saul seems to have no doubt that a medium can be found, and his attendants can name one immediately. En-dor. Josh. 17:11, 12 attests to a persistent Canaanite influence at En-dor, which is about four miles (6 km) northeast of Shunem (v. 4 note). Saul's recourse to En-dor takes him behind Philistine lines.

Probably this is Samuel himself, not merely an apparition. The consternation of the medium shows that the figure is something outside her usual experience of magic arts. The narrator calls it simply "Samuel," and what the figure says is consistent with Samuel's pronouncements when he was alive (esp. ch. 15). For some reason the Lord allows Samuel to visit Saul. It is clear from the medium's reaction that she cannot compel him to appear.

Apparently Saul recognizes Samuel when the woman describes his mantle. Robes have symbolized the fate of Saul's kingship in a variety of ways, and mention of Samuel's mantle recollects the devastating pronouncement of 15:28 (see also 18:4; 24:4–6).
Saul's egotism is on display in this verse: he uses the first-person pronoun six times in his response to Samuel.
That is, among the dead (31:2–4).
See note on 1:7.

Much has changed since Saul's first encounter with Samuel, when he was designated as the one to deliver Israel from the Philistines (9:16) and was treated to a festal meal by the prophet (9:22–24). Now in his last encounter with Samuel, on the eve of his own death and the crushing Philistine defeat of Israel, Saul is treated to a fatted calf by a medium.

This notice resumes the account initiated in 28:1, 2 but suspended in order to relate Saul's visit with the medium (28:3–25). Aphek. Probably the same Aphek mentioned in 4:1 (note), twenty-eight miles (45 km) north of Gath. The Philistines assemble their forces at Aphek before continuing their northward march (v. 2). The site is located on the main highway called the "Great Trunk Road." Jezreel. North of Mount Gilboa, a few miles south of Shunem, and forty miles (64 km) northeast of Aphek.
See note on 4:6. I have found no fault in him. This judgment is a measure of Achish's gullibility, not David's sincerity (27:8–12).
The other Philistine commanders are less gullible than Achish and perhaps still carry painful memories of mid-battle defection in an earlier war with Israel (14:21).
See note on 18:7; 21:11. Apparently this song is famously known even in Philistia.

A protest of genuine innocence when spoken to Saul (26:18), the question is now no more than a ruse. David has indeed done much (27:8–12) — if Achish is willing to see it. that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king. As in 28:2, David deals in ambiguities apparent to the reader, if not to Achish. The ambiguity here is the identity of "my lord the king." It could be Achish, Saul, or possibly God Himself.
Achish's grossly misplaced confidence makes him appear practically a fool. On the expression "angel of God," see 2 Sam. 14:17, 20; 19:27.

See note on 27:6. Amalekites had made a raid. See notes on 15:2, 8. Having been the victims of David's forays (27:8), the Amalekites have taken the opportunity of David's absence from Ziklag to retaliate. the Negeb. See note on 27:10.
A remarkable evidence of the Lord's providential protection of David (v. 19; 26:12), whose own practice has been quite different (27:9).

This turn of events is especially troubling, inasmuch as concern for the safety of their families may have motivated the retreat of David and his men to Philistine territory in the first place (27:1 note).
**LORD** his God. See note on 23:16.
See note on 22:20.

Seasonal rivers (or wadis) from the vicinity of Beersheba and south converge to form the brook Besor, which runs northwest to empty into the Mediterranean. David and his men have come to the ravine some thirteen miles (21 km) south of Ziklag.
Their exhaustion is not surprising after a march of more than sixty miles (nearly 100 km) from Aphek (29:1–11) to the brook Besor.

The Cherethites were probably from Crete. They are often mentioned alongside the Philistines (Ezek. 25:16; Zeph. 2:5). The "Cherethites and Pelethites" served under the command of Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, as professional troops loyal to David (2 Sam. 8:18; 15:18; 20:7, 23) and, for a short time at least, to Solomon (1 Kin. 1:44). They seem to have been the king's bodyguard (2 Sam. 23:20, 23). the Negeb of Caleb. Caleb, son of Jephunneh, is first mentioned in Num. 13:6 as one of the spies chosen to scout out the land of Canaan. He is commended in Num. 14:24 as one who followed the Lord "fully" and who therefore would receive an inheritance in the Promised Land. His inheritance included Hebron (Josh. 14:13, 14; Judg. 1:20).
This is further, striking evidence of the Lord's watchful care over David's affairs (v. 2 note).
See note on v. 9.
See note on 2:12, where the same Hebrew expression is used.

**LORD** has given us. David recognizes that the successful rescue is not his doing but the Lord's (vv. 2, 19 and notes). This leads him to reject the idea that the frontline troops have a right to more spoil than those who stayed behind.
Probably he is thanking them for the help he received in escaping from Saul (v. 31), though it is also in this area that David's kingship is first officially recognized (2 Sam. 2:1–4).

As v. 31 says, these cities are within the range of David's roamings as a fugitive. All of them are in the south of Judah. This Bethel (v. 27) should not be confused with the more northern city of the same name (7:16 note).
See note on 28:4.
See 14:49. For a listing of all four sons of Saul, see 1 Chr. 8:33. Only one of Saul's sons remains alive after the battle (see 2 Sam. 2:8).

See note on 14:6. Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. While some praise Saul's action as worthy of a tragic hero, the tenor of the books of Samuel points in another direction. To be commended are those who, like David, in times of distress find strength in God (23:16; 30:6), and who, like Jonathan, yield fully to His will (18:4, 28, 29; 19:4; 20:31; 23:17 and notes).
On the qualified sense of "all," see note on 15:8.

The fertility goddesses of the Canaanites. Beth-shan. Located in the Jordan Valley some sixteen miles (26 km) south of the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee), this border city of the territory of Manasseh is listed in Josh. 17:11, 16; Judg. 1:27 among those cities that resisted Israelite occupation and remained Canaanite and Philistine strongholds.
See note on 11:1.

This courageous act of the "valiant men" of Jabesh-gilead is an expression of gratitude for their rescue by Saul, recounted in ch. 11. It is regarded as shameful in Saul's era for the dead to remain unburied.

2 Samuel.note: See 1 Sam. 30:1; note on 1 Sam. 27:6.

In the wake of Israel's devastating defeat (1 Sam. 31:1), the messenger takes on the appearance of mourning (cf. Josh. 7:6; 1 Sam. 4:12). His claim to have had a hand in Saul's death (v. 10), however, shows that he expects at least this item of news to please David.
Chariots often carried archers in those days (cf. Saul's injury, 1 Sam. 31:3).

In light of 1 Sam. 31:4–6, it seems probable that the Amalekite happened upon Saul's body before the Philistines and, in the hopes of receiving a reward from David, has fabricated a part for himself in Saul's death. Others have suggested that Saul's act of falling on his sword might only have wounded him and that the Amalekite's account is therefore plausible. In either case, the Amalekite expects to receive a different response from David than what he actually receives. crown \... armlet. Royal regalia is proof of Saul's demise. The crown in view is presumably a lighter version of the heavy state crown. The way in which Saul's regalia come into David's possession is a stark contrast to Jonathan's voluntary surrender of his robe and weapons to David (1 Sam. 18:4 and note). This contrast epitomizes the radically different responses of Saul and Jonathan to the divine will with respect to David and the house of Saul (e.g., 1 Sam. 18:28, 29; 19:4; 20:30, 31; 23:17, 18).
The Amalekite is clearly subject to the laws of Israel because he is an alien who resides in the land of Israel (Lev. 19:33, 34; 24:22).
LORD's anointed. By not sharing David's conviction about the sacrosanct status of "the LORD's anointed" (1 Sam. 24:6; 26:9), the Amalekite signs his own death warrant (vv. 15, 16).
David's severe reaction to the Amalekite's story provides evidence that David was not involved in Saul's death (cf. 4:10).

The lament opens with an introduction presenting the refrain, "How the mighty have fallen!" The first section exhorts the people to mourn for Saul and is marked by the references to "the daughters of the Philistines" (v. 20) and the "daughters of Israel" (v. 24). The second section (vv. 25, 26) expresses David's personal mourning for Jonathan. The lament closes with a final repetition of the mournful refrain.
See note on Josh. 10:13.
This phrase, which refers to Saul and Jonathan (v. 17), is repeated as a refrain in vv. 25, 27. "Mighty" appears also in v. 21 in parallel to "Saul."

David implores his listeners not to let the news be heard among the Philistine cities lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice over Israel's defeat, in the same way that the daughters of Israel earlier rejoiced over the defeat of the Philistines (1 Sam. 18:7).

It was customary to condition and preserve leather shields by rubbing them with oil (Is. 21:5). It may be more than coincidental that the particular wording is associated with royalty. Not only were kings "anointed" (1 Sam. 2:10 note) for their office, but the word "shield" is sometimes used in the OT as a figure for "sovereign" or "chieftain." Beneath the literal meaning of the words is perhaps the implication, "sovereign Saul, no longer anointed with oil."
The intent of this line is to praise Saul's military prowess.
A color that represents prosperity, wealth, and luxury (Prov. 31:21).

David's praise of Jonathan's love (cf. 1 Sam. 18:3) does not mean that love between friends is inherently superior to marital love. Rather, the point seems to be the astonishingly selfless quality of Jonathan's love for David. David himself does not prove selfless in his relations with women (3:2 note). Modern attempts to find in this verse evidence for a homosexual relationship between Jonathan and Saul have no exegetical warrant. Sadly, many people in our hyper-sexualized culture find it inconceivable that people of the same gender can have deep, loving friendships with one another without transgressing boundaries into sexual intimacy. Scripture, however, frequently extols the bonds of brotherhood and sisterhood, friendships that exhibit sacrificial love without any hint of eroticism (Prov. 17:17; 18:24; 4:9–12).
Probably stands for Saul and Jonathan. Cf. the designation of Elijah and Elisha as "the chariots of Israel and its horsemen" (2 Kin. 2:12; 13:14).

LORD. Though aware of his divine appointment as Israel's next king, David seeks the Lord's guidance, as he has done so often before (e.g., 1 Sam. 23:2, 4, 9–12; 30:7, 8). Hebron. Located nineteen miles (31 km) southwest of Jerusalem, Hebron has the highest elevation of any town in Israel and is strategically well suited for the inauguration of David's rule over Judah. Hebron was a Canaanite royal city when the Israelites came from Egypt (Josh. 10:3), but its links with the people of God extend back to the patriarchs (e.g., Gen. 13:18; 23:2, 19; 35:27). Under Israelite rule, it becomes both a Levitical city and a city of refuge (Josh. 21:11–13).

See note on 1 Sam. 25:40–44. Jezreel. Listed in Josh. 15:56 as one of the hill country villages south of Hebron, this Jezreel is not the better-known Jezreel in the north (v. 9). Carmel. See notes on 1 Sam. 15:12; 25:2.

On anointing, see note on 1 Sam. 2:10. David has already been anointed by Samuel (1 Sam. 16:3, 12, 13) and is now anointed again, this time as king over Judah. He will be anointed a third time, as king over Israel (5:3).

LORD. David's commendation of the Jabeshites for their kindness to Saul accomplishes two things: it shows he has no malice toward the now-deceased king, and it sets the stage for his own bid for leadership over the Gileadites east of the Jordan River.

Abner's installation of Saul's son Ish-bosheth as king over Israel results in war between the houses of Saul and David. 2:8 Ish-bosheth. Ish-bosheth is the only son of Saul left alive after the defeat on Mount Gilboa. The name "Ish-bosheth" ("man of shame") is probably a later alteration of the other names by which this son of Saul is known in the OT, Ishvi (1 Sam. 14:4) and Eshbaal (1 Chron. 8:33; 9:39), the change being made to avoid any association of Saul's son with the Canaanite god Baal. As will become apparent, this last surviving son of Saul is little more than a pawn in the hands of Abner. brought him over to Mahanaim. Abner brings Ish-bosheth across the Jordan River, probably in an effort to escape Philistine pressure. Two sites near the Jabbok River have been suggested for Mahanaim, one seven miles (11 km) and the other seventeen miles (27 km) from the river.
The way specific parts are listed suggests that Ish-bosheth's control of these areas is more complete than his control of Israel as a whole.
This is the length of time that Israel and Judah are a divided monarchy between the death of Saul and their unification under David.
See note on 5:4, 5.
Gibeon is a Benjaminite town, now called el-Jib, about five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem.
See note on v. 18. pool of Gibeon. Archaeologists have unearthed this structure, which served as a water storage facility for the town.
Abner suggests a form of representative combat similar to the contest between David and Goliath (1 Sam. 17:4 note). Large-scale bloodshed occurs on both occasions (vv. 17, 31).

According to 1 Chr. 2:16, Zeruiah is one of David's two sisters, which makes her sons his nephews. Joab. Joab plays an important role throughout David's reign, serving as commander of David's forces (8:16). Though an ardent supporter of David, Joab at times proves to be uncontrollable (3:39), acting in his own interests (3:26, 27) and even defying David's orders (18:5, 9–14). Joab is later executed by King Solomon (1 Kin. 2:28–35). Abishai. Abishai serves alongside Joab in David's army (10:10; 18:2; 23:18). Asahel. Also listed among David's mighty men (23:24), Asahel's relentless pursuit of Abner in this present episode will lead to Asahel's violent death (v. 23).

Abner's attempts to avoid striking down Asahel may be motivated not simply by fear of reprisal from Joab but also by a desire not to erect unnecessary barriers to an eventual compromise with David. See note on v. 26.

Abner's reference to "their brothers" may suggest a shift in a more conciliatory direction; perhaps Abner senses that David cannot be stopped. Abner prefers truce to defeat, especially if he can remain autonomous.
See notes on 1 Sam. 13:3; 2 Sam. 18:16; 20:22.
The disparity between the number of casualties suffered by David's troops and by the Benjaminites is a token of things to come.
A twenty-three-mile (37 km) journey after a battle is duly impressive.

At least in the northern tribes, the transfer of power to David after the death of Saul is not unopposed. A key figure supporting Saul is Abner, Saul's military commander who installed Saul's surviving son, Ish-bosheth, as king in Mahanaim (2:8, 9). But the tide is running in David's favor (2:30, 31 note).

The list of six sons born to David (vv. 2–5) amplifies the statement in v. 1 that "David grew stronger and stronger," while the wrangling between Abner and Ish-bosheth over a concubine (vv. 6–11) dramatizes the final statement in v. 1 that "the house of Saul became weaker and weaker." 3:2 sons were born to David at Hebron. As the list that follows reveals, David takes additional wives in Hebron. In 5:13–16, after David's arrival in Jerusalem, yet more wives and concubines are added, and at least eleven more children are born to David (cf. 1 Chr. 3:1–9). While the narrator offers no explicit evaluation of David's behavior (ancient Near Eastern kings commonly multiplied wives and children), it violates the standards of Deut. 17:17.
David's marrying a foreign wife from the small Aramean kingdom of Geshur may be politically motivated, giving him an ally north of Ish-bosheth's shaky realm.

Abner's appropriation of Saul's concubine amounts to a claim on the throne (12:8 note; 16:21 note; 1 Kin. 2:22). The reader is not told whether Ish-bosheth's suspicion is well-founded or simple paranoia. Whatever the case, Abner uses the accusation as an occasion to shift his allegiance to David (vv. 8–10).
has sworn to him.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} See notes on 5:2; cf. 1 Sam. 13:14; 15:28; 24:20.
A proverbial expression for the whole country (Judg. 20:1).
Ish-bosheth's reaction indicates that Abner is in a position not only to make a threat but also to carry it out.
Abner means either that the land is his own, as one who controls it and can give it to David, or that the land is David's by right, and that David should enlist Abner's help to secure it.

Returning David's wife Michal to him (1 Sam. 18:27) will not only make right Saul's wrong of giving her to another in David's absence (1 Sam. 25:44) but will also strengthen David's claim to the throne over Saul's former realm. The restrictions of Deut. 24:1–4 do not apply in this situation, since David's separation from Michal was involuntary.

The insecurity of Ish-bosheth's position is evident not only in his fear of Abner (v. 11) but also in his inability to resist David's orders. a hundred foreskins of the Philistines. David refers to the bride price that Saul set for Michal (1 Sam. 18:25); he actually paid twice that amount for her hand in marriage (1 Sam. 18:27).

A vivid glimpse of suffering caused by deeds outside the man's control. Bahurim. Tentatively identified with a site about one-and-a-half miles (2 km) east of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin. Bahurim is the hometown of Shimei, son of Gera (16:5; 1 Kin. 2:8).

See note on v. 1. Apparently Ish-bosheth and Abner are all that have stood in the way of harmonious relations between David and Israel. Abner here steps aside, and Ish-bosheth will not stand long without him (ch. 4).
David is now recognized as the recipient of a commission like the one first given to Saul (1 Sam. 9:16).
See 5:3. in peace. The repetition of this phrase twice more in vv. 22, 23 underscores that David is not involved in Abner's death; see also vv. 26, 28, 29, 37.
Joab's agitation at the thought of Abner's peaceful departure is apparent in his words to David.

According to the first-century historian Josephus, this site is located two-and-a-half miles (4 km) north of Hebron. But David did not know about it. This note is another confirmation of David's innocence in the death of Abner (vv. 21–23, 28, 29, 37).

An ironic death because Abner earlier killed Asahel by stabbing him in the stomach (see 2 Sam. 2:23). for the blood of Asahel his brother. See also v. 30. In 2:18–23 Abner's slaying of Asahel is depicted as essentially a matter of self-defense, and the battle context of Abner's action makes it doubtful that Joab has the right to act as an "avenger of blood" (14:11; cf. Num. 35:16–25; Deut. 19:11–13; Josh. 20:3). Joab may also want to eliminate a potential rival in David's court (see his murder of Amasa in 20:10).

David's decision only to utter a curse upon Joab's house rather than take direct disciplinary action may be a result of the ambiguous circumstances of Joab's crime. More likely, however, such factors as Joab's considerable power and reputation, and his familial relationship with David influence his decision. Ultimately Joab's crime does not go unpunished, although Solomon's actions in having Joab killed are questionable (1 Kin. 2:5, 6, 28–35).
This is David's second lament (see 1:17–27).
That is, "too hard" or "ruthless." See note on v. 29; cf. 16:10; 19:22.

The death of Abner affects Ish-bosheth and "all Israel" the same way, but for different reasons. Ish-bosheth's courage fails because he knows that Abner's death means the loss of the backbone of his government. Israel, on the other hand, is "dismayed" by what seems to be a rejection of their friendly overture to David (3:17–21).

The Benjaminite origin of Ish-bosheth's assassins is stressed (two verses are dedicated to establishing it), perhaps to show that disenchantment with the house of Saul extends even into his own tribe.

Although Beeroth is one of the four major cities of the Gibeonites (an Amorite people who duped Joshua into making a peace treaty with them; Josh. 9:17), Josh. 18:25 indicates that the town was allotted to Benjamin. King Saul attempted to annihilate the Gibeonites (21:1, 2), and this aggression may explain the flight of the Beerothites to Gittaim.

See 3:21. The covenant establishing David's rule over the northern tribes likely consists of regulations for the kingship (cf. 1 Sam. 10:25), including their rights and responsibilities to one another and to the Lord (2 Kin. 11:17). That this covenant does not end the sense of separate identity felt by Israel and Judah is evident in the revolt of Sheba (20:1) and particularly in the dissolution of the united kingdom under Rehoboam (1 Kin. 12:16). they anointed David. In the OT, a stereotyped formula often introduces the account of a king's official tenure in office (e.g., 1 Sam. 13:1; 2 Sam. 2:10; 1 Kin. 14:21; 22:42). In this case it appropriately marks David's assumption of power over all Israel.

A city of great antiquity (occupied as early as the third millennium B.C..), Jerusalem is in the tribal region of Benjamin, near the northern border of Judah. The city is mentioned in extrabiblical texts as early as the twentieth century B.C. in Egypt. The city was earlier conquered by Judah (Judg. 1:8), but neither Judah nor Benjamin have been successful in permanently dislodging its Jebusite inhabi­tants (Josh. 15:63; Judg. 1:21). David may well think that Jerusalem's strategic location and relatively independent status makes the city well suited to the establishment of a national capital that will not imply favoritism to any particular region. Jebusites \... said to David. The Jebusites' taunt, whether suggestive of overconfidence or simply of a determination to fight to the last man (even be he blind or lame), reflects the hostility between the Jebusites and David (see v. 8; 1 Sam. 17:54 note).

This marks the first occurrence of "Zion" in the Bible and the only one in Samuel. The name originally designated a fortified mound located at the southern end of the Ophel ridge. Eventually, the name came to be used in an extended sense for all of Jerusalem (2 Kin. 19:21; Is. 2:3) and even for the entire nation of Israel (Ps. 149:2; Is. 46:13). The name occurs frequently in Israel's poetic and prophetic literature, where it is often presented as the place of God's mighty acts of salvation and judgment (e.g., Ps. 14:7; Is. 4:4; Lam. 4:11).

Archaeologists have uncovered the remains of a complex water system in Jerusalem; it was built to bring water into the settlement from the Gihon Spring that was located outside of the city. This may be the shaft that Joab and his men use to penetrate the city (1 Chr. 11:6).
Heb. "fill." It perhaps refers to terraces that support buildings on top of them. It is mentioned in numerous passages (Judg. 9:6, 20; 1 Kin. 9:15, 24; 11:27; 1 Chr. 11:8; 2 Chr. 32:5).

Just as chs. 3, 4 detail how "the house of Saul became weaker and weaker" (3:1; 3:2–11 note), so chs. 5–10 show David growing "stronger and stronger" (3:1). The fundamental reason for David's success is that the Lord is with him (1 Sam. 16:18 note).

In David's time, Tyre is a Phoenician port city about thirty-five miles (56 km) north of Mount Carmel and twenty-five miles (40 km) south of Sidon. Hiram's generosity to David may be motivated by the impressiveness of David's recent accomplishments, but it also involves an element of self-interest. Tyre needs the inland trade routes controlled by David and the agricultural produce of central Palestine (cf. Ezra 3:7). Hiram's friendship with Israel continues well into Solomon's reign (1 Kin. 5:1–12; 9:11).

had established him king.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} See note on v. 10. for the sake of his people Israel. David understands not only that his kingship is dependent entirely upon God but also that it is intended for the benefit of God's people (v. 2; 8:15).

The Hebrew here is difficult, but cf. the explanation given in 1 Chr. 13:10 "because he put out his hand to the ark." It may be that the punishment relates not only to Uzzah's touching the ark (Num. 4:15, 20) but also, more importantly, to the irregular way the ark is being carried (v. 3 note; 1 Chr. 15:13–15).
The reader is not told whether the main cause of David's anger is Uzzah's death, Uzzah's recklessness, or his own cavalier handling of the ark.

That is, a man of Gath. Whether the reference is to the Philistine city of Gath (1 Sam. 4:1 note; 5:8 note) or to Gath Rimmon (a Levitical city in Dan or Manasseh; Josh. 21:23–25) is uncertain. Obed-edom is frequently referred to as a Levite in Chronicles (e.g., 1 Chr. 15:17–25; 16:5, 38; 26:4, 5, 8, 15; 2 Chr. 25:24).

LORD. David will not accept Michal's indictment. It is not before the "female servants" (that is, for their eyes) but "before the LORD" that he has celebrated. David pointedly mentions that the Lord displaced Saul and chose him instead.

Or, "I will humble myself even more than this." Unlike Eli and his sons (1 Sam. 2:29, 30 and notes) and Michal's father Saul (1 Sam. 15:12, 30 and notes), David is willing to be abased that the Lord may receive the honor due Him. The motif of David's humility recalls Hannah's remarks in 1 Sam. 2:7, 8. by them I shall be held in honor. David replies that he has no reason to feel embarrassed before the maids. This is either because of the direct decision of the Lord or because David excludes Michal from marital relations. To be childless in this era is a reproach (1 Sam. 1:5, 6).

Mentioned here for the first time, Nathan the prophet will also play a significant role in ch. 12 and 1 Kin. 1. See also 1 Chr. 29:29; 2 Chr. 9:29; 29:25. in a tent. David apparently views his palace as symbolic of his now-established rule (5:11, 12), and he proposes that God's rule should be similarly symbolized with a permanent dwelling.

David's plan seems reasonable to Nathan, but he is quick to reverse himself when ordered by the Lord (v. 4). Nathan is no flatterer (12:7–14). the LORD is with you. This repeated statement gets at the heart of David's early life and early kingship (1 Sam.16:18; 17:37; 18:14, 28; 2 Sam. 5:10).

The theological and historical significance of the divine promise to David recorded in these verses (par. 1 Chr. 17:3–15) can hardly be overestimated. Indeed, the promise of an enduring Davidic kingdom has been called the summit of the entire OT. Looking back, it takes up the promises of blessing made to Abraham and his elect seed (Gen. 17:16) and brings them to rest on David (vv. 9, 10, 12). Looking forward, it prepares for the messianic hope that inspires Israel's faith before and after the exile in Babylon (Is. 11:1; Jer. 23:5, 6; Zech. 3:8; 6:12). The hope for a Messiah culminates in the coming of Jesus Christ (Is. 9:1–7; Luke 1:32, 33, 69, 70; Acts 2:30, 31; 13:22, 23; Rom. 1:1–4; 2 Tim. 2:8; Rev. 22:16).

Cf. 3:18; Ps. 89:3. The Lord's reference to David as "my servant" places him in a select company that includes Abraham (Gen. 26:24), Moses (Num. 12:7, 8; Deut. 34:5), Caleb (Num. 14:24), and Joshua (Josh. 24:29).

God has accompanied His elect people throughout their wanderings (vv. 6, 7). Not until He has planted them in their place (v. 10) and they enjoy "rest" (v. 11) that exceeds what they already have under David (v. 1) will He allow a permanent house to be built for His name (v. 13).

See note on 1 Sam. 16:18. a great name. The declaration of a great name recalls the divine promise made to the patriarch Abraham in Gen. 12:2. Cf. 8:13, where David "made a name for himself," possibly an implied criticism because David promotes his own name (on promoting one's name, cf. Gen. 11:4).

will make you a house.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Having declined David's offer to build Him a house (i.e., a temple; v. 5), the Lord counters with the gracious announcement that He will instead establish a house (i.e., a dynasty) for David.

A double prophecy that is first fulfilled in Solomon, but the everlasting nature of David's throne finds its culmination in the Messiah (see Acts 2:30). who shall come from your body. The same words were spoken to Abraham in Gen. 15:4.

It was "for his great name's sake" that the Lord refused to reject His people after their sinful request for a king (1 Sam. 12:22). Now He announces to David that his own son, who will succeed him as king, will build a temple "for my name." For an explication of the significance of God's name, see Ex. 34:5–7 and note on 1 Sam. 17:45.

The full significance of this promise, expressive of the special relationship that the Lord establishes with the Davidic kings (Pss. 2:7; 89:18–37), is ultimately realized in Christ (Mark 1:11; Acts 13:33; Heb. 1:5). 7:14 I will discipline him. As a father, the Lord will discipline the royal son when he does wrong, but His covenantal love will never be taken away from David's line. Though the punishment is severe, extending even to the loss of land and temple (1 Kin. 9:6–9), God's promise to establish forever the throne of David cannot fail. This promise will increasingly come to be understood in messianic terms (Is. 9:7; 11:1–5; Jer. 33:14–26; Mic. 5:2–5).

LORD. Presumably David sits in front of the ark, the symbol of the Lord's presence (Ex. 25:22; 30:6; Deut. 10:8; Josh. 6:8). In this era, it is not usual to sit while praying (Deut. 10:8). Who am I. Having offered God a house (i.e., a temple), David is overwhelmed by the Lord's declaration that He will build David a house (i.e., a dynasty). The humility evident in David's "Who am I" agrees with his recognition that it is the sovereign Lord who has been with him (1 Sam. 16:18 note) to bring him this far.

This phrase is difficult to interpret. The parallel at 1 Chr. 17:17 reads quite differently: "\[you\] have shown me future generations." The likely sense is, "this is for the benefit of mankind." Like the covenant with Abraham (Gen. 12:1–3) and like the purpose of the crossing of the Red Sea (Ps. 66:5, 6), the covenant with David has implications for all humanity.

David is moved by consideration of his unique status and that of his house (vv. 18–21) to contemplate the uniqueness of his God. He is the only true God, and in His unmerited favor He has chosen David and the nation of Israel itself to be the people through whom His great name will become known (Ex. 15:11–13; Deut. 7:6–8).

In this summary of David's victories, pride of place is given to his defeat of the Philistines, Israel's archenemy (3:18; 1 Sam. 9:16) and against whom David's successes far surpass those of his predecessor, Saul (1 Sam. 14:52). See note on 5:25. Metheg-ammah. The name is otherwise unattested.

David executes two-thirds of his Moabite opponents and reduces the survivors to tributary status. The cause of David's ruthless treatment of a people whom he earlier trusted (1 Sam. 22:3) is not stated. Moabites. See notes on 1 Sam. 22:3. David's great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite (Ruth 4:21, 22).

This name appears to be a compound of "Hadad," the Syrian storm-god or Baal, and "ezer," meaning "help." "Hadad" is found elsewhere in compound names of Syrian monarchs (1 Kin. 15:18). Though defeated by David, Hadadezer later assists the Ammonites in their opposition to David (10:15–19). Zobah. A region in Syria to the east of Zobah (8:3) and west of the Euphrates River Valley.
LORD. David's action is perhaps in preparation for the temple to be built by Solomon (cf. 1 Chr. 22:1–5, 14; 29:1–5, 16–19).

The slaughter of eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt is credited to Abishai in 1 Chr. 18:12. It may be that Abishai receives credit as one of David's generals, possibly to remove the implied criticism of David, who makes a name for himself. See also Ps. 60 and its title.
gave victory to David wherever he went.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} This clause repeats v. 6, and it highlights the theme of the chapter.

As the prototypical theocratic king, David subjugates Israel's enemies (vv. 1–14), but he knows that he is called to be just (23:3). His descendants do not always follow his example, despite prophetic exhortation (Jer. 22:3). to all his people. See note on 5:12.

Zadok is a Levite priest descended from Aaron through Eleazar (1 Chr. 6:3–8, 50–53). He becomes the sole high priest in Solomon's administration (1 Kin. 2:35). From that time on, the Zadokite priests form one of the most important and influential priestly families (Ezra 7:1, 2; Ezek. 40:46; 44:15). Ahimelech the son of Abiathar. According to 20:25 and 1 Kin. 4:4, Zadok and Abiathar are David's priests (see 15:24, 35; 19:11). It was earlier reported that Abiathar, "one of the sons of Abim­elech," joined David during his exile from Saul's court (1 Sam. 22:20). It seems likely, therefore, that the names of father and son have somehow been reversed here (as also in 1 Chr. 18:16). Abiathar is a descendant of Eli through an Ahitub different from Zadok's father (1 Sam. 14:3; 22:20). His removal by Solomon for having supported Adonijah's bid for the throne (1 Kin. 1:7, 8) brings to final fulfillment the judgment on the house of Eli (1 Sam. 2:31 note; 1 Kin. 2:26, 27). Seraiah was secretary. Variations in the recording of this name (20:25; 1 Chr. 18:16; possibly 1 Kin. 4:3) may suggest a non-Israelite origin — perhaps Egypt, where the scribal tradition was well established. The scribe was among the highest ranking civil servants (2 Kin. 12:10; 18:18).

A man of outstanding military credentials (23:20–22), Benaiah demonstrates his intense loyalty to David and Solomon (1 Kin. 1:8, 36, 37), and, after carrying out Solomon's order to execute Joab, becomes commander-in-chief of Solomon's army (1 Kin. 2:34, 35; 4:4). Cherethites and the Pelethites. See note on 1 Sam. 30:14. priests. This is an office for which they are not clearly eligible. He had been a servant in the house of Saul, but now he says to David, "I am your servant." He comes back into the story in 16:1–4 and 19:16–30.

Mentioned also in 17:27–29, Machir appears to have been a wealthy man in a good position to host a descendant of Israel's first king. Lo-debar. This city has been tentatively located in Gilead about four miles (6 km) northwest of Mahanaim, Ish-bosheth's short-lived capital east of the Jordan River (2:8 note), and ten miles (16 km) south of the Sea of Galilee.

It has been suggested that David's act is somewhat self-serving, since the arrangement enables him to keep Mephibosheth under surveillance. But this suggestion is unlikely for several reasons. The text offers no hint of such a motive; Mephibosheth's crippled condition makes him less of a threat; and David surely knows from experience that it is dangerous for a rival to be at the king's court (cf. 16:3, 15–23).

The focus is not on Bathsheba herself so much as on her status as the wife of another man. Eliam. If Bathsheba's father is the same as "Eliam the son of Ahithophel" (23:34), this might help to explain Ahithophel's later betrayal of David in favor of Absalom's conspiracy (15:12; 16:15), which ostensibly is motivated by a sense of David's failure to provide justice for the people (15:4, 6). Notice especially the nature of Ahithophel's advice in 16:20, 21. Uriah. Uriah is a Hebrew name meaning "the LORD is my light." He is a member one of David's elite forces called "The Thirty" (23:24–39).

Despite David's efforts, Uriah does not do what he considers wrong. It is possible that Uriah knows about David's relationship with Bathsheba (perhaps from the messengers of v. 4), but this is unlikely in view of his willingness to carry a letter from David to Joab (v. 14). Uriah explains his abstinence in v. 11. Since sexual activity is a source of ritual impurity under the old covenant, obedient soldiers exercise abstinence during a military exercise (1 Sam. 21:5).

Uriah's insistence that he will not fare better than his fellow combatants again underscores by contrast the reprehensible nature of David's sin. Even though the Lord Himself (as symbolized by the presence of the ark) is on the field of battle, the king is in Jerusalem (vv. 1, 2 and notes).
See note on v. 8. Uriah still remains faithful to his duty and does not go home.
