The rich man is David, and the poor man is Uriah. A similar injustice is later perpetrated by Ahab and Jezebel against Naboth (1 Kin. 21:1–14).
The verse ends with the Hebrew word for "daughter," which is also the first syllable of the name "Bathsheba."
Nathan's parable has succeeded; in pronouncing judgment on the rich man, David has condemned himself. His response is an exclamation, not a legal decision. He mentions death first, then restitution.

Ex. 22:1 orders fourfold restitution for stolen sheep. Some commentators have detected here a hint of David's subsequent loss of four sons: the first son of Bathsheba (vv. 14, 18), Amnon (13:28, 29), Absalom (18:14, 15), and Adonijah (1 Kin. 2:24, 25).

In a manner typical of prophetic judgment speeches (1 Sam. 2:27–36 note), Nathan begins with an accusation that includes a description of the Lord's providence (vv. 7, 8), a question, and an indictment (v. 9). He concludes by announcing the judgment and the penalties corresponding to the crime. 12:7 I anointed you. Cf. Samuel's indictment of Saul (1 Sam. 15:17).

It is uncertain whether this statement is to be taken literally (only one wife and one concubine of Saul are mentioned; 3:7; cf. 1 Sam. 14:50) or as simply referring to the full extent of David's inheritance of Saul's kingdom. On the matter of kings acquiring their predecessors' harems, see 3:7 and note.
This same idiom appears in 11:25, 27. You have struck down Uriah. Because David causes Uriah to die in battle, he is as guilty as if he had murdered him with his own hand.

As Uriah was killed by violence, the house of David will be plagued by violence. Absalom kills Amnon (13:28, 29); Joab kills Absalom (18:14, 15); and Solomon orders the deaths of Adonijah (1 Kin. 2:24, 25) and Joab (1 Kin. 2:29–34). In addition, as David has committed sexual sin, there is sexual sin in his household (2 Sam. 13:1–15).
The prophecy is fulfilled by the rebellion of Absalom (chs. 15–18). lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. This prediction is fulfilled in 16:21, 22.

LORD. When charged by God's prophet, David responds with an immediate and unqualified confession; cf. Saul's confessions in 1 Sam. 15:24, 25, 30 (notes). Ps. 51, according to its superscription, is a fuller picture of David's repentance. you shall not die. See notes on 11:5; 12:5.
See note on 1 Sam. 1:7.

Like Eli, but unlike Saul, David humbly accepts the Lord's discipline (15:26; 16:11; cf. 1 Sam. 3:18 and notes). His humble response probably explains why his dynasty is established unlike the dynasty of Saul.
That is, in the place of the dead (1 Sam. 28:19 note; Gen. 37:35).

Bathsheba is called David's wife for the first time (11:3 note). She has been referred to as "the wife of Uriah the Hittite" for most of the story in chs. 11, 12 (11:3, 26; 12:10, 15). Solomon. This name is likely derived from the Hebrew word for "peace" (cf. 1 Chr. 22:9). Another possibility is that it means "replacement"; the birth of Solomon compensates for the loss of the first child.

See text note. This name confirms that "the LORD loved him" (v. 24) and bodes well for the future of the Davidic house. Despite the sin of David and his descendants, the Lord's favor will not be withdrawn (7:14 note).
The narrative once again returns to the Ammonite campaign (11:1 and note). This time it is not David who sends for Joab, but Joab who sends for David (v. 27).
Joab's concern may be prompted by an interest in David's reputation and the propriety of having the king receive the captive crown.

A crown weighing as much as seventy-five pounds ("a talent") would have been too heavy to wear except for brief ceremonies. The crown could have been from a statue of Milcom or Molech. The same Hebrew letters translated as "their king" can also be read as "Milcom" (i.e., Molech, the chief god of the Ammonites; see 1 Kin. 11:5, 33).
Subjugation of defeated enemies is common practice for David (8:2) and in the culture of the ancient Near East generally (Ex. 1:11; Josh. 9:22–27; 1 Kin. 9:20, 21).

David's sons follow their father's example of sexual misconduct (Amnon, vv. 1–22) and murder (Absalom, vv. 23–39). 13:1 Absalom and Tamar are siblings, having been born to David and his wife Maacah. Amnon is the eldest son of David, and he is a child of Ahinoam; thus Amnon is a half-brother of Tamar.

Both the words used for the "cakes" and their preparation ("make") are cognates of the Hebrew word for "heart" and may have an amorous connotation. A more common word for food is used by Jonadab in v. 5 and by David in v. 7. Sadly, David seems to miss the innuendo in Amnon's overture. in my sight. This emphasis (also in vv. 5, 8) is suggestive of a lustful aspect in Amnon's request.

Tamar's desperate appeal to Amnon points first to the distinctive moral standards of Israel ("such a thing is not done in Israel," v. 12), then to the claims of human decency ("my shame"), then to Amnon's self-interest ("you would be as one of the outrageous fools"), and finally to marriage as a better means of fulfilling Amnon's desire (v. 13). But he does not listen (v. 14). Incest is immoral in Israel but practiced in the surrounding nations (Lev. 18:1–3, 6). 13:12 do not violate me. The verb is used elsewhere to describe acts of rape (Gen. 34:2; Deut. 22:24, 29) and sexual violence (Judg. 19:24; 20:5).
It is uncertain whether David would allow such a marriage (see Lev. 18:9, 11; 20:17; Deut. 27:22) or whether Tamar is simply trying every possible argument.
With keen psychological insight, the narrator notes that Amnon no sooner violates Tamar than he is suddenly repulsed by the victim of his crime.
A rude and abrupt way of referring to Tamar. Cf. Amnon's terse dismissal of her (v. 15).
A garment of similar description was given to Joseph by his father, Jacob (Gen. 37:3).

Absalom's ability to discern the wrong suffered by Tamar suggests that Amnon's infatuation with her has not been a deep secret. hold your peace \... do not take this to heart. Though seeking to calm his sister, Absalom will soon seek revenge against Amnon (vv. 22, 32).

That David is furious at Amnon's violation of Tamar is understandable; that he takes no disciplinary action is not (1 Sam. 3:13 and note). The Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls add, "He would not hurt Amnon because he was his eldest son and he loved him." Whether original or not, the sentence accurately highlights a weakness in David's handling of his sons (14:24, 33; 1 Kin. 1:6 and notes). It is David's duty as father and as king to "administer justice and equity to all his people" (8:15 and note). His failure to do this contributes to the greatest political crisis of his life — Absalom's rebellion. One of Absalom's complaints is that David is slow to provide justice for his people (15:4–6).

This site is some fifteen miles (24 km) north of Jerusalem. Absalom may choose this location to facilitate his imminent escape to relatives in Geshur, across the Jordan River (v. 37). Absalom invited all the king's sons. The invitation is to participate in the feasting that accompanies the shearing of sheep (cf. 1 Sam. 25:4–8).
Amnon is the oldest son and crown prince, but even so his being singled out by Absalom arouses suspicion. David questions the request: "Why should he go with you?"
David sends not only Amnon but the rest of his sons, perhaps to deter Absalom from taking revenge against Amnon.

In one stroke Absalom will avenge his sister Tamar and move himself closer to the throne (3:3; 15:1–6). He will also become a murderer, repeating his father's sin as Amnon, also like David, engaged in sexual immorality. David's sons are demonstrating the same moral failings as their father.
See note on 18:9.
Jonadab seems to know something about Absalom's plans.
Absalom's maternal grandfather (3:3). Geshur. See note on v. 23. Absalom flees here to seek the protection of his maternal grandfather (3:3).
It is hard to determine what emotions or reactions precisely are specified in these sentences.
Later known as the birthplace of Amos, Tekoa is a town ten miles (16 km) south of Jerusalem.

The tale that the wise woman concocts raises not only the issue of blood revenge (v. 11; 3:27; cf. Num. 35:16–25; Deut. 19:11–13; Josh. 20:3) but also the continuance of her family line on its ancestral property, for her enemies propose to execute the surviving son. As she points out, this will leave her with no name or descendant, something that Israelite law seeks to avoid (Deut. 25:5–10). The woman skillfully introduces in her fictional story the same dilemma that David has. His duty to avenge the blood of Amnon conflicts with his anxiety that Absalom, now presumably his heir, not be cut off. Cf. Nathan's parable in 12:1–4.
The woman is either expressing her willingness to shoulder whatever blame might arise or is requesting, in polite court language, permission to speak further (1 Sam. 25:24).

your God.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The woman requests and secures an oath from David, in the name of the Lord, that "the avenger of blood kill no more." As was the case in Nathan's parable (12:1–6), a judgment is elicited from David's own mouth that will then be used to judge him (v. 13).

The woman seems to mean that God does not desire to take away lives but is ready to see the banishment ended. Some translations read, "God will not take away the life of someone who arranges for a banishment to end."

While the woman has accomplished her objective of pleading for Absalom, she now returns to the matter of her son, perhaps hoping that David will continue to believe her story and not discover that she and Joab have conspired together (vv. 1–3).
The woman flatters David by praising his judgment. See also v. 20; 19:27; cf. 1 Sam. 29:9.
See note on 13:37.
David allows Absalom to return to Jerusalem, but the estrangement continues.
As with Saul before him, Absalom is described in exclusively physical terms (1 Sam. 9:1, 2 and notes).

See note on 18:18. daughter whose name was Tamar. That only the daughter's name is recorded is sometimes taken as implying that Absalom's sons all died young, but the significance of this notice may lie elsewhere. The daughter's name is the same as the sister whose violation has brought Absalom into conflict with David.
The same amount of time that Absalom waited before taking revenge on Amnon (13:23).

Absalom hopes to win David over, and he does not expect to be executed even if David cannot be assuaged. David has not taken any dire action so far in the affair, and Absalom had some justification for killing Amnon. In effect, his request is that he should be completely punished or completely forgiven and not be left in between.

The narrative ends abruptly. Though David's action is sometimes referred to as the "kiss of reconciliation," it is doubtful that a real reconciliation is effected. Ironically, by giving kisses to those who approach him with petitions, Absalom will soon steal away the hearts of the people and launch a rebellion against his father (15:5, 6).
See notes on 8:4; 1 Sam. 8:11. Adonijah later does the same thing when he attempts to succeed David on the throne (1 Kin. 1:5).
See note on 13:21.

Four years from the meeting of v. 33 equates to six years from Absalom's return to Jerusalem (14:28). Hebron. See note on 2:1. Hebron is Absalom's birthplace (3:2, 3) but also the place where David was first anointed king over Judah (2:4) and subsequently also over Israel (5:3).
See note on 13:23.
Though employing a standard expression (e.g., 1 Sam. 1:17; 20:42; 29:7), David's farewell to Absalom adds a touch of irony to the story, since Absalom is planning to make war.
See note on v. 7. David first ruled here, and thus Absalom is attempting to usurp the throne in the very heart of David's power.
See note on 11:3 ("Eliam"). Giloh. A town in the hill country of Judah (Josh. 15:48, 51), probably not far from Hebron.
Heb. "the far house," perhaps denoting a well-known landmark on the outskirts of the city.

See note on 1 Sam. 30:14. These are David's bodyguards (1 Sam. 28:2). six hundred. This number, which occurs frequently in military contexts (e.g., Judg. 3:31; 18:11; 20:47; 1 Sam. 13:15), may designate a standard military unit. Gittites. That is, from Gath. Perhaps David won the loyalty of these troops during his time in the Philistine region ruled by Achish of Gath (1 Sam. 27).
This foreigner becomes one of David's trusted military commanders, alongside Joab and Abishai (vv. 21, 22; 18:2, 5, 12).
Presumably this is to be understood figuratively, not literally, and consequently refers to a recent action.
Ittai and his men are evidently mercenaries, but Ittai's loyalty is still outspoken.
A valley running from north to south along the eastern side of Jerusalem and separating Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives. David and his entourage are heading into the Judean wilderness.
See note on 8:17. ark of the covenant of God. See notes on 1 Sam. 3:3; 4:3.
David clearly resists any magical understanding of the ark's power (cf. the elders of Israel, 1 Sam. 4:3). Rather, he casts himself on the Lord's mercy.
David humbly accepts the Lord's will (10:12 note; 1 Sam. 3:18), yet this does not prevent him from taking steps to secure his survival (vv. 28, 32–36).
Zadok, Abiathar, and their sons will prove useful to David's cause in 17:15–21.
Probably the region along the western shore of the Dead Sea; see 17:16.
See note on v. 23. barefoot \... head covered. Signs of grief and sorrow (Esth. 6:12; Is. 20:2–4; Jer. 14:3, 4; Mic. 1:8).

No sooner does David pray that Ahithophel's counsel be confounded than he is presented, in the person of Hushai, with the means of accomplishing his objective. the Archite. The Archites are of Canaanite descent (Gen. 10:15–17), and their territory is west of Bethel (Josh. 16:2) in the land of the Benjaminites.
Probably an official counselor. See 1 Chr. 27:33.
Introduced in 9:9, 10 as the steward of all Saul's possessions after his death. Mephibosheth. See note on 4:4.
While David appears to believe Ziba's tale of Mephibosheth's treachery, he will change his ruling after hearing Mephibosheth's side of the story (19:24–30).

See note on 3:16. Shimei. As a kinsman of Saul, Shimei may hold David responsible for the deaths of Abner and Ish-bosheth (vv. 7, 8; on David's innocence, see 3:21, 26, 28; 4:9, 12 and notes). He may also resent David's permitting seven of Saul's descendants to be executed by the Gibeonites (21:1 note). As a resident of Bahurim, moreover, Shimei may be upset by David's treatment of Michal, Saul's daughter, for at Bahurim her second husband was ordered to cease following her as she was being taken back to David (3:16).
Lit. "a man of Belial." A strong word of abasement (1 Sam. 1:16; 2:12) that describes a person as a scoundrel.

has avenged on you.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Shimei is correct that divine retribution plays a part in David's distress, but it is not because of any injustice to the house of Saul. It is the result of David's sin against Uriah and Bathsheba (12:11).
See note on 2:18. dead dog. See notes on 1 Sam. 24:14; 2 Sam. 9:8.

David refuses to silence Shimei for several reasons. The Lord has prompted him to curse (v. 10); if his own son wants to kill him, how much more a kinsman of Saul; if the cursing is unjust, the Lord may repay David with good (v. 12). David's ready submission to God's judgment is consistent with his character (12:20–23; 15:26).
See note on 11:3 ("Eliam").
See note on 15:32.

Absalom's suspicion of David's "friend" (v. 16; 15:37) elicits from him a clever reply that he will be loyal to the one whom the Lord and all Israel have chosen. Moreover, it is a natural thing for one who has served a father to serve his son also.

To remove any thought among Absalom's followers of a reconciliation with David, Ahithophel counsels Absalom to lie with the concubines David has left behind (15:16). This will make clear Absalom's desire for the throne (3:7 note; 12:8 note; 1 Kin. 2:22). Whatever the motivation, such behavior is detestable to God (Lev. 18).
This action fulfills the judgment announced by Nathan in 12:11, 12.
See note on 15:32.
Absalom explains Ahithophel's advice to Hushai.

After declaring Ahithophel's advice "not good" (v. 7), Hushai offers an alternative plan, emphasizing not quick action but overpowering numbers (vv. 11–13). The plan he suggests will gain time for David to escape across the Jordan River (vv. 16, 22).
See Judg. 20:1; 1 Sam. 3:20.

Hushai's simile evokes a sense of the all-encompassing power of a blanketing mass attack and also tends, by its use of serene imagery, to lessen the sense of urgency and to suggest that the victory will be effortless.
had ordained.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Though the Lord does not openly intervene, He is far from inactive. to defeat the good counsel. An answer to David's prayer in 15:31.

In 15:27–29 David sends them, along with their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan, back to Jerusalem in order to gather and convey information to him (15:35, 36). For general information on Zadok and Abiathar, see note on 8:17.
See note on 15:28.

See note on v. 15. En-rogel. A spring outside the walls of Jerusalem, probably on the south (Josh. 15:7; 1 Kin. 1:9). A female servant. Drawing water is a normal task for a young woman in that day, and these visits to the spring will not be noticed.
From David's recent trip through Bahurim, the site of Shimei's cursing (16:5–14), he would know who his supporters are. On Bahurim, see note on 3:16.

See 15:12 and note. hanged himself. Ahithophel's suicide is presumably prompted not only because his most recent advice is ignored but also because he knows Absalom's chances of success have become slim. Neither can there be any reconciliation with David (16:21 and note).
See note on 2:8.

According to 1 Chr. 2:13–17, Amasa is David's nephew. This makes Amasa a cousin of both Absalom and Joab (2:18 note). Absalom appoints Amasa to replace Joab as commander of the army, and David will later do the same (19:13). Amasa's tenure will be short, however, for Joab is never slow in dealing with a competitor (20:9, 10). Abigail. Amasa's mother is either David's sister (1 Chr. 2:15–17) or half sister since she is here described as "the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah." Nahash. Presumably a different Nahash than the Ammonite "Nahash from Rabbah" in v. 27.

Like Hanun, Shobi is a member of the Ammonite royal family (10:1, 2), but unlike Hanun, he is friendly toward David and may even be David's appointee to govern the city of Rabbah after its capture (12:26–31). Rabbah of the Ammonites. See note on 11:1. Machir. See note on 9:4. Barzillai. For more on this benefactor of David and David's attempt to reward him, see 19:31–39; 1 Kin. 2:7.
These are standard military units (Ex. 18:21; Num. 31:14; Deut. 1:15; 1 Sam. 8:12; 22:7; 29:2).
In David's era, it is a conventional practice to divide troops into three parts (1 Sam. 11:11). Abishai. See note on 2:18.

In response to David's emphatic pronouncement in v. 2, the troops are adamant that he must not accompany them. Perhaps they fear that David's feelings for Absalom (v. 5; 18:33–19:7) or simply his advancing age (21:15–17) might prove a liability in the campaign. They recognize, moreover, that the death of David would mean sure defeat, as Ahithophel earlier pointed out to Absalom (17:2, 3).
That is, in Mahanaim (17:24, 27). See note on 19:8.

Though the territory of Ephraim is west of the Jordan, the present context implies that "the forest of Ephraim" is east of the Jordan in Gilead (17:24; 19:15). Ephraim may have taken some territory in the east.
The enemy will be lost in the unfamiliar, rough terrain. Some might take the opportunity to desert, and others will become easy prey for more experienced soldiers.

Mules are the royal mount of choice in this era (13:29; 1 Kin. 1:33). his head caught fast in the oak. The text does not say that Absalom's famous hair is caught in the branches, but it seems likely (14:25, 26 and note).
Joab has no qualms about violating David's express command (v. 5).

The man obviously does not share Joab's cavalier attitude toward David's orders. Moreover, he astutely concludes that if he kills Absalom, Joab will deny having any part in it and leave him to take the blame.
See note on 1 Sam. 13:3.
Such burial is often reserved for criminals or enemies (Josh. 7:26; 8:29).

Cf. Saul's action in 1 Sam. 15:12. In life Absalom envisaged for himself a king's career and erected a pillar of remembrance in his own honor; in death he is branded a traitor and buried under a pile of stones. King's Valley. Probably near Jerusalem (Gen. 14:17). no son. Absalom's three sons, mentioned but not named in 14:27, presumably were not yet born or were already deceased when Absalom erected his monument.
Ahimaaz previously served as a messenger for David (15:36; 17:15–21) and wishes to do so again.

It can be inferred from v. 27 that there is a correlation between the messenger chosen and the content of the message. Joab's decision not to send Ahimaaz may be prompted by a desire not to appear as personally taking too much pleasure in Absalom's death.
Cush is the area south of Egypt.

Were he fleeing the battlefield he would not likely be alone, nor would he be approaching so energetically and openly (cf. 19:3, which speaks of people "who are ashamed when they flee in battle" and so steal into the city).
See note on v. 20.

The text literally says, "Is it peace with the young man Absalom?" Absalom's name means "father of peace," but there is nothing in the text to indicate that he lives up to his name. I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was. Ahimaaz conceals his knowledge of Absalom's death (v. 20).
The Cushite offers a conventionally phrased response (cf. 1 Sam. 25:26), which David readily understands (v. 33).
The awful repetition in David's outburst conveys his anguish at the loss of his son (19:4). In spite of all the harm that Absalom has caused, David's grief blinds him to everything else (19:5 note).

What might, under different circumstances, be an understandable display of grief is totally unacceptable here. Joab forcefully declares to David the demoralizing effect his behavior is having on those who have just saved his life. If the actions of later usurpers are any guide, Absalom's success could have cost the lives of David and his whole household (1 Kin. 15:29; 16:11, 12; 2 Kin. 10:6, 7, 17).
Joab practically threatens to lead a rebellion himself if David does not correct his behavior and show his troops proper honor.

Heeding Joab's words, David takes his place in the gate of Mahanaim (18:4 note), the same spot where he earlier gave orders concerning the treatment of Absalom (18:5). The two gateway scenes provide a frame for the account of the death of Absalom. Archaeologists at the site of Tel Dan have uncovered a gate complex that includes an ashlar-constructed platform to support a throne for judges.

See note on 17:25. commander of my army \... in place of Joab. David's promotion of Amasa over Joab appears to be politically astute and magnanimous, since Amasa sided with Absalom and deserves a traitor's death. Nevertheless, this promotion will cost Amasa his life (20:8–10).
See note on 1 Sam. 13:4. It is the location of the first encampment of the Israelites in Canaan during the conquest period (Josh. 4:19).
See 16:5–14 and notes. Bahurim. See note on 3:16.

Strictly speaking, the "house of Joseph" includes only the descendants of Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48:5, 20; Josh. 17:17). The expression sometimes appears to be used, however, to describe all the northern tribes (1 Kin. 11:28; Amos 5:6; Zech. 10:6). In the present context, even Benjamin, Shimei's tribe, is included (cf. Ps. 80:1, 2).
LORD's anointed. A grave offense. See note on 1 Sam. 2:10.
For a similar sentiment under similar circumstances, see 1 Sam. 11:13.

Although David will remember his oath, he will not forget Shimei's offense and on his deathbed will remind Solomon of it (1 Kin. 2:8, 9). Solomon has Shimei executed, although the grounds for his doing so are questionable (1 Kin. 2:36–46).

See note on 4:4. neither taken care of his feet. Mephibosheth's neglect of personal hygiene signifies his distress over David's predicament, and he may also have intended this neglect to serve as evidence of his loyalty upon David's return.
See note on 14:17.
David is either unwilling to call Ziba to account for his betrayal or uncertain of the truth of Mephibosheth's story, so he settles for a compromise arrangement.

In light of the circumstances and of David's words in 1 Kin. 2:7, it is reasonable to assume that Chimham is a son of Barzillai. The later place-name "Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem" (Jer. 41:17) may suggest that a land grant is part of Chimham's reward.

Whereas there are ten northern tribes, there are only two southern tribes, Judah and Simeon. The northerners feel slighted. you despise us. The north-south hostility so much in evidence will fuel Sheba's revolt (ch. 20) and eventually bring about the division of the kingdom (1 Kin. 12). See note on 1 Sam. 11:8.

Lit. "a man of Belial." A common expression in the books of Samuel to describe someone as a "good-for-nothing" (1 Sam. 1:16; 2:12; 10:27; 2 Sam. 16:7; 23:6). See note on 1 Sam. 2:12. Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. From the same tribe as Saul, Sheba may even be his relative. no portion in David. See note on 19:43. Although the aggressive behavior of the men of Judah is certainly a factor, residual allegiance to Saul must also play a part in the mass withdrawal of support from David among the northern tribes. every man to his tents. This archaic turn of phrase should not be taken to imply that the Israelites at this stage in their history are still tent dwellers. See Judg. 19:9, which renders the Hebrew word for "tent" simply as "home."
See 15:16; notes on 16:21, 22.
See notes on 17:25; 19:13. three days. This is a limited, though not impossible, amount of time for the task set by David.

The reason for Amasa's delay is not stated. Perhaps he does not entirely support David's cause or, alternatively, is unable to gain an immediate following among the Judahites, whose loyalties may still have be with Joab (v. 11 and note).

Though Amasa is proving unsatisfactory, David is still unwilling to reinstate Joab (19:13), so he addresses Joab's brother Abishai instead. By the end of the episode, however, Joab will have retaken his former position, regardless of David's wishes (vv. 13, 23). your lord's servants. They are called "Joab's men" in v. 7.
See note on 1 Sam. 30:14. mighty men. They are presumably the same as those listed in 23:8–39.

This is possibly a well-known landmark, similar to others mentioned elsewhere in Samuel (15:17; cf. 1 Sam. 19:22; 20:19). The large stone may be an altar (cf. 1 Sam. 14:33, 34), and some have suggested a link with the "great high place" in Gibeon (1 Kin. 3:4). Gibeon. See note on 2:12. it fell out. Whether the sword falls to the ground or into the folds of Joab's tunic (possibly girded up for marching), is not stated. See note on v. 10.
This is a normal gesture in administering the kiss of greeting and is not likely to arouse suspicion.

It is unclear whether this is the sword that fell and was retrieved, either from the ground or the folds of Joab's tunic (v. 8 note), or a second weapon that has been concealed on Joab's person (in which case the dropped sword was a decoy). At any rate, Joab is able to catch Amasa completely off guard and kill him, as he killed Abner (3:27).

Two things might be inferred from this summons. Joab continues to enjoy the personal loyalty of at least some of the troops, despite his having been ousted by David (19:13), and Amasa's loyalty to David is not beyond question. See note on v. 5.

This city is mentioned also in 1 Kin. 15:20; 2 Kin. 15:29. On the kingdom of Maacah, see 10:6 and note. Abel is usually identified with a site about twelve miles (19 km) north of Lake Huleh and four miles (6 km) west of Dan.

The Judahites construct a siege ramp, then drive a battering machine to the top of the tell and try to knock down the city wall. Such a siege ramp, which Sennacherib uses against the town in the eighth century B.C.., has been found at the Judean city of Lachish.

The phrase "a mother in Israel" is one of veneration and honor (Judg. 5:7). This "peaceable and faithful" city deserves to be treated with respect rather than destroyed as a rebellious traitor. Such a city is central also because it has "daughter" villages around it (Judg. 1:27). the heritage of the LORD. That is, Israel — its land and its people — as a whole and in its parts (14:16; 21:3; cf. 1 Sam. 10:1 and note; 26:19).
This name may apply to a geographical area that extends into Benjaminite territory, or else Sheba, although of Benjaminite ancestry (v. 1), is living in Ephraim.

This summary of David's officers parallels the list in 8:15–18, with several differences. The opening formula regarding "David's reign" (8:15) is lacking, as is any mention of David's sons (cf. 8:18). Seraiah (8:17) is here called Sheva (v. 25), and two new names are added to the list: Adoram and Ira (vv. 24, 26). 1 Kin. 4:1–6 indicates that many of David's officers continue in their duties during at least the early part of Solomon's reign. 20:23 Joab was in command of all the army of Israel. See note on v. 6. Having regained his former position, apparently without protest from David, Joab retains it until he is executed by Solomon for treason (1 Kin. 1:7; 2:22, 28–35). Benaiah \... the Cherethites and the Pelethites. See note on 1 Sam. 30:14.

After serving not only under David but also under Solomon (1 Kin. 4:6 note), Adoram will be stoned by "all Israel" during the early days of King Rehoboam (1 Kin. 12:18). forced labor. The Hebrew word translated "forced labor" here and in 1 Kin. 12:18 is used to describe the hard labor imposed on subjugated peoples, similar to the work the Israelites were forced to do in Egypt (Ex. 1:11) or what the surviving Canaanites had to do after the Israelite conquest (Josh. 16:10; Judg. 1:28). It also describes the labor done by conscripts from Israel itself on the building projects of Solomon (1 Kin. 9:15). Neither Adoram nor forced laborers are included in the first summary of David's government (8:15–18), which may suggest that forced labor is not introduced until later on in David's reign (e.g., 12:31). Jehoshaphat \... recorder. That is, perhaps a "royal herald" (see 8:16 note).
He is a high-ranking official, perhaps akin to secretary of state (8:17 note).

Ira is not mentioned elsewhere in the OT, unless he is "Ira the son of Ikkesh" (23:26) or "Ira the Ithrite" (23:38), both listed among David's mighty men (23:24–39). Jairite. Some have attempted to associate "Ira the Jairite" with the Levitical city of Jattir (Josh. 21:14). Others refer to "Jair the son of Manasseh" (Num. 32:41; Deut. 3:14) or to "Jair the Gileadite" (Judg. 10:3).

Not uncommon in the land of Canaan (Gen. 12:10; 26:1; Ruth 1:1), famine is often recognized in the Bible as a manifestation of God's judgment (e.g., 24:13; Deut. 32:24; 2 Kin. 8:1; Ps. 105:16; Is. 14:30; Jer. 11:22; Ezek. 14:21; Rev. 6:8). in the days of David. The time frame is stated quite generally. Perhaps the famine should be placed about the time that Mephibosheth came to David's court (v. 7; ch. 9) and before Absalom's rebellion (16:5 note), but this is uncertain. on Saul and on his house. Saul tried to annihilate the Gibeonites (v. 2; 4:3 note), though obviously with only partial success.

Israel's treaty with the Gibeonites is recorded in Josh. 9. Although Israel was remiss in entering into such a treaty without inquiring of the Lord (Josh. 9:14), they still felt obliged to honor their word (Josh. 9:19). in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah. Saul's attempt to annihilate the Gibeonites was motivated by nationalistic, not religious, zeal. He may have wanted to rid his home tribe, Benjamin, of unwanted Amorite survivors. For Saul's ancestral association with Gibeon, see 1 Chr. 9:35–39.

In David's era it is considered a disgrace when the bodies of the slain are allowed to become carrion for birds and beasts (Deut. 28:26; 1 Sam. 17:44, 46; Ps. 79:2; Is. 18:6; Jer. 7:33; 16:4). Rizpah guards the bodies until they can be buried (vv. 11–14).

David is prompted by Rizpah's vigil to gather the bones of the recently slain (so the Septuagint's translation of v. 13), and of Saul and Jonathan as well, and to give them a proper burial in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father. The bones of Saul and Jonathan were previously interred in Jabesh-gilead (1 Sam. 31:12, 13).
An almost identical statement occurs in 24:25 after the lifting of the plague brought on by David's census.

These verses describe briefly the defeat of four Philistine champions at the hands of David and his men. While it is difficult to locate these events chronologically with any precision, their literary placement provides a fitting preface to David's song of praise (ch. 22).

The term "Rephaim" is sometimes applied to such peoples as the Emim, Zamzummim, and Anakim (Deut. 2:10, 11, 20, 21), all distinguished for their size and strength. According to Josh. 11:21, 22, the Anakim were driven from the hill country of Israel and Judah by Joshua but remained in the Philistine cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. three hundred shekels. That is, just over seven pounds. Goliath's spearhead weighed twice as much (1 Sam. 17:7).

See note on 2:18. lamp of Israel. "Lamp" is used as a metaphor for guidance, blessing, proclamation, and revelation (1 Sam. 3:3 note). Here the metaphor expresses the belief that Israel's hope for blessing resides in David and his house (1 Kin. 11:36; 15:4; 2 Kin. 8:19).
See note on v. 16.

The corresponding verse in 1 Chr. 20:5 contains the words "brother of." It has been suggested that "Elhanan" is another name for David (as "Jedidiah" for Solomon, 2 Sam. 12:24, 25). This would make 2 Samuel say that Elhanan (David) killed Goliath, but it makes 1 Chr. 20:5 difficult, unless Elhanan (David) killed both Goliath and Lahmi. Neither Samuel nor Chronicles supposes that anyone except David killed Goliath, and it remains unclear why they introduce the name Elhanan in two verses.
See note on v. 16.
David was directly involved in the encounter with Ishbi-benob (vv. 16, 17).

David's song of praise (which appears also in Ps. 18, with minor variations) and the prayer of Hannah form a fitting frame for the books of 1 and 2 Samuel (1 Sam. 2:1–10 note). David's song focuses on the Lord's deliverance of David. It may be outlined as follows: introductory praise of God as "savior" (vv. 2–4); the psalmist's distress (vv. 5, 6); the psalmist's petition (v. 7); the Lord's response in cosmic demonstration (vv. 8–16) and personal rescue (vv. 17–20); the psalmist's innocence (vv. 21–25) and the Lord's faithfulness (vv. 26–30); the Lord's deliverance (vv. 31–37) and the psalmist's resultant victories (vv. 38–46); concluding praise of God as Savior (vv. 47–51). Ps. 144, also ascribed to David, shows many similarities in theme and language. This verse is the title or superscription to this song of David, and it is nearly identical to the heading of Ps. 18. all his enemies. See 8:1–14; cf. 5:8; 7:1, 9, 11; 18:32. from the hand of Saul. See 12:7; cf. 1 Sam. 18–31 (esp. 18:9–11; 19:2, 10, 11, 15, 16).

See notes on 1 Sam. 2:1, 10.
See v. 17. The image of overflowing water recurs frequently in OT poetry as a symbol of distress and destruction (Pss. 32:6; 69:1, 2, 14; 144:7; Is. 43:2; Jon. 2:5).

Being in a narrow or tightly confined space is a common figure for distress. In v. 20 (note) relief is described as being brought into a "broad place." From his temple. This perhaps means God's heavenly sanctuary (1 Kin. 8:27, 38, 39; Ps. 11:4; Is. 6:1; Jon. 2:7; Rev. 11:19; 14:17; 15:5), but "temple" can be used of the tabernacle (1 Sam. 1:9).
Cf. the imagery used to describe the awesome power of Leviathan in Job 41:18–21.
thundered.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} See 1 Sam. 2:10; 7:10. The Lord's voice is often likened to thunder (Job 37:4, 5; 40:9; Ps. 29:3; Is. 33:3). Most High. See Gen. 14:19 and notes.
For similar imagery, see Deut. 32:23, 42; Job 6:4; Ps. 64:7. Lightning is sometimes described as the Lord's arrows (Ps. 77:17; cf. Hab. 3:11; Zech. 9:14).
See note on v. 5. The verb is used in Ex. 2:10 to describe how Moses was drawn out of the waters of the Nile.

David is not laying claim to righteousness or sinlessness in any absolute sense. Rather, he asserts his blamelessness with respect to his enemies and his confidence that the Lord rewards those who seek to be faithful to Him (v. 26; 1 Sam. 26:23). If this were not the case, David would surely be classed among "the haughty" (v. 28).

See the theme of divine reversal of fortunes in Hannah's prayer (1 Sam. 2:1–10 and note; esp. v. 7). This theme is important throughout the books of Samuel, as both Saul and David are exalted from humble origins.
Cf. notes on 21:17; 1 Sam. 3:3. The sense of this word here is probably "blessing."
See v. 2 and note.

This is possibly a reference to the many perils that David has experienced at the hands of Saul, Absalom, and others. The corresponding verse in Ps. 18:43 reads simply "the people," as does the Septuagint translation of this verse.

The mention of the Lord's "king" and His "anointed" is reminiscent of the closing verse of Hannah's prayer in 1 Sam. 2:10. After the dynastic promise of 2 Sam. 7:5–16, David can speak confidently of God's unfailing mercy to his descendants forever. The dynastic theme is the transition to ch. 23, where David celebrates the "everlasting covenant" he has with the Lord (23:5).

That is, his last poem. See 1 Kin. 2:1–10 for David's final instructions to Solomon. oracle. Or "utterance." The Hebrew word is often, though not exclusively, associated with prophecy (e.g., 1 Sam. 2:30; 2 Kin. 9:26), an association not inappropriate for David (v. 2 and note; Acts 2:30). the sweet psalmist of Israel. Another translation of the Hebrew is "the beloved of Israel's protector."

The Lord revealed to David the essential character and glorious benefits of the ideal theocratic king. Only in Christ, the greater Son of David, will such qualities of character be fully displayed and such benefits fully realized (7:4–17 note). 23:2 The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me. Other references to David acting or speaking under divine inspiration include 1 Chr. 28:9–19; Matt. 22:43; Acts 1:16; 4:25. David's empowerment by the Spirit is recounted in 1 Sam. 16:13.
See v. 32; notes on 22:2; 1 Sam. 2:2. justly. Righteous rule is possible only for one who lives in a right relationship with God. On what it means to "fear" God, see note on 1 Sam. 12:14.
The benefits of righteous rule are enlightenment, fruitfulness, and refreshment. For a fuller development of similar themes, see Ps. 72.

David's confidence rests not in his own righteousness but in the everlasting covenant made with him by a gracious God (7:11–16; 2 Chr. 13:5; 21:7; Ps. 89:3, 4, 28, 29; Is. 55:3; Ezek. 37:25, 26). covenant. Refers to 2 Sam. 7:4–17.
The Hebrew term is "Belial"; see note on 1 Sam. 2:12. The focus here may be on those who have opposed the rule of David.

The presentation of David's "mighty men" in these verses forms a counterpart to the much shorter description of Davidic champions in 21:15–22. According to v. 39, the warriors listed should total thirty-seven. They are presented in two sets of three (vv. 8–12 and 13–17), plus Abishai (vv. 18, 19), Benaiah (vv. 20–23), and the thirty-one listed in vv. 24–39. However, the "three" of vv. 13–17 are apparently to be counted among "the thirty" (v. 13; v. 24 note) and not separately. Thus, this list contains thirty-six mighty men, and Joab makes thirty-seven. A similar list is given in 1 Chr. 11:10–47 with more than fifteen additional names and no summary total. 23:8 eight hundred. 1 Chr. 11:11 has "300," possibly a copyist's error. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

brought about a great victory that day.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} This statement, repeated in v. 12, serves as a reminder that whatever the heroic qualities of the human agent, it is God who ultimately brings victory (8:6, 14; cf. 1 Sam. 14:15, 23; 19:5).
Destroying crops is a common tactic of war (Judg. 6:3–6, 11).
See note on 5:18.
See note on 1 Sam. 23:14.

LORD. The brave exploit of the three men is a testimony to their devotion to David, while David's refusal to drink (v. 17) what has been procured at such great risk to his loyal followers is testimony to his love for them.
See note on 2:18.
See note on 8:18.
David's bodyguard is presumably composed of Cherethites and Pelethites (1 Sam. 30:14 note).

See note on 2:18. the thirty. "Thirty" may be a round number. Not surprisingly, more of David's men are from the tribe of Judah than from any other. Elhanan. He is not necessarily the same Elhanan as in 21:19 (note).
David receives support even from Saul's hometown (1 Sam. 10:26; 11:4).
Not the same as Benaiah in vv. 20–23.

By concluding the list of David's mighty men with Uriah, the victim of David's great sin in ch. 11, the chapter ends with a poignant reminder that David is, like all men, a sinner and in need of God's forgiveness (ch. 12). This theme is continued in the next chapter. thirty-seven in all. See note on vv. 8–39.

This chapter is a fitting conclusion to the books of Samuel. David is shown for what he is, a sinner, but a sinner who is ready to repent and to cast himself upon God's mercy (12:13 and note). Another appropriate note on which to end these books is the association of the threshing floor of Araunah (vv. 18–25) with Mount Moriah, the future site of the temple (Gen. 22:2; 1 Chr. 22:1; 2 Chr. 3:1). 24:1 Again. If a specific occasion is in view, a probable one is the famine of 21:1. he incited David. The antecedent of "he" is the Lord (cf. 1 Sam. 26:19). According to 1 Chr. 21:1, however, it is Satan who moves David. At issue here is the mystery of the presence and practice of evil. The Scripture is clear that God is not the author of evil (James 1:13–15), but it also teaches that the wicked acts of men and of Satan do not fall outside God's sovereign determination. number Israel and Judah. Taking a census does not appear to be wrong in itself (Num. 1:1, 2; 4:1, 2; 26:1–4), but see Ex. 30:11, 12. This act of census may point to a lack of trust on David's part, or even to a desire to gain control of God's providence by making an inventory of His apparent resources. That the report (v. 9) emphasizes military strength may suggest that David wants to take more territory than what the Lord has granted him.
A proverbial expression for all the land.
The reason for Joab's reluctance is not stated. It can as easily be political as religious, since the people might take a census as a sign that David plans to raise taxes or draft more soldiers.
These verses indicate that the census is begun in the south, east of the Jordan River, and continues in a counterclockwise direction through the land, finally arriving in Beersheba.
Most of this time is needed for taking the census; the travel itself can be accomplished in a matter of weeks.

1 Chr. 21:5 has "1,100,000" and "470,000," respectively. On this difference, see notes on 1 Chr. 21:5 and Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues. The Hebrew word for one thousand can mean "unit," and therefore the figures may indicate that there are eight hundred military units in Israel and five hundred military units in Judah.

It is uncertain precisely when David's plea for forgiveness is granted, but perhaps God does it before Gad's arrival (vv. 11–13). Nevertheless, as in the case of David's sin against Uriah and Bathsheba, forgiveness does not mean that sin will have no further consequences (v. 13; 12:13, 14). What is David's sin? Perhaps it is pride that he has such a large army or that he puts his hope in the size of his army rather than in the Lord.
See 1 Sam. 22:5.
The Lord sends Gad to confront David, just as He earlier sent the prophet Nathan (12:1 and note).

Implicit in the threat of pursuit by foes is loss of life by the sword, as 1 Chr. 21:12 makes explicit. Famine, sword, and plague are the OT's triad of woes regularly threatened for impenitent covenant breaking (Lev. 26:23–26; Deut. 28:21–26; 32:24, 25; 1 Kin. 8:37; 2 Chr. 20:9; Is. 51:19; Jer. 14:12; Ezek. 6:11, 12).

LORD. Technically, this allows either the first or third option, that is, famine or plague. The inference is sometimes made that David's choice is selfish, but all three options, including flight before enemies, will cost lives (v. 13 note). David's motivation is entirely different, for he has learned that the Lord's mercy is great (v. 16; cf. Ex. 34:6, 7; Neh. 9:17; Pss. 30:5; 86:14–16; 103:8–10; Is. 54:7, 8; 60:10; Hos. 11:8, 9; Joel 2:13).
See v. 2.
LORD. See note on Gen. 16:7. On the Lord's angels as agents of judgment, see Ex. 33:2; Ps. 35:5, 6; Matt. 13:41; Acts 12:23. threshing floor of Araunah. See note on 24:1–25.

The heart of David, like the heart of God (v. 16), is grieved by the suffering he sees among his people, his "sheep." As their shepherd-king, he is moved to compassion and, not knowing that God in His mercy has already stayed His hand (vv. 16, 21), asks that the hand of judgment fall upon him alone. David deserves punishment for his sin, and the people are innocent. David's offer as a guilty person to suffer in the place of innocent "sheep" is not a very close analogy to Christ's death for the sake of His sheep (John 10:11), although the language is similar. Unlike David, Christ was personally innocent and died for the guilty.
See note on 1 Sam. 10:8.

my God that cost me nothing.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} While God's grace and forgiveness are free, David understands that proper worship of God is never to be cheap or careless (cf. Mal. 1:6–14; 2 Cor. 8:1–5). The consistent testimony of Scripture is that God deserves our best, the "firstfruits" (Num. 18:12; Deut. 18:3–5; 26:10; Neh. 12:44; Prov. 3:9). fifty shekels of silver. 1 Chr. 21:25 records a much larger sum of six hundred shekels of gold, possibly referring to a larger transaction of which the fifty shekels is a part.

LORD. According to 1 Chr. 22:1, this is the location for the future Solomonic temple. burnt offerings and peace offerings. See note on 1 Sam. 10:8. the LORD responded to the plea for the land. An almost identical statement is made in 21:14.

1 Kings.note: Solomon succeeds David as king in spite of political turmoil and intrigue by Adonijah, Abiathar, Joab, and Shimei. 1:1 old and advanced in years. As 1 Kings begins, David is about seventy years old (2 Sam. 5:4; 1 Kin. 2:11).
Shunem is sixteen miles (26 km) southwest of the Sea of Chinneroth (Galilee), near Mount Gilboa (Josh. 19:18; 1 Sam. 28:4; 2 Kin. 4:8).

This underlines David's frailty and suggests that he no longer has the physical strength to be king. Since David does not have sexual relations with Abishag, Adonijah's later request to marry her (2:17) is not against the law of Deut. 22:30.

Probably the oldest living son of David (2 Sam. 3:2–5; 13:28; 18:14). As such, he may believe that he will succeed his father. However, Deut. 17 emphasizes that the king should be the one chosen by God. Adonijah, who strives to make himself king, is rejected by God (cf. Abimelech in Judg. 9). chariots and horsemen. Like Absalom before him (2 Sam. 15:1), Adonijah signals his ambitions and positions himself to take the throne.

As in dealing with his other rebellious sons, David makes no attempt to either question or discipline Adonijah. But his patience and forgiveness seem only to invite further rebellion (2 Sam. 13:32, 39; 14:33; 18:5). very handsome. Handsome features are an asset for someone aspiring to the throne (1 Sam. 9:2; 16:12; 2 Sam. 14:25, 26), but God looks at inward qualities (1 Sam. 13:14 note; 16:7).

Joab is the commander of the army of Israel and one of David's longtime supporters (2 Sam. 2:13; 8:16; 18:2; 20:10, 23). His relationship with David has been strained by his harsh actions in putting down rebellions (2 Sam. 18:5; 19:5–8, 13; 1 Kin. 2:5, 6). Abiathar the priest. Abiathar and Zadok are the two high priests appointed by David (1 Sam. 22:20–22; 2 Sam. 8:17 note).

Benaiah is the commander of the Cherethites and Pelethites, mercenary forces who have functioned in large measure as David's royal guard (2 Sam. 8:18; 20:7; 23:20; 1 Chr. 18:17). Nathan the prophet. The most prominent prophet during David's reign (2 Sam. 7:1–17; 12:1–15). Shimei. A different man from the one referred to in 2 Sam. 16:5–8; 1 Kin. 2:8, 36–46. Perhaps this person is "Shimei the son of Ela," one of Solomon's governors (4:18). mighty men. See 2 Sam. 23:8–39.

Again, Adonijah follows the example of Absalom (1:5 and notes; cf. 2 Sam. 15:7–12). This activity appears to be a coronation sacrifice and banquet (1:41; cf. 1 Sam. 9:22–24; 2 Sam. 15:10–12). En-rogel. This spring is located south of the city. Because of their importance to the city, springs are considered to be an appropriate place for such activity (cf. 2 Sam. 17:17).

Queen mothers can play an influential role in the affairs of state (2:19; 15:13; 2 Kin. 10:13). As Solomon's mother, Bathsheba has a major interest in seeing that Adonijah is thwarted in his plans to become king.

Since contenders for the throne in the ancient Near East often sought to consolidate their positions by eliminating all potential rivals, Nathan's advice conveys a sense of urgency (cf. 15:29; 2 Kin. 10:11; 11:1).

Nathan's advice plays on the ambiguity and instability inherent during a coup attempt. Actually David is still king, but Nathan's words underscore the fact that Adonijah has also publicly claimed this status (vv. 5, 9). By confirming Bathsheba's concerns, Nathan underscores the gravity of the situation to the "very old" king (v. 15).

In Israel an oath taken in the Lord's name constitutes a sacred obligation and, as such, is considered inviolable (Ex. 20:7; Lev. 19:12; Josh. 9:15, 18, 20; Judg. 11:30, 35; Eccl. 5:4–7). For the oath, see 1 Chr. 22:9, 10.
Only a public declaration that Solomon will succeed David as king will suffice to turn back Adonijah's claim to the throne.

Nathan incisively attacks the issue. Either David has privately affirmed Adonijah as heir apparent (and hence Nathan, Zadok, and Benaiah have been shunned), or David has not done so (and hence Adonijah has rebelled against his father).
Solomon will be the offspring through whom God will fulfill His promise of establishing the throne of his kingdom forever (2 Sam. 7:12, 13).

Mules and donkeys are used as mounts of royalty (Judg. 10:4; 2 Sam. 13:29; 18:9; Zech. 9:9). David is therefore making a public declaration that Solomon is the heir. The triumphal entry of Christ may be a symbol of His kingship as the son of David (see Matt. 21:1–11). Gihon. The Gihon spring, located about one-half mile (0.8 km) north of En-rogel (v. 9), is a major supply of water for Jerusalem in this era (2 Chr. 32:30; 33:14). Due to topography, En-rogel is not visible from Gihon; however, the two are within earshot (v. 41).

Priests (Ex. 28:41; 29:4–9; Lev. 4:3, 5, 16), kings (1 Sam. 2:10; 9:16; 10:1), and occasionally prophets (1 Kin. 19:16), were anointed in ancient Israel. The Hebrew for "anointed" became a technical term for the Lord's anointed, usually with royal connotations. The title is usually transliterated "messiah." The Gk. word for "anointed" is christos ("Christ," Matt. 1:17). Although Solomon receives God's promises to David, those promises are fully realized only with the coming of Jesus Christ. blow the trumpet and say, "Long live King Solomon!" A public celebration of Solomon's new status as crown prince (cf. 1 Sam. 10:24; 2 Sam. 15:10; 16:16; 2 Kin. 9:13; 11:12), or perhaps David and Solomon have a co-regency for a short time.

Although made up of twelve tribes, the nation is composed of two major units, Israel in the north and Judah in the south. When David became king, he had to command assent from both Judah (2 Sam. 2:4) and Israel (2 Sam. 5:3). As heir to the Davidic dynasty, Solomon becomes king of both areas at once. This description may also highlight a long-standing division between the north and the south that later results in two separate monarchies at the death of Solomon.
See note on v. 8.

In ancient Israel both priests and prophets could officiate at the anointing of a king (1 Sam. 9:16; 16:12; 2 Kin. 9:1–3; 11:12). tent. A reference to the tent David pitched (2 Sam. 6:17) to house the ark of the covenant (Ex. 37:1–9); not the same as the tabernacle of Moses (Ex. 35:4–29; 36:8–38; 1 Kin. 3:4; 1 Chr. 16:39; 21:29).
See note on v. 33.
David praises God (v. 48) because his prayer for succession has been granted (cf. Gen. 47:31).
The guests at Adonijah's coronation festival are afraid because their attendance at the feast signifies that they are part of the rebellion.

These are projections resembling horns at the four corners on the top of the altar (Ex. 27:2; 29:12; Lev. 4:7; Ps. 118:27). The place of sacrifice is sacred, and Adonijah is seeking sanctuary there before God in the hope that he will not be killed (Ex. 21:12–14; 1 Kin. 2:28–34).
Solomon spares Adonijah on condition that he conduct himself as a loyal citizen of Solomon's kingdom.

David, like Jacob (Gen. 49), Moses (Deut. 31:1–8), Joshua (Josh. 23), and Samuel (1 Sam. 12) before him, gives a final speech before his death. These speeches mark the transition from one era to another and the transfer of authority.

A euphemism for death (Josh. 23:14). Be strong, and show yourself a man. These instructions are suitable either before a warrior goes into battle or before a person undertakes a difficult task (Deut. 31:7, 23; Josh. 1:6, 7, 9, 18; 1 Sam. 4:9).
David admonishes Solomon to be faithful to God and so experience blessing (cf. Deut. 4:40; 6:2; 8:6, 11; 10:12–11:1).

David's instructions to Solomon echo God's promises to David through the prophet Nathan in 2 Sam. 7:8–16 and reaffirmed in David's prayer in 2 Sam. 7:18–29. Here David underscores the need for covenant faithfulness (cf. 8:25, 26; 9:4, 5). with all their heart and \... soul. An allusion to Deut. 4:29 and 6:5. When Jesus is asked what is the greatest commandment, He likewise quotes from Deut. 6:5 (Matt. 22:35–40).

Joab is the most successful, but also the most unscrupulous, of David's generals (1:7 note). David calls on Solomon to see to it that the crimes Joab has committed against his rivals Abner (2 Sam. 3:22–30) and Amasa (cf. 2 Sam. 20:4–10) do not go unpunished. The way Joab tricked Abner and Amasa and murdered them was unlawful (Deut. 19:1–13; 21:1–9). This may, in reality, be not mere vengeance on David's part but a political move to protect Solomon from Joab, who is particularly dangerous, violent, and without scruples.
To enjoy a position of honor at the court and share in the bounty of the state (2 Sam. 9:7; 19:28; 2 Kin. 25:29; Neh. 5:17).
He cursed and stoned David, who was running from his son Absalom (2 Sam. 16:5–8). Shimei later begged for pardon, and David promised that Shimei would not die (2 Sam. 19:16–23).
Cursing a ruler violates God's law (Ex. 22:28; cf. 1 Kin. 21:10).

One of David's major accomplishments was to capture Jerusalem, which became the nation's capital. The city afterward bore the name of David in his honor (2 Sam. 5:7). David's city was located on a spur between the Central Valley and the Kidron Valley. Solomon later expanded the city to the north to include the Ophel and Mount Moriah, the site of the temple complex.
David ruled c. 1010–970 B.C.. During his last years he may have shared the throne with Solomon (1:38–40).
This is wishful thinking on Adonijah's part (1:7–10). it was his from the LORD. Adonijah claims to recognize the sanctity of Solomon's reign, but his request for Abishag suggests otherwise.

In the ancient Near East, a large court and family were a sign of royal status. Abishag remained a virgin while she stayed with David (1:1–4), so Adonijah would not be technically breaking the law by marrying her (Deut. 22:30). LORD. There are a number of similarities between the tabernacle and the temple, although the temple is twice the size of the tabernacle (Ex. 26:15–30; 36:20–34). Both are divided into three main sections: a vestibule, a sanctuary (the Holy Place), and an inner sanctuary (the Most Holy Place). This three-part structure is common in other ancient Near Eastern temples. Israel's sanctuary differs radically from a pagan sanctuary because it has no idols or standing stones. At its center is the ark of the covenant containing the Ten Commandments, the moral will of God that orders Israel's life (Deut. 10:4, 5; 1 Kin. 8:6–9).

As the city of Jerusalem expanded northward along the Ophel ridge, it was necessary to build supporting earthworks for the city's fortifications. The Millo (lit. "filling") was apparently such a restraining structure constructed east of the palace to fill in a depression along the top of the ridge (v. 24; 11:27; cf. 2 Sam. 5:9; 2 Kin. 12:20; 2 Chr. 32:5). Archaeologists have uncovered a stepped-stone structure on the Ophel ridge that perhaps served as the Millo. Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer. These towns are strategically located along major trade routes. Hazor is ten miles (16 km) north of the Sea of Chinneroth (Galilee); Megiddo is at the opening onto the Jezreel Valley of a strategic pass through the Carmel ridge. Gezer is twenty miles (32 km) west of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavation has revealed identical Solomonic gates and outer-wall systems at each of these sites. It remains the capital city until the destruction of Israel by the Assyrians in 722 B.C.. Assyrian documents of the eighth century B.C.., long after the death of Omri, refer to Israel as "the land of Omri."

Politically and militarily, Omri is quite successful. The Moabite Stone, an inscription from one of Israel's neighbors, states that Omri subjugates Moab and captures Medeba during his reign. However, he receives little attention in 1 Kings because his success is not of interest to the author, who is more attentive to religious failure in the north than to political or military success.

In the Canaanite nations of Ahab's day, a king can seize property and personal belongings at his pleasure, because in theory all the property is owned by the royal family and only entrusted to their subjects. In Israel, God owns the land (Ex. 19:3–8; Lev. 25:23), and the people hold it as His stewards (Num. 14:8; 35:34; Deut. 1:8). The powers of an Israelite monarch are limited, in contrast to the powers of a Canaanite king (Deut. 17:14–20; 1 Sam. 8:9–19; 10:25). When Ahab wants his neighbor's vineyard, his thought is to negotiate a purchase (cf. 16:24).

Israel had peace for three years after the two-year war between Syria and Israel described in 20:1–34. During this peace, Had­adezer (Ben-hadad II) of Syria, Ahab of Israel, and ten other kings formed a coalition to ward off an Assyrian invasion led by Shalmaneser III. Assyrian records report that in the major battle of this campaign fought at Qarqar, Syria, on the Orontes River (853 B.C.), Ahab contributed two hundred chariots and ten thousand soldiers. Assyria's claim to have won a great victory seems to be an exaggeration, because the Assyrians withdrew and did not try to invade again for about four years.

In Ahab's day, that highway is a major thoroughfare between Egypt and Syria.

Athaliah is a devoted Baal worshiper, and the diplomatic marriage introduced state-sponsored Baal worship to Judah, corrupting the worship of Yahweh (2 Kin. 11).

Jehoram of Judah and his father, Jehoshaphat, probably rule together as co-regents for approximately five years (853–848 B.C.). If so, "the second year of Jehoram" (1:17) is the same as "the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat" (3:1). twelve years. 852–841 B.C.

Probably this is the capital of Moab (Is. 16:7, 11; Jer. 48:31, 36), about eleven miles (18 km) east of the Dead Sea and fourteen miles (23 km) north of the Valley of Zered, which is at the southern tip of the Dead Sea.

This grisly act is meant to induce the god Chemosh to deliver the Moabites from certain defeat. Child sacrifice is expressly forbidden in Israel (Ex. 34:20; Deut. 18:10); nevertheless, two later kings of Judah (Ahaz and Manasseh) apparently practice it (16:3; 21:6).

See note on 1 Kin. 20:35. my two children to be his slaves. The Mosaic law allows taking children as bond-servants (or slaves) for a limited period of time (Ex. 21:2, 7; Lev. 25:39–46; Deut. 15:12–18). Unfortunately, this provision was often abused (Neh. 5:5–8; Jer. 34:8–22; Amos 2:6; 8:6). Such situations fall under the rights of redemption (Lev. 25:23–55; cf. Ruth 4:1–12). Apparently, this widow has no kinsman-redeemer to act on her behalf, and thus she seeks Elisha's intervention.

Throughout the Bible, God's grace to childless women, such as Sarah (Gen. 17:16–19), Rebekah (Gen. 25:21–26), Rachel (Gen. 29:31; 30:22–24), and Elizabeth (Luke 1:5–25), shows His love and compassion for the those in need.

Ancient Israel had a lunar calendar, and a festival was celebrated at each new moon (Num. 10:10; 28:11–15; Ezra 3:5; Neh. 10:33; Is. 1:13, 14; Amos 8:5). The law does not permit work on the Sabbath and possibly not on the new moon either (Ex. 16:23; 20:8–10; 1 Sam. 20:5; 1 Chr. 23:31).

Jehoram probably reigned together with his father, Jehoshaphat, for five years before becoming the sole monarch of Judah (1:17; 1 Kin. 22:42). This verse marks the death of Jehoshaphat and the beginning of Jehoram's (Joram's) independent rule (848–841 B.C.).

Usually Judah's kings are evaluated with reference to their predecessors. Jehoram is purposely compared to the "house of Ahab" because he imitates their policies. Ahab introduced and sanctioned Baal worship in the northern kingdom of Israel, and now Jehoram does the same in Judah. the daughter of Ahab. Jehu's demand takes the form of a pun. In Hebrew "head" can mean part of the body or it can mean "leader" or "chief." It is uncertain whether Jehu is asking for the death of all Ahab's male descendants or for the leaders among the royal princes.

The leaders of Samaria take no chances; they carry out Jehu's command literally. In this way another component of Elijah's prophecy comes to pass (1 Kin. 21:21–24). This drastic action is not unknown in the ancient Near East: its purpose was to wipe out any descendant that might seek retribution at a later time.
Assyrian kings, such as Ashurbanipal II and Shalmaneser III, intimidated populations by leaving heaps of heads by the city gates.
Jehu's actions go far beyond the mandate of Elijah's oracle (1 Kin. 21:21–24) and the oracle delivered personally to Jehu (9:7–10).

In an inscription on the Black Obelisk, the Assyrian ruler Shalmaneser III (854–824 B.C..) records that "Jehu, son of Omri" paid him tribute of silver, gold, and other articles. On the same obelisk, Jehu, or one of his messengers, is portrayed as bowing before the Assyrian king. If the engraving is of Jehu, then it is the only known pictorial representation of an Israelite king from antiquity. Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. See note on 1 Kin. 11:41.

Jehoiada the priest leads a coup against the usurper Athaliah, mother of Ahaziah, and installs young Joash (Jehoash), son of Ahaziah, as rightful king of Judah. 11:1 Athaliah. A daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, she has been dedicated to seeing Baal worship flourish in Judah (8:18; 11:18). Athaliah's attempted purge of the royal house of Judah brings the dynasty of David to the brink of extinction.

If, as is likely, she is not a daughter of Athaliah, Jehosheba is a half sister of Ahaziah. In 2 Chr. 22:11 she is identified as the wife of Jehoiada the priest (cf. vv. 4, 9). Her actions stand in contrast to the disloyalty of the leaders of Samaria (10:1–7). Joash. The son of Ahaziah and consequently a grandson of Athaliah. Also known as Jehoash. in a bedroom. Joash (Jehoash), less than a year old (vv. 3, 21) and not yet weaned, is providentially saved from Athaliah's persecution.

The writer acknowledges that Athaliah controls Judah for at least six years, but because he regards her reign as illegitimate, he does not dignify it with the usual introduction and conclusion (cf. vv. 1, 20 with 11:21–12:3, 19–21). These articles may be part of the spoils David captured from King Hadad­ezer of Zobah (2 Sam. 8:3–11). If so, these spears and shields were dedicated by David to the Lord (2 Sam. 8:7, 11) and have been stored in the temple since their capture. Another explanation is that they were David's personal spears and shields. Displaying these armaments is probably a symbolic act that indicates that the military leaders have aligned themselves with the Davidic line and its beliefs in opposition to Athaliah and her support of Baalism in the land.
This refers either to the Sinaitic covenant as a whole (Ex. 25:16; cf. 2 Kin. 23:3) or to a more limited document that specifies the duties and limitations of kingship (Deut. 17:14–20).
