In this section the Chronicler makes use of 1 Kin. 12–2 Kin. 17, but about half his materi­al comes from other sources. His record of the period of the divided monarchy does not rehearse the harsh condemnation of the northern tribes found in Kings, focusing instead on events in Judah, the location of the temple, and the Davidic king. Throughout this section, the writer reports how the conditions in the kingdom depend on the king's faithfulness to God and the guidance he gives to the nation. As the original readers considered these events, they could see clearly the choices for blessing and curse in their own day. 10:1–12:16 In describing Rehoboam's reign (931–913 B.C.), the Chronicler makes broad use of Kings (cf. 10:1–11:4 with 1 Kin. 12:1–24; 12:9–16 with 1 Kin. 14:21, 25–31) while presenting the material in accord with his own theological understanding and emphasis. The account is presented in two parts (10:1–11:23 and 12:1–14), each narrating a problematic situation, prophetic encounter, and divine blessing. The conclusion is a notice of Rehoboam's wars with Jeroboam and his death (12:15, 16). The chapters impress on the readers God's curse against pride and infidelity and the benefits of living in humility and obedience to the prophetic word (20:20 note). 10:1–11:23 The first section recounting Rehoboam's reign focuses on the initial three years of his rule (11:17), in which there is conflict (ch. 10), obedience to the prophetic word (11:1–4), and divine blessing (11:5–23). 10:1–11:4 is derived from 1 Kin. 12:1–24 (notes); the Chronicler adds 11:5–23. 10:1 all Israel. In the discussion of the period of the divided monarchy, this expression and others like it can refer to: the southern kingdom alone (11:3; 12:1; 24:5; 28:23); the northern kingdom alone (10:16; 11:13; 13:4, 15); or both kingdoms together (18:16; see 1 Chr. 11:1 note; 2 Chr. 29:24 note). The last usage is found here. The gathering of all the tribes is for recognition of his kingship. Shechem. An ancient and important settlement, situated in the hill country of Ephraim, thirty-four miles (55 km) north of Jerusalem. In Rehoboam's day, the city has been a center for the northern tribes since the time of Joshua, who had renewed the Mosaic covenant there (Josh. 24:1).
He was the foreman of the forced labor in Ephraim and Manasseh who fled to Egypt (1 Kin. 11:26–28, 40).
The northern tribes are not prepared to accept Rehoboam's rule without negotiating the terms of their allegiance to him.
Rehoboam seems out of touch with the mood of the nation and requests three days' respite to formulate his response to the situation.
Possibly a metaphorical usage for a scourge with pieces of metal in the whip.

might fulfill his word.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The author points out that Rehoboam's reaction must be seen in the light of God's sovereign purposes. Ahijah's prophecy concerning Jeroboam (1 Kin. 11:29–39) is fulfilled by this turn of events. Divine sovereignty extends over the sinful actions of human beings (1 Chr. 21:1 note).
The northern tribes alone. See note on 10:1. to your tents, O Israel. A declaration of rebellion, renouncing Rehoboam's authority. Cf. 1 Chr. 12:18.
Further evidence of the extent to which Rehoboam is out of touch with the mood of the ten northern tribes.
Obviously incorporated from the source the Chronicler is using. See note on 1 Chr. 4:41.
Not all the territory of Benjamin becomes part of the northern kingdom (see 1 Kin. 12:21).
The prophet appears twice in Rehoboam's reign (see 12:5–8). To Rehoboam's credit and benefit, both times the king listens to the prophet's word.
The phrase makes clear who is included. See note on 10:1.
See note on 10:15. God does not permit Rehoboam to reunite the people by force.

The Chronicler gives three illustrations of divine blessing to demonstrate the wisdom of Rehoboam's response to the prophetic warning (20:20 note). The text mentions fortifications and military strength in Judah and Benjamin (11:5–12), the defection of Levites from the northern kingdom (11:13–17), and the increase of his family (11:18–23). Most of this material is found only in Chronicles. 11:5 built cities for defense. Rather "rebuilt," as the cities previously existed. An indication of divine blessing. See note on 1 Chr. 11:5. The cities lie close to Jerusalem but mainly to its west and south. Rehoboam feels threatened by Egypt rather than by the northern kingdom.
See note on 10:1.

The Chronicler does not repeat the account found in Kings about how Jeroboam establishes idolatrous worship centers at Dan and Bethel (1 Kin. 12:25–33) but assumes that the reader knows.that Jeroboam rejects priests and Levites who are faithful to Jerusalem as the proper site for worship. The Levites whose ancestral property is located throughout the northern tribes are prepared to forgo it for conscience's sake, and they move south to Jerusalem. The theme of faithful Israelites defecting to Judah appears several times in the periods of the divided and reunited kingdoms (13:8–11; 15:9; 30:10–12). After the return from exile in Babylon, these accounts are a precedent for Israelites from the northern kingdom to join with the returned exiles, since the restoration is centered in Jerusalem (1 Chr. 9:3 note; see Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).
Not mentioned in Kings but see Lev. 17:7.

LORD. Mere outward engagement in religious ceremonies does not constitute true seeking, which requires inward devotion joined with obedience to the Lord's demands. Those in the north who have a true regard for the Lord and His worship join the Levites who have moved to the south.
Rehoboam enjoys God's blessing because he and his subjects imitate the faithfulness of David and Solomon during the early years of his reign.

The Chronicler frequently mentions family increase to demonstrate God's blessing (1 Chr. 13:13 note). 11:18 Mahalath. The Chronicler notes that she is descended from David on both her father's and her mother's side. Jerimoth married his cousin Abihail.

See note on 13:2. The Absalom mentioned here is probably not David's son (see 2 Sam. 14:27). If this Absalom is David's son, he may be the grandfather of Maacah through his daughter Tamar (2 Sam. 14:27), who presumably becomes the wife of Uriel (13:2).
This appointment is typical of the co-regencies (overlapping reigns between father and son) that prevail in Judah and provide a clear line of succession there.

By dispersing his sons throughout Judah and settling them there rather than keeping them at court, Rehoboam tries to forestall plotting against his chosen heir and also strengthens royal control of the land.

For the second major portion of the account of Rehoboam's reign (10:1–12:16 note), the historian expands the account of 1 Kin. 14:25–28. He reports Rehoboam's disobedience in his fourth year and divine retribution by means of Shishak's invasion in his fifth year (12:2). 12:1, 2 abandoned the law \... unfaithful to the LORD. Three years that witnessed consolidation of Rehoboam's rule in the south are followed by a fourth in which the king and nation fall prey to pride and self-reliance. See 1 Kin. 14:22–24 for more details on their apostasy involving adoption of Canaanite idolatry and associated immoral practices. See also note on 1 Chr. 16:40. 12:1 all Israel. The southern kingdom alone as embodying the covenant community. See note on 10:1.

The author adds these verses to complete the parallel with Rehoboam's previous encounter with Shemaiah (cf. 11:2–4; 10:1–11:23 note). 12:3 1,200 \... 60,000 \... without number. See note on 1 Chr. 19:7. "Sukkiim" are Libyan mercenary forces, who are mentioned in Egyptian texts.
Rehoboam's newly strengthened fortress towns (11:5–12) prove incapable of resisting the might of Egypt.
First appears in 11:2; here he tells the leaders of Judah that they have brought this attack on themselves by their religious compromise (see 1 Chr. 28:9; 2 Chr. 15:2).
See also vv. 7, 12. This event illustrates God's response to Solomon's prayer (7:14 note). It remains a standing principle of devout conduct (1 Pet. 5:6).

Although Shemaiah modifies his first warning, God's sovereign plan is not overturned. Prophetic warnings are designed to stir repentance. If successful, the threat of judgment is often removed, postponed, or softened (Jer. 18:1–12; Joel 2:12–14; Jon. 3).
The glory of Solomon's kingdom has already faded, and the people are forced into surrendering its trappings, which are taken as plunder to Egypt.
The key lesson the Chronicler wants to impress on his audience is that while Rehoboam continues to suffer for his sins, God graciously establishes his kingdom and blesses the nation.
Probably a reference to the sins of Rehoboam's fourth year (vv. 1, 2 note). This observation is not found in 1 Kin. 14:29–31.
See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features. Some of the additional sources from which the Chronicler derives his information.

The account of Abijah's reign in Chronicles (13:2–21) differs considerably from that in Kings (1 Kin. 15:3–5). Chronicles emphasizes the positive side of Abijah's reign, while the writer of Kings focuses on the negative side (1 Kin. 15:3). The Chronicler reports Abijah's speech against the northern kingdom (13:4–12) and his prayerful reliance on God in battle (13:14). 13:1 Abijah. He reigned 913–910 B.C.., during the rule of Jeroboam I in the northern kingdom (930–909 B.C.). His name is spelled Abijam in 1 Kin. 15:1–8.

A variant spelling of "Maacah" (see 11:20; 1 Kin. 15:2). Maacah is apparently the granddaughter of Absalom through his daughter Tamar and her husband, Uriel of Gibeah. war between Abijah and Jeroboam. 1 Kin. 15:6, 7 mentions this war, but Chronicles has more details, including the drawing of battle lines, Abijah's speech, the battle itself, and its outcome.

Judah is greatly outnumbered, highlighting the power of God at work on behalf of faithful Judah (1 Chr. 12:23 note; 1 Chr. 19:7 note). The seemingly high numbers are in line with those recorded in 1 Chr. 21:5.

Abijah's speech against the northern kingdom makes clear that David's dynasty is approved by God and that the temple worship in Jerusalem is established by God. 13:4 Mount Zemaraim. In the border regions between Judah and Israel, probably in the territory of Benjamin (see Josh. 18:22).

The revelation embodied in the covenant and its institutions create additional obligations upon those who are aware of it. The rebellion of the north is still a recent event, and those addressed by Abijah should not suppress the truth they learned earlier. a covenant of salt. Probably symbolic of the permanence of the covenant because of salt's preservative qualities (Lev. 2:13; Num. 18:19).
Abijah appeals to the northern army by blaming Jeroboam for the rebellion against Rehoboam.
Abijah explains that Rehoboam's offense against the northern tribes (10:1–17) is the result of his youth (in fact, he is forty-one years old) and inexperience (see 1 Chr. 22:5; 29:1; 2 Chr. 12:13).

LORD. Despite Rehoboam's offense, to oppose David's dynasty was to resist God Himself. "Withstand" is literally "to strengthen oneself before," but it was a false confidence despite the larger army of the north.
The Chronicler has already mentioned the defection of these Levites as an indication of God's blessing on Rehoboam (11:13–17 and notes).

In contrast to the northern kingdom, Judah has remained fundamentally loyal to the temple, priests, and Levites (but see 12:1, 2). As Hezekiah's later reforms indicate, Judah's faithfulness does not endure (29:4–11 note; 30:6–9 note).
Abijah's speech refers to his care for proper worship, and is an important message for the original readers of Chronicles during their reestablishment of worship in Jerusalem after the exile.
LORD. In his dedicatory prayer, Solomon spoke of praying to God in battle (6:34 note). Prayer appears here as the decisive factor in the battle (1 Chr. 4:9 note).
In this context, the northern kingdom.

See note on 1 Chr. 20:4. This is the same verb as "to humble oneself" (see 7:14). Those who do not voluntarily humble themselves before God will be made to bow. because they relied on the LORD. Reliance on the power of the Lord instead of on human strength is a dominant theme in Chronicles (16:2 note).

The outcomes for Jeroboam and Abijah indicate whether God approves or disapproves of them. Jeroboam never recovers from his defeat. Abijah, however, grows stronger and has many children (1 Chr. 13:13 note).
Iddo was mentioned in 9:29, and his "story" or "record" is another source used by the Chronicler. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features.

This account of Asa's reign is considerably longer than that of 1 Kin. 15:9–24 (forty-eight verses as compared to sixteen). Asa's reign is presented in two parts: years of fidelity and blessing (14:1–15:19) and later years of infidelity and curse (ch. 16). Within these two parts there is a pattern of contrasting parallels: Asa's growing prosperity (14:1–7) is balanced by the concluding section on his illness and death (16:11–14). This change of circumstances is explained in the central section where Asa is first presented as reliant on God and successful in war (14:9–15). This is followed by words of prophetic commendation and royal reform (ch. 15). By way of contrast, in his later years Asa relies on human power and allies himself with a foreign king (16:1–6) and so incurs prophetic condemnation (16:7–9), to which he reacts harshly (16:10). Again the Chronicler is drawing on the past to make the options more vivid for his own and succeeding generations. 14:1 A transitional verse, moving from the reign of Abijah to that of Asa. the land had rest. See note on 1 Chr. 22:9. Asa has a lengthy reign, from 911 to 870/869 B.C. In his first ten years, his reforming zeal is blessed with national security (911–900 B.C.).

Asa removes pagan high places (see 1 Kin. 3:2 note) from both Jerusalem and "all the cities of Judah" (14:5), but 15:17 (1 Kin. 15:14) indicates that he does not continue his initial efforts throughout his life. A similar explanation holds for the descriptions of Jehoshaphat's removal of high places (see 17:6; 20:33).
LORD. See note on 7:14. keep the law and the commandment. See note on 1 Chr. 16:40.

It is later noted that "the high places were not taken out of Israel \[= Judah\]" (15:17; 1 Kin. 15:14). Possibly the emphasis here should be on "the cities of Judah" with high places in the countryside remaining. More probably Asa's early reforms have only a superficial impact on the people, and later in his reign there is a resurgence of Canaanite practices.

Apparently this means that there are no major wars in this period. The writer says later that Asa captures some towns in Ephraim during this time (15:8). the LORD gave him peace. Chronicles presents peace in Asa's reign as a blessing for devotion and obedience to God (14:2–16:14 note; 1 Chr. 22:9 note). 14:6, 7 He built \... Let us build. God also assists Asa's building projects (1 Chr. 11:5 note).

When Zerah attacks, Asa seeks the Lord and gains victory, fulfilling Solomon's request in his prayer (6:34 note). This battle directly contrasts with Asa's later battle against Baasha (16:1–6; see 14:2–16:14 note). 14:8 Asa's army totals 580,000. The attacking army is nearly twice as large ("a million men," v. 9). On these large numbers, see note on 1 Chr. 12:23.

Possibly a general of Pharaoh Osorkon I, second ruler of the Twenty-Second Dynasty of Egypt. Ethiopia (or Cush) in the Bible is the remote region south of Egypt, corresponding to modern-day northern Sudan (1 Chr. 1:8). This invasion seems to occur shortly before Asa's fifteenth year (see 15:10). a million men. See note on 1 Chr. 19:7. Mareshah. About twenty-five miles (40 km) southwest of Jerusalem.
Asa expresses his utter inadequacy for battle against Zerah (20:12 note). we rely on you. Reliance on the Lord's power is the key to Asa's victory (16:7 note).
A Philistine city that lies twenty miles (32 km) southwest of Mareshah. The area around Gerar seems already to be under Egyptian control.

As the army returns from Gezer (see v. 11), Azariah proclaims the principle of retribution so often illustrated in this account of the divided monarchy. Faithfulness to God will bring blessing; disloyalty will result in chastisement.
See notes on 7:14 and 1 Chr. 28:9.

That is, without His presence and blessing. "Without a teaching priest" implies they are neglecting their duties in this respect (Lev. 10:11), so there is no true knowledge of the law or obedience to it. Probably a reference to the days of the judges so that "Israel" is the whole nation.
LORD. See note on 7:14.

Asa responds to the prophet with further reforms (v. 8) and an assembly of covenant renewal (vv. 9–15); he goes so far as to depose Maacah, his relative, because of her religious apostasy (vv. 16–19). 15:8 repaired the altar of the LORD. The great bronze altar in the outer courtyard. Exactly how it was damaged is not known.
Israelites from the northern tribes (11:14 note) defect and join Asa as he suppresses idolatry and reestablishes true worship in Jerusalem.
Probably coincides with the celebration of the Feast of Weeks/Pentecost in May/June 895 B.C.

A renewed pledge of adherence to the Sinai covenant as a seal of their wholehearted participation in their special relationship with the Lord. Significant for the Chronicler is that Asa (15:12), Jehoiada (23:16), Hezekiah (29:10), and Josiah (34:30–32) all lead the nation in such renewals, celebrating God's goodness to His people over the generations. In this way, the author emphasizes to his contemporaries the importance of adhering to their similar commitments (Ezra 10:3–5; Neh. 9:38).
The law of Moses prescribes capital punishment for those who seek other gods (Ex. 22:20; Deut. 13:6–16).
See note on 1 Chr. 22:9.

His grandmother has the same name (11:20), so "mother" may be used in an extended sense. In either case, Asa does not let family connections compromise his loyalty to the Lord. at the brook Kidron. Outside Jerusalem, to the east.
See note on 14:3.

See note on 14:6. 15:19–16:1 thirty-fifth year \... thirty-sixth year. Kings reports that Elah succeeded Baasha in Asa's twenty-sixth year (1 Kin. 15:33; 16:8), Zimri in Asa's twenty-seventh year (1 Kin. 16:10, 15), and Omri in Asa's thirty-first year (1 Kin. 16:23). Consequently, this battle could not have taken place in the thirty-sixth year of Asa (16:1) since Baasha would have been dead for ten years. No simple solution to this difficulty has been found. One suggestion is that an original "twenty-fifth" and "twenty-sixth" was inadvertently changed through a copyist's error (see Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues). A plausible alternative is that the Chronicler's source here used a chronology dating from the division of the kingdom, so that the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years of the kingdom correspond to what is elsewhere be expressed as Asa's fifteenth and sixteenth years, respectively. Understood in this way, it eliminates the problem of Baasha's waiting for ten years until 885/884 B.C. before trying to stem the flow of his subjects to the south, which began in 895 B.C.

Asa's battle with Baasha of Israel begins his downfall. He seeks the assistance of Ben-hadad of Syria, in sharp contrast with his battle against Zerah when he relied on the Lord (14:2–16:14 note). 16:1 Ramah. On the border between the two kingdoms, five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem. Baasha is trying to prevent further defections to the south.

\... to Ben-hadad.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Asa's actions are wrong on two counts. First, he takes from the temple treasuries, showing disregard for the temple and its worship (see 28:21). Second, he allies himself with a foreign power instead of relying on the Lord. He compounds this fault in that the foreign alliance is against northern Israel. The Chronicler demonstrates many times the benefits of relying on God (1 Chr. 5:20; 2 Chr. 13:18; 14:11–15; 16:7, 8; 32:20–22). He also deplores foreign alliances and points to their dire consequences (18:1; 19:2; 20:35–37; 22:3–9; 25:7; 28:16–21; 35:21 note), a suitable warning to those engaged in rebuilding the nation after the return from exile in Babylon.

An international treaty, here one between equals. Asa's payment is not tribute but a bribe to induce Ben-hadad to repudiate his alliance with Israel. Making this covenant is a sad reversal of the scene found in 15:12.

–6 Ben-hadad captures several cities in the far north of Israel, and this diverts Baasha's attention from his southern border. Asa is therefore able to take over the newly constructed border post at Ramah, reusing its building materials on other sites nearby. The record is one of success for Asa's political strategy.

In contrast to the earlier episode of Azariah's encouragement and Asa's reforms (ch. 15), Hanani is sent to deliver a prophetic rebuke to King Asa, who reacts negatively (14:2–16:14 note). This is the first recorded persecution of a prophet. 16:7 you relied. This verb occurs three times in vv. 7, 8 (elsewhere in Chronicles only in 13:18; 14:11). It points to seeking God's assistance in a time of national crisis. Even though a measure of military success is achieved, the whole enterprise is flawed because it is not based on faith in God and what He will achieve for His people. escaped you. Baasha deserts his position before the arrival of Asa and Ben-hadad, cutting short Asa's victory (16:5).
Hanani refers directly to the contrast with Asa's victory over Zerah (14:8–15). "Ethiopians" means people from south of Egypt (see 14:9 note). The Libyans are from North Africa, west of Egypt.
Hanani threatens divine judgment because of Asa's infidelity (1 Chr. 28:9 note; 2 Chr. 14:6 note).
Presumably those who agree with Hanani the prophet.
. Not the canonical books of Kings but an earlier court chronicle.

Asa's rejection of the prophetic word leads to his disease and death (14:2–16:14 note). thirty-ninth year. 872/871 B.C., two years before his death in 870/869 B.C. physicians. Asa continues to turn away from the Lord and rely on human strength. The OT does not hesitate to prescribe medical treatment for physical maladies (2 Kin. 20:5–7 and the use of balm in Jer. 8:22; 51:8), but it never divorces natural remedies from seeking divine assistance (Deut. 32:39).
These fires are not cremations but memorials honoring deceased kings. Cf. the honor bestowed on Asa with the response to Jehoram's death (21:19).

The account of Jehoshaphat's reign incorporates most of the record in Kings (cf. 1 Kin. 22:1–35 with 2 Chr. 18:2–34; 1 Kin. 22:41–46, 49 with 2 Chr. 20:31–36) but is twice as long, adding some material and a summary of his reign. The Chronicler views Jehoshaphat positively in general. In his earlier reign, Jehoshaphat is faithful (17:3–9) and faces battle (18:1–19:3). Later he again is faithful (19:4–11) and again faces battle (20:1–30). The Chronicler once more brings out the need to respond properly to God's Word (18:4–27; 20:14–21) and the power of effective prayer (18:31; 20:5–17). Also, foreign alliances are to be avoided as they substitute reliance on human scheming and power for faithful trust in the Lord. Jehoshaphat is portrayed as a man of faith who is somewhat naive (18:29) and whose otherwise creditable desire to promote good relations with the north and a changed religious outlook there leads him to make several unwise moves. 17:1 Jehoshaphat. He reigned 873–848 B.C. Jehoshaphat was probably co-regent with Asa for three years (873–870/869 B.C.) because of Asa's illness (16:11–14; see 20:31 note). At the beginning of his reign, there continued to be hostility toward the northern kingdom, which was by that time ruled by Ahab.
See note on 14:6.

The Chronicler hints that David's later ways (2 Sam. 11–21) were different. the Baals. This reflects the Baal worship of Canaan and Phoenicia, which is being promoted at this time in Israel by Ahab and his wife, Jezebel (1 Kin. 16:31).
See note on 14:3. Just as in the reign of his father, Asa (14:5; 15:17), the king's initial removal of these sites of pagan worship is later reversed due to popular attachment to them (see 20:33).

This teaching mission probably takes place just after Asa's death (17:1 note). 17:7, 8 officials \... Levites. The royal officials are accompanied by Levites, whom Moses ordained to be teachers of the people (1 Chr. 26:29–32 note; 2 Chr. 19:5–11 note).
LORD. The identity of this book is uncertain. It may include the entire Pentateuch, but in light of the nature of Jehoshaphat's reforms (19:4–11), it certainly includes Deuteronomy.
LORD. Fear of the divine power displayed in Jehoshaphat's military strength gives him peace with other nations (1 Chr. 14:17 note). Some indeed pay him tribute (v. 11).
See note on 1 Chr. 11:5.
For these large numbers, see note on 1 Chr. 12:23.

In contrast to his early years, Jehoshaphat comes under God's curse because he ignores the prophetic warning and makes an alliance with the northern kingdom (16:2 note; 20:20 note). 18:1 he made a marriage alliance. The author refers to the marriage of Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram to Athaliah, daughter of Ahab (21:6; 22:2). In Kings, Ahab (874–853 B.C.) represents the depths of apostasy in the northern kingdom (1 Kin. 16:30). See note on 16:2; 19:1–3.

Probably near the end of Ahab's reign. induced. The Hebrew expression can have the connotation of enticing to apostasy (Deut. 13:6; 1 Chr. 21:1). Ramoth-gilead. A city thirty miles (48 km) east of the Jordan River, closer to the Sea of Galilee than the Dead Sea. Moses set it apart as a city of refuge in Israel (Deut. 4:43; Josh. 20:8), but it was captured later by the father of Ben-hadad, the king of Syria against whom Ahab fought several battles. Ben-hadad eventually agreed to return the city to Israel, but he failed to do so (1 Kin. 20:1–34).
Jehoshaphat tries to still his conscience and regain some initiative in the situation by requiring the Lord's approval for the proposed enterprise.

Jehoshaphat perceives that though the prophets are presenting themselves as prophets of the Lord (see "another"), they are not speaking by divine direction. He therefore asks for a genuine prophet to inquire of the Lord's will.
Zedekiah's enacted prophecy may be an attempt to invoke the Mosaic blessing of the Joseph tribes in Deut. 33:17.
An attempt to coerce Micaiah to fall in with the majority viewpoint and say what the king wants to hear, but Micaiah rejects such compromise (v. 13).
The mocking, ironic tone of Micaiah's response is evident to Ahab.
LORD. Micaiah's vision of heavenly deliberations (see Job 1:6–12; Is. 6:1–8; Zech. 3) demonstrates that the sovereignty of God extends over evil events (1 Chr. 21:1 note).
A singular form, referring to Ahab.
The designation of a court official who enforces royal orders rather than a member of Ahab's family (see Jer. 36:26; 38:6).

In contrast to Rehoboam (11:4) and Asa after his first battle (15:1–8), Jehoshaphat pays no attention to the prophet's warning. As a result, Jehoshaphat barely escapes with his life (18:31). See note on 20:20.
Ahab tries to make Jehoshaphat a target for the enemy, and, unsuspectingly, Jehoshaphat does not see the danger he is in.

The writer adds to the words of 1 Kings 22:32 the explicit statement that "the LORD helped him," recalling the request of Solomon's dedicatory prayer (6:34 note; 7:14 note). Even though Jehoshaphat is engaged in an enterprise that the Lord has not sanctioned, when he cries out in prayer, he receives divine assistance.
The writer does not repeat the details of Ahab's death found in 1 Kin. 22:36–40.

Jehoshaphat escapes death after crying out to the Lord (18:31). Even so, Jehu rebukes him for his sin. God earlier chastised Jehoshaphat for depending on a foreign alliance (16:7–10 note; 1 Chr. 28:9 note).
LORD. This does not interdict compassion for the lost (Matt. 5:44) but does forbid compromise with God's enemies and involvement in their schemes (Ps. 139:21, 22).
Jehoshaphat is guilty of inconsistency, but despite that, the Lord will bless him.
Jehoshaphat personally travels throughout the kingdom from Beersheba in the south to the northern border with Israel to draw the people back to allegiance to God.
Jehoshaphat establishes a system of courts throughout Judah to enforce the Mosaic law (1 Chr. 26:20–32). He earlier sent out leaders, Levites, and priests to teach (17:7–9).
This does not mean that their decisions are inspired but that God approves of the work of the courts in general and wants their decisions to be made according to His law.

Jehoshaphat also sets up a supreme court in Jerusalem to hear appeals. The king's arrangements provide for religious cases to be heard by the chief priest and civil cases by a royal administrator. Zebadiah is not the same individual as the Levite of that name in 17:8. Details of such judicial arrangements were of interest to the Chronicler's postexilic readers because the Persians granted them the right to organize local courts.

This battle is not found in Kings. Jehoshaphat responds to a serious military threat with exemplary reliance on the Lord (cf. his approach to the battle in 18:1–19:3). This incident probably occurs shortly after the defeat at Ramoth-gilead. 20:1 Moabites \... Ammonites. The descendants of these enemies are still a threat to Israel after the return from exile in Babylon (Neh. 2:19; 4:1–3; 13). Meunites. Members of an Arabian tribe who live south and east of the Dead Sea, including in the territory of Edom (1 Chr. 4:41; 2 Chr. 26:7). Possibly at this time they are dwelling in Mount Seir (v. 10), probably located in the south of Edom.

See note on 1 Chr. 19:7. Edom. Although virtually all Hebrew manuscripts read "Aram," that is, Syria (text note), there is no mention of Aram in the context. The Hebrew for Edom and Aram differ only in one letter, so there may have been a tendency for copyists to accidentally misread "Edom" as "Aram." See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues. Engedi. On the west shore of the Dead Sea, en route to Jerusalem.
Jehoshaphat responds immediately by calling Judah to fast and seek the Lord; these actions recall Solomon's dedicatory prayer (6:34 notes).

Jehoshaphat's assembly follows the liturgical pattern often associated with prayers of lament: corporate prayer is offered (vv. 5–13); there is an oracle of deliverance from God (vv. 14–17); and the people respond with praise (vv. 18, 19).
Jehoshaphat applies Solomon's dedicatory prayer explicitly to his situation (6:12–42 and notes).
Confession of human impotence, humility, and reliance on divine power appear also in Asa's prayer (14:11 note).
Human effort in Israel's warfare is by divine power. The prophet reminds Jehoshaphat that human responsibility depends on the sovereignty of God (v. 17).

The strategy and outcome of this battle forms a striking contrast to Jehoshaphat's previous battle (18:28–34 and notes). 20:20 the wilderness of Tekoa. Tekoa lies twelve miles (19 km) south of Jerusalem. The mountain pass of Ziz (v. 16) begins north of Engedi and stretches inland to end near Tekoa. believe his prophets, and you will succeed. 2 Chronicles frequently emphasizes the importance of trusting and obeying the prophetic word. See notes on chs. 10–12; 14:2–16:14; 18:1–19:3; 24:19; 25:1–13; 25:15, 16; 28:5–15; 36:15 (see also Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Jehoshaphat's instruction contrasts with his earlier rejection of Micaiah (18:1–32).
See note on 5:13.

The Lord causes the enemy army to be attacked (by whom is not clear), but the result is that in the ensuing melee the various contingents of the enemy force engage in mutual destruction (see Judges 7:22).
See note on 1 Chr. 4:41.

The Chronicler supplements the record of Jehoram's reign in Kings (2 Kin. 8:16–24); in Kings, the assessment is negative. Jehoram reigned as co-regent with Jehoshaphat from 853 to 848 B.C. (2 Kin. 1:17; 3:1) and by himself from 848 to 841 B.C.. He murdered his brothers (21:2–7); Edom and Libnah rebelled against him (21:8–10); he fell into idolatry (21:11); and Elijah prophesied an impending judgment (21:12–20).

The murder of Jehoram's brothers recorded here is additional to the account in Kings (2 Kin. 8:16–22). On the other hand, Kings describes how Solomon disposed of Adonijah, an event omitted from Chronicles (1 Kin. 2:24). king of Israel. As sole monarch (21:1–20 note).

The house of David is on the brink of annihilation. Jehoram deserves to die, but God preserves his life to fulfill His promise of a permanent dynasty to David. Despite the sins of individual descendants of David, the Davidic line will never be entirely rejected (1 Chr. 17:7–14 note). a lamp. In this era, lamps are kept burning in a tent to provide light in the darkest of surroundings. In this and the following reign, the Davidic dynasty falls to new lows and is maintained only by God's grace.

God's displeasure toward Jehoram becomes evident when these two nations subject to Judah successfully rebel against him. 21:8 Edom. Jehoshaphat subjugated Edom through righteous dependence on God (20:1–30). Jehoram, however, fails in his attempt because he rebels against God (v. 10).
See note on 1 Chr. 4:41. Libnah. An area between Judah and Philistia.

This episode illustrating the depths of Jehoram's sin is additional to the account in Kings. 21:11 made high places. The only mention of the prophet in Chronicles; compare the lengthy account of his prophetic activities in 1 Kin. 17–2 Kin. 2. Elijah's translation must have occurred shortly after he wrote this letter in 848 B.C. Elijah gives the reason for impending judgment, that Jehoram has not taken his father or grandfather as role models, but the corrupt kings of the northern kingdom.

The judgment against Jehoram is twofold. First, God promises "a great plague" on the people and on Jehoram's family, a threat fulfilled by the attacks of Philistines and Arabs. Second, Jehoram becomes terminally ill, as prophesied (v. 15). The emphasis is on immediate retribution (1 Chr. 28:9 note; Introduction: Theology of 2 Chronicles).
Lit. "near the Cushites," possibly meaning nomads in the area between Judah and Egypt (for the normal use of "Cush," see 1 Chr. 1:8).
This is a variant spelling of the name Ahaziah (22:1).
Cf. the response to Asa's death (16:14). Jehoram (21:20), Joash (24:25), Ahaz (28:27), and Manasseh (33:20) die in ignominy. Amon is assassinated (see 33:24).
Chronicles supplements the record given in 2 Kin. 8:24 of Jehoram's death and burial with details that reveal his utter disgrace. eight years. See note on v. 5.

The record of Chronicles ties Ahaziah (841 B.C.) closely to his father Jehoram (21:4–20). Both kings are deeply influenced by Athaliah and so are evaluated negatively (21:6; 22:3, 4). In both reigns, the Davidic dynasty barely escapes annihilation (21:16, 17; 22:7–9).

The Hebrew text reads "forty-two years old" (text note), but that would make him older than his father (21:20). The correction is made based on 2 Kin. 8:26. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

Chronicles presents Ahaziah's rapid downfall as divine chastisement for his alliance with the northern kingdom (16:2 note). He is under the influence of his mother (v. 3) and of northern counselors of the house of Ahab (v. 4), a truly toxic combination bent on promoting iniquity.
Also known as Joram (later in this verse, and v. 6). He was Ahaziah's uncle. Hazael. See 1 Kin. 19:15; 2 Kin. 8:7–15.
It is Ahaziah's contacts with Joram that are divinely used to bring about his downfall.
Kings reports that Elisha anointed Jehu to destroy the house of Omri (2 Kin. 9:1–10:31). The death of Ahaziah is part of this judgment.

Ahaziah receives an honorable burial, presumably in Jerusalem, not because of his character but out of respect for his grandfather Jehoshaphat. no one able to rule. The only male survivor of the Davidic dynasty is Joash, still an infant.

The Chronicler follows the record of 2 Kin. 11 closely. Athaliah is the only queen to rule in Judah (841–835 B.C.). No formal statements are made regarding the beginning and end of her reign, because she is treated as the usurper that she is, and the account of her reign focuses on opposition to her. The life of the young heir to the throne, Joash, is preserved by his aunt, Jehoshabeath (22:10–12). Seven years later, Jehoshabeath's husband, Jehoiada the high priest, gathers sufficient support to have Joash crowned (23:1–11). Athaliah is executed (23:12–15), and Jehoiada takes action to reverse the religious decline that prevailed during her reign (23:16–21). 22:10–12 Jehoshaphat's marriage alliance (18:1 note) finally yields its most dire consequence: the Davidic line from which the Messiah will come is almost rendered extinct. With a ruthlessness typical of the apostate north, Athaliah assassinates any who pose a threat to her hold on power.
(Jehosheba, 2 Kin. 11:2) is the daughter of the previous king, Jehoram. Her husband, Jehoiada, may well be much older than she (see 24:15).

The Zadokite priest Jehoiada resists Queen Athaliah and gains the military support necessary for temple and political reform. The account in Kings focuses more on the royal guards, whereas the Chronicler brings out the involvement of the nation as a whole and of the temple officials.
This verse expands the account in Kings, depicting Joash's widespread support in Judah (1 Chr. 11:1 note).

–10 Jehoiada is well aware of Athaliah's ruthlessness and takes steps to ensure the young king's safety, both in his refuge in the temple and when he leaves it. He is able to double the number of priests and Levites in the temple precincts by staging the coup when the guards are scheduled to change duty.
Probably the text of the covenant made in 23:3, reflecting the requirements of Deut. 17:18–20, and possibly also the role of Jehoiada during any continuing regency.
See note on 1 Chr. 15:16. Treason. Athaliah is oblivious to her position and has no inkling of there being any surviving son of Ahaziah.

The scene may be read in two ways, as the text note indicates. Probably Athaliah walks out of the temple (note "went," not "was brought"). As one whose philosophy takes "might" to be "right," she recognizes the inevitability of her doom.
See note on 15:12. This acknowledges the Lord's sovereignty in all matters pertaining to the kingdom and leads to the eradication of Baal worship in Jerusalem.
Probably a shrine to Baal erected for Athaliah (see 1 Kin. 11:1–8).

This account emphasizes more than 2 Kin. 11:18 that the new temple order under Jehoiada and Joash is according to Mosaic and Davidic design. This provides an obvious lesson for the restored community regarding worship in the second temple.
See note on 1 Chr. 22:9.

Joash reigned 835–796 B.C. This account should be compared with 2 Kin. 12, to which vv. 15–22 are a lengthy supplement. The Chronicler carefully notes the watershed in Joash's reign, which occurs at the death of Jehoiada, so that Joash's reign is described in two periods: years of faithful obedience (vv. 1–16) and years of treachery ending in assassination (vv. 17–27). This account is followed by those of two other reigns, Amaziah (ch. 25) and Uzziah (ch. 26), where good beginnings are not maintained and later disobedience leads to disgrace and failure.

Joash's positive accomplishments are the result of the influence of Jehoiada (24:14). After Jehoiada's death, Joash turns away from the Lord (24:17–19; see 26:5). The Chronicler illustrates the importance of mutual support between king and priest (22:10–23:21 and 24:1–27 notes).

The evidence of 2 Kin. 12:6 locates Joash's initial concern for refurbishing the temple sometime before the twenty-third year of his reign. Since the Levites do not act by then (possibly because they do not wish temple donations diverted from their own upkeep, see 2 Kin. 12:7), the king takes further steps to move the work forward by allowing donations to be made at the temple itself (vv. 8–10).

Chronicles (23:18, 19 note) emphasizes the need for proper Levitical order more than 2 Kin. 12:1–3. money \... from year to year. This requirement is the half-shekel tax of Ex. 30:11–16; 38:24–26 (see 24:9).
See note on 1 Chr. 16:40.
She has no offspring. These men are her followers, who have adopted her practices and have desecrated the temple.
The generous and joyful giving of the officials and people is a good example for those engaged in restoring temple worship after the exile (1 Chr. 29:1–9 note).
–16 The death of Jehoiada marks the turning point in Joash's career. His contribution to the life of the nation is recognized by according him the equivalent of a state funeral.
He gives his consent to the proposals of the princes and leaders of Judah that Canaanite worship should again be permitted. Joash is portrayed as being easily influenced by those around him.

The repetition of the same Hebrew verb denotes action contrary to the terms of the covenant. When the people and their kings are no longer obedient to the Lord and fail to observe His requirements, He treats them (temporarily) as though they have no covenant affiliation to Him in order to force them to reconsider and amend their apostate behavior. See note on 1 Chr. 28:9.
Apostasy is tied to the rejection of God's prophets (20:20 note), whom He sends to warn His rebellious people of their need to repent.

In the spring, when ancient armies usually campaign. The vengeance of the Lord that Zechariah invoked is not long in coming. Chronicles frequently mentions military defeat as the judgment of God against sin (1 Chr. 10; 2 Chr. 13:1–16; 18:33, 34; 21:16, 17; 25:14–24; 28:1–5; 33:1–11). Here the impact of the invasion particularly affects "the princes of the people," most probably the group that initiated the return to paganism in v. 17.
The tables are turned against Judah as was threatened in the covenant (Deut. 28:25; 32:30; 1 Chr. 28:9 note).
Joash is not accorded the honor extended to his guardian Jehoiada (v. 16).

Jehoshaphat earlier defeated Ammon and Moab (20:1 note). This information about their nationality is not noted in Kings, but it is significant in terms of the opposition being encountered in the Chronicler's time.
See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features.

The account of Amaziah's reign (796–767 B.C.) should be compared with 2 Kin. 14. Note that the details of the mercenaries and the war against Edom are recorded only in Chronicles (vv. 5–16). The Chronicler shows how foreign alliances, response to prophetic instruction, and idolatry affect Israel's military security. The account describes fidelity and infidelity, much as in the reports about Joash (22:10–24:27) and Uzziah (ch. 26). 25:1–13 Amaziah. He is not devoted wholeheartedly to the Lord, but he responds properly to prophetic warning (20:20 note). Details of Amaziah's halfheartedness are not recorded here (see 2 Kin. 14:4).
See 1 Chr. 16:40. In observing this limitation, which does not accord with the way vengeance is taken in the nations surrounding Judah, Amaziah honors the requirements of the Lord.

His action is breathtakingly perverse. He abandons the God who has given him victory and worships the gods of those he defeated (perhaps with the intention of placating them).

In contrast with his earlier repentance at the prophetic word (25:7–10), Amaziah rebuffs the prophet and receives a stern warning (20:20 note). 25:16 God has determined to destroy you. See note on 1 Chr. 28:9.

Amaziah reacts to the Israelite raids on his territory (v. 13) by challenging the Israelite king, Joash/Jehoash (793–753 B.C.), to fight. Joash responds at first with a parable in which he compares Amaziah to a thistle seeking a favor from himself as a mighty cedar. A wild beast is a reference to the marauding soldiers. Joash argues that Amaziah has become bigheaded and should be content to stay at home.
The sovereignty of God includes hardening the hearts of sinners so that they no longer respond to warnings (1 Chr. 21:1 note; see also Ex. 3:19; 4:12; 7:3, 4).
West of Bethlehem.

From the northwest corner of the city wall to the northeast corner.

Amaziah's folly leads to plotting against him by unspecified parties. His flight to Lachish (thirty miles \[40 km\] southwest of Jerusalem) is insufficient to extricate him from their hands.

The Chronicler adds a long section (vv. 5–20) to the brief notices about Uzziah in 2 Kin. 14, 15. His account is in four stages: rise to power (vv. 1, 2); obedience and blessing (vv. 3–15); disobedience and curse (vv. 16–20); summary and death (vv. 22, 23). 26:1 Uzziah. Uzziah reigned 792/791–740 B.C.. In 2 Kings he is frequently, but not always, called "Azariah." The chronology of his reign is best understood as presenting him at the age of sixteen as co-regent with his father in 791 B.C., an arrangement that lasts until 767 B.C., when Uzziah begins to rule in his own name. His reign ends with another co-regency (see 27:1 note). The preposition translated "instead of" may also mean "below, underneath."
Or Elath. This port on the Gulf of Aqaba was repossessed by Edom during Jehoram's reign (21:8–10).

The historian compares Uzziah with his father, whose reign was also divided between blessing and curse. The Chronicler again omits the notice in Kings about the failure to remove the high places (2 Kin. 15:4).

LORD. See note on 7:14. in the days of Zechariah. An unknown royal advisor, unlikely the Zechariah named in Is. 8:2, since "in the days of" suggests that Zechariah died during Uzziah's reign and so he could not have been an advisor to his grandson Ahaz (king at the time of Is. 8; see Is. 7:1). Joash was obedient as long as Jehoiada was alive, and Uzziah does well under Zechariah's tutelage (24:2 note). God made him prosper. Covenant obedience brings covenant blessing. Both Israel under Jeroboam II and Judah enjoy a period of prosperity at this time. Uzziah focuses on territory to the south of Judah.
Uzziah is blessed in international conflict (vv. 6–8), domestic affairs (vv. 9, 10), and military strength (vv. 11–15).
Uzziah's blessing recalls Jehoshaphat's victory (20:1–30).
See note on 1 Chr. 19:1.
A reversal of the destruction in Amaziah's defeat (25:23). See note on 1 Chr. 11:5.
For the large number, see note on 1 Chr. 12:23.

This episode shows the Lord's judgment against Uzziah's pride. As with Rehoboam (12:1), initial success leads to disregard for God and His law. Uzziah's leprosy is mentioned only briefly in 2 Kin. 15:5. It may be that Uzziah is claiming to be a priest-king similar to those in surrounding nations and is punished for his presumption and faithlessness. For "unfaithful," see note on 1 Chr. 2:7. 26:16 when he was strong. Moses warned Israel to be careful not to let success make them proud and self-reliant (Deut. 8:10–18).

An otherwise unknown chief priest. He and eighty courageous priests deliver God's judgment to Uzziah. The Chronicler highlights for a third time the role of priests as instructors of royalty (24:2 and note).
Burning incense is restricted to the priests in Mosaic legislation (Ex. 30:7–9; Num. 16:39, 40). See theological note "Civil Government" on p. 2004.
He refuses to accept the rebuke of the priests and to repent. It is this obduracy that leads to his being struck with a skin disease, which entails ceremonial uncleanness.
LORD. Uzziah is quarantined and kept out of the temple, in accordance with the law of Moses (Lev. 13:46; Num. 5:1–4).

See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features. The Chronicler notes that Isaiah also records Hezekiah's reign (32:32), though that reference, unlike the one here, may refer to his canonical prophecy.
Uzziah is buried away from the royal family in relative dishonor because of the curse of leprosy.

In contrast to the records from Joash to Uzziah, where each reign has a balance of obedience and disobedience (22:10–24:27 note), the Chronicler's evaluation of Jotham is fully positive. This is followed with a negative treatment of Ahaz (ch. 28). Chronicles points out that faithfulness to God is the way to success in construction projects and military conflict, providing a vital lesson for the postexilic community trying to rebuild life in the Promised Land. The Chronicler draws on 2 Kin. 15:32–38, with additional material from other sources in vv. 3–6. 27:1 Jotham \... sixteen years. Reigned 750–732 B.C. Jotham reigned during the period of his father Uzziah's leprosy (750–740 B.C..) and had co-regency with his son Ahaz (735–732 B.C.). For six years he was the sole monarch. The figure "sixteen years" here and in v. 8 probably refers to his co-regency with his father and his independent reign. Adding his four years with Ahaz, who probably took over the reins of government, brings the total to twenty years (2 Kin. 15:30).

Unlike his father Uzziah, Jotham does not violate priestly regulations (26:18 note). the people still followed corrupt practices. The historian explains that the people and not Jotham are guilty of continuing corruption (see 2 Kin. 15:35), probably meaning worship at the high places.
Jotham rebuilds this gate on the north side of the temple. wall of Ophel. To the south of the temple. Ophel is the northern part of the original city of David.

This record of victory over the Ammonites highlights God's approval of Jotham. The payment for three years may be in compensation for tribute previously withheld, or it may indicate that attacks on Judah from the north occur because Jotham's attention has been diverted from enforcing these payments.
See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features.

The account of Ahaz in 2 Kin. 16 is supplemented here, esp. in vv. 5–21. Ahaz's reign contrasts sharply with his father's (ch. 27 note), and the account focuses on how his infidelity led to military defeat. 28:1 Ahaz. Ahaz reigned together with Jotham, 735–732 B.C.., and then as sole monarch for sixteen years, 732–715 B.C.. If he was twenty when he took office, he was thirty-six when he died, and he would have been only eleven when his son Hezekiah was born (29:1). Some ancient sources give the figure "twenty-five" instead of "twenty" for his age at succession. did not do what was right. Ahaz possesses no redeeming features; his reign is one of utter disaster from the beginning.
As regards their religious policy of adopting Canaanite practices. In this Ahaz goes farther than others.

To the south of Jerusalem, outside the city walls. Later known as Gehenna. In Ahaz's day, the site is used by Jerusalem for rubbish disposal, and there are many fires there. burned his sons. Ahaz's apostasy is so complete that he practices human sacrifice. See Lev. 18:21; Deut. 12:31; 18:10; 2 Kin. 16:3; 17:17; 21:6; 23:10; 2 Chr. 33:6; Ps. 106:37, 38; Is. 57:5; Jer. 7:30, 31; 19:5; 32:35; Ezek. 16:20, 21. Human sacrifice is characteristic of the worship of the Ammonite god Molech. Though 2 Kin. 16:3 has simply "son," the plural "sons" is also found in some early Greek manuscripts.

Ahaz is defeated in battle as a divine judgment on his flagrant apostasy (v. 5). 28:5 king of Syria \... king of Israel. Rezin (king of Syria) and Pekah (king of Israel) join forces against Ahaz (2 Kin. 16:5, 6; Is. 7:1–17).

Turning from his usual focus on the southern kingdom (Judah), the Chronicler reports that citizens of Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, obey when a prophet speaks to them. This obedience is an instructive contrast to the apostasy of Judah, the southern kingdom. Oded. An otherwise unknown prophet, and not the same Oded as in 2 Chr. 15:1.
Lit. "your brothers." Oded still acknowledges the bond that links north and south.

The treatment accorded to the captives by these high-ranking men from Samaria is echoed in the parable of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:30–37). It is ironic that Israel listens to the Lord and His prophet, whereas Judah and its king are set on going their own way.

Ahaz is thoroughly shaken by events (Is. 7:2) and decides to negotiate with the king of Assyria, Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 B.C.), to intervene on his behalf. In addition to the hostility of Syria (Aram) and Israel to the north, Ahaz faces the Edomites to the south and east (v. 17) and the Philistines to the southwest (v. 18).
See note on 1 Chr. 2:7.

Inviting Assyrian help proves disastrous. Though Judah is not occupied by the Assyrians at this point, and though Assyrian advances against the alliance of Damascus and Samaria remove the northern threat, Judah has to pay tribute, and the spiritual blight from the Assyrian connection is devastating.

LORD. See note on 16:2. did not help him. Tiglath-pileser's intervention gives temporary relief to Judah from the threats of Syria and Israel (2 Kin. 16:7–9), but Judah becomes subservient to Assyria.
The blows that come upon Ahaz in God's providence do not induce in him a spirit of repentance but rather one of intensified spiritual hardness and obstinacy.
Ahaz visits Damascus (2 Kin. 16:10–16), but it is baffling why he chooses to worship the gods of a people who have been conquered by the Assyrians.
Ahaz's changes in the temple are discussed further in 2 Kin. 16:17–18.
See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Literary Features.
A note of dishonor. See note on 21:19.

The reign of Hezekiah (c. 727–c. 696 B.C.; cf. 2 Kin. 18:1, 2; 21:1 notes; Is. 36:1 note) begins a new era in the history of Israel and Judah. The northern kingdom has been destroyed by the Assyrians, and only Judah remains. Hezekiah is portrayed as bringing together representatives from both kingdoms so as to form a single, reunited kingdom with one king and one temple in Jerusalem. 29:1 Hezekiah. The Chronicler devotes more attention to Hezekiah than to any other king except David and Solomon. He uses material from 2 Kin. 18–20, but he supplements it extensively with other details, including an lengthy account of Hez­ekiah's temple reforms and Passover celebration (29:3–31:1). Hezekiah's reign appears as a return to the glory of Solomon's kingdom. In particular, Hezekiah's Passover reunites the separated kingdoms under a Davidic king. This anticipates the future that the Chronicler believes awaits the restored people in postexilic Israel.

The Chronicler's assessment of Hezekiah is totally positive, and he passes quickly over Hezekiah's failings as not relevant to the lessons from history he is trying to teach. Although David is mentioned here, the Chronicler repeatedly compares Hezekiah to Solomon.

Hezekiah ruled as junior partner with his father Ahaz for fourteen years from 729 B.C. As soon as he becomes sole ruler in 715 B.C., Hezekiah reverses the actions of his father, Ahaz (28:25 note), and restores the gold ornamentation stripped from the temple doors (2 Kin. 16:8, 9).

Chronicles typically gives attention to matters concerning the priests and Levites (1 Chr. 6:1 note). 29:4–11 Hezekiah's speech stands in contrast with Abijah's earlier assessments (13:6–12 notes). Judah is no longer different from Israel; both have forsaken God. Judah must repent as well.
Two key terms in the Chronicler's vocabulary, for which see notes on 1 Chr. 2:7 and 1 Chr. 28:9, respectively.
As Ahaz did (28:24).
Hezekiah asserts that Judah and Jerusalem are under the curse of God for their neglect of the temple.

During the reign of Ahaz, many from Judah were taken into exile by the Syrians (28:5–8) and Edomites (28:17). These events foreshadowed the Babylonian captivity to come (36:15–23), making the reign of Hezekiah a persuasive example for restoration after exile.

The anger of God turns Hez­ekiah toward Him in repentance, not away from Him in fear. make a covenant. Hezekiah proposes that the people reaffirm their commitment to the Sinai covenant. See note on 15:12.

The Chronicler mentions representatives of the three divisions of the tribe of Levi (v. 12) and the three families of singers (vv. 13, 14). Hezekiah's reforms are widely supported by the Levites and in accordance with the order established under David and Solomon (1 Chr. 6:1 note).
A prominent leader of the Kohathites (Num. 3:30).
The historian offers these details to demonstrate that Hezekiah's renovation is in strict accordance with Mosaic legislation.
Two days after the regular date of the Passover.
Hezekiah's dedication of the temple is reported in three parts: sacrifices brought by the leaders (vv. 20–24), arrangement of music (vv. 25–30), and sacrifices brought by the people (vv. 31–36).
Sacrifices are made on behalf of the royal family, the priests and Levites, and the people. All three groups are involved in the apostasy under Ahaz (2 Kin. 16).

In connection with the reunited kingdom (chs. 29–36), the expression "all Israel" (30:1; 31:1; 35:3) refers to both Judah and the refugees from the northern tribes (1 Chr. 11:1 note; 2 Chr. 10:1 note). Hezekiah orders sacrifices to be offered not for Judah only (v. 21) but for all the descendants of Israel. This desire to unite is clearly expressed in his arrangements for the Passover (30:1–6).
See note on 1 Chr. 15:16.
After the sacrifices are offered on behalf of the community as a whole, individuals are invited to bring personal offerings.
These sacrifices are fewer in number but still a reminder of what Solomon offered when the temple was dedicated (7:4–6).
The restoration of the temple takes less than three weeks (vv. 3, 17), evidence that God is working in the people.

Kings emphasizes the Passover under Josiah (2 Kin. 23:21–23) without discussing the celebration arranged by Hezekiah. The Chronicler exalts this celebration that reunites the northern and southern tribes in temple worship. Such reunion is recorded because of its striking relevance for those working for the restoration of Israel in the time after the return of the exiles from Babylon.

Hezekiah follows the good example of David (1 Chr. 13:1). the second month. Normally, the Passover and the feast of Unleavened Bread are observed in the first month (Ex. 12:2, 6; Deut. 16:1–8; see 2 Chr. 35:1). However, exceptions are made for travelers or those who are unclean during the designated time of celebration (Num. 9:9–13). Hezekiah applies the exception generously to the entire nation (v. 3).
From the southern to the northern extremities of the land, including the territory of the former northern kingdom of Israel.

Hezekiah sends the same letter to both Israel and Judah (v. 6), addressing them as "Israel," the covenant community. His letter contrasts with Abijah's speech to the northern kingdom (13:4–12). By Hezekiah's day, Judah and Israel are both in need of repentance and renewal. 30:6 return to the LORD. See note on 7:14. the remnant of you who have escaped. Ezra.note: The book of Ezra deals with two sets of events, separated by more than half a century. In chs. 1–6, the focus is on the twenty-three years from the edict of Cyrus to the completion of the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem (538–515 B.C.), though two later incidents are mentioned in 4:6 and 4:7–23. The account is in two main sections: the return of the exiles (chs. 1; 2) and the rebuilding of the temple (chs. 3–6). 1:1–4 By beginning with the decree of Cyrus, Ezra picks up the history of redemption where Chronicles leaves off. Verses 1–3 repeat, with minor differences, the closing words of 2 Chronicles. 1:1 first year. Beginning in 559 B.C., Cyrus ruled Anshan, a territory to the north of the Persian Gulf. He extended his rule over Medo-Persia around 550 B.C.., and, after conquering lands as far as Lydia in the west of Asia Minor, in October 539 his armies entered Babylon. The reference here is to 538 B.C. The spring of that year marked the start of the first year of his reign over his enlarged empire.

Jewish advisors may have helped to write the decree. 1:2 The LORD, the God of heaven. A title identifying the Lord as the supreme authority and power, whose rule from on high was not constrained by any earthly boundary (5:12; 6:9, 10; 7:12, 21, 23; Neh. 1:4, 5; 2:4, 20; Dan. 2:18, 19, 37, 44; Jon. 1:9). "The God of heaven" was a divine title used by the Jews particularly in dealings with foreigners. has given me \... has charged me. Cyrus's testimony to the sovereignty of God is probably a diplomatic formality for him, since the famous Cylinder of Cyrus says similar things about other gods (1:3 note). a house at Jerusalem. This "house" refers to the temple but in the end will include the city and the people of God. The rebuilding of the house of God is a dominant theme in Ezra and Nehemiah (see Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Without the temple and its associated sacrifices, the spiritual needs of the community cannot be properly met.

Cyrus's policy of religious toleration and support for the Jerusalem temple was similar to his treatment of other subject peoples. His purpose was to enlist the gods of these peoples in his own service (note the motivation of Darius in 6:10 and of Artaxerxes in 7:23). The Lord's controlling purpose, however, was to continue the progress of his provision of salvation. of all his people. The exiles return to Jerusalem with the articles for the temple according to the decree of Cyrus. The Lord keeps His promise that after chastening His people for breaking the covenant, He would bring them back to the Promised Land (Deut. 30:1–5). Those who return are the legitimate successors of the pre-exilic community, and God is continuing to work for and through them.

This list of exiles who return may not appear theologically important, but the repetition of the same list, with some variations, in Neh. 7 suggests otherwise. First, the Lord knows His people personally. The covenant relation between the Lord and His people is a bond of intimate friendship. Second, common people are vital to the accomplishing of God's redemptive plan (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Not only the religious and political leaders but also the common people are important in rebuilding the house of God. In fact, "the rest of the people" contribute more to the rebuilding than do "the heads of the fathers' houses" and the governor (Neh. 7:70–72). Third, the enumeration resembles that found in Numbers (1; 26) and Joshua (18; 19). As the Lord formed the covenant community after the exodus from Egypt, so He re-creates it after the return from Babylon. However, for the moment they remain "the people of the province" (v. 1), a subdivision of the vast Persian Empire. They have returned home, but they are still without political freedom.

His name means "offspring of Babylon," a reference to his birth in exile. He is a descendant of David, the son of Shealtiel (3:2) and a grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chr. 3:17). The genealogy of Jesus is traced through him (Matt. 1:12, 13; Luke 3:27). He is probably recognized by the Persians as the civil leader of the restored community. He is responsible for laying the temple's foundation (3:8–10). Jeshua. As high priest at the time of the restoration (Hag. 1:1; Zech. 3:1), Jeshua, a variant spelling of Joshua, is the spiritual leader of the community. His grandfather Seraiah, high priest when Jerusalem fell to the Babylonians in 586 B.C., was executed at Rib­lah along with other notable citizens (2 Kin. 25:18–21; Jer. 52:24–27). However, Seraiah's son Jehozadak was spared and taken to Babylon (1 Chr. 6:15), and now Jehozadak's son has returned to Jerusalem. Nehemiah. The laity are mentioned ahead of the clergy in keeping with the emphasis in Ezra and Nehemiah on the significance of the common people in rebuilding the kingdom (2:1–70 note). The twelve leaders of the first return (see Neh. 7:7; only eleven are named here, as Nahamani is omitted) collectively represent the twelve tribes that make up the real Israel (see 6:17; 8:24, 35).

The next groups are officially associated with the temple service: priests (vv. 36–39), Levites (v. 40), singers (v. 41), gatekeepers (v. 42), temple servants (vv. 43–54), and Solomon's servants (vv. 55–57).
