This final verse closes the section by echoing v. 1, in which they "came" and "returned"; in v. 70 they "lived in their towns." The Lord has returned the people of promise to their ancestral homes in the Land of Promise.

The people rebuild the altar, resume the sacrifices (3:1–6), and then rebuild the temple itself (3:7–6:22). Spurred on by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah (5:1–2) and blessed by God (5:5), they succeed in spite of opposition from the peoples around them (ch. 4) and from the governor of "the province Beyond the River" (5:3–6:12). 3:1–6 The exiles' merely returning to Judah is insufficient. The worship of the Lord has to be resumed even though there is time only to build an altar at the site of the former temple. 3:1 the seventh month. Tishri (September–October), the month of the Feast of Booths (Lev. 23:33–44). The desire to celebrate this feast (3:4) no doubt provided the stimulus needed to rebuild the altar. The year is not stated. The decree permitting the Jews to return was issued in Cyrus's first year, March 538–February 537 B.C., possibly in the summer (see 6:1, 2 note). After that, time was needed to organize the return, for the actual journey, and for an initial period of resettlement. In what follows the date 536 B.C. is assumed, but a case can be made for a year earlier or later. as one man. The decision to reinstitute the worship of the Lord in proper form is unanimous.

The only place where Jeshua is mentioned first, as is appropriate for the priestly task of erecting the altar. Here and in v. 8, Sheshbazzar may have delegated Zerubbabel to represent him because of his belonging to the house of David (see 2:2; 5:14–16). It had been prophesied that one of David's offspring would be involved in building the temple (2 Sam. 7:12, 13). burnt offerings. Burnt offerings were the primary offerings (Lev. 1), but others are also in view (v. 5). The burnt offering was the continuing basis on which a sinful people could live in the presence of a holy God (Ex. 29:42), looking forward as it did to the sacrifice of Christ as the final sacrifice that brings sinners into the presence of God (Heb. 10:19–20). as it is written. The written Word is a powerful tool used by God to accomplish His redemptive plan.

They have the courage to build the altar and lay the foundation of the temple. But their resolve will soon be tested (4:4, 5), and the work will stop (4:24). the peoples of the lands. While some restrict this phrase to Judeans who never suffered exile (see 2 Kin. 25:12), it is more probably a reference to surrounding nations, including those groups settled by the Assyrians in the territory of the former kingdom of Israel to the north (see 2 Kin. 17:24).

Not only is the Feast of Booths celebrated from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the month, but the entire sacrificial system is set in motion because the sacrifices are a part of maintaining the covenant relationship (Heb. 9:22). So important are the sacrifices that they are started before the temple itself is finished.

The workers are supervised by the Levites (v. 8), who are under the direction of the leading families in the community (v. 9). 3:7 Steps are immediately taken to secure the craftsmen and materials to begin rebuilding the temple. The language of v. 7 recalls the materials assembled for Solomon's temple (1 Chr. 22:2–4; 2 Chr. 2:8–16).

Ziv (or Iyar, April–May), the same time of year that Solomon began building the original temple (2 Chr. 3:2). Seven months have elapsed from 3:1 in procuring supplies. The year is probably 535 B.C. to supervise the work of the house of the LORD. This phrasing is virtually identical to the language used about Solomon's temple (1 Chr. 23:4).

The focus of the narrative is the response of the people rather than the mechanics of construction. If the return of the temple articles has encouraged the spirits of the people (1:9–11 note), much more does the laying of the foundation confirm their faith in God, who has promised restoration after exile (Deut. 30:1–5). Their expression of praise echoes exactly the dedication of Solomon's temple (2 Chr. 5:13).

The tears of the older members of the community are not tears of joy but tears of disappointment because of the contrast between this small beginning (see Zech. 4:10) and the splendor of Solomon's temple. Similar disappointment will later call for rebuke (Hag. 2:1–5), but for the moment the joy of the Lord is the strength of many.

News of what is happening in Jerusalem has spread quickly and attracted hostile attention. Work on the temple is delayed for more than a decade. The prophet Haggai also sheds light on events in this period, but he focuses on the reluctance of the people to continue rebuilding the temple in difficult economic circumstances. Ezra shows that their disinclination to proceed is also significantly influenced by external opposition. Indeed, in later years similar antagonism hampers attempts to refortify Jerusalem (vv. 6–23). Consequently, from here through to the end of Nehemiah the record is one of malice, harassment, and hostility. Whenever the cause of God moves forward, it encounters opposition. 4:1 the adversaries. Though these people come with outward expressions of good intentions, they are referred to as "adversaries," since they are real­ly intent on undermining the work of restoration. Political factors play a part in this conflict. Only the returnees have authorization from Cyrus to undertake construction (1:2–4), and the leaders in Judah may be reluctant to accept the assistance of unauthorized persons lest the Judahites get into trouble with the empire. Ultimately, however, the trouble is religious. The adversaries include people from various places who were transplanted into Samaria, the area north of Judah, after the destruction of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 B.C. (4:9, 10 note). They worship many gods and incorporate worship of the Lord into their polytheism (2 Kin. 17:24–41). The animosity between the Jews and the Samaritans who descend from these adversaries continues into the NT era (see John 4:1–42).

The incident that led to this is described in 2 Kin. 17:24–28, but the polytheism practiced by the peoples in Samaria does not warrant them adding "as you do" (cf. 2 Kin. 17:29–41). Esarhaddon. Assyrian policy involved substantial resettlement of subject peoples. In addition to the influx after the fall of Samaria (see 3:3) and at a later period (see v. 10), there were also settlements in the north under Esarhaddon (681–669 B.C.).

The discrimination is not racial or political but religious. From the early days of living in the Promised Land (Judg. 3:6) and throughout their history (2 Kin. 17:7–17), the Israelites made alliances with foreigners that led them into idolatry and ultimately to exile from the land (2 Kin. 17:18–23). The failure of the returnees to separate themselves from the indigenous population became a problem before long (Ezra 9; 10). The same principle of religious separation is still operative under the new covenant (2 Cor. 6:14–7:1).

The "adversaries" of v. 1 (see 3:3). discouraged \... made them afraid. The word "discouraged" is lit. "made hands limp" (see Neh. 6:9). These verbs are participles, indicating that this behavior extends over a considerable period of time.
Perhaps these are Persian officials. The obstructive efforts of the adversaries cause a delay in the work from the time of Cyrus (550–530 B.C..) until the second year of Darius (522–486 B.C..).

This material is a separate section, describing later opposition to the Jews during the reigns of Xerxes (486–465 B.C..) and Artaxerxes I (465–424 B.C..). The narrative justifies calling the neighboring peoples in v. 1 "adversaries." Additionally, it shows that the opposition is not a brief and passing problem but a foretaste of prolonged opposition — to the people of God in rebuilding God's ''house" (the temple) and to the city and the nation in general. 4:6 Ahasuerus. Ahasuerus (Xerxes) succeeded Darius and was king of Persia from 486 to 465 B.C. they wrote an accusation. The subject of the verb is not specified, but the context shows that the troublemakers are a later generation of the "adversaries" of v. 1. Nothing is said about the nature of the accusation.

Artaxerxes I, successor to Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and king of Persia from 465 to 424 B.C.. wrote to Artaxerxes. There is no information about the content of this letter, but considering the context, it is doubtless an effort to prevent rebuilding the wall. Aramaic. The language of international diplomacy in the ancient Near East.

This section is written not in Hebrew but in Aramaic, the language of the original documents cited in this section. The correspondence expresses the concern of various Gentile officials about the progress of the Jews' work. 4:8 scribe. Scribes are high officials who write official correspondence and keep archival records for the provincial government (7:6 note).
The opposition does not come from a few but is broadly based.

Probably Ashurbanipal, the last successful king of Assyria (668–627 B.C..), who transplanted various peoples into Samaria. This practice began after the fall of Samaria in 722 B.C., probably under Sargon II (2 Kin. 17:24). Beyond the River. An extensive area west of the Euphrates, including Aram, Phoenicia, and Palestine.

This term came into common use after the exile because the majority of the returnees were from the tribe of Judah. from you. "From you" (singular) refers to Artaxer­xes and may point to the group who returned with Ezra. finishing the walls. See note on 4:6–23. The reference is to the walls and foundations of the city, not the temple.
The complainants cloak their motives by expressing concern for the revenues of the Persian Empire. They predict that if Jerusalem is walled, it will again rebel and cease paying taxes.
Lit. "we have salted with the salt of the palace." Probably a way of referring to the covenantal obligation of a vassal to his overlord (see Lev. 2:13; Num. 18:19; 2 Chr. 13:5).
The various Aramaic documents used in writing this section of Ezra would be kept in a similar archive. a rebellious city \... was laid waste. See 2 Kin. 18:7; 24:1.

Obviously an exaggeration, these words are intended to sway Artaxer­xes. This letter is written at a time when there is great unrest in the western provinces of the empire. The implied threat is probably that rebellion in Jerusalem will tip the balance of power in favor of those who oppose Persia.
The king is not given a summary of the letter; it is read to him word for word, probably translated from Aramaic into Persian.

Israel received tribute from other nations under David and Solomon. Now, even though they have returned to the Land of Promise, God's people must submit to the rule of the ungodly (9:9 and note). The initial phase of the restoration is less than what the prophets expected (e.g., Isa. 60:1–3; Mic. 4:1–5), leaving the full restoration of God's people in the hands of the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

It is probable that the destruction of these newly built walls ("by force and power," v. 23) is the subject of the report that Nehemiah receives in Neh. 1:3. until a decree is made by me. The complainants do not get all they want. The possibility of Jerusalem's walls being rebuilt is not entirely ruled out, but it is dependent on future imperial policy. Such a decree to rebuild the walls is made by Artaxerxes when he gives permission to Nehemiah to return and perform the work (Neh. 2:1–9).

After the section dealing with opposition to the rebuilding of the wall (vv. 6–23), the author returns to the topic of vv. 1–5, rebuilding the temple. The author uses a technique called "repetitive resumption," in which the substance of vv. 4, 5 is repeated, not to add new information but to mark vv. 6–23 as a digression. the second year \... of Darius. April 520 B.C.

In the same year referred to in 4:24, the second year of Darius, Haggai begins to prophesy in August (Hag. 1:1). Three weeks later, work resumes at the temple site, and Zechariah's ministry commences two months after Haggai's (Zech. 1:1). Work on the temple proceeds not because of a decree from Darius but because of the preaching of God's prophets and the obedient response of God's people (Hag. 1:14, 15). 5:1 over them. Both the people (Deut. 28:10) and the prophets (Jer. 15:16) belong to God.

The work that resumed under God's direction is soon put to the test and threatened with a prohibition order by the Persian authorities (vv. 3, 4). However, in God's providence, the people are allowed to continue until a directive is received from the emperor. The letter sent to him (5:6–17), the record of Cyrus's decree (6:1–5), and Darius's permission to proceed (6:6–12) are all duly recorded. There is, however, the additional and unexpected benefit of state provision for the rebuilding work and for future sacrifices. 5:3, 4 As soon as the work on the temple resumes, the Persian officials in control of the area investigate whether the activity has been duly authorized. Large-scale construction work might be connected with the considerable political unrest throughout the empire in the early years of Darius's reign, so the officials want to make sure the Jews are not intent on rebellion. These officials are not as hostile as those at a later date (4:7–9) and are presented as acting honorably throughout the incident.

His watchful and preserving oversight. This time God chooses to intervene, and the officials permit the work to continue until they hear from Darius. Here, as throughout Ezra and Nehemiah, God becomes involved through the actions of people (see 1:1 note).
When Ezra draws up this account of earlier events, he makes use of his official position in the Persian administration to access the state archives to obtain the material.

Judea is a sub-province in the Persian Empire, not an independent political state. prospers in their hands. It prospers due to the care of God (v. 5), the preaching of the prophets (vv. 1, 2), and the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua (v. 2).
The question underscores Judah's lack of independence.

Tattenai's report to the king is comprehensive and includes the reply of the Jewish leaders to the questions of the Persian officials (vv. 3, 4). 5:11 God of heaven and earth. A fuller form of the more frequent title "God of heaven" (1:2 note). a great king of Israel. Solomon built the original temple in the years 966–959 B.C.. (1 Kin. 6:1, 38).

God used Nebuchadnezzar to punish Israel for breaking the covenant. Chaldean. The Chaldeans lived in southern Mesopotamia and established the Neo-Babylonian Empire by overthrowing the Assyrians in 612 B.C.. The new empire continued until it was overthrown by the Persians in 539.
Here is the answer, on the human level, to the question posed in 5:3.

See note on 1:8. As the Persian appointee, his role is emphasized in dealing with another Persian official, even though the work has in fact been delegated to Zerubbabel (see Hag. 1:12–14; Zech. 4:9).
The work is not done continuously but experiences a break of about seventeen years (4:24 note). The Jewish elders view the work as suspended, not abandoned.

This is the second reference to an archival search, underscoring the theme of the power of written documents (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). The search mentioned earlier (4:15) stopped the building of the wall. This second search (recorded later, but occurring earlier) will result in the completion of the temple.

A search of the royal archives unearths an official copy of Cyrus's decree, which Darius then endorses. God overrules the interference of the officials so that the work proceeds with state protection and support. 6:1, 2 Darius responds to Tattenai's request. The search begins in the treasury at Babylon, but the decree is found in Achmetha (Ecbatana), almost three hundred miles (480 km) northeast of Bab­ylon, and probably the city from which Cyrus issued the decree when he stayed there in the summer of 538 B.C.

This copy of the decree differs somewhat from that in 1:2–4; e.g., God's name ("LORD") is not used. The copy in 1:2–4 is what the heralds proclaimed to the Jews, while this copy is the minutes kept as an official record. 6:3 Its height shall be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits. These dimensions are larger than those of Solomon's temple (1 Kin. 6:2). They may give the maximum size allowed rather than the size planned.
Probably the layer of timber provides a measure of shock-proofing against earthquakes (see 1 Kin. 6:36; 7:12). The cost is to be met from state funds, something not mentioned in 1:2–4.
Having found Cyrus's decree, Darius issues a second decree reinforcing it. In God's providence, the opposition of Tattenai and his associates turns out for the good of the project (see Gen. 50:20).
Unlikely to be a reference to a member of the Persian administration; most probably Zerubbabel is in view.
As a result of the opposition, provision is also made for continuing the temple services.
See note on 1:3.

This decree thwarts those opposing the temple rebuilding effort, and it features the customary ancient Near Eastern curses on anyone who changes an official document (see Rev. 22:18, 19). As a result of the opposition they have faced, God's people are granted irrevocable support to rebuild the temple. impaled on it. Execution by impalement was a common Persian form of capital punishment.
Darius orders that his decree be carried out "with all diligence" (6:12), i.e., with care and thoroughness, and the Persian officials are careful to comply (see the diligence of the builders, 5:8).

God has worked through the leadership of the community (see 5:5). Note that there is no mention of Zerubbabel. As with his predecessor Sheshbazzar, we are never told what becomes of him. the prophesying of Haggai \... and Zechariah. The preaching of the prophets moves the people to start the work again (5:1, 2) and to complete it. God \... Cyrus. The same word is used for the command of God and the Persian kings' decree, a singular form treating the edicts of the various kings as essentially one in purpose — that of God. God's sovereign decree does not negate human responsibility but rather establishes it. The reference to Artaxerxes, who reigned in the next century, may seem out of place, since the temple proper was completed before he became king. However, the temple is not explicitly mentioned in the Aramaic text of v. 14, so the reference could be a preview to the finishing of the rebuilding of the entire "house of God," including the community and the wall that were rebuilt under the authority of Artaxerxes (7:11–26; Neh. 2:1, 8).

Use of the name of the month may reflect Ezra's source (see Neh. 1:1). The date corresponds to March 12, 515 B.C.., nearly four-and-a-half years after the work began in earnest (Hag. 1:15), twenty years after the restoration work was first started (3:8), and almost exactly seventy years after the Solomonic temple was destroyed in 586.

This designation focuses on their status as the covenant people of God (see v. 21). the dedication of this house of God. With the solemn assignment of the completed temple for the worship of the Lord, a major milestone has been reached. The parenthetical section of 4:6–23 has already given a preview of trouble to come. The dedication of the wall (Neh. 12:27) and the final reforms (Neh. 13) will complete the restoration of the Jewish community.

The number of offerings is small in comparison to those of Solomon (1 Kin. 8:62, 63), but the reference to "12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel" points to the ideal unity of the community (see 2:2; 1 Kin. 18:31). Reference to a sin offering indicates their awareness of sin and of their need for faith in God, who keeps His covenant of love (Deut. 7:9).

The written text prescribes the sacred duties, and the chastened and restored community is careful to carry out all covenantal obligations. Contrary to many reconstructions of these events, this verse makes clear that the restored community had the Book of Moses in its possession long before the arrival of Ezra. The first Aramaic section of Ezra ends with this verse.
The first celebration of the Passover since the destruction of the temple seventy years earlier. The date of this Passover is April 21, 515 B.C.., a month after the completion of the temple (v. 15).

While this may include Gentiles (see Num. 9:14), it is more likely that the writer is referring to people of Judah (and possibly of the former northern kingdom) who were never deported and have remained in the land since the rest of the population went into exile. In large measure, they have assimilated to pagan practices, but if they repent of this and separate (a key issue for the holy people; see Introduction: Theology of Ezra), then are incorporated into the covenant community and allowed to participate in its worship. to worship the LORD. Lit. "to seek the LORD." They have renounced pagan practices and now seek to ascertain God's will so that they might order the whole of their lives by it. "To seek God" is virtually a technical term for a true worshiper and diligent follower of the Lord.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread lasted throughout the week after the Passover (Lev. 23:6–8). The restored people in the rebuilt temple are once more enjoying fellowship with their God. Their joy is the Lord's gift to them through His control of the actions of pagan kings, both Cyrus (1:1) and here Darius. the king of Assyria. The reference is to Darius. The Assyrian Empire ceased to exist a century earlier, and by this time its former territory is under Persian control. Mention of Assyria probably indicates that the judgment on Israel, begun through that regime, is now reversed.

Only in these closing chapters are we introduced to Ezra, after whom the book is named. We are also permitted to read parts of his personal memoirs. These certainly include 7:27–9:15, where the "I" and "me" refer to Ezra. Since the words "such a thing" in 7:27 link back to his letter of commission in 7:12–26 this letter was likely preserved among Ezra's personal documents as well. The remaining material in these chapters was probably added by whoever drew the source material together into the book we now have. 7:1–10 These verses are an introductory summary of Ezra's return to Jerusalem, about which greater detail is provided later in the chapter. Here the focus is on Ezra's credentials and the secret of his competence as a leader. 7:1 Now after this. Nearly sixty years have passed between the events at the end of ch. 6 and those at the beginning of ch. 7. The only information we have on this period from Ezra and Nehemiah concerns opposition in the days of Ahasuerus (4:6 note) — the events in the book of Esther also occur during this period (Esth. 1:1). Artaxerxes. Artaxerxes I, king of Persia from 465 to 424 B.C.. Some scholars have understood the reference to be to a later Artaxerxes, thus setting Ezra's ministry many years subsequent to that of Nehemiah, but such scenarios are at variance with the scriptural account. Ezra. The lengthy introduction of Ezra (vv. 1–10) signals his importance for what follows. The first information given about Ezra is his ancestry. The genealogy spanning seventeen generations is full but not complete (six more names may be added on the basis of 1 Chr. 6:3–15); the phrase "son of" is often used to mean "descendant." Ezra's line goes back to Aaron, establishing his priestly authority for his subsequent actions. Seraiah was high priest when Jerusalem fell (see 2:2), and so he is not Ezra's immediate father but a more remote ancestor. Hilkiah was the high priest under Josiah (2 Kin. 22:4).

Not all the pious exiles returned with Sheshbazzar in 538 B.C.. Ezra's family did not. Probably, Ezra was not yet born at the time of the first return. He grew up in Babylon, where most of the exiles lived. a scribe skilled. In the OT, scribes were often government officials who composed official documents (4:8 note; 2 Sam. 8:17; 1 Kin. 4:3), administered temple treasuries (2 Kin. 12:10, 11; 22:3, 4, 9; Neh. 13:13), served as court emissaries (2 Kin. 18:18–37), and provided literary functions such as taking dictation (Jer. 36:32). Ezra is a high-ranking official in the Persian administration (v. 25), but his most important qualification is as a teacher of God's law (vv. 10, 11, 14; Neh. 8:1–9). that the LORD \... had given. The "Law of Moses" is divine in origin (see 2 Tim. 3:16). The reference here is to the first five books of the Bible. the king granted him all that he asked. The actions of responsible human beings are traced back to the sovereign action of God: Ezra takes the initiative and asks. The content of his petition is not specified but presumably corresponds to what he was granted in his letter of commission (vv. 12–26). Artaxerxes grants his request because God providentially gives success to Ezra's endeavor.
Ezra is not alone but is leading a second group of returning exiles. the seventh year. 458 B.C..

The trip takes place in the spring, when there is ample water along the way. It takes nearly four months, from April 21 to August 4, and covers about 850 miles (1370 km), proceeding north along the banks of the Euphrates before turning south.
Success is attributed to God's providence. This or a similar expression occurs frequently in Ezra and Nehemiah (see 7:6, 28; 8:18, 22, 31; Neh. 2:8, 18).

Ezra's goal in going to Jerusalem is now given. As a diligent hearer and doer of the Word (James 1:22), Ezra's goal is to teach others to do the same. to study \... to do \... to teach. Lit., "to seek." Only here is the Hb. verb "to study" (lit. to seek") used with "the Law" as its object. Ezra seeks to know more about God and His will (see 6:21 note) through studying His Word. Ezra is a model reformer in that he first follows God's precepts himself (see Ps. 119:100) and then, having studied and put into practice the law, Ezra is equipped to teach others (see Ps. 51:13).

A copy of a letter from King Artaxerxes records his commission of Ezra to return to Jerusalem to inquire about the spiritual state of the people (v. 14), to provide supplies for the temple (vv. 15–24), and to arrange for the administration of justice (vv. 25, 26). Included is a specific directive to local Persian officials to provide Ezra with all that is necessary (vv. 21–23). 7:11 letter. The letter (vv. 12–26), written in Aramaic (4:7 note), gives Ezra the authority to carry out the reforms recorded in the following chapters. The letter may have been written by Ezra and then signed by Artaxerxes, or Artaxerxes may have had Jewish advisors help compose the letter, as some of the details seem to indicate.

A title used by Persian monarchs to indicate their supremacy over all subject kings. That God is the true King of kings is implicit in the book of Ezra (1:1 note) and explicit elsewhere in Scripture (Rev. 17:14; 19:16). scribe. See note on v. 6.

This phrase describes them in their religious status as the covenant community and may well indicate Jewish input to the drafting of the letter. As in the original decree of Cyrus in 1:3, the permission to return extends to all who are willing.

This refers to the inner cabinet who had special access to the king (see Esth. 1:14), a feature of Persian administration documented by Greek historians. to make inquiries. Whereas Cyrus commissioned the first returnees "to build" a temple, Artaxerxes commissions Ezra to inquire about the spiritual condition of the people. His efforts will help rebuild the community of God's people, God's "house" (Num. 12:7). It may be that the verb is a technical term, implying more than inquiry and having the sense "to examine" or "to superintend."
Artaxerxes' knowledge of the details of Israelite worship indicates that Ezra or Jewish advisors wrote the letter themselves or assisted in writing it (1:2–4 note).
Conformity to God's will is a major theme in the rest of the book.
The generosity of Artaxerxes is like that of Darius (6:9). The amounts involved are enormous, but the Persian Empire is very wealthy.

See note on 1:3. Egypt, with Greek assistance, rebelled against Persia in 460 B.C., and the unrest was not totally suppressed at the time Ezra traveled to Jerusalem. It suits Artaxerxes to strengthen a loyal community as a buffer state.
Exemption of temple personnel from taxation is not uncommon. Again, note the indications of Jewish input in the details of temple personnel.

Ezra's role is twofold: exercising governmental authority and teaching the law of God (7:6 note). all the people \... Beyond the River. The Jews who have returned to Judah and Jerusalem. Ezra is not given authority over other nationalities.

The two are not identical. The distinction between religious and civil law is more important for the Jews in exile under a foreign civil power than during the monarchy, when the state was of the same religion as the people. The second Aramaic section of Ezra ends with this verse. let judgment be strictly executed. Ezra himself is not given the authority to punish; the "officials and the elders" exercise it in 10:8.

Ezra reverts to Hebrew in his doxology. He expresses his joy at God's endorsement of the enterprise. 7:27 put such a thing \... into the heart of the king. The actions of Artaxerxes are traced to the sovereign action of God.

"Steadfast love" translates the Hb. word hesed, which refers to God's covenant loyalty. The same word occurs in 9:9. Artaxerxes's favor toward Ezra is due to God's covenant loyalty to His people. "To me" is the first reference to Ezra in the first person, evidence of Ezra as the source of these "memoirs" (Introduction: Author). to me. The first reference to Ezra in the first person, evidence of Ezra as the source of these "memoirs" (see Introduction: Author). the hand of the LORD. Ezra's awareness of God's providential control is a source of encouragement for the tasks that lie ahead (see v. 9).

Not all the exiles returned in response to the decree of Cyrus in 538 B.C.. A second but significantly smaller group returned with Ezra about eighty years after the first return. Many of these returnees in Ezra's day are related to those who have already gone back to Jerusalem. Allowing for the later contingent of Levites (vv. 15–20) and women and children, the second group numbers between four thousand and five thousand, about a tenth the size of the original group.

The narrative of Ezra's return relates four matters: finding Levites prepared to return to Jerusalem (vv. 15–20); spiritual preparations for the journey (vv. 21–23); practical arrangements for transporting the valuables (vv. 24–30); and the actual journey and arrival in Jerusalem (vv. 31–36). 8:15 the river that runs to Ahava. Probably a canal connected to the river Euphrates, but its exact location is unknown. none of the sons of Levi. Ezra wants more Levites for service in the temple (v. 17) and perhaps to help with the sacrifices mentioned in v. 35. He may also want Levites to be part of the caravan to the Promised Land — just like they were at the time of the exodus from Egypt and the first return from Babylon (1:2 note). The Levites also have responsibility for teaching the law, a task that needs to be carried out.
Ezra selects a group of influential men to persuade some Levites to return with him. Meshullam may be the same individual as in 10:15, 29.

The location is not certain, but it could be Ctesiphon on the river Tigris north of Babylon. Obviously there is a settlement of Levites there. However, both earlier (Deut. 12:5; Jer. 7:2, 3) and later, "the place" refers to a holy place, and it may be that Casiphia is the site of a sanctuary. There is a Jewish sanctuary at Elephantine, Egypt, at this time. Levites would be concentrated at such a sanctuary, explaining why Ezra sends the delegation to Casiphia. Iddo is probably the leader at the sanctuary, but that is not conclusively established.

Ezra does not weary of ascribing his success to God's providential control (7:9 note). Thirty-eight Le­vites are persuaded to return along with three key Levitical leaders and 220 temple servants ("Nethinim"). Just as the Lord stirred the spirits of Cyrus (1:1), the first returnees (1:5), and Artaxerxes (7:27), so His good hand moves these Levites to accept Ezra's call.
Fasting is an aspect of humbling oneself for the purpose of requesting something from God (2 Chr. 20:3). a safe journey. Safety from bandits, among other dangers, is in view (v. 31).

Ezra testifies to God's providential control not only before the saints but also before Artaxerxes. It seems inconsistent with this testimony to ask for a military escort. See note on Neh. 2:7–9 for a contrast between Ezra and Nehemiah on this point.
Not then and there with words but throughout the journey with actions (vv. 31, 32).
Twelve priests and twelve Levites, perhaps as representatives of all Israel (see v. 35). Ezra is not reluctant to delegate responsibilities to others.

The total contribution listed in v. 26 is enormous, such that critics have doubted the authenticity of the list. However, the Persian kings are known for their great wealth and generosity toward the religions of subject peoples. There are also wealthy Jewish families in Babylon at this time.
For the enormous amounts involved, cf. 7:22.

LORD. Holiness is an attribute of God (Lev. 19:2) and, by extension, of anyone or anything belonging to Him, especially priests (Lev. 21:6), Levites (Num. 3:11–13, where "consecrated" means "dedicated" to God), and temple articles (Ex. 30:22–29). Ezra's strict command arises from the spiritual threat that contact with the profane represents for the holy.

According to 7:9, Ezra began to gather fellow Jews and depart from Babylon on the first day. The difference is due to the delay (until April 19 458 B.C..) experienced in order to find the needed Levites. he delivered us. That is, God keeps them from being attacked or ambushed rather than rescuing them after they are waylaid. Again Ezra attributes his success to God's providential control. The fasting and prayer for a safe journey are answered with the arrival of people and possessions in Jerusalem (vv. 21, 32).
Cf. the similar rest of Nehemiah in Neh. 2:11 (see Josh. 3:2).
These temple officials may also be mentioned in Nehemiah (Neh. 3:4, 21; 11:16; 10:9, respectively).

Just as the provisions were made (7:17), so the sacrifices are offered. This is a picture of complete success. Again, the number "twelve" signifies completion (v. 24 note). The impersonal style of vv. 35, 36 probably indicates that these verses were inserted into the memoir by the compiler of the book.

So that there will be no misunderstanding, the officials in surrounding areas of the empire are informed of the royal warrant for what Ezra is about to do, A "satrap" is a ruler of a province of the empire; "governors" are high-ranking officials under a satrap.

Return to the Land of Promise is a means, not an end. The people are to aim at worshiping God and enjoying fellowship with Him. That requires adherence to God's covenant requirements. Ezra must direct the community as to how to deal with intermarriage with surrounding peoples. The books of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther reflect an acceptance of Persian overlordship and the need for a minority group to relate to the political authorities of their day. However, such cooperation with others cannot be at the expense of compromising their overriding loyalty to the Lord. The danger of interfaith marriages is assimilation to the surrounding culture and religion and the loss of their distinctive commitment to the Lord alone. 9:1–15 Four-and-a-half months after arriving in Jerusalem (see 10:9), Ezra is informed about the prevalence of marriages with women of surrounding nations (vv. 1, 2). This causes him great personal distress (vv. 3–5) as a result of which he engages in confession and prayer (vv. 6–15). 9:1 the officials approached me and said. Ezra has come to teach the law (7:10 note) and has not adopted a confrontational approach to any irregularities he detects in the life of the community. But now some of the leaders come to him to report certain sins. Probably these leaders are not from the party who returned with Ezra but from the earlier returnees. Possibly they are responding to Ezra's teaching, which has sensitized them to what is wrong in the land. have not separated themselves. The point is the difference of religion, not race, as the following verses indicate (vv. 10–12; 4:3 note). Marriage to a foreign woman who maintains the beliefs of her people brings polytheistic worship of pagan deities into the family circle and undermines the covenant commitment of future generations. the peoples of the lands. Of those listed, only the Ammonites, Moabites, and Egyptians are present in the days of Ezra. The others were in the land during the conquest under Joshua, and the mention of them could have brought to mind the original prohibitions against intermarriage (Ex. 34:10–16; Deut. 7:1–4). with their abominations. Instead of "with," it is preferable to retain "according to" or "like" in the translation. The idolatrous practices of the nations in Ezra's day are compared to those encountered among the heathen when Israel first entered the land.

The problem is not intermarriage of different ethnic groups but the confusion of those set apart as holy by covenant with the Lord with those who are outside the covenant and therefore unclean (8:28 note; 9:11 note). "Holy race" or "holy seed" reminds the people that the Messiah will come from them. the officials. The word for "officials" here is the same as in v. 1. Not all the leaders are guilty of leading people to sin; some of them are leading the way to reform.

A typical way of expressing grief (2 Sam. 13:19). pulled hair from my head and beard. An unusual action. Some years later, Nehemiah encounters the same sin, but rather than pulling out his own hair, he pulls out the hair of the offenders (Neh. 13:25). sat appalled. Sitting inactively is a natural and accepted response to overwhelming tragedy (Job 2:13). "Appalled" denotes an intense inward reaction of numbing shock because the covenant people have begun to compromise their fidelity to the Lord. It was such behavior that led to the judgment of the exile.
There is a group that has not intermarried but fears the Lord and keeps His law (see Is. 66:2). the evening sacrifice. Mid-afternoon, a time of prayer as well as sacrifice (Ps. 141:2).

See 1 Kin. 8:54. Kneeling expresses humility before the majestic Lord (Ps. 95:6), and spreading the hands often accompanies petitions (Ps. 28:2). Ezra has gone to the temple, as 10:1 makes clear. For similar prayers of confession of national sin and intercession, see Neh. 1:4–11; 9:5–37; Dan. 9:3–19.

Previously, Ezra was ashamed to ask Artaxerxes for protection on the return trip (8:22). Now his shame is of a different kind, disgrace joined with the guilt that results from sin. our iniquities \... our guilt. Ezra is acutely aware of the people's sin and guilt before God. Note also the sudden shift from "my" to "our." Though Ezra is not guilty of marrying into paganism, he identifies himself with the people in their sin, as does the Suffering Servant of Isaiah (Is. 53:12; 2 Cor. 5:21).
There is a sense of corporate solidarity and mutual responsibility that spans the generations of the covenant community.

The status of the returnees as the recipients of God's favor is in jeopardy. The same word is repeated later in the verse ("brief \... a little") to emphasize how marginal and tenuous the situation is. favor has been shown by the LORD \... a remnant. Justice demands the absolute end of the people of God, but grace preserves a remnant. Through this remnant the Messiah will come, and redemption will be accomplished. secure hold. The word translated "secure hold" means a stake that holds a tent in position (Judg. 4:21) or a nail that holds up objects that are hung on it (Is. 22:23–25). The Lord has given Israel a place in His temple, like the peg of a tent, and has made Ezra someone who could be trusted with burdens. brighten our eyes. An idiom for increased vigor (Ps. 13:3).

Though restored to their land, the people of God are not politically independent like they were during the monarchy (4:19–23 note). God has not forsaken us. God's promise not to forsake the nation is, in its outer, typological aspect, conditional (10:5 note). If Israel forsakes God and the covenant by disregarding the law, she will forfeit the blessings and experience the curses (Deut. 28:20; 29:24, 25; 31:16, 17). Even so, God has promised never to finally desert Israel, through whom Christ comes. See Lev. 26:44, 45; Ps. 89:30–37; Is. 54:7; Rom. 11. the kings of Persia. Specifically Cyrus (550–530 B.C..), who issued the decree to return; Darius (522–486 B.C.), who confirmed the decree; and Artaxerxes (465–424 B.C..), who commissioned Ezra to teach the people. protection in Judea and Jerusalem. Does not refer to the wall built later by Nehemiah but instead is a figure for the protection afforded the returnees (note the figurative language in v. 8 and that the wall of Nehemiah is not built around all of Judah).
Forsaking the commandments means that covenant curses can fall upon the people at any time (v. 9 note).

Moses was the prophet who gave the command initially (Deut. 7:1–3). The words are not a quotation of a single text but a summary of the theology of separation taken from numerous texts, including Lev. 18:25; Deut. 4:5; 7:3; 18:9; 27:3; and 2 Kin. 21:16. Intermarriage with people outside the covenant introduces a relentless temptation to corrupt or abandon worship of the true and living God (see Deut. 7:3, 4; Judg. 14:1–4; 1 Kin. 11:1–4; 2 Cor. 6:14).
The restoration is on the basis of grace and the promise of the Abrahamic covenant (Deut. 4:25–31). So also was the initial entrance into the land (Deut. 9:5).

Ezra fears that the current covenant breach might result in ultimate judgment. Though judgment will later come upon the nation (Luke 20:9–19), even then there will be a remnant according to grace (Rom. 11:1–5).
Ezra's conclusion is that even now the people live only because of God's grace.

Ezra's prayer is heard by the crowd gathered at the temple. Their reaction parallels that of Ezra, incorporating grief (v. 1), confession (v. 2), and repentance (vv. 3–17). One man acts as the catalyst to induce a spiritual reaction and as a channel for articulating their response. 10:1 Ezra \... weeping. Other leaders set the pace for sin (9:2). Now Ezra sets the pace for repentance, not by exhorting the people to mourn but by mourning himself and pricking their consciences. The bitter weeping of a substantial section of the population shows that they appreciate the gravity of the situation.

Ezra's confession in 9:13, 14 becomes the confession of the people through one of their leaders, Shecaniah. If his father, Jehiel, is the same person listed among the sons of Elam in v. 26, Shecaniah is aware of the problem in his own family circle. there is hope. Shecaniah encourages Ezra that all is not lost. In contrast to Ezra's despair, he argues that there is still a way to recover from the existing situation.

Not an entirely new covenant but the renewal of the Mosaic covenant in terms of an oath (v. 5) to keep the stipulation regarding intermarriage (Deut. 7:3; see Jer. 34:8–22 for a similar covenant renewal). to put away. This is not the usual Hb. phrase for divorce and is used only here. The Hb. expression in v. 2 ("have married \... women") is not the usual phrase for marriage, and is used in the same way only in Neh. 13 in an analogous situation. The writer's choice of language seems to indicate that he does not regard the unions as legitimate marriages or the sending away as actual divorce. Alternatively, the language used may indicate that this is a special situation in which divorce is preferable to the more serious transgression of allowing the holy seed (9:2) to be debased by intermarriage, thereby imperiling the people's role as those through whom the Messiah will come. according to the Law. The law does not provide explicitly for this exact situation. The phrase may refer to sending a woman and her children away along with some provisions (Gen. 21:14) and certain legal rights (Deut. 21:10–14).

As the recognized leader of the community, Ezra is responsible for formulating and coordinating their response. He is assured of the backing of the people in taking steps to renew their engagement to the covenant.

Ezra responds to the encouragement of Shecaniah and puts his advice into practice. Ezra's action may not constitute a universal norm. He is dealing with a situation of defiance of the covenant, whereas Paul in 1 Cor. 7:12–14 is dealing with marriages entered into before conversion. made \... all Israel take an oath. The covenant is conditional, as the swearing of the oath by the Israelites and not by the Lord indicates (9:9 note; Jer. 34:8–22).

Located in the temple. Jehohanan is also called "Johanan" (Neh. 12:23); he is the grandson of Eliashab. neither eating bread nor drinking water. A total fast was rare (Deut. 9:18). The fast indicates that Ezra does not think the exiles are immune to the covenant punishments on the basis of an oath alone. the faithlessness of the exiles. "Faithlessness," see 9:1, 4. "The exiles" (golah) refers to those who have returned from exile.

Ezra was given authority to act in this way by the king (7:26), but it is not said that he issued this proclamation, which would be publicly delivered by a herald. Ezra's preferred mode of operation (see vv. 1, 2) is to wait for others to respond to the lead he has given them by his teaching and example. Verse 8 suggests that the officials and elders take the initiative on this occasion.

Owing to the reduced territory of Judah, three days are sufficient for any who want to travel to Jerusalem. forfeited \... banned. Lit. "caused to be separate" (see 9:1). Failure to comply will result in the loss of property and excommunication (7:26). If the call for separation from entanglement with those outside the community (see Introduction: Theology) goes unheeded, there will be forcible expulsion from the community.

See note on 1:5. the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month. December 19, 457 B.C., during the rainy season. At this time, Jerusalem is colder than most of the countryside around it, and rainfall in the region is more concentrated than in temperate climates. all the people. The people as a whole respond to the proclamation. trembling because of this matter. Ezra's spiritual distress has spread throughout the populace (v. 1 note), though physical conditions play a part as well.

Lit. "give thanks and praise to." When a person confesses sin and trusts in God for mercy, praise is given to God. In Ps. 103, the psalmist "blesses" God by confessing who God is and what He has done. do his will. Confession must lead to repentance (v. 6 note). Separate yourselves. See note on 9:11 (see Num. 16:21; 2 Cor. 6:14).
Not only do all the men assemble and express their distress (v. 9), but they also agree with Ezra as to their sin and guilt.
Not an attempt to escape the responsibility to repent but an expression of genuine concern that the repentance be carried out well.
Local knowledge should lead to better-informed judgments as well as more rigorous supervision of the verdict.
They probably oppose the delay, though they oppose the sending away of the foreign women. Meshullam may be among those who errs in this matter (v. 29), though the name is common in this period.

It takes from "the first day of the tenth month" (December 29, 458 B.C.) until "the first day of the first month" (March 27, 457 B.C.). The problem is so widespread that the commission takes three months, not a single day (v. 13), to scrutinize all the cases.

Ezra carefully lists the members of the high priest's family (v. 18) first, then other priests (vv. 20–22), then the Levites (v. 23), and finally the rest of the community (vv. 25–43). There is no cover-up of the misconduct of the influential. From this list of those guilty of intermarriage, it is evident that the individual who sins cannot find sanctuary within the larger community (Deut. 29:19–21). But for those who will avail themselves of the sacrifice provided by God, there is always forgiveness (v. 19).

Nehemiah.note: The central focus of these chapters is undoubtedly Nehemiah's success in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem and in securing the defenses of the city. But this is no mere construction project. It is an act of faith, sustained by prayer on the part of Nehemiah (1:5–11; 2:4; 4:4, 5; 5:19; 6:9, 14) and also of others (4:9). Such prayer is needed because of the opposition and harassment they face from surrounding peoples (2:10, 19; 4:1–14; 6:1–14). There are also internal difficulties within the community (ch. 5). But God uses Nehemiah's leadership skills to ensure the completion of the work. 1:1 The words of. This introductory phrase does not settle the question as to whether the book of Nehemiah was originally composed separately from Ezra. It may indicate the beginning of personal records or memoirs by Nehemiah (see Introduction: Author). Nehemiah. The name means "the LORD has comforted." Chislev. Corresponds to November/December. Unlike Ezra, who uses ordinal numerals to designate the months (e.g., Ezra 7:8, 9; 10:9, 17; but not Ezra 6:15), Nehemiah employs their Babylonian names. twentieth year. If the reference is to the years of Artaxerxes\'s reign (which would correspond to 446 B.C.), there is a conundrum. Regnal years are customarily calculated from the month of Nisan, the first month of the year (March/April). Since 2:1 is dated clearly as occurring in March 446 B.C, 1:1 would then occur after 2:1, not before it. Obviously, Nehemiah is using some other basis for his calculation, perhaps from the month of Artaxerxes\'s succession (July/August). However, this proposal remains uncertain, as there are no parallel examples of such dating in other sources. Even emending the text is impossible since there are no attested textual variants, and any change would be speculative. At present, there is not enough evidence to be sure of the precise dating of these events. We know that they happened, but we just cannot presently identify exactly when. See Introduction to Ezra: Date and Occasion. Susa. This city is a winter residence of the Persian kings (Esth. 1:2 note).

A short form of Hananiah, it means "the LORD is gracious." A certain Hananiah who was head of Jewish affairs is mentioned in the Elephantine papyri and is believed by some to be the brother of Nehemiah (7:2). He and his companions may have been sent to Jerusalem as part of an official mission to survey what had happened there.

It is less likely that this refers to the destruction 140 years earlier in the days of Nebuchadnezzar (586 B.C.). Nehemiah's shocked reaction indicates that this is of more recent origin, most probably the result of the events recorded in Ezra 4:7–23.

Fasting is here connected with mourning (1 Sam. 31:13) as well as with making a request of God (Ezra 8:21 note). Nehemiah is a man of prayer (2:4; 4:4, 9; 5:19; 6:9, 14; 13:14, 22, 29, 31), and here he brings before God his concerns over the dismal news from Jerusalem. the God of heaven. See notes on Ezra 1:2; Dan. 4:37.

In his prayer, after addressing God as supreme and the God of the covenant (v. 5), Nehemiah pleads for a response despite the sin of the people, past and present (vv. 6, 7). In vv. 8, 9 Nehemiah frames his petition on the basis of God's word to Moses (see Deut. 7:9) and on Solomon's temple prayer (see 2 Chr. 6:40). In addition, he mentions God's past deliverance of the people (v. 10) before concluding with the needs of his immediate, personal situation (v. 11). From the start, Nehemiah is not concerned merely with a building project. He has in view the furtherance of God's redemptive purposes. 1:5 In calling on God Nehemiah captures both His transcendence and His immanence. The true God is not only far above His people as the God of heaven (v. 4 note); He is near His people as the God of the covenant (Deut. 4:7). who keeps covenant and steadfast love. Nehemiah bases his petition on the constancy of God to His self-commitment, not on any merit the people possess. For "steadfast love," see note on Ezra 7:28.
The prayer of one particular day (v. 11), after four months of prayer and fasting (1:4; 2:1 note). "Day and night" means "continually" (Josh. 1:8; Ps. 1:2).

In his intercession Nehemiah speaks in solidarity with his people (see Ezra 9:6–15). Continuing enjoyment of the blessings of the Mosaic covenant is conditioned on the obedience of the people to the Lord's statutes. If Israel flagrantly and impenitently breaks His commands, the result is the imposition of the curses of the broken covenant. Nehemiah recognizes that Israel's disloyalty has led to forfeiture of the covenant blessings, and the result has been exile (Ezra 9:9 note).

A common petition (Deut. 9:27; Ps. 132:1; Jer. 14:21), particularly in Nehemiah (5:19; 6:14; 13:14, 22, 29, 31). It does not imply divine forgetfulness but rather calls for God's intervention and action based on His ongoing commitment.

The Mosaic covenant promises restoration of a remnant after exile (Deut. 30:1–5) on the basis of the covenant made with Abraham (Deut. 4:25–31). Such restoration must be accompanied by repentance and confession just as Nehemiah voices here (see Lev. 26:40–45). make my name dwell there. The name of God symbolizes God Himself, as He reveals Himself to His people. A place for His name to dwell is a place for Him to be with His people and to receive their worship (Deut. 12:5 note). Though the place is unspecified in Deuteronomy, Nehemiah recognizes it as Jerusalem, in keeping with Israel's history (see 2 Chr. 6:6).

A reference to the exodus (Ex. 32:11; Mic. 6:4). The people belong to the Lord because of His past intervention on their behalf when He saved them and claimed them for Himself. Even though they have rebelled against Him, He in His grace and forbearance has not dropped His claim on them, so His commitment can function as the basis for Nehemiah's petition.

The fear of the Lord is the proper response to God's self-revelation. To fear God is to know Him (Prov. 9:10), trust Him (Ps. 34:11, 22), obey Him (Prov. 8:13), and show Him reverence. "Delight" shows this is far from a coerced reaction. this man. Artaxerxes I. cupbearer. A member of the royal court whose responsibility is to choose wine (2:1) and safeguard it from poison. As the cupbearer, Nehemiah has the complete confidence of the king. This, combined with his constant access to the king, secures for him prestige and influence at court.

The date is March/April 445 B.C.., four months after Nehemiah received the report about Jerusalem (1:1 note). Nehemiah has continued to pray for a favorable opportunity to approach the king, and on the occasion of some festivity ("wine was before him") Artaxerxes gives an opening for him to speak.

A courtier with a sad face or anxious expression might well be implicated in a palace intrigue. Nehemiah is unaware that his prayer vigil has affected his looks. very much afraid. Nehemiah fears the king's wrath (Prov. 16:14) either because he is sad in the king's presence, especially on a festive occasion, or because he is about to ask the king to reverse a previous decision (Ezra 4:21). Nehemiah may also fear that he will be refused the permission he seeks.
A brief, spontaneous prayer based on a life of prayer (see 1:4–11).

Rebuilding the city is one aspect of rebuilding the "house of God" (see Num. 12:7), a major theme in Ezra and Nehemiah (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Themes). It is the focus of Neh. 1:1–7:3. Though Nehemiah mentions Judah, with characteristic tact he does not name Jerusalem, which was the subject of a previous, generally negative decree of Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:21, 22).

Opinions differ as to whether this indicates the meal is held in private or whether it brings out the influence the queen might have on the king's response. How long \... given him a time. It may seem doubtful that Nehemiah requests the twelve-year absence presumed in 5:14, but his request to rebuild his personal residence (v. 8) indicates that more than brief leave is in view. No matter how long of a leave Nehemiah asks for specifically at this point, the leave is certainly extended over the years. Possibly Nehemiah makes short visits to the royal court to report to the king.

Nehemiah now makes his specific requests. letters. The two references to letters in vv. 7, 8 are part of a major theme in Ezra and Nehemiah: the written word is an effective instrument used by God to accomplish His redemptive purpose (Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

The scope of the building project becomes clear: fortress, walls, and a governor's residence. The interval of four months has involved more than prayer. Nehemiah has been checking up on who is in charge of the king's forest, possibly located six miles (10 km) south of Jerusalem. It is also possible that the fortress is located north of the temple to protect its most vulnerable aspect. Nehemiah has a clear idea of what will be needed. the good hand of my God. Nehemiah acts as a responsible human agent in making the request, but the success is from God's sovereign good pleasure (Ezra 7:6), a theme that expresses the overarching message of Ezra and Nehemiah (Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Themes).

In Nehemiah's era, the chief Persian administrators are probably located in Damascus, and Nehemiah presents them with his credentials as he travels to Jerusalem. The military escort befits his status as governor of the subprovince of Judah (see Ezra 8:22).

A Babylonian name meaning "Sin \[the moon god\] gives life." Sanballat and his descendants served for more than a century as the governors of Samaria, the area north of Judah. He may have worshiped the God of Israel in some fashion (2 Kin. 17:24–41), since the names of his sons, Delaiah and Shelemiah, end with a short form of "Yahweh." "Horonite" may indicate that he came from Beth-Horon, about ten miles (16 km) northwest of Jerusalem or, less probably, from Horonaim in Moab. Tobiah. Probably the governor of Ammon, east of Judah, where his family remained influential for centuries. His name means "the LORD is good," indicating that he, too, may have worshiped the God of Israel (6:17, 18; 13:4). His son Jehohanan (6:17, 18) also had a Yahwistic name and was married to the daughter of an influential Jewish leader (3:4, 30; 6:18). Their religion was probably syncretistic. heard. References to the enemies having "heard" will punctuate the rest of 1:1–7:3 like a refrain (v. 19; 4:1, 7, 15; 6:1, 16). The conflict escalates until it is resolved in 6:16. displeased them greatly. The opposition has a political aspect in that Nehemiah's presence reduces their control over Judah. But it is religious at its root (v. 20 note; Ezra 4:13 note).

Soon after returning to Jerusalem, Nehemiah conducts a nighttime inspection of the walls and, aware of God's blessing upon him, encourages the population of the city to rebuild them. 2:11–16 Nehemiah's three-day wait after arriving in Jerusalem invites comparison with Ezra (Ezra 8:32). Ezra acts publicly; Nehemiah secretly (that Nehemiah has "told no one" is emphasized in v. 12; see v. 16).
A ministry of the Holy Spirit, similar to "stirred up" (Ezra 1:1, 5), except that Nehemiah consciously recognizes the divine origin of the burden he feels and the project he envisions.

Some of the damage is from Nebuchadnezzar's day. Lack of maintenance has caused further erosion and decay of the terraces surrounding the city, perhaps at the Millo (1 Chr. 11:8 note) on the east of the city. Nehemiah has to turn back rather than circumnavigate the city, especially at night.
Much of the city has lain in ruins for almost 150 years (1:3 note). An earlier attempt to rebuild the wall was stopped (Ezra 4:7–23). Nehemiah's presence will change all that.

Nehemiah's acknowledgment of God's sovereignty as the ultimate source of his plan does not exclude the providentially ordered actions of the king (v. 8 note). Let us rise up. Nehemiah's initiative meets with wholehearted support on the part of the leaders of Judah; by now the reader knows that this response, too, is governed by God's purpose (Ezra 1:5 note).

Sanballat and Tobiah are well informed about what is going on in Jerusalem (see 6:17). Geshem the Arab. This third opponent of Nehemiah was probably an Arab chief controlling a substantial area south of Judah, stretching to Egypt and over into Arabia. Nehemiah is pictured as virtually surrounded by enemies — Sanballat to the north, Tobiah to the east, and Geshem to the south (4:7, 8 note). The first tactic that they employed was demoralization of the people by ridiculing their proposals and insinuating that they were engaged in rebellion. Such allegations had worked a few years before (see Ezra 4:12, 13).

The material of this chapter probably existed independently, perhaps as an official report, before Nehemiah incorporated it into his memoir. The chapter underscores an important theme of Ezra and Nehemiah: the people of God as a whole and not just the great leaders are vital for accomplishing God's redemptive purpose. All of God's people worked together to rebuild the wall: clergy and laity, craftsmen and tradesmen, by town and by family, each contributing to the completion of the whole (see Eph. 4:16). 3:1 Eliashib. The grandson of Jeshua, the high priest during the days of Zerubbabel. Sheep Gate. The gate at the northeast corner of the city (see John 5:2) used to bring sacrificial animals into the city. That may well be why this gate is "consecrated." The description in the following verses moves counterclockwise until the Sheep Gate is mentioned again in v. 32. Tower of the Hundred. This is somewhere on the north side, the area with the poorest natural defenses. Tower of Hananel. A tower on the north side.

Repeatedly in this description "next" occurs, emphasizing that Nehemiah's allocation of work areas has been carefully planned to avoid gaps. the men of Jericho. Similar groups are found in vv. 5, 7, 27. Though their own homes are elsewhere, they recognize the importance of the work going on in Jerusalem. Perhaps they are allocated sections of the wall where there are few houses.
A main gate on the north side (2 Chr. 33:14; Zeph. 1:10), this is probably the gate used by merchants (see 13:16).
Lit. "made strong." It is possible that sections of the wall remain standing here and need only to be restored. Elsewhere it is a matter of rebuilding from the ground up.
Though the text presents an amazing picture of unanimity, it notes realistically that not all of God's people are in harmony with what the Lord is doing through Nehemiah.
Traditionally rendered "the Old Gate," it is on the northwest corner of the city. Possibly to be identified with the Gate of Ephraim (8:16; 12:39), which is not mentioned here.
On the west side of the northern half of the city. It probably leads off from the wall that is being repaired.
Probably others too, such as Jedaiah, work on the sections near their homes.

Probable causes of the economic stress mentioned are that Judah has been cut off from trading with neighbors; farmers are away from their fields because they have stayed in Jerusalem (4:22); there is a famine (v. 3); and previous administrators have burdened the people (v. 15). Times are so bad that children are being sold into slavery, houses and vineyards are being mortgaged, and money is being borrowed at interest. The crushing realization for Nehemiah is that the people of God themselves are forcing these intolerable measures on each other, not foreigners. The doctrine of the perspicuity (clarity) of Scripture is that the things necessary for salvation can be understood from the Bible without special techniques or higher education. This then leads into renewed obedience to the truth (vv. 13–18).

In this prayer of praise, the Levites (vv. 4, 5) address God on behalf of the people, extolling Him as creator (v. 6) and redeemer (vv. 7–12), lawgiver and disciplinarian, savior and judge (vv. 13–31). On the basis of His character and covenant, they petition God to take notice of their distress (vv. 32–37) in preparation for their covenant renewal (9:38–10:39 and note). The sequence of 9:5–10:39 resembles the form of ancient covenants: preamble identifying the overlord (vv. 5, 6), historical prologue (vv. 7–37), acceptance of the covenant (9:38–10:29), and covenant stipulations (10:30–39).
The Septuagint inserts "And Ezra said" (text note). Whether the prayer is uttered collectively by the Levites or by Ezra, its theology reflects his instruction over the preceding decade.
The people praise God for choosing Abraham and giving him the covenant of promise (Gen. 12–22).

A reference to God's oath to Abraham (Ex. 6:8).

In the Hebrew text, this word is last in the verse; it occurs also at the beginning of the prayer in v. 6, marking vv. 6–31 as unit. At this point in the prayer, the celebration of God's faithfulness in history gives way to a petition for similar divine action in the present.

The petition is that God will do again what He did in the past: see the distress of His people and come to their aid. kings of Assyria. These are the Neo-Assyrian kings whose presence was felt in Syria-Palestine from c. 850 B.C.., culminating the attack of Tiglath-pileser III (Pul) on Israel (2 Kin. 15:19), which led to the overthrow of the northern kingdom. Afterward came the Neo-Babylonian kings in the late seventh century and then the Persian kings in the mid-sixth century.
The execution of the covenant curses throughout Israel's history was in perfect harmony with the principle of divine justice, which lay at the foundation of the Mosaic covenant (Ezra 9:9 note).

The leaders who renewed the covenant are listed. Surprisingly Ezra is absent, being treated as a member of the priestly family of Seriah (10:2; see Ezra 7:1). This list of eighty-four names, about half of whom are not mentioned elsewhere, reinforces one of the major themes of Ezra and Nehemiah: the people of God as a whole, not just the great leaders, are vital for the accomplishing of God's redemptive plan (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Themes). Nehemiah and Zedekiah are joined together as representing the civil power. Many of the priestly names are those of families rather than individuals.

The whole community (vv. 28, 29) pledges fidelity to the terms of the covenant, specifically identifying and applying those parts of the Mosaic ordinances that are under the most severe pressure in their contemporary circumstances (vv. 30–39). 10:28 all who have separated themselves. See Ezra 6:21. This renunciation of heathen practices may additionally point in this context to those who acted on the issue of intermarriage (Ezra 9; 10).

The swearing of the oath by the people (9:15; Ezra 10:5 note) emphasizes the distinctively legal nature of the Mosaic covenantal arrangement as compared to the Abrahamic covenant in which the oath is taken by God alone (Gen. 12:1–3; 15; Heb. 6:13–18). As the apostle Paul later reveals, the Mosaic law was a kind of "guardian" that did not annul the covenant of promise already made with Abraham (Gal. 3:17, 24). Throughout the history of redemption, all God's covenantal arrangements call for obedience springing from faith in God and willingness to observe the terms of the covenant. This is true even for the Abrahamic covenant, wherein reception of its blessings required faith that bore fruit in obedience. However, under none of God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the new covenant church are people saved by their works of obedience. Justification is always and only by faith in the Lord's promises (Rom. 4:1–12). a curse. Covenant ratification involves a self-maledictory ceremony in which subscribers acknowledge the penalties that will be imposed on any who violate the covenant's terms and invoke such penalties on themselves if they act unfaithfully (see Deut. 28:15–68; Jer. 34:18).

Particular pledges of obedience are elaborated. (1) The avoidance of intermarriage (v. 30; see Ezra 9:2). (2) Keeping the Sabbath and the sabbatical year (v. 31; Ex. 20:8–11; Lev. 25:1–7). (3) Support for the service of the temple (vv. 32, 33). In Ex. 30:11–16 the levy is a half-shekel, but there it seems to be a particular, rather than an annual, levy. Alternatively, the difference could be from the use of a new monetary system under the Persians, or it could be a concession to the hard economic times. (4) Provision of wood for the fire on the altar (v. 34), not specifically required previously. (5) Donation of the firstfruits (vv. 35–37; Num. 18:12, 13; Deut. 26:1–11). (6) Payment of tithes (vv. 37, 38; see Lev. 27:30; Num. 18:21–24). (7) The Levites additionally tithe the tithes they receive for the temple service (vv. 38, 39).

The pledge to maintain the temple and its services as specified in the preceding verses is an index of the renewed spiritual commitment of the people. Rebuilding the house of God is a major theme in Ezra and Nehemiah (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

Apart from the chief men of the nation and temple personnel, few people were settled in Jerusalem at the completion of the wall repair because the ruined state of Jerusalem discouraged settlement there (7:4). A balanced community, however, requires a wider spread of population, and the repair of the wall and gates has made it less of a hardship to reside there. Because it is difficult to relate this appointment to those in 3:9, 12, or 7:2, some have supposed that "second" relates to the Second Quarter of the city (see 2 Kin. 22:14), a residential area on the western hill; however, archaeologists are uncertain if that area was occupied at this juncture.

Priests (vv. 10–14), Levites (vv. 15–18), and gatekeepers (v. 19) are all resident in Jerusalem after the wall is repaired. The same priestly lines are referred to in 1 Chr. 9:10–13, with some names variously spelled. The total of 1,192 priests in Nehemiah differs from the 1,760 of 1 Chr. 9:13, but the reasons for this are unclear. There are also unexplained differences regarding the Levite family leaders compared to 1 Chr. 9:14–16 and regarding the gatekeepers (1 Chr. 9:17–22).
The ridge south of the temple.
The reference may be to David (12:24; 1 Chr. 25) or to King Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:21–24), the latter being more likely because of the information given in v. 24.

A list of those who resettled the area surrounding Jerusalem. It links with Ezra 2:21–35, binding Ezra and Nehemiah into a whole. The list is not comprehensive but points to the extent of settlement in Judah. Cf. Josh. 15.

These lists of priests and Levites who serve in the Jerusalem temple during the Persian period may make for challenging reading, but they are a significant part of the picture being presented: legitimacy through continuity. The priestly offices are hereditary, and genealogical lists establish the validity of contemporary incumbents in the postexilic period. The restored community wants to ensure that every aspect of its worship corresponds to what God desires. 12:1–9 This list of priests (vv. 1–7) and Levites (vv. 8, 9) who returned under Zerubbabel connects the end of Nehemiah to the beginning of Ezra, uniting the whole work. In total twenty-two chiefs (leaders) of the priests are listed, whereas David appointed twenty-four priestly divisions (1 Chr. 24:7–19). Perhaps two lines died out during the exile. 12:1 Zerubbabel \... Jeshua. See note on Ezra 2:2. Ezra. Not the same Ezra as the leading figure of Ezra and Nehemiah. That Ezra returned eighty years after Zerubbabel (Ezra 7:6 note).
For antiphonal singing, see v. 24.
Gives the high-priestly line. Eliashib is high priest in Nehemiah's day (see 3:1). Scholars dispute whether the line is continued to the time of Darius II or Darius III (see v. 22).
This list is repeated with certain variations from vv. 1–7. The name Hattush (v. 2) is omitted, and there are a number of spelling differences.

A list of heads of Levitical families. 12:22 Darius the Persian. May be Darius II (423–404 B.C.) or Darius III (336–331). According to the first-century historian Josephus, Jaddua was high priest at the time of Alexander the Great (around 330 B.C.), which would support the latter identification. However, the Jaddua mentioned by Josephus need not be the one intended here. Moreover, Josephus often proves unreliable in his discussion of the Persian period.
Probably an official temple record (see Ezra 4:15).
Makes clear that the arrangements are divinely sanctioned. Persian kings were ordinarily interested in ordering the affairs of temples according to local custom.

The temple itself was dedicated earlier (Ezra 6:16). This ceremony is for the completed wall surrounding God's "house" (the temple as such and the community). In this section Nehemiah writes in the first person (vv. 31, 38, 40). Apart from 12:44–47 where third-person references to Nehemiah recur, the remainder of the book is drawn from his memoirs. 12:27 sought the Levites. The dedication could not take place without the help of the Levites, who are included in the preceding lists (vv. 1–26) and now live outside Jerusalem. The significance of the event is obvious to those making the careful arrangements for it.
Hence the list in 11:22, 23.

Ritual purification is a representation or symbol of moral purity (Lev. 16:30). 12:31–39 A grand procession takes place, apparently beginning at the Valley Gate on the western wall (3:13). Part of the procession, led by Ezra (v. 36), moves counterclockwise (v. 31), passing the Dung Gate, the Fountain Gate, and the Water Gate before proceeding to the temple. The other part of the procession, accompanied by Nehemiah (v. 38), moves clockwise (v. 38), passing the gates on the north side of the city before going to the temple. For the locations, see ch. 3 and notes.
A visible demonstration of what has been achieved and evidence that the walls are sturdily built. These groups weigh much more than a fox (see 4:3).
Because of his priestly descent, Ezra is qualified to lead the choir, whereas Nehemiah as a lay official follows (v. 38).

The people rejoice because God has given them cause to do so by His sovereign work through human agents (see Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Primary Themes). It is an echo of the joy experienced ninety years before when the temple foundations were laid (Ezra 3:13). This time, however, there is no weeping. the women and children. Including women and children underlines the great size of the celebration (3:12 note; 5:1 note).

These verses show that the people honored their pledge (10:39) and not neglected the house of God after the excitement of the day of celebration was over. Possibly "the days of Nehemiah" (v. 47) indicates this was added later to Nehemiah's memoir. 12:44 storerooms. They adjoin the main temple building to the north and south.
See 1 Chr. 25; 2 Chr. 8:14.
The people of God as a whole, not just the great leaders, are vital for accomplishing God's redemptive plan.

These further excerpts from Nehemiah's memoirs relate to his second period as governor (see v. 6). He was recalled to the Persian court in 433 B.C. (5:14 note). His return may reasonably be dated after 430 B.C.. and certainly before Artaxerxes' death in 424 B.C.. How long he remained governor is unknown. It is known that another individual became governor of the Persian subprovince of Yehud (Judah) before 407 B.C. On his return Nehemiah quickly realizes that in his relatively brief absence, the conduct of the people has deteriorated considerably and that he must take stern measures to maintain the spiritual strength of the community. 13:1–3 The pledge of general obedience to the law of Moses (10:28, 29) includes separation from neighboring peoples (10:28). Deut. 23:3–6 requires the exclusion of any Ammonite or Moabite from an assembly of the people for worshiping the Lord. However, the people have not conformed to this aspect of the law even though the exclusion of "those of foreign descent" is in keeping with the pledge in 10:28, 29. In view is religious, not racial or political, separation (Ezra 4:3 note). It probably does not include those who have professed allegiance to the Lord. Members of the nations excluded from the assembly of Israel could be included if they put their faith in Yahweh, the covenant Lord of Israel and only true God. Ruth the Moabite, ancestor of both David and Christ, is a prominent example of this reality (Ruth 1:1–18; 4; Matt. 1:1–17). 13:1 On that day. The reference may well be to a celebration of the Feast of Booths in a sabbatical year when the law is read to all the people (Deut. 31:9–13). The chronological references in vv. 4, 6 make clear that it is after Nehemiah's first term as governor, but it is unclear how the incident relates to his second term of office.
The story of Balaam is found in Num. 22–24.
Though Ezra is not on the scene, his labor is still bearing fruit (10:1–27 note). Once more (see 8:13–18), hearing the Word of God leads to renewed obedience, the obedience of separation.

The final commitment not to neglect the house of God (10:39) was violated during Nehemiah's absence (v. 11), as were the commandments governing both the pledges for the storehouse and the tithes (10:37–39). Reform is needed upon Nehemiah's return. 13:4 Eliashib. Though this Eliashib is possibly the high priest (3:1 note), it is more likely that another priest with the same name is intended, since the high priest is not likely to be placed in charge of the storehouse. Tobiah. See note on 2:10. He is well connected with the Jerusalem upper classes, having himself married into one of them, while his son marries into another. He is a daring and persistent character who attracts significant supporters.
It is because of a lack of tribute to the temple that the room is empty and can be made available for Tobiah's use.

See note on 5:14. Nehemiah returned to the Persian court in 432 B.C. king of Babylon. Some Persian kings used this title after the conquest of the Babylonian Empire (Ezra 5:13), but it was less common by Nehemiah's day. Its use here may indicate that the king of Persia was then in residence in Babylon. I asked leave of the king. This expression need not imply reappointment as governor, but the actions Nehemiah subsequently takes make it virtually certain that he has resumed his former status.

Cf. Matt. 21:12, 13. Nehemiah allows no compromises and takes immediate remedial action. What has been devoted to the Lord should not be used for personal gain and certainly not to benefit those who are antagonistic to His cause.

While he is clearing Tobiah's possessions out of the temple, Nehemiah probably asks why such a large storeroom is empty in the first place. It is apparent that the people have lapsed in their giving to maintain the temple ministry. 13:10 portions of the Levites. Links this section to the pledge in 10:37. The Levites possess no land (Num. 18:20–24; Deut. 14:29; 18:1), though some may have private income (Deut. 18:8).
