The dependence of the Levites on the support of the people may explain the reluctance of many Levites to leave Babylonia (Ezra 8:15–20). Lack of support from the people means that the Levites and singers are forced to leave the temple and support themselves by working elsewhere.

See note on 5:7. Nehemiah's direct action challenges those responsible, not the Levites who left but the temple officials who have permitted such a situation to arise. forsaken. The pledge not to neglect the house of God (10:39) was violated in Nehemiah's absence.
They do so in keeping with the pledge in 10:37.

See Acts 6:1–5; 2 Cor. 8:16–21. A carefully balanced set of representatives: a priest, a scribe, a Levite, and a layman. Zadok is a short form of the name Zedekiah, probably a reference to the individual named in 10:1.

The fourth use of "remember" in a prayer (1:8 note) and the second of four prayers by Nehemiah with the theme "remember me" (5:19 note). my good deeds. Not a boastful expression but "my acts of covenant loyalty." Nehemiah is motivated not by self-advancement but by zeal for God's cause and all that pertains to it.

Sabbath observance was a problem in preexilic times (see Jer. 17:19–27; Amos 8:5). It brought the Lord's demands on His people's time into tension with their perception of their economic best interests. The problem seems to have become prevalent during Nehemiah's absence. 13:15 Sabbath \... bringing \... sold. Three links with the pledge in 10:31 that was violated. The people in the countryside were working on the Sabbath to make the most of the grape harvest (late July/September), and they were also bringing produce into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. It is not said they are selling the produce on the holy day; indeed "on the day when they sold food" suggests that Nehemiah's remonstrance is on a day other than the Sabbath.

These men are one of the "peoples of the land" in view in 10:31. Fish is a significant element in the diet in that day. It is preserved by drying or salting. The Tyrian community in Jerusalem is selling to Jews on the Sabbath.
Again, a direct approach to those responsible for permitting the covenant violations, reminding them of what happened in the past (see Jer. 17:19–27).

The Israelites usually counted days from sunset to sunset (Lev. 23:32; Esth. 4:16; Dan. 8:14 text note). Nehemiah's direct action extends to closing the entrances of the city to traders from Friday evening. When they do not get the message, he spells out the consequences of further attempts to get around the situation, possibly through setting up a market outside the city wall.

Though he first used members of his entourage to enforce the regulations, Nehemiah now hands the matter over to the proper custodians of this aspect of God's law for permanent implementation. 13:22 Remember. See note on v. 14.

Ezra dealt with the perennial problem of intermarriage in 457 B.C. (Ezra 9:1 note), and in 445 B.C. the people gave solemn commitments regarding it (10:30). It is difficult to see how this problem could arise if Ezra was alive in the preceding decade. 13:23 Ashdod. The Persian province between Yehud (Judah) and the Mediterranean; the area of Philistine settlements. See note on 4:7, 8. Their language may be a variant of Aramaic.

It is not just the affront to God involved in such marriages that enrages Nehemiah; it is the corrosive effect on future generations. The problem is not primarily linguistic but concerned the ability of the next generation to hear and learn from the Hebrew Scriptures. The family, which should be the key building block of the covenant community, is being undermined. It is interesting to compare Malachi's assertion from this period that God seeks godly offspring from the marriages of the covenant community (Mal. 2:15).

Nehemiah's action can be contrasted with that of Ezra (Ezra 9:3). shall not give. Ezra actually dissolves the illegitimate unions (Ezra 10:3 note), whereas Nehemiah only attempts to prevent such unions in the future through adherence to the terms of their earlier commitment (10:30) and by adding the words "or for yourselves."

The argument is from the greater to the less: "If Solomon was not spared, how much less will we be spared." The reference "to sin" pertains to Solomon's involvement in pagan cults brought to Jerusalem by some of his many wives. The problem is not with foreign women who renounce their gods and pledge fidelity to the Lord, such as Ruth the Moabite (see Ruth 1:16). To be avoided is the insidious influence of a mother committed to worship of the pagan gods.
His marriage is doubly grievous, first, because a high priest in particular is not to marry a foreigner (Lev. 21:14), and second, because Sanballat is an enemy (2:19; 4:1; 6:1).

The sixth use of "remember" in a prayer (1:8 note) and the third imprecatory prayer (4:4, 5 note). Any corruption of the standards of behavior that should prevail in the covenant community is serious, but when the treachery emanates from those responsible for promulgating and maintaining those standards, the situation is doubly shameful and dangerous.

Contributions of wood are made in keeping with the pledge in 10:34, 35. Remember me. See note on v. 14. The book does not end on the high note of 12:27–47 but on the note of failure to carry out the pledges of 10:30–39 and the continuing need for reform. The people of God have not arrived at a resting place. Ezra and Nehemiah show the devotion of the faithful to the temple of God and the community surrounding it, a devotion that comes to maturity in Christ and His church (1 Cor. 3:5–17; Eph. 2:21, 22; 4:16; Heb. 3:1–6).

Esther.note: This section introduces the workings of the Persian Empire and makes clear its vast extent and massive resources. However, the conduct of the king is presented as arbitrary and somewhat incompetent. 1:1–22 The anger the king displays against Vashti and her disappearance from the royal court sets the scene for Esther to become queen, and thus to be in a position to influence the affairs of the empire for the benefit of her people. 1:1 Ahasuerus. Also known as Xerxes (486–465 B.C.), Ahasuerus is the Persian king mentioned in Ezra 4:6. He is renowned for consolidating his father Darius's empire, for his successful building projects, and for his wars against the Greeks from 480 to 470 B.C. India. The area watered by the Indus River, in modern-day Pakistan. Ethiopia. Heb. "Cush," the region south of Egypt, now part of northern Sudan (see 1 Chr. 1:8). No mention is made of the northern or western boundary where Ahasuerus failed to fully conquer the Greeks. 127 provinces. The reference here to the large number of divisions within the thirty larger administrative districts, or satrapies, in the Persian Empire is intended to impress.

This acropolis is a fortified palace 120 feet (36 m) above the surrounding city of Susa, which is the most significant of the four Persian capital cities and the royal winter residence. It has been excavated several times since 1851.
The year is 483 B.C. About this time, Ahasuerus is planning his forthcoming invasion of Greece, which may account for the large military presence in the capital.

For 180 days, the king ostentatiously displays the royal wealth. The extravagant, seven-day outdoor feast is the climax of the celebrations. The elaborate details about the drinking vessels and the abundance of the wine highlight the king's lavish generosity. All is intended to impress and intimidate, but events will show where control really lies.

This term is employed nineteen times in Esther to refer to royal decrees. Micromanipulation of conduct is characteristic of bureaucracies, ancient and modern. Here the concession is made that each individual is free to drink as much or as often as he pleases.

This name, not found elsewhere, may be related to the Persian word meaning "the beloved" or "the best." Extrabiblical sources name Ahasuerus's queen as Amestris. Vashti may have been a popular or an alternative name. Another proposal is that Ahasuerus had other queens.

Reasons for Vashti's disobedience are not given in the Hebrew text, though early Jewish interpreters explained that she was commanded to appear naked, wearing only her crown, or that she had some disfigurement. The queen's courageous refusal to obey introduces the theme of obedience and disobedience. The weakness of the regime has been exposed from within, from the top — and by a woman. That a woman would show the regime's weakness is ironic considering the lower place of women in the eyes of the culture of that day.

This expression usually refers to astrology, though in this context it probably means "the proper course to follow" (see 1 Chr. 12:32). The satirical flavor of the narrative is evident as the king, who has just displayed all the power and glory of his magnificent kingdom, proves incapable of formulating a response to this affront to his self-esteem and has to consult experts on matters of law and justice and to go to the nobles for advice on how to deal with his wife's behavior. the seven princes of Persia and Media. The king's inner circle of advisors (see Ezra 7:14).

The counselor (as well as the king, v. 10) is probably somewhat intoxicated after the extended banquet. He exaggerates the situation, deftly avoids the king's role in the affair, and proposes a disproportionate and unenforceable response, which gives massive exposure to the whole incident.

The permanency of royal law is an important feature in the development of the story (4:11; 8:8). The plan to banish Vashti and to give her position to someone better — more beautiful or more obedient (or both) — has be carried out. The legal structures of the empire are brought into operation to ensure that defiance does not spread.
This is more a piece of court flattery than concern with the difficulties of communication.

The Persian postal system, renowned for its efficiency, is used to publish the irrevocable royal edicts (3:12–14; 8:9, 10; see 9:20, 30). master in his own household. Indeed, the biblical standard is that the husband is the head of the household, but he must exercise his authority in the right spirit: not a display of domineering bullying but of care and love modeled on that of Christ (Eph. 5:22–25).

Steps are taken to replace the deposed Vashti (vv. 1–4). Then Mordecai and Esther are introduced (vv. 5–7). Esther is one of many young women coerced into the process of selecting a new queen (vv. 8–11). Details of the procedure (vv. 12–14) lead into an account of how Ahasuerus is captivated and overwhelmed by Esther (vv. 15–18). Around this time, Mordecai becomes aware of a plot against the king, which his information helps to foil. He does not, however, receive any immediate reward (vv. 19–21). 2:1 After these things. Combining the information in vv. 12, 16 with that in 1:3 suggests that approximately three years have past, during which time Ahasuerus was away from Susa, fighting the Greeks (482–480 B.C.). abated. The use of the same rare verb in 7:10 suggests a parallel between the dismissal of Vashti and the hanging of Haman. he remembered Vashti. The king may have regretted his actions, but it was too late; the legislation made his actions permanent.

Probably his personal assistants, not the senior advisors of 1:13, 14. If Ahasuerus does indeed regret deposing Vashti, he may be uninterested in listening to those who suggested it. be sought out. This is not a competition that one chooses to enter but a commandeering exercise on the part of the empire to acquire whatever it wants, no matter the human cost involved.
For the unsuccessful young women it will lead to a life of widowhood, imprisoned in the royal harem.

A name derived from Marduk, the Babylonian city-god. Mordecai may also have a Jewish name, like Esther (Hadassah, v. 7). The discovery in ancient texts (including one dated c. 485 B.C.) of the Babylonian personal name Mardukaya, as well as the discovery of an archive of texts in Nippur containing the names of Jews from the time of Artaxerxes I and Darius, point to the authenticity of Mordecai's name and to the historicity of the events behind the story. Mordecai was a Jew living in the citadel, which presumably implies that he was a Persian official. Jair \... Shimei \... Kish. The names in his genealogy may refer to Mordecai's remote rather than immediate ancestors (Shimei, 2 Sam. 16:5–14; Kish, 1 Sam. 9:1, 2; 1 Chr. 8:33). Kish may well have been an earlier ancestor rather than the one carried into exile, who in that case would be Jair. The reference is not to Mordecai personally — that would have made him about 120 years old. Mordecai's connection with Saul, who was also a Benjaminite, takes on great significance when we encounter Haman, Mordecai's enemy, who was a distant relative of Agag, the Amalekite, Saul's enemy (3:1 note; Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

Also known as Jehoiachin, the second-to-last king of Judah, who was taken to Babylon in 597 B.C. while still a young man. This may mean that Mordecai's family was among the Judean nobility (2 Kin. 24:6–17; 25:27–30).

Esther's Hebrew name, meaning "myrtle." Esther. Perhaps derived from the Persian word for "star," or a form of Ishtar, a Babylonian goddess. The family information given shows that Esther was not Mordecai's niece but his cousin. Since Esther became his adopted daughter, she was presumably younger than Mordecai.
This brings out the initial vulnerability of Esther. She had no option in the matter.

A secular use of the Hebrew word for "covenant loyalty," hesed (Ex. 15:13 note). The idiom is normally used with the more passive verb "found" (e.g., Gen. 39:4); the active verb "won" suggests that Esther took advantage of the opportunities in her new situation. Hegai's attitude is also a first sign of God's providential care of Esther (see v. 17; 5:2; cf. the more explicit references to God's providence in Dan. 1:9). Hegai's speedy arrangements and provision of the "best place in the harem" mark Esther as the woman most likely to succeed in the selection process. her portion of food. Esther's reception of special portions of food contrasts with her intentional fast in 4:16. Life in the harem is highly regulated, as in the empire as a whole. Unlike Daniel, Esther does not follow Jewish dietary laws or declare her background (v. 10).
The elaborate preparations are in keeping with the other excesses of the court (1:4–8).
The place reserved for concubines, the king's mistresses.
the tenth month \... the seventh year. Corresponds to December 479/January 478 B.C., four years after 1:3.
Ahasuerus is completely captivated by Esther and makes her queen immediately.

Esther's accession to the throne, which is celebrated with a banquet, contrasts with Vashti's banquet in 1:9. a remission. Lit. "a giving of rest." Perhaps a declaration of a public holiday, but remission of taxes is attested as a royal concession in the Persian Empire. This, along with giving gifts (probably food) and other favors, foreshadows the great banquet and rest for the Jews in 9:16–18, 22. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

It is unclear what this refers to; perhaps a second selection of a concubine or part of the celebrations at Esther's feast. at the king's gate. This expression (see v. 21; 3:2; 5:9, 13; 6:10, 12) may imply that Mordecai has been promoted in the royal service, a move that not only enables him to discover the conspiracy to assassinate the king (v. 21) but which also may be what incites Haman's jealousy (5:13). The king's gate is a large structure that houses key elements of the royal administration. Sitting there does not depict the attitude of a bystander or a supplicant but of a court official.
These personal bodyguards control access to the king's private quarters and so have easy access to him.

Lit. "on a tree." Refers to impalement on a wooden stake, a Persian and Assyrian form of execution. To the Jews, this is a sign that the two officials are under God's curse (Deut. 21:22, 23 and note), confirming the appropriateness of Mordecai's loyalty to the pagan king. recorded in the book of the chronicles. Mordecai is not rewarded at this time (see 6:1–11); instead, the account of Haman's promotion is given (3:1). Since Persian kings were usually scrupulous in rewarding exceptional service, the fact that the king grants no prize to Mordecai in this instance demonstrates God's providential control. Ahasuerus's failure to reward Mordecai at this point allows the king to reward him later, providing evidence of God's overruling Haman's wicked plans in order to bring about the evil man's downfall (Est. 6:1–13).

A crisis is precipitated as events take a threatening turn. Unexpectedly and with no explanation stated, Ahasuerus promotes Haman (not Mordecai, as 2:22 might lead the reader to expect) to second position in the empire. However, Haman and Mordecai are soon found opposing each other (vv. 1–6). Haman abuses his position of trust to dupe Ahasuerus into promulgating a decree of genocide against the Jews (vv. 7–14). Again Ahasuerus is portrayed in a poor light as he makes decisions without securing adequate information. 3:1 After these things. The precise time lapse from 2:17 depends on one's understanding of 3:7. Four, or more probably five, years have now passed. Haman the Agagite. The antagonist of this story bears the Persian name Haman and is the son of the Persian Hammedatha, but the true significance of the man is found in the identification of Haman as "the Agagite." This suggests that Haman has an important association with Agag, the king of the Amalekites, the archenemies of Israel, who were opposed by Saul (1 Sam. 14:47–15:35). God called on the ancestors of Mordecai and Esther to blot out the Amalekites, and the presence of one of them in the days of Esther shows that the job remains unfinished (Ex. 17:8–16; Deut. 25:17–19). Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin, failed to obey God immediately and kill Agag. Now, Esther and Mordecai, also from the tribe of Benjamin, are left to deal with his descendant.

Mordecai's refusal to honor Haman cannot be explained on the basis of OT law, since Jews do not regard bowing before kings and other honored persons as a violation of the first and second commandments (Ex. 20:3–6; 1 Sam. 25:23; 2 Sam. 18:28; 2 Kin. 4:37). Mordecai and Haman are best understood as representatives of two hostile nations — Israel and its enemy Amalek, a nation under the divine curse (v. 1 note), respectively. Mordecai's refusal to bow down to his hereditary enemy because he (Mordecai) "was a Jew" is understandable (v. 4). Similarly, Haman's seemingly excessive passion to destroy the entire Jewish nation for Mordecai's insolence is explained (v. 6). Ultimately, this hostility is a particular manifestation of that divinely imposed conflict between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent in Gen. 3:15.

It is strange that only at this point does Mordecai take a stand, since there are many other objectionable features of life in the royal court in Susa. Still, a late stand is better than no stand at all.
"Fury" is the same word translated "anger" (1:12; 2:1). Haman shares the character trait with Ahasuerus. Indeed, there is a play on how similar the name Haman sounds in Hebrew to "fury" (hemah).

Haman's vehement passion will not stop at half-measures in seeking revenge. He will deal not simply with Mordecai but with his whole race. So the continuation of the covenantal line of promise that is to produce the Messiah comes under threat, as the Persians control the lives even of those Jews who have already returned to Jerusalem.

Haman uses the ancient practice of casting lots (1 Sam. 14:41, 42; Prov. 16:33) to determine the most propitious time to set in motion his plan to destroy the Jews. The lots probably take the form of small clay cubes. The plural form of Pur — Purim — is the name of the celebration that commemorates the death of Haman, the enemy of all the Jews (9:23–32). they cast it month after month. There are two understandings of what is related here. (1) The process of casting lots takes place daily for almost a year (475 B.C.). (2) More probably, on one day in the first month of the year (early April 474 B.C.) lots are cast for each month and day in succession until the last month of the year emerges as propitious. This, too, is part of the Lord's providence to allow time for the deliverance of His people. Haman is prepared to endure that delay to ensure the success of his scheme, but he approaches the king immediately to set his plan in motion.

Haman's speech is a calculated blend of truth ("scattered abroad and dispersed") and falsehood ("they do not keep the king's laws"). If Mordecai and Esther are anything to go by, the Jews are largely prepared to assimilate. Without naming the Jews, Haman uses vague and unsubstantiated allegations to imply that they threaten to be a disruptive influence in the empire.

Yet another of the king's impulsive responses authorizes Haman to issue royal edicts (see Gen. 41:42). The repetition of Haman's full name together with the phrase "the enemy of the Jews" underlines the terrible predicament of the Jews at this point. Haman has been able to manipulate the king with ease.

The king is not refusing Haman's offer. It seems to be understood that Haman will recoup this enormous expense by appropriating the assets of those killed. The king is authorizing him to do so — and expects the promised payment to the royal treasury (see 4:7).

The impersonal imperial administrative machine swings into action to process Haman's plans. The elaborate, descriptive language (e.g., the multiple verbs in the edict "to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate") highlights the painfulness of the senseless edict and emphasizes the extreme danger to God's covenant people. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes. 3:12 the thirteenth day of the first month. The significance of this day — the eve of the Passover celebration — would not be lost on any Jew. Now it would not be a commemoration of divine deliverance but the start of an ominous shadow cast over the Jews. It has been calculated to correspond to April 17, 474 B.C.
On March 7, 473 B.C., almost a full year later. to plunder their goods. To be compared with the Jews' refusal to plunder (9:10, 15, 16).

While the king and Haman callously feast, the city, not just the administrative classes in the citadel, is in a highly agitated state. There is probably a measure of sympathy for the Jews, but equally there is surely bewilderment as to what the future might hold for other people groups as a result of Haman's influence over the emperor.

The royal decree issued as a result of Haman's plot plunges the Jewish community, near and far, into deep mourning (vv. 1–3). Esther becomes aware of the threat to the Jews only through the information passed on by Mordecai. Then the initiative in events moves from the king and his courtiers, first to Mordecai and then to Esther. Mordecai orders Esther to approach the king to induce him to intervene in the situation (vv. 4–9). After Esther sets out the difficulties involved in his proposal (vv. 10, 11), Mordecai warns her that her life too is in danger (vv. 12–14). Esther then prepares to act, hazarding her personal safety (vv. 15–17). 4:1 all that had been done. Mordecai keeps himself well-informed about what goes on in court. His knowledge is not confined to the public decree. He has insider information. 4:1–3 tore his clothes \... bitter cry \... fasting \... ashes. These responses by Mordecai and by Jews in every province are conventional signs of intense grief and horror at the reception of bad news in a society that does not despise public displays of emotion (see Gen. 37:29, 34; Dan. 9:3; Jon. 3:6). The Persians responded similarly after their defeat by the Greeks at the battle of Salamis. sackcloth. Rough garments, often of goats' hair, worn in mourning or distress.

Esther's life in the palace has become so detached from the rest of her people that she does not know about the decree and the danger they are in. But she does know that Mordecai's action indicates that something is very much amiss. Her initial concern is for Mordecai personally.
His name may mean "the good one," or perhaps "courier." He certainly acts in a trustworthy manner.

See 3:12–14. Mordecai makes sure that Esther not only is given a copy of the edict but also has it explained to her (perhaps translated) before he charges her to entreat the king for mercy for her people. Mordecai's previous command that Esther conceal her identity as a Jew is reversed (2:10).
Persian kings live under perpetual fear of assassination, and this practice gives clear direction to the royal bodyguards as to how to deal with an unexpected visitor.

Mordecai subtly alludes to his belief that God, in His sovereignty, has providentially ordered the events of Esther's life to put her in a position where she can act to deliver all the Jews. Mordecai believes that the sovereign God will bring relief and deliverance to the Jews, that Esther could be the means through which that deliverance will come, and that God is not restricted to this plan if Esther decides to remain quiet. However, it is striking that Mordecai manages to communicate those things without directly mentioning the Lord's name once.

Esther now takes the lead in shaping the response to the crisis (see Mordecai's compliance in v. 17). Go, gather \... fast on my behalf. With conviction, faith, and fear, Esther directs that a fast be undertaken on her behalf. Prayer normally accompanies religious fasting (Deut. 9:9; Judg. 20:26, 27; 2 Sam. 12:16; Ezra 8:21–23; Dan. 9:3) but is left out here. However, fasting itself contains an implicit appeal to God to save His people from destruction. three days, night or day. Usually, fasts are prescribed for only one day. This unusually long fast points to the seriousness of the situation and effectively contrasts with the feasts that stand at the beginning and end of the book (1:3, 5, 9; 2:18; 9:17, 18). against the law. See v. 8. Esther's dilemma reintroduces the theme of obedience, since obedience to Mordecai means disobeying the law of the land. if I perish, I perish. Given Ahasuerus's temper, there is a significant possibility that he will not accept her. Yet in obedience to Mordecai's request, Esther resigns herself to her fate (see Gen. 43:14).

The scene switches from the bleak world outside to the splendor of the court, from the fasting of the Jews to the feasting of the palace. After she overcomes the initial hurdle of an audience with Ahasuerus, Esther cautiously and successfully manipulates events to achieve her purpose. 5:1 Wearing royal robes that undoubtedly enhance her beauty (cf. the mourning attire in 4:15, 16), Esther dares to approach the threshold of the imperial throne room. To emphasize that Esther is entering another world, the narrator repeats the word "king" three times and the word "royal" twice.
Ahasuerus grants Esther's request for an audience. The immediate threat to her life has been removed, but the situation remains far from resolution.

This generous offer reflects a courtly convention and should not be taken literally (v. 6; see Mark 6:23). Esther's first request is that the king and Haman attend a banquet (v. 4). Her second response (v. 8) effectively obliges the king to grant her petition. But it is not until 7:2–6 that Esther finally answers the king's question. Esther's delaying tactics not only demonstrate her wisdom and sense of control but also raise the suspense in the story.
Esther does not move too fast. The inclusion of Haman would occasion no surprise due to his recent promotion.

Esther's second response effectively obliges Ahasuerus to grant her petition, but it is not until 7:2–6 that Esther reveals what that is. Subtly, she makes the second banquet seem like the king's idea.

Haman's elation at the honor extended to him as the only guest at an intimate meal with Ahasuerus and his queen is shattered when he again witnesses Mordecai's defiant attitude toward him (v. 9). At a gathering of family and friends to boast about his status (vv. 10–12), Haman reveals his irritation with Mordecai. His wife and friends advise him to use his influence with the king to have Mordecai eliminated (v. 14). 5:9 filled with wrath. The same expression as "filled with fury" (3:5). Mordecai has evidently removed his sackcloth and is back at his post.
Though infuriated, Haman unexpectedly does not openly react to Mordecai's snub and pretends not to notice it.
Haman does not give details of what has happened but makes his vexation with Mordecai clear.

Haman was content to leave Mordecai's fate to be determined by the general decree against the Jews (3:6), but now his wife and friends urge him to act immediately against Mordecai. fifty cubits high. Whether hanging or impalement is in view, the height of about seventy-five feet (23 m) is excessive (but then, so was much else connected with the Persian court). Possibly the gallows is to be erected on top of something else so that Mordecai's demise will be a public spectacle. Then go joyfully. The ruthless policy of arranging a political assassination so that he can enjoy a banquet and his new status at court appeals to Haman.

This chapter constitutes the watershed in the narrative. Events begin to turn around for the people of God through a striking series of events, each plausible when considered in isolation, but their combination reveals the working of a higher hand. The king has a bout of insomnia (v. 1). He is reminded that Mordecai has never received any reward (vv. 2, 3). Even though it is still night, Ahas­uerus calls for a royal advisor (v. 4). Haman is in attendance because he is eager to have Mordecai executed (v. 5). Haman, thinking the conversation is about himself, advises the king how to honor a favorite courtier (vv. 6–9). But, far from receiving the accolade himself, Haman is ordered to bestow it on Mordecai (vv. 10, 11). Utterly frustrated and humiliated, Haman returns home (vv. 12, 13). 6:1 the king could not sleep. Lit. "the sleep of the king fled," but we are not told why. The hand of God is at work. The chronicles of eastern kings are tedious, but the intention is probably to induce the king to sleep.

There does not seem to have been any particular reason to read the account of a five-year-old conspiracy (see 2:19–23). Again the hand of God is at work. To enhance their personal safety, Persian monarchs richly rewarded informers (see 2:23), and Ahasuerus is perturbed that Mordecai has been overlooked.

He has spent the night supervising the construction of the gallows for Mordecai, so ironically he is there at dawn to request Mordecai's death just as the king is seeking advice on how to honor Mordecai.

In a further ironic turn, the king — unintentionally — does not reveal the identity of the one to be honored (see Haman's intentional concealment of the identity of the people to be destroyed, 3:8). Assuming that he himself is the focus of the king's favor, Haman unveils his personal dream list, which focuses not on material gain or position but on public acclaim and adulation (see Gen. 41:42, 43). He wants to be treated as if he were king and for all Susa to know about it.
Though Ahasuerus has no idea of the hostility between the two men, others are likely well aware of it.
Just days before, Mordecai was there wearing sackcloth (4:2).
A deliberate contrast between Mordecai's returning to his post and Haman's returning home utterly dejected and forlorn.

Haman's wife and advisors give voice to the belief that the Jewish people are indomitable and, perhaps, even to the view that their God is the living God. See the predictions about the fall of Amalek before Israel (Ex. 17:16; Num. 24:20; Deut. 25:17–19; 1 Sam. 15; 2 Sam. 1:8–16; cf. predictions of others fearing God's people and the Lord in Josh. 2:11; Dan. 6:26, 27; Ezek. 38:23). See also Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

The pace quickens. Haman is hurried to the banquet before he has time to think (6:14). On this occasion, Esther reveals the plight of her people (vv. 3, 4) and denounces Haman as the would-be perpetrator of genocide (v. 6). Haman's attempt to win a reprieve from the queen is misinterpreted by Ahasuerus (vv. 7, 8), and Haman is sentenced to die on the gallows he has prepared personally (vv. 9, 10). 6:14 hurried to bring Haman. The affairs of the court are always carried out in haste. It was oriental custom for servants to escort guests to special functions. Events have spun out of Haman's control; Esther is now in charge.

As on the first occasion (5:5) wine is drunk after the banquet (5:6). Queen Esther. Ahasuerus's use of her title here (as in 5:3) indicates his favorable disposition toward her. The title is also used in vv. 1, 3, 5 and 7, emphasizing her dominant role in this scene.

The drama of the scene is heightened by Esther's slow unveiling of her twofold petition for her own life and for her people to be spared, corresponding to the king's twofold offer to grant her wish and her request (v. 2). Esther does not name her people, but the fate awaiting them makes her nationality obvious.

A reference to Haman's initial bribe (3:9; 4:7). destroyed \... killed \... annihilated. The Hebrew verbs are precisely those used in the initial decree (3:13). Esther identifies with her people but does not yet come completely into the open. She skillfully uses passive verbs in her description to avoid implicating the king. not to be compared. The Hebrew is somewhat difficult to translate. Esther seems to argue that Haman's financial offer (3:9) will not compensate for the king's damages (i.e., lost revenue from the Jews). Appealing to Ahasuerus's self-interest is virtually certain to sway him.

Esther's tactics have completely won over the king. When he angrily demands to be told who has threatened the queen and her people, Esther makes no mention of the king's own decree but points to Haman as the instigator of the genocidal atrocity. "Foe" and "enemy" point not just to hostility to Esther and her people but to Ahasuerus's interests as well. terrified. Haman is gripped with sudden, overwhelming fear as he realizes that there is no way out. The king and queen are united in opposing him.

It is improbable that Ahasuerus wants a place to cool off. Though Esther has not named him personally, the decree went out with his authority, and the whole situation reflects badly on him. He needs time to work out how to extricate himself without losing face.

It is the custom to recline on couches at a feast in this era. Haman's violations of etiquette seal his fate and provide Ahasuerus with a neat way out of the tricky situation he finds himself in. covered Haman's face. The court attendants understand the implications of the king's word, that is, his verdict regarding Haman's guilt.

As always, the king welcomes the advice of others — here, the eunuch Harbona (1:10; see the speech in 5:14). The order to hang Haman on the gallows intended for Mordecai is the great ironic reversal of the story. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

Though Haman, the main adversary of the Jews, has been removed from the scene, the story is not over. The edict to annihilate the Jews is still in place with all the inescapable fixity of the laws of the Medes and Persians. Esther again approaches the king (v. 3) and asks for the law to be revoked (v. 5). Ahasuerus gives Esther and Mordecai permission to proceed as they think best (v. 8), and Mordecai formulates a decree (v. 9) that effectively counters the impact of Haman's edict by authorizing the Jews to take action against any who attack them (vv. 11, 12). Both the Jews and the general population of Susa celebrate Mordecai's new prominence and his countermeasure (vv. 15–17). 8:1 On that day. Seemingly the same day that had begun with the king's sleeplessness (6:1). gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman. According to Persian custom, the property of a traitor ("house" implies all his possessions) is confiscated by the crown. Here Esther receives compensation for the wrong done to her. Mordecai came before the king. Mordecai is given official status (see 1:14) and effectively takes over Haman's official and personal position.
In her second appeal to Ahasuerus, Esther abandons her cool, calculating approach, and resorts to emotional entreaty.

Esther presents her case carefully and with a liberal dose of flattery. Two of the conditional clauses relate to the king's assessment of the situation and two to his personal regard for Esther, which is in reality the only leverage she has with him.
The "you" is emphatic. Ahasuerus does not want to think through the details of rectifying the situation. Typically he delegates others to act in his name with full authority.

The new decree, issued two months and ten days after the first (3:12), is almost identical to Haman's first decree (3:12–15). The date is June 25, 474 B.C. There are still eight months and twenty days to go until Haman's decree will take effect. It cannot be formally revoked, but Mordecai's strategy nullifies its effect by permitting the Jews to defend themselves. 8:9 and also to the Jews. An addition to the original decree to ensure that the Jews knew they could take appropriate action.
The additional details regarding the speed and reliability with which the second decree is to be conveyed indicate the urgency of the situation (see v. 14).

Repeats the terms of the original decree (3:13). children and women included. While this might relate to the families of their attackers, it is more probable that it again repeats the language of 3:13 and refers to the families of the Jews.
Retaliation is authorized to punish any who take action against the Jews. Those who act on the basis of Haman's edict will share his fate.

Whereas after the first edict Mordecai had torn his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes (4:1), the situation is now completely reversed, and he is dressed with regal splendor, and not just for a single parade (see 6:11). Blue and white are Persian royal colors. The majority reaction in the city shows that anti-Jewish feeling is not widespread throughout the population.
The conversion of those from other nations who fear the Jews marks a climax in the story (see Josh. 2:9; Ex. 15:14–16; Ps. 105:38).

The day set for the implementation of Haman's decree, March 7, 473 B.C. (see 3:13), arrives. Despite the promulgation of countermeasures, some still attack the Jews. In Susa, five hundred enemies are killed (v. 12), and at Esther's request the action is continued for another day, which leads to three hundred more deaths (vv. 13–15). Throughout the provinces of the empire, many who attack the Jews are slain, but the Jews refrain from plundering their property. 9:1 the reverse occurred. The theme of ironic reversal is again emphasized. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

Fear of the God of the Jews is behind the Persians' pervasive fear of the Jews (see Ex. 15:14–16). The reversal (v. 1 note) is so complete that all the officials who were to have enforced the extermination of the Jews now aid them. They are acutely aware of who has come to enjoy royal favor.

The extent of the killing is emphasized (vv. 6–11), but so is the Jews' not plundering their enemies (v. 10). Their refusal to plunder recalls the plundering of the Amalekites that led to Saul's demise (1 Sam. 15:17–19). This contrast (see 8:11) suggests the propriety of their conduct in this final encounter with the Amalekites, despite the extent of the killing. It seems that the Jews are acting in accordance with the rules pertaining to a war of the Lord (Num. 31:1 note; Josh. 6:17).
This significant detail is repeated in vv. 15, 16 to emphasize the restraint that the Jews exercise. It is a deliberate decision not to enrich themselves at the expense of their enemies.

Esther's requests for further vengeance (v. 13), which may be due to widespread anti-Jewish sentiment in the city, leads to a second day of bloodshed in Susa (v. 15). Notably, the emphasis in the narrative is on killing enemies, not just on winning a victory. Esther is operating in accordance with the directives applicable to a war of the Lord (see Josh. 8:29; 10:26).
The bodies of the dead sons (v. 12) are displayed as a warning and a sign of ultimate dishonor (2:23 note).

The slaughter of a further seventy-five thousand enemies emphasizes the extent of the antagonism toward the Jews throughout the empire, which in turn explains the celebrations that follow. relief from their enemies. The rest granted to the Jews at this time becomes the basis for the annual celebration of Purim (also v. 22). Such rest was earlier closely associated with blotting out the memory of the Amalekites (Deut. 25:19).

The difference of the day on which the feast of Purim is held is first explained (vv. 17–19). The further record (vv. 20–32) shows how important it is to the writer to establish that Purim is to be celebrated by each new generation of Jews. There is no mention of God. The feast is based on the edict of Mordecai and Esther (v. 31).

The additional day of bloodshed in the capital leads to two different dates for the observance of Purim. It is still the case that the Jews celebrate it on the fifteenth in Jerusalem, but on the fourteenth elsewhere.

The exchange of gifts, usually food (v. 22), enables even the poorest Jew to join in the celebrations (Deut. 16:11, 14; Neh. 8:10, 12) and is a further instance of providential care for the oppressed, here within the Jewish community itself.
He does this by incorporating the information in the letters of instruction he sends regarding the festival.

This brief summary of the events of the preceding chapters focuses, not on Esther and Mordecai, but on the king and Haman, and pre­sents Haman as the archetypal adversary of all Jews, past and present (3:10; 8:1; 9:10).
A plural form of pur, a Babylonian term for "lot" (see 3:7).

Esther along with Mordecai sends a final official letter regarding Purim that carefully places the feast within the setting of the more established Israelite practices of fasting and lamentation (v. 31). In this way, Purim is made an official religious celebration of the Jews, a task the writer of Esther seems to view as important because of the non-Mosaic origin of the feast.

The epilogue mirrors the introductory statements about the reign of Ahasuerus (1:1, 2). Though the Lord granted the Jews relief from impending annihilation, the political structures of the world continue to dominate their lives. The salvation of God's people is not yet complete, even though they now have a powerful advocate in the royal court. True deliverance awaits the coming of one able to do far more than Esther and Mordecai. 10:1 The extent of Ahasuerus's power is brought out by his ability to impose taxation throughout his land empire and on the cities of the eastern Mediterranean, such as those of the Phoenicians, whose economies were based on maritime trade.

The historicity of the narrative is emphasized by citing Persian official records as sources of further information about Ahasuerus and the status he conferred on Mordecai, who continued to work within the official structures of the empire. For some reason, Esther's name is not included in the postscript.

Mordecai is esteemed as an ideal Jewish statesman, recalling the status of Joseph (Gen. 41:40) and Daniel (Dan. 2:48; 5:29; 6:28). His importance as a model for the Jews and in the establishment of Purim is acknowledged in the apocryphal book of Maccabees, where Purim is called "the day before Mordecai's day" (2 Macc. 15:36).

Job.note: In the prose prologue, the narrator provides the reader with essential background information for understanding the central poetic speeches. There are two basic points being made: what befalls Job is not a consequence of sinful behavior on his part, and all that occurs is under the sovereign control of God. 1:1–5 The prologue (chs. 1; 2) begins with a depiction of Job as blessed by and devoted to his God. 1:1 Uz. An extended region east of Judah, perhaps on the edge of the desert but conducive to raising crops (v. 14) and livestock (v. 3). Job is not a nomad but an elder in a major town (29:7). Job. The meaning of his name is uncertain, but see note on 6:27; 13:24. There is no mention of his family line, implying he is not an Israelite. His standing before God is based not on inherited privilege but on personal commitment. blameless and upright. "Blameless" means acting with integrity, springing from a wholehearted commitment to God. "Upright" describes one whose conduct is habitually ethically correct. This is ordinary language and means not that Job was sinless but that he is genuine in his religious profession. feared God and turned away from evil. Job's character embodies awe and respect for God, shunning all who would offend Him. This verdict is endorsed by God in 1:8 and 2:3.

Job is blessed with a large family. Retribution theology (Introduction: Genre) would argue that this is a sign of Job's righteousness and that its loss a sign of his sin. As this book will reveal, however, this kind of retribution theology is far too simplistic to explain God's providential dealings with his people.
Patriarchal wealth is measured by numbers of livestock (see Gen. 30:43).
There was a prearranged program for these festivities, perhaps in connection with their birthdays.

Job is rightly concerned for the spiritual welfare of his children. offer burnt offerings. By this means of grace the patriarch Job, like Abraham (Gen. 15:9, 10), fills the role of priest for the family, consecrating his children to God. In the epilogue Job again plays an intercessory role (42:8, 9). cursed God in their hearts. The Hebrew reads lit. "blessed God," but that is a euphemism to avoid uttering "curse" next to "God." Cursing God is a sin in which Job himself will be tested (v. 11).

The writer reveals the developments in heaven and their consequences on earth that lead to Job's suffering, first regarding his possessions and family (vv. 6–22) and then his physical well-being (2:1–10). 1:6–12 The first of two scenes in heaven depicting the divine council and focusing on an encounter between the Lord (Yahweh) and Satan. As the text note indicates, throughout chs. 1; 2 Satan is not a proper name but a descriptive term meaning "the adversary." While some argue that he is merely an angel who functions as the Lord's observer of affairs on earth, "also" (1:6) indicates that his presence is intrusive. Additional information will be revealed in later ages about his character, but here Satan is obviously more than a prosecutor. He opposes the will of God, in keeping with the role of the serpent in Gen. 3. In v. 9 he questions Job's religious motivation. The use of Yahweh, the covenant name of God, throughout chs. 1; 2 (also in 38:1; 40:1; 42) indicates that God is in a loving and merciful covenant relationship with Job. 1:6 Satan. See theological note "Satan." He is not a free agent but needs divine permission to proceed.
It is the Lord who initiates the interchange. Satan constantly scrutinizes human affairs to identify the vulnerable.
Job is honored by God, who approves of him as a true and faithful servant, i.e., one keeping the solemn oaths of the covenant relationship. It is God, not Satan, who singles out Job for testing.
Satan does not dispute Job's integrity but argues that Job's conduct is motivated by what he gets out of it rather than by a sincere attachment to the Lord.
Satan also insinuates that the only way God can get people to worship Him is by bribing them with protection and prosperity.
The question is whether Job, who was so sensitive to the possibility of his children's cursing God, will now sin that way himself.
The adversary is allowed to test Job, but at this point, only with regard to his possessions and family. Satan's activities are restricted to what is permitted by the Lord.

Satan delivers an assault on Job's possessions, servants, and, climactically, his children. Each time he leaves a single survivor to bring word to Job, but while one messenger is still relating his catastrophic news, another comes to tell of a further dire blow. Even so, Job remains steadfast in his belief that God is good.
The Sabeans were a tribe from the south Arabian desert. The Chaldeans were at this time a marauding tribe from north Arabia. Their descendants later became the rulers of Babylon.

Job utters a wisdom poem that portrays the discernment of quiet submission to the secret will of God. Everything belongs to the creator who gave it. God's people must praise Him for whatever He does with what is His. The word "blessed" (v. 21) is the same used in v. 11 for "cursed." By employing it here, the author is emphasizing how Job, though grief-stricken, has frustrated Satan's predictions in v. 11. However, v. 22 implies the testing is not yet over.
Further developments in heaven — another round of accusations from Satan — precede more suffering for Job on earth.

"Integrity" lit. "blamelessness." The sudden change from the words of 1:6–8 at the end of 2:1–3 shows how the adversary, who has lost the first round, is humiliated by God through a bit of irony. The same word ("for no reason," 1:9) Satan had used to accuse Job is used here, translated "without reason." It is the adversary who has done wrong, not Job.

Satan suggests that even Job's statement of faith in 1:21 is nothing but a ploy. Job is willing to sacrifice anything for his own skin. If God will only stretch out His hand and strike Job's body, then he will curse God to His face.

God permits the adversary to be used as His instrument to strike Job, a fact that bears on the problem of evil. Satan, as a creature, is reined in. He is allowed to go only as far as God permits. The word translated "spare" can be translated "safeguard"; it would appear that Satan is being held responsible for Job's life.

Notwithstanding Satan's divinely permitted (and divinely limited) attacks on Job's body, Job holds firm to his conviction that God is praiseworthy. 2:7 loathsome sores. We have no way of knowing the exact nature of the disease that affects Job's skin. But it is disfiguring and painful.
Perhaps by trial and error the ancients learned that the ashes were a place where disease would not spread. Or it may simply have been a way of lamenting.

Job's wife is unaware of God's guarantee that Job's life would not be taken. She does not doubt his integrity and may be speaking out of a misplaced sympathy, considering death to be preferable to the agony her husband is suffering. Whatever her motives, her intervention increases the pressure on Job to succumb to the temptation.

The Hebrew word for "foolish" or "fool" has to do with faithlessness and religious apostasy, as in Ps. 14:1 (see also Ps. 53:1). It is more an ethical judgment than an intellectual one. Job did not sin with his lips. This stress on the purity of Job's speech is an anticipation of the contrast that will come in the dialogue, where Job's words are less pure.

In the final paragraph of the prologue, Job's friends arrive to comfort him in the midst of his terrible suffering. They live in different localities, and the time taken for news to reach them, to make arrangements for the visit, and to travel to Job implies that his sufferings were already prolonged when they arrived (see 7:3). They are introduced as a group, and they share a similar outlook. Although they will become highly critical of Job, their visit is well-intentioned.
An indication of the severity of Job's physical affliction. wept \... robes \... sprinkled dust. Cultural expressions of distress and anxiety.

This behavior, tied to the number of completeness (seven), expresses the most intense form of grief they can display. For the practice of mourning seven days over the dead, see Gen. 50:10. By conforming to Near Eastern protocol, which demands that Job should be the first to break the silence, the friends exhibit sympathy and wisdom in a way that they fail to do when they actually do speak.

Job breaks the weeklong silence with a fiercely emotional lamentation. He expresses the same kind of depression that overtook the psalmist (Ps. 88) and Jeremiah (Jer. 20:14, 15), whose bitter lament is similar to Job's in language.

Job does not curse God, but he goes so far as to question God's wisdom in giving him life. It is also significant that although Job is mentally and spiritually at the breaking point, it does not cross his mind to take his own life.

Job wishes for the nonexistence of the day of his birth. This curse would reverse creation and introduce darkness rather than light into that day. If the day had never existed, then neither would Job.
Refers to the night of v. 3; the thought is that it would be better for Job if he had never been conceived.

Job refers to enchanters who claim they can rouse the seven-headed monster of the deep (41:1 note). The thought may be that the monster will cause an eclipse by swallowing the sun or the moon. No sun would indicate no calendar day on which Job's birth could occur.
That is, of the night of his conception. The morning stars are to be extinguished rather than usher in the dawn. "Eyelids of the morning" personifies dawn, a dawn that Job wishes had never come.

Verses 3–10 are set in the form of curses, while these are rhetorical questions, perhaps uttered more musingly. Job gives vent to his frustration, asking why he did not die at or just after birth (vv. 11, 12, 16) so as to escape his present agony. Since that did not happen, in vexation he moves on to ask rhetorically why he should not now experience premature death (vv. 20, 23).
Either those of his mother as she holds him in her lap or of his father who acknowledges him as his legitimate son (see Gen. 50:23).

At this early stage of divine revelation, Job's view of existence after death is colored by what will be absent in death. There will no longer be the striving of the mighty after greater achievements (vv. 14, 15) or harassment from the wicked (v. 17) or maltreatment of the oppressed (v. 18). Death, the great leveler (v. 19), brings an end to earthly agony — including that of Job.
Job is speaking under intense emotional pressure; his thought here is not consecutive but reverts to the theme of vv. 11, 12.

Job generalizes from his situation to include all who suffer. Unlike 1:10, the divine hedge in v. 23 is one that prevents an afflicted individual from seeing a way of escape from his situation. Job questions how living is worthwhile for one engulfed by misery. 3:20 the bitter in soul. Those experiencing intense inward vexation and distress about God's providential dealings with them (7:11; 10:1; 27:2 and notes).
That is, an experience of physical suffering and spiritual desolation such as has overwhelmed Job.

The weeklong silence has been broken by Job's anguished outburst (ch. 3), after which his friends can no longer keep silent. They speak in turn, probably in order of seniority, and Job responds to each contribution. All the speakers accept a simplistic "retribution principle," whereby God controls the world by punishing anyone who sins and rewards whoever does what is right. Job's friends, however, hold that the reverse is also true: whoever suffers has sinned and whoever is blessed is righteous. As such, there is a one-to-one correspondence between sin and suffering; since Job is suffering so greatly, he has sinned greatly. At first they just hint at this (5:8; 8:6; 11:14), but when Job fails to accept their analysis, they become more open and ferocious in their attacks. Though ultimately it is true that God punishes (impenitent) sinners and rewards (those whom He mercifully declares to be) righteous people, Job's friends err in believing that every instance of suffering is an application of this principle. 4:1–5:27 The name Eliphaz means "my God is gold," but that does not contribute to understanding the present account. He comes from Teman in Edom, a locale with a reputation for wisdom (Jer. 49:7).

Eliphaz is the least caustic of Job's three friends, at least in his first speech. Compare these opening words, which assume Job is innocent (v. 7), with 22:1–11, where he is fully convinced Job is getting what he deserves. Job is complimented for being a wisdom teacher who in the past has helped the discouraged (vv. 3, 4), but in v. 5 he is warned lest he fails in his suffering to apply to himself what he once taught others.

Lit. "your fear." Eliphaz acknowledges the genuine piety that controls Job's life (see 1:1). His question is put in such a way as to encourage Job that his present distress will not last. According to Eliphaz's theology, any interruption of the good fortune of the pious can only be temporary.

Eliphaz assures Job that God will preserve the righteous and bring the wicked to an early grave. However, even from the death of Abel (Gen. 4:8–11; 1 John 3:12), and especially in the death of Christ, it is evident that the retribution principle is not the only factor determining God's providential rule.

Eliphaz bases his advice on personal observation (5:3 note; 15:17 note), but personal observation and experience is a limited basis for wisdom. sow trouble reap the same. Such wisdom cannot be denied, but does it apply to Job? Is retribution imposed as immediately as Eliphaz implies? This approach also fails to allow for the activity of divine grace, where we reap what we have not sown.
Five different words are used to describe lions. Their strong appearance does not mean that they can thwart the operation of universal law. No more can the wicked escape divine judgment.

Although Eliphaz is unsure of the identity of the one who visited him in his night vision (v. 16), he is certain he received authoritative, supernatural revelation. It is always necessary, however, to test the genuineness of such an experience (see 1 John 4:1).

It is unclear where the message Eliphaz heard ends. The ESV extends the quotation to the end of v. 21, but it may only consist of v. 17, in which case the remaining verses expand on what Eliphaz heard. 4:17 in the right before God. Although this may also be translated "more righteous than God" (text note), that rendering is implausible in this context. Eliphaz is not (yet) implying that Job has become so conceited. The rhetorical questions emphasize human moral inadequacy. Whether weak ("mortal man") or strong ("man" at the height of his powers), "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Rom. 3:23). Job therefore has no ground for complaint against God (see 9:1 for Job's rejoinder).
Even angels are not exempt from divine criticism and rebuke, so Job should not expect to avoid it.
A reference to the human body (10:9; 33:6; cf. Gen. 2:7). Job shares the frailty of all mankind, and his departure will attract as little attention as a moth being swatted.
That is, their death is without any purpose and therefore meaningless. They "perish forever" (v. 20) with no rationale for their lives.

Eliphaz asserts that no other being, human or angelic, is in a position to extend help to Job as he endures the troubles that are common to mankind. The idea of mediatorial assistance is a theme that Job will repeatedly take up later (9:33; 16:19, 20; 19:25). 5:1 To which of the holy ones will you turn. None of the "sons of God" (1:6), the holy angels, would dare to help Job or could do so in the light of the assessment of 4:18.

An intense emotional reaction to circumstances, such as that displayed by Job in ch. 3. "Jealousy," envy of the lot of others, perhaps reflects Job's desire to have been stillborn (3:16). Although Eliphaz is speaking in general terms, there is no doubt that he is alleging Job's behavior to be that of "the fool" and "the simple," wisdom language for those lacking spiritual insight.
Eliphaz views himself as approving of, and participating in, the retribution that will inevitably overturn the fortunes of the wicked.
Even though it is presented as a proverbial truth, the implied reference to Job's family is still insensitive (see 1:18, 19).
Eliphaz's point is that trouble does not spring up spontaneously like a weed but is inevitably reaped by those who sow it.

Lit. "the sons of Resheph fly upward." Resheph was the god of pestilence, lightning, and destruction. A similar idiom is used in Song 8:6, where love is described as "flashes of fire." In other places the idiom is used for bolts of lightning (Ps. 78:48) and of pestilence (Deut. 32:24; Hab. 3:5). From the day an individual is born, any activity generates frustration and woe as inevitably as a fire generates sparks.

Since Eliphaz cannot conceive of another being intervening effectively, he advises Job to appeal to God for assistance. In general, this is good advice, but implicit here is the misplaced assumption that Job has deliberately sinned in a heinous manner. For Job to seek God would require repentance and a request for forgiveness, but Job knows that he has not acted in a reprehensible fashion. 5:8 commit my cause. Hints at a legal interpretation of the dialogues (9:3 note).

Paul cites the first line of this verse in 1 Cor. 3:19 to establish divine superiority over those who consider themselves to be wise. The problem with Job's counselors is not so much ignorance of the truth as the wrongheaded and partial application of it.
A reference to slander (see v. 21).

Eliphaz informs Job why he should not despise God's dealings with him. Whoever accepts divine correction will be restored and blessed (see Prov. 3:11, 12). This reference to the disciplinary nature of human suffering is the only place in the speeches of the three counselors where the subject is even broached. Job is only at the first stage of a process that will lead to healing and recovery (v. 18). In vv. 19–22, the second line reinforces the theme of the first line. 5:17 the Almighty. The first of thirty-one times that "the Almighty" is used in Job to render the Hebrew term Shaddai (Gen. 17:1 note). The title is most commonly thought to be derived from an Akkadian word meaning "mountain" and conveys the thought that God is mountain-like, that is, enduring, imposing, majestic, and awe inspiring. The rendering "Almighty" dates back to the Septuagint and associates this name of God with his supreme power and total sovereignty over creation.
A poetic expression meaning "many."

This may well be figurative language describing an Edenic condition before the curse imposed after the fall. Job's physical environment would no longer frustrate his attempts at cultivation. Alternatively, some read this as "in league with the offspring of the field" to reflect the other side of the parallelism that reads, "the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you." Since wild animals often kill domestic animals, this fits the context, where in v. 22 Eliphaz says Job has no need to fear the beasts of the earth.
Considering that Job has lost all his children, the statement is both unnecessary and cruel.
At this point neither Job nor Eliphaz can imagine that this statement will come true for Job (see 42:16, 17).

Eliphaz commends to Job the conclusions reached by wisdom teachers (including Eliphaz) regarding the blessings that come to the repentant. However, the generalization, which is an expression of simplistic retribution theology, is not invariably true, and, crucially, his advice to Job to repent is based on a complete misunderstanding of the origin of Job's sufferings.

Job often does not directly respond to the arguments of his friends. Here he begins with introspective soliloquy before upbraiding Eliphaz for uttering presumptuous, insensitive, not to mention false, words about him (6:14–30); then in ch. 7 he addresses his complaint to God.
Job speaks out of his anguish and argues that if the extent of his suffering were accurately assessed, it would be seen as more than sufficient to warrant his complaints.
Job excuses his raging by fantasizing that God has become his enemy. He shares Eliphaz's presupposition that this suffering is divinely imposed, but Job does not know why.
Job's questions expect a negative answer. The vehemence of his speech has arisen from his distressing circumstances.
Eliphaz has offered him no real food (v. 5), i.e., words of comfort. What was supposed to be good food (words of comfort from friends) has made Job sick.

Job does not contemplate suicide. Rather, he affirms that the only comfort left to him is the exquisite release from pain that death, sent by God, would bring. He strongly affirms continued faith in God. This passage shows that Job believes in a blissful afterlife.
As a weaver cuts a thread, so would God bring Job's earthly existence to an end.

The first of Job's affirmations of innocence (see 9:21; 16:17; 27:6). He has lived by God's words (commands) and is unaware of how he has offended God and brought such suffering on himself. Such a declaration does not ring true as far as his friends are concerned. For them Job's suffering clearly proves otherwise.
In a series of rhetorical questions, Job affirms that he is drained of strength and unable to endure much longer.

Job complains that his friends have acted improperly in not displaying toward him kindness or steadfast love, that is, the protection and assistance appropriate to a committed relationship. Even though Job knows he is innocent, he still needs companionship and sympathy. Their response has been deficient.

Intensifies their insensitivity. It reminds one of Judas (John 13:18) or the disciples (Matt. 26:40). torrent-bed. In the rainy season a wadi turns into a raging torrent, but in summer, when water is needed, it dries up. In his extended metaphor (6:15–20), Job pictures desert travelers seeking water from such wadis, only to be disappointed.

Plural, referring to the three counselors. Even though Job had not sought costly favors from them, they were afraid to help him. They would rather maintain their theology than allow for an exception. Such an admission would deprive them of the satisfaction they derive from their ability to analyze the circumstances of life.
Job asks his friends to give him real help by providing direct evidence of the wrongdoing they allege he must have committed.

The difference between Job and his friends is summed up here. The speeches of the friends are formally correct but do not necessarily apply to Job. Indeed, the friends falsely accuse Job of having lived a sinful life. Job insists on speaking honest words about his life: he has never forsaken God or lived in a profligate way.
Later, Job will speak of his loving care for the fatherless (31:16–22). His name possibly means "without a father."
Lit. "is in it." The "it" is their insistence that he is suffering for his sins. Either he or they must be wrong.
In vv. 6, 7 Job spoke of their words as bad food. Here he pleads that they change what they are feeding him.

Job reverts to soliloquy in which he at first reflects on the harsh lot of mankind in general (vv. 1, 2) before describing his own circumstances (vv. 3–6). Whereas the shadows of evening bring relief to the slave toiling under the sun and a hired hand can expect due payment, in his despair Job has nothing to look forward to (v. 6). 7:1 hard service. The terminology often refers to military service, but here it describes the inescapable rigors of life in general.
Job's malady may be a combination of diseases. Repulsive symptoms, however, have appeared all over his skin, the largest and most sensitive bodily organ.
The term "hope" skillfully extends the weaving metaphor of the preceding line; there is a similarly spelled word meaning "cord" or "thread" (see Josh. 2:18).

The singular form of the verb "remember" (v. 7) shows that God is now being addressed as Job sets out the brevity of earthly existence for himself and for mankind generally. Comparable sentiments about life as "a breath" are found in the Psalms (see Pss. 39:4–6; 62:9; 144:3, 4). But reflecting on human transience turns the psalmists to God, whereas Job reacts bleakly and holds out no hope for himself. 7:7 never again see good. Worse than pain is the loss of hope for a return to health.
The language of appearance. Job is not developing a doctrine but merely stating what all observe. Later, Job will show he believes in the possibility of resurrection (14:12–15).

Job refuses to go quietly and sets out the grounds of his complaint regarding God's unremitting and harsh treatment. 7:11 will not restrain my mouth. Like the psalmist who had to give vent to his emotionally distraught feelings (Ps. 39:3), Job insists on complaining out of his "bitterness of soul" (3:20 note). Note that here he complains to God, not to man.

The Hebrew uses "sea" as a proper name here without the definite article. This is poetic language for the boisterous Canaanite deity Yam (sea). Job does not worship Yam, but he knows the story about him. a sea monster. Possibly a reference to Tiamat, who, according to Babylonian myth, was overcome and held captive by the god Marduk to create the ordered world of human existence. Job complains that God is treating him in a disproportionately harsh fashion. set a guard. An instance of dramatic irony in the light of the prologue, esp. 2:6. God had been guarding Job but not in the restrictive manner Job thought.
Job imagines that God is actually doing all this. The reader knows from the prologue that God permitted Satan to do it. Yet that permission is within God's sovereign ordination.
Job sees death as the way out, but Satan has not been permitted to go that far, nor would death serve Satan's purpose of getting Job to curse God to His face.
Again, Job imagines that God is the one who torments him. We know from the prologue, however, that God has a high and holy purpose in permitting Satan to touch Job.

A similar thought is expressed positively in Pss. 8:4 and 144:3. The psalmist marvels that God cares so much for the creature He has made in His own image. But Job, in his distress, wishes that God would leave him alone.
Subject to scrutiny and examination (23:10 note).
Job thinks God is too critical and eager to find faults. For what sin is God punishing him so severely?

Though Job will stress his integrity (i.e., his honest commitment to godliness and righteousness), he never denies being a sinner. Job argues that if he has committed such heinous sin as to warrant his suffering, God should deal with the matter immediately and forgive him. That God does not implies that He must prefer to punish rather than forgive. But Job's agony is so intense that without immediate relief, his death seems inevitable.

This short contribution reveals Bildad to be a blunt and unfeeling person. He has failed to hear Job's cry for compassion (6:13, 14, 26). His message to Job is forthright: he and his family have received what they deserve. Now if only Job will repent of the shameless deeds that brought on this disaster, he can be restored to even greater prosperity and happiness than he had before. 8:1–7 Bildad reveals his impatience at Job's attempts to clear himself and at his failure to accept the counsel offered to him. 8:1 Bildad the Shuhite. Bildad's name may be an Aramaic compound of the names of two gods, Baal and Hadad. Shuah was a son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen. 25:2), whose descendants were located in northeast Arabia. Like the other counselors, Bildad is not of Israelite descent.

A strong accusation, picking up on and intensifying Job's expression in 6:26. It is unlike the tone of Eliphaz, who attempted a soft approach at first (4:2). On the basis of Job's suffering, Bildad is sure that Job's protestations are all bluster, with no real content.
Bildad rebuts what he infers is Job's position, that God is unjust. "Pervert" conveys the thought of twisting what is straight out of shape.
Bildad expresses himself with a veneer of sensitivity, though it is clear what he really thinks. Those who offend God die, and conversely those who die young must have offended God grievously.

In Bildad's mind, God has mercy only when human beings deserve it. Mercy, however, cannot ever be deserved. In Bildad's interpretation of the situation, he is offering Job a way out of his misery. He not only urges repentance but also points to good works as the basis of enjoying God's favor.

Eliphaz appealed to revelation as his authority, even though that revelation was somewhat enigmatic (4:12–17). Bildad appeals to human tradition. He has not invented his theology but inherited it from former generations whose views were accorded great respect in the ancient Near East.

Bildad sets out in general terms traditional teaching regarding conduct and rewards. Illustrations drawn from the natural world show the invariable connection between cause and effect. Without water, plants cannot grow.

This Hebrew word occurs eight times in Job (8:13; 13:16; 15:34; 17:8; 20:5; 27:8; 34:30; 36:13) and refers to someone who is arrogant and defiant in rebellion against God and so is profane or defiled by sin. Obviously, Bildad sees Job as a case in point.
The hope of the godless provides no more substantial a foundation for life than a spider's web.
The description is of a prolific plant with shallow roots. If such superficial support is removed, the plant collapses. Similarly, the success of the wicked soon passes.

The heart of Bildad's theology of suffering. As standard wisdom it is not wrong. Ps. 1:6 teaches that the Lord cares about the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish. Bildad's error is that Job's suffering indicates Job is godless. take the hand of evildoers. An action associated with providing guidance and security.

Job does not give an item-by-item rejoinder to all that Bildad has said, though he does display an awareness of Bildad's points. Job starts with a discourse on God's power and wisdom (9:1–13) but shifts to questioning His justice (9:14–35). In 9:28–31 he begins to direct his words to God, which continues through ch. 10.

Job makes extensive use of legal terminology because he considers that God is treating him as guilty of some offense. Job is unable to mount an effective challenge against God because of the power God possesses. 9:2 Truly I know that it is so. Job has no quarrel with Bildad's view that God punishes the wicked and cares for the righteous (Ps. 1:6). But why then is he suffering? Job accepts the retribution principle just as much as Bildad and the other friends, which is why he has an insoluble problem. Convinced as he is of his integrity and acutely aware of his suffering, Job's presuppositions can lead him to conclude only that God has unfairly perceived him as guilty. But how can a man be in the right before God? Job is concerned about the impossible task of trying to establish a case before, and against, God.

This term introduces a significant theme in Job — initiating litigation against God. "To contend" is to lodge a complaint or accusation against someone. Job is uncertain if this is possible to do against God. He does not anticipate that God Himself will be his cross-examiner at the end of his story (38:3; 40:7).

The creative initiative and overwhelming power of the God whom Job worships far exceed anything attributed by pagan mythology to their gods, singly or combined. Job reverently asserts that the one true God is unique and supreme. Job is challenged to learn this lesson anew in chs. 38–41. Here Job's perception of God's power leads him to conclude that he is incapable of mounting a successful challenge to God's ways.
The earth is described poetically as having subterranean architecture.
The reference is to an eclipse of the sun and the disappearance of certain stars over the seasons.
The poetic figures in this verse refer to God's creation and control of the forces of nature.
Job refers to various constellations, emphasizing God's creative power and thus the foolishness of contending with Him (see 38:31, 32).

Job accepts that God is present in creation, but he has been unable to catch sight of Him to present his case. Job's situation is frustrating because no one can reverse God's actions or demand an explanation of them — something Job himself is (inconsistently) doing.

Job argues that God is too stubborn to listen to his arguments and review his case. Rahab. Rahab is the Semitic sea monster defeated at creation in the myths of non-Israelite peoples. See 26:12. "The helpers" are associated demonic powers involved in maintaining the turbulence and disorder of the sea. In Ps. 87:4 and Is. 30:7, Rahab also functions as a symbol of Egypt.

Job has no doubt about his innocence and desires an audience with God to prove it. But he concludes that even if that were granted, he would still lose because he would become so confused that he would be unable to present his case effectively. Indeed, God's power is such that He would overwhelm Job.

These verses represent a low point in Job's speeches. As happens to many who suffer greatly over a long period, Job is tempted toward fatalism. He wavers between hope and doubt and even accuses God. 9:21 I am blameless. Job is not self-deluded when he characterizes himself in this way (see 1:1, 8; 2:3). I regard not myself. If God is no longer interested in treating him equitably, Job does not care whether he lives or dies.

This is symbolic not of impartiality but of their indifference to administering justice. God is unjust in treating the blameless and the wicked alike (v. 22). He even allows the wicked to prosper and have the upper hand (see Ps. 73). if it is not he, who then is it. These sad but profound words reflect Job's belief in the absolute sovereignty of God, apart from which he would not feel such perplexity. But as things stand, Job finds God and His actions utterly impenetrable and unjust.

In despair, Job focuses on his situation. His days pass as rapidly as a runner, a swift but fragile boat, and an eagle swooping to bring a violent end. Time is running out to have his situation resolved. Putting on a brave face will not help alleviate his suffering if God still condemns him (vv. 27–29).

A plant-based extract used in laundering clothes. No matter what efforts Job might make to cleanse himself of the great sin his friends are convinced he has committed, it will accomplish nothing. God will continue to treat him unfairly (v. 32).

Eliphaz taunted Job with the thought that no heavenly being would think of defending him (5:1). Here Job recognizes his inadequacy in dealing with God and expresses a longing for another to intervene (text note) and also regrets that there is no one who can bring both parties together. He will return to this theme again (see 16:19–21; 19:23–27; see also 33:23–27). Job touches a profound truth: that sinful man needs an arbiter who can reach both God and man. Although not a direct prediction, this verse foresees the need of the "one mediator between God and men" (1 Tim. 2:5).

Since there is no one else to do it, Job sets out his case against God. He does not claim to be sinless, but according to the terms of the simplistic retribution theology to which he subscribes, he does want to prove that he has done nothing to deserve his suffering. Yet while Job is driven to voice severe complaints against God, he does not curse or abandon Him. 10:1 I loathe my life. Job expresses wearied frustration with his life of suffering (see 7:16; 9:21).
