Not only is Job willing to die, he is seeking death as his only means of escape (6:8, 9). Nothing worse can happen, so he will complain freely and bitterly (see 3:20).

He speaks on the assumption that the traditional view of suffering held by the counselors is correct. He has not been able to deliver himself from this view. Therefore, he has wrongly concluded that God is angry with him but has refused to specify the grounds for His treatment of Job.
Lit. "Is it good?" A better translation may be, "Is it right?" favor the designs of the wicked. See 9:24. No wonder God will later accuse Job of discrediting His justice (40:8).

Here is irony. Job knows God is omniscient and does not have to search out sins as a human prosecutor does. God knows Job is innocent, yet He has made Job His helpless victim. Job accuses God of hounding Him and acting like a bully.

Like the author of Ps. 139:13–16, Job understands that God fashioned him in the womb, gave him life, and blessed him. In another context, vv. 11, 12 would constitute grounds for praise, but here Job cannot understand how God can treat him so badly. Job is leveling a charge of inconsistency against God.
Job seems to say that his plight is a divine punishment planned from the beginning of his life. He does not understand that God's plan in his suffering is something other than punishment.
All this is predicated on the mistaken assumption that his ordeal is due to God's punitive wrath. In Job's mind, nothing he does can relieve him of God's unremitting hostility toward him.

Though "my head" is not expressed in the text (text note), it is readily supplied. The thought is either of Job's getting up off the ground or his achieving some measure of success in prosecuting his case against God. Three metaphors are used to show God's reaction were that to happen: (1) He would renew His attacks on Job like a lion; (2) He would provide additional witnesses against him in court (v. 17); and (3) He would resume His attacks on Job with fresh troops (v. 17).

Job again wishes he had never been born (see 3:10). His unremitting pain has rendered his life worthless. His tone is no longer the patient resignation of 1:21 but of embittered protest at the treatment he has received at the hand of God.

Notice the difference between Job's present description of that place as a land of darkness (using four nouns of similar meaning to intensify the picture), while in 3:13–19 he looked on it as being a place of peace and rest. This proves that Job's emotional raging must not be used as a basis for constructing normative OT or Christian theology. The rule of interpretation to be observed is that when Job or the counselors are in agreement with the testimony of the rest of Scripture, their statements may be accepted. But in the dramatic flow of the book, neither he nor they can be relied on as a sure source of theological formulations and their correct applications. All of them say much that is correct, but they apply it wrongly to the situation at hand.

Zophar, the most severe of Job's counselors, now speaks his mind on Job's plight and bluntly presents recommendations based on the assumptions that Job has spoken presumptuously regarding his character (v. 4) and that he is willfully concealing his wrongdoing and refraining from confessing serious sin. Zophar speaks in a cold, rationalistic fashion, seemingly more concerned with putting Job in his place than extending him any comfort. 11:1 the Naamathite. Possibly from Arabia; not from the Naamah mentioned in Josh. 15:41, which was in the western foothills of Judah.
Zophar is indignant with Job and mocks him because he has said much without true substance.

Not an exact quotation of Job, who has not said he was sinless (see 7:21; 13:26). He has claimed not to have led the kind of sinful life that might deserve such severe suffering, but he has also admitted that no mortal can be righteous before God (9:2).

The image is of something folded double so that its full extent is not immediately revealed. God's wisdom is far greater than Job supposes. If God were to expose all of Job's sin, it would be far greater than Job imagines. Far from a divine audience leading to Job's vindication, it would leave him liable to greater punishment. less than your guilt deserves. The words reflect Zophar's supposition of the enormity of Job's sin.

Zophar picks up on Job's reference to God's wisdom (9:4) and argues that Job cannot fathom the wisdom of God, who is inaccessible and inscrutable. Verses 7–9 are an eloquent expression of the transcendence of God, which Zophar then misapplies. Job therefore cannot successfully oppose God in court. Ironically, Zophar has no doubts about his own perception of God. It is this misperception that is corrected in the epilogue (42:7–9).

God is capable of assessing who is "worthless," a term implying deceitful behavior. "A stupid man" is empty-headed and without spiritual capacity; it would take a miracle to make him see sense. Zophar speaks in general terms, but he is clearly taking aim at Job.

While this is good advice for a profligate sinner, it does not properly apply to Job. Like Bildad, Zophar makes no allowance for mercy. Instead he argues that Job has to become righteous before God will accept him and give him the benefits of restoration.

Zophar is arrogant to think he knows why Job is suffering. We know from the prologue that it is not because Job sinned. Job was called by God to join that grand company of innocent sufferers for the glory of the Lord.
Zophar contrasts the end of the wicked to the blessedness of the righteous (vv. 15–19). He implies that if Job persists in his current attitude, he can expect to share the fate of the wicked.

Job's long speech starts with a blast of sarcasm against his counselors, which continues to 13:19. Beginning in 13:20, Job turns to God, creating a major break in the speech. Job's inclination to talk to God (to pray) stands in notable contrast to the counselors, who never say a word to God but only talk about Him.
The forms in vv. 2, 3 are plural. Job replies caustically to the insinuations of his friends. They think they know everything, but he is their equal.

Job agonizes over being made a laughingstock, even to his friends. He remembers times of familiarity with God and contrasts them with what has come upon him, while evildoers and idolaters live in ease and security. Job claims that divine administration of justice is awry.
The translation is uncertain, but the thought seems to be that they can easily control and manipulate the gods they worship.

The forms in these verses are now singular, probably referring to Zophar alone. ask the beasts \... the earth. Like Eliphaz, who called upon revelation to support his arguments, and Bildad, who called upon tradition, Job calls on every creature in the universe to bear witness to his argument that the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer.

LORD. Only here in the poetic discourses is Yahweh, the covenant name of God, used. While some take this as evidence of a later insertion into the text, its rare occurrence points to its significance. God is acting even in these circumstances with personal care and attention. Its use is not anachronistic, though its full significance has not yet been revealed. Job uses the name in 1:21, where he also acknowledges that calamities come from the Lord.
Can also be translated as a question: "Shouldn't wisdom be found among the aged?" The verse is ironic and aimed at the counselors, who are old but have not become wise.

In this unit of poetry, Job expounds the doctrine of God's sovereign freedom. Some have interpreted this as subtle criticism of God for mismanaging the universe. According to that view, God is limited and needs to be "forgiven" by His creatures. But throughout this book, even when Job is raging over his suffering and suggesting doubts about God's justice, he always takes for granted that God is sovereign and that man can make no effective objection to what He does. Job wrestles with a mystery, one too deep for his shallow counselors. This part of the speech may be provoked by Zophar's question in 11:7, "Can you find out the deep things of God?" The poem may also be a reply to Eliphaz's hymn in 5:1–26, where only good things happen to good people. Such an idea is refuted in this stanza.

Job's understanding of how God can reverse the circumstances of the wise and powerful is implicitly turned on his friends. Though they are old and considered to be wise, God has left them in the dark when it comes to considering what has overwhelmed Job.

Job acknowledges that he has listened to his friends (v. 1), but he is just as capable as they ("you" is plural) are and dismisses their counsel as worthless. While Job states that he wants to argue his case with God (v. 3), he does not do so immediately and continues to address his friends. They have not listened to him or heard what he has been saying (v. 6), and therefore they have failed to diagnose his situation correctly. They can only expect divine rebuke for their mishandling of the situation (v. 10).
An audience with God would bring matters into the open.
The arguments the friends have advanced to justify God's present treatment of Job are without substance and unable to withstand pressure.
Job returns to the thought suggested in v. 3. He has decided that he must have an audience with God, no matter the consequences.
He is fearful that he might not survive an audience with God.

Often quoted as the supreme expression of trust in God. Job is confident that he will have an audience with God and that this will bring about his deliverance — "the godless shall not come before him." Moreover, v. 18 makes clear that Job is positive about his being vindicated when he comes before the Lord. The words "in the right" imply that Job will be demonstrably vindicated in his claim that he is innocent of the counselors' false charges. Job's outlook is fluctuating. Earlier, in despair, he claimed that God would not acquit him (9:28). in him. The ESV translation follows the marginal reading of the Masoretic Text ("I will hope in him") whereas the text note follows the body of that text ("I have no hope"). The latter rendering makes the utterance an expression of Job's desperation as he sets out his case against God. Both readings make sense in the context, but the former is more probable in light of the positive note Job strikes in v. 18.

The verb "grant" (v. 20) and the references to "you" and "your" (vv. 20, 21) are singular, addressed to God. This is in contrast to the second-person plural references in v. 17, addressed to the counselors.

Job trusts that his sins do not include the sort of unbridled wickedness that might justify his terrible suffering. He too accepts the counselors' basic premise of the retribution principle, but what he is suffering is disproportionate to any offense he has committed. Here Job views himself as the defendant in a case brought against him by God and demands that the charges be specified. See notes on 11:4 and 29:7–17.

To withdraw the blessing of spiritual access to God. and count me as your enemy. This is the delusive fantasy with which Job is struggling. God has not considered Job His enemy. There is a play on Job's name, which has the same consonants as "enemy." This, however, does not establish that the name Job means "enemy" or "one experiencing enmity."
Frail, worthless objects that are unable to resist outside forces. This is how Job perceives himself.
Job considers that God can have against him only failures of the distant past, and he is at a loss to see why they are exposed now, and why they warrant such extreme treatment.
Probably the opening line of the poem in 14:1–6. In this poem Job's mood slumps into despondency, and he imagines that God is constantly punishing human beings for their misdeeds.

Job laments the futility and brevity of life. Under God's scrutiny, an individual's failings are readily exposed. Although Job speaks generally, he really has his own situation in view (see v. 3), and he begs God to let him have peace to enjoy his few remaining days (see 7:19).

Having concluded that death is the only escape from suffering, Job suggests that God let him die and then raise him up after His anger has cooled down. The reader, however, knows God was never angry to begin with. This chapter does not clearly teach a doctrine of resurrection (yet see v. 14), but it shows an awareness of the subject. 14:7–12 Job contrasts the experience of a man and a tree. A tree may be cut down and new shoots spring from its stump; there is no such hope for a man to have a second chance in this world. Death is final.
Job is doubtful that God will inflict a temporary death, and he concludes that He will not. But he believes in God's ability to do it. For Sheol, see note on Prov. 1:12.

Many argue that in light of the preceding verses, Job's question expects a decidedly negative answer. However, Job is looking beyond reentry into this life on earth. He is groping toward true postmortem existence. The doctrine of the resurrection had not yet been revealed with clarity and fullness in Job's day, but he senses that there must be more than mere annihilation after death. I would wait. Here, and in succeeding verses, some translate "would" as "will." The "service" of which Job speaks is in the state of death. renewal. A form of the word translated "sprout again" in v. 7. Job is looking for an experience in some way analogous to the tree enjoying new life.

Ordinarily translated "now." Between the two lines of the verse Job is contrasting his present experience of divine scrutiny with what he expects in the future when God calls him and he answers. His sin will no longer confront him because it will be divinely sealed. Job's thinking is still conditioned by his acceptance of a simplistic retribution theology. He can explain his agony only by supposing there is some heinous offense of which he is unaware. His hope for the future arises through God's graciously finding a way of dealing with his sin.

Having glimpsed a graciously provided future, Job slumps again into despair and concludes that the world will go on as it has in the past, and those suffering like him will continue to have little hope. Indeed, he declares that God goes so far as to destroy man's hope (v. 19). All that will be left is the isolated introspection of those wrapped up in suffering (v. 22).

The three friends are dissatisfied with Job's failure to accept their assessment of his situation, an assessment based on arguing back from his suffering. In the second cycle of speeches, they maintain their verbal barrage against Job with increased vigor and bitterness. By describing the wicked and their fate, they hope Job will be induced to recognize his position and act in terms of their conclusions. Job, however, continues to maintain his innocence of any wrongdoing commensurate with the suffering he is enduring, and he continues to protest that God is acting unjustly. Increasingly, Job adopts the stance that a direct encounter with God will enable him to get the record set straight. 15:1–35 As before, Eliphaz leads off the cycle of speeches, moving away from the tactful approach he used in chs. 4; 5.

Although Eliphaz begins by speaking of "a wise man," it is clear that he is referring to Job, whose speech he disparages as irreverent and lacking content. 15:2 the east wind. The fierce sirocco, which blows in from the Arabian desert and scorches everything, producing no benefit for man, animal, or plant.
More than peer pressure has moved Eliphaz; it is also the raging coming from Job's lips.
Annulling or negating true piety. It is not just Job's past conduct that Eliphaz finds condemning but also his present behavior. Hidden, inner sinfulness is shaping Job's speech.

Eliphaz resorts to a series of rhetorical questions dripping with sarcasm to insult Job. 15:7 the first man. Since in Job's era wisdom is associated with age, Adam is viewed as possessing special wisdom and insight (see Ezek. 28:12, 13). Job has no well-founded claim to great wisdom.
Eliphaz returns to Job the very sarcasm Job used on him in 12:2.
He continues to answer Job using Job's own words. See 12:3; 13:2.
Job's irony in 12:12 is not lost on Eliphaz. He assures Job that all the elders are on the side of the counselors, not Job's.

Eliphaz's meaning is unclear. Possibly he means that his gentle counsel to Job has been given to him by God, and he is hurt that Job has not responded as expected to his exhortations. If so, Eliphaz has not grasped the full extent of Job's anguish.
Eliphaz considers that Job's emotions have got the better of his reasoning.

Eliphaz harks back to the oracle he received in 4:17. Cf. vv. 15, 16 with 4:18, 19. Fallen human beings are inherently flawed and therefore liable to experiences such as that which Job is undergoing. But Eliphaz does not know the facts of Job's situation as revealed in the prologue.

Based on personal experience (v. 17) and what the sages of old had perceived (v. 18), Eliphaz assures Job that the wicked are terrified throughout their lives by their fate (vv. 20–24). He particularly emphasizes the defiant attitudes of the wicked (vv. 25–27) and the calamitous end that awaits them (vv. 28–35). Whatever possessions they amass will soon be destroyed. Note how "flame will dry up" and "fire consumes" (vv. 30, 34), "the destroyer will come upon him" (v. 21), "his possessions spread" (v. 29), and "houses \... heaps of ruins" (v. 28) all match elements of Job's experience in ch. 1. Eliphaz uses shock tactics to force Job to recognize that this picture of the wicked fits him.
The thinking of the ancient sages was not affected by alien philosophies.
It is the defiance exhibited by the wicked that brings misfortune upon them. Job claimed that God was attacking him (7:20; 13:24), but Eliphaz asserts that reality is the other way around.
In Job's world, fat was a sign of prosperity and abundance (see Ps. 73:7). The thought is of self-indulgent affluence.
A grim, poetic description, but by affirming that these things happen to the wicked, Eliphaz goes beyond observable fact and thus fails to convince Job of his assertions.

Job begins by disparaging his friends' attempts to help him (vv. 2–5) and then complains about God's unfair treatment (vv. 6–9) in attacking him (vv. 10–17). He then expresses with a measure of confidence that a witness in heaven will pre­sent his case (vv. 18–21). But for all his seeming confidence, Job is a broken man at death's door (16:22–17:2). He is scornful of his friends' attitude (17:3–5) and traces it back to what God has done to him (17:6, 7). Such unfair divine behavior depresses the righteous, though they seek to carry on regardless (17:8, 9). Job, however, is without hope and can only wait for death (17:11–16).
They have not provided support for Job but have only increased his trouble and anxiety because they have failed to connect with the specific facts of his situation.
Job has grown weary not of the length of their speeches, but of their failure to say anything helpful.

The thought is rather, "I would strengthen you." Job imagines his own situation and that of his friends reversed. In that event, Job would not mimic their heartless and mocking behavior (v. 4) but would instead provide them with true comfort.
Job is exhausted by the torment he has endured, but he still maintains that he does not deserve such agony (see v. 17).
Again Job imagines God as his adversary. In v. 9 he compares God to a ferocious beast that has attacked him.
Job has had to endure the ignominy of human insults and abuse because God has exposed him to such disrespect.

The problem to be resolved, as far as Job is concerned, is God's violent action against him, like an attacking army. Though Job is wrong in assuming God is hostile toward him, it is the only explanation he can formulate. This is one of the low points of Job's ordeal.
The earth is personified as a witness to Job's unceasing suffering — indeed, his impending death. Job pleads that there be no cover-up of his cry for justice.

Job believes he has a witness in heaven, a notion that was summarily dismissed by Eliphaz in 5:1. But the thought has tremendous meaning for Job. He looks not for someone greater than God but for one who will present his case sympathetically to Him. It is not yet clear who Job expects this witness/advocate to be (19:25 note), but ultimately such a figure is only found in Jesus Christ (1 John 2:1). Job seems to express confidence in God as the source of justice and mercy.

The Hebrew may be understood in various ways. The ESV follows the more frequent meaning of the terms, in which case Job is emphasizing his utter aloneness (17:2 and note). However, there is substantial evidence to support a rendering such as "My intercessor is my friend." The term translated "intercessor," "interpreter," or "go-between" is translated "mediator" in 33:23, and the plural as "mediators" (Is. 43:27). If that is the case, the activity of the go-between is described in v. 21.

In his distress, Job looks for relief through death. Through his tears, he can only perceive his friends, who are adding to his sorrow by their unsympathetic attitude (17:2). Job, however, boldly pleads with God to guarantee that he will be vindicated before his friends. 16:22 This verse goes better with ch. 17 (13:8 note), a fact that serves as a reminder that the chapter divisions are not original. Job longs for death as a release from his constant pain (14:13), although he expects to live "a few years" longer. He does not entertain any assurance of respite and considers himself to be at death's door.
The reference must be to the three friends, possibly others also. He cannot escape their antipathy.

The question may well imply that Job wants God to vindicate him, i.e., to prove to the counselors that he is in the right. This would support the idea that in 16:19–21 the advocate Job is searching for is God Himself. While Job has been driven to conclude that God is persecuting and wronging him, he still feels that the resolution to his situation can be provided only by God Himself.
The minds of the counselors.

Job cites a proverb that asserts that those who act for a reward will be punished. This is a veiled threat to the friends who falsely accuse Job in order to alleviate their unease that their theology cannot explain Job's circumstances.

Job can see no hope for himself in this life and again looks forward to death. 17:6 Since God has not vindicated him, he continues to hold God responsible for his frightful condition. See 30:10. byword. A negative example and therefore exposed to disdain and ignominy (see 30:9).

The symptoms of his disease include boils, other skin problems, and nightmares (2:7; 7:5, 14). Here and in 19:20 there is weight loss; and in 19:17, bad breath; in 30:30, fever; and in 30:17, pain day and night.
Job is in effect expressing strong disapproval of the way his friends have viewed his situation.

Again Job sarcastically challenges the counselors to diagnose and remedy his situation. He is sure they will be exposed as lacking wisdom because of the foolish optimism of the contorted arguments they present (v. 12).
Job appears to remember Zophar's words in 11:17.
Sheol is envisaged as an underground city, the gates of which are held shut by wooden beams.

Bildad speaks out of irritation that Job continues to disparage the advice given by the friends (vv. 2–4). He makes no appeal for Job to respond but impatiently repeats his earlier exposition on the destiny of the wicked (see 8:8–19), emphasizing that the wicked will be identified by the way they live (vv. 8–10).
Bildad accuses Job of using words to cover up his unwillingness to accept the reality of his situation.
Bildad's sense of self-importance has been offended by Job's accusation that animals could instruct the friends (12:7–9).

Bildad alleges that Job's emotions are destroying him and that Job sees his situation from the wrong perspective. The universe is not going to change to accommodate Job. He should admit his guilt and find relief by confessing his sin.

Bildad never identifies Job as the target of this description of what befalls the wicked, but there is no doubt about what he is saying. Bildad remains sure that the wicked get paid in full for their sin, and since Job's suffering is dire, his sin must be heinous.
Six different terms for "trap" are used to drive home the argument that the wicked (that is, Job) will be betrayed by their own scheming (v. 7).
An obvious reference to Job's physical condition. the firstborn of death. Probably refers to the onset of a physical malady that is obviously going to prove fatal.

The Canaanites understood death as a god with one lip touching the earth and the other touching the heavens so that he swallowed up everything. According to Bildad, "the firstborn of death," following in the footsteps of his father, eats away the skin and devours the limbs of the wicked. According to Is. 25:8, the Lord will "swallow up death forever."
Both the physical dwelling of the wicked and his family line will vanish. Lack of descendants was viewed as a mark of great shame.
An instance of the figure of speech known as a merism. Opposites are cited to indicate totality — everyone everywhere.
Job's refusal to accept the arguments set before him has led Bildad to conclude that Job is unrighteous and unsaved.

In his fifth response to his friends, Job accuses God of wronging him and not listening to his plea for justice (vv. 6, 7), of stripping him of honor and attacking him (vv. 9–12), and of alienating his kinsmen and friends (vv. 13–20). Job is wrong on all points. He is wrestling with God over the apparent meaninglessness of his suffering, which is actually the work of the Adversary but ordained by God to accomplish a higher purpose. The counselors, on the other hand, reduce God and His acts to an impersonal formula. They are incapable of empathy with the agony of Job's predicament or of showing him any mercy. After pleading for sympathy from his friends (vv. 21, 22), Job's mood swings from deep dejection to confidence that he will see God and be vindicated by Him (vv. 23–29). 19:1–12 In despair, Job accuses his friends of verbal assault, which intensifies his agony (vv. 2–5), and he then declares that God has brought about his troubles (vv. 6–12).
A round number used as an idiom for "many times."
Job is not admitting that he is at fault but is making a concession for the sake of argument.
Job's cry expresses his need for help because he has been bodily attacked, but his cry is unanswered. God has remained silent.
This is no longer the protective fence of 1:10 but a barrier that prevents Job's escape from his torment.
God has deprived Job of every vestige of status and respect in the community where he was formerly held in high esteem (29:7–11; 30:1, 9, 10).
Earlier the image of a tree provided Job with a measure of hope (14:14), but here the tree is not cut off at ground level but totally uprooted. Even so, this applies to Job's hope, not his life.
Job is wrong in his perception of God as hostile toward him (see 16:10–14).

Job further accuses God of isolating him and leaving him exposed in his time of suffering by alienating his friends and relatives. 19:13 my brothers. Probably more than blood relatives but includes associates or companions.
Job has become a social outcast, ridiculed even by children whose behavior defies conventional requirements of respect for the elderly.
Includes the three counselors who, though present with Job, speak to him in such a hurtful fashion.

This idiom has entered the English language through the Bible, but it is hard to see how the phrase suggests a narrow escape. Alternatively, some suggest that the phrase should be understood as "with only my skin or gums remaining." His body is so physically run down that his teeth have fallen out, and only his gums remain.

Job poignantly begs for the friendship and empathy he needs, but nothing of the sort is possible from his counselors, who have only added to his misery. the hand of God. Refers to God's acting powerfully, often on behalf of His people, but here perceived by Job to be acting against him.

Job's mood swings for a little from the depths of his misery, and in faith he desires that his cause will be vindicated by a permanent memorial (vv. 23, 24). He confidently affirms that his situation will be rectified through the activity of a "Redeemer" (vv. 25–27). The text is variously understood, and the precise meaning of his affirmation is disputed. Many scholars deny that the passage has any eschatological significance. They argue that Job does not anticipate bodily resurrection but instead yearns for no more than to see God before he dies so that God will vindicate him. Such a conclusion is often based on the perception that belief in an afterlife did not arise until much later in the OT. This view is improbable. Even though in the earliest times not much information was disclosed about life after death, an awareness of it existed, albeit dimly (e.g., Gen. 5:24). Under the pressure of his experience, Job's vision has moved from the world around him to future realities. Even if v. 25 is not understood as direct messianic prophecy, there can be no doubt that these words are an expression of indomitable faith that rises above the immediately perceptible because of trust in God. His words are ultimately fulfilled in Christ. 19:23, 24 Job has an important message that he wants permanently inscribed for posterity. Through the inspiration of the Spirit, his words are preserved for all time in the Bible (see Mark 14:9).

The Hebrew word translated "Redeemer" can also be rendered "avenger," "guarantor," "vindicator," or "kinsman-redeemer" (Ruth 2:20 note). Job's words are clear, but from his perspective, who will help him? The prologue reveals that God is not Job's enemy. Indeed, God will become his vindicator (42:7). Job elsewhere seems to think of the Redeemer as a third party (16:19–21). at the last he will stand upon the earth. In Job's mind, this vindicator will be both heavenly (16:19) and earthly (able to stand on the earth). "Stand upon the earth" is literally "rise upon dust." In this context, where death is prominent, Job imagines that after his death, his vindicator will bear witness to others regarding his integrity.

Job is aware that the disease racking his frame will prove fatal if left unchecked. in my flesh. The meaning of the preposition "in" (lit. "from") could be either "from my flesh," i.e., while Job lives, in this life or possibly in a postmortem experience; or "apart from my flesh," possibly in a disembodied state (text note). Since the book does touch on the idea of resurrection in ch. 14, it seems likely that when death is spoken of in v. 26, resurrection is in view, and the translation should be "in" my flesh. What is certain is that Job believes he has a Redeemer who loves him and for whom his heart yearns (v. 27). The whole passage is strongly evocative of every sinner's need for the one mediator who is both God and man (1 Tim. 2:5, 6).

Job emphatically anticipates personally witnessing this vindication, whether with the eyes of a resurrected body or with spiritual perception. My heart faints within me. In his anguished condition, Job yearns even more intensely for the resolution of his perplexity.

In the light of the eternal destiny that awaits them, Job solemnly cautions his friends not to misjudge his situation or continue their pursuit of him (see v. 22). His warning is similar to that of Christ in Matt. 7:1–5. The root of the matter. He is the cause of his own misfortunes. the sword. The instrument of divine justice.

This speech is Zophar's final contribution to the exchange of views between the friends and Job. It consists of another eloquent statement of the fate of the wicked. In it, Zophar expresses the truth of the moral governance of the world by God but fails to make a correct application of it.

Feeling personally insulted by Job's words, Zophar again sets out the view that the joys of the wicked soon vanish. A godless individual will quickly perish, particularly because of his inflated self-esteem (vv. 5–7). 20:2 my thoughts. The term applies to anxious or disquieting thoughts. Zophar has been upset by Job's vigorous rebuttal of the counsel extended to him. my haste within me. Job's closing words in 19:28, 29, threatening impending judgment, have not been lost on Zophar.
Job's claim was that God had closed the friends' hearts to understanding (17:4), a thought Zophar indignantly counters.
The allusion seems to be to the tower of Babel (see Gen. 11:4) and implies that Job is as arrogant a sinner as there has ever been (see v. 4).

Portrays the children as having to beg from the very people their father had oppressed, or, less probably, presents them as having to make restitution to the poor. give back his wealth. Repeatedly Zophar mentions the wealth of the wicked (also vv. 15, 18, 21, 22, 26), insinuating that Job acquired his former wealth dishonestly.

–19 Zophar argues that even though a wicked man displays an insatiable relish for ill-gotten wealth, it will poison him, and he will be forced to relinquish it. He will have to disgorge what he had taken such pains to obtain (see Eccl. 2:18–23).
A coarse expression of the operation of retributive justice: what a man swallows poisons him and has to be vomited up.
"Curds" refers to curdled milk, a much-appreciated form of yogurt. The sinner will be deprived of the delicacies he expended so much effort to acquire.
Misuse of wealth and power to oppress the less fortunate is characteristic of the ruthlessness of those who cherish material prosperity (see Amos 2:6–8; 8:4–6).

–29 Zophar emphasizes that God does not let a wicked person escape the consequences of his actions. Divine wrath will change their ease and prosperity into distress and calamity. 20:20 knew no contentment. Zophar argues that the wicked man (implicitly, Job) always craves more and will consume anything he can.

No matter how hard the wicked man tries to escape punishment, even the heavens and the earth will give evidence against him, a clear reference to Job's wish in 16:18–21. Zophar is convinced that the miserable turn Job's circumstances have taken is a sure indicator that he is no longer in God's favor.
Lit. "produce." It is possible that the word rendered "possessions" should be understood as "a flood"; that is, "a flood carries away his house." In either case, the picture is that of a total loss.

What Zophar teaches will ultimately come to pass, but, sadly, he has no word to say about God's mercy. Even in his earlier speech in 11:13–20, where he called on Job to change his ways, there was no mention of mercy. According to Zophar, people receive God's blessing only by earning it.

Job's sixth speech closes this second cycle with a firm rejection of the friends' arguments that the wicked always suffer in this life. Unlike his other responses, Job makes no appeal to God. Throughout the chapter he uses plural forms when referring to his friends (but see v. 3 note), though he does rebut Zophar's allegations from the previous chapter. Note how he alludes to their very words: cf. 20:11 with 21:7; 8:19 with 21:8; 18:5 with 21:17; 5:4 and 20:10 with 21:19; and 20:5–7 with 21:28–30.

After another plea that his friends actually listen to what he has to say rather than just repeating their preconceived, simplistic notions (vv. 2, 3), Job calls on them to "look" (v. 5) at his misery. Surely they should be compassionate about one in such a piteous state. 21:2 let this be your comfort. The solace they offer him. They should at least extend to him the consolation and support he would receive if they took seriously what he was saying. Note the similar phrase in v. 34, bracketing this speech.

Unlike the other verbs in the chapter, this is singular, addressed to Zophar, and ironically conceding to him the right to continue his bitter attacks if only he will first actually listen to what Job has to say about his situation.
If they have any compassion, Job says, they will stop accusing him and lying about him.
Job is probably referring to the condition he is in. If he shudders at it, should not his friends shudder with him?

Job insists that the available evidence about the prosperity and longevity of the wicked refutes Zophar's argument that they die young (e.g., in 20:11). It is simply not the case that they always receive their recompense in this life. The wicked flourish (vv. 7–13) even while they defy God (vv. 14–16). 21:7 Why do the wicked live. Job admits that he is perplexed by the ease and grandeur enjoyed by the wicked. He has no answer (see Ps. 73:3). The counselors assume that they know exactly what is going on (see John 9:41).
Bildad earlier claimed that they would have no offspring (18:19).
God does not chastise them but allows them to prosper.
The prosperity of the wicked continues even though they openly flout God.
In a series of rhetorical questions, Job points out that it is not the case that "the light of the wicked is put out," as Bildad claimed (18:5).

The prosperity of the wicked cannot be evaded by saying that God will punish their children. It has already been claimed they will have no children, and once they die, they are unaffected by the suffering of their offspring. It is the wicked themselves who should experience divine punishment.

Job picks up earlier assertions of Eliphaz (see 4:18; 15:15). Job's high view of God only makes his problem more perplexing. He acknowledges the inscrutability of God's action when one person dies young and prosperous while another lives long in deprivation and adversity. Though all lives end in death, their spiritual condition cannot be judged by external circumstances.

Job anticipates that his counselors will try to discount his argument by asking where wicked, wealthy people have lived. He inquires in return if they have quizzed the widely traveled. Is he accusing his friends of living in ivory towers, out of touch with what is obvious to others? It is not difficult to find instances of evil men enjoying relief from calamity and popularity and thus not being openly denounced.
Job has found no satisfactory explanation of his condition in what his friends have said to comfort him. All their arguments are deceptive and unreliable.

In this final cycle of speeches, Bildad's contribution is brief (25:1–6), and Zophar does not speak at all. Although attempts have been made to find the missing speech in ch. 26, it is more probable that the intention is to show the exhaustion of the friends. In these chapters they openly accuse him of sin (22:5–9; 25:5, 6), of which he needs to repent (22:21–23). But Job cannot do what they urge and maintains his integrity because he does not know of any sin to be confessed. 22:1–30 Eliphaz begins the third cycle of speeches (22:1–26:14), listing Job's sins and calling on him to repent.

Eliphaz does two things: he emphasizes the transcendence of God (vv. 2–4) and lists the many sins of which he considers Job to be guilty (vv. 5–9). His sin explains his situation; he is being appropriately punished. 22:2, 3 Eliphaz reacts to Job's statement that God allows wickedness to go unpunished, and he also says that human uprightness adds nothing to God. Eliphaz espouses such a transcendent view of God that it pictures Him as unconcerned with the details of life on earth (see vv. 12–14) and with Job's situation. It is therefore pointless for Job to be so obsessed with vindication. His suffering is what he deserves. 22:3 The sense may be, "Would it please God if you were vindicated?" Since all comes from God, we have nothing to give back to Him that is not His in the first place.

Eliphaz reaches the conclusion Zophar and Bildad have already expressed — that Job's sins are endless. In the light of the following line, "your evil" refers to Job's wrongdoing rather than to the misery he is enduring.

Here is a direct personal attack on Job for specific sins, especially social sins against the poor and widows. Later Job will emphasize his social righteousness (chs. 29; 31). Eliphaz has no evidence to substantiate these allegations against Job. He is simply arguing back from the intensity of Job's suffering.

Eliphaz makes no secret of his conviction that Job had adopted the lifestyle of the wicked before disaster struck him (v. 15). 22:12–14 Eliphaz attacks Job's complaint that God is absent (13:24). It is not unnatural for Job, in the midst of suffering, to complain that God is either too observant and intrusive to leave him alone (7:17–19; 10:8; 16:9) or too far away. It looks as though Eliphaz attributes words to Job twice — vv. 13, 14 (clearly so), and perhaps also v. 17 or vv. 17, 18 — and counters both of them.

Once more Eliphaz presents the fate of the wicked in simplistic terms. They die prematurely (v. 16). Despite their rejection of God (v. 17; see 21:14, 15), He has abundantly blessed them (v. 18). 22:15 old way. That of living in defiance of God.

Eliphaz rejects Job's claim that God prospers the wicked. It is best to understand Eliphaz as reflecting what Job said but claiming that the prosperity of the wicked is followed by disaster. Eliphaz employs Job's phrase from 21:16 to describe Job's own position.
The rejoicing of the righteous is evidence of the fall of the wicked. "Mock" recalls divine mockery in Ps. 2:4.

In his final entreaty to Job, Eliphaz sets out to an even greater extent the blessings he will enjoy if only he repents (vv. 21–23). He should also renounce claims to his wealth as being his own (v. 24). Eliphaz remains convinced that Job is guilty (v. 30), and his advice is grounded on that assumption. Consequently, what he says fails to comprehend the nature of Job's situation.
The words are ironic. It is Eliphaz himself who will be delivered through Job's intercession (42:7–9).

Job does not take up what Eliphaz has just said until ch. 31. Instead he gives vent to matters immediately weighing upon him. He wants to present his case directly to God (23:1–7), but God will not grant him a hearing and is acting unfairly toward him (23:8–17). Furthermore, there are many aspects of divine implementation of justice that leave Job confused and mystified (ch. 24). 23:1–12 Job's thoughts vacillate. In ch. 9 he doubts God would give him a hearing. In ch. 13 he is convinced he will get a hearing and be vindicated. In 17:1 he is convinced that only death awaits him but also that his counselors will not triumph, and that he will be vindicated (17:10–16). That conviction reaches its zenith in 19:25–27, and from then on he never again doubts it, as these verses and especially ch. 31 prove.

Job probably has his friends in view. What they have said has not connected with his situation or relieved his distress. my hand is heavy. The idiom denotes weariness and inability to act. His grievous condition has drained Job of strength.
Refers to where God acts as judge. 23:3–9 Job has not been successful in ascertaining why God has afflicted him (see 9:10, 11).
If he were to receive an audience with the Lord, Job would set out why he considers himself innocent of any offense that warrants the imposition of such suffering.
"Contend" implies engaging in legal argument (9:3 note). Job believes that the arguments he could present would be so convincing that God would declare him innocent.

Though Job knows God is present, he is unable to sense His presence (vv. 8, 9). He is now certain he will get a hearing (v. 10) that will vindicate him because he has obeyed God's Word. 23:8 Job's God is invisible, but He has an all-seeing eye (v. 10). The four directions of movement in vv. 8, 9 are all-inclusive, possibly representing east, west, north, and south, respectively.

For "tried," see "test" (7:18). Job confidently expects to come out of the process of divine trial completely vindicated. Job has in view not God's using this experience to advance his spirituality, but the expectation that when he is granted a hearing, divine scrutiny of his conduct will endorse his claim that he has done nothing to merit his suffering. Chapter 42 shows that the outcome is not quite as Job anticipates here.
Job responds to Eliphaz's injunction to "agree with God" in 22:21 by insisting that he has always lived in harmony with God's ways and treasured God's Word.

Lit. "one," perhaps signifying "unique." Job returns to asserting his confidence in God's sovereign control. Even though he does not understand, he affirms that God will surely accomplish what He desires for Job. This consideration seems to undermine his confidence in appearing in court before Him (v. 15).

Job's friends think they understand all about God and His ways and therefore are able to predict what God will do. Job realizes that there is much he does not understand about God, and he is therefore daunted and dismayed before Him.

Despite the ordeal he is undergoing, his lack of comprehension of what is occurring, and his overwhelming dread before God, Job considers that he has no option but to continue to plead to be heard and vindicated.

Job has not yet learned the important lesson that justice in this world does not operate mechanically but according to the will of God. If it were not so, the human race would have perished long ago. This chapter alternates between descriptions of the fortunate wicked and the sufferings of their victims, with emphasis on the sufferings. Job wants the wicked to be judged so that those who know God will see it and know that God is just. The chapter shows Job's hatred of wickedness. 24:1–12 Job reverts to his earlier theme that the unrighteous prosper (ch. 21) while God does not intervene in judgment. Job lists the crimes of which the wicked are guilty (vv. 2–4, 9, 13–17, 21) and here particularly details the deprivation and injustice arising from their exploitation of the poor and defenseless (vv. 5–12). 24:1 see his days. The days in view are the times when God intervenes in the flow of human history to judge wickedness and ensure that justice prevails in human affairs. Job complains that this does not happen immediately, even though the wicked sin flagrantly. The prophets later talk about "the day of the LORD" as a future time of judgment on the nations and blessing of His people (see Joel 2:1, 2; Amos 5:18–20), when God will openly display His control of affairs.
Job's most sweeping allegation against God — that He is not concerned about administering justice (9:24 note; cf. Ps. 50:21; Lam. 3:34–36).

Job focuses on the misconduct of the wicked, singling out murder (v. 14), adultery (v. 15) and theft (v. 16). Throughout he emphasizes the covert nature of their activities, as the wicked operate in darkness and shun both the light of day and the light of truth.

Often considered an unannounced quotation from the counselors since the views expressed here seem more consistent with their position than Job's (24:18 note). Others think the whole chapter is an attempt by early editors to make Job sound more orthodox. But Job may have a reason for seeming to adopt the counselors' stance. 24:18 You say. A translator's addition to clarify that vv. 18–24 are the words of the counselors. Job is expostulating against his friends' inability to see what is so obviously happening: the imposition of divine judgment is delayed. The friends continue to hold that the wicked are carried away as swiftly as something floating on a stream or perhaps like a bubble or eddy on the surface of the stream.

These seem to be Job's words, emphasizing the wrongdoing of the wicked (v. 21) but claiming that God prolongs their lives and grants them prosperity. Still, Job argues, their thriving condition lasts only for a little. God deals with them not immediately but gradually.

These verses must be connected with v. 1 in order to understand the point of the chapter. Job is trying to show that though the wicked are punished, this punishment takes place little by little, while the righteous want to see justice meted out completely and immediately. Job's thought anticipates the "day of the LORD" doctrine of the prophets, which looks for the final judgment day. Conversely, Job claims to be suffering wrongfully, yet God will not hear him because He has not set times for judgment. Even so, Job holds to God's justice and expects vindication eventually, though he would rather it come more speedily.
This is a veiled threat to his friends. If God's justice does not operate with immediate effect, then they too must be fearful and not presume (see 19:29; 27:7–13).
Bildad makes no new argument but repeats what has already been said about God's dominion and power (vv. 2, 3) and about His moral purity, which is in marked contrast to mankind's (vv. 4–6).

Human impurity is a given, but missing here is a hint of grace. Paul, who developed the doctrine of the total depravity of man in Romans, did so as a background for God's marvelous grace. Bildad does not think in terms of grace.

Bildad risks overstating the depth of human worthlessness because he has a pessimistic view of man (see Eliphaz in 15:14–16). The doctrine of total depravity is not pessimistic. Even in their sinful condition, human beings retain the image of God, giving each person dignity and value. Furthermore, Bildad's sweeping generalization does not begin to connect with the specifics of Job's circumstances.

This chapter falls into two distinct parts: vv. 1–4 and vv. 5–14, which has led some to say that only the opening verses are Job's while the rest of the chapter is Bildad's, or is a third speech by Zophar, thus identifying three speeches of the counselors in the third cycle.
"You" in these verses is singular; Job explicitly addresses Bildad and scathingly mocks his ineffective attempts to strengthen or enlighten him regarding what is happening.
Job suggests that Bildad's words have some source other than God.

These verses celebrate God's omnipotence. They are not unlike Job's words in 9:5–10 and need not be assigned, as they sometimes are, to one of the counselors. Job will not take second place to his friends when it comes to acknowledging God's sovereign dominion. His problem concerns the equity of God's actions. 26:5 The dead. Lit. "the Rephaim," a term variously used but here referring to the shadowy existence of those who have departed this life (see Is. 14:9). 26:5, 6 Unlike the Canaanite gods, who each have a restricted domain of power, the true God controls even Sheol (Prov. 15:11), the supposed domain of Mot, the god of death.

Job's purpose here is not to teach the science of space or weather but to glorify God through the mysteries of His work in nature. The whole created realm continues in existence solely by God's sustaining power.

Another word, "throne," is spelled the same way in Hebrew (text note); if it is applied here, it would indicate God's refusal to disclose all that is decided in His heavenly council chamber. The context favors a description of divine control of the natural realm.
Possibly a reference to the mountains, which often reach into the clouds and appear to support the sky.

God rules the supposed dominion of Yam, the Canaanite god of the sea. Jesus Christ showed He is the true God of His people when He calmed the sea in Matt. 8:23–27. Rahab. A mythical Canaanite monster of the deep, similar to Leviathan, capable of wreaking havoc. This poetic imagery enriches the concept of God's great power over the boisterous sea (Ps. 89:9, 10).

A further description of the Canaanite sea god (v. 12 note). Every conceivable power is under the control of the one true God. This will be finally demonstrated when Satan is overwhelmed by the power of Christ (John 12:31; Rev. 20:7–10).

Job is aware that such phenomena only hint at the full extent of divine power. Since even there, God's ways lie beyond human comprehension, Job's friends are presumptuous to suppose that they can unerringly interpret God's dealings with him.

The structure of the book of Job at this point is much disputed. There are two issues: How ch. 28 relates to the surrounding chapters and whether a third speech by Zophar is found in ch. 27. Given that the author is meticulous elsewhere in noting who is speaking, he is unlikely to have been negligent here. There are two clear introductory formulas in 27:1 and 29:1, which bracket chs. 27; 28 and designate them as Job's speech. (For further details, see notes on these verses and the introduction to ch. 28.) When Job becomes aware that his friends are not going to speak again, he takes the opportunity to conclude their interchange by reasserting his innocence (ch. 27) and by setting the whole debate in a broader context, the need for true fear of the Lord (ch. 28). Thus, along with ch. 3, where Job also speaks, these chapters function as brackets to enclose Job's disputation with the three counselors. 27:1–23 Job rounds off the discussion by insisting once more on his innocence (vv. 2–6) and by describing the destiny of the wicked (vv. 7–23). Using words similar to those employed by his friends, Job calls the fate of the godless to fall on them. Since his expression resembles that of his friends, attempts have been made to reconstruct a third speech of Zophar from vv. 7–23. That misses the point that Job likewise accepts a simplistic version of retribution theology. It also fails to account for the language of vv. 11, 12. 27:1 Job again took up his discourse. While this indicates continuity of speaker from ch. 26, it also suggests that some interval has occurred from the preceding speech (see 29:1). Note the repeated use of a similar formula to introduce various distinct speeches of Balaam in Num. 23; 24.

These verses are directed at the counselors ("you" is plural in v. 5). With a most solemn oath founded on God's existence, Job denies their false accusations and at the same time asserts his integrity. As long as he lives, Job will not admit to wrongdoing in the way his friends are urging (v. 5). He has no qualms of conscience regarding his conduct (v. 6). 27:2 God \... Almighty. Job does not deny the existence or power of God, but the qualifying clauses he adds to the divine name express his frustration and grievance regarding the justice of God's dealings with him. For "soul bitter," see note on 3:20.

Job poses four rhetorical questions that emphasize the hopeless condition of the godless. He calls for his friends who have falsely accused him of being wicked to share their fate. 27:7–10 Curses like these are found in the Psalms (Pss. 109:6–15; 139:19–22). See Introduction to Psalms.

The pronouns are plural and can be accounted for only by supposing Job is speaking to his friends. They do not fit in with attempts to identify here a speech of one of his friends. Rather, Job claims to be able to instruct them regarding "the hand of God," that is, how God will intervene in judgment.

Job turns to discuss the fate of the wicked, a topic addressed at length by his counselors. His comments show that he understands it as well as they do. He has never disputed the ultimate fate of the wicked; it is their immediate punishment that he denies, in contrast to Zophar's assertion (20:5; 21:7). But Job makes the counselors and not himself the implied objects of the destiny described.
A reference to death in military conflict.
Though the wicked think they erect solid structures as homes, those homes will in fact prove to be insubstantial and transient.

Gestures of derision at the helpless state of the wicked. While vv. 22, 23 may extend the description of the east wind, as the ESV margin notes, the subject may well be God so that these lines directly detail His scornful dismissal of the wicked.

A different type of wisdom literature is presented in ch. 28, a kind of standard wisdom like that found in the book of Proverbs. The lack of an introductory formula indicating the speaker might indicate that this is an insertion by the author of Job, reflecting on the lack of wisdom displayed so far in the dialogue. However, the text does not indicate a change of speaker from ch. 27, so it is probable that ch. 28 is spoken by Job. After his extended yet unsatisfactory dialogue with his friends, he experiences a period of relative tranquility in which he muses on how to find wisdom — the capacity to make right decisions and cope with life. Job's reflective mood continues into ch. 29, where he recalls his past happiness before he is again overwhelmed by his present distress (chs. 30; 31). The subject of the poem is the elusiveness and surpassing value of true wisdom. It may be analyzed as having three stanzas (vv. 1–12, 13–20, 21–28), though the refrain in vv. 12, 20 is transitional and may also be read with what follows. The refrain asks the key question, "Where shall wisdom be found?" and the answer is provided in the concluding verse of the poem (v. 28). 28:1–12 Job reflects on the great skill and tenacity with which mankind has gathered hidden treasures from the depths of the earth. However, such technological exploits must be surpassed to acquire wisdom.
The darkness of underground caverns can be dispelled by lamps or torches, but this might be an implied contrast with other forms of darkness — intellectual and spiritual.
Envisions miners being lowered down shafts using ropes.

Likely not a reference to volcanic activity. It is a contrast between fields above ground and the upheaval and rubble hidden in the mine workings below ground. It is like debris from a burned building.
Or "lapis lazuli" (text note). Both are highly prized, blue gemstones.
Mining is a human achievement that sets mankind apart from animals.
This transitional verse emphasizes that technological know-how is incapable of providing spiritual insight.

The principal theme of this stanza is the value of true wisdom, even though weak, mortal man fails to appreciate its worth (v. 13). It cannot be found by exploring ocean depths (v. 14) or by trading in the marketplace. Wisdom is not for sale.
The closing stanza of the poem contrasts the inability of the created realm to find wisdom with God's complete grasp of it.
The place of destruction (26:6 note). Abaddon and Death are personified; they have only heard a rumor (from those who have died?) that wisdom exists.

–27 God understands the way to it. As creator, God alone knows where true wisdom is to be found. There is nothing hidden from His scrutiny (v. 24). From the very beginning, He established how mankind should live.

Mankind can acquire wisdom only from God, and He has not concealed it. It is obtained through obedience to His revealed will (Deut. 4:5, 6; Prov. 8:4–9; 9:10). For the NT application, see Col. 2:2, 3 and Eph. 3:8–10. fear of the Lord. This key phrase of wisdom teaching (see Ps. 111:10; Prov. 1:7) embodies respectful acknowledgment of God's existence, authority, and standards. "Lord" here is Adonai, "sovereign master" (the sole occurrence of the term in Job), and not Yahweh, the covenant name of God. This advice has universal applicability. turn away from evil. Includes both a positive attitude toward God and avoidance of all that is contrary to His commands (see Prov. 3:7). If Job is here reproaching his friends for failing to show proper respect for God, there is irony in the fact that he is also condemning himself by his self-righteous presumption in challenging God, which becomes even more evident in the following chapters.

There now follow three monologues. In the first of these, Job summarizes his case against God (chs. 29–31). Then Elihu intervenes to object to the way in which God's justice has been inadequately defended and presents his perspective on the situation (chs. 32–37). Finally, God Himself speaks to resolve the situation (chs. 38–41). 29:1–31:40 Job addresses God in the form of a case presented in court. He first establishes the loss he has suffered as he looks back poignantly to the affluence and respect he previously enjoyed (ch. 29). In ch. 30 he expresses his gloom and dismay at his loss, especially the loss of friendship with God. In ch. 31 he defends himself and delivers a final oath of innocence, which he feels should settle matters once and for all in his favor. 29:1–25 Job sues for restitution of what he has lost. In effect, this chapter expands on his affirmation of his previous circumstances, "I was at ease" (16:12). 29:1 took up his discourse. This does not necessarily indicate a change of speaker but may indicate a new division or the passage of time before the start of a new speech (27:1 note).

Job bemoans the loss of God's favor. He nostalgically yearns for what he formerly enjoyed (note the repetition of "when"). 29:2 months of old. Job's prosperity obviously extended over a considerable period of time.
Light symbolizes God's blessing. This illustration is based on a lamp dispelling the gloom inside a tent.

Lit. "in days of my autumn/winter." The point of the metaphor is unclear. It may well indicate the time when Job was enjoying the produce of his labor and fellowship with God. That, of course, was precisely what Satan pointed to as the reason for Job's piety. the friendship of God. Lit. "the council of God." Pictured is a scene of familiarity such as is found in Gen. 18, particularly vv. 17–19. Job always viewed God as the source of his good fortune, the root of which was his intimate relationship with God.
Job recalls the happiness of family life while his children were still alive and gathered around him.
Choice luxury goods. Job enjoyed an abundant lifestyle.

Job was once a figure of standing, respected throughout the community. When he spoke, his sage advice caused others to fall silent (vv. 9, 10). 29:7 the gate of the city. Where the commercial and legal business of the community was conducted in the ancient Near East.

Job recalls the noble reputation he had built as a practitioner of what the NT calls "pure and undefiled" religion (cf. vv. 12–16 with James 1:27). He was respected not just because he was rich, powerful, and wise, but because of his compassionate intervention on behalf of the vulnerable (contrary to Eliphaz's allegations in 22:6–9).
This verse is the center point of the chapter, an emphatic assertion of Job's call for vindication.
Those who preyed on others in dire need are compared to wild animals. The action Job took rendered them incapable of inflicting injury.

In light of his past deeds, Job had expected to be vigorous in the later years of his life. This reflects the fact that he too accepted a simplistic version of retribution theology. 29:18 in my nest. A picture of security and absence of worries. In such circumstances, Job had expected to enjoy continuing respect and to die in peace.
The image changes to that of a tree, nourished by its access to water (see Ps. 1:3; Jer. 17:8).
Job remembers his former dignity and honor. The advice he gave was eagerly awaited and readily accepted.
Job had merely to look at those who were uncertain, and they were encouraged.

"But" and "And now" (30:1, 9, 16) move the time frame from the past of ch. 29 to the present. Here, point for point, Job laments how the blessings he enjoyed were taken away from him. In ch. 29 he dealt with honor from man, blessings from God, and his own benevolent deeds. This chapter describes how all that has been reversed. 30:1–8 Job describes those who ridicule and insult him. Previously, the young men of the community had treated him with esteem (29:8). Now, contrary to ancient deference to elders, they display utter disrespect by mocking him. Moreover, Job's shame is intensified because those who mock him are not just young but the offspring of disreputable scoundrels.

The group Job describes are those eking out an existence in marginal land on the edge of the community, such as runaway slaves or absconding criminals. They have to eat the poorest of food and live without permanent homes or adequate shelter. These verses are a good example of the discursive style of the poet.

Job bewails the dishonor he receives from these criminals (see 29:7–10, 21–25). Even such social misfits and outcasts consider themselves more fortunate than Job and are not slow to insult him as he sits on the city rubbish heap.
Likely an analogy of a loosened bowstring, which is therefore incapable of being used effectively (cf. 29:20). Alternatively, the cord may be what once held up his tent (see 29:4).
Job is no longer respected or safe in the situation to which God has brought him (cf. 29:7–11). 30:12 cast up. The image is that of an army conducting a siege. See "wide breach" (v. 14).

Job is physically in pain (vv. 16–19), but worse still is the spiritual trauma arising from the recognition that it is God who is subjecting him to this treatment and refusing to pay attention to his pleas for relief (vv. 20, 21). Cf. 29:2–6, 18–20.
The Septuagint reads, "He seizes my garment." Job is talking again as if God is his enemy.
Symbols of abject humiliation. Job, however, may have been literally covered by them (2:8 and note).
"You" is singular, referring to God. Job accuses God of abusing His position by ignoring Job's petition and need.

See 29:11–17. Job again describes his intense physical and emotional pain. Though he comforted others in the past (v. 25), he now receives no assistance from his friends. They forget his former kindness. As a conse­quence, he is drained physically and emotionally (vv. 27–31).
His affliction has caused his skin to darken (see v. 30).
In his agony, Job has uttered sounds like the wailing of jackals or the groans of ostriches (see Is. 13:21; Mic. 1:8).
Job's life is no longer regaled by music. He hears only the shrill tones of mourning and weeping.

Uppermost in Job's mind is the false accusation that he is a man of exceptional wickedness, suffering no more than what he deserves. To counter this allegation, Job employs a legal procedure that is common in his day: he calls on the gods to impose a curse on him if he is guilty of the charges. So Job solemnly rebuts various forms of misconduct and sets out the sanctions God should impose on him if he is lying. Although this is a protestation of innocence, it is not the self-righteousness of the Pharisee in Luke 18:11, 12. Like the psalmist, Job is the victim of false accusation, so vindication has become his passion. Job's thinking is governed by a simplistic principle of retribution. If he has acted sinfully, then he will accept that he has been justly cursed. However, the converse proposition is implicit: since he has not acted inappropriately, he should be acquitted and reinstated in divine blessing. Job's logic is irrefutable. Like his friends, however, he has illegitimately extended the scope of the retribution principle and is attempting to use it to force God into acting as he demands. It is this coercive approach to God that Job has later to repent of (see 42:6). 31:1–4 Job declares that he had determined not to sin with his eyes (1 John 2:16). God would have been aware of such transgression (v. 4) and would justly punish it (v. 3). However, Job may be speaking of more than ordinary lust. He may have in view worship of the fertility goddesses so popular in OT times. The word translated "virgin" (v. 1) is used of the goddess of fertility in Canaanite writings. She was a kind of Venus and was called the "maiden Anat" in the city of Ugarit.

Job clears himself of avarice in his business dealings. In v. 6 he declares his "integrity," not an assertion of sinless perfection but of genuine probity and honesty. He therefore does not shrink from being weighed in God's balances.
The penalty Job sees as appropriate is a curse of reversal and frustration (see Deut. 28:30–41).
Job clears himself of adultery. If he had violated another man's wife, then the curse should have come on his own marriage.
Grinding grain is viewed as the most menial of tasks in this era.
Job acknowledges that adultery is so serious an offense that it merits the sanctions of human and divine justice.
Job clears himself of injustice with respect to his servants. If he had rejected their claims for fair treatment, he would have no grounds for complaining about God's treatment of him.
Job disregards the class structures of his society and recognizes the basic equality before God of master and servant alike (see Prov. 22:2).
Job clears himself of neglect of the needy and abuse of the helpless (see 29:12–17).

Probably not a threat to strike them but rather a gesture employed in taking an oath. Job had not given false evidence to deprive them of their rights even though his "help" was "in the gate"; that is, even though he knew of some who would support him in whatever action he took in public affairs (see 29:7).
The curse that should befall him would render him incapable of raising his hand to subscribe to a false oath (v. 21).
Job avoided social injustice because he dreaded the penalty God would rightly impose on it.
Job clears himself of idolatry with regard to gold or the gods. 31:24, 25 Though Job had enjoyed considerable affluence (1:3), he had not made it his source of confidence for living.
Worship of the sun and the moon was widely practiced throughout the ancient Near East.
Kissing one's hand was a recognized devotional gesture in the ancient Near East (see 1 Kin. 19:18; Hos. 13:2).

The structure of Job's thought is somewhat complex here. Verses 29–34 and 38–40 continue to present in conditional form the behavior he has avoided. On the basis of his assertion of innocence, he breaks off in the central verses (vv. 35–37) to express his basic demand. He wants a hearing with God. If he has been responsible for such misconduct, then, in terms of his simplistic retribution theology, he ought to be indicted and punished; if not, he deserves his day in court to clear his name. Job appears supremely confident that he would be successful in achieving such an outcome. 31:29–34 Job clears himself of hatred, selfishness, and hypocrisy. He had not harbored malevolent attitudes toward those who opposed him (see Ps. 35:13, 14; Matt. 5:43–47).
Members of Job's household looked out for those who would benefit from Job's benevolence, including travelers passing by (v. 32).
"As mankind does," or possibly "as Adam did" (text note), in which case the reference is to Gen. 3:8.
Behavior Job has avoided. He has not covered up his transgressions or avoided people out of fear of public opinion.

The climax. The repeated "Oh, that I had" embody Job's perception that having his case heard will lead to his vindication. He views God as his adversary and attaches his binding signature to his challenge to God to issue specific charges against him.
Job would proudly wear God's written indictment, a sign that he considers any accusations against him easily refutable.
Job has already expressed confidence that God would accept him if he had an opportunity to present his case (13:14–16). In the end, this is possible only through grace.

Job again denies that he had ever abused his position as a wealthy landowner. He had not misappropriated the crops of his tenants or imposed on them unreasonable conditions. If he had, then his fields would have rightly become unfruitful and overgrown with weeds.

Job closes his case. The rest is now up to the Judge. Job apparently thinks that his protestation of innocence will force God to act, but there is no immediate response. God neither affirms Job's innocence nor imposes any penalty for perjury. Instead, the way is open for Elihu's intervention in the following six chapters.

These chapters present the second monologue, that of the young man Elihu, who, unlike the others, has a Hebrew name (32:2). Commentators do not know what to make of him. Many dismiss him as wordy, self-important, and irrelevant, and say he merely reiterates what has already been said. Indeed, some critics believe these chapters are additions to the original text, since Job makes no reply to Elihu, and he is ignored in the epilogue. Both views are defective. The author of Job gives Elihu a formal introduction (32:1–5) and accords six chapters to what he has to say. That is difficult to square with an easy rejection of his contribution. Furthermore, Elihu is not mentioned in the epilogue (ch. 42), not because he is irrelevant, but because he is not guilty of the same errors as the other three. Elihu's critique centers on Job's words uttered during the dispute. He quotes Job but does not accuse him of having lived a wicked life. He stresses an issue neglected by the three friends: the disciplinary and redemptive role of suffering. Eliphaz alone has touched on suffering as discipline (5:17). 32:1–5 The narrator introduces Elihu's four speeches on Job's situation with an explanation for why Elihu injects himself into the debate. 32:1 righteous in his own eyes. Job has stoutly insisted upon his innocence despite his suffering. Since the friends have been unable to induce Job to adopt their analysis of his situation, they view him as incorrigible and intransigent. There is no point in saying anything more to him.

The genealogy shows the narrator considers Elihu (his name means "He is my God") a significant figure. Nothing is known about Barachel, but there was a Ram who was an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chr. 2:9, 25), and there was a Buz connected with Abraham (Gen. 22:21). burned with anger. Elihu does not want to see God's justice compromised, and he sees Job's focus on his innocence as doing that very thing.

According to ancient Jewish tradition, the original reading ("condemned Elohim") was changed by pious convention to "condemned Job," so as to avoid writing a blasphemous thought. Elihu's anger with the friends seems to arise from their failure to establish that God is acting justly.
According to the conventions of the time, older men speak first.

Elihu's introduction, including his reason for speaking, runs to 33:7. He appears to have a warmer personality than the counselors, who never called Job by his name (see 33:1, 31). 32:6–10 Elihu first addresses all four who have spoken thus far. He deferentially explains why he is speaking despite his youth. God has given him something to say. 32:6, 10, 17 my opinion. Lit. "my knowledge." Elihu claims more than an alternative viewpoint. He has definite, God-imparted insight into the situation and so can contribute at a different level. Moreover, he is sure that he will be able to convince the others that his approach is right.

These phrases are in apposition in the parallelism and have the same reference. Elihu claims that the experience and observation of age don't really impart knowledge (v. 9) but insight from God, which is accessible also to the young. "The spirit in a man" may here refer to the Holy Spirit as the source of wisdom (see Gen. 41:38; Ex. 31:3).

Elihu next focuses on the three counselors. He listened to their addresses, but they failed to convince Job that he was in the wrong (v. 12). 32:11 you searched out what to say. Possibly the earlier rounds of speeches extended over days with the participants using the gaps to develop more effective arguments.
The friends could not rightly claim to possess wisdom beyond what God has revealed.
Elihu claims he is going to follow a different line of argument in answering Job.

Elihu no longer addresses the counselors, whom he refers to as "they" (v. 15). Instead he engages in a soliloquy that the others, especially Job, are intended to overhear. Elihu is mainly concerned with establishing his right to speak.

Elihu's speeches are longer than the combined addresses of any one of the three friends. 32:18–20 the spirit within me. Probably Elihu's inner being. He is ready to burst because there is so much he is eager to say. A wineskin required a vent so that the gases produced by the fermenting wine could escape without rupturing the wineskin.
Since Elihu disagrees with both Job and the friends, he will not favor either side in the dispute.

Elihu turns to address Job directly and pleads that Job listen to him. 33:1 hear \... listen. Elihu has perceived that the counselors were not listening to Job and that Job himself is not in a frame of mind to listen to anyone. Hence Elihu's repeated injunctions to listen (33:1, 31, 33; 34:2, 10, 16, 34; 36:2, 10–12; 37:14). Job. Elihu addresses Job by name three times (vv. 1, 31; 37:14) and names him seven other times (32:12, 14; 34:5, 7, 35, 36; 36:16). In contrast to the three counselors, who never mentioned Job's name, Elihu's approach displays a measure of empathy. However, he also appears condescending at times and overconfident in his ability.
See note on 32:8. Elihu goes beyond acknowledging that he too is a creature, dependent on God, to hinting that his message has a divine origin.

Elihu urges Job to respond to what he has to say, but Job never takes up his challenge, perhaps due to fatigue or to acceptance of the accuracy of what Elihu is saying. It is also possible that Job is resentful of Elihu's intervention and dismissive of his contribution.

Lit. "I am as your mouth with respect to God." Job had been looking for an intermediary (9:33 note); Elihu claims to fulfill that role, though he does so with a measure of modesty, acknowledging his frail origins. Even so, it is difficult to see how he thinks his presence might terrify Job (v. 7).

Elihu sets out the substance of his argument, and he begins by summarizing Job's view of himself (v. 9) and of God's attitude toward him (vv. 10, 11). 33:8 your words. Verbatim quotation was not the expected norm in ancient Near Eastern culture. Elihu's summary fails to clarify that Job has never spoken of himself as absolutely sinless (see 7:21; 14:17). His claim of innocence concerns only the gross allegations made against him by the counselors (see 13:23).
A fair summary of Job's utterance in 13:24, 27. He does feel that God is hostile toward him.

Elihu proceeds to correct Job's perception of God. The counselors have already mentioned God's transcendence, but Elihu approaches matters from a different perspective. Despite His transcendence, God does communicate with mankind through revelatory dreams (vv. 15–18) and through suffering (vv. 19–22). 33:12 in this you are not right. Job's perception of his relationship with God is not well founded. Elihu does not conjure up errors in Job's past life but focuses on what he has said in the interchange of views with his friends. God is greater than man. Job has acknowledged the sovereignty and majesty of God. Therefore he is inconsistent when he alleges that God is doing wrong and when he demands that God explain himself. Elihu does not argue that greatness justifies injustice, but he hints that there may well be more behind Job's experience than any human can appreciate.
That is, enter into a legal dispute with an individual (9:3 note). Job has argued that God is not responding to his arguments.
Contrary to Job's perception, God has been speaking, but Job has not been listening, possibly because God has been speaking in ways Job did not anticipate.

The expression is equivalent to "reveals the truth to them." God may send warnings in dreams so that an individual is kept alive. terrifies them with warnings. This rendering follows the Septuagint. The Hebrew may be understood as "seals/confirms their instruction"; that is, dreams reinforce what men already know (see Ps. 16:7).
Elihu diagnoses Job's fault as pride. Elihu also points out that God may speak to prevent wrongdoing as well as to pronounce sentence against sins.
