Not the ordinary word for a sword, but one that signifies a weapon, particularly a missile such as a spear. "Perishing," too, is unusual in that it signifies going or passing over, presumably to death. Some prefer to understand the line as embodying mythological references, identifying "sword" as a term for a "canal" or a "river" on the way to the realm of the dead.

Elihu adds another channel of divine communication with mankind — suffering — through which God gains an individual's attention and compels him to think about final realities. "Rebuke" (v. 19) is part of a disciplinary process intended to bring reformation. Unlike the counselors, who saw no place for grace or mediation (5:1), Elihu knows God provides both. He also introduces the possibility of an angelic intermediary to plead with and for an individual.
Possibly a reference to angels who announce death (see Ps. 78:49).

Elihu pictures a hypothetical scene in which an angelic mediator (see Job's earlier desire for such a figure, 9:32–35) intervenes on behalf of an individual, bringing to him divine truth and pleading with God to deliver him. This will be done on the basis of a "ransom" (v. 24), but it is not specified precisely what this will be. 33:23 an angel. The term basically means "messenger." If here it refers to a superhuman being in general, the thought is not dissimilar to that of Gen. 48:16 (see also "the messenger of the covenant," Mal. 3:1). Moreover, "one of the thousand," or rather "one from a thousand," points to the rarity, indeed the uniqueness, of the one in view here (see 9:3). He may well be identified with "the angel of the Lord." In his intervention in the dispute between Job and his friends, Elihu himself faintly prefigures this unparalleled messenger. a mediator. By introducing God's redemptive purpose in Job's suffering, Elihu substantially realigns the discussion. what is right for him. The messenger's declaration may be understood in two ways. It may consist of the true standard of right conduct (as in v. 27), which may be the means of bringing an individual to faith (see Gal. 3:19–24). Alternatively, "his uprightness" may be that of God Himself, which is perfectly disclosed by Christ as the consummating revelation of God (John 1:18). In either approach, the uprightness presented by the mediator exposes the inadequacy of mere human righteousness and points to the need for God's merciful provision of what is lacking.

–28 The outcome of the angelic mediation is that the sufferer is restored to physical health. This is accompanied by renewed spiritual vitality evidenced by prayer (of repentance, see v. 27) to God and restoration of a right standing before God (v. 26). "Sees his face" (v. 26) denotes a familiar relationship. The restored individual then witnesses to the gracious treatment he has received from God (v. 27, 28). "Look upon the light" refers to enjoyment of life (see v. 30).

This is the culmination of the gracious provision of a ransom appropriated through a prayer of confession. Divine acceptance of the repentant sinner leads to full restoration. As with "his uprightness" in 33:23, in "his righteousness" the personal pronoun may refer to the individual or to God. If that of the individual, this meshes with Job's desire to be declared righteous before God. More probably, however, it refers to God's righteousness, in the sense of the transformation that enables Job to act rightly for God.

God's dealings with an individual may effect his deliverance from death and open up the possibility for further enjoyment of life. Elihu emphasizes that God's dealings with an individual in this life are instructive, though he leaves room for punitive suffering as well. Elihu does not, however, really cover Job's situation, for there is no punitive element in what has come upon Job. Elihu urges Job to consider what he is saying and to set out any difficulties he has with the argument because Elihu desires Job to be set right through God's redemptive grace, but Elihu's assumption that Job needs to be set right in this specific instance is mistaken. Ultimately, Job's travails foreshadow the sufferings of Christ, who, though sinless, "learned obedience through what he suffered" and thus proved Himself to be rightly equipped to serve as high priest (Heb. 5:7–9). Through his suffering, Job will also be equipped to act in a priestly role and pray for his counselors (42:8).

After a pedantic introduction (vv. 2–4), Elihu quotes words from Job that are easy to refute (12:4; 13:18; 27:2, 6). His thesis is that no one is really innocent, so God denies no one justice (vv. 14, 15). The bulk of this second speech is a defense of God's goodness and justice (vv. 10–30). Elihu closes with another condemnation of Job's words and a call for repentance (vv. 31–37).

The expression implies that others are addressed as well as Job and his friends. This is quite possible since the reader does not learn Elihu was present and observing the earlier dialogues until ch. 32.

A fair representation of Job's claim in 27:2. "I am in the right" (see 9:15, 20; 27:6) is a demand that he should be pronounced righteous, that is, innocent of any major sin commensurate with his suffering. The following two occurrences of "my right" take up the term of v. 4, "what is right," an idea closer to "justice" or "just cause" (see 19:7; 27:2).
Elihu accuses Job of having an insatiable propensity to expose himself to ridicule by maintaining his innocence while suffering as he is.

Elihu is probably not making allegations about Job's previous conduct but is asserting that his present accusations against God render his speech and outlook indistinguishable from those of the wicked.

A number of passages are reflected here, but principally 21:15, though that is not Job's own sentiment but his description of the outlook of the wicked. Job has, however, repeatedly argued that God treats the righteous and the wicked alike (see 9:22; 21:17; 24:1–12).
For the next twenty-one verses Elihu expounds this theme. In moments of extreme stress Job said practically the opposite (10:3; 12:4–6; 21:7, 8; 24:1–12).

A clear statement of the retribution principle, which is not wrong in itself as long is it is not viewed simplistically. What is flawed is taking that principle as the exclusive key to understanding God's present providential dealings.
Because God does not depend on anyone for His status, He is sovereign and necessarily in the right.

Elihu is right: God's continual common grace is necessary for any of His creatures to continue to exist. However, the survival of any individual or of humanity as a whole is not a matter of just recompense for their deeds but is grounded in God's inscrutable purposes.

Elihu turns to Job ("you" is singular in these verses) and takes up his query as to why the innocent do not see God's judgment of the wicked (24:1). Elihu's answer is that all, including those in positions of social prominence, are under God's impartial scrutiny, though this is not always evident to the eyes of humanity.

Elihu points to God's omniscience (v. 21 echoes Job's expression in 31:4). He has no need to gather further facts to arrive at a verdict (vv. 21–24) and so does not need to respond to Job's demand for a hearing. God overthrows the wicked suddenly (v. 25) and conspicuously (v. 26). Moreover, no one has the right to condemn God if He does not act immediately (v. 29). The ruler of the universe has to take into account far more than we can comprehend. God does act to prevent the godless from overturning His sovereign purpose (v. 30).
A difficult verse that seems to deal with Job's complaint by asserting that God is acting as judge even though to human perception He is "quiet" and "hides his face."

Elihu asks two questions, of which the first is posed in general terms. He asks if anyone suffering punishment for sin has ever repented. In v. 32 he supposes that the real nature of the offense may be unknown to the sufferer.

Elihu's second question is pointedly directed to Job. He must decide whether to persist in his demands for divine explanation and restitution. "Declare what you know" ("keep to the facts") rather than speculate about what has not been revealed. Elihu urges Job to abandon his wrongheaded thinking and to approach God in a respectful fashion.

In a further attempt to persuade Job, Elihu muses about the verdict of a hypothetical group of wise men who unsurprisingly echo Elihu's viewpoint. The presuppositions of Job's arguments are invalid (v. 35). If a thorough scrutiny of all that he has said were to occur, it would make clear that his thinking has become aligned with the spiritually rebellious (v. 36). Moreover, Job is acting disrespectfully to the wise by clapping his hands in derision to silence them and by making lengthy accusations against God (v. 37).

Elihu addresses Job and takes up his allegation that God has not rewarded him, even though Job is innocent of gross misconduct. Elihu defends divine sovereignty by arguing that God is not affected by Job's sin or by his innocence (vv. 6, 7). Furthermore, God may withhold an answer to the pleas of mankind because of human pride (vv. 12, 13).

Elihu questions Job's consistency in saying that God will vindicate him while at the same time saying it makes no difference whether he has lived a sinful life. 35:2 to be just. Lit. "in accordance with justice." It is my right before God. Lit. "my righteousness from God." Presumably Job expects a divine verdict regarding his innocence.
This question resembles Eliphaz's words in 22:3 but may be extrapolated from Job's words in 9:14–31.
The heavens and the clouds are higher than Job; how much more so is God?

Elihu argues that what happens on earth is incapable of affecting the essential blessedness of God. Human claims of righteousness do not sway God, though He does respond to trust and faith. Elihu has not grasped that Job wants to see God's ways vindicated in the prosperity of those who trust in Him.
Human sin does affect the sinner, and his personal conduct does make a difference to his life (see v. 3).

Job complained in ch. 23 that God has been indifferent to his situation and has not answered his prayers (24:12; 30:20). Elihu counters with some good advice (especially vv. 9–11). But some of it does not apply to Job (v. 12). In times of misery and hardship, people cry out for relief but not always with due recognition of who God is and what He can do. Their cries are self-centered, and do not acknowledge the blessings God has bestowed (v. 11). Cries for relief from distress are not the same as prayer.
God is able to give joy even in the darkest set of circumstances.
Without due recognition of who God is, cries to Him are spiritually empty. They express human arrogance and pride, and so God does not respond (see James 4:1–3).

Elihu criticizes what Job has said and its effect on his relationship to God. Job is inconsistent in saying that he does not see God while also claiming to wait for Him and saying that his case is in God's hands. His presumption leaves his pleas unanswered.

Elihu sets out Job's earlier argument that God does nothing about wickedness (24:1–17). But Job meant only that God's action need not be in this life. Elihu argues that Job's speech was empty in that it was not based on a proper recognition of divine punishment of sin. Elihu views God as continuing to extend grace to Job.
Elihu argues that Job speaks presumptuously, without due recognition of God's sovereign plan (see 34:35, 37) and that this is also God's verdict (38:2).

In his final contribution, Elihu focuses on Job's suffering from the perspective of God's perfect righteousness and absolute power. He speaks of God's justice and power in His dealings with mankind (36:1–26) and then of His sovereignty and benevolence in His dealings with nature (36:27–37:24). God's instruction alerts people to their sin, and whoever ignores it does so at his own peril (37:24).
Elihu opens the speech with a wordy apology in which he reasserts his credentials (see 32:6–33:7; 36:1–4).

Elihu is full of self-confidence regarding his grasp of the situation. He is certain of his ability to proclaim God's "righteousness," probably here referring to God's ability to deliver a correct verdict on human affairs.
If Elihu is describing himself, this is sheer conceit. It may, however, be a divine epithet (see 37:16) with Elihu presenting himself as God's spokesman.

Elihu struggles with Job's complaint about the wicked who prosper and the righteous who suffer (v. 6). With this in mind, he dwells on God's power, goodness, justice, and mercy. But all this is in the context of the simplistic view of suffering that views it as being always in direct proportion to sins while righteousness is always blessed. Only the last judgment will reveal this; cf. John 9:2, 3 with Rom. 2:6; 2 Cor. 5:10. 36:5 Behold. This focus particle occurs four times in this speech to introduce statements about God's power (see vv. 22, 26, 30).

Elihu sides with the three friends in their understanding of divine retribution. God's action toward the unrighteous and the righteous is to be seen in this life. As was clear in 27:13–23, Job affirms that God practices justice. However, he has argued that this might not happen in this life and that certainly God is not acting fairly in his case.
Elihu emphasizes the benefits God bestows on the righteous, making them the equal of kings.

God uses affliction to alert even the righteous to their sin and their arrogant self-sufficiency. If they respond in obedience, then they will once more enjoy prosperity (v. 11). Not listening to God will lead to death. Unlike the three friends, Elihu focuses on Job's spiritual attitude and does not presume there is heinous sin from his past to be unmasked and confessed.
Possibly "cross the river" (33:18 note).

Elihu continues to argue that God's justice is immediately evident in His dealings with "the godless" (see 8:13), who are spiritually insensitive and refuse to yield to God or cry out to Him. God also deals appropriately with the afflicted when He uses their suffering as a means of spiritual discipline and education (v. 15).
A reference to individuals who engage in depraved sexual rituals at idolatrous sanctuaries (see 1 Kin. 14:24; 15:12). A shameful end is described.

Elihu shifts his focus from general principles to Job's particular situation and assures him of God's good purpose in his suffering. He sternly admonishes Job to receive God's divine discipline, with its promise of deliverance from distress. Job's reaction to this experience of divine wrath will give proof of his true inner disposition.
The rendering of vv. 18–20 is difficult. Elihu asks Job to accept the great ransom of 33:24 and not persist in defying God and demanding that He act.
Refers either to "night" as the time when people use the cover of darkness to sin (24:13–17) or to the night of death. Neither will provide adequate shelter for Job.
Job's conduct in complaining against God is wrong. He should bear his affliction without complaint.

Elihu now returns to his opening thesis (v. 5) concerning the sovereignty of God, whose purpose is always good. God uses the circumstances of life to teach (v. 22), and no one is able to sit in judgment over Him (v. 23). It is pointless for Job to maintain his self-righteous stance over against Him. He should instead learn the lesson he is being taught and repent.
In view seems to be the heavenly display of God's greatness. Job has shown his awareness of God's greatness but not of his inconsistency in criticizing Him.
Elihu's graphic description of God's awesome majesty displayed in His control over the forces of nature is somewhat like God's first speech (see ch. 38).
The scope of "judge" here is more general than giving a verdict. In view is the total administration of their affairs.
Probably a reference to the approaching storm.
A difficult passage to translate. Possibly the thought is that if the cattle are restive before the thunder of God, Job should much more take notice.

Elihu also is affected by the magnificence of the thunderstorm. It seems that there is an actual storm approaching, with which the whirlwind of ch. 38 is associated. The chapter division is probably introduced here because of Elihu's reference to his own reaction.
The verb is plural, indicating that up to v. 14 Elihu is speaking also to Job's companions.
The term implies that which is truly extraordinary and therefore beyond human comprehension. It has the same origin as "marvelous" (5:9; 9:10).
Sealing a document means that no more can be added to it. Extending that thought to the human hand implies that individuals are unable to work, possibly because of the bad weather being described.
Elihu may have in mind more than natural storms; he may be generalizing to include the storms of life. for love. persistent, loyal love; here, seeking to reclaim through warning.

Here the link with the divine speeches (chs. 38–41) becomes more pronounced, as the young counselor begins to cross-examine Job about God's power and righteousness. His concluding words anticipate the appearance of God in the heavens (vv. 21, 22).

Elihu's rhetorical questions have exposed Job's ignorance of how God controls natural forces. It is therefore preposterous that mankind can draw up a watertight argument to overthrow God's judgment. "Darkness" refers to lack of comprehension. The implication is that Job's action in ch. 31 is deficient and necessarily misguided.

If looking at the sun in the heavens dazzles human vision, how much more so do human attempts to view the splendor of God. Out of the north. Possibly a reference to the north as the home of the gods (see Ps. 48:2), an idea prevalent in the surrounding culture. The subject of the verb may be "God" or "gold." If the former, the thought is that "He comes with golden splendor."

Elihu has warned Job to show humility before God and not to become narrow-minded in his self-perception and thus to fail to show due reverence and respect to God. In many respects, Elihu here sides with the theology of the friends' simplistic principle of retribution.

In His appearance to Job, God does not mention the subject of Job's suffering, much less give the reason for it. What the Lord says is far more important than Job's suffering, which the Lord knows He will shortly remove. Nor does Job receive the bill of indictment he has wanted (31:35), for there is none. Job learns he must rest his case, including his desire for vindication, in the hands of a sovereign and good God, who is not his enemy (1 Pet. 4:19). God has come not to stand in the dock but to preside over the court. Job does not confront God; the Lord confronts him. 38:1–40:2 The Lord calls on Job to withdraw his accusations against the Almighty by exposing his weakness and foolishness. The divine interrogation contains a measure of sympathy. God questions Job so that Job may come to a greater measure of self-knowledge. His lack of clarity about God reflects a lack of clarity regarding himself. In a series of questions about the natural world, the Lord reveals to Job just how little he actually knows. If Job does not understand God's ways with nature, how can he understand His ways with mankind? Job has displayed impatience and presumption, of which he should repent. True piety is not based on comprehending all about God but on trust in His wisdom and goodness. 38:1 the LORD. The divine covenant name is used again, as in the prologue, showing that the author was an Israelite. Job and his counselors use other divine epithets such as "God" and "the Almighty." Job 12:9 is the only place where Job or the counselors use the covenant name "Yahweh," and some manuscripts have "God" even there. Job was evidently not an Israelite. The use of the name highlights the personal dealings of the Lord with Job as one in a saving relationship with Him. the whirlwind. Presumably associated with the storm Elihu had seen coming (37:22).
God accuses Job of speaking without knowledge (see 34:35; 35:16) and therefore of obscuring what ought to be done in his situation.
Although God has appeared as Job requested, there is no doubt about who is in charge. Job had expected that he would be able to demand answers from God (31:35).

In His cross-examination of Job, the Lord reveals Himself as sovereign over the natural world. He is creator (38:4–15) of the earth (vv. 4–7), of the sea (vv. 8–11), and of day and night (vv. 12–15). He is Lord of inanimate nature (38:16–38) and of animate nature (38:39–39:30). What does Job know about these things? Job has to accept that he is the creature, not the Creator. 38:4 Where were you. Highlights Job's finitude. He obviously was not around when God, as a master builder, constructed the earth. Since he did not see the plan, there are obvious gaps in his knowledge of its execution.
The irony here and in vv. 18, 21 is not sarcasm (intended to hurt), but a reminder that God is the creator.

For the personification of natural forces as God's angels, see Ps. 104:4 and Heb. 1:7. morning stars. Possibly Venus and Mercury. They are personified, not deified. "The sons of God" are angelic beings (1:6; 2:1). Both join in acclaiming the power and wisdom of the Creator (see Ps. 148:2, 3).
God controlled the sea and ordained its boundaries (Gen. 1:9, 10; Ps. 33:7; 104:9; Jer. 5:22). The origin of the oceans is described in terms of giving birth.
God determines the daily cycle of light and darkness and uses the change to curtail the activities of the wicked during the night.
The light of the wicked is darkness (Is. 5:20; Luke 11:35).
Job's limitations are further exposed by listing locations he has never explored: the depths of the sea, the realm of the dead, and the wide expanse of territory throughout the earth.

The "gates" stand for dominion (Matt. 16:18). The Lord is sovereign over this invisible realm, which no living person has ever seen (17:16). According to the pagan religions of Canaan, the god Mot was ruler of the realm of the dead, but Job knows otherwise (see 26:6).
Light and darkness are personified as living in houses, but Job does not know where and he cannot tell where the sun goes when it sets (vv. 19–20).
This is irony, affirming that Job was not present when these aspects of creation were instituted. Only God is eternal (see 36:26).
Job does not know how snow or hail originate. They are viewed as kept in divine storehouses and released by God as a means of intervention in earthly affairs (v. 23; see Josh. 10:11).
. Probably refers to lightning, since this section is about weather. "The east wind" is the storm wind coming from the desert.
Again God puts Job in his place by stressing who is in control of rain and ice. 38:25 cleft a channel. Not a course for a river to flow but a path in the sky along which the rain clouds come.

In a world where rainwater is precious, God impresses on Job His sovereign freedom to do what perplexes those who don't appreciate the distinctions between the sovereign God and themselves. Nature does not exist simply for mankind.

God alone has dominion over the cosmic forces that constrain the cluster of stars called "Pleiades" in the constellation of Taurus and those making up the belt of the hunter Orion. Job acknowledged this in 9:9.
An unknown constellation, not mentioned in 9:9. the Bear. It is uncertain which star with "its children" makes up this constellation to which Job refers.
Job's inability to direct rain (v. 34) and lightning (v. 35) further demonstrates the limitations of his power and knowledge.

The Hebrew word translated "mind" occurs only here, and its meaning has been in question since ancient times. In one traditional translation, the verse asks who gave wisdom to "the ibis" and "the rooster," birds that were thought to announce the coming of the rain and the flooding of the Nile.

The questions shift from inanimate to animate creation, a sampling of God's creatures great and small. Beginning here with lions and ravens, the full list comprises five animals and four birds (38:39–39:30). Job does not sustain the animal realm; God does (see Luke 12:24), and therefore He will surely not neglect the needs of human beings.

God reminds Job of His creative, wise, and sustaining work even in the barren hills where man can scarcely live. This reminds Job of his ignorance by contrast. The "mountain goat" is probably the ibex, which retreats into inaccessible areas to give birth.

This creature was greatly admired for its freedom and its ability to live in "the arid plain" and "the salt land" around the Dead Sea (v. 6). Job has no ability to control the movements of such animals or to sustain them.

This now-extinct animal, the aurochs, was already rare in Palestine in Job's day. These large, powerful creatures resisted domestication. They were hunted to extinction in the ancient Near East by the Egyptians and the Assyrians, though they survived longer in Europe, where they also became extinct. The aurochs is the ancestor of modern domesticated cattle.

The flightless ostrich may have wings, but their wings are not used as expected. "Of love" may well be a reference to "a stork" or "heron," which nests in trees (Ps. 104:17) and has strong wings (Zech. 5:9). In contrast, the ostrich nests on the ground, exposing her young to danger. The mother bird may desert her nestlings (Lam. 4:3).

Though the ostrich cannot fly, it runs faster than a horse. Job has complained of paradoxes in his life; God shows him natural paradoxes that are resolved only in the secret (or revealed) purposes of the self-existent God.

Probably this is the war horse, by reputation the strongest and most intelligent animal but still only partly domesticated. Since Job's strength is inferior to that of the horse, he is unable to compete with the creator of the horse.

The final lesson from the natural realm concerns birds of prey. "Toward the south" (v. 26) refers to the migratory instinct of the sparrow hawk, which passed through the region on its way south. In light of v. 30, the vulture may be intended here.

In addition to the mysterious migratory instinct of birds (v. 26), these words speak of the phenomenal eyesight of eagles. If Job cannot understand or regulate so many features of the created realm, he is in no position to call God to answer for His conduct. Furthermore, the natural realm witnesses to God's concern and provision for it. This runs contrary to Job's allegation that God is uncaring and distant.

This conclusion of the first speech should be compared to its opening with a rebuking question (38:2) and a challenge that Job respond (38:3). Both are directed toward Job's bold but erroneous utterances during his moments of doubt.
Job abandons his obsession with being vindicated. It is his turn to speak, but he has no argument to present. He is brought low before the Almighty.

Job has become aware of his insignificance before the Creator, who controls all. There is no response Job can give. He abandons his earlier self-confidence (10:2; 13:22; 14:15). However, silence before God is not necessarily linked to repentance. Job still seems petulant, overwhelmed by what God has said but not prepared to give up his defiant remonstrance. Even so, God does not give up on Job but speaks to him again.

The same introduction (cf. 40:6 with 38:1) points to the awesome location of the speech. The Lord opens His second discourse (40:6, 7) as He did in 38:1–3, but here he challenges Job with a new line of reasoning about whether God is just in judging the wicked. In His first speech, God revealed Himself as Lord of nature, but here He shows Himself to be Lord of the moral realm. Job cannot act to administer justice. He should be content to leave such matters in God's hands. The divine speech is vehement, stripping away Job's pride.
This section emphasizes God's power over pride and wickedness (vv. 11, 12).

Heb. "nullify my justice." Not only is Job asserting his innocence; he is challenging the integrity of God's administration of the world. Will you condemn me. Job has been prepared to judge God and pronounce a guilty verdict (19:6) because of his sense of self-righteousness and the incomprehensibility of certain aspects of his situation as he perceived it.

Ironic commands meant to underline Job's incapacity to acquire for himself even the garb of divine majesty, far less exercise real power; they highlight his incapacity to judge God's dealings with mankind.

Job had complained that God does not punish the wicked (21:29–31; 24:1–17) — at least not quickly enough — so God ironically suggests that Job undertake the task and so exposes Job's arrogant presumption. If Job could perform that role, God would grant that Job possessed the capacity to remedy his situation. Otherwise Job should rest content with God's way of acting.
Job needs more than vindication before others. He has wronged God. It is his relationship with God that is at stake.

The monsters in these verses, Behemoth and Leviathan, probably represent forces of evil that God can control but before which Job is helpless. As to whether these are real or mythical animals, it seems best to regard them as hyperbolized portraits of something real in the natural realm. However, they also function in an ancient Near Eastern context as symbols of chaos, death, and evil. The power of these animals has sinister and dangerous overtones. If Job cannot control these animals, how can he grapple with the mysterious powers of evil that they represent? 40:15 Behemoth. Since Job is called on to look at Behemoth, which God created, it may be that a real creature is in view. The Behemoth has many points of similarity with a hippopotamus. It is herbivorous (v. 15) and therefore not a threat to other animals (v. 20). The hippopotamus's stomach muscles are far stronger than those of an elephant (v. 16). Its tail, though relatively small, stiffens when the animal is startled or running (v. 17). It was the largest mammal known in the region (v. 19). The Hebrew root is used for "cattle," but the plural form here implies "the beast beyond comparison," particularly in terms of its size and strength. Parts of the description, especially v. 19, go beyond any natural creature such as the hippopotamus or the crocodile. In any event, the Lord's speech indicates that whatever the forces of this creature, it is no more than a plaything in comparison to His unfathomable power.
The habitat described may be the marshy ground near Lake Huleh, which lay to the north of the Sea of Galilee.

The description fits a hippopotamus lying almost totally submerged in water. Its eyes and nostrils do not present a target that a hunter could use to spear and kill it. Less probable is the idea of a domesticated Behemoth led around with a hook in its nose.

Another creature similar to Behemoth, but whereas Behemoth is a beast from the land, Leviathan comes from the sea (see Rev. 13). Leviathan is given the longest treatment of any creature and is even more terrifying than Behemoth. It is mentioned as a climax; it attacks humans (v. 8). The description of its back (vv. 13, 15–17, 23), its teeth (v. 14), its chest and undersides (vv. 24, 30), and the way it causes turmoil in the water (v. 31) all fit with a crocodile as the origin of the representation. Again, the poetic description is anchored in nature but symbolizes something even more terrifying. Like Leviathan in Is. 27:1 and Ps. 74:14, the imagery denotes threatening powers in the heavenly and earthly realms (Rev. 12:7; 13:1). 41:1–11 The implements available to mankind are insufficient for capturing Leviathan. It is so fierce it cannot be tamed as a pet, and no one is able to talk with one (vv. 3–5).

God created and controls these massive creatures, so His might is far greater than theirs. Arguing from the lesser to the greater, if Job or any other human cannot dominate the creatures of God, how do they think they can supervise and direct Him?

It is unlikely that Leviathan is a mythical dragon that breathes fire. It is more probably a hyperbolic portrayal of a crocodile emerging from water. "His sneezings flash forth light" may imply no more than the water vapor it expels when it clears its nostrils after being submerged, seen against the sun as spray.
If the crocodile's presence and movement terrifies strong men, how does Job think he is able to contend with the creator of such an awesome beast?
The point of the comparison is uncertain; perhaps it is to the foam and froth on the surface of a container of boiling liquid.

This fits exactly the lines introducing Behemoth and Leviathan in 40:11, 12. Job cannot humble the arrogant wicked by looking down on them (40:11–14), but Leviathan can. How much more can God look down on Job's proud assertiveness against the Lord Himself? If Job cannot tame these creatures whose might makes them seem contemptuous of other beings and whose presence conveys a constant threat of destructive force, his posturing against God is quite absurd. God, the creator, can deal with these animals and any evil they may symbolically represent. In fact, that is exactly the case throughout the book: Job has (unknowingly) been engaged in a struggle with Satan, whom he has no power to defeat. However, Satan and his forces of evil have no more power than God allows them. He is able to treat them like tame household pets.

Appropriately, Job is now more than humbled: he must repent for his rash words and doubting of God's justice during his deepest suffering and his audacity in thinking he could institute proceedings against God. Because of his experience, his repentance is unforced and sincere as he acknowledges the full dimensions of God's sovereignty and confesses his folly in questioning God's goodness and justice.
See theological note "Omnipresence and Omnipotence" at Jer. 23:24.

Job quotes God's question in 38:2 to admit his fault in speaking beyond what he knows. He responds to both discourses, not just the second one. He now accepts his limitations and concedes God's sovereign wisdom.
Job again quotes God, this time the challenge with which God began His two speeches (38:3; 40:7). In doing so, Job is admitting that he cannot answer God's questions.

Job cannot see physically through the whirlwind out of which God speaks (38:1; 40:6); he expresses a deeper meaning. He had known God with words, but he now experiences His living presence in his inner being. He meets Him as Savior and friend and, above all, God. His disposition to argue through ignorance and presumption has been overwhelmed and removed.

More probably, "I reject myself," "I recall my former opinions." Acknowledging how faulty and rash his speech has been, Job rejects the accusations he had made against God. Throwing dust and ashes over oneself was an accepted expression of humility (2:12 and note). Job grieves over the offense of his sin and is truly repentant. While not accepting his friends' argument that his great suffering has been caused by great sin, Job admits he has not maintained his initially correct attitude toward God (1:21, 22; 2:10) but has become unwarrantably resentful and accusatory (see 34:37). Now Job is willing to trust God, accepting that His ways, while inscrutable, are nevertheless right — even in the calamities that had engulfed him.

The drama introduced in the prologue now comes full circle. The epilogue is written in prose, matching the introductory chapters. 42:7–9 The Lord rebukes Job's counselors and accepts Job's prayers on their behalf. As the eldest among them, Eliphaz represents the others. 42:7 My anger. The Lord's attitude toward the friends is similar to Elihu's reaction in 32:3. what is right. Since God has rebuked (and forgiven) Job for his sinful words, why does He say that Job said what was right while the counselors did not? On the one hand, Job throughout was determined to speak honestly before God. He did not succumb to the threat of disowning Him. On the other hand, though the counselors sincerely tried to defend God and their words were often formally blameless, they were less than upright and honest. The counselors failed in their arrogant assumption of why Job was suffering and in falsely accusing Job of sins of which he was not guilty. They thought they knew all about God, when actually their views were inadequate. That God accepts Job's prayer on their behalf indicates His gracious forgiveness of them also. my servant Job. This phrase, repeated four times in vv. 7, 8, emphasizes Job's restored position as devoted and obedient to God, enjoying fellowship with Him (see 1:8).

We often assume that praying for one's detractors is teaching from the NT, but it is here in Job. In this way Job foreshadows Christ, who, when nailed to the cross, prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34).

The sequence in these verses is significant. The friends are first brought back to God through the instrumentality of Job's intercessory prayer on their behalf. It is in his restored capacity as the servant of the Lord that Job acts. He is then further blessed in that he is abundantly honored by the Lord.

blessed.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} "Bless" reintroduces a term used six times in the prologue, as Job is restored and those who refused to be near him in his dark hour (19:13–20) are forgiven. The number of animals he possesses is double what he lost (v. 10; 1:3), and his seven sons and three daughters replace his family who died. Commentators have objected to this restoration, since so many through the ages have suffered without experiencing such blessing. But God allowed Satan to strike Job to prove that His servant would remain true. The reader knows that Satan was proved a liar: Job never cursed God (1:11; 2:5), and God was glorified. It was the good pleasure of God to reward His servant. The "steadfastness of Job" was known to God (James 5:11). Job's cry, "I will argue my ways to his face" (13:15) can be compared with Jacob's, "I will not let you go unless you bless me" (Gen. 32:26).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Pss. 1; 2 Ps. 1 provides the purpose of the book of Psalms as a manual for living the blessed life, while Ps. 2 provides the overall message of the book in terms of God's reign through His messianic king.
Psalm.note: Ps. 1 provides the purpose of the book of Psalms as a manual for living the blessed life, while Ps. 2 provides the overall message of the book in terms of God's reign through His messianic king. Ps. 1 Like the gateway to a sanctuary, one of the relatively few wisdom psalms introduces the whole collection. Before having close conversation with God, the reader's attitude toward the law of God has to be considered. The righteous person loves and studies it; the wicked person hates it. 1:1 Blessed. A stronger word than "happy" (see Deut. 33:29; 1 Kin. 10:8; 2 Chr. 9:7; Eccl. 10:17; Is. 32:20). To be "blessed" is to enjoy God\'s special favor and grace. walks not \... nor stands \... nor sits. The righteous person is described by what he avoids. There is a downward progression in the verbs "walks," "stands," and "sits." way. A common metaphor in the Wisdom Literature for lifestyle (Prov. 1:15).

"Tree" is a symbol of the blessed life (Prov. 3:18). planted. An image of endurance; the tree will not be blown away like chaff. streams. An image pointing to resources. As the tree drinks from the stream, the righteous drink from "the instruction of the LORD." fruit. Unlike the chaff, which is good for nothing, the righteous live lives of purposeful productivity. prospers. The Hebrew word is broader in scope than English "prospers," which tends to be restricted to finances. The Hebrew word means "succeeds" (Is. 55:11), which fits well with "in all that he does."
The contrast is strong. The wicked are compared to dead and rootless plants. A puff of wind carries them away.

knows the way.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The two ways of life are determined by one's relation to the Lord. Jesus has fulfilled the role that we could never fulfill, and He is also the model to imitate. Ps. 1 shows us a picture of Christ, the perfect blessed man, and it calls us to be increasingly like Christ. perish. The sense is "comes to nothing." As chaff is good for nothing, the wicked way of life comes to nothing (see 112:10).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 2 The theme of kingship pervades this psalm, which gives the overall message of the book: the Lord reigns. While most of the kingship psalms focus on either divine or human kingship, Ps. 2 masterfully integrates both, contrasting the divine King and His human counterpart with the hostile "kings of the earth." The psalm has no title, but the NT ascribes it to David (Acts 4:25). The NT frequently quotes and alludes to this psalm (Matt. 3:17; 17:5; Acts 4:25–27; 13:33; Rom. 1:4; Heb. 1:5; 5:5). Jesus Christ is the Son of David and the Son of God; the promises given to David come to fulfillment in Him.
Psalm.note: The theme of kingship pervades this psalm, which gives the overall message of the book: the Lord reigns. While most of the kingship psalms focus on either divine or human kingship, Ps. 2 masterfully integrates both, contrasting the divine King and His human counterpart with the hostile "kings of the earth." The psalm has no title, but the NT ascribes it to David (Acts 4:25). The NT frequently quotes and alludes to this psalm (Matt. 3:17; 17:5; Acts 4:25–27; 13:33; Rom. 1:4; Heb. 1:5; 5:5). Jesus Christ is the Son of David and the Son of God; the promises given to David come to fulfillment in Him. 2:1–3 In these verses the wicked plot against the Lord and His anointed king. 2:1 plot. The underlying Hebrew word was used in 1:2, where the righteous "meditate" on the Lord's instruction so as to obey it. In contrast the wicked "plot" to rebel against it.

The nations are being organized by their political leaders. his Anointed. Heb. mashiach ("anointed") is the origin of Eng. messiah. The Davidic king was anointed with oil as a symbol of the Holy Spirit's descent to empower the king for office. While the contemporary Davidic king is undoubtedly in view for the psalmist, the ultimate reference of the song is to Christ, the King of kings.
A metaphor for rebellion.
The Lord answers His enemies with the installation of the King. 2:4 sits. That is, sits enthroned as king (29:10). laughs. The kings of the earth are no match for the King of heaven.

The Lord counters the plotting of the kings by pointing to the establishment of His messianic king, prefigured by the previous kings in the line of David. Zion, my holy hill. Zion is a hill north of the Davidic city of Jerusalem. It is important not because of its size but because it is the location of the temple, the place of God's special covenant presence; hence "my holy hill." Jerusalem as a whole is sometimes called "Zion." Earthly Zion was a token of the heavenly Zion. Much of the symbolism of the temple pointed to heavenly realities.

The divine speech addressed to the divine Son (cf. Heb. 1:5), with David as witness, reflects the promise of 2 Sam. 7:14 — the Davidic covenant, which had in view not merely David's earthly descendants but also the divine Son of whom David was also an ancestor.

The poet sets the alternatives before everyone. 2:10 be wise \... be warned. Like the call to wisdom issued throughout the book of Proverbs, the call here is to embrace the wise path that leads to life and to avoid the foolish path that leads to death.

To kiss the Son is an act of submission (cf. 1 Sam. 10:1; 1 Kin. 19:18). The word "Son" is not the usual Hebrew term but an unexpected Aramaic term. perish \... Blessed. The same words used in 1:6 and 1:1, respectively. All are invited to choose between the two ways, one of rebellion against the Son, which leads to death, and the way of trust, which leads to the blessed life.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 3 Surrounded by trouble and crying out to the Lord in distress, the psalmist expresses deep trust in God. The psalm was originally composed when David fled from Absalom and battled against revolt (see 2 Sam. 15:13–37). The military terminology throughout the psalm may indicate that it continued to be used in warfare after David's day.
Psalm.note: Surrounded by trouble and crying out to the Lord in distress, the psalmist expresses deep trust in God. The psalm was originally composed when David fled from Absalom and battled against revolt (see 2 Sam. 15:13–37). The military terminology throughout the psalm may indicate that it continued to be used in warfare after David's day. 3:1–3 These verses (second-person address to the Lord) focus on the psalmist's enemies. 3:1 Many \... rising. The number and nature of the foes betray the royal origin of the psalm. The foes of the nation are also the king's foes.
Here, "salvation" means deliverance in battle.
A common image for protection, e.g., 7:10; 18:2; 28:7. lifter of my head. An expression of encouragement (see 110:7).

These verses (third-person address to the Lord) focus on the psalmist himself. 3:4 holy hill. That is, Zion (see 2:6 note). God designated Zion as the place where His people could approach Him through sacrifice.
As in Ps. 91, the psalmist is able to sleep in the war camp, though the enemy surrounds him.

These verses (third-person address to the Lord) focus on the psalmist's God. 3:7 Arise. This expression is typical of psalms sung at the beginning of war. God fights for His people against their flesh-and-blood enemies. you strike \... you break. In keeping with the first two imperatives, "Arise" and "Save," these verbs are better interpreted as imperatives as well. On this cry for retributive justice, see Introduction: Special Issues.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 4 Like Ps. 3, this psalm was composed in distress, and the psalmist exhibits a deep confidence in God. Both psalms meditate on faith in the night (vv. 4, 8). The righteous have nothing to fear because God hears their prayers and cares for them. The righteous are not without sin but are in covenant relationship with God.
Psalm.note: Like Ps. 3, this psalm was composed in distress, and the psalmist exhibits a deep confidence in God. Both psalms meditate on faith in the night (vv. 4, 8). The righteous have nothing to fear because God hears their prayers and cares for them. The righteous are not without sin but are in covenant relationship with God. 4:1 This verse focuses on prayer. 4:1 Answer me \... my righteousness. The imperative verbs show the boldness of the psalmist in prayer. He can fearlessly call on God because he knows that God is his righteousness (Jer. 23:6).

These verses focus on exhortation. 4:2 my honor be turned into shame. It seems that the psalmist is angry at men who turn away from God to serve the false gods of the nations. vain words. Lit. "empty things." seek after lies. The idols of the nations are lies because they don't really exist. They are the figments of sinful imagination.
Those in covenant with God, the recipients of God's lovingkindness.
Cf. Eph. 4:26. These are the sacrifices prescribed in Lev. 1–7, offered with a righteous attitude without which all sacrifice or worship is unacceptable (Ps. 40:6–8).

Focuses on prayer. 4:6 good. "Good" is bounty or prosperity. The skeptics taunt that there is none. The psalmist responds to their doubts with an appeal for God to reveal Himself, which will bring the psalmist more joy than the physical blessings of grain and new wine that the skeptics are seeking. light of your face. An image of divine favor. The phrase resembles the priestly blessing found in Num. 6:25, 26.
God's intimate presence allows the psalmist to sleep peacefully and with full confidence. His heart is filled with spiritual blessing.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 5 This lament petitions the Lord in the midst of distress. However, the psalmist also expresses trust in the Lord's protection. The psalmist's distress is caused by the evil speech of the wicked.
Psalm.note: This lament petitions the Lord in the midst of distress. However, the psalmist also expresses trust in the Lord's protection. The psalmist's distress is caused by the evil speech of the wicked. 5:1–7 Prayer offered: request (vv. 1, 2a) and reason (vv. 2b–7). 5:1 groaning. The Hebrew word implies a kind of muttering or scarcely audible speech, as would accompany reflection (1:2).
David, Israel's king, addresses God as his king. He knows that his own kingship is a reflection of God's.
Morning follows the night of the previous psalms (4:8).
A poetic understatement. God hates sin (v. 5; 11:5). evil may not dwell. God is holy, "set apart" from all evil. Sinful people may not come into His presence without a substitutionary sacrifice.

The writer knows that he is different from the wicked only because of God's grace. His sin would destroy him if God did not have compassion on him as he approached God's presence. "Steadfast love" is Heb. hesed, God's covenant loyalty. enter your house. The psalmist protests his innocence by stating his desire to worship the Lord. "Your house" and "your holy temple" may refer to the site where the temple would be built or, more likely to the tabernacle of the psalmist's own time (1 Sam. 1:9).
Prayer repeated: request (v. 8) and reason (vv. 9–12). 5:8 your way. The path of safety that God opens is also the path of obedience to His will.
Note how evil speech brings death. throat is an open grave. "Throat" is a metonym for speech, and "open grave" is a metonym for stench: "their speech stinks."
The psalmist calls upon God to punish the wicked because they are guilty. Sin often brings retributive consequences.
A piling up of refuge imagery.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 6 An individual lament. As with many laments, the psalmist expresses his trust in the Lord at the end of the psalm. The occasion of the psalm appears to be a severe illness (vv. 2, 5). This psalm is one of seven penitential psalms (along with 32; 38; 51; 102; 130; 143).
Psalm.note: An individual lament. As with many laments, the psalmist expresses his trust in the Lord at the end of the psalm. The occasion of the psalm appears to be a severe illness (vv. 2, 5). This psalm is one of seven penitential psalms (along with 32; 38; 51; 102; 130; 143). 6:1–4 A series of requests. 6:1 rebuke \... discipline. The psalmist begs the Lord to refrain from verbal and physical punishment. Though God disciplines His people (Heb. 12:1–13), it is for correction and not destruction.
The psalmist experiences suffering, probably a serious illness. Some take the language as figurative for spiritual distress.
The psalmist boldly asks how long God will permit his suffering to continue. He desperately seeks relief from the one who is able to give it.

LORD. The psalmist feels as if God has turned away from him. the sake of your steadfast love. The word translated "steadfast love" indicates God's devotion in binding Himself to His people by His covenant (see 5:7).

A series of reasons for the surrounding requests. 6:5 no remembrance. A similar statement is expressed in 30:9. The doctrine of resurrection, like the doctrine of the Trinity, is implicit in the OT but not developed fully until the NT. The living observe that the dead are silent and do not take part in worship. Sheol. This word is found most often in poetic passages that reveal the thoughts and fears of the living but are not presentations of a doctrine of resurrection or of the intermediate state. See note on Is. 14:9–11. "Sheol" is used most often in the OT simply to refer to the grave.

A request coupled with confidence in the Lord. 6:8 you workers of evil. This reference, along with the reference to "foes" in the preceding verse, is abrupt. It is possible that the foes are people, like the "friends" of Job, who blamed the patient's sickness on his sin.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 7 A lament and psalm of refuge by an innocent person beset by enemies. As one falsely accused of murder could find sanctuary in the house of God and appeal his case to God's judgment, so the psalmist commits his case to God. His protestations of innocence refer to specific charges and are not a claim to sinlessness. See Pss. 11; 17; 26; 27; 31; 71.
Psalm.note: A lament and psalm of refuge by an innocent person beset by enemies. As one falsely accused of murder could find sanctuary in the house of God and appeal his case to God's judgment, so the psalmist commits his case to God. His protestations of innocence refer to specific charges and are not a claim to sinlessness. See Pss. 11; 17; 26; 27; 31; 71. 7:1–9 A prayer for deliverance (vv. 1, 2 and vv. 6, 7) and a confession of innocence (vv. 3–5).

Though not found in Israel today, lions lived there in ancient times. In Scripture the lion often symbolizes power, cruelty, and ruthlessness (Is. 5:29; Nah. 2:11, 12). When used of Christ, the metaphor of the lion refers to strength, glory, and authority.
He is not afraid to invoke a curse on himself, since he knows he is innocent.
See note on 3:7.

There is a judicial setting in this psalm of refuge. God must judge between the psalmist and his opponents. according to my righteousness. Refers to a particular situation and not a general sinlessness.
A confession of God's justice (vv. 10–13) and the outcome of wickedness (vv. 14–16), followed by a vow of gratitude (v. 17).
These terms express the conviction that a sinner reaps what he sows. Sin brings retribution.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 8 The subject of this creation hymn is the majesty of God as revealed in the created order and the majesty of humanity, God's supreme creation. The psalm is arranged concentrically: the majesty of God's name (v. 1a), heaven (vv. 1b–3), the central questions (v. 4), earth (vv. 5–8), and the majesty of God's name (v. 9). This structure teaches the centrality of humanity and the ultimacy of deity. Verses 4–6 are applied to Jesus in Heb. 2:6–8. He was perfect man as well as God. Jesus is the head of redeemed humanity and is restoring human dominion over creation (Gen. 1:28). See also 1 Cor. 15:27 and Eph. 1:22.
Psalm.note: The subject of this creation hymn is the majesty of God as revealed in the created order and the majesty of humanity, God's supreme creation. The psalm is arranged concentrically: the majesty of God's name (v. 1a), heaven (vv. 1b–3), the central questions (v. 4), earth (vv. 5–8), and the majesty of God's name (v. 9). This structure teaches the centrality of humanity and the ultimacy of deity. Verses 4–6 are applied to Jesus in Heb. 2:6–8. He was perfect man as well as God. Jesus is the head of redeemed humanity and is restoring human dominion over creation (Gen. 1:28). See also 1 Cor. 15:27 and Eph. 1:22. 8:1 LORD. The personal, or covenantal, name of God revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Ex. 3). our Lord. A title that can also be translated "governor" or "master." He is our Lord because He has established His covenant with His people. how majestic is your name. The repetition of this line at the end enhances the high note of reverence that pervades the psalm. "Name" signifies the character or reputation of God. 8:1b–3 These verses focus on God's glory in the heavens.
Note the contrast between the weak and the strong. However, because of God, whose praise they sing, the weak silence the powerful. See Matt. 21:16.
The almost limitless universe is described as the work of God's fingers, emphasizing the power of God.

See 144:3. In the vastness of the universe and against the greatness of God's power, man seems to be little but is actually exalted in status. The Hebrew word translated "what" is translated "how" in vv. 1, 9. The answer to the question is found in the majesty of God. Humanity, created in the image of God, is majestic. man \... son of man. The Hebrew terms refer to humanity in general and then to individuals in particular. What is humanity as a whole, let alone mere individuals whom God has crowned with such majesty?

Focuses on humanity's dominion on the earth. All that humanity is has been derived from the gifting of God. 8:5 heavenly beings. The Hebrew word elohim, here translated "heavenly beings," usually means "God," but it can mean "divine beings" (text note). If God were in view, one would expect, "You have made him a little lower than Yourself." See Heb. 2:7. crowned. A royal term. Humanity has a royal majesty. glory and honor. Psalms regularly uses this pair, as well the pair "splendor and majesty" for royalty, both divine (24:7–10; 96:6; 104:1; 111:3; 145:4–13) and human (21:5; 45:3). God imparted a royal majesty to humanity in creation.

The "cultural mandate" of Gen. 1:28 divinely confers on humanity the royal authority and responsibility for governing earthly life. under his feet. In the ancient world an image of dominion over and protection of that which is under the feet.
This poetic line focuses on the majesty of God's name (see v. 1a).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Pss. 9; 10 Originally a single psalm (note the lack of a title for Ps. 10). Together they form a single acrostic (see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry) that is concentrically arranged: a hymn of praise to the divine King (9:1–12), a plea for the Lord to come to the aid of His people (9:13–20), a lament concerning the wicked (10:1–11), a plea for the Lord to come to the aid of His people (10:12–15), and a hymn of praise to the divine King (10:16–18).
Psalm.note: Originally a single psalm (note the lack of a title for Ps. 10). Together they form a single acrostic (see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry) that is concentrically arranged: a hymn of praise to the divine King (9:1–12), a plea for the Lord to come to the aid of His people (9:13–20), a lament concerning the wicked (10:1–11), a plea for the Lord to come to the aid of His people (10:12–15), and a hymn of praise to the divine King (10:16–18). 9:1–12 These verses are a hymn of praise to the divine King. 9:1 wonderful deeds. The Hebrew word refers to the great acts of God, His intervention in human affairs, as at the exodus from Egypt.
A statement of future hope, not past reality.
The psalmist's confidence is not in himself but in God's character as the righteous judge.
To be remembered no more, contrasted with God's name (v. 2), which will be praised forever.
See 2:4.
This refers to God putting everything into right order; see 96:11–13 and 98:7–9.
See note on 2:6. The afflicted should know that God is present with them in the world.
Lit. "seeks blood." God does not let wickedness go unpunished (Gen. 9:6; Nah. 1:2–6).
These verses are a plea for the Lord to come to the aid of His people. 9:13 gates of death. See note on Prov. 1:12. This verse is the first sign of the psalmist's present distress.
Contrasted with "gates of death" in the previous verse. The psalmist will praise God for answered prayer in the most public places in Jerusalem, the "daughter of Zion."
See 7:14–16. The wickedness of such enemies will come back to haunt them.
Further defined in the second half of the verse as "all the nations that forget God." Sheol. See notes on 6:5 and Prov. 1:12.

The phrase "the poor and needy" (35:10; 74:21; Prov. 31:9; Ezek. 18:12) is a fixed expression in the OT, and the words also appear frequently in parallel (72:12; Job 24:4; Is. 32:7; Amos 8:4). The meaning is frequently literal poverty, but the words are also used figuratively to express total dependence on God (40:17; 86:1; 109:22; also Matt. 5:3 and Luke 6:20). Poverty is not itself meritorious, but God gives special attention to the cries of the oppressed (12:5; 72:4 note). Jeremiah equates bringing "justice and righteousness" to the "poor and needy" with knowing God (Jer. 22:15, 16). This was an explicit responsibility of those in power.
See note on Ps. 3:7.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 10 See note on Ps. 9.
Psalm.note: See note on Ps. 9. 10:1–11 The center of Pss. 9; 10; a lament concerning the wicked. 10:1 Why \... do you stand far away. The psalmist is more troubled by the apparent absence of God than by the presence of enemies.
The wicked person's ethical judgments are upside down. He should bless the Lord and reject the greedy.
From the perspective of the oppressed, it appears that the oppressor has no troubles (73:12).
This attitude of self-trust brought trouble to the psalmist himself (30:6). Confidence must be in God, not in one's own ability.
Sins of speech are the focus of attention. Rom. 3:14 alludes to this verse.
The metaphor of the wicked in ambush is well known from Proverbs (Prov. 1:11). stealthily. The wicked prefer to work in darkness, not in light (John 3:19).
The wicked is a hunter of the helpless.

These verses are a plea for the Lord to come to the aid of His people. 10:12 Arise, O LORD. See note on 3:7. lift up your hand. The metaphor refers to God's active intervention in behalf of the psalmist.
In the ancient Near East, the fatherless and the widow were extreme examples of helplessness because they had no kinship protection.
These verses are a hymn of praise to the divine King. 10:16king. God is covenant Lord; see Introduction: Characteristics and Themes. nations. Those who worship other gods and persecute God's people.
The lament concludes with a strong statement of trust in God, who delivers the weak from oppression. Men terrify, but God overrules the wickedness in men.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 11 Another psalm of refuge that shows how to respond when the world around us is collapsing.
Psalm.note: Another psalm of refuge that shows how to respond when the world around us is collapsing. 11:1 to your mountain. Possibly, "from your mountain." If it is "to your mountain," then the advice is to flee the city for a mountain fortress. If it is "from your mountain," then the reference is to Zion. In either case, David is being advised by others to find salvation elsewhere than in God.
While the psalm may have had an original military setting and thus would have found appropriate use during periods of war, the image could also refer to other types of affliction.
That is, of the kingdom conceived as a political entity; including its economy, military, and the like.

These verses focus on the Lord's righteous rule as the object of faith. 11:4 throne. As king of the universe, God is in control (9:7). Nothing escapes His notice. Not even the actions of the wicked are beyond His purview.

Reminiscent of the judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:24). Evil will be completely burned up. the portion of their cup. There is a cup of God's blessing (23:5) as well as a cup of His wrath. The wicked will drink wrath to its dregs (75:8). Jesus Christ took His people's punishment upon Himself by drinking the cup of God's judgment.
God will make His presence known to His people in the darkness. In the resurrection of the just this hope will be realized.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 12 A plea for help in view of the abysmal state of the world. The psalm is concentrically arranged: the earth is in trouble (v. 1), the speech of the wicked (vv. 2–4), the Lord speaks (v. 5), the speech of the Lord (v. 6), and the earth is in trouble (vv. 7, 8).
Psalm.note: A plea for help in view of the abysmal state of the world. The psalm is concentrically arranged: the earth is in trouble (v. 1), the speech of the wicked (vv. 2–4), the Lord speaks (v. 5), the speech of the Lord (v. 6), and the earth is in trouble (vv. 7, 8). 12:1 This verse focuses on the earth/world in trouble. 12:1 the godly one is gone. Like Elijah in 1 Kin. 19:14, the psalmist feels alone in his devotion to the Lord.

These verses focus on the speech of the wicked. 12:2 Everyone utters lies. Lit. "they speak lies," or "emptiness," including outright falsehoods, but also insincere and irresponsible talk, which cheapens and corrodes all human communication.
"Cut off" usually means to be excluded from the community, so the sense may be more than "stop their speaking."
Speech is often used as a weapon (see 3:2; 4:2; 5:9; 10:7).
This verse contains what the Lord Himself says. 12:5 poor. See 10:8–11. arise. See note on 3:7. God promises to act.
This verse focuses on the speech of the Lord. 12:6 pure. The promise in v. 5 can be relied upon because it is pure truth.
These verses focus on the earth/world in trouble. 12:7 keep \... guard. In spite of the apparent chaos in the world, the believer is confident in God's superintending care.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 13 A lament expressed from the perspective of an individual. The situation of distress is not clearly defined, allowing multiple applications. If "enemy" is taken literally, warfare is in view. Or the psalmist may be ill and near death (v. 3).
Psalm.note: A lament expressed from the perspective of an individual. The situation of distress is not clearly defined, allowing multiple applications. If "enemy" is taken literally, warfare is in view. Or the psalmist may be ill and near death (v. 3). 13:1, 2 These verses focus on the expression of dark feelings with regard to God, self, and others. 13:1 How long. See note on 6:3. The fourfold repetition expresses his anguish and frustration. God could resolve the issue in a moment but is letting it drag on. forget \... hide your face. The psalmist feels abandoned by God (see 22:1).

These verses focus on the psalmist's requests regarding God, self, and others that arise from the feeling of vv. 1, 2. 13:3 Consider \... answer. The psalmist wants God to pay attention. light up. The psalmist wants physical sustenance rather than illumination of some sort. This same language is used of Jonathan after he ate some honey and was revived (1 Sam. 14:27, 29; see also Ps. 38:10).

These verses focus on the psalmist's faith and God's character. 13:5 But I have trusted. The Hebrew emphasizes the pronoun "I" and thus the psalmist's faith. steadfast love. Faith is founded upon God's covenant loyalty. shall rejoice. The Hebrew grammatical form expresses the resolve of faith. salvation. Faith is founded upon God's saving deeds (9:1).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 14 This psalm has an attitude of quiet meditation that focuses on the fool: the fool's character (vv. 1–4) and the fool's fate (vv. 5–7). See Ps. 53, which is an alternate version of Ps. 14.
Psalm.note: This psalm has an attitude of quiet meditation that focuses on the fool: the fool's character (vv. 1–4) and the fool's fate (vv. 5–7). See Ps. 53, which is an alternate version of Ps. 14. 14:1–4 These verses focus on the fool's character. 14:1 fool. The fool may be highly intelligent by the world's standards but is oblivious to the true nature of reality (Eccl. 2:14). To be called a fool is a moral judgment (see Prov. 1:22 note). There is no God. The fool denies the existence of God, which is practical atheism. God is held to be unconcerned about the affairs of the world and especially the affairs of the individual. corrupt. Note Paul's use of this psalm in Rom. 3:10–18. Foolishness points to lack of morality, not absence of native intellect. none who does good. Refers to doing good absolutely, with one's motives governed fully by a desire to honor the Lord (v. 3; Eccl. 7:20; Rom. 3:12). Until our glorification, sinners cannot do good in this perfect, absolute sense. However, sinners can do good relatively. In comparison to others, some people can rightly be called "good." (Prov. 12:2; 13:22; 14:14; Rom. 2:10; 3 John 11). Relative acts of good are insufficient to save us, for God demands absolute perfection for our justification. Only Christ can provide this perfection (Matt. 5:48; Rom. 3:21–26).
Fallen man does not actively seek God.
Absolute language used to communicate relative truth. as they eat bread. The wicked exploit people frequently and without feeling guilt. It is as natural to them as eating bread.

Those who would shame others will themselves experience shame. his refuge. God can overrule the wicked plans of evildoers for the good of the afflicted. This principle is stated by Joseph (Gen. 50:20) and is applied to the crucifixion in Acts 2:22–24.
Fools will experience none of this. out of Zion. The place where God most personally and directly revealed His presence.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 15 Reminiscent of Ps. 1, this psalm focuses on the requirements for approaching God's presence at the sanctuary. It is similar to 24:3–6. The two passages (cf. also Is. 33:14–16) have been called "entrance liturgies," since they answer the question, "Who can enter the holy place of God?"
Psalm.note: Reminiscent of Ps. 1, this psalm focuses on the requirements for approaching God's presence at the sanctuary. It is similar to 24:3–6. The two passages (cf. also Is. 33:14–16) have been called "entrance liturgies," since they answer the question, "Who can enter the holy place of God?" 15:1 Raises the question as to the qualifications for entering God's presence. tent. Before the temple was built, the symbol of God's dwelling with His people was a tent. holy hill. Mount Zion, where the temple was located.
The qualifications for entering God's presence. The ten requirements for entrance are ethical, not formal or liturgical.
Alternatively, "and does not falter." The point is the same: when he promises, the righteous person fulfills his word.

See Deut. 23:19, 20. A foreigner, but not a fellow Israelite, could be charged interest. Loans were intended to relieve extreme need, and interest on such loans was a form of exploitation. 15:5b shall never be moved. This verse issues a promise to those who meet the qualifications for entering God's presence. Cf. the boast of self-reliance of the wicked who say, "I shall not be moved" (10:6). Stability in life is a good thing. The question is whether God or self will be relied upon for the stability.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 16 This psalm expresses confidence in the Lord and presents numerous perspectives on what trust is.
Psalm.note: This psalm expresses confidence in the Lord and presents numerous perspectives on what trust is. 16:1, 2 Teaches that trust is reliance on the Lord. 16:1 Preserve me. An invocation of the Lord and a plea for help. This line indicates that the psalmist is in crisis.
Teaches that trust is devotion to the Lord. 16:3 saints. Lit. "those who are set apart," God's elect people.
Teaches that trust is delight in the Lord. 16:5 portion \... cup \... lot. Three metaphors that describe life as a gift of God.

Teaches that trust is learning from the Lord. 16:7 bless. To bless the Lord is to praise Him in response to the blessings He has granted. heart. Lit. "kidneys" (text note). Like "heart," it stands for the core of a person's being.
Teaches that trust is rejoicing in the Lord.

The immediate application of this psalm is to David and the OT saints. It refers to deliverance from the immediate threat of death, but it points prophetically to the Son of David whom the historical David reflected and anticipated. Both Peter and Paul recognized Jesus as the ultimate fulfillment of this psalm (Acts 2:25–28; 13:35).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 17 A psalm of refuge titled "Prayer," and the nature of this psalm as a "prayer" is underscored by the concentric arrangement that has prayer in the outside frame and in the center: prayer for vindication (vv. 1, 2), affirmation of the psalmist's innocence (vv. 3–5), prayer for protection (vv. 6–8), description of the psalmist's accusers (vv. 9–12), and prayer for deliverance and blessing (vv. 13–15).
Psalm.note: A psalm of refuge titled "Prayer," and the nature of this psalm as a "prayer" is underscored by the concentric arrangement that has prayer in the outside frame and in the center: prayer for vindication (vv. 1, 2), affirmation of the psalmist's innocence (vv. 3–5), prayer for protection (vv. 6–8), description of the psalmist's accusers (vv. 9–12), and prayer for deliverance and blessing (vv. 13–15). 17:1, 2 Prayer for vindication. 17:1 free of deceit. The psalmist is not denying that he is a sinner. He is denying specific charges made against him (see Ps. 7:8).
Affirmation of the psalmist's innocence. 17:3 tried my heart. Here, the "heart" is the hidden center of a person's being, but God can read the heart.
God's will, disclosed in the law of God.
These ways, as spelled out in God's Word, are to be contrasted with the "ways of the violent" (v. 4).
Prayer for protection.

The Hebrew word denotes God's love toward those with whom He is in covenant relationship. Savior. The psalmist could look back over the history of Israel and see how many times God had saved His people in distress. The exodus from Egypt is the prime example of God's saving love in the OT.

Lit. "little man," and then pupil, since one can see a reflection of oneself, a "little person," when one looks into the eye of another. A term of endearment well captured by the English expression "apple of the eye" (Deut. 32:10; Prov. 7:2; Zech. 2:8).
Description of the psalmist's accusers.
An alternative translation is "their fat," a caricature of their physical appearance.
The enemy has taken the initiative to destroy the psalmist.
When used as a negative metaphor, the reference is to ruthlessness and cruelty. Cf. 7:2; 10:9; 22:13.
Prayer for deliverance and blessing. 17:13 Arise. See note on 3:7.

Refers to the righteous and uses the blessing of children as synecdoche for the experience of blessing in general. leave their abundance. "A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children" (Prov. 13:22).
The psalmist will know God's presence, hinting at his resurrection in the "likeness" of God (1 John 3:2).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 18 This psalm thanks the Lord for a great deliverance. The strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry) are arranged concentrically: opening praise of the Lord as refuge (18:1–3), what the Lord does for the king (18:4–19), central praise of the Lord as refuge (18:20–30), what the Lord does through the king (18:31–45), and concluding praise of the Lord as refuge (18:46–50). The opening and closing strophes and the central strophe show the main point of the psalm: the praise of the Lord as refuge. This same psalm appears in 2 Sam. 22 with minor differences.
Psalm.note: This psalm thanks the Lord for a great deliverance. The strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry) are arranged concentrically: opening praise of the Lord as refuge (18:1–3), what the Lord does for the king (18:4–19), central praise of the Lord as refuge (18:20–30), what the Lord does through the king (18:31–45), and concluding praise of the Lord as refuge (18:46–50). The opening and closing strophes and the central strophe show the main point of the psalm: the praise of the Lord as refuge. This same psalm appears in 2 Sam. 22 with minor differences. 18:title See Introduction: Author; Characteristics and Themes. The title unambiguously attributes this psalm to David. 18:1–3 Opening praise for the Lord as refuge. 18:1 love. Not the usual Hebrew word for love; it emphasizes intimacy, expressing David's personal devotion. See 116:1.
Connotes protection. When David fled from Saul, he could find refuge in the caves and cliffs of the dry streambeds.

What the Lord does for the king. 18:4 cords of death. The tentacles of death rise up from Sheol, the underworld, to drag the psalmist down. torrents of destruction. The powers of evil and death are frequently likened to an overwhelming flood (46:2 note; 69:1, 2 notes; Is. 28:15, 17, 18; Matt. 16:18).
The place of God's special presence. At the dedication of the temple Solomon indicated that the proper response to trouble was to pray to God in or while facing the temple (1 Kin. 8).

When God reveals Himself as a warrior, nature convulses (Is. 24:4–13; Nah. 1:5). mountains. The hills symbolize all that is firm and established in the world, but they shake before the might of God (see Ex. 19:18).
The nostrils and mouth are standard figures of speech for anger (text note). Smoke and fire often accompany a theophany (a visual self-revelation of God; Gen. 15:17; Ex. 19:18; Nah. 1:6).

God is pictured as coming with the storm clouds into battle. This portrayal is frequent in the Bible (68:4; 104:3; Nah. 1:3; Dan. 7:13). In the NT, Christ is portrayed as coming in the clouds (Mark 13:26; Rev. 1:7).

Angelic beings first mentioned in Gen. 3:24. Their role in Gen. 3 and their symbolic representation at key places in the tabernacle (Ex. 26:1, 31) indicate that they are guardians of God's holiness (cf. Ezek. 1; 10).
Thunder; cf. 29:3–9.
Lightning.

When God appears as a defender of His people, the waters representing chaos and evil shrink back. Cf. 77:16–19 (reflecting on the exodus from Egypt); Nah. 1:4; Rev. 21:1. rebuke. God controls the chaotic waters of the sea (104:7; 106:9). Jesus shows Himself to be the second person of the Trinity by silencing the chaotic waters with His rebuke (Luke 8:22–25).
Symbolic of trouble and distress (32:6; 69:2).

This may be an allusion to the exodus and the conquest of Canaan. God delivered Israel from many waters (Red Sea) and brought them to a broad place (the Promised Land). The broad place contrasts with a narrow one, from which it would be hard or impossible to escape from an enemy.
Central praise of the Lord as refuge.
LORD. God's covenant law.
The term translated "merciful" has reference to God's special lovingkindness toward those with whom He is in covenant relationship.
A constant teaching of the OT and the Psalms, most notably 113:7–9.
A glimpse at the original inspiration of the verse. It appears as if the psalmist is waging war.

LORD. His revelation to His people. Since this is a psalm of David in a warfare setting, perhaps the reference is more specifically to 2 Sam. 7, the Davidic covenant, where the Lord promises to be David's Father and God.
What the Lord does through the king. 18:31 but the LORD. The use of these rhetorical questions is emphatic: there is no one like the Lord (Ex. 15:11).
Bows were constructed primarily of wood, at times reinforced with metal. The bronze bow is meant to suggest the psalmist's God-given strength.
Paths are narrow and rocky in Israel, permitting slippage and injury to a soldier. The divinely enabled, steadfast faith of David is illustrated.
See text note and Josh. 10:24. Ancient Near Eastern tablets and stone memorials show enemies under the feet of conquerors and bowing before their captors.
LORD. Indicates that the psalmist was battling fellow Israelites.
David's personal imprint is strong here. God granted him victories over neighboring nations that were brought under his rule (2 Sam. 8:1–14).
Concluding praise of the Lord as refuge.
Quoted by Paul in Rom. 15:9 as fulfilled in Christ, who brings the Gentiles to join in His praise of God the Father.
At his coronation, the king was anointed with oil by the priest. Jesus Christ, David's Lord and descendant, ultimately fulfills this psalm.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 19 The psalm praises the Lord for His two great gifts to humanity: creation and the law. To use modern terminology, the psalm speaks of God's general revelation in nature and His special revelation in Scripture.
Psalm.note: The psalm praises the Lord for His two great gifts to humanity: creation and the law. To use modern terminology, the psalm speaks of God's general revelation in nature and His special revelation in Scripture. 19:1–6 Celebrates God's revelation in creation. 19:1 heavens. The psalmist uses creation language here; cf. Gen. 1:1–8, where this word has been translated "expanse." See theological note "Divine Revelation" on next page.
This metaphor claims that the creation, specifically the heavens, constantly attests God's power and goodness.
