These verse show the need for transformation. 51:10 Create. The verb is the same one used at Gen. 1:1 for the creation of the world, a verb that focuses on the newness of the thing created. The psalmist knows that the redirection of his desires and thoughts can come about only through the intervention of God. See theological note "Repentance" on p. 1964.

The OT does not make a full disclosure of the personhood of the Holy Spirit. David understands that his spiritual well-being depends on God's presence with him. He fears that the Spirit of anointing for kingship may be taken away from him, as the Spirit was taken from Saul (1 Sam. 16:14). See theological note "The Personality of the Holy Spirit" on p. 1889.
David suffered from a spiritual dullness that led to moral bankruptcy. To prevent such disaster in the future, he prays for joy.
If forgiven, David promises to use his life to help others find forgiveness (see Ps. 32).
David has already spoken of God's justice in condemning sin (v. 4). Now, the same justice overcomes sin and condemnation through grace, as explained in Rom. 3:21–26 and epitomized in 1 John 1:9.
See 50:9. The Bible values heartfelt obedience above outward religious conformity (40:6–8; Mic. 6:6–8). As v. 19 shows, this does not condemn sacrifices as such.
The restoration of the king leads to blessing for the people.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 52 This psalm, like Ps. 49, is an instructional poem that expresses confidence in the Lord, like a psalm of trust; pronounces judgment on the wicked, like a lament; and uses wisdom language. The psalm focuses on the question of personal security: will it be found in oneself (vv. 1–7) or in God (vv. 8, 9)?
Psalm.note: This psalm, like Ps. 49, is an instructional poem that expresses confidence in the Lord, like a psalm of trust; pronounces judgment on the wicked, like a lament; and uses wisdom language. The psalm focuses on the question of personal security: will it be found in oneself (vv. 1–7) or in God (vv. 8, 9)? 52:title The historical title refers to the event recorded in 1 Sam. 22:6–23. In effect, the title identifies Doeg with the boastful, wicked man and David with the righteous psalmist. However, the psalm itself is not so specific and continues to be immediately relevant to the people of God. 52:1–7 These verses ask about the wisdom of finding security in self. 52:1 boast of evil. As if evil deeds will provide all that one needs. mighty man. A soldier or warrior.
More exactly, "confused." The Wisdom Literature consistently teaches that confusion is on the side of the wicked and order on the side of righteousness.

This verb may seem strange as associated with laughter. The meaning, however, is not fear in the sense of dread but rather in the sense of reverence and awe. The righteous see the justice of God's judgment against the wicked.

This man is the opposite of everything the psalms stand for. Throughout the psalms people are urged to find their security in God, not themselves. God is the power behind His people in all their victories. trusted in \... riches \... sought refuge in his own destruction. Relied on self for security.

These verses encourage the wisdom of finding security in God. 52:8 olive tree. Reminiscent of Pss. 1; 92. Olive trees can live for hundreds of years. I trust in the steadfast love of God. The psalmist found security in God.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 53 Cf. Ps. 14. A meditation on the wickedness of the fool. God will destroy the fool and restore Israel's fortunes. Ps. 53, in contrast to Ps. 14, uses "God" rather than the more specific, covenant name "LORD" (Yahweh) to refer to the deity. This variation fits the broader context, since Ps. 53 is in Book 2 of the Psalter, which uses the broader term rather than the covenant name.
Psalm.note: Cf. Ps. 14. A meditation on the wickedness of the fool. God will destroy the fool and restore Israel's fortunes. Ps. 53, in contrast to Ps. 14, uses "God" rather than the more specific, covenant name "LORD" (Yahweh) to refer to the deity. This variation fits the broader context, since Ps. 53 is in Book 2 of the Psalter, which uses the broader term rather than the covenant name. 53:1–4 See notes on 14:1–4.

In the OT, God often fights for His people against their flesh-and-blood enemies. With NT revelation the underlying spiritual conflict to save His people from sin becomes the dominant theme, although the fundamental conflict has been at the spiritual level from the beginning (Gen. 3:4, 5).
An expression of hope for deliverance from evil.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 54 The psalm is prayer and praise for the power of God, which sustains and delivers from opposition, and has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): a prayer for vindication (vv. 1–3), an affirmation of faith (v. 4), and praise for deliverance (vv. 5–7).
Psalm.note: The psalm is prayer and praise for the power of God, which sustains and delivers from opposition, and has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): a prayer for vindication (vv. 1–3), an affirmation of faith (v. 4), and praise for deliverance (vv. 5–7). 54:title The historical title locates the inspiration of the psalm in David's pre-monarchical days. He wrote the psalm after being betrayed by the Ziph­ites (1 Sam. 23:19; 26:1). 54:1–3 These verses are a prayer for vindication. 54:1 vindicate me. Identifies his complaint as a judicial one. David had been unjustly betrayed by the Ziphites, his countrymen from Judah.
Though they are countrymen, he does not know them personally.
This verse is an affirmation of faith. 54:4 God is my helper. See 33:20; 44:26; 124:8. John Calvin routinely used 124:8 at the beginning of worship.
These verses offer praise for deliverance.
A sacrifice of thanksgiving and a thanksgiving psalm were customary responses to God's deliverance of His people. See 22:22 and note.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 55 Like many laments, this psalm bemoans the attack of enemies. Most unusual is the sorrow over betrayal by a friend. The psalm descends to the pits of despair but turns at the end toward the Lord with hope. The macrostructure of this psalm is not clear, so it is best to read it in a series of small units. The psalm anticipates the suffering of Christ, who was betrayed by Judas, a disciple of His inner circle (Matt. 26:47–56).
Psalm.note: Like many laments, this psalm bemoans the attack of enemies. Most unusual is the sorrow over betrayal by a friend. The psalm descends to the pits of despair but turns at the end toward the Lord with hope. The macrostructure of this psalm is not clear, so it is best to read it in a series of small units. The psalm anticipates the suffering of Christ, who was betrayed by Judas, a disciple of His inner circle (Matt. 26:47–56). 55:1–5 An opening cry for help
The psalmist refers to enemies in general terms because he knows that his song will be used by other people in other situations (v. 22).
Expresses the psalmist's urge to flee. 55:6 I would fly away. The writer has the urge to escape the source of his distress but is unable to do so.
Bemoans the reign of violence. 55:9 divide their tongues. The psalmist alludes to the judgment the Lord brought upon the wicked generation who built the tower of Babel (Gen. 11:1–9).
Lawless men are loose and active on the walls, the main defense of the city.
This description of an ancient city of Israel, presumably Jerusalem during David's reign, could be applied to today's lawless cities.
Bemoans betrayal by a friend.
The terms become increasingly intimate, from "a man, my equal" to "my companion" to the climax, "my familiar friend."
The worst hurt of all is that the close friend was a fellow worshiper in the house of God.
A prayer for justice.
A statement of confidence. 55:15 down to Sheol alive. That is, into Sheol, the grave.
While the psalm conceivably had its origin in battle, it is more likely that the battle is a metaphor for the struggles that the psalmist feels with his enemies and friends who surround him.
God hears the psalmist's prayers from His kingly throne in heaven.
The psalmist describes the willful breaking of a formal agreement between friends. A covenant is a solemn agreement under sanctions.
A powerful, poetic description of hypocrisy and deceit.

Shows the psalmist's ultimate recourse. 55:22 never permit the righteous to be moved. See 121:3. The context of the psalm shows that there is no unqualified promise that the righteous will always be happy and prosperous. The psalmist sings this lament to the Lord because he is in despair. The verse must mean that God will not leave the righteous in the fallen position forever but will vindicate them in the end.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 56 The psalm has characteristics of both the lament and the psalm of confidence. The psalmist expresses fear and faith, but faith prevails in the end.
Psalm.note: The psalm has characteristics of both the lament and the psalm of confidence. The psalmist expresses fear and faith, but faith prevails in the end. 56:title The title is difficult to fit into David's life as it is known from the Historical Books. The closest parallel is 1 Sam. 21:10–15, when David was feigning madness before the king of Gath in order to escape him. 56:1, 2 A prayer for mercy. 56:1 Be gracious. A common prayer in the laments (see 4:1; 6:2; 31:9; 41:4, 10), sometimes translated, "have mercy" or "be merciful" (51:1; 57:1).
The enemies, like ruthless animals, treat the psalmist as their prey.
Moves from fear and faith. 56:3 When I am afraid. Experiencing fear from time to time is not unusual for God's people.
Describes the psalmist's trouble.
Moves from need to confidence. 56:7 cast down the peoples. The parallelism of this verse suggests that the enemies are the foreign nations that surround Israel.
The psalmist is calling upon God to hear and remember his prayer.
The psalmist remembers God's covenant promises, such as Deut. 28:7, a promise that God will scatter the enemies of His people.
These verses, like vv. 3, 4, move from fear to faith.

A vow to give thanks once the psalmist is delivered. 56:12 render thank offerings. When the psalmist's prayer is answered, he promises to return to offer his thanks. He would do this by offering sacrifices and singing thanksgiving songs similar to Ps. 34. See 22:22 and note.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 57 Like Ps. 56, Ps. 57 expresses both lamentation and confidence, with confidence being the final note. The refrain in vv. 5, 11 divides the psalm into two stanzas and gives the ultimate perspective of confidence prevailing over adversity. There are four concentrically arranged strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 1–3), confidence (vv. 4, 5), confidence (v. 6), and God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 7–11).
Psalm.note: Like Ps. 56, Ps. 57 expresses both lamentation and confidence, with confidence being the final note. The refrain in vv. 5, 11 divides the psalm into two stanzas and gives the ultimate perspective of confidence prevailing over adversity. There are four concentrically arranged strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 1–3), confidence (vv. 4, 5), confidence (v. 6), and God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 7–11). 57:title The psalm was composed before David was king, when he was hiding from Saul in a cave. Many scholars relate the psalm to 1 Sam. 24, but a closer parallel is 1 Sam. 22:1–5, when David fled to the cave of Adullam. 57:1–3 These verse express trust in God's steadfast love and faithfulness. 57:1 Be merciful. See note on 56:1. shadow of your wings. The image of God as a mother bird protecting her young from trouble communicates God's compassion for His people (see Ruth 2:12). See note on maternal representations of God at 131:2.
The word translated "steadfast love" indicates God's devotion in binding Himself to His people by His covenant.
Expresses confidence in the face of opposition. 57:4 lions. Lions were numerous in the ancient Near East and in Palestine. They often symbolized power and ruthlessness.

Expresses confidence in the face of opposition. 57:6 net \... pit. Like a hunter, the enemy sets snares for the psalmist. The principle that evil people are ultimately caught by their wicked schemes is a theme that runs through the Psalms and the Prophets. See 7:14–16; 34:21; 35:8; 37:15. fallen into it themselves. One reaps what one sows (Gal. 6:7; cf. 2 Cor. 9:6; Hos. 8:7; 10:12).
These verses express praise for God's steadfast love and faithfulness. 57:7 steadfast. Nothing can swerve the psalmist from his faithful intention to offer up his hymn of praise.
He will praise the Lord through the night, until dawn arises.
God is more than the God of Israel. He is king of the universe, and the psalmist will praise God's great deeds throughout creation.
See v. 3.
See v. 5.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 58 Psalms of lament often contain curses directed against the evil and unjust. The objects of the psalmist's scorn seem to be human rulers (v. 1 note), especially unjust judges. The psalm has two stanzas; the first (vv. 1–5) addresses the problem of injustice, while the second (vv. 6–11) points to a resolution. Early Christian tradition associated this psalm with the high priest and the Sanhedrin as they condemned Jesus (Matt. 26:57–68).
Psalm.note: Psalms of lament often contain curses directed against the evil and unjust. The objects of the psalmist's scorn seem to be human rulers (v. 1 note), especially unjust judges. The psalm has two stanzas; the first (vv. 1–5) addresses the problem of injustice, while the second (vv. 6–11) points to a resolution. Early Christian tradition associated this psalm with the high priest and the Sanhedrin as they condemned Jesus (Matt. 26:57–68). 58:1–5 These verses articulate the problem of injustice in the world. 58:1 gods. The word "gods" could be used for the corrupt judges of this verse, according to the example in 82:1 (text note).

David recognized this of himself in 51:5. All are born with a nature that re­bels against God — the doctrine of original sin. David means that the wickedness of the evil judges in particular extends back to the beginning of their lives.

The psalmist likens the wicked rulers to snakes. The story of the fall (Gen. 3), initiated by the Serpent, sharpens the image. The rulers' words are as distinctive as the venom of the serpent, and they turn a deaf ear to logical arguments and even divine judgments that may be addressed to them.
These verses point toward a solution to the problem of injustice.
Bring to nothing their evil schemes that seek violence against the innocent.

Eternity will show that God's judgment of the wicked is just. This judgment will cause rejoicing since the alternative would be unthinkable: heaven populated with God's enemies (Rev. 16:5, 6; 19:1–3; 21:27).

When the wicked prosper or the righteous suffer, faith is shaken. The covenant promises of Deut. 28 provide for curses on the wicked and blessings for the righteous. The last judgment will set things right again.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 59 The psalm is a lament and is symmetrically arranged in two stanzas with three matching strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): petition with reasons (vv. 1–5), the enemy as dogs (vv. 6, 7), a statement of assurance (vv. 8–10), petition with reasons (vv. 11–13), the enemy as dogs (vv. 14, 15), and statement of assurance (vv. 16, 17). The quasi refrain that marks the end of each stanza provides the theme of the psalm: "O my Strength \... my fortress" (vv. 9, 17).
Psalm.note: The psalm is a lament and is symmetrically arranged in two stanzas with three matching strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): petition with reasons (vv. 1–5), the enemy as dogs (vv. 6, 7), a statement of assurance (vv. 8–10), petition with reasons (vv. 11–13), the enemy as dogs (vv. 14, 15), and statement of assurance (vv. 16, 17). The quasi refrain that marks the end of each stanza provides the theme of the psalm: "O my Strength \... my fortress" (vv. 9, 17). 59:title The psalm comes from the period before David became king. Saul set a watch over David's house, hoping to kill him; but David's wife Michal, the daughter of Saul, helped David escape (1 Sam. 19:11–17). 59:1–5 These verses offer a petition with reasons.

The psalmist is not saying that he is without sin; he is asserting that the enemy has no cause against him. This was true of the original situation, where David had committed no aggression against Saul's kingship. See Ps. 26.
This divine title indicates that God has heavenly armies at His command. nations \... plot evil. The enemies come from the nations outside of Israel but also from within.
These verses portray the enemy as dogs. 59:6 like dogs. The enemies are like a pack of dogs who roam the streets of the city and make them unsafe. Dogs were not valued in the ancient Near East.
These verses are a statement of assurance.

God will lead the way in the fight against the enemy. In the time of Joshua, the ark, symbolic of God's presence, led Israel into the Promised Land. look in triumph. For now, the enemy gloats over the psalmist, but the psalmist expects a reversal.

These verses offer a petition with reasons. 59:11 Kill them not. The psalmist desires to prolong the suffering of the enemy. This will make them an example to the rest of Israel that evil doesn't pay.
Words are powerful and can bring either great blessing or tremendous harm.
The ultimate goal of the destruction of the enemy is that the glory of God's justice may be seen.
These verses portray the enemy as dogs; see v. 6.
These verses are a statement of assurance.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 60 The psalm laments a military defeat and asks God why He has rejected the people. For the most part, the community voice dominates, and the psalm addresses God with the first-person plural.
Psalm.note: The psalm laments a military defeat and asks God why He has rejected the people. For the most part, the community voice dominates, and the psalm addresses God with the first-person plural. 60:title This psalm has the longest title in the Psalter, referring to the events recorded in 2 Sam. 8 and 1 Chr. 18. The Historical Books, however, tell only of the conclusion of the battle's victory. The title and the psalm suggest that David experienced setbacks on the way to victory. The Historical Books and the psalm differ on the number of Edomites killed in the Valley of Salt, probably through a copyist's error. The psalm associates Joab with the victory, while 2 Sam. 8:13 names David, and 1 Chr. 18:12 lists Abishai. All three were high commanders in the army and could be credited with the victory. 60:1–5 States the problem faced by the psalmist and his request. 60:1 rejected us. When God rejects His people, He abandons them and leaves them to the mercy of the enemy. It is only with God's approval that the people of Israel have any reason for confidence.

A frequent image in the Prophets. The cup that makes a nation stagger is the cup of judgment (Jer. 25:15–38; Nah. 3:11). Jesus drank the cup of wrath to its dregs in behalf of His people (Matt. 26:39 and par.).
The verse is a token of hope for the faithful. God gives protection to His people from the weapons of the enemy.

Contains a reminder of God's promises. 60:6 God has spoken in his holiness. The divine oracle was probably spoken through a prophet associated with the temple (text note). The gist of his message is that victory will be forthcoming, a message borne out by the report in 2 Sam. 8. I will divide. The following verses exult in the inheritance of the Promised Land. Shechem \... Succoth. These names are the first two places that Jacob occupied after returning from his encounter with Esau (Gen. 33:17–20). They are on opposite sides of the Jordan River.

Both areas are located, at least in part, in the region of the Trans­jordan. Ephraim \... Judah. The two most powerful tribes in Israel. They were frequently rivals, but here they are united as parts of God's army.

Moab and Edom were east of Judah, and Philistia was west of Judah on the Mediterranean coast. These countries were traditional enemies of Israel, but in this song God exults in His power and authority over them. cast my shoe. A gesture of contempt, or possibly a claim to ownership (Ruth 4:7).
Raises the psalmist's questions and his faith in a good outcome. 60:9 me. Likely the king, who speaks on behalf of the nation.
The psalmist confesses that it is only through God's power that they will win the victory. This is the primary attitude that motivates Israel's wars in the OT.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 61 The psalm has two strophes (vv. 1–4 and 6–8; see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry). Both contain petitions and end with reference to vows.
Psalm.note: The psalm has two strophes (vv. 1–4 and 6–8; see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry). Both contain petitions and end with reference to vows. 61:1–5 A prayer for help.

The psalmist means that he is at a distance from the sanctuary on Mount Zion and feels himself to be far from God. rock. He comes to the critical recognition that he does not have the strength to rescue himself; he can only turn to God in trust.

God has protected the writer in the past against his enemies. This phrase leads us to believe that the psalmist is not only physically distant from the temple but is also engaged in a military action for which he needs God's help.

The psalmist yearns for God's fellowship. See v. 2. shelter of your wings. Some see here a metaphor for God's compassion, as in the protection of the mother bird for her young. However, David's reference to the familiar wings of the cherubim portrayed on the ark of the covenant seems more likely.

In the process of petitioning the Lord, the psalmist has made promises of obedience. See 22:22; 1 Sam. 1:11. heritage. As a member of God's community, he receives the promises of the covenant, including the land of Israel and the promise of God's protection.

A prayer for the king. 61:6 life of the king. Israel's king was the center of the social order in Israel. The stability of that office affected the stability of the society as a whole. The earthly king was a symbol of the divine King. When Christ came, His gospel announced the kingdom of heaven.
Jesus Christ, David's greater Son, fulfilled this verse. steadfast love. Specifically, lovingkindness toward those with whom God is in covenantal relationship.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 62 Raises the question of the ultimate source of one's well-being: wealth and power, or God. The answer lies in the center of the poem (v. 7): "On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God." This central line is preceded by an eight-line stanza (vv. 1–6) that expresses quiet confidence in God and is followed by another eight-line stanza that encourages confidence in God, not in wealth or power (vv. 8–12).
Psalm.note: Raises the question of the ultimate source of one's well-being: wealth and power, or God. The answer lies in the center of the poem (v. 7): "On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God." This central line is preceded by an eight-line stanza (vv. 1–6) that expresses quiet confidence in God and is followed by another eight-line stanza that encourages confidence in God, not in wealth or power (vv. 8–12). 62:1–6 The verses express quiet confidence in God. 62:1 waits in silence. Lit. "is silent." To wait quietly is a challenge when there is trouble all around.
Portrayals of God's protection from the dangers of life. See note on 28:1. I shall not be greatly shaken. The psalm lays hold of the promise given, for example, in 55:22.
The modern idiom is to "kick a man when he's down." The wicked continue to take advantage of the weak.
The wicked add hypocrisy to violence.
His hope to be saved from the enemy.
See note on v. 2.
Expresses confidence in God alone. my glory. The psalmist's sense of dignity and reputation in the community.

These verses encourage ultimate confidence in God, not in wealth or power. 62:8 O people. The psalmist turns to the faithful in the congregation and encourages them to put their trust in God alone. pour out your heart before him. One's deepest and most private thoughts and feelings are safe with God.

The Hebrew word for "breath" is translated variously in different contexts. It is the most characteristic word of Ecclesiastes, where it is often translated "vanity." The point in this verse is that people are meaningless and without consequence in and of themselves. The psalmist takes comfort in this; his persecutors, in reality, are not significant.
Doubt arises when people become rich through evil means (Ps. 73). In this psalm, the author clearly sees that such riches are transitory.

God is not only able to save the psalmist; He desires to do so. render \... according to his work. The psalmist has a long-range perspective here, since at present the righteous are often at the mercy of the wicked. From the NT we understand that there will be many unresolved injustices in the present life until Christ returns.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 63 Guides us in the search for answers when we find ourselves in the "wilderness," the times in life when we experience desolation in the form of sorrow, confusion, loneliness, barrenness, or lifelessness. Verses 1–4 take us on the search, and verses 5–11 guide us to the destination.
Psalm.note: Guides us in the search for answers when we find ourselves in the "wilderness," the times in life when we experience desolation in the form of sorrow, confusion, loneliness, barrenness, or lifelessness. Verses 1–4 take us on the search, and verses 5–11 guide us to the destination. 63:title The setting of the psalm is the desert of Judah. 63:1–4 These verses take us on the search. 63:1 earnestly \... thirsts. The search here is reminiscent of that in Pss. 42; 43. my flesh. The book of Psalms permits no false spiritualization. The whole person, not merely the nonphysical aspect of the person, yearns for God.
The psalmist remembers the place of God's appointment, and the vision of God's "power" and "glory" entrusted to him there. See 42:4.
The unchanging love God shows toward those joined to Him by His covenant.
These verses guide us to the destination. 63:5 satisfied. Only in praise to God, in intimate communion with Him, will the psalmist feel spiritually content.
The destiny of the search is the presence of God. watches of the night. The psalmist has confidence in the Lord when he is most vulnerable to fear and attack.
God may be compared to a mother bird who protects her young, but see note on 61:4.

Though far removed from the sanctuary, the place where he has experienced God's presence, the psalmist still enjoys intimate communion with Him. Clinging to the Lord means finding in Him one's only hope (Deut. 10:20; 11:22).
The first indication in the poem of the psalmist's distress.
God's justice wins. Those who love God will continue to praise Him, but the wicked will be stifled.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 64 A lament that is loosely arranged in a concentric pattern: a prayer for relief (vv. 1, 2), a description of distress (vv. 3–6), a description of deliverance (vv. 7–9), and a promise of rejoicing (v. 10).
Psalm.note: A lament that is loosely arranged in a concentric pattern: a prayer for relief (vv. 1, 2), a description of distress (vv. 3–6), a description of deliverance (vv. 7–9), and a promise of rejoicing (v. 10). 64:1, 2 These verses are a prayer for relief.

These verses are a description of distress. 64: 3 like swords \... bitter words like arrows. The Bible consistently teaches that words are powerful and can be used for good (Prov. 25:15) or evil (Prov. 12:18; 25:18). Frequently in the laments, words are used as weapons.
They do not fear men, and by their question they show they do not fear God. They think their acts go unnoticed, forgetting that there is a just God in heaven who watches their every move (Ps. 2).
To their other crimes, these evildoers add the sin of pride.

These verses are a description of deliverance. 64:7 shoots his arrow. Cf. v. 4. Some of the same words are used to highlight the reversal. The wicked who try to shoot the righteous are themselves struck by the arrows of God.
Cf. v. 3. God reverses the effects of their tongues. They want to use their tongues against the psalmist; they finally incriminate themselves.
Seeing God's justice, the world will be startled by the judgment of the wicked. People of the world will reconsider their own acts in the light of God's dealings with the wicked.
This verse is a promise of rejoicing. rejoice \... refuge \... exult. God's people can rejoice because God is their refuge. Cf. 5:11.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 65 A hymn of praise to God for sending rain in answer to prayer, since Israel's agricultural economy depended on rainfall, the amount of which was commonly variable. There are three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): praise for God's presence (vv. 1–4), praise for God's awesome deeds (vv. 5–8), and praise for God's provision (vv. 9–13).
Psalm.note: A hymn of praise to God for sending rain in answer to prayer, since Israel's agricultural economy depended on rainfall, the amount of which was commonly variable. There are three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): praise for God's presence (vv. 1–4), praise for God's awesome deeds (vv. 5–8), and praise for God's provision (vv. 9–13). 65:1–4 These verses offer praise for God. 65:1 Praise is due to you. In the Masoretic Text, lit. "praise is silence," which makes no sense. The Masoretes who produced the Masoretic Text added vowel points to assist readers centuries after the prophets penned the original consonantal text. Here it appears that the Masoretes made an error when they added the vowel points, but that does not affect the inspiration of the texts, since only the consonantal text is inspired. A slight revocalization of one word results in "is due/fitting." The opening words set the tone of the psalm. in Zion. The location chosen by God for the temple and the place toward which praise is directed. See notes on 50:2; 128:5; 129:5; and especially 2:6. vows. When Israel brought petitions before the Lord, they frequently promised to offer sacrifices in response to answered prayer.

That is, when overwhelmed by sin. our transgressions. The psalmist moves seamlessly from the individual to the group. God in His grace, however, forgives; this is a source of great joy to the psalmist.
See note on 1:1. you choose. God's free grace is the source of blessing, and the highest blessing of all is to enjoy His fellowship (16:11).

These verses offer praise for God. 65:5 awesome deeds. God is not a distant deity who has nothing to do with His creation. He answers prayer by intervening in history and in the lives of His people. ends of the earth. In the theologies of the surrounding lands, it was thought that there were different gods for different localities; e.g., Marduk of Babylon and Baal of Ugarit. The psalmist knows that the Lord is not simply another god among many; He is the God of the universe.

A symbol of firmness and strength. God's creation of them shows His power and greatness (46:2, 3 and notes). girded with might. God is clothed with power as a divine warrior who conquers the enemies of Israel (Ex. 15; Josh. 5:13–15; Judg. 5).

The seas represent chaos and evil (77:16–19 and notes), often the chaos and evil of surrounding nations who attack Israel (Dan. 7). tumult of the peoples. God's victories in Israel's history are an application of His cosmic victory at the time of creation.
A deeper meaning of this verse was brought to light in the coming of Christ and the preaching of the gospel throughout the world.

These verses offer praise for God. 65:9, 10 water it. Describes the onset of the "early rain" (Deut. 11:14) in October and November. Cf. 1 Kin. 17–19, the time of Elijah, when God cursed His rebellious people by withholding the rain.

bounty. Refers to abundant rain. This verse describes the heavy rains of December through February. wagon tracks overflow with abundance. The "wagon tracks" refer to God's chariot that brings rain; cf. 104:3, where God "makes the clouds his chariot. He rides on the wings of the wind" to bring rain.
Describes the time of the "later rain" (Deut. 11:14) in March and April.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 66 A sequel to Ps. 65, which focuses on God's awesome deeds in creation (v. 5). Ps. 66 focuses on God's awesome deeds in redemption (v. 3). There is a shift at v. 13 from the community to the individual.
Psalm.note: A sequel to Ps. 65, which focuses on God's awesome deeds in creation (v. 5). Ps. 66 focuses on God's awesome deeds in redemption (v. 3). There is a shift at v. 13 from the community to the individual. 66:1–12 Focuses on the community at worship.
Great and fearful. cringing. When God appears as a warrior, the enemies have reason to fear they will be destroyed (Josh. 2:11).

The psalmist invites the hearer to remember God's great acts in history (46:8). awesome in his deeds. The next verse tells us that this awesome deed for all of humanity was the crossing of the Red Sea. While this event was for Israel in the short term, in the long term all of humanity was in view.
The first phrase of this verse refers to crossing the Red Sea (Ex. 14; 15). The second may refer to the crossing of the Red Sea or, less likely, to crossing the Jordan forty years later (Josh. 3).
A general truth, but there may be an allusion to the exodus. A context of Israel's more recent testing is also possible.

God occasionally laid difficult decisions before His people to see whether they would be obedient to Him in spite of their suffering (Ex. 15:25). as silver. When silver is refined, it is purified; the dross is taken away. When God tests His people, those who are not obedient are taken away while the faithful remain steadfast.
The Lord has brought the psalmist and the faithful through a period of affliction.
A possible reference to recent salvation from distress, but there may also be an allusion to Israel's conquest of Canaan.

Focuses on the individual at worship. 66:13 perform my vows. The psalmist expresses his individual thanks. Apparently, God had recently saved him from some distress. While he was suffering, he promised to worship God with sacrifices if God heard his prayer (22:22 note).
Often, the fulfilling of the vow leads to public praise, witnessing to God's salvation.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 67 The psalm is concentrically arranged: blessing for the nations (vv. 1, 2), the nations glorifying and enjoying God (vv. 3–5), and blessing for the nations (vv. 6, 7). The universal scope of this psalm is striking, even in a book where such far-reaching vision is not rare.
Psalm.note: The psalm is concentrically arranged: blessing for the nations (vv. 1, 2), the nations glorifying and enjoying God (vv. 3–5), and blessing for the nations (vv. 6, 7). The universal scope of this psalm is striking, even in a book where such far-reaching vision is not rare. 67:1, 2 A prayer for God to bless His people for the sake of the nations. 67:1 his face to shine upon us. The psalmist picks up the standard priestly blessing found in Num. 6:25. The thing promised in the blessing is that God will be present.
God is sovereign over all, not merely of a particular country.

These verses are a prayer for God to be glorified and enjoyed by the nations. 67:3 Let the peoples. The psalmist's desire to see peoples from many different nations praise the Lord was begun in a new way when the crucifixion and resurrection of Christ broke down "the dividing wall of hostility" (Eph. 2:14).
A promise that God will bless His people for the sake of the nations.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 68 The psalm celebrates the reign of God, though it has an enigmatic quality, owing both to the rare vocabulary it contains and to the seemingly disconnected nature of the various sections. Yet there are common themes and attitudes in the psalm. It has a hymn-like mood of joy with frequent allusions to community worship. God appears as a warrior at its center. His victory over His enemies as expressed here is used by Paul in Eph. 4:7–13 as a picture for Jesus' victory over the forces of Satan at His ascension.
Psalm.note: The psalm celebrates the reign of God, though it has an enigmatic quality, owing both to the rare vocabulary it contains and to the seemingly disconnected nature of the various sections. Yet there are common themes and attitudes in the psalm. It has a hymn-like mood of joy with frequent allusions to community worship. God appears as a warrior at its center. His victory over His enemies as expressed here is used by Paul in Eph. 4:7–13 as a picture for Jesus' victory over the forces of Satan at His ascension. 68:1 God shall arise. See Num. 10:35. These were the first words Moses spoke each day before Israel marched during the wilderness period. As he spoke, the ark of the covenant was raised to lead the procession.
The two images call on God to deal with the enemy quickly.
Better, "rides on the clouds." See v. 33, where God "rides in the heavens"; see also the reference to rain in vv. 8, 9 and the reference to God riding His cloud/chariot to bring rain in 104:3.
Widows and orphans were particularly vulnerable in ancient society. God commanded Israel to care for them (Ex. 22:22; Deut. 10:18; Ruth 4:14, 15).
Since the family was the center of Israelite society, those outside of its structure were alone and often needy.
The reference is to the forty years of wilderness wanderings.
God made the earth shake at Sinai (Ex. 19:18, 19).
An essential blessing in a land without rivers for irrigation. Long droughts had devastating effects (1 Kin. 17–19).
A military term.
See Judg. 5:30.
The Bashan mountains are physically majestic, far more imposing than Zion, but the latter's glory surpasses the former's. That is because Zion's majesty is spiritual, not physical.
In Eph. 4:8 Paul writes "gave gifts." In a procession of triumph, the victor would receive and distribute gifts.
God cares for His people and is constantly in touch with their needs. Cf. Is. 46:1–4, where the prophet decries the inability of the idols to care for their worshipers.
The Lord saves His people from illness and from death in battle. In Jesus Christ His people learn that He, by His resurrection, delivers from death by obtaining eternal life for them.
Likely a reference to the defeat of Og, king of Bashan in the period before the conquest of the land (Deut. 3). depths of the sea. God delivered Israel from death at the Red Sea (Ex. 14).
After being led by God in battle, the army would return to the city of Jerusalem, carrying the ark with them (Ps. 24). Worshiping crowds would accompany it to the temple.
Jerusalem's prestige has a single, spiritual cause: God chose it as a special place of His dwelling in that era (Deut. 12; 2 Sam. 7; cf. Is. 22:1, 2).
More than a verbal assault, to "rebuke" a nation is to destroy it. beasts \... reeds. Either the crocodile or the hippopotamus, both symbols of Egypt.
A traditional ally of Egypt (Nah. 3:9). Cush is the remote land south of Egypt, including parts of modern Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Sudan.
The psalmist poetically alludes to the heavens as God's war chariot.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 69 The cry of a soul that has been in distress for a long time and yet still trusts in God to bring salvation. This psalm is well known because of its application in the NT to the anguish of Jesus, God's righteous servant, as He sought His Father's will during His earthly ministry.
Psalm.note: The cry of a soul that has been in distress for a long time and yet still trusts in God to bring salvation. This psalm is well known because of its application in the NT to the anguish of Jesus, God's righteous servant, as He sought His Father's will during His earthly ministry. 69:1–4 Describes an overwhelming flood. 69:1 waters. The psalmist pictures his distress as one slowly sinking down in a river. The raging waters are a frequent biblical illustration of social or personal chaos. See notes on 18:4; 46:2, 3.

The poetic language in this section can be compared to a water ordeal, in which a person suspected of a crime might be cast into a river. The river was expected to overwhelm and carry away the guilty but to release the innocent.
Articulates how God knows the psalmist's humiliation. 69:5 wrongs I have done. Although the psalmist is innocent of the charges alluded to in v. 4, he does not claim to be without sin.

The psalmist is concerned not for himself only but for others in Israel who might be injured in some way through his sins. His power and prominence in society increases the likelihood that his sins will affect others.

This verse is applied to Jesus as He cleared the temple of money changers (John 2:17) and by doing good attracted the hatred of the wicked. Enmity directed toward God may cause suffering for those who are being conformed to Him (Rom. 15:3).
When the psalmist performs religious acts such as fasting, he must bear the brunt of ridicule from rich and poor alike (v. 12).
A prayer for the flood not to overwhelm the psalmist.
See v. 2. pit. See Prov. 1:12; Is. 5:14; and notes.
Articulates how God knows the psalmist's humiliation.

The bitterness of gall is proverbial. When the psalmist suffers such maltreatment, he responds with a curse (vv. 22–29). The metaphor became a reality when Jesus Christ was offered vinegar at His crucifixion (John 19:29). He responded with compassion for those who tormented Him.
The psalmist asks for the death of the wicked (v. 28). Peter cited this verse in connection with the death of Judas Iscariot and the void he left among the disciples (Acts 1:20).
The enemy furthers the pain of the afflicted. If God chastises someone, this is no excuse for others to increase his pain.
A prayer for rescue for the praise of God.
The transition from pain and the call for judgment to resolute praise is abrupt. Such compression of thought is not unusual in biblical poetry.
An ox was the most expensive sacrifice possible in ancient Israel. God is concerned with genuine praise, not wealth (50:12–14, 23; Hos. 14:2; Rom. 15:6; Heb. 13:15).
The way to God is open to the humble poor.
The last verses were probably added later than David, during or shortly after the exile of the Jews to Babylon in the sixth century B.C.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 70 The psalm is nearly identical to 40:13–17 and is concentrically arranged: the psalmist needs rescue (v. 1); prayer regarding those who search for the psalmist (vv. 2, 3); prayer regarding those who search for the Lord (v. 4); and the psalmist is poor and needy (v. 5).
Psalm.note: The psalm is nearly identical to 40:13–17 and is concentrically arranged: the psalmist needs rescue (v. 1); prayer regarding those who search for the psalmist (vv. 2, 3); prayer regarding those who search for the Lord (v. 4); and the psalmist is poor and needy (v. 5). 70:title This title is used elsewhere only for Ps. 38. 70:1 Make haste \... to deliver me. In his desperate plight, the psalmist boldly asks the Lord to come to his rescue.
These verses are a prayer regarding those who search for the psalmist.
That is, the Lord. The theme of the strophe is a prayer regarding those who search for the Lord.
This verse focuses on the psalmist as poor and needy.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 71 A lament that articulates both sorrow and joy (2 Cor. 6:10). Given the close connection of Ps. 71 with Ps. 70 (a psalm of David), it is possible to read Ps. 71 as written by David in his "old age" (v. 9) BACK TO PSALM 71:1
Psalm.note: A lament that articulates both sorrow and joy (2 Cor. 6:10). Given the close connection of Ps. 71 with Ps. 70 (a psalm of David), it is possible to read Ps. 71 as written by David in his "old age" (v. 9)
See note on 31:1.

While the form of the verb in Hebrew is typical for a past action, here in the context of a number of imperatives it is used as an imperative. my rock and my fortress. God is the psalmist's only place of protection. See note on 61:2.
The language of the psalmist shows that he is now an older man (see v. 9). He is in a position where he can look back over his life and ponder his relationship with God.
The psalmist confesses that God created him for a gracious purpose.
Like Job's friends, the psalmist's enemies have come to the wrong conclusion about his suffering.
He can look back over his long life and see how God has saved him in the past. His memory serves as a bulwark of devotion.
Uninterrupted praise cannot adequately express God's mercy; His salvation is beyond comprehension.
It is the duty of the older members of God's community to teach the young what God has done for His people.
God's righteousness is so great it cannot be contained. It is without limit. who is like you. A rhetorical question — to ask it is to answer.
The psalmist knows that life is hard and that God has not sheltered him from every difficulty. Nonetheless, he has confidence that God will deliver him.
Job is an example of someone restored after a time of intense suffering. But this kind of restoration does not always happen during earthly existence (Luke 16:25; Rom. 8:18; 2 Cor. 4:17).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 72 A prayer for the king, composed of three strophes (vv. 1–7, 8–14, 15–17; see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry); a benediction (vv. 18, 19); and a postscript (v. 20). Some of the language goes beyond what applies literally to the earthly king, anticipating the Messiah.
Psalm.note: A prayer for the king, composed of three strophes (vv. 1–7, 8–14, 15–17; see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry); a benediction (vv. 18, 19); and a postscript (v. 20). Some of the language goes beyond what applies literally to the earthly king, anticipating the Messiah. 72:title See Introduction: Author. The Septuagint understands the title to name Solomon as the subject rather than the author of the psalm. The traditional understanding of the Hebrew is that the title indicates authorship. 72:1–7 A prayer for a righteous and prosperous reign. 72:1 justice \... righteousness. God, the divine king, is the source of all justice and righteousness. If the human king is to have such qualities, he must receive them from God.
The human king receives his calling from the divine King.
Heb. shalom. Under the terms of the Mosaic covenant, a just and righteous reign should also be a prosperous reign. See note on 122:6.
The king had a special responsibility to the vulnerable in society. God has a special concern and love for the poor, and the earthly king must take special care of them. See note on 9:18.

For the sun and moon in an image of longevity, see 89:36, 37. As applied to an earthly king, this is a poetic overstatement. The language looks forward to the one King who will live forever (Luke 1:33; Heb. 7:16; Rev. 11:15).
Better, "prosperity" for Heb. shalom in this psalm (see v. 3).

A prayer for a worldwide reign. 72:8 from sea to sea. There is an allusion here to the promised boundaries of Ex. 23:31, but the language far exceeds any achievement of any earthly king of Israel and so looks forward to the Messiah's reign.
He will subdue the rebellious tribes of the desert.
These places were considered remote. Tarshish is usually associated with Tartessus in Spain. Sheba and probably Seba are in southern Arabia.
A prayer for a long reign.

The verse recalls the Abrahamic promises of Gen. 12:2, 3. The king is a focal point for the society of God's people, for he represents the people and is the heir of the promises. In Jesus Christ these promises come to fulfillment.

A doxology that concludes Book 2 (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). The doxology in all likelihood is an independent poem. Blessed be. God is blessed in response to all the blessings he has granted in Pss. 42–72.

A postscript. Ps. 72 is the last psalm of a Davidic collection that was incorporated in the book of Psalms as the process of collecting continued. This verse cannot be applied strictly to every psalm in Pss. 1–72.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 73 The psalm begins with an assertion that God is good, a belief won only after long struggle with what is observed in the world, especially the prosperity of the wicked. This important theme is also treated in Pss. 37; 49; and the book of Job. Based on the threefold use of Hebrew ak in v. 1 ("truly"), v. 13 (not translated), and v. 18 ("truly"), the psalm is divided into three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): the crisis of faith (vv. 1–12), the turning point in the crisis (vv. 13–17), and the resolution of the crisis (vv. 18–28).
Psalm.note: The psalm begins with an assertion that God is good, a belief won only after long struggle with what is observed in the world, especially the prosperity of the wicked. This important theme is also treated in Pss. 37; 49; and the book of Job. Based on the threefold use of Hebrew ak in v. 1 ("truly"), v. 13 (not translated), and v. 18 ("truly"), the psalm is divided into three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): the crisis of faith (vv. 1–12), the turning point in the crisis (vv. 13–17), and the resolution of the crisis (vv. 18–28). 73:1–12 These verses articulate the crisis of faith. 73:1 God is good. What clouded the psalmist's heart and troubled his relationship with the Lord has been resolved but only through struggle.
An obedient life is often compared to a walk along a straight path (Prov. 1–9). The psalmist describes doubt and skepticism with the image of falling off a path.
The prosperity of the wicked leads to the deeper sins of pride and violence.
A figure for a heart made insensitive by overindulgence (1 John 2:16).
The proud are not afraid to talk as if they had created the world themselves, leaving God behind (Acts 20:22).
These verses articulate the turning point in the crisis. 73:13 in vain. Shows the poet's attitude before he resolved the issue in his mind.
If he had broadcast his doubts and complaints before coming to a solution, he would have instilled doubt in the community of God.
The prosperity of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous.
The change came for him when he entered the presence of God revealed in the temple. their end. Though the wicked may prosper for a time, their final lot is destruction.
God will come in judgment against the wicked. When He does, their prosperity will seem like a dream.
His negative emotions blocked clear thinking about God and His ways.
God is close to the worshiper to counsel and guide him.
While some take this as a reference to eternal glory, a reference to earthly fame and reputation is more likely.
An example of hyperbole to emphasize the fact that God is the psalmist's ultimate desire (cf. 16:2 note).
The presence of God is the ultimate resolution to the problem of the prosperity of the wicked.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 74 A lament for the destruction of the temple in 586 B.C. comparable to the mournful poems of Lamentations. It articulates those times in life when circumstances offer no evidence that God is present or in control. The psalm has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): the agonizing "why?" (vv. 1–11), an affirmation that God is king (vv. 12–17), and petitions that God remember His people (vv. 18–23).
Psalm.note: A lament for the destruction of the temple in 586 B.C. comparable to the mournful poems of Lamentations. It articulates those times in life when circumstances offer no evidence that God is present or in control. The psalm has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): the agonizing "why?" (vv. 1–11), an affirmation that God is king (vv. 12–17), and petitions that God remember His people (vv. 18–23). 74:1–11 These verses express the agonizing "why?" of the psalmist. 74:1 why do you cast us off forever. Israel's defeat at the hands of the Babylonians indicated that God had abandoned His chosen people and would protect them no longer. The prophets describe God's abandonment of His temple, blaming it on Israel's sin and unbelief (e.g., Ezek. 9–11). See note on 22:1. sheep. The writer appeals to this metaphor of intimate relationship between God and His people in order to plead for restoration. See 23:1.

The psalmist means more than mental recall; he wants God to act on His ancient covenant promise to save His people. Mount Zion. The location of the temple and the place where God made His presence known in a special way. See 2:6; 50:2; 128:5; 129:5.
The psalmist asks God to survey and react to the damage the enemy inflicted on His possessions. When Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 586 B.C. he ordered the sanctuary to be demolished.
The worst fear is that God will be silent in the face of destruction. This psalm was likely written soon after the event, since a number of prophets were active during the period of restoration.
The psalmist tries to persuade God by arguing that His reputation is in danger. Asaph is distressed by God's apparent inactivity.
These verses are an affirmation that God is king. 74:12 Yet God my King. Faith sees the invisible (Heb. 11:1).

The poet alludes to a popular concept of creation and applies it to the Lord. These three "monsters" occur in this same order in a related text discovered at ancient Ugarit in Syria. In that text, the monsters are defeated by the goddess Anat at the time of creation. The defeat of the "Sea" refers to God's work of creation in the first place and then, perhaps, alludes to the exodus, as is clear from the references to creation in vv. 16, 17 and the Ugaritic parallels. The psalmist's use of this imagery is not meant to endorse the popular myth but to say that the God of Israel is the creator of all. The gods of the Near East are nothing because they do not exist. See 18:4; 29:3, 10; 46:2, 3; 69:1, 2; Jer. 14:22; 1 Cor. 8:4. Implicit in this affirmation of faith is the request for God to do in the psalmist's presence what He did at the time of creation — eliminate the obstacles to a well-ordered life.
These verses offer petitions that God remember and not forget His people. 74:18 Remember. The third strophe opens with a call for God to remember.
The writer appeals to God's covenant, knowing that His patience is not exhausted despite the disobedience that led to the fall of the northern kingdom in the eighth century B.C.
See note on 7:6.
The strophe closes with a call for God to not forget His enemies and their opposition to Him.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 75 A song of thanksgiving that has four strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): communal thanksgiving (v. 1), a divine oracle (vv. 2–5), a prophetic oracle (vv. 6–8), and individual thanksgiving (vv. 9, 10). The theme of casting down the wicked and lifting up the righteous is also found in Hannah's song (1 Sam. 2:1–10) and Mary's words of praise (Luke 1:46–55).
Psalm.note: A song of thanksgiving that has four strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): communal thanksgiving (v. 1), a divine oracle (vv. 2–5), a prophetic oracle (vv. 6–8), and individual thanksgiving (vv. 9, 10). The theme of casting down the wicked and lifting up the righteous is also found in Hannah's song (1 Sam. 2:1–10) and Mary's words of praise (Luke 1:46–55). 75:1 We. The psalm begins as a communal thanksgiving, though at the end an individual speaks for the community. name. See 8:1. wondrous deeds. God's great acts in history (Rev. 15:3, 4).
These verses are a divine oracle. 75:2 judge with equity. God's judgments are always just, and He knows the secrets of the heart.
God provides the underlying stability of the world order.
This common metaphor is one of a powerful horned beast proudly lifting up its head in defiance and anger. God warns the wicked not to act in this way against Him.
These verses are a prophetic oracle. 75:6, 7 God \... executes judgment. God and not any person in any other place determines what shall stand.
See note on 11:6.
These verses are individual thanksgiving. 75:9 But I. An individual, probably the king, now speaks.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 76 A psalm of Zion that focuses more on the God of Zion than on Zion itself. There are four strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): God is known among His people (vv. 1–3), God is majestic in battle (vv. 4–6), God is awesome in judgment (vv. 7–10), and God is awesome among the nations (vv. 11, 12). From the NT perspective, this song praises God for His victory at the cross and looks forward to the great final victory over evil at the end of the age (Rev. 19:11–21).
Psalm.note: A psalm of Zion that focuses more on the God of Zion than on Zion itself. There are four strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): God is known among His people (vv. 1–3), God is majestic in battle (vv. 4–6), God is awesome in judgment (vv. 7–10), and God is awesome among the nations (vv. 11, 12). From the NT perspective, this song praises God for His victory at the cross and looks forward to the great final victory over evil at the end of the age (Rev. 19:11–21). 76:1–3 These verses teach that God is known among His people.

Salem is the ancient name for Jerusalem. God's tabernacle is His sanctuary. The tabernacle was a tent, but the temple that replaced it could still be called a "tent" poetically. Zion. The mountain where the temple was situated (2:6).
God defeated the enemy at Jerusalem. A good example of such a battle is the siege by Sennacherib in 701 B.C. (2 Kin. 19; Is. 37).
These verses teach that God is majestic in battle. 76:4 Glorious. See John 1:14.
God has destroyed powerful soldiers; they are no match for Him.
God's rebuke is the word of His powerful judgment. At His rebuke the forces of chaos and evil flee before Him, and peace reigns (Nah. 1:4; Matt. 8:23–27; 17:18).
These verses teach that God is awesome in judgment.
God's wrath brings praise because it is directed against the wicked and unjust, who afflict the poor and vulnerable (9:18 note).
These verses teach that God is awesome among the nations. 76:11 vows. See Lev. 27.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 77 An individual prays on behalf of the community (vv. 7–9). A deep lament (vv. 1–9) is followed by eloquent reflection on the exodus (vv. 10–20).
Psalm.note: An individual prays on behalf of the community (vv. 7–9). A deep lament (vv. 1–9) is followed by eloquent reflection on the exodus (vv. 10–20). 77:1–9 These verses are a lament.
A common gesture of prayer was reaching out toward heaven.
The days when God was near and acted to save Israel from distress.
The Lord had promised to be with His people, and His people had to obey in gratitude for His presence. Though God is longsuffering, at times His patience runs out (1 Sam. 4; Lam. 1–5; Ezek. 9–11).
It is impossible that God should cease to be merciful, but the distress of life elicits these questions in the psalmist.

This reflection on the exodus provides light for the psalmist in the darkness of lamentation. 77:10 I will appeal to this. This verse provides a crucial transition in the psalm. By remembering God's great acts in the past, the poet builds confidence in the present and for the future. years of the right hand. When God's power was seen to act for them (Ex. 15:6).
As the writer remembers God's great acts in the past, he is reminded of God's attributes: holiness and unique power.
The context shows that the psalmist has in mind the deliverance of Israel from Egypt.

In this poetic remembrance of the exodus, the waters of the Red Sea are personified. In this way the crossing of the Red Sea is pictured as a battle against the waters of chaos (18:4; 29:3, 10; 46:2, 3 and notes).
God's action was from above, not controlled by the constraints of earthly conditions.
The crossing of the Red Sea was a violent conflict; in this verse, the mood is calm as the Shepherd of Israel leads His people through the desert (23:1).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 78 A historical psalm with the express purpose of passing on instruction (v. 1) about God's justice and mercy and about the response of faith and obedience. After a wisdom-based introduction (vv. 1–8), there are two recitations of history: vv. 9–39 and vv. 40–72, both of which begin with God's acts in Egypt.
Psalm.note: A historical psalm with the express purpose of passing on instruction (v. 1) about God's justice and mercy and about the response of faith and obedience. After a wisdom-based introduction (vv. 1–8), there are two recitations of history: vv. 9–39 and vv. 40–72, both of which begin with God's acts in Egypt. 78:1–8 This introduction provides the purpose of the poem. 78:1 teaching. From the Heb. word torah, which here means instruction, not law. See note on 1:2.
The writer will recount the events of the past in a poetic way designed to instruct the hearts of distant generations.
Instruction was disseminated in his family from generation to generation (Deut. 6:4–9; 32:7).

God established a relationship with His people based on grace alone. In this context He gave them laws to live by so that they could show their gratitude to Him. These laws are summarized in the Ten Commandments (Ex. 20; Deut. 5).
See note on v. 3.
The object of the history lesson is not merely antiquarian but to deepen the faith and obedience of God's people (see 105:45).
These verses are the first of two recitations of Israel. 78:9 Ephraimites. Cf. vv. 67, 68, where the choice of Judah is coupled with the rejection of Ephraim.
God promised to protect His people if they obeyed the terms of His covenant but to destroy them if they disobeyed (Deut. 27:9–28:68).

Chief among the great acts of God was the deliverance from Egypt by which God rescued His people from slavery and brought them into their own land. The Red Sea crossing was the greatest demonstration of God's power in the past and, accordingly, was often called to memory by psalmists and prophets.
Israel grumbled about the food in the wilderness time and time again, and God provided for their needs (Ex. 16).
God's provision of water in the wilderness should have led to faith and trust. Instead, the Israelites tested the Lord by asking for food (cf. John 6:25–58).

Rebellion against the Lord led to His judgment (Num. 11:1–3). After judging the people, He returned with His grace (vv. 23–39), but the people responded to grace only with further rebellion (vv. 40, 41). This is the story of Israel throughout the OT, perhaps best represented in the book of Judges (see Judg. 2:6–23). Heb. 12:1–12 reminds us that God chastises those whom He loves.

The same word as that found in the opening of Ecclesiastes: "vanity" (Eccl. 1:2). It describes the world apart from God and under the curse of the fall. Apart from God, humanity has nothing — only the fear of death and the void.

See v. 10. God initiated a relationship with Israel through His grace and then revealed His will to them through His law, including the curses and blessings of the covenant. The people disobeyed the law and brought on themselves God's judgment.
These verses are the second recitation of Israel's history. 78:40 often they rebelled. Examples include Num. 11; 14; 16.
He lists six of the plagues of Egypt.
God blessed them with the Promised Land, but they quickly forgot Him.

Israel fought, but the faithful knew that it was God, the divine warrior, who actually won the victories against the enemies. The story of the defeat of Jericho was a model for the battles of the conquest under Joshua (Josh. 5:13–6:27).
They did not keep His law in the desert, nor did they keep it in the Promised Land. See Judg. 2:10–15.
The height of their rebellion was to worship false gods.
Soon after entering the Promised Land, the tabernacle was set up in Shiloh (Josh. 18:1), twenty miles (32 km) northeast of Jerusalem, in the tribal territory of Ephraim.
During Samuel's youth, God punished Israel and its leaders, particularly Eli's sons, by abandoning Israel in battle and allowing the Philistines to capture the ark (1 Sam. 4; 5).
God had left Israel temporarily and seemed to be asleep. An unusual figure of speech explains how He began to act.
The rejection of the tribe of Ephraim refers to the abandonment of the Shiloh sanctuary and perhaps also the rejection of Saul's monarchy.
Jerusalem succeeded Shiloh as the designated location for the worship of God. Mount Zion. See note on 2:6.
Recalls David's humble origins (1 Sam. 16:11–13).
The psalm climaxes on a positive note with a faithful king in Jerusalem, the place of God's special presence.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 79 The destruction of the temple (v. 1) dates this psalm to the period after the Babylonian defeat of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. The psalm articulates the agony of that disaster. The problem (vv. 1–5) is followed by a series of petitions (vv. 6–12), and the psalm ends with a promise of praise (v. 13).
Psalm.note: The destruction of the temple (v. 1) dates this psalm to the period after the Babylonian defeat of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. The psalm articulates the agony of that disaster. The problem (vv. 1–5) is followed by a series of petitions (vv. 6–12), and the psalm ends with a promise of praise (v. 13). 79:1–5 These verses describe the problem of the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem. 79:1 the nations have come into your inheritance. Because the people disobeyed God's covenant, He did what He had warned them He would do (Deut. 28:15–68), sending a foreign nation against them. Both city and temple were destroyed at this time (2 Kin. 25; 2 Chr. 36:15–23; Lam. 1–5).
The faithful also suffered at the hands of the Bab­ylonians. The psalmist singles out the death of the faithful as he appeals to God for restoration.
This is a prayer to God to change a hard situation. See 6:4; 13:1–2; 74:10; 80:4. jealousy. A synonym for anger.

These verses contain a series of petitions. 79:6 Pour out your anger on the nations. The poet calls for a reversal, asking God to turn His wrath from Israel to the nations God was using to punish them. In the end the Lord answered the psalmist's prayer, restoring Israel and destroying Babylon.
This psalm may have been written some time after the destruction of Jerusalem. The chief sin was idolatry, turning to false gods.
The writer knows that God has a special place in His heart for the oppressed and vulnerable, so he reminds the Lord of those who need Him (9:18 note).
This verse is a promise to praise God. 79:13 generation to generation. See 78:4.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 80 A prayer for restoration to God's favor that depicts the Lord as both Shepherd and Vinedresser of Israel. The theme is stated in the refrain of vv. 3, 7, 19: "Restore us \... Let your face shine, that we may be saved!" The psalm is concentrically arranged: asking for the Shepherd's favor (vv. 1–3), lamenting the Shepherd's anger (vv. 4–7), lamenting the Vinedresser's apparent neglect (vv. 8–14a), and asking for the Vinedresser's favor (vv. 14b–19).
Psalm.note: A prayer for restoration to God's favor that depicts the Lord as both Shepherd and Vinedresser of Israel. The theme is stated in the refrain of vv. 3, 7, 19: "Restore us \... Let your face shine, that we may be saved!" The psalm is concentrically arranged: asking for the Shepherd's favor (vv. 1–3), lamenting the Shepherd's anger (vv. 4–7), lamenting the Vinedresser's apparent neglect (vv. 8–14a), and asking for the Vinedresser's favor (vv. 14b–19). 80:1–3 These verses are a prayer for the Shepherd. 80:1 Shepherd. God is Israel's shepherd (Ps. 23) because He guides His people and provides for them (77:20; 78:52, 71, 72; 79:13). In the ancient Near East, "shepherd" was not an unusual title for kings. cherubim. Above the ark of the covenant, in the Most Holy Place of the temple, the wings of the cherubim stretched out over God's throne (Ex. 25:22; Num. 7:89). shine forth. An allusion to the priestly benediction in Num. 6:24–26. The psalmist is calling upon God to reveal His gracious presence to them.
The mention of these significant tribes of the northern kingdom may indicate that the psalm was composed in the last days of that kingdom.
In this first occurrence of the refrain, God is addressed simply as "God." See v. 7.
These verses lament the Shepherd's anger. 80:4 how long. See 79:5.
Their mourning is so continuous that it is like their daily food and drink.
In this second occurrence of the refrain, God is addressed as "God of hosts." See vv. 3, 19.

These verses lament the Vinedresser's apparent neglect. In reality, the Lord had not neglected Israel but had allowed the nation to reap the destruction it had sown in its disobedience. 80:8 vine. Israel is the vine God transplanted from slavery in Egypt to the fruitful soil of Palestine (Is. 5:1–7; John 15:1, 2).
The lowly vine became so great through the blessing of God that the mountains and the giant cedars were covered with its shadow (Luke 13:19).
The Mediterranean and the Euphrates. The language is reminiscent of the promises made to Abraham.
The psalmist knows that no matter what human army actually defeated Israel, God had allowed it. God seemed to be turning His back on the people He had created.
These verses are a prayer for the Vinedresser's favor.
Though the reference might be to Israel, it is more likely to the Davidic king and ultimately to the Messiah.
God of hosts.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} In this third occurrence of the refrain, God is addressed as "LORD God of hosts." See vv. 3, 7.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 81 The psalm begins with praise to God (vv. 1–5a) and ends with preaching by God (vv. 5b–16), providing a sermon that reveals God's heart.
Psalm.note: The psalm begins with praise to God (vv. 1–5a) and ends with preaching by God (vv. 5b–16), providing a sermon that reveals God's heart. 81:1–5a These verses offer praise to God.
The psalms teach us by example to worship with exuberance.

The Bible occasionally mentions a special celebration that took place at the time of the new moon (1 Sam. 20:5, 18; 2 Kin. 4:23; Is. 66:23; Ezek. 46:1, 6; Amos 8:5). Frequently, the new moon festival is mentioned along with regular Sabbath observance; see also Col. 2:16, 17.
The language may be Egyptian. Another translation is "a voice we did not know," referring to the verses following. 81:5b–16 These verses are a sermon by God.
God responds to the cries of His people. 81:6 I relieved \... the burden. With specific language, God reminds Israel of its slavery in Egypt.
God warns of danger.

God promises abundance. 81:10 I am the LORD your God. Strongly reminiscent of the preamble to the Ten Commandments (Ex. 20:2). The relationship of grace came before revelation of the law. I will fill it. Much of Israel's history, as recorded in Joshua through Chronicles, is the story of God's people looking for satisfaction without God. If they were worried about rain, they turned to Baal (1 Kin. 18). If they were worried about enemies, they wanted a strong king (1 Sam. 8). They kept forgetting they had a God who could and would fulfill all their needs easily.
God lets us suffer consequences.
See Rom. 1:24.
God's compassion for Israel is clearly seen in this verse.

God longs to bless us. 81:16 finest of the wheat \... honey from the rock. God longs to satisfy us with the finest of wheat, not just manna, and with honey from the rock, not just water from the rock.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 82 This short psalm presents some difficult problems. Chief among them is the "gods" mentioned in vv. 1, 6. A number of scholars take this as a reference to angelic powers, lesser spiritual beings who make up God's heavenly council. A second interpretation understands "gods" literally, as deities made subordinate to Yahweh. The most probable interpretation is that the "gods" are human judges. The Hebrew word elohim ("gods") is used of human judges in Ex. 21:6; 22:8, 9. Within Ps. 82 the human nature of these gods is indicated by vv. 6, 7. A rough paraphrase is, "As judges, people may call you 'lord,' but you are as mortal as anyone else."

A number of scholars take this as a reference to angelic powers, lesser spiritual beings who make up God's heavenly council.
