It may be the heavenly assembly (including only spiritual powers), or it may include earthly kings.
See note on 9:18.
God is the judge, so human judges functioning as His agents can be called "gods." Jesus quotes this line in reference to himself in John 10:34.
Since the human judges were failing to reflect His justice, God Himself would have to do it.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 83 The community lament has two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): a prayer for God's action (vv. 1–8) and a prayer for God's vengeance (vv. 9–18). The psalm is a model prayer for the Christian's spiritual warfare. Instead of calling upon the Lord to destroy one's flesh-and-blood enemies, He is called upon to vanquish the spiritual forces of evil.
Psalm.note: The community lament has two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): a prayer for God's action (vv. 1–8) and a prayer for God's vengeance (vv. 9–18). The psalm is a model prayer for the Christian's spiritual warfare. Instead of calling upon the Lord to destroy one's flesh-and-blood enemies, He is called upon to vanquish the spiritual forces of evil. 83:1–8 These verses are a prayer for God. 83:1 do not keep silence \... hold your peace \... be still. Three negative imperatives bring out the passion of the plea. The heart of the covenant is the promise that God will be present with His people. To the psalmist's eyes, God is absent from His people if they are defeated before the enemy.

The nations involved in the plot against Israel are listed in vv. 6–8. Attempts have been made to identify the historical situation behind the psalm, but no time period is known in which all of these enemies were actively hostile toward Israel at the same time. The closest is Jehoshaphat's war recorded in 2 Chr. 20, but there is no mention of Assyria there.
Moab and Ammon (Gen. 19:30–38).

These verses are a prayer for God. 83:9 Midian. God enabled Gideon to destroy the Midianites (Judg. 7). Sisera \... Jabin. Jabin was a king of Canaan, and Sisera was his general early in the period of the judges. God delivered the Israelites from them through the work of Deborah (Judg. 4; 5).

Two leaders who were destroyed by Ephraimites during Gideon's battle against the Midianites (Judg. 7:25–8:3). Zebah and Zalmunna. Midianite kings who were captured and executed by Gideon (Judg. 8:4–21).

The land of Israel, where the shepherd God settled His sheep, the people of Israel. The quote is ascribed to Israel's enemies in order to highlight the blasphemous nature of their plots against Israel.
God's wrath is often compared to a violent storm (18:7–15; Nah. 1:3).
The psalm supplies a redemptive reason behind the judgment. As God judges the wickedness of the attackers, they will see their folly and turn to Him.
The Hebrew words used sound similar to the most common title of the Canaanite god Baal. The poet is asking God to judge the nations so that they will know that He, not Baal, is the only God.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 84 A pilgrimage psalm (see Pss. 120–34) that expresses a deep longing to be in the presence of God. While Christians do not travel to a special location to be in God's presence (John 4:21–24), the psalm articulates their yearning to experience Christ's nearness.
Psalm.note: A pilgrimage psalm (see Pss. 120–34) that expresses a deep longing to be in the presence of God. While Christians do not travel to a special location to be in God's presence (John 4:21–24), the psalm articulates their yearning to experience Christ's nearness. 84:1 your dwelling place. The temple, the place which God chose to reveal His presence to the people (Deut. 12; 1 Kin. 8).

The true object of the psalmist's devotion is not the temple building itself but the God who revealed Himself there. Israel was often tempted to forget God and rely on the external trappings of religion (Jer. 7).

Note the playful envy expressed by the psalmist. He is jealous of the birds who are able to build their homes near the altar. In this way, he expresses his deepest longings to be as close as possible to God.

See note on 1:1. Blessed are those who experience God's presence. your house. The temple, being the place of God's appointment on earth, is like heaven on earth. From a NT perspective, this verse gives a glimpse of the unending happiness of heaven.

See note on 1:1. Blessed are those who find strength in God to experience His presence. whose strength is in you. Their vitality in life is found in God's power, not in their own. highways. People living outside of Jerusalem made special trips to the temple to enjoy God's presence in worship. The Songs of Ascents (Pss. 120–34) were probably used during these journeys (120:title).

The name of a valley otherwise unknown. There is a similar sounding Hebrew verb meaning "to weep." Others identify the noun as a certain kind of tree that flourishes in dry places, such as the balsam or aspen. The context indicates that the valley is arid but transformed by the presence of the joyful pilgrims. early rain. The reference to the early rains probably connects this psalm with pilgrimage to the Feast of Booths (see Zech. 14:16–19), which was celebrated in the fall with the onset of the rainy season.
The location of the temple, the ultimate goal of their pilgrimage. See notes on 2:6; 50:2; 74:2; 137:1.
Shield is a metaphor for the king in his role as protector of his people. The king is not only the political leader of Israel but also the reflection of God's kingship on earth.

The metaphor comparing God to the sun praises Him as the source of light and energy. The burning rays of the sun in the dry country east of the Mediterranean make it a suitable portrayal of God's power. shield. God is the ultimate source of protection. No good thing does he withhold. See Rom. 8:28–39, esp. v. 32.
See note on 1:1. Blessed are those who trust in God to experience His presence.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 85 Recalls the past when God's people experienced His restoration (vv. 1–3) and the present when restoration is needed again (vv. 4–7). The promise of restoration and a word of exhortation follow (vv. 8, 9), along with a description of the restoration in terms of rain that will result in a bountiful harvest (vv. 10–13).
Psalm.note: Recalls the past when God's people experienced His restoration (vv. 1–3) and the present when restoration is needed again (vv. 4–7). The promise of restoration and a word of exhortation follow (vv. 8, 9), along with a description of the restoration in terms of rain that will result in a bountiful harvest (vv. 10–13). 85:1–3 These verses recount a past experience of restoration. 85:1 favorable to your land. A number of occasions in biblical history are illustrative for the psalm. Perhaps most appropriate, though the psalm could have already been in existence for many years, was Judah's return from Babylonian captivity in the sixth century B.C.
The people's misfortunes came from their sin before God. Forgiveness of sins means that God's wrath will be stilled. The necessary repentance is also the gift of God's grace.
These verses recount a present need for restoration. 85:4–7 Restore us again \... revive us again. Based on God's restoration in the past, the psalmist prays for restoration in the present.

These verses recount the promise of restoration and a word of exhortation. 85:8 me. The community has been speaking as a unit up to this point ("us"), but now an individual steps forward. Whoever he is (priest or prophet), he speaks on behalf of God. he will speak peace. The word for "peace" (Heb. shalom) indicates health and wholeness, and, like "steadfast love" (v. 7), it is a word intimately associated with the covenant. God promises the restoration of intimate relationship with His people. saints. Formed from the same root as "steadfast love" (v. 7) and denotes those who are the objects of God's covenant love.

These verses describe the promised restoration. 85:10 meet \... kiss each other. This verse has long been interpreted to refer to the reconciliation that Jesus Christ effected between God's justice, which cannot tolerate sin, and His mercy, which does not rejoice in the death of the wicked (Ezek. 33:11; 2 Pet. 3:9). Justice and mercy came together in the cross of Christ. See theological note "The Holiness of God" on p. 172. peace. The well-known Heb. shalom, which denotes wholeness and health. (see v. 8).
The future restored relationship with God will join God's blessing from heaven with the faithfulness of His people on earth.

In context, "good" refers to fall rains that start the agricultural year and enable a bountiful harvest; see 65:11. yield its increase. Fertility of land in an arid climate is an indication of God's care and love for His people.
This attribute of God is personified as a herald who proclaims God's way before Him (cf. 23:6).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 86 A prayer for help in time of trouble concentrically arranged: save Your servant (vv. 1–4); God's steadfast love (vv. 5, 6); trouble (v. 7); the nations will glorify God's name (vv. 8–10); teach me to honor Your name (v. 11); the psalmist will glorify God's name (vv. 12, 13); trouble (86:14); God's steadfast love (v. 15); save Your servant (vv. 16, 17).
Psalm.note: A prayer for help in time of trouble concentrically arranged: save Your servant (vv. 1–4); God's steadfast love (vv. 5, 6); trouble (v. 7); the nations will glorify God's name (vv. 8–10); teach me to honor Your name (v. 11); the psalmist will glorify God's name (vv. 12, 13); trouble (86:14); God's steadfast love (v. 15); save Your servant (vv. 16, 17). 86:title See note on Ps. 17. 86:1–4 These verses are a prayer for God to save His servant.
The psalmist recognizes his inability, but he knows where true strength lies.
The poet knows that God's answer to his prayer is a manifestation of God's unmerited grace. God owes him nothing.
An idiom for trusting in God; see 24:4; 25:1.
These verses focus on God's steadfast love.
This verse focuses on the psalmist. 86:7 day of my trouble. For this expression see 77:2.

These verses promise that the nations will glorify God. 86:8 none like you. The psalmist sees that no god of the surrounding nations can be compared with the Lord in what He is or does. This confession of God's uniqueness is not a tacit admission that other gods exist (see v. 10). The psalmist is comparing the foreigners' vain imaginations with the reality of Yahweh.
Yahweh is the God of all the nations, even though they may not recognize Him. God gives them their existence and whatever blessings they have.
The center of the poem and a prayer for God to teach the psalmist to honor His name. 86:11 unite my heart. A united heart is one totally set on God.
These verses promise that the psalmist will glorify God.
This verse focuses on the psalmist. 86:14 they do not set you before them. Something that the godly do; see 16:8; 54:3.
This verse focuses on God. 86:15 See note on v. 5.
These verses are a prayer for God to save His servant.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 87 The psalm glorifies Jerusalem as the city of God (vv. 1–3), which is the spiritual home of all the nations (vv. 4–7), and is similar to Pss. 46; 48; 76. The unique contribution of Ps. 87 is to give a glimpse of the universal character of God's worship. Its universalistic language brings to mind the future day when the Gentiles should be "fellow heirs" in the gospel (Eph. 3:6).
Psalm.note: The psalm glorifies Jerusalem as the city of God (vv. 1–3), which is the spiritual home of all the nations (vv. 4–7), and is similar to Pss. 46; 48; 76. The unique contribution of Ps. 87 is to give a glimpse of the universal character of God's worship. Its universalistic language brings to mind the future day when the Gentiles should be "fellow heirs" in the gospel (Eph. 3:6). 87:1–3 These verses portray Jerusalem as the city of God. 87:1 holy mount. God is omnipresent: He is everywhere. Nevertheless, God met His people in an intimate and special way at Zion (2:6 note). he founded. This refers to the building of the temple on Mount Zion, north of the city of David and towering over it.

The point is not that God hated other parts of Israel but that He blessed Jerusalem with His presence. After the temple was built, there was only one designated place for the official worship of God — Jerusalem (Deut. 12).
Referring to the divine pronouncement to follow in the next few verses.

These verses portray Jerusalem as the spiritual home of the nations. 87:4 those who know me. There were occasional foreigners, such as Rahab and Naaman, who worshiped the Lord during the OT period (cf. Ex. 12:38). This amazing verse looks forward to seeing entire foreign nations bowing down to God. mention. This formal introduction to the divine pronouncement uses the idea of the "book of the living" (69:28; cf. Ex. 32:32; Ps. 139:16; Is. 4:3; Rev. 21:24–27). Rahab and Babylon. Rahab is a name for Egypt (Is. 30:7). Egypt and Babylon were the two superpowers who continually fought against Israel. Philistia. Israel's traditional enemy on the Mediterranean coast west of Judah. Tyre. An affluent sea power north of Israel. Cush. Biblical Cush is the remote region south of Egypt, including parts of modern Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Sudan.
Refers metaphorically to a spiritual birth in Zion, which is the spiritual birth mother of peoples from all over the world.
See note on v. 4.
Physical thirst stands for spiritual thirst (42:1, 2), which can only be satisfied in Jerusalem, God's chosen place.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 88 Of all the laments in the Psalter, this psalm most vividly expresses the distress of the psalmist. The writer's distress can be heard from beginning to end, because his pain has lasted from his youth (v. 15) until the present. Most laments turn to confidence and praise at the end, but in this one the only glimmer of hope is that the psalmist is concerned to pray at all. He refers to God as "my salvation" (v. 1). A Christian is not, as such, free from the suffering of this world. On the contrary, the Christian lot commonly is suffering and pain but the believer finds so­lace in the suffering and resurrection of Christ (Phil. 3:10). BACK TO PSALM 88:1

See note on 6:5.
His condition is so bad that people treat him as if he were already dead.
The psalmist's unhappiness is reminiscent of the suffering of Job.
An attitude of prayer. Though God afflicts him, or perhaps because God afflicts him, the psalmist knows there is only one refuge for him — God.
See 6:5; 30:9; and notes.
For water as a figure of trouble, see notes on 18:4, 15.
His closest friends have abandoned him (v. 8), and God is distant (v. 14), leaving only darkness nearby. This is the only psalm that ends on such a downcast note (Ps. 88 note).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 89 The psalm opens joyfully but turns to lament. It opens with confidence in God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 1–37) and closes with doubts about God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 38–51). The issue at the heart of the psalm is the Davidic covenant. In 2 Sam. 7:4–17 (cf. 1 Chr. 17:1–15) God established a covenant with David in which He promised that the special relationship would pass on to David's obedient sons God's language was bold; He promised that the covenant would last "forever" (2 Sam. 7:13). But this promise was not without conditions upon the recipients. If they sinned, they would be punished (1 Kin. 8:25; 2 Sam. 7:14). David's son Solomon began his slide into apostasy by admitting the religious cults of his foreign wives (1 Kin. 11). The continuing disobedience of the Davidic kings resulted in the Babylonian exile and an end to that period of Israel's monarchy in the sixth century B.C. But the substance of the promise was not canceled; Christ came to take the throne of David forever (Is. 9:7; Luke 1:32; 22:30).
Psalm.note: The psalm opens joyfully but turns to lament. It opens with confidence in God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 1–37) and closes with doubts about God's steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 38–51). The issue at the heart of the psalm is the Davidic covenant. In 2 Sam. 7:4–17 (cf. 1 Chr. 17:1–15) God established a covenant with David in which He promised that the special relationship would pass on to David's obedient sons God's language was bold; He promised that the covenant would last "forever" (2 Sam. 7:13). But this promise was not without conditions upon the recipients. If they sinned, they would be punished (1 Kin. 8:25; 2 Sam. 7:14). David's son Solomon began his slide into apostasy by admitting the religious cults of his foreign wives (1 Kin. 11). The continuing disobedience of the Davidic kings resulted in the Babylonian exile and an end to that period of Israel's monarchy in the sixth century B.C. But the substance of the promise was not canceled; Christ came to take the throne of David forever (Is. 9:7; Luke 1:32; 22:30). 89:1–37 These verses express confidence in God. 89:1 steadfast love. The wonders of God's devotion to His people in the love of His covenant with them. faithfulness. God is not fickle or capricious but will keep the promises He makes. Hope in the fulfillment of God's promise to David is what will motivate the lament at the end of the psalm (vv. 38–51).

The heavens are personified; the reference is to the beings in heaven, such as the cherubim and the angels. God is so great that even these powerful spiritual entities fall to their knees in adoration. assembly. The angels and other spiritual beings in heaven are God's divine assembly through whom He works His will.

Having mentioned spiritual beings, the psalmist is quick to point out the uniqueness of God. The writings of the Canaanites and Mesopotamians also mention an "assembly of the holy ones," but that was an assembly made up of different gods. The God of Israel is not the best of such gods but wholly different from them. The OT expresses His transcendence in numerous places (Is. 44:6).
Like Leviathan, Rahab is a sea monster of Near Eastern mythology, standing for forces of evil and chaos (Job 9:13; Ezek. 29:3 and note). Frequently the name Rahab is applied to Egypt (87:4 and note).
Unlike the heathen gods, the Lord is the creator of the world.
Hermon in the far north is the highest peak in Israel. Tabor is a mountain of distinctive shape standing in the Megiddo plain, a landmark of the boundary of three tribes.
As king, God is responsible for the administration of law in the land. He does not judge arbitrarily. go before you. See 85:13.
The king. The metaphor of the horn is associated with that of the bull, which stands for strength. God is the one who endows the human king with power. This thought is specified in the next line.

The exact words of this vision are not found elsewhere in Scripture, but the allusion is probably to the prophetic insight of Nathan in 2 Sam. 7, if not to the initial divine word given to Samuel concerning David's kingship (1 Sam. 16).
The king had sacred responsibilities, both political and religious. God promises to give David the strength he needs to carry out his divinely given tasks.
These two key words reverberate throughout the psalm, beginning in v. 1 (v. 1 note).

A reference to the intimate relationship established between God and David in 2 Sam. 7:14 (see Ps. 2:7). The king played an important role as mediator of the Davidic covenant between God and His people. This special function made the apostasy of later kings especially heinous.

Calling David the "firstborn" means that he was first in rank in the covenant community, the head of a household (Gen. 4:4; 25:31 and notes). David in particular foreshadows Christ, uniquely the Son of God by nature and head of the church (Eph. 1:22; Heb. 3:6).

The dynasty of David as an earthly political enterprise was long-lived but not eternal. It fell because of the sins of David's successors. Superseding it, as the reality casting a shadow, is the eternal kingdom of Jesus Christ.
God's will as summarized in the first five books of the OT. Deut. 17:19 commands the king to be well versed in God's law and obedient to it.

God's promises stand forever. The Davidic covenant has a conditional element, as this psalm points out in v. 32, but its ultimate fulfillment does not depend on human response. David and the psalmist knew that it would be fulfilled but could not know everything about how that would occur (Acts 2:29–31; 1 Pet. 1:10, 11).

These verses express confidence that God can deliver the king. 89:38 But now. Signals the start of the new, contrasting section. you have cast off. The focus of the psalm shifts to the present and the great rift in the relationship between God and the king. your anointed. An unspecified Davidic successor to the throne.
The psalmist is outspoken, speaking boldly in his appeal to break God's silence.
God's absence is experienced through the victory of their enemies.
The most poignant line in the poem. The psalmist agonizes over the seeming absence of God's love.

A doxology that concludes Book 3 (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). The doxology in all likelihood is an independent poem. Blessed be. God is blessed in response to all the blessings He has granted in Pss. 73–89.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 90 This psalm, the only one ascribed to Moses, affirms that the absence of the Davidic king (Ps. 89) does not mean the absence of God or His steadfast love. God Himself always has been and always will be "our dwelling place" (v. 1). The poem has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): an affirmation of faith in the Lord as the eternal refuge of His people (vv. 1, 2); a lament for the pain and trouble of human existence (vv. 3–11); and a concluding series of requests (vv. 12–17), at the heart of which is "Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love that we may rejoice and be glad all our days" (v. 14).
Psalm.note: This psalm, the only one ascribed to Moses, affirms that the absence of the Davidic king (Ps. 89) does not mean the absence of God or His steadfast love. God Himself always has been and always will be "our dwelling place" (v. 1). The poem has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): an affirmation of faith in the Lord as the eternal refuge of His people (vv. 1, 2); a lament for the pain and trouble of human existence (vv. 3–11); and a concluding series of requests (vv. 12–17), at the heart of which is "Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love that we may rejoice and be glad all our days" (v. 14). 90:1, 2 These verses are an affirmation of faith in the Lord as the eternal refuge of His people. 90:1 you have been our dwelling place. The psalmist begins by affirming the truth that God Himself, not the Davidic king, is the ground of hope.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR 90:2 from everlasting to everlasting. The psalmist affirms the eternal existence of God. God's work of creation (Gen. 1) brought the whole universe into existence; God Himself had always been there. See theological note "The Self-Existence of God" on next page. BACK TO PSALM 90:2
Psalm.note: The psalmist affirms the eternal existence of God. God's work of creation (Gen. 1) brought the whole universe into existence; God Himself had always been there. See theological note "The Self-Existence of God" on next page.
These verses lament the pain and trouble of human existence. 90:3 to dust. God's judgment returns the descendants of Adam to the dust in death.
God is not subject to time but is its creator.
The brevity of human life is likened to a dream, highlighting the contrast of finite lives with God's eternity.
People commit sins they think they can hide, such as envy, hatred, and lust. But before God there are no secrets (Heb. 4:12, 13).

To a young person, seventy years seems like a long time. But before God's eternity and in human retrospect, it is brief. toil and trouble. A touch of hyperbole to underscore the human condition, since not all the days of all humans are "toil and trouble" (cf. 16:2; 51:4; 73:25 notes).
Only Jesus Christ, who drank the full cup of God's wrath for sinners, knows the full power of death.
These verses offer up a series of requests.
See note on 6:3.
See 30:5 for the hope of restoration "in the morning."
Not moral evil, but trouble, affliction, or calamity; see 27:5; 34:19; 35:26.
God must act to redeem and restore. their children. Moses contemplates a generation entering the Promised Land.

our God. In the midst of life in the wilderness, only the blessing of God's presence can give meaning and joy. establish the work of our hands. Wanderers in the wilderness may leave no monuments, but God can give eternal significance to the deeds of hands that serve Him.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 91 A refuge psalm that provides God's people "through all the generations" (90:1) with an antidote to fears and anxiety. There are three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): an affirmation that God is our refuge (vv. 1, 2), a description of how the Lord is our refuge (vv. 3–13), and a confirmation by God Himself that He is, in fact, our refuge (vv. 14–16).
Psalm.note: A refuge psalm that provides God's people "through all the generations" (90:1) with an antidote to fears and anxiety. There are three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): an affirmation that God is our refuge (vv. 1, 2), a description of how the Lord is our refuge (vv. 3–13), and a confirmation by God Himself that He is, in fact, our refuge (vv. 14–16). 91:1, 2 These verses are an affirmation that God is our refuge.
These verses are a description of how the Lord is our refuge. 91:3 he will deliver you. God is present and able to deliver His people.

Psalms of confidence often have a metaphor for God's compassion at their core. God is likened to a mother bird who protects her young. his faithfulness. God's steadfast love and the certainty that He will keep His promises sustain the psalmist.
Perhaps a reference to plagues that could sweep through an encampment. arrow. The literal setting of battle can be taken figuratively for the struggles of life.
See note on 90:15.

God often works His will through His spiritual attendants, the angels. 91:12 they will bear you up. Satan quoted this passage to Jesus in the wilderness (Matt. 4:6), tempting Him to jump from the top of the temple. Satan's aim was to turn faith into presumption.
These verses are a confirmation by God Himself that He is, in fact, our refuge. 91:14 holds fast to me in love. God's promise of protection comes to those who have faith in Him.
See, e.g., Deut. 6:2 and Prov. 3:1, 2.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 92 A hymn that has the exaltation of the Lord at its heart (v. 8). This central verse is preceded by seven lines with fifty-two words that praise God (vv. 1–4) and affirm the fleeting nature of the prosperity of the wicked (vv. 5–7), and it is followed by seven lines with fifty-two words that affirm the downfall of the wicked (vv. 9–11) and the ultimate prosperity of the godly, who praise God (vv. 12–15).
Psalm.note: A hymn that has the exaltation of the Lord at its heart (v. 8). This central verse is preceded by seven lines with fifty-two words that praise God (vv. 1–4) and affirm the fleeting nature of the prosperity of the wicked (vv. 5–7), and it is followed by seven lines with fifty-two words that affirm the downfall of the wicked (vv. 9–11) and the ultimate prosperity of the godly, who praise God (vv. 12–15). 92:1–4 These verses focus on the praise of God. 92:1 Most High. This title is similar to one commonly given to Baal in Canaanite religious texts. Applying it to the God of Israel is a kind of taunt directed toward anyone tempted to worship Baal (83:18).
In His covenant with His people, God pledges to love them faithfully. He is the author of the terms of the covenant that bind Him and His people together (136:1 and note).
The psalmist concentrates on God's acts in time and space. God is not out of touch with created reality but works through such reality to demonstrate His love for His people.

These verses teach the fleeting nature of the prosperity of the wicked. 92:5 How great \... thoughts are very deep. The contemplation of God's acts and thoughts are overwhelming. They lead to reverent fascination and humble devotion.
The psalmist does not deny that the wicked appear to prosper in this world. doomed to destruction forever. The pro­sperity of the wicked is short-lived; see 37:2; 73:18–20.

The heart of the poem. 92:8 but you, O LORD, are on high forever. In contrast to the fleeting prosperity of the wicked is the eternal exaltation of God. Those who are truly prosperous will enjoy a prosperity that is as eternal as God's exaltation (v. 14).

These verses affirm the downfall of the wicked. 92:9 your enemies shall perish. As the psalmist meditates on the greatness and justice of God, he comes to the sure conclusion that the wicked will be destroyed.
The horn of an animal is used in the Bible as a symbol of power. The wild ox raises its horn with pride and confidence. Cf. 75:4; 89:17; 132:17; 148:14 and notes.

These verses focus on the praise of God for the ultimate prosperity of the wicked. 92:12 palm tree \... cedar. A strong contrast is drawn between the flourishing of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked (v. 7). The wicked are like fragile grass, whereas the righteous are strong, vital, and productive trees. A similar contrast is found in Ps. 1.
LORD. The source of the vitality of the righteous is not themselves but God.
The horizon of the ancient poets was often limited to this life, but the NT extends that horizon into eternity.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 93 This short poem stands at the head of a group of psalms that praise God as king (93; 95–100). Cf. Pss. 24; 46.
Psalm.note: This short poem stands at the head of a group of psalms that praise God as king (93; 95–100). Cf. Pss. 24; 46. 93:1 The LORD reigns. This phrase and its slight variants may be found throughout this section of the Psalter (96:10; 97:1; 98:6; 99:1). God is king, with omnipotent power and sovereign control over the world. the world is established. This word of assurance is based on the fact that the King has created and maintains the world. The forces of evil, disorder, and chaos (vv. 3, 4) will not overwhelm the world.

God has no beginning; He is uncreated. This conception of the eternal kingship of God stands in stark contrast with the theology of Mesopotamia and Canaan. In these neighboring regions, the power of the gods varied according to changes in the political arena.
An ancient symbol of the forces of chaos and evil. See notes on 18:4, 15.
The stability and order that exists because of God's eternal kingship is shared with humanity through the revealed law.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 94 The psalm provides us with five perspectives for dealing with oppression and injustice.
Psalm.note: The psalm provides us with five perspectives for dealing with oppression and injustice. 94:1–7 Shows that vengeance belongs to God. 94:1 God of vengeance. See Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19; Heb. 10:30.
See notes on 3:7 and 7:6; theological note "The Holiness of God" on p. 172.
See note on 6:3.
They should be ashamed and silent, but instead they shout their evil accomplishments from the rooftops.
See note on 9:18.
The wicked in their prosperity believe that God does not care what they do.

Teaches that God knows what is happening when there is oppression and injustice. 94:8 be wise. The wicked will be wise when they shed the illusion that God does not know their evil schemes or that He is unable to do anything about them.
The Lord knows even the secret thoughts hidden away in the heart (90:8).
Shows that true happiness is available even in the midst of injustice and oppression. 94:12 Blessed. See note on 1:1.
The psalmist recognizes that there is often a delay between a wicked act and its punishment. The unrighteous may prosper for a time. However, that they will pay for their crimes is a certainty.
God may discipline the righteous (v. 12) to return them to conformity to His will, but He will never leave them.

Shows that the Lord can be looked to for protection from the wicked in times of injustice and oppression. 94:16 for me. The psalm takes on a personal note as the author prepares to mention how God delivered him.
Specifically, God's love for those in covenant with Him.

Shows that people reap what they sow. 94:20 wicked rulers. A king who perverts justice. A king of Israel was to reflect the kingship of God, particularly God's justice and compassion. The psalmist refers to an Israelite king who did not seek the will of God. There are many such examples from the history of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
See Prov. 1:18 for the principle that one reaps what one sows.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 95 The psalm calls believers to respond in two ways to God, who is creator and king.
Psalm.note: The psalm calls believers to respond in two ways to God, who is creator and king. 95:1–7a Calls for worship of God as creator and king. 95:1 let us. A worship leader, such as a priest, calls on the congregation to worship the Lord together with him.
As the supreme God of the universe, all sovereignty is His. The reference is to popular Near Eastern mythology, not the actual existence of such gods (48:2; 74:13 and notes).
In His power.
As in v. 4, complementary terms are used to indicate the whole earth.
Our Creator is our redeemer, and "maker" refers in this context to God's act of redemption whereby He "made/created" a people for Himself and became their King. See also Is. 54:5; Hos. 8:13, 14.
Calls for submission to God, who is creator and king.
An ever-present day.

These place names may be translated "quarreling" and "testing." They sum up Israel's attitude toward God during the forty years of wandering in the wilderness. For the history see Ex. 17:1–7 and notes; Num. 20:1–13.

Those who rebelled against the Lord in the wilderness never entered the Promised Land. Heb. 3:7–4:7 cites this passage and applies it to the Christian's life. Professing Christians must heed God's Word, or they will not enter God's eternal rest.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 96 The psalmist calls on all nations to proclaim God as their king. The psalm contrasts God with the lifeless idols of the nations (vv. 4–6). The theme of God's universal kingship is similar to that seen in Ps. 47; 93; 97; 99; and particularly Ps. 98. 1 Chr. 16:8–36 records the thanksgiving song of David when he brought the ark to Jerusalem, a song composed from Pss. 96; 105. See esp. 1 Chr. 16:23–33 for Ps. 96. The intensity of the psalm builds over three strophes (vv. 1–6, 7–10, and 11–13; see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry).
Psalm.note: The psalmist calls on all nations to proclaim God as their king. The psalm contrasts God with the lifeless idols of the nations (vv. 4–6). The theme of God's universal kingship is similar to that seen in Ps. 47; 93; 97; 99; and particularly Ps. 98. 1 Chr. 16:8–36 records the thanksgiving song of David when he brought the ark to Jerusalem, a song composed from Pss. 96; 105. See esp. 1 Chr. 16:23–33 for Ps. 96. The intensity of the psalm builds over three strophes (vv. 1–6, 7–10, and 11–13; see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry). 96:1–6 These verses call us to sing to the Lord. 96:1 new song. See note on 33:3. all the earth. Since God is king of the whole earth, not merely of Israel, the writer calls on all His subjects to praise Him. It is not until Christ returns that substantial numbers from the nations join in the universal chorus of praise.
God's acts in history provide marvelous events for which to praise Him, e.g., He "made the heavens" (v. 5).

LORD. A standard affirmation in worship (35:27; 40:16; 48:1; 145:3). feared above all gods. That the Lord is "to be feared above all gods" (v. 4) is not an affirmation of polytheism but a denial of it (see 95:3; 115:4).
See note on 8:5. strength. See 93:1.
These verses call us to sing to the Lord as King.
See Lev. 2. The word is also used for the tribute due a king (2 Kin. 17:4).

reigns.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The psalmist proclaims God's kingship among the nations. shall never be moved. For this image of the earth as unshakable from the time of creation onward, see 93:1; 104:5. judge \... with equity. God does not rule according to whim but according to justice and righteousness. As there is stability in creation, so there is stability in justice.
These verses call us to sing to the Lord as the judge of the earth. 96:11 heavens be glad \... earth rejoice. This verse and the one that follows personify the whole creation.
The sense is that He comes to put everything back into proper order, which is why the creation is rejoicing in vv. 11, 12.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 97 Verses 1–6 describe the King when He appears in His world; vv. 7–9 describe various reactions to the Lord's appearance; vv. 10–12 teach those who love God how to respond to His appearance and reign.
Psalm.note: Verses 1–6 describe the King when He appears in His world; vv. 7–9 describe various reactions to the Lord's appearance; vv. 10–12 teach those who love God how to respond to His appearance and reign. 97:1–6 These verses describe the appearance of the King. 97:1 The LORD reigns. For God as king, see note on 93:1. the earth. The psalm calls on all the earth to praise God. This call to the nations has taken on a whole new meaning after the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
See Pss. 18; 29. The visible revelation of God (i.e., in theophany) was sometimes in the context of a storm-like event. Such a manifestation helped God's people to appreciate His awesome power.
See note on 46:2, 3.
These verses describe various responses to the King's appearance. 97:7 shame. The response of those who do not honor the King is shame at His appearance. who make their boast \... idols. See 96:4–6.
The people of God know that the judgments of God will remove the wicked and so bring about their liberation.
These verses teach the righteous how to respond to the King. 97:10 hate evil. Evil is that which is out of accord with the King's ways and is not to be chosen as a way of life.
As the earth is to rejoice in the King (v. 1), so are His people.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 98 A royal psalm, like Pss. 47; 93; 95; 96; 97; 99. The theme of deliverance is divided into past (vv. 1–3), present (vv. 4–6), and future (vv. 7–9).
Psalm.note: A royal psalm, like Pss. 47; 93; 95; 96; 97; 99. The theme of deliverance is divided into past (vv. 1–3), present (vv. 4–6), and future (vv. 7–9). 98:1–3 These verses focus on celebrating the King's reign in the past. 98:1 new song. See note on 96:1. marvelous things. Translated "wonderful deeds" in 9:1 (9:1 note). worked salvation. In its OT context the reference is to a military victory. It is appropriate today to apply the verse to a spiritual victory, since it is a great victory by God over "the cosmic powers" (Eph. 6:12).
More than mere memory, God's remembrance includes His favorable action.

These verses focus on celebrating the King's reign in the present. 98:4 a joyful noise. This section demonstrates the enthusiastic worship of a people who have deep love for God. Their worship is active and noisy.
These verses focus on celebrating the King's reign in the future. 98:7 sea. Nature is here personified as praising the Lord (96:11, 12). He is creator of all, animate and inanimate (95:5).
See notes on v. 7; 46:2, 3.
See note on 96:13.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 99 A royal psalm (Ps. 93 note). "The LORD reigns" is the governing theme of the psalm, and the threefold use of "holy" (vv. 3, 5, 9) shows that holiness of the King is the focus of praise. There is an obvious strophic break at the end of v. 5, and vv. 6–9 are tied together by the repetition of the idea that God "answered" His people in vv. 6, 8.
Psalm.note: A royal psalm (Ps. 93 note). "The LORD reigns" is the governing theme of the psalm, and the threefold use of "holy" (vv. 3, 5, 9) shows that holiness of the King is the focus of praise. There is an obvious strophic break at the end of v. 5, and vv. 6–9 are tied together by the repetition of the idea that God "answered" His people in vv. 6, 8. 99:1–5 These verses call us to praise the holy King, who reigns. 99:1 The LORD reigns. See notes on 5:2 and 93:1. cherubim. Cherubim are spiritual beings who dwell in heaven with God. They are guardians of God's holiness, as witnessed by their role in protecting the post-fall garden (Gen. 3:24). Cherubim were symbolically represented in the tabernacle, both in the innermost curtain (Ex. 36:35), and in the Most Holy Place (Ex. 37:1–9). Later, Solomon added cherubs made of wood overlaid with gold in both the Most Holy Place and the inner sanctuary (1 Kin. 6; 2 Chr. 3). The psalm refers to the cherubim of God's throne with their outstretched wings above the ark of the covenant. let the earth quake. At God's special self-revelations (theophanies), reverberations like those of a natural earthquake were sometimes felt throughout the earth. See theological note "The Incomprehensibility of God" on p. 630.
The location of the temple. See note on 3:4.
See note on 8:1. Holy is he. God is set apart from all His creatures, which is evident from His uncreated nature, His power, and His moral perfection.
See note on 96:10.

These verses call us to praise the holy King, who responds. 99:6 Moses \... Aaron \... Samuel. Three of the most prominent leaders of Israel in the period before the monarchy. All three served as mediators between God and His people. called upon his name. The emphasis in this section is that God speaks to His people when they turn to Him for help in prayer. he answered them. God responds to His people.

God responds to His people. avenger of their wrongdoings. For their own good, and to preserve His holiness, God may punish His people for the sins they commit. Israel knew this, because God gave foreign enemies power over them when they persisted in unbelief. This reflects God's corrective punishment.
See note on v. 3.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 100 This psalm brings the celebration of the Lord's kingship in Pss. 93–100 to a conclusion, calling on "all the earth" (v. 1) to worship Him.
Psalm.note: This psalm brings the celebration of the Lord's kingship in Pss. 93–100 to a conclusion, calling on "all the earth" (v. 1) to worship Him. 100:1 all the earth. As in the preceding royal psalms, the call goes out beyond the chosen people to all the peoples of the earth. God is their king too, regardless of whether they are aware of it.
God is not a despotic king who forces His people to serve Him. Loving service is a grateful response to the grace of God.
See note on 23:1.
Those of the temple. This psalm may have been sung during a festive entry into the temple precincts.
God's lovingkindness to people in covenant with Him.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 101 In this psalm the king promises to live a life of obedience, pursuing holiness and seeking to root out evil from his kingdom. David could not live up to his ideals. He failed time after time, though he lived a life of repentance. Many believe that Ps. 101 was written by David and later used as a coronation psalm, beginning with Solomon. If so, high ideals at the beginning of his reign degenerated into disobedience and, in the case of Solomon, open apostasy. Christ alone could offer perfect obedience in the flesh.
Psalm.note: In this psalm the king promises to live a life of obedience, pursuing holiness and seeking to root out evil from his kingdom. David could not live up to his ideals. He failed time after time, though he lived a life of repentance. Many believe that Ps. 101 was written by David and later used as a coronation psalm, beginning with Solomon. If so, high ideals at the beginning of his reign degenerated into disobedience and, in the case of Solomon, open apostasy. Christ alone could offer perfect obedience in the flesh. 101:1 justice. The reference is to God's judgments. The psalmist praises the Lord for them because they are consistent and righteous, not arbitrary.
As defined by the law of God. See Mic. 6:8 for the classic description.
The psalmist strongly repudiates wicked deeds. He will not tolerate them in his presence. In this he seeks to emulate God, who will not tolerate an unrepentant sinner in His presence.

The psalmist will actively oppose unrighteousness in his area of authority. haughty look \... arrogant heart. The heart is the foundation of a person's being and character. The "look" refers to demeanor. See 131:1.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR 102:title The title is unusual in that it does not give a specific historical occasion but the situation (affliction) in which the psalm finds appropriate use. The title also teaches us the best way of working through feelings of being overwhelmed by trouble. The psalm has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): Pour out your complaint before the Lord (vv. 1–11), put your focus on the Lord (vv. 12–22), and pray with confidence to the Lord (vv. 23–28).
Psalm.note: The title is unusual in that it does not give a specific historical occasion but the situation (affliction) in which the psalm finds appropriate use. The title also teaches us the best way of working through feelings of being overwhelmed by trouble. The psalm has three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): Pour out your complaint before the Lord (vv. 1–11), put your focus on the Lord (vv. 12–22), and pray with confidence to the Lord (vv. 23–28). 102:1–11 These verses show how to pour out complaint before the Lord.
The psalmist wonders at the withdrawal of God's friendship. He knows it is a sign of God's wrath, since God promised to be with His obedient covenant people.
Points to the pain and suffering of life in general and the pain of a raging fever in particular.
His suffering is not only spiritual and psychological but also physical.
He is silent in his affliction and without friends or supporters.
As is typical in a lament, unnamed but real enemies are a source of distress to the psalmist. Because the enemies are unnamed, the psalm has timeless application to all generations.
The psalmist knows the ultimate cause of his suffering: God's anger. He never disputes the justice of that anger, but he turns to God for relief.
These verses show how to put one's focus on the Lord. 102:12 forever. Over against the fragility of the psalmist's life stands the constancy and eternity of the Lord.
See notes on 3:7 and 7:6. Zion. See 2:6; 3:3. The references to the destruction of Zion have led many commentators to place the psalm just after the Babylonian captivity.
As Jerusalem rises up from destruction, all who see it will praise the Lord.
Though God is above heaven, He enters the world to help the afflicted (9:18; 72:4 and notes).
These verses show us how to pray with confidence to the Lord. 102:23 shortened my days. Through the sickness that now threatens the psalmist's life.

God existed before His work of creation. The author of Hebrews applies vv. 25–27 to Christ (Heb. 1:10–12). There the argument is that however great the angels are considered, they are created and not eternal. But Christ, the second person of the Trinity, exists through all eternity.
See theological note "The Self-Existence of God" on p. 938.
The poet's hope is with the future generations. Though he suffers now in the present, he sees a brighter future.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 103 The first of four psalms of praise and thanksgiving that bring Book 4 to a close. This psalm begins and ends with invitations to praise God (vv. 1, 2, 20–22), which surround the actual praise of God (vv. 3–19).
Psalm.note: The first of four psalms of praise and thanksgiving that bring Book 4 to a close. This psalm begins and ends with invitations to praise God (vv. 1, 2, 20–22), which surround the actual praise of God (vv. 3–19). 103:1, 2 Calls the psalmist himself to praise God.

These verses contain the praise of God called for in vv. 1, 2, 20–22. 103:3 forgives all your iniquity. The primary benefit of grace is the forgiveness of sins (Acts 13:38). God is compassionate toward His repentant people. heals all your diseases. God's saving benefits are for the body as well as the soul.
That is, from death. steadfast love. See note on 92:2.
God provides everything that is constructive and wholesome for His people.
See note on 102:2.
By referring to Moses, the psalmist calls to mind all of God's blessings associated with the exodus, the wilderness wanderings, and even the conquest of the Promised Land.
When God forgives sins, He completely removes them. The height and breadth of His mercy are vast.
The comparison of God to a compassionate and loving father is developed in Rom. 8:12–17. See Ex. 4:22, 23; Hos. 11:1, 8, 9.

God knows people better than they know themselves. we are dust. According to Gen. 2:7, God formed Adam from the dust of the ground. The consequence of sin is that humans die as surely as the animals (Eccl. 3:19). Yet God has mercy on us. See theological note "Human Beings as Body and Soul" on p. 1948.

There is a reciprocal relationship between divine initiative and human response. God first loves His people, then they love Him in return as shown in the faithful obedience of their lives (Rom. 5:8; 1 John 4:10–12).
The obedience of those who keep God's covenant shows the reality of His mercy. They walk in devoted fellowship with the Lord, who loves them in His covenant of grace.
See theological note "Providence" on p. 1045.
Calls the angels to join in the praise of God. 103:20 Bless. See note on v. 1.
A reference to the divine army, which includes the angels, the cherubim, and other heavenly creatures.
The final line forms an inclusion with the opening line.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 104 The psalm is a creation hymn of matchless beauty. The psalm opens with praise for the majesty of God, who is the kingly creator (vv. 1, 2a). Two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry) follow with praise for the stability of the universe God has made (vv. 2b–9) and for God's abundant provision in the world (vv. 10–30). The psalm concludes with praise and prayer for the Creator's glory (vv. 31–35).
Psalm.note: The psalm is a creation hymn of matchless beauty. The psalm opens with praise for the majesty of God, who is the kingly creator (vv. 1, 2a). Two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry) follow with praise for the stability of the universe God has made (vv. 2b–9) and for God's abundant provision in the world (vv. 10–30). The psalm concludes with praise and prayer for the Creator's glory (vv. 31–35). 104:1, 2a These verses praise God for His majesty as the kingly Creator. 104:1 O my soul. See note on 103:1. clothed. This section develops the metaphor of the creation as God's garment. This emphasizes the distinction between the Creator and the creation and implicitly disparages worship of any aspect of the creation, however glorious it may seem (cf. Rom. 1:22–25). splendor and majesty. See note on 8:5.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR 104:2 light. A reference to the first day of creation (Gen. 1:3).
Psalm.note: A reference to the first day of creation (Gen. 1:3). 104:2b–9 These verses praise God for the stability of the universe He has made. heavens. A reference to the second day of creation (Gen. 1:6–8).
See 18:9 and note.

God's heavenly servants have an awesome appearance. How much more powerful must God, their creator, be. This verse may be a polemic against Baal worship, since Canaanite mythological texts describe the servants of their god as flames of fire.
The world is stable and ordered, not chaotic. God's control of the world is comforting to those who recognize it.

God created the waters and ordered them in rivers, lakes, and oceans. In the religions of the surrounding nations, the sea is a symbol of chaos and disorder. Their pantheistic theology deifies the sea and sets it against the gods of order. The Bible uses this imagery but disallows the polytheistic theology (18:4; 46:2, 3; 74:13–15; Nah. 1).
The Greek word used in the Septuagint for "rebuke" is also used in Matt. 8:26 when Jesus rebuked the sea, demonstrating that He is the Creator.
The flood was thus an act of de-creation.

These verses praise God for His abundant provision in the world. 104:10 springs. God provides water from the terrestrial sources in the form of springs and streams; see the waters below the firmament in Gen. 1:7.

The words "lofty abode" translate the same Hebrew word translated "chambers" in v. 3. God provides water from celestial sources in the form of rain; see the waters above the firmament in Gen. 1:7. 104:14 You cause the grass to grow. A reflection of the third day of creation (Gen. 1:9–13).

God's kindness is exhibited in His provisions for daily life (Acts 14:17; 1 Tim. 4:3, 4). "Food" refers to grain, wine comes from grapes, and oil from olives. This triad stands for a whole year's agricultural produce and is in this order owing to the order of harvesting; see, e.g., Deut. 7:13; 11:14; 14:23; 18:4.
A reference to the fourth day of creation (Gen. 1:14–19).
What appears to be purely natural — lions seeking their prey — is an act of providence.
God has given His creation a wonderfully ordered rhythm.
See notes on Prov. 8:22–31. The divine answer to Job (Job 38–41) contains many examples of God's wisdom in creation.
The fifth day of creation (Gen. 1:20–23).

The psalmist's imagination is caught up with God's mysterious sea. On its surface ships glide to and fro from distant ports, while underneath lurks the monster Leviathan, here a poetic symbol of God's creative power (Job 41).
God is omnipresent, i.e., everywhere (Ps. 139). However, in His anger God withdraws covenant blessings, and this is experienced as divine absence.

Perhaps better translated "wind," referring to the west wind that carries the rain that renews the land at the end of the dry season. If "Spirit," this is a likely allusion to Gen. 2:4-8 and the creation of man on the sixth day.

These verses conclude the psalm with praise and prayer for God's glory. 104:31 glory of the LORD. "Glory" here is not abstract but concrete and refers to God's glorious creation, as it is paralleled by God's "works."
Hills are the symbol of stability and firmness (46:2, 3), but God's mere touch sets them aflame.
LORD. The psalmist rejoices in the Lord by rejoicing in the Lord's creation, in which the Lord Himself also rejoices (v. 31).
The psalmist would like to see the removal of everything that opposes the godly order he has so eloquently described. 104:35 Bless. The final line forms an inclusion with the opening line.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 105 While Ps. 104 praises God for His acts in creating the world, this song meditates on His acts in the world's continuing history. The first fifteen verses are quoted (along with Ps. 96 and part of Ps. 106) in 1 Chr. 16, perhaps indicating use of the psalm in worship. The poem falls into two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): vv. 1–6, which invite the singing of God's praise, and vv. 7–45, which are the content of that praise.
Psalm.note: While Ps. 104 praises God for His acts in creating the world, this song meditates on His acts in the world's continuing history. The first fifteen verses are quoted (along with Ps. 96 and part of Ps. 106) in 1 Chr. 16, perhaps indicating use of the psalm in worship. The poem falls into two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): vv. 1–6, which invite the singing of God's praise, and vv. 7–45, which are the content of that praise. 105:1–6 These verses invite the singing of God's praise. 105:1 among the peoples. Israel cannot hide its light "under a basket" (Matt. 5:15). True people of God gladly bear witness to God's grace throughout the world.

Those acts of grace and judgment that God performs in history. God enters history and acts graciously in behalf of His people, remarkably so in the life, death, resurrection, and ascension of His only begotten Son.
Seek to live in His presence. The psalmist often testifies of the horror associated with the withdrawal of God's friendship (22:1; 28:1).
"Remembering" God's works is more than recalling what they were; it means reacting with faith and obedience to what they mean.
These verses contain the content of the praise that is offered.

As in v. 5, remembrance involves doing as well as knowing. In this case, God acts in the present based on the promises given to Abraham. covenant. The specific covenant here is the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 12:1–3; 15; 17).
God reaffirmed His covenant relationship with the descendants of Abraham. See Gen. 26:3.
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived in the Promised Land as resident aliens. They wandered from place to place in Canaan.
Abraham is referred to as a prophet in Gen. 20:7.

God promoted Joseph to a position of power in Egypt. 105:16 he summoned. God directed the events in Egypt so that when famine threatened that country, Joseph was in power and able to save many people (Gen. 50:20).
See Gen. 46. land of Ham. Another name for Egypt.
The psalmist emphasizes the ninth plague by naming it first.
These are the third and fourth plagues in reverse order of their actual occurrence in Egypt.
The fifth and sixth plagues are unmentioned by the psalmist. The plague of hail was the seventh.
The tenth and final plague, after which Egypt allowed Israel to leave Go­shen.

God's great mercy and generosity may be seen here. As a slave nation in Egypt, the Israelites had little to call their own. Through the plagues, however, God struck fear into the hearts of the Egyptians so that they not only let Israel go but were willing to hand over their valuables to encourage Israel's exodus (Ex. 12:33–36).
The manna. God's providential mercy went beyond bringing them out of Egypt — He provided for them in the wilderness by giving them food and drink.
The Abrahamic covenant included the promise that God would make Israel "a great nation" (Gen. 12:2).

The retelling of the history of Israel is for a purpose: to learn from it to obey God (see 107:43 note). The covenant relationship between God and His people is established and maintained by God alone as His work of grace. His people (indeed, all humanity) are responsible to reciprocate not merely in the formal observance of particular commands but appropriately with all of their being (Mark 12:29–34; cf. 10:20–22).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 106 While Ps. 105 is mainly concerned with God's redemptive acts, this psalm focuses on human sin.
Psalm.note: While Ps. 105 is mainly concerned with God's redemptive acts, this psalm focuses on human sin. 106:1 Praise the LORD. Hb. Hallelu yah, "You (plural) praise Yah." he is good. Though the writer is concerned about Israel's suffering, he knows that its source is in Israel's sin and not in God's character.
The psalmist has no doubt that God will come to aid His chosen people, but he does not assume that he will personally enjoy God's blessing. He turns to God in prayer for this.
An introductory statement that gives the theme for the body of the psalm down through v. 39. Israel has deliberately and constantly rebelled against the Lord.

The poet stands amazed at the stubbornness of his people. He remembers that a previous generation doubted God's power — even though they had just witnessed the ten plagues — when they were caught between the Egyptian army and the Red Sea (Ex. 14).

By personifying the Red Sea, the psalmist makes it a part of God's defeat of the powers of chaos. he led them through. In spite of their sin, God saved them. God's persevering love in the face of rejection is a major theme here, and indeed throughout the Bible.
The people's faith and thanks were short-lived. As remembrance (105:5 note) includes obedience, so forgetting leads to disobedience.
See Num. 16.
They put a metal idol in the place of God and worshiped it. As Paul points out (Rom. 1:21–23), idolatry consists in worshiping any part or aspect of creation as God.
Ham is another name for Egypt, and the works are preeminently the ten plagues.

See Ex. 32:11–14. Moses interceded in behalf of the people and saved them from the wrath of God. In this, he foreshadowed the work of Jesus Christ, who not only prayed for His people but died to save them.
They despised the Promised Land by not having faith that God could give it to them (Num. 13; 14).
This gesture accompanies a formal oath, showing God's determination to judge the sons of Israel.

The language is derogatory; worshiping a foreign idol is like becoming a beast of burden. Baal of Peor. Baal was a god of the eastern Mediterranean region at the time Israel was entering the Promised Land. Baal took slightly different characteristics in each local worship site and so is often identified by the region. sacrifices offered to the dead. This could refer to funeral rituals of some sort. Canaanite funeral rituals involved heavy drinking, feasting, and obscene lust. The whole incident, initiated by Balaam, is reported in Num. 25.

When Israel took the fateful steps toward idolatry, Phinehas took a violent step to bring Israel back to the way of God. As a result, God made a covenant with his family to give them the priesthood. Similar language is used in connection with the covenant promises given to Abraham (Gen. 15:6) and inherited by the church (Rom. 4:3). However, the sense of the phrase "counted to him as righteousness" is not the same in 106:31 as it is in Gen. 15:6 and Rom. 4:3. In Gen. 15:6 and Rom. 4:3, the righteousness in view is the individual's right standing before God that secures eternal life. This righteousness is the perfect righteousness of Christ imputed to us by faith in Him alone (Rom. 4:4, 5; 2 Cor. 5:21). Ps. 106 concerns the righteous reward that Phinehas received, namely, a perpetual priesthood (Num. 25:10–13). Phinehas, no less than anyone else, received a right standing before God only through faith. He was not declared righteous before the Lord on the basis of His obedience. But like us, His justifying faith produced the fruit of obedience. We are justified by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. Good works follow faith, but they in no way secure for us our righteous standing before the Lord (cf. James 2:14–26 and notes).
See Num. 20:1–13.
By not trusting God to provide for their survival in the wilderness.
The spiritual reality behind the lifeless idols is demonic, a world of hostility to the one God.
Joining themselves to a false god is spiritual adultery.
God's promises express the commitment that causes Him to continue with His people even though they turned their backs on Him. On remembrance, see note on 105:5.
LORD. God is blessed in response to all the blessings He has granted in Pss. 90–106.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 107 This community thanksgiving accompanied the offering of sacrifices (v. 22). The date of its original composition is not certain. The psalm opens with an invitation to "give thanks" (vv. 1–3), followed by four examples of God's steadfast love (vv. 4–32), each containing an invitation to "give thanks," and closes with a hymn of thanksgiving and a concluding exhortation to lay hold of God's steadfast love (vv. 33–43).
Psalm.note: This community thanksgiving accompanied the offering of sacrifices (v. 22). The date of its original composition is not certain. The psalm opens with an invitation to "give thanks" (vv. 1–3), followed by four examples of God's steadfast love (vv. 4–32), each containing an invitation to "give thanks," and closes with a hymn of thanksgiving and a concluding exhortation to lay hold of God's steadfast love (vv. 33–43). 107:1–3 These verses are an invitation to "give thanks." 107:1 he is good. See vv. 1, 8, 15, 21, 31, 43. steadfast love. God's covenant devotion, by which He binds Himself to His people.
The situation after the Babylonian exile seems to be in view here.
These verses provide four examples of God's steadfast love. 107:4–9 Example one: God guides those wandering in the wilderness to a city.
This section is the first of four that illustrate God's readiness to answer the prayers of His people.
Example two: God delivers His imprisoned people to freedom.
God chastises His wayward people in order to elicit their repentance. See Heb. 12:1–13.
\... he delivered them.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} See v. 6.

Example three: God saves foolish rebels when they call on Him. 107:17 fools. Not because they were without natural intelligence but because they refused to face the reality that the Lord is God. "Foolishness" is an ethical-spiritual category, not an intellectual one.
It seems that a physical malady, some kind of sickness, is in view here.
As early as the creation account (Gen. 1:3), it is clear that God's word is powerful and effective.
This verse points to public worship in the temple.
Example four: God rescues those in trouble on the seas.
LORD. The mystery, power, and beauty of the sea, with everything that lives in it, testifies eloquently to God's wisdom (Gen. 1:9, 10, 21).
The ship as it rises and falls on the waves.
\... he delivered them.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} See vv. 6, 13, 19.
God shows His divine power and might by controlling the chaotic sea. See notes on 18:4, 15. Christ demonstrated His power from on high when He stilled the waters (Mark 4:35–41).
These verses form a hymn of thanksgiving and a concluding exhortation to lay hold of God's steadfast love.

God does not arbitrarily bring destruction upon His people. Here the reason is identified as the people's sin. A historical example may be found in 1 Kin. 17, where God determined to withhold rain and dew from Israel because Ahab and Jezebel had turned the nation toward Baal.
The ultimate reference is to the conquest in which God gave the land of Canaan to Israel. They passed from the hard conditions of the wilderness wanderings into the pleasant land of Palestine.
Perhaps a reference to the Babylonian exile.
The retelling of the history of Israel is for a purpose: to learn from it the steadfast love of God (see 105:45 note).

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 108 This psalm was composed from two previous psalms. The first five verses are from 57:7–11, and vv. 6–13 are from 60:5–12. There are only minor changes of wording, but the overall effect of the psalm is quite different. Pss. 57; 60 include elements of complaint; this psalm is a statement of assurance. The psalm is comprised of two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): thanksgiving to God for His steadfast love (vv. 1–5) and dependence on God for His help (vv. 6–13).
Psalm.note: This psalm was composed from two previous psalms. The first five verses are from 57:7–11, and vv. 6–13 are from 60:5–12. There are only minor changes of wording, but the overall effect of the psalm is quite different. Pss. 57; 60 include elements of complaint; this psalm is a statement of assurance. The psalm is comprised of two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): thanksgiving to God for His steadfast love (vv. 1–5) and dependence on God for His help (vv. 6–13). 108:1–5 These verses offer thanksgiving to God for His steadfast love. 108:1 steadfast. The psalmist has resolved to praise the Lord, and nothing can cause him to swerve from his resolve to offer up his hymn of praise.
See note on 57:8.
The psalmist realizes that God is more than the God of Israel. He is the king of the universe, and as a result, the psalmist will witness to God's great deeds throughout the universe.
Specifically, the mercy God has for the people who are in covenant relationship with Him.

God is so great that not even the heavens can contain Him (1 Kin. 8:27). He is transcendent, yet in special ways (presently by the Holy Spirit) He is also immanent in that He compassionately condescends to dwell with His people.
These verses focus on dependence on God for His help.

The divine oracle was probably spoken through a prophet associated with the temple. The sense of His message is that victory is forthcoming. Shechem \... Succoth. These two places are associated with Jacob in Gen. 33:17–20 as the first two places the patriarch occupied after returning from his encounter with Esau. They are on opposite sides of the Jordan River.

Both these areas are located, at least in part, east of the Jordan River. Ephraim \... Judah. The two most powerful tribes in Israel. They were frequently rivals, but here they are united as parts of God's army. scepter. See Gen. 49:10.
See 60:8 and notes.
Likely the king, who speaks on behalf of the nation.
The writer confesses his confidence that through God's power they will be victorious.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 109 The psalmist stands before a corrupt court, falsely accused of a crime. In his distress, he turns to God for help, asking Him to reverse the roles and allow the psalmist to judge the court, and one person in particular (either the judge or the accuser). The poet does not conceal his strong feelings against his enemies (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes).
Psalm.note: The psalmist stands before a corrupt court, falsely accused of a crime. In his distress, he turns to God for help, asking Him to reverse the roles and allow the psalmist to judge the court, and one person in particular (either the judge or the accuser). The poet does not conceal his strong feelings against his enemies (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). 109:1 Be not silent. See note on 83:1.
The legal language here and elsewhere in the psalm reveals that the psalmist is a defendant in a courtroom setting.
See note on 35:12. for my love. What makes the writer's plight so poignant is that his attackers were once friends but have turned treacherously against him.
The penalty for falsely accusing someone of a certain crime was the penalty corresponding to that crime (Deut. 19:16–21).

As this accuser brought false charges against the psalmist, so Judas Iscariot sought Christ's death by turning Him over to the Jewish authorities. Afterward, Judas killed himself in remorse. Peter understood that this psalm was fulfilled in that situation and cited it as a replacement was sought for Judas among the disciples (Acts 1:20).
Among people who depended heavily on their relatives for social support, this verse was a hard-hitting curse, calling for punishment on the accuser and on his family.
The curses focus on eradicating the accuser's family line. To have descendants stretching into the distant future was extremely important in ancient Israel.
Once again the psalmist invokes the principle that the unrighteous will receive the penalty they are trying to call down upon another. See note on v. 6.
The psalmist appeals to God's reputation (8:1). He belongs to God, and if he should die at the hand of the wicked, it will appear as if God can do nothing about evil.
In disgust.
The Hebrew word for "steadfast love" refers salvation to God's covenant faithfulness.
Instead of finding an accuser at his right hand, the psalmist finds his support in God.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 110 There can be no doubt that this psalm looks forward to Christ. Jesus Himself cites it to show that David knew that its ultimate fulfillment would come in one greater than he (Mark 12:35–37 and par.). Even before Christ's coming, a prophetic-messianic interpretation of the psalm was well known among Jewish interpreters. Nevertheless, like all other royal psalms, Ps. 110 does address the time in which it was first composed. It is likely that it was sung at the time of the coronation of the king. The composition seems to have been written after David defeated Jebus (Jerusalem) and celebrates his victory and enthronement in that city, explaining why he also inherits the royal priesthood of Melchizedek. Focusing on two divine oracles, the first (v. 1) shows the close, but subordinate, relationship that the human king bears to the divine King. The NT writers cite this oracle to demonstrate Jesus' post-resurrection glory and to point to the struggle between God and the spiritual powers of evil (Acts 2:34, 35; 1 Cor. 15:25; Eph. 1:20; Col. 3:1; Heb. 1:13; 1 Pet. 3:22). The second oracle appointed the king as a priest, but as a special type of priest. As opposed to the hereditary Aaronic priesthood, this priesthood is descended from Melchizedek (Gen. 14:18–23), whose mysterious origins are related to Jesus Christ, the Great High Priest (Heb. 5:6; 7:17; 8:1; 10:12–14).

As the translators indicate with the use of small capital letters, this is God's name. Lord. This title is often used for God but can also be addressed to a king or other respected person. The NT makes clear that King David refers to his son — who is also the Son of God — as his "Lord" (Mark 12:35–37). The promised Messiah descended from David but is greater than David. right hand. The place of honor. After His resurrection, Jesus was exalted to the right hand of God in heaven. enemies. In the OT they were physical flesh-and-blood enemies of Israel. In the NT the battle is intensified, as Jesus fights against the invisible, cosmic powers of evil. footstool. A place of disgrace, symbolizing subjugation. After a victory, Near Eastern leaders would humiliate their defeated enemies by stepping on their heads or necks (Josh. 10:24–26).
God will enlarge the King's authority. Zion. See note on 2:6. scepter. A common symbol of governmental power and authority.
A difficult phrase in the Hebrew. The image compares the dew, which appears suddenly during the night and is present in the morning, with the eager and mysterious appearance of the king's troops.

The regular priesthood of Israel was from Aaron, and its duties were limited to religious worship. Little is known about Melchizedek, but it appears that he combined the functions of king and priest (Gen. 14:18–20). David also combined these functions to an extent, as he offered sacrifices and helped prepare for the temple building in addition to ruling as king (1 Chr. 16:1–3; 17; 22:1–26:19). Jesus Christ is both king and priest, though not descended from the line of Aaron (Heb. 5:6; 7:17; 8:1; 10:12–14).
A title of respect (v. 1 note).
God often used the human king to bring His judgment upon the nations through warfare. As applied to Jesus, this verse anticipates the last judgment that will take place at the end of time.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. The king finds refreshment during the battle and can carry on God's work of judgment.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 113 With its opening "Praise the LORD!" this psalm continues the theme of praise found in Pss. 111; 112, and it contains two strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry): vv. 1–3 (the Lord is to be praised) and vv. 4–9 (the incomparable Lord is to be praised). Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 114 Jewish tradition assigned this psalm to the eighth day of Passover. In eight short verses and with virtually unrivaled poetic subtlety, the psalmist describes the tremendous power of God's visual self-revelation (theophany) at the time of Israel's salvation from Egypt and entry into Canaan (Ex. 13:21). Stories evoke responses. The psalm begins with a brief story about God (vv. 1, 2), then tells of creation's response to this story (vv. 3, 4) and raises a question as to why this particular response was drawn out (vv. 5, 6), before providing its own answer to the question in the form of an imperative (vv. 7, 8).

Lit. "Precious in the Lord's eyes is the death of his loved ones." Since the psalmist lived to write this psalm, the sense seems to be that God's loved ones are so precious that He keeps them from dying. This interpretation finds confirmation in 72:14: "From oppression and violence he redeems their life, and precious is their blood in his sight." Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 118 This psalm concludes the section associated with the celebration of Passover (Pss. 113–18). As the last song of the group, it may have been the final psalm in the mind of Jesus as He celebrated Passover with His disciples (Mark 14:26). Jesus quoted vv. 22, 23 about Himself (Mark 12:10, 11; Matt. 21:42; Luke 13:35; cf. Acts 4:11). The people greeted Jesus' triumphal entry with shouts of joy taken from this psalm (Mark 11:9, 10; Luke 19:38; John 12:13). The main speaker is likely the king (vv. 5–21), but the psalm as a whole is a liturgy with other speakers as well (vv. 21–27). The references to altar, temple, and procession (vv. 19, 20, 27) show that it was used in corporate worship. This is a psalm of thanksgiving in which the psalmist expresses his deep distress, how he prayed to the Lord, and how the Lord rescued him.

Psalm.verse_ref: STUDY NOTE FOR Ps. 119 As Ps. 117 has the distinction of being the shortest chapter in the Bible, so Ps. 119 is the long­est. The psalm is an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The eight poetic lines of each stanza begin with the same Hebrew letter.
Psalm.note: As Ps. 117 has the distinction of being the shortest chapter in the Bible, so Ps. 119 is the long­est. The psalm is an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The eight poetic lines of each stanza begin with the same Hebrew letter. The number eight may be connected with eight Hebrew words that appear throughout the psalm concerning its main theme. The words are translated variously as "law," "testimonies," "precepts," "statutes," "commandments," "rules," and "word." In five stanzas all eight Hebrew words occur, and every stanza has at least six of the eight. Verse 97 is perhaps the theological heart of the psalm, as it expresses the psalmist's love for God's law. The psalmist also has a deep desire to live in keeping with this law. Yet the psalmist also recognizes that he has strayed from time to time from the standard set forth in the law. While the emphasis of the psalm is on love for and obedience to the law of God, this is balanced to some degree by an awareness of the need for forgiveness. The law is a faithful expression of God's character. God sent His Son to keep the law for us. The law no longer condemns us, setting us free to accept it as our own guide for pleasing the One who died in our place. 119:1 Blessed. See note on 1:1. who walk. A metaphor for the activities of daily life. law of the LORD. The law, or Torah, refers to the first five books of the Bible as a unit, or to the legal sections of those books. Here the latter is meant: the Ten Commandments and the other laws of the Pentateuch.
The psalmist is not speaking of a mere external adherence to the law. He calls for obedience that comes from a deep-seated faith in the Lord.

to act.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} With the direct honesty characteristic of the psalmist, he tells God that He has delayed His judgment long enough. The wicked deserve the punishment they are about to receive.

It is not clear whether the writer refers to the initial act of revelation, the process of interpreting God's Word, or applying the law to his heart. Perhaps all three are intended as a single process bringing light, hope, and understanding to the dark soul.
The concept is the same as 42:1, 2.
