Note the parallel closing at v. 6. his sanctuary \... his mighty heavens. Given that poetic lines usually say something similar twice with a difference in the second colon, the "sanctuary" would be on earth. Earthly worship needs heavenly worship added to it to begin to do justice to the worship of which God is worthy.
This verse gives reasons why God should be worshiped.
A wonderful array of instruments for the praises of God.

See Gen. 2:7. Life is represented in the breath. The breath is also the means of speech, prayer, and praise. Praise the LORD. See v. 1. Doxology is the destiny of the Psalms, and it is the destiny of the saints because it was the destiny of the Savior: "Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?" (Luke 24:26).

Proverbs.note: The introduction to the book, with v. 1 as the title, vv. 2–6 as the purpose, and v. 7 as the theme. 1:1 proverbs. The Hb. word translated as "proverb" has a range of meanings, but it is usually applied to an aphorism or maxim in a wisdom context. The prologue (1:1–7) applies to the whole book and the variety of wisdom sayings it contains, all broadly classified as "proverbs." Solomon. Although Solomon wrote many proverbs (1 Kin. 4:32), the words of sages other than Solomon are included under this heading (e.g., Agur, 30:1; and Lemuel, 31:1). Even in the materials attributed to Solomon, something other than direct authorship may at times be involved. Note that the "words of King Lemuel" were not authored by Lemuel but taught to him by his mother and then associated with Lemuel. So, too, at least some of the "proverbs of Solomon" could have been taught to him by others and then associated with him as Israel's quintessential wise man. The roots of proverbial traditions in folk experience make it unlikely that Solomon was the exclusive originator of all the proverbs he put into writing (Introduction: Author). king. Wisdom was a royal enterprise in the ancient Near East. The queen of Sheba came to listen to Solomon's wisdom (1 Kin. 10:1) and the "men of Hezekiah king of Judah" copied some of the proverbs (Prov. 25:1).

Explicit reference to the purpose behind this collection suggests that some kind of formal educational use was being made of such materi­al, although evidence for wisdom schools (groups gathered around prominent teachers) in Israel is not strong. 1:2 wisdom. The purpose of Proverbs is to guide the reader into wisdom, a word with many nuances. It refers fundamentally to living in keeping with the order that God built into the world so as to survive and thrive. James 3:15–18 distinguishes heavenly wisdom from earthly wisdom; the former is defined very much in terms of the fruit of the Holy Spirit, while the latter is the opposite. instruction. The word suggests moral and intellectual discipline. It often means the learning of wisdom. insight. Or discernment, the ability to read between the lines and make correct distinctions.

These words can be used in religious and ethical contexts as well as in temporal affairs. At times, biblical wisdom shows concern with worldly matters, but it always does so within the framework of divine design in the created order.

Sound judgment. simple. The word is paralleled in this verse by "youth"; it refers to those who are untutored, inexperienced, and easily deceived (1:10), not to those lacking intellectual powers. Wisdom is a matter of practical godliness. discretion. The word suggests making right decisions with understanding.

Wisdom was institutionalized in the ancient culture in that the wise called upon people to improve their wisdom. Succeeding generations were to learn from those who went before (v. 8). Note the typical parallel structure of this verse in which almost synonymous phrases are joined. guidance. This Hb. word, used only in Proverbs and Job, highlights the importance of right thinking and experience in decision making.

These different words may be used synonymously, as in Hab. 2:6, but probably here they are distinct forms of wisdom sayings, having as a common characteristic an enigma that challenges the intellect (1:1 note). saying. Sometimes rendered "parable." The parables of Jesus are somewhat different from what is found in the book of Proverbs, although they show the influence of Wisdom Literature. riddles. Probably a broad but identifiable type of wisdom literature. The word is used of Samson's riddle (Judg. 14:12–19), of an allegory (Ezek. 17:2), and of the sayings used to test Solomon (1 Kin. 10:1).

LORD. The main theme of Proverbs and ancient Israel's decisive contribution to the human quest for knowledge and understanding. The fear of the Lord is the only basis of true knowledge. This fear is not distrustful terror of God but rather the reverent awe and worshipful response of faith to the God who reveals Himself as the Creator, the Savior, and the Judge. Although Israel's covenant relationship with God receives little overt attention in Proverbs, the use of the divine name most closely associated with the covenant, "Lord" (Hb. Yahweh; cf. Ex. 3:15; 6:3 and notes), is significant. It indicates that God's redemptive covenant with His people and the special revelation that accompany it are foundational for true wisdom. In Deuteronomy, "fear the Lord" means living by the stipulations of the covenant in grateful response to God's redemptive grace (Deut. 6:2, 24). The temple built by Solomon later became the visible expression of Israel's covenant relationship with the Lord, which again is described as the "fear" of the Lord (1 Kin. 8:40, 43). There is an important link through Solomon and the temple between biblical wisdom and the covenant theology found elsewhere in the OT. is the beginning of knowledge. See also 2:4–6; 9:10; 15:33; Job 28:28; Ps. 111:10. The Hebrew means either the starting point of knowledge or its best part. The former is in view here, not as in a starting point that one leaves behind, but as in mathematics, where one uses the numbers learned at the beginning in all of the later courses. While in His common grace God enables unbelievers to know much about the world, only the fear of the Lord enables one to know what anything means ultimately. Relying on this light, wisdom pursues the task of reflecting on human experience.

The first collection of proverbs in the book. It consists of longer poems that have as their primary function admonishing the youth mentioned in 1:4 to choose the way of wisdom. 1:8–19 The first instructional poem, wherein the parents call the son to avoid the wrong path. 1:8, 9 The instruction form of ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature typically begins with a call for attentiveness. Father and mother were both involved in home instruction. 1:8 instruction. See note on 3:1. teaching. Hb. torah in Proverbs refers mostly to human teaching (3:1; 4:2; 6:20, 23; 7:2; 13:14; 31:26). Four times torah echoes divine instruction (28:4, 7, 9; 29:18) and is translated "law." The human instruction in the book is at the same time divine instruction.
These metaphors portray the effect of wisdom: the garland is a symbol of victory (4:9) and the pendants are a symbol of luxury (Judg. 8:26).

Summarizes the instruction. The "if" will be expanded in vv. 11–14 and the "do not" in vv. 15–18. "If \... then" clauses are common throughout the book (see 2:4, 5). entice. The Hb. verb is related to the noun translated "simple" in 1:4. The simple are easily enticed.

The realm of death is here depicted as ready to swallow its victims. Elsewhere, this poetic term denotes a realm where corruption is father and the worm is mother (Job 17:13, 14), a domain with gates (Is. 38:10). It is a land of no return (Job 7:9), silence (Ps. 94:17), darkness (Ps. 143:3), and forgetfulness (Ps. 88:11, 12). See notes on 9:18 and Is. 14:9–11.
Proverbs does not forbid or discourage wealth — only the use of evil to get it. However, the ultimate wealth is wisdom itself (2:4; 3:13–16; cf. Job 28:12–19).
After the extended conditional clause (vv. 10–14), the address is repeated to reinforce the command to avoid evil people.
This verse is almost identical with Is. 59:7 and is partly quoted by Paul in Rom. 3:15 as part of his demonstration that all are sinners.

This saying is introduced to strengthen the reasons for the author's counsel. The apparent meaning is that even a bird will avoid a trap once it has knowledge of it. Those who are tempted should do the same.
One reaps what one sows. These "lie in wait" and plan to "ambush" others (v. 11), not knowing that they "lie in wait for their own blood" and "set an ambush for their own lives."

Such folly is contrary to the true order of the world, which, though fallen, is still under God's sovereign rule. This expression of inevitable retribution is based on the observable order of causes and consequence. Apparent interruptions in this pattern prompted other biblical writers to address the problem of the prosperous wicked and the suffering righteous (Job 1–42; Ps. 73).

These verses make up the first wisdom poem in the opening collection and focus on wisdom's rebuke of the simple, with vv. 20, 21 as the setting, vv. 22–27 as the sermon, and vv. 28–33 as the significance. 1:20 Wisdom is portrayed as an open-air preacher similar to the caller in Is. 55. Personified as a woman, she calls on the simple to repent of folly and to seek wisdom before it is too late. Personification of wisdom is found also in 3:14–18; 8:1–36; 9:1–12.

The town gate was the public forum for counsel and judgment (Deut. 22:15; 25:7; Ruth 4:1, 11; 2 Sam. 19:8). It is the place where the elders of the town often met. This is the fitting location for the figure of wisdom to call people to heed her counsel.

See v. 4 and note. There has been a development of thought. At issue is not merely gaining more insight but a deliberate choice between two ways. Wisdom and folly, righteousness and wickedness, are constantly opposed in Proverbs as the only two options for life (cf. Matt. 7:24–27). scoffers. The precise meaning of this word, used mostly in Proverbs, is difficult to determine. The mocker (or scoffer) is a person who resists the discipline of the wise (9:7, 8; 13:1; 14:6; 21:11; Ps. 1). fools. Unteachable people. knowledge. See 1:7. In Wisdom Literature, "knowledge" is often a synonym for wisdom.

Proverbs recognizes wisdom as both a divine gift and a human task. The former is seen in 1:7, where the fear of the Lord grows from the grace of God in redemption. Redemption involves renewal of the mind as well as regeneration of the soul (Rom. 12:1, 2; 1 Cor. 1:18–2:6).
The rejection of wisdom's message has its parallels in the rejection of God's grace by Israel.
Here wisdom speaks with full authority. As God's counsel, her counsel and advice are not open to debate (2:6; 8:14).
"He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision" (Ps. 2:4).
Storm imagery is frequent for divine judgment in the OT (e.g., Jer. 23:19; Jon. 1:9–12).

True wisdom is an aspect of God's saving grace, and there comes a point of no return for those who reject it. This truth reinforces the urgency of the message. No one can expect God's favor and at the same time scorn the gifts He offers (Deut. 1:45; 1 Sam. 28:6; Ps. 18:41).

A synonym for wisdom, explained here by the phrase parallel with it, "the fear of the LORD" (1:7 note). Wisdom comes from above (James 3:17) as God's gift in redemptive revelation. This is true even when it must be desired and strived for (2:4–6; Heb. 5:7, 8; James 1:5).
The relationship between deed and outcome is observable in natural cause and effect. Here the image is not one of pleasure after a full meal but of disgust at being glutted.
Indifference or willful neglect. complacency of fools. The ignorant self-satisfaction of the willfully unteachable, who see no need to learn anything from anyone.
This verse stands in direct contrast with v. 32. Wisdom brings life and security. To embrace wisdom is to embrace all that promotes life.

The second instructional poem of the first collection, with a focus on how wisdom will keep one safe. The poem is an acrostic, with vv. 1–11 governed by aleph (the first letter of the first half of the Hebrew alphabet) and vv. 12–22 governed by lamed (the first letter of the second half of the Hebrew alphabet). The aleph stanza is divided into three strophes (Introduction to Hebrew Poetry), each beginning with a word that starts with aleph: "if" (vv. 1–4), "then" (vv. 5–8), and "then" (vv. 9–11). The lamed stanza is also divided into three strophes, each beginning with a word that starts with lamed: "delivering \... from" (vv. 12–15), "delivered from" (vv. 16–19), and "So you will walk" (vv. 20–22). 2:1–11 The development of wisdom. 2:1–4 The conditions for developing wisdom. 2:1 receive. The first condition is the acceptance of wisdom (1:3). treasure. The Hb. word has the sense of hiding something of value so as to protect it, and the means of hiding is memorization (Ps. 119:11).

The second condition is submission. To stretch out the heart is to submit. In Josh. 24:23 and 1 Kin. 11:2–4, such submission is a human responsibility, whereas in 1 Kin. 8:58 and Ps. 119:36, it is a matter of divine sovereignty. The heart is the seat of reason and the will. Today's popular distinction between heart knowledge and head knowledge does not apply here. The usual OT contrast is between a formal or outward compliance lacking true assent of will and a willing, wholehearted compliance.
The third condition is humility. As wisdom called out (1:21) and raised her voice (1:20), humility responds in kind.

The fourth condition is desire. "Seek" and "silver" are rather common terms in the Hebrew Bible, but "search" and "hidden treasure" are rare. The movement from the common to the rare underscores the need for deep desire if one is going to develop wisdom. hidden treasures. Note the similar image used by Jesus in Matt. 13:44.
The first result of meeting the conditions is wisdom in one's relationship with God. 2:5 you will understand \... knowledge. Wisdom starts with the knowledge of God.

gives wisdom.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} No matter how much we are engaged in the task of searching for knowledge through our human experience in the world, the source of all wisdom is God (Job 28). He must provide the wisdom necessary for the proper interpretation of reality (3:5). from his mouth. Although their emphasis is different, both Deuteronomy and Proverbs recognize that the underlying foundation of knowledge is the Word of God (Deut. 8:3). Even before sin had entered the world, Adam and Eve needed God's revelation in order to know themselves and their relationship to creation (Gen. 1:28–30).
The character of God, which the wise come to know (v. 5), is the basis of morality. Standards of integrity and righteousness are expressions of wisdom.
People who show that they possess the fear of the Lord by imitating His covenant love.

The second result of meeting the conditions is wisdom in one's relationship with others. 2:9 righteousness and justice and equity. Terms that articulate what should govern how we treat others. every good path. The Wisdom Literature is important to our understanding of God's guidance of our lives. It points to the task of gaining wisdom so we can make decisions that are responsible and consistent with our covenant status as God's people (1 Pet. 2:9).
Resourcefulness or prudence.

The deliverance by wisdom. 2:12–15. Deliverance from evil men, from their evil speech and apostasy. 2:12 evil. The Hb. word is masculine and refers to evil men, not to evil in general, as is made clear by the word "men" in the second half of the verse. perverted speech. Words of rebellion that overturn truth. Later proverbs will have much to say about speech.
The evil men turn away from the right path (see v. 17).

Deliverance from evil women, from their evil speech and apostasy. 2:16 forbidden woman. Adultery is a radical departure from God's order for human relationships (5:1–23; 6:20–29; 7:1–27). The Hb. term is "foreign" or "strange" woman. In this context, it means a woman who is foreign to the proper marital relationship, a harlot or adulteress. smooth words. As evil men use perverted speech (v. 12), evil women use seductive speech.

The evil woman turns away from the right path (see v. 13). companion. Her husband. covenant of her God. If the "forbidden woman" is a non-Israelite (v. 16 note), "covenant" may refer to a marriage witnessed by some foreign god. More likely, the woman is an Israelite who transgresses the requirements of the covenant given at Sinai, particularly the commandment against adultery (Ex. 20:14).

In OT Wisdom Literature, life is not mere existence but a way characterized by true relationships that conform to God's design. Death is not only the end of physical life but an irreversible descent into the disorder of moral perversity (cf. 5:23, where "dies" is parallel with "led astray").
This note of finality highlights the seriousness of breaching standards that are not merely social customs but creation ordinances of God.
Deliverance from" evil people creates space for walking in the way of good people.

The promise of land was a basic part of the covenant God made with Abraham, Moses, and the people (Gen. 13:15 and note; Ex. 20:12; Deut. 1:8; 26:1–9). These promises foreshadow the promise of eternal life (Hb. 11:16) and the meek's inheriting the earth (Matt. 5:5). The conditional aspect of the covenant is reflected here (Gen. 17:2 note) — the upright and the wise inherit the land, but the wicked are removed (Deut. 28).

These verses are the third instruction in the first collection and focus on one's relationship with God by holding on to the teaching (vv. 1–4), centering on the Lord (vv. 5–10), and accepting God's discipline (vv. 11, 12). The repetition of "my son" in vv. 1, 11 marks the boundaries of the section, and the consistent use of couplets evidences the internal unity. 3:1–4 The first two couplets focus on holding on to the teaching ("do not forget," keep," "let not \... forsake," "bind," and "write"), which advances the acceptance of the teaching in 2:1. 3:1 teaching. See note on 1:8. commandments. This word is also found in the law. As is typical of the parallel phrases of Hebrew poetry, the second half of the verse repeats the idea of the first half, clarifying it or expanding on it. Essentially, this verse means to memorize the commands and then put them into practice.

Refers to quantity of life. years of life. Refers to quality of life. The normal expectation is that wisdom will lead to a long, prosperous life, which is the blessing of God (Ex. 20:12; Deut. 6:1–3). peace. Heb. shalom. The term denotes general well-being, a harmony of relationships, wholeness, and health (v. 8). In the OT, the blessings of God are seen primarily in terms of this present life. It was not easy to reconcile this perspective with the suffering of the righteous or the prosperity of the wicked. The revelation that would come with Christ, especially in His resurrection from the dead, was still far in the future.

Metonyms for the teaching and commandments of v. 1, since it is the latter that are characteristically bound and written (6:20, 21; 7:2, 3; Deut. 6:8). The teachings and commandments in Proverbs are characterized by love and faithfulness.
Reputation is the sense (text note). Jesus lived this out, as it is written, "Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man" (Luke 2:52).

LORD. Rely entirely upon the Lord's Word and promises as revealed through the sage (2:6; 16:20). See note on 1:7. lean \... understanding. The text warns against relying exclusively on one's own understanding, but does not prohibit using it.

This is the practical expression of the mind that submits to God and knows Him. he will make straight your paths. The straight path is the path of the righteous (2:20) that leads to life (12:28) and is to be contrasted with the crooked path (2:15) that leads to death (2:19). The straight path is also the level path (15:19); both are metaphors for freedom from obstacles (see 3:23; 4:12).
Summarizes the idea that the human mind with its intellect and reason is independently capable of reaching a true understanding of reality, without dependence upon God's revelation.

Lit. "navel" (text note), which may be a figure of speech where a part stands for the whole, and thus refers to the outer body. Since one cannot see the bones, they may serve as a figure for the inner person. Together, "flesh" and "bones" stand for the whole person.

To esteem one as having importance. wealth \... firstfruits. The poet moves from the general (material wealth) to the specific (the best part of one's wealth). Honoring God with the right use of material things expresses gratitude for His favor and recognizes that He controls the natural order and its processes.

The three basic products for the ancient Israelite farmer were grain, wine, and oil (Deut. 11:14; 12:17; Hos. 2:8; Joel 2:24). Barns full of grain and vats full of wine symbolize prosperity on all levels.

The repetition of "my son" (3:1) signals the end of this instructional poem. discipline. Although the instruction of God will require chastisement, this correction is not calculated to harm or anger His children. But because chastisement is difficult, specific encouragement not to rebel against it is necessary.
Discipline is the expression of the Father's love for His children. Heb. 12:3–11 explains that God's correction is better than that of an earthly father; cf. Luke 11:11–13.

Another wisdom poem. This one focuses on the benefits of wisdom, both the blessings of wisdom (vv. 13–18) and its effectiveness (vv. 19, 20). 3:13–18 The repetition of "blessed" in vv. 13 and 18 marks the beginning and end of this section, and it focuses attention on the main theme: the blessings of wisdom. 3:13 Blessed. The Hb. word ashrey, used almost exclusively in the Wisdom Literature, refers to well-being in every area of life (see Ps. 112). The one who finds wisdom, like the one who meditates on God's instruction (Ps. 1), is blessed.
Job 28 describes wisdom as a treasure. Ps. 19:10 refers specifically to the revealed law.
See v. 2 and notes. One of the reasons that wisdom is better than wealth is that wisdom brings wealth as well as long life and honor.

Probably not a specific allusion to the tree of life in Gen. 2:9, though the author would have known of it. In the literature of the time, the flourishing tree was a common figure for continuing blessings. The metaphor is used again in 11:30; 13:12; 15:4. More important is the theme of "life" in Proverbs. "Life" in the Bible is essentially linked to our relationship with God. Disruption of the proper relationship with God, the source of life, leads to death (Gen. 2:17). Wisdom is concerned with proper relationships with God, other people, and nature.

These verses are linked to vv. 13–18 by the repetition of "wisdom" and "understanding" in vv. 13 and 19 and focus on the effectiveness of wisdom. 3:19 by wisdom \... by understanding. God's wisdom is so effective that it was used to create earth and heaven. earth \... heavens. God's wisdom produced the well-ordered world of earth beneath and heaven above, implying also all creation between earth and heaven.

An instructional poem that focuses on wisdom and relating to our neighbor: wisdom's benefits (vv. 21–24), the good neighbor (vv. 25–32), and wisdom's outcomes (vv. 33–35). 3:21–24 These verses focus on the need to hold on to wisdom (v. 21) and the benefits that will result (vv. 22–24). 3:21 See notes on v. 1 and 1:4.

Here as elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, the word for "soul" refers to the whole person. adornment. The Hb. word is a common term for "favor." Wisdom brings "favor \... in the sight of God and man" (3:4).
See note on 3:6.
not be afraid. Part of wisdom is the avoidance of life-threatening situations, not by refusing to face danger when necessary but by pursuing right relationships and an orderly existence.
In context, the sense seems to be the ruin that might be brought about by a wicked neighbor.
The Lord will protect the righteous from a wicked neighbor.
Contains a series of commandments ("Do not") about relating to our neighbor, the first and the last containing explanatory clauses ("for").
Devious people are alienated from God, but those who are righteous enjoy intimacy with the Lord.

The commands of vv. 25–32 have come to an end, and this instructional poem ends by spelling out the two outcomes of one's choices in life. 3:33 Here the typical proverbial contrast between the righteous and the wicked (cf. 10:2, 3, 6, 7, 11, 16) is related to God's blessings and curses. This parallels the covenant theology of Deuteronomy, in which faithfulness is rewarded by the blessings of God (Deut. 11:26–29; 28:1–19).
See James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5.

These verses are wisdom passed down from a grandfather to his son and then to his grandson, focusing on the need to embrace wisdom. 4:1 sons. The first of four occurrences of "sons" in place of the usual "son" (see 5:7; 7:24; 8:32). The shift is probably an indicator of the fact that Proverbs is a compilation of various collections of wisdom teaching.
Or "learning," as in 1:5. The Hb. term emphasizes the receptive activity of the learner; it stems from the same root of the verb translated "receive" in 1:3.

The wise continue the tradition of wisdom by passing on to succeeding generations the wisdom they learned from their parents. Ps. 78 is a wisdom psalm that has this same transgenerational approach to the teaching of wisdom. Age and experience are not absolute authorities, but they are important and must be highly regarded (Lev. 19:32).

Note the parallel structure in this verse, where the second line says almost the same as the first yet with some development of thought. "Do not forsake" becomes the positive injunction to "love." Wisdom is far more than an accumulation of facts. It involves trust and commitment.

This embrace of the need for wisdom goes hand in hand with the fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom (1:7), for it is only in fearing God that we realize our need for wisdom. whatever you get. Jesus used a similar saying about how one should seek the kingdom of God (Matt. 13:45, 46).
One benefit of wisdom is that wisdom brings other benefits. See note on 1:9.

These verses, marked out at the beginning by "Hear, my son" (see 4:1, 20), focus on wisdom and the two ways: the way of wisdom (vv. 10–13, 18) and the way of the wicked (vv. 14–17, 19). 4:10 accept. See 1:3. years \... many. See note on 3:2.
The metaphor of life as a way or a path is common in Israelite wisdom. Wisdom and uprightness go together, showing the moral side of wisdom, as do folly and wickedness (10:18; 14:16; 24:9).
The path of wisdom is the straight path (3:6 note).
Life cannot exist without wisdom. In the NT, Christ is called our wisdom (1 Cor. 1:30) and our life (Col. 3:4).

Wisdom typically contrasts opposing ways and ideas (esp. in the concise proverbs of chs. 10–22). This teaching device accentuates the path of wisdom by opposing various aspects of it to the path of folly and evil. Here vv. 11–13 contrast with vv. 14–17, and v. 18 with v. 19.
Evil is like an addictive drug. Those who embrace it find that without their daily dose they are unable to sleep.
Eating and drinking image the joy and satisfaction of life elsewhere (Eccl. 2:4 note), but the wicked pervert these blessings.
These verses use imagery of an ever-increasing light to characterize righteousness and an impenetrable gloom for wickedness (John 8:12; Eph. 5:8–13)., 19

Builds on the previous section and culminates in a call to stay on the right path. 4:20 my son. Typical at the beginning of a new section. be attentive \... incline your ear. The language of submission to God's instruction (2:2 note).
The seat of reason and the will (2:2 note).
Wholeness and soundness that include the body (3:8).
Our thoughts shape the way we speak and live. See Matt. 12:35; Mark 7:21; Rom. 2:29.
"Crooked" and "devious" characterize the speech of the wicked (2:12, 16) as well as their general lifestyle (2:15). What is on one's lips is a reflection of one's life.
Keeping the eyes straight on the path of wisdom is the responsibility of the one who trusts the Lord to make the path straight (3:6).
See note on 4:12.
See Deut. 5:32.

These verses focus on wisdom and two women, an adulteress and one's wife: an instruction to stay away from the forbidden woman (vv. 1–6), a second instruction to stay away from her (vv. 7–14), an instruction to embrace one's wife (vv. 15–19), and a concluding instruction to stay away from the forbidden woman (vv. 20–23). The repetition of "forbidden woman" in vv. 3, 20 serves to tie these sections together as a unit. Wisdom urges us to avoid the life-destroying adulteress and to find sexual and emotional satisfaction in the bonds of marriage. 5:1–6 Describes the character of the forbidden woman. On the surface she is sweetness and light, but underneath is the bitter taste of death. 5:1 be attentive \... incline your ear. The language of submission to God's instruction (4:20 note).
The sense seems to be that his lips should be involved with holding on to knowledge by means of the recitation of Scripture rather than being involved with "the lips of a forbidden woman" (5:3).

While her lips are associated with speech in the next line, it is hard not to hear a reference to her seductive kiss as well. In contrast with v. 2, the seducer begins with deceptive words of charm. Cf. the sweetness of true love in Song 4:11.

The phrase speaks of the end result for one who lets himself be seduced. bitter as wormwood. A plant especially bitter to the taste, wormwood is used as a metaphor for the experience of affliction (Deut. 29:18). two-edged sword. The smoothness of her words is deceptive (v. 3), and the liaison leads only to injury.

Not merely a matter of an early demise brought about by dissolute living, death in this context is all that does not promote life as defined by God. Sheol. The place of the dead, the grave. Disorderly life leads to physical death. See note on Is. 14:9–11.
The moral censure here is inseparable from the wisdom idea that folly and wickedness involve a rejection of God's order and plan for things.
These verses provide a more detailed description of the results of immorality and the price it exacts.
The wise will make a conscious choice to avoid any contact with immorality and keep out of the way of temptation.
Both should be gained through wisdom (3:16), not lost through folly. the merciless. Perhaps the outraged husband of the adulteress (6:34, 35).
This verse may refer literally to the high cost of keeping a mistress (a "foreigner"). More likely, the warning is that immorality takes away wealth and strength.
Both should find healing through wisdom (3:7, 8), not demise through folly.
Sexual immorality epitomizes the way of folly that rejects the discipline of wise instruction.
In view here is either public disgrace or punishment by the covenant community.

These verses are similar to the love poetry of the Song of Solomon. 5:15 Drink water \... cistern. The context suggests that this is a metaphor for marital relations with one's wife. flowing \... well. In Song 4:15, the young woman is described with the same language.
The imagery suggests the wastefulness of male promiscuity. "Spring" is used to refer to the young woman's sexuality in Song 4:12. Cf. "garden fountain" in Song 4:15.
The image could refer either to male or female sexuality. Whichever is the case, the point is clear.

See, e.g., Song 1:3; 4:5; 7:3. intoxicated. The Hb. word is predominantly negative, as in "go astray/sin" (Lev. 4:13). It comes to mean "stagger" in association with drunkenness (Is. 28:7). Here it is used positively, as in Song 1:2, where the kiss is like wine, which can intoxicate, and in Song 5:1, which also compares sexual union to drinking wine, saying, "Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!" 5:19–23 In these verses, which are linked to the previous by the repetition of "intoxicated," the text returns to a final warning about the forbidden woman (see 5:3). Up to this point, the warnings against adultery have not referenced God's law. Similar warnings can be found in other wisdom traditions. Now the writer explains that the natural consequences of folly, and especially sexual folly, are punishments ordained by God.

Or "takes note of." Our behavior is under constant scrutiny. The text does not say that every sin is visited with an immediate penalty. Rather, God oversees the created order so that sinners are captured by their folly (vv. 22, 23).
One reaps what one sows. See note on 1:18.
See notes on v. 5 and 2:18.

These verses offer advice on three types of men: the foolish helper (vv. 1–5), the lazy man (vv. 6–11), and the worthless man (vv. 12–15). The section concludes with a treatment of seven characteristics of bad men in general (vv. 16–19). 6:1–5 The foolish helper. 6:1 pledge for a stranger. Such an agreement to guarantee another's debt is unwise because it involves matters quite beyond the guarantor's control (11:15; 17:18; 22:26).
Borrowing money is one thing, but to provide security for another is to walk into a trap of one's own making.
By accepting responsibility for another's debts, one allows another to take control of one's life. hasten. See text note. This is not the time for pride.
There must be an unremitting effort to have the contract annulled.
The imagery of creatures hunted and trapped heightens the sense of urgency.

The lazy man. These verses are an object lesson based on the industry of the ant. The underlying assumption is not only that the universe is orderly but also that there are points of analogy between even the lowly insect world and humans. Solomon's nature proverbs may have drawn other such analogies (1 Kin. 4:33). 6:6 ant. See 30:25. The ant's industry gives the appearance of prudent activity. sluggard. Suggests a lazy person whose inactivity expresses an attitude of folly (10:26; 13:4; 15:19; 19:24; 20:4; 26:16).
This proverbial saying is linked with the previous saying (vv. 6–9) to provide an application of it. The same saying is later linked with a different object lesson (24:33, 34).

The worthless human. The form suggests a proverbial saying that has been expanded to apply to a specific situation. A string of descriptive clauses is added to the main thought: the worthless person stirs up discord. 6:12 worthless person. Lit. "man of Belial," a phrase of uncertain origin and meaning. It probably indicates a base and worthless person, with an element of active malevolence.
The wicked do not speak plainly and openly but make veiled suggestions and signs that sow seeds of distrust and dissension.

Such people, in time, bring destruction upon themselves. The OT reveals that God will ultimately punish the wicked (24:19, 20) and reward the righteous (23:17, 18; 24:15, 16), but it does not present a fully developed doctrine of punishment in the afterlife. The prosperity of the wicked was a continuing problem (Pss. 37:7; 73:3–14). The NT clearly indicates that the righteous judgment of God falls on the wicked, whether in this life or the next (Luke 16:23, 24; Rev. 14:10–12; 20:15).

These verses are the first of the numerical sayings in Proverbs (cf. 30:15–31). The form of these sayings suggests a kind of riddle with an answer provided, not to dispose of the question but to invite further appropriate answers. Wisdom literature often lists things together that are perceived as having something in common. Relationships are established in surprising ways, and the process of discerning orderly relationships in the universe increases wisdom. This unit is quite distinct from the previous ones (vv. 1–15) but is probably placed next to them for development of the theme of "bad people." Whereas v. 15 expresses the perspective of an unspecified natural retribution, this saying implies that the Lord renders judgment (5:21–23 note). 6:16 six \... seven. The use of successive numbers is a common device in Hebrew poetry (Job 5:19; Amos 1:3).

Another warning against adultery (chs. 5; 7; 30:20). The form of this section is essentially that of the instruction but with considerable variation. Some quite elaborate word pictures are used to heighten the urgency of the warnings (vv. 23, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31). Verses 21 and 23 depend on Deut. 6:8 and Ps. 119:105, which refer to the law. The law provides a clear framework for revelation, showing Israel the proper response to God's covenant relationship with her. Wisdom works within that framework to describe the bounds of human responsibility. The law condemns adultery and prescribes a penalty for it (Ex. 20:14; Lev. 20:10). Wisdom shares this opposition to adultery and adds its own warnings about the inevitable disaster that such folly brings. 6:20 See 1:8. commandment. See note on 3:1.
For the old covenant responsibility to write the teachings on the heart, see 3:3 and Deut. 6:6, 8.
See notes on 3:23, 24; cf. Deut. 6:7. Wisdom is comprehensive in its effects on one's life. they will lead you. See notes on 1:5; 2:9; and 3:6.

In Ps. 119:105, the same metaphor is applied to the law. The wise person accepts the revealed law and examines nature and the experiences of life in dependence upon it. In this way, wisdom supplements the law from its own perspective.
See notes on 2:16 and 5:3.
The lustful desire of the heart is the start of the progression of folly. The connection between the desire and the act is not as stark as in Matt. 5:28, but it is present.
Although consorting with prostitutes is self-destructive, adultery is worse. It is not only a violation of marriage but also a direct attack on it.
Wisdom in Proverbs emphasizes the expected results of folly, but also, from time to time, goes behind the natural cause-and-effect chain to the overarching purpose and judgment of God.

The person driven by hunger to steal is still subject to the law, but people can understand such need. By contrast, adultery has no such extenuating factors and brings utter disgrace. The law required restoration of four times the theft; "sevenfold" exaggerates this for emphasis (Ex. 22:1).
The offended husband's jealousy leads to fury and to a merciless revenge that no offer of compensation can avert. The forces that drive human relationships are often at the center of wisdom thinking.

These verses are made up of three parts, linked by the common theme of adultery. The first (vv. 1–5) and third (vv. 24–27) are in the form of instructions, and both warn about involvement with the adulteress. The middle section (vv. 6–23) appears as a dramatic narrative that functions as an imaginative reinforcement of the instructions. 7:1–5 A warning from the father to the son. 7:1 commandments. See note on 3:1.

See notes on 2:18 and 3:2. apple of your eye. Lit. "the little man of your eye," a reference to the pupil, in which the image of the observer is reflected, and an expression of endearment. The pupil admits light to the eye and must be protected from all harm (cf. Deut. 32:10; Ps. 17:8; Zech. 2:8).
See 3:3 and notes. The procedures outlined in vv. 1–3 are an aspect of wisdom's method. The traditions are handed down in order to mold life and character.

One should think of wisdom and understanding as one's close relatives. This image is intended to depict the desired intimacy with wisdom rather than to contrast with the adulteress of v. 5. For the metaphorical use of "sister" as a term of intimacy, see Song 4:9, 10, 12; 5:1, 2.
These verses tell a story to illustrate the warning given in 7:1–5.
See note on 1:4. The young man is naive and unskilled in the art of living. The teaching of wisdom is aimed at such an impressionable type (1:2–4).
The movement from twilight to evening to night to dark underscores the increasing intensity in the alluring setting.
Seduction involves a deceitful show that attracts the victim while at the same time concealing the real intent.
The same verb used for the men in 1:11, 18 who were trying to seduce the young man to join their gang.
The food from these religious offerings provided opportunity for gluttony (Lev. 7:12–18). See 17:1; 21:27.
Flattery assuring the young man that he was specially chosen for this treat.
Aromatic spices used for perfuming garments and beds. See Song 1:13; 3:6; 4:14.
The most fraudulent proposition of all. To suggest that casual and illicit sex can satisfy deep longings for mutual, loving commitment is a destructive lie.
The woman is aware that this illicit relationship involves them in deceit. They vainly hope to avoid the jealous husband's rage (6:33–35).
The seductive power of words is a constant theme (2:16; 5:3; 6:24; 9:16, 17). It stands in contrast to the healing power of wisdom's words (2:1–6; 3:1, 2; 5:1, 2; 7:24, 25).

The dumb animal is unaware of its fate and allows itself to be led. as a stag is caught fast. See text note. The uncertainty of this line does not obscure the overall sense of the verse: the young man has walked into a trap.
A mortal wound.
These verses apply the story told in vv. 6–23 to the sons.
See note on 2:2. do not stray into her paths. The wise man's prescription is to keep one's thoughts (heart) from adultery and to stay away from places where there is temptation.
A motive for prudence is to avoid the carnage that results from folly.

Wisdom again calls out to the simple to invite them to embrace her in a way that parallels her call in 1:20–33. In 1:20–33, her call was rejected, but the response in 8:1–36 is left open, since the function of 1:8–9:18 is to get the young man to choose his path in life — toward folly or toward wisdom. In this majestic poem, wisdom is personified as the supreme teacher who teaches on her own authority. The personification is most probably a poetic device to express more vividly the authority of wisdom. Although it is premature to see personified wisdom (esp. in vv. 22–31) as a direct portrayal of a divine being, there is no doubt that the revelation of Jesus Christ as the wisdom of God shows us the significance of a wisdom that is its own absolute authority (1 Cor. 1:24, 30; cf. John 1:1–18; Col. 1:15, 16; Heb. 1:1–4). The poem progresses from a call of wisdom (vv. 1–11) to the effectiveness of wisdom in the world (vv. 12–21) to the divine origin of wisdom and its place in the totality of creation (vv. 22–31) to the final appeal that equates wisdom with life (vv. 32–36). Behind human wisdom is the original, uncreated wisdom of God, by which He established all created things in their proper relationships to God and to one another. This means that human wisdom is valid and life-affirming insofar as it works within the context provided by divine special revelation (ch. 4 note). 8:1–11 Wisdom's call. 8:1–3 See notes on 1:20–33.

The Hb. word usually applies to males, which fits the context of the address of Lady Wisdom to males, but extends to all humanity (1:5 note). Wisdom, in the role of the instructor, ultimately addresses not sons or pupils but all people. There is no elite class in the matter of learning wisdom; it is for all. children of man. This refers to individuals, so the movement from "men" to "children of man" is from humans as a whole to individuals. The individual is not lost in the group.
See notes on 1:4, 22.
Princely or valuable things. what is right. The moral element is implied.
Denotes what is utterly reliable. It is the opposite of wickedness. Proverbs relates truth to wisdom in several places, and here the word of wisdom is described in a way suggestive of divine origin.
See note on v. 18.

Wisdom is a self-consistent reality. One must be attuned to it in order to learn it. This is another way of saying that all truth is God's truth, and without the knowledge of God, we cannot know the absolute truth. Cf. the wisdom of Jesus in Matt. 13:10–16; Luke 11:52.

The comparison of wisdom to the most desirable emblems of wealth is a way of emphasizing its value (2:4; 3:14, 15; 8:19–21; Job 28:17). The warning against crass materialism is obvious — and against creation-denying asceticism as well — since the comparison presumes the goodness of wealth.
Wisdom's effectiveness. 8:12 See 1:4 and note.

LORD. See 1:7; 2:5; 3:7; 9:10 and notes. Wisdom reminds us that the search for an ethic based solely on experience is futile. Education and experience must build on the basis of the faithfulness and hope provided by God's covenant promises. Ethical systems without the absolute standard of right, goodness, and truth revealed in the Scriptures cannot survive (Ps. 36:9). Pride \... I hate. Wisdom echoes the hatred that God has for evil (6:16; Deut. 12:31; 16:22; Ps. 5:5; Is. 61:8; Jer. 44:4).

Advice derived from wisdom and experience; also, plans made by joint deliberation on a course of action. The same word is used for the mind of God concerning His plans and purposes (Is. 5:19; 19:17; 25:1; 28:29). Wisdom has access to this counsel.

The proper function of human rulers is defined by the order of God's creation as revealed in the Word of God (Gen. 1:26–28). Wise rule begins with the fear of the Lord (Deut. 17:18–20; 1 Kin. 3:6–9; 4:29–34). The Messiah will rule by perfect wisdom (Is. 11:1–3).

The statements contrast with wisdom being hidden from fools (1:28, 29). Wisdom cares for her own (4:6, 8, 9). those who seek me \... find me. See 2:4, 5; 3:13–15. This anticipates the final appeal of the poem (vv. 35, 36) and suggests a relationship between wisdom and the grace of God that causes Him to draw near to us (Is. 55:6). Jesus, Himself the final revelation of divine wisdom (1 Cor. 1:24, 30; Col. 2:2, 3), possibly alludes to this verse in Matt. 7:7.

See 3:2, 16. Solomon's early reign was an example of the material and social benefits of wisdom (1 Kin. 10:1–9). righteousness. This means obedience to God's law, extending to the cultivation of right relationships between God, people, and creation. See Rom. 12:18; 1 Tim. 2:1–4.
See note on vv. 10, 11.

Wisdom's origin. This hymn-like section presents wisdom as the basis of design in the universe. The focus is unusual, but this view of wisdom does not go against the theology of the covenant and God's saving acts in Israel. The sages were also men of the covenant (1:7; 2:20–22 and notes). The method of wisdom is to emphasize the biblical theology of creation as the basis for understanding our lives as redeemed people of God. 8:22 The LORD. The proper name of God as the redeemer and the author of the covenant (Ex. 3:15 and notes). God's redemptive covenant with Israel underscores His commitment to creation, for the covenant promises culminate in Jesus Christ — the great seed of Abraham (Gen. 12:7; cf. Gal. 3:16) and son of David (2 Sam. 7:16; cf. Luke 1:32) — through whom the broken and fallen creation is redeemed (Rom. 8:20–22; 2 Cor. 5:17 note; Col. 1:15–20; Rev. 21:1). possessed me. The sense is probably "fathered" (text note). The figurative use of "fathered" is intended to indicate that the wisdom spoken of comes from the very essence of God; it is divine wisdom in the fullest sense. beginning of his work. "Beginning" takes us back to Gen. 1:1 and focuses on wisdom's role in creation. the first of his acts of old. The act of creation.
Wisdom's role before the creation of the universe.

The wise plan of God precedes His action. The reference to being "brought forth" suggests that wisdom is uniquely the child of God, but this is still a poetic device and does not refer to a new divine being.
Wisdom's role at the time of the creation of the universe.
The two sources of water for the ancient Israelite, rain and springs. See note on 3:20 and Gen. 7:11; 8:2.
For God's bounding of the sea, see Job 38:8–11; Ps. 104:9.
The meaning of this term is debated but the best interpretation is that it serves as an adverb meaning "constantly." Wisdom was constantly at God's side in the creative process.
Wisdom reflects the satisfaction expressed in the divine declaration that creation is very good (Gen. 1:31). 8:32–36 Wisdom's final appeal.
See note on 3:13. The blessings of God on obedience are a feature of covenant theology (Deut. 28:1–14). Here the word describes the rewards of wisdom (3:13–18).
The pupil attends at the house of the teacher, eager to learn whatever wisdom will impart.

The benefits of wisdom are equated with life itself. To be truly alive is to be rightly related to God, other people, and the created order. See notes on 3:2, 18 and notes. favor from the LORD. That is, acceptance and goodwill. The sage is not describing an alternative way of gaining acceptance other than that provided in the covenant community and sacrifices. Rather, he describes the richness of the believers' fellowship with the Lord as their lives are molded by true wisdom (12:2).
To hate wisdom is to hate life and therefore to love death.

These verses consist of two competing invitations, one from wisdom (six lines) and the other from folly (six lines), corresponding to the two competing invitations in 1:8–19. Both wisdom and folly are portrayed as women calling people to enter their houses. Wisdom invites the simple to eat of her life-giving food (vv. 1–6). Folly offers food that leads to death (vv. 13–18). In between are two matching sections of three lines each (vv. 7–9 and vv. 10–12) that contrast the scoffer and the wise. 9:1–6 Wisdom's invitation that contrasts with vv. 13–18. 9:1 her seven pillars. The significance of "seven pillars" is not clear. It may simply indicate the architectural splendor of the house. However, "seven" often symbolizes perfection or completeness and so may here represent the perfection of divine wisdom.
Probably a mixture of wine and spices (Song 8:2).
Wisdom's servants are sent out to summon any who will hear her invitation to life. from the highest places. The invitation is open and universal (Is. 52:7).
See 1:4 and note. Note the competing call of folly in v. 16. lacks sense. Lit. "lacks heart," the will to think and act rightly.
A banquet is the right setting for the food distributed by wisdom. The banquet motif is later used to portray the blessings of the redeemed (Is. 55:1, 2; Matt. 22:1–13; 26:29; Rev. 19).

These verses contrast the wise and the fool in terms of teachability. 9:7 scoffer. The scoffer has gone beyond a simple lack of judgment and has made a conscious decision for evil. gets himself abuse. The effort to correct such a person will fail and may backfire. he who reproves. This parallel phrase is synonymous in meaning with the first part of the verse.

Here the parallel structure is antithetic (i.e., the two parts are contrasted opposites). reprove a wise man. While a fool shuts out wisdom, a wise person is glad for the opportunity to shut out folly. Wisdom perceives the positive side of correction; wisdom is not defensive and easily offended but humble and responsive.
Wisdom recognizes an important principle of human nature: there is no standing still; one progresses in the direction of one's choice. Wisdom accumulates more wisdom (cf. Matt. 13:12).

These verses contrast the wise and the fool in terms of their respective outcomes. 9:10 The fear of the LORD. See 1:7 and note. Holy One. Lit. "holy ones" or "saints." The translation here is based on the parallel with "the Lord" in the previous line (cf. 30:3, where the same plural form is used).
See 3:2 and note.
That is, you will benefit (3:13–18; 4:9–13; 8:34, 35).
Folly's invitation that contrasts with vv. 1–6. 9:13loud. See 7:11, 12. seductive and knows nothing. The sensuous appeal of folly contrasts with wisdom as the teacher.
Folly counterfeits the actions of wisdom so as to appear wise (cf. v. 3).
Folly's entreaties further imitate those of wisdom (cf. v. 4).

Anything forbidden, especially illicit sex (5:3, 15; 7:16–18). bread eaten in secret. Because it is stolen or forbidden. A perversity in human nature is stirred up by prohibition and the law (Rom. 7:7–11).

Hb. rephaim, of uncertain derivation. The word is used eight times in the Bible, all in Hebrew poetry, referring to the spirits of the departed. Sheol. See 1:12; 5:5; 7:27 and notes. In Proverbs, Sheol is the fitting destination of fools, not because it is a place of torment, as hell is later described (Rev. 14:9–11), but simply because those who go there have lost the possibility of relationship with the living God. See also 2:18 and note.

These verses consist mainly of single-sentence proverbs and are intended to teach those who embrace wisdom how to live out that wisdom in all of life. The unity of the section is marked by the heading in 10:1, "The proverbs of Solomon"; the shift to "the words of the wise" in 22:17; and the fact that the section contains 375 proverbs, the numerical equivalent to Solomon's name in Hebrew. There is no evidence that these are a form of wisdom literature from a different time than the longer instructions of chs. 1–9. They are simply different forms and function in different ways. Aphorisms are often stated without qualifications; they are thus often misinterpreted as promises rather than proverbs. The wisdom of Proverbs presupposes and builds upon the special revelation of God in the Mosaic law (1:8 note). The Hebrew sages assumed that, given human intelligence and the gift of God's wisdom in His self-revelation, God's people can discern the order and relationships that make for a meaningful and productive life. The wisdom of Proverbs is the fruit of experience and reflection, stressing the need to think through and apply human knowledge and the Word of God to all affairs of life in a responsible way. As is sometimes the case in the Bible, the chapter divisions are rather arbitrary and do not aid the analysis of the text. The individual sentences can be classified according to their literary structures and themes. Chapters 10–15 consist mainly of contrasts between opposites, as indicated by the conjunction "but" introducing the second line of most of these proverbs. This common literary device uses contrasting pairs such as "righteous" vs. "wicked" and "wise" vs. "fool." Occasional grouping of sentences according to theme and form is evident in the book, a method that aids memorization but does not assist the interpretation of the mostly independent sayings. Each sentence has its own social setting and special aim. Much like folk sayings in other societies, some of the sayings have been separated from their contexts in order to provide concise, practical guidelines for living. 10:1 The proverbs of Solomon. See Introduction: Author.
See note on 8:18. In this chapter, about half the verses contain a contrast between the righteous and the wicked. delivers from death. See 2:18; 3:18 and notes.
There is a correlation between righteousness and life both in the covenant promises of God and in general life experience. The suffering of the righteous is not in view, however (cf. 1:19 note).

See 6:6–11; 13:4; 15:19; 24:30–34. A frequently used wisdom theme, poverty itself is no shame, but poverty due to laziness is. 10:5 prudent son. Family relationships and obligations are primary concerns in wisdom literature.
The unspecified blessings leave the application open to a range of situations, but, as in v. 22, the goodness of the Lord is experienced.
How the righteous person is remembered after death.

The wise person is teachable and receives the commands of wisdom (2:1; 3:1 and notes). babbling fool. Fools do not know when to be silent and listen. They lack the discipline of wisdom and promote their own downfall (v. 14 note).
The one who attempts to pervert the truth will be exposed and disciplined by God.

See 6:13 and note. babbling fool. See v. 8 and note. This phrase does not seem to correspond to the first line, either as a parallel or a contrast. The Septuagint reads, "but the one who boldly reproves makes peace."
The image is similar to "tree of life" (3:18 note). The words of the wise, like a well, are a source of life (Ezek. 47:1–12; Rev. 22:1–3).

Suggests the rejection of the good order, indeed the dissolution (cf. 1 John 3:15) of human relationships. Such hatred causes the fragmentation of society. love. Suggests seeking the best for others. Love is the greatest expression of ordered relationships. covers. In order to promote harmony of relationships, love covers over those matters that cause friction. This verse is alluded to in James 5:20 and 1 Pet. 4:8.

Those who are perceptive reveal their character in the wisdom of their words. Those who lack sense simply involve themselves in strife. The parallel suggests that foolish talk is the cause of their problems.

The wise person, though no longer the pupil, will continue to learn. See notes on 1:5 and 9:9. Only a fool claims to know everything. mouth of a fool. Note how often the fool is portrayed as a babbler (vv. 6, 8, 13, 18, 19, 31, 32). The book of James, the wisdom book of the NT, also explores this theme (James 1:26; 3:1–12). Knowing when to speak and when to keep silent is a prominent wisdom theme (11:12 note; 26:4, 5; Job 38:2; 42:1–6).

The image is that of security against the uncertainties of life, a benefit of building wealth over time (13:11). poverty of the poor. The poor do not have much defense against unexpected financial downturns in life.
The outcome or reward of righteousness is life (3:2, 18 and notes; cf. Rom. 6:23). sin. Sin or its consequence, punishment, is opposed to life.

The form of this verse, synonymous parallelism, differs from the parallel of opposites (antithetic parallelism) found in much of this chapter. Again the subject is foolish speech (lying or slander), and the one who engages in such action is either malicious or foolish (v. 14 note). Such foolishness is not lightly regarded, because this folly is actually sin (Ex. 20:16).
Here the word is parallel with "tongue." The mind, will, and character of the wicked are the source of futile words (Matt. 15:18, 19).
See vv. 11 and 17. The wisdom of the righteous has good effects upon others, but fools cannot even sustain themselves.

In the OT context, this is materi­al wealth, a result of Solomon's wisdom (1 Kin. 4:22–28; 10:4–13). Wealth is not wisdom's goal but is often wisdom's reward (v. 2). adds no sorrow. The book of Proverbs lays down the basic teachings of wisdom and leaves the exceptions for the most part to books such as Job and Ecclesiastes.
The wicked's fear of punishment. The meaning seems to be that God's righteous judgment is inevitable. desire \... granted. Cf. Ps. 37:4

The form of this proverb, synonymous parallelism, differs from the parallel of opposites (antithetic parallelism) found in much of this chapter. The comparison turns on what is common to the three pairs (see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry). The lazy person is a distasteful irritant to his employer.

LORD. See 1:7; 9:10 and notes. Harmony with God, here recognized as coming through the provisions of the covenant, means harmony with life. As in the fifth commandment, the blessings of God are seen in terms of a lengthy and fruitful life in the Promised Land (Ex. 20:12; Deut. 5:16 note). See 2:20–22; 3:2 and note.

States a basic principle of covenant theology rather than an observation on human life. The wisdom writers remind us that the source of all true knowledge and wisdom is the self-revelation of God in His creative, providential, and saving works, and especially in the Scriptures.

See v. 27. Another proverb grounded in God's covenant with Israel. The "land" is that promised to Israel, and its possession is basic to life. Possession of the land was conditional upon the response of faith to the covenant promises.
See note on v. 14.
Honesty and fair dealing are basic to covenant ethics. Reference to the Lord indicates that covenant relationships are in view.

Wisdom recognizes the importance of self-control. Arrogance and pride are easily recognized by others who will then withhold honor. with the humble is wisdom. Because humility involves the realistic appraisal of one's place in relationship to others, it promotes a wise sense of the true order of things.

The Hb. word indicates a state of moral goodness in life. Guidance in living is put in its ethical framework. A right relationship to the Lord leads to a right course in life. crookedness. This lifestyle destroys a person because God's order cannot ultimately be resisted.

The saying anticipates not merely natural and impersonal retribution in life but a personal judge and His wrath. Wealth cannot secure anyone from God's wrath (Luke 12:13–21). righteousness. See note on 8:18.
The sense is almost identical with v. 3.

An apparent reference to God's providential intervention. Proverbial sayings often state what is generally true, but not without exceptions. The suffering of the righteous (e.g., Job) shows that while a degree of order is perceptible in human experience, such order is not invariable since God is sovereign and pursues His eternal purposes. Trusting in God's goodness, even when His goodness is not immediately seen, alone addresses the problem of the righteous sufferer. See note on 10:1–22:16 and Introduction to Hebrew Poetry.
See 10:13, 14, 18 and notes. knowledge. Wisdom and knowledge as the way to life enable one to escape the ways of the godless (vv. 4, 6, 8).

A viable society must have some recognition of right and wrong, and of reward and retribution. Without descending to vindictive revenge, there is a proper rejoicing when the perpetrators of evil, corruption, and human misery are destroyed.
The corporate implications of behavior are apparent: righteous lives strengthen the community, while the wicked corrupt and overthrow it.

See note on 10:14. Gossip and derision easily destroy another's reputation, but they do not advance the reputation of the gossiper. The wise know when to keep silent (v. 13; 12:23; 13:3; 17:28; 18:2, 6–8; Eccl. 3:7).
A variation on v. 12, this verse notes that maintaining confidences strengthens relationships, but a fool's gossip destroys them (10:14 and note).
See 15:22; 20:18; 24:6. Counsel or advice was a feature of the emergence of wisdom in political life during the reign of David (2 Sam. 15:30–17:23).
See 6:1 and note.

These opposed parallel thoughts (antithetic parallelism) perhaps teach the desirability of respect over mere wealth (22:1; cf. Eccl. 7:1) and show that the book is not unaware of exceptions to its basic teaching that the righteous prosper. Alternatively, the sense may be that the gracious woman retains honor as surely as the ruthless acquire riches.
Describes one who behaves rightly toward others. There is a legitimate self-interest expressed in the command to "love your neighbor as yourself" (Lev. 19:18). What is best for others is best for us.
See 10:2, 16; cf. 1 Cor. 9:6–11. The reward may be material or spiritual. The principle is the lasting value of the rewards of righteousness.

The ways of righteousness and evil, worked out in specific detail in many sayings in the chapter, are here stated in the broadest terms. The underlying principle is explained in Deut. 30:15–20. In this verse, "righteousness" and "evil" are used broadly to include the order in the world created by God and discerned by experience (8:18 note).

The legal terminology indicates that the judgment of God, not merely natural retribution, is involved. In the same way, there is a judicial act of God involved in the escape of the righteous from judgment.
See 10:24, 25, 28–30. The contrast of the righteous and the wicked is seen in their destinies.
These verses make the general point that the generous person is blessed while miserliness leads to ruin (v. 17 note).
The generosity of v. 25 is illustrated by the community-minded merchant who puts the needs of others ahead of his own interests.

See v. 17 and note. The one who "seeks good" is either the benefactor of society who receives community approval in return or the seeker of righteousness who receives the approval of God (cf. Matt. 5:6).
See v. 4 and note. When possessions are seen to ensure life, God is excluded, as are right relations with others. The result is a life of diminished quality.

The parallel thoughts of this verse are not obvious unless we understand the first line to mean a reckless use of the family wealth that brings ruin on the household. The fool inherits nothing ("wind"; see Eccl. 5:16) and must be the servant of the one who has managed his finances well.

The metaphor is curiously mixed. The result of righteousness is life. See 3:18 and note; 13:12; 15:4. captures souls. Lit. "takes souls" or "takes lives." The usual meaning of the phrase is to kill or take away life. To accommodate this, the Septuagint renders the clause, "But the souls of the lawless are taken away before their time." The translation is uncertain.

The form of this proverb, using intensification ("how much more"), is typical of wisdom (15:11; 17:7; 19:7, 10; 21:27). the righteous is repaid. Not even the righteous escape the scrutiny of judgment. The Septuagint translation reads, "If the righteous one is scarcely saved" (as quoted in 1 Pet. 4:18). on earth. Or "in the land" (2:20–22 note). how much more the wicked. If the sins of the righteous are judged, obviously those of the ungodly are judged as well. The principle of human responsibility is clear: even the righteous must accept that they are responsible for their folly.

Lit. "loving discipline, loving knowledge." The form of this proverb, like 13:3 and 14:2, groups things that belong together without explicitly stating the relationship. These are then contrasted with their opposites. The wise person accepts correction and consequently grows wiser, but the one who cannot accept criticism goes nowhere.
See note on 8:35. LORD. See note on 1:7.
See the extended appraisal of the virtuous wife at 31:10–31.
The character of a person establishes principles for action. There is an implicit warning against trusting people on the basis of appearances.
See 1:11. Stresses the power of words for good or evil. delivers them. They will rescue the victims of the wicked.
See 10:25 and note.
The display of mastery in life wins praise. twisted mind. Suggests an inability to think straight, a mind that is more muddled than evil.

A number of proverbs have this form of direct comparison using the "better \... than" formula (15:16, 17; 16:8, 19, 32; 17:1, 12; 19:1). to be lowly. A person of no social standing or reputation. have a servant. The Septuagint renders the first half of this verse, "Better is a man in dishonor who works for himself." The meaning is either "Better humble prosperity than poverty concealed by pretense" or "Better to work without esteem than to go hungry while dreaming of affluence."

God takes account of our treatment of animals (1 Kin. 4:33). This is consistent with concern for the right order of things in the world. righteous. See note on 8:18. mercy \... is cruel. The wicked person is incapable of kindness even toward his livestock.
A variation of v. 9, this verse contrasts the benefits of honest hard work with fantasies that produce nothing. See 6:6–11; 20:4; 24:30–34; 28:19.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, but the basic contrast — the benefits of righteousness against the effects of wickedness — is plain.

The limits of human understanding must be acknowledged in the light of God's wisdom and sovereignty. The fear of the Lord (1:7 note) puts us in touch with the revealed wisdom of God. These verses are a collection of wisdom sayings mainly in the form of instructions (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). The unity is marked by the use of "words of the wise" at the beginning of the section and "sayings of the wise" at the beginning of the next section (24:23–34). There is evidence that the first part (22:17–23:11) has drawn upon the Egyptian wisdom of Amenemope (cf. 4:1–27 note). If so, these insights have been consciously appropriated under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit as admonitions that assist one in meeting covenant obligations to "trust \... in the Lord" (22:19). The author of Proverbs, like the historians of the Bible, was not prevented in principle from using existing materials in the course of writing what God inspired. All truth is God's truth, and there was a place for using existing materials insofar as it communicated truth. 22:17–21 These verses introduce the larger section by exhorting the hearer to pay attention and listen and also indicate some of the benefits of such learning. 22:17 apply your heart. –29:27 These verses are another collection of Solomonic proverbs and contain a number of couplets, sayings composed of two poetic lines, e.g., vv. 2, 3; 4, 5; 6, 7; etc. 25:1 proverbs of Solomon. See Introduction: Author and note on 1:1. Hezekiah. Wisdom was a royal enterprise in the ancient world (1:1 note). Hezekiah was king of Judah at the time of the destruction of the northern kingdom of Israel. He vigorously carried out reforms of Judah's corrupt religious practices. This introduction to a new section of the book shows that Hezekiah not only promoted a return to the law of Moses but also encouraged the wisdom movement by literary activity. copied. The development of a scribal class in Israel was dictated by the religious and administrative needs of the nation. The Hb. word used here indicates transmission and may mean committing oral tradition to writing or transcribing something already written.

Wisdom of the royal court observes an unspoken protocol. It rebukes conceit and self-seeking that overreach and lead to humiliation. It is better to start out with humility and then be exalted. Jesus adapted this instruction to speak of our place in the kingdom of God (Luke 14:7–11).
The principle can apply more widely to the need for prudence in speech that reflects on the character of others.
Do not involve others in a dispute.

Lit. "Apples of gold in settings of silver, a word fitly spoken." The importance of well-chosen words, a common wisdom theme, is highlighted by their comparison with objects of fine craftsmanship.

A similar comparison of ideas is found in v. 11. Two pieces of jewelry are set alongside a good relationship between the wise teacher's rebuke and the receptive pupil. The implied comparison says either that a rebuke is as valuable as fine gold jewelry or that a wise rebuke and a receptive ear go together like matched jewelry.
The imagery is not of an unseasonable snowfall, which would be disastrous for the harvest, but of refreshment (cf. v. 25).

–33 A collection of somewhat longer wisdom poems, including a number of numerical says. The unity of this collection is marked by the title in 30:1, "The words of Agur," and the title of the following collection in 31:1, "The words of King Lemuel." 30:1–6 These verses are a poem that contrasts the limits of human wisdom with the reliability of divine revelation. 30:1 Agur son of Jakeh. His identity is unknown, but many consider him to be a foreigner. See note on 22:17–24:22 and Introduction: Author. The oracle. It is possible that the Hb. word is a place name, "Massa" (also in 31:1), and that both Agur and Lemuel were Ishmaelites from Massa, thought to be in Arabia (Gen. 25:14). I am weary \... worn out. These lines are difficult; see text note.

This statement is not mere modesty or humility but a recognition of the mystery of the being and ways of God such as is found in Job and Ecclesiastes. The writer is acutely conscious of the bounds of human knowledge and wisdom. God is not an object for our investigation or speculation but the infinite and personal creator in whom we must trust. There may be a note of irony in the profession of ignorance here, but v. 4 indicates the meaning.

These questions express the conviction that knowledge based solely on observation of creation can never fully comprehend God. In Job 28, the same point is made, as it is in the course of God's answer to Job in 38:1–40:2.

With these words, Agur gives and assessment of God's Word within the framework of Israel's law and prophetic writings. He quotes Ps. 18:30 and echoes Deut. 4:2. The full knowledge of God comes through special revelation and is received by faith (1:7 note). 30:5 proves true. Tried and found to be utterly reliable.
A prayer that reflects the desire to learn from the kind of wisdom found in Proverbs.

The request is for a sufficiency that avoids both extremes of poverty and unnecessary riches. Jesus may have had this verse in mind when He taught His disciples to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matt. 6:11).
LORD. People who have an excess of material possessions, if they are not careful to cultivate piety, may forget their dependence on the Lord (Deut. 8:10–18; Luke 12:16–21).

The first of several numerical sayings in this collection. On the form of these numerical sayings, see notes on 6:16–19.

Interrupts the numerical sayings of this section. The eye that mocks. The contemptuous look can be as poisonous as words. The words portray the fate of the corpse that lies unburied, with special attention to the offending eye.

The second numerical saying shows four ways that cannot be understood, either because they leave no traces or because they are so easily, yet mysteriously, mastered. Some suggest that the emphasis is on the fourth way, human sexual relations, of which the other three may be metaphors.

Like v. 17, this verse interrupts the numerical sayings of this section. eats and wipes her mouth. The expression is a metaphor for sexual intercourse (7:18; 9:17) — her adultery has become as natural to her as eating.

–23 The third numerical saying of this section focuses on unbearable aspects of life. 30:21 the earth trembles. The four items in vv. 22, 23 hardly seem able to produce such dire consequences in the natural order. This is likely a figure of speech for an intolerable state of affairs.

The fourth numerical saying of this section. If this saying went no further than natural history, it would still fulfill a purpose of wisdom: the perception of order and of how things work together. Many proverbs show an interest in nature as a parable on human life (e.g., 6:6–11). The fact that wisdom is ascribed to these creatures implies some unity with human existence. The creatures are wise because they are able to surmount some serious inherent weakness and so to survive well. These gifts of wisdom, to each according to its kind, are given by the Creator of all. 30:24 small. Vulnerable, in the sense of easily hurt. wise. That is, having the skill to survive.

The fifth numerical saying of this section. The inclusion of a king with the animals suggests a human parallel with nature and the underlying coherence of all creation. The observation of rule and order in both animal and human society indicates that both are products of the same Creator's genius.
, 33 A final proverb that closes the words of Agur. 30:32 put your hand on your mouth. That is, stop talking; cease your scheming and provocation.

–9 These verses are a discrete unit that contains advice to the king. Wisdom was a royal enterprise in the ancient world; see note on 1:1. 31:1 The words of King Lemuel. While these are the "words of King Lemuel," he is obviously not the author, since he was taught them by his mother. Similarly, "the Proverbs of Solomon" (1:1) do not all necessarily come directly from Solomon, but many of them would have been taught to him and left for him to pass on. Lemuel was not an Israelite king; see note on 30:1. The nature of this section (vv. 1–9) suggests an Egyptian or perhaps a Bab­ylonian origin. Its intention is apparently vocational, the equipping of the ruler for his task. The form is similar to the instructions of chs. 1–9 (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). In this case, the teaching is given by the mother (1:8; 4:1, 3). While the father may have been the principal teacher of the children, godly women also took that role (cf. 14:1 note), and there were in Israel noteworthy wise women (2 Sam. 14:2; 20:16).
The expression may refer to a vow made in anticipation of the birth (cf. 1 Sam. 1:11).
The parallel indicates that fornication is perhaps in view.

The king's responsibilities give him no leisure to be confused by wine. strong drink. This translation may lead the reader to think of distilled beverages such as whiskey, but there is no evidence that the ancients knew the distillation process. They did understand fermentation, and ancient beer recipes have been discovered. So when paired with "wine," beer is in all likelihood the meaning.
While the king must avoid using alcohol as a means of escape from the concerns of high office, it may be given to those whose suffering is too much to bear.
The king's task is to uphold righteousness in society. In Israel, this task was viewed in the context of the covenant with the Lord (Deut. 17:14–20).

Some include vv. 10–31 in the words of King Lemuel, but they are better taken as a concluding poem for the entire book. This section, which has no title, matches the opening section, 1:8–9:18, which also has no title. In 1:8–9:18, two women vie for the heart of the young man. In 31:10–31 only one woman remains, Wisdom. This section is primarily a final portrayal of Lady Wisdom in all her beauty. Secondarily, it is a poem extolling the virtues of a wife who exemplifies the principles of wisdom, both practically and spiritually. The sequence of virtues is governed more by the demands of the acrostic (the first word in each verse beginning with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet) than by logic. Yet the overall effect is of a coherent description of a woman beautified by her virtues of practical wisdom and charity. That the household described is well-to-do underscores the rewards of wisdom. 31:10 excellent wife. The Hb. word translated "excellent" has connotations of power (see v. 17) and is used in military contexts. Ruth is the only woman given this appellation (Ruth 3:11; see Prov. 12:4). It is perhaps not coincidental that in the order of the Hebrew Bible the book of Ruth follows the book of Proverbs. who can find.
