LORD. Up to this point, the poem concentrates on practical wisdom. Now the basis of all true wisdom is emphasized, as the book of Proverbs ends where it begins: the fear of the Lord. Observation of the created order can provide some wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom. 1:20–23), but only the self-revelation of the Creator enables us to know and appreciate the God-centered meaning of reality. True wisdom is seen as the life lived in wholehearted obedience to God's revelation in His Word and world, which is "the fear of the Lord" (1:7 and note). This trust is the foundation and continuing path of wisdom for both men and women as it brings us to final perfection in Christ.

Ecclesiastes.note: This verse is the title to the book. Few books in the Bible have such titles; see Prov. 1:1. 1:1 Preacher. Hb. qohelet (Introduction: Title). The text emphasizes the Preacher's function as gatherer of the covenant community (Ex. 35:1) or as composer of proverbs (Eccl. 12:9) for the purpose of teaching. The Preacher addresses God's people, not unbelievers. son of David. See Introduction: Author.

This verse states the theme of the book. Few books in the Bible have such an explicit statement of the book's theme; see Prov. 1:7; Luke 1:1–4; John 20:30, 31. 1:2 Vanity. The Hb. word translated "vanity," which occurs thirty-eight times in Ecclesiastes, means "breath," "vapor," or "fleeting" and in the context of the book refers to that which is frustrating, temporary or perplexing (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). "Vanity of vanities" is a Hebrew way of expressing the superlative. The Preacher is here clearly using hyperbole to encourage the reader to face the vanity of life; elsewhere in the book, he commends finding satisfaction, the opposite of frustration in life, and presumes that the reader will understand and not be perplexed by his message. All. This word is qualified by the phrase "under the sun" (v. 3) and means everything people experience with their senses (v. 8).

These verses focus the reader's attention on the frustrations of life and provide the first explanation of the meaning of "vanity." Despite our engaging in all of life's activity, we seem to get nowhere in the end. Although there may be some satisfaction in accomplishments, death can seem to make them meaningless because death comes to all, and our enjoyment of them seems to end at death. Only when one is rightly oriented to the Creator do we understand the true significance of our earthly lives (12:13, 14). 1:3 gain. The idea that life's labor is unprofitable, presented here as a rhetorical question, is stated directly in 2:11. under the sun. This phrase, which occurs twenty-six times in Ecclesiastes, is synonymous with "under heaven" and "on earth" and refers to life as adversely affected by the fall (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). Paul's equivalent is "the present evil age" (Gal. 1:4). From the perspective of "under the sun," life is often frustrating and perplexing. By contrast, from the perspective of the resurrection, life's labor is not in vain (John 6:27–29; 1 Cor. 15:58).
People are constantly starting over (like the sun in v. 5), while by contrast, the earth (to which every person returns) abides.

The Hb. word (shoep) translated here as "hastens" means "to pant" (text note). The picture is that of the sun panting as it circles the earth, only to repeat the process day after day — a picture of exhausting, frustrating activity.
An image that communicates the same idea as the Preacher's recurrent refrain "striving after wind," both of which speak of the frustrations of life.
People's experiences often fail to fill or satisfy them, just as waters never fill the sea; hence, life can be frustrating.
The lack of satisfaction articulates the theme of frustration — always wanting more and never having enough.

Cultural endeavors cannot reverse the futile and frustrating process of repeating what has already been done, because all die and their works are forgotten by humanity. under the sun. See note on 1:3. The Preacher reminds the reader that this present life is the sphere of frustration.
No remembrance is a curse (Ps. 83:4; Jer. 11:19), and on this frustrating note the first section comes to a close.

In this first half of the Preacher's monologue or autobiography, he rehearses his search for escape from the vanity of life. 1:12 –18 Continuing the theme of life's frustrations and introducing the related theme of life's perplexities, these verses show how the Preacher began his search for escape. 1:12 king \... in Jerusalem. See Introduction: Author. If anyone could find satisfaction and meaning in life, a king could. But not even a king can escape the vanity, the fleeting and perplexing nature of life.

Even wisdom, as wonderful and beneficial as it is, cannot totally protect people from the vanity of life (8:17). Life is at times frustrating and perplexing even for the wise. unhappy business. Human existence includes divinely imposed burdens (Gen. 3:16–19; Rom. 8:22, 23). Jesus makes them bearable (Matt. 11:28–30). God. Hb. Elohim. This term for God focuses on His transcendence and fits with the universal scope and application of the book's teaching (12:13, 14). God's personal covenant name (Hb. Yahweh, conventionally rendered "Lord") is not used in this book. The forty occurrences of "God" in the book underscore the fact that God is very much involved in life, even in its apparent vanity. 1:13, 14 under heaven \... under the sun. See note on 1:3. God is active in this world as it has been adversely affected by the fall, but God is not subject to the vanity of life, as He is "in heaven" (5:2), not "under heaven."
The failure to straighten is frustrating, and the failure to count is perplexing.

Since only David ruled over Jerusalem before Solomon, many have questioned the Solomonic authorship of Ecclesiastes (Introduction: Author). If Solomon is indeed the author, this phrase would refer to the pre-Israelite kings of Jerusalem (e.g., Adoni-zedek; Josh. 10:1). In any case, the point being made is that even the Preacher in his lofty position could not figure out life.
See note on 1:14.

Ironically, wisdom can at times add to the frustration of life. The more one knows, the worse off one can be; ignorance can be bliss. If even the king with all his resources could not escape the vanity of life, ordinary folk should not be surprised if they cannot escape either.

See Prov. 31:4, 5.
The implied reference is to a king and his kingdom. Such sloth and indolence could well characterize the young king of v. 16.

The Preacher commends joy in life. Such laughter and gladness could well characterize life under the nobility of v. 18. everything. Means that money is needed for both food and wine, or that money provides for all of life's basic needs (cf. 7:12).
A metaphor for a spy or an informer.

These verses teach the benefits and uncertainty of human industry. 11:1 bread upon the waters. Possibly a reference to grain trade by sea or to Egyptian agricultural practice in which seed is placed in the Nile River at its low point and then takes root and grows when the river overflows its banks.
An admonition to spread the risks one takes (v. 6). you know not. Uncertainty is a reason for diversity in financial management. See v. 6.
The reality of uncertainty is not an excuse for laziness.
Here again is an affirmation of God's incomprehensible, secret counsel (8:17 note).
See notes on 3:11; 6:12.

These verses teach that youthful life is to be lived to the fullest and governed by discretion. This is because youth is followed by old age, and this present life will be followed by an inevitable meeting with God (12:7). 11:7 Light is sweet. For the young in particular; cf. 12:1, 2.
The joys of the present life should be held loosely, in the awareness that such joy is temporary. vanity. See note on 1:2.

The Preacher encourages young people to live life to the fullest but does not encourage mindless self-indulgence; he gives a sober warning that God will bring everything into judgment (12:14; Matt. 12:36).
To the extent that God enables them, young people should live life to the fullest. vanity. See note on 1:2.

The Preacher's comments on aging and death, using the extended metaphor of a house that is falling down. He contrasts the deterioration of the house with the permanence of nature. It is best to take the metaphors here for their overall effect rather than speculate on the meaning of each individual figure. As the following notes indicate, some associations are clearer than others. 12:1 Remember. Living life to the fullest (11:7–10) includes living in relation to the Creator. evil days. If God is forgotten in youth, pleasure will be unknown in later years.
The phrases here probably refer to parts of the body as members of a household.
Their white color is associated with the hair of the aged. eternal home. Refers not just to the grave but also to the presence of one's Creator and Judge (v. 7).
Describes a lamp broken in a fall that was caused by a break in a silver chain. Broken vessels and severed cords suggest the frailty that comes with aging.
Human existence continues beyond death.

These verses form the epilogue of the book. Verse 8 repeats 1:2 and signals the beginning of the conclusion, as does the return of references to the Preacher in the third person. "Fear God and keep his commandments" (v. 13) is the moral compass in all of life's perplexities, frustrations, joys, and satisfactions. 12:8 Vanity. See note on 1:2. A final reiteration of the Preacher's refrain.
In addition to being wise, the Preacher was an excellent teacher, student, and scholar.
The Preacher was concerned not only with truth but also with beauty in communicating the truth.
The words of Ecclesiastes are God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16).

To fear God is the logical conclusion drawn from the body of the book; the Preacher lays the basis for this conclusion at numerous points (3:14; 5:7; 8:12). Loyal submission to the rule of God is the central and summary admonition of the Bible's Wisdom Literature (Job 28:28; Prov. 1:7; 9:10). See Introduction to the Wisdom Literature. the whole duty of man. Perhaps better translated as "the duty of everyone." For the same Hebrew expression translated "everyone," see 3:13; 5:19.
God's judgment of thoughts and deeds is a dominant theme throughout the book (3:17; 8:12, 13; 11:9; 2 Cor. 5:10).

Song Of Solomon.note: See Introduction: Title; Author.

Third-person expressions in 1:2, 4 ("Let him kiss me \... The king has brought me") open and close these verses, which are otherwise in the second person ("your love \... your name"); this shifting of persons is common in Hebrew and prominent in the Song. Note the sensuous nature of the language, which includes touch, taste, and smell.
The oil is the fragrant oil just mentioned, and having been poured out, would have filled the room with its aroma.

This is the first of five occurrences of the word "king" (1:4, 12; 3:9, 11; 7:5). Here in v. 4, there are two possibilities for the meaning: either the "king" is just that, a king, who has tried to win the young woman's affections, or he is her lover, whom she romantically fantasizes to be her king. The latter interpretation is to be preferred (Introduction: Author). chambers. The word "chambers" here as elsewhere refers to the bedroom, the most intimate of rooms. We will exult and rejoice in you. We meet for the first time the female companions of the young woman. They are referred to as the "daughters of Jerusalem" (1:5), "daughters of Zion" (3:11), and "young women" (6:9). Here they serve to confirm the young woman's appraisal of her beloved (see v. 2).

A self-description wherein the young woman expresses displeasure with her deeply tanned skin, perhaps because it makes her appear to be an ordinary laborer. 1:5 tents of Kedar. Bedouin tribes that live on the edge of the desert make their tents of dark goat hair, as was apparently the case with the tribe of Kedar. Kedar was seen as an exotic land (Jer. 2:10; 49:28).

The young woman provocatively inquires as to where she can meet the man at noon (v. 7); then the man indirectly but suggestively provides her direction. 1:7 like one who veils herself. "Veils" has the same negative connotations here as it does in Gen. 38:14, 15. The young woman does not want to be mistaken for a prostitute.

The first descriptive admiration of the young woman by the man. 1:9 a mare among Pharaoh's chariots. Egyptian chariots were drawn by stallions. An ancient military strategy was to insert a mare into the mix in the hopes of distracting and confusing the stallions. The man uses the image to express his crazed passion for the young woman.

In v. 4, the "daughters of Jerusalem" echo the young woman's praise of her lover; here they respond similarly to his praise of her. The plural subject "we" goes against taking this verse as a speech of the young woman's lover using courtly language, since "we" is consistently used by various groups at other points in the book (6:1, 13; 8:8).

The young woman's lover is again presented as a king, as indicated by the following verse. on his couch. Lit. "in his surroundings." The surroundings may not be a literal couch but may refer to the outdoors (see, e.g., 1:16, 17; 6:2; 7:11–13).

A gum resin native to South Arabia; it is exotic and valuable. Mixed with olive oil, myrrh was used as an expensive perfume. between my breasts. The sachet between the breasts is an image of intimacy.

Henna bushes produce a substance that is applied to the body as an ointment or perfume. Engedi. This lush oasis is halfway down the western shore of the Dead Sea and contributes to the lush images of intimacy, and Engedi's location between the hills mirrors the sachet between the breasts.

These verses express mutual admiration, as is clear from the repetition of "Behold, you are beautiful." 1:15 your eyes are doves. Doves occur in the ancient Near East as a symbol of lovemaking or seduction. Here they evoke the young woman's seductive power (see also 4:1). The young woman uses the same image in 5:12 (cf. also 6:9).
The Hb. word translated "green" means verdant, flourishing, or luxuriant, and it contributes to the lush images of intimacy.
The cedar and pine trees provide the privacy for intimacy that would be provided by a literal house.

The Hebrew indicates a plant of the bulb family, like a crocus or daffodil (text note). See Is. 35:1, 2. Sharon. This plain extends south from Mount Carmel along the Mediterranean coast. Here the young woman modestly compares herself to familiar wildflowers.
In these verses, both the young man and the young woman praise each other as standouts among their peers.

Lit. "house of wine" (text note). The setting is outdoors (1:12 note). The lover's "house" to this point has been the forest (1:16, 17). Now they move to a different "house," namely, the young man's vineyard, his "house" of wine. The expression continues the royal imagery from 1:4, 12 (the shepherd is a king) and the comparison of love and wine from 1:2. his banner. An emblem typically used to mark out one tribe from another (Num. 2:3, 10, 18, 25). Banners were also used to muster troops for battle. It has been suggested that the word is used here for something like a sign for an inn. The young man is unabashedly advertising his love for the young woman.

Raisins or raisin cakes are associated elsewhere in the OT with religious rites, sometimes even in a pagan context (2 Sam. 6:19; Hos. 3:1), which has led some commentators to suppose that the Song originated as the script of a pagan fertility rite involving ritual sex (cf. Hos. 4:11–14). But the lovemaking in the Song has no obvious cultic dimension. The raisins here, like the apples, are simple aphrodisiacs. The young woman calls for raisins and apples to renew her vigor.
For the role of this verse in the structure of the book, see Introduction: Literary Features.

For comments on this refrain, see Introduction: Literary Features. Here the refrain is a reminder that the lovemaking should await the right time with the right person. The broader context of Scripture indicates that the right time is marriage, and the right person is one's spouse.

The image of the shepherd lover as a gazelle or a young stag on the hills introduces and concludes these verses, which describe another outdoor rendezvous between the two lovers (see 8:14). 2:8 leaping. Reflects his joy and excitement to see her. over the mountains. The mountains and hills are symbolic of the obstacles that must be surmounted so the lovers can be together.
Known for its speed and agility, the gazelle serves well as an image for the woman's excitement as she longs for her lover to come to her.
Spring is a time of fertility, and thus the images of spring in these verses contribute to the picture of an intimate rendezvous.
The switch to the feminine form of the possessive pronoun "your" suggests that vv. 14, 15 should be assigned to the shepherd.

The foxes are the one negative element in the otherwise idyllic spring setting of vv. 10–15, and they perhaps represent aggressive suitors who threaten the relationship of the young woman and her beloved. They could also represent her brothers. The imperative with no specific subject is like a passive ("May the foxes be caught"), and the whole verse is a wish by the lovers that nothing should be allowed to interfere with their lovemaking.
In view of the context, this is most likely a metaphor for lovemaking. See notes on 2:15; 6:2.

Traditionally, these lines have been taken with what follows, but they seem to make better sense when read with v. 16. The lovers have been together through the night, and when day breaks they must part. The young man's return to the hills marks the end of the unit that opened in v. 8 (2:8–17 note). Alternatively, she may have declined his invitation to sexual love that is offered too soon.

This seek-and-find story has a more ominous counterpart in 5:2–8. 3:1 On my bed by night I sought \... found him not. The young woman is not with her lover but alone on her bed, and the verb "sought," repeated twice, underscores her intense desire to be with him, while the fact that she "found him not" indicates at least some level of tension or frustration within her.
The young woman is not passive but boldly takes the initiative to go out and find her lover.
The presence of watchmen patrolling the city streets indicates that it is night, and their role is more positive here than in 5:7.

The passionate search is over, he is in her arms, and she will not let him go. my mother's house \... chamber. Again the young woman takes the initiative, bringing her lover to the "chamber" of her mother, and since the young woman was conceived in this chamber, it is obviously a place of sexual intimacy.
This second occurrence of the refrain, like the first one (2:7), follows a scene of lovemaking and is another reminder that lovemaking should await the right time with the right person.

This is the fourth time that the young woman has pictured her lover as a king (1:4, 12; 2:4). These verses celebrate the joy of the regal wedding day (v. 11). Given that the Song is not a drama with a tight plot and that sexual intimacy has already taken place several times, we are not to interpret these verses as describing a wedding that is chronologically sequential to the previous material. Dischronologization (not ordering events chronologically) is common in both Hebrew prose and poetry.

Solomon's men formed a bodyguard for protection from marauders, especially as weddings were celebrated at nightfall. But the verse has a double reference. There is also the "night" introduced in 3:1, which was spoiled by the young woman's own "terror by night." These fears are banished, at least for a time, by the splendid vision of Solomon with his fighting men.

An alternative name for Jerusalem (see 1:5 for "daughters of Jerusalem"). the crown. This is not the king's crown but the sort of garland worn by brides and grooms at ancient weddings. The custom was abandoned by Jews in their sorrow caused by the tragic war with Rome and the loss of Jerusalem (A.D. 70). A rabbinic proverb states that "a bridegroom resembles a king." his mother. The mother plays a prominent role in the Song (1:6; 3:4; 6:9; 8:1, 2, 5). There is no reference to a father, which is in keeping with what we find in other love poetry in the ancient Near East. the day of his wedding. The real Solomon had many weddings (1 Kin. 11:3). The one day in view here may be a romantic ideal or a fond remembrance.

In these verses, the young man admires the beauty of the young woman (see "beautiful" in v. 1 and v. 7). 4:1 beautiful \... beautiful. The repetition indicates a superlative beauty. Your eyes are doves. In the ancient Near East, doves were a symbol of lovemaking or seduction. Here they evoke the young woman's seductive power (see also 1:15). The young woman uses the same image in 5:12. behind your veil. The veil not only conceals but also reveals and thus intensifies the passion. Gilead. A high plateau east of the Jordan River, compared for its beauty to the Lebanon mountains (Jer. 22:6; Zech. 10:10) and known as a place of fertility (Num. 32:1; Jer. 8:22; 46:11).

The location of this tower is unknown. It is not the present-day tower of David just inside the Jaffa gate of Jerusalem, since that tower is no older than the time of Herod the Great. The young woman's neck is adorned with jewelry as the famous tower was adorned with shields.
The young man's freedom to mention the young woman's breasts shows the great intimacy of their relationship.

The time when the lovers must part is approaching (2:17 note). mountain of myrrh \... hill of frankincense. Frankincense, like myrrh, was an imported aromatic spice (cf. Matt. 2:11). After the literal mention of the young woman's breasts in v. 5, the "mountain" and "hill" could be a poetic reference to the same.

–5:1 These verses (united by the sixfold use of "bride," the underlying Hebrew word of which is used only here in the Song) begin with the young man imploring the young woman to come to him (v. 8) and end with their union (4:16b–5:1). 4:8 Lebanon \... Amana \... Senir \... Hermon. All these sites are in the remote north of Palestine. We are not meant to think of the young woman as living on the summit of Mount Hermon. Rather, the place names are symbols of the inaccessibility that the wooing is meant to overcome. my bride. The word is used six times in this section (vv. 8, 9, 10, 11, 12; 5:1) and nowhere else in the Song, and thus serves to unite these verses.
In ancient Near Eastern languages, "sister" was commonly used by lovers as a term of endearment and affection. It expressed a closeness between people who were not members of the same family.
The compliment of 1:2 is returned, and it reflects reciprocity in love and affection.
These two terms are used together more than forty times in the OT, most commonly of the Land of Promise as great blessing.

Images of the young woman's sexuality and likely her virginity, both of which seem inaccessible to her beloved (v. 15). spring \... fountain. Having mentioned her breasts (v. 5), the young man now makes poetic reference to the most intimate area of the young woman's body.
The image of the enclosed garden is further developed (v. 12 note). In context, "shoots" seems to allude to the young woman's thighs.

This image expresses that the young man would like his lover no longer to be a "garden locked" or "spring locked" (v. 12 and note). This is an implicit invitation to sexual union as the consummation of their marriage.
The young woman unlocks her "garden" to her beloved bridegroom (v. 12 note). Consummation in the Song comes in the context of marriage.

The young man immediately accepts his beloved's invitation. Eat \... drunk with love. The speakers are not specified, but the ESV's "Others" is in all likelihood correct. The chorus of young women joins in to celebrate the beauty of love.

These verses give a different perspective on love and sex than that found in the preceding verses. Here the focus is on risk and disappointment (see Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). The final verse is the third repetition of the key structuring phrase "I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem" and brings the third major section of the Song to a conclusion. 5:2 I slept \... A sound. Whether the young woman was deeply asleep and dreaming or sleeping lightly is less relevant than the fact that the sound of her beloved knocking awakened her. Open to me. These verses are full of double entendre. "Open to me" is a request not only for entrance into the room but also for sexual union.
The young woman begins to contemplate the risk involved in opening herself to her beloved.
The young woman is aroused by her beloved's actions.

Having contemplated the risk involved in the relationship, the young woman decides to run the risk. 5:5 liquid myrrh. Myrrh in its virgin, liquid state, exactly as it flows from the tree, is a rare and precious substance (cf. Ex. 30:23). It is not clear from the Hebrew whether the girl has applied it liberally to herself before going to the door, or whether her lover has left it on the door latch as a token of his love. The repetition of the exact expression in v. 13 marginally favors the latter.
they beat me. Rather than describing physical abuse, these verses are better understood as describing the young woman's mental and emotional pain.

This third occurrence of the refrain like the first two (2:7; 3:5) follows a scene of disappointment and frustration. This refrain is slightly different from the others in that it expresses the depth of desire the young woman has for her beloved despite her disappointment and frustration. Implicitly, it functions like the other refrains to teach the young women that love and sex should await the right time with the right person (i.e., with one's spouse).

These verses are a sequel to the previous verses, as indicated by the repetition of language in 5:6 ("beloved" and "sought") and 6:1 ("beloved" and "seek"). The young women want to join the young woman in the search for the young man.
Used of Esau (Gen. 25:25, 30) and David (1 Sam. 16:12; 17:42) as men of the outdoors.

The compliment of 1:15 and 4:1 is returned (1:15 note). The contrast with "locks \... black as a raven" in the previous line is striking. Her description suggests that her beloved displays both strength and gentleness. bathed in milk. Probably refers to the whites of the eyes. The description of the eyes in this verse is an example of mixed metaphor.
Lit. "dripping flowing myrrh." See note on v. 5.
The exact stone cannot be determined. In Ex. 28:20, the same type of stone is set in gold on the breastpiece worn by the high priest.
The relationship between man and woman in the Song is broader than lovemaking, although that is central to it. It involves companionship as well.
This language echoes 5:6 and shows the willingness of the women to aid the young woman in her search for the young man.
The young woman reveals that she knows where her lover has gone: "to his garden" where "he grazes among the lilies," language used previously for sexual intimacy (2:16).

These verses express admiration for the young woman by her beloved. Note how the boundaries are marked by the repetition of "banners," a word that in the Song occurs only here and in 2:4. 6:4 Tirzah. This city, six miles (9.7 km) northeast of Shechem in central Palestine, is in a setting of great natural beauty. It was the capital of the breakaway northern kingdom for approximately fifty years after Solomon's death. It continued to be a place of political intrigue until it was destroyed in the seventh century B.C. (1 Kin. 14:17; 15:21; 16:8–18; 2 Kin. 15:14–16). The positive reference to Tirzah here, particularly in parallel with Jerusalem, may support the traditional view that the Song originated in the time of Solomon, before hostility between the northern and southern tribes led to the division into two separate kingdoms, but see Introduction: Date and Occasion.
See note on 4:1.

The two references to queens and concubines indicate that vv. 8 and 9 belong together. In her beloved's eyes, the girl is more beautiful than all the women of Solomon's harem (8:11, 12 and notes). 6:8 sixty \... eighty. At its peak, Solomon's har­em contained many more wives and concubines (1 Kin. 11:3), and there is already a suggestion of its future growth in the expression "virgins without number." concubines. A concubine was not an illicit or casual partner but a wife of secondary status (Gen. 25:6; 36:12; Judg. 20:4).

The young woman is praised here. dawn \... moon \... sun. The young woman is described in language reminiscent of an ancient Near Eastern goddess. awesome as an army with banners. The phrase is an exact repetition of the last line of v. 4. The praise given here is that of the girl's beloved and concludes the unit (vv. 4–10).

These two verses are in all likelihood a short, independent poem in which the young woman recalls an experience of intimacy with her beloved. 6:11 The word translated "orchard" is the feminine form of the same word elsewhere translated "garden" (e.g., 5:1). The orchard, like the garden, is a private place for intimacy.

The core of these verses (7:1–9a) is another instance of the young man's admiration of the young woman. This core is surrounded by an introductory exchange between a group of men and the young man (6:13) and the young woman's response to her beloved's admiration (7:9b–10). 6:13 Return. The speakers are most likely male, as indicated by the response of the young woman, "Why should you \[masculine plural\] look \... ?" They are possibly the watchmen of 5:7 from whom the young woman presumably fled earlier. Shulammite. The designation probably refers to the young woman's hometown (Shunem) with a variant spelling of "Shunammite" (1 Kin. 1:3, 15; 2:17–22). The interchange of l and n in Semitic languages is well attested. two armies. Or Mahanaim (text note). Mahanaim is the name of a town east of the Jordan River (Gen. 32:2). The nature of the "dance before two armies/Mahanaim" is unknown.
"Noble" here is the same word found in 6:12. There, the young woman speaks of herself as noble; here, her beloved speaks of her as such. In everyday life, she is a country maiden (1:5, 6).

This city east of the Jordan River opposite Jerusalem was captured by the Israelites in the time of Moses (Num. 21:25, 26). Excavations have revealed large reservoirs near the city, perhaps the pools mentioned here. gate of Bath-rabbim. Bath-rabbim ("daughter of many") is probably the name of the gate, possibly one of the gates of Heshbon. tower of Lebanon. The identity of this tower is not known. The great height suggested by "looks toward" or "looks over" Damascus has led some to take it as referring to the Lebanon mountains (cf. v. 5).

There are two places with this name in the OT. One is in the relatively arid south, in the hills west of the Dead Sea (1 Sam. 15:12). The other is the famous mountain where Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal (1 Kin. 18), in the lush north. The latter is on the Mediterranean coast, due west of the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee), and is probably the Carmel in view here in this favorable comparison. a king. The young man fancies himself a king enchanted by the beauty of his princess (v. 1; cf. 1:4, 12; 6:12).
Images of lovemaking (v. 7; cf. 5:1).
Here, similarly to 4:16, the woman responds to her beloved's wooing with a willingness to yield to his overture.

–13 In these verses, the woman takes the initiative and offers to give her love to her beloved. 7:11 Come. The young woman invites her beloved to the sexual encounter. fields. The "fields" are once again the location of intimacy (6:2, 3).
The young woman yields not out of compulsion but out of will and desire.

The mandrake plant has purple flowers and an orange, tomato-like fruit, and residents of the ancient Near East believed it to be an aphrodisiac (Gen. 30:14–16). our doors are all choice fruits. The doors are metaphorical for the meeting place of the lovers outdoors (v. 12). For a similar mixing of plants and architectural terms, see 1:17.

These verses express the intense desire of the young woman for her beloved. 8:1like a brother. The key word is "like." She does not, of course, wish that her lover were actually her brother but only that she would have the freedom to kiss him in public and go with him anywhere without attracting comment.
See note on 3:4. she who used to teach me. The daughter learned about marriage and its attendant joys from her mother, who taught her about the marriage covenant.

This verse is identical to 2:6 and precedes the last occurrence of the refrain (Introduction: Literary Features), which serves to remind the young women that the lovemaking should await the right time with the right person.

These verses continue the expression of the woman's intense desire for her beloved, begun in vv. 1–4. 8:5 Who is that coming up from the wilderness. This clause is an exact repetition of 3:6, but there it is used in reference to the arrival of the young man. Here it is used in reference to the arrival of the young woman. The speakers may be the chorus of young women. leaning on her beloved. This simple statement captures an intimate and typical pose of lovers. apple tree. Presumably this does not refer to any particular apple tree but evokes the outdoor image associated with sexual intimacy throughout the book. I awakened you. That is, "began to woo you" or, better, "aroused you." The speaker is the young woman, and she is addressing her beloved. was in labor. The verb translated "was in labor" could be translated "conceived." The sequence would then be natural: aroused, conceived, bore. See Ps. 7:14, where this verb is translated "conceived" and is followed by "pregnant" and then "gives birth." This is the only verse in the Song where the reproductive results of sex are in view; elsewhere, the focus is on physical (and emotional) pleasure.

A signet made of metal or stone and worn on a necklace over the heart or on an armband (Gen. 38:18). heart \... arm. This pair signifies the entire person. strong as death. Love is as strong as the most powerful, negative human experience. In vv. 6, 7, the emotional side of love comes to clear expression, whereas the emphasis throughout the book is on the physical side. jealousy. In parallel with "love," jealousy here is not a vice but a virtue that seeks to protect the relationship, like the jealousy of God (Ex. 20:5; Ezek. 39:25; John 2:17). Like God's love, the love being celebrated tolerates no rivals.

The young woman has encountered numerous obstacles to love along the way (e.g., 2:8; 4:8), but her love has enabled her to surmount them all. wealth. Wealth without love is of little value (Prov. 15:17; 19:22), and true love cannot be purchased.

An exchange between the young woman and her protective brothers. 8:8 no breasts. Probably not to be taken literally but to be read as a metaphor for the brothers' perception of their sister as being too young for marriage. spoken for. I.e., asked for as a prospective bride.
Metaphors for virginity and promiscuity. The brothers will honor the sister if she is a virgin but will rein her in if she is promiscuous.

The young woman allays the fears of her brothers by confirming her virginity. towers. The young woman counters her brothers' perception that she is too young for marriage. Rather than having "no breasts" (v. 8), her breasts are "like towers." peace. The Hb. shalom here has the sense of well-being. By implication, the Song points to the marriage relationship as a place where such fulfillment is found. This points finally to Christ, for the ups and downs of marriage cause us to look for the one Spouse who fully satisfies our deepest need for love.

These verses, spoken by the young woman, are difficult, but the sense seems to be that her love cannot be purchased. 8:11a vineyard at Baal-hamon. Some interpreters have regarded this vineyard as a metaphor for Solomon's harem, but the designation of a specific place suggests otherwise. The location of Baal-hamon is unknown, as is the reason for the reference, other than as a place of intimacy. for its fruit. The keepers would pay Solomon a thousand pieces of silver for selling the fruit.

These verses conclude the book with one final articulation of mutual desire. 8:13 you who dwell. The Hebrew makes clear that "you who dwell" refers to the young woman. companions. Perhaps the young women and the brothers. let me hear it. The young man is eager to be alone with his beloved.

Isaiah.note: Refers to the entire book of Isaiah. "Vision" means that the book is a revelation from God. Isaiah. "The Lord saves." kings of Judah. See Introduction: Date and Occasion. Isaiah's prophetic career spanned at least the period from 740 B.C. (the year King Uzziah died) until 681 B.C., the death of Sennacherib.

Chapters 1, 3, and 5 depict a covenant lawsuit scene. Here an abbreviated historical prologue recalls the Lord's good purposes, and an indictment follows. The whole of creation will bear witness against Israel that the Lord had warned them they would be judged if they broke their covenant with Him (Deut. 30:19; 32:1). LORD. The Hb. name "Yahweh" is usually represented in English translations as "Lord," using small capitals. This name signifies the personal revelation of God to Israel and His solemn promise to be their God (Ex. 3:15). Children. They were the Lord's children by creation, by election, and by covenant (45:11; 49:7; 64:8; Deut. 32:6, 18; Mal. 2:10). The background for this is Moses's writing in Deut. 32:1–9. rebelled. Rebellion is willful transgression against the Lord's sovereign and gracious rule (1:28; 43:27; 48:8; 59:13). Rebellious children could be subject to the death penalty (see Deut. 21:18–21).
Even unintelligent domestic animals know where their food comes from. Not so Judah.

An emphatic particle used in contexts of lament (1:4), but more often in threats ("woe"; cf. 3:9, 11; 5:11, 18, 20, 21). The staccato lament decries the folly and evil of God's children. sinful nation. At the exodus, Israel had been called to be a holy nation (Ex. 19:6). Rather than being "my people," they are a people laden with iniquity. Rather than being God's children, they are children who deal corruptly. the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah's special designation for the Lord calls attention to His unique and awe-inspiring splendor. The phrase occurs twenty-six times in Isaiah (e.g., 5:19, 24; 41:14, 16, 20; 60:9, 14). See also "the Holy One of Jacob" (29:23), "Holy One" (10:17; 40:25), and "your Holy One" (43:15).

Further preaching only hardens impenitent sinners. Sin is at its root irrational. 1:5, 6 struck \... wounds. The people were unable to recover from God's chastisement. The imagery of the suffering nation has its counterpart in the suffering of God's Servant (53:4, 5), who endured the judgment of God in His own body vicariously (that is, as a substitute for others). There are explicit verbal connections between the two passages.

A personification of Jerusalem. Zion was the hill that David captured (2 Sam. 5:7), but this Hb. idiom often stands for all of Jerusalem or even all of Judah and Israel. booth. A temporary shelter used by watchmen during harvest to prevent valuable crops from being stolen or damaged by marauding animals. See note on 4:6.

of hosts.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} A designation for God that presents Him as a divine warrior (13:4; 30:27; 40:10; 42:13, 25; 59:17; 66:15, 16), the commander over all troops whether in heaven or on earth. Ultimately, Israel's survival is not due to the enemy's weakness, but to God's sovereign power. a few survivors. The Lord will not overturn His promise. Even in the midst of judgment He will preserve a remnant. Paul quotes this verse in Rom. 9:29, presenting the idea of a remnant taken out of a larger group as an expression of the electing grace of God. In Rom. 9:27, Paul quotes from Isaiah's teaching about the remnant at 10:20–23. See also Is. 4:3; 7:3 and note; 11:11, 12, 16; 28:5; 37:31, 32; 46:3. Sodom \... Gomorrah. God's people have become like the wicked inhabitants of Canaan, whose cities were destroyed (1:10; Gen. 18:20, 21; 19:24, 25). The fate of Sodom and Gomorrah typifies the terrible judgment of God on the kingdoms of this world (3:9; 13:19; Luke 17:28, 29; 2 Pet. 2:6–10; Jude 7; Rev. 11:8). Apart from Lot and his daughters, no one survived this judgment.

The central visible observances of OT religion. Although God ordered them to be performed, they were of no value without obedience from the heart (vv. 16, 17; 1 Sam. 15:22, 23; Ps. 51:16, 17; Mic. 6:6–8; Matt. 23:23). do not delight. The Lord's distaste for sacrifices offered by those who do evil (v. 16) is expressed with increasing sharpness: "I cannot endure" (v. 13); "my soul hates" (v. 14).
Although these festivals were required by God's law, when performed merely as a ritual, they became an abomination to the Lord.

When the people of the ancient Near East prayed, they often spread out their hands as a gesture of petition. Yet in Judah's case these same hands were stained with innocent blood: the people praying were implicated in the wider sins of their society. Their behavior hindered their prayers (cf. 1 P et. 3:7). They needed to wash themselves before they could come to a Holy God in prayer.
Concern for the needy is a practical demonstration of true godliness (v. 23; 58:7; Ps. 9:18 note; Jer. 22:16; James 1:27).

When a declaration of judgment is expected, the Lord issues a gracious offer of mediation. The language has legal overtones of attempting to resolve a dispute. scarlet. Depicts hands "full of blood" (v. 15). white as snow. God can take away the stain of sin without compromising His righteousness because Jesus Christ bore God's punishment for sinners (53:4–6; Rom. 3:21–26).
God's Word is a two-edged sword: eternal life (v. 19) or eternal death (v. 20; 66:24).

Godliness is demonstrated by perseverance, stability, and consistency in doing God's will. Through the purifying process, the Lord will renew a remnant who will again constitute a "faithful city" (v. 26), for He is faithful (49:7; 55:3). whore. The metaphor shifts from unfaithful children to an unfaithful wife. A whore in religion is an idolater, someone who has forsaken God to serve idols (Jer. 2:20; 3:1; Ezek. 16:23–30; Hos. 2:2; 3:1). The sins listed (vv. 21–23) are evidence that God's people have forsaken Him. justice \... Righteousness. Justice means right relations between people. It is violated by murder, rebellion, stealing, and bribery (vv. 21–23). True justice will defend the cause of orphans and widows as much as the cause of those who can pay bribes and give rewards. The enemies of justice may even pass laws that facilitate their wrongdoing (10:1). These are specific examples of the "scarlet sins" mentioned in v.18. Despite all such obstacles, God promises to restore righteousness to the earth (v. 26; 32:1; 33:5, 6; 42:1–4).
Represent Jerusalem's unjust rulers (v. 23). Silver contaminated with dross and watered-down wine are symbols of spiritual pollution and impurity.
God's law strongly condemns bribery, which fosters injustice and discrimination (5:23; cf. Ex. 23:8; Deut. 16:19).

of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The lengthy and exalted title focuses on the Lord's power. God, the Sovereign, will restore justice by removing His enemies, the unrighteous leaders of Jerusalem. It is striking that the Lord's enemies are among His own people.

The new age will be a restoration, bringing miraculous continuation and renewal to the covenant community. A purified leadership and people will live in harmony with God's will (24:23; 32:1). city of righteousness. The new community is made up of men and women who practice righteousness and demonstrate a commitment to God and to other human beings (1:21 note).

The righteous and faithful city is identified as Zion rather than Jerusalem, a title that emphasizes the spiritual purpose of Jerusalem as the home of the temple. redeemed. Ransomed, transferred, or freed from ownership by another through the payment of a price. The penitent, who turn their backs on idolatry and injustice, find freedom from Satan, sin, and death through the righteousness of Christ imputed to them.

What people hold in honor will be exposed as worthless. Sinners will see how wrong they have been when they come to ruin (26:11; 44:9, 11; 65:13; 66:5). oaks \... gardens. Places of fertility rites and pagan worship that the people have chosen in preference to serving God (65:3 and note; 66:17).

Drought and fire are metaphors for judgment. Water in Isaiah signifies free, gracious, and bountiful salvation (11:9; 32:2; 41:18; 55:1; 58:11). The absence of water signifies separation from God's blessings (3:1; 50:2). It is a particularly apt image because what the fertility rites promised to deliver was the much-needed rain. They were incapable of doing so, as the Lord made clear in the days of Elijah (see 1 Kin. 17; 18).

See note on 4:4. Unlike the purifying judgment of fire in v. 25, for some the Lord's judgment will simply be destructive. There is redemption for those who repent but ruin for those who persist in their rebellion.

–4 An oracle almost identical to Mic. 4:1–3. Isaiah and Micah were contemporaries, so it is not surprising that their messages would have significant overlap. Since the Lord was the ultimate author, He could deliver His revelation to His messengers directly or through another legitimate prophet. 2:2 in the latter days. An indefinite reference that may include a lengthy process of fulfillment, including the reigns of Hezekiah and Josiah, the period of restoration after the exile, the first coming of our Lord, the present age, and the glorious consummation (Jer. 23:20; 30:24; Ezek. 38:8, 16; Hos. 3:5). The phrase designates a new epoch that for the prophet lies in the hidden future. The new epoch alters history in every dimension and is the goal toward which events are striving. The apostle Peter relates this time to the new age begun at Pentecost by using the phrase for an introduction to his citation of Joel 2:28–32 (Acts 2:17). mountain. The Temple Mount is a metaphor for the Lord's kingdom that will be exalted above all other kingdoms (cf. 11:9; 65:25; 66:20). Mount Zion and the temple on it were symbols of heaven and the heavenly sanctuary (Heb. 9:24). These earthly representations have passed away (Heb. 8:13); through the priesthood of the ascended Lord, the church comes directly to the heavenly reality (Heb. 12:22–24). highest of the mountains. Pagans worshiped their gods at mountain shrines. Israel's God, who is worshiped on Mount Zion, will establish Himself in the eyes of all races and nations as the only true and living God, even as He is worshiped today. Although Mount Zion was not physically imposing, its spiritual significance was out of all proportion to its size. See note on Ps. 48:2.

They encourage one another to worship God from regenerate hearts (John 3:3–8). out of Zion. The prophet proclaims the new era in which Jews and Gentiles will serve one King (11:10–12; 27:13; 56:3–8; 66:19–23). Zion, or Jerusalem, stands for God's throne (1:8 note). the law \... the word of theLORD. Represent the media of revelation that belong to the priest and the prophet respectively. The scenario depicts a radical transformation from the situation in 1:3, where Israel herself does not know the Lord's word.

In this renewed Jerusalem, the Lord will establish the justice that has been so lacking, not only for His own people but for the whole world (see 1:27). The redemption of Israel takes place through the salvation of the nations, not their destruction (cf. Ps. 47). swords into plowshares. Cf. Joel 3:10. The instruments of war are transformed into implements of human flourishing.

Stands for God's blessings, presence, and revelation (9:2; 30:26; 42:6, 16; 60:1–3). The Lord is the light in blessing and in judgment (10:17; 60:19, 20; cf. John 1:4; 8:12). People who exchange His light for the darkness of their corrupt minds (5:20; 8:20), will experience His judgment and live in the darkness of separation from God (5:30; 13:10; 59:9; cf. John 3:19, 20). Isaiah's message to his original audience is that if the peoples of the world will walk in the Lord's ways in the last days (v. 3), should not the house of Judah walk in the light now?

Isaiah condemns syncretism, the mixture of religions. These verses contrast the light with all the things the people have adopted from the nations: magic, greed, warfare, and idolatry. The key words are "full" or "filled." 2:6 things from the east \... Philistines. The pagan cultures on either side of Judah. Philistia was to the west; Babylon and Assyria were to the east. The law condemns all forms of magic and divination (Lev. 19:26; Deut. 18:10, 11). Such abominations finally lead the Lord to abandon His people.

They relied on their own military strength (30:16; 31:1, 3), as well as alliances with foreign nations (see v. 6), rather than on the Lord (Ps. 20:7). Israel's kings were forbidden to multiply horses and chariots (Deut. 17:14–20), though Solomon was probably the worst offender in this respect (see 1 Kin. 10:26).
Isaiah contrasts the powerlessness of human-created idols with the power of the uncreated God in 44:6–20.

At God's judgment people may seek shelter, but no one can hide from Him (Rev. 6:16). the terror of theLORD. The Lord is far more awe-inspiring and fear-provoking than the Assyrian kings, despite the claims they made in their annals that their appearance induced terror in their enemies.

The contrast between the exalted God and the weakness of humanity is a central theme in Isaiah's call narrative (Is. 6). in that day. The day of the Lord brings judgment on the godless, but blessing and salvation to the godly (Joel 2:31; Zeph. 1:7; 2:13–18). Isaiah's reference encompasses historical events (the fall of Israel, Assyria, Judah) and the coming judgment and salvation (3:7; 7:18–25; 11:10, 11; 24:21; 27:1).

Large, impressive trees with valuable wood (Ezek. 27:5, 6). They symbolize the permanence and splendor of nature and are natural symbols for pride (cf. Ezek. 31; Dan. 4). But just as the mighty cedar can be felled, the most exalted human beings are subject to God's judgment.
Symbolize pride at being first in trade and commerce (23:1, 8).
See note on 2:11.
As terrified humans seek refuge from divine wrath by hiding in holes in the ground and caves, they will discard their idols to the subterranean creatures that surround them.

One must trust God, who gives breath, not those who are dependent on Him. In the face of many very real dangers on all sides, the Judean kings were often tempted to trust in human allies rather than in the Lord (see Is. 7).
The chaotic conditions result in a lack of the most basic supplies of food and water. See note on 1:30.
The Lord will remove every kind of leader that Isaiah's audience is trusting to secure their society: warriors, sages, magicians, and other prominent people. See note on 11:2.
Because they have trusted in their leaders rather than in God, the nation will be ruled by inexperienced people who are unable to govern wisely. A fitting punishment.
The collapse of civilization comes with communal strife: rich against poor; young against old. Normal social structures will be overthrown.

In a collapsing society, someone who has as little as a decent suit of clothes will seem prosperous enough to be made a ruler. But when the people try to draft such a person, he will reply that his wealth is only an illusion; he has no better answers than they have.
The fall of Jerusalem (586 B.C.) was a partial fulfillment of this prophecy, as was the devastation caused by Sennacherib's siege of the city in 701 B.C.
Israel has no sense of shame, defying God and acting as if the covenant does not exist. See 1:9, 10.
Even though both righteous and wicked alike are affected by the siege and fall of Jerusalem, the Lord distinguishes between these two groups.

As in v. 4, the punishment for trusting in human leaders is the replacement of those leaders by unprepared and ill-equipped stand-ins. O my people. See note on 40:1. On the lack of leadership and its consequences, see 3:4–7 and notes.

In the OT, the metaphor of a vineyard is an important symbol for the temple, temple city, or even the entire Land of Promise. Israel can therefore be referred to as God's vine or vineyard (e.g., Ps. 80; Is. 5:1–7; 27: 2–6; Jer. 12:10; Ezek. 15; 17:3–10; 19:10–12; Hos. 9:10; 10:1). The Lord's people are His vineyard, yet those He has placed in leadership over the vineyard have neglected and abused it.
Cf. the actions of these rulers with those of the ideal Davidic king in 11:3–5.

These women live to the fullest, flaunting their wealth at the expense of those around them. The ornaments are meant to impress others and to supply magical protection from sudden disaster. This outward adornment reflects an inner attitude of pride and self-sufficiency (1 Pet. 3:3, 4). It is the feminine equivalent of the confidence that the men place in their extensive supply of leaders (3:2, 3). Both groups will be stripped of the things in which they place their trust.

The destitution threatened by the day of the Lord is expressed with words associated with bloodshed, war, and captivity. Far from having an abundance of unnecessary ornaments, in that day the women will lack the basic necessities of bread, clothing, and a husband.
Jerusalem is personified and joins in the lament.
The day of judgment. See note on 2:11.

The term has two possible senses. One is literal, corresponding to the parallel phrase "fruit of the land." In this case it is speaking of a glorious restoration of the remnant of God's people on the day when the Lord acts. However, Hebrew parallelism is not always synonymous but often has an "and what's more" character. The other possible sense of "branch" is as a messianic title: Jesus Christ is the fulfillment of the promise as He yields glorious spiritual fruit (11:1–5; Jer. 23:5; Zech. 3:8; John 15:1–8). The remnant find life and blessing in Him (6:13). Because Jesus humbled Himself, He is crowned with glory (52:13; 53:12; Phil. 2:9–11). This verse and the ones that immediately follow provide an important background for chs. 5 and 7, where the vineyard of the Lord is treated in greater depth. Note that 4:2–6 conveys the idea that the Lord's faithful remnant will be called holy. glorious. Displaying the splendor and brightness of God. The glory of God is revealed in all His works, but especially in the Messiah (Ps. 19:1; John 1:18). the survivors. A remnant (1:9 note).

Represents Jerusalem as a whole. See note on 1:8. holy. Consecrated to God, the Holy One of Israel (1:4 note; 62:12). Holiness is a key theme in Isaiah (see ch. 6). recorded. Their names are written in the book of life (Ex. 32:32, 33; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Rev. 20:12).

This judgment will be one of purging, a theme that will appear again in ch. 27. daughters of Zion. Wealthy women who flaunted their affluence. See note on 3:16. spirit. Possibly this is the Holy Spirit, but more likely it refers to the process of purification (cf. 28:6). burning. Signifies judgment (1:25–31; 10:17; 30:27; 42:25). Through the process of refining fire, consuming the faithless and purifying the faithful, God will produce a holy Zion.

In the new act of redemption, the Creator of heaven and earth (40:26; 42:5; 45:12, 18) will renew everything for the sake of His people. God gives the glory of the messianic age; it does not come from human effort or skill (Jon. 2:9; Eph. 2:4–10). A significant theme in this chapter is God's act of recreating His people and being their dwelling place. cloud \... smoke \... shining of a flaming fire. Unlike the burning of the fire of judgment in v. 4, this cloud and fire signal God's protective presence, as at the Red Sea (Ex. 13:20–22), over the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34–38), and in the wilderness (Num. 9:15–23). Here His presence covers a restored and sanctified Mount Zion (2:2 note). a canopy. Jewish weddings include a canopy over the bride and bridegroom as part of the ceremony (see Joel 2:16).

The annual Feast of Booths recalled Israel's wandering in the wilderness and the temporary shelters that they lived in during that time. The Lord will once again provide for His people's needs as He did in the past. shade. God protects His people. See note on 30:2. refuge. In contrast to human deceptions (28:15, 17), the Lord provides effective shelter from the storm (25:4; cf. Pss. 14:6; 46:1; 62:7; 94:22).

Cf. 3:14 note. This vineyard song should be read with the one in ch. 27.The owner and the vineyard stand for God and His people, though that would not have been obvious at first hearing. The language is reminiscent of Song of Songs (e.g., Song 2:15, 16). The song is ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ, who replaces sour grapes with new fruit (Matt. 21:33–44; John 15:1–6).

Images that reinforce the expectation of an abundant harvest; the vineyard is protected against pests and intruders (see Song 2:15). Any deficiency in the harvest is therefore due to the grape vines themselves. wild grapes. Lit. "stinking or sour things."

God decrees desolation and destruction for His people by removing their hedge of protection because of their unfaithfulness and unfruitfulness. God will withdraw His covenant protection from them (cf. Matt. 21:40, 41).

The weeds represent God's curse (7:23–25; 32:13), that is, the anarchy following war (3:4, 5). God can also turn curse into blessing, replacing the briers and thorns with the pine tree and myrtle (55:13). no rain. Rain in its proper season is a covenant blessing, while drought is a covenant curse (see Deut. 11:17).
of hosts.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} See note on 1:9. justice \... bloodshed \... righteousness \... an outcry. The last words in each line rhyme in Hebrew.

The first of six exclamations of woe, proclaiming God's displeasure with greed, drunkenness, and other sins. The first woe condemns greed. add field to field. The land belonged to God (Lev. 25:23), had been allotted to specific families by patrimony (Num. 33:54), and was the basis of livelihood. Deprived of their land, small farmers in Israel were forced to become day laborers or slaves.
God's judgment targets the rich in their greed and self-indulgence. They were not content with a modest living. Mansions provide no protection from His eye (24:10 note).

The bath is a liquid measure of about six gallons. In comparison to its size, the vineyard will produce practically nothing. Likewise, a homer of seed (six bushels) yields only an ephah (half a bushel) of produce. The land will be cursed. Instead of their vast landholding yielding increased profits, the land would produce little (Deut. 28:38, 39).

The second woe condemns drunkenness. See note on 24:11. Although wine was a common beverage in times when water was not safe to drink, overindulgence is a characteristic of social corruption and moral laxity (chs. 22, 28; Amos 4:1–3; 6:6, 7). It is clear that other people are doing the work on the large estates while the landowners sit back and expected to reap the profits.
See note on 40:1. exile. The exile with all its miseries is threatened as a judgment on the people, who have shown no knowledge of the right way to behave.

Lit. "the grave," used almost exclusively in poetry. See Prov. 9:18 and note. Isaiah portrays death as a terrible beast that devours everyone without regard to social class, both the "honored" and the "multitude" (v. 13). In Isaiah, "Sheol" often emphasizes the notion of a shadowy place of nonlife that constantly threatens the unfaithful.
See note on 1:21. The contrast between God and His people is immense even though they are supposed to be a holy people (Ex. 19:6).

The third woe condemns those who mock God as they sin. It imagines them dragging a load of their own sin that is so heavy that they need a cart just to contain it, even while they scoff at the idea that the Lord will act to judge sin. They misconstrue God's patience (2 Pet. 3:3, 4).
A favorite title for God in Isaiah. See note on 1:4.
The fourth woe condemns moral corruption that reverses good and evil. darkness \... light. See notes on 2:5 and 5:30.

The fifth woe condemns pride and self-righteousness. wise in their own eyes. An expression for irrational, arrogant autonomy. A revelation from God, who alone knows all things, is the only firm foundation for knowledge (Prov. 1:7).

The sixth woe condemns those who pervert justice. mixing strong drink. Refers to wine and beer with spices added. Once again, as in 5:11, Isaiah speaks of overindulgence. These men are skilled in preparing exotic drinks, but they neglect weighty matters like guilt and innocence.
See note on 1:23. Bribery involves injustice and greed, as in 5:8.

See note on "burning" at 4:4. In a dry climate, the merest spark is enough to set the stubble ablaze at certain times of the year. the law \... the word. These are central in Isaiah's vision of the latter days (see 2:3), but God's own people reject them.

At the revelation of God's anger, nature quakes (2:19; 13:13; 24:18, 19; Ezek. 32:6–8 note). For a contrasting image of redemption, see 54:10. streets. See note on 24:11. his anger has not turned away. God is not reconciled, and His wrath hangs over the disobedient (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4; 31:3).

This description of the Assyrian army closely matches its portrayal on ancient Assyrian reliefs. 5:26 signal. A signal flag (11:10, 12; 18:3; 49:22; 62:10). Like a commander in battle, the Lord summons the nations to execute His judgment (10:5). Like a pet dog, they come at His whistle. nations far away. Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon. The imperial Assyrian army was made up of mercenaries hired from all over the Assyrian Empire. The professionalism of such mercenary armies would have been terrifying to militia armies such as Judah's.

See note on 2:11. darkness. The people who once possessed the light (2:5) are now walking in great darkness. This metaphor for depression, alienation, and judgment (8:22; 42:7; 47:5; 60:2) teaches that all who twist justice by living in darkness (5:20; 29:15) will suffer the darkness of God's judgment. By contrast, the light of God will dawn on the needy (9:2; 29:18; 42:7; 49:9; 58:10; 60:1, 2). The Lord is sovereign over darkness and light (45:7). distress. Lit. "sorrow," "narrowness." God delivers His own from such confinement (25:4; 63:9).

Having suffered from leprosy (2 Chr. 26:16–21), he died in 740 B.C., signaling the end of a long period of relative peace and prosperity. I saw. Isaiah describes a "theophany," a visible manifestation of God. God's coming is often attended by such phenomena as earthquakes, smoke, fire, and lightning (13:3 note; 29:6; 30:27–31; Ex. 19:18, 19; Pss. 18:7–15; 50:3; 97:2; Mic. 1:3, 4; Nah. 1:3–8; Hab. 3:3–15). the Lord.Adonai, lit. "Sovereign." Cf. note on 1:2. throne. The Lord rules heaven and earth from His throne. The death of the earthly king did not affect the ultimate fate of the universe. The choir of seraphim (6:2 note) and the splendor of God's holiness inspired the prophet throughout his ministry. the train of his robe. The very edge of His garment was greater than the temple. the temple. The heavenly temple, after which the temple in Jerusalem was patterned (cf. Rev. 4:1–8).

A Hb. word probably meaning "burning ones" (cf. the fiery serpents in Num. 21:6). Representations of angelic creatures with six wings have been discovered in the Near East by archaeologists. covered his face. The seraphim have no glory to compare with God's, and they cannot look on Him directly. covered his feet."Feet" can also be translated "legs." This may be an indication of modesty. flew. The seraph does the Sovereign's will. Here it is to praise Him.

A threefold repetition is the strongest sort of superlative. It is the only one of God's attributes that is repeated in this way. Nothing is as holy as God. See note on 1:4. LORD of hosts. Originally a military title, its scope is extended to denote divine control over all the created realm. See note on 1:9. whole earth. This announcement explains the cosmic perspective of the prophet. God is King of the world, and His salvation and judgment extend to all nations (11:4, 9, 12; 42:1, 4, 5; 65:17; 66:1; cf. Luke 2:14). glory. See note on 4:2, "glorious." God's glory filled the earthly tabernacle and temple at key moments of the dedication ceremonies, representing the Lord symbolically taking up residence there (Ex. 40:35; 1 Kin. 8:11). The whole earth is full of God's glory because He indwells the whole cosmos, not merely a small building on Mount Zion.

Isaiah is astonished by the glory of God; like Peter he becomes afraid (cf. Luke 5:8). He pronounces an oracular curse upon himself. His conviction of sin is specific: he has unclean lips. The fact that others around him suffer from the same condition compounds his sin rather than alleviating it.

The altar from which the live coal is taken is not described. The stress is on the purification necessary for approaching God. The altar symbolizes purification by blood, and the fire, purification by the Spirit. The blood of Christ and the ministry of the Holy Spirit sanctify believers today.
The purification is specifically applied to the point of his sin — his lips — making the prophet acceptable as a minister of God's words (Jer. 1:9).

The Lord permits Isaiah to listen in on the sessions of the royal, heavenly court ("us"). From this moment on, Isaiah is a servant of God's court and proclaims God's message to kings and people alike (cf. 1 Kin. 22:19, 20; Jer. 23:18, 22). Having been freely forgiven, Isaiah volunteers without waiting to hear the nature of his commission.

Isaiah's mission is paradoxical in its effect, as is the proclamation of the Word of God (Matt. 13:13–15; Rom. 11:7–10, 25). The prophetic word closes the way of God to those who are rebellious, proud, and hypocritical (29:13–16; 65:1–7), but opens it to the deaf, blind, humble, and poor (29:18, 19).
Isaiah is asking how long the message of judgment must go forth until he can be a "herald of good news" (40:9).

The land will be laid waste, and even the remnant who will be saved will be further purified by suffering (1:9 note). stump. The Middle Eastern terebinth and oak trees can produce new shoots even when they appear to have been cut or damaged beyond all hope. There is a glimmer of hope for God's people, but it is only to be found on the far side of judgment.

Oracles of judgment and hope associated with the war between Judah and a coalition of Israel and Syria (734–732 B.C.). Ahaz, king of Judah, was seriously threatened by the alliance of Pekah, king of Israel, with Rezin, king of Syria (2 Kin. 16:5–18; 2 Chr. 28:16–21). They threatened to invade Judah if Ahaz would not help them against Assyria.

This expression means the current head of the house, Ahaz. It recalls the Lord's covenant with David, granting him an eternal offspring and kingdom (2 Sam. 7:12–16). The attempt to replace his dynasty with another ("the son of Tabeel," v. 6) cannot succeed because God's promises are at stake. The rival claimant doesn't even deserve to be mentioned by name in the text. shook. Ahaz, the proud king, has been unable to calm his people. The response of the leader has created panic among the people (22:3 note).

"A remnant shall return" (10:20–22) is a name representing a promise of salvation and life for the faithful beyond the imminent doom of the unfaithful. Judah may suffer, but a remnant will remain (see 6:13). the conduit of the upper pool. Water supplies are crucial in case of a siege of the city.
Two kingdoms are about to be destroyed: Damascus in 732 B.C. by Tiglath-pileser III, and Samaria in 722 B.C. by Sargon II.

GOD. This title combines the Hb. word for "lord, sovereign" with the covenant name Yahweh, represented by "God," using small capitals (cf. 25:8; 28:16; 40:10; 52:4; 65:13). shall not come to pass. The Lord voids the counsel of kings (8:9, 10; 40:23; Ps. 33:10, 11).

That is, less than the span of a normal human life (see Ps. 90:10). God will fulfill His promises after Ahaz's death (2 Kin. 17:24–41). The northern kingdom will actually be conquered by the Assyrians much sooner than that.

A play on different meanings of the same Hb. word. Faith means knowing God's promise, assenting to it intellectually, and trusting Him to keep it. The threat to Ahaz's kingdom provides him an opportunity for him to trust in God and see God deliver him.

A sign will authenticate the prophetic message concerning the future. Normally, asking for a sign is a mark of weak faith (as in the case of Gideon in Judg. 6); however, here God condescends to Ahaz's weakness and offers him a sign. deep \... high. Nothing is outside the Lord's sovereignty; no sign is too great for Him to accomplish (Deut. 10:14; Ps. 139:8; Rom. 8:39). I will not put the LORD to the test. Ahaz makes his refusal sound spiritual, quoting Deut. 6:16, but in reality he has already made up his mind to place his faith in the chariots and horsemen of Assyria rather than in the Lord.
See note on 7:2.

This Hb. word occurs seven times in the OT. It means a young woman of marriageable age, who in ancient Judah and Israel was normally a virgin (Gen. 24:43). The Septuagint translates the Hb. word with a Gk. term that specifically means "virgin." The NT understands the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's promise to be the Virgin Mary (Matt. 1:23). Immanuel. "God with us." Conveys God's promise to save, bless, and protect His children. The identities of the virgin and the child have been the subject of considerable discussion, and three major interpretations exist. First, some find the prophecy exclusively fulfilled in the prophet's own lifetime. Some of these interpreters, especially Jews of the second century A.D., have understood the prophecy to mean Ahaz's wife and her child, Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:2). But, as Jerome (c. A.D. 400) pointed out, Hezekiah was already born. Others identify the woman as Isaiah's wife or a woman betrothed to him (8:3). The child is then Isaiah's son, Maher-shalal-hash-baz. However, the Hb. term translated "virgin" would not normally be used for a woman who was already a mother (of Shear-jashub, 7:3). If it means someone engaged to the prophet, then one must assume that his first wife had died prior to this prophecy. Further, this interpretation requires that the child have two different names: "God Is with Us" (Immanuel) and "The Spoil Speeds, the Prey Hastens" (Maher-shalal-hash-baz; cf. 8:3). In that case, the point of the immediate fulfillment would be that God's presence with His people brings judgment as well as salvation. Second, in the light of the NT, the traditional Christian interpretation identifies the child directly as the Messiah, a divine personage whose birth is above nature (and so of the same miraculous order as the sign of v. 11). This approach equates the child named "Immanuel" with the child possessing God's titles in 9:6, and with the "branch" of ch. 11. According to Matthew, the virgin is Mary and the child is Jesus Christ (Matt. 1:22, 23). However, v. 16 seems to require the birth to be imminent. A third interpretation is to consider the prophecy to be typological, with a two-stage fulfillment: an immediate but partial realization in Isaiah's day and a later definitive one in the birth of Jesus Christ, who secures God's throne forever. The difficulty that remains is determining the partial fulfillment. Some opt for the birth of Isaiah's son Maher-shalal-hash-baz (8:1–3), while others take the initial reference to be to a nameless teenage mother, who hears and believes God's promises and thus names her son "God Is with Us" in spite of the threatening circumstances. Her faith contrasts with the conduct of King Ahaz, the son of David who refuses to trust God's promise entirely, but an ordinary birth falls short of the radical nature of the sign envisaged in v. 11.

Not typical food for infants, but they point to a time when people will have to live off unworked fields (v. 22). The child is identified with the remnant. when he knows how to refuse the evil. The boy is not just able to distinguish between right and wrong, but he actively chooses what is right, in contrast to the failed leadership of Israel that has been insensitive to social and spiritual values (5:11–23). What is true of this child in an imperfect and lesser way is perfectly and fully true of Jesus Christ (42:1–4).

Before the time required for a child to reach an age of adult moral accountability — twelve years — Pekah and Remaliah will both be defeated. In this understanding, "boy" points primarily to Isaiah's son and secondarily to Christ.
The consequences of Ahaz's unbelieving trust in Assyria will be devastating not only for Syria and Israel, but for Judah as well.

See note on 2:11. The fall of Damascus, of Samaria, and the devastation of Judah are foretastes of the events of the last judgment. fly \... bee. These insects swarm in great numbers, like the hordes of invaders.
Traditional hiding places will provide no escape (2:19).

Shaving the head is a sign of mourning (15:2) and a way of humiliating conquered enemies (2 Sam. 10:4, 5). It is a way of systematically "de-manning" the captives, which is why the "feet" (the lower part of the anatomy from the waist down) is also shaved. Ahaz has hired Tiglath-pileser of Assyria to help him against Syria and Israel, but the Lord will use Assyria to humiliate Judah instead (v. 17).
The land will be so depopulated that this limited food will seem abundant. curds and honey. See note on v. 15. The remnant will have something to eat, but it will not be much.
The cultivated land will return to weeds and be barely fit for grazing. This represents God's covenant curse on the land (see 5:6 note).
Probably a polished piece of wood like a signboard. The meaning of the name is explained in v. 4.
Two witnesses are necessary to attest to legal documents or transactions.

Isaiah refers to his wife in this way perhaps because of her association with him as a prophet, or perhaps because she was a prophet in her own right (Judg. 4:4; 2 Kin. 22:14). Maher-shalal-hash-baz. The name means "the spoil speeds, the prey hastens," which signifies the rapid devastation of Syria, Israel, and Judah, but also the presence of God with the remnant and the impending fulfillment of God's word of promise. The similarities between the sign of his birth and the sign of Immanuel are striking, perhaps because his birth is an immediate testimony to God's long-term promise.

Judah. waters of Shiloah. Might refer to a stream flowing from the Gihon Spring (2 Chr. 32:30). It is a symbol of the Lord's faithful but unspectacular provision, which the people have despised (cf. 1:30 note; Jer. 2:13; Zech. 4:10). rejoice. The people may be looking forward to the fall of Rezin, king of Syria, without considering that the word of judgment applies to Judah as well.

The Euphrates, standing for the Assyrian invaders. The mighty Euphrates contrasts with the soft waters of Shiloah (v. 6). In Isaiah's day, it regularly burst its banks and flooded the surrounding area of Mesopotamia.

The implication is that Assyria will almost, but not quite, annihilate Judah. At the height of the Assyrian invasion in 701 B.C., Jerusalem escapes, but barely (37:33–36). O Immanuel. See v. 10; note on 7:14. Isaiah bestows the name of the virgin's child on Judah as the object of God's care.
Syria and Israel.
See note on 11:2. God is with us. Hb. "Immanuel." God is with the remnant of Judah, which will not be destroyed (v. 8 notes; 7:14 note).
Isaiah has had an experience of inner compulsion from the Spirit of God (Ezek. 1:3; 3:14).
The people considered Isaiah a traitor because he said that Ahaz and his administration were wrong to rely on Assyria.

It is not people (v. 12), but the Lord who is the object of fear. The kings of Syria and Israel seem dangerous to Judah but the Lord can bring their threat to nothing. Even Assyria can do nothing without the Lord's permission. He is the ultimate authority to whom all must submit, in whom all must trust, and to whom everyone must render an account (12:2; 33:6; 50:10; 59:19; Pss. 25:12–15; 34:11–14).

A place of refuge. a stone of offense. The sign of Immanuel, which Ahaz rejected, will be a vital test of faith. To those who trust the Lord and believe His promise, He will be a sanctuary. But those who refuse to trust in the Lord will stumble over this sign. both houses. Judah and Israel.

This could refer to God's revelation (1:10) to Moses (Deut. 4:44, 45), to Isaiah, or to both. disciples. Isaiah's followers are to write down and seal his prophecy like a law so that it can be known later whether it fails or is fulfilled by events (vv. 1, 2, 20). This is the test of a true prophet (Deut. 18:21, 22; Jer. 28:9), through whom God is known and trusted. In the midst of the destruction, God preserves the holy seed (see 6:13).

See 25:9; 26:8; 30:18; 33:2; 40:31; 49:23; 64:4. hiding his face. The covenant God, who is presently leaving His people to themselves, is also free in bestowing grace on those who repent (54:8; 64:7; Deut. 31:18; 32:20).
The children's names are significant (7:3; 8:1, 3 and notes).

God's law prohibits diviners (Is. 2:6 note). chirp and mutter. The mediums promise contact with the dead, who in the popular understanding of Judah are insubstantial and weak-voiced. Isaiah regards calling on them as contemptible, as well as useless.
See note on 8:16. dawn. Light stands for God's blessing. See note on 2:5.
An image of despair (5:30 note; 50:10).
Being in the north, these regions in Galilee were the first to suffer from the Assyrian invasion of 732 B.C. (2 Kin. 15:29).

See note on 2:5. deep darkness. The Assyrians cast their terrible shadow over the land and the people (cf. Pss. 23:4; 44:19; 107:10). Yet there is hope; the certainty of that hope is expressed in the "prophetic perfect" ("have seen"), speaking of the future light as if it has already happened.
God opens up a new future for the humble (29:19) where gloom had previously existed (35:10; 51:3; 61:7). This new joy finds expression in the metaphors of harvest and of victory (cf. 5:10; 8:4).

Figures of oppression (10:27; 14:25; 47:6; cf. Matt. 11:29, 30). day of Midian. A reference to Gideon's defeat of the Midianites, which was accomplished by God's mighty power in spite of Gideon's own weakness (10:26, 27; Judg. 6:7; 7:22–25).
The debris left from battle can be removed and burned when the fighting stops. God will bring an end to war (2:4; Ps. 46:9, 10; 2 Cor. 10:4).

The good news is the birth of Jesus Christ. The four royal names express both His divine and human qualities, giving assurance that He is indeed "Immanuel" (7:14). born \... given. The verbs are consistent with His humanity and deity respectively. the government shall be upon his shoulder. He will carry the burden of rule and authority (cf. 22:22). Wonderful Counselor."Wonderful" might be more accurately translated "miraculous" because it typically describes God's mighty works. The role of a counselor is to provide wisdom (Jer. 18:18). This coming King will possess divine wisdom. Mighty God. As a warrior, God protects His people (10:21; Deut. 10:17; Jer. 32:18). This attribute of divine power is ascribed to the coming King.
