For the importance of this verse in the interpretation of the Seventy Weeks passage, see note on Dan. 9:27. Everlasting Father. The coming King possesses divine eternity: He is from ancient times, and He will not need a successor to follow in His footsteps (cf. 2 Sam. 7:13; Mic. 5:2). Ancient kings often referred to themselves as the fathers of their subjects. This name reveals the divine, eternal care that the coming King will have for His people. Prince of Peace. His government brings divine peace to the earth (2:4; 11:6–9; Ps. 72:7; Zech. 9:10; Luke 2:14).

He is a descendant of David (11:1 note), and he will establish the kingdom of God in "justice and with righteousness" (1:21 note); his reign will endure forever. No earthly son of David, such as Hezekiah or Josiah, ever lived up to this grand description. zeal. God guarantees that He Himself will fulfill this promise; it will not depend on human power or decisions (37:32; 42:13; Zech. 1:14).
The Lord will judge Israel (the northern kingdom) and its capital, Samaria. The northern kingdom is also sometimes called Ephraim. (Judah is the southern kingdom, with Jerusalem as its capital.)
Their motivation has been to preserve and glorify themselves. Compare also their words "we will \... we will" in v. 10 (Gen. 11:3, 4; Is. 5:21).

The people think the challenges they face are minor setbacks rather than the beginning of the end. They imagine that they are going to start rebuilding with better materials, when in reality destruction lies ahead.

The Assyrians (7:1 note; 7:20 note; 8:7 note) would attack Syria from the north, and the Syrians and the Philistines would attack Israel from the east and west, respectively. The Lord will raise up many enemies. 9:12 his anger has not turned away. This refrain is also found in 9:17, 21; 10:4 (cf. 31:3). See note on 5:25. The hand that once delivered Israel from the Egyptians is now extended to strike His own people.

They have been unresponsive to divine discipline (Amos 4:6, 8–11). They have not depended on the Lord or sought Him with diligence; instead, they have persisted in their rebellion (8:19; 11:10; 31:1; 55:6; 58:2; 65:10).

Represent the civil and religious leadership, as explained in v. 15 (cf. 3:1–3; 30:10 note). The same imagery, including the "palm branch and reed," is used to represent Egyptian leaders in 19:15. Because they are opposites, they also imply judgment for everyone else in between.

See note on 1:17. The gravity of God's anger is vividly expressed when it is said that He will have no mercy on the fatherless and widows. Not even the most helpless members of society will escape. everyone is godless and an evildoer. Sin is found in every person, even the fatherless and widow, and it corrupts both their thoughts and their deeds (Gen. 6:5; 8:21). The Lord's total destruction is just.

Pride, narcissism, and greed destroy the fiber of society, especially the covenant relationship among the tribes. Before the revelation of this oracle, Manasseh fought Ephraim (Judg. 12:4), and together they battled Judah during the war with Israel and Syria. Sin is self-destructive: as a fire, it consumes the land; as a person, it eats its own arm. Even this, though, does not exhaust God's wrath against sin.
The principle of retribution is an important biblical teaching. People reap what they sow, whether to destruction or benefit (Gal. 6:7, 8).

See note on 1:21. On social injustice, see 1:23. poor \... fatherless. The object of the Lord's special care. See 1:16–18; 11:4; Ps. 9:18 and notes. my people. It is significant when the Lord identifies His people as belonging to Him. See note on 40:1.
The day of the Lord (2:11 note). from afar. The desolation brought by the Assyrians.

God makes the nations serve Him as instruments of His will, but they continue to be responsible for their acts (5:25; 7:20 and notes). God's anger is against those who administer His kingdom on earth corruptly, both rulers and people (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4, 25).
Includes Israel and Judah (v. 11).
Human rulers have their own reasons for acting, yet they end up doing exactly what the Lord has purposed from the beginning (cf. Ezek. 38:10).

Assyria conquered these cities: Calno (Calneh; cf. Amos 6:2) in 738 B.C.; Carchemish in 717 B.C.; Hamath in 738 and 720 B.C.; Arpad in 740 B.C.; Samaria in 722 B.C.; and Damascus in 732 B.C. Cf. 36:19; 37:12, 13. In each pair, the first city is further away from Assyria than the second; the boast is that Assyria will continue to extend its sphere of influence wider and wider.

Assyria boasts of its power, demonstrated in the destruction of nations with far more impressive idols than Jerusalem and Samaria (cf. Dan. 4:30; Luke 12:18–20). The irony is rich: Jerusalem and Samaria ought not to have idols at all, but should trust in the Lord. In reality, though, their trust is in idols that cannot measure up even in an idol contest. kingdoms. See note on 13:4.
The Assyrian assault is itself part of God's work. Zion. Jerusalem. See note on 1:8.
A restatement of vv. 5–11. For similar expressions of pride, see 14:13, 14; Ezek. 28:2–5.
See note on v. 5. It is ridiculous for a tool to boast about its mighty accomplishments.
The Lord can destroy the tool when its usefulness is over.
A symbol of God's blessing. See note on 2:5. it will burn and devour. Cf. 9:18.

See note on 4:2. What people think should be honored or despised means little before God's fiery judgment. forest \... fruitful land. The Assyrian pride will end quickly like thorns in a fire. Little will remain (v. 19).

The day of God's judgment. See note on 2:11. remnant. The Lord will preserve a faithful few out of the destruction. See note on 1:8. him who struck them. The remnant will no longer put their faith in Assyria, as Ahaz did in ch. 7.
Recalls God's promise to Abraham (Gen. 22:17; cf. 1 Kin. 4:20). Paul cites this verse in Rom. 9:27. decreed. God is determined in His judgment (v. 23; 28:22).
GOD of hosts. The Lord's military title. See notes on 1:9, 24.
A word of encouragement for the remnant in Judah (37:6; 41:10, 13; 43:1). See note on 35:4.
The one to fear is not the Assyrian king, but the Lord who is bringing the Assyrians in judgment on Judah. destruction. The instruments of destruction will themselves be destroyed.
Two examples are taken from the history of redemption: the defeat of Midian at the rock of Oreb (a Midianite leader; Judg. 7:25), and the victory over Egypt at the Red Sea (Ex. 14:26–28).
See 9:4. Their prosperity will be such that, like a muscular ox, the yoke will not be able to contain their neck.

Describes a march to Judah from north to south through the cities mentioned. The last, Nob, is within sight of Zion. For a similar portrayal of Assyria's invasion, but from the southwest, see Mic. 1:10–16.
The Assyrians may inspire Judah with terror, but the Lord will intervene.
The Assyrians are portrayed as a forest that the Lord is going to cut down (v. 18 note). Majestic One. See 33:21.

All that will be left of the Davidic dynasty after God's judgment is a stump. The privileged sons of David, no less than Assyria, will be like trees that have been chopped down (10:33, 34; cf. Jer. 22:30). But in spite of this judgment on Judah, the Lord will raise up new leadership from David's dynasty (Jer. 23:5, 6; Matt. 1:1). The remaining stump will be living, and it will send forth a shoot, a branch that will bear fruit. Jesse. David's father (1 Sam. 16:10–13). David inaugurated a great kingdom, but the greater David (Ezek. 34:23–25; Zech. 12:7–10), now only a tender plant (53:2), will rule an incomparably greater kingdom. branch. See note on 4:2.

LORD. As the fourfold repetition emphasizes, the same God-given endowment of the Spirit that brought David his successes (1 Sam. 16:13; Ps. 51:11) will empower the Messiah (42:1; 61:1; Luke 3:22). The Spirit is the creative agent for establishing God's kingdom (Gen. 1:2; Judg. 3:10; 6:34; 1 Sam. 10:6 and notes). rest upon him. The Spirit came in a powerful way on saints in the OT to equip them for service: Moses (Num. 11:17); certain elders (Num. 11:25, 26); Joshua (Deut. 34:9); the judges (Judg. 3:10; 11:29; 13:25); kings (1 Sam. 11:6); and prophets (1 Sam. 10:10; 2 Sam. 23:2; 1 Kin. 22:24; 2 Kin. 2:15; Mic. 3:8). The Spirit is the divine agent of restoration (32:15; Joel 2:28–32). wisdom. Solomon prayed for wisdom and understanding (1 Kin. 3:9), the administrative skills needed to govern the people in righteousness and justice. See Introduction to the Wisdom Literature. counsel. Authoritative plans and decisions. Human counsel may or may not be in accord with God's plan (30:1), but the Messiah's counsel is by "the Spirit" (see 9:6). knowledge. Refers to wise and submissive living in accordance with the will of God (33:6; 53:11). It is a perfection of God (40:14). fear of theLORD. Fearing God includes obeying His commandments out of faith that the Lord will keep His threats against transgressors (Prov. 1:7 note).
See note on 2:4.

See note on 1:21. poor \... meek. Those who long for divine righteousness and justice (25:4) because of oppression by the rulers of this earth (3:15; 10:2; 32:7; 61:1). They are the afflicted, oppressed, and humble whom Jesus blesses (Matt. 5:3–10; cf. Ps. 19:8 note). equity. The Hb. word also means "level" or "straight" (40:4). God's judgment is balanced and fair. rod \... breath. With great power and authority (Pss. 2:9; 82:8; Rev. 6:15–17; 20:11, 12) the Messiah will conquer by His word (49:2; 61:1; Heb. 4:12; Rev. 19:15).
See note on 1:21; cf. 25:1; 33:6. the belt of his loins. In antiquity, people wore long flowing robes that could be tucked into a belt in order to prepare for vigorous action (cf. Eph. 6:14).

Carnivorous animals, remade with natures that protect what they formerly devoured, effectively portray the wonderful peace on earth in the new age ruled by the Messiah (see 2:4). The devouring nations, such as Assyria, will no longer assault God's people. The vision corresponds to reconciling love already visible in the church (Eph. 2:14–18), which will be consummated in the new heavens and new earth (Rev. 21:4, 24–27).
Mount Zion (cf. 2:2–4). the earth shall be full. See Hab. 2:14.

The day of God's judgment. See note on 2:11. root of Jesse. See note on v. 1 (Rev. 22:16). signal. Here, a sign of hope (cf. John 12:32), in contrast to 5:26 (see note). glorious. Displaying God's glory. See note on 4:2.

The first time God reclaimed His people from Egypt through the exodus; the second time will be from the exile (51:9–11). remnant. See note on 1:8. The Lord will lead His children from wherever they are distressed.

The remnant will come from all of the known world (24:15; 42:4, 10; 51:5; 59:18, 19; cf. Matt. 24:31). The nations listed in v. 11 are located geographically on all sides of Israel and Judah: Assyria, Elam, and Shinar are to the east, in and around Mesopotamia; Egypt, Pathros, and Cush are to the south; Hamath is north, and the coastlands are to the west.

The era of restoration will witness a reconciliation of the disunited and hostile tribes. When the remnant later returns to the land after the exile, the people offer sacrifices on behalf of all twelve tribes (Ezra 6:17; 8:35).
Represent freedom from the oppression, subjugation, and harassment that had characterized Israel's experience in the land (cf. 54:3; Mic. 5:6 note for a similar use of Assyria).

The second exodus will come by another miracle similar to the parting of the Red Sea (vv. 11, 12). However, this deliverance will be even greater, dividing the Euphrates into seven channels, not merely into two. scorching breath. See Ex. 14:24–27 and Is. 11:4. in sandals. The water of the great Euphrates will become so shallow that people will be able cross without even taking off their shoes.
The Lord provides an image to confirm the certainty of His salvation (19:23; 35:8, 9; 40:3–5; 57:14; 62:10). Just as He led His people out of Egypt, so He will lead them out of exile.

Isaiah's new hymn at the second exodus corresponds to that of Moses at the first (Ex. 15). 12:1 in that day. The day of God's judgment. See note on 2:11. I will give thanks. The prophet speaks as a representative of the people of God. The reason for praise is God Himself. that you might comfort me. Comfort is a key feature of the second half of Isaiah's prophecy. See 40:1.

See Ex. 15:2. He is the source and the initiator of salvation (49:6, 8; 51:6, 8; 56:1; 62:1). the Lord God. There is a double reference to the covenant name of God (Ex. 3:15) in the designation Lord God (Yah Yahweh). This is a poetic device to emphasize the certainty of the salvation He provides.

The salvation of the Lord always brings joy (35:10; 51:3, 11; 61:3), as God removes the causes for sorrow and anxiety. water \... wells. Salvation is compared to an abundance of water (Pss. 1:3; 65:9; 104:10–13; 107:35) coming "from the wells of salvation" (41:18; cf. John 4:14).
God's glory is a key theme in Isaiah. See 2:11, 17; 33:5.
An allusion to "triumphed gloriously" (Ex. 15:1) and a synonym for "exalted" (v. 4). made known in all the earth. See 11:9.

Isaiah prophesies concerning the day of the Lord and what it means for the nations. Babylon and Assyria are treated together in the first oracle (13:1–14:27) because Babylon became the crown jewel of the Assyrian Empire and subsequently replaced it. Assyrian kings had themselves crowned as kings of this renowned city. Babylon was regarded as an epitome of religion and culture, and as such Babylon represents the kingdoms of this world. Peter and John continue to use Babylon as a symbol for ungodly nations (1 Pet. 5:13; Rev. 14:8; 16:19; 17:1–18:24). 13:1 oracle. The Hb. word can mean a literal weight, corresponding to the idea that the prophetic word is a heavy responsibility for the prophet who must deliver it. On the other hand, the word can also mean simply a message or oracle, without the suggestion of weight. It is often used for judgment oracles, but it can also refer to other prophetic messages.
The Lord directs the nations like a military commander. See note on 5:26. gates of the nobles. Implies that the city is proud.
The armies God uses as instruments of judgment.

The great noise indicates the exercise of God's power (30:30, 31; 33:3; Ps. 29:5–9). kingdoms, of nations. The Lord is the commander of human kingdoms. In Isaiah's era, Bab­ylon thinks of herself as "the glory of kingdoms" (13:19) or the "mistress of kingdoms" (47:5) and rules over others with great force (14:16).

The Lord's kingdom is universal. The Medes and the Persians eventually destroy Babylon (see v. 17). Significantly, the prophet foretells the destruction of Babylon many centuries before it happens. weapons of his indignation. See note on 10:5.
Describes the terror of the day of the Lord. 13:6 the day of theLORD. Also called "the day" (v. 13); see note on 2:11.
The people will be utterly helpless, lacking the strength to resist their enemies (Jer. 6:24; Ezek. 7:17).
The Bible often uses this imagery to convey intense pain and suffering (21:3; 49:24; 50:43; Ps. 48:6; Mic. 4:9; cf. Rom. 8:22).

Imagery for God's cosmic judgment (24:23; Joel 2:10, 31; Matt. 24:29; Rev. 6:12–14). The Lord reigns over the entire cosmos. light. See note on 2:5. The ancients worshiped the heavenly bodies, but Scripture teaches that God is the creator of them all (Deut. 4:19). Darkness symbolizes judgment. The imagery is also used for the final destruction of the world (34:3).
See note on 29:20.
Ophir produced particularly fine gold in the ancient world, gold fit for royalty and temples (see 1 Chr. 29:4; Ps. 45:9).

These expressions depict the coming of God in judgment against His creation. The shaking of the world symbolizes the overthrow of all that unbelievers exalt as rivals to God (2:12–18). The king of Babylon is described as one who makes "the earth tremble" (14:16).
The attractiveness of Bab­ylon will become a phantom when people realize how short-lived human kingdoms are.
The terrors brought by war.

Inhabitants of the Zagros Mountains, east of Babylon and Assyria. They were never subjugated by Assyria and joined Babylon in the conquest of Assyria (612–609 B.C.). For the dating of this prophecy it is significant that Persia, which conquered Media in 549 B.C., is not mentioned.

See note on v. 4. Chaldeans. Chaldea was part of Babylon and the home of the dynasty founded by Nebuchadnezzar's father, Nabopolassar. "Chaldeans" sometimes serves as an alternative name for the Babylonians. Sodom and Gomorrah. The fate of these cities is a perpetual reminder of the total destructiveness of the Lord's judgment. See note on 1:9.
The measure of God's judgment on human pride. Centuries after this prophecy, Babylon is finally laid waste as described.

Or owls. It is not always easy to identify the specific kind of bird in view in the OT. 13:21, 22 wild animals \... jackals. Babylon becomes unfit for human habitation; only wild animals haunt the site (34:11–15; Jer. 50:39; 51:37; Zeph. 2:14, 15).

Election is God's choice, and He is free to set Israel aside or to choose Israel again for a new future (41:8, 9; 44:1, 2; 45:4; 65:9; Ex. 19:6; Deut. 7:6; cf. Rom. 9–11). Babylon's downfall is the necessary prerequisite for the restoration of God's people. sojourners \... will attach themselves. See Is. 56:3.
Instruments of God's plan of redemption (55:5; 60:1–18; 61:5–7; 66:19, 20; cf. Ezra 1:1–8).

A taunt against the king of Babylon. Victors in the ancient world frequently sang taunt songs against their victims (v. 7; 12:1; Ex. 15:1). 14:3 rest. As in the first exodus, God will liberate the people from oppression.

The Hb. term has a range of meanings, including brief sayings like those in the book of Proverbs, and a figurative poem like the one here. The form of the song as a lament is ironic, as if the end of Babylon were a tragic death. king of Babylon. A chief representative of oppressive human power.
The symbol of oppressive power is broken by God.
Instead of "the song of the ruthless" (25:5), a new song of salvation will be heard in response to God's judgment and deliverance (24:14, 16; 26:1, 19; 44:23; 49:13). See note on 12:1–6.

Nature responds to God's acts of judgment and restoration (55:13; 60:13; cf. 37:24). The trees may also represent the surrounding nations, which are now left to flourish in peace. no woodcutter. Ancient Near Eastern kings boast in their annals of the magnificent trees they cart off from pillaged lands to build their splendid palaces.

Isaiah uses the popular conception of the realm of the dead with its shadowy figures welcoming newcomers in an ironic description of Babylon's fall and her descent into the lower regions. The use of these conventional ideas is poetic, and is not intended as a theology of the afterlife. See 5:14 and note; Prov. 1:12; 9:18 and notes. 14:9 thrones. The defeated kings had thrones in their royal graves. By contrast the king of Babylon is given a bed of maggots (v. 11).

Represents in an exaggerated way the fall of Babylon, with all its imperial ambitions, into destruction (cf. Lam. 2:1; Luke 4:6; 10:15). Cf. the claims and fate of the king of Tyre in Ezek. 28. O Day Star, son of Dawn. Lit. "shining one, son of dawn." Probably refers to the planet Venus, rising in the morning and climbing toward the top of the sky, only to be overtaken by the sun. In the ancient world, observations of this astronomical cycle gave rise to several myths. Babylon seems to have thought of itself as fulfilling such a heavenly destiny and becoming an eternal and universal empire. But with the appearance of God (v. 22), Babylon's light will be extinguished. Traditionally, this passage has also been seen as a picture of Satan's fall from grace.

According to Canaanite myths, the god El presides over an assembly of gods on Mount Zaphon in Syria. The king of Babylon is ready to claim this exalted honor for himself. far reaches of the north. A traditional rendering of Hb. zaphon. Ps. 48:1, 2 mentions "the far north" as belonging to the Lord alone, rather than to El or Babylon.

See Gen. 14:19, 20. This is a restatement of v. 13. People may claim rule over the entirety of God's kingdom, but God is still sovereign. The greater their pride, the greater their fall. The conflict between nations is not part of a conflict between rival deities, as in ancient Near Eastern mythology, but an unequal battle between the Most High God and mere humans.
See vv. 9–11 and notes. Death and entry to Sheol is the ultimate proof of the emptiness of the king of Babylon's claims to be a god (see Ezek. 28:2).
See note on 13:4.
Babylon has used the power of which it was so proud for destruction and cruelty.

The satirical contrast introduced in v. 9 is taken up again. The conquered kings are pictured in honored rest, while proud Babylon is thrown out like unhealthy refuse. To be deprived of a proper burial was regarded as a great misfortune in the ancient world.
Unlike Israel, Assyria has no remnant (v. 30; cf. 15:9; 17:3 and 1:9 note).
See note on 13:21, 22. In modern Hebrew, the word means "hedgehog," but it is possible that in ancient Hebrew, a type of bird is meant. The same word also appears in Is. 34:11 and Zeph 2:14.

The oracle shifts from distant deliverance to the more immediate threat of Assyria. The imminent demise of the Assyrian army in the days of Hezekiah will provide a lesson in the Lord's sovereign power over history (see Is. 36; 37). yoke. See note on 9:4.
These verses concluding the section that began at 13:1 are an eloquent statement of God's irresistible hand of judgment extended over the whole earth (43:13).
Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. Ahaz dies in 715 B.C., fourteen years before the siege of Jerusalem (2 Kin. 18:13).

See note on 10:5. Around the time of Ahaz's death there is a Philistine revolt against the Assyrian emperor Sargon. broken. This weakness in Assyria's hegemony is temporary. adder \... flying fiery serpent. There is no need to identify the snakes with particular kings, like Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, or Ashurbanipal. The idea is that Assyrian strength will go on for more than one generation despite successions of kings. The next generation will be more fearsome than the previous.
The object of the Lord's special care. See 11:4; Ps. 19:8 and notes. remnant. See note on v. 22.
The Assyrian invasion.

The Philistines seek to create a coalition with Judah and other nations to rebel against the Assyrians, but God's response through Isaiah is clear. God will protect His own, in spite of the political and military turmoil, without the need for external alliances.

This oracle of judgment against Moab is probably delivered around the time of Sargon's defeat of Moab in 715 B.C. See also 11:14; 25:10; Jer. 48; Ezek. 25:8–11; Amos 2:1–3; Zeph. 2:8–11. The oracle concerns Moab's distress (ch. 15) and the response to Moab's distress (ch. 16). 15:1 oracle. Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. Moab. Moab is a nation east of the Dead Sea, between the Ammonites and the Edomites. In the ancient world, her relations with Judah are often tense. Ar \... Kir. The city of Ar is on the Arnon River, and Kir is the capital of Moab.

Dibon is a site north of the Arnon River devoted to the worship of the Moabite god Chemosh. The high places are the sites of pagan worship. Nebo \... Medeba. Nebo is a village north of the Arnon River, not far from the mountain where Moses went to look at the Promised Land (Deut. 34:1). Medeba is five miles (8 km) to the southeast. baldness. The customs of mourning include cutting the hair and shaving.
In the public places, where people gather. sackcloth \... tears. Mourning customs (v. 2; 22:12; Jer. 4:8; 41:5; 48:20, 34; Lam. 2:10).

These two towns are close together, about six miles (10 km) north of Medeba (v. 2). Heshbon was captured by Israel under Moses (Num. 21:23–26). Jahaz. Located on the Arnon River, about twenty miles (32 km) south of Heshbon (Num. 21:23; Jer. 48:34).

Isaiah has noticeably more sympathy for Moab, Ruth's homeland (16:11), than for the other nations. Zoar. The Moabites flee to Zoar, as their forefather Lot had done (Gen. 19:23–30). Their escape route appears to go south, away from the invaders coming from the north. Luhith \... Horonaim. Unidentified cities probably close to Zoar (Jer. 48:3, 5, 34).
Possibly a seasonal stream southeast of the Dead Sea (Jer. 48:34).
Possibly the Zered River on the border between Moab and Edom (v. 8).
A city on the Arnon River. a lion. The fugitives go from trouble to trouble (cf. Amos 5:19) in their flight southward. They finally turn to Judah in the west for asylum (16:1–5).

The Moabites are shepherds (Num. 32:3, 4), and can send lambs as tokens of their submission (cf. 2 Kin. 3:4). from Sela. The fugitives are either at Sela, a naturally fortified site in Edom or at a mountain stronghold (Hb. sela means "rock," or "cliff"). The tribute is sent from their outpost to Judah. Zion. See note on 1:8.
The fugitives became refugees fleeing to the south (15:8, 9).
The prophet requests protection from the heat of the day.
Assyria.

God made a covenant with David (55:3; 2 Sam. 22:51; Ps. 89:28; see 54:8). In Jesus, the Son of David, the nations find shelter (Acts 15:16, 17). throne \... tent of David. Hope lies in the Lord and in His promises to David (9:2–7; 11:1–9; Amos 9:11, 12).
A delicacy associated with celebrations generally, and with pagan worship particularly (Hos. 3:1).
These places are not far apart (15:4; Jer. 48:32). vine. The imagery of the vineyard is applied here to Moab (cf. 5:1–7). Jazer \... the sea. Jazer is the extreme north of Moabite territory.
Isaiah is moved by the desolation of the fine vineyards for which Moab is well known. Elealeh. See 15:4.
Trampling the grapes is generally a time of great celebration (see Jer. 25:30).
Describes deeply felt sorrow (v. 9; 21:3, 4; cf. Jer. 48:36). See note on 15:5.
Often the sites of pagan sanctuaries.
spoke.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} This summary regarding Moab's distress is in prose form. Either it is a revelation in the past or a reference to the oracles in 15:1–9 or 15:1–16:12.

The desolation of Moab is at hand. Perhaps this is a reference to the quelling of the rebellion against Sargon, king of Assyria, around 715 B.C. like the years of a hired worker. Impatiently. glory. The prophetic word applies to all who exalt themselves and trouble the people of God. Salvation is in the Messiah (v. 5), but those who seek refuge for political or economic reasons will not find shelter in Zion.

This oracle of judgment concerning Damascus may be dated to the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734–732 B.C. 17:1 oracle. Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. Damascus. Besides being the capital of Syria, it is also the commercial hub along the trade routes between Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Arabia. Damascus is captured by Tiglath-pileser III in 732 B.C.
This city is located on the Arnon River (2 Kin. 10:32, 33). Syria's political control extends at times to the Arnon.

The "strong cities" (v. 9) of Israel are already weakened by 732 B.C. (9:1 note) and cease to exist in 722 B.C. The northern kingdom of Israel has allied itself with Syria against Judah (see 7:5, 6). remnant. Unlike Israel, Syria has no remnant. like the glory of the children of Israel. Normally, this would be a good thing. However, the following verses make plain that their former glory has been brought low.
A lush valley southwest of Jerusalem, it is the gateway to the western plains (Josh. 15:8; 18:16; 2 Sam. 5:18, 22; 1 Chr. 14:9).
Olive trees are beaten with sticks to shake loose the ripe fruit. Only a few olives on the topmost branches remain out of reach of the long staves.

The faithful remnant look to their Creator. The promise seems broader and more inclusive than one made simply to Israel, especially in a context relating judgment upon the nations (see 2:2–4). Maker. The prophet contrasts the works of God with those of His creatures. See note on 2:8.

The Canaanite goddess Asherah is a fertility goddess, symbolized by sacred groves and poles (27:9; Ex. 34:13; Deut. 16:21; Judg. 2:13). Incense altars are also often used in pagan worship (see Ezek. 6:6).

Describes apostasy (Deut. 4:9, 23; 8:11, 14, 19; 32:18). It is not simply a description of mental states but of actions that flow from those thoughts. Rock. See 8:14, 15; 26:4; Deut. 32:4. refuge. The Lord alone is the strength of His people (25:4; 27:5), in contrast to military and political solutions (v. 9; 23:11, 14; 30:2). the vine-branch of a stranger. Israel has worked diligently to cultivate relationships and alliances with her neighbors, as a farmer might cultivate an exotic seedling. Yet in the process they have forgotten the Lord, who is the nation's true refuge. As a result, all of this hard work will come to nothing.
Perhaps this alludes to a pagan practice in which potted plants are forced to sprout in order to secure fertile crops. harvest. The end will bring nothing but disaster.

The destructive power of the nations appears to be like that of the "seas" and "mighty waters" (8:7 note). In ancient Near Eastern myths, the sea represents chaos and death (Ezek. 28:2; 32:2 and notes). Yet the Lord is the one who truly thunders with power (Ezek. 1:24): when He acts, the seemingly-powerful nations are blown away before Him like chaff (see Ps. 1:4).
To be driven away as chaff (cf. 29:5; 41:15, 16; Ps. 83:13) reveals a lack of life, value, and stability. mountains. In Isaiah's day, grain is winnowed on windy hilltops.

An unforeseen series of troubles (24:17, 18) appears on the day of the Lord's wrath (22:5). The Lord still protects His people. He is "God with us" (8:10 note) who repays the nations for the evil done to His people. Yet none of this precludes the suffering of His people: on the contrary, the nations will only be crushed after they plunder Judah.

A cry of woe. See note on 1:4. land of whirring wings. This may mean either a land of "many insects" or "many ships" (so ancient translations). Lush lands are known for the quantity of their insect life. The frantic buzzing of the insects provides an image of the desperate diplomacy presented in these verses. Cush. The biblical Ethiopia is the remote region of southern Egypt and beyond, including Nubia, south of the fourth cataract of the Nile. The Nubian Shabako ruled over lower Egypt from 715 B.C. (twenty-fifth dynasty). His administration tried to extend his influence northward into the delta region.

Papyrus boats that the Nubians can use to send messengers to incite the nations to rebel against Assyria. a nation tall and smooth. Possibly refers to the impressive appearance of the nation or nations that the remote Nubians are trying to stir up. The specific nation is not identified, perhaps because the general hubbub of international diplomacy is in view here.

Those addressed in this oracle will observe what the Lord is doing. signal. See note on 5:26. Trumpets are also commonly used as signals in war during this era. The Lord is the one who gives the signal to begin this conflict.

The Lord patiently observes the rebellion of the nations (Ps. 2:1–4). clear heat \... cloud of dew. Expressive of the silent stillness as God waits to act, in contrast to the buzzing but fruitless activity of the nations (see 25:5).

These verses contain two images of God's judgment. First, there is the pruning of the vines before harvest to encourage the development of the grapes, "shoots," and "branches." Second, there is the carcass on which the "birds of prey" and the wild animals feed (cf. 31:5). For a body to be left unburied as food for the wild animals and birds is a sign of judgment.
The nations offer tokens of submission to the Lord (13:4 note; 16:1 note). tall and smooth. See v. 2 and note. the place. The temple is the OT sign of God's presence and reign (Deut. 12:5, 11).

An oracle of judgment concerning Egypt. In contrast to ch. 20, the language of ch. 19 is symbolic, not historically specific. 19:1 oracle. Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. the LORD is riding on a swift cloud. An ancient Near Eastern image of deity. The cloud forms the Lord's chariot-throne (see Pss. 18:10; 68:33). the idols of Egypt will tremble. The exodus represented the Lord's earlier victory over the gods of Egypt (Ex. 12:12).
Egypt spends much of the eighth century B.C. in civil war.
On idolatry and divination, see 2:6, 8; 8:19 and notes.
Egypt, too, will be subjugated; perhaps this is an allusion to Pharaoh's cruelty before the exodus (Ex. 6:9). LordGOD of hosts. See note on 1:9.

This spells economic disaster for a country whose life depends on the Nile. God can easily dry up Egypt's many waters (see Ezek. 30:12). This is also a direct assault on Pharaoh's claim, as a god, to regulate the flow of the Nile.
In the ancient world, Egypt served as the breadbasket of many countries because of the regular flooding of the Nile (Gen. 41:57).
God's judgment against Egypt falls on the important industries of fishing (v. 8) and flax products, for which ancient Egypt was famous.

The meaning of this Hb. word is uncertain. Some believe it is a metaphor for the nobles as the "foundation" of the society in contrast to those "who work for pay." Others suggest "weavers" of cloth. The point is that all aspects of the society will suffer greatly.

Also known as Tanis, this is a city in the Nile Delta (Num. 13:22; Ps. 78:12, 43) and Egypt's capital at the time. foolish. God turns the wisdom of the wise into folly. counselors \... stupid counsel. In contrast to the wise and effective counsel of the coming Branch; see 11:2. son of the wise, a son of ancient kings. This sarcastic remark taunts Egypt's claim to wisdom (cf. 1 Kin. 4:29–31).
These words addressed to Pharaoh continue to stand as a polemic against human pride (1 Cor. 1:20).
These include political, economic, and religious leaders. Memphis. This city in Lower Egypt is its ancient capital.
Judgment is frequently compared to drunkenness in the OT (Is. 51:21–23; Jer. 25:15, 16): a state of staggering and confusion that ends with vomiting, falling down, and being unable to get up.
Judgment will extend from the civil and religious leaders down to the bottom of society. See 9:14, 15.
For the hand of the Lord's judgment, see 14:26, 27.
Given the difference in their relative sizes, this is a remarkable prophecy. This will remove the temptation for Judah to seek military alliances with the Egyptians.

Not just one but five cities will turn to the Lord. language of Canaan. Shows how great a change is in view, because anything Canaanite is an abomination to the ancient Egyptians (Gen. 43:32; 46:34). swear allegiance to theLORD. Submit completely to God. City of Destruction. Probably refers to Heliopolis ("City of the Sun"; see text note). Jewish scribes parodied the name by changing the Hb. word for "sun" to the almost identical Hb. word for "destruction."

The altar (v. 19) signifies their commitment to the Lord (cf. Gen. 12:8; 28:22; Josh. 22:26–29), while the pillar will be a memorial commemorating God's great work (cf. Gen. 28:18–22). savior and defender. As in the days of the judges, God will fill these roles to deliver His people from oppressors (Judg. 2:18; 3:9, 15).
Divine discipline will draw the Egyptians to the Lord (30:26; Hos. 6:1; 14:1, 2, 4). If He can do these things for the Egyptians, how much more will He do for His own people?

Building this link between Egypt and Assyria symbolizes the removal of the alienation between them (cf. 11:16 note). Egypt to Assyria. These two great cultures find unity in a common commitment to the Lord. Since they are at opposite ends of ancient Israel's universe (Assyria in the north, Egypt in the south), the implication is that all of the other nations of the world will likewise be included in this hope-filled future.
Israel, Egypt, and Assyria will join in the patriarchal promises (Gen. 12:2, 3).

Each will share in full covenant membership, signified by three designations: "people" (cf. 10:24; 40:1 note; Ps. 100:3; Jer. 11:4; Hos. 2:23); "work of my hands" (60:21; Pss. 119:73; 138:8); "inheritance" (cf. Deut. 32:9).

Sargon II, king of Assyria from 722 to 705 B.C. Ashdod. This Philistine city rebels against Assyria at the encouragement of Shabako, the Nubian king (18:1 note) in 713 B.C. It falls in 711 B.C. An inscription mentioning Sargon by name has been unearthed at Ashdod. The lack of Egyptian help for her former allies serves as a potent lesson to all of the folly of relying on Egypt.

The Lord orders Isaiah to be partially clad like a prisoner of war going into exile. Sackcloth is a garment for times of mourning (15:3; 22:12; 37:1, 2; 58:5) and a distinctive prophetic garment (2 Kin. 1:8; Zech. 13:4). Several prophets perform similar kinds of sign-acts, designed to display their message in pictorial form, especially when their audience is hostile or unreceptive (cf. Ezek. 4).

Refers to a position of trust and honor before God. Moses was God's friend and servant (Ex. 14:31; Num. 12:7, 8; Deut. 34:5). Abraham (Ps. 105:42); Jacob (Ezek. 28:25); Joshua (Josh. 24:29); David (37:35; 2 Sam. 3:18; Ps. 132:10); the Suffering Servant (52:13–53:12); and groups of people such as the prophets (44:26) and restored Israel (41:8, 9; 43:10; 44:1, 2, 21; 45:4; 48:20) are also reckoned as the Lord's servants. God's servants may suffer, but they are promised a great heritage as servants of the Lord (54:17; 65:8, 9, 13–15; 66:14). three years. It could designate the time that Isaiah walks about as a sign or the duration before the sign will be realized. sign and a portent. The prophetic style of life (8:18; cf. Deut. 13:1, 2; Jer. 32:20) demonstrates the folly of relying on Egypt, for Egypt, like any nation, is vulnerable.
Esarhaddon fulfills this prophecy in 671 B.C.

Ashdod is one of the Philistine cities on the coastal plain. in that day. The day of judgment. See note on 2:11. in whom we hoped. Egypt's fate will persuade the people that no ally can help them escape.

Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. wilderness of the sea. This is probably a sarcastic parody. Babylon's southern region on the Persian Gulf, known as "Land of the Sea," will become a wilderness or as good as a wilderness to anyone looking for salvation from there. Neither the wilderness nor the sea is able to sustain life.

The prophet is overwhelmed by what he sees. betrays \... destroys. In the course of waging war, nations change sides and break former alliances. Elam \... Media. Elam is a major region of Persia and allies itself with Media in 700 B.C. Perhaps as a part of Assyria's army (5:26 note), Elam helps to conquer Babylon in 689 B.C. But Elam and her allies certainly conquer Babylon in 539 B.C. (11:11; 13:17 and notes). the sighing. Could refer to the groan of Babylon under Assyrian domination or to the groan of the nations under Babylonian control. The former is more likely because Babylon does not again become dominant in the region until 605 B.C.

The expressions in these verses convey great psychological suffering on the prophet's part (16:9–11; 22:4; cf. Dan. 8:27; 10:16, 17). The report of Babylon's fall may distress Isaiah because now no one can rescue Judah from Assyria. The image of a woman in labor is a common one in the prophets for extreme pain and anguish.
Prepare for battle.
Isaiah is God's watchman in Judah.
Probably signs of an approaching army.

Finally, the seductive power of Babylon, her religion (17:7–9; 27:9; 46:1–13), and her culture have come to an end (13:19). See Rev. 14:8; 18:2. all the carved images of her gods. Not only has Babylon been defeated but her gods as well (cf. 19:1).
Judah is portrayed as an oppressed people, much like the grain under the threshing sledge (28:27, 28; 41:15, 16; Amos 1:3). See note on 40:1.

Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. Dumah. An oasis in Edom at the intersection of the roads from the Red Sea to Palmyra and from the Persian Gulf to Petra. The name means "silence" or "stillness" in Hebrew, representing the future of the once bustling land of Edom. Seir. A significant mountain in Edom, which represents the whole land (cf. Ezek. 35). The Edomites ask the prophet what the future will hold.

The future holds both hope and judgment, specifically, relief from Assyrian domination followed by oppression from Babylon. However, the vagueness of the response implies that deliverance may yet be a long time in coming.

Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. concerning Arabia. In Hebrew this sounds like "at evening." Dedanites. Dedan is an oasis two hundred miles (320 km) south of Dumah (Ezek. 27:20; 38:13). For safety, they will pass the night in the thickets rather than in more conventional lodging places.

An oasis located ninety miles (145 km) north of Dedan (Jer. 25:23). The desert peoples provide food and water for the fugitives from the battle. The fact that fugitives appear in these remote locations is a sign of how intense the battle will be.

Arabia's glory will be directly affected by what happens in Babylon. according to the years of a hired worker. See note on 16:14. Kedar. Arabia, including Syria; the area inhabited by Bedouin tribes (Jer. 49:28, 29).

An oracle of judgment concerning the Valley of Vision, Jerusalem. The placement of an oracle concerning Jerusalem in the midst of oracles against foreign nations may be explained by the historical association of Jerusalem with Babylon. Jerusalem trusted in Babylon during the Assyrian hegemony, but ultimately was taken into captivity by her former ally. The occasion for this particular oracle may be Ashdod's rebellion and the Assyrian campaign in 711 B.C., or the lifting of the siege on Jerusalem after the devastation of Judah in 701 B.C. Much of it looks back on past events. 22:1 oracle. Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. valley of vision. May be intended as an insult, to the effect that the city built on a hill (2:1) is now a valley, and though they think they can see, they are actually blind. to the housetops. The Assyrians having left, the people gather on the housetops for purposes of socializing and celebrating (v. 13).
The noisy and excited citizenry has not seen what the prophet has seen. They have become complacent (32:13; Zeph. 2:15; 3:11). not slain with the sword. They have run away (v. 3).

The people were once governed by unreliable and selfish leaders who now have abandoned them to save their own lives (2 Kin. 25:4–6). The prophet is critical of human leadership and of people who have no understanding of what is happening around them (1:23–26; 3:13–15; 9:14–17; 19:13–15; 28:7–13; 29:15).
His sorrow is too deep for consolation. See note on 21:3, 4. The deliverance from Sennacherib is only a temporary reprieve from judgment, which will still come in the end.

The day of the Lord. See note on 2:11. tumult and trampling and confusion. A vivid description of desolation and destruction, providing a dramatic contrast to the joyful tumult of v. 2 (cf. 18:2, 7; Deut. 28:20; Ezek. 7:7; Amos 3:9; Zech. 14:13). battering down \... shouting. There is frenzied anxiety and screams of anguish.
See notes on 11:11; 21:2. These nations to the east of Babylon join Assyria in the siege of Jerusalem (5:26 note).
When the Lord removes His divine protection, all human preparations will prove useless. the House of the Forest. This is apparently a storeroom for weapons next to the temple (1 Kin. 7:2–5).

Jerusalem. lower pool. Possibly the pool of Siloam. Hezekiah put buildings around it to ensure that people in Jerusalem could reach it while at the same time denying access to enemies outside (Luke 13:4; John 9:7, 11).

Probably the Gihon Spring, also known as the "upper pool" (7:3; 36:2). did not look \... see him. While busying themselves with planning and fortifying Jerusalem, the people forgot the Lord. planned it long ago. God planned the future of Jerusalem when He determined long before to create it (37:26). No one can change His plan or avert His judgment.
Repentance would have been the appropriate response to the assault, but it was not forthcoming.

This is the spirit of revelry (v. 2). It should be contrasted with the proper joy of God's people (35:10; 51:11). wine. See 24:11. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. A proverbial expression of materialistic despair that sees no future beyond this life (1 Cor. 15:32; cf. Luke 12:19, 20).
God's judgment upon Jerusalem still stands (Amos 7:1–9). The sacrificial system does not cover unrepentant sin.

Isaiah questions Shebna's preparation of a royal tomb in the hillside. As steward over the royal household, Shebna holds an important position and should be providing leadership, not working on luxuries for himself. A tomb that may perhaps have been Shebna's, cut in the rock, has been excavated in the Kidron Valley.
This ironic expression challenges Shebna's presumption.

Shebna is insignificant and is readily overthrown (cf. Jer. 22:26). There you shall die. What good will an elaborate tomb be if Shebna dies in exile? chariots. Emphasizes Shebna's luxurious way of life.
By 701 B.C. Shebna is demoted to serve as secretary, and Eliakim assumes Shebna's office (36:3, 22).
See note on 20:3. God regards Eliakim (36:3, 11, 22; 37:2) as His servant, a special designation for one close to God.

Garments for a person in high office. It is ironic that proud Shebna will lose his high position and be replaced by someone who is content to be the Lord's servant. father. He will be a godly leader who serves the people well, unlike Shebna, whose only concern is his own interests.
The symbol of his authority as steward to oversee the royal house. Cf. Matt. 16:1; Rev. 3:7, 8.
The Lord is the one who strengthens and upholds His servants. throne of honor. He will bring honor to his family and offspring, in contrast to Shebna ("shame of your master's house," v. 18).
A metaphor for those who depend on God's servant.

Even though Eliakim is faithful, he will not avert God's judgment on Judah. No matter how godly their leaders happen to be, people should not place their faith ultimately in leaders who are merely human. Even godly leaders do not always succeed in their efforts.

An oracle of judgment concerning Tyre and commercial systems that do not take God into consideration (cf. Ezek. 27; 28). The language is general and symbolic, not historically specific. 23:1 oracle. Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. Tyre. A prominent Phoenician port on the Mediterranean. Judah has had a longstanding relationship with Tyre, for Solomon traded with Hiram of Tyre (1 Kin. 5:1, 8–11), and Phoenician sailors manned Solomon's fleet (1 Kin. 9:27). ships of Tarshish. These large vessels of the merchant fleet (1 Kin. 10:22; Ps. 48:7) traverse great distances to the Phoenician colonies along the Mediterranean coasts. is laid waste. The fall of Tyre will require the ships to find another port. Cyprus. A port of call on the return voyage.
Tyre and Sidon are the two most important Phoenician cities, both Mediterranean ports. The fall of one will affect the other.
The Nile valley of Egypt, which is famous in the ancient world for its grain exports (cf. 19:7).
The sea laments the loss or destruction of its children. Hearing this, Sidon should not be overconfident.
Tartessus in Spain (Jon. 1:3). The nations join in the lament.
Tyre is known for her revelry (22:2 note), origin, far-reaching influence, wealth, and fame (v. 8).

of hosts.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The Lord's military title. See 1:9 and note. purposed. Throughout his prophecy, Isaiah seeks to bring to light God's counsel (11:2 note). The Lord is against the proud and self-exalting.
Or perhaps "overflow your land." The Nile overflows its banks every year, leaving rich alluvial deposits that make the surrounding land suitable for farming.
God is Lord of land and sea. Canaan. Canaan includes Tyre and Sidon.
The inhabitants of Sidon (cf. 37:22; 47:1).
Another name for the Bab­ylonians. See note on 13:19. The Assyrians defeat Babylon in 689 B.C. Isaiah refers to the defeat as an example for Tyre.

A period of time ordained by God; "seventy" signifies fullness. It is not possible to determine the specific time to which the prophecy refers, but it is the same length of time prophesied for Judah's exile (Jer. 25:12). song of the prostitute. A street song concerning a prostitute.
Like an aging harlot, Tyre forms economic alliances with anyone who enriches her, regardless of ethics.

LORD. Tyre, too, will acknowledge the sovereignty of the Lord by paying tribute (Deut. 2:3–35; Josh. 6:17, 19). Normally the wages of a prostitute cannot be consecrated to the Lord (Deut. 23:18); here, the old prostitute will herself finally be sanctified. abundant food and fine clothing. The wealth of the nations builds up the kingdom of God (45:14; 60:5, 11; 61:6; 66:12; Hag. 2:7, 8).

This section is often called an "apocalypse," which is a genre in which something hidden is revealed, often filled with symbolism and having to do with cataclysm and judgment. The prophet holds before sinners and godly people the clear teaching that the day of the Lord brings judgment on creation and the fullness of salvation for the saints. God's plan of redemption includes restoration from exile, the blessings of Christ in the church, and the establishment of God's kingdom in all nations. Chapter 24 focuses on God's overthrow of the corrupted earth; ch. 25, on the praise that comes to Him in response; and chs. 26 and 27 on God's interaction with His people. Brilliant assonances, impossible to translate, enhance the prophetic message. 24:1 the LORD will empty the earth. This is not annihilation, but a situation in which human structures can no longer operate (v. 3). desolate. All human resources are removed (Nah. 2:10). twist its surface. The world is filled with disturbances and distresses; creation itself experiences the wrath of God (Lam. 3:9). scatter. God will judge the people more severely than He did at Babel, when He scattered them by confounding their languages (Gen. 11:8, 9).
God will judge everyone, without making social distinctions of inferior or superior.
A word of judgment. See note on 1:19, 20.
People in their pride elevate themselves above God (2:11, 12, 17).

The days of Noah will return to the earth (Gen. 6:5, 11–13). The earth itself is considered to be in danger of judgment due to the sins of those who live on it (Jer. 44:22; Rom. 8:20–22). Sin pollutes the surrounding environment. they have transgressed \... the everlasting covenant. This includes, but is not limited to, the covenant with Noah (Gen. 9:16). All of God's laws, written and unwritten, have been set aside and treated as worthless.

The consequence of breaking the covenant is receiving the curses attached to it. left. This Hb. word is also translated "survivors" (1:9) and "remnant" (10:20, 21). As in the days of Noah (Gen. 6:8, 18), "few" will remain.

The prophet explains what the universal day of the Lord will be like. There will be sorrow instead of laughter (vv. 8–11; cf. 22:2, 13 notes). The makers of music and song will stop in the middle of their act (cf. 5:12), while the alcoholic beverages associated with celebration will be set aside.

That is, the city of desolation or desolate city, made like the chaotic state of the world in Gen. 1:2 and unable to support life. It may possibly refer to Jerusalem, but in context it most likely means civilization in general. house. What used to be a place of private security and enjoyment of life (5:9; 6:11; 13:16, 21; 32:13) will be closed.
In addition to its role in celebrations, wine is also used to dull pain (see Prov. 31:6).
Olive trees are beaten to bring down the ripe fruit. See note on 17:6.

The new song is in response to God's act of salvation (cf. ch. 12; 35:6; 42:10–13; 44:23; 49:13; 52:8, 9; 65:14). See v. 16; note on 14:7. majesty. They sing of the greatness of the Lord as over against human pride.
A call to give God the recognition worthy of His name (25:3; 43:20; Ps. 22:23; Rev. 4:8–5:14). See note on 37:16.

The nations will also join in, from both the east and the west. But I. Isaiah, filled with tension as he looks forward to God's salvation, sees the corruption and devastation all around him and is unable yet to join in the universal hymn of praise. traitors. The Hebrew evokes a sense of widespread corruption. Deception is everywhere.

Those who escape one form of God's judgment will be caught in another. windows \... are opened. The judgment is like the flood, encompassing the whole inhabited world (cf. Gen. 7:11; 8:2). foundations \... tremble. The image of an earthquake is expanded in vv. 19, 20 and is an expression of a theophany (6:1 note; 13:13 note; Ps. 99:1 note).
Elsewhere, drunkenness is an image of God's judgment on nations (Is. 51:21–23; Jer. 25:15, 16). Here, the same image applies to the created order itself.
These include the gods of the nations, Satan's hosts, and human powers (cf. Eph. 6:11, 12). They are reserved for punishment and will be cast out from God's presence (2 Pet. 2:4; Rev. 17:8; 20:10).

See note on 13:10. Many of the ancient Near Eastern neighbors of Judah and Israel worship these as deities, but they are insignificant in comparison to the Lord of Glory. Zion. See note on 1:8. As those in Noah's ark found rest on Mount Ararat, so the remnant will find rest on Mount Zion. The elders who once led God's people astray (3:14; 9:14, 15) will be replaced by elders who govern wisely.

A personal affirmation of confidence in God, which is made all the more stark when compared with the sadness of 24:16 (7:13; 49:4, 5). exalt \... praise. The prophet speaks as representative of the people. See note on 12:1. wonderful things."Wonderful" in the sense of being "wonders" or "miracles": things that no one apart from God can do. faithful. See notes on 1:21; 11:5. The Lord is the sovereign king who makes plans and then faithfully carries them out.
In light of His wonderful acts of deliverance, the nations will be forced to acknowledge the Lord (24:14–16 and notes). ruthless nations. Oppressive, tyrannical nations. See notes on 19:24; 29:20.
See note on "refuge" at 17:10. poor \... needy. The object of the Lord's special care. See note on Ps. 9:18. shelter \... shade. God protects his people. See 4:6; 30:2.
Like "storm" in v. 4, this is a metaphor for oppression and persecution. ruthless. The oppressors, troublers, and seducers of God's people.

Isaiah envisions the grand banquet that will celebrate God's victory. 25:6 mountain. Zion, the mountain of the Lord (vv. 7, 10). See note on 2:2. for all peoples. The guests come from all nations (24:14–16; Rev. 14:6). rich food \... aged wine. Ps. 23:5; Matt. 8:11; Luke 13:29; Rev. 19:9. Part of each Israelite's annual tithe was devoted to feasting in the Lord's presence, foreshadowing this final banquet (see Deut. 14:22–26). The Lord's Supper serves a similar function for Christians.
Possibly refers to the grave as the covering for the dead.

Paradoxically, the devouring "mouth," from which no one can escape, will itself be swallowed up (5:14; Prov. 1:12 note). LordGOD. See note on 7:7. tears \... reproach. All mourning will be removed (30:19; 35:10; 61:2–5; Rev. 7:17; 21:4), even death and sin, which is the sting of death (1 Cor. 15:54).

The prophet identifies himself with the people of God (26:13; 40:3; 61:6). waited. See note on 8:17. To be able to say this in the future, of course, requires Isaiah's original hearers to wait patiently for the Lord in their present. The confident expectation of the Lord's final deliverance will help them as they wait. be glad \... salvation. See 12:1–3 and notes.

The hand of judgment (9:12 and note; 9:17, 21; 10:4). on this mountain. Zion. See note on v. 6. Moab. Here Moab represents all the proud nations, as does Edom in 34:5–17; 63:1–6; Obad. 1. in his place. May also be read "under Him," i.e., the Lord.
As Moab attempts to escape from the dunghill, he is depicted as trying to swim away. pride \... skill. See 5:21.

A new song of salvation. See note on 14:7. city. The city of God is the community of the redeemed (1:26; 2:2; 60:18 and notes; Pss. 46:4; 48:1–3, 12, 13; Rev. 21:2, 10). It is also the positive counterpart of the wasted city of 24:10. salvation as walls and bulwarks. Since God is with His people, He provides salvation and security (12:2 note). God is like a wall protecting His people from disgrace (49:16).

The gates open for the triumphant entrance of the glorious King and His people (Pss. 15; 24:7, 9; 118:19, 20), in contrast to the wasted city, where every house is closed up (24:10). the righteous nation. Cf. Isaiah's description of Judah as a sinful nation in 1:4.

The peace of God that the righteous receive and promote (v. 12; 32:17, 18; 55:12; 66:12) will not be extended to the wicked (48:22; 59:8). This peace is found in Immanuel (9:6; 11:6–9; 14:7 and notes). As the previous chapters make clear, it is not a peace that stems from the absence of difficulties; rather, it is a peace that guards their hearts and minds in the midst of great trials. stayed \... trusts. See 2:22; 8:12, 17.
See 8:14, 15; cf. 1 Sam. 2:2. Cf. the shattered earth in 24:19.
As Nebuchadnezzar discovered (Dan. 4:37).
Those whom the Lord protects (see 25:4).

This statement is a magnificent expression of what God desires: children who do His will, love Him, and wait trustingly for His full salvation. Though they are poor and needy, what they most desire is the Lord Himself, not merely deliverance from their problems.
God's common grace (Matt. 5:45; Luke 6:35) is evidenced in His blessings in nature, procreation, health, and prosperity (Acts 14:17).
The hand of judgment (9:12 and note; 9:17, 21; 10:4; 25:10). fire. See note on "burning" at 4:4.
See note on v. 3.
God's people have been subject to foreign powers, but the Lord remains their only true King.
Notice the contrast with v. 19 (cf. 14:22, 30). remembrance. Their names, dynasty, and memorials are forgotten.
Describes the experience of restoration in earthly terms, fostering hope in the final restoration (9:3; 54:2).

This expression of futility is due to the failure of the godly to establish God's kingdom (49:4). They have suffered like a woman in labor, but without the fruit of bearing a child. deliverance in the earth. The hope of God's people both before and after the coming of Christ is the renewal of the earth and its transformation into a kingdom of peace and righteousness (cf. 12:2 note; 42:4; 2 Pet. 3:13).

This message of hope for the future of "your dead" contrasts with v. 14, which declares the demise of their oppressors (cf. Ezek. 37:11, 12). The OT expresses faith in the resurrection of the body since death is an invasion of God's created order (25:8 note; Job 19:26; Pss. 49:15; 73:24–26; Dan. 12:2; Hos. 13:14).

The remnant (vv. 7–9; 40:1 note). enter \... hide. As He protected Noah behind doors of safety (Gen. 7:16), so here God protects His own as they await His salvation. a little while. This "little while" is as long as God's judgment lasts. The present suffering is not worthy to be compared to the eternal glory that follows (v. 19; 54:7; Ps. 30:5; 2 Cor. 4:17; 2 Pet. 3:9). fury. See 10:5 and note.

The day of judgment. See note on 2:11. Leviathan \... dragon. The OT employs this image of a multiheaded serpent to denote evil, autocratic powers (Ps. 74:14; Is. 30:7 note; 51:9; Ezek. 28:2; 32:2 and notes) and to assure the godly that the Lord will punish all such human expressions of power and resistance to His kingdom. Behind earth's tyrants is Satan, and behind the elect is Christ (Gen. 3:15; Rom. 16:20; Rev. 12:1–6). The threefold description of the Lord's sword matches the threefold description of the monster, and thus assures us of the Lord's victory.
Portrays the coming transformation. 27:2–6 This song of the vineyard sharply contrasts the parable of the fruitless vineyard in 5:1–7. For the vine and vineyard, see 3:14; 61:5; 65:21.
He provides for all of their needs by His blessing and steadfast protection of His people (cf. Ps. 121:4, 5).

The Lord is ready to forgive and to reconcile people to Himself. Would that I had thorns. Enemies or difficulties simply serve to provide the Lord with opportunities to show His love and care for His people. burn. See note on 4:4.
God welcomes all who are reconciled to Him (26:3).

Indicators of a good and productive vine (John 15:1–8). the whole world. The people of God (Jew and Gentile) make up the kingdom of God (1 Pet. 2:9–12). Israel's blessing will mean blessing for all (Rom. 11:12).

The Lord has dealt more graciously with His people than with their oppressors. God fatally struck the nations, but even though Israel has been judged, the nation will be restored (10:5–23; 13:19–14:2; 47:4, 5).
The east wind brought dust and scorching heat from the desert, destroying vegetation. Here it is a metaphor for God's wrath (cf. Jer. 18:17).

By undergoing God's discipline (v. 7), Jacob — i.e., Israel — will pay its debt to divine justice for its idolatry. The proof that the discipline has been effective will be the destruction of the places where the people have worshiped idols. This atonement and new obedience illustrates on a national level what Christ accomplishes in a perfect way on behalf of a greater number (John 11:52). Asherim. Sacred trees used in pagan worship. See note on 17:8.
The city of man, which is under God's judgment (26:1 note).

The mighty city will become as brittle as dried-out branches. people without discernment. The city is inhabited by foolish idolaters (2:8 note; Rom. 1:20–23). he who made. The Lord created them. See note on 22:11. he who formed. A frequent designation of God as creator, ruler, and redeemer of His people. The verb denotes planning ("purposed"; 46:11); authority, as of an artisan over his materials (41:25); creation and providence (45:18); and the formation of a new people (43:1, 21; 44:2, 21; 49:5; 64:8). favor. The undeserved grace of God (26:10; 30:18, 19; 33:2).

Can refer to separating grain (by flailing the stalks; Ruth 2:17) or olives (by beating the branches; Deut. 24:20). It is frequently used as a metaphor for separating and gathering God's people from the world. river \... Brook. That is, the Euphrates and the Wadi el-Arish, defining the boundaries of the territory of Canaan given by promise to Abraham (Gen. 15:18). Assyria and Egypt will be connected by a highway (11:16; 35:8, 9) that leads from both to Jerusalem. God's people who have been scattered to exile in different locations (see v. 8) will once again be united in worship of the one God in Jerusalem.

Like the banner (11:10), the trumpet is used for summoning troops (Ex. 19:16, 19; 1 Sam. 13:3; 2 Sam. 6:15; Matt. 24:31; 1 Thess. 4:16). lost. Possibly refers to the oppressed and scattered remnant (Jer. 50:6; Ezek. 34:4–6), to the dead (25:8; 26:14, 19), or to both. mountain. Zion (2:2 note), the place of God's throne (14:13) and His blessed presence (25:6, 7). These promises are both already realized (e.g., Heb. 12:22) and still to come (e.g., Rev. 21:2, 3).

An oracle of woe on the occasion of Ephraim's fall (722 B.C.). This is the first of six sections of woes (1:4 note) in chs. 28–33 (28:1; 29:1, 15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1). 28:1 proud. Human arrogance stands in opposition to the "majesty" (same Hb. word) of the Lord (26:10). crown. A symbol of royalty (Ezek. 21:26) or deity (2 Sam. 12:30), or if translated "wreath," a sign of social status or celebration (e.g., a garland worn at a wedding; Song 3:11). The reference is to Samaria and its debauched leadership. Israel is like a fading flower, soon to fall. drunkards \... wine. See 24:11.

Assyria. hail \... waters. Elsewhere in Isaiah, Assyria is frequently likened to a powerful storm that the Lord is bringing upon His people (7:2; 17:13; 28:17; 29:6; 30:30; 32:19). For God's protection, see 4:6.

The June figs are delightful because they foreshadow the September harvest (Hos. 9:10; Mic. 7:1; Nah. 3:12). Because only a few appear, they are certain to be picked and eaten. Ephraim, with all her possibilities of achievement, will be exiled, and the fruit of her labors will be enjoyed by the Assyrians.

The day of judgment. See note on 2:11. crown of glory. Unlike Ephraim's trampled crown (v. 3), the Lord will be an enduring crown for the faithful remnant of His people. remnant. The Lord promises to preserve his people. See note on 1:9; cf. 10:19–23.

As such, He will be the Spirit of transformation (32:15; 44:3–5; 59:21; 61:1). See notes at 4:4; 11:2. Paul also contrasts being drunk with wine to the work of the Spirit (Eph. 5:18). The "spirit of justice" prevails in the messianic age (11:1–5; 42:1–4). justice. See note on 1:21.
See v. 1; 24:11. priest and the prophet. The leaders of God's people have become sensual, hard of heart, and confused (29:9–14; cf. Zeph. 3:4).
The leaders speak these words against Isaiah, mocking his oracles of judgment as being baby talk, too simple for their subtle and advanced minds to stoop to heed.

The foreign language of the oppressors (33:19; Jer. 5:15). Since the Israelites have failed to heed the clear warnings of the prophet in their own language, the Assyrians will become Israel's teachers in spite of their harsh and convoluted foreign speech. For Paul's application of the verse to "speaking in tongues," see 1 Cor. 14:21, 22.

Israel could not enter the full rest in Canaan (Deut. 12:9) because of unbelief (Ps. 95:11). The hope for rest lies in the promises to Moses (1 Kin. 8:56) and to David (Ps. 132:8, 14, 17). Instead of enjoying the rest that comes by faith, Israel will be punished by her enemies.

LORD. This revelation will come to Israel through the discipline of foreigners, who will teach Israel the simple and basic lesson of sin and judgment that they have refused to heed from the lips of Isaiah. precept upon precept. Isaiah throws the taunts of the religious leaders (v. 10) back at them. fall backward. The word of God through the prophet will have a hardening effect on many of its hearers, leaving them confirmed in their unbelief, as the Lord warned Isaiah in 6:10.
The foolish and wicked rulers of the southern kingdom, Judah, who are following the same path as their northern counterparts.

They have chosen to ally themselves with Egypt for the purpose of remaining independent (30:2), but the choice is deadly, as if they have made a pact with Sheol itself. lies \... taken shelter. Their confidence is false; the Lord is the true shelter for His people, not Egypt (4:6 note).

GOD. See note on 7:7. stone \... sure foundation. See note on 8:14, 15. The sure foundation is Jesus Christ (cf. Ps. 118:22; Rom. 9:33; 10:11; 1 Cor. 3:11; Eph. 2:20; 1 Pet. 2:4–8). This is the only solid and sure refuge in the day of distress (see 4:6). not be in haste. The decision of Isaiah's original audience to make an alliance with Egypt was hasty and futile; deciding to trust in the Lord is the opposite.
See note on 1:21. The plumb line defines what is true and upright. hail \... waters. See note on v. 2.

The Assyrian army marched through Israel many times. terror. Divine judgment in human history brings people face-to-face with God's power. to understand the message. The people have been deliberately blind to the prophet's words of judgment (vv. 7–13).
The things people depend on for safety are neither adequate nor comfortable.

In the past the Lord struck the Philistines (2 Sam. 5:19, 20) and the Canaanites (Josh. 10:10) at these places. work \... alien. It goes against the way things should be for the Lord to turn against His own people.
Judah (v. 14) should heed the prophet's words and repent while there is still time. decree. God ordains the events of history. See 10:22, 23.
As timing is important for success in farming, so God has times for grace and for judgment. 28:23 Give ear \... hear. The prophet issues the call of divine wisdom (1:2; Prov. 1:8; 4:1; 5:1).
Probably rye (Ex. 9:32). The comparison follows the natural order of plowing, breaking up the clods, harrowing, and sowing (vv. 24, 25).
The wise farmer pays attention to the Lord's lessons in the natural world. Likewise, should not Judah learn His ways in judgment and salvation?
The different grains require different treatment; the Lord adjusts His judgment to circumstances and does not "plow continually" (v. 24).

See note on 11:2. The scoffing rulers foolishly mock the one who is wonderful in counsel (cf. 9:6 note). Yet the Lord is wiser than any good farmer (see v. 26) and knows exactly the methods to use to cultivate His harvest — when to judge and when to restore His people.

An oracle of woe against Jerusalem. As the text note indicates, "Ariel" may mean "altar hearth," which would refer to Jerusalem's role as home of the temple (see v. 2). 29:1 Ah. An exclamation of woe. See note on 1:4. David. Jerusalem's status as the city of God arose out of David's occupation of it and his act of bringing the ark of the covenant there (cf. Ps. 132). year \... feasts. Points out the repetitious and tiring observance of empty rituals. Even though God commanded these observances, if the people perform them merely by rote, they are useless. See note on 1:11–15.
That is, like an altar hearth where the sacrifices are consumed by fire.
God refers to Assyria's siege of Jerusalem in 701 B.C., but makes it clear that He Himself is the true enemy that assaults His people.
Like the voice of a ghost, as if Jerusalem has died. These images describe Jerusalem's experience of humiliation (2:10; 8:19).
See note on v. 20. suddenly. Jerusalem's fortunes will instantly change when the Lord turns from being their enemy to become their deliverer.
The language of theophany. Nature rages when the Lord of the heavenly armies appears (cf. Ex. 19:16–19; Judg. 5:4, 5; Ps. 18:7–15; Ezek. 32:6–8 note).
The downfall of Judah's adversaries will be so rapid that their earlier menace will seem like a bad dream.

Even this astonishing act of judgment and deliverance will not open the blind eyes of Judah's leaders or soften the hard hearts of the people. Even though they have not been drinking, they are as out of touch with reality as if they were drunk.
See note on 30:10.

If a document is sealed, it doesn't matter whether someone can read. Likewise, when the Lord has closed someone's eyes (see 6:10), it doesn't matter whether that person claims spiritual knowledge or is ignorant.
God desires expressions of devotion from the heart and hates empty and insincere ritual (see Matt. 15:8, 9; 1 Cor. 1:19; Col. 2:20–23).
God will shatter human wisdom and planning, overturning the normal and expected course of events with miraculous interventions (30:1–5; 31:1–3).

This oracle of woe against Jerusalem's sages begins the third section of woes in chs. 28–33 (28:1–13 note). 29:15 counsel \... deeds. They oppose the plans and works of God (11:2 note; Pss. 10:11; 64:5, 6). They try to manipulate God rather than submit to Him, and they claim that the Lord does not see or know what they are doing (cf. Ps. 73:11).

The forests of Lebanon will become fields, and fields will become forests. Judgment brings about such reversals; "the last will be first, and the first last" as a demonstration of God's sovereign power in salvation (Matt. 20:16; Luke 1:52, 53; John 9:39).

The day of judgment. See note on 2:11. deaf \... blind. These words are used here as figures for the people's former spiritual conditions. The "deaf" are those formerly deaf to the message of God (42:18, 19; 43:8; cf. 6:10; 29:9). The "blind" formerly wandered from and did not discern the ways of God (42:7, 16; 56:10; 59:10; Lam. 4:14). The restoration of the spiritually deaf and blind is fulfilled today in Christ (61:1; see Matt. 11:5). book. See notes on vv. 11, 12.
See Ps. 9:18 note. the Holy One of Israel. See note on 1:4.

The powerful and tyrannical oppressors of this world (13:11; 25:3–5; 29:5; 49:25; cf. Pss. 37:35; 86:14; Ezek. 28:7; 30:11; 32:12). scoffer. Common in Wisdom Literature, this term designates a hardened and cynical person (28:14; Ps. 1:1; Prov. 1:22; 3:34; 9:7, 8; 21:24). watch to do evil. Such a person is identified in v. 21.
The gate is the place where legal cases are heard and justice rendered. The wicked are undermining that system of justice.

God accomplished redemption for Abraham by election and by covenant, in spite of his failures, promising him and his descendants the hope of the divine presence (cf. Josh. 24:14; Acts 7:2–4). The Lord will faithfully fulfill those promises. ashamed. Humiliated in defeat.

Jacob's hope lies in God's gracious dealing with his offspring from generation to generation (49:20–22; 54:1, 13; 65:23). They will be transformed from offering meaningless worship to having a true awe for the Lord, from being blind and deaf to accepting instruction.

A cry of woe. See note on 1:4. stubborn children. Hezekiah's counselors (cf. 1:2 note). carry out a plan. The Hebrew can be translated "weaving a web" or "pouring out libations." Either refers to making political alliances. not of my Spirit. Their human plans (v. 2) oppose the plans of the Spirit of God. They are trusting in human resources such as horses and chariots rather than in the Lord. add sin to sin. Stubbornness is increasing (1:2–4) from the plan to act independently of God to the sin of injustice (v. 12; 10:1–4 notes).

In 701 B.C. Judah counted on Egyptian troops for help against Sennacherib (20:5, 6; 2 Kin. 8:21). This was a perennial temptation for God's people. shadow. God alone provides His people with protection from danger (4:6; 16:3; 25:4, 5; 51:16; cf. Pss. 17:8; 36:7; 91:1; 121:5).

The Lord promises to deliver those who trust in Him (54:4; 61:7) from this experience of utter failure.Relying on human resources is not only ineffective in the day of distress, but it is a shameful denial of the Lord.
Possibly Judah's ambassadors who went to Zoan (19:11 note) and to Hanes. Hanes is either a major city fifty miles (80 km) south of Cairo or the name of the palace in Zoan.

Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. a land of trouble and anguish \... fiery serpent. The wilderness, through which Judah's emissaries have to travel to get to Egypt, contained many dangers. In fact, during the wilderness wanderings, the Lord safely brought His people through precisely these dangers (Deut. 8:15). Why make the risky journey again, at great expense, to solicit help from a worthless ally, when the Lord stands ready to deliver them from all dangers?

The name "Rahab" alludes to a chaos monster defeated by the gods in Canaanite creation mythology (Ezek. 28:2 and note). The prophet mocks both the mythical monster and Egypt with a title meaning roughly "Rahab, who does nothing."
The oracles concerning the folly of dependence on Egypt are to be written down as a witness to future generations. The Lord's ability to predict the future is a key proof of His power (see 44:7, 8).
See 1:2. instruction. The law that they are rejecting is the godly wisdom taught by Isaiah (cf. Prov. 2:1–5).

The preaching of many prophets conforms to the expectations of the people, who preferred to hear "smooth things" (9:15; 28:7; 29:10; 44:25; 1 Kin. 22:8; Jer. 6:14; 14:13–16; 20:9, 10; 28:8, 9; Ezek. 13; Hos. 9:7–9; Amos 2:12; 7:12, 16; Mic. 2:6–11; 3:5, 11). Others, like Isaiah, spoke by inspiration of the Spirit and under compulsion of a divine vision, and were often unpopular as a result.
See note on 1:4.

Even though they refused to listen to God's prophets, they will still hear from Him words of judgment. word. That is, the word of God through Isaiah (vv. 8, 9). oppression and perverseness. Jerusalem's leaders are unprincipled, and their diplomacy has resulted in oppression.

Their stubborn resistance to the Lord and dependence on Egypt will bring about their downfall. a high wall, bulging out. Ezekiel likewise compares the false prophets to a wall about to collapse and fall on the people who trust in them (Ezek. 13:9–12).
See Jer. 19:1–12.

GOD. See note on 25:7. the Holy One of Israel. The one they want to hear no more about in v. 11. rest \... quietness. The Lord can give His people what they have searched for in Egypt, if they will just repent and return to Him, quietly trusting in His power to deliver them. be saved \... strength. The Lord is the strength of His people, and He will be victorious (12:2 note).
They depend on military strength and stratagems (2:7 note; 31:1, 3). Yet others may have a stronger military and better strategy.
This is a reversal of God's promise to give His people victory and a sign that they are under the covenant curse (Lev. 26:7, 8; Deut. 32:30; Josh. 23:10).

waits.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The Lord is patient with His people even when they resist Him and run away. He is compassionate as well as just. justice. God upholds His kingdom in His patience (1:21 note).

See notes on 25:7, 8; cf. Rev. 7:17; 21:4. as soon as he hears it. Like the father of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32), the Lord is quick to listen for the voice of His returning people. It is they who are hard of hearing.
For God's instruction, see 28:11–13; 29:11, 12. After the difficulties and shortened rations of His judgment, they will once again see His salvation (29:24).

On Isaiah's polemic against idolatry, see 2:8. When God becomes their teacher, they will throw away their former idols. defile. Desecrate (2 Kin. 23:4–8). unclean things. Lit. "menstrual cloths," which are defiled and defiling according to the law of Moses because of their contact with a loss of human blood (cf. Lev. 15:19–24).

These blessings will come in response to the repentance apparent in the preceding verses (v. 20; cf. Deut. 28:11, 12), and be in sharp contrast to the bread of adversity that was their former food (see v. 20). Even the oxen and donkeys will dine on rich fare rather than the normal hay. In that day. The day of judgment. See note on 2:11.

Previously the home of pagan worship sites (see Jer. 3:6). Now there will be rivers flowing from them, like the river that flows from the heavenly temple (cf. Ps. 46:4; Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13). day of the great slaughter. The day of the Lord (cf. 34:2, 6; Jer. 12:3; 19:6; 46:10; Zeph. 1:7, 8). towers. Symbols of human pride (2:12–17).

Here the exaggerated figure indicates that the light of God's presence is with His people (2:5 note; 42:16; 60:19; Rev. 21:22, 23). binds up \... heals. God disciplines, but He remembers and heals the wounds of His people (19:22; 57:18; 61:1; Ps. 147:3; Jer. 3:22; 30:17; but cf. Is. 6:10).
LORD. The covenant name represents God (12:2 note; cf. Ex. 3:14). lips \... tongue. Isaiah uses the resources of poetry to depict the angry power of God to judge and to direct the nations.
This celebration is like that of pilgrimage feasts, which are famous for their singing and dancing (see v. 32). mountain. See note on 2:2.
The expensively purchased Egyptians will not fight, but the Lord will.

Hb. "Topheth." A pit on the south side of Jerusalem where children have been sacrificed and a continual fire burned to consume the refuse that was thrown there (57:5; 2 Kin. 23:10; Jer. 7:31, 32; 19:6, 11–13). the king. All human powers and authorities, including the king of Assyria.

Judah thinks that she will be delivered by Egyptian horses and chariots (30:2). Even if Egypt were to supply these resources, Judah would be placing her trust in the wrong refuge (see Ps. 20:7). look to. One way of seeking the Lord is to consult His prophets (29:9, 10; 30:1). the Holy One of Israel. See note on 1:4.
This prophetic sarcasm ridicules the royal counselors: the Lord's wisdom will prevail over all so-called human wisdom. disaster. He is sovereign in judgment (45:7).
