This model of poetic parallelism contrasts flesh and spirit, creature and Creator (2:22; Ps. 56:4; John 4:24). The chariots and horses of the Lord always prevail over human enemies (see 2 Kin. 6:15–17).
The Lord is as determined as a lion, and He is not scared away by human adversaries. Assyrian kings likened themselves to lions, proverbial for their strength and ferocity.
The Lord cares for His people like a mother bird (Ex. 19:4; Deut. 32:11, 12). Can Egypt make the same claim of dependability and care? God's faithfulness ought to lead the people to repentance.
The day of judgment. See note on 2:11. idols \... hands. On Isaiah's polemic against idolatry, see 2:8.
Assyria will come to an end by God's hand and at His time, not by human stratagems (37:36).

Assyria will look for a place to hide (Rev. 6:16). This prospect must seem unthinkable to the nations at the height of Assyria's power and military domination. fire \... furnace. See 4:4, 5 and notes; 10:17; 30:27, 30, 33.

The peace and harmony of godly leadership. 32:1 king \... princes. The Messiah (9:1–7; 11:1–9) and godly leaders (1:26; 1 Pet. 5:2). Reigning in righteousness is a far cry from the kind of leadership the people are used to (1:21; 5:7).
The protective role of the king and his cohorts results from their dependence on the Lord (4:6 note), in contrast to any reliance on Egypt (30:1, 2, 12; 31:1, 3).
This is in dramatic contrast to 6:9, 10; 29:9, 10; 30:1, 2; 31:1. The people will be transformed. See note on 29:18.
The fulfillment of 29:24.
One effect of spiritually blind eyes being opened is that they see clearly the distinction between good and evil, wisdom and folly (cf. Eccl. 10:16, 17).
Bad leaders do not care about the needs of the people and so leave them hungry and thirsty.
See note on Ps. 9:18.
He stands in contrast to the fool, who is willing to oppress the needy (vv. 5–7).

The people are confident of succeeding in their schemes. One aspect of this is the rise of a class of wealthy and foolish women, who live off the labor of others and complacently close their eyes to the needs of the community (vv. 5–7; cf. 3:16–24; Amos 6:1; Zech. 1:15). complacent. The same Hb. word is rendered "trust" in v. 17 and "secure" in v. 18. The false security based on their confidence in Egypt and on the wealth of their households contrasts with the true security based on trust in God.
Poor harvest is an indication of God's judgment; their affluent lifestyle is about to come to an end.
Signs of mourning and sorrow.
Everything will become a wasteland (cf. 5:5, 6; 16:8–10; 24:7–13; 34:13–15). Thorns and briers result from the covenant curse (see 7:23). exultant city. See notes on 22:2, 13.

The Holy Spirit transforms everything according to God's order. He is the Spirit of renewal and restoration. See 11:2; 28:6; 42:1; 61:1; Ezek. 36:27; Joel 2:28, 29. from on high. The Spirit is above all earthly powers (Ps. 93:4; Luke 24:49; Eph. 4:8). wilderness \... forest. See note on 29:17. Just as fruitful land becomes barren under God's curse, so His blessing can make the barren land blossom.
See note on 40:1.
See note on 28:2. God is going to judge the "forest" of Assyria (see 10:18).

This sixth and final oracle of woe in chs. 28–33 is against Assyria. By focusing on Assyria's defeat and Judah's exaltation, the Lord, the King of Judah, is exalted. 33:1 destroyer \... betrayed. Though the reference is to Assyria in the historical context (cf. 10:5, 12, 24; 14:25; 30:31; 31:8; 2 Kin. 18:13–16; 19:32–37), the metaphor of the destroyer represents any power opposed to God.

This verse begins a prayer for mercy during the hour of judgment. Isaiah models the patience and trust to which he called the people (see 30:15). Rather than looking to the arm of Egypt, he looks daily for the arm of the Lord.
See Num. 10:35.
The spoils go to the Lord, victor over the nations (23:18).
See note on 32:15.

See note on 12:2. Zion's treasure. See text note. Probably the meaning is that the best gift a person can receive from God is the pure faith that is formed in response to the revelation of God's grace (Ps. 130:4; Prov. 9:10; Luke 5:10). This is a treasure that cannot rot or fade away, and that no thieves or invading armies can steal.

With all of Judah's false hopes gone (vv. 7–9), the Lord acts to destroy Assyria. 33:7 heroes. Perhaps this sarcasm is directed at the three officials who have conversed with Assyria (36:3, 22). cry \... weep. Human ploys have failed. International trade, diplomacy, and military expeditions have come to an end. The Assyrians have accepted gifts and tribute from Judah, but they treacherously continue their siege.
Probably a reference to Assyria's commitment to leave Judah in return for receiving tribute, which it has not kept.
Areas famous for their fertility have become like deserts (2:13; 29:17; 32:13 and notes). For the transformation, see 35:1, 2.
The time for divine intervention and the glorious establishment of His kingdom has arrived.
An image of hard work and toil that brings no reward.
These similes explain how completely Assyria will be destroyed (cf. 27:4; Amos 2:1).

People will confess that God's judgments in history are wise and powerful, and they will submit to His sovereignty. far off \... near. See 57:19. These statements include all people no matter their nation or tribe. All will see the greatness of God's glory and power.
This realization by sinners challenges them to repent and live in harmony with God's holy presence (Pss. 15:1; 24:3). consuming fire. See Heb. 12:29.

These phrases describe conduct of the godly (Pss. 1:1, 2; 15:2–5; 24:4; Gal. 5:22–25; Eph. 5:1; James 3:13–18). There is a fitting godliness that marks out the people of God, with whom He is pleased to dwell. bribe. Bribery leads to injustice and oppresses the poor. See note on 1:23.
With God. fortresses \... water. He enjoys divine protection (cf. Ps. 18:1–3) and provision (49:10; 55:1, 2; 62:9; 65:13; cf. 30:20).

The arrival of God's kingdom and Messiah will be of greater splendor than any previous manifestation (32:1 note). For the wicked, the coming of the king is something to be dreaded (see v. 14), but for the godly it is their greatest longing.

Isaiah describes the misery of exile from home and oppression by foreigners, which on the day of the Lord's appearing provides reasons for thankfulness and relief among the godly. For the speech of foreigners, see 28:11.
The exile has ended. Jerusalem enjoys stability and prosperity (54:2; cf. Rev. 21:1–3).
God provides for all the needs of the citizens of His kingdom (41:18; 48:18). galley \... majestic ship. The kingdoms of this world can no longer intimidate and harass God's people.
See notes on 2:4; 12:2; cf. 44:6; 51:4; Pss. 46; 48; 96–99; Zeph. 3:15, 17. As their true judge and lawgiver, as well as their savior-king, the Lord provides the justice for which the people long.

In contrast to the eternally solid tent cords of future Jerusalem (v. 20), in their present state the people of the Lord are compared to a drifting ship with loose and ineffective ropes. In the future, though, even the weakest people will share the spoils of victory.
See note on v. 14. Those who dwell in the renewed Zion will do so not because of their personal righteousness but because they have been forgiven their iniquity.

See notes on 5:25; 10:5. Those who oppose the Lord face His judgment. devoted them to destruction \... slaughter. They are consigned to complete destruction through holy war, as the Canaanites were (Josh. 6:17). In ch. 34, the fate of the nations in general, and Edom in particular, form a dramatic contrast to the future of God's people in ch. 35. Judgment forms the dark backdrop against which God's deliverance of His own shines all the more brightly.
The blood of the slain will be so great it will create mudslides (v. 7). This is imagery of the day of the Lord on earth (cf. Ezek. 39:4).
See Heb. 1:10–12; 2 Pet. 3:12. As the Lord stretched out the heavens at creation (42:5), in the end He will roll them up (Mark 13:24, 25; Rev. 6:13).
The Lord's avenging sword moves from demolishing the pantheon of heaven to Edom in particular. Edom. Represents the nations who oppose God's people (63:1–6; Ezek. 35; Obad. 10–14; cf. Rev. 18:2).

See Rev. 19:15. lambs \... goats \... rams. Sacrificial animals. In some OT sacrifices, the animals take the place of sinful people in receiving the punishment of death for sin. In the absence of a sacrifice for the nations, the people themselves must die for their sins. Bozrah. An important city in Edom thirty miles (48 km) southeast of the Dead Sea.
Refer to the Edomite leaders.

The day of the Lord is the time when the Lord establishes His kingdom on earth by delivering and glorifying His saints as well as by punishing the wicked and the oppressors of His children (2:11 note; 35:4; 59:17, 18; 61:2; 63:4).
Alludes to the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:24–28; Ps. 11:6; Jer. 49:17, 18; Rev. 14:10, 11). Burning fire is a common image in the Bible for the enduring fate of the wicked.
God's judgment is everlasting (66:24; Matt. 18:8, 9; 25:41, 46; Mark 9:43, 48).

See note on 14:23, where the ESV translates the word for "porcupine" as "hedgehog." In the context of this verse, a kind of bird seems more likely, perhaps a bittern. The land will be left empty of life, except for a few birds. confusion \... emptiness. The same Hb. words are rendered "without form and void" in Gen. 1:2. God has decreed the desolation of powers that oppose His order. He will bring disorder on those who have wreaked havoc with His order. The measuring line was often used in construction projects but could also be used for the demolition that preceded such new beginnings.
Aspects of the covenant curse (5:6 note).
Possibly an owl.
LORD. Probably the prophecy of vv. 1–15. The Spirit will ensure the fulfillment of the prophetic announcement. The mouth of the LORD has commanded. See 40:5.
As God distributed the Promised Land by lot (Josh. 18:10), so He has divided Edom among the unclean animals (v. 11). Even seemingly random events in history are under the Lord's control.

See note on 40:3. The presence of God's Spirit of restoration transforms nature and people, renewing that which has been corrupted by sin (32:15 note). This sharply contrasts the previously cultivated land of Edom, which is now a wilderness (ch. 34). Trusting in the nations makes a fruitful land barren, but trusting in the Lord makes a barren land fruitful. the crocus. A desert flower that blooms with the coming of rain every spring, possibly an asphodel. See Song 2:1.

Areas known for their rich forests, which serve as symbols of abundance (see 33:9). our God. For the revelation of God's kingdom, see notes on 6:3; 33:17, 21. The real glory belongs to the Lord, not to the most fruitful places on earth.
The issue is fear, not merely tiredness (cf. Ezek. 7:14–18).

This admonition often occurs as an assurance of deliverance from oppressors (7:4; 8:12 note; 10:24; 37:6; 41:10, 13; 43:5; 51:7). vengeance \... save. God will bring complete deliverance to the oppressed and establish justice on earth (34:8 note). In earlier chapters, the Lord's coming with vengeance was not good news, since He came in judgment on His own people. In this announcement He comes to save.

These transformations are evidences of a supernatural restoration and are associated with the ministry of Jesus (Matt. 11:2–6; 12:22; Mark 7:37; Luke 7:21, 22; Acts 3:8). They are a reversal of the curse of Is. 6 (cf. 29:18). waters. See note on 1:30. Cf. John 7:37, 38.
See 34:13. reeds and rushes. Cf. 19:5, 6.

See note on 11:16; 40:3; cf. 33:8. Way of Holiness. Only those who have been cleansed and consecrated are privileged to walk on the road of salvation that leads to Zion (4:3 note). The image combines a safe return from exile with a safe pilgrimage journey to Zion. even if they are fools. The Lord's new highway will guard even those whose natural tendency is to go astray (see 53:6) through their own folly.

Cf. 13:21, 22; 34:11–15. Wild animals are part of the covenant curse (see Lev. 26:22). 35:9, 10 redeemed \... ransomed. These two Hb. words often appear as parallels (Jer. 31:11; Hos. 13:14), and are almost synonymous (for the difference, cf. Jer. 31:11 note). Both words are used to describe God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt. (Cf. Ex. 6:6, where "redeemed" represents the same Hb. word translated as "redeemed" in Is. 35:9, and Ex. 13:15, where "redeem" represents the same Hb. word translated as "ransomed" in Is. 35:10.)These terms play an important role in Isaiah's description of the future deliverance from the exile as a new exodus (51:10, 11). The Lord is the "Redeemer" (41:14 and note; 49:26) who will forgive Israel's sins (44:22; Ps. 103:3, 4).

This historical bridge between chs. 1–35 and 40–66 directly parallels 2 Kin. 18:13–20:19. It records the fulfillment of Isaiah's predictions that the Lord would judge Judah by bringing the Assyrian army to the gates of Jerusalem and would then judge that proud army by destroying it there, preserving a faithful remnant in the city. Hezekiah's faith contrasts with the response of his father, Ahaz, to the prophetic word. Hezekiah by faith accepts a sign when confronted with illness (38:7, 8); Ahaz refused to ask for a sign (7:12). Yet even Hezekiah falls into the same temptation to trust in the nations as his forefathers did, seeking to impress the envoys from Babylon with his resources (ch. 39). The result is the inevitability of exile. Thus, the first two chapters of the bridge (36; 37) deal with the main subject of the first half of the book of Isaiah — Assyria — while chs. 38; 39 transition to the subject of the second half of the book — Babylon. Because of this concern, the events seem to be presented out of chronological order: before Sennacherib moved west to attack Judah, he had already defeated Merodach-baladan and the Babylonians, so Merodach-baladan would have had no reason to seek an alliance with Judah. Isaiah arranges his material thematically, placing the visit of Merodach-baladan after the defeat of Assyria even though the visit happened before Assyria's defeat at the hands of the angel of the Lord (37:36–38). 36:1 fourteenth year. The precise chronology of the reigns of Hezekiah and his father, Ahaz, is difficult to determine, and scholars disagree on the dating (Introduction to 1 Kings: Chronology; 2 Kings 16:1 note). These notes assume that Hez­ekiah rules alongside Ahaz as co-regent from c. 727–c. 715 B.C. and is sole king from c. 715–c. 696 B.C. (2 Kin. 18:1, 2 and notes). While some explain the "fourteenth" year as a copyist's error for "twenty-fourth," it is more probable that Isaiah is referring to the beginning of Hezekiah's independent rule in 715 B.C., which would make 701 B.C. the king's fourteenth year as the sole ruler of Judah. Sennacherib. King of Assyria from 705 to 681 B.C. The events recorded here are also recorded in his royal annals, and they make no claim that he destroyed Jerusalem, thereby providing external evidence for the biblical account. fortified cities. Sennacherib states in his annals that forty-six such cities were conquered during this campaign (2 Kin. 18:13 note).

The royal counselor for military affairs. According to 2 Kin. 18:17, the king also sends his "Tartan" ("commander in chief"; cf. Is. 20:1) and his "Rab-saris" ("chief officer"). Lachish. In Isaiah's day, this fortress town in the western hill country of Judah guards an important road that led into the highlands south of Jerusalem (Jer. 34:7). The reliefs from the Assyrian royal palace at Nineveh depict the brutality of this siege. great army. According to 37:36, 185,000 troops are killed in the siege of Jerusalem; the full army is much larger than that. upper pool. Isaiah earlier met Ahaz there (7:3).
See 22:19. Joah \... recorder. An important office holder and the official spokesperson of the kings.
An official title of Assyrian kings that is equivalent to "emperor." By contrast, Hezekiah is named without a title (vv. 13, 14).
The challenge to choose between loyalty to Assyria, other political powers, or to the Lord is the essential message of Isaiah (12:2 note).

Hezekiah has depended on Egypt for support until now (30:2, 6, 7, 13; 31:1, 3 and notes). But as Isaiah has said, Egypt can never deliver Judah because she, too, is under divine judgment (19:1–15; 20:3–6). Cf. Ezek. 29:6, 7. Trusting Egypt is like trusting one's weight to a broken reed, which can provide no support even if it is whole.

Hezekiah has removed many pagan and idolatrous sites in Judah (2 Kin. 18:4; 2 Chr. 31:1), no doubt to the dismay and anger of many Judeans, who would view them as authentic forms of worship. The Assyrian envoy is therefore understandably confused about the nature of Hezekiah's reforms. this altar. In line with the requirements of Deut. 12, this charge focuses on the requirement to worship exclusively at the temple of Solomon.
Judah does not have cavalry. Assyria, on the other hand, is known for its overabundance of cavalry.
said to me.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} He is trying to appeal to the religious people of Judah. Ironically, the Lord is indeed sovereign over his coming (see 10:5, 6).
For many centuries, Aramaic was the international language of diplomacy and commerce, while the ordinary people of Judah only spoke Hebrew ("the language of Judah").
The unpleasant result of a long siege.
The Assyrian messenger gives the king of Assyria several exalted titles but doesn't recognize Hezekiah's position.
These words testify to Hezekiah's public expression of faith in God. trust in theLORD. This theme has been at the heart of Isaiah's preaching in chs. 7–35.

Lit. "make a blessing" (text note). The Rabshakeh appeals for renewal of a political covenant with Assyria. Cf. 27:5. eat \... drink. He tempts them with food and drink (37:30 note) in the midst of a harsh siege (v. 12). The Assyrians project a proverbially ideal and happy life (cf. 1 Kin. 4:25), but the Lord alone can fulfill what they promise.

The phrase reflects the Assyrian policy of exiling a rebellious population to a new location and replacing them with another population (cf. 2 Kin. 15:29). In this way, they hope to disrupt old alliances and disconnect peoples from their heritage, making them less able to mount effective resistance.
To the Rabshakeh, one god is much like another. He is about to find out that Judah's God is quite unlike the gods of the nations.
These expressions of mourning or repentance over the Assyrian insults signify humility, dependence, and a need for God, contrasting dramatically with Ahaz's response to Isaiah's prophecy in ch. 7.
See 22:15–25. senior priests. Representatives of the leading priestly families (Jer. 19:1).

This is a time of adversity when the loyalty of people is tested (cf. 25:4; 26:16; 33:2). birth \... no strength. Hezekiah admits the futility of human strategies in a time of acute crisis (26:17, 18).

your God.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Hezekiah humbly makes no personal claim on the Lord's favor but relies on Isaiah's role as prophetic intercessor. the living God. These words express Hezekiah's renewed faith and zeal for the Lord's name. remnant. The nation has been greatly reduced (1:9 note; 6:11).

The king of Assyria has not merely insulted Hezekiah but the Lord Himself. Hezekiah's humble trust in the Lord's deliverance will not be disappointed, for the Lord is sovereign even over what rumors the king of Assyria heard and how he responds to them.
See vv. 37, 38. Isaiah encourages Hezekiah to continue to trust the Lord, as he had encouraged Ahaz years earlier (7:4).

Sennacherib renews his attempt at persuading Hezekiah to submit to and depend on Assyria. By making folly of the gods of the nations, he challenges Hezekiah to stop trusting in the Lord. But as Sennacherib will discover, the Lord is not like the gods of the nations. This will also become an important lesson for the Jewish exiles in Babylon to remember as they are surrounded by seemingly powerful national gods. 37:8 Libnah. A city in the western hill country of Judah a few miles north of Lachish (36:2 note).
Egypt is ruled by an Ethiopian dynasty at this time. Tirhakah commands the Egyptian troops in 701 B.C. He becomes sole king about 689 B.C. For "Cush," see note on 18:1.
Sennacherib assails the Lord's ability to deliver Judah (v. 4 note).
Sennacherib claims that his god is with him because the Assyrian success goes back several generations. Gozan \... Eden. Cities in Mesopotamia.
Cities in Aram (Syria). The extent of Sennacherib's conquests is made plain. Yet the Lord is mightier still.

Hezekiah doesn't respond to Sennacherib's boast; instead, he turns to the Lord in prayer (38:2). Unlike Ahaz, Hezekiah confesses his complete trust in the Lord as the king, the creator, and the redeemer. The theology of this prayer summarizes Isaiah's vision of God.

God is with His people and rules over them (1 Sam. 4:4; 2 Sam. 6:2; Pss. 80:1; 99:1), truths represented by His presence in the Most Holy Place of the temple in Jerusalem, which contains the ark of the covenant with the wings of two cherubim above it. The Lord's throne itself is invisible, but the ark is the footstool of that throne, while the cherubim form the heavenly bodyguard and pull the divine throne-chariot (see Ezek. 1). you are the God, you alone. Hezekiah attributes deity exclusively to the Lord (44:8; 45:5, 6, 14, 22; 46:9). kingdoms. See note on 13:4. The Lord reigns over all human kingdoms. made heaven and earth. There is a distinct emphasis in Isaiah's prophecies on the Lord as the sovereign and absolute creator of all (27:10, 11; 42:5; 45:12, 18). The Lord is the God who made heaven and earth and everything that they contain, including the Assyrians.
Unlike the gods of Assyria, the Lord sees, hears, and acts (see Is. 44:18).
On Isaiah's polemic against idolatry, cf. 2:8.

our God.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} In prayer, Hezekiah appeals to the unbreakable relationship between God and His people. He asks God to act not simply for the sake of His people but for the honor of His own name among the nations.

LORD, the God of Israel. A formal title for the one whose covenant is with the twelve tribes of Israel. The title indicates that the Lord has accepted the identification as "the Lord our God" (see v. 20).

Hebrew literary convention speaks of cities and people as young women (47:1; Lam. 2:10; Amos 5:2). Declaring that the mighty Assyrian army will be overthrown by a mere slip of a girl adds a note of scorn. Zion. See note on 1:8. despises \... wags her head. She expresses rejection and derision in this manner (Ps. 22:7; Jer. 18:16). This taunt song in vv. 22–29 is similar to the one in 14:4–21.
Assyria has exalted itself against the Lord. Jerusalem may be a mere girl but she has a powerful friend.

This poetic expression, emphasizing superiority and pride (14:13, 14), is usually reserved for deity. to cut down its tallest cedars. The proud were compared to mighty cedars in Lebanon in 2:13. Assyria's pride is likewise preparing it for a fall (see Ezek. 31:3).
Absolute claims of authority over creation are an insult to God's prerogatives. In this case, Assyria is boasting of achievements that it has not yet accomplished, always a dangerous strategy.

Assyria is nothing but a tool to advance God's plans. Therefore, the empire has no cause for boasting over its achievements. heaps of ruins. Assyria has accomplished God's will among the kingdoms of this world (10:5–19; cf. Ps. 37:1, 2; Mic. 4:11–13). See note on 27:10.
Grass seeds might sprout even on a rooftop, but grass can never prosper there without a proper depth of soil.
God is sovereign over Assyria. The empire can never escape His scrutiny (cf. Ps. 139). What is comforting for God's people should be frightening for their enemies.
God has seen what Assyria has done, holds her responsible, and decides her punishment. hook. Assyrian monuments show their captives pierced with hooks or rings.

The overthrow of Assyria and the restoration of a remnant will be a witness to God's faithfulness in working out His plans (7:11 note). eat their fruit. What Assyria promised (36:16), the Lord alone can fulfill. Even though there will be two years of difficult struggle, the Lord will sustain them through it.

See note on 1:9. The Lord's response picks up the language of Hezekiah's request to Isaiah in v. 4. root \... fruit. These events will fulfill God's promise to restore His vineyard (27:6 note). This restoration began in 701 B.C. and still continues, as all who are in Jesus Christ are grafted into the vine and become part of God's vineyard (John 15:1–8).
See 9:7.

See note on 31:5. Sennacherib does not succeed in his siege of Jerusalem. God is faithful to the promise made to David (8:8, 10; cf. 2 Sam. 7:16), and His pledge to defend His own glory (v. 20). servant. See note on 20:3.

LORD. Jerusalem's deliverance comes by supernatural means, as did the death of the firstborn in Egypt (Ex. 12:12; cf. 2 Sam. 24:16). behold. This Hb. word often introduces surprising or noteworthy events, including miracles and dreams.

Sennacherib's death in the temple of Nisroch contrasts with the life Hezekiah finds in the temple of the Lord (vv. 1, 14). Even in their own house, the gods in whom Sennacherib has placed his trust are unable to protect him. struck him down. Twenty years later, his own sons murder him (681 B.C.). Ararat. A mountainous region in the extreme eastern part of modern-day Turkey. Esarhaddon. King over Assyria from 681 to 669 B.C.

Refers to the general time of the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem, though v. 6 shows that these events actually occur before the siege, which takes place c. 701 B.C. (cf. 36:1–39:8 and 36:1 notes). you shall not recover. If God actually means to kill Hezekiah immediately, there is no need for this warning. The prophetic word gives Hezekiah opportunity to ask for healing and receive it.
The king places his confidence in God's righteousness.

This petition is a moving expression of loyalty to the Lord (33:14–16). Hezekiah has instituted significant reforms among the people. in faithfulness \... a whole heart. See 10:20 and note. wept bitterly. Hezekiah is apparently without a male heir. He lives an additional fifteen years (v. 5). Manasseh, his successor to the throne, is twelve when Hezekiah dies (2 Kin. 20:21–21:1).

Assuming that Hezekiah dies in 696 B.C., Hezekiah's illness and recovery occurred c. 711 B.C. If, as some scholars suggest, Hezekiah's reign extends to 686 B.C., that would put the king's illness before c. 701 B.C. The difficulty of dating Hezekiah's reign makes certainty on this point impossible until further extrabiblical evidence is discovered. See note on 2 Kin. 20:1.
See 37:33–35. The Lord is not simply healing Hezekiah for the king's own sake but to enable him to be part of the deliverance from Sennacherib through his prayers.

Given Ahaz's earlier refusal to seek a sign, it is ironic that the Lord chooses an instrument named after him to reveal this sign to Hezekiah. The "dial" appears to be a stairway with steps calibrated with the movement of the sun to give a rudimentary means of telling time via the casting of shadows.
Verses 10–20 form a hymn combining elements of lament (vv. 10–15) and thanksgiving (vv. 16–20; 2 Chr. 29:30; Prov. 25:1). In this hymn, Hezekiah acknowledges the Lord's deliverance.
Hezekiah expresses his anguish over the reality and sting of death (Ps. 55:4). He is perhaps in his late thirties at this point. See notes on "Sheol" at 5:14; 14:9–11.

LORD. Hezekiah is fearful over the possibility of being left in Sheol (5:14 and 14:9–11 notes). At this difficult point in his life, he does not seem to share the confidence that the psalmist expresses in Ps. 139:8.
Hez­ekiah offers many metaphors for vexation with the brevity of life, as if God were his enemy (cf. Pss. 22; 32:3, 4).

In the face of the mystery of providence, Hezekiah is at least looking in the right direction. His sickness is oppressing him like a harsh taskmaster. He knows that the Lord has the power to deliver him from such oppression, yet so far he has not seen the Lord's deliverance.

Hezekiah acknowledges that ultimately even his bitter suffering has been for his good (Rom. 8:28). God graciously delivers him from his sickness at exactly the right time, even though Hezekiah had wished for an earlier deliverance. pit of destruction. Hb. sheol; see notes on 5:14; 14:9–11. cast all my sins. Sometimes in the Bible, personal sin is the immediate reason for sickness, but not all sickness is directly caused by one's own sin. Often, sickness simply provides the opportunity for God's mighty works to be displayed (John 9:2, 3).

Hezekiah emphasizes communal and personal praise in response to God's acts of salvation in this life. How can anyone praise God in the shadowy existence of Sheol? Praise is offered only in the land of the living.
The story of God's acts of redemption are to be told from generation to generation (cf. Ex. 12:25–27).

Hope is alive (cf. Pss. 6:9; 22:22–24), as Hezekiah expects to join in the communal praise (vv. 18, 19). stringed instruments. Musical accompaniment assists the singing of psalms (cf. Pss. 33:1–3; 150). For Hezekiah's Passover celebration, see 2 Chr. 29. house of theLORD. The temple on Mount Zion was the place God specially designed for worship from the time of Solomon until the time of the new covenant church.
All healing is of God. He may mediate it through medicine.
Sometime after Hezekiah's illness but before the events recounted in chs. 36; 37 (38:1 note).

These arms and wealth evidence Hezekiah's ability to support Babylon in its rebellion against Assyria. The envoys have not merely been sent to inquire after Hezekiah's health. Hezekiah's sin in seeking to court an alliance with the Babylonians is all the more striking given that it occurs in the context of his trusting in the Lord and receiving great deliverance from sickness.

Isaiah comes to speak for God and questions Hezekiah. Hezekiah's answers are evasive. He avoids the question about what the envoys said and instead focuses on the fact that they came from a far country, a phrase that elsewhere describes people coming from a distance to see the Lord's works of judgment or deliverance (1 Kin. 8:41, 42).
His action suggests he is trusting in his might and political alliance with Babylon, not trusting in the Lord.
This phrase introduces the prophetic charge and judgment. LORD of hosts. See note on 1:9.

Isaiah predicts the Babylonian exile. Fittingly, all of the things that Hezekiah showed the Babylonians will be carried away by the Babylonians. The Assyrians whom Hez­ekiah fears are not the real enemy. The Lord is the one whom Hezekiah should be fearing.
See 2 Kin. 24:15. eunuchs. See Dan. 1:3–6.

See note on v. 5. good \... in my days. This response has a negative note, as the king shows little concern for his own descendants or for his people, or for the messianic promise of the coming Son of David. Though the Babylonian exile does finally end, the prophetic word is clear that there "is no peace \... for the wicked" (48:22; 57:21). God's peace will extend to the children of Zion (66:12, 13). Indeed, given the chronology of these chapters, Hezekiah is not even right about his own times, since the Assyrians arrive on his doorstep shortly after he says this.

Isaiah originally addressed these words to the future exiles in Babylon to encourage them to flee from there and return by faith to the Promised Land (e.g., 48:20, 21). The encouragement partially arises from the supernatural character of his words (e.g., 41:21–27). These prophecies, originally delivered more than a century and a half before the end of the exile (see Introduction: History of Interpretation), astonish their audience by predicting Israel's (i.e., Judah's) immediate deliverance from Babylon by Cyrus (e.g., 44:24–45:13), the coming of the suffering Christ to save them from their sins after they return to the land (42:1–7; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12), and Israel's final salvation in the last days (51:6). The near, more remote, and most remote prophecies merge together on the canvas. From Isaiah's perspective, the restoration after the exile inaugurates the new age, and this first taste of salvation through God's servant, Cyrus, coalesces with the greater salvation that the Christ, God's Servant, will bring His people. Today, the elect have even more confidence in these words of prophecy because they have been fulfilled in Christ and are being fulfilled in His church (2 Pet. 1:19). These chapters lay the foundation for Isaiah's theme of a new exodus. Numerous passages in this section of Isaiah (40:3–11; 41:17–20; 42:14–17; 43:16–21; 44:1–5, 27; 48:20, 21; 49:8–12; 50:2; 51:9, 10; 52:11, 12; 55:12, 13) develop a paradigm to demonstrate that the exodus theme has become "eschatologized." That is, the exodus imagery has developed now into the expectation of a promised future event, which is developed on the basis of God's past action in delivering His people. Isaiah is teaching that the foundational salvific event in Israel's history now becomes a paradigm for a new salvation event that will be far more significant than even the epochal deliverance of the Israelites from Egypt. 40:1 Comfort, comfort. The verbs are plural in form. God is addressing His heavenly court and the prophetic messengers who participate in it (v. 6; 44:26). Other heralds will be encouraged to spread the good news (vv. 9–11; 52:7), which is the reverse of Isaiah's earlier commission in 6:9–13. The repetition is for emphasis and occurs in 51:9, 17; 52:1, 11; 57:14; 62:10. This good news of the Lord's care and concern for His people contrasts starkly with Hezekiah's lack of concern for anyone but himself in 39:8. my people \... your God. Though they have rebelled, they are still treated as the people of God. The phrase occurs frequently in Isaiah (1:3; 3:12, 15; 43:20; 51:4, 16; 53:8; 58:1; 65:10, 22). See notes on 43:1.

Isaiah refers to the exile of Israel and Judah of which he has spoken repeatedly. The suffering of the exile is the a result of sin. See note on 27:9. double for all her sins. God has judged the punishment to be sufficient ("double" in the sense of exactly matching, like an actor's "double"), and is ready to forgive (43:25; 44:22; 48:9).

Though the voice may include earlier prophets, such as Isaiah, it finds consummate fulfillment in the ministry of John the Baptist (Matt. 3:3; Mark 1:2–4; Luke 1:76; 3:4, 5; John 1:23). Since the word of the Lord is effective in bringing to pass what it declares (see v. 8), the role of the messenger is crucial. The gospel of Mark opens with these words of Isaiah. wilderness \... desert. Metaphors for alienation and anguish (14:17; 27:10; 64:10). God alone can transform the desert into a blooming and fruitful oasis, a metaphor for the fullness and joy of His salvation (32:15, 16; 35:1, 6; 41:18, 19; 43:19, 20; 48:21; 51:3). They also remind Israel of God's faithfulness to them in the first exodus. prepare \... make straight. "Prepare" means to "remove every obstruction" (57:14). God will remove all obstacles at His coming, but He expects His people to prepare for the kingdom (62:10) and requires the nations to assist the progress of His salvation. way \... a highway. See note on 11:16. Here these are metaphors for human hearts that must be prepared through repentance (35:8–10; Luke 3:3–9). When that happens, God's glory appears on earth to accomplish a second exodus of His people from bondage.
At the Lord's appearance, nature submits to His will. He removes all obstacles and prepares a road by which the royal procession advances in the establishment of the kingdom.

God's kingdom is "revealed" in acts of salvation and judgment. The restoration from exile manifests God's glory, but it is most clearly revealed in Jesus Christ (Ezek. 44:1–3; Luke 2:30, 31; John 1:14). all flesh \... together. The revelation of His kingdom is public and visible in creation, in Christ, in the church, and in the new earth (Gen. 9:17; Matt. 2:1–11; 16:27; 24:30; Acts 28:28; 2 Cor. 3:18). mouth. See note on 1:20. This affirmation is expanded in vv. 6–8.

An angelic voice addresses Isaiah (6:6–9). All flesh is grass. Human existence is temporary, its glory fleeting. God's judgment ("when the breath of the Lord blows upon it") terminates it (cf. Ps. 90:5, 6).
His wrath is likened to the destructive east wind (Ps. 103:16; Jer. 4:11; Ezek. 17:10).

Not just the Scriptures in general (though they will likewise endure); rather, the Lord's word of judgment and blessing that is declared before the time of its realization and certainly comes to fulfillment. Just as the scheming plans of the Judeans could not stave off the judgment of the exile, the power of the Babylonians cannot prevent their deliverance.

The typical place of encounter with God (cf. Ezek. 40:2). Zion. See note on 1:8. good news. The gospel. God has come to rescue His enslaved people. As in ch. 2, God's word streams forth from Zion. The good news is that the Lord is coming in power to reign, bringing rewards to those who have faithfully endured the period of hard service (v. 10; see vv. 12–26), and that the Lord is coming in gentleness as a good shepherd, bringing protection and care to His sheep (v. 11; see vv. 27–31).

He arrives to inaugurate His kingdom on earth (35:4 note; 43:15; 44:6; 52:7–10). arm. This metaphor describes the power of God as manifested in acts of deliverance and vengeance (v. 11; 48:14; 51:5, 9; 53:1; 59:16; 63:5, 12; Ex. 15:16; Pss. 44:3; 89:13; 98:1; 136:12). reward. The spoils of victory here are the delivered people themselves. The rescued exiles both foreshadow and merge into the messianic community.
These are the expressions of the tender, shepherding care of the divine King (Pss. 23:1–4; 78:52; 80:1; Jer. 31:10; Ezek. 34:11–16; Mic. 2:12; John 10:11).
The Lord is the sole creator of the universe. What part of that creation can therefore withstand His will? a span. A hand's breadth used as a measure.
The Creator is sovereign over all human powers — which are as nothing before Him (2:22).
Famous for its dense cedar forests (2:13 note).
The Lord is incomparable to the gods of the nations, which are only idols and have no real existence or power (v. 25; 46:5).
Possibly chains that keep the idol from toppling over. On Isaiah's polemic against idolatry, see 2:8.

This charge is directed at rejection of God's revelation (52:6 note). These rhetorical questions parallel those in vv. 12–14. beginning \... foundations. God's glory and power are revealed in nature, which is His creation (Rom. 1:20).

This is either the horizon or the hemisphere of the sky over the earth. From the Lord's perspective, the rulers of the nations are as nothing (cf. vv. 15–17). tent. God's creation is compared to a tent He has pitched (42:5; 44:24; 51:13; Pss. 18:11; 19:4).

This verse develops the imagery introduced in vv. 6, 7. carries them off like stubble. Stubble and chaff are the unwanted byproducts of harvesting and are blown away in the breeze. See notes 17:13; 29:5.

God encourages His people to look above the apparently overwhelming nature of their present problems to see the greater nature of His sovereign power. If He is able to shepherd the stars in the night sky, is He not able to shepherd His own people? This parallels the call in v. 10: "Behold the Lord God." calling \... might. The Lord knows and upholds His creation.

Isaiah has in mind the remnant in exile. The regular and distinctive paralleling of the names Jacob/Israel in Isaiah 40–66 is not coincidental but connects back to the patriarchal narratives. Jacob himself received the new name "Israel" after his life-changing encounter with God at Peniel, representing the transformation that God had accomplished in his heart. Yet he continued to also bear his old name, Jacob ("deceiver"), which aptly described his old nature. Jacob/Israel was simul justus et peccator: "at the same time justified and a sinner." So too the postexilic Israel that Isaiah addresses will be at the same time renewed by God and restored to a new relationship with Him, but also a struggling and weak people who need continual exhortation to pursue obedience as well as constant encouragement to trust in God's faithful love for them. hidden \... disregarded. In His anger, God hid His face from them (49:14; 54:8), but in His grace He is powerful to deliver (8:17 note). This verse poses the question on the lips of the discouraged people in exile to which the entire chapter is the answer. The exiles feel that they are out of the Lord's sight and that He has given up on them.
See note on v. 21. everlasting God. The Creator is sovereign over time and space (9:6; 40:22). He does not \... grow weary. He has not given up on His people as the exiles feared.
All human strength has limits, but the Lord's power is unlimited.

Like Isaiah himself. See notes on 8:17; 26:8, 9. mount up \... run \... walk. These verbs give a vivid picture of the spiritual transformation that comes through faith, supernaturally infusing people with the Lord's strength so that like Him they do not faint or grow weary. This good news can give the Lord's people the courage to wait patiently for the Lord's salvation.

All nations are called upon to acknowledge the Lord's sovereignty and discern His hand in history. coastlands \... peoples. See notes on 24:16; 40:15. The coastlands represent the most distant nations, who are invited to observe the Lord acting to deliver His people. their strength. The nations may try to match the strength that has been given to God's people, but it will not be enough to prevail against them (40:31).

Namely, Cyrus the Great of Persia (reigned 559–530 B.C.; v. 25; 44:28; 45:1 and notes). Cyrus conquered Babylon and issued the decree permitting the Jews to return to their homeland (Ezra 1:1–4). victory. Cyrus is victorious in establishing a new order (1:21 note; 44:24–45:5, 13; 46:11). gives \... makes. Cyrus's victories are the Lord's doing on behalf of Israel (43:3). nations \... kings. The nations are under the Lord's authority, and they must acknowledge His name to participate in His plan of redemption (45:1; 49:22, 23; 60:3, 16). The Lord raises up kingdoms and sets them down in turn.
Cyrus's conquests are rapid (cf. 46:11).

God has ordered human history from the beginning of time, even the sinful actions of powerful pagan rulers. What the Lord is doing now is nothing less than a new creation (cf. 41:20). I, the LORD \... I am he. A most significant formula of divine self-identification (41:13; 42:8; 43:3, 10, 13, 15; 44:24; 45:3, 5, 6; 46:4; 48:17; 49:23; 51:15; 60:22; note the use of "I am" in John 6:35; 8:12, 58; 9:5; 10:7, 9, 11, 14; 11:25; 14:6; 15:1, 5). first \... last. These words give assurance that everything is always under the Lord's control (44:6; 48:12; cf. Heb. 13:8; Rev. 1:8, 17; 2:8; 21:6; 22:13).

Fear leads to rebellion in response to the Lord's challenge of v. 1. The natural response for pagans to external threats is to construct more and better idols, yet even the most glorious idols have no real power.
On Isaiah's polemic against idolatry, see 2:8.

These names describe the dual nature of God's people. See note on 40:27 (v. 14; 40:27; 42:24; 43:1, 22, 28; 44:1, 5, 21, 23; 45:4; 46:3; 48:1, 12; cf. Luke 1:54). my servant. See note on 42:1–9. chosen. See note on 14:1. God's election of His people is irrevocable and gives them hope in spite of finding themselves in exile. Abraham, my friend. Abraham is the only OT character to receive this title (cf. 2 Chr. 20:7).

An assurance of the Lord's deliverance. See notes on 35:4; 10:24. I am with you. This is the reality summed up in the name "Immanuel" (8:8, 10; 43:2, 5; cf. Acts 18:9, 10). I am your God. The basic promise of the covenant (vv. 13, 14; 43:1, 5; 44:2, 8; 51:12; Gen. 17:7; 21:17; 26:24; Deut. 20:1; 31:6, 8; Lev. 26:12; Jer. 32:38; Ezek. 37:27; 2 Cor. 6:16). strengthen \... uphold. The Lord is present in graciously delivering, exalting, and vindicating His children (v. 13; 42:1; 44:2; 49:8; 50:7). See note on 40:31. righteous right hand. He establishes order on earth by His power, as He did at the exodus (63:12; Ex. 15:6). The result will be the vindication of His people.
See note on 1:29.

The same word occurs at Job 25:6 and Ps. 22:6. It typically refers to an insect grub and is a symbol of something with no power to defend itself and no attractiveness to draw others to protect it. Redeemer. The Hb. term designates the family protector. For a distressed family member, among other things, the redeemer avenges a murder (Num. 35:19) and redeems family property and those who have become slaves (Lev. 25:23–49; Ruth 2:20 note). See also 35:9, 10 and note. the Holy One of Israel. See note on 1:4. The Lord, the Holy God, stoops to deliver His own people even though they have no holiness of their own (43:14, 15; 45:11; 47:4; 48:17; 49:7; 54:5; 57:15).

A board studded with iron or stone teeth that is driven over the wheat to separate the grain from the chaff so that it can be winnowed. mountains \... hills. Represent the many enemies of Israel (vv. 11, 12; cf. 42:15). The image of a threshing sledge grinding the mountains and hills into small pieces shows the scale of God's judgment.
The returning exiles and all who seek God's favor (11:4 note; Ps. 9:18 note). Their lack of resources causes them to throw themselves wholly on the Lord.
An abundance of water ("rivers \... springs") and vegetation ("cedar \... cypress") pictures a transformation of creation (12:3; 35:1 and note; 43:18–20; 49:9–11; 55:13).
See note on 4:5.
God renews the challenge issued in v. 1. The idols are being brought before the heavenly court and asked to prove their power, if they can.

The idols cannot even appear in court without the help of the nations who have to carry them in. what is to happen \... outcome. The Lord alone plans, declares, and executes. See note on 11:2. former things. See 42:9; 43:9; 46:9; 48:3. These include past prophecies of events, especially God's abandonment of Israel and Judah as recorded in chs. 1–35. They might also include the Lord's earlier acts of salvation. Fulfilled prophecy is a key evidence of the Lord's existence and power. things to come. See 42:23; 44:7; 45:11; 46:10. These are prophecies of the Lord's favor and the full establishment of His kingdom, as in chs. 40–66.
God taunts the pagan gods for their complete inability to act in any direction. They have no power to terrify anyone, unlike the Lord.
God condemns those who turn away from Him.

The Lord shows His sovereignty over the nations. north \... rising of the sun. Cyrus came from Persia in the east and conquered Media in 550 B.C., becoming master of territories north of Babylon. He executed the Lord's will (45:4, 5; 2 Chr. 36:23; Ezra 1:1–4). From an Israelite and Judean perspective, he also came from the north, as nations outside of that region came into the fertile crescent from the north when they were executing campaigns in the area. he shall call on my name. Although Cyrus was not a believer, he acknowledged the existence of the gods of subject nations in his decree. In this case, his words were truer than he knew. potter. See note on 27:11.

Probably refers to Isaiah (40:1 note). good news. The gospel of God's grace (40:9 note). In this case, the specific news of their deliverance from exile in Babylon under Cyrus, which Isaiah had declared long ago.
The nations and their idols are impotent. The Lord needs no one to advise Him for He has all wisdom in Himself.
The Lord's assessment of idols is that they are empty, worthless (40:18–20; 41:7, 21–24; 44:9).

This is the first of four "Servant Songs" in chs. 40–55 celebrating the Servant of the Lord (49:1–7; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12; cf. ch. 61). 42:1 Behold. The third in a sequence. See 41:24, 29. The idols and the nations are nothing: the alternative is found in "my Servant." my servant. See note on 20:3. Isaiah has already identified the covenant people Israel as the Servant of the Lord (41:9; cf. 42:19; 43:10; 44:2; 45:4; 48:20). Now he introduces another application of the expression to describe an individual who, by divine empowerment, stands in contrast to the ineffective nullities of idolatry (41:24, 29). This individual will succeed where Israel has failed in her divinely allotted mission. Furthermore, as the supreme embodiment of Israel, he is able to provide the salvation that the nation needs. Isaiah's focus on this individual becomes clearer throughout the following chapters, culminating in the prophecy of 52:13–53:12. The impact of the Servant's ministry is not confined to Israel, but also embraces the nations. He brings justice and light to the nations, and so accomplishes what Isaiah earlier attributed to the Messiah (42:1, cf. 11:2–4; 49:6, cf. 9:2–6), with whom he is to be identified. Unlike Israel, which has been disobedient and has suffered for her own sins while nonetheless complaining of being abandoned by the Lord (40:27; 49:14), this prophetic figure is obedient, suffering in silence for Israel's sins and looking forward in hope to final vindication. Ultimately, the servant imagery is fulfilled in Jesus (Matt. 12:15–21). But just as Isaiah envisaged a servant role for the people after the Servant completes his task (54:17; 56:6; 65:8, 9; 66:14), those who acknowledge Christ as their Savior are called on to emulate his example of servanthood (1 Pet. 2:21–25). uphold. See note on 41:10. The Servant's strength does not come from Himself but from God (cf. 40:30, 31). chosen. See note on 14:1. delights. The Servant pleases God and is an object of His love and favor (60:10; 62:4; Matt. 3:17; Mark 1:11; Luke 9:35). The Lord is able to use other servants, such as Cyrus (45:1), in whom He takes no such pleasure. justice to the nations. God institutes His universal kingdom of justice and righteousness. "Justice" is emphatically repeated three times in vv. 1–4.
The Servant does not clamor for attention but speaks in a spirit of gentleness and patience.

This metaphor is appropriate for the poor and needy (Ps. 9:18 note). Ancient kings boasted about their ferocity and the way in which they brought subject nations to their knees. Rather than break the weak, however, the Servant will heal them. burning wick. Represents people who are close to losing faith and hope.

The Servant will practice godliness on earth (cf. 2:2–4). He will be greater than Moses (Deut. 18:15–18; Acts 3:22–26), mediating a new covenant that enables people to keep His law (v. 6; 2 Cor. 3:3; Heb. 8:7–13). For the coastlands, see note on 41:1. wait. See note on 8:17.

God the creator is above all creation because He made everything (4:5 note). The God who created everything has the power to fulfill His promises. breath \... spirit. The Creator and Sustainer of life (Ps. 104:30; Acts 17:24, 25) will enable the Servant to transform the earth with new, spiritual life.

These expressions parallel "chosen" and "uphold," respectively, in v. 1. covenant for the people. Jesus Christ, as God's Servant, brings the new covenant to His people (see 53:4–6; Jer. 31:31–34; Heb. 8:6–13; 9:15). This new covenant (Jer. 31:31) is also called the "covenant of peace" (54:10) and the "everlasting covenant" (55:3; 61:8). light for the nations. The recipients of God's light are a new community of light-bearers in a dark world (9:2; 49:6; 51:4; 60:1–3; Luke 2:30–32; Acts 26:17, 18, 23).

The Babylonian exile is described as a kind of dark prison. Israel's salvation from exile prefigures a spiritual deliverance through Christ from the blindness, bondage, and darkness of sin (5:30; 29:18; 51:14 and notes). Blindness is a theme in this chapter (see v. 16, 18, 19)

Include the judgments prophesied against Damascus, Samaria, Nineveh, and Judah, as well as the Lord's deliverance of His people from Egypt (41:22 note). new things. Include renewal of the covenant, restoration to the land, the messianic kingdom, inclusion of the Gentiles, and the new heaven and earth (41:22 note). declare \... tell. God plans, proclaims, and executes. His word will come to pass (11:2 note; 40:8). Unlike the idols of the nations, the Lord both speaks and does.

Represents the specific praise that the redeemed sing in response to a specific new act of deliverance, just as Moses and Miriam sang a new song after they witnessed God's acts of salvation (Ex. 15:1, 21; cf. Is. 12:1–6 and notes; Ps. 149:1; Rev. 5:9; 14:3). end of the earth. Wherever God's children may be found (11:12), including the former Gentiles.
See note on 21:16 (60:7; Ps. 120:5; Jer. 2:10; 49:28, 29). Sela. See note on 16:1. These, too, are Gentile areas that will join in singing the Lord's praises.
The Lord receives acclamation from His subjects (v. 8; 24:14–16 note; 1 Pet. 2:9).

Assurance comes from knowing that when the Lord's zeal is stirred, He will accomplish His plan (9:7 note). mighty man \... man of war. Isaiah describes the Lord as the Divine Warrior in whom hope lies (1:9; 5:26 and notes). See note on Dan. 9:27. cries out. The Hb. word here is different from the one in v. 2. This is a battle cry or call to arms, not a cry of distress.

God promises to be with His people and lead them, as He did Israel in the wilderness (Ex. 13:21, 22). darkness \... into light. See 9:2. rough places into level ground. See 40:4. No obstacles, whether within His people (their blindness) or external challenges, can prevent the Lord's plan from being put into effect.
They are "deaf" because they have not listened (v. 23), and "blind" because they have refused to see the hand of God in their history (v. 20; 48:3–6).

See note on 42:1. The Lord exclaims at the blindness and deafness of Israel, who has been as weak spiritually as her neighbors. Those who are supposed to be the light to the nations are unfit for the task. In order to redeem His people, the Lord Himself will have to take the form of a servant and embrace His people's weakness (see Phil. 2:8–11).
There is nothing wrong with God's law: it is holy, righteous, and glorious. Yet given Israel's failure to keep it, it became a curse rather than a blessing to His people (see Rom. 7:12, 13).
These conditions have come about because they have rebelled against the law of the Lord (v. 24).
See note on 41:8.

God in effect fought against His own people through the Assyrian and Babylonian devastation of Samaria and Judah. Yet even this act of judgment has not changed them; the law and its curse are ultimately powerless to change hard hearts.

God will establish a new and transformed community. 43:1 created. See note on 4:5. formed. God is Israel's creator as well as her redeemer. See note on 27:10, 11. Fear not. The Lord will deliver His people. See note on 10:24; 35:4. redeemed. See note on 35:8, 9. called \... name. The Lord has called them to be His people and He knows them by name — an expression of His personal care for them (cf. 45:3; 49:1; 62:2; John 10:3; Rev. 2:17). The basic blessing of God's covenant is expressed in Jer. 30:22: "You shall be my people, and I will be your God." See also Ex. 6:7; Lev. 11:45; Jer. 11:4.

These words describe the affliction through which God will bring His people to safety (Ps. 66:6, 12). Water and fire are opposite dangers, and so they encompass every danger in between. Passing through the waters recalls the exodus from Egypt (Ex. 14), while fire often represents the Babylonian exile (29:6). Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were literally protected from the fire (see Dan. 3, esp. v. 27).

Seba is probably South Arabia, or Eritrea. For Cush, see note on Ps. 68:31. The Lord connects the idea of redeeming His people with a concrete ransom, in this case the wealth of several nations combined.

God's people are exalted by election (49:5; Ex. 19:5; Deut. 7:6–8). In spite of their repeated sin and rebellion against Him, for which they have been judged, the nation still belongs to the Lord, and He will not let them go.

–7 east \... west \... north \... south \... everyone. The Lord will bring His people back from the four points of the compass to which they have been scattered. In spite of their sin, they are still His beloved children.
Here again is the community of rebels. See notes on 29:18; 42:18, 19. Spiritually "blind" and "deaf" Israel fulfills the Lord's prophecies in spite of her sin.

The whole world is called to the Lord's courtroom to hear His vindication of Himself as He demonstrates that He alone is able to predict the future before it happens. In this case, He demonstrates His power through the redemption and return of His own people. former things. God's earlier prophecies. See note on 41:22.

OT Israel partially fulfilled this mandate as they returned from exile. Yet it is more completely fulfilled under the new covenant as the church, the new Israel, is commissioned to be witnesses, bringing the good news to all nations (Acts 1:8). servant. See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1.

Is. 40–48stresses the powerlessness of the idols that have surround the Jews in exile in Babylon. Here, the Lord goes further to declare their nonexistence. The idols of the nations don't merely do nothing; they are nothing.
The Lord alone from old willed the redemption of His people (40:21; 41:4). deliver from my hand. See Deut. 32:39. The Lord's power to judge is what proves His power to deliver His own people.

See 35:9; 41:14 and notes. Babylon. The Lord's deliverance specifically includes Babylon as the place from which His people will be delivered long before they are exiled there. The oracles in Is. 40–66, though originally addressed to the postexilic community, were revealed before the exile (cf. 40:1–55:13; 56:1–66:24 notes). Chaldeans. The Babylonians. See note on 13:19.
Isaiah refers to the crossing of the Red Sea (Ex. 14; 15).
The prophet recalls the chariots of Egypt that were destroyed before the face of the Lord, proving the assertion made in v. 13 (cf. 31:1).

In comparison to the return from Babylon, even the exodus from Egypt will seem relatively unimportant (42:9 note). God's action in the past has become the basis for understanding a future event. See note on 40:1–55:13. wilderness \... desert. See note on 40:3. rivers. See note on 41:18.

Creatures associated with desolate areas (34:11–15). See note on 13:20–22. water. Recalls God's provision in the wilderness during the first exodus (Ex. 15:22–26; 17:5, 6). See note on 1:30. my chosen people. See notes on vv. 1, 3.
Instead of presenting offerings and sacrifices in response to the Lord's great grace to them, the people were hardened in their sins and finally went into exile.

The people followed more than one religious practice, but these were not necessarily offered to God. They were weary of serving Him, even though His demands on them were not burdensome. However, they had both burdened and wearied the Lord with their many sins (v. 24), and were finally exiled from the Promised Land. On the emptiness of sacrifices which are mere external rituals, see note on Jer. 7:21–23.
An aromatic plant, possibly sugarcane.

A repetition for emphasis. blots \... remember. God forgives sin, as Israel experienced after the incident of the golden calf (Ex. 34:6, 7; cf. Luke 5:21). The Lord graciously promises to forgive and to establish His word (37:35; 42:21; 48:9, 11).
They stand condemned, unable to refute God's charge. Cf. 1:18.
Jacob was the father of the twelve tribes (Hos. 12:2, 3). mediators. The religious leaders, including prophets and priests.
Judah has been disgraced by the destruction of the temple and the exile of her people, because it was a divine judgment upon their many sins (63:18; cf. 2 Kin. 25:18–21).
See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1. chosen. See notes on 14:1; 43:3.

See note on 27:11. from the womb. God likens Himself to a mother who has conceived and will give birth (v. 24; 42:14; 66:9). Fear not. See notes on 10:24; 35:4. Jeshurun. A poetic name for Israel meaning "upright one" (cf. Deut. 32:15).

This passage develops the promises in 28:6; 32:15. The Spirit lives in the children of the covenant today (Ezek. 36:26, 27; Joel 2:28, 29; Acts 2:38, 39). blessing on your descendants. The Spirit will also confirm God's promises. For the connection between water and the Spirit, see Mark 1:8–10. The blessings of forgiveness and the Holy Spirit are for believers and their children, and those who by faith receive these blessings at the first Pentecost of the new covenant church are also baptized (Acts 2:1–41).
Many will participate in the new age of restoration as Gentiles and Jews together confess the name of the Lord and are joined together as the true Israel of God (cf. Ps. 87:4–6).
The Lord confronts the idols. On Isaiah's polemic against idolatry (vv. 9–20), see note on 2:8. 44:6 Redeemer. See note on 35:9, 10. first \... last. See note on 41:4.
God demonstrates His sovereignty over history through predictive prophecy. See 41:22, 26.
See note on 43:10. Rock. See note on 8:14, 15; Deut. 32:4, 15, 31.
See note on 41:29. Their witnesses. The "witnesses" could be the idols or their makers. Neither has any power of sight or understanding (Ps. 115:8).
The setting is a court of law (41:21).
An idol may be a work of art. But even the finest craftsman's mortality is revealed in his hunger and thirst. How can a human make anything that is greater than himself (cf. 40:28)?
The carpenter makes his god in his own image (Deut. 4:16; Rom. 1:22, 23). Yet the true God has made us in His image (Gen. 1:27).
The same substance is burned and venerated. How can the same thing be both firewood and a deity?
They are utterly foolish (v. 9; 6:9, 10). The idol-worshiper becomes as blind and helpless as the idol that he worships.
The prophet employs ridicule to expose the foolishness of idolatry.
The conclusion: idolatry is a deception, a hoax. "A lie" is a common term in the prophets for an idol.
The Lord alone is redeemer (35:9, 10; 41:14 and notes).

All creation will praise God for His salvation of Israel. The natural order that furnishes materials such as wood and metal from which humans make idols is not as dumb and blind as human idol-worshipers are. Instead, it glorifies its creator. glorified. God will glorify the redeemed, who in turn will lead many to praise the Lord for His mighty acts (4:2 note; 49:3; 55:5; 60:21; 61:3). Creation may rightly praise God, but the greatest praise that God receives is from those who have experienced His redemption.

The Lord's care for His people started before they were born (Ps. 139:13). His redemption is therefore not based on our works, but solely on His electing grace (see Rom. 9:11). This is why He blots out our many transgressions and redeems us (v. 22).
False prophets. diviners. Divination was strictly forbidden in Israel (2:6; 8:19 and notes).

These refer to the Lord's revelations of His plan (11:2 note). He declares ahead of time His purposes through His servants, the prophets (Amos 3:7). servant. See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1. ruins. The regions devastated by Babylon. The restoration of Judah is the beginning of a new stage in the history of redemption.

Possibly a reference to the crossing of the Red Sea (43:16, 19 and notes). The prophecy may have found a literal fulfillment when Cyrus diverted the water of the Euphrates River and marched his army through the water gates that allowed it to flow through the city of Babylon (45:2 note).

Kings were often called shepherds in the ancient Near East (2 Sam. 5:2; Jer. 3:15; cf. Mic. 5:4). The postexilic community is to know that Cyrus rules by God's decree. Raising up a pagan ruler to fulfill the Lord's purpose of bringing His people back to their homeland is as astonishing and miraculous an event as drying up rivers or providing water in the wilderness. Jerusalem \... temple. These are rebuilt by Cyrus's royal decree (Ezra 1:2–4; 6:3–5).

This title is not used elsewhere of anyone outside Israel, and its application to Cyrus would have shocked Isaiah's original audience. It stresses the fact that the Lord can use anyone to accomplish His purposes, even pagan emperors. Identifying Judah's deliverer by name many years ahead of time is a clear mark of the Lord's sovereign power to predict and control the future. right hand I have grasped. He rules by the Lord's authority and has been commissioned by Him for a particular task (41:2; 48:14; cf. Pss. 2:8, 9; 110:1). nations \... kings. See note on 41:2.

Bronze and iron are the hardest known materials at the time the prophecy is given; nothing can withstand the Lord's Servant (cf. Ps. 107:16). doors. The prophecy may have had a literal fulfillment when Cyrus used the gates that allowed the Euphrates to flow through Babylon (44:27 note).
Precious metals come from deep mines (Job 28:1–6). Cyrus plundered the fabulous wealth of Lydia in 546 B.C. call you by your name. The Lord has raised up Cyrus and knows him (cf. 43:1 note).

See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1. Cyrus's success is not for his own sake but a means to God's greater end, which is the deliverance of His people from exile. chosen. See note on 14:1. name you. As God's "shepherd" (44:28) and "anointed" (v. 1), Cyrus has a title of honor. you do not know me. Cyrus is an unbeliever.
The two opposites, the eastern and western horizon, encompass everyone in between.

See note on 27:11. light \... darkness. The Lord asserts His power over two fundamental poles of reality, whose separation was the first step in the process of creating the world (Gen. 1:3, 4). The opposing terms "well-being" and "calamity" include the political realities that Cyrus will disturb in fulfilling the counsel of God.

Creation must prepare itself for the Lord's act of redemption, described by two synonyms: "righteousness" and "salvation" (12:2; 26:17, 18 and notes). In Prov. 3:20, showers of rain are associated with creation, but whereas the earth sprouted green plants in the beginning, now it will sprout with salvation and righteousness.

The image of potter and clay is a common one for the Lord's sovereignty over His people. He is their creator and, as such, He has the right to assign them their purpose and determine whether they are fulfilling it. Indeed, like a potter, the Lord literally formed the first man, Adam, from the dust of the ground (Gen. 2:7; cf. v. 12). Human beings have no rights independent of those assigned to them by the One who created them, and to seek such autonomy is to place oneself under a judgment curse ("woe"). Cf. Jer. 18:6; Rom. 9:20, 21.

Isaiah moves seamlessly from describing creation to describing history, for the same God is sovereign over both (cf. Is. 40). The same power that made the universe out of nothing is now exercised in redeeming His people from their bondage. not for price. Although the Lord gives Cyrus a handsome reward (v. 3) for ransoming His people (43:3), this is not the reason Cyrus has liberated them.
See notes on 43:3; Ps. 68:31. Distant nations will come to worship the one God (Zech. 8:23; Eph. 3:6).

God is said to hide Himself when He seems not to be present to help His people (8:17; 54:8). He is also "hidden" in the sense that He is unaccountable to anyone, and His ways are often mysterious (55:8, 9; Ps. 77:19 note; Rom. 9:20; 11:33, 34).
God is unlike people and idols, who can never secure the future for themselves or for others (cf. Heb. 5:9).

This word is translated "without form" in Gen. 1:2. This was the beginning, not the end of creation. In the same way God does not invite people to seek Him to no purpose. He will carry through with what He has begun (55:11; 66:9) and answer those who seek Him (55:3; Matt. 11:28; Heb. 11:6). Just as He created the world to be peopled, so will His new heavens and new earth must be peopled with a redeemed humanity.

The Lord's revelation is unlike pagan oracles, which are obscure and ambiguous. The Lord's revelation is clear and public, through the words of His prophets, though the outworking of His promises might not conform to human expectations (48:16). Nonetheless, it will be effective in bringing His chosen people into a true relationship with Him.
See v. 14 and note.

God's promises are guaranteed by His own name, for there is no one greater by whom to swear (14:24; 62:8; cf. Gen. 22:16; Ex. 32:13; Heb. 6:13–18). a word that shall not return. None of the Lord's words shall be ineffective. See 55:11. every knee \... every tongue. The goal of redemptive history is to bring Israel's offspring to repentant submission before the Lord's majesty (v. 14 and note; Rom. 14:11; 1 Cor. 15:25; Phil. 2:10, 11). Yet Israel's offspring will include the ends of the earth as well, for God includes the Gentiles in His salvation (see v. 22).

Babylonian gods. Bel means "lord" and probably refers to Marduk, the most powerful god in the Babylonian pantheon, while Nebo (or Nabu) is the god of wisdom. In reality, neither has any true power or wisdom to offer.

The idols are dead weight, lifeless burdens on the animals that have to carry them, unlike the Lord who lifts His people up on eagle's wings (see 40:31). The idols cannot even save themselves from going into captivity, let alone those who worship them. On Isaiah's polemic against idolatry, see 2:8.

The small group that is saved out of the judgment. See note on 1:9. birth \... womb. The Lord's care is like that of a mother for her children — tender, attentive, and with the best interests of His people in mind (44:2 note; 49:5; cf. Deut. 1:31; Hos. 11:3, 4).
Unlike the powerless idols, the Lord is constant in His care for His people, from before their birth to their old age (Ps. 71:9, 18). I am he. See note on 41:4.
A god that cannot move can do nothing to save or to judge.
See notes on 41:22; 42:9. This includes the Lord's past acts of deliverance of His people and judgment on His enemies in which He demonstrated real power to direct the course of events.
Unlike Bel and Nebo (see v. 1), who have neither power nor wisdom, the Lord's power establishes what His wisdom decrees. No power in earth or heaven can stand against His sovereign will.
Cyrus; see 41:2.

These are the transgressors of v. 8. As some in the first exodus looked back to Egypt (Num. 14:3), some in the second exodus remain in Babylon, doubting that the Lord could really bring about His promised salvation and restore the glory of His people — at least at any time in the near future (cf. Hag. 1:2).
See note on 1:8.

An oracle regarding the fall of Babylon, never to rise again. Her fall is the mirror image of Zion's restoration, and it matches Jerusalem's original fall (see 3:16–26). 47:1–3 Babylon, the queen of nations, is commanded to descend from her throne and become a menial slave girl. In contrast, Zion, a captive slave girl, will be commanded to ascend her throne (52:1, 2). God has used the Babylonians to bring judgment on His own people, but they are proud and assume that their gods have given them victory. 47:1 virgin daughter of Babylon. The city of Babylon and its inhabitants. On the idiom, see note on 1:8. Chaldeans. Babylonians. See note on 13:19.
All Babylon's privileges and status will be removed. She will be humiliated.
See notes on 35:9; 41:14, as well as the promise in 43:14 to judge Babylon.
Her boast is based on her contempt for the truths that God rules history and that He will judge her for her cruelties (v. 6; Rev. 18:7). Her society and politics have no regard for the true God.
The Babylonians claim godlike power and self-existence for themselves, a glory that the Lord will not share with anyone (see 45:5, 6, 18, 21, 22; 46:9).

Babylon's losses will occur suddenly. loss of children and widowhood. Bereft of her husband and children, Babylon has no hope for the future and is consigned to slavery and extinction (cf. 49:21–23; 54:1–6). your many sorceries \... your enchantments. The Babylonians are famous in Isaiah's day for the study of magic, so much so that "Chaldean" comes to be a term for those who practice divination. Yet they place their trust in these things in vain.
Babylon's traditions of religion, magic, and divination. See note on 44:25.
Their vaunted wisdom (see v. 10) will be of no value to them.
Isaiah mocks their confidence in divination.
Babylon depends on omens from the heavenly bodies for her decisions (Dan. 2:2).
See Rev. 18:17–19. Babylon's astrologers practice their craft to save Bab­ylon from these prophecies (v. 13), but they cannot even save themselves (Dan. 2:10–13).
Babylon's trading partners, who will be unable to assist her when the day of judgment comes.

This final and urgent appeal is designed to lead deaf and blind Israel (vv. 6, 8; cf. 42:18–20; 46:3–12; 51:1) to recognize God's ways in creation and in history (vv. 12, 16). but not in truth or right. It is possible to be descended from Israel but not be part of the true Israel; the true Israel is known by sincere faith in the Lord (Rom. 2:28, 29; 9:6–8).
of hosts.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The Lord's military title stresses His power to act, so His name is not merely a label but an expression of His character and power.
See notes on 41:22; 42:9.
Parts of the body associated with stubbornness (see Deut. 31:27; Ezek. 3:7).
The Lord alone decrees and executes His will according to His word. Yet His people are stubbornly attached to their idols, even after years of exile.

The evidence speaks for itself, if only they will believe God's word. In the past the problem was that they were blind and deaf to the Lord's message (see 6:10). new things, hidden things. An era of salvation and kingdom righteousness begins with the restoration from exile, including God's raising up Cyrus to set the Jews free (45:1), but these prophecies look forward ultimately to Christ's coming and the growth of His kingdom in its fullness (45:15; Rev. 1:19).
See 1:2.

The exile has been a period of refining (1:22, 25; cf. Ezek. 22:18–22; 1 Pet. 1:7). Difficult though it was, their trial was not as severe as the refining of silver, which involves extremely high temperatures.

The Lord does everything for His own glory, which is good news for undeserving rebels. He will fulfill His original purpose for Abraham and his offspring in spite of their continual rebellion against Him.

Cf. Babylon's boast in 47:8, 10. The Lord is truly the One who was there in the beginning and whose kingdom will never come to an end. The Creator of all things will accomplish His purpose for the universe, which is to have a sanctified, holy people that belong to Him and serve Him.
loves him.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Cyrus (41:2, 25; 45:4; 46:11 and notes).
The Lord gives Cyrus his status and success.

The Lord is the eternal God who speaks and acts (see vv. 12, 13). The last part of the verse refers to one of those acts, sending "me" (the Servant \[see 49:1–3\]) and His Spirit. Some see this verse as a reference to the Trinity. Christ is the servant who came into the world, sent by the Father and the Spirit. Salvation is the work of the triune God.
See notes on 35:9; 41:14. who teaches you to profit. Unlike the idols, whose service is without profit (44:9), serving the Lord is not a wasted endeavor.

God reveals a compassionate longing for His people to find their peace in living for Him. Because they have rebelled against the Lord, they have experienced great and needless pain and loss throughout their history (see 1:5, 6). river \... waves of the sea. These similes represent abundant life (66:12; Amos 5:24). righteousness. See note on 1:21. Peace and righteousness go together (v. 22; 26:3 note; 32:17; 54:13, 14; 60:17; Ps. 85:10; Heb. 7:2).
The promise first made to Abraham (Gen. 12:2; 22:17).
The prophet remembers the exodus from Egypt and how God provided for His people then (41:17–20; 43:19–21; 44:3; cf. Ex. 17:6; Ps. 105:41).

See note on v. 18. This is true both for the nations and for those who claim to be the Lord's people but are simply going through the motions (48:1, 2). Rest can be found nowhere other than in the Lord.

The second of the four "Servant Songs" (42:1–9; 49:1–7; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). 49:1 called \... name. The faithful Servant is called "Israel" (v. 3; 43:1; 44:2, 24; 45:3 and notes). He is distinct from unfaithful Israel, and He Himself has a mission to the tribes of Jacob as well as the task of accomplishing Israel's unfulfilled mission to the Gentiles (vv. 5, 6; 42:18; 46:12; 48:1 and notes).

The Servant conquers through preaching (11:4 note; 51:16 note; 61:1). God's words are effective (40:8; 45:19; 55:10, 11). sharp sword \... polished arrow. These metaphors portray the effectiveness of the word, which in the NT context is explicitly the word of Christ (Eph. 6:17; Heb. 4:12; Rev. 1:16; 2:12, 16; 19:15).
See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1.

The Servant's complaint is fulfilled in Christ's rejection and suffering (42:2 note). right. See 40:10; cf. Gen. 15:1. The Servant triumphs through weakness and is vindicated (50:8) and rewarded after His death and resurrection (53:8–10).
See note on 27:11. bring \... gathered. One purpose of the Servant is to reconcile the Jews to God.

A second purpose of the Servant is to bring the gospel to the nations (Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47; 26:23). He fulfills the call of Abraham (Gen. 12:3; 22:18) and of Israel (Ex. 19:5, 6). Today the ascended Christ brings the gospel to the nations through His body, the church (Matt. 28:18–20; 1 Pet. 2:9, 10). to the end of the earth. See Acts 1:8.

See note on 41:14. servant of rulers. Paradoxically, the King who humbles himself to become a servant of rulers will Himself receive their homage (4:2; 45:24; 52:15). God will exalt the despised and rejected Servant.

This time stands in contrast to the day of vengeance (12:2; 34:8 and notes; cf. 35:4; 59:17, 18; 61:2; 63:4; 2 Cor. 6:2). a covenant to the people. See note on 42:7. The God who covenanted to give Abraham the land will fulfill His promise through His Servant. establish \... apportion. This restoration begins with the return from exile (44:26; 45:8 note).
Those still in exile. See notes on 42:7; 51:14; 61:1. darkness. See notes on 5:30 and 9:2. feed \... pasture. The Servant is Israel's shepherd and king (40:11).
Isaiah alludes to the exodus from Egypt (42:16; 48:21; Ex. 15:13).
See notes on 11:16 and 40:4.
The salvation of true Israel is in view here (11:11 note). Syene. Hb. sinim, which the Dead Sea Scrolls relate to Syene, which is Aswan, in southern Egypt (cf. Ezek. 29:10; 30:6).
See note on 14:7. Creation, which has witnessed the Lord's acts of judgment, will now burst into praise, so great is the Lord's salvation of His people.

God seemed to have abandoned Judah during the exile (40:27; 54:7). Yet it is even more impossible for God to forget those with whom He had entered a covenant than for a mother to forget her own child. "Remembering" here includes not merely calling someone to mind but appropriately acting on that thought.

Though the Lord's memory is infallible, He had written a permanent reminder on His hands to constantly remind Him of His people. walls. See note on 26:1. City walls form the core of the city's defenses, so if the Lord remembers the walls of the city, she cannot fall. Rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem is a crucial step to removing Judah's shame after the exile (see Neh. 1).
Zion's children (see v. 20).

The prophecy of vv. 19–21 looks beyond the return at the time of Cyrus. Nehemiah later builds only a small city, but the promised blessing bursts the boundaries of such historical realities. The prophecy is fulfilled in the new Israel, the church (54:1–3; Zech. 2:4, 5).
