These northern locations will be among the first to see an invader from the north.
It is as if Judah's enemies already own the land.
As representative of the people, the prophet himself feels deeply the pain that will come upon them.
This cry is common in psalms of lament (e.g., Ps. 13:1).

These are moral categories, not just intellectual categories. Original wickedness is strengthened by habit and practice (9:5). God's people have become like children left to their own devices, children who will not learn to do what is right.
Cf. Gen. 1:2, 14, 15. Creation itself is undone by His judgment.
The same phrase is used in Gen. 2:5. Again creation is being returned to its original chaos.
Covenant blessings are now reversed (Deut. 8:7–16).

A vivid repetition of the harlot metaphor. Instead of repenting and turning to the Lord, Judah has persisted in pursuing her former lovers, Assyria and Egypt, hoping in vain that they will provide deliverance for her. lovers \... seek your life. These lines express the ironic truth of Judah's self-deception.
Jerusalem is personified as a woman in labor (Lam. 1:6 note). Woe \... murderers. Jerusalem utters her pathetic, dying breath.

This search is an allusion to Abraham's prayer for Sodom (Gen. 18:22–32) and an implicit answer to Jeremiah's prayer for the city (later forbidden; 7:16). But the city of Jerusalem is so totally corrupt that not even one righteous man can be found.

The people's determination not to repent is the chief frustration of the prophet (cf. Ezek. 3:7–9). This is not just the attitude of the poor and uneducated people but of the noble and powerful classes as well.

Such breach of God's covenant brings the covenant curses of assault by wild animals on the people (Lev. 26:22). A person might possibly escape from one of these animals, but an attack by all three together will surely be fatal.
The motive for following false gods is the delusion that the gods of the land of Canaan have the power to make it fertile. The Lord claims the land's fertility as His own sphere (Hos. 2:8, 9 notes).
Religious prostitution slips over into actual adultery in the worship of the fertility cults. See a similar description in 2:23, 24.
Again the courtroom metaphor is used; an appeal to witnesses is implied. The Lord's justice must be accomplished.

This hint that punishment will not be final is one of several such clues in the early part of the book (12:14–17; 16:14, 15; and 23:3 note). are not the LORD's. In the same breath, Judah's covenant status is annulled (Hos. 1:9 note). The apparently irreconcilable needs of judgment and salvation are both evident here.

Wrong belief about God is related to every kind of untruth (9:3–6). He will do nothing \... famine. These words summarize the attitude of the people, reinforced by the oracles of the false prophets. See 28:2–4.
The people claim that far from having the Spirit (Hb. ruah), the prophets are but wind (also ruah).
That Judah's enemies will consume the bounty of the land is a reversal of covenant blessing. See Deut. 7:13 for the promise of the very things now to be lost.
See Prov. 1:7. who have eyes \... hear not. See note on Is. 6:10. The people become like the idols that they serve (Is. 44:18).

Jeremiah argues from God's power in creation (Job 38–41; Rom. 1:18–20). The people's folly is visible in their trust in powerless idols instead of fearing the all-powerful God, who truly controls the seasonal rains upon which their lives depend (see 3:3).
The nature of wickedness is to entice even the innocent into it. Prov. 2:12–19 describes its alluring speech.
Jeremiah moves from specifically religious sins to social evils, for the two are closely related.

This description symbolizes self-centered wealth, cf. Ps. 73:7. fatherless \... needy. See note on Ps. 9:18. These people are often oppressed in Jeremiah's day because they have no one to be their advocate.

Not only are the prophets and priests teaching what was false, but such teachings are exactly what the people want. They want no one to confront them about their sinful behavior. Such comfort is shortsighted because it deliberately ignores what will happen in the end.

This territory bordering Jerusalem to the north is part of the southern kingdom of Judah. Normally, people would flee to a fortified city in a crisis. In this case, Jerusalem is actually the most dangerous place to be, so people flee from it. Tekoa. A city in Judah, the home of Amos (Amos 1:1). Beth-haccherem. An unknown location in Judah. Most likely, Tekoa and Beth-haccheremwere to the south and west of Jerusalem, so if an enemy from the north reaches them, he already has Jerusalem surrounded. north. See note on 1:14.
See note on 2:2. Though a personification of Jerusalem (4:31 note), the simile has in mind the city's refined women (Is. 3:16–26).
These "shepherds" are enemy officers with their troops (the "flocks") taking possession of the land (cf. 4:15).
These are unusual times to attack; the enemy's strength is such that he is free to attack whenever he likes.
A new oracle is addressed to the as-yet-unidentified force, which will act as the Lord's instrument of judgment. oppression. The rich and powerful of Jerusalem have oppressed their own people.
Judah cannot help pouring out her wickedness because that is her true nature (cf. Matt. 7:16).

Farmers are not supposed to glean everything but to leave something behind for the poor (Deut. 24:19–22). Babylon, however, may "glean" Judah completely (cf. 5:10). The Lord has deeper purposes behind the permission He gives (23:3 note). The curse is not absolute, for God does spare a small remnant to fulfill His covenant of redemption (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). See note on 11:23.
They are as deaf to the Lord's word as uncircumcised pagans would be.

These opposites include everyone in between, showing that judgment will be as comprehensive as the spread of sin, which affects everyone in the community. The prophets and the priests, who are supposed to be the watchmen, are themselves implicated in the evil.

More than absence of war, peace means individual and social well-being that is the consequence of covenant-keeping. Repetition is a way of emphasizing something in Hebrew. The message of false prophets might be attractive but it cannot bring true peace (Mic. 2:6), whose counterpart is righteousness.
This phrase describes the traditional religious life of the Israelites from the time of Moses; it is the task of priests and prophets to direct the people.
The prophets (Is. 21:11; Ezek. 3:17; Hab. 2:1). Those few prophets who do faithfully declare the Lord's word are ignored by the people.
See 2:4; Mic. 1:2.

Expensive ingredients used in religious rituals (Ex. 30:23–38). Sheba is located in distant southwest Arabia during Jeremiah's era. burnt offerings are not acceptable. This indictment is important in the Psalms and Prophets (Ps. 40:6–8; Is. 1:11–15; Mic. 6:6–8). Defiant, unrepentant sinning cannot simply be atoned for by the regular offerings (see Num. 15:30, 31; Matt. 23:23).
Those who seek to approach the Lord while their hearts are devoted to idols will not find access to Him (see Ezek. 14:1–5).
Babylon (1:13, 14 note). From the perspective of those living in the Promised Land, Babylon is at the ends of the earth.
See the description of Babylon in Hab. 1:6–11. Though the Babylonians are God's instrument, He does not approve of their cruelty.
A slogan that Jeremiah uses repeatedly (see 20:3, 10; 46:5; 49:29). The mere report of the approach of such a fearsome enemy is utterly demoralizing.
Such mourning will be especially intense, as without a son the family's name would be lost (see Zech. 12:10).
Elsewhere in the book, the Lord Himself is the One who tests both the people (9:7; 17:10; 20:12) and Jeremiah (11:20; 12:3). The prophet acts as God's agent here (see Mal. 3:2, 3).
Lead is used in the process of refining silver. The process of refining Judah has yielded nothing of value.

Probably the gate leading to the inner court of the temple. Pilgrims may recite passages like Ps. 15 at this entry point to the temple, reminding one another of the need for purity among those who approach the presence of the Lord. Jeremiah stands in the central place of Judah's worship to proclaim its falsehood. The power of this action is heightened because Jeremiah himself is a priest. Alternatively, the Lord may have chosen this location because of its exposure to numerous people. all you men of Judah \... to worship the LORD. Possibly this prophecy is delivered on one of the great annual feasts (Ex. 23:14–18), for that is when every Israelite male is to be present.

OT believers were not saved by their works, but their actions revealed the true nature of their hearts (Matt. 7:16–18). this place. The Promised Land. The force of Jeremiah's appeal here, perhaps a shock to complacent Judah, is that they cannot take the land for granted.

LORD. The repetition gives emphasis and sounds as if the worshipers view it as a magic formula that will automatically protect them. This false confidence in the inherent power of the temple to protect Jerusalem may stem in part from the Lord's dramatic deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib and the Assyrian army in the days of Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:13–19:37). Some of the psalms also promise protection for the Lord's city (e.g., Ps. 46), yet this promise cannot be disconnected from the need for God's people to be faithful to their covenant commitments to the weakest members of the community.

The conditional language echoes that of the Mosaic covenant (Deut. 13:1–3; 14:28, 29). The law warns that if Israel breaks the covenant, she cannot expect the Lord's protection but will be sent into exile (Deut. 28:25, 26).
An allusion to five of the Ten Commandments (cf. Hos. 4:2), with a climactic stress on the first (Ex. 20:3).
See Deut. 12:5; 1 Kin. 8:43, where the "place" is identified as the Jerusalem temple. delivered. False worship yields false security.
A secure place to which robbers return to divide their spoils. Jesus accused the Jerusalem temple of His own day of the same thing (Matt. 21:13).

Shiloh was a central place of worship for all Israel before David made Jerusalem the capital (Josh. 18:1; 1 Sam. 1:9). Since Shiloh is no more in Jeremiah's day (it was probably destroyed by the Philistines because of the sins enumerated in 1 Sam. 2), it is a good demonstration of the prophet's point that even a place where the Lord has made His name to dwell is not immune to His judgment. Just as the glory of God went into exile from Shiloh when the ark was captured (see 1 Sam. 4:22), so it can leave Jerusalem and go to those already in exile (see Ezek. 8–11). In that event, the city will be left unprotected. The same thing has happened already to the northern kingdom, the offspring of Ephraim (v. 15).

Lit. "and I spoke to you, rising up early and speaking," which is meant to express the continuation of the action. Cf. 2 Chr. 36:15, 16. you did not listen. An important theme in the book (6:17; 11:7, 8; 25:3; cf. 2 Kin. 17:13, 14). The statements in vv. 13–15 add a note of finality to the prophet's message.

Such prohibition is ominous because one of the roles of the prophet is to intercede. (Abraham served as an intercessor and Moses did as well; cf. Gen. 20:7; Ex. 32:11–14.) The prohibition is repeated at 11:14 (cf. 15:1; 1 John 5:16). A key element in Jerusalem's deliverance in the days of Hezekiah was the intercession of the prophet Isaiah (Is. 37:4–7).
A picture of the universal hold idolatry has on the people. queen of heaven. A name for the Babylonian goddess Ishtar (44:19, 25). The cakes apparently bear her image (see 44:19).

The worship of Ishtar, a fertility goddess, is supposed to ensure agricultural success. Yet a breakdown in the relationship between the Lord and His people will affect negatively the fertility of humans, their domestic animals, and all of their crops.

God is not interested in sacrifices without the inner worship of the heart; thus, the people might as well eat the sacrifices themselves if they offer them that way. This prophetic condemnation of empty ritual is all the more remarkable because the sacrificial system revealed to Moses is still in force in Jeremiah's era. Jeremiah is not alone in speaking this way (cf. 1 Sam. 15:22, 23; Is. 1:11–15; Hos. 6:6; Amos 5:21–25; Mic. 6:6–8).

This portrayal of Judah strongly suggests a native disposition toward evil in the human heart. The word "stubbornness" in Hebrew may more properly be rendered "self-reliance." Jeremiah uses this term more than any other biblical author.
See note on v. 13.

This command is in the grammatical feminine and personifies Jerusalem as a woman (cf. 2:1, 2). The Nazirite vow involves allowing the hair to grow unchecked as a sign of consecration to the Lord (Num. 6:2–8). The cutting off and throwing away of Jerusalem's hair therefore represents her de-consecration and rejection by the Lord because of her defilement. The Lord has rejected and forsaken His previously chosen city.

This verse is evidence of the presence of a foreign cult in the temple itself, as under Manasseh (2 Kin. 21:7). Josiah removed the abomination, but it has been returned by the time this oracle is given, possibly in the time of Jehoiakim (Introduction: Author; Date and Occasion). Ezekiel also describes such defilement (Ezek. 8:3–12). Such practices explain Jeremiah's reference to Judah's persistent rebelliousness.

The usual name for pagan cult centers (2 Kin. 23:8, 9). Topheth. Lit. "place of fire." This is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, where children are sacrificed to the foreign god Molech in Jeremiah's day. Offering the firstborn child is practiced by Israel's neighbors in Jeremiah's day, but in Israel the firstborn child is to be "redeemed" by substituting an animal for sacrifice (Ex. 13:2; 34:19, 20). Child sacrifice is expressly forbidden (Lev. 18:21; 20:2–5). See also 2 Kin. 23:10 and note. The reference may be meant to undercut a perverted notion among some that child sacrifice fulfills an ancient Mosaic custom (cf. Ex. 22:29). Valley of the Son of Hinnom. Southwest of Jerusalem; its equivalent name in Greek is Gehenna, or "hell" (Matt. 5:22 note).

See 1 Kin. 14:11 and note. Exhuming remains (8:1) inflicts an even greater dishonor than leaving a corpse exposed to scavengers, and it is a way of defiling sacred places so that they could no longer be used for that purpose (2 Kin. 23:16, 18).
The irony in this curse is that they worship these heavenly bodies (2 Kin. 21:3–5). Is. 40:25, 26 declares the Creator to be greater than these created things.
Life in exile will be so traumatic that even death will be better (see Deut. 28:64–68).

Just as it is normal for people to get up again after they have fallen down, so ought it be normal for God's people to repent when they sin. Yet instead of turning away from their sins and repenting, they have turned toward them in a headlong rush like a horse charging into battle.

The created order perfectly obeys the laws that God has laid out for it; thus, birds never refuse to migrate at the proper time. Yet the Lord's people, who out of all humanity ought to be most obedient, do not know or obey His rules.
The wise are a group, perhaps the same group as the "scribes"; cf. 2 Sam. 8:17; Ezra 7:6 and notes. It is likely that the oral traditions of some scribes have in Jeremiah's day distorted the law.

Unlike the wisdom expounded in Proverbs, the wisdom of these scribes is empty, having no real knowledge of the Lord's Word. They may know what it says, but failing to do what it says betrays a lack of wisdom. See Deut. 4:6. The same was true of the scribes of Jesus' day (see Matt. 23).

The motive for the false prophets is greed. If they pretend that there is no real problem in society and that there is peace between God and His people, they are more likely to be popular. See note on 6:14.

The vine symbolizes Judah (2:21). However, the language also suggests a loss of fertility, a blessing of God that the people have attributed to other gods (Hos. 2:8, 9). They will personally suffer the covenant curses, whose reality they have strenuously denied.

The word is the same as for "gathering" the harvest in v. 13. Yet there is no safety in numbers, even in the fortified cities. Once they understand that the Lord is judging them for their sin, it will be too late to repent. The ones who insist on seeking their water from broken cisterns (2:13) will be given poisoned water to drink. This recalls the judgment at Marah in the wilderness, where the water was too bitter to drink, though on that occasion the Lord graciously healed the water (Ex. 15:22–25).
This may be taken literally, as a kind of plague (cf. the "poisoned water," v. 14; Num. 21:6), or as a figure of speech for the enemy.
The Hebrew in this phrase is problematic; this rendering comes from the Septuagint (text note).
The false confidence of 7:10 has been shattered by unfolding events.
Jeremiah participates in the suffering of the people (14:2). Likewise, the Lord does not delight in the judgment of the wicked (see Ezek. 18:23).

Gilead is known for its medicinal products in Jeremiah's day (46:11), but the balm that one could normally expect to find there is absent. no physician \... restored. For the healing metaphor and false healers, see 8:11. The desire for a physician is an appeal to God as such; He will come at the right time in the person of Christ, the Great Physician (30:17; cf. Luke 4:18, 19).

A key interpretive question here is determining who is speaking. It seems that the Lord Himself is offering this lament, though it could also be from Jeremiah. In either case, Jesus shares the sympathy for the people expressed in these verses (Luke 19:41).
This statement is jolting, especially if God is the speaker; however, the grammatical form of the verb shows that the action has not taken place.

This is a military simile; their bow is falsehood, and they go out wielding it as if to battle. The focus of this section is the sins of the tongue. declares the LORD. God concurs with Jeremiah's estimation of the moral condition of the people (vv. 1, 2). The Lord's attitude is expressed through the prophet.
See note on 6:27–30.
Such peace (Hb. shalom) is a true basis for society, and a product of covenant faithfulness; its opposite is falsehood, which is unfortunately the actual basis of their society.

Jeremiah weeps particularly for the desolation of the land God gave His people to be rich and populated, but which is desolate. See Mic. 1:8. The Lord also grieves for the destruction of the land, but justice must be done.
The lack of inhabi­tants marks the land as cursed (cf. Ps. 44:19; Is. 13:21, 22).
This language is reminiscent of the concept of wisdom as God-given knowledge (Prov. 1:2–5). The idea of wisdom as a recommendation of Israel among the nations (Deut. 4:6) has now been overturned.
See Deut. 4:8.
See note on 7:24. The people have developed an atrophy of the will by continually refusing to do what is right.
They are aware of their existence, but they have never had a relationship with them (cf. Deut. 28:36; Ezek. 32:9).
The weeping theme is taken up again (vv. 1, 10), with the OT's clearest allusion to professional wailing women employed to lead in mourning for the dead (Amos 5:16).

The actions of death are poetically personified as a stealthy thief or a conquering army. children \... young men. See 6:11; Lam. 5:13–15 and notes. Death usually carries off older people, but now it will remove the children and young men as well, leaving the community without hope for the future.

See theological note "Knowledge of Self and Knowledge of God." Wisdom, might, and riches are natural places for sinful human beings to place their trust. Yet none of these things can withstand the outpouring of God's wrath.

See 4:4. Israel is outwardly circumcised, but inwardly uncircumcised. Some of the surrounding nations also practiced circumcision, but not as a covenant sign of belonging to the Lord. Because Israel and Judah are uncircumcised in their hearts, they are effectively in the same condition as the nations. Cf. Jer. 4:4, 6:10; Deut. 10:16, 30:6; Rom. 2:25–29; 4:9–12; 9:8; Gal. 5:6; 6:15.

Terror characterizes the worship of false gods. Worship of heavenly bodies (8:2 and note) carries with it special fears related to the occurrence of unusual phenomena. A biblical understanding of creation should take away these fears, accepting such phenomena as God's created order (Gen. 1; Is. 40:26). Yet God's people can also be overawed by such events.
This word, used elsewhere by Jeremiah for idols (cf. v. 8), conveys their emptiness (2:5). They are as powerless to inflict harm as scarecrows are (v. 5).

Although some idols are cast in precious metals (Ex. 32:4; Neh. 9:18), more often they are carved out of wood and decorated with gold or silver as described here (Is. 40:18–20). The most common household idols are molded from clay and fired like pottery (Judg. 18:17; Is. 30:22; 42:17).

In contrast to the powerlessness of the idols, the Lord is great and mighty. The biblical fear of God involves more than the dread of God's judgment. It includes awe, reverence, and adoration in response to God's majesty and holiness (Ps. 2:11, 12).
The language is like that of the OT's Wisdom Literature.

The former is in Spain, but Uphaz has not been identified. Since it is brought from such distant locations, presumably this silver and gold are of particularly fine quality. Violet and purple are colors associated with wealth and royalty because the dyes used to make them are especially expensive in Jeremiah's era.

See Deut. 5:26. everlasting King. See note on v. 7; cf. Ex. 15:18; 2 Sam. 7:13. The eternity of God's kingdom is affirmed, even though the house of David is about to come to its historical end. wrath \... indignation. Cf. Ps. 97:5.

This verse is in Aramaic (text note), the international language of the period, and reflects the testimony to be delivered to the nations in a way they can understand. The saying also incorporates a play on the similar sound of "make" and "perish" in Aramaic.

Jeremiah appeals to the power of the true God in creation in his argument against foreign gods. For creation's being accomplished by God's wisdom, see Prov. 8:22–31, a passage that foreshadows Christ as the preexistent wisdom of God (Col. 1:15; 2:3).
See Pss. 29:3, 4; 135:5–7. The Lord's control of the rain directly counters claims made for the Canaanite god Baal (see 1 Kin. 17:1). God alone has power over rain, clouds, lightning, and wind.

For the Lord as one's portion or inheritance, see Num. 18:20; Ps. 16:5. Originally this referred specifically to the Levites, but later it is used more broadly to describe what God promised Israel in His covenant with them. The same God who created the universe also summoned Israel into existence and gave them their land as an inheritance.

See Jeremiah's cry in 4:19–21. He empathizes with his audience. The medical metaphor is a favorite in Jeremiah (6:7; 14:17; 30:12, 13, 15, 17). The exile is now inevitable; Judah's wound is incurable.
The sorrows of losing children fill in the picture of the desolation of exile (16:3–5). The picture of Judah as a tent is also found in 4:20.
Not only are the idols and the ones who worship them stupid (cf. 10:14), but the leaders ("shepherds") are as well (cf. 4:22 note).
Babylon (1:13, 14 note).
This thought is found also in the Wisdom Literature (Prov. 16:9).
Distinguishes between a corrective chastening, as promised in 2 Sam. 7:14, 15, and a judgment that represents casting someone off forever (see Ps. 6:1)
This verse may be a citation of Ps. 79:6, 7.
Judah's idolatry is a violation of the covenant and will result in captivity as part of the curses of the covenant.

The commands of God in the Mosaic covenant (Deut. 1:1). If the people were unfaithful to the Mosaic covenant, they would lose possession of the land, though their salvation was always a work of God's grace. covenant. A covenant is a solemn agreement between two or more parties. It is the kind of relationship into which God freely entered first with all mankind (Gen. 9:1–17), then with Abraham as the father of Israel (Gen. 17:1–21), then with Israel at Sinai (Ex. 19–24), then with David (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Ps. 89:3), and finally with the whole people of God in the new covenant (31:31–34 notes). The goal of the covenant is for the Lord to have a holy people belonging to Himself (see v. 4).
See Deut. 27:15–26.
Israel's formative but painful experiences in Egypt.

The covenant with Abraham was in the form of a divine promise (Gen. 15:17–21; cf. Deut. 4:31). Under the terms of the Mosaic covenant, the temporal blessings of the Abrahamic covenant (i.e., the possession of the land) were administered on the basis of Israel's obedience (Ex. 19–24; Lev. 26; Deut. 28), but the Abrahamic blessing of eternal salvation was administered in the same way it is administered under the new covenant — on the basis of Christ's obedience. Under both covenants, the obedience of believers demonstrates the vitality of their professed faith; it is not the means by which they secure their righteousness before God (Rom. 3:21–26; James 2:14–26). a land flowing with milk and honey. See Ex. 3:8; Deut. 6:3. So be it. Hb. amen. Indicates acceptance of the terms laid down. See Deut. 27:15–26.
For the blessings that accompany obedience to the Sinai covenant and the curses for disobedience, see Lev. 26 and Deut. 28.
This could be resistance to the Lord's words through Jeremiah, or opposition to Josiah's reform. Either way, the word "conspiracy" has overtones of rebellion against a king (see 2 Kin. 15:30; 17:4).
Again, the covenant is traced back to the promise to the patriarchs (v. 5 and note). Judah's present breach of it is consistent with the pattern of Israel's history (see esp. the book of Judges).

When the inevitability of judgment finally dawns on Judah, the people will cry out to the Lord, only to find Him deaf to their pleas. When they cry out to their idols, they will discover that they are unable to help them.
Incense was used in pagan worship and also in worship of the Lord (1:16; 7:9; 18:15; Ex. 30:7–9). It was one of the simplest offerings to make and could be offered in a variety of locations.
Since the Lord already determined that He would judge His people, there is no point in Jeremiah's interceding for them. See note on 7:16.

Judah, also in 12:7. The term of endearment is in line with the courtship and bridal imagery of 2:2; 3:1. in my house. See 7:10, 11; Ezek. 8:6–13. sacrificial flesh \... exult. The Hebrew is difficult; the criticism, however, is of unacceptable worship that produces a falsely based joy in God's salvation.
The Lord had planted and provided for Israel in a way that should have established her fruitfulness. However, she had turned out dry and barren. Paul uses a similar image for Israel in Rom. 11:17–24.

A simile drawing on the practice of sacrifice (see Ps. 44:11). Jeremiah often uses the language of the psalms of lament (see Introduction to the Psalms). As a type of Christ, Jeremiah prefigures the sufferings of Christ in his life (Is. 53:7). tree with its fruit. Meaning Jeremiah and his message, or an emphatic reference to his life. cut him off \... remembered no more. Not to be remembered, by having no children, is the worst of fates for the people of Jeremiah's day. Those who tried to cut off Jeremiah's remembrance are themselves forgotten, while through his prophecy, Jeremiah is remembered today.

Jeremiah is not asking for the Lord to judge his personal enemies but for the Lord to establish His justice in the face of attempts by the wicked to suppress it, which is a common theme in the psalms of lament (e.g., Ps. 78:9, 10). See Introduction to the Psalms: Special Issues: The Curses of the Psalms.

They are from Jeremiah's own town (1:1). The details of the plot reveal that his worst opposition comes from those closest to him (Ps. 69:7–9; Matt. 10:36, citing Mic. 7:6). In this respect also, Jeremiah prefigures Christ (John 7:2–5; Acts 1:15–20).
This threat of total extinction contrasts the fate of those who plot against Jeremiah, the Lord's chosen prophet, with that of Judah in general (see 4:27; 5:10; 6:9, and notes).

–3 Why does the way of the wicked prosper. The psalmist asks the same question in Pss. 37 and 73. Here, instead of pleading the Lord's case against the people, the prophet pleads his own case with the Lord. Since God is sovereign, the wicked must have been planted by Him (see 1:10). They are growing like a green tree, while Jeremiah himself continues to suffer.

The Lord gently rebukes Jeremiah by making comparisons from the lesser to the greater, from what is easy to what is comparatively more difficult. If the prophet is struggling now, what will he do when the opposition to him gets much greater?
God's "heritage" includes both the land given to Israel (Deut. 4:21) and the people themselves. See vv. 8, 9; 2:7. beloved. See 11:15 and note.

This first of a series of similes (cf. vv. 9, 10) shows how Judah's nature has been changed. I hate her. As often in the Bible, "hate" is the only alternative to love (Mal. 1:2, 3). It includes the action that flows from the feeling, not merely the feeling itself.
Foreign rulers. pleasant portion. See Is. 5:7.
The land of Canaan, once the royal garden of God has been turned into a desert.
The verse exposes the lie of the prophets' false proclamations of peace (6:14).

Though the Lord uses Judah's enemies to punish her, these foes themselves will also be judged. pluck up. When God judges Judah's enemies by removing them from their own lands, He also will deliver and restore Judah. Chs. 30–33 develop this theme.

This marks an astonishing turn in thought, anticipating a restoration and salvation of all the peoples of the world. Jeremiah looks forward to the inclusion of the Gentiles in God's salvation (46:26; 48:47; 49:6), as do other prophets (e.g., Is. 42:6). The promise of the Abrahamic covenant cannot be nullified by Israel's disobedience; God is determined to bless all nations through Abraham and his seed.
See Is. 19:25 for an equally surprising use of "my people" — for Egypt.

The loincloth symbolizes the close relationship between God and His people. Linen is expensive in Jeremiah's day, so this is a costly garment. Several of the prophets, especially those called to address hostile audiences such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel, perform these kinds of sign-acts that are designed to display their message in pictorial form .

A nearer location than the river in Mesopotamia may be intended (possibly Parah, Josh. 18:23, which is close to Anathoth). The similarity of name nevertheless suggests the Euphrates and therefore the Babylonian exile.
The loincloth's predictable ruin depicts the corruption of the people, who are no longer fit for a relationship with the Lord — or anything else for that matter.
The Lord spells out the meaning of the symbolic act as an illustration of His covenant with all Israel.

Wine is here used as a symbol of God's wrath (25:15–29). As with the sign-act, the parable depicts an obvious truth and then applies it to Judah's situation. The leaders of Judah will be filled with drunkenness and then smashed against one another like clay wine jars, destroying them in the process.

Probably Jehoiachin and his mother, Nehushta (2 Kin. 24:8). This prophecy is thus close to the time of Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Jerusalem in 597 B.C. (Introduction: Author; Date and Occasion). The queen mother exercises a position of power and influence in society (1 Kin. 15:13). The poem takes the form of a lament, acting as if they are already dead. has come down. See 22:24–26. This judgment spells the end of the Davidic dynasty, and seems to conflict with the promise to David (2 Sam. 7). However, see 33:14–26 for the future fulfillment of the Davidic covenant.

These cities along the southern border will be the last to see the Babylon invaders, who will approach from the north. If they are surrounded, the whole country is overrun. Judah's pride in her own resources is hollow (v. 17).
See 4:6.
A picture of public shame, as of a prostitute or an adulteress. The punishment fits the crime (see 3:8, 9). Compare the similar judgment on the Lord's adulterous people in Ezek. 16:36 and Nah. 3:5.

A rhetorical question expecting a negative answer. Ethiopians in the Bible come from Cush, the southern part of Egypt, and have dark skin. It is typical of Jeremiah to assert Judah's inability to repent and obey the Lord — hence his new covenant theology (31:31–34 and notes). See theological note "Free Will" on p. 1293.
Recalls the lot cast for the division of the land (Josh. 14:2). Now it signifies expulsion from the same land. lies."The lie" is a common derogatory term for idols.

The people are so hardened in their sin that God will not answer Jeremiah's prayer for deliverance from the punishment of drought, the sword, famine, and plague — four of the covenant curses threatened in Lev. 26:19–26. In answer to Jeremiah's question as to whether God has rejected Judah completely (14:19), God replies that the coming judgment is inevitable because of Judah's sin, but He assures Jeremiah of personal deliverance from his enemies. 14:1The word of the LORD that came. This is not the normal Hebrew phrase that introduces a prophetic oracle, for the first part of this chapter is more of a lament over the drought than specific instructions from the Lord.
A sign of mourning.
The Lord either gives or withholds the rain (Deut. 11:10–15; 28:12).
These hardy wild animals are used to withstanding the normal variations in rainfall in the Promised Land. However, even they will be unable to survive the drought.
The Hebrew word also means "pool," a striking word in time of drought.

This calling explains the meaning of "for your name's sake" in v. 7. The Lord's honor is at stake in the fortunes of His people. Yet they cannot simply assume that He will always rescue them from trouble, no matter how they have behaved.

LORD. God responds directly to the prayer of vv. 7–9. Often in a lament, there is an assurance of deliverance after confession and supplication. In this case, however, since there is no real repentance, the Lord responds by confirming the judgment against them. this people. Significantly, God does not use "my people."
See 7:16 and note. Here the prohibition follows the intercession in vv. 7–9.

Ritual for its own sake — even ritual ordained by God Himself — does not move God (7:21–23 note). sword \... famine \... pestilence. The first of fifteen appearances of this combination in Jeremiah (e.g., 15:2). This is a typical summation of the horrors that judgment can bring (Deut. 32:24, 25).
Those who falsely prophesy peace (6:1–4; 8:11). Jeremiah pleads on behalf of the people whom they have misled.

The prophet's plea (v. 13) misses its mark: the people should have tested the prophets by their prophecies (Deut. 13:2, 3; 18:21, 22). Jeremiah's own words are themselves tragically vindicated by the events surrounding Jerusalem's fall. none to bury. See 7:33.

The prophet's sorrow represents the Lord's heartbreak over having to judge His own people in this way, just as Jesus later weeps over hard-hearted Jerusalem (Matt. 23:37). The prophet laments the way in which God's people have changed from a virgin daughter to a wanton prostitute. However, there are no tears of repentance in the eyes of those to whom the prophet speaks.
Because of the false prophets' teaching (v. 13 and note).
The temple is in view (see 2 Kin. 19:15; cf. 1 Kin. 8:27). your covenant. Jeremiah recalls the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Gen. 15:12–21; 26:3–5; 28:13–15; Lev. 26:42–45).

God identifies two great prophets who were archetypal intercessors for Israel (Ex. 32:11–14; 1 Sam. 12:23). Note also Elijah in 1 Kin. 17:1. Prayer for the people is again prohibited (7:16; 11:14), and the prayer just offered (vv. 19–22) is specifically rejected.
See 1 Kin. 21:23; note on 7:33.

A son of the reformer King Hez­ekiah (2 Kin. 20:21) and one of the most wicked kings (2 Chr. 33:1–9). Even after the reforms of his grandson Josiah, Judah's punishment and exile continues to be linked to him (2 Kin. 23:26). See Introduction: Author; Date and Occasion.

The people claim that God has rejected them (14:19), but the reality is the exact opposite. The phrasing in the Hebrew is emphatic: "You \[the people\] have rejected me." going backward. See 3:22. I am weary of relenting. Such promises as in 31:20 are for the moment in the background.

Winnowing involves separating the grain from the chaff by throwing both into the air with a special fork; the lighter chaff is blown away by the wind, while the heavier grain falls to the ground. See 4:11, where the metaphor is used slightly differently. Here it means punishment (cf. Is. 41:16).
The Babylonians are so confident that they don't try to conceal their plans but attack in broad daylight (see 6:4).

A picture of blessing (Ps. 127:5) is reversed. rest of them \... to the sword. Even the remnant left by the destruction is threatened with death. Cf. Is. 6:13, where a similar thought is finally softened by the promise of the "seed."

These words describe the role that has been assigned to Jeremiah as the prosecutor of the Lord's case against His people (see 2:9). I have not lent \... borrowed. Lending money at interest is forbidden in Ex. 22:25, but was nonetheless a common exploitative practice in antiquity. If Jeremiah has taken advantage of people in that way, or has borrowed money and been unable to repay it, people will have good reason to hate him (Prov. 22:7). The people's hatred for him, therefore, is groundless.
How can Jeremiah be expected to change Judah's stubborn heart? See 13:23 and note, as well as 28:10–13. from the north. Babylon, Judah's enemy, will come from the north (see 1:13, 14).
This prophecy is fulfilled for Jeremiah at 43:4–7.
Recalls the sweet side of the bittersweet task of receiving God's words (Ezek. 3:1–3). I am called by your name. This phrase is applied to the people in 14:9.

No doubt this is literally true, partly due to his enforced celibacy (16:2). But there can also be a profound sense of loneliness for the unwelcome prophet; cf. Elijah in 1 Kin. 19:10 and Jesus in Matt. 26:37, 38. indignation. When he ate the scroll — i.e., received God's words — the prophet internalized the Lord's anger toward His people. Cf. note on v. 16.

The wound is Judah's in 14:17. The whole phrase is applied to Judah in 30:12, together with a promise of healing (30:16, 17). See also 10:19, where it is used of Jeremiah. a deceitful brook. Jeremiah accuses the Lord of behaving like an unreliable stream that dries up during the summer months when there is no rain (see 20:7).

Jeremiah is prohibited from marrying and taking part in other normal activities as a sign of coming judgment (ch. 16). A sharp contrast is drawn between the destinies of those who trust in people and those who trust in God (17:1–18).

The prohibition is related exclusively to Jeremiah's role as a prophet of Judah's fate (1 Cor. 7:26). Even priests and those who take Nazirite vows are normally free to marry in the prophet's era. Jeremiah will be childless, a sign that there is no immediate future for Judah. A day is coming when many who have married will lose their spouses and children in the Babylonian invasion.
See note on 14:12.
In the coming judgment on Jerusalem, so many people will die that normal funeral practices will be suspended. Jeremiah is to act out the Lord's lack of compassion toward His people.
These pagan practices are forbidden in Deut. 14:1. Such paganism has become so common in Judah that it must be specifically banned in this passage.
After v. 2 and v. 5, there is yet a third symbolic prohibition.
See also 7:34. Such sounds are typical of times of peace and hope (Matt. 24:38, 39; cf. 33:10, 11).

Jeremiah's extraordinary behavior is intended to provoke people to ask questions about the causes of the coming judgment. The answer is a combination of the sins of the fathers (14:20) and the even greater sins of the present generation (31:29, 30; Ezek. 18:2–4).

God will send them into exile (see Deut. 28:36, 64). serve other gods. With a punishment to fit the crime, the people who have served other gods in the land the Lord gave them will be made to serve these same gods in the homelands of those gods. There, the people will finally discover that these gods can provide no benefit.
Judah is pictured as the prey of the Lord. every mountain and every hill \... clefts of the rocks. There will be no escape (23:24; Is. 2:19).
This is normally be good news for God's people. See theological note "The Omniscience of God" on p. 1041. Here, however, it means inescapable judgment.
The Hebrew word for "double" may mean an exact match, in the same way that one might speak of an actor's "double."

ORD, my strength. Unlike the rest of God's people, Jeremiah still finds refuge in the Lord. The nations too will ultimately reject their own gods ("the lies"; 13:25 note) and come to the Lord, underlining the extreme foolishness of Judah's continuing commitment to her idolatry.
LORD. Knowing the Lord's name here means recognizing His authority and power through His acts of judgment.

Judah's heart of stone is so hard that only a tool of the hardest material can possibly write on it. on the tablet of their heart. This metaphor recalls tablets for writing laws. See 31:33, where the law will be written on the heart, and Prov. 3:3; 7:3. In the new covenant, Christ writes the law on His people's hearts by His Spirit (2 Cor. 3:3). on the horns of their altars. These altars should commemorate atonement for sin, but where the sin is unforgiven, they continue to remind God of the sin itself.
See notes on 2:20; Ex. 34:13; Deut. 7:5. Asherim are living trees or wooden poles in pagan sanctuaries that represent the fertility goddess Asherah.
In Jeremiah's era, pagan worship takes place on "high places" such as mountaintops. However, in some cases, the high places are located within towns and cities.
The Promised Land (2:7).
Two different Hb. words for "man" are used here. The second word (adam) focuses on the weakness of mere humanity in contrast to the power of God (cf. Ezek. 28:2).
The Lord repays trust because He is by nature trustworthy (Is. 7:9). The close similarity between vv. 7, 8 and Ps. 1:1–3 suggests that trust in the Lord entails obedience to His law.
This image is a potent symbol of strength in a dry country, and a reminder that true fertility is to be found in the Lord's blessing, not in the Canaanite fertility gods Baal and Asherah (Ps. 1:3).
In the OT, the "heart" is more than the seat of emotion. It represents the basis of character, including the mind and the will (4:19; Prov. 4:23; 16:23). See theological note "Free Will."

Lit. "kidneys." In ancient Hebrew idiom, these organs represent the seat of the emotions. Together with "heart," "mind" indicates a person's secret thoughts and feelings. No human being can completely uncover someone else's thinking, but the Lord weighs every secret intention and is able to dispense perfect justice to all. Given the corrupt state of every human heart, it is not good news that the Lord will judge each one according to the fruit of his or her deeds.

In the prophet's day, people commonly believe that partridges steal the eggs of other birds, but the hatchlings return to their natural parents. In the same way, a person will not be able to retain riches unjustly gained. and at his end \... fool. On the transience of riches, see Prov. 23:4, 5. In the Bible, "fool" indicates someone with a moral deficiency, not a mental one.

See note on 14:21; Ps. 99:1. from the beginning. This implies that Zion was chosen as God's throne even before the temple was built (Ex. 15:17). The mountain where the temple was built was the same one on which Abraham was to offer up Isaac (Gen. 22:2; 2 Chr. 3:1).
They will soon be forgotten. Cf. the thought of Ex. 32:32. the fountain of living water. See 2:13.
The psalmist sometimes uses the language of sickness to describe broader difficulties and trials. The Lord's deliverance from such trials comes as healing.
LORD. With this taunt, Jeremiah is accused of being a false prophet (Deut. 18:21, 22), though he has been a faithful shepherd and not a hireling. See Mic. 7:10; 2 Pet. 3:2–4.
Prayer for judgment upon his enemies is common in Jeremiah (11:20; 12:3; 15:15). The words are reminiscent of his call (1:17). double destruction. See note on 16:18.
This location is not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture.
The message is given at the gates because of their role in commerce (see Neh. 13:15, 19).

Carrying a load is forbidden on the old covenant Sabbath since it is a form of work. Bringing loads through the gates of Jerusalem necessitates further work in the form of selling on the Sabbath. keep the Sabbath day holy. Specific appeal is made to the Sabbath commandment, which is a central requirement of the Lord's covenant with His people, distinguishing them from their neighbors (Ex. 20:8–11; Deut. 5:12–15; Neh. 10:31; Is. 56:2). The exile is in part a punishment for Israel's failure to keep the Sabbath, as well as an opportunity for the land to enjoy its Sabbath rest (see Lev. 26:34, 35; 2 Chr. 36:21).

This prophecy presents a picture (partly repeated in 22:4) of the restoration of the Davidic dynasty, the social structure, and the worship, which all center on the temple. See also 23:5, 6; 30:9; 33:14–26. All that is threatened for Judah, therefore, can be reversed.

Just as a potter remolds a marred pot, God will remold His people by disciplining them in exile (18:1–17). Jeremiah portrays God's judgment by breaking a clay jar (ch. 19), and he is mistreated because of his unpopular message (18:18–23; ch. 20).
Apparently in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, near the Potsherd Gate (19:2); hence the command to "go down." See also 7:31.
The potter has freedom with respect to his plans. The spoiling of his first intention is not final.
The analogy with Israel follows. The use of "Israel" recalls God's historic purposes of election for the whole people, purposes to which Judah is now heir.

The potter illustration (vv. 2–4) shows that the Lord's purposed judgment may be revoked by that nation's repentance. Judah cannot rest simply in being the Lord's chosen people if by her actions she continues to rebel against Him. From one perspective, the Lord does not change His mind, for He is unchanging and outside of time (Num. 23:19). Yet human actions of faithfulness, repentance, or rebellion have meaning and significance nonetheless.

The people's hard-heartedness is demonstrated by their refusal to repent even when Jeremiah pleads with them. They would rather remain committed to their rebellion and perish than turn to the Lord and live. However, the prophet's words also contain a message of hope for the next generation: even in exile, they can repent and receive the Lord's blessing.
See note on 14:17. very horrible thing. One of the strong terms used for idolatry (v. 15; cf. 5:30).
The slopes of the mountains in Lebanon are always covered with snow, and the waters that flow from them never run dry. In terms of faithfulness and consistency, Judah has been the exact opposite.
See note on 11:13. ancient roads \... side roads, not the highway. See note on 6:16. The "side roads" are narrow and dangerous.
A gesture of astonishment and mockery.
Cf. 4:11. my back, not my face. Withheld favor (2:27). God will turn His back on them.

The Lord's claim in v. 12 that the people prefer their own plots or plans to obeying the Lord proves true; instead of repenting in response to the prophet's words, the people plan to harm him. priest \... wise \... prophet. Three means of receiving the Lord's wisdom are through the teaching of the Mosaic law (priests; Deut. 33:8–11), reflection on God's creation (wise men), and the declaration of the word of the Lord (prophets). The people are denying that the Lord has really turned His back on them, as Jeremiah maintains in v. 17.

This is legal language. Jeremiah's opponents are not merely slandering him with their tongues but are plotting to kill him (v. 23). Anyone who brings a false charge against someone else, such as accusing Jeremiah of being a false prophet, is subject to the penalty they seek for him (see Deut. 19:18, 19).
Cf. Ps. 35:12; 1 Pet. 2:19–24. dug a pit. They have a murderous intention (v. 22). See Jeremiah's actual experiences in 37:16; 38:6. stood before you \... for them. See note on 15:1.
The word for flask in Hebrew (baqbuq) is onomatopoeic, mimicking the sound of liquid being poured from a long, narrow-necked decanter of some sort.

See note on 18:2. Potsherd Gate. A gate on the south of the city, possibly the Dung Gate (Neh. 2:13). It may be where potters deposit their broken wares, which makes it an appropriate location for the sign.
The words closely resemble 2 Kin. 21:12, which also concerns judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. The judgment is severe and shocking to anyone who hears of it.
Child sacrifice is more often related to the worship of the god Molech in the OT, but here it is linked to the worship of the Canaanite fertility god, Baal.
See note on 7:31.

The Hebrew verb for "make void" has the same root as "flask" in v. 1, and thus again is onomatopoeic (lit., "I will empty"). Additionally, the Hebrew word for "plans" is used in 18:18 for the "counsel" that Judah expects to continue from the wise and in 18:23 for their "plotting" to kill Jeremiah. Another term is used for "plans" or "plots" in 18:11, 12, 18. the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth. Deut. 28:26 threatens the curse of dead bodies' being left exposed to the birds and wild animals (cf. 7:33). Scholars have shown how important a proper burial was to the ancient Israelites. Therefore, this is an ultimate dishonor (cf. 2 Kin. 23:13–16, 19, 20).
a thing to be hissed at \... and will hiss. Jeremiah frequently combines noun and verb forms from the same Hebrew root in the same verse. This stylistic device is a common feature of his writing.
Such a horror occurs during the siege of 586 B.C. (Lam. 2:20 and note).

The climax of the scene is another symbolic prophetic action (13:1–11 and notes). The earthenware flask shatters on impact (Ps. 2:9). The metaphor is familiar to the residents of the ancient world whom Jeremiah is to address.
Unlike the soft clay of ch. 18, Judah is so set in her ways that she cannot be reshaped (lit., "healed") but only destroyed. Men shall bury \... no place else to bury. See 7:32.
See 8:2 and note; also 2 Kin. 23:4, 5. This probably relates to the worship of the Astarte/Ishtar, the "queen of heaven" (7:18, 19). defiled like the place. Josiah defiled Topheth (2 Kin. 23:10).

LORD's house. Jeremiah repeats his main message in the temple in Jerusalem to ensure that it reaches a wider audience, triggering immediate opposition from the priests who are in charge of the temple.

The name is apparently common (cf. 21:1; 38:1, each text possibly referring to a different man). Note that senior priests are among Jeremiah's audience in the valley (19:1), and Pashhur is perhaps among them.

Pashhur's duties as governor of the temple include restraining those whose actions disrupt temple worship (29:26; Deut. 25:2, 3). Yet he does nothing about the idolatrous practices that Jeremiah identifies in 7:30, all the while persecuting the prophet by having him beaten and confined. Jeremiah's prayer in 15:18 shows that faithful prophetic preaching is dangerous. the prophet. This title affirms Jeremiah's status as a true prophet, despite the legal action against him. the upper Benjamin Gate. A prominent gate into the temple.

–6 Terror on Every Side. See 6:25. The people should be afraid to be associated with Pashhur, because he is a highly visible example of why the Lord's anger is falling on them. He has abused God's prophet openly while tolerating false prophets. As a result, he and his companions will become living examples of the truth of Jeremiah's threats of exile.

Jeremiah did not foresee the trials that his task would bring, and he received his call (esp. perhaps 1:7, 8) as an overpowering compulsion (4:10). He laments his struggles in prayer, wrestling with God, his enemies, and himself. In saying that God has deceived him, he uses the same verb used of the Lord's strategy in using false prophets to tell King Ahab what he wanted to hear (1 Kin. 22). However, God is not using Jeremiah like one of those false prophets but rather like Micaiah, telling the painful truth to those who do not want to listen.
A compulsion he cannot control makes him utter his message of coming wrath (see Amos 3:8; 1 Cor. 9:16; 2 Cor. 5:14).
See 6:25. If Jeremiah were deceived and his message were false, then the authorities could act against him.

As is typical in laments, the prophet turns from describing the difficulty of his situation to expressing his confidence in God's power and protection. He anticipates that the Lord will act to vindicate him.

Unlike Jeremiah's earlier laments (11:18–20; 15:10), this time there are no words from the Lord designed to encourage Jeremiah. He feels alone in his depression. Normally the person who brings a father the good news of the safe arrival of a baby boy is blessed, but here the prophet curses him. The Spirit has permitted this record of Jeremiah's near-total despair to be preserved for the encouragement and consolation of believers in Christ: great faith is not incompatible with deep struggles. The prophet's words are like Job's (Job 3:1–26).
Sodom and Gomorrah, whose fate is proverbial (Gen. 18; 19; cf. Is. 1:9; Amos 4:11).

These chapters narrate the end of the Davidic dynasty, making it clear that disaster and exile are God's judgment on the sins of Judah's kings and people. Jeremiah denounces false prophets who lead the people astray (ch. 23), but also sounds a note of hope as God promises to gather a remnant of His people from captivity under the leadership of "a righteous Branch" from David's house (23:3–8). The twin messages of judgment and future restoration are repeated in Jeremiah's vision of two baskets of figs (ch. 24). 21:1 Zedekiah. The name means "the Lord is my righteousness." See note on 1:2. sent to him. Zedekiah maintains a vacillating dependence on Jeremiah without the moral courage to obey his warnings (37:3, 21; 38:5, 14, 19, 24–26). Having been placed on the throne by the Babylonians, he has only a tenuous hold on power, especially after he rebels against them. Pashhur. Not necessarily the same Pashhur as in 20:1 (see note) or 38:1. Zephaniah. A priest and the son of Maaseiah (29:25, 29; 37:3; 52:24), not the same as the prophet Zephaniah (Zeph. 1:1). In 2 Kin. 25:18, he is called "the second priest."

A request for guidance. Not all such inquiries are sincere attempts to seek the Lord (see Ezek. 20:1–3). Nebuchadnezzar. King of Babylon, 605–562 B.C. His name is formed with "Nabu" (or "Nebo"), a Babylonian god (Is. 46:1; Dan. 1:1). The variant form "Nebuchadrezzar" (text note) matches the Babylonian spelling more closely. making war against us. Zedekiah has been a vassal of Nebuchadnezzar (37:1), but he rebels against Babylon in 589 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar finally lays siege to Jerusalem in 587. wonderful deeds. The miraculous works of the Lord in the past for His people, perhaps especially His deliverance of Jerusalem from the Assyrians in the days of Hezekiah (see 2 Kin. 18, 19).
Chaldea is part of Babylon and the home of the dynasty founded by Nebuchadnezzar's father, Nabopolassar. For this reason, "Chaldeans" sometimes serves as an alternative name for the Babylonians.

The language depicts the Lord's power in war, especially during the exodus, now horrifyingly turned against His people (Deut. 4:34; 5:15; 7:19; Amos 5:18). anger \... fury \... great wrath. See Deut. 29:23.
See note on 14:12.

In Deut. 30:19, Israel is given the choice between long life in the land if she obeys the Lord or exile if she is disobedient. However, since the people and their fathers have already chosen the way of disobedience and death, the choice for Jeremiah's generation is simply between death for those who remain in Jerusalem and exile for those who surrender to the Babylonians.
In contrast to the Lord's good plans for those already in exile (29:11).
Now begins a section of oracles directed toward the last kings of Judah.
See 9:24. This requirement of justice is expected both of the earthly king and the messianic King (23:5; 2 Sam. 8:15; 1 Kin. 3:28; Ps. 72:1, 2).
The residents of Jerusalem are confident in its inaccessible location, yet they will find their confidence misplaced, as the Jebusites did before them (2 Sam. 5:6, 7).

A word for any of the kings, serving as the prelude to a demonstration of their virtually unbroken failure. They sit on David's throne but they do not follow his example. As in 17:25, the future of the Davidic dynasty is tied to the faithfulness of the nation's kings.
Three of the most powerless groups in the community, whom the kings must protect (Ex. 22:22–24).
See Gen. 22:16; Is. 45:23 and notes. this house. See 2 Sam. 7, where the promise was first made to David. "House" can refer to David's family as well as to a physical building.
These are fertile regions (cf. 8:22 and note). In the prophet's day, Lebanon is well-watered and rich in forests, especially cedar, which was used for the Jerusalem temple (1 Kin. 5:6–10).
Lit. "consecrate." Language normally used of war undertaken by God for His people is used, shockingly, of a foreign army arrayed against God's people (6:4, 5; 21:4, 5).
Josiah and his son Shallum (v. 11). Shallum, also known as Jehoahaz, reigns briefly and is exiled to Egypt in 609 B.C. (2 Kin. 23:30–34). This saying probably dates from that year.
Expensive architectural touches paid for by oppressive taxation of the poor.
The contrast is between kingship seen as the exercise of justice (Josiah) and kingship as an opportunity for getting wealth (Jehoiakim).
See note on Ps. 9:18. Knowing the Lord requires being faithful to His commands (Mic. 6:6–8; John 14:15, 17).
Jehoiakim. dishonest gain \... innocent blood \... oppression. Jehoiakim is guilty of all of the evils Jeremiah condemns (6:13; 7:6; 19:4; 21:12; and cf. 26:20–23).
The extreme shame of no burial, rather than the kind of burial given to family members or respected leaders. See 7:33; 8:1, 2 and notes; cf. 15:3.

These mountainous regions lie to the north, northeast, and southeast, respectively. Jerusalem is pictured as wailing for help to former allies (her "lovers"), themselves now powerless before Babylon, leaving Jerusalem to cry alone.
The wind often represents the Lord's judgment (e.g., 4:11); the shepherds are Judah's kings. See note on 2:8.

In the present context, this phrase is a figure for Jerusalem. (The phrase itself is related to the close trade connections between Jerusalem and Lebanon.) The temple and palace were built with cedar from Lebanon (v. 6 note). The name connotes Judah's pride and false sense of security.

Oracle against Jehoiachin (here called "Coniah"), after whose brief reign (December 598–March 597 B.C.) the first major deportations to Babylon occur. 22:24 signet. Represents the identity of the owner and is used to sign important documents. To reject it is shocking. This indicates a temporary end to the promise to David and his line. Jehoiachin is the last in the direct line of Davidic kings. Zedekiah, who succeeded him and who reigns when the Babylonians destroy Jerusalem, was Jehoicahin's uncle. Later, the same language is used to promise a renewal of the Davidic kingdom (Hag. 2:23).
See note on 21:4.
See 13:18 and note. For other instances of "hurl," see 1 Sam. 18:11; Jon. 1:4. into another country. This reference to exile in Babylon is fulfilled in 597 B.C. (29:2; 2 Kin. 24:15).
Jehoiachin is like the shattered clay vessel of ch. 19.

In this address to the land, the Lord expresses His grief over His inheritance that has been defiled by Judah's sin (2:7 and note; 12:4). The triple repetition adds emphasis, as with the triple repetition of "holy" in Is. 6.

Though Jehoiachin had seven sons (1 Chr. 3:17, 18), none of them will reign as king over Judah. Promises of future Davidic kingship (e.g., 23:5, 6) are fulfilled beyond the scope of the historical Israelite and Judahite kingdoms — in Christ the Son of Man (Dan. 7:13 and note) and the greatest son of David (Matt. 22:41–46). Even the promise to Zerubbabel (Hag. 2:23), Jehoiachin's grandson (1 Chr. 3:19), finds fulfillment in Christ, since Zerubbabel never reigns as king. After Zerubbabel, the monarchy is essentially abandoned until the coming of Christ (Mic. 5:3).

The kings of Judah. It is typical of the prophets to use language imbued with shepherd imagery in order to criticize royalty. Elsewhere, shepherd imagery is used positively to speak of exemplary leadership (cf. Ps. 23).

The failure of the kings requires the Lord Himself to take control in a new way (24:7 note). remnant. The gathering of the remnant shows the continuing care of the Lord for His people and His determination to fulfill His covenantal purposes. In the present context, the doctrine of the remnant suggests first of all the breaking off of certain of Judah's branches (vv. 1, 2; cf. Rom. 11:17–24) following the king's neglect and the due punishment (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). bring them back to their fold. The Lord Himself is now the Shepherd (Ps. 23; Ezek. 34:11), a role that Jesus takes up in the NT (John 10:14).
Under the Shepherd there will be true shepherds who will faithfully administer the kingdom in the new age (Mic. 5:5; 1 Pet. 5:2–4).

This messianic promise is a fulfillment of the promise to David (2 Sam. 7:12; Matt. 1:1, 17) and follows repeated indictments against Judah's shepherd leaders. Despite the coming judgment, the Lord will install a future Davidic king. 23:5 a righteous Branch. A messianic term. See Is. 4:2; 11:1; and Zech. 6:12, where Zerubbabel is a type of Christ. execute justice and righteousness. See note on 21:12. This messianic King will be quite unlike Zedekiah and Jehoiakim.

Until this point in old covenant history, the exodus from Egypt has been the paradigm of deliverance. This future salvation from the north country (Babylon) will so far exceed the Egyptian experience as to replace it as the new paradigm of redemption.

See theological note "The Prophets of God" on p. 279. like a drunken man. Judgment is frequently compared to drunkenness in the OT (Is. 51:21–23; Jer. 25:15, 16): a state of staggering and confusion that ends with falling down and being unable to get up. As a prophet, Jeremiah identifies with those against whom he is prophesying and feels within himself the judgment that is coming upon them. The false prophets have no such compassion or empathy.

These groups are supposed to communicate the Lord's will to the people through bringing the word and teaching the law. If these men are ungodly, how can God's people be expected to find the way of truth?

Right belief and right action are inseparable in the OT; it is no accident that those who have not heard God's revelation actively encourage evil. See 29:21–23. This may refer to spiritual adultery as well as to physical adultery. The prophets of the southern kingdom of Judah have become just like the prophets of the old northern kingdom of Israel, which has long since been destroyed by God's judgment. like Sodom \... like Gomorrah. See 20:16; Is. 1:9 and notes. The comparison of Jerusalem to Sodom and Gomorrah is shocking and ominous.
See Jer. 9:15. The imagery in these verses describes a shocking reversal. Instead of a rich banquet, the Lord serves a meal of bitterness and poison.

LORD. The Hebrew word translated "council" here and in v. 22 may also be translated "counsel," depending on whether the emphasis is on God's deliberations with the heavenly "council" (1 Kin. 22:19–22; Job 1:6) or on the "counsel" resulting from those deliberations. The word is translated "secret" in Amos 3:7.
LORD. Entering the presence of the Lord is often likened to experiencing a storm or a tempest (see Job 38:1; Ezek. 1:4).
This does not refer to the end times, but rather to the fact that subsequent events will show the truth of a prophet's words. Jeremiah's prophecies are later vindicated by the fall of Jerusalem.
See 14:14. yet they ran \... prophesied. The prophets are a picture of zeal in their self-serving propagation of falsehood. See theological note "Prophets" on p. 279.
See note on v. 18.
Nothing, near or far, can escape God's knowledge (Ps. 139:2; Amos 9:2, 3). The Lord is not tied to a particular geographical location, as the pagan gods are.
See theological note "The Omnipresence of God" on previous page.

The dream is one way in which a revelation might come to a prophet (Num. 12:6; cf. Joel 2:28); yet such claims should always be treated with due suspicion and tested against the rest of God's revelation (Deut. 13:1–3).
The false dream is to the true prophetic word as straw is to wheat; only the wheat has any value. The question "What has straw in common with wheat?" probably reflects a contemporary proverb.
There can be no mistaking the true word because of its inevitable effects (Amos 3:8).
For a case of prophetic jealousy, see 1 Kin. 22:24.

\... and declare, 'declares the]{.rsb-studynote-bold} LORD.' The false prophets disguise their own words as words from God by using the prophetic formula. Alternatively, the Septuagint, instead of "and declare, 'declares the Lord,'" has "and sleep their sleep," which comes from a different but related Hebrew root.

This word is typically used in judgment oracles. The people's desire for a message from God might sound spiritual, but it is actually a rebellious refusal to listen to the clear word that He has already declared to them.

A vision of two baskets of figs, one representing those exiled to Babylon and the other those who will resist exile and with it the Lord's purpose of judgment and salvation. This prophecy reveals that it is too late to avert the exile by repentance (21:9). 24:1 Jeconiah \... to Babylon. The first large deportation was in 597 B.C. (2 Kin. 24:14–16). Jeconiah is yet another name for Jehoiachin, who is also known as Coniah (22:24). placed before the temple. Represent an offering of the firstfruits: the good figs are accepted while the bad figs are rejected.

Those who remain behind in Judah regard the people sent into exile as self-evidently under God's judgment. However, this vision reveals that the exiles are the remnant that will be preserved for God's purposes ("good figs"), while those who remain in Judah are beyond redemption and can only be destroyed by judgment ("bad figs," vv. 8–10).
See note on 21:4.

The Lord's plan for the exiles is positive: to build them up and plant them, not to tear them down or uproot them (cf. 1:10). The vocabulary of this section displays many similarities to the account of Jeremiah's call in 1:4–19.

The Lord's answer to His people's inability to maintain the covenant relationship is that He Himself will intervene and create in them a new capacity for knowing Him. they shall be my people and I will be their God. Use of the basic covenant formula (32:38; Lev. 26:12) shows that this answer is nothing less than a new covenant. The theology introduced here is developed at 31:31–34.

Some people flee to Egypt before, during, and after the Babylonian invasion (see ch. 43). Yet even though these people have escaped the judgment of God on the earthly plane, they are not included in the good figs. The future of the Lord's people lies with those undergoing the exile in Babylon.

Jeremiah predicts seventy years of Babylonian captivity for Judah as judgment for persistent sin, and he warns the neighboring nations as well of judgment at the hands of Babylon (ch. 25). His message meets opposition from false prophets, priests, and the people (chs. 26–29). 25:1 fourth year of Jehoiakim. The Babylonian armies move down the Mediterranean coast in 605 B.C., and Judah becomes a vassal state. This is the same year in which Jeremiah dictates a message of judgment that his scribe, Baruch, reads to King Jehoiakim (ch. 36).

See 1:2 and notes. persistently. Jeremiah's persistence is part of a long prophetic mission to Israel. He has been preaching for twenty-three years at the time this oracle is given. The faithful prophets Uriah (26:20–23), Zephaniah, and Habakkuk are also prophesying during this time. Like his predecessors and contemporaries, Jeremiah does not receive a positive response to his ministry (7:13 and note).

An apt summary of what all of the faithful prophets of the Lord said to the people. Jeremiah's message to the old covenant community is that obedience to the Mosaic covenant is essential if the people are to stay in the land God has given them.

Babylon and her allies (1:15; 6:1). Nebuchadnezzar \... my servant. See also 27:6. He is God's "servant" in the sense of being appointed as an agent of His judgment. Even though Nebuchadnezzar has his own sinful motivations for his actions, the Lord can overrule his purposes to accomplish His goals. In the same way, Cyrus is called God's "anointed" for the purpose of releasing the exiles to return to their land (Is. 45:1). The Lord is able to pronounce doom and blessing ahead of time in very specific terms, naming individuals, because He is the sovereign God who controls the outcome of all events. surrounding nations. See vv. 19–26. The judgment on Judah is only the beginning of a general judgment. everlasting desolation. Hb. olam often means everlasting but sometimes simply means a lengthy period of time (Is. 58:12; Jer. 5:15). The following verses make it clear that the land will be restored after seventy years.

See 29:10. This period may be counted in round figures from 605 B.C. (v. 1; Dan. 1:1) to 538 B.C., when the exiles begin to return home after Cyrus's decree (2 Chr. 36:20–23; Dan. 9:1, 2). In Zech. 1:12, the prophecy seems to be applied to the time between the destruction of the first temple in 586 B.C. and its rebuilding in 515 B.C., so it may simply represent the span of a person's lifetime. The seventy years allow the Lord's word of judgment to have full effect before new salvation can be experienced. 25:12 punish the king of Babylon. This prophecy is developed further in chs. 50; 51. The agent of punishment is in turn punished for its own sins, in particular the brutality of its conquest (50:18; cf. Is. 10:5–7, 12). Babylon falls to the Medes and Persians in 539 B.C., and over succeeding centuries becomes increasingly impoverished and insignificant.

In the Septuagint, the "oracles against the nations" from chs. 46–51 occur after this phrase. The order of these oracles also differs between the Hebrew and Greek texts. This phrase indicates that Jeremiah's oracles will be written down and preserved for future generations.
Possibly Persia and its allies, but more likely a general statement of the principle that agents of God's judgment are themselves subject to judgment (v. 12 note).
See note on 23:9.

God's judgment is first visited upon His chosen people, as befits those who are most privileged (25:29; Amos 3:2). The other nations that Jeremiah goes on to list are the same as those who are the subject of the oracles in chs. 46–51, except for Damascus. The nations are ordered from south to north according to their geographic locations.

This list of Philistine cities omits Gath, apparently already destroyed (Amos 1:6–8). Ashdod was partially destroyed by the Egyptians during the seventh century, roughly one hundred years or so before this oracle is given. See also 47:1–7.
The principal cities of Phoenicia, both ports on the Mediterranean coast. See Ezek. 28:1–23.
Tribes living in northern Arabia (Is. 21:13, 14). "Buz" is probably an Arabian tribal group as well.
Unknown. Media. Having themselves been defeated by Cyrus and incorporated into his empire, the Medes participate with the Persians in the conquest.

Hb. "Sheshach" (text note). This word is an allusion to Babylon based on the word "Babel," using a code that substitutes for each consonant the corresponding one from the alphabet written in reverse. In English, e.g., ABC would become ZYX.

Jerusalem; see notes on 7:10–15. The Lord will not punish His own people while ignoring the wickedness of other nations. An important factor in the theology of judgment against the nations is that the honor of God's own name is at stake in the fate of His people.

Wine production at this time involves stomping on the grapes in large vats. Those who tread the grapes have their clothes covered with red juice, which forms a potent image of judgment in the Bible (see Is. 63:1–6; Rev. 14:19, 20). Since this is a joyful event, it is also associated with happy shouts.
A legal action in which the Lord claims His right to punish the guilty (2:9 note).
See note on 2:8. roll in ashes. A symbol of mourning.
See v. 30 and note on 2:15. Here Jeremiah refers to the Lord going out in judgment against His own people (Amos 3:8).

Possibly his first year (609–608 B.C.). The previous chapter records oracles and events from Jehoiakim's fourth year, so it is clear that Jeremiah's prophecies are not recorded in chronological order. The fuller account of the temple sermon in 7:1–15 is not dated. This date formula brings Jehoiakim into the foreground as one who rejects Jeremiah's words (ch. 36).
–6 Summarizes the sermon delivered in ch. 7. 26:2 the court. Probably the inner courtyard.

This phrase is used in handing down the sentence for capital crimes (Ex. 21:15–17; Deut. 18:20). Jeremiah is evidently held to be a false prophet because of the people's belief that God's temple can never be destroyed. The people's response to the Lord's messenger is indicative of their attitude to the Lord (see Matt. 21:35, 36).

These individuals have legal duties in the royal administration, and their arrival indicates that formal proceedings against Jeremiah are about to begin. New Gate. The gates of a city are the normal place for court hearings in ancient Israel and Judah (Ruth 4:1; Prov. 31:23).

Jeremiah's defense is that the Lord gave him the message to prophesy, but that defense can only be evaluated with the benefit of hindsight. Yet to execute him before seeing his message fulfilled or falsified is to risk incurring the guilt of shedding innocent blood.

Cf. v. 11. This verdict is a remarkable vindication of Jeremiah's authenticity as a prophet. Crucially, the people, who at first sided with the priests and the prophets against Jeremiah (v. 8), seem to have joined the officials in defending Jeremiah's right to speak.

His precedent is cited in support of the judgment just given, because as a result of his prophecy that Jerusalem would fall (Mic. 3:12), the people repented of their sin. King Hezekiah prayed for Jerusalem and avoided defeat by the Assyrians in 701 B.C. (cf. Is. 37:14–38). Unfortunately, though Jeremiah's life is spared, the people of his day do not follow Hezekiah's example in repenting before the Lord.

The story of Uriah shows that Jeremiah is not alone in his preaching. It also stresses that Jeremiah's escape is not the most important point of this chapter, but rather Judah's opposition to the word of God through his prophets. Uriah dies but Jeremiah lives to complete his God-ordained ministry. Compare the various fates of the heroes of faith in Heb. 11:32–38.

Contrast his action on Jeremiah's behalf in 36:12, 25 — an evidence of shifting roles that put Jeremiah's safety into question. The Egyptians placed Jehoiakim on the throne, which perhaps explains how he is able to extradite the prophet Uriah from there.
The cemetery is located east of Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley (2 Kin. 23:6).

An official under Josiah (2 Kin. 22:12, 14); his support may be the decisive factor in Jeremiah's deliverance. His father, Shaphan, was a key reformer in Josiah's time (2 Kin. 22:3–14), and at least three brothers of his also engage in public affairs: Elasah (29:3), Gemariah (36:10–12, 25), and Gedaliah, who governs Judah after Jerusalem's destruction (39:14; 40:5–16).

Most manuscripts have "Jehoiakim," though some do have "Zedekiah." It is clear from the rest of the chapter that Zedekiah is the correct attribution. The scribal error probably came from the similarity between the opening of this chapter and 26:1. The entire verse is missing from the Septuagint.
As in chs. 13 and 19, Jeremiah is to perform a sign-act visibly depicting his message. In this case, he is to wear a yoke symbolizing submission to the Babylonians.

The Hebrew has "Send them," which may suggest that the prophet is to send yokes to each of the envoys. Edom \... Sidon. See 25:21, 22; these nations are under the Lord's judgment as well. envoys who have come \... to Zedekiah. Probably they have come to discuss rebellion, in league with Egypt, against Nebuchadnezzar.
See 21:5. have made the earth \... give it to whomever it seems right. With an argument from creation, the Lord claims rights over all nations. See Dan. 2:38; 4:25 (also Nebuchadnezzar).

Even mighty Nebuchadnezzar must do the Lord's bidding. the beasts of the field. The Lord will make even the wild animals obey Nebuchadnezzar, putting him in a position like that of Adam before the fall. Humans will similarly have to submit to the Babylonian leader.
Nebuchadnezzar's chosen successors, not necessarily those who are physically his offspring.
See note on 14:12. These covenant curses will descend even on the surrounding nations if they disobey the Lord's word through His prophet.

All these serve merely to bolster the political system, in this case with an exhortation not to submit to Babylon, which is exactly the same message of the false prophets in Judah. These false prophets and other classes are forbidden in Israel (14:14; Lev. 19:26; Deut. 18:10, 11).
Judah and its neighbors can still avoid total exile by accepting God's judgment of submission to Babylon. The Lord is the One who will decide whether they stay in their land or go into exile.

Jeremiah pleads with Judah to accept dominion by Babylon and the exile of some of its leaders (Jehoiachin and those taken in 597 B.C.; cf. 2 Kin. 24:15, 16) as part of God's plan for her ultimate salvation (24:5).

This false message is proclaimed by Hananiah (28:1–3). vessels of the LORD's house. These vessels are eventually carried off, some in 605 B.C. (Dan. 1:1, 2), some in 597 B.C. (2 Kin. 24:13). They are brought back to the temple as part of the return in the days of King Cyrus (Ezra 1:7–11), which occurs seventy years later, not "shortly" after they are taken to Babylon.

A large bronze tank that contains the water for the priests to wash in (2 Chr. 4:2). It represents the Lord's victory over the forces of chaos, which were symbolically calmed and placed within the Lord's house.
The fate of exile for a fixed time (25:11; 27:7) is now applied to the temple vessels.

Since Zedekiah's reign began in 597 B.C., the events recounted here and in ch. 27 (27:1 note) occur in 593 B.C. Gibeon. Hananiah's hometown is a few miles (about 5 km) west of Jeremiah's home in Anathoth.
Hananiah directly challenges Jeremiah's message (27:16–22).
Since just over four years have already passed (v. 1), Hananiah predicts that they will be gone no more than seven years. Contrast Jeremiah's seventy years (25:11, 12).
