A Hebrew way of saying, "May it be so." Jeremiah's first response reflects his love for the land and people. He takes no pleasure in predicting the destruction of Jerusalem. But the message God has revealed to him gives him no confidence that Jerusalem will be spared.
Jeremiah includes Hananiah with himself among the prophets and reminds him that the Lord's message has been principally judgment, while false prophets inevitably preach the popular message of peace.
Hananiah responds to Jeremiah's sign act with one of his own, breaking Jeremiah's yoke. Jeremiah does not immediately respond since as a true prophet he needs the Lord's authorization to speak.
Hananiah's symbolic act cannot frustrate the Lord's will. Hananiah dramatizes Judah's resistance, which will only make the inevitable servitude harsher.
See note on 27:6.

The same Hebrew word as "sent" (v. 15), an ironic play on words since this "sending" is to his death. you shall die \... rebellion. Hananiah will not even live the two years necessary to prove his prophecy false. He will die within the same year, for he has rebelled against God (Deut. 13:5). His death should vindicate the truth of Jeremiah's prophecy about Babylon — if the people have ears to hear.
He is likely from the same family that has defended Jeremiah (cf. 26:24). Gemariah the son of Hilkiah. Possibly the son of the high priest at the time of Josiah's reforms.
The Lord is sovereign over their fate, not the Babylonians.
An act of commitment to their new lives, showing acceptance of the Lord's judgment and recognizing that they are going to be in Babylon for an extended period (cf. Ezek. 8:1).

Peace (6:14 and note) is the chief covenantal blessing. The Jews previously have prayed for and sought the welfare of Jerusalem (Ps. 122:6–9); for the duration of the exile, they are to seek the welfare of their Babylonian home instead. pray. The Lord's blessing can come on any nation through the prayer and action of His people; cf. Abraham (Gen. 20:17), Joseph (Gen. 37–50), and Daniel (Dan. 1–6).
Their exile is not permanent. Just as the Lord fulfilled His promise to Joseph to visit His people and bring them out of Egypt (Gen. 50:24), so He will bring them back from Babylon.
In contrast to His plan to judge those who remain in Jerusalem, the Lord plans blessing for those who are already in exile.

Echoes Deut. 30:3–5 (similar in turn to Deut. 4:29, 30). bring you back. Implies a restoration of the relationship between the Lord and His people. See 30:3, 18; 31:23; 32:44; 33:7, 11, 26; 48:47; 49:6, 39.
False prophets are in Babylon among the exiles, just as they are in Judah.
Zedekiah. That Zedekiah still rules in Jerusalem, albeit as a Babylonian vassal, may be a focus of false hope for the exiles.
Cf. ch. 24.

A method of execution particularly associated in the OT with the rule of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 3:6). The Lord earlier carried out the penalty of death for false prophecy on Han­aniah (see 28:17); the same penalty will be carried out on Ahab and Zedekiah in Babylon. Their deaths in the fire are in striking contrast to the Lord's ability to preserve Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
A technical term for a particularly offensive crime (see Gen. 34:7; 2 Sam. 13:12).

She­maiah wants the authorities in Jerusalem to act against Jeremiah, presumably because his letter is having an impact on morale among the exiles. Zephaniah is in charge of temple security (see 21:1), an important position within the royal administration. He may be the brother of the Zedekiah who is prophesying in Babylon, since their father's name is the same. Jeremiah was earlier placed in the stocks by Pashhur (20:2). However, Zephaniah takes no action beyond reading the letter aloud (v. 29).
Jeremiah prophesies that the exile will last seventy years (v. 10; 25:11, 12). build houses \... plant gardens. Shemaiah cites Jeremiah's letter (v. 5).
The threat to Shemaiah parallels that made against Hananiah (28:15, 16). Even though he lives among the exiles, he will not share in the good plans that the Lord has for them (see v. 11).

After many chapters declaring judgment on God's people, these chapters contain promises of restoration and of the new covenant (31:31–34). The certainty of restoration is portrayed in Jeremiah's purchase of a field (ch. 32). These prophecies relate to Israel and Judah, not just to Judah alone (cf. Ezek. 37:15–28). In the NT the gospel goes to Samaria, as well as to Jerusalem and Judah, before going out to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).

Most of the prophets delivered their messages orally. Jeremiah is told to write these words of hope in a book (or rather a scroll) since their validity will only be vindicated many years in the future. Also, in written form, his words can be transmitted to those who are in exile in Babylon.
The anguish of childbirth is a picture of the suffering under the Babylonian armies (4:19, 31). Yet it is also a picture that leaves open the possibility of a new beginning.

The day of the Lord; see Amos 5:18; 8:9. Amos's generation expected it as a day of deliverance, but had to learn that it would bring judgment. Jeremiah has told his contemporaries about the coming judgment, but he also has a message of a positive future on the far side of that judgment. The image of a yoke that in chs. 27; 28 spoke of their subjugation by the Babylonians is now reversed to speak of their ultimate restoration. The Davidic line, whose end was anticipated in 22:30, will nonetheless have a future heir.

See Is. 41:8, 10; 43:1; 44:1, 2. The name "Jacob" communicates God's continuing choice of His people in spite of their continuing sin by reminding them of God's faithfulness to their very flawed ancestor. He will discipline His people but not destroy them. none shall make him afraid. Cf. v. 5. This promise is a fulfillment of covenant blessing (Lev. 26:6).
See 8:22. Yet since the Lord inflicted the wound and He is the Great Physician (Ex. 15:26), He can still restore them to full health (see v. 17).
Nations with which they had made political alliances.
A reference to Israel's origins in the wilderness period (see Num. 24:5). the city. Jerusalem. It will be rebuilt on its ruins (lit. "tel").
Probably an allusion to the time of David (v. 9). congregation. A technical term denoting the political or religious assembly of the covenant people.

Whereas Judah is ruled by a foreign power during its exile, Jeremiah looks forward to the restoration of her political independence and special relationship with the Lord (v. 22). In view of v. 9, this promised leader will be from the line of David.
The day when God acts to rescue His people (see 30:8). all the clans of Israel. See 30:3.

The remnant through whom God's purposes will continue (v. 7; 6:9 note; 23:3 note). Cf. 15:2. wilderness. Judah's exile in Babylon and subsequent restoration are sometimes compared with Israel's wanderings in the wilderness before entering the Promised Land (see Is. 40:3, 4; 43:19, 20). Like the first exodus, this restoration will be a demonstration of the Lord's power to save. After the unbelieving generation has perished, a new, believing generation will enter God's rest.

This phrase probably carries forward the previous verse's allusion to Sinai (Ex. 19–24). loved \... everlasting love. The Lord's love for Israel is the ground of His election of them (Deut. 7:6, 7). The everlasting character of the covenant is affirmed in Gen. 17:7. faithfulness. See note on 9:24; cf. 16:5. This verse provides another sign of the reestablishment of the broken covenant.

Cf. 18:13–15, where Israel's "virginity" has been squandered. See also 2:20, 22. In the new covenant, the stain of defilement is finally cleansed. Though Israel has repeatedly been unfaithful, the Lord cannot abandon His love for her (see Hos. 1–3). tambourines. More precisely, they will adorn themselves with timbrels, small pieces of metal that jingle musically as they dance. dance. Such dances are acts of religious celebration (Judg. 21:19, 20).

This promise signifies the covenant blessing of fertility (Deut. 7:13; 28:4; cf. Deut. 28:30). Samaria. The capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, or the northern kingdom as a whole. Its people were deported by Assyria in 722 B.C., long before Jeremiah's ministry.

Instead of crying out warnings about approaching enemies, the watchmen will shout encouragement to the people to make the annual pilgrimages. Ephraim \... let us go up to Zion. Not as previously, to the apostate northern shrines of Jeroboam at Bethel and Dan (1 Kin. 12:26–33), but to the Lord's sanctuary on Mount Zion because of the people's renewed relationship with him. Under the old covenant, the answer to the woman of Samaria's question as to where worship should take place was clear: Mount Zion (see John 4:20).
Babylon. The blind \... she who is in labor. The weakest and most vulnerable members of the community, who are least able to endure a long journey (cf. Is. 40:11).

The physical return will be matched by spiritual turning to the Lord as well. lead \... brooks of water. See Ps. 23:2; Is. 48:21; 49:10. straight path. See Ps. 23:2; Is. 40:4. father \... firstborn. See 3:4; 31:20; Ex. 4:22; Hos. 11:1–4. A declaration of status rather than chronology since Ephraim was actually Joseph's second son, born after Manasseh. God, however, chose Ephraim to be first; God's election is what is crucial (Gen. 48).

These verbs are closely related in Hebrew. The word translated "ransomed" means "to set free by paying a ransom," and it is used of the Lord's act of liberating Israel, His firstborn son, from Egypt (Ex. 4:22; Deut. 7:8; 9:26). The second verb ("redeemed") is a technical term related to the responsibility of a close relative to purchase or "redeem" property that would otherwise be alienated from a family (32:8; Ruth 2:20 note). It is also used of God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt (Ex. 6:6, 7). The way that God has redeemed us to Himself through the ransom of Christ (cf. 1 Tim. 2:5, 6) is explained in the NT (see theological note "Atonement" on p. 1983).

In Deut. 7:13, God promises to bless His people with an abundance of these staple crops if they keep the terms of the Sinai covenant. Here, He promises to bless them with these things in spite of their unfaithfulness. The result will be great joy for all ages and classes of people, including the priests, who were frequent targets of rebuke in the earlier chapters.

Ramah is in the region assigned to the tribe of Benjamin, close to where Rachel, the favored wife of Jacob and the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, may be buried (1 Sam. 10:2). Rachel's weeping over the destruction of the northern kingdom in 722 B.C. represents the mourning of all of the mothers of Israel over their lost offspring. Yet the Lord promises that their parenting will not have been in vain. There will be a restoration of their children from the exile. These words are quoted in Matt. 2:18 concerning Herod's slaughter of the innocents.

For the people of Ephraim (the northern kingdom) to return, they must first repent. When they do, they will find the Lord more than ready to receive them back, like the father of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32).
A symbol of grief and remorse.
Israel must remind itself of the way to return not only to its land, but also, more importantly, to God.

See Is. 42:9. a woman \... a man. The saying is obscure, but possibly the picture is of the security provided by a mother's protecting her son or a woman's faithfully embracing her husband, in contrast to Israel's past wandering.

The section began by talking about Ephraim's return; it ends with words about Judah's return, underlining the fact that both nations are to be restored together. O holy hill. Jerusalem was the target of considerable prophetic rebuke in earlier chapters, yet she will be restored to her former glory.
These words of restoration seem like a wonderful dream to the prophet. In contrast, many prophetic dreams are threatening and troubling (e.g., Dan. 8:27).
Both words are from the same Hebrew root. This makes an allusion to the promise of Gen. 15:18, where the Hb. word for "seed" is translated "offspring."

The exiles use this proverb to blame previous generations for the disaster of the exile (Ezek. 18:2), possibly based on a misunderstanding of Ex. 20:5 and Num. 14:18. Certainly, the sin of previous generations was a factor in the exile (see 2 Kin. 23:26, 27), but the proverb incorrectly assumes that the present generation is blameless.

The principle that each person is judged fairly is elaborated at length in Ezek. 18:4–32 (cf. Deut. 24:16). The point is that this generation fully deserves the punishment of the exile, even though the nation's guilt has been continuous (7:13; 11:7, 8). The Lord never judges unjustly.

Picking up themes that Moses first expounded in Deut. 30:1–14, Jeremiah prophesies that God will make a new covenant with His people. As the making of the old covenant (Ex. 19–24) followed the redemption from Egypt (Ex. 12–15), so the making of the new covenant will follow the redemption from exile and from sin (v. 34). 31:31, 32 The new covenant will stand in contrast to the old covenant in that the consummated new covenant cannot be broken by human sin as the old was (v. 32; Heb. 8:7, 8). The guarantee that it will not be broken is the grace that is mediated by Christ through His death and resurrection (Heb. 9:12–15; 10:1–4, 10–18). 31:31 new covenant. See theological note "Covenant" on p. 37. See also 1 Cor. 11:25; 2 Cor. 3:6; Heb. 9:15; 12:24. with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Using both names stresses the unity of God's covenant people.

Under the old covenant, the law of God was engraved on tablets of stone and placed in the Most Holy Place; under the new covenant, God will write His law on the hearts of His people through the work of His Spirit. The people, then, are like the temple in that the law of God is within them, but with the difference that they are a living temple, made of living stones (2 Cor. 3:3; 1 Pet. 2:5). See theological note "Covenant" on p. 37. after those days. Without being specific, the prophet speaks of a time after the exile. The NT shows that the time arrived with Christ, the Messiah. I will. God will take the initiative to renew His people. my law. The law of Moses requires obedience from the heart (Deut. 6:6) but provides no enablement for that obedience (Deut. 5:29; 29:4). It does mediate forgiveness and hope, especially through the sacrifices that point to the final sacrifice of the Messiah. The law is a system of "types and shadows," that is, of significant elements foreshadowing Christ and inviting trust in God through Him. I will be their God, and they \... my people. This declaration is the summary of God's blessings promised in His covenant (Lev. 26:12; cf. 7:23).

See theological note "Knowledge of Self and Knowledge of God" on p. 1278. For I will forgive. The basis of the promises in vv. 32, 33 will be a new work of redemption that secures the forgiveness of sins (see Heb. 10:1–17). remember their sin no more. The continuing cycle of sacrifices under the old covenant provided a constant reminder of sins (Heb. 10:3, 4, 11). The words "no more" underscore that the satisfaction made for sins in the redemption to come will be perfect, making any further sacrifices unnecessary. This passage is echoed in a series of new covenant passages including Is. 59:21; Jer. 32:37–41; Ezek. 11:17–20, 36:22–26. These passages all communicate common themes of the new covenant: restoration, the giving of a new heart, an internalized Spirit with new obedience, God's swearing the oath for keeping the covenant, and the everlasting nature of the new covenant.

The enduring order of the heavenly bodies is made the measure of God's commitment to His people (33:20, 21, 25, 26). The exile looks like the end for Israel and Judah, but their existence depends on the Lord's faithfulness, not their own.

Jerusalem. Tower of Hananel \... Corner Gate. Opposite ends of the city, signifying its entirety (cf. 2 Chr. 26:9; Zech. 14:10, 11). The restoration of Jerusalem will be the first sign of the fulfillment of the new covenant promise.
Unidentified locations in Jerusalem. Since the Tower of Hananel and the Corner Gate are at the northeast and northwest of the city, these two may be on the southern edge of Jerusalem.
The Valley of the Son of Hinnom (7:31 note).
587 B.C. This chapter recounts the first of several exchanges between Jeremiah and Zedekiah in this period. See 21:3–7; 34:1–7; 37:3–8, 17–20; 38:14–28.

Jeremiah's prophecies of judgment against Jerusalem are regarded as treasonous, especially while the city of Jerusalem is being besieged by the Babylonians. Yet Zedekiah still consults Jeremiah privately (37:11–21).
See note on 21:4.

Jeremiah's hometown; see 1:1. right of redemption by purchase is yours. Hanamel may be selling the field because of debt and asking Jeremiah to be the close relative who redeems (31:11 note; see Lev. 25:25–28). By normal standards, it is absurd to buy a field when the whole land is about to be lost. Yet Jeremiah is instructed to make sure that every aspect of the deal is witnessed and carefully recorded, providing a sign that land ownership still has a future in Judah.
Probably a normal price, though under the circumstances the field is worthless.

A sealed clay jar cannot protect important documents from moisture and insects for a long time. Here, the action is as important as the result. If Judah ceases to exist as a nation in the Babylonian assault, then these title deeds will be of no value.

The significance of the purchase is that Judah will again possess its historic land and enjoy normal life in it. It therefore symbolizes that aspect of the new covenant promise (29:14 and note; 31:38–40).

OD. Jeremiah does as he is instructed, but he is puzzled by the Lord's plans. The Lord is the creator of everything and sovereign over all. He is just and gracious, as the echo of Ex. 34:6, 7 makes clear. Yet He also judges each one appropriately, in contrast to the people's claim in 31:29. Will not the people's unfaithfulness result in the destruction of Judah? Why should Jeremiah buy a field if that is the case?
See Ex. 7:3. and among all mankind. This confession emphasizes God's rule over the whole world.
This description is repeated from Deut. 26:8. See also v. 20; Ex. 15:14–16.

The Lord's response to Jeremiah's question (v. 17–25) begins with His sovereignty and power. Since He is the sovereign Lord of the universe, He is able not only to judge the people of Judah for their sin but also to transform them into a new people and restore them to their land.
Typical elements in Jeremiah's accusation against Judah (1:16; 7:18; 19:13; cf. Deut. 31:29).
Probably the title of a god (rather than a proper name) worshiped by the Phoenicians, Moabites, Ammonites, and others in a ritual involving child sacrifice (Lev. 18:21; 20:2–5; 2 Kin. 23:10).

Jeremiah reaffirms Moses's promise of restoration from exile (Deut. 30:3–5). The suddenness and improbability of this promise, after the tirade of vv. 26–35, is explained by the rhetorical question, "Is anything too hard for me?" (v. 27; cf. v. 17).
Their actions will at last be in line with their beliefs, and both will be in line with the Lord's commands.
See 31:31–36 and notes.
These regions represent the territorial extent of Judah at the time of the exile (17:26; 33:13).
See note on 10:12. God's role as creator is here the basis of His power both to judge and to save (32:17). The LORD is his name. God's name denotes His character, rather than merely being a title.
A similar phrase in Is. 48:6 also speaks of salvation as a new creation. See Dan. 2:47.

A sign of the desperate nature of the defense of Jerusalem. During the Babylonian siege, houses and even royal palaces are destroyed to reinforce the walls at the points where they are under assault by siege ramps.

The change in the Lord's purpose is not motivated by any change in Judah but by His decision. See 30:8, 16; 32:36, for similar transitions. Human attempts to save the city will be unavailing; the Lord will accomplish His purpose to cleanse and restore the people (see 31:34).
The Lord acts to judge and redeem His people for the sake of His own glory throughout the whole world.
Cf. 7:34; 16:9. These typical circumstances of joy — weddings and bringing thank offerings to the temple — are symbols of the joy that will be brought about by the new covenant.

The exile leaves much of Judah desolate and uninhabited. Its restoration will bring back the normal activity of the shepherds, who know each member of their flock personally and count them individually into the sheepfold at night.

In addition to literal shepherds, the Lord will restore Israel's shepherd, their king. The promise is similar to 23:5, 6, but with an added focus on Jerusalem. Now Jerusalem will be called "The Lord is our righteousness," as will the Messiah. God's people will be made holy as He is holy.
This promise is not finally to restore the monarchy but to inaugurate the messianic kingdom (23:5; 30:9; 2 Sam. 7:12–16; cf. 1 Kin. 2:4).

The priests' role is essential to the administration of the covenant (Ex. 28; 29; Deut. 10:8; 18:1). They also have a covenant of their own with the Lord (Num. 25:12, 13; 1 Sam. 2:30, 35). Yet with the destruction of the Jerusalem temple, that covenant seems to be in jeopardy. The promise of a perpetual priestly ministry is fulfilled in the new covenant by Christ Himself (Heb. 5:6–10; 7:11–25), and in believers who by their union with Him become priests (1 Pet. 2:5, 9).

The permanence of the institutions now envisaged is in stark contrast with 7:1–15. Such permanence is only comprehensible in the framework of the everlasting new covenant — though the need for faithfulness is never set aside (32:40 and note).
In these promises concerning the messianic kingdom, the promises to Abraham are also fulfilled (Gen. 22:17; cf. 15:8).
The reference to these "clans" is ambiguous. It could refer to the kingdoms of Israel and Judah (v. 14) or to the royal family of David and the priestly family of Levi (vv. 17, 18).
The new covenant fulfills the covenant with Abraham that embraces all peoples (Gen. 12:3). See note on v. 22.

These chapters narrate scenes of rejection of the word of the Lord through His prophet that leads to final judgment on Judah. King Zedekiah is condemned for going back on his promise to free slaves (ch. 34), and the people of Judah are reproved for failing to learn a lesson from the example of the faithful Rechabites (ch. 35). King Jehoiakim earlier rejected Jeremiah's message and burned the prophet's scroll (ch. 36) 34:1, 2 all the kingdoms of the earth \... I am giving this city. Vassal nations are required to join in battle with their overlord. The forces against Jerusalem are overwhelming. Yet Zedekiah's principal problem is not the size of the Babylonian army but rather that the Lord is giving him into Nebuchadnezzar's hand.

Zedekiah's precise fate was left obscure in 21:4–7; 32:3–5; but see 52:11. The point here is that he will not die in battle. It is a limited mercy, however. Zedekiah later sees his own sons put to death before the Babylonians put out his eyes (2 Kin. 25:7). At this point, he can yet have an easier fate if he listens to Jeremiah and surrenders to the Babylonians.

Fortified cities of Judah (2 Chr. 11:5, 9). The verse gives a glimpse of the last days of Judah. Jerusalem knows the enemy is closing in as the outlying cities fall one by one to the Babylonians. A pottery fragment dating from this period carried this message to the commander at Lachish: "We are watching for the signals of Lachish \... we cannot see Azekah."

According to Ex. 21:2–11; Lev. 25:39–55; Deut. 15:12–18, slaves are to be released in the last year of a seven-year cycle. There is little evidence that this biblical law has been observed regularly at other times, yet perhaps in a desperate attempt to win the Lord's favor, the people obey it now. Zedekiah's "covenant" (or solemn undertaking) reflects his ambivalence between listening to Jeremiah and listening to his own political advisers.
These two verbs effectively portray Judah's fickleness (3:6, 14 notes). This probably happened when the Babylonians withdrew briefly to deal with an approaching army from Egypt.

See Gen. 15:18 and note. This sort of action accompanies the making of a covenant. It illustrates the penalty that will fall on a person who breaks the covenant. In this case, their dead bodies will be left unburied as food for the birds and wild animals (see Deut. 28:26).
The material in this chapter predates the previous chapters, which describe events during the reign of Zedekiah.
Most of what is known of this clan is in this chapter. house of the LORD \... chambers. Rooms used for storage (1 Kin. 6:5; Neh. 13:4, 5).
One of two people who share the prophet's name mentioned in the book (see 52:1).

Another name for a prophet (1 Kin. 12:22). keeper of the threshold. An important position in the temple, controlling access to the sacred space. In 2 Kin. 25:18, the three keepers of the threshold are mentioned right after the high priest and the second priest.

The vow taken by Jonadab the son of Rechab commits his descendants to a nomadic life of impermanent lodging and abstention from wine. This life is a voluntary commitment not required by the Mosaic law (Deut. 6:10, 11; 7:13). It may function as a reminder that the Promised Land and its blessings are only symbols of the spiritual inheritance that God has prepared for His people. The faithfulness of the Rechabites to this human decree from two hundred years earlier stands in sharp contrast to Judah's unfaithfulness to the Lord's decrees. 35:7 that you may live many days. The style of the command echoes the style of Deuteronomy (e.g., Deut. 11:9; 25:15).

See 33:17, 18. Such a promise might be expected for a king, and even for priests, but not for the obscure Rechabites. It is used here to contrast ominously with what Jehoiakim and the Davidic dynasty can expect. The Rechabites' faithfulness receives its reward. In Neh. 3:14, a Rechabite is listed among those rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem with Nehemiah.
That is, 605 B.C., the year of Nebuchadnezzar's first move against Jerusalem (25:1 note).

This account is an important guide to understanding how prophetic books were written. Jeremiah's oracles were spoken over a long period (25:3) and are here gathered into a collection (Is. 8:16 and note). Since Jeremiah continued to prophesy after this date, the scroll is not the book of Jeremiah in its final form but rather an earlier edition.
The Lord takes no pleasure in judging the guilty, but longs for people to repent and live (see Ezek. 18:23).
The second mention of Jeremiah's scribe (32:12). His activity suggests that he had a role in compiling the book of Jeremiah.
He probably is banned from the temple area because of his unpopularity with the authorities (26:2–11). The Lord's word cannot be so easily restricted, however.
December 604 B.C.

See note on 26:24. the New Gate. This is where judicial cases would be heard in Jeremiah's era (see 26:10). Reading from a room in the upper courtyard, Baruch can be seen and heard by the people down below. Since the king has proclaimed a fast (v. 9), there are larger crowds in the temple than usual.

This family was also involved in Josiah's reforms (2 Kin. 22:12). Those reforms began with a rediscovery of the Book of the Law in the temple; perhaps they hope for a similar response on this occasion. If so, their hopes are not realized.

Baruch is no longer the reader, as he is presumably in hiding (v. 19). The absence of Jeremiah and Baruch puts the focus on Jehoiakim's response to the words themselves and suggests that Jeremiah's supporters are not optimistic about the outcome. Jehoiakim has already had the prophet Uriah brought back from Egypt and executed (26:23).
This takes place in December (v. 9 note).
The contrast with Josiah's response to the Lord's word could not be stronger (2 Kin. 22:11–13).

Not necessarily the son of the reigning king, but he is of royal blood. the LORD hid them. Instead of seeking the Lord in repentance, Jehoiakim seeks to kill the messengers, just as he earlier killed the prophet Uriah (26:23). Yet the Lord's power is evident in His ability to protect His servants, even within the capital city itself.
God's revealed word cannot be invalidated by the destruction of a scroll. Indeed, the new scroll of judgment will be even longer than before (v. 32).
His son Jehoiachin's rule lasts only a few months (22:30 note; 2 Kin. 24:8).

These chapters recount Jeremiah's last warnings before the fall of Jerusalem and his imprisonment for his unpopular message. His repeated advice to surrender to the Babylonians is ignored, and he remains imprisoned until the fall of Jerusalem. 37:1, 2 Zedekiah \... reigned instead of Coniah. The Babylonians place Jehoiakim's brother Zedekiah on the throne, thus fulfilling the previous oracle. See 2 Kin. 24:17, 18. The year is 597 B.C. Yet neither the new ruler nor the wealthy landowners ("the people of the land") pay any more attention to Jeremiah than Jehoiakim did.

See 21:1, 2. The request for the Lord to act is inevitably doomed, given the people's refusal to listen to His words. In any event, the Lord has already instructed Jeremiah not to pray for the people (7:16).

See 34:10, 11. Egypt and Babylon are in contention for the region. Many in Judah are looking to Egypt for support (24:8); the Babylonians have withdrawn to counter the Egyptian advance. Jerusalem's relief is only temporary, however, as Jeremiah prophesies (v. 7). On the Chaldeans, see note on 21:4.

While the siege is temporarily lifted, Jeremiah tries to access a piece of land that belongs to him, perhaps the field he purchased from Hanamel in 32:1–15. However, he is arrested at the city gates, accused of deserting to the Babylonians.
The second mention of such punishment (20:2).
Lit. "a cistern house" (see 38:6).

Perhaps he hopes that Jeremiah's dismal surroundings will make him more compliant. Jeremiah's message for the king is unchanged, however, and is vindicated by the events that Zedekiah himself can see.

The court is less severe than the "dungeon" (v. 16; see 32:2). Jeremiah is also given a daily ration of food until the resources of the city are exhausted by the siege. Zedekiah here shows a measure of respect for God's prophet.

There are many similarities between this chapter and ch. 37. They may be parallel accounts of the same events, though there are some differences, including there being no account of Jeremiah's arrest in ch. 38 and the mention of the house of Jonathan the secretary in 38:26. 38:1 Jucal. A variant of "Jehucal" (37:3).

Since Zedekiah owes his position to the Babylonians and has rebelled against them, his political position is weak and his power is limited. In the face of strong opposition, he chooses not to protect Jeremiah.
Likely a deep pit with only a small opening in the top. Whether it is empty from water shortage or disuse is not clear. They may be hoping Jeremiah will die there. the king's son. See note on 36:26.

The name means "king's servant," and he holds a position of responsibility in Zed­ekiah's household. It is revealing of Judah's spiritual state that a foreigner from Ethiopia (that is, the southern part of Egypt) rescues the Lord's prophet and not one of Abraham's descendants according to the flesh. eunuch. The word can refer to an castrated male or simply a court official, since certain court roles are normally filled by eunuchs in this era. king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate. Probably he is hearing civil suits (2 Sam. 15:2–4). See 37:13.
A touching glimpse of Ebed-melech's kindness.

This entrance is not mentioned elsewhere. It is perhaps for the king's private use. The whole encounter smacks of secrecy. Jeremiah is understandably concerned about the king's intentions, given Zedekiah's earlier failure to protect him.
Jeremiah has no new message for Zed­ekiah. He merely confirms what he has already told him (27:1–15).
Zedekiah fears people instead of fearing the Lord.

The loss of a harem is a humiliating consequence for a king defeated in war. Your trusted friends. Lit. "men of your peace." These "friends" include the officials who have counseled war (vv. 1, 4) and the false prophets (8:11). The expression ironically confirms Jeremiah's criticism of them. sunk in the mud. As Jeremiah was in v. 6.
Zedekiah's inability to guarantee Jeremiah's safety (unless his own officials are not told of their conversation) highlights the king's political weakness.
July 586 B.C. (52:5–7; 2 Kin. 25:2–4 and notes). Though commentators disagree on the exact duration of the siege, it probably lasts eighteen to thirty months.

This fulfills 1:15. The gates of the city are where rule and authority are exercised. The officials' names are formed with those of Babylonian gods (Nebo, Nergal). Nergal-sar-ezer may be Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law, who later succeeds him as king.

When the inevitable breach of the city wall finally occurs, it is probably on the north side. At that point, King Zedekiah attempts to flee to the south, to the Arabah, the wilderness region that includes the Jordan valley. However, the Babylonians overtake him near Jericho, which is less than twenty miles (30 km) from the city. Zedekiah's fate is also described in 2 Kin. 25:1–12.

The majority of the people are exiled to Babylon. However, some of the poorer people are left behind to work the vineyards and the fields so that the Babylonians can continue to receive their tribute.

How much of the prophet's message the king knows is unclear; he probably regards him as a Babylonian sympathizer (though see 25:12). It is ironic that the faithful prophet of the Lord is treated more favorably by the Babylonians than by his own people.

The Ethiopian eunuch receives his reward for rescuing the prophet from the cistern (see 38:7–13). His actions demonstrate that he trusts in the Lord. In Acts 8, another Ethiopian eunuch trusts the Lord and receives his reward.

Even though Nebuchadnezzar issued orders for Jeremiah's protection, in the chaos after Jerusalem's fall he is taken to the staging center at Riblah for deportation with the other prisoners. Apparently, the commander of the imperial guard intervenes personally to release Jeremiah. From a Babylonian perspective, Jeremiah's prophecies are useful propaganda, but it is clear that Jeremiah has no personal affinity for the Babylonians.
See 26:24. Gedaliah is receptive to Jeremiah's understanding of events and will presumably welcome his support.

Fugitives and small military groups emerge from hiding and congregate at Mizpah, where they are able to gather in the harvest alongside the poor Judahites whom the Babylonians have left behind. At the moment of judgment, there is a glimpse of future blessing in the land. Contrast the drought conditions during parts of Jeremiah's earlier preaching (14:1–6 and notes).

The returnees bring news of a plot against Gedaliah's life. It is backed by the Ammonites, an anti-Babylonian group in the Transjordan.Unfortunately, even though the proposed assassin is identified by name, Gedaliah does not believe the reports.

This hospitality emphasizes the treachery of Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the man who was named in the earlier reports (40:15). Ishmael is of royal blood and may harbor ambitions of taking the throne. This passage seems to expand the account in 2 Kin. 25:25.

Important religious centers in the former northern kingdom that fell in 722 B.C. The men are a remnant of Israel's population who have been making regular pilgrimages to Jerusalem for the great feasts (in accordance with Ex. 23:14–17). The time of year (the "seventh month"; see v. 1) is the Feast of Booths. Compare the group that comes from Bethel shortly after the return from exile in Zech. 7:2, 3. The slaughter of these pilgrims is a senseless massacre. with their beards shaved \... bodies gashed. Signs of mourning for the fall of Jerusalem. Not all of them are legitimate under the Mosaic law (see Deut. 14:1). the temple of theLORD. Although the temple has been destroyed, the Temple Mount is still regarded as holy.
Mizpah (v. 6).
Members of Zed­ekiah's court, not just the king's own daughters. Ammonites. As part of the former alliance against Babylon (27:3), the Ammonite action is itself under God's judgment (27:8; 49:1–6).

Jeremiah is taken to Egypt by Jewish survivors fleeing from possible Babylonian reprisals. 41:11 Johanan the son of Kareah. He brought the original intelligence about plans for a coup to Gedaliah in 40:15.

Ishmael took all of the citizens of Mizpah with him on his flight to Ammon (v. 10) so he has been unable to travel quickly. Gibeon is a mere three miles (5 km) from Mizpah. The great pool there also saw a bloody battle after the death of Saul (2 Sam. 2:13).
Two men are presumably lost in the skirmish (see v. 2), but Ishmael himself gets away.
–18 Gedaliah's death creates a power vacuum. The former military officers who take over fear Babylonian reprisals and decide to flee to the relative safety of Egypt.
Likely the same person as Azariah the son of Hoshaiah in 43:2.

–6 pray to the LORD your God for us. Jeremiah was absent from Mizpah for the coup but on his return the people ask him to seek guidance from the Lord on their behalf, as Jacob did before going down to Egypt in Gen. 46:1–3. Their pledge to listen whether the Lord's words are "good or bad" shows that they already have a plan of action in mind, namely, going down to Egypt. As it turns out, they have no intention of listening to Jeremiah's words unless they agree with what they have already decided to do. Such an attitude will inevitably end in judgment.
Jeremiah is unable to give the people immediate direction, which must test their patience and trust. They have no idea when or how the Babylonians might respond to their attempts to flee to Egypt.

This promise of blessing for the remnant left behind during the exile is a new theme in Jeremiah's message (24:8; 40:6). The Lord declares that He will build them up and not pull them down (see 1:10). I relent. Having carried through the threatened judgment on Jerusalem, the Lord's attitude is now changed toward those who remain in Judah. Instead of bringing further judgment upon them, He will protect them from the Babylonians.

The Lord's word is still against seeking refuge in Egypt (Deut. 17:16). The issue, as ever, is false trust and the delusion of safety in human power and calculation (22:20, 22; 30:14). Those who remain in Judah will experience the Lord's blessing, but those who go down to Egypt will find the sword, famine, and pestilence following them there (14:12 note).

See note on 42:1. You are telling a lie. Though the people swore to respect whatever Jeremiah said as the Lord's word, they reject his prophecy as a lie. Previously, they were happy to accept the lies that the false prophets presented as the truth. It is not clear why they blame Bar­uch, Jeremiah's scribe, for the unfavorable message.

–7 In spite of Jeremiah's words of warning, the army officers who are now in charge take everyone down to Egypt. Those who liberated the people from Ishmael soon become as oppressive as the leader they have replaced. Jeremiah and Baruch are forced to go down with them.
Jeremiah's prophetic ministry continues in Egypt by means of another sign act.

Jeremiah sets large stones in the pavement near Pharaoh's palace (lit. "the king's house"; it may be a government building or a residence owned by the king). On that exact spot, he declares, Nebuchadnezzar will set up his royal throne when he invades Egypt, complete with a canopy to protect him from the sun. The message for the Judeans is clear: running away to Egypt will not help them evade the grasp of the Babylonians.
See note on 25:9.

Characteristic examples of Egyptian religious architecture. The temple of Heliopolis is only a few miles (about 5 km) from Tahpanhes. The Egyptian gods are powerless to protect their sacred objects, for the Lord has given the land into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar invades Egypt in 568–567 B.C., as Jeremiah has foretold.

Those who have taken Jeremiah to Egypt are not the only Jews there. Other groups have migrated or been exiled there at different times. Some are in lower (northern) Egypt, in Migdol and Memphis, while others are in upper (southern) Egypt, where there is a Jewish temple at Elephantine (Syene). This latter group carries on a considerable correspondence with the temple authorities in Jerusalem after the exile. Many of these dispersed Jewish groups seem to have brought with them the idolatry and disregard for the prophetic word that, prior to Jerusalem's fall, dogged those who remained in Judah.
Idolatrous worship of other gods.

Possibly this oracle threatens that the restoration promised in 5:10 and 23:3 may not be carried out. Those who share the idolatrous practices of Jerusalem will share its fate of complete destruction.
Israel was supposed to be a blessing to all nations of the earth (Gen. 12:1–3).
The implication is that they have also forgotten the judgment that resulted. Similarly, 2 Kin. 17:18–20 uses the judgment of the northern kingdom as a warning to Judah before her fall.

See Num. 30:6–15. The women have evidently taken the lead in worshiping the "queen of heaven," the goddess Astarte or Ishtar (7:18), likely because these cults appeal to women's fertility, just like other ancient pagan religions do. Yet the men are clearly implicated by their approval of these pagan practices. The practices amount to a denial that Jerusalem's destruction was the work of the Lord; instead, the people blame the city's downfall on their failure to offer enough sacrifices to their goddess.
The requirements of the Mosaic covenant (Deut. 11:1, 32; 12:1).

The people are scrupulously faithful to the promises they have made to their idols, yet their idols cannot help them or harm them. At the same time, they have failed to fulfill their vows to serve the Lord.
Pharaoh Hophra (reigned 589–570 B.C.) was killed by his enemies during a military revolt; his death is used as a sign that all the Lord's prophecies against the refugees in Egypt will come to pass.

This chapter contains God's promise to Bar­uch to spare his life, a promise made many years prior to the events of ch. 44. 45:1 fourth year of Jehoiakim.605 B.C., the year in which Baruch prepared the first scroll of Jeremiah's words for public reading (36:1–3).

Baruch had evidently suffered along with Jeremiah as a result of Jeremiah's prophetic commission (cf. 11:18–23). See 36:19; 43:3. When he said, "Woe is me!" he was declaring himself to be under the covenant curse (cf. Is. 6:5). rest. See Deut. 12:9; Ps. 95:11.

The servant is not greater than his master (John 15:20); since the people have rejected the Lord, they are likely to reject Jeremiah and Baruch as well. as a prize of war. Like Ebed-melech, his faithfulness would not go unrewarded by the Lord (cf. 39:15–18).

This section of Jeremiah comprises a series of judgment oracles against the surrounding nations. These declare the Lord's sovereignty over all nations and assure His own people that the negative promise of the Abrahamic covenant — "him who dishonors you I will curse"(Gen. 12:3) — is still in place. The Septuagint places these oracles after 25:13.

Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Neco at the battle of Carchemish on the upper Euphrates River in 605 B.C. and brought to a close Egypt's political and military influence over Palestine and Syria. Nonetheless, the Judeans continued to harbor vain hopes of help and support from the Egyptians, and the Egyptians in turn encouraged those hopes (see Ezek. 29). fourth year of Jehoiakim. See 36:1; 45:1. This links the oracle with the preceding chapter. The ascendancy of Babylon over Egypt is significant in the life of Judah in her final years, and the oracles recorded here are originally spoken before Babylon reaches the height of its power over Egypt.

These orders to the Egyptian army mock her military pretensions. They have all of the military equipment that they need, yet they will end in full retreat, proving the words of Eccl. 9:11: "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong."
See Jer. 6:25.
At Carchemish (v. 2 note).
Mercenaries from Africa and Greece testify to Egypt's power, but human strength is unavailing on the day of the Lord's vengeance.
See note on 8:22. virgin daughter of Egypt. Suggesting vulnerability and innocence, though it could be meant ironically. See its use in connection with Israel in 14:17; 18:13.
See 2:16; 43:8; 44:1. These are fortified cities close to the eastern border and thus will be strategic targets for Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar's assault is also prophesied in Ezek. 29:17–21.

The Septuagint's reading is preferred by many interpreters: "Why has Apis run away?" Apis is the sacred bull of ancient Egypt, worshiped as an incarnation of the god Ptah, especially at Noph (Memphis; v. 14). Alternatively, it could be a reference to the mercenaries they hired in v. 9.

See Gen. 22:15–18. the King. For God as king, see 8:19; 10:7, 10; 48:15; 51:57; Deut. 33:5. In the oracles against the nations, God's true kingship is contrasted with the vain pretensions of earthly kings. the LORD of hosts. This title for God is often used in military contexts. Tabor \... Carmel. These mountains in northern Israel stand at the eastern and western boundaries of the strategic plain of Megiddo and tower impressively over their surroundings.
The Egyptian capital will be laid waste, just like Jerusalem (see 9:12).

This may be an ironic allusion to Egyptian worship of the bull Apis (v. 15 note). Their mercenaries, too, are fattened calves ready for the slaughter (see v. 10). biting fly. Nebuchadnezzar. from the north. See 6:1.
The Egyptian crown contains serpents as emblems of strength, but here the serpent will slink silently away.
Amon is the chief Egyptian god. Thebes is in the south, suggesting even deeper penetration by Babylon. The Lord's judgment is not just upon Pharaoh and Egypt but upon the gods of Egypt as well.
The promise of restoration for Egypt also appears in Is. 1:16–25; 27:13. It is fulfilled on the day of Pentecost when visitors from Egypt are among those added to the church (Acts 2:10)

The prophecy against Egypt is intended to encourage Judah. Though Judah is under the Lord's judgment for their sins, He has not forgotten His people, nor is He finished with them. Those who have assaulted them will be judged as well. Even though their journey through life might be painful and bitter like Jacob's was (Gen. 47:8, 9), the Lord is still with them. Cf. Is. 41:8–14; 43:1–5.

The Egyptians attacked Israel's old enemy the Philistines on several occasions, including an assault before the Battle of Megiddo in 609 B.C. and also in 601 B.C. Yet the Philistines' downfall will not come at the hands of the Egyptians but rather the Babylonians, the "waters \... rising out of the north" (1:13, 14 note).

These Phoenician cities afford natural protection to the Philistines farther down the Mediterranean coast, though it is not known whether alliances ever exist between them. Caphtor. The Philistines' place of origin, usually identified as Crete.
Ritual mourning practices for pagans include cutting themselves and shaving their heads.
LORD. This instrument of the Lord's judgment is unsheathed against His own people in Ezek. 21:9–17. Now it will come on their neighbors.

This chapter records the oracle against Moab; cf. Is. 15; 16; Ezek. 25:8–11; Amos 2:1–3. Moab was Israel's enemy (Judg. 3:12–14; 2 Kin. 3:4–27). It was an ally of Judah against Babylon (27:3), but supplied troops for Nebuchadnezzar against Jehoiakim (2 Kin. 24:2). Its defeat by Nebuchadnezzar may have come in 582 B.C. after a rebellion. 48:1 Nebo \... Kiriathaim. Originally these towns were allocated to the tribe of Reuben (Num. 32:3, 37, 38; Josh. 13:15, 19). Since they are in the northern part of Moab, they will be overrun first in a Babylonian invasion.

A village northeast of Mount Nebo; it was also assigned to Reuben (Num. 32:37; Josh. 13:17). 48:2–5 Madmen \... Horonaim \... Luhith. A similar reference to Luhith and Horonaim occurs in Is. 15:5. Horonaim also appears on the Moabite Stone, from the ninth century B.C. The name "Madmen" is a play on words: it sounds like the Hebrew word for "silence."
Junipers are hardy evergreen trees that cling to life in hostile environments.
A god of Moab worshiped by Solomon (1 Kin. 11:7, 33; 2 Kin. 23:13). Images of defeated gods were often carried off into exile.
Probably Nebuchadnezzar.

The wine left to age represents Moab's complacency. Moab has been left untouched while the surrounding nations are invaded. Its ease and security will vanish as quickly as a bottle empties when overturned.

Possibly a reference to the name "El Bethel" used for the Lord in Jeroboam's apostate worship at Bethel (1 Kin. 12:28–30). That cult did not prevent the Assyrians from plundering the land in 722 B.C. (2 Kin. 18:9–12).
Like Egypt, Moab puts its confidence in the power of its soldiers (see 46:3–6). Its trust will be equally misplaced.

A lament for Moab (cf. 2 Sam. 1:19). The prophets sing laments for those who are not yet dead as a sign of the certainty of their coming downfall (cf. Ezek. 19). The scepter and the staff are symbols of Moab's power, now broken.
Southeast of Dibon, this border fortress on the Arnon River (v. 20) is here pictured anxiously watching the flight of the refugees.
The region along the Arnon. It is the most important river in Moab in Jeremiah's day.
Drunkenness is a symbol of Judah's judgment (see 25:15–29); now it is Moab's turn to be judged.
Moab mocked Judah for her fate, asserting that she deserved to be destroyed for her sins. Although that was true, Moab was no better and in no position to look down on Judah.
See Is. 2:10.

See Is. 16:8. This area at the northern end of the Dead Sea is famous for its orchards and vineyards. The joyful shouts of those treading the grapes will be replaced by shouts of anguish and pain (see 25:30).
These local places of pagan worship will be eliminated from Moab, just as they have been destroyed in Judah (see 17:3).
The music of the flute often accompanies ceremonies both joyful and sad.
Signs of mourning. See note on 41:5.
It is customary in Jeremiah's day to offer incense upon rooftops as an act of worship (2 Kin. 23:12).
Nebuchadnezzar (Ezek. 17:3).
Derived from Num. 21:28, 29, but Jeremiah redirects Balaam's prophecy against the Amorites by applying it to Moab.
Like Egypt (see 46:26), even Moab can repent and be added to the Lord's people.

A prophecy against the Ammonites. See Ezek. 25:1–7; Amos 1:13–15. Ammon, an old enemy of Israel (Judg. 11:4–33; 1 Sam. 11:1–11; 2 Sam. 10; 1 Kin. 4:13–19), is located in Transjordan just north of Moab. Like Moab, it was part of an alliance against Babylon (27:3), and like Moab it supplied troops to Nebuchadnezzar against Judah (2 Kin. 24:2). Its hostility to Gedaliah (40:13–41:3) suggests a rebellion against Babylon, probably leading to an attack that virtually ends its existence as an autonomous nation. 49:1 Milcom. Chief god of the Ammonites, also known as Molech (32:35 note; 1 Kin. 11:5). Gad. This Israelite tribe settled in the Transjordan before the conquest of the Promised Land proper (Num. 32). The Ammonites took it from them more than a century before the time of Jeremiah, claiming that it belonged to their god, Molech.
This city is identified with modern Amman in Jordan. It is the capital of the Ammon­ites; once it is reduced to ruins, the Israelites will reclaim their inheritance.

As a border town, it may have belonged to Ammon at some time also (Judg. 11:26). Ai. Not the city of Ai familiar from the events of Josh. 8. Its location is unknown. Milcom shall go into exile. See note on 48:7. The Lord is judging Moab's gods as well as Moab itself.
Reminiscent of the phrase "terror on every side" (see 6:25; 20:3; 46:5).
See note on 48:27. This message should encourage the Lord's people in exile as well. If Egypt, Moab, and Ammon can be restored, how much more the Lord's own people?

A prophecy against Edom. See also 27:3; cf. Is. 21:11, 12; Ezek. 25:12–14; Amos 1:11, 12; Obad. 1–16. Edom, the descendants of Jacob's estranged brother Esau, is an old enemy of Israel (2 Sam. 8:13, 14) and has caused special bitterness by assisting Babylon against Judah. 49:7, 8 Teman \... Dedan. These regions represent the northern and southern limits of Edom (see Ezek. 25:13).
Cf. Obad. 5. Both of these groups tend to leave something behind no matter how careful they are. Yet when the Babylonians come, there will be nothing left.

The image of bitter wine for the judgment of God is common in the Prophets (see 25:15–17; 34:5, 6). "Those who did not deserve to drink the cup" may be a reference to faithful Judeans who, like Baruch and Jeremiah, have been caught up in the destruction of their homeland nonetheless.
The capital of Edom.
The Edomites are confident that the inaccessibility of their cities will protect them. Yet no natural advantages can protect a city from the wrath of the Lord.

In Jeremiah's day, lions roam the lush terrain of the Jordan valley and threaten shepherds (1 Sam. 17:37). In 4:7, the roaring lion was Nebuchadnezzar. Here it is the Lord, the One whose wrath stands behind Nebuchadnezzar.
Probably Nebuchadnezzar (as 48:40), though the Edomites are also conquered decisively by Arabs during the sixth century B.C.

A prophecy against the city-states of Syria (Aram), of which Damascus is the most significant. Syria impinges chiefly on the northern kingdom of Israel in the Assyrian period (1 Kin. 20; Amos 1:3–5). The three states named here fell to Assyria in the eighth century B.C. 49:23 Damascus \... Hamath \... Arpad. Major Aramean city-states. Hamath and Arpad are both north of Damascus and will therefore be the first to be affected by a Babylonian invasion.
This is not a personal name but rather a dynastic title that identifies the ruler of Syria as the son of the god Hadad.

A prophecy against Arabian kingdoms. Arab nomadic tribes pose a periodic threat to settled communities in the ancient world (Judg. 6:1–6). The present prophecy may be occasioned by an Arab uprising against Nebuchadnezzar in 598 B.C. They have few cities, so the judgment is aimed at the markers of wealth in their community — tents, flocks, and camels. 49:28 Kedar. An Arab tribe well known in the OT period (Gen. 25:13; Is. 21:16, 17; 42:11). Hazor. Also in the Arabian desert, and not the well-known Hazor in northern Israel. This name may designate a number of Arab settlements, including Teman, Buz, and Dedan (25:23, 24). people of the east. Another designation for Arab tribal peoples (Judg. 6:3; 7:12; Job 1:3).
These nomadic peoples typically live in unwalled towns, not depending on fortified cities. See the description of Laish in Judg. 18:7. They are no match for a well-armed invader.
Animals known to haunt desolate ruins (see Mal. 1:3).

A prophecy against Elam, an important power to the east of Babylon, subjugated by Assyria but resurgent in the Babylonian period. The prophecy possibly relates to a Babylonian containment campaign against Elam in 595 B.C. Unlike the other prophecies in this section, the oracle against Elam is dated to the beginning of Zedekiah's reign in 597 B.C. At that time, some in Judah may have hoped that a resurgent Elam would neutralize the Babylonian threat and result in the swift return of those already exiled.
Elam is famous for its archers.
Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of Elam has nothing to do with the gods of the Babylonians. It is a sign of the Lord's sovereign rule over all nations.

The prophecy against Babylon (cf. Is. 13:1–14:23; 21:1–9) is the climax of the book. The previous prophecies have served Jeremiah's purpose of showing that Babylon will prevail over "all the nations" for a period (27:7). Babylon has appeared up to this point as the instrument of God's wrath. Finally, however (as in 25:17–26), "the word that the Lord spoke" is uttered against Bab­ylon itself to show that its own time of judgment must come (25:11, 12). The Hebrew text of Jeremiah has placed the prophecy (actually delivered in 593 B.C.; cf. 51:59 note) at this point in the book so that the judgment on Babylon can occupy the climactic position. The relative length of the prophecy also shows how important Babylon is in the theology of the book.

Merodach, or "Marduk," is the creator and chief deity in Babylonian myth. He is also called Bel, an early form of the word "Baal" ("lord"). See also Is. 46:1. He is nothing more than a powerless idol, however.

See 1:14; 6:1. Normally in the book of Jeremiah, the enemy from the north country is Babylon. The tables are now turned on Babylon. The nation in question is not specified, but see 51:27, 28, where it is clear that the reference is to the Medes and the Persians.
The report of Babylon's impending downfall is good news for God's own people, who will then be able to return to worship the Lord at Zion, the site of the temple in Jerusalem.

This claim on the part of the enemies of God's people is refuted by the surrounding oracle of judgment against Babylon. God will hold those who assault His people to account even though He has brought these nations in judgment against them.

When the day of Babylon's judgment comes, it will be time for God's people to return home to Judah. See Is. 48:20; Zech. 2:6. The edict issued by Cyrus in 539 B.C., shortly after Babylon's destruction, allows the Jews and other captured peoples to go home.
Cyrus is mentioned as the leader of this alliance of the Medes and Persians in Is. 41:25; 45:1. Members of the alliance are named in 51:27, 28.
The Lord's continuing concern for His promises to His people is clear. Those who assault Israel will pay the price (see Gen. 12:3).
Babylon is personified. last of the nations. She who has seemed invincible will be completely devastated (Is. 14:12–17).
The references to the kings of Assyria and Babylon make it clear that "Israel" here is not the former northern kingdom but the original people of God, made up of all twelve tribes.
The most fertile parts of Israel, famous for their livestock (see Amos 4:1).
The Lord promises to do something in the future that will remove completely the sins of His people. Cf. Zech. 3:9.
These words are puns on Babylonian place-names (Marratu, Puqudu). The Hebrew words mean "double rebellion" and "punishment."
Hammers are used for breaking up rocks (23:19). Here the hammer itself will be shattered.
The Persian defeat of Babylon is unexpected.
Babylon's army (46:15 note).

Jewish escapees from Babylon will return to Jerusalem, where they will testify to the Lord's deliverance. vengeance for his temple. The burning of the temple (52:13) was the definitive destruction of Jerusalem. The Lord ties His vengeance on Babylon specifically to that.

Unlike in the fall of Judah, there will be no remnant surviving the fall of Babylon. the Holy One of Israel. This name for God is frequent in Isaiah (cf. Is. 1:4 note). No one can defy the true and living God and escape the consequences.

–38 The people of Israel are oppressed \... they refuse to let them go. The background for these verses is the exodus, when God brought Israel out of captivity in Egypt. Similar language is now applied to the oppressive Babylon. A new exodus will ensue in which God will subdue the Babylonians and deliver His people once more.
See note on 31:11. When the Lord steps in as their advocate, the result is rest for His people and unrest for her tormentors.

–40 the Chaldeans. See note on 21:4. Everything in which the Babylonians might trust — wise men, diviners, warriors, horses and chariots, mercenaries, treasures, the waters that surround the city — will prove to be unworthy of such trust. The ruins will be abandoned to wild animals such as hyenas and ostriches (or possibly "screech owls"; the exact identity of the bird is not clear). Its downfall will be as complete and permanent as that of Sodom and Gomorrah.
Compare the almost identical description of the Babylonian armies coming against Judah in 6:22–24. Now they will be invaded by such an oppressor.
Cf. 49:19–22, where Babylon's assault of Edom is described in similar terms.

A coded reference to "Kasdim" or the Chaldeans (text note), another name for Babylon. It uses the same code as the name "Sheshach" in 25:26 and 51:41 (text notes), in which the last letter of the alphabet is substituted for the first, the second last for the second, and so on.
Babylon is to be treated according to the rules of holy war. No one is to be spared alive and no plunder is to be taken, for everything belongs to the Lord.
See note on 50:8.
Babylon has been the agent of the Lord's destruction of many nations (25:15). Now she herself will have to drink from that bitter cup.
The sudden destruction of this seemingly invincible city is a symbol of the end for all of God's enemies. See Rev. 18:2.
Babylon is finally conquered by an alliance of Medes and Persians, including Darius the Mede (see Dan. 6; Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). See also Is. 13:17; 21:2.
Babylon is renowned for its irrigation channels, fed by the Euphrates River. In the same way, the great prostitute of Rev. 17:1 sits on many waters.
See Gen. 22:16 and note.

–19 The Lord's power and wisdom, which are evident in His work of creation, will be harnessed to the task of Babylon's destruction with equally impressive results. Cf. 10:12–16. In comparison to Him, the idols of the nations are worthless and powerless. They will be destroyed along with all those who trust in them.

Apparently addressed to Babylon, vv. 20–23 should be taken together with vv. 24–26. Babylon has been God's "hammer" (50:23) against the nations, but Bab­ylon's own sin will later cause it to be judged.

In Dan. 2:35, a small stone becomes a mountain that fills the entire earth. Here Babylon begins as an enormous mountain that destroys much of the earth but then shrinks into a rock that can be rolled off a cliff and then burned. No foundation stone or cornerstone will come from it (cf. Is. 28:16).
Districts of Media that are now summoned to join the fight against Babylon.
Babylon's sacking of Judah (cf. 21:10) is being avenged by her Median conquerors.
A possible route of escape from the city of Babylon is blocked.

This figure both personifies Babylon and alludes to its women, made vulnerable by defeat. See 50:42; Lam. 1:6 and note. a threshing floor. An area that has been trodden hard and flat, where the harvested wheat is taken to be beaten with sticks to separate the grain from the chaff.

Hb. tannin. Used to describe the great sea creatures in Gen. 1:21 and the multi-headed sea monster Leviathan in Ps. 74:13. It is often an image of something far more terrifying than a normal creature.
See 50:15. The metaphors of revenge and courtroom judgment are mixed here.
See note on 9:11.
The Hebrew has "Sheshach" here (text note); cf. notes on 25:26; 51:1.

See note on 50:2. Instead of the nations flowing to Bel, in the last days they will flow to Zion, to the Lord (see Is. 2:2). what he has swallowed. Bel has "swallowed" the nations taken into exile and their treasures (see v. 34). Judah's treasures are later restored by Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:5–11). wall of Babylon. An enormously wide double wall, further protected by an intervening moat.

God's people should be prepared for the coming day when they will leave their exile and return home. Though it is still many years distant and there will be conflicting reports at the time,they should maintain a constant state of readiness for the Lord's day of judgment on Babylon, which would be their own day of deliverance.

The exiles express their grief over the occupation of the temple by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 B.C., perhaps feeling that this defilement can never be cleansed. Yet they must continue to remember Jerusalem even though they are far away in exile. Cf. Ps. 137.
Probably a reference to its lofty ziggurats, symbols of its religious pride (Gen. 11:4).
is a God of recompense.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Unlike the idols, which can say and do nothing, the Lord acts to defend His people and judge their enemies (see vv. 35, 36).
The Ishtar Gate is known for its great height. labor \... the nations. The labor of subject nations in building Babylon's fortifications will be of no use when God brings His judgment.

An official in Zedekiah's administration, he is responsible for this expedition's lodging en route. He is the brother of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe (32:12). went with Zedekiah \... to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign.593 B.C. The expedition may be in response to a summons to explain Zedekiah's part in the uprising against Nebuchadnezzar (27:3 note). Jeremiah knows the ultimate destiny of Babylon even as he urges his countrymen to submit to Nebuchadnezzar (38:1–3).
It may contain the prophecies in chs. 50 and 51. See 36:2.
This final symbolic act (13:1–11 note) reinforces the last word of Jeremiah that Babylon will fall as completely and comprehensively as a scroll tied to a stone and cast into the Euphrates.

The final chapter of Jeremiah is an appendix, largely drawn from 2 Kin. 24; 25, describing the fall of Jerusalem and reminding the reader that Jeremiah's prophecies have been fulfilled. Despite its message of divine judgment for sin, the book of Jeremiah ends (as does 2 Kings) on a hopeful note by calling attention to the mercy shown to King Jehoiachin of Judah while in Babylonian exile (52:31–34; cf. 2 Kin. 25:27–30). The section of 2 Kings dealing with Gedaliah's assassination is omitted here because it was dealt with in chs. 40; 41. 52:1 Jeremiah of Libnah. Not Jeremiah the prophet, who is from Anathoth (1:1).

LORD. In the book of Kings, all of the kings of Israel and Judah are evaluated for their faithfulness in pursuing the pure worship of the people, centralized in the temple in Jerusalem. Zedekiah is judged a failure on this account.
The fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple are also described in Jer. 39:1–10.
2 Kin. 25:8 has the "seventh day." One or the other text could be a copyist's minor error. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

These are added to the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar has already taken from Jerusalem (see 27:16). They are returned to Jerusalem in the time of Cyrus (Ezra 1:7), providing a line of continuity between the first and second temples.
2 Kin. 25:17 has "three." See note on v. 12.
2 Kin. 25:19 has "five." See note on v. 12.

These verses refer to the two main deportations of Jews to Babylon in 597 B.C. ("the seventh year") and 586 B.C. (the "eighteenth year"; "nineteenth" in v. 12 is due to an alternate way of counting). A third, smaller deportation is also mentioned, perhaps in response to the assassination of Gedaliah. The numbers here are smaller than those in 2 Kin. 24:14, 16, and may count only adult males or only the leading figures of Judah.

–34 twenty-fifth.2 Kin. 25:27 has "twenty-seventh." See note on v. 12. 52:31 Jehoiachin. The kind treatment of the former king of Judah by Evil-Merodach (also known as Amel-Marduk) on his accession to the throne in 562 B.C. provides a glimmer of hope for the restoration of God's people that Jeremiah prophesied. The absence of any reference to the decree of Cyrus permitting the people to return home in 539 B.C. suggests that the book of Jeremiah reached its final form before that date.

Lamentations.note: The chosen city of Zion, once exalted, has been humbled for her sins. 1:1 How lonely. The word "how" often begins biblical laments, contrasting the present disaster with previous prosperity. The first verse sets the theme of the lament: Jerusalem's loss of greatness. The city, once favored, is desolate from the Babylonians' plundering (Is. 1:21–26). widow. Widowhood and solitude (Jer. 15:17) are typical pictures of abandonment. Israel's husband is the Lord; she is therefore not a widow because of her husband's death but because of the consequences of her unfaithfulness to God with her pagan lovers (see v. 2). slave. Slavery is contrary to God's ultimate design for Israel. They became a nation when God delivered them from slavery in Egypt so that they could serve Him (Deut. 6:20–25; Jer. 2:14; Deut. 15:12–18). The blessings of living in the Promised Land and serving according to the law are replaced with the punishments of exile and forced labor because the people have flagrantly and impenitently broken the covenant they accepted when they left Egypt (Ex. 24:7, 8; Deut. 28:47–50).

A word often used ironically in reference to Judah's idolatrous neighbors, with whom she has consorted willingly (Jer. 3:1). none to comfort. See also vv. 7, 9, 16; cf. the comfort promised in Is. 40:1. Here there is no limit to the effects of the Babylonian ravages. friends. Her former allies who have abandoned her in her hour of need.

For the fall of Judah, see 2 Kin. 24:20–25:30; Jer. 39–45, 52. exile. The ultimate humiliation for the covenant people (Deut. 28:63–68). no resting place. The Lord promised and provided His people rest from their enemies (Deut. 12:9; 2 Sam. 7:1, cf. Deut. 28:65). Israel and Judah's unfaithfulness has left them without rest.

A picture of ancient Israel's regular worship life. roads to Zion. In the past, people who lived at a distance would travel these roads in pilgrimage to the temple (Ps. 84:5), but now that temple has been destroyed by the Babylonians. festival. The three main yearly gatherings for worship are Unleavened Bread/Passover, Weeks (Pentecost), and Booths (Ex. 23:14–17; Lev. 23:4–44). Under normal circumstances, Jerusalem is crowded, and priests preside over the vibrant celebrations. The exile now makes this impossible. her priests groan. The priests are those most affected by the destruction of the temple. virgins have been afflicted. A sign of defeat; cf. Jer. 31:13.

See other complaints in Jer. 12:1; Ps. 73. Here the complaint comes with a confession of sin. As the Prophets foretold, Judah's unfaithfulness has brought her to grief. the Lord has afflicted her. Jerusalem's destruction is not the result of the great power of the Babylonians and their gods; it is the Lord's judgment upon the people. In this lay their hope: the One who has wounded them can bind up those wounds (see Hos. 6:1).Their Judge's covenant faithfulness endures forever (see 3:22–24).

This phrase personifies Jerusalem (Jer. 6:2), but it might also allude to the women of the city, who feel its anguish most keenly. all her majesty has departed. The glory of God, which once inhabited the Most Holy Place of the temple in Jerusalem, has abandoned it and gone into exile with those in Babylon (see Ezek. 8–11).
The bitter present contrasts with an earlier, happier time, possibly the days of David and Solomon. none to help her. Cf. Ps. 46:5.

The idea that sin has caused the exile is developed, first with images of ritual impurity. filthy. Probably refers to menstruation, which, like other bodily emissions of life fluids, renders a person temporarily unfit to stand in God's presence (Lev. 15:19–33). The consequence of Judah's sin is similar, if not more severe: being cut off from God's worship, and perhaps also suffering public humiliation (cf. Jer. 13:22, 26). Jerusalem's spiritual adultery, in which she has stripped before her lovers, is fittingly punished by an unwilling uncovering. In the day Lamentations is written, prisoners of war, both male and female, are often stripped naked as an act of extreme humiliation. Cf. a similar sequence in Ezek. 16:36–39.

The image of ritual uncleanness intensifies. she has no comforter. Since she has been deaf to the warnings of His prophets, the Lord is deaf to her appeals (see Jer. 11:11). O Lord, behold. An element of appeal to the Lord, a normal part of the lament form (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes), is now introduced.

The temple's true purpose is to attract the nations to worship the God of Israel (1 Kin. 8:41–43), but now it has brought invaders who desecrate it. those whom you forbade. Since God's people have not protected the sanctity of the temple but allowed uncircumcised Gentiles to enter it (see Ezek. 44:6–8), God has brought Gentiles to destroy it.
This vivid picture of desolation hints at food shortages.

The sufferer imagines that his suffering is unprecedented. Yet no one seems to sympathize. the day of his fierce anger. A grim confirmation of Amos's prophecy that on the day of the Lord His anger will be against His own people (Amos 5:18).
Zion knows that the Lord Himself has afflicted her (Ps. 88:13–18). Her downfall is like that of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:24). he spread a net. Cf. Ezek. 17:20.
See Jer. 27, 28.
The Lord, formerly a warrior on Israel's behalf (Deut. 9:1–3), has turned His might against His own people, trampling her like grapes in a winepress (see Is. 63:1–4).
See Jer. 9:1. a comforter is far from me. There is no one to help, no one to comfort — a dominant theme in these verses (2, 7, 9, 17).

A historic name for Israel, derived from the name of the nation's ancestor (Gen. 32:28). his neighbors should be his foes. The presence of Judah as an unclean thing among the nations falsifies her intended role as a witness to the holiness of God (Ex. 19:5, 6).
Zion justifies the Lord's punishment by an admission of sin (see Ps. 51:4). Yet the thought shifts quickly again to her slavery.
The nations around Judah fail to help her in her time of need. priests and elders. See Jer. 2:8.

Zion appeals to the Lord because of her enemies' gloating. Their insults are deeply offensive to Judah's status as God's covenant people — and therefore to God Himself. According to the Abrahamic covenant, their insults demand a divine response (Gen. 12:1–3). day. The day of the Lord now becomes a day of terror for Zion's enemies. Zion's lament follows an established prophetic pattern: the enemies who administer God's judgment finally come to suffer judgment themselves (Jer. 25:15–38).
Zion finally asserts that her enemies merit judgment as much as she does. my groans. The petition to punish, however, does not diminish Zion's deep distress.

The second lament over Zion's loss of glory begins, and the poet portrays the Lord's anger with her. 2:1 How. Cf. 1:1 and note. He has cast down \... the splendor. Israel's fall into disfavor is compared to a falling star (Is. 14:12). has not remembered. Judah is astonished that the promise to David is now apparently void (cf. Ps. 89, especially vv. 38–51). Isaiah assured the people that God would protect Zion (e.g., Is. 37:35), and the people of Judah has absolutized these promises, forgetting their obligation to keep the terms of God's covenant with them (Ex. 24:1–3). his footstool. A term normally used for the ark of the covenant (1 Chr. 28:2; Ps. 132:7) or for the earth (Is. 66:1). It is here applied to Zion (cf. Ps. 99:5).
Cf. Ex. 34:6, 7. strongholds. The strength of the fortified cities of Judah once symbolized God's blessing in response to Judah's covenant faithfulness (2 Chr. 10:4–12).
The language vividly contrasts Judah and her enemies, as well as Judah's life as it should be and as it is. a flaming fire \... consuming all around. Cf. Ex. 3:2.

The harmful arrows meant for God's enemies (Deut. 32:42) are now aimed at His people (Hos. 5:10; Jer. 6:11; 7:20). like an enemy. See note on 1:15. poured out his fury. This holy war imagery is classically used of God's judgment on the nations (Ps. 69:24).
See note on 1:6.

References to the temple. the Lord has made \... forget festival and Sabbath. See note on 1:4. This can be rendered "The Lord has made appointed feasts and Sabbaths forgotten things in Zion," an ironic justice since the people first forgot the Sabbaths themselves (Amos 8:5; Jer. 17:19–27). king and priest. The Lord's wrath is poured out on the sacred place, the sacred festivals, and the sacred people. Everything holy is swept away by His wrath.
God's judgment destroys not only the place of His dwelling, but Israel's means of approaching Him in worship. The shouts of triumphant enemies replace the cry of worshiping assemblies.
To survey the city for destruction (Is. 34:11; Amos 7:7, 8). In Zech. 1:16, the Lord promises to do the same thing when He restores His chosen city.
Not only are the religious institutions destroyed, but the Lord withholds revelation. The prophetic vision that accompanies preaching of the law has ceased (Jer. 8:8–10; 18:18; 1 Sam. 3:1).

Conventional gestures of mourning (1:14; Job 2:12, 13). Here they are undertaken by old men and young women, implying the comprehensiveness of the mourning. 2:11 My eyes are spent with weeping. Cf. this natural suffering because of the agony of his people with Jer. 4:19, and note the pictures of desolation that accompany the prophet's expressions of anguish (Jer. 4:31). my bile. Lit. "my liver," which in Hebrew thought is one of the key locations of the emotions.
The poet is especially moved by the sight of suffering children.
The meaning seems to be, "What can I tell you about suffering, you who have suffered so much?" No ready answers occur to someone who has witnessed sorrows such as these. comfort. See note on 1:2.

The thought advances from v. 9; prophets are now said to have prophesied falsely. The complex problem of false prophecy is a recurrent theme of the Prophets (Jer. 5:12, 13; 23:9–40; 28). Deut. 18:21, 22 furnishes one of the criteria by which prophets may be judged true or false.
The beauty of the chosen place is extravagantly expressed (Pss. 50:2; 48:2), but it is by scoffers who mock the ruin and agony of Jerusalem.

In vv. 2 and 5, God Himself is said to have swallowed up the people. As this verse makes clear, He has done this using Judah's enemies as His agents. The verse also shows how the nations proudly attribute their victory over Judah to their own strength.

God's purposes of judgment were declared via Moses in the curses of the covenant (Lev. 26:23–39; Deut. 28:15–68). Judah's present has happened in accordance with God's known purposes. See 1:18; 2:8. might. See note on v. 3.
There is irony in this futile cry to the city wall, a symbol of the nation's imagined strength. day and night. Cf. Deut. 28:67.
See note on v. 12.

The theme of the suffering of innocent children reaches the height of pathos (Jer. 19:9). Its power as an appeal to God is enhanced by the knowledge that God knows motherly affection (Is. 66:13). As extreme in its own way is the outrage of sacrilege: the Lord's anointed ones are killed in His sanctuary. This is only possible because the temple in Jerusalem has already been desecrated by the people's idolatry (see Ezek. 8; 9). priest and prophet. For the sins of priests and prophets, see 4:13.
The horror of death in youth contrasts with the blessing of attaining a good age (Job 42:17).

This contrast between summoning to the joy of a feast and summoning to disaster is starkly powerful. terrors on every side. See Jer. 6:25; 20:10. day of the anger of the Lord. The poem ends where it began — without alleviation of the dark picture.

As an individual expresses the grief of the community, hope and consolation are sustained by a knowledge of God's compassionate love. This central chapter is three times as long as each of the surrounding chapters, highlighting its importance. 3:1 I am the man.
