Five hundred cubits is the sum of the lengths of the north outer gateway (50), part of the outer court (100), the north inner gateway (50), the inner court (100), the south inner gateway (50), part of the outer court (100), and the south outer gateway (50). Unlike the less-regular design of the tabernacle and Solomon's temple, Ezekiel's temple complex is itself square.

The prophet had an earlier vision of the glory of the Lord departing from the city (10:18–22; 11:22–24); now in his vision he witnesses its return. The glory comes from the east, the direction to which it had departed (11:23). Unlike its slow and halting departure, the return of the glory is sudden and rapid, accompanied by the characteristic roar of many waters (see 1:24), leading the prophet once again to fall on his face. The glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple when they were dedicated (Ex. 40:34, 35; 1 Kin. 8:10, 11; 2 Chr. 5:13, 14; 7:1, 2; cf. Is. 60:1–3). See note on 11:22–24. The temple of the restoration period, built by Zerubbabel, is not built according to Ezekiel's vision. It is a rebuilt version of Solomon's temple, though lacking its earlier splendor (Ezra 3:12, 13; Hag. 2:3). Yet Haggai prophesies that the glory of Zerubbabel's temple will exceed that of Solomon's (Hag. 2:7–9), because God's presence will be there. Ultimately, this is fulfilled in Christ and His temple, the church.

The Jerusalem temple is understood as the place where God had His throne, where He is enthroned in the Most Holy Place above the ark, which is His footstool (1 Sam. 4:4; 2 Sam. 6:2; 2 Kin. 19:15; 1 Chr. 13:6; Pss. 80:1; 99:1; 132:13, 14; Is. 6:1; 37:16). The significant part of the affirmation is that this temple will be the Lord's throne forever; the sins of His people will never again drive Him away from His sanctuary. the dead bodies of their kings. In the past, Israel's kings defiled the temple both by their spiritual adultery and by placing memorial markers for dead kings in the grounds of the temple of the living God. In the future, the kings will be put in their proper place at a greater distance from the residence of the great King, God Himself.

The patterns for Israel's past sanctuaries have come from God; likewise, the plans for the temple in Ezekiel's vision are of divine origin. See note on 40:1–48:35. This vision is not intended to provide the blueprint for a building project; rather, it has a message for Ezekiel's contemporaries. As they study the plan, they are to be convicted of their sins and ashamed of their iniquities. By permitting and restricting access to particular groups of people and raising the general standards of holiness throughout the sacred space, Ezekiel communicates the same message of the necessity of absolute holiness that he has proclaimed elsewhere in more direct form.

Ezekiel's temple vision is the only body of ritual law in the Bible not from the mouth of Moses. Like Moses, Ezekiel receives this law on a high mountain (40:2; Ex. 25:9, 40). This law is not intended to replace the laws of Moses, with which it cannot be harmonized. Rather, it is another way of making the same fundamental points as Ezekiel's visionary temple. Here, theology is described in the form of legislation.

See note on 40:5. altar. The altar is built as a series of platforms, each smaller than the one below, similar to a step-pyramid or ziggurat. The ancient rabbis had many discussions about this altar since its construction contradicts the command that the altar should not have steps (Ex. 20:24–26). The steps ascend the east side to prevent any repetition of the sun worship in 8:16, where the people turned their backs on God. The importance of the sacrificial aspect of temple life is emphasized by the massive size of the altar and its location at the geometric center of the entire temple complex.
See Ex. 29:16; Lev. 4:6; 5:9. The new altar must be consecrated before it can be put into use (2 Chr. 7:8, 9). A similar procedure was followed when the altar of Solomon's temple was consecrated.
See note on 44:15.
See Ex. 29:14; Lev. 4:12, 21; 8:17; 9:11; 16:27. The writer of Hebrews interprets these instructions as an aspect of Christ's offering of Himself (Heb. 13:11–13).

The prophet has been in the inner court (43:5), but he is now taken to the eastern gate. That gate will remain closed because the glory of the Lord has entered the temple through it (v. 2; 43:4; cf. Ps. 24:7–10). That the gate is closed may also imply that the Lord will never leave the temple again (43:7, 9).

Since the gate is closed, the gateway becomes a room; in this room the prince will be allowed to eat his portion of sacrificial meals. In Ezekiel's vision it represents the special relationship the promised king will maintain with the Lord. See note on 37:24.

While some portions of the OT emphasize restrictions on the participation of foreigners in Israel's worship (Ex. 12:43; Lev. 22:25; Neh. 9:2; Jer. 51:51), other passages anticipate the participation of foreigners (47:22, 23; cf. 1 Kin. 8:41, 43; 2 Chr. 6:32, 33; Is. 56:3, 6–8; cf. Zech. 14:21; Eph. 2:12, 19). Similar restrictions on foreigners characterize other writings from the period after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 4:1–3; 10:10–44; Neh. 13:1–9; Hag. 2:14). The issue in this passage is not merely that these people are foreigners but that they are uncircumcised — that is, they have not become part of God's people. Most likely, this refers to the practice of using foreign mercenaries to guard the temple (2 Kin. 11:14–19), a role that the Lord specifically assigns to the Levites (Num. 1:53). In the New Israel of the new covenant, the church, all such distinctions between Jew and Gentile have been removed, as Jews and Gentiles together become part of the one new people of God in Christ (Eph. 2:11–18; 3:6).

The tasks that have wrongly been delegated to uncircumcised foreigners will once again be performed by the Levites (Num. 1:50–53; 3:6, 8, 28–32; 1 Chr. 23:24–32; 2 Chr. 8:14, 15). Though the Levites were involved in the people's sin of idolatry and therefore could not enter the inner court as the priests would, they yet retained an important role. The priesthood itself was restricted to the line of Zadok, who has persevered in faithfulness to God (v. 15; 40:45, 46). The reward for that past faithfulness is closer access to God's presence, while those who were unfaithful are kept at a distance from the Lord.

Zadok served as high priest alongside Abiathar during the reign of David (2 Sam. 15:24–29; 20:25). Abiathar was dismissed because he supported Adonijah against Solomon (1 Kin. 1:7; 2:26), but Zadok supported Solomon and became the only high priest. The priesthood had earlier been restricted among the Levites to the descendants of Aaron (Ex. 28:1; Lev. 8:2–7; 9:1–24; Num. 20:25–28; 1 Chr. 6:48–53), and Ezekiel foresees a further restriction to one family from Aaron.

The corollary of increased access for the Zadokite priests is heightened responsibility in ritual holiness. Their behavior is far more strictly regulated than that of the people as a whole. They have to wear only linen rather than wool so that they will not be defiled by the emission of sweat. They cannot come into contact with the realm of the dead, whether by contact with a dead body or by observing ritual mourning practices (see Lev. 21:1–12). The priests are not to drink wine when on duty, since priestly mistakes can have fatal consequences (see Lev. 10:9). They can marry only a virgin or the widow of a priest so that there will be no question as to the priestly bloodline of any children of the marriage. Again, the prophet insists on a radical distinction between holy and the common, the unclean and the clean (v. 23).
For the judicial role of the priests, see 1 Chr. 26:29; 2 Chr. 19:8–11.

The rest of Israel will receive a share in the reallocated Promised Land (see 47:13–48:35), but the priests will receive no share of their own since the Lord is their inheritance. They are to be provided for through the regular offerings and sacrifices made at the temple.
The prohibition against eating meat of an animal found dead is part of the priests' radical separation from the realm of death.

The allocation of the land will be taken up in greater detail in ch. 47. The concern here is the sacred precincts, where the priests and Levites will live. Ezekiel describes a sacred area in the middle of the land, a square of 25,000 cubits (about 8 miles; 13 km) on a side, further subdivided into three strips of land (cf. Rev. 21:16). The northern zone (about 25 square miles; 65 square km) is set aside for the use of the Levites. The central zone contains the sanctuary and is set apart for the priests. The southern zone, about half the size of the other two, is given to the city itself. The area east and west of the eight-mile square is given to the prince, while the area north and south is to be divided among the other tribes. Interestingly, in Ezekiel's vision the temple itself is outside the city proper, maintaining a buffer zone against the sacred being defiled by the entry of the profane. The key element in the restoration of the land is to maintain the purity necessary for the Lord to dwell in the midst of His people. It is also the Lord who distributes the land, not the princes.

The prince's primary responsibility was to establish justice and righteousness among the people. The prince himself was assigned enough land to meet his own needs and to support the ministry of the temple without burdening the people. The measures he uses to collect the people's tithes and offerings for the temple are to be just, instead of adjusting the scales to secure profit for himself. Apparently the use of false weights and balances was common prior to the exile (Lev. 19:35, 36; Deut. 25:13–16; Prov. 11:1; Amos 8:5; Mic. 6:10–12).
Ten baths or ephahs make a homer, or about fifty gallons (190 L).
A shekel is about two-fifths of an ounce (11 g); a mina of sixty shekels is about a pound and a half (0.7 kg). The mina is normally fifty shekels.

Israel's princes are also responsible to make offerings on behalf of the people (vv. 13–17). The people will give offerings in kind to the prince, who in turn provides them to the sanctuary (cf. 2 Chr. 30:24). See notes on 37:24; 44:3.

These regulations cover aspects of the ceremonial observances of New Year's Day (vv. 18–20), Passover (vv. 21–24), and Tabernacles (v. 25) in the seventh month. This legislation represents dramatic modifications of earlier liturgical practice, replacing the three distinctive festivals of the Mosaic calendar with two festivals that are virtually identical. The central focus of both festivals is on purification from sin, a central theme in these chapters.
Compare the consecration of the altar in Ex. 29:35–37.
A liquid measure of about one gallon (3.6 L).

The prince will be allowed to enter as far as the inner threshold of the eastern gate into the inner courtyard on festival days; on other days he will enter and leave with the ordinary people (vv. 9, 10) unless he is making a freewill offering (v. 12). The prince has special privileges with reference to the eastern gate in the outer courtyard (44:1 note; 44:3 note), though nothing like the control over worship exercised by the kings before the Babylonian exile (e.g., 2 Kin. 16:10–12). From his vantage point at the threshold of the inner gate, the prince will have a full view of the inner courtyard and the great altar; but entry to the inner court is restricted to priests and Levites. In contrast, the ordinary people are to offer their worship outside the gateway to the inner court, separated from the inner court by eight steps and a corridor that is ninety feet long.
The specifications for this offering differ from the Sabbath offerings in Num. 28:9, where two lambs and no ram are required.
The first day of the month. The specifications again differ from earlier legislation (Num. 28:11).
The prince accompanies the people as they pass through the temple, acting as their representative in worship.

Whereas most of the preceding regulations concern offerings on particular days of the OT liturgical calendar, God is to be worshiped every day in Israel (vv. 13–15). The provisions for these daily offerings differ from earlier practice (Num. 28:3–8; 2 Kin. 16:15; 1 Chr. 16:40; 2 Chr. 13:11; 31:3). The meal imagery of these sacrifices depicts the regular table fellowship and communion between the Lord and His people.

In redeeming Israel from Egypt and later Babylon, God removed them from the place of bondage but also secured for them an inheritance in their own land. The land was supposed to be inalienable (Lev. 25:14–17, 23, 24; 1 Kin. 21), representing the permanence of the redemption and inheritance that God provided (1 Pet. 1:4). These verses address the previously common temptation for the prince to acquire additional lands with which to provide for his children or to reward his loyal servants, thereby oppressing the ordinary people.
Most likely a reference to the Year of Jubilee (Lev. 25:8–17; 27:24; Is. 61:1, 2).

OT worship combines sacrifice and prayer with eating and social activity. These regulations specify the places where the Levites prepare offerings for the sacrificial meals that are eaten by worshipers. The tour of the temple ends where it began, at the outside of the outer court.

The courtyard of the tabernacle had a large basin or laver where the priests washed (Ex. 30:17–21). Solomon's temple housed a much larger Sea (1 Kin. 7:23–26). This Sea was used for ritual washing (2 Chr. 4:6), but it also symbolized the primeval ocean, no longer a menacing symbol of chaos (28:2 note) but subjected by God to the service of His temple. In Ezekiel's temple vision, these earlier basins are replaced by a life-giving river (Rev. 21:1; 22:1, 2). The tabernacle laver and the temple Sea stand south of the altar in the sanctuary courtyard; the river likewise originates from south of the altar. This passage should be compared with others that speak of a river in the city of God (Ps. 46:4) or describe the eruption of a stream in the city (Joel 3:18; Zech. 14:3–8). Since the temple in part symbolizes paradise, Ezekiel's river recalls the rivers issuing from the garden of Eden (Gen. 2:10–14).

The river brings life everywhere it goes, transforming Israel into a paradisiacal garden. It brings life to even the lifeless salt waters of the Dead Sea, recalling the transformation of the dry bones in ch. 37. What is more, this unearthly river grows dramatically from small beginnings to become a mighty torrent that is impossible to cross. The exiles are to notice this and remember that the work of God often begins in small ways but culminates in grandeur (Zech. 4:10; Matt. 13:31, 32). Jesus appealed to the images used in this passage to describe Himself. He told the Samaritan woman that He is the source of life-giving water (John 4:10–14). When the disciples were surprised that Jesus was talking with a Samaritan woman, He spoke to them of an unending harvest that had already begun (John 4:27–38), drawing on Ezekiel's picture of trees bearing twelve crops a year. John also records Jesus' saying that He is the source of streams of living water, adding the comment that Jesus was speaking of God's Spirit (John 7:37–39).
From one side of the Dead Sea to the other. A mark of the new life in the sea is the abundance of fish where previously there were none.
The swamps and marshes will be left for salt. Salt is a useful commodity and under the old covenant is often used in covenant-making ceremonies because of its unchanging character.

In Ezekiel's vision, the land will be divided equally among the twelve tribes. Since the tribe of Levi receives its territorial inheritance inside the sacred precincts of Jerusalem (45:1–8 note), the number twelve is maintained by substituting for Joseph the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48:1–6). Israel and Judah are now reunited into a single nation (see 37:15–28).
This is the land God promised to the patriarchs (Gen. 12:7; 15:18–21; 22:17; 28:4), and that was possessed during the reigns of David and Solomon (1 Kin. 8:65; 1 Chr. 13:5; 2 Chr. 9:26).

The boundaries detailed here (vv. 15–20) mention a number of sites that are not known, but they roughly correspond to other such lists of sites (Num. 34:1–12; 1 Kin. 8:65). The eastern and western borders are easy to identify: on the east, the boundary begins in the headwaters of the Jordan south of Damascus, down the Jordan River, and along the western shore of the Dead Sea; on the west, the border is the Mediterranean Sea. The northern and southern borders are more difficult to establish: in the north, the line begins near Tyre and proceeds east to a point north of the Sea of Galilee; in the south, it runs from a point below the Dead Sea to the Brook of Egypt (the Wadi el-Arish) on the Mediterranean coast. Strikingly absent is the Transjordan, the area east of the Jordan River. Although this is historically the home of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, it is not part of the original land promised to Moses.

In Ezekiel's vision, the allotment of the land among the tribes is different from what it was before the exile. Each tribe is allotted a horizontal strip of land connecting with the eastern and western borders, aligned with the sacred east-west axis of the temple. The statuses of Jacob's wives and of the individual tribes seem to be the determining factors in the arrangement of the tribes (cf. Num. 2, 3). The northernmost tribes (Dan, Asher, and Naphtali) are traditionally located in the north; the southernmost tribe (Gad, v. 27) is historically a northern tribe. These four tribes are the sons of Leah's servant Zilpah and Rachel's servant Bilhah (Gen. 30:3–8, 10–13); as such they are located at the outer extremities of the tribal allotments in Ezekiel's vision. Judah is the closest tribe north of the sacred area in the center of the land (vv. 8–22; 45:1–8). Judah is historically a southern tribe; by presenting the tribe of David as part of the northern tribes, Ezekiel may be saying in effect that the North will have a portion in David (cf. 2 Sam. 20:1; 1 Kin. 12:16; 2 Chr. 10:16). Judah is in the place of honor that normally belongs to the firstborn, Reuben. Reuben is located immediately north of Judah. Next are the two tribes of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, descendants of Jacob through the favored wife Rachel. The nearest tribe south of the sacred area is Benjamin. Its favored place reflects the favored status of Rachel and balances the favored position of the Joseph tribes in the north. The remaining three southern tribes (Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun) are the descendants of Leah. Historically, Issachar and Zebulun hold allotments in the north.

This description is an elaboration of 45:1–8. The length of the description of this single portion compared to the brief description of the portions for the tribes highlights its central importance. The holy strip is not in the geographical center of the land, since there are seven tribes to the north and five to the south. Nonetheless, the spiritual center of the land has moved considerably north of the old location in Jerusalem.
See note on 44:15.

The city has twelve gates named for the twelve tribes (cf. Rev. 21:12–14). The focus on the exits of the city underlines the theme of access that runs through these chapters. Since one gate is named after Levi, Ephraim and Manasseh are replaced by their father Joseph. Unusually, the three most important gates face north, rather than east, so that they can open toward the temple. The city is a visible symbol of unity for the twelve tribes, and presumably contains residents from each tribe.

The city that used to be known as Jerusalem now receives a new name to match its transformed status. From the beginning of the OT, God revealed His intention to be with His people. He walked and spoke with them in the garden of Eden and dwelled in sanctuaries built in their midst. The promise of a child named Immanuel points to a day when God would be "with us" (Is. 7:14 text note). The NT ends in much the same way as the book of Ezekiel ends. John, too, describes the city of God, and a time when God will live with human beings face-to-face (Rev. 21:3); he ends with the prayer, "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus" (Rev. 22:20).

Daniel.note: 605 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar defeated a coalition of Assyria and Egypt at Carche­mish and initiated Babylon's rise to international power. After the battle of Carchemish, Nebuchadnezzar advanced against Jehoiakim (2 Kin. 24:1, 2; 2 Chr. 36:5–7) and took some Judeans captive, including Daniel. This was the first of three invasions of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar. The second was in 597 B.C. (2 Kin. 24:10–14), and the third in 586 B.C. (2 Kin. 25:1–24). In the book of Jeremiah, Nebuchadnezzar's attack is dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year instead of the third (Jer. 25:1; 46:2). The difference occurs because in the Babylonian chronology, which Daniel apparently used, the king's reign was officially counted from the first day of the succeeding new year, rather than from the actual date of his accession to the throne. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. Neb­uchadnezzar led the Babylonians to victory at Carchemish as crown prince and commander of the army. Shortly after this victory, he assumed the Babylonian throne when his father Nabopo­lassar died (626–605 B.C.). Nebuchadnezzar's reign (605–562 B.C.) is the historical context for much of Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.

Israel's defeat by the Babylonians is not to be explained simply by analysis of military and political factors. God is at work in the affairs of the nations, and the message to Daniel's original audience is that He has used the Babylonians to judge His own people for their transgressions (2 Kin. 17:15, 18–20; 21:12–15; 24:3, 4). Under the terms of the covenant made at Mount Sinai, the Lord threatened to exile His people if they were unfaithful (Lev. 26:33, 39). The length of their tenure in the land in spite of their unfaithfulness is a sign of the Lord's mercy. Their unfaithfulness culminated in the destruction of Jerusalem and exile of the majority of the remaining population by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 B.C. the vessels of the house of God. These same temple vessels are brought out by Belshazzar for his feast in Dan. 5 and will be returned to Judah with the exiles in the time of Cyrus (Ezra 1:7). the treasury of his god. Marduk (or Bel) is the chief god of the Babylonian pantheon (cf. Jer. 50:2).

Like the temple vessels and sacrifices, they have to be perfect to appear in the presence of the king. The exiling of these royal and noble offspring fulfills Isaiah's prophecy to King Hezekiah in 2 Kin. 20:17, 18. literature and language of the Chaldeans. Babylonian literature was written in Akkadian, using wedge-shaped characters impressed with a stylus on soft clay tablets that were later fired to make them permanent. Thousands of these tablets have been discovered by archaeologists. The Babylonians worshiped many gods, and their culture was filled with magic, sorcery, and astrology. The common commercial language of Babylon was Aramaic, which was used especially in the court of the king during the time of Daniel (see 2:4 and note).
KingJehoiachin later receives such a provision under the rule of the Babylonian king Evil-merodach (2 Kin. 25:27–30). These provisions are designed to create a culture of dependence on the king.

These Hebrew names contain the word "God" (el) or a shortened form of God's covenant name, "Yahweh" (Ps. 50:1 note). Daniel means "my judge is God"; Hananiah, "Yahweh is gracious"; Mishael, "Who is what God is?"; and Azariah, "Yahweh has helped."

Suggestions for the meanings of these names include: Belteshazzar, "May Bel protect his life" (Bel is another name for Marduk, the chief Babylonian god; cf. 4:8); Shadrach, "the command of Aku," (the Sumerian moon god); Meshach, "Who is what Aku is?"; and Abednego, "servant of Nebo" (a Babylonian god). These name changes are a further step in Babylon's attempt to reshape their religious and cultural identity.

The reason for Daniel's conclusion that he and his friends will be defiled by the king's food is not given. Perhaps it involves violation of the dietary laws of Moses (Lev. 11; 17). Yet it does not appear that they permanently abstain from Babylonian food, as would be required if the issue were obedience to the kosher laws. More likely, this is a concrete way of affirming their dependence upon the Lord by vowing to eat only foods that grow naturally and to drink only water rather than to consume the rich food and wine provided by the king.
This is a specific answer to Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple in 1 Kin. 8:50.

That is, they are fatter — an unexpected result of a low-calorie lifestyle. The obedience of Daniel and his friends to God and their refusal to compromise their faith in a heathen environment are rewarded with God's blessing (cf. Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4).

God's blessing is not limited to physical well-being, but also includes outstanding intellectual development during their three years of Babylonian education. He thus enables them to be a blessing to their pagan neighbors and to build up the city where they have found themselves (cf. Jer. 29:5–7) while remaining true to their beliefs. visions and dreams. With a view to what follows in the book (chs. 2; 4; 5), Daniel is distinguished from his companions in his ability to interpret dreams and visions, much as Joseph was in the court of Pharaoh (Gen. 40:8; 41:16).
That is, after the three years mentioned in v. 5.

The term translated "magicians" is also used in Gen. 41:8, 24, and Ex. 7:11. The word translated "enchanters" occurs only here and in 2:2 and can be rendered "conjurer" or "soothsayer." Whatever means these royal advisers use to gain knowledge, Daniel and his friends are able to demonstrate superior insight on the matters they were questioned about.

Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 B.C., sixty-six years after Daniel had been taken captive to Babylon. Daniel lived through the entire period of the Babylonian captivity. Cyrus issued a decree in the first year of his reign permitting the Jews to return to their land, and to take with them the vessels from the temple that had been seized by Nebuchadnezzar (Ezra 1:7–11). The statement does not mean that Daniel died in the first year of Cyrus (10:1), but rather that the Lord was faithful to protect Daniel all the way through the exile. Kingdoms might rise and fall, but the Lord preserves His own.

Since the Babylonian system counts Nebuchadnezzar's reign officially from the first day of the year after his actual accession, his "second year" could mean the end of Daniel's three years of training (1:5). Otherwise the events took place during his training. his sleep left him. It was widely believed in the ancient Near East that the gods spoke to human beings in dreams. The dreams of a king had particular significance for the fate of the whole people.

See note on 1:20. sorcerers \... Chaldeans. "Sorcerers" practice divination or witchcraft (Ex. 22:18; Deut. 18:10; Is. 47:9, 12; Jer. 27:9). Here, "Chaldeans" probably means a class of soothsayers and astrologers, rather than the name of an ethnic group (as in 1:4; 3:8; 5:30; 9:1). These are part of Nebuchadnezzar's specialist staff of dream interpreters.

From here until the end of ch. 7, the text is written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew. Ezra 4:8–6:18; 7:12–26 are also written in Aramaic. There has been much speculation about why these verses are in Aramaic, but no generally accepted conclusion has been reached.

Normally, the king would tell his advisors the dream so that they could suggest an interpretation. Here, Nebuchadnezzar formulates a test to see whether the advisors to the court have the access to hidden knowledge that they claim. If they cannot tell him the dream, then he will have no confidence in their interpretation (cf. v. 9) and will execute them.

The wise men confess that they cannot do what the king asks. Only the gods have such power, but the gods, they protest, do not reveal such things to anyone (cf. Ex. 8:18, 19). They are diviners, not prophets: they discern patterns in events but do not claim access to the minds of the gods. Indeed, in their theology, such knowledge is impossible since the gods do not make their dwelling among men. Israel's God is unique in this respect (see Is. 57:13).

Nebuchadnezzar's furious response expands the group subject to punishment to include the whole class of wise men, including Daniel and his friends. With remarkable confidence, Daniel asks for an appointment to see the king, even though he has yet to receive revelation from God.

Daniel also realizes that human wisdom is insufficient to meet the king's demand (v. 11 note). Only divine revelation can provide the answer. Fortunately, unlike the gods of the Babylonians, Daniel's God is able and willing to reveal what will happen in the future (Is. 44:8; 45:21; Amos 3:7).
See theological note "The Will of God."
Daniel alludes to the content of the dream.
Job 28 is a carefully drawn picture of wisdom as "hidden from the eyes of all" (Job 28:21) and inaccessible without God.
Daniel urges the king to be merciful to the wise men even though their inability to know the dream has been exposed.
Arioch is eager to claim credit for finding someone who can interpret the king's dream.

Just as Joseph did in Egypt (Gen. 40:8; 41:16), Daniel attributes his knowledge of the dream to God. Daniel's God has revealed to this young man what astrology, magic, and the occult cannot discover. in the latter days. This expression seems to range in meaning from the "end time" or eschaton(Gk.; cf. Ezek. 38:16) to simply the future in general (Gen. 49:1; Deut. 4:30; 31:29). Here it covers the entire sweep of world history from Nebuchadnezzar onward.
There is a progressive decrease in the value of the materials in the image from the head to the feet.
Some interpreters view the mixture of iron and clay in the feet of the image as representing a second phase of the fourth kingdom different from the legs of solid iron (cf. vv. 41–43).

The four kingdoms have been widely understood since the Jewish historian Josephus (writing in the first century A.D.) to be the empires of Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome. Others understand them to be Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece, a sequence in agreement with the liberal critical view that the book was written during the period of Greek ascendancy in the Middle East. Darius's appeal to the single "law of the Medes and Persians" (6:12; cf. 5:28) agrees with the first order of empires. The only certain identification between the portions of the image and specific world empires is Nebuchadnezzar (Babylon) as the head of gold. It is plausible that four represents completeness here: rather than seeking to describe particular kingdoms, the sequence describes the consistent downward trend in world history, not toward greater glory and unity but toward greater dishonor and chaos until the kingdom of God arrives on earth and fills it with its glory. The rock that crushes all of the kingdoms of this world is Christ (Luke 20:18). He is the mystery of the ages, the One in whom God will unite all things in His glorious kingdom (Eph. 1:9, 10).

The elements of the fourth kingdom cannot preserve their union. One possible interpretation of the image is that the iron represents the culture and laws of imperial Rome, while the clay represents the divergent political and social traditions of its many parts. The fourth kingdom, though strong, is as temporary as those that precede it and lacks the glory of the earlier kingdoms.

The most natural interpretation is that the kings are the rulers of the four powers making up the image just described. The other possibility is that they are a sequence of several rulers of the fourth kingdom only. a kingdom that shall never be destroyed. The eternal kingdom is the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ (Is. 9:7; Luke 1:33; Heb. 1:8; Rev. 11:15). This kingdom was inaugurated and preached at the first coming of Christ (Matt. 12:28; 24:14; Mark 1:15) but does not come in its fullness until His second coming. See theological note "The Kingdom of God" on p. 1823.

In a reversal of roles, Daniel is exalted to a position of honor by the Lord's intervention on his behalf, from which he and his friends will be able to promote the peace and welfare of the city of Babylon where God has placed them (Jer. 29:5–7). For the king's reaction, cf. Acts 14:11; Rev. 22:8.

Nebuchadnezzar's statement does not necessarily mean that he recognizes Israel's covenant Lord, Yahweh, as the only God. His exclamation is that Yahweh is superior to other gods. Lord of kings. Nebuchadnezzar confesses that the God of Israel is supreme over human rulers and kingdoms. This is the unifying theme of Dan. 1–6 (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

The Babylonian Empire is divided into provinces. Daniel is appointed ruler (cf. 3:2) of the province where the capital city is located. Joseph and Mordecai also rose as Jews to political power in a foreign land. See Gen. 41:37–44 (Joseph) and Esth. 8:1, 2 (Mordecai).

Although the narrow proportions might suggest an obelisk rather than a statue, the monument is called an "image." It is probably a figure standing on a pedestal. The gold is probably plating, the fabrication of the image being much like that described in Is. 40:19; 41:7; Jer. 10:3–9. It reflects the enormous statue that Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream in ch. 2, except that it is entirely made of gold, as if Nebuchadnezzar is asserting that there will be no other kingdoms after his. It is not clear whether the image represents Nebuchadnezzar himself or one of his gods. He set it up. Eight times in this chapter we are told that this is the image that Nebuchadnezzar set up, making it clear that it is merely an idol made by man, not a god with transcendent powers. the plain of Dura. Probably about six miles (10 km) south of Babylon. Since it is set up on a plain in Babylon (lit. Of the six terms for musical instruments, the three translated "lyre," "harp," and "bagpipe" are borrowed from Greek. The third empire is symbolized by the "leopard," known for its quickness. Alexander the Great (356–323 B.C.) conquered the Persian Empire with great speed. Alexander died suddenly at age thirty-three, and the empire he established was divided into four parts (Macedonia under Cassander, Thrace and Asia Minor under Lysimachus, Syria under Seleucus, and Egypt under Ptolemy). However, many other empires have also been militarily swift and fierce, so the identification of the leopard with Alexander, though likely, remains uncertain.

This last "beast" cannot be identified with any earthly animal. It is exceedingly powerful and terrifying, with great iron teeth that crush its enemies. The ten horns are prior in time to the "little horn" that uproots three of them, symbolizing another phase of the fourth kingdom. Many interpreters suggest that the little horn in some way represents the Antichrist (2 Thess. 2:3, 4, 8). If so, this is the first reference in Scripture to the Antichrist. Linguistically, the Aramaic phrase here translated as "son of man" means either "a human being" as opposed to the preceding "beasts" or a divine being. In light of the application of the phrase to Jesus, both are likely in view. Daniel's "son of man" is a divine-human ruler, specifically the God-man, Jesus Christ.

The "son of man" is Christ, the Messiah, and the word for "serve" implies acts of worship. Daniel recounts the revelation he received concerning the prophecy of Jeremiah about the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolation (Jer. 25:11, 12; 29:10). Significantly, the revelation follows Daniel's prayer confessing the sinfulness of God's people and the justice of Jerusalem's desolation, and his seeking the favor of God for the restoration of the city and the temple. 9:1 the first year of Darius the son of Ahas­uerus. Interpreters differ on the dates of the beginning and ending of the seventy-year period, and on whether it is to be understood as a round number for a human lifetime or exactly seventy years. Some date the period from 586 B.C. (the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar) to 516 B.C., when the restoration of the temple was completed under Zerubbabel (Ezra 6:13–18). Others date the beginning of the period to the year of Daniel's own captivity (605 B.C.; 1:1 note), which suggests that Daniel recognizes the end of the seventy years is imminent. Either way, it is clear that Daniel's prayer is motivated by reading Jeremiah's prophecy, especially in view of the fall of Babylon, which Jeremiah anticipated. Daniel sees that two things are to happen according to Jeremiah (25:11, 12; 29:10–14): the fall of Babylon and the restoration of the people to the Promised Land. The first has happened at the time of Daniel's prayer, but the second has not. Therefore, Daniel beseeches the Lord to accomplish the second. God responds to the prayer with an answer to this and even more.
These are signs of repentance and mourning over sin.

Daniel's prayer is rooted in a covenantal understanding of the Lord's relation to His people (blessing for obedience, cursing for disobedience, especially vv. 5, 7, 11, 12, 14; cf. Lev. 26:14–45; Deut. 28:15–68; 30:1–5). For a similar prayer, see Neh. 9. The prayer has four parts: (1) worship (v. 4); (2) a confession of sin (vv. 5–11); (3) recognition of God's justice in His judgment on sin (vv. 11–14); and (4) a plea for God's mercy based on concern for His name, kingdom, and will (vv. 15–19). The prayer is grounded on God's promises (v. 2) and offered in a spirit of contrition and humility (v. 3). It is a model for the appropriate elements of effective prayer.
See note on 8:16. Gabriel's arrival is proof that Daniel's prayer has been heard and his request for the Lord's favor has been approved.

The interpretation of these verses is disputed at many points. There are two fundamental approaches to the interpretation of the "weeks" (lit. "sevens"): as symbolic periods of time or as literal periods of time. In the symbolic view, the seventy years of punishment (v. 2) are multiplied seven times in accordance with the covenantal curses (Lev. 26:18, 21, 24, 28). Jubilees, a Jewish book from the intertestamental period, also structures the whole of history into periods of 490 years. Adherents of the literal view fall into three categories. As with other prophecies in Daniel, some commentators interpret the verses with reference to the time of Antiochus IV. Other interpreters may be divided into two categories: (1) those who interpret the passage as having its primary focus on events associated with the first coming of Christ and shortly thereafter (first-coming view); (2) those who interpret the passage as having reference to events associated with both the first and second comings of Christ, necessitating an unstated time interval between the two (second-coming view). Within each of these broad categories, individual interpreters differ on specific details. 9:24 Seventy weeks. Most interpreters view the units of "seventy weeks" (lit., "seventy sevens") as representing 490 years (9:24–27 note). These so-called seventy weeks of years are then divided into three subunits of 49 years ("seven weeks," v. 25); 434 years ("sixty-two weeks," v. 26); and 7 years ("one week," v. 27). Interpreters differ over whether these subunits are to be viewed as a continuous sequence or as having time intervals between them. More important, the main point of Gabriel's answer is that Daniel's request for God to deal with the sin and wickedness of the Lord's people will be answered in the affirmative, though not immediately. The seventy years of which Jeremiah spoke and which are now nearing an end will be extended into a longer period of "seventy times seven" years (cf. Matt. 18:22). Notice that six purposes are to be achieved within the "seventy weeks." These are divided into three pairs: (1) the first and second purposes deal with the sin of the old covenant community; (2) the third and fourth purposes deal with the inauguration of the messianic period; and (3) the fifth and sixth purposes express that everything will be fulfilled.

The Hb. term translated "word" may mean either "word" or "command." This ambiguity has given rise to multiple interpretations for the beginning of the "seventy weeks": (1) Some interpreters understand it to be the decree issued by Artaxerxes I in the seventh year of his reign (457 B.C.; Ezra 7:12–26). Forty-nine years later (408 B.C.), the streets and wall around Jerusalem were completed (v. 25). (2) Other commentators understand the "seventy weeks" as beginning in 587 B.C., the time of Jeremiah's prediction (his "word") that Jerusalem would be rebuilt (Jer. 31:38; 32:15, 37, 44). Forty-nine years later would be 538 B.C., the year that Cyrus permitted the Jews to fulfill Jeremiah's prophecy by returning to Palestine (Ezra 1:1–4). (3) Since ancient times, many interpreters have also understood the "seventy weeks" symbolically. Proponents of this view note a sabbatical pattern in the six purposes of the seventy weeks (9:24 note), culminating in the work of the Messiah described in the final week. to the coming of an anointed one, a prince. Advocates of interpretation (1) in the previous note understand "anointed one" to be a reference to Jesus. Linking the "seven weeks" (forty-nine years) and the "sixty-two weeks" (434 years) as a continuous sequence yields 483 years, from 457 B.C. to A.D. 27, or approximately the beginning of Christ's three-year public ministry. Others take the 483 years to begin with the "command" of Artaxerxes I in the twentieth year of his reign (444 B.C.; Neh. 2:1), instead of the seventh year of his reign (Ezra 7:12–26) in 457 B.C. Using a 360-day lunar year (as in the Jewish calendar), this approach reaches a date for the crucifixion in A.D. 33. This date for the crucifixion is possible but not certain. Advocates of interpretation (3) in the previous note also believe Jesus to be the "anointed one," though the specific chronology in this verse is understood symbolically. Advocates of interpretation (2) in the previous note understand "anointed one" to refer to Cyrus (also called the Lord's "anointed"; Is. 45:1). This view separates the "seven weeks" and the "sixty-two weeks." The "seven weeks" elapse between the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. and the decree of Cyrus in 538 B.C. The "sixty-two weeks" (434 years) is the time when the city is to be rebuilt, somewhere between 538 B.C. and A.D. 70 (Jerusalem's destruction at the hands of the Roman general Titus). This view requires a time interval between the two periods of "weeks."

Certain details in 11:36–12:3 cannot be harmonized with the events surrounding the death of Antiochus IV. For this reason, some interpreters understand these verses to describe the Antichrist, who like Antiochus IV will persecute God's people just before the second coming of Christ (cf. 12:1–3). These verses describe the character of the Antichrist, his activities, and the destiny of God's people. This understanding requires a time interval between the events depicted in 11:21–35 and those in 11:36–12:3. Consequently, other interpreters have understood vv. 36–39 as a summary of Antiochus's religious policies; vv. 40–45 as a description of how his ambition led to his defeat; and 12:1–3 as an anticipation of his defeat. The anticipated invasion of the Holy Land may be presented as a parallel to Nebuchadnezzar's earlier invasion, using the names of the nations of that time, sparing Israel's old enemies (v. 41), and climaxing in the anticipated defeat of Egypt itself (vv. 42, 43; cf. Ezek. 29). At his proudest moment, Antiochus was destroyed at Mount Zion in the heart of the Holy Land (vv. 44, 45). Antiochus's defeat in 12:1–3 is described in terms of the absolute end of history. Because of the difficulties in interpreting 11:40–12:3, it is hard to discern how literal or metaphorical they are, and their interpretation must be speculative. The increasingly severe prophecies of judgment symbolized in the names of the three children are now dramatically reversed. 1:10 sand of the sea. A clear reference to the ancient patriarchal promise of innumerable descendants (Gen. 22:17; 32:12; cf. Gen. 13:16; 15:5; 26:24; 28:14). You are not my people. The promise of restoration to these people is fulfilled at least in part when remnants of the north are later joined with the south during the reign of Hezekiah (2 Chr. 30:11, 18) and after the exile (1 Chr. 9:3; Ezra 8:35). The NT applies this promise to the church, the true Israel, composed of both Jews and Gentiles (Rom. 9:24–26; 1 Pet. 2:9, 10). For the apostles, the remnant of ethnic Israel was evidently a model for the remnant of the nations: what applied to the former applied to the latter. Children of the living God. This unique expression suggests the kind of intimate relationship God desires with Israel, one in which God gives life (as opposed to the lifeless relationship Israel has with Baal). In Is. 40:18–20; 44:9–20; 46:5–11, dead idols are contrasted with the living God. The living relationship is now provided in Jesus Christ (Matt. 16:16; Rom. 9:26).

This reveals the completeness of reconciliation between both kingdoms and the Lord. Ultimately, this reunion takes place under Christ, the son of David (Matt. 1:23; 2:6, 15). they shall go up from the land. Israel's restoration begins in the return from exile. The phrase may also refer to resurrection from death (Ps. 71:20; Is. 43:6). the day of Jezreel. See note on 1:4.
Hostile siblings Israel and Judah will be fully reconciled, and the horrible indictments contained in the names "Lo-ammi" (1:9 note) and "Lo-ruhama" (1:6 note) will be reversed.
God brings a case against Israel in which the children are to accuse their mother. she put away. Repentance and reconciliation are the final goals of God's judgment (vv. 9–23).

If repentance does not take place, the unfaithful wife (Gomer/Israel) will be publicly exposed (v. 10) and left destitute, traditional punishments for an adulteress (Ezek. 16:37–39; Nah. 3:5–7), though less severe than the death penalty (Deut. 22:22).
See 1:2. God's love and mercy (1:6) will also be withdrawn from the children who, like their mother, are charged with promiscuity.
The unfaithful mother (Israel) has looked to Canaanite fertility religion and not to the Lord (v. 8) to provide the staples of life.
The woman's initiative, representing all Israel, is stressed. my first husband. The early period of intimacy in reference to the Lord is remembered fondly (cf. 11:1–4).

Israel has credited the Lord's agricultural and commercial gifts (Deut. 7:13; 11:14; 28:1–12) to Baal. In texts discovered at the ancient north Syrian city of Ugarit, Baal is seen as the god of the storm and worshiped as the provider of rain and fertility.

Though not punished with death (v. 3 note; cf. Ezek. 16:37–40), the unfaithful and forgetful lover is severely chastised through a series of dramatic reversals in which God's gifts are withdrawn: failed harvests, exposure, and the end of festivals. 2:9 take back. The Hebrew indicates a forceful, snatching action.

The Hb. word translated as "Sabbath" (shabbat) is derived from the verb meaning "stop" or "cease," making a sarcastic pun with "put an end to" regarding the Sabbaths. appointed feasts. The festivals have become occasions for religious syncretism in which the worship of the Lord and Baal are intermingled. See Introduction: Occasion.
The prostitute's wages, which are in fact gifts from the Lord (v. 8), are to be destroyed.

On pagan goddesses in the region, jewelry emphasizes the erotic areas of the anatomy. A tie between idolatry and jewelry is made in Gen. 35:4. her lovers. In vv. 7, 10, 12 these are probably synonymous with the Baals. The essence of the charge against Israel is that she has forgotten the Lord, whom she should love (cf. 4:6; 13:4–6). See theological note "Syncretism."

There Israel is to love God alone (v. 16; cf. Jer. 2:2). speak tenderly to her. Lit. "speak to the heart," an idiom used elsewhere for wooing, speaking kindly, and coaxing (Gen. 34:3; Judg. 19:3; Ruth 2:13).

Lit. "Valley of Trouble," this area is near Jericho and is the site of the stoning of Achan (Josh. 7:24–26). Though associated with sin and death, this valley is to be transformed into a "door of hope."

The Hb. word baal can mean "master" or "husband" and can also refer to the pagan god Baal. Israel's use of the noun baal in reference to the Lord blurs the distinction between the two. In the future, Israel will be so zealous to stamp out anything associated with Baal worship that the word baal itself, in all its senses, will be avoided (v. 17).

Taking up the same theme in a later era, Jeremiah explains the covenant as entailing a new heart (Jer. 31:31–34). with the beasts. In Hosea's day, wild animals are a threat, particularly after invading armies ravage the land, but the future kingdom will be secure and peaceful, free from the threat of wild animals (Is. 11:6–9) and invasions (Ps. 46:9; Is. 2:4; Mic. 4:3). The language may be figurative for a transformed humanity, with the resulting peace and security attending the renewal to be consummated at Christ's return.

Betrothal is the final step in the courtship process and involves paying a bride-price to the bride's father. Here the qualities of righteousness, justice, love, mercy, and faithfulness are a sort of bride price that guarantees the permanence of the relationship. righteousness. God's righteousness is expressed both in His fairness and in the salvation He bestows on His people (10:12; Amos 5:7). justice. This term can denote the legal decisions and relationships by which justice and fairness are established and restored (5:11; 6:5; 10:4; Amos 5:15, 24; Mic. 6:8). steadfast love. See note on Ex. 15:13; 34:6. mercy. The term can refer to compassion, heartfelt sensitivity, and love (1:6; Gen. 43:14; Deut. 13:17; 2 Sam. 24:14).

This quality includes dependability, truthfulness, and steadfastness in one's relationships (Ps. 88:11; 89:1, 2, 5, 8, 24; 92:2; 98:3). Christ, by His active obedience, provides these covenant virtues for His people. By the Holy Spirit He inscribes His own nature on their hearts (2 Cor. 3:3). know. The essence of the new covenant relationship involves knowing the Lord intimately (Jer. 31:34). Today Christ mediates this new covenant and renders the old covenant relationship obsolete (Heb. 8:7–13).

The Lord will graciously answer Israel's cry as she learns again to answer His appeals (v. 15). the heavens. The Lord will show that He, not the storm-god Baal, commands the cycles of nature whereby the land becomes fertile and produces the crops that were earlier withheld (v. 9). See Introduction: Occasion.
See note on 1:4, in which Jezreel is a sign of curse, in contrast to its function as a sign of blessing here.

The promises of restoration come to a climax as Jezreel is redeemed (v. 22; cf. 1:4, 5), Lo-ruhama (1:6 note), is shown God's love and Lo-ammi (1:9 note) becomes God's people. I will sow. This is a wordplay on the name "Jezreel." You are my God. See Rom. 9:23–26 and 1 Pet. 2:9, 10 regarding the fulfillment of these promises.

Hosea recounts his reconciliation with his wife Gomer as an anticipation of God's reconciliation with Israel. 3:1 love \... even as the Lord loves. God's apparently unreasonable request to Hosea is patterned after His own loyal, protective, and bountiful love for undeserving Israel. cakes of raisins. These delicacies, made from raisins pressed together, are associated with special occasions (2 Sam. 6:19), and may serve in Baal worship as an aphrodisiac (cf. Song 2:5).

An act of redemption on Hosea's part. Christ similarly fulfilled this picture of love in action when He redeemed His saints from the slave market of sin. shekels. The payment, roughly half in silver and half in produce, amounts to about thirty shekels and approximates the price of a slave in Ex. 21:32. The NT teaches that Christ's blood is the cost of redemption from the penalty of death (1 Pet. 1:18).

The waiting period until the coming of Christ, the great and final King of the Davidic dynasty (v. 5). without king \... household gods. Israel's basic political and religious institutions, both legitimate (sacrifice and ephod; Ex. 28:31) and illegitimate (sacred stones or pillars and idols or teraphim; Deut. 16:21, 22; Zech. 10:2), are going to be removed as punishment.

Many Israelites later repent with a full desire for intimacy with God, such as the Jews who repent at Pentecost (Acts 2:38–41). David. This reference points to Jesus Christ, Son of David (1:11 note; cf. 2 Sam. 7:12–16; Matt. 1:1; Rom. 1:3). the latter days. A reference to the period extending from the first coming of Christ until His second coming and beyond. See note on Mic. 4:1.

In this striking example of a prophetic lawsuit against Israel for violating the terms of the covenant, Hosea gives an overview of the Lord's case against Israel and then focuses on the consequences of the nation's rejection of the knowledge of God. 4:1 faithfulness \... knowledge. See notes on 2:19, 20.
These sins constitute violations of the foundational covenant document — the Decalogue (Ex. 20:2–17; Deut. 5:6–21). Five of the commands of the Decalogue are listed here.
Human sin results in crises within the natural order that endanger all of life (Lev. 18:28; Is. 24:4, 5).

Attention shifts to the sins of the priests, whose failure to instruct the nation in God's law has corrupted Israel (v. 6; cf. Deut. 31:9–13; 33:10). 4:4 let no one contend. Or, "let no man bring a charge." According to the Mosaic law, the priests are entrusted with the task of rendering legal judgments (Deut. 17:9–13). But because of the general lack of knowledge and respect for God's law in Israel during Hosea's time, there is no point in bringing charges against another because the verdicts will not be honored (the people are "like those who contend with the priest" \[text note\]; i.e., they do not respect his decisions and teaching).
The nation of Israel (2:2, 5; Is. 50:1).

The nation will lose her covenant relationship with God through lack of covenant knowledge (vv. 8, 12). knowledge. Knowledge of God is inseparable from the law of God (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). The priests, who are responsible for teaching the law, and their descendants are to be punished for ignoring or forgetting the law (vv. 4–10 note).

Or, "they will change their glory." Ultimately, the Lord is Israel's glory (Is. 60:19; Jer. 2:11). In Rom. 1:23, Paul condemns the sin of exchanging God's glory for something corruptible. shame. Idols or false gods (Deut. 32:16, 17).

In a literal sense, the priests, who eat portions of the animals sacrificed for sin (Lev. 6:26), encourage the people to sin so that they will have more to eat. In a figurative sense, the priests are gratified by the people's sin.
No one is spared from judgment (cf. Is. 24:1–3). People naturally follow their religious leaders for good or ill.
Food will not satisfy (v. 8), and illicit sex will not produce increase. They have left the Lord, the source of life, to practice harlotry (vv. 12, 18; 2:4; 6:10; 9:1), just as Gomer has done.
Lit. "take away the \[people's\] heart," i.e., their ability to judge and think clearly (cf. Prov. 31:4, 5).

Lit. "their wood." This may refer to the Asherah pole beside a Canaanite shrine (Deut. 16:21; Judg. 6:25–32), to some other deity (Hab. 2:18, 19), or to a sacred tree thought to give oracles (Judg. 9:37). staff. Probably a divining rod, or perhaps a small figurine of Asherah. spirit of whoredom. Their spiritual adultery is caused by an intoxicating and seductive power that draws them continuously into sin (cf. "spirit of confusion" in Is. 19:14; "spirit of deep sleep" in Is. 29:10).

It is not that God refuses to punish the harlots and adulteresses at all (since the people as a whole will be judged), but that He will not allow them to be punished while the men who patronize them go free (cf. Gen. 38:24–26).

The theme of prophetic lawsuit against Israel continues as further charges of covenant disobedience are leveled (4:1–19 note). 4:15 Gilgal. This important Israelite sanctuary near Jericho is situated across the Jordan from Baal-peor. Gilgal was the first place Israel camped during the settlement under Joshua. From the time of the conquest, Gilgal has been an important place of worship (Josh. 4:19–5:12; 1 Sam. 10:8; 11:12–15). Later in Israel's history, Gilgal becomes associated with wicked and syncretistic religious practices (9:15; 12:11; Amos 4:4). Beth-aven. Lit. "house of wickedness" or "house of deception." This is a contemptuous nickname for Bethel ("House of God") — a royal, but apostate, sanctuary for the northern kingdom (1 Kin. 12:28–33; Amos 4:4; 5:5; 7:13). One of Jeroboam's calves was located here (1 Kin. 12:29). As the LORD lives. This orthodox oath (Judg. 8:19; Ruth 3:13; 1 Sam. 14:39) is forbidden here because they are lying (v. 2), or because it is being misused by linking the Lord to Baal worship. The Lord's name is not to be associated with the practices of those sites.
The Israelites are kicking against all of the Lord's efforts to care for them (cf. Jer. 31:18).

Because Ephraim is by far the largest and most centrally located of the ten northern tribes, the northern kingdom of Israel is sometimes called Ephraim (Deut. 33:17 note). From the time of Joseph to the time of Samuel, Ephraim was expected to be the tribe that provided leadership for Israel. leave him alone. The plural verb here may indicate an address to other prophets or to other Israelites.

A wordplay on the Hb. word meaning "wind" or "spirit" is probably intended. Not only is a destructive storm wind of divine judgment about to sweep away the people (Job 1:19), but also "the spirit of whoredom" (v. 12; 5:4) is leading them to ruin. The Israelites are caught up in a gale of idolatry.

The fate of the northern kingdom is bound up with that of its leaders. The priests are responsible to teach the law (4:6), and the royal house is responsible for administering justice. snare. The leaders have trapped their foolish subjects. Mizpah. Probably the Mizpah in Gilead where Jeph­thah was made ruler and a syncretism between the gods of Ammon and the Lord prevailed (Judg. 10:17; 11:8–33). Tabor. A famous mountain site located on the northeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley (Judg. 4:6). These and other northern sites have become high places of the pagan cult of Baal in Hosea's day.
See note on 4:17.
See note on 4:12. They "know not the Lord" truly (4:1, 6), nor can they return or repent (cf. Jer. 13:23).
The sins of the people testify against them in the Lord's covenant lawsuit against His people (4:1–19 note).
They will not find the Lord through the offering of their ritual sacrifices (4:13; 1 Sam. 15:21–23; Is. 1:11–17; Mic. 6:6–8).

Like an unfaithful wife and mother, Israel is giving birth to children who are literally and religiously illegitimate (4:6, 13, 14). new moon. The festivals bring judgment instead of the Lord's blessing on their wombs and crops as they have imagined would happen (cf. Is. 1:13, 14).

These commands sound the watchman's cry to warn of an approaching enemy (Judah) from the south (cf. 8:1). The Syro-Ephraimite war described in 2 Kin. 16:5–9 and 2 Chr. 28:5–21 seems to be the context behind this warning. See Introduction: Occasion. Gibeah \... Ramah \... Beth-aven. These Benjaminite towns lie in a straight line running north from Jerusalem: Gibeah, three miles (5 km); Ramah, five miles (8 km); Beth-aven (Bethel), eleven miles (17 km). At various times in their history, they are claimed by one kingdom or the other (1 Kin. 15:16–22).
The boundaries separating family property are marked by stones (Deut. 19:14; 27:17; Job 24:2; Prov. 22:28; 23:10). See note on Num. 27:1–11.

Like a moth, or possibly like an infection (some suggest that the Hb. word translated "moth" means "pus"), God will bring inexorable and unpleasant decay upon sinful Ephraim and Judah. A moth eats garments, and dry rot destroys the timbers of a building.

Instead of turning to the Lord for healing from their miseries inflicted by an enemy (cf. Is. 1:5–9; Jer. 30:12, 13), Israel has turned to Assyria. Assyrian records speak of the tribute paid by two of Israel's kings, Menahem and Hoshea (cf. 2 Kin. 15:17–20; 17:3).
Even with Assyrian help, Israel and Judah are helpless prey before the powerful lion, the Lord (13:7; Amos 1:2; 3:8).
In His anger, God removes His saving presence from the people until they truly repent (3:5).

The response of this song of repentance echoes the imagery of 5:11–14. The prophet includes himself in this call to repentance, so there is yet opportunity for restoration. 6:1 let us. The priests may be quoted here, much as Israel was quoted in 2:7. return. The call to return to the Lord is one of the central messages of the book (2:7; 3:5; 5:4, 15). True repentance and conversion bring reconciliation that includes healing of wounds (cf. Deut. 32:39).
This may simply denote a short period of time. Some, who view this as a prediction of Christ's resurrection, understand Paul to allude to this verse in 1 Cor. 15:4. live before him. See Ps. 16:11.

Like the call to return (v. 1), the call to true knowledge of the Lord is central to Hosea's message (2:8, 20; 4:1, 6; 5:4; 6:6). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes. as the dawn \... as the showers. These similes compare God's reliability to the recurrent events of nature that revive.
Continuing the use of images from nature, God laments the temporary, transitory quality of Israel and Judah's covenant love in contrast to His own faithfulness (v. 3).

Like the light of the sun whose rising dispels the darkness and dries up the dew, God's justice consistently and inevitably goes forth (cf. Ps. 37:6), exposing the sins of those who have broken the covenant.
Covenant faithfulness or loyalty, not mere ritual, is required of the covenant people (Mic. 6:6–8 and notes).

These verses catalog a number of crimes associated with specific places that are infamous in Hosea's day. Though the details are now lost, the record serves to indict the whole nation (v. 10). 6:7 like Adam. Several possible interpretations of this reference have been proposed: (1) the first man, Adam (Gen. 3); (2) a place identified with the ancient site Tell ed-Damiyeh on the Jordan River (Josh. 3:16), paralleling Gilead and Shechem (vv. 8, 9) and suggested by "there" in the second half of the verse; and (3) humanity. Because the elements of a covenant were present in God's relationship with Adam, the doctrine of God's covenant with Adam does not depend upon the interpretation of this text. See note on Gen. 3:1-24.

This is a mountainous region in the northern Transjordan, but the word may refer to the city of Ramoth-gilead. evildoers. The term is used frequently in the Psalms to indicate the enemies of the righteous and of the Lord. tracked with blood. This may allude to the fifty men of Gilead involved in the assassination of Pekahiah (2 Kin. 15:25).
An important religious and political center, Shechem is located in Ephraimite territory between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal (Deut. 27:4, 12–14; Josh. 8:30; 20:7; 24:1; Judg. 9:6; 1 Kin. 12:1).

The phrase suggests a religious sin or the involvement of priests or prophets in gross wrongdoing (Jer. 5:30, 31; 18:13–15; 23:14). whoredom. A common figure here for religious infidelity (7:4 and note).
A metaphor for God's judgment (Jer. 51:33; Joel 3:13; Matt. 13:39–43).
Both terms refer to the northern kingdom, of which Samaria is the capital (4:17 note). The Lord's grace shines a light on Israel's sins.
They have deceived even themselves (cf. Gal. 6:7).
The royal leaders should provide moral leadership, but they have savored instead the evil and treachery of those around them (2 Kin. 15:8–30).

They have left the Lord, to whom they were allied in the covenant, and have joined themselves with other gods and other foreign allies (2:4; 4:12–14; Jer. 9:2; 23:10–14). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes. like a heated oven. The figures of an oven, a baker, and fire present a graphic word picture of the self-propagating passion, treachery, and wickedness that infests the political life of Israel during its last days and leads to the series of violent assassinations of its kings (2 Kin. 15:8–30). The assassination of Pekah by Hoshea (2 Kin. 15:30) may be the occasion of the remarks in vv. 4–7.
A royal celebration becomes an occasion for drunkenness, which in turn fuels more wickedness (1 Kin. 16:9, 10; Prov. 31:4, 5; Amos 6:6).
Those plotting against the king, perhaps the priests (6:9).
Even amid unrest that has seen four kings assassinated within twenty years (2 Kin. 15:8–30), none of the leaders have called upon God.

A reference to Israel's shifting alliances with Egypt, Philistia, Aram, and Assyria. a cake not turned. In this sarcastic figure for foolish national policy, Israel is compared to a useless half-baked cake that cannot be eaten because she has refused to turn to the Lord.

They have made Ephraim poor by exacting tribute. he knows it not. This repeated phrase stresses Israel's ignorance of how politically weak and drained she has become. Lack of knowledge of God is here followed by a lack of self-knowledge and by self-deception.
Israel's blindness is attributed to stubborn arrogance that testifies against her (5:5). Turning back to the Lord is Israel's only hope (2:7; 3:5; 5:4; 6:1; Amos 4:6–12).

In Hosea's era, the dove is reputed to be witless and easy to trap. Egypt \... Assyria. Like a dove, Israel has fluttered from one nation to another seeking security and protection: Menahem submitted to Assyria and paid a vast tribute (2 Kin. 15:17–20); Pekah formed a coalition with Syria-Damascus against Assyria (2 Kin. 15:29, 37; 16:5); and Hoshea shifted his allegiance from Assyria to Egypt (2 Kin. 17:3, 4).
The Lord's net of judgment will come down upon flitting Israel.

This term from commercial law meaning "buy back" (Lev. 27:27–31) is used also of Israel's deliverance from bondage (13:14; cf. Ex. 13:15; Deut. 7:8; 9:26; 15:15; Mic. 6:4). lies. This may refer to the false ideas about the Lord that has been imported into Israel's religion, to insincere words of repentance (6:1–3), or more generally to the broken promises of the covenant.

A responsible and loyal response, as suggested by a similar expression used in a contemporary Assyrian treaty. wail upon their beds. This phrase could mean that they cry out to their gods on the beds of fertility-cult prostitution. gash themselves. Cutting oneself is a pagan Canaanite ritual to cause Baal to intervene in one's behalf (1 Kin. 18:26–29).

See Ps. 78:57. insolence of their tongue. These are directed against God and His prophets (6:5). Egypt. The Egyptians will soon mock at the fall of those who have solicited their help only intermittently.

The urgent call for alarm (5:8) indicates that Assyria, like an eagle or vulture, is rapidly approaching to administer God's judgment. the house of the LORD. The temple in Jerusalem is at the very heart of the land of God's people. my covenant \... my law. Rebellion against the terms of the covenant is tantamount to rebellion against God Himself (4:6; 6:6, 7; 7:13; 8:12).
As they cry for help, the Israelites claim to know God, but their actions belie their words (6:1). They truly do not know the Lord (5:4).
This comprehensive term describes all the blessings under God's covenant. It may even refer to the "Good One," God Himself (Amos 5:14, 15; Mic. 6:8).

Israel's independence from God in the political sphere is apparent in her refusal to consult God in her choice of leaders. This leads to a series of conspiracies and violent assassinations (7:3–7; cf. 2 Kin. 15:8–30). idols. In making gods of silver and gold, Israel expresses her defiant rejection of God (v. 5; cf. Ex. 20:3–6; 34:17; Lev. 19:4).
A symbol of fertility and strength, the bull was frequently worshiped in the ancient Near East and is itself here described as the object of worship (10:5 note).
This proverbial saying emphasizes the dire cause-and-effect relationship between sin and punishment (10:13; cf. Job 4:8; Prov. 11:18; 22:8; Gal. 6:7–9).

Probably a reference to Hoshea's submission to Assyria in his attempt to keep the power that he seized following his murder of Pekah (7:11; cf. 2 Kin. 15:30; 17:3). wild donkey. Using a wordplay between the Hb. for "wild donkey" and the Hb. name Ephraim, Hosea condemns Ephraim (Israel) for stubbornly rejecting the Lord's company.
This gathering is for judgment, not restoration (Joel 3:2; Zeph. 3:8). the king and princes. The king of Assyria (Is. 10:8).
Although built to atone for sin, northern altars instead have become places to sin.
God threatens them with captivity, here symbolized by the land where Israel was once enslaved (9:3; cf. Ex. 1:8–14; Deut. 28:68).
Israel's confidence that buildings and fortifications bring spiritual, political, or military security is misguided. fire. See Amos 1:4, 7, 10, 12, 14.

Because of divine judgment on her covenant disobedience, Israel will not enjoy the fruit of the land (Deut. 28:18), nor will she celebrate the annual agricultural feasts (Deut. 16:1–17 and notes). 9:1 threshing floors. The flat, open area used for threshing wheat and barley is also a place where Israel has prostituted herself by indulging in sensual activities related to the fertility worship of Baal.
This device is used for both wine and oil.

LORD. Also called the Lord's "house" (8:1; 9:15), the Promised Land is owned by the Lord and not by Baal — or even by Israel (Lev. 25:23 and note). Exile from this land is another consequence of Israel's idolatry. return to Egypt. See note on 8:13. unclean food. Other nations and the food they produce are considered unclean (Ezek. 4:13; Amos 7:17).

Food in the house of mourners is unclean because of contact with a dead body (Num. 19:11–22; Deut. 26:14). house of the LORD. They will be unable to sanctify their food through sacrifice while in exile.
. A probable reference to the annual fall harvest Feast of Booths or Tabernacles (Lev. 23:33–43; Deut. 16:13–15).

The Assyrian invasions. Memphis shall bury them. Here poetically paired with Egypt, this Egyptian city is known for its great cemeteries, tombs, and pyramids. precious things of silver \... tents. The abandoned tents and valuables may be religious shrines and idols, or their personal property in general.

In their sin, the Israelites have considered the Lord's prophets to be foolish and idle talkers. man of the spirit. Used in parallel with "prophet," this is probably another expression for "man of God" (1 Sam. 10:6; 1 Kin. 18:12; 22:21–28; 2 Kin. 2:9, 16). mad. The Hb. word indicates a nonsensical babbler or madman (1 Sam. 21:13–15; 2 Kin. 9:11; Jer. 29:26).

The prophets keep watch over Israel (5:8; cf. Jer. 6:1; Ezek. 3:17; 33:1–7). But the one who has sounded the alarm now finds himself hunted like an animal and an object of hostility. the house of his God. The temple (8:1 note).

A town infamous for the gang rape of the Levite's concubine and the war that followed (Judg. 19–21). The gravity of Israel's former sins also shows how deeply they require a complete renewal of their nature.

An unusual and delicious find. first fruit on the fig tree. The early fig that ripens on the previous year's sprouts is not only very tender but quite uncommon (cf. Is. 28:4). These images stress how exceptional and pleasing was the Lord's initial covenant relationship with Israel. Baal-peor. A reference to Israel's sexual and spiritual adultery in the wilderness (Num. 25 and notes) — behavior that is paralleled by Hosea's contemporaries. became detestable. By joining themselves to Baal-peor, the god of shame, the Israelites themselves became detestable.

Possibly her political and military power, but the context suggests that it is her large population. The blessing on Joseph and Ephraim had made them fruitful (Gen. 48:16; 49:22–26). no birth. The practice of fertility religion generates a fertility curse, not a blessing (Deut. 28:18).

Hosea responds in prayer, asking that God's fertility blessings be withdrawn (Gen. 49:25; Ex. 23:26; Deut. 28:4, 11). The prophet can only agree with God's righteous judgment. Israel has sought fertility from Baal, but Hosea prays that the God of Israel will answer with infertility.

See note on 4:15; cf. 12:11. drive them out of my house. Although the emphasis here is upon expulsion from the temple, this punishment parallels God's banishment of the Canaanites (Ex. 23:29, 30; 33:2; Josh. 24:18; Judg. 6:9). See note on 8:1.

"Ephraim" sounds like "fruit" in Hebrew, and the wordplay ironically underscores the tragedy of Ephraim's fruitlessness (Gen. 41:52). The name of this leading northern tribe is often used in Scripture for the entire northern kingdom of Israel.

Unlike the people who have turned away from God, the prophet has remained faithful to the covenant. wanderers. Having wandered from God (7:13), the Israelites, like Cain, are destined to be exiled, with no true home (Deut. 28:64, 65).

In this section, unlike in the preceding and following sections, the Lord does not speak, but the prophet speaks about Him. 10:1 more his fruit increased \... more altars he built. Israel has given the credit for prosperity to their idols, and they have devoted more resources to the pagan cult whenever their prosperity has increased.
The covenant requires single-minded devotion to the Lord (Deut. 6:5); Israel's divided loyalties call forth the judgment predicted in the covenant curses pronounced by Moses (Deut. 29:14–29).
Whether the king is still on the throne and about to be deposed, or he has already been deposed, he is useless without God's blessing.
Or "wormwood," as the Hb. term is translated in Amos 6:12.

The capital city of the northern kingdom. calf of Beth-aven. The calf and its priests (2 Kin. 23:5; Zeph. 1:4) are probably not representative of a foreign deity. Rather, they exemplify a highly perverse form of worshiping the Lord in Israel (cf. 8:5 note; 13:2 note; 1 Kin. 12:31–33). This is likely a reference to the calf of Bethel erected by Jeroboam I (cf. 4:15). mourn. Hosea mocks the pious emotions that the people manifest for an idol.

See 4:13–15. Cover us \... Fall on us. The words speak of overwhelming devastation from the Lord. The people would rather die than face further judgments from Him. The passage is quoted by Jesus in Luke 23:30, and it is alluded to in Rev. 6:16.
See note on 9:9.
May refer to the past sin at Gibeah and the present sin of Israel, to Israel's religious sin and political faithlessness, or simply to Israel's repeated and unyielding transgressions.

Both kingdoms are in view. trained calf \... loved to thresh. A positive image of Israel's original calling as a teachable animal without a muzzle and free to eat as it threshes the harvested grain because it willingly does what it is told (11:4; cf. Deut. 25:4; Prov. 12:10; Jer. 50:11). fair neck. That is, a strong neck capable of arduous work. Israel has not fulfilled the Lord's expectations. The easy yoke of covenant blessings will be replaced by the hard yoke of covenant curses in order to teach them obedience.

See note on Ex. 15:13. Sowing what is right and good brings a harvest of blessing from the Lord. Here is another call to repentance from the prophet. break up your fallow ground. When virgin and fallow ground is plowed, it produces a particularly abundant harvest. rain righteousness. God must give the harvest (1 Cor. 3:6, 7).

Instead of cultivating a fruitful relationship with God, Israel has planted, reaped, and eaten wickedness and dishonesty (8:7; Gal. 6:7–9). Because you have trusted in \... your warriors. The punishment God will bring (a military defeat) is directly related to Israel's sin of depending on its own military power and not on the Lord (Jer. 9:23, 24).

Hosea's original audience must remember this now-unknown event as particularly brutal. Shalman is an unknown figure. He has been identified variously as Shalmaneser III of Assyria (859–824 B.C..), Shalmaneser V (727–722 B.C..), and Salamanu, a contemporary Moabite king. Beth-arbel is often identified with the site of Irbid in Gilead.
Often ironically called "Beth-aven" by Hosea (4:15 note; 5:8; 10:5). At dawn. The time for battle to begin.

In language as tender as the story of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32), God, the loving parent, proclaims His compassion for Israel. In spite of rebellion, God's election cannot be defeated. Beyond judgment there is hope. 11:1 loved. The language of love is used to describe both the father-son relationship and the covenantal relationship between a suzerain and vassal in ancient Near-Eastern treaties (Deut. 6:5; 7:8, 13; 10:15; 23:5). out of Egypt I called my son. Here and in v. 4, reference is made to God's deliverance of Israel from slavery in Egypt (Ex. 4:22). Jesus, as the true Israel, was also brought out of Egypt (Matt. 2:15).

The Hebrew of this verse is difficult to translate. The meaning may be that the pagans or their gods, the Baals, have tempted Israel, causing the nation to depart from the Lord. Alternatively, those who are called may be the prophets, whose messages are ignored as Israel went after other gods.

Probably a reference to God's tender leading of Israel through the wilderness to the Promised Land as a father leads a little child. I healed them. God spared Israel from harm during the formative wilderness period (Ex. 15:26).
The imagery apparently returns to Israel as a work animal (10:11), but here God is pampering the creature by easing the yoke and reins on it.

The Hb. word for "not" here seems to indicate that Israel will not return to Egypt (symbolic for bondage; cf. 8:13 note), but such a reading appears to conflict with 8:13; 9:3; and 11:11. Some render this phrase as a rhetorical question ("shall he not return?"), while others emend the Hb. word for "not" to mean "to it." Another reading, however, is indicated by the context of divine mercy in this passage (vv. 4, 8). Israel shall not return to Egypt (i.e., to her status before God called her as His covenant people, Deut. 4:34), but she will be punished for her sins by Assyria. In other words, she will not return to the oppression of Pharaoh but will come under the oppression of the king of Assyria. Egypt \... Assyria. See notes on 8:13; 9:3. Though deserved, the effect of this judgment is tempered in v. 11.

With fortified cities they are self-reliant (8:14). gates. Some suggest that this difficult Hb. word refers to people, specifically to false prophets who supplied the military counsel mentioned later in the verse.

Here God is speaking directly to Israel. The contrast with vv. 5–7 heightens the impact of this deeply personal declaration of relentless compassion. Admah \... Zeboiim. These two cities on the plain near the southern end of the Dead Sea (Gen. 10:19; 14:2, 8) were destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:23–25), thus becoming examples of God's wrath (Deut. 29:23; Jer. 49:18).
Holiness denotes God's moral perfection. Men seek revenge, but God works salvation.
LORD. Restoration, not destruction, is the goal of God's judgment of His covenant people.

God compassionately tempers the effect of the judgment pronounced in v. 5.
