Although the people have breached the Mosaic covenant and deserve to experience its curses without mitigation, God promises that they will be restored to the land. from Egypt \... Assyria. Again Egypt and Assyria are paired to symbolize the judgment of God's people through exile (8:13 note; 9:3; 11:5).

This section accuses Israel of betrayal and pronounces judgment. Recurrent themes are the past treachery of Israel (artistically linked with episodes from the life of Jacob) and the rejection of the word of the Lord as spoken by the prophets. 11:12 surrounded me with lies. The northern kingdom lacks integrity before God. Judah still walks with God. The Hebrew is difficult to translate. As rendered here, Judah is viewed positively and contrasted with Ephraim (i.e., Israel). But some translate the phrase to speak of Judah as "unruly against God," and thus like Ephraim.

See Prov. 15:14; Is. 44:20. wind \... east wind. These images of futility (Job 15:2; Eccl. 1:14) and destruction (13:15; cf. Jer. 18:17) are applied to Israel's alliances with Assyria (5:13; 7:11; 8:9; 14:3; cf. 2 Kin. 17:3) and Egypt (7:16 note; cf. 2 Kin. 17:4). Such alliances are not merely poor foreign policy but expressions of faithlessness against the Lord. falsehood. Examples of deception include Israel's vacillation between Assyria and Egypt (7:11), and playing off the latter against the former (2 Kin. 17:3, 4). oil. Gifts are often given when making covenants.

As in 4:1, the Lord acts as plaintiff, judge, and prosecutor in a court scene, bringing a covenant lawsuit against His people. He calls for punishment (v. 2) but also reconciliation (v. 6). Jacob. That is, Israel (10:11; cf. Gen. 32:28).
The Hebrew here is the root for "Jacob" (Gen. 25:26) and is translated "cheated" in Gen. 27:36.

The Hb. root for "strive" is given as the source of the name "Israel" in Gen. 32:28. In tenaciously seeking God's blessing, Jacob set a positive example for the nation (v. 6). Bethel. The place where God made Himself known to Jacob (Gen. 28:12–19; 35:1–15). See note on 4:15.

LORD, the God of hosts. A doxology, similar to those in Amos (Amos 4:13; 5:8, 9; 9:5, 6), here reminds Israel that the covenant God of the patriarchs (the Lord) is the God of hosts, the commander of Israel's armies, and sovereign over all creation (Zech. 1:3 note). memorial name. See Ex. 3:15.
Like Jacob, who returned to Bethel to fulfill his vow (Gen. 35:1–15), Israel must return to the Lord.
The merchant Ephraim has been dishonest and cruel.

your God \... Egypt.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} The statement is one of self-presentation. It introduces the following expression of God's will to His covenant people (Ex. 20:2; Deut. 5:6). tents \... appointed feast. A reference to the Feast of Booths, when the people live in booths in memory of Israel's time in the wilderness after leaving Egypt (Lev. 23:43). Just as Israel was judged with forty years of wilderness wandering (Num. 14:33), here Israel is threatened with the "wilderness" of exile from the land.

No one can plead ignorance as an excuse (6:5; 12:13). visions. A mode of revelation to the prophets (Num. 12:6; Job 33:14–16). parables. These "parables" are figures of speech bearing divine messages (2 Sam. 12:1–4; Ps. 78:2; Is. 5:1–7; Ezek. 17:2–10).

This region east of the Jordan, bordered by Moab on the south and Bashan on the north, is a place of illegal sacrifices, bloodshed, and idolatry. It is conquered by Assyria in 734–732 B.C.. (6:8; cf. 2 Kin. 15:29). Gilgal. See note on 4:15. heaps on the furrows. Large stones struck by the farmer's plow are piled in heaps.
Paddan-aram (Gen. 28:2, 5). served \... guarded. Hosea compares Jacob's service to secure a wife from a foreign country with God's rescue of His people from Egypt.

The first prophet is clearly Moses (Deut. 18:15; 34:10–12) and the second probably is as well. The preserving prophet could, however, be a later prophet such as Samuel (Jer. 15:1) or Elijah (1 Kin. 19:9–18).

Again God's covenant faithfulness (v. 13) is contrasted with Israel's faithlessness. The Lord has been provoked by the worship of pagan gods (Deut. 32:21), but here even more offenses seem involved. bloodguilt. A reference either to murder itself (4:2; 5:2; 6:8) or, as in ancient legal texts, to any capital crime. The verse concludes the lawsuit, and is parallel in structure to v. 2, which introduces the section. Covenant election entails covenant responsibility.

This begins an announcement of judgment for sins past (v. 1) and present (v. 2). Ephraim. See note on 4:17. Baal. See 2:7, 8, 17; 9:10; 11:2. died. Because of its idolatry, the northern kingdom (Ephraim) is regarded as spiritually dead and lifeless.

The collective picture is of small statues of calves molded of bronze and overlaid with silver (Ex. 32:4, 8; 34:17; Lev. 19:4; Deut. 19:16). The calf idol is Canaanite and linked with Baal worship, but the idolaters probably also associate it in their own minds with the Lord (8:5, 6; 10:5 and notes). kiss. An act of devotion, adoration, or appeasement (1 Kin. 19:18).
See 6:4. Something that is fleeting and insubstantial.

See note on 12:9. you know no God but me. This statement contrasts with the idolatry of v. 2. The statement, reminding Israel that the covenant relationship is exclusive, is cast in the language of the first commandment (Ex. 20:2, 3; Deut. 5:6, 7) and adds the idea of "knowing" God. Other so-called gods are worshiped, but only the one true God can be "known" (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Further linkage to the covenant requirements of the Decalogue is evident in the description of Israel's idolatry (vv. 1, 2), a clear violation of the second commandment (Ex. 20:4–6; Deut. 5:8–10).

Israel is represented in corporate solidarity by the Hb. singular word for "you." This form of the pronoun emphasizes the personal nature of God's covenant relationship with His people. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes; note on Gen. 17:7. wilderness. During the difficult wilderness wanderings, God knew His people and was preparing them. Similarly, God will use the "wilderness" of exile to reclaim Israel (2:14–16).

Describes a step-by-step process of descent in morals and worship (Deut. 32:10–18; Jer. 2) due to material prosperity and self-reliance. forgot. This pitiful climax stands in sharp contrast to the former days of knowledge (cf. vv. 4, 5 and notes; cf. Deut. 8:11–20).

This startling comparison of God to ferocious wild beasts that devour the flock echoes the covenant curses for disobedience (Lev. 26:21, 22; Deut. 32:24; Ezek. 14:21). These images depict the severity of divine judgment (5:14; cf. Prov. 17:12; Jer. 5:6; Lam 3:1–18).

Israel's destruction is explained here in terms of the nation's rebellion against her Divine Helper. There is no help like God (Ex. 18:4; Deut. 33:26–29; Ps. 10:14; 54:4; 115:9–11; 121:2–8; 146:5). To oppose Him is to invite destruction.

On Israel's request for a monarchy, see 1 Sam. 8. On that occasion, the people's asking for a king meant that they had rejected God as King (1 Sam. 13:9, 10). Their sense of security in having a king was a delusion.

Though describing past action, the Hb. verb tense suggests an ongoing process of giving and taking. The king is not specified. Perhaps this is a reference to the royal assassinations of Hosea's time (3:4; 7:7; 8:4; 10:3; cf. 2 Kin. 15:8–31; 17:1–6), to an early king such as Saul (who was alive when kingship was first requested), or even to all of the kings of the north (all twenty of whom "did what was evil in the sight of the Lord").

Lest they be diminished or forgotten, transgressions are figuratively tied up and then stored in a safe place for future retribution (7:2; 9:9; cf. Deut. 32:34, 35; Job 14:17). Ephraim. See note on 4:17.

The predicament of Israel facing certain judgment is vividly compared to that of a mother and child during an unsuccessful birth (cf. 2 Kin. 19:3). This complex word picture compares Israel both to the mother (who faces sorrow and certain death) and to the child (who stubbornly refuses to be safely delivered). an unwise son. Israel is depicted as a fetus that fails to position itself properly in the womb for delivery. This surprising figure relates to the theme of failure to acknowledge God.

The Hb. for "pity" can have the sense of "repentance" or "regret." God will not "repent" (i.e., change His mind) of His intention to vanquish death for His people. Paul quotes part of this verse in 1 Cor. 15:55.

Refers to Ephraim, whose name is from the same Hb. root as "fruitful" (9:16 note). east \... wind of the Lord. Cf. 12:1 and note. Here this destructive force is a symbol for Assyria as God's weapon of judgment against Israel (Introduction: Occasion; Is. 10:5, 6).

The capital city and driving force behind the northern kingdom's rebellion. fall \... dashed \... ripped. Figurative language for destruction (vv. 3, 8, 15) here gives way to chilling expressions of hard reality.

The prophet speaks to the people, urging repentance, before conveying God's promise of blessing (vv. 4–8). 14:1 Return. This thematic exhortation to return (2:7; 3:5; 6:1; 7:10; 12:6) is now addressed to those who have already fallen because of their sins.

Words of confession accompanied by obedience please God, not half-hearted sacrifices (5:6; 6:6; 8:11–13). A precise wording for confession is suggested in vv. 2, 3. the vows of our lips. Or, "fruit of our lips" (text note). The Hb. words for "bull calves" (here rendered "vows") and "fruit" are similar. Cf. Prov. 12:14; 13:2; Heb. 13:15.

Israel is to give up trusting in foreign political powers (5:13; 7:11; 12:1), in her own military strength (10:13; cf. Ps. 33:16, 17), and in idolatrous and syncretistic religion (2:8, 13; 3:1; 4:12; 8:5, 6; 10:5, 6; 13:2). orphan finds mercy. This expression alludes to the earlier theme of loss and restoration of love illustrated by Hosea's marriage and his daughter, Lo-ruhama (1:6; 2:2–4, 14–23). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

The promise of healing begins to be realized when Israel returns from its sixth-century exile in Babylon. It finds much greater fulfillment in Jesus Christ and His church, and is consummated at His second coming. apostasy. Israel's characteristic unfaithfulness (4:10–12; 5:4; 7:4; 11:7) will be healed by the great Healer, whose anger is now turned away. love them freely. In this love song, we hear again the deep affection of God for His elect. This undeserved love is what the NT calls grace (Rom. 5:15; Eph. 2:5, 8).

In this section, resplendent with the language of love, colorful metaphors drawn from plant life — a blossoming lily (Song 2:1, 16), a deeply rooted, sprouting and fragrant cedar of Lebanon (Pss. 92:12; 104:16), a splendid olive tree (Ps. 52:8; Jer. 11:16), a shade tree (Song 2:3; Ezek. 17:22, 23), flourishing grain (2:8, 22), a flowering vine (10:1; cf. Is. 5:1–7) and the fruit of the vine — depict a vigorous, renowned, stable, and prosperous Israel flourishing under God, who is likened to the life-giving dew (Deut. 33:13).
Like a tree renowned as a symbol of life (cf. Gen. 3:22; Rev. 22:2), God will give fruit to fruitless Ephraim (9:16 note).

This epilogue challenges every generation to consider carefully the ways of the Lord that are presented in the book (cf. Ps. 1; 18:21; Prov. 10:29). The choices that Israel — and every generation of God's people — faces are also set before the reader: wisdom or folly; discipleship or rebellion; life or death. The wise will "choose life" (Deut. 30:19, 20).

Joel.note: **LORD**. This short and simple title announces that what follows is the Lord's revealed word, and compares most closely with Jon. 1:1. More extended titles for individual prophetic books are found in Jer. 1:2; Ezek. 1:3; Hos. 1:1; Mic. 1:1; Zeph. 1:1; Hag. 1:1; Zech. 1:1; Mal. 1:1. Joel. His name means "Yahweh is God." Pethuel. The only occurrence of this name in the Bible.

Two crises confront Judah as a consequence of the people's sins: (1) the recent devastation of the land by locusts (1:4–8) and drought (1:10–12, 16–20); and (2) the imminent assault on the land by the army of the Lord (2:1–17). If the people are to be delivered from these calamities, they must repent of their sins and return to the Lord. 1:2–20 Joel appeals to elders (v. 2), drunkards (v. 5), farmers (v. 11), and priests (v. 13) to ponder the meaning of the recent locust plague and drought, and to repent. This variety of different types of people reflects the idea that all the men and women in Judah are to consider their situation and circumstances. 1:2 Hear \... give ear. This series of commands calls the people to recognize the personal and spiritual significance of the locust invasion. The repetition of thought in the first and second lines and in the third and fourth lines illustrates the parallelism typical of Hebrew poetry. elders. This term designates the community and religious leaders. The same term used in 2:28 seems to refer to age, hence the translation "old men." all inhabitants of the land. The entire population of Judah and Jerusalem is called to listen.
Reports of God's judgments, as well as His mercies, are to be passed on to future generations (cf. Deut. 4:9; 6:7; 32:7; Ps. 78:1–8).

The poetic repetitions in every line emphasize the thoroughness of the locusts' destruction. The variety in the names of the locusts may refer to their different stages of development, although color differences or differences in type and regional origin may be reflected here and in 2:25. When locusts are understood to be an instrument of divine punishment, repentance is the appropriate response (Deut. 28:38; Amos 7:1; Is. 33:4).

The first call to respond is given to the drunkards. These represent the attitude of many who are oblivious to things that have spiritual significance. Only the alert are able to respond rightly to God's judgment. Even the drunkards are to understand that there will be no wine for them after the locust devastation.

Personal pronouns are used throughout the book and point to the covenant relationship that binds the Lord not only to the land and its vines and fig trees, but also to His people (1:7; 2:13, 14, 17, 18, 23, 26, 27; 3:2, 3, 17). powerful \... lioness. The locusts are compared to an invading nation that has the consuming passion of a lion (cf. 2:4–9; Rev. 9:7–9). Locusts and armies are often compared in ancient times. Mythical literature from the ancient city of Ugarit likens a large army to locusts (cf. Judg. 6:5; Prov. 30:27; Jer. 51:14, 27; Nah. 3:15–17).
The locusts' teeth have effectively stripped the most valuable trees of the Lord's land. These trees are symbols of prosperity in the OT (Mic. 4:4).

The mourning is to be like that of a young woman who has lost her beloved before marriage. sackcloth. This coarsely woven material was often made of goat's hair and worn during times of mourning. See v. 13; cf. Gen. 37:34; 2 Sam. 3:31; 1 Kin. 21:27; Is. 32:11, 12.
These offerings, which the Mosaic law prescribes as offerings that must be made twice daily (Ex. 29:38–42; Lev. 2:1, 2; 23:13), are lacking because the crops have been destroyed.
The ingredients needed for the daily offerings traditionally appear in this order (2:19; cf. Hos. 2:8). dries up. Drought accompanies the locust invasion.

Five kinds of trees are noted, leading up to the climactic statement that all the trees of the field are dried up. gladness dries up. In an agricultural economy, human joy withers along with the vegetation.
The priests are given precise instructions about how to respond to God's judgment.

The priests are to provide leadership in the community by proclaiming a public fast so that the entire nation can stop all regular activities for a time (probably for a day; cf. Judg. 20:26; 1 Sam. 14:24; Jer. 36:6–9) to acknowledge God's judgment and to repent.

**LORD**. A thematic phrase in Joel (1:15; 2:1, 11, 31; 3:14) and in other OT prophetic books (Is. 13:6, 9; Ezek. 13:5; Amos 5:18, 20; Obad. 15; Zeph. 1:7, 14; Mal. 4:5). Here (and in 2:1, 11) it refers to a day of the Lord's wrath against Judah, though later in the book it refers to the Lord's wrath against the nations and His blessing of His people (2:31; 3:14). The magnitude of the devastation points to an even more ominous day of judgment. destruction from the Almighty. This phrase can be translated "might from the Almighty," capturing the sense of the Hb. wordplay shod ("destruction") from shaddai ("the Almighty"; Is. 13:6).
Joel reinforces his point about the nearness of the day of the Lord by reminding his audience again of God's judgment, which is evident in the drought conditions all around them.
**LORD**, I call. The prophet himself begins the lamentation. The devastation is from the Lord, and He is the source of restoration.

Even the animals join Joel in his cry (Job 38:41; Pss. 104:21; 147:9). fire has devoured. Divine judgment is often depicted as fire (Deut. 32:22; Pss. 50:3; 97:3). The metaphor describes the effects of drought (cf. 2:3, where the "fire" of locust devastation is depicted).

Joel urges "all the inhabitants of the land" (v. 1) to prepare for an imminent assault by the army of the Lord. Contrite hearts among the people may bring God's compassion and blessing (v. 14). 2:1 a trumpet. The ram's horn (Hb. shofar) was used in warfare and to signal danger. All tremble at the trumpet blast signaling the coming of the day of the Lord (Amos 3:6; Zeph. 1:14–16). Zion \... my holy mountain. Jerusalem, the location of God's earthly residence.

This vivid word picture of the coming day of the Lord (cf. Zeph. 1:15; Amos 5:18, 20) corresponds to descriptions of the Lord's appearances in the past (Deut. 4:11; 5:22, 23; Ps. 97:2). great and powerful people. Complex metaphors of an army and locust invasion combine to depict the judgment and devastation to occur (1:6 note).

The invaders raze the land. The bold contrast between "the garden of Eden" and this wilderness (Gen. 13:10; Is. 51:3; Ezek. 28:13–19; 31:8, 9, 16–18; 36:35) highlights the horror of the inescapable invasion.
Again the army of judgment is figuratively depicted as a locust invasion (1:6 note; cf. Rev. 9:1–11).
The army is disciplined, ruthless, and successful. The "city" (v. 9) is finally overrun (cf. the Egyptian plague of locusts in Ex. 10:6).
Such divine judgments are accompanied by a shaking and breakdown of the natural order. All creation is disturbed (v. 31; cf. Jer. 4:23–26; Ezek. 32:7, 8; Nah. 1:5; Hab. 3:6, 10).
The relentless army is the Lord's. He commands and His forces obey. The day of the Lord is great (2:31; Zeph. 1:14), dreadful (Mal. 4:5), and unbearable (Nah. 1:6; Mal. 3:2).

The Lord invites His people to escape by returning to Him with their whole hearts. There is yet time for them to repent and to be restored. fasting \... weeping \... mourning. The visible signs of repentance (Ezra 10:1–6; Esth. 4:3; Jon. 3:5–9). with all your heart. The repentance of God's people must be complete and undivided.

See theological note "Legalism" on p. 1713. gracious \... steadfast love. The call to return to the Lord is based on the Lord's compassionate nature as revealed through the dramatic self-revelation of His character to Moses in Ex. 34:6, 7, a description frequently repeated throughout the OT (e.g., Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Pss. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Jon. 4:2).
God's sovereignty and freedom in forgiveness are seen in vv. 13, 14 (cf. Ex. 33:19; 2 Sam. 12:22; Lam. 3:29; Jon. 3:9; Zeph. 2:3). See note on Gen. 6:6.

Further instructions for returning to the Lord include a fast and an assembly (v. 15), a gathering and consecration of all the people, including the elders, children, nursing infants, and even those about to marry (v. 16). The staccato quality of the Hebrew poetry in these verses emphasizes the urgency of the situation.

Specific instructions are also given to the priests who are to weep and offer prayers of intercession. Between the vestibule and the altar. This site in the temple is the usual place for priestly intercession (1 Kin. 8:22; Ezek. 8:16). your heritage. The priestly lament appeals to the Lord's sense of ownership and pride in His covenant people (Deut. 9:26, 29; Pss. 44:11–14; 74:2; 79:10; 115:2; Mic. 7:10). 2:18–3:21 The Lord, the God of the covenant, promises to renew the land and His people, as they respond in repentance to the crises of 1:2–2:17. The redemptive renewal of God's people will someday lead to the final devastation of Zion's enemies and the final exaltation of Zion itself.

Repentance will bring renewed fruitfulness to the land. 2:18 Then. Here begins the Lord's response to the people's anguish, which marks a decisive turn in the text. Some translations (e.g. KJV, NASB, NIV 1984) use future tenses to translate the verbs in this verse, but this indicates that the Lord's changed attitude has not yet occurred. A change in subject, mood, and tense takes place at this point, however, showing that the Lord has already reacted; what the people are waiting for are the blessings He will provide.
The prayers of God's people will be answered with the staples of agricultural produce — "grain, wine, and (olive) oil" (1:10; 2:24).

Some interpreters have understood this to be a reference to the locusts of ch.1. More likely it refers to a large and mighty army that becomes the Lord's instrument of judgment. Unlike most locust invasions (which came from the east or south), foreign military invasions often came from the north in ancient Israel. Cf. the references to the enemy from the north in Jer. 1:14, 15; 4:6; 6:1, 22; Ezek. 38:6, 15; 39:2.
Even the land and the wild animals are urged not to be afraid, and they are exhorted to be glad and rejoice with the people of Zion in the agricultural abundance from the Lord.

This is a very difficult phrase to translate. "The early rain" (Hb. moreh) may also be rendered "the teacher" or "that which instructs." Although Joel uses the same word later in the verse in the sense "early rain," it is not the normal term for such rain (Hb. yoreh). Most modern translations opt for rain/early rain in both occurrences as more appropriate to the passage, in that agricultural blessings associated with reversal of drought are mentioned first, and spiritual blessings are dealt with later (vv. 28–32). However, that does not account for Joel's unusual word choice. Some authors continue to prefer a rendering such as "the teacher for righteousness" and find here a direct messianic prophecy, as did many early commentators. The Qumran community, which copied the Dead Sea Scrolls, derived from this phrase their title for their founder or leader: the Teacher of Righteousness. More likely, Joel's play on words is less direct: the coming rain and the resumption of the usual agricultural cycle will be a medium of divine instruction for the people regarding the Lord's faithful provision for His repentant and restored people. early rain \... latter rain. The autumn and spring rains respectively, both of which are needed for agricultural prosperity.
See note on 1:4.
Abundance should lead to praise (cf. Deut. 8:10; Hos. 13:5, 6).
Restoration leads to a new realization that the Lord is in Israel, that He is the covenant God and there is no other.

Joel prophesies concerning the unprecedented outpouring of God's Spirit that will occur before the coming of the day of the Lord. There are three strophes (see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry) that begin with the same grammatical construction: the first strophe (2:28, 29) expresses the outpouring of God's Spirit; the second strophe (2:30, 31) addresses the cosmic signs that are the harbinger of the day of the Lord; the third strophe (2:32) describes the ultimate security of the Lord's people. 2:28, 29 Moses prayed that Israel as a whole would be a nation of prophets (Num. 11:29), and Joel now predicts this as part of Israel's glorious future. Peter proclaimed that the vision began to find fulfillment at Pentecost with the coming of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:16–21), who empowers believers to bear witness to Jesus Christ (Acts 1:8). By introducing this prophecy with "the last days" (Acts 2:17), Peter links it with other prophecies regarding Israel's messianic future and so teaches that Pentecost inaugurates the promised new age (cf. 1 Pet. 1:10–12).
The universal scope of events heralding "the great and awesome day of the Lord" is emphasized. See also Is. 13:10; Ezek. 32:7, 8; Amos 8:9; Zeph. 1:14–17.

LORD. A reference to the worship of the Lord (Gen. 12:8; Ps. 105:1). Salvation is found only in returning to the true and exclusive worship of God. Paul quotes this verse in Rom. 10:13 with regard to the inclusion of the Gentiles into the salvific plan of God. survivors. These are those the Lord who have responded in faith to His calling. There is a hint here that divine intervention on that day does not exempt those in Zion and Jerusalem from scrutiny and judgment.

Joel prophesies the coming of that day of the Lord in which God will with finality judge Zion's enemies and make Zion a source of everlasting blessing. 3:1 in those days. In parallel with "at that time," this announcement marks the beginning of a further series of promises for God's people (Jer. 33:15; 50:4, 20).

Restoration will include the judgment of Israel's enemies ("all the nations") for their injustices against God's people and land. Valley of Jehoshaphat. This place is identified as the "valley of decision" in v. 14. It is commonly believed to be located at the site of the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem between the city and the Mount of Olives. scattered \... divided. Following deportation of the people, the land was redistributed to others. The particular historical event referred to here is not clear. The deportations of 722, 701, 598, and 586 B.C., or even smaller deportations involving border wars (e.g., Amos 1:9, 10) are possibilities.
Following the casting of lots for prisoners (Obad. 11; Nah. 3:10), defenseless children were traded and sold for purposes of debauchery (Amos 2:6).

The legal charge against Tyre and Sidon (coastal Phoenicia) and the regions of Philistia (coastal Palestine, Josh. 13:2, 3) concerns their involvement in capturing and trading Israelites as prisoners of war. Both regions sold Israelites as slaves to the Greeks (v. 6) and to Edom (Amos 1:6, 9).
The land's silver and gold, as well as its inhabitants, belongs to the Lord (Hag. 2:8).
God's restored people will inflict His punishment on Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia.
These are merchants from the distant land of Sheba (1 Kin. 10:1–13; Jer. 6:20).
Joel issues a bitterly ironic invitation to battle to those nations that the Lord will defeat.
This is the opposite of Is. 2:4 and Mic. 4:3. Here agricultural tools are to be turned into weapons of warfare.
The Valley of Jehoshaphat (v. 2 note) is the place of the great battle (v. 14 note).

Like grain ready to be cut down with the sickle (Is. 17:5) and like grapes waiting to be pressed (Is. 63:3), the wicked nations are ripe for a harvest of judgment (cf. Rev. 14:15, 18, 20). winepress is full \... vats overflow. The full winepress and overflowing vats emphasize the enormous wickedness of the nations massed in the valley for judgment. This is a reversal of the promise made to Judah in 2:24.

The Valley of Jehoshaphat is now identified as the "valley of decision" where the Lord's judgment will be passed upon multitudes. near. The imminence of the day of the Lord as a day of judgment is again underlined (1:15; 2:1, 31).
Nature responds to the Lord's appearing on the day of judgment (2:10, 31; Amos 5:18).

**LORD** roars. The Lord's voice is so powerful that even the earth and the sky tremble (Ps. 29:3–9; Jer. 25:30; Amos 1:2). refuge \... stronghold. Yet in the midst of the extraordinary manifestations of the Lord's anger against the nations, the Lord protects His covenant people (Is. 25:4; Ps. 46:1).

Judah's experience of the Lord's protection in the midst of His wrath will deepen her knowledge of the reality of God's presence in her midst (in Zion, the Lord's holy and inviolable hill (2:27; cf. Ps. 46:4; Is. 8:18; 52:1, 2; Zech. 2:10; 8:3; Rev. 21:3).

The final scene of the drama is one of paradisiacal prosperity and blessing (cf. 2:19–26). fountain shall come forth. The temple itself will be the source of a life-giving stream (Ps. 46:4; Ezek. 47:1–12; Rev. 22:1, 2), which will water even the dry and barren valley where acacia trees grow.
Egypt (1 Kin. 14:25, 26; 2 Kin. 23:29) and Edom (Obad. 9–14), here representing all of Israel's enemies, will be in ruins after this judgment.
In contrast to her enemies, Judah and Jerusalem are blessed and promised perpetual habitation of the land (Jer. 17:25; Zech. 12:6) because "the Lord dwells in Zion" (v. 21).

Amos.note: Amos introduces himself and his prophecy, specifying the time when God's word came to him. The words of Amos. The prophet's messages are introduced with this formula (cf. Jer. 1:1). Amos is God's covenant lawsuit messenger, bringing God's suit against disobedient Israel. shepherds. The Hb. term probably refers to keepers of a particular kind of sheep known for its unusually fine wool. The king of Moab is noted as owning such sheep (2 Kin. 3:4). Tekoa. This village was five miles (8 km) south of Bethlehem. Because of its good pastureland, it supported many shepherds with their flocks. the earthquake. Since this earthquake was remembered in a region prone to seismic activity, it must have been of considerable magnitude, and it would have acted as a reminder of divine judgment, as in Zech. 14:5.

LORD. See note on Ex. 3:15. roars. As a shepherd, Amos knows well the terrifying roar of a lion on the attack (1 Sam. 17:34–37). The Lord Himself roars from Zion to announce His judgment (Jer. 25:30; Joel 3:16). These opening words of judgment set the tone for what follows. pastures \... withers. The Lord's judgment will affect the whole land, from the pastures to the forested top of Carmel, rich in orchards and vineyards (Lev. 26:19; Deut. 28:23, 24).

This series of prophecies begins with six Gentile nations: Syria, Philistia, Phoenicia, Edom, Ammon, and Moab. Some of the transgressions mentioned here have nothing to do with Israel or Judah. The sins listed are crimes against humanity and therefore God Himself. After addressing the sins of the Gentile nations, the oracles dramatically turn against Judah (2:4, 5) and Israel (2:6–16). 1:3 For three transgressions \... for four. This refrain, repeated with each prophecy, is an example of parallelism using ascending numbers for emphasis (cf. Ps. 62:11; Mic. 5:5). This standard device in ancient Near Eastern poetry is not intended to be taken literally, but means "for many transgressions." Damascus. David defeated and garrisoned this royal city of Syria (2 Sam. 8:6). During Solomon's reign Damascus broke free, with Rezon as king (1 Kin. 11:23–25). sledges of iron. The threshing sledge was a wooden board with teeth of iron or basalt fixed on the underside. An ox would pull the sledge over the grain while the driver stood on it. This symbol portrays how the Syrians treated Gilead with extreme cruelty (2 Kin. 13:7).

This refrain (1:7, 10, 12, 14; 2:2, 5) in each of the messages is also found in Hosea (8:14) and Jeremiah (17:27; 21:14; 50:32). Fire was widely understood in the ancient Near East to be an instrument of divine judgment. It was often used in warfare, and was considered one way that a god purged a rebellious people. This pagan understanding also reflects a truth revealed in Scripture: the true God will in fact judge by fire (2 Pet. 3:7 note). Hazael. The king of Syria (c. 841–801 B.C.), whose reign was predicted by the prophet Elisha (2 Kin. 8:13). strongholds. Fortified citadel-palaces of the nobility. Ben-hadad. A throne name, like "Pharaoh" in Egypt. Probably the third king with this name is meant. The first assisted Judah's king Asa against Israel's Baasha (1 Kin. 15:18–20). The second, Ben-hadad II, was assassinated by the usurper Hazael (2 Kin. 8:14, 15). Hazael's son, Ben-hadad III, was contemporary with Jehoahaz of Israel (2 Kin. 13:25). It was he who made Israel's army "like the dust at threshing" (2 Kin. 13:7).

The verb is often used to indicate annihilation by war (Josh. 23:4; Is. 10:7). the inhabitants. The Hb. term is lit. "the one who sits," possibly a reference to the king rather than the whole population. The same word is used of God sitting or enthroned as king in Pss. 2:4; 22:3 ("enthroned"); 29:10. Valley of Aven. Lit. "Valley of Wickedness." Possibly it refers to ancient Syrian Heliopolis, now called Baalbek, in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon. It was apparently a center for sun worship. The phrase itself may be an indirect reference to a pagan deity. Beth-eden. Probably a district about two hundred miles (320 km) northeast of Damascus (not to be confused with the Garden of Eden; cf. Gen. 2:8 note), and ruled by a Syrian vassal king. The point of the parallelism between the Valley of Aven and Beth-eden is to indicate that not only Damascus, but its territories as well, will be undone. Syria \... to Kir. The original home of the Syrians (9:7), Kir will become their place of exile.

The southernmost of the five Philistine royal cities, which are Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath, and Gaza. Located between Egypt and Canaan, Gaza was a natural center for trade. whole people. That is, an entire group of exiles (also v. 9). The Philistine trade included slaves. Prisoners of war usually became slaves, but here a whole population was sold into slavery. The apparent reference is to the capture and sale of Israelites during the reign of Jehoram (2 Chr. 21:16, 17). to Edom. Edom is an alternative name for Esau, the brother of Jacob/Israel (Gen. 25:30). Although originally closely related to the Israelites, the Edomites received Israelites as slaves from the Philistines. For its role in the Edomites' sin against their brother Israelites, Gaza, which stands for Philistia as a whole, is now sentenced.

A strong and prosperous Philistine capital city located eighteen miles (29 km) northeast of Gaza. Ashkelon. The third royal city, located halfway between Gaza and Ashdod on the Mediterranean coast. Ekron. The fourth royal city of the Philistines, located on the border of the territories allotted to Judah and Dan (Josh. 15:11, 45, 46; 19:43. Gath, the fifth royal city, is not mentioned because it had already been defeated by Hazael at the time Amos wrote (2 Kin. 12:17). Assyria was the primary instrument of judgment against all these cities, and all four are subsequently mentioned in Assyrian annals as vassals of Esarhaddon (681–669 B.C.) and Ashurbanipal (668–627 B.C.).

One of two major Phoenician cities (the other is Sidon) mentioned in the Canaanite Amarna letters (fourteenth century B.C.). The name itself means "flint." Tyre was built on a large rock in the sea and was considered virtually impregnable until the fourth century B.C., when Alexander the Great conquered the city by building a causeway to it. delivered up a whole people. See notes on v. 6. did not remember the covenant. This phrase denotes the keeping of covenant obligations and is a standard phrase in ancient international covenants or treaties (cf. Gen. 9:15; Ex. 2:24; Lev. 26:42). Amos is asserting that Tyre did not keep its treaties with Israel. of brotherhood. In the ancient Near East, kings entering into treaties styled themselves "brothers." So Hiram of Tyre called Solomon "my brother" (1 Kin. 9:13; cf. 1 Kin. 5:12), as he had a background of treaty relations with David (2 Sam. 5:11). Later, Ahab continued the close relation with Phoenicia by marrying Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, the king of Sidon (1 Kin. 16:31).

See note on v. 6. This listing of events from the reign of Jehoram possibly includes Edom's revolt and collusion with the Philistines and Arabs, who attacked Judah and entered Jerusalem, plundering the palace and deporting the royal household (2 Chr. 21:16, 17; Obad. 10–14).

Teman is a grandson of Esau (Gen. 36:11, 15). His descendant clan apparently gave its name to a region in the south of Edom, and to a village some fifteen miles (24 km) from Petra. Here, the region is meant. Teman was famous for wisdom (Job 2:11; Jer. 49:7). Bozrah. The northernmost Edomite city, some thirty-five miles (56 km) north of Petra. By mentioning its northernmost and southernmost regions, Amos consigns all of Edom to destruction.

The Ammonites descended from Ben-ammi, the offspring of the trickery and incest of Lot's younger daughter (Gen. 19:34–38). They lived between Aram and Moab. ripped open pregnant women. This particular atrocity was practiced by others, including Hazael of Syria (2 Kin. 8:12), Menahem of Israel (2 Kin. 15:16), and Assyria (Hos. 13:16). The apparent purpose was to eliminate descendants who might try to reclaim the land. enlarge their border. Ancient Near Eastern kings typically boasted that they extended the borders of their land. By doing so they fancied that they carried out the desire of their gods.

A short form of the fuller reference, "Rabbah of the Ammonites" (Deut. 3:11; 2 Sam. 12:26). This location is the modern Amman in Jordan near the spring that feeds the Jabbok River. The site is easily defended because it is surrounded by deep valleys and it has easy access to water sources. tempest \... whirlwind. In Scripture, the figure of a violent and destructive storm is often used for the tumult of battle, as well as for the anger of God, or indeed for both at once (Pss. 83:15; Is. 5:28; 17:13; 29:6; 66:15; Jer. 4:13; 23:19; 25:32).

According to regular Assyrian practice, a conquered king, his household, and his officials were taken together into exile. Under Shalmaneser III (858–824 B.C.), Assyria conquered Ammon, making it an Assyrian vassal.

According to Jewish tradition, these are the bones of the Moabite king Mesha. Such burning indicated special contempt and was thought to deprive the dead of peace in the afterlife. Josiah burned the bones of false priests on the altar at Bethel (2 Kin. 23:15, 16).

Probably the name of a major Moabite city and religious center (Jer. 48:41). The exact site is uncertain. Alternatively, the Hb. word might mean "towns," as the Septuagint translators understood it. Moab shall die amid uproar. The Hb. word used for "uproar" expresses a double entendre. It is associated both with the din of battle and with an archaic name for Moab, "the sons of tumult" (cf. Jer. 48:45). trumpet. This is the ram's horn (Hb. shophar), the signal horn of ancient warfare.
See note on 1:5.

The five oracles against pagan nations are concluded, and the southern kingdom of Judah is now addressed. Divine judgment moves ever closer to the northern kingdom of Israel, where Amos himself has prophesied (v. 6). rejected the law \... statutes. For rejecting God's revealed law, and so God Himself, they are particularly worthy of judgment (Deut. 4:39, 40). Judah's covenant privileges imply greater responsibility (cf. Luke 12:48). after which their fathers walked. "To walk after" is an idiom meaning to follow in obedience as a vassal or servant. Judah is following lies, and serving as the vassal of false gods or demons (Deut. 32:17; Rom. 6:16; 1 Cor. 10:20).

See note on 1:4. Jerusalem. The name means "city of peace." The Hb. word for "peace" (shalom) denotes not only the absence of war, but also the presence of prosperity and wholeness. Because Judah had not sought integrity in the Lord, she will see destruction, not peace. This prophecy is fulfilled more than 150 years later, when Nebuchadnezzar II conquers Jerusalem and burns every notable building, including the king's palace (2 Kin. 25:8–10).

The indictment of the northern kingdom begins — Israel is guilty of social injustice, sexual immorality, and religious abuses (vv. 6–8). sell the righteous for silver. A reference to the corrupt judicial system. Judges are willing to convict the innocent upon payment of a bribe. the needy. The Lord has a special concern that their rights be protected (Ex. 23:6; Jer. 5:28), but they are being sold into slavery even for insignificant debts (here symbolized by a pair of sandals). Slavery in ancient Israel, though permitted in some forms, is carefully limited by the law of Moses (see Ex. 21:2; Deut. 15:12; 1 Pet. 2:18 and notes).

Amos decries uncontrolled sexual passion. Such behavior is contrary to God's original intention (Gen. 2:21–24; Matt. 19:4–6), and it profanes God's holy name (Lev. 18:24). The Mosaic law prohibits sexual union among individuals closely related by blood (Lev. 18:6–18). While the Mosaic law does not mention this specific situation (the sharing of a common prostitute), the basic principle still applies. This is perhaps a reference to cultic prostitution; cf. v. 8.

They have engaged in fertility cult prostitution beside the altars, further profaning the Lord's name. There are many altars in Israel, including those at Bethel (3:14), Dan (8:14), and Gilgal (Hos. 12:11). Their sins of sexual license and idolatry are compounded in that they have slept on clothing taken as pledges for loans to the poor. Such garments are not to be kept overnight (Ex. 22:26; Deut. 24:12, 13).

Faithful to His covenant promises (Gen. 15:16–21), the Lord drove out the Canaanites (simply called "the Amorite" here) from the Promised Land. See note on Gen. 10:16. like \... the cedars. The description recalls the report of the twelve spies (Num. 13:32, 33), but also God's wrath against all that is lofty and proud (Is. 2:12–18). fruit above \... roots beneath. A poetic expression for complete destruction.
By reminding them of His covenant faithfulness (cf. Gen. 50:24; Ex. 3:8), the Lord presses His case against Israel's unfaithfulness.

The Lord sovereignly raises up prophets (Deut. 18:15–22), judges (Judg. 2:18), priests (1 Sam. 2:35), and kings (2 Sam. 7:12). The prophets serve as covenant lawsuit messengers, sent to recall the people to obedience. Nazirites. See note on Num. 6:1–21. The OT mentions Samson by name as a Nazirite (Judg. 13:4, 5). Samuel was probably a Nazirite as well (1 Sam. 1:11 note). The three basic vows of the Nazirite are to abstain from consuming alcoholic drinks, touching dead bodies, and cutting one's hair.

In contrast with the Lord's faithfulness, Israel has sought to defeat God's purposes by commanding His messengers not to prophesy, and by making the Nazirites drink wine (in violation of their vow). They have shown contempt for both the Lord and His law.
Just as a cart bogs down from the pressure of its contents and so becomes immovable, so Israel will be unable to flee (v. 14).
A vivid picture of helplessness: the fleet of foot will not escape, and the strong will not stand their ground.
All units of the army will fail before God's anger.

Even the bravest warriors cast away not only armor and weapons but also every impediment, including clothing, in the panic of their useless flight. Such naked flight is an utter humiliation. in that day. This phrase often indicates the Lord's day of judgment (Zeph. 1:7 note). Here it refers to the approaching day of Assyrian conquest.

God prosecutes a lawsuit against Israel through His servant Amos (cf. Hos. 4:1–19). 3:1 Hear this word. This solemn command occurs again in 4:1 and 5:1, and echoes commands to hear and obey the Lord in the original covenantal documents (Deut. 4:1; 5:1; 6:3). It occurs regularly in covenant lawsuit material (Jer. 2:4; Hos. 4:1).

In addition to cognition (Gen. 4:9), the Hb. word for "know" has a wide range of meaning, including sexual relations (Gen. 4:1). Here the term denotes God's sovereign choice, or election, of Israel as the object of His loving concern within a unique covenantal relationship (Ex. 19:4–6; cf. Deut. 7:7, 8). therefore. The Lord's gracious oversight of His people includes punishment for their sins precisely because He loves them too much to allow them to sin without discipline (Prov. 3:11, 12).

Amos presents a series of rhetorical questions, to which the answer in every case is quite clear. Their purpose is to emphasize that the message of Amos comes from the Lord. 3:3 walk. To "walk together" with someone here means to agree with his or her destination and route. Implicitly, the prophet "walks" with the Lord.
A silent hunter, the lion roars only after its victim's fate is sealed. Just as there is reason for the lion's roar, so also there must be a cause behind the prophet's utterance.
No bird is caught in an unbaited trap.

See note on 2:2. Siege is a fearful prospect in Amos's era, for it often results in starvation of the populace, followed by all the horrors of conquest: rape, pillage, slaughter, and burning. disaster. Lit. "evil." The OT teaches that the Lord is the creator of peace and of calamity (Is. 45:7). This does not mean that God is the author of evil, but rather that He sovereignly brings disaster or adversity on individuals and nations as just punishment. The curses pronounced in Gen. 3:14–19 show that the Lord brings such punishment.

The God who acts also reveals Himself and interprets His actions to and through the prophets. God revealed His plans for Sodom and Gomorrah to Abraham, the first "prophet" so designated in Scripture (Gen. 18:17; 20:7). his servants the prophets. Moses, the supreme OT prophet, is called "the servant of the Lord" (Deut. 34:5). Subsequent prophets are characterized by the similar phrase, "my servants the prophets" (Jer. 7:25; Ezek. 38:17; cf. Dan. 9:10).
Just as a lion's voice evokes fear, the voice of the Lord compels the prophets to proclaim His word (Deut. 18:18; cf. 1 Cor. 9:16).

The command is in the plural and apparently directed at the Lord's servants the prophets. Ashdod \... Egypt. Amos poetically summons the pagan nobility to look upon the injustice that reigns in Samaria. Israel (the northern kingdom) should have been more righteous, not less, than her pagan neighbors. It is ironic that these pagans should be called as witnesses to Israel's misbehavior. mountains of Samaria. Samaria is surrounded by mountains, from which the spectators are asked to view her. tumults. Or, "disturbances," as the word is translated in 2 Chr. 15:5. Such conditions result from sin and are the opposite of "peace" (Hb. shalom).
The ill-gotten gains from their violent and thieving behavior. The rich have plundered and looted the poor.
Assyria. The thought of this verse echoes the substance of the covenant curse for disobedience (Deut. 28:52).

According to ancient laws, shepherds are to demonstrate their diligence by rescuing a portion of a sheep taken by wild beasts (cf. Gen. 31:39 and note). The sheep of Israel will only be saved in a mutilated condition — in fact, the nation will be destroyed. with the corner of a couch. The rich recline idly on couches (as the Romans later did at their banquets), enjoying the luxury they have extorted from the poor (6:4).

The command here (in the plural) may be to the pagans who have been summoned as witnesses, or to the Lord's messengers, who are commanded to summon the pagan witnesses (v. 9 note). Or perhaps it is merely a general call to creation to be a witness to the broken covenant.

The phrasing here recalls the original covenant documents (Ex. 32:34). altars of Bethel. This is one of the primary worship centers at the time of Amos. More than a century before Amos's ministry, Jeroboam I made a golden calf for Israel to worship at Bethel in the north, as an alternative to worship at Jerusalem in the south, and installed an altar there (1 Kin. 12:25–33). Both altar and sanctuary were later destroyed by Josiah (2 Kin. 23:15). horns of the altar. In Amos's day, a fugitive can gain asylum by grasping the horns of the altar (1 Kin. 1:49–51), though the Israelites have been known not to observe this privilege (1 Kin. 2:28–35). Even this last resort for sinful Israel will be cut off.

The possession of both a summer and a winter house is a great luxury, affordable only by kings and the very wealthy. The Lord will destroy these multiple houses and decorated mansions. Assyria, God's instrument of judgment (Is. 10:5, 6), is expert at such destruction and plunder, as the vast wealth of Nineveh during this period amply testifies (Nah. 2:9). houses of ivory. Excavations at Samaria have uncovered a hoard of ivory pieces in the royal acropolis of the city. Most of them were found in the "ivory house" constructed by Ahab (see 1 Kin. 22:39). Many of the ivories are small plaques intended to adorn furniture, such as the "ivory beds" mentioned in Amos 6:4.

Through His servant Amos, God prosecutes a second covenant lawsuit against Israel. 4:1 Hear this word. See 3:1 and note. cows of Bashan. The wealthy women of Samaria, who have been raised and cared for like the prime cattle of Bashan, a fertile area east of the Jordan River (Deut. 3:1 note) and northeast of the Sea of Galilee.

The same phrase occurs one other place in the OT (Ps. 89:35). No oath can be greater or more final (Heb. 6:13, 14). fishhooks. The Assyrians of this period frequently lead prisoners by ropes attached to rings or hooks in their noses or lips.
This location is unknown.

These were important sites in the earlier history of Israel. Bethel was a sanctuary during the period of the judges, and Samuel judged both there and at Gilgal (1 Sam. 7:16). They became centers of syncretistic worship during the period of the divided kingdom (5:5). every three days. Although the Hb. word for "day" can stand for a year or for an unspecified longer period (Gen. 1:5 note), three literal days seem to be meant here. Israel's religious observances go even beyond what the law requires. Though enthusiastic about ritual, they have no living relationship with God.

The covenant law makes it clear that they are not to burn leavened bread as a sacrifice (Lev. 2:11; 6:17; 7:12). Amos sarcastically urges them to continue in their disobedience. for so you love. In the ancient Near East, the term to love had special significance in covenants: the vassal's "love" for the sovereign entailed obedience (Deut. 6:5; cf. John 14:15). The nation's disobedience has made it apparent to Amos that Israel loves rituals and idolatry rather than the Lord.

This section reviews what the Lord has done in punishment to warn His people and draw their attention back to Him. The emphatic phrase "I also" indicates the change of subject. All the disasters mentioned are threatened in the covenant document (Deut. 28). Israel should understand this and repent. But as the refrain repeats, "you did not return to me" (4:6, 8, 9, 10, 11). 4:6 cleanness of teeth. Their teeth are clean because they have nothing to eat. The covenant stipulations threaten hunger and want as a penalty for disobedience (Deut. 28:47, 48).

The winter rains from October through February are essential for the crops to begin their growth. The spring or "latter" rains of March and April will provide for mature growth (Jer. 5:24). The Lord promises these rains if Israel obeys His commands (Lev. 26:3, 4), but also warns that He will withhold them if they flagrantly and impenitently disobey Him (Lev. 26:18, 19; Deut. 28:23, 24).

The Lord threatens these in the covenant document (Deut. 28:22; cf. Hag. 2:17). locust. The Hb. word for this destructive insect probably derives from the verb meaning "to cut" (cf. Joel 1:4; 2:25). Ironically, the punishment described here is what the Lord had inflicted on Egypt (Ps. 105:34, 35), whose Pharaoh rebelled against God. Rebellious Israel has received the same punishment, and like Pharaoh has not repented.
The Lord had threatens a plague in His covenant with Israel (Deut. 28:21), along with all the diseases of Egypt (Deut. 28:60, 61). killed. Yet another covenant curse fulfilled (Ex. 22:24).

Similar or identical phrases are used in prophecies against Babylon (Is. 13:19; Jer. 50:40) and Edom (Jer. 49:17, 18). The devastation of Sodom and Gomorrah provides a symbol of God's judgment against sin (see Gen. 19:24, 25; Deut. 29:23 note). Here, God promises to overthrow Israel with equal thoroughness. a brand plucked out of the burning. Despite God's repeated mercy to His people (e.g., 2 Kin. 13:3–5; cf. Zech. 3:2), they remain ungrateful and unrepentant.

The phrase echoes Ex. 19:15–17, where, after three days of sanctification, the people met the Lord at Sinai. Then they met a God who was graciously forging a covenant with them. Now they will meet a God who is coming to judge their covenant disobedience.

This verse is in the form of an ancient Near Eastern divine or royal title: a series of titles or epithets used to describe the deeds or powers of a god or king. Here they describe the great King, who is abundantly able to carry out the curses He originally threatened in the covenant (cf. Is. 44:24–28). the Lord, the God of hosts. See note on Zech. 1:3.

. This literary section is made up of many short prophetic oracles. 5:1 Hear this word. See 3:1 and note. lamentation. As though in mourning for the dead, Amos pours out a lament for Israel. This literary device is frequently used in OT prophecy (e.g., Jer. 7:29; Ezek. 19:1; 26:17; 27:2; 32:2).

This term is used in other laments (e.g., 2 Sam. 1:19, 25, 27; 3:34; Lam. 2:21). Amos later uses the word to describe the "fallen" booth or house of David (9:11). virgin Israel. This kind of personification is used of Israel (cf. Jer. 18:13; 2 Kin. 19:21) and of other nations such as Babylon (Is. 47:1) and Egypt (Jer. 46:11).
The drastic military reversals described here perhaps echo the prophecy of such disasters in the covenant that are the punishment for flagrant, impenitent idolatry (Deut. 32:15–18, 28–30).

This is a passionate plea for repentance and a call to turn back to God. The Lord has promised to meet those who would seek Him, even in exile (Deut. 4:29; cf. Lam. 3:25). Tragically, the Lord's people often do not seek Him (Is. 9:13; Jer. 10:21).

See note on 4:4. Beersheba. This ancient city (Gen. 21:31–33; 26:23–25; 46:1–5) is located fifty miles (80 km) south-southwest of Jerusalem, and is apparently a destination for religious pilgrims from the north in Amos's day (8:14). Later, in the seventh century B.C., Josiah destroys the high places "from Geba to Beersheba" during his reform (2 Kin. 23:8). Excavations have revealed an Israelite temple here that was used from the ninth century onward. The temple has a structure similar to the temple in Jerusalem. It appears to have been created by the Israelites as a center for worship, but that temple is nowhere sanctioned by God's law. Gilgal \... exile. The words form an alliterative wordplay in Hebrew.

See note on 1:4. house of Joseph. Ephraim and Manasseh, the tribes descending from Joseph (Gen. 48:15 note), whose tribal areas contain Bethel (Ephraim) and Gilgal (Manasseh), both mentioned in v. 5. These northern sanctuaries will be destroyed. Beersheba, in the south, will escape the fire of judgment that will sweep through the northern kingdom. none to quench it. The Lord's judgment fire cannot be extinguished (Is. 1:31; Jer. 4:4; Matt. 3:12).
These often occur together in the OT as qualities of life the Lord desires (v. 24; Is. 5:7). wormwood. An herb found in Eurasia and North Africa that is poisonous in its pure oil state.

See note on 4:13. This majestic description of the Lord contrasts starkly with the previous verse. Pleiades. A star cluster in the constellation Taurus that features six or seven prominent stars visible to the unaided eye. In many ancient Near Eastern cultures, the stars were thought to be personifications of deities. Orion. In classical mythology, the constellation Orion is "the Hunter." In Job also, the Pleiades and Orion are named together as evidences of God's incomparable power and wisdom (Job 9:9; 38:31).

This verse contrasts with vv. 11, 12, which are in the second person. Such shifts of person are common in ancient Near Eastern writings of all kinds, and no significant difference of tone seems intended here. who reproves \... who speaks the truth. A reference to those who reprove falsehood in court and bear true witness there. Israel has come to hate such men, presumably because they threaten practices of corruption and dishonest gain (2:6 and note). in the gate. Much of a city's legal business in this era is transacted in its gate, a large passageway with adjoining rooms. Excavations at Iron Age cities such as Gezer and Megiddo have uncovered benches inside the gateways; this is where the elders of the city sat and deliberated (cf. Ruth 4:1, 2).

These are costly to build, in contrast to the mud brick houses in which many people live (cf. Is. 9:10). you shall not dwell \... you shall not drink. The curse of futility (failure to enjoy the fruit of one's labor) fell on the Canaanites as Israel dispossessed them from their cities (Deut. 6:10, 11). Now Israel will suffer the same fate, according to the words of Deut. 28:30 (cf. Is. 65:21–23; 1 Cor. 15:58).

Israel needs to realize that the Lord knows what they seem to imagine that He does not know (cf. Ps. 73:11; Job 22:13, 14). bribe. The Hb. term can refer to a common bribe (1 Sam. 12:3) or to a ransom for loss of life (Ex. 21:30).
This phrase explains why the prudent will be silent: the times will be so bad that the truth will not be tolerated.

For this thought of effective repentance, see Is. 1:16, 17. In 5:4 they were commanded to "Seek me," for only God is good (Matt. 19:17). that you may live. Obedience to the Lord will bring them security and prosperity (Deut. 28:1–14); but the verse points to a deeper truth, that to know God is life itself (John 17:3). God \... with you. This is the deepest need of God's people, expressed prophetically in the name Immanuel ("God is with us," Is. 7:14; cf. Matt. 1:23). as you have said. Israel complacently claims that the Lord is with them, despite their rebelliousness, simply because He has made a covenant with them (cf. Matt. 3:9).

See note on v. 10. remnant of Joseph. The northern kingdom of Israel is dominated by the tribe of Ephraim, descendants of one of Joseph's sons (Deut. 33:17 note). Though Israel is relatively prosperous and strong, the phrase anticipates the future, after God's judgment, when He will graciously restore a remnant of the people.
This possibly refers to professional mourners, who were common in the ancient Near East.

The laments over Israel will be taken up in every part of the land, since every part will be punished. I will pass through. The same verb appears in Ex. 12:12, where the Lord speaks of His impending judgment on Egypt. Ironically, because Israel has become as pagan as Egypt, He must now "pass through" Israel in judgment as well (7:2 note).

This second portion of ch. 5 discusses the day of the Lord and His rejection of Israel. 5:18 the day of the LORD. Ultimately, this is the great and terrible "day of the Lord" when He comes in judgment (cf. Is. 2:12; 13:6–13; Obad. 15; Zeph. 1:7, 14). Every OT judgment is also a "day of the Lord," and anticipates that final day. Joel describes it as a day of terrible judgment and destruction (Joel 1:15–20; 2:11). This time of judgment contrasts sharply with the redemptive outpouring of God's Spirit (Joel 2:28–32). darkness, and not light. The Lord alone has power to make day as dark as night, both literally and figuratively, in judgment (v. 8).
Amos vividly portrays the futility of trying to escape the Lord's judgment (Is. 24:17, 18).

In addition to denoting physical light, the Hb. word for "brightness" is associated with the Lord (Ps. 18:12; Is. 4:5) and with the righteous (Prov. 4:18, 19; Is. 60:3; 62:1). There will be no light of righteousness in the land, and no brightness from the Lord's favorable countenance. Judgment will be black and total, engulfing the whole land.

For a similar condemnation of empty ritual and sacrifice without repentance, see Mic. 6:6–8 (cf. Matt. 5:23, 24; 1 Cor. 13:3). 5:21 I hate, I despise. Two Hb. words here combine to express the attitude more forcefully than either could by itself. The result can be translated, "I reject with utter hatred." I take no delight. The language refers to burnt offerings. In the Mosaic covenant, the Lord declares that if His people are disobedient and unrepentant, He will "not smell" the fragrance of their offerings (Lev. 26:31).

The word for "noise" has a wide semantic range in Hebrew, but here it communicates a loud clamor or din (cf. 1 Sam. 14:19; 1 Kin. 18:41). The songs of the people are a loud disturbance, not pleasing to the Lord.

See note on v. 7. ever-flowing stream. The streams, or wadis, of the Middle East are rocky watercourses through which torrents rush in the rainy season, but which are dry at other times. The Lord desires righteousness that is like His own — dependable, strong, and constant.

Offerings were brought to the Lord during the wilderness wanderings (Ex. 18:12; Lev. 9:8–24). The question emphasizes that such offerings were not of primary importance to the Lord then, and they are not of primary importance in Amos's time either. Rather, He wants worship in spirit and in truth accompanied by true repentance.

Sikkuth (or Sakkuth) is an Assyrian deity associated with the planet Saturn. Kiyyun (or Kaiwan) is a Babylonian term for Saturn. Amos here refers to idols associated with astral deities that are carried in cultic processions. The Septuagint translates the Hebrew for "Sikkuth your king" as "tabernacle of Moloch" (the Hb. letters are similar), a reading quoted by Stephen in Acts 7:43. that you made for yourselves. OT attacks on idolatry often focus on the merely man-made nature of the idols (Is. 44:9–20; Jer. 10:1–5; Mic. 5:13).
Banishment beyond Damascus in Syria implies exile to Assyria, as the prophet's audience well understands. Exile far from home is the worst of the original covenant curses (Deut. 28:36, 64).

Zion (Jerusalem) and Samaria are the capitals of Judah and Israel, respectively. Like his contemporaries Hosea, Isaiah, and Micah, Amos is given prophecies that address both the southern and northern kingdoms (Is. 9:8–10:4; Hos. 6:4–11; Mic. 1:5). first of the nations. The same ironic Hb. phrase occurs in Num. 24:20 (referring to Amalek). Israel has become powerful and prosperous under Jeroboam II, and might fancy herself the first among the nations.

The identity of this city is uncertain, but it may be the Calno mentioned in Is. 10:9, which was conquered by Sargon II of Assyria in 710 B.C. Hamath the great. Located north of Dan on the Orontes River in Syria, it was restored to Israelite control by Jeroboam II (2 Kin. 14:23–25). Gath. One of the five major Philistine cities (1:6 note), Judah's Uzziah recaptured Gath from Syrian control (2 Kin. 12:17; 2 Chr. 26:6). Are you better \... is their territory greater. The precise historical context and meaning of this verse is debated. Some suggest that Calneh, Hamath, and Gath have been conquered at the time of this prophecy, and that Israel should therefore not expect to escape conquest either. Others contend that Amos mentions other flourishing capitals of the region to show that Israel is as great as they, perhaps implying that Israel's territory is not so small that aggressors will ignore it and attack these other cities instead.
Israel has enthroned violence, such as extortion and abuse of the poor, as a way of life, while also denying that the day of judgment is coming.
A symbol of wealth and luxury (3:15; 1 Kin. 10:22). calves \... stall. Choice calves are kept in stalls and fattened for special occasions. Such is the normal fare for the wealthy of Samaria.
An ironic comparison with David's musical interests. Unlike the Israelites, who pursue frivolous musical endeavors, David composed many psalms to the glory of the Lord (2 Sam. 23:1).

That is, from large bowls or basins. The same Hb. word is used for the large bowls before the altar at the temple (Num. 7:13; Zech. 14:20). The prophet's hyperbole vividly portrays the excesses of the city. Joseph. See note on 5:6.
This phrase is a Hb. wordplay on the earlier phrase, "first of the nations" (v. 1). Israel fancies herself the first among the nations, but will find herself leading the exiles.

A series of judgment pronouncements follow the indictments of vv. 1–7. 6:8 sworn by himself. Similar to oaths in Gen. 22:16; Ex. 32:13; Is. 45:23, here indicating that the judicial sentence is unalterable (Heb. 6:13 note). The Lord has no higher authority to swear by than Himself. pride of Jacob. This refers both to Israel's pride and to the very thing in which they have taken pride — their military strength. The word translated "strongholds" has the sense of "fortified palace" or "citadel."
The meaning seems to be that small remnants hoping to escape will be found and killed.

Lit. "a man's kinsman and his burner," probably one and the same individual. Fear of epidemics may require cremation instead of burial in this era. Or, the burning could be a fire in honor of the dead (Jer. 34:5). must not mention the name of the LORD. Previously, one might mention or invoke the Lord's name for help, since He is the God of Israel's covenant. But on the day of judgment one may not do this because the God of the covenant is coming in judgment (cf. Is. 48:1).

commands.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} "Behold" frequently introduces noteworthy events. Here it signals the pronouncement that the Lord is rousing Assyria, His instrument of judgment, to come against Israel (cf. Is. 10:5, 6). great house \... little house. Both the great houses of the wealthy and the small houses of the poor will be shattered by the coming judgment. This is a figure of speech called a merism, in which two opposites are all-inclusive: its use here demonstrates a total judgment. Here, as it often does in Hebrew, the word for "house" can also mean "household" or "family."

Obviously not; no one runs a horse on such treacherous footing. Neither will one plow on rocks. But Israel's injustice is just as absurd. A suggested reading of the second question, "Does one plow there with oxen," requires a different word division in the Hebrew and is attested by no ancient version. It is better to take "rocks" as understood, although not explicitly stated, in the second query.

Lo-debar is a border town in Gilead, Karnaim a city on the plain of Bashan on the way to Damascus. They are both on the east side of the Jordan River. Both were apparently retaken from Hazael by Jehoash (2 Kin. 10:32, 33; 13:25), but later conquered by Assyria (2 Kin. 15:29). Respectively, the names mean "nothing" and "horns." A wordplay is intended, by which Amos says that Israel rejoices in the conquest of nothing (the conquest of Lo-debar, soon to be taken by Assyria, is short-lived), and boasts of having taken "horns" (symbolic of military strength in the ancient Near East) by their own strength. Their conquests amount to nothing, and their strength will melt away before the Lord's judgment.
Assyria. Lebo-hamath \... Brook of the Arabah. The northern and southern boundaries of the kingdom as restored by Jeroboam II (2 Kin. 14:25).

This long section contains four visions (7:1–3; 7:4–6; 7:7–9; 8:1–3) and an autobiographical section related to the third vision (7:10–17). The first two visions have the following structure: (1) the Lord gives the vision; (2) Amos intercedes; (3) the Lord relents. Conversation between the Lord and His prophet is an integral part of the visionary experience. 7:1 locusts. This Hb. word, occurring only here and in Nah. 3:17, denotes swarming locusts just hatched. latter growth \... king's mowings. This verse seems to indicate that the first crop (the "king's mowings") represents the king's share (cf. 5:11; 1 Kin. 12:4), while the farmer and his family depend on the second harvest for survival. Destruction of this second crop by locusts places the population at risk of starvation.

The Hb. word for "grass" is general; all vegetation is destroyed, not just crops. In Hebrew, the whole phrase echoes the description of the locust plague in Ex. 10:12, 15 ("every plant in the land"). The Lord will punish Israel just as He punished Egypt before the exodus. please forgive. Amos mediates and then pleads for God to show compassion on Israel.

Moved by intercessory appeal, the Lord is willing to relent concerning an intended punishment (cf. Ex. 32:12, 14; Joel 2:13; Jon. 3:10; Jer. 18:8). See note on Gen. 6:6. He has sworn that He will relent if the people repent.

See note on 1:4; Is. 66:15, 16. great deep \... land. The "great deep" could be the Mediterranean Sea, although the same phrase is also used of the chaotic subterranean waters (Gen. 7:11 note), and of the Red Sea at Israel's crossing (Is. 51:10). The prospect of a fire that will devour sea and land echoes the covenant judgment warning in Deut. 32:22. The language exceeds what happened in the OT, but foreshadows the last judgment (cf. 2 Pet. 3:10; Rev. 21:1), of which all previous judgments are but types.

This and the fourth vision (8:1–3) have the same structure: (1) the Lord gives the vision; (2) the Lord questions Amos; (3) Amos replies; (4) the Lord explains and judges. Similarly structured visionary experiences are recorded at Jer. 1:11–16. a wall built with a plumb line. Most interpret this image to portray Israel as being judged in order to see if the people up to God's standard. Others, following another analysis of the words (the word translated "plumb" resembles the Akkadian, or Assyrian, word for "tin"), render this "a wall of tin." The same "wall" symbolism in Egyptian literature stands for military capability (cf. "wall of bronze," Jer. 15:20; and "iron wall," Ezek. 4:3). If this second interpretation is correct, the use of an Akkadian word for the metal indicates the source of the military power that the Lord will use to judge Israel. with a plumb line in his hand. See note above. Many interpret this phrase as a reference to God's covenant law, His standard of judgment. Others render this phrase "with tin in his hand," a probable reference to Assyrian power, anticipating that He will put "tin" (i.e., Assyrian power) in the midst of His people (v. 8).
No longer will the Lord pass over their transgressions (Mic. 7:18).

These high places are traditional sites of pagan Canaanite worship (Deut. 12:2; 2 Kin. 17:10–12). The sanctuaries are for idolatrous or syncretistic worship. The appearance of these pagan worship centers in Israel demonstrates that the people did not meet God's standards. house of Jeroboam \... sword. Jeroboam himself might not die by the sword, but his household or family will be affected. Apparently, Jeroboam later died a natural death (2 Kin. 14:29), his son Zechariah was murdered (2 Kin. 15:10).

This autobiographical section apparently relates to the third vision, telling the reaction of Amaziah to the prophecies of Amos. 7:10 the priest of Bethel. Amaziah is probably the chief priest at the shrine of Bethel, and a representative of the priestly status quo. Amos has conspired. The political implications of the prophet's preaching are apparent. Jeremiah, too, was wrongly considered a traitor because of his prophecies against Judah (Jer. 26:11; 37:11–13; 38:1–6).
Probably an allusion to the prophecy in v. 9. Amaziah misquotes Amos so as to make Jeroboam feel more personally threatened.

Probably this means "earn your living by prophesying there in Judah." Although it is appropriate for a prophet to be paid for his work (1 Sam. 9:6–8; but cf. Mic. 3:5, 11), Amaziah accuses Amos of being merely a prophet for hire. Amaziah's commands here are an example of the sin of commanding the prophets not to prophesy (2:12).

From the time when Jeroboam I established idolatry at Bethel (3:14 note) the kings of Israel have had a major influence on the cult. Amaziah is concerned for the sanctuary of his earthly king rather than for the sanctuary of the great King, the Lord. Ironically, Amaziah as the religious official is concerned only about protecting his earthly interests — and he charges Amos with conspiring against those interests (v. 10). A future generation of priests likewise puts to death Jesus, the greatest of the prophets, out of a wrong concern to protect their own kingdom and temple (John 11:48).

Unlike other prophets, Amos's original vocation was not the prophetic ministry, nor is he one of the so-called sons of the prophets (i.e., disciples of the prophets; 1 Kin. 20:35; 2 Kin. 2:3, 5, 7, 15). He is not a paid professional prophet. Amos may also be signifying that he is performing this function by the election and call of God. herdsman. See note on 1:1. dresser of sycamore figs. One who treats the fruit by appropriate cutting to ensure superior sweetness once the fruit is ripe. Amos is skilled in more than one trade (1:1 note).

took me \... my people Israel.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Amos flatly rejects Amaziah's accusation (7:12) and stresses his divine call to prophesy. The same phrasing is used for the Lord's choice of David as king (2 Sam. 7:8). The prophet's allusion to David's call indicates that the Lord has the sovereign right to choose both kings and prophets — and that His prophets have every right to prophesy at the "temple of the kingdom" (v. 13).
See 2:12 and note; 7:12, 13.

Either by being ravished at the fall of the city, or out of desperation after the loss of family and wealth (cf. Deut. 28:30). your sons and your daughters. Sons and daughters are often punished along with parents for covenant transgressions (Deut. 28:32, 53; Jer. 5:17; Ezek. 24:21). Violent death is a typical covenant punishment (Is. 3:25; Jer. 39:18). die in a unclean land. Exile will be especially distasteful for the priest Amaziah: by living in a pagan land, he will become ritually unclean. See note on Lev. 11–16. Israel \... land. Amos sarcastically quotes Amaziah's own words from v. 11 back to him.

The Hb. words for "summer fruit" and "end" are similar, and are skillfully brought together here for effect. The vision of summer fruit indicates that the "end has come" for Israel. In addition, the appearance of summer fruit also denotes the end of the harvest period. never again pass by them. See note on 7:8.

The Lord will no longer tolerate the noise of the temple songs (5:23), which will turn to the wailing of bereavement when the Lord comes in judgment. that day. See note on 5:18. many dead bodies. An abundance of corpses is typical in defeated cities in the ancient Near East, especially when conquered by the Assyrians (Nah. 3:3).
God charges Israel with social injustice, commercial dishonesty, and indifference to holy days.

The New Moon festival is celebrated every fourth week, with various offerings (Num. 28:11–15). The Sabbath, observed every week, is founded on God's acts of creation (Ex. 20:8–11) and redemption (Deut. 5:12 note). Work is forbidden on these days. ephah small \... balances. Such dishonest business practices are against the Lord's law, and will result in His judgment (Lev. 19:36; Deut. 25:14).

See notes on 2:6. chaff of the wheat. Lit. "the refuse of the wheat." By mixing the chaff with the actual kernels of wheat, the estate owners cheat the buyers of their grain. These owners add to the good wheat that which falls the floor and is supposed to be discarded in the wheat threshing process.

This phrase may refer to the Lord Himself, or to the land of Israel, which is elsewhere called "our heritage \... the pride of Jacob" (Ps. 47:4). The oath in this verse dramatically introduces the forthcoming punishments. See note on 6:8.

Each year the Nile rises and overflows its banks, flooding the countryside and leaving rich deposits of silt. The imagery is used here to depict a coming flood of judgment — the upheaval of the Assyrian invasion (cf. Is. 8:7, 8).

See note on 5:18. I will make \... darken. Though such idolatry is strictly prohibited by the covenant (Deut. 4:19), Judah and Israel have engaged in star and sun worship (5:26 note; 2 Kin. 23:5, 11). The assertions here affirm that the Lord alone is God, and the sun is merely one of His creations (Gen. 1:16 and notes). the earth. Or, "the land," since the land of Israel is to be punished. The phrase directly recalls the plague of darkness that the Lord brought upon the land of Egypt (cf. Ex. 10:21, 22; Ps. 105:28). Here again, the Lord is about to judge Israel in a manner similar to His judgment of Egypt.

This coarse material is worn as a sign of mourning to indicate that the pleasures of life no longer matter to the mourner (Gen. 37:34; 2 Sam. 3:31). baldness on every head. Shaving the head is a sign of mourning. It is prohibited in the Sinai cov­enant (Lev. 21:5; Deut. 14:1), perhaps because it is a pagan practice of bodily disfigurement that disgraces God's image (Is. 15:2, 3; Ezek. 27:30, 31). Ironically, it is prophesied for Israel and Judah (cf. Is. 3:24; Mic. 1:16). bitter. A term describing the ultimate consequences of sin (2 Sam. 2:26; Prov. 5:4).
This curse stems from the covenant law (Deut. 32:20; Hos. 3:4). So also in the period of the judges, when sin abounded (Judg. 21:25), "the word of the Lord was rare" (1 Sam. 3:1).
A standard phrase in the ancient Near East denoting "the ends of the earth," this lit. means "from the Mediterranean to the Persian Gulf."
Even the young and robust will be at the end of their strength (cf. Is. 51:20). thirst. The focus is on physical extremity (cf. 4:7, 8), though spiritual thirst may be in view as well (v. 11).

This is likely a play on words: the Hb. word for "guilt" sounds like the name of the Canaanite goddess Asherah, the consort of Baal. To swear by a god in the ancient Near East of Amos's day implies the recognition and worship of that god. Israelites are commanded to swear only by the Lord (Deut. 6:13; 10:20; cf. Jer. 5:7; Zeph. 1:5).

In the other four visions, Amos was an intercessor or respondent to the Lord's questions (7:1–8:3 note; 7:7 note). In this vision, however, Amos has no active role but simply records what he sees. 9:1 Strike the capitals. That is, of the pillars. The command seems to be for an angel (cf. 2 Sam. 24:16; 2 Kin. 19:35) to destroy the temple by striking its pillars, bringing their capitals down on the heads of those within (cf. Judg. 16:29, 30).

Although the people may think that they can escape judgment, they will not find refuge from God's pursuit. 9:2 Sheol \... heaven. This pair poetically expresses the comprehensive nature of God's dominion (Ps. 139:7–12; Is. 7:11).

See 1:2 and note. bottom of the sea. In contrast with the height of Mount Carmel. Since Carmel is on the coast of Israel, further flight will lead one into the sea. serpent. This sea monster is perhaps the Leviathan of Is. 27:1. These lines of poetry assert the Lord's sovereignty over all creation; none can escape His justice.
One of the covenant curses for disobedience (Deut. 28:41).

This section constitutes a short divine title (4:13 note), identifying the Lord as judge. 9:5 touches \... melts. For similar expressions of the Lord's awesome power, see Ps. 46:6; 104:32; Nah. 1:5. rises \... sinks. See note on 8:8.

Lit. "like the sons of the Ethiopians," the dark-skinned tribes south of Egypt (Gen. 10:6). Sinful Israel has rejected the covenant and is no more privileged than the Ethiopians, who are in a far land and do not reside where God has chosen to make His name dwell, namely, the Promised Land. Egypt \... Caphtor \... Kir. By making Israel's exodus from Egypt poetically parallel (and hence implicitly equal) to His dealings with other nations, God tells Israel that she has become no better than the pagans. Caphtor. Crete. Syrians from Kir. See note on 1:5.
Israel. not utterly destroy. A graciously chosen remnant will survive.
