The Lord will scatter His people among the nations, first by means of Assyria, which often resettles conquered peoples in different parts of its empire. as one shakes. Figuratively separating the wheat (the faithful) from the chaff (the sinners), the experience of exile will serve to purify the nation of Israel (v. 10).
Denial of judgment, like denial of guilt, is characteristic of sin.

Amos concludes with an oracle of promised restoration ordered as follows: (1) reconstruction (v. 11); (2) conquest (v. 12); (3) fruitful abundance (v. 13); (4) rebuilding and replanting (v. 14); (5) enduring security (v. 15). Amos assures his readers that once the judgment of exile is past, restoration is as certain as was dispersion. 9:11 In that day. Possibly "the day of the Lord." It is here depicted as the time of Israel's deliverance (Zeph. 1:7 note). booth. The "booth" represents the dynasty of David that, to the eyes of the prophet, is as good as fallen. But the tabernacle of David will be rebuilt. In Jesus, the greater Son of David, the dynasty of David has been reestablished (Matt. 1:1; Acts 15:16, 17).

Though subject to divine judgment (1:11, 12), a remnant of Edom will be brought under the redemptive kingship of David's Son. Edom, and indeed all the nations, will benefit from coming under the dominion of this future King (Ps. 2:8). In Acts 15:16, 17, James applies this passage to God's taking a people for Himself from among the Gentiles and including them in the church. and all the nations. The addition of this phrase points to the fulfillment of the covenantal promise to Abraham that he would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4, 5). who are called by my name. This phrase tells us that some, not all, from every Gentile group will come under the dominion of David's Son. Only those who bear God's name among all the nations will be included. The phrase (lit. "upon whom My name is called") indicates subordination to His name and sometimes is used of Israel's subordination to God's covenant lordship (Deut. 28:10; Jer. 14:9). Amos foresees that the Lord will take possession of the remnant of all nations and will reign over them in a covenantal relationship through His messianic King (Acts 15:13–17).

A prediction of abundance, indeed more than abundance, follows the prophecies of disaster and desolation. The culmination of the Lord's redemptive work through David's greatest son, the Messiah, is portrayed in terms of endless cycles of fruitfulness that are reminiscent of Eden but surpass it (cf. Joel 3:18).

Lit. "turn the captivity of my people," a recurring phrase in the prophetic covenant lawsuits (Jer. 29:14; Ezek. 16:53; Hos. 6:11). rebuild \... inhabit \... plant \... drink. These blessings reverse the earlier futility curses (see 5:11 and note).

The Lord promises lasting safety for His people. God's covenant with David promises an eternal kingship (v. 11; 2 Sam. 7:10). David's greatest son, Jesus Christ, will guarantee redeemed Israel's permanent blessedness. the land that I have given them. See note on Gen. 13:15. The phrasing harks back to God's cov­enant with Abraham and his descendants (Gen. 12:1, 7; 13:14–17; 15:18; 17:8). The physical Promised Land is but a type of the New Israel's life in Christ; it points forward to the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb. 11:13–16; 12:22–24) and eternal inheritance (1 Pet. 1:3–5). The covenant land promise finds final fulfillment in the new heavens and the new earth (Rev. 21:1–22:6).

Obadiah.note: A supernatural revelation to the prophet's inner sight or hearing. Obadiah introduces the message he received from the Lord about Edom. Thus says the Lord GOD. God revealed the content of the prophecy (cf. 2 Pet. 1:21). This raises the moral quality of its severity above human vengefulness to the purity of divine justice. Edom. The bitterness between Edom and Israel began in the patriarchal period. God blessed Isaac and Rebekah with twin sons, Esau and Jacob (Gen. 25:21–26; cf. Mal. 1:2, 3; Rom. 9:10–13). The personal rivalry between Jacob and Esau (Gen. 27), from whom the nations of Israel and Edom descended, developed into longstanding national conflict (Ex. 15:13–15; Num. 20:14–21; 1 Sam. 14:47; 2 Sam. 8:13, 14; 1 Kin. 11:14, 15; 2 Kin. 8:20–22; 14:7), though Israel was directed to treat the Edomites with consideration (Deut. 23:7, 8). The descendants of Esau settled in the largely mountainous area stretching south from the shore of the Dead Sea for one hundred miles (160 km) to the Gulf of Aqabah, Because of its hostility, Edom also symbolically represents the enemies of God's people (Is. 63:1–6). Let us rise against her. Speaking for his people, the prophet sees divine significance in the news of a conspiracy against Edom. Behind the human plot the Sovereign Lord is at work. That such news has reached Obadiah's ears in connection with this vision is no coincidence; it is a token of the prophecy's fulfillment.

God declares war on Edom, resolving to have it humiliated (vv. 2–4) and looted (vv. 5–7) by other nations. No wise statesman or brave warrior in Edom will withstand the assault (vv. 8, 9). Edom, which has been cruelly indifferent to Judah's woes (vv. 10–14), will fall.

The Hebrew word for "rock" (sela) is also the name of a fortress city in the rocky heights of Edom (probably to be identified with the later Petra). The rugged mountain terrain of Edom deters invasion from without and encourages complacency within. 3, 4 Edom's arrogant question ("Who will bring me down?") is answered with God's solemn resolve ("I will bring you down").
Once ordinary robbers loot enough to satisfy themselves, something is left behind, but the armies the Lord will bring against Edom will exhibit no such restraint.

The conspiring nations of v. 1 turn out to be Edom's own allies. It is a matter of justice that Edom should be betrayed by friends, having stabbed his "brother Jacob" (v. 10) in the back. Probably these past tense verbs refer with absolute certainty to future events that will engulf Edom.
Though wise and mighty, Edom is no match for the Lord.
The personal name of a descendant of Esau (Gen. 36:11), which is also used for the Edomite nation.

Edom is doomed because she broke the law of brotherly compassion by joining, in malicious merriment, with God's enemies as they destroyed Judah. The interplay between "your brother" in v. 10 and the invading "strangers" and "foreigners" here is powerful. The exploitation of a brother's adversity has shown that Edom's true loyalty is toward getting ahead in the world, in disregard of moral and spiritual absolutes. The seeds of Edom's moral character were sown by her ancestor Esau, who showed that he cared more for earthly enjoyment than for God's kingdom by despising his birthright of covenant blessings and marrying Hittite wives (Gen. 25:29–34; 26:34, 35; cf. 27:46–28:1). Translated into NT terms, Edom embodies the spirit of "the world" (1 John 2:15–17) and serves as a symbol for the enemies of God and His people.

The day of divine retribution will destroy all God's enemies and vindicate His people, through whom He will execute judgment. 15 day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. For the day of the Lord, see Is. 2:11, 12. Now the prophet sets the judgment of Edom against the larger backdrop of God's moral reckoning with all nations. This episode with Edom is only a small preview of God's judgment; He will not stop until He has cleansed His world of all His enemies. The connection between Edom and the rest of the nations is their shared rebellion against God.

The Edomites' drunken revelry on the sacred temple mount in Jerusalem is answered in kind with the cup of God's wrath forced to the lips of Edom and of all the nations that have desecrated the things of God (cf. Jer. 25:15–29).
No longer the victim of pillaging armies, Mount Zion will again be holy, pure, cleansed for God.

The survivors (v. 14) of Judah will rise up like a blazing fire of divine wrath to consume Edom, leaving her not a single survivor. Although powerful in Obadiah's day, from God's perspective in that same day Edom is as good as dead. the LORD has spoken. Like a signature, this clause emphasizes the finality of God's intentions. He has committed Himself.

God's exiled people will return to occupy the land of their inheritance, and its boundaries will be restored and expanded. 19 God promises His people that the boundaries of the Davidic kingdom will be restored in the south ("Mount Esau," the territory of the Edomites), the west ("the land of the Philistines"), the north ("the land of Ephraim and \... of Samaria"), and the east ("Gilead").

While some understand this term as referring to those who have been saved, the Hebrew term is active. It seems to describe the Lord's provision of deliverers for His people, like the judges of old (Judg. 2:16; Neh. 9:27). Their rule will bring peace and security to the land. This verse foreshadows the Messiah and His dominion when this promise is consummated (Rev. 11:15). the kingdom shall be the LORD's. While all created reality is the Lord's right now (Pss. 47:2; 145:13), Obadiah is making a different point here — that the kingdom will be the Lord's because He will judge His enemies and deliver His people with finality. God will be all in all (cf. 1 Cor. 15:28), and His glorious, triumphant people will reign forever with Him. In this promise, Judah will find hope for a future without Edomite persecution. Here, too, the church finds hope for the future, when "the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ" (Rev. 11:15).

Jonah.note: The book of Jonah falls into two main divisions, each introduced by the sentence, "Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah." The first division comprises two sections: the call, flight, and judgment of Jonah (ch. 1), and the thanksgiving psalm (ch. 2). 1:1–17 This passage depicts Jonah's disobedient response to his commission as a prophet to go to Nineveh, but it does not tell us Jonah's reason for fleeing from God (which is not revealed until 4:2). Here we witness Jonah's interaction with the Gentile sailors, which involves a theme prominent in the book's second division — the Lord's mercy to Gentiles. Despite Jonah's disobedience and hypocrisy, the sailors do not despise Jonah's God, but see the clear hand of the God of Israel and respond in worship. In contrast with Jonah, the Gentile sailors are careful to avoid personal sin before God (v. 14). The prophet of God is judged, but the Gentiles are spared, an event that foreshadows the response and sparing of the Ninevites in the book's second division. 1:1 Now the word of the **LORD** came to Jonah. With some variations, wording like this is used some 112 times in the OT to describe the giving of a divine message to a prophet. Jonah the son of Amittai. The recipient of the Lord's revelation is Jonah ("dove"), the son of Amittai ("loyal" or "faithful"). This designation identifies the prophet as the historical character of 2 Kin. 14:25, who proclaimed that Jeroboam II (793–753 B.C.) would recover territory from the Syrians to the north. Contrast Jonah's message to Jeroboam's kingdom with the words of Amos and Hosea, who prophesied during the period of Israel's spiritual decline in the latter part of the eighth century (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

The Lord's sovereignty over all the nations is implicit in the command to Jonah. He is the "Judge of all the earth" (Gen. 18:25). The last capital of the Assyrian Empire, Nineveh was on the east side of the Tigris River directly opposite the modern city of Mosul in northern Iraq. The site has been extensively excavated and boasts a long and rich history. It is noteworthy that Assyria exacted tribute from an earlier Israelite king named Jehu (841–814 B.C.;2 Kin. 10:34 note). So from the perspective of the book's original audience, who lived in the eighth century B.C., Assyria is still feared in the memory of the Israelite people, even though the military threat of the Assyrians had temporarily subsided. call out against it. Though it is not disclosed here, Jonah understands that his pronouncement of the Lord's judgment on the feared and hated Assyrian Empire is reversible (4:2 note). He knows that his message offers the opportunity for repentance. their evil has come up before me. In the later prophecy of Nahum (seventh century B.C.), the Assyrian capital of Nineveh is the focus of divine wrath and is depicted as the embodiment of evil and cruelty (Nah. 3:1–7). In Nahum's day, the Assyrian war machine is guilty of horrendous atrocities. In 612 B.C., that empire would itself fall victim to a cruel destroyer.

Precise identification of this Tarshish is difficult, though it is often taken to be the mining port of Tartessus in southern Spain. Sometimes, however, the term designates distant Mediterranean coastlands in general. In either case, Jonah has fled in the opposite direction from Nineveh. from the presence of the **LORD**. Because God is present even "in the uttermost parts of the sea" (Ps. 139:9), escape is impossible.

**LORD** hurled a great wind upon the sea. Jonah's God is creator and lord of the sea (Gen. 1:10, 21; Ex. 14:21; Mark 4:41). The ferocity of the storm is evident from the fear of these seasoned sailors and the fact that the ship is in danger of breaking up.

The casting of lots was a common form of divination in the ancient world, a device used to discover the will of the gods. This method of discerning the will of the true God was not forbidden in ancient Israel, for the Lord rules even over lots (Lev. 16:8–10; Num. 26:55; Josh. 18:6–10; Judg. 20:9; 1 Sam. 10:19–21; Neh. 10:34, 11:1; Prov. 16:33, 18:18; cf. Acts 1:24–26).

See note on Gen. 14:13. Jonah identifies himself in ethnic terms. The term "Hebrew" is commonly used by Israelites to identify themselves to foreigners (Gen. 40:15; Ex. 1:19; 3:18; 10:3). I fear the **LORD**. Jonah also identifies himself in religious terms. The word order focuses attention on the divine name. The Lord his God is not just a personal, family, or national deity. He is the supreme and sovereign God, creator of land and sea. the God of heaven. An old title (Gen. 24:3, 7) also commonly used in the Persian period after the exile (2 Chr. 36:23; Ezra 1:2; Neh. 1:4, 5; 2:4).

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}**LORD** appointed. The same Hebrew word also occurs three times in 4:6–8. Each instance indicates a startling example of God's sovereignty over the natural world. God's mercy is also displayed, as Jonah is saved in spite of his stubborn disobedience. a great fish. The species of whale or fish that swallows Jonah cannot be identified with certainty. Suggestions have included the sperm whale or a large shark. The fish is God's instrument to rescue Jonah from the depths of the sea ("the belly of Sheol"; 2:2). three days and three nights. Jesus referred to the book of Jonah to communicate truths regarding His own message and mission (Matt. 12:38–41; 16:4; Luke 11:29–32). He spoke of the "sign of the prophet Jonah" not only with reference to the three days and three nights that Jonah was in the fish (Matt. 12:39, 40), but also with regard to the efficacy of Jonah's preaching. Without benefit of a miraculous sign, the Ninevites recognized Jonah's message as one with divine authority, and they responded in repentance.

Jonah's response to God's judgment is framed as a thanksgiving psalm (v. 9). The cry of the prophet focuses on the desperate character of his situation by using terms typical in poetic descriptions of death or nearness to death. In his plight he looks to the Lord's holy temple, the physical token of the Lord's saving presence with His people. The psalm is a moving testimony to the heart of Israel's faith and to the heart of the prophet, but he still has much to learn. His vision of God's mercy is still too narrow at this point, as the final chapter of the book reveals. 2:1 Jonah prayed. Consistent with OT narrative style, the Jonah story is interrupted with a poem (vv. 2–9), a psalm of thanksgiving and celebration for the Lord's deliverance and mercy. The literary structure is typical of a thanksgiving psalm: (1) petition for deliverance (2:2); (2) review of crisis (2:3–6); (3) review of deliverance (2:6, 7); and (4) praise for deliverance (2:8, 9).

Using the poetic device of parallelism, Jonah's psalm is introduced in two couplets that tell of the prophet's prayer and the Lord's answer. Jonah acknowledges that he has been rescued "out of the belly of Sheol." Personified in this instance as having an insatiable appetite, "Sheol" can refer either to death itself or to the realm of the dead where the wicked go.

These verses contain a vivid recollection of the near-death crisis, its causes, and its results. Jonah's plight is the Lord's judgment on his disobedience. The brush with a watery grave is presented with graphic imagery: entanglement in seaweed, the silence of deep water, and waves swelling high above the victim.

For the prophet, the ultimate horror of death is separation from the presence of the Lord (Ps. 88:4, 5, 10–12). yet I shall again look upon your holy temple. The Jerusalem temple is the earthly location of the divine presence. Jonah longs for the communion with God that the temple affords. The prophet laments losing the same divine presence that he earlier sought to escape (1:3, 10).

Jonah was at death's door. His slow, silent descent through the depths, like a journey to the underworld, brought him to "the gates of death" just before his rescue (Ps. 9:13). you brought up my life from the pit. Here "pit" is used to describe the realm of death (Job 33:22, 24; Ps. 49:9; Is. 51:14). Despite the hopelessness of the circumstances, the repentant prophet is rescued from the realm of the dead and restored to communion with God.
**LORD**. The context indicates that this prayer is answered. The importance and effectiveness of prayer are again emphasized, as in v. 2 (cf. Heb. 4:16).

Recalling the ineffectiveness of the sailors' prayers and of their gods (1:5), Jonah condemns those who put their faith in idols. forsake their hope of steadfast love. This may be an indirect reference to the Israelites. The word translated "steadfast love" is hesed, which often describes God's covenant faithfulness to His people. This verse warns that those who worship idols abandon God's hesed toward them.

**LORD**. Like Joshua before him (Josh. 24:14, 15), Jonah declares his loyalty to the Lord and extols Him as the only source of salvation and deliverance. In imparting salvation to Jonah, the Lord moves the prophet from disobedience to repentance; in imparting salvation to the Ninevites, He will move them from idolatry to faith (3:5–10); in imparting salvation to the Gentiles in the new covenant era — as under the old covenant — He sovereignly moves them to faith and repentance (Acts 11:17, 18).

**LORD** spoke \... it vomited Jonah. Again creation responds obediently to the sovereign commands of the Creator (1:4, 15, 17). By grace, the fish has served as God's instrument to deliver Jonah to safety.

In this second division of the book, Jonah preaches the message God has commanded, and the people of Nineveh respond with genuine repentance (ch. 3). When the Lord turns from threatened judgment, the real reason Jonah fled the first time is revealed in the text: he feared that God would show mercy to the hated Assyrians (4:2). In the object lessons that follow, the wideness of the Lord's mercy and compassion is revealed (4:5–11).

Having learned that the call of God is irrevocable (cf. Rom. 11:29), Jonah responds to the Lord's renewed commission. Nineveh was. Some have suggested that the use of the past tense ("was") indicates that the city no longer existed at the time of writing. Given the city's destruction in 612 B.C. by the Medes and Babylonians, this interpretation would date the narrative sometime after the late seventh century B.C. The past tense does not preclude an eighth-century date, however, for it may simply indicate the status of the city when the prophet arrived. an exceedingly great city, three days' journey. Many commentators interpret these phrases as a reference to the physical size of Nineveh. Archaeological exploration has shown that the city was between seven and eight miles in circumference. Others suggest that the first formula should be translated "a very important city," or "a great city to God" (emphasizing its significance rather than size). The second expression (lit. "journey of three days") could indicate the duration of visit appropriate (in terms of ancient Near Eastern diplomatic protocol) for an emissary to such an important city. Alternatively, the expression "the great city" (1:2, 3:2; 4:11) could refer to "Greater Nineveh", a region that also included the cities of Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen (see Gen. 10:11, 12).

Jonah's worst fears are realized (cf. v. 10; 4:1, 2) when the people believe, repent, proclaim a fast, and adorn themselves in sackcloth (the traditional mourning garb of the ancient Near East). The repentance is swift and citywide. The narrator indirectly cites this repentance on behalf of the Ninevites to indict his Israelite audience for their lack of repentance and for their lack of zeal for holiness and righteousness.

An unusual way to refer to the king of Assyria. In the light of Assyrian politics during the mid-eighth century B.C., the term "king" can be used here of a strong provincial ruler who exercises control over the region of Nineveh. During this period, the authority of the king of Assyria is somewhat limited. he arose \... and sat in ashes. The king's response is as immediate and spontaneous as that of his subjects. Royal authority gives way to penitent humility. He exchanges his robes for sackcloth and his throne for a bed of ashes (cf. Job 42:6; Is. 58:5).

With the royal edict mandating prayer, mourning rites, and a fast for man and beast, Nineveh's repentance is complete. The inclusion of animals points to the thorough and genuine nature of their repentance. Later, it is customary among the Persians to include domestic animals in the rites of mourning.
This royal admonition addresses the most prominent of Nineveh's sins. Physical violence and social injustice are hallmarks of the Assyrian Empire during the biblical era (Nah. 3:1).

The king gives personal and corporate expression to the hope that genuine repentance may avert the divine judgment. The structure of 3:5–9 conforms to the typical OT pattern of reporting corporate repentance (Jer. 36:3; Joel 2): (1) threat of judgment; (2) penitent response; and (3) divine decision to withhold punishment.

The prophetic warning (v. 4) had an implied condition, namely, that judgment was imminent — if the city did not repent. In turning "from their evil way" the Nine­vites have met that condition. God relented. When the Bible narrates God's actions, it often does so in anthropomorphic terms, i.e., ascribing to God human characteristics. This change in God's actions does not imply a change in His sovereign will. The Lord's apparent change of mind (i.e., His sovereign choice to carry out His own action in a way that is appropriate to a human response) is fully compatible with God's sovereignty and immutability, since He ordains the means as well as the ends of His sovereign will (Jer. 18:7–10). See note on Gen. 6:6.

The book concludes with angry Jonah receiving a lesson in divine mercy and compassion from God Himself. Strikingly, the text does not explain how Jonah responds to this instruction. Instead, it ends leaving the reader with the contrast between Jonah's resentful attitude and God's great mercy to the Ninevites. 4:1 it displeased Jonah exceedingly. The Hebrew is particularly vivid (lit. "it was evil to Jonah as a great wrong"). Jonah expresses his emotion in the strongest language possible: his greatest fear before going to Nineveh was that the Lord would bestow forgiveness on Israel's most-hated enemy (v. 2), and this forgiveness is what has occurred.

The reason for Jonah's initial flight to Tarshish is revealed. Despite his blatant disobedience and narrow-mindedness, Jonah understands the character of God. Here he is echoing an important statement describing God's mercy to an undeserving Israel (e.g., Ex. 34:6; Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 103:8; Joel 2:13). Only here and in Joel 2:13 is the reference to divine repentance ("he relents over disaster") included (3:10 note), an inclusion appropriate to the context of Nineveh's repentance and deliverance.

Grateful for his own deliverance, Jonah still refuses to accept that of the Ninevites. Hoping that the Lord will execute judgment, Jonah leaves the city for a vantage point from which to view its destruction.

**LORD** God appointed a plant. See note on 1:17. Probably because of the shortage of timber in this dry region, Jonah's shelter is not adequate to provide protection from the hot Near Eastern sun. The type of vegetation provided is uncertain. Although some suggest the castor oil plant, which grows quickly to a height of fifteen feet (4.5 m), a climbing plant, like a gourd, is more likely.

The same divine hand that in mercy provided the great fish and the shade now brings a worm to kill the plant and a hot east wind to torment the bitter prophet. Jonah struggles to understand why God acts as He does, providing protection one day and removing it the next. The episode with the plant mirrors larger events. The plant provided temporary shelter to Jonah and Nineveh's repentance means that Israel is temporarily safe from Assyria's violent invitation. However, just as the plant falls away and Jonah suffers, a future generation of Ninevites will, within decades, revert to the empire's typical behavior and destroy the northern kingdom of Israel. Jonah cannot understand why God would permit this to happen. He cannot accept that God is willing pardon the people of Nineveh, who deserve to be punished for their wickedness.

The divine intention of the object lessons is revealed here. God's magnificent compassion for the people and animals He creates and sustains (v. 11) is contrasted with Jonah's petty concern for the plant (v. 10). The reader may recall Jesus' compassion as He looked upon the multitudes (Matt. 9:36; Mark 6:34; 8:2), and His statement in Matt. 10:29 that not a sparrow will fall to the ground apart from the Father's will. In its infancy, the largely Jewish NT church later wrestles with this issue of the wideness of God's mercy raised here in the book of Jonah, as the Lord opens the hearts of the Gentiles to obey the gospel (Acts 11:18; 15:14; 28:28).

Micah.note: The name Micah is an abbreviated form of Micayahu ("Who is like Yahweh?"). The town of Moresheth is located near Gath in the Shephelah, or foothills, of southwestern Judah. which he saw. The divine message to Micah takes the form of a supernatural revelation to the prophet's inner sight or hearing. The verb "saw" is related to the word "vision" (Nah. 1:1).

This prophecy has four parts: summons of the nations to attend the trial (v. 2); a symbolic vision of God overthrowing creation (vv. 3, 4); an accusation against the two capital cities (v. 5); and the divine sentence for Samaria to be destroyed (vv. 6, 7). 1:2 all of you \... against you. God's judgment of Samaria (vv. 6, 7) exemplifies and prefigures His judgment against all people who commit idolatry and social crimes. his holy temple. That is, His heavenly abode (Ps. 11:4).

Behind the march of the Assyrian army, the prophet sees the hand of God (cf. Is. 10:5, 6). The depth of divine judgment against Jerusalem and Samaria is vividly portrayed as a destruction of the created order itself. 1:3 high places. Whoever controls Israel's heights controls the land. This probably refers to such mountains rather than to the Canaanite shrines known as "high places."
These words link the symbolic vision with the historical overthrow of Samaria (vv. 6, 7), which is located on a hill (1 Kin. 16:24).

"Jacob" and "Israel" often occur together in Micah, referring to the entire covenant people. Sometimes "Jacob" represents the people as a whole (2:12; 3:1, 8, 9). The second occurrence of "Jacob" in this verse points to the northern kingdom of Israel (with its capital, Samaria) as distinct from Judah (with its capital, Jerusalem). In this book "Israel" generally designates Judah as representing the whole nation.

Ancient Near Eastern fertility religions involved ritual prostitution, an activity strictly forbidden to Israel (Deut. 23:17). The wealth that has been paid to the temple prostitutes and used to make idols will be taken by the Assyrians and used in the same way.

This lament has three parts: an introduction stating Micah's resolve to mourn Judah's exile (vv. 8, 9); a main body with a series of wordplays on the names of Judah's stronghold predicting Judah's fall and exile (vv. 10–15); and a conclusion calling the house of David to join in mourning rites because it will go into exile (v. 16). stripped and naked. A symbolic act referring to the threat of captivity (Is. 20:2–4).
Assyria's King Sennacherib reached Jerusalem's gate but did not take the city (v. 12; see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

Micah's lament over the fall of David's house recalls David's lament over the fall of Saul's house under similar circumstances (2 Sam. 1:20). The Philistine city of Gath should not be given reason to rejoice over the coming calamity.

Its location is unknown. The name sounds like a word for "beautiful" and is an ironic wordplay on the fate of its citizens taken into exile. Zaanan \... out. Despite its name, which echoes the Hebrew for "come out," this town will cower behind its wall and not "come out" to battle. Beth-ezel. Lit. "adjoining house." The Hb. word ezel resembles a verb meaning "withdraw" or "withhold." This town will withhold its protection from Judah because it has been annexed by the conqueror.
Though it has longed for good, this town, whose name sounds like "bitterness," will experience the harshness of defeat.

A major fortress town of Judah located twenty-six miles (42 km) southwest of Jerusalem, Lachish house a contingent of chariots. Here the reference to "steeds" (the Hb. term resembles "Lachish") perhaps implies that the chariots will be used for flight rather than for fighting. the beginning of sin. The precise nature of this sin is not explained. Many suggest that it involves the import of Egyptian horses for use in war (5:10; Deut. 17:16; 1 Kin. 10:28, 29), inducing Israel to rely on her military strength rather than on the Lord. daughter of Zion. A personification of Jerusalem (Zeph. 3:14 note).

This allusion to the dowry given by a father to his daughter as she departs for her husband's house (1 Kin. 9:16) is motivated by the similarity of Moresheth to the Hb. term for a "woman who is betrothed." The inhabitants of Moresheth-gath (the prophet's hometown, about twenty miles \[32 km\] southwest of Jerusalem and six miles \[10 km\] northeast of Lachish) will depart into exile. Achzib shall be a deceitful thing. The town's name closely resembles the Hb. term for "deceitful," a word used for the "deceitful brook" in Jer. 15:18. The town of Achzib (nine miles \[14km\] east of Gath) will disappoint the king of Judah.

The term sounds like Mareshah, another fortress town in the foothills south of Jerusalem, lying five miles (8 km) northeast of Lachish. The "conqueror" undoubtedly refers to Assyria. glory of Israel \... Adullam. As David fled to the wilderness cave at Adullam (2 Sam. 23:13), so the leaders ("glory") of Israel will flee. The body of the lament (vv. 10–15) begins and ends with literary references to David's career (v. 10 note).
A culturally recognized sign of bereavement that in normal circumstances is forbidden to Israel (Deut. 14:1).

This prophecy has three parts: (1) the accusation — evil and violent men unethically seize sacred property and destroy its owners (vv. 1, 2); (2) the sentence — the Lord sentences them to exile (v. 3) and loss of their lands to invaders (v. 4); and (3) the conclusion — the robbers are cut off from the covenant people (v. 5). The accusation and sentence are linked by a play on words involving "who devise wickedness" (v. 1) and "I am devising disaster" (v. 3), which are virtually identical expressions in Hebrew. As the powerful have taken fields away from Israel's families (vv. 1, 2), so the Lord will send an enemy army to wrest the Promised Land from them (vv. 4, 5). 2:1 in the power of their hand. They misuse their status to perpetrate oppression.
A family's property is a permanent, sacred trust from God (Lev. 25:10, 13). See note on Num. 27:1–11.
A reference either to God giving their land to the Assyrians or to the Assyrian conqueror distributing their fields to others as booty.
After the Babylonian exile the land will be redistributed (cf. Num. 26:55; Josh. 18:8–10), but neither the oppressors nor their descendants will then be present to claim an inheritance.

In this prophecy, Micah defends his message against those who seek to silence him. Micah rebuffs their command to cease (v. 6). Then the Lord accuses the powerful of exploiting the defenseless (vv. 8, 9) and sentences them to exile because they have defiled the land (v. 10). Finally, the people are condemned for desiring false prophets who tell them what they want to hear (v. 11). 2:6 The Hebrew of v. 6 is difficult to translate. Some suggest that Micah confronts false prophets who support the land robbers and who have sought to silence him. In support of this interpretation, the Hb. phrase rendered "thus they preach" (lit. "drip \[words\]") can be translated "they prophesy." Others argue that the greedy and corrupt leaders themselves have tried to silence the prophet.
From this point to the end of the chapter, Micah directly relays the word of the Lord.
The oppressed belong to Israel's middle class (Introduction: Date and Occasion).
The people have grown so spiritually inept that they will easily be deceived by a charlatan or false prophet.

Micah concludes the first section of his prophecy with a brief oracle of salvation. Expositors differ as to the particular event primarily in view. Some consider the passage to foreshadow the eventual return from the exile. The Lord will make a breach in the defenses of their captors and lead His flock back from the lands where they have been dispersed to the sheepfold of Jerusalem. Alternatively, the passage may refer to the divine deliverance extended to Jerusalem when Sennacherib overran much of the land in 701 B.C. This interpretation receives significant support from the similarity of language between 2:12, 13 and Isaiah's prophecy, "Out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant," which definitely refers to 701 (2 Kin. 19:29–31; Is. 37:30–32). The Lord will gather the people into the city for their preservation. He will then break out of the besieged city to deliver them by decimating the Assyrian army (2 Kin. 18:17–19:37). Either reading of a deliverance of God's chosen remnant anticipates the greater triumph of the Messiah, the great Shepherd-King (5:2–5). 2:12 Jacob \... Israel. The second interpretation above requires these to refer to Judah as representing the whole nation (1:5 note), whereas the first interpretation is not restricted in this way.

The three prophecies of this chapter announce the rejection and punishment of Israel's incompetent, corrupt leadership. First, the leaders' treatment of the oppressed people is likened to cannibalism (vv. 1–4). Second, the false prophets who led the people astray are condemned (vv. 5–7) and contrasted with Micah, who prophesies true revelations from God (v. 8). Finally, the corrupt political and religious leaders are condemned and their complacency is castigated (vv. 9–12). 3:1 And I said. An editorial addition indicating that Micah edited his own book (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). It marks the start of the second cycle of prophecies in this work (chs. 3–5). Jacob \... Israel. Both terms designate Judah as the covenant people (1:5 note).
Just as the magistrates have refused to hear the cries of the oppressed, so God will refuse to hear their cry in the time of judgment.
These false prophets are opportunists, tailoring their pronouncements of peace and security to the desires of those who feed them. See Jer. 28.
Those who have prophesied falsely will be judged and shamed by God's silence.
Micah is divinely inspired not to lull the people into a false sense of security and divine favor, but to expose their iniquity with insight and boldness.

Possibly to be related to the expansion of Jerusalem to accommodate refugees from the north and to the building projects undertaken during the reign of Hezekiah. The prophet Isaiah also highlights the corruption that exists within the city of Jerusalem during this era (Is. 1:14, 15, 21–23).

This prophecy is given in the days of Hezekiah (Jer. 26:17–19). Hez­ekiah's repentance and faithfulness (cf. Is. 36–38) mean that the complete fulfillment of Micah's words in the judgment of Jerusalem is delayed until 586 B.C.

Micah's prophetic vision shifts from impending judgment in the short term to the "latter days," when the messianic reign of God is established in Zion. The first part of this oracle (vv. 1–5) is virtually identical to Is. 2:1–5 (see notes there for further comment). 4:1 the latter days. (cf. Is. 2:2–4) The expression points to a new epoch, which, though in the hidden future, decisively alters the course of history. Here it refers to the messianic age, consummated in the new heaven and earth (Rev. 21; 22). mountain of the house of the LORD. As part of the old covenant, the earthly religious center has been eclipsed by the coming new order (Heb. 8:13). as the highest of the mountains. Pagan gods in Micah's day also have sacred mountains with temples. By being raised above them, God's eternal house (here symbolized by the temple on Mount Zion) will be established among the nations as the center of true worship.

See note on v. 1. assemble \... gather. The same verbs as in 2:12, indicating that this prophecy is a development and expansion of what was said earlier. and those whom. Perhaps better translated "even those whom," a further description of the same group.

Just as God preserved a remnant that survived Sennacherib's invasion (2:12, 13 note), so also a remnant will survive the later Babylonian exile. strong nation. A prophecy that finds final fulfillment in the church (1 Pet. 2:9, 10).

Jerusalem (i.e., the new Jerusalem; Rev. 21, c.f. Heb. 12:22) will become a fortified tower around which the inhabitants will gather for protection. Isaiah anticipates a similar transformation of Jerusalem (Is. 65:17–25).

This prophecy explains that Israel's present distress (the "now" of vv. 9, 11) will bring glorious salvation — liberation from the later Babylonian exile (vv. 9, 10) and release from Sennacherib's siege (vv. 11, 12).

The pain of judgment (exile, loss of king and land) for the remnant must precede the birth of the messianic age that will follow. to Babylon. Micah's vision goes beyond the immediate Assyrian threat to Judah, and anticipates what happens more than a century later when there is no deliverance for Jerusalem from the Babylonians.
The focus is again on the circumstances of Micah's own day. many nations. The Assyrian imperial army consists of mercenaries from many nations.

This prophecy also moves from present distress ("now"; v. 1) to the Messiah's coming and victory (vv. 2–5). See Introduction: Christ in Micah. 5:1 cheek. This insult to Israel's leader signifies that Jerusalem will fall to its Babylonian attackers, and all power to resist will be gone (cf. 2 Kin. 25:4–7).

Contrasts the coming ruler with the current humiliated representative of David's line in v. 1. Bethlehem Ephrathah. Lit. "house of bread, fruitful." The previously undistinguished town of David's birth (1 Sam. 16:1–13), situated five miles (8 km) southwest of Jerusalem. Though the Davidic line of kings would temporarily cease (v. 3), God would yet raise up a ruler from David's family to reign forever — Jesus Christ Himself (2 Sam. 7:12–17; Matt. 2:6). for me. All occurs to advance the divine plan. from ancient days. This expression can also be translated "from days of eternity." Indeed, "from of old" is rendered "from everlasting" in Hab. 1:12, where it is applied to God Himself (cf. "eternal God," Deut. 33:27). Israel was without a Davidic king from the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. until the coming of Christ. she who is in labor. A reference either to Mary, the mother of Jesus, or to the faithful remnant (see 4:10). rest of his brothers. Thousands of Israelites were converted after Pentecost (Acts 2:41, 47).
The messianic ruler is assigned the LORD's role (2:12) of caring for the flock.

The ruler as "Prince of Peace" (Is. 9:6; cf. also Zech. 9:10) will provide completely for the well-being and security of His people. It is this aspect of Christ's mission on which Paul reflects in Eph. 2:14. the Assyrian. After the first line of what is now designated v. 5. Micah switches his focus back to contemporary conditions. Assyria, the besieging nation of v. 1, here represents all enemies opposed to God's kingdom. seven \... eight. Seven is the number of perfection. There will be a more-than-sufficient supply of leaders to expand Christ's kingdom.
A reference to an ancient king, whose empire included both Babylon and Assyria (Gen. 10:10, 11).

This oracle has two parts: a prophecy that the remnant will become God's instrument of life and death (vv. 7, 8), and a petition for God to defeat all His foes (see v. 9 and note). These statements find fulfillment in the church (2 Cor. 2:14–16). 5:7 delay \... wait for. As rain proceeds from the divine initiative, so the remnant depends on God to refresh the earth.
This verse is perhaps better translated as a petition for divine victory ("Let your hand be lifted against"). How the Lord accomplishes this victory is described in the following section.

God will cleanse His people (vv. 10–14) and cut off the pagan nations (v. 15). God's salvation cannot come except by stripping His people of all vain and false military confidence (vv. 10, 11), sorceries (v. 12), and idolatry (v. 13).

God's vengeance will take place when He reveals His full sovereignty by delivering His people and punishing their guilty oppressors. Only the sovereign Lord Himself has the ultimate right to use force to protect His kingdom, and the exercise of force by an individual or community without divine authorization springs from unbelief (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19–21).

The third cycle of Micah's oracles (chs. 6, 7) opens with a classic example of the prophetic covenant lawsuit in which the Lord pleads the terms of the covenant against His disobedient people. The message opens with a judgment scene in which the Lord is plaintiff, Micah is His envoy, the mountains are witnesses, and Israel is the accused (vv. 1, 2). God's own covenant faithfulness is then attested as He first gives Israel opportunity to voice any complaints (v. 3) and then recounts His mighty acts of deliverance (vv. 4, 5). The demand for covenant righteousness is then proclaimed — a righteousness consisting not merely in empty ritual but in heartfelt obedience (vv. 6–8). 6:1 Arise, plead your case. The Lord commands Micah, as His representative, to prosecute God's case against the people. Micah obeys the command (v. 2). mountains. The Lord uses the enduring mountains as witnesses to the covenant mediated by Moses (see Deut. 4:26; 30:19 and note; 31:28; 32:1).
The Lord recognizes them as being in covenant bond with himself.

These verses are framed by references to Egypt (from which Israel was delivered) and Gilgal (where Israel entered the Promised Land, Josh. 4:19). All God's saving acts during Israel's formative period are included: the Passover and exodus, guidance by the pillar of fire and cloud, miraculous provision of food and water, the provision of able leaders ("Moses, Aaron, and Miriam"), and victory over enemies. God's wonderful provision for His people during this period foreshadows the church's experience with Christ (John 6:33; 1 Cor. 5:7; 10:1–4).

Through the rhetorical escalation of sacrifices ("calves \... thousands of rams \... rivers of oil \... my firstborn"), Micah displays the absurdity of Israel's dependence on empty ritual and sacrifice to earn divine favor. Such reliance shows a profound misunderstanding of God's grace, for Israel's salvation from Egypt (and ultimately from sin and death) was free and not earned (vv. 4, 5). Moreover, Israel's covenant obligations entail social justice and mercy, not mere liturgy (v. 8). See also Amos 5:21–24.

Or "prudently." These three divine requirements cover relationships with others, an individual's inner attachment to the standards of the covenant, and a lifestyle that gives due acknowledgment to God in every aspect of conduct.

This prophecy consists of an address to Jerusalem (v. 9), an accusation of falsity in business dealings and speech (vv. 10–12), and a judicial sentence of disease and ruin (v. 13–15). The covenantal context is apparent as the punishment reflects the covenant curses specified in the Mosaic law (v. 15; Lev. 26:20; Deut. 28:40, 51). Those who live in rebellion against their covenant king will find every endeavor blighted as He frustrates them from achieving what they want.
The bitter conditions foretold in these verses reflect the futility curses described in Lev. 26:26; Deut. 28:30, 31, 38–40.
Omri and Ahab ruled over the northern kingdom during the ninth century B.C.. Notorious for their wicked deeds, they actively promoted the worship of Baal throughout Israel.

Micah laments that no righteous are found (vv. 1–4), and he bemoans the resulting social and national confusion that is both the result and punishment of their sin (vv. 4–6). Particularly striking is the description of the breakdown of family order. Micah concludes, however, with his confidence that beyond God's judgment lies salvation (v. 7). 7:1 I have become \... summer fruit. In his search for the righteous, Micah compares himself to a vinedresser searching for choice fruit after the best of the season has past.
One characterized by loyalty to the covenant (cf. text note on 6:8). no one upright. This verse explains the allegory of v. 1.

As with a person searching for choice fruit but finding only briers and thorns, a righteous person cannot be found. watchmen. A metaphor for the prophets who have announced the coming judgment (Ezek. 3:17; 33:7).

This passage is later used in Jewish extrabiblical apocalyptic literature to describe the conflict that will accompany the final day of the Lord. Jesus quotes v. 6 in describing the conflict associated with His coming (Matt. 10:35–39; Luke 12:51–53).

This concluding hymn consists of four stanzas: (1) Lady Jerusalem in her fallen status confesses her sin and her faith in the Lord (vv. 8–10); (2) the prophet promises that she will become a sheepfold offering salvation to the world under judgment (vv. 11–13); (3) Micah prays that the Lord will again miraculously shepherd His people (v. 14), which the Lord promises to do (v. 15), and Micah then prophesies that the unbelieving enemy will be conquered (vv. 16, 17); and (4) the people celebrate God's forgiveness and faithfulness with a hymn of praise (vv. 18–20). 7:8 darkness. A dungeon without light is an apt figure for a city under divine judgment.
The Lord's righteousness will be manifested in faithful Israel's salvation (vv. 8, 9) and her unbelieving enemy's destruction (v. 10).

See 4:1, 6; 5:10–15. The last day is symbolically depicted by the restoration of Jerusalem's city walls (v. 11) and the extension of the boundaries of the land to limits prophesied by Moses and enjoyed under David and Solomon (v. 12; Gen. 15:18; Ex. 23:31; Deut. 11:24; 1 Kin. 4:21, 25).
The Euphrates.
Outside the elect's secure borders is universal judgment. The last judgment is ultimately in view.
Fertile areas east of the Jordan renowned for their cattle and sheep.
These are signs of humiliation in the face of overwhelming divine power. They will no longer taunt Israel or listen to the vain boasts of others.

Micah, whose name means "who is like the Lord?" (1:1 note), perhaps employs a wordplay on his own name to emphasize God's pardoning grace. because he delights in steadfast love. The word used here (and in v. 20) for "steadfast love" is the familiar Hb. term hesed. It refers to God's utter commitment to the covenant relationship that He sovereignly instituted and that persists despite the waywardness of His covenant partners. He delights to display His resolute and effective commitment by securing pardon and acceptance for them — no matter the cost or difficulty involved. He will thus ensure that the relationship disrupted by their sin will be consummated in accordance with His purpose.
As God began Israel's journey by casting the Egyptians into the Red Sea (v. 15; cf. Ex. 15:1–5), He will conclude her history by casting His people's iniquities into the depths.
God's loving fidelity to the patriarchs is the basis of the church's hope (Rom. 4:17; Gal. 3:7–9, 29).

Nahum.note: Title of the book. See Introduction: Title and Author; Date and Occasion. oracle \... vision. "Oracle" focuses more on the contents of a weighty prophecy of judgment (Hab. 1:1 note), whereas "vision" relates to the process by which God communicates to the prophet's inner perception. Nineveh. In Nahum's day, it is the capital city of the Assyrian Empire and situated on the east bank of the river Tigris at its confluence with the river Khosr. Repeatedly, it is described as "a great city" in Jon. 1:2; 3:2–4; 4:11. Here, Nineveh stands for Assyria as a whole and conveys the idea of evil forces arrayed against the people of God.

The introductory hymn (vv. 2–8), which in the Hebrew forms an incomplete acrostic poem, movingly describes the Lord as the Judge of all, with power to accomplish His will. 1:2, 3 The Lord's character forms the key to what follows. The repetition of "the LORD" emphasizes that it is the God of the covenant who is described. 1:2 jealous. This attribute refers to God's passionate reaction against any infringement on His holiness or any attempt to share His glory. His jealousy demands undivided loyalty and reveals itself as wrath against rejection of Him or His lordship. avenging \... avenging \... takes vengeance. True to His nature, the universal Judge leaves no sin unpunished and metes out the just deserts of the wicked (Deut. 32:35). The threefold repetition of the Hebrew word for "avenge" strongly emphasizes an inescapable and appropriate retribution. adversaries \... enemies. Those who oppose God's sovereign reign over the whole earth. 1:3 slow to anger. A well-known confession of God's patience with sinners (Ex. 34:6; Jon. 4:2). great in power \... by no means clear. God's patience never implies that He is weak or that He condones evil (Gen. 18:25; Ex. 34:7).

The prophet offers a poetic portrayal of the power of the Lord as manifested in His control of nature on occasions of intervention in behalf of His people (Ex. 14:21, 22; Ps. 18:7–15; Matt. 8:26). The godly Israelite recognizes the Lord's work in nature. But nature is not confused with God or worshiped as God; it is the theater of His revelation.

These words vividly portray the power of God in subjecting the forces of nature, as at the crossing of the Red Sea (Ex. 14). sea \... rivers. Used here as poetic parallels (Is. 50:2; Ps. 74:12–15). The fertile pastures of Bashan to the northeast of Judah, the vineyards of Carmel to the northwest, and the forests of Lebanon to the north all wither when the hot desert wind, sent by the Lord, blows over them (Is. 33:9).

The displeasure of the approaching Lord fills the earth and its creatures with terror. All creation seems threatened when even the seemingly permanent things ("the mountains \... the earth") tremble and disappear.
The rhetorical questions emphasize the irresistibility of God's anger. Divine wrath is compared to fire (Deut. 4:24; Ps. 11:6; Heb. 12:29).

Whereas the subject matter of vv. 4–6 concerned nature, the focus now returns to God and His enemies (vv. 2, 3). 1:7 good. The term denotes the Lord's benevolence as the source of all true human well-being and prosperity, and is particularly a confession of His abundant covenant blessings and kindness (Ps. 73:1). The Lord's people experience His awesome power as holy love. When help is needed He is an impregnable fortress (Ps. 46).

Striking images of severe, all-encompassing judgment. The metaphor of a flood is used in Is. 8:6 of an invading army, but here it might literally anticipate what actually contributes to Nineveh's collapse (2:6). of the adversaries. A wordplay, since this may also be heard as "of her place," most probably hinting at Nineveh — brought out more fully below.

The downfall of the wicked, represented by Nineveh, will culminate in the comfort of God's people, Judah. 1:9 plot. All Assyrian strategies will be futile. Their struggle and their plans are against the Lord, who has decided on their destruction and will bring it about once and for all (Ps. 2).

Perhaps a reference to Ashurbanipal (see Introduction: Date and Occasion), or, more probably, to Sennacherib, the most powerful Assyrian aggressor against Judah (2 Kin. 18:13–18). "From you" is a feminine form referring to the city of Nineveh. worthless. The Hb. word suggests something demonic.

A comforting divine message assures God's people that the downfall of Assyria implies the end of their humiliation. 1:12 Thus says the LORD. A well-known prophetic-messenger formula. "They" refers to the Assyrians, and "you" to Judah.
Vivid poetic images of emancipation (Jer. 2:20; Ps. 2:3). God will break the power of the Assyrian oppressor.

The word emphasizes authority and certainty. "You" possibly refers to the Assyrian emperor, whose fate reflects that of the nation as a whole. your name. The elimination of one's name from memory reflects common Near Eastern curse formulas. Complete loss of power and prestige awaits the Assyrians. house of your gods. The temple and other objects of Assyria's trust and pride will also be destroyed. grave. The term denotes the final undoing of Nineveh, its king, and its people in 612 B.C.

This section is written in the prophetic present tense. Events still future are pictured as if already present, and events even more distantly future are portrayed as occurring at the same time with those happening much earlier. This vivid prophecy of judgment is a poetic "vision" (1:1; cf. Num. 12:6–8), and is not a precise and detailed historical account of events that later take place in 612 B.C. 1:15–2:2 See Is. 52:7. The approach of a herald of "good news," whose feet tread "the mountains" of Judah, will initiate a new period of grateful service to the Lord. The good news is summarized in the meaningful word "peace" (Hb. shalom), signifying not only the end of hostilities but also the return to normal, abundant living conditions and general well-being. This passage, together with Is. 53:1, is picked up by the apostle Paul in Rom. 10:15, 16. Keep \... vows. Periods of national crisis or foreign oppression often make celebration of the important temple feasts difficult, if not impossible, during the old covenant era. The "vows" made in the previous period of distress should now be fulfilled (Ps. 116:14, 17–19).

In sharp contrast to the call for Judah to celebrate, Nahum resumes his address to Nineveh with the ironic exhortation that it should prepare for an attack. has come. Nahum speaks as one whose "vision" (v. 1) permits him to be an eyewitness of the attack on Nineveh. scatterer. The Assyrians, who have destroyed many nations, including Israel, by scattering them over the face of the earth, will experience a similar fate. In August 612 B.C., the combined forces of the Medes and Babylonians destroyed Nineveh, and shortly afterward the Assyrian Empire collapsed.

God will restore the oppressed people to the happiness implied by the name "Israel." Jacob received this new name as a sign of his spiritual maturity and his willing acceptance of the destiny God intended for him from the beginning (Gen. 32:27, 28).

Probably a reference to the Lord's army (v. 2). The warriors and chariots of the attackers will fulfill His purposes. The armies of Assyria herself earlier were God's instruments to accomplish His purposes of judgment (Is. 10:5–7). red \... scarlet. These terms emphasize the awe-inspiring appearance of the approaching army, whether the color refers to their actual robes or to the bloodstains on them. Red colors were favored by the Babylonian army (Ezek. 23:14). spears are brandished. The Hebrew is difficult but conveys the general impression of ready eagerness for war.
Nineveh is a beehive of frantic soldiers. streets. Possibly open fields or plains outside the city; if so, the verse speaks of the approaching army and its chariots of war.

This may refer to the Assyrian king and his nobles, especially the military commanders. Alternatively, this verse may describe the attackers and their frenzied siege of Nineveh. The Hb. word here rendered "siege tower" usually refers to a movable structure shielding the besiegers of a city, technically known as a "mantelet" (text note).

The city of Nineveh was on the bank of the Tigris River, and a smaller river flowed through the city. Conflicting ancient accounts ascribe the fall of Nineveh to flooding when the enemy redirected the dams and sluices of the water system. The description in Nahum is manifestly poetic, however. The term "gates" could simply refer to the five gates opening (cf. 3:13) in the direction of the Tigris River with its tributaries and canals. palace. The seat of political and military organization.

Nineveh is personified as a woman, a queen, going into exile. Her "slave girls," the inhabitants of the city, mourn the fate of their mistress. Alternatively, "she" might refer to the goddess Ishtar, whose image is taken as plunder while the girls who served in her temple bewail their loss.
This striking image is often taken to portray Nineveh's full population and prosperity. Now it is drained away.
The Assyrian royal annals make numerous references to plunder being taken from conquered cities.
The merciless devastation creates terror and paralysis among the once-mighty Ninevites.

This closing section is a taunt song in which the striking image of a pride of lions that meets with destruction is employed to describe the imminent reversal of Nineveh's fortunes. God is the author of Nineveh's humiliation and disappearance. 2:11 Where. This rhetorical question emphasizes how the famous city will be reduced to oblivion. the lions' den. An apt image for Nineveh as the home of the aggressive and ruthless Assyrians, particularly since extant Assyrian texts often pre­sent the king as a lion.

The real secret of Nineveh's full and final downfall is revealed. Confrontation with Israel's almighty covenant God is fatal to the Assyrian Empire. I am against you. The opposite of the good tidings of salvation, "I will be with you" (Ex. 3:12; Josh. 1:5; Is. 43:2, 5). messengers. The voices of the Assyrian envoys dictating terms and exacting tribute will be permanently silenced from the face of the earth.

The expression of woe that opens this chapter controls its mood until the last verse. The various parts all contribute to its literary unity, and together they emphasize the irreversible doom of Nineveh. The prophet no longer focuses on Israel and Judah alone, but places the fate of Nineveh in a universal perspective. 3:1–7 These vivid scenes of violence, death, and destruction confirm the city's expected doom. The charges against Nineveh (vv. 1–4) and her penalties (vv. 5–7) are set forth in stark detail. 3:1 bloody city. The phrase emphasizes the merciless cruelty openly boasted by the Assyrians in their official records. lies. Deceitful diplomacy characterizes their international dealings (Is. 36:16, 17). plunder. See 2:12, 13. Friendly negotiations serve as a cover for rapacious behavior. In their insatiable lust for more they have moved constantly from one victim to another.

These poetic verses provide one of the most vivid portrayals of a battle scene in the OT. The staccato beat, economy of words, and gruesome detail all contribute to the image of action that reduces whole populations to "heaps of corpses" (v. 3). Views differ as to whether this describes how Assyria conquered other nations, or, more probably, how enemy forces will assault Nineveh with a savagery that matches her own previous conduct.

With a change of imagery, Nineveh is likened to a beautiful and seductive "prostitute" for whose favor "nations" and "peoples" are sacrificed. Service of the gods, warfare, and commerce are closely intertwined. Seduction by Nineveh's power and pomp implies apostasy from true religion and subjection to her "charms," a term probably indicating the totality of pagan religion (Is. 47:12, 13).
Retribution by the universal Judge is inevitable. See 2:13. lift up your skirts. The public humiliation by which harlots are punished in this era (Jer. 13:22; Hos. 2:3).
The image of the harlot is continued. She will be made an object of scorn and an example to deter others from doing the same.

The sight is so terrible that people will retreat from it in horror. So dreadful and truly deserved will be the disaster that no one will be found to mourn or comfort the nation in its downfall. who will grieve for her. The rhetorical question expects the answer "no one" and emphasizes that even those who have reluctantly supported Nineveh will have no regrets at her downfall.

The fall of Thebes was a well-known event that marked the peak of Assyrian expansion. If such a city could be overwhelmed, it is presumptuous for Nineveh to assume that she is invincible. 3:8 Thebes. The Greek name for No-amon, the city of the Egyptian god Amon. This ancient and magnificent metropolis of Upper Egypt fell to the Assyrians in 663 B.C. Located on the Nile some four hundred miles (645 km) up the Nile valley from Memphis, it may have had moats and canals as defenses. There is probably a figurative element in Nahum's emphasis on the sea. In Scripture, a river or sea is often an emblem for strength that only God can overcome (Ex. 15; Ps. 114:3–5; Is. 23:3, 4; Matt. 8:27). Alternatively, "sea" may be a Hebrew usage for any extensive body of inland water, such as the Nile, which was near Thebes (Is. 19:5).

The region to the south of Egypt. Egypt. The land to the north of Thebes. Though its extensive resources had been available to defend Thebes, they were insufficient to avert disaster. Put. Traditionally identified with Libya to the west, though others suggest an African location in the region of modern-day Somalia.
Such brutal practices were carried out to deter future uprisings among subjugated peoples (cf. 2 Kin. 8:12; Ps. 137:9; Is. 13:16; Hos. 10:14).

Apparently a figurative reference to the cup of the Lord's anger, from which all who defy Him are forced to drink (Is. 51:17–23; Lam. 4:21). Nineveh in her distress tries to hide and find refuge, but only the Lord provides refuge in times of trouble (1:7). Compared to Him, even the most powerful are weak and vulnerable (vv. 12–17). you will go into hiding. This could also be translated "you will be concealed." After its destruction in 612 B.C., the site of Nineveh remained abandoned until archaeological excavations commenced in the mid-nineteenth century A.D.
This telling image emphasizes that the normally impregnable fortresses are now not only desirable but also easy to take.
In the face of the approaching army, all the Assyrian troops are like women (i.e., not trained for warfare). All barriers to slow the enemy's advance, such as gates and bars, have been removed.
Frantic efforts need to be made to "strengthen \... forts" and to prepare for a lengthy period of siege. The imperatives are ironic; vv. 14–17 reflect the mood of a derisive taunt song.
Even the most strenuous efforts to avoid invasion are useless. The city and its people succumb to fire and sword.

Assyria's international trade and commerce bring people and wealth to Nineveh during the biblical era. Under pressure from outside, the self-interest of these traders has become clear. Having gathered like locusts, they seize what they can and disappear.

See text note. These two terms are rare in Hebrew and may be Assyrian loanwords. They probably represent important officials in the government of the vast empire. When things become dangerous they run away. Riches, power, and organization fail miserably as the nation collapses. sun rises. The appearance of the Lord's judgment will scatter His enemies as dramatically as the heat of day rouses and disperses sleeping locusts (cf. Ps. 84:11; Mal. 4:1–3).

The finality of divine judgment on the cruel oppressor will lead to universal rejoicing. These verses are reminiscent of funeral dirges and taunt songs of the period. 3:18 shepherds. A well-known metaphor for leaders indicates the subordinate rulers of the Assyrian king. asleep \... slumber. Striking euphemisms for death. Your people \... gather them. The pastoral image is extended to the people (or perhaps the army) as a flock of sheep. In the absence of shepherds, the people are scattered (cf. 1 Kin. 22:17).

Habakkuk.note: Often a technical term for a prophecy of judgment against a foreign nation (Is. 13:1; 15:1; Nah. 1:1; cf. Mal. 1:1 note). Habakkuk the prophet. See Introduction: Title and Author. saw. The divine message took the form of a supernatural revelation to the prophet's inner consciousness with no less clarity or vividness than physical sight or hearing (Mic. 1:1).

Habakkuk's first complaint: The prophet is grieved and shocked by how the wicked prosper at the expense of the righteous. The wicked in the covenant community no longer live like a chosen and saved people (Ex. 19:4–6). But Habakkuk is even more concerned about the Lord's apparent inactivity. Breach of the covenant is supposed to bring curses and judgment (Deut. 28:15–68). He therefore appeals to the Lord in language reminiscent of the psalms of individual complaint to redress a seemingly hopeless situation. Habakkuk's passionate dialogue and anguished wrestling with the Lord dominate the first part of the book (1:2–2:20). 1:2 how long. This impatient question, characteristic of the psalms of lament (Pss. 13:2; 62:3; Jer. 47:6), indicates both importunity and perseverance in the prophet's appeal to the Lord, the final judge in matters of covenant disobedience. shall I cry. This indicates the loud cry of someone in deep distress (Pss. 22:24; 30:2). Violence. This term summarizes the deliberate, brutal, and insensitive infringement of the rights and privileges of members of the covenant community. "Destruction" (v. 3) is concerned more with damage to property than malicious personal assault. you will not save. Habakkuk painfully observes the Lord's seeming indifference and inactivity in the face of undeserved suffering.

The question continues the complaint (cf. Lam. 5:20). iniquity. Lit. "labor" or "toil" that leads to distress, exhaustion, and despondency. strife and contention. Unchecked wickedness results in a divided community riddled with suspicions, accusations, and personal attacks.

Lit. "the law is numb." The word for "law" (Hb. torah) denotes the divinely revealed standard for covenant life. The power and influence of the wicked have rendered the law ineffectual because just judges cannot be found. Even so, there is still a righteous remnant in the land. the wicked. Those in Israel who spurn the Lord's will and law. They dominate society in Judah, preventing the righteous from receiving justice. 1:5–11 God's first response: The Lord is already at work. He will send the Babylonians to judge His people. He uses strange instruments against His unfaithful people — the terrifying Babylonians (cf. Is. 10:5, 6).

At the time of Habakkuk's complaint to God, the Babylonians have not yet come to a position of power in the ancient Near East. Everyone will be surprised by the coming of the Babylonians to punish the wicked in Judah.

The sovereign God of Israel controls every power in history, including the aggressive Chaldeans. Chaldeans. Also called Babylonians, or Neo-Babylonians, the Chaldeans took control in Babylon in 626 B.C. as the power of Assyria declined. They played a key role in the destruction of Nineveh, capital of Assyria, in 612 B.C. After routing the Egyptian army in 605 B.C., they established an empire that lasted until the Persians captured the capital city of Babylon in 539 B.C.
This describes the arrogance of the coming enemy whose standards of action and honor are entirely self-determined and self-centered, with no respect for the rights of others, let alone God.

Vivid images portray the speed and resolution of these fierce and overpowering warriors. evening wolves. Ravenous because they have not eaten all day, and therefore ferocious and unflinching in identifying and devouring prey.
The intimidating Babylonian armies look at obstacles as challenges and treat their opposition with contempt. pile up earth. Siege ramps built by attackers to gain access to a fortified city's walls.
Or "this his power is his god." Pride, especially the deification of one's own power, is offensive to God, who alone deserves our worship.

Habakkuk's second complaint: We do not know what length of time has elapsed between Habakkuk's complaints. He expresses his perplexity at the Lord's plan to use the wicked Babylonians to punish Israel because it seems to be in flagrant opposition to God's own revealed character. 1:12 from everlasting. As the eternal God of history and Lord of His people, He is free to choose the agents of chastisement. In faith, Habakkuk begins by setting out what he is sure of — God's character. my God, my Holy One. A personal relationship to the incomparable God, the Holy One, turns confusion into conviction that the present anguish will not be the end. We shall not die. This voices faith's confidence that the Lord will fulfill His covenant commitment to Israel (Jer. 31:36; 33:23–26). O Rock. This ancient Mosaic name for God emphasizes divine dependability and protection (Deut. 32:4 note).

How can the holy and all-powerful God, to whom sin is totally repugnant, permit evil to go unchecked and unpunished? traitors. Lit. "those acting treacherously." The reference is to the Babylonians. Habakkuk cannot fathom how the holy God can use such an unscrupulous and wicked nation to punish Judah, whose conduct is by comparison "more righteous."

A bold accusation by Habakkuk. If the Lord tolerates the evil actions of the Babylonians, He becomes responsible for the fate of their victims. like the fish. Imagery of Babylon as a fisherman catching helpless fish is developed in vv. 14–17. Fishing was an important activity in Babylonia, which was located in the region of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and was bordered on the south by the Persian Gulf. Some ancient Near Eastern wall reliefs portray victorious rulers carrying captives in fishnets. no ruler. There is no one to protect them. Kings in the ancient Near East were seen as the protectors of their people (1 Sam. 8:20). An implicit accusation may also be present here, since the Lord is the ultimate king and protector of His people (Deut. 33:5; Is. 63:18, 19).
The instruments of their success are idolized and worshiped (v. 11 note).

God's second response:Habakkuk receives an answer to his painful questions of 1:12–17. God will show that He is just and the justifier of those who have faith in Him. The final outcome of history will be worship of the one holy and just king (v. 20). The destiny of nations and individuals alike will be determined by their attitude toward God as expressed in persevering and faithful dependence or haughty rejection (Pss. 1; 2:2, 3). In the meantime, God calls on His people to live through persevering faith. 2:1 A transitional verse. Habakkuk's anguished questioning drives him to the fount of all wisdom to wait for an answer. His words express his determination to wait for an answer. God is sovereign in word as well as in deed — His revelation cannot be forced. watchpost \... tower. Military terms figuratively depict the prophet as a watchman on the lookout for a word from God (Is. 62:6, 7; Ezek. 3:16; 33:1–9).

In order that it might be preserved and transmitted (cf. Jer. 30:2; Nah. 1:1) as a long-term witness because the Lord's intervention will take time to develop. vision. See note on 1:1. so he may run who reads it. Perhaps a figure (though some suggest that Habakkuk actually writes an oracle on large tablets) indicating that Habakkuk's prophecy is to be publicized. Either the writing is to be so clear that a courier who is running with the tables can read them, or that its clarity will enable passersby to read without difficulty (i.e., "that one may read it swiftly").

A fixed period must elapse before the prophecy will be fulfilled, but this should not be regarded as failure or deception. Rather, this time can be endured with the Lord's guarantee of approaching fulfillment. Judgment on the Babylonians came (long after Habakkuk's vision) through Cyrus on October 29, 539 B.C.

The Lord here discloses the essential distinction He makes between the wicked, the Babylonians, and the righteous, the remnant of Judah. The wicked take paths that lead to death and defeat; the righteous by faith take a path that leads to life and victory. His distinction and the promise it contains for the righteous bring a word of comfort to Habakkuk. It also marks the turning point in his personal struggle over the Lord's use of the wicked Babylonians as a rod of judgment against His people. puffed up. The Babylonian king and kingdom, the embodiment of wickedness in the world. Habakkuk earlier described their arrogance (1:7, 10, 11). by his faith. Or "by his faithfulness." In context here, the Hb. word denotes steadfast reliance on the Lord, a trust that perseveres. In the midst of a land filled with wickedness (1:2–4) and subject to the wrath of God, the Lord promises that a righteous remnant in Judah will trust in the God who remembers mercy in His wrath (3:2). The Hebrew recalls the words of Gen. 15:6 and applies them to Habakkuk's situation. By faith, Abraham waited patiently for the fulfillment of God's promises (Heb. 6:15), and now Habakkuk and the remnant must wait patiently as well (v. 3; 3:16). Here Paul finds scriptural proof for the doctrine of justification by faith (Rom. 1:17; Gal. 3:11), and Habakkuk's word of comfort has been a key text for Protestant faith since the sixteenth century.

The arrogance and insatiability of the Babylonians is compared to a drunkard besotted with wine. Sheol \... death. It is proverbial in Habakkuk's day that death is like a devouring mouth always ready for more to die (Prov. 1:12; 27:20; 30:15, 16).

This section of woes forms a distinct literary unit. Prophetic judgments are presented here in a taunt song, a poetic form that mocks the defeated. 2:6–8 The first woe. Those who plunder others will themselves be plundered. 2:6 all these. Judah and all those who have suffered under the Babylonian oppressor. The prophecies of woe in vv. 6–20 are depicted in such general and proverbial terms that they acquire a universal applicability to the struggle of the persecuted righteous against the wicked. Woe. The Hebrew word is apparently an interjection derived from the funeral lament (sometimes rendered "Alas"; cf. 1 Kin. 13:30), but is often used in prophecies of judgment. pledges. The heavy tribute exacted by the Bab­ylonians is figuratively depicted as articles taken in security for debts.
The violence and bloodshed through which the Babylonians have gained their plunder cries out to be avenged (v. 11; cf. Gen. 4:10).

The second woe condemns those who seek security and economic gain at the expense of others. 2:9 nest on high. Birds of prey often make their nests in high and inaccessible places. Likewise, the Babylonians consider their position in world history to be secure (Is. 14:13, 14; 47:7).

A striking personification. This cry against injustice will emerge from building materials stolen from others or purchased with unjust gain. 2:12–14 The third woe pronounces judgment on the ruthless but futile efforts of the tyrant to perpetuate his fame.

Babylonian inscriptions confirm the high premium placed on building activities. Nebuchadnezzar, who used subjugated peoples as forced laborers, took special pride in his building of Babylon (Dan. 4:30). Such projects involved loss of life and were paid for with the spoils of war.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold} \... nothing. God sovereignly ensures that the efforts of the proud to perpetuate their own glory amount to nothing. Instead, the "earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord" (v. 14).
No longer merely the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34, 35) or the temple (1 Kin. 8:11), but the whole earth will acknowledge divine glory.
The fourth woe pronounces judgment on Babylon's sadistic and humiliating treatment of others.
]{.rsb-studynote-bold}'s right hand. This biblical metaphor indicates divine retribution (Is. 51:17–23). What the Babylonians have done to others will be done to them (vv. 7, 8).

Military campaigns usually caused extensive damage to plants and animals. Trees supplied building materi­al and firewood (Deut. 20:19, 20); wild and domestic animals were killed for food. Many cedar trees were lost during the Babylonian campaign against Lebanon (Is. 14:8). God's concern for His creation should be noted.
The fifth woe denounces idolatry, the worship of false gods, as futile and foolish (Is. 44:9–17; 57:12, 13).

Lit. "palace," the heavenly sanctuary from which the Lord, the Great King, rules His world (Ps. 11:4). let all the earth keep silence. A sharp contrast is drawn between the silent idols (v. 19) and the living God, before whom all others must keep silence. The woes of judgment on the proud and wicked culminate in the universal silence of worship in the glorious presence of the incomparable God (v. 14; Ps. 46:10).

This chapter records the persevering prayer of Habakkuk. In moving hymnic style, Habakkuk responds (vv. 16–19) to the Lord's revelation (2:2–5) of His imminent intervention in history on behalf of His people (vv. 3–15). As the Babylonians represent the proud and wicked on their way to ruin, Habakkuk now exemplifies the righteous faithful persevering and already rejoicing in hope of the Lord's promise of life. 3:1 prayer. Here perhaps a synonym for hymn (Ps. 72:20). The musical and liturgical notations in the heading, text, and conclusion of this prayer are like those commonly found in the psalms. See Introduction to Psalms: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

The invocation or prologue to the hymn. heard the report. Habakkuk's patience in standing before the Lord (2:1 note) is rewarded by a vision based on God's mighty deeds in the past. revive it. Habakkuk's prayer is that the Lord would be as present and active as He was in the time of Moses. in wrath remember mercy. A prayer for the gracious combination of divine judgment tempered by mercy.
