Habakkuk's prayer portrays a theophany, or visible self-manifestation of God, using imagery found in the traditional descriptions of God's appearances at the exodus from Egypt, at the giving of the covenant law at Sinai, and during the conquest of Canaan (Ex. 15:1–18; Deut. 33:2, 3; Judg. 5:4, 5; Pss. 18:10; 68:7, 8, 24; 77:16–20). 3:3 Teman. The name of Esau's grandson represents the land of Edom (Amos 1:12 note). Mount Paran. A mountain in the wilderness of the Sinai peninsula (Deut. 33:2). The imagery of vv. 3–7 is that of God's march to His holy mountain and, subsequently, His act of leading His people to take possession of the land He had won for them.
Habakkuk pictures ominous dimensions of God's coming in judgment (Deut. 28:21, 22).
These are possibly alternative names for one people or area, perhaps for nomads from the Sinai peninsula.

The prophet here directly addresses God. The approaching Lord is the invincible divine warrior who demonstrates His lordship over the cosmos. Similar poetic imagery is known from Canaanite and other mythologies. 3:8 rivers ... sea. The Lord has demonstrated His power over the river Nile (Ex. 7:14–24), the Jordan (Josh. 3:14–17), and the Red Sea (Ex. 14:21–30).
See Josh. 10:12, 13.

The Lord of nature also has absolute power over the forces of history. He comes to deliver His people and judge the wicked. 3:12 threshed. An agricultural image derived from the way grain was threshed by violent beating or trampling (Amos 1:3 note).

In the past the Lord came out of His sanctuary for the salvation of His people in distress. This is what Habakkuk is expecting Him to do again. for the salvation \... anointed. Or, "to save Your Anointed." Perhaps a synonym for the chosen people of Israel (cf. Ps. 105:15), but more probably a reference to the Davidic kingship as it comes to final expression in the Messiah (Ps. 132:10).
Habakkuk refers again to the exodus history in which God displayed His undisputed dominion over natural and historical forces.

Together with v. 2, this verse encloses the hymn of vv. 3–15 with autobiographical references at beginning and end. my body trembles. Habakkuk describes in physical terms the profound effect that the divine self-revelation has had on him (cf. Jer. 4:19). The Lord has answered his painful questions and will hear his prayer. I will quietly wait \... of trouble. Awed by the divine majesty, Habakkuk can rest in the assurance that the Lord will judge the wicked.

Even when crops and herds fail (a horrifying thought in the context of an agricultural economy), and society lives with hunger and poverty, Habakkuk's trusting expectation will not be crushed. Hope and trust transform his fear of the future into the desire to rejoice always in God his Savior (Rom. 8:35–39).

, the Lord, is my strength.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} Total dependence on the sovereign covenant Lord is Habakkuk's key to life. feet like the deer's \... tread on my high places. This striking figure portrays the strength and confidence that the Lord imparts to the righteous (Is. 40:29–31). choirmaster. See note on v. 1.

Zephaniah.note: Superscription. See Introduction: Title and Author; Date and Occasion. word of the LORD. The phrase refers to revelation received from the Lord and communicated through a prophet.

The prophet begins with an announcement of universal judgment (vv. 2, 3), and quickly particularizes it against Judah and Jerusalem (v. 4). Three specific sins are denounced: idolatry (v. 4), syncretism (v. 5), and religious indifference (v. 6).

Cf. Matt. 13:41, 42. The coming judgment is compared to that of the Genesis flood by use of the phrases "man and beast" and "birds of the heavens" (cf. Gen. 6:7; 7:23). This prophecy will be consummated at the end of history (2 Pet. 3:3–7).

This phrase refers to the power of God unleashed against His antagonists (2:13; Ex. 3:20; Deut. 4:34; Is. 5:25). remnant of Baal. All that remains of Baal worship will be destroyed. This statement may mean that a religious renewal is already under way in Zephaniah's era and that Baal worship is in decline.

The phrase "host of heaven" is frequently connected with Baal or Asherah (2 Kin. 17:16; 21:3, 5; 23:4, 5; 2 Chr. 33:3, 5). Baal worship and the worship of the stars were sins that had contributed to the demise of the northern kingdom in the eighth century B.C. (2 Kin. 17:16). Altars were apparently erected upon the roofs of the houses (2 Kin. 23:12; Jer. 19:13). Milcom. Or "Molech." Worship of this Ammonite god, which involves the hideous practice of child sacrifice, is strictly forbidden (Lev. 18:21 note; 20:2–5; cf. 1 Kin. 11:5; 2 Kin. 23:10; Jer. 32:35).
]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. See 2:3.

See Ps. 46:10; Hab. 2:20; Zech. 2:13. The prophet calls for trustful submission to the sovereign, covenant God. The command to "be silent" is often linked to being in the presence of the holy God. the day of the LORD. This term occurs frequently in the OT prophets. It can refer to any specific time when the Divine Warrior, the Lord of Hosts, is glorious in victory: against Babylon through the Medes (Is. 13:1–14:27), against Egypt through Babylon (Ezek. 30:2–4), or against Israel through Assyria (Is. 10:5, 6, 20, 24). This day of the Lord's vengeance against the wicked is also depicted as the time of Israel's deliverance (Is. 34:2–35:10) when the Lord decisively defeats all of Israel's opposition (2:2, 9; 3:8–20; Joel 3:14–16). It is also the day of final judgment (Amos 5:18–20). Cf. notes on Ezek. 7:7 and Amos 5:18. the LORD has prepared a sacrifice. The imminent judgment coming upon Judah is compared to sacrifices. The nation is a sacrificial lamb (Is. 34:6; Jer. 46:10; Ezek. 39:17–19). consecrated his guests. The invited guests may be the nations who serve as the divine instrument of judgment (Is. 10:5–10; Hab. 1:6). The consecration of guests is necessary to maintain the holiness of the Lord (Ex. 19:10; 24:9–11), and recalls elements of the covenant ritual at Mount Sinai (vv. 15, 16 note).
The sons of the king and other royal officials. Their lack of commitment to the covenant is evidenced by their adoption of foreign customs and attire, a sign of religious disloyalty.

Many take this verse as referring to religious malpractice. They identify the threshold as that of a pagan sanctuary, and consider the allusion to be to a Philistine religious practice that is being imitated (1 Sam. 5:5), with "master" referring to their god (text note). Alternatively, it may be social injustice that is in view. The expression may indicate the speed with which unscrupulous servants enter houses to seize whatever they can and carry it off to their masters.

Cries of anguish come from all parts of the city, depicting the extent of the evil and the judgment. The Fish Gate is on the north side of the city (2 Chr. 33:14) and the Second Quarter is to the east of the temple (2 Kin. 22:14).

Possibly a name given to a depression in the Tyropoeon Valley that runs north to south through the center of Jerusalem. This is a district where markets are found in Zephaniah's day. The wealthier merchant class is singled out for its greedy and corrupt business practices (Amos 8:4–6).

The investigation of the Lord takes place before the destruction. The Lord will make a thorough inquiry, and there will be no escape from this divine scrutiny (Ps. 139; Amos 9:1–4). who are complacent. See text note. The prophet draws a word picture from the wine-making process. Like the sediment of wine, which settles and thickens if left undisturbed, the citizens of Jerusalem have become settled (confirmed) in their indifference toward God. Because they are thoroughly complacent toward God, they regard Him as morally indifferent toward good or evil, and therefore inactive in human affairs.
The curse of the broken covenant frustrates the endeavors of those flagrantly defying the Lord's standards (Deut. 28:30; Amos 5:11; Mic. 6:15).

Zephaniah elaborates further on the day of the Lord, setting the stage for his strong plea for repentance in 2:1–3. The prophet's staccato style emphasizes the speed with which the day approaches and the devastating nature of the judgment it brings. 1:14 the mighty man cries aloud there. The day will strike terror into the soldier, even the stouthearted man of war.

The day of the Lord is presented in frightful images recalling the theophany that accompanied the establishment of the Mosaic covenant at Mount Sinai (Ex. 19:16), the terms of which Judah has broken. Some suggest that "day of the Lord" here can be regarded as the day of His covenant, when the Lord establishes His covenant or enforces its provisions.

The scope of the prophecy widens to anticipate the final, all-consuming day of the Lord affecting "all the earth" (v. 18). they shall walk like the blind. One of the covenant curses found in Deut. 28:28, 29. they have sinned. The reason for the Lord's judgment of Judah is stated in general terms. See note on 3:1–5.

Neither their silver nor their gold. See Ps. 49:6–9; Prov. 11:4; Matt. 16:26; Luke 12:13–21. jealousy. See Ex. 20:5; 34:14; Deut. 4:24. God's jealousy presupposes His covenant love. He has redeemed a people to make them His "treasured possession" (Ex. 19:5). God's covenant love demands the absolute loyalty of His people.

As the Lord's representatives to enforce the covenant, the OT prophets often warned God's people (Is. 1:16–20; 55:1–6; Hos. 2:4, 5; 4:15; Amos 4:12; 5:5, 6; Mic. 6:8). 2:1 Gather together. They are called to assemble in order to hear (cf. Is. 34:1; Jer. 4:5; Joel 2:15, 16; 3:11). The call to hear these severe warnings is itself an act of divine grace, for the warnings are designed to elicit repentance. shameless. Spiritually insensitive and no longer capable of evaluating their own conduct in accordance with divine standards.

LORD. See 1:6 and Is. 55:6, 7. Here this seeking of the Lord is further defined as "seek righteousness; seek humility." A similar pattern is evident in Amos, where the prophet commands, "Seek the LORD," and later, "Seek good, and not evil" (Amos 5:6, 14). perhaps you may be hidden. The prophet's tentative words here express both his hope that the "humble" remnant (v. 3) will find refuge from the Lord's wrath (cf. Is. 55:7) and his pessimism that the "shameless nation" (v. 1) will actually repent. Cf. Amos 5:15.

This section consists of four prophecies of judgment directed against the foreign nations. Such messages are meant to assure God's own people that His sovereign purposes extend over their enemies (1:5, 6) and that these nations are also morally accountable for their actions (Amos 1:3–2:3; Mic. 1:2). 2:4–7 This prophecy is directed against Philistia, a territory to the southwest of Judah, on the Mediterranean coast. 2:4 As in Amos 1:6–8, only four of the five main cities of the Philistines are mentioned (1 Sam. 6:17). Possibly the fifth, Gath, no longer exists when Zephaniah is ministering.

The same word of doom later pronounced upon Jerusalem (3:1). It often introduces a prophecy of judgment. Cherethites. A term for people associated with the Philistines who originated in Crete (2 Sam. 8:18; Ezek. 25:16).

The judgment of the nations will be accompanied by God's preservation of a remnant from His people (Deut. 32:27 note) who have survived the devastation. Other references in Zephaniah to the remnant occur in v. 9 and 3:9–12. restore their fortunes. This widely employed phrase refers to Israel's future salvation beyond the judgment (Deut. 30:3; Ps. 14:7; Jer. 30:3, 18; 32:44; Amos 9:14). It refers in some instances to the physical return of exiles but in other instances to a more general restoration of fortunes (e.g., Job 42:10).
.These nations occupy territory to the east of Judah, on the far side of the Dead Sea, and are inveterate foes of God's people during the OT era.

That is, of the covenant people, now represented by Judah (3:13–15), as the northern kingdom was exiled a century before Zephaniah's ministry. Sodom \... Gomorrah. These ancient cities symbolize sin and serve as types of God's final judgment on sinners (cf. Gen. 18:20 note; Is. 1:9; Amos 4:11; Matt. 10:5; 2 Pet. 2:6). Ironically, both Moab and Ammon are descended from Lot and his daughters, whom God rescued when destroying Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:15–38). the remnant of my people shall plunder them. See v. 7.

Their land lies to the south of Egypt and is mentioned here to indicate the universal sway of the Lord. my sword. A reference to the Lord's use of a foreign power (possibly Babylon; cf. Ezek. 30:4, 5) to overwhelm them.

These verses foretell the destruction of once-mighty Assyria, which is located to the northeast of Judah. Throughout Josiah's reign, Judah is emerging from the domination of the retreating Assyrians. 2:13 destroy Assyria. Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 B.C. This verse indicates that Zephaniah prophesied prior to that date (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

This boast is phrased in language similar to what the sovereign Lord alone rightly may use (Deut. 4:39; Is. 45:5, 6; 47:10). Such self-deification meets with ruin, and those Assyrians who boasted become objects of scorn.

The references here to prophets, priests, the sanctuary, and the law indicate that the prophet is addressing Jerusalem. The general accusation of 1:17 now becomes specific. Jerusalem's sins are particularly heinous because they are committed against the righteous covenant God who has graciously revealed Himself to His people (v. 5; Amos 2:4, 10–12; 3:2). 3:1 Woe to her. See 2:5.

The people have ignored God's voice revealed in the law (Deut. 31:9–13), through the prophets (Jer. 7:23–28; Hag. 1:12), and through the sages (Prov. 1:8). she accepts no correction. See v. 7. Failure to receive correction leads to death (Prov. 5:23), but openness to it leads to life (Prov. 6:23; Jer. 2:30; 5:3; 7:28; 32:33; 35:13; Ps. 50:17). draw near. The Hb. verb here means "to approach God properly in worship" (cf. Lev. 10:3). Worship must come from the heart, not just the mouth (cf. Is. 29:13; John 4:24). Jerusalem has not availed herself of the opportunities she possesses on account of the Lord's presence in the temple "within her" (v. 5).

The decline of the nation is accelerated by corrupt leadership, of which four main groups are named here (compare Mic. 3:9–11). The king is not mentioned, which may reflect the reforming character of Josiah's rule. 3:3 officials within her. See note on v. 5. roaring lions. The images of the unclean lion and wolf here describe the predatory and fierce nature of corrupt government officials. Instead of fulfilling their proper roles in protecting and giving stability to society, they have been devouring the people and taking advantage of them.

Zephaniah contrasts the presence of the righteous Lord within Jerusalem and the presence of corrupt and unrighteous leadership within her (v. 3). The essence of God's covenant commitment is the promise of His presence with His people (Ex. 29:42–46 note; Num. 14:14; Is. 43:2). Here, God's presence threatens judgment (Hos. 11:9), but the same phrase in 3:17 signifies salvation.

Attention shifts from Jerusalem to the surrounding nations. The prophet notes God's previous judgment of the nations (v. 6), which should be a lesson to Jerusalem (v. 7), before turning to the future judgment that awaits (v. 8).
See v. 2.
Addressed to the "humble of the land" (v. 2:3). The Lord's judgment will come in a way that anticipates the final day of the Lord.

The dramatic reversal: judgment is the prelude to restoration and purification both in Israel and among the nations (vv. 9, 12, 13). In a closing hymn of praise (3:14–20), the prophet sings of the future reign of the Lord, His victory over His enemies, and His love for and presence with His people. The church may sing this song now in celebration of Christ's victory on the cross (Col. 2:15) and in anticipation of His triumph when He returns (2 Thess. 1:5–10). 3:9 change \... a pure speech. To purify the lips is either to cleanse from sin in general (Is. 6:5) or to remove the names of foreign gods from the lips of a worshiper (Hos. 2:17). of the peoples. The Gentiles will also call on His name (Is. 52:15; 65:1; 66:18). all of them may call upon the name of theLORD. In contrast with the idolaters of 1:5, 6. See Gen. 4:26; 1 Kin. 18:24; Jer. 10:25; Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21; Rom. 10:12, 13.
These are contrasted with the proud and haughty of v. 11.

See note on 2:7. shall do no injustice. The remnant will be like God. Identical words are used of the Lord in v. 5. A primary goal of salvation is ever-increasing conformity to the image of God (Matt. 5:48; 1 Pet. 1:15, 16; 2 Pet. 1:3, 4). and speak no lies. In contrast with the deceitful idolaters of 1:9. graze and lie down. A common prophetic phrase (cf. Is. 49:9; Jer. 50:19; Ezek. 34:14; Mic. 7:14) that portrays the security that comes to the Lord's sheep from trusting Him and acknowledging His kingship (v. 15). none shall make them afraid. See Mic. 4:4.

This personification of Jerusalem is based on the practice among poets of personifying places and objects in terms of grammatical gender. The word for "city" in Hebrew is feminine, and the prophet speaks of Zion as "daughter."

The basis for the rejoicing in v. 14 is that the judgments against God's people are removed and the enemies that threaten them are overcome. This prophecy finds final fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who satisfied God's judgment against sin and overcame the enemies of God through His death on the cross (Rom. 3:23–25; Col. 2:15 note). The King of Israel \... in your midst. The promise of God's dwelling in the midst of His people points forward to Christ, the King of Israel (John 1:49) and incarnate glory of God (Ex. 26 and John 1:14 notes).

This delight is grounded in the character of God, who "delights in steadfast love" (Mic. 7:18). he will quiet you by his love. The phrase translated "quiet you" may also be rendered "is quiet" or "rests." In the larger context, God has been revealed as the Divine Warrior who is "mighty to save." The former war cry (1:14) is now quieted by victory and the loving relationship between God and His people. The Lord's purging and transforming work of grace creates a renewed people who acknowledge His rule and trust in His name (v. 12).
The repeated first-person verbs emphasize the Lord's initiative and sovereign determination to accomplish this restoration.

See v. 20. The phrase goes back to Deut. 26:18, 19, where Israel as the Lord's special people is privileged to represent Him and be the tangible means whereby praise, honor, and glory are given to the Lord (cf. Is. 43:7; Jer. 13:11; 33:9). Paul sees the church in this role (Titus 2:14), as does Peter (1 Pet. 2:9–12).

Haggai.note: Each of Haggai's sermons is carefully dated, which is an uncommon feature among the biblical prophets. These dates connect the events described in the book with the wider backdrop of world history. This oracle occurred probably on August 29, 520 B.C., when stability was returning to the empire after a time of unrest following Darius's accession. The sixth month was the time for harvesting the fruit trees, after harvesting the other crops, so it was a natural time to assess the success of the agricultural year. The first day of the month, the "new moon," was a festival day, when crowds would likely have gathered at the site of the temple. Haggai's message was addressed publicly to the leaders so that the people could respond as well (1:12). Zerubbabel. He may be the same person as Sheshbazzar (cf. Ezra 1:8), since both are said to have rebuilt the temple. Sheshbazzar could be an official Persian name. However, it is perhaps more likely that they were separate individuals. Zerubbabel was the grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chr. 3:19) and a descendant of David (2:23 note), appointed by the Persians as the governor of the province of Yehud (Judah). Joshua the son of Jehozadak. See 1 Chr. 6:15. A descendant of Zadok the priest. Under Persian rule, Zerubbabel had responsibility over the daily civil affairs of the region. As high priest, Joshua dealt with religious matters.

An expression of implied displeasure (2:14). Verses 2–11 indict the spiritual indifference and misplaced priorities of God's people. the time has not yet come. Their objection is not to the rebuilding itself, but to the timing of it. The objections may be seasonal, since it is harvesttime when Haggai is ministering, or more generally economic, because their land is in trouble (cf. vv. 10, 11). The Persian army is making preparations at this time for an assault on Egypt, to which the empire's vassals, including Judah, are expected to contribute. There seems to be a general discouragement about the future. Such excuses show that they are not pursuing God's kingdom and righteousness (cf. Matt. 6:33). the house of the LORD. The Jerusalem temple is the dwelling place of God's special presence with His people during the old covenant era (1 Kin. 8:27–30). Today God is graciously present in His temple, the church (1 Cor. 3:16, 17).

Haggai reveals the hypocrisy of their objections by a rhetorical question. The houses probably have elaborate wooden walls and ceilings (1 Kin. 7:3; Jer. 22:14). They are living in comparative luxury while God's house lies in ruins. More specifically, since the word "paneled" elsewhere is usually used with reference to the temple, they apparently have precisely the resources to build their own houses that they claim are lacking to build God's house.
The people may be blaming God for the lack of fruitfulness, but the issue is their own lack of obedience.

Their economic and social hardship is the effect of God's covenant curse on their disobedience (Lev. 26:20; Deut. 11:8–15; 28:29, 38–40). God has frustrated their efforts because of their lack of concern for His glory. These kinds of futility curses are common in ancient Near Eastern covenant treaties. a bag with holes. The people are compared to a laborer who takes the wages for which he has worked hard and deliberately puts them into a bag with holes, so that much for which he has worked is lost on the way home. As a result, their lives are frustratingly unfulfilling.

God's purpose in the enterprise is the special joy He will take in this edifice and the appropriate honor He will thereby receive from His people. Their lack of concern for rebuilding indicates their lack of spiritual health.
The focus of their lives is on building their own personal fortunes and families rather than building God's kingdom.

The drought on Judah's crops is God's curse on their agriculture, in keeping with His covenant (1:6 note; Deut. 7:13). The Hb. word translated "ruins" in v. 9 sounds like the Hb. word for "drought" here. Haggai's play on words reinforces the point that the drought is God's response to their neglect of His house.

A common term used by the prophets for those of God's people who remain faithful to Him in the midst of unbelief (Is. 10:22; cf. Zech. 13:9). Using this term here focuses attention on the fact that God has brought them through the judgment of the Babylonian exile. Paul later points to a faithful remnant in Israel — Jews who have embraced Christ (Rom. 11:5). voice of the LORD \... words of Haggai. They recognize God's word through the voice of the prophet. God's revelation always accomplishes its intended purpose (Is. 55:1; Heb. 4:12). the people feared the LORD. Given the consequences for unfaithfulness that they have already received, this is a wise and appropriate response.

As the people repent of their sin, they receive the greatest assurance possible, the presence of God. God's gracious presence with His people is the heart of the covenant relationship (Zech. 8:8 note).

God Himself brings about His people's response by His presence with them. Haggai emphasizes the internal response by the threefold repetition of "spirit." God's Spirit works efficaciously through His word, which Haggai has given, in order to achieve His sovereign purpose (cf. Is. 55:11). The outworking of repentance is renewed obedience.
Probably September 21, 520 B.C., just twenty-three days after the initial oracle.

The Lord again speaks to the people, this time encouraging them to continue building. Reports about the magnificence of the now-destroyed temple of Solomon are apparently a source of discouragement (v. 3). The Lord first assures them of His continued presence with them — a promise for the present (vv. 4, 5). Second, He assures them about the future goal of their project (vv. 6–9). Though it appears humble in comparison, the glory of this temple will finally far outstrip Solomon's temple because it will be graced by the presence of the Messiah Himself (v. 9 note). 2:1 seventh month \... twenty-first. October 17, 520 B.C. The year is not explicitly mentioned; presumably, it is still the second year of Darius (see 1:15). According to Lev. 23:33–43, this is the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, during which God's people are to rejoice in God's provision for them in the wilderness and the blessings of the harvest. It is once again the time of a major assembly, giving the prophet an opportunity to address a large group of people. There is not much to rejoice in this year, however, since their harvest is meager (1:11). Solomon's temple was also dedicated at the time of the same festival (1 Kin 8:2).

Haggai's first sermon was addressed to the leaders because they had to initiate the work. The common people are included here because this message is intended to encourage them about the task at hand. Remembering the first exodus and wilderness wandering is particularly poignant for this group of people who have just recently experienced their own exodus from Babylon.

Verses 1–3 suggest that the people are discouraged by the new temple's relative lack of splendor (cf. 2 Chr. 3; 4) and by the difficulty of the task ahead of them. Although the rebuilt temple is similar in its dimensions to the old one, it lacks the physical splendor and the political significance of Solomon's temple. It also lacked the spiritual glory (Hb. kabod) of the Lord, which departed from Solomon's temple in the days of Ezekiel before its destruction by the Babylonians (Ezek. 10).

Threefold repetition adds emphasis to the command. Similar commands accompanied the building of Solomon's temple (1 Chr. 22:13; 28:20; cf. Gal. 6:9) and the entering of the land under Joshua (Josh. 1:6). I am with you. The Lord's presence and His sustaining strength guarantee the ultimate success of their labors. This promise is at the heart of God's covenant relationship with His people (Ex. 33:15, 16; cf. Heb. 13:5).

God's covenant promises, made with His people in the exodus from Egypt, now assure them of His presence (cf. Ex. 33:12–17; Num. 11:16, 17). His mighty Spirit is present, just as in the days of the great deliverance from Egypt (cf. Zech. 4:6).

As is common in the Prophets, the near and distant future are telescoped, or compressed together. Here references to the glory of the second temple are juxtaposed with a picture of the final universal judgment on the cosmos. While this shaking may be prefigured by political events occurring shortly after the time of Haggai (e.g., the defeat of Persia by the Greeks), the ultimate shaking of the created order is still to come (Heb. 12:26–28). The Feast of Booths (or Tabernacles), with its reenactment of the wilderness period, always had a forward-looking focus, anticipating the greater fulfillment of God's promises. It was an annual reminder that the earthly land of Canaan was not their real home. This longing would have been intensified during times of difficulty, such as in the days of Haggai. The language of shaking the earth is typical of theophanies, when the presence of the Lord is manifested on earth. Here the ultimate appearing of the Lord is in view.

Though the Hb. term translated "treasures" could refer to a person (i.e., the Messiah), the immediate context here favors a reference to the things desired by all nations (i.e., the things precious to them), especially since the Hb. verb is plural. Verse 8 speaks of such precious things, and the decree of King Darius, during whose reign Haggai ministered, alludes to precious things being contributed to the temple building project (Ezra 6:3–5, 8, 9). Here Haggai probably echoes Isaiah's promise of an Israel made rich by the wealth of the nations (Is. 60:5). In other words, he speaks of the messianic age. fill this house with glory. God's intention is to honor Himself by manifesting His glorious presence before "all nations." As God's presence fills the temple, the nations come to the light (Is. 2:3–5; 60:3).

As the sovereign possessor of all things (cf. Pss. 24:1; 50:9–12), God will bring about both His own glorification and His people's inheritance of the nations' wealth (Is. 60:5). As Haggai delivers this prophecy, much of the silver and gold that was looted from the temple by Nebuchadnezzar has not yet been returned. See note on v. 7.

The tabernacle and temple are filled with God's glory (Ex. 40:34, 35; 1 Kin. 8:10, 11), and Haggai anticipates this happening again when the temple is reconstructed. This promise of greater glory is realized in Christ, the greatest manifestation of God's presence and glory (Mal. 3:1; John 1:14). in this place I will give peace. This peace (Hb. shalom) means more than the absence of conflict. It implies prosperity and a sense of total well-being, nothing short of full salvation. Christ gives peace to believers now (John 14:27), but ultimate fulfillment awaits the time when the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of the New Jerusalem (Rev. 21:22).

This date has no particular significance in terms of the festival calendar, but it is the most important date in the book, being repeated three times (2:10, 18, 20). Its significance comes from the event noted in v. 18, the symbolic refounding of the temple. The sequence of time is important for interpreting the third message, which begins on a note of judgment (vv. 10–14). The people repented and began the work on September 21, 520 B.C. (1:15), and Haggai brought a message of encouragement on October 17 of the same year (2:1–9). Here, on December 18, he brings another cautionary message. It is not enough to rebuild the temple; the deeper issue of the people's defilement before a holy God must be dealt with.

This portion of Haggai's third sermon, emphasizing the extensive defilement of the people and their efforts, builds on an object lesson taken from the Mosaic ceremonial law. One of the primary tasks of the priests is to teach the law, answering questions about its content and meaning (cf. Deut. 33:10). The questions that the Lord tells Haggai to direct to the priests are designed to show that while ceremonial holiness is not transferable (v. 12), ceremonial defilement is (v. 13). Haggai then applies the lesson of the preceding questions to his hearers (v. 14). They have defiled the work of the temple and their offerings because their estrangement from God is deeper than they realized. The mere presence of a rebuilt temple will not render them holy as a people (cf. Jer. 7:3–7); God demands genuine change of heart and life, not mere outward conformity.
This word signals a transition from indictment to blessing, as a result of the rebuilding of the temple. In spite of their past defilement, the holy God is determined to bless them (v. 19).

This verse draws on Amos 4:9 and Deut. 28:22. Such natural disasters and lack of agricultural productivity, the bitter fruit of disobedience to the Lord's covenant (1:6 note; Deut. 28:22), are God's way of getting His people's attention. Yet as in the time of Amos, these judgments have not yet brought the people to repentance.

The seed for the next year has already been planted but it is too soon to anticipate by normal means what the outcome will be. the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree. The four main fruit trees in Israel. I will bless you. God's grace will nonetheless overcome the sin and defilement of His people. Though He chastises them, in the end mercy triumphs over judgment. This is the outworking of the Lord's promise in v. 9.

The last of Haggai's sermons, given the same day as the previous address (v. 10), returns to the theme of the latter-day glory of the temple (v. 6 note). Again, future events are telescoped as Haggai interweaves mention of the coming Messiah (v. 23) with references to the shaking of the cosmos and God's final victory over the nations (vv. 21, 22). When God ultimately shakes all things, then everything will be as it should be.

The military and political powers of the nations finally submit to God's lordship (Dan. 2:44; 7:27). The nation is left unspecified since all nations must bow to His rule. The language is saturated with traditional themes and images recalling the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, the destruction of the Egyptian chariots in the exodus, and the conquest of the land under Joshua. God will again do the great things He has done for His people in the past.

See note on Zech. 12:3. my servant. Like his ancestor David, Zerubbabel is God's chosen representative to accomplish His work. Isaiah speaks of a greater Servant who will come, whom Zerubbabel foreshadows (Is. 42:10). Jesus is the descendant of Zerubbabel (Matt. 1:12) and also the Servant of God (Acts 4:27, 30). signet ring. A symbol of authority, ownership, and power. Before the exile, Jeremiah used the term to describe the rejection of the Davidic king Jehoiachin (Jer. 22:24). Yet here the Lord reverses that earlier oracle, declaring that Zerubbabel represents a continuing future for the line of David. The Lord is not, after all, finished with that family. A new shoot will yet emerge from the stump of Jesse (Is. 11:1). No action is demanded of Zerubbabel or his hearers in response to this oracle. They are not summoned to throw off the yoke of their Persian oppressors. They are simply to wait with confident hope for the decisive saving work that the Lord will do in His appointed time. More than five hundred years later, God accomplished this final salvation through His Son, Jesus Christ, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared the Son of God in power at His resurrection (Rom. 1:1–4).

Zechariah.note: Zechariah sets the stage for the record of night visions that follows in 1:7–6:8. 1:1 the eighth month, in the second year of Darius. October–November 520 B.C. Cf. the dates in Hag. 1:1, 15 to see how the two prophets ministered during the same time (cf. Zech. 8:9). Zechariah began his ministry two months after the returnees from Babylon began to rebuild the temple. This is the first of three dates in chs. 1–8, dividing these chapters into three sections: 1:1–6; 1:7–6:15; and 7:1–8:23. Zechariah, the son of Berechiah. See Introduction: Title and Author; Date and Occasion. His name means "the LORD remembers." Iddo. A man by this name led one of the priestly families who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:4). Like some of the other prophets, Zechariah possibly came from a priestly family.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold} was very angry with your fathers. Verses 2–6 are a preface to the eight night visions of 1:7–6:8. They introduce a key distinction between the past and the present. The Lord was very angry with their fathers, the generations prior to the exile, because of their failure to repent in response to the prophets' preaching. However, a different outcome is possible for the postexilic generation if the people respond and repent.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold} of hosts. A divine title used extensively by the postexilic prophets Zechariah, Haggai, and Malachi. It has military connotations (God as leader of Israel's armies; cf. 1 Sam. 17:45), but it also highlights God's sovereign kingship and power over all creation. Return to me \... I will return. Repentance involves a wholehearted turning away from sin and a turning to God. God's return will then bless His people with His presence (1:16; 2:11). The people have physically returned from exile, but they have not yet been transformed spiritually.

The preexilic prophets (e.g., Isaiah, Jeremiah). Return from your evil ways. As well as being a general summary of the preaching of all of the prophets, this quotation almost exactly matches Jer. 25:4, 5. they did not hear or pay attention to me. Their fathers showed obstinacy and rebellion (2 Kin. 17:13–15). As a consequence, the curses of the covenant (Deut. 28:15–68) came upon them for their disobedience.
Both obedient and disobedient alike suffered and perished in the catastrophe of the fall of Jerusalem. Even the prophets do not live forever, unlike the Lord's word, which they proclaim (see v. 6).

See note on Is. 20:3. they repented. See Neh. 9:1–10:27. Unlike their fathers, who listened to the preaching of the prophets without a response and so faced judgment, Zechariah's hearers repent. They can therefore expect to find the Lord turning to them as well (see v. 3). purposed to deal with us. The Hb. word suggests that God's punishment of the preexilic fathers was in accord with a plan.

These verses record the first of eight night visions that Zechariah saw in the course of one night (v. 8). The visions are organized so that the first and last (6:1–8) correspond to one another in the imagery of horses and chariots. This first one emphasizes God's commitment to His covenant people; He is the rebuilder of Jerusalem and its protector against pagan forces in the outside world. The vision calls God's people to look beyond their present circumstances and place their trust in the promises of God. 1:7 the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month. Like Haggai, Zechariah's visions are carefully dated, all of them occurring on this day, during the night.

The horses and horsemen are carefully concealed from normal view among evergreen bushes in dark surroundings. These are the Lord's scouts sent out to patrol the earth and observe what is happening while remaining hidden themselves. red horse \... red, sorrel, and white. The significance of these colors is uncertain. Hebrew has fewer color terms than English; as a result, "red" is a normal color for a horse.

This interpreting angel (1:19; 2:3; 3:1; 4:1) should be distinguished from the "Angel of the Lord" (v. 12 note; 3:1). The interpretations he gives should be used as a guide to understanding the meaning of the visions.

The self-assured nations stand in contrast to the Jewish state struggling under Persian rule. Yet God assures His people that these proud nations will experience judgment (cf. Obadiah's words about Edom's false security, Obad. 3, 4, 8).

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. See note on Gen. 16:7. Many, though not all, scholars identify this angel with the "man riding on a red horse" (v. 8). seventy years. A reference to the prophecy of Jer. 25:11, 12, where the Babylonian exile was announced.
Words that reflect God's love for His people and reaffirm His commitment not to forsake them (Heb. 13:5). The Lord not only sees what is happening, but He also cares about the needs of His people.
The first expression of the theme of God's jealousy in the book (8:2). God's zealous love for His chosen people moves Him to act in their behalf. A similar theme is expressed in Zeph. 3:9–20.

Notice the contrast with v. 2, where God's past anger with His own people is expressed. Here God's love for His own (v. 14) moves Him to protect them by bringing judgment on the nations who have persecuted His people beyond measure.
The building work on the temple, begun under Haggai, is a key mark of the Lord's favor and determination to dwell with His people.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold} will again \... choose Jerusalem. A common theme in the visions (2:12; 3:2). God's choice of Jerusalem distinguishes it from all other cities. The result of His choice is to bring prosperity to Judah ("My cities shall again overflow with prosperity"). The repeated use of "again" reminds Zechariah's hearers that this blessing has been nothing less than the Lord's plan for His people from the very beginning.

The second vision focuses on the four horns. The "horn" was a symbol of power and pride in the ancient Near East (Ps. 75:4, 5). This vision is the counterpart of the first: Zion will be rebuilt, and the nations that feel secure will be destroyed. The identification of the four horns could be the same as those of Daniel's prophecies (Dan. 2:36–45; 7:17–28), and so the horns correspond either to Babylonia, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome, or to Assyria, Babylon, Egypt, and Persia (10:10, 11). The horns could also have a broader significance and refer to "the four corners of the earth" (Rev. 20:8). That is, they could refer to all of the world powers that elevate themselves against God's people at whatever time in history. This would then match the significance of the number four in the description of the craftsmen.
The four craftsmen come to overthrow the power of the nations. This is symbolic of God's judgment coming on the nations that have persecuted His people.

Zechariah's third vision describes a man with a measuring line. This vision emphasizes God's protection of His people with His own personal presence (v. 5 notes). Jerusalem's walls are not rebuilt yet, and the city is subject to attack from roving bands. 2:1 a measuring line. An implement that symbolized rebuilding in Jeremiah's portrayal of a restored Jerusalem (Jer. 31:39). The act of measuring is a precursor to building. The word is different from the more general term used in Zech. 1:16.

The OT prophets envision a time when Jerusalem will be the center of worship for the nations (v. 11; 8:20–23; Is. 2:1–4) and the city will overflow with people. The youth's measuring task will thus be fruitless because the city's boundaries will be infinitely expandable to accommodate the needs of the population. multitude of people and livestock. See note on v. 11.

The prophets portray the day of full restoration as a second exodus with the imagery of the pillar of fire (Is. 4:5, 6). As Israel was once protected from her enemies by God Himself, so He will again guard her from oppressors. The obvious drawback of Jerusalem being unwalled is thus alleviated. the glory. God's presence is far more than protection; it is the source of all blessing for His people. The essence of the renewed covenant is, "I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (Jer. 31:33). The return of God's glory to His chosen city is a key theme in Ezek. 43. Like the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34, 35) and the temple (1 Kin. 8:11), Jerusalem will be filled with God's glory.

In this section, the prophet speaks to the Jews in Babylon (vv. 6–9) and in Jerusalem (vv. 10–13). 2:6 the land of the north. Babylon. Even though it is geographically east of Judah, it is regarded as being in the north by Zechariah's contemporaries since that is the direction from which travelers from Babylon approach Judah. I have spread you abroad. A reference to God's judgment of Judah in the exile as punishment for covenant disobedience (Deut. 28:36, 49, 50). The time of judgment is over; the time of restoration has come (v. 7). the four winds of the heavens. The four points of the compass.
See note on Deut. 32:10.
This promise assumes the sanctification of the people and land through the blood of the everlasting covenant (3:9 and 8:8 notes; Heb. 13:20).

The extent of the vision transcends anything the Jews could accomplish in their day. The vision captures a time when salvation will not be limited to the Jewish nation but will extend God's grace to the world (cf. Is. 56:3–5). That day has come in Christ's inauguration of the kingdom of God.

An expression used only here in the Scriptures. Judah will be holy because God will dwell there (cf. Ezek. 37:26–28). Zechariah is envisioning the fullest realization of God's promise to Abraham (Gen. 12:3; 15:5).

All people should revere God because of the great salvation declared in this chapter (Hab. 2:20). The nations that previously oppressed God's people are struck dumb. he has roused himself. For the purpose of judgment. God will both judge the nations that have oppressed His people and provide a safe home for His people.

The fourth vision concerns Joshua, the high priest (Ezra 3:2), and deals particularly with the problem of an impure priesthood. It begins by showing God's solution to the problem (vv. 4, 5) and ends by showing how God promises to wipe away the sin of all His people (vv. 8, 9). 3:1 A courtroom scene similar to that in Job (Job 1:6–12). Satan has come to accuse Joshua of his unworthiness for the priesthood. The Hb. term satan means "adversary" or "accuser" (text note); here it may be descriptive (i.e., not a proper name). standing. Joshua assumes the position of the accused party in the presence of the angel of the Lord, who is serving as the judge. Accusation is a favorite ploy of Satan against believers. It differs from the conviction of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit convicts of sin in order to move us to repentance and forgiveness. Satan's goal is condemnation and destruction, not redemption.
The fire is a metaphor for the exile from which the people of God have been snatched. Amos 4:11 uses the same expression to speak of the danger from which God redeems His people.

The basis of Satan's accusations that Joshua is unworthy. If the high priest is unclean, who can make atonement for sin? If he cannot make the atonement, how can the people be forgiven? The answer is given in a twofold manner below.

God makes Joshua fit for the priesthood by giving him new, clean garments. This foreshadows the work of the coming Branch (v. 8), who will fulfill a priestly function and provide clothing of righteousness from His own merit (2 Cor. 5:21; Col. 2:13, 14).
The turban is part of the high priest's dress. A new, clean turban completes the restored garments, indicating that God has taken away the reproach on the priesthood (Ex. 28:36–38).

These men foreshadow the coming Servant because they are priests, and He will act as a priest by making atonement for sin (v. 9 note). my servant. A title of honor initially used for Moses (Num. 12:6–8). The term also is used as a title in Isaiah, sometimes for Israel (Is. 41:8; 44:1, 2) and sometimes (as here) for the Messiah, the Servant who will redeem His people (Is. 42:1–7; 52:13). the Branch. A Messianic title combining the offices of priest and king (6:12 note: Is. 4:2 and note).

Possibly a reference to the Messiah. Several OT passages about the stone are interpreted as messianic in the NT (Ps. 118:22; Is. 8:14; 28:16; Matt. 21:42; 1 Pet. 2:6–8). Alternatively, it may be a reference to the inscribed gemstone associated with the priestly turban in Ex. 28:36–38. seven eyes. The mixture of images is difficult to interpret but these eyes are symbols of God's omniscient and watchful care (also used in 4:10). If the stone is a gemstone, the word translated "eyes" may also be translated as "facets." remove the iniquity of this land. God will take away His people's sin through the Branch. The priestly system in the OT was never intended actually to cover sin but only to prefigure the One who would truly deal with humanity's sin (Heb. 10:1–18). in a single day. The Day of Atonement (Lev. 16:30; 23:28) was an annual reminder of sin (Heb. 9:7–10), but Christ on a single day (Good Friday) made full and final atonement for the sins of God's people (Heb. 9:11–14).
An expression for peace and prosperity (1 Kin. 4:25; Mic. 4:4). The ultimate state of God's kingdom is in view.

The fifth vision describes a golden lampstand and two olive trees. The main problem addressed in the visions is how the work of rebuilding the temple will be completed. God's answer is that Joshua and Zerubbabel are only finite and limited human beings. The power for completing the task will come from God Himself.

The lampstand is probably used to remind the people of the lampstand in the tabernacle and the temple (Ex. 25:31), although its shape is different than the shape of the lampstand found in those sanctuaries. The lampstand represents the Lord's favor shining on His people, and perhaps recalls the Servant who will be a "light for the nations" (Is. 42:6; 49:6). seven lamps \... seven lips. The numbers in this verse are somewhat confusing, but they probably mean that there are seven lamps on the stand with one bowl to hold the lamp oil. Seven tubes from the bowl fed the lamps, while the bowl itself is filled from the olive trees (v. 12).
See v. 14 and note.
Zechariah's question does not receive an immediate reply, though the angel's counter-question suggests that he ought to know. It is answered in v. 14.

The key verse for understanding the vision. Zerubbabel. The previous vision addressed Joshua; here, the focus is on Zerubbabel, as is evident from the repetition of his name in vv. 6, 7, 9, 10. Not by might \... power. Military strength or any other form of power (apart from God). God's people are repeatedly told not to depend on military power and foreign alliances to accomplish their calling (Is. 31:1–3; Ps. 20:7–9). by my Spirit. The Spirit of God is often portrayed in the Prophets as the One who enables God's servants to do God's work and overcome obstacles (cf. Hag. 2:5). Even the coming Servant of the Lord, the Messiah, is described as empowered by the Spirit (Is. 11:2; 42:1; 61:1).

The text does not identify who or what precisely this is, perhaps because any and every obstacle — whether practical, political, or spiritual — must yield to the all-surpassing power of God. Nothing can stand in the way of God's purpose to restore His presence to the midst of His people (cf. Is. 40:4). the top stone. The "chief" stone could either be the capstone, which completes the temple, or a ceremonial stone, which marks the formal beginning of the building project. Either way, the point is that having begun the building program, Zerubbabel will see it through to a successful conclusion. Grace, grace to it. The temple is completed amid shouts that ask for God's favor to rest on it. The phrase is repeated for emphasis (Is. 40:1 note).
Zerubbabel started the work, and he will finish it. Zerubbabel's finished temple building ultimately points toward Christ and His temple (cf. John 2:19–22).

It is easy to be discouraged with the meager results and progress evident in Zechariah's day. The people of Judah were discouraged at the laying of the foundation of the second temple (Ezra 3:10–12) and also at the rebuilding in Haggai's day (520 B.C.; Hag. 2:3). The question in this verse reminds us not to judge God's work by human standards. Even these skeptics will be brought to rejoice over God's faithfulness. plumb line. Lit. "tin stone." Older translations, following the Septuagint, understand this as a plumb line; however, it may be a special brick of semiprecious metal that forms part of the temple's foundation. eyes of the LORD. See notes on 3:9 and 2 Chr. 16:9. The seven lamps on the lampstand represent the Lord's watchfulness over the interests of His restored people. The temple that is being rebuilt by Zerubbabel will serve as the foundation for a new relationship between the Lord and His people.

Some aspects of the vision are not obvious, but the function of these elements is clear: to transmit an endless supply of oil from the trees to the lampstand, ensuring that the lamps will never go out. The Lord's favor toward His people is eternal and His blessing inexhaustible.

Lit. "sons of new oil" (text note). The two trees are characterized by great fertility, which enables them to supply the lampstand abundantly. The trees are symbols for two members of the divine council; they stand beside the Lord. Traditionally, many interpreters have identified the two trees as Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest. However, it is perhaps more likely that they either represent Haggai and Zechariah, who as prophets have access to the Lord's presence, or they picture the Lord's heavenly servants, who are tasked with supplying unlimited divine assistance to the renewed temple. Lord of the whole earth. God is sovereign over all the affairs of people (Is. 40:15, 23, 24). Similarly, the title "Lord of hosts" shows that all the powers of the cosmos are at His disposal (1:3 note).

The sixth vision concerns a flying scroll. It teaches that the Lord who loves and restores His people is also righteous and will punish wickedness. This vision and the one to follow are warnings, but they are also encouragements that God will deal with the problem of sin in the land, whether by judgment or removal.

A large open scroll for all to read its words. As the context implies, the words on it are words of covenant curse. Its large size is appropriate for its task of going out over the whole land to deal with every sin (v. 3).

The curse contained in the Law (Deut. 28:15–68). As in Hag. 1:1–11, the prophet emphasizes that, under the Sinai covenant, the obedience of God's people brings blessings while disobedience brings God's curses. everyone who steals \... swears falsely. The curse is probably not directed at just two sins, but these are representative of the iniquity of the whole land (cf. Lev. 19:11–12). False swearing violates the third commandment, and theft violates the eighth commandment. They may also be connected since a suspected thief may have been required to swear an oath of self-imprecation when accused of a crime under the old covenant. The Ten Commandments summarize the whole moral law and are a revelation of God's own character.

God's Word will accomplish its intended purpose (Is. 55:11). Those who break God's law will surely suffer the consequences of their sin that this curse brings. Scripture regularly emphasizes the certainty of judgment (Rom. 2:3; 1 Thess. 5:1–3; Heb. 2:3). The threat of destroying a person's house for breaking the covenant is found in both biblical and extrabiblical texts (cf. Ezra 6:11).
The seventh vision, featuring the woman in the measuring basket, stresses God's sovereign removal of wickedness from the land (v. 11 note). God's holy nature cannot tolerate sin in His people.

See text note. The ephah is a unit of dry measure equivalent to about one bushel (36 L; see Judg. 6:19; Ruth 2:17). Clearly, such a basket will not contain an adult, but precise realism is not necessarily characteristic of prophetic visions (Num. 12:6–8 and notes). going out. The wickedness of the people is going to be removed from the land once for all.

A simple but effective means of keeping the contents of the basket restrained. Lead may be used because it is a base metal and therefore suitable for this task. a woman. Wickedness is personified by a woman, perhaps because the Hb. word used for "wickedness" is grammatically feminine, or because Israel's idolatry is often characterized by the prophets as prostitution (Ezek. 16:25; Hos. 2:2). She may represent an image of an enthroned female deity such as Asherah.
There is no danger of wickedness being allowed to get free.

God's agents for removing wickedness out of the land. God's covenant faithfulness removes the sin of His people far from them (Ps. 103:11, 12; Mic. 7:19). wings of a stork. Storks are large birds that migrate through Israel in a northward direction each year.

This older name for Babylon is used possibly to evoke the Tower of Babel as a symbol of opposition to God (Gen. 11:2). Shinar, not Jerusalem, is the appropriate place for iniquity because Jerusalem is the dwelling place of the Holy One of Israel (2:10–13; 8:3).

The last vision, the four chariots, recalls the four horses of the first vision (v. 1 note; cf. 1:7–17). Yet whereas the horses in ch. 1 were concealed, representing the Lord's invisible scouting parties, here the horses are pulling chariots, symbolic of powerful intervention on the Lord's part. The intelligence-gathering phase is over, and it is time for the Lord's deliverance to begin. The order and colors of the horses do not have any special significance. The author of Revelation uses similar imagery in his portrayal of the four horsemen (Rev. 6:1–6). 6:1 mountains of bronze. These brightly shining mountains probably symbolize the gate to heaven, though some suggest that the bronze reflects the bronze pillars of the temple (1 Kin. 7:13–22). In the first vision the riders went from the presence of God (1:10). Here the chariots are God's emissaries of judgment who emerge from between the bronze mountains.

The Hb. word for "wind" can mean "spirit." Zechariah may be intentionally drawing on that ambiguity to say that as the winds cover the earth, so the angels of God cover the earth with God's presence and power (cf. v. 8 note). the LORD of all the earth. The sovereign God commands His heavenly hosts to do His will (4:14 note).
The eager horses portray the immediacy of God's judgment.

The north is here representative of Israel's enemies because the geography of Palestine demands that anyone in the ancient world attacking from the east, including the Persians, must come by way of the north. rest. If God judged the north country, then all other lands are securely under His judgment, and His protection of His people is complete. His Spirit can therefore rest, and so can His people.
This section is an appendix to the visions, offering additional comments on the fourth and fifth visions.
These returning exiles have an important part to play in the renewal of the community (cf. v. 15).
A composite crown is unusual; this may represent the foreshadowing of the fulfillment of the promise of Hag. 2:8, or it may anticipate the exceptional presentation of v. 13.

A messianic title, the importance of which explains its occurrence here and in 3:8. Isaiah first used the term to denote the Messiah (Is. 4:2). Jeremiah then developed it as a title for the Davidic descendant who will rule on David's throne (Jer. 23:5, 6; 33:15, 16).

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. The Messiah in His kingly function will build the temple. This is meant to encourage the Jews of Zechariah's day, but its fulfillment can be found in Jesus, who has promised to build His church as a temple (John 2:19–21; 1 Cor. 3:16, 17; Eph. 2:19–21). And there shall be a priest on his throne. The ESV rendering supposes that Zechariah is given a vision of two individuals on two thrones: the Messianic descendent of David who builds the temple, and beside him a priest, seated on another throne. This would envision a twin concern for the Davidic monarchy and the Levitical priesthood working together, as is also expressed in Jer. 33. Priests are needed to serve alongside the king, offering sacrifices in the rebuilt temple. Alternatively, the text may be understood to express two aspects of the status and activity of one person sitting on a single throne (cf. the composite crown in v. 11); it would then be rendered "and it is he who shall be a priest on his throne." Zechariah is given the astounding insight that this one individual will combine the offices of priest and king, which have been kept separate in Israel up until the prophet's day. This messianic prophecy anticipates the NT's disclosure of Christ as being at the same time High Priest (Heb. 4:14; 7:24; 9:11) and King (Matt. 22:41–46; Heb. 1:8).

These are the nations who join in the Messiah's task of rebuilding the temple. This reflects Haggai's teaching that the nations will bring their wealth to the temple (Hag. 2:7 note). Since the church of Christ is the temple in this age, Gentiles build the temple by building the church, the living body of Christ on earth (1 Pet. 2:5).

This chapter deals with a question from the residents of the land about continuing to fast. The question shows their lack of understanding of the real issue of obedience. Zechariah answers that obedience is better than sacrifice (cf. 1 Sam. 15:22). 7:1 fourth year \... fourth day \... ninth month. December 7, 518 B.C., a little more than two years after the visions in chs. 1–6. This is the seventh and last date in the books of Haggai and Zechariah.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. A delegation comes from Bethel to inquire whether they should continue to fast in mourning for the destruction of the temple. The temple was destroyed in the fifth month (586 B.C.), according to 2 Kin. 25:8–15. Now that the temple is being rebuilt, is there any reason to continue to mourn its destruction? The question is answered by the prophet in 8:18, 19. Chapter 7 shows that the restored community in Jerusalem is outwardly religious but is missing the fruits of true religion. True religion should result in good deeds that flow from the heart (James 1:26, 27). See notes on vv. 9, 10.

Two fasts are in view here. The first commemorates the fall of Jerusalem (cf. 7:2 note), and the other mourns the assassination of Gedaliah, the governor of Judah appointed by the Babylonians (2 Kin. 25:25 note). seventy years. It has been sixty-eight years since the destruction of the temple; Zechariah here speaks in round numbers. was it for me. Zechariah's emphatic question points out the hypocrisy of their fasting; their fasts are motivated by self-interest rather than a desire to please God. They have not learned the lessons that the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple were intended to teach.
See note on Gen. 12:9.

Zechariah calls on the people to do what their fathers did not. True justice means applying God's Word to the problems, both personal and social, confronting the restoration community. They must deliver the oppressed and punish the oppressor.

These groups are easily exploited. God loves them (Ex. 22:21; Deut. 10:18) and orders provision for their care (Deut. 24:17–22), since they are, after all, "your brothers." God also pronounces curses on those who exploit them (Deut. 27:19). Injustices done to these groups are mentioned in Ps. 94:6 and Is. 10:1, 2. devise evil \... in your heart. The outward problem of mistreating others springs from inward hatred and disregard for others (Matt. 5:21, 22).
The generations leading up to the destruction of Jerusalem.

God's judgment, the Babylonian exile, was in proportion to their disobedience. The prophets repeatedly emphasize that formal acts of worship are nullified by disobedience. See esp. 1 Sam. 15:22 and Is. 1:13–15.
The disobedience of their forefathers brought about God's judgment. Zechariah wants the people to understand that continued disobedience will be answered with judgment.

This chapter is a picture of the ultimate state of the kingdom of God, when God brings His final and fullest blessings on His people. Similar to Isaiah's portrayal of the future (Is. 65:17; 66:5–24), it gives the postexilic Jews hope that the Lord is still determined to bless them. Since the coming of Christ into the world, the beginning of these blessings is seen, but their full realization awaits the new heaven and earth (Rev. 21:1).
God's zeal, or jealousy, for His people (not of them) is born of His covenant love and commitment to them (1:14), which in turn demands their wholehearted loyalty to Him.

Faithful observance of God's law was rarely true of Israel, even in Zechariah's day. The prophet foresees a time when God's people will reflect His character in their dealings with one another (vv. 16, 17). See also Ex. 34:6, 7. holy mountain. Mount Zion will be holy because God's presence will dwell there in a special way. The prophets repeatedly emphasize the day of salvation as a day of renewal of God's presence (2:5, 11).

A picture of God's covenant blessings, in which the complementary images of God's blessing of long life (Ex. 20:12) and the joy of children playing reflect a state of shalom, that is, total well-being.

The Hb. word denotes something beyond human strength and understanding, typically with reference to a divine action. For other examples of this emphasis, see Gen. 18:14 ("hard") and Judg. 13:18. remnant. Those faithful to God in the midst of disobedience. Paul speaks of "a remnant, chosen by grace" in Rom. 11:5. The elect of God are preserved to serve Him faithfully. See notes on Is. 1:9 and Mic. 2:12.
The covenant renewal of God's people involves restoration from foreign lands. See Deut. 30:1–5; Jer. 30:8–11.

This personal relationship is the essence of God's covenant with Abraham and his descendants (Gen. 17:7 and note) and of the new covenant (Jer. 31:33). It is the source of all other covenant blessings.

The blessings of God's final renewal are expressed in agricultural terms appropriate to the covenant promise of land. Because old Israel's life in the land is a type of new Israel's life in Christ (Gen. 13:15 note), Christians today experience the blessings of God's covenant renewal through Jesus (Matt. 26:28; 1 Cor. 11:25) and look forward to the total renewal of God's covenant blessings in the new heaven and earth (Rev. 21:1–22:5).

Previously, while they were under God's wrath, their name was used as a curse word. Now that God has returned to their midst, their name will be regarded as a blessing among the nations (cf. Gen. 12:3).
See note on 1:6.

The people are called on to order their lives in keeping with God's ethical standards. The godly behavior described here contrasts with the ungodliness that characterized much of Israel's history; truth and righteousness will reign in this final era of blessing (Amos 5:24).

This verse relates to the question in 7:3 and its reply. The fasts mentioned commemorate various aspects of Jerusalem's destruction. fourth. The fast commemorating the fall of the walls of Jerusalem, the beginning of the end for the city (2 Kin. 25:3, 4). See notes on 7:2, 5. fifth. This marks the date of the fall of Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kin. 25:8). seventh. This marks the date of Gedaliah's death (2 Kin. 25:25). tenth. Nebuchadnezzar began his siege of Jerusalem in the tenth month (2 Kin. 25:1; Jer. 39:1–10). love truth and peace. Love is an action in the Bible, not just an emotional feeling. Therefore, to love truth and peace means actively to pursue the things that support these.
These verses depict a great pilgrimage by the Gentile nations to Jerusalem, implying the extension of God's salvation beyond the borders of Israel (14:16–20; cf. Is. 2:1–4; Mic. 4:1–3; Mal. 1:5).
See Is. 2:2–4; Mic. 4:3.

Emphasis is laid on the great numbers (v. 22, "many peoples") of Gentiles that will come to worship the true God. Rev. 5:9 speaks of the redeemed from "every tribe and language and people and nation." Salvation then is worldwide, not in the sense that every human being is redeemed, but that the children of God are chosen from every language and ethnic group of the world. God is with you. The attraction of worship is the presence of God in the midst of His people (1 Cor. 14:24, 25).

The prophet turns his attention to the future of God's kingdom, developing his theme in two lengthy oracles (chs. 9–11; 12–14). The first prophecy of the book's latter half focuses on the coming of God the King in judgment. The opening verses (9:1–8) portray God as an avenging warrior who comes to take possession of His land by destroying all the pagan enemies who lie in His path (cf. Is. 9:6 note). He comes from the north to Jerusalem (cf. 9:14–17, where God is pictured as coming from the south to Jerusalem), an event that leads to the proclamation of 9:9. Some interpret the picture of a northern invasion as describing Alexander the Great's conquest of Palestine in 333 B.C. That may be, but its greater meaning concerns God Himself coming to avenge His people. See Introduction: Genre and Literary Features. 9:1 oracle of the word of the LORD. This phrase is used three times in the OT (here, 12:1, and Mal. 1:1, which links this section of the book with the book of Malachi). Here it may carry the sense of a burden, i.e., the prophet is under strong compulsion to deliver a message of judgment from God. land of Hadrach. Known as Hatarikka in Assyr­ian cuneiform inscriptions, this is the northernmost city listed in vv. 1–8. The description here is rather general, and a specific fulfillment ought not to be sought. Damascus. The capital of Syria, Israel's neighbor to the north.

Located on the Orontes River north of Damascus. Tyre and Sidon. Phoenician cities on the Mediterranean coast. Both were commercial centers throughout the biblical period. Their description as "very wise" may relate to shrewdness in business. Judgment of these cities is a common prophetic theme (Jer. 47:1–7; Ezek. 28:11–23).
The source of Tyre's wealth and security.

Strong cities of Philistia will not be able to withstand the power of the approaching Warrior — God Himself. These cities are marked out for judgment many times in the OT (Is. 14:28–32; Ezek. 25:15–17; Amos 1:6–8).
The object of this comprehensive judgment on Israel's enemies is to make life safe for her.

This important OT prophecy finds fulfillment both in Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem (Matt. 21:1–11; John 12:12–16) and in His messianic reign (v. 10 note). 9:9 O daughter of Zion. A common title for God's holy city and people, which personifies her as a young woman (Is. 1:8 note; 62:11; Zeph. 3:14). your king. The royal descendant of David promised repeatedly (2 Sam. 7:12–14; Ps. 132:11; Is. 9:7; 11:1–5; Jer. 23:5, 6; 33:15–22; Ezek. 34:23, 24; 37:24, 25). righteous. See Ps. 72. on a donkey. A sign of His coming in peace more than a sign of humility. Wealthy people ride donkeys in this era (Judg. 10:4), but horses are the mount of choice for military activities.

A reference to the provision in God's covenant for covering sin (Ex. 24:8; Matt. 26:28). 9:13 O Greece. Lit. "O Javan" (Gen. 10:2). This does not necessarily refer to the Maccabean wars (second century B.C.) of the intertestamental period, or indicate that the author lived in that period. During Zechariah's lifetime, Javan encompassed many of the coastal Mediterranean nations, and thus naturally later came to denote the Greeks.
In contrast to the earlier image of shattering the threatening weapons of Judah's enemies, the Lord will make His own people into a powerful weapon, uniting Judah and Israel together.

The God of Israel is now portrayed as the Divine Warrior, coming from the southern region of the desert riding on the storm clouds (2 Sam. 22:8–16; Ps. 29). Since Mount Sinai was the place He appeared when He brought the people out of Egypt, the OT sometimes depicts God as coming from that region.
God's people will be exuberant with a holy joy because of God's victory and presence (Acts 2:13–21; Eph. 5:18).
God's people rest secure as sheep under His care (13:7; Ezek. 34:11–24; 37:24). Like carefully protected crown jewels, they will become glorious as a result of God's presence (2 Cor. 3:18).

This chapter is a rebuke to the people of Judah, especially its leaders, for seeking wisdom and advice from idols (v. 2). God's answer to their waywardness is that He Himself will be their shepherd. The Messiah is often portrayed (like David) as the Shepherd-King (Ezek. 34; Jer. 23:1–8). 10:1 Ask rain from the LORD. See note on 8:12. Given its arid climate, the Israelite agricultural economy is crucially dependent upon rain for its success. The constant temptation of the people under the old covenant is to look elsewhere than God for sustenance, especially to Baal, who is said to be in control of the weather and fertility.

Occult attempts to tell the future — and in this context, to provide the blessing of rainfall — are forbidden for God's people (Deut. 18:9–14), who are to derive their wisdom from the word of God (Prov. 1:7). lack of a shepherd. Israel's and Judah's leaders are often rebuked for their godless leadership of God's people (Ezek. 34:1–10).
Because of God's help, Judah will be strong like a horse arrayed for battle (v. 6).

Symbolic references to the Messiah. Jesus is from the tribe of Judah (Heb. 7:14) and came in fulfillment of the promise of a Ruler who would conquer every other ruler. See notes on Gen. 49:10; Is. 28:16; Mic. 5:2.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold} their God. Another strong reaffirmation of the covenant bond between God and His people. God saves His people because of His eternal commitment to them (8:8 note; Jer. 31:33). Though they were cast off for a while because of their sins and exiled in Babylon, that could not be the end of the story.

As the shepherd whistles for his flock (cf. Is. 7:18), so God will recall the exiles from foreign lands (Deut. 30:1–10). The Lord earlier used the same signal to summon their enemies in judgment upon them (Is. 5:26; 7:18). as they were before. As the Israelites earlier multiplied (Ex. 1:7), in fulfillment of God's covenant promise to Abraham (Gen. 15:5; 17:6).

God's mighty act in summoning the exiles is depicted in language recalling Israel's exodus from Egypt (Is. 43:16, 17). The sea is a classic symbol of the forces of chaos in the OT, while Gilead and Lebanon are noted centers of fertility.
Following His guidance and wisdom in all that they do (Deut. 6:4–9; Mic. 4:5).

Scholars debate whether this small poetic section belongs with what precedes (chs. 9; 10; God's judgment against the nations) or with what follows (11:4–17; God's judgment against Israel for their rejection of the Shepherd). The metaphors of large oaks, dense forests, and ravaging lions are drawn from the plants and animals of the Jordan Valley. The language is consistent with a number of judgments in Israel's history, but the preeminent judgment comes to those nations and individuals who reject the Good Shepherd, Jesus Christ (Acts 4:24–28).
Often used as a symbol of Lebanon (1 Kin. 5:6; Ps. 104:16). Bashan. The fertile area northeast of the Dead Sea (Deut. 3:1 note).

The actors are difficult to identify with certainty in this section, although the general teaching is clear. The prophet is appointed to represent a good shepherd, who forsakes the flock because he is rejected (v. 9). As a good shepherd, the prophet is a type of the coming messianic Shepherd, Jesus Christ, who came as the Good Shepherd and laid down His life for His sheep (John 10:11–18). 11:4 Become shepherd. A command given to Zechariah. the flock doomed to slaughter. The people of Israel, who were about to be left without good leadership.

These words were appropriate before the Babylonian exile (Jer. 13:14; 15:5; 21:7); they occur here because of the continued rebellion of the people (Matt. 21:33–46). If the Lord has no pity on His people, no one else will show them pity either.

Or "grace." This word is also used of God Himself (Pss. 27:4; 90:17). The staff is symbolic of the grace that God has shown His people in His covenant (v. 10). Union. Or "unity." The unity of the divided nation (v. 14) is part of the promise of the new covenant (Jer. 30:3; 31:27, 31; 33:7).
These shepherds are difficult to identify. They could be symbolic of all leaders who fail to meet God's standards. In time, the Good Shepherd of God's choice will depose all other rulers (Rev. 2:27).
The prophet as shepherd expresses his disgust with the rebellion and disobedience of the flock. He will therefore leave the flock to its deserved fate.
The divinely imposed obligation on the nations not to injure God's people Israel (cf. Ezek. 34:25; Hos. 2:18). With the removal of God's favor toward Israel, the nations can afflict the flock of God.
Apparently the price of a slave (Ex. 21:32). Jewish officials paid Judas thirty shekels of silver to betray Jesus (Matt. 26:14–16).

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. Zechariah rejected the derisory wage that they offered. Throwing it to the temple may represent a rejection of the temple's activities as well. This prophecy was fulfilled when Judas threw down the thirty pieces of silver on the floor of the temple (Matt. 27:1–10; cf. Jer. 19:1–13).
The dissolution of the covenant nation because they rejected the Good Shepherd.

With the rejection of the Good Shepherd, worthless leaders take His place (cf. Ezek. 34:1–10). The loss of the "arm" and the "right eye" indicates the loss of power and insight necessary for leadership (v. 17). Some suggest that this prophecy refers to the Jewish leaders who led the nation into disastrous rebellions against Rome after the death of Christ (A.D. 66–74, 132–35). Because of the Lord's faithfulness to His own promises, He will not leave His people forever in the hands of false shepherds.

The second oracle of the book's latter half focuses on God's judgment of the nations, climaxing with the salvation of Jerusalem and the final celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles. 12:1 oracle of the word of the LORD. See note on 9:1. who stretched out the heavens. As the Creator, God has the power to make all things new (2 Cor. 5:17; Rev. 21:5).
A common OT image of God's wrath as a cup from which the nations will drink (Is. 51:17; Jer. 25:15–17, 27–29; Ezek. 23:32–34).

The day of the Lord (14:1). This phrase occurs numerous times in chs. 12–14, and indicates the fullness of God's judgment of the world and the final salvation of His people. Jerusalem a heavy stone. Like the object of an ancient weight-lifting competition, Jerusalem will not be easily moved.
These images are drawn from the covenant curses of Deut. 28:28.
More images of Judah's devouring power (cf. Judg. 15:1–8). Yet their power comes not from themselves but from the Lord of hosts.

The highest human glory, to be like David, the man after God's own heart, will be commonplace. Meanwhile, the line of David will reach even higher glory — divine glory — in the person of Jesus Christ.

Describes God's gracious Spirit who produces repentance and humility in God's people. The OT prophets emphasize that God's renewal of the covenant (Jer. 31:31–33) entails renewal through His Spirit (Is. 59:21; Ezek. 36:26, 27; 39:29; Joel 2:28, 29). look on me \... whom they have pierced. In the original context, this piercing is metaphorical; the Lord is stabbed to the heart by His people's unfaithfulness. Ultimately, though, the metaphor became reality in the person of Jesus, to whom all people must look if they are to be saved. Many passages in John's gospel speak of faith in terms of "seeing" (cf. John 6:40). as one mourns for an only child. With great intensity.

This could describe an intensity of mourning similar to pagan mourning rites or, alternatively, if Hadad-rimmon is the name of a place near Megiddo, it could describe the deep national mourning that followed the death of Josiah in battle (see 2 Chr. 35:24).

Every family will be affected by this mourning, with leadership provided by the Davidic line, represented by the family of his son, Nathan (1 Chr. 14:4), and the priestly line of Levi, represented by the family of his grandson, Shimei (1 Chr. 6:16, 17)

See note on 12:3. fountain \... from sin and uncleanness. The picture of a cleansing fountain indicates the abundance of forgiveness (cf. Jer. 2:13). Ultimately that abundance of forgiveness is found in Jesus and the Spirit (John 7:37–39).

Because of their idolatry, the people need to be cleansed; with the fulfillment of their cleansing, their attachment to idolatry will disappear. The Lord promises to cleanse His people not just from the guilt of sin but from its power as well.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. False prophecy includes both prophecy in the name of a false god and presumptuous speech in the name of the Lord (Deut. 13; 18:20–22). False prophets are to die by the sword according to the Mosaic law (Deut. 13:12–15). Removing these false prophets will also help the people to be faithful to the Lord.
False prophets will deny that they are prophets for fear of punishment, and will refuse to wear the traditional clothing symbolic of the prophet (2 Kin. 1:8; Matt. 3:4).
