Probably wounds that are self-inflicted during idolatrous worship. Several OT texts suggest that such practices are customary in pagan worship during that era (Lev. 19:28; 21:5; Deut. 14:1; 1 Kin. 18:28). The accused prophet contends that his wounds are inflicted by friends, and are not the result of idolatrous worship.

These verses envision God's chosen Shepherd, who suffers at the hand of God (v. 7). Out of this judgment emerges the true people of God (v. 9). This ranks among the clearest pictures of Jesus and His suffering church in the entire OT. 13:7 Strike the shepherd. Astonishingly, God strikes His own chosen Shepherd, as He earlier struck the worthless shepherd (see 11:17). Jesus is the Shepherd who is stricken and afflicted (Matt. 26:31–35; Mark 14:27–31; Luke 22:31–34). the sheep. God's people suffer along with their Shepherd (2 Cor. 1:5 note). against the little ones. Possibly an indication of God's judgment against His sheep. The Hb. word rendered "against" can also be translated "upon," indicating God's protection of the "little ones" in the midst of suffering.

The judgment sifts the true believers from the untrue. A common prophetic theme is that God's judgment will distinguish between the proud and humble (Zeph. 3:11, 12), between the true and false sheep (Ezek. 34:17–22).
The outcome of this time of testing will be the purification of God's people, not their destruction.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. The OT prophets proclaim a "day of the Lord" for judgment and deliverance, both of which are present in this passage (Introduction to Zephaniah: Characteristics and Primary Themes). This will be a time of severe testing for God's people (cf. 13:9).

Experiencing the Lord's favor does not always mean avoiding trials. Sometimes God calls His people to go through the most terrible of circumstances. Yet none of this is outside His sovereign control and care.

This is the classic language of theophany (the appearing of God). Cf. 1 Kin. 19:11. When the Lord comes in judgment, even the mountains cannot maintain their integrity. What human can stand before Him? The valley that is created is aligned along the sacred east-west axis of the temple.

Clearly a place close to Jerusalem; its precise location is unknown. in the days of Uzziah. This event is mentioned in Amos 1:1, 2. holy ones. An expression found also in the NT (Jude 14; cf. Matt. 25:31). These are God's chosen servants, the angelic host (perhaps humans as well), coming to Jerusalem to liberate it from pagan aggressors. This day of battle ushers in the eternal bliss of God's special presence among His people.

Like the first day of creation, before light and darkness were separated. God Himself will be the permanent light of the city (Is. 60:19, 20; Rev. 21:25; 22:5). Natural light from the heavenly bodies will have ceased (v. 6). No matter how intense the trials, the focus is on the greater reality of God's presence.

As the result of the Lord's presence, a refreshing stream of running water brings healing to those who seek refuge in the Lord. Such water symbolizes the blessings of salvation (Is. 55:1–5; Ezek. 47:1–12; John 4:10–14). Believers in Jesus receive the living water only He can give (John 7:37–39; Rev. 22:1).

With the final victory, God's sovereignty over all is manifested. the LORD will be one and his name one. These words clearly draw on Deut. 6:4, Israel's foundational confession (Mark 12:29 note). Only on this day of victory will the full meaning of this confession be understood.

This extensive geographical description is designed to stress that the whole land of God's people will be claimed by God Himself. In the language of theological geography, the land will be flattened so that Mount Zion can be properly and uniquely exalted (cf. Is. 40:4).
This fearful plague may recall the plagues on Egypt (Ex. 7–12), as well as the covenant curses God proclaims upon disobedience in the Mosaic law (Lev. 26:16; Deut. 28:22).

The plague will extend even to the (military) animals belonging to the heathen enemies of God. Zechariah is emphasizing the fact that the destruction of God's enemies will be final and complete. Even now, Christians enjoy victory in faith (1 John 5:4) and await the final subjugation of God's enemies by Christ (1 Cor. 15:24–28).

The last part of the book pictures the universal blessing that God will bestow in the final state. 14:16 everyone who survives. The people in the pagan nations are not all destroyed. Some are converted and come to worship the true and living God in Jerusalem (6:15; 8:23; and notes). Feast of Booths. The worship of the Gentiles is expressed in terms of this feast because it is one of joy and thankfulness to God for His blessings, as well as celebrating His reign as king (Lev. 23:33–36, 39–43; Num. 29:12–34; Deut. 16:13–15). The feast occurs during the fall harvest season and therefore might symbolize the ingathering of the Gentiles.

Prayer for rain may have been part of the liturgy of the Feast of Booths (or Tabernacles). Certainly, the Lord's ability to provide or withhold rain is a key aspect of His sovereignty (see 1 Kin. 17, 18).
Egypt may perhaps be singled out for a particular form of punishment because its harvests are not dependent upon local rainfall but upon the regular inundation of the Nile.

]{.rsb-studynote-bold}. Originally inscribed on the high priest's turban (Ex. 28:36–38) to express dedication, the phrase is now applied to everything in Jerusalem, even the horses' bells and cooking pots, because God's presence sanctifies all around Him.

Malachi.note: The people of Israel, back in their land after the exile, are not convinced that God loves them. This section is God's response to that cynical doubt. The Lord reminds Israel that Jacob, her ancestor, was chosen by God while Esau, Edom's forefather, was rejected. Therefore, although Israel has experienced the Lord's wrath for just a little while, Edom is a "people with whom the LORD is angry forever" (1:4). Furthermore, while Israel is heir of the everlasting promises of their covenant Lord, Edom will never rise again. The Lord's judgment on Edom will be cause for praise in Israel. 1:1 oracle of the word. Is. 13:1; Nah. 1:1; Hab. 1:1; Zech. 9:1; 12:1. Normally used in prophecies of judgment, "oracle" may point to the urgency felt by the prophet in issuing his proclamation. On this urgency, see also Jer. 20:9; Amos 3:8. Malachi. This could be either a personal name or a title (Introduction: Title and Author).

God's electing love is sovereign and unconditional. It is expounded principally in Deuteronomy, where the verbs "to choose" and "to love" are parallel, showing that love is not a feeling but the behavior that flows from a committed relationship (Deut. 7:6–8). God's love is manifested in the covenant He initiates with His people. The nearness of God to Israel was to be the source of awe and amazement (Deut. 4:7, 8). God's love begins in eternity (Jer. 31:3) and is manifested in His covenantal dealings with Abraham, Israel, and David (Gen. 17; Ex. 19:5, 6; 2 Sam. 7). God's election of Jacob continues to have relevance for His dealings with Israel in the period of Malachi's ministry. Properly understood, God's love does not lead to moral complacency but to moral zeal. However, Israel's complacency and the people's cynicism about God's love have led to the moral crises that Malachi addresses. See theological note "Predestination." How have you loved us. The response of Malachi's hearers might be surprising given all that the Lord has done for His people throughout the OT. Yet at this point in their history, perhaps a century after the return from the exile, it reflects the difficult challenges of life in a vassal state of Persia. The people are asking, "Where are all of the great blessings God has promised through His prophets?" Jacob. One of the titles for God in the Psalms is "the God of Jacob" (Pss. 20:1; 46:7; 75:9; 76:6; 84:8). God's electing love is unique because He loves sinners, who by nature are the objects of His displeasure and wrath (Luke 15:2; Rom. 5:6–8; Eph. 2:1–3). The history of Jacob and Esau in Genesis clearly points to God's choice of Jacob despite his lack of merit (Gen. 25:21–34; 27:1–40; Rom. 9:10–13).

Although there is a usage of the verb "hate" which means "to love less" (Gen. 29:31; Luke 14:26), the context immediately following suggests that here "hate" means active rejection, displeasure, and disfavor manifested in retributive justice. Like love (1:2 note), hatred is not merely an emotion but a covenantal term that includes the actions that flow from it. It is not merely that Esau (and the nation that comes from him, Edom) suffers the absence or lessening of blessing, but that he receives judgment that works its way out in the course of history. For this usage of "hate," see Ps. 5:5; Is. 61:8; Hos. 9:15; Amos 5:21; Mal. 2:16. See theological note "Predestination and Reprobation" on p. 1997. Neither Jacob (Israel) nor Esau (Edom) deserves God's love. Both merit destruction. Yet because of God's electing love for Jacob, Israel will be restored after her deserved punishment at the hands of the Babylonians, while Edom will have no such restoration. This distinction should encourage the Jews of Malachi's day to recognize the Lord's utterly undeserved mercy to them. laid waste. Probably a reference to the occupation of Edom by the Nabatean Arabs.

God is the sovereign Lord of history, whose redemptive purposes are accomplished both inside and outside ancient Israel (v. 11; Gen. 17:4–6). The fact that there is still a territory that could be called "Israel" in Malachi's day is a mark of God's faithfulness to His promises. In contrast, the land of Edom will disappear forever.

A major reason for the Lord's anger with Israel is the priesthood's attitude toward God's name at the altar and toward God's law in teaching and judging. At the altar, they offer diseased or imperfect animals in sacrifice, thereby reversing the intent of their labors and bringing curse and defilement where they should bring blessing and cleansing. In their teaching and judging, they violate the covenant with Levi (2:8), showing partiality and causing many to stumble. 1:6 honor. If normal fathers and masters expected honor, how much more does God deserve honor? God is in Himself infinitely glorious, and He must receive the recognition of His people (Pss. 29:1, 2; 57:5, 11). despise. The opposite of honoring and fearing the Lord (cf. 2 Sam. 12:9, 10). The word is used often in Proverbs (1:7; 15:20; 23:22).

The reference is to animal sacrifices (v. 8). "Polluted" means ceremonially unclean and therefore unacceptable to God. God is not offended merely by ceremonial imperfections but by the attitude of contempt behind such imperfect sacrifices (Gen. 4:3–5 and notes; Heb. 11:4). The priests' task is to teach the law and to oversee the sacrifices, so they are culpable for allowing the people to bring such defective offerings. the LORD's table. This phrase and the similar phrase in v. 12 occur only here in the OT, both times referring to the altar.

The law expressly prohibits such offerings (Lev. 22:22; Deut. 15:21). Only unblemished animals are suitable, prefiguring the perfect atonement that Christ would ultimately make for sin. to your governor. It is normal in Malachi's culture for a visitor to bring a gift to a superior; someone who brings a defective animal as a gift, however, should hardly expect to receive a favorable welcome.

Even worship that is offered in the right location in the name of the true God is not acceptable if it comes from a defiled heart. The Lord prefers that no offerings be presented on His altar rather than such defective ones.

In contrast to the despising of His name by the priests (v. 6), God promises the future triumph of His glorious kingdom. "From the rising of the sun to its setting" and similar phrases often point to God's future judgment of the entire world and the restoration of His order (Ps. 50:1; Is. 45:6; 59:19). in every place. The imperfect sacrifices being offered during the prophet's time (vv. 7, 8) are contrasted with the pure offerings of worship in the future (Is. 2:2–4; 66:19–21; Zech. 14:16–21). The promise of this verse is being fulfilled even now as Christ gathers His royal priests from among the nations (1 Pet. 2:9; Rev. 5:9, 10), and it will be consummated in the future as the nations gather to worship God in purity (Rev. 21:27).
In the similar phrase in v. 7, "the LORD" is the divine name, Yahweh. Here it is "Lord," the same word for "master" in v. 6, underlining the lack of respect that is being shown to God.

Laws regulating offerings given in response to a vow require the giving of a perfect offering. This text implies an attempt to deceive the Lord by promising a costly offering when in trouble but then giving a less-expensive offering after deliverance has been granted (cf. Ps. 76:11). I am a great King. God is not only their Father (1:6; Ex. 4:22) and their Master but also their King. The idea of God as King arose early in OT religion (Ex. 15:18; Num. 23:21; 24:7; Deut. 33:5). See Pss. 93–100.
The priests are supposed to be the representatives of the people as well as their spiritual leaders. The following verses show how they have failed to act in accordance with their priestly calling.

See Deut. 28:20. I will curse your blessings. The blessings are either the physical and material blessings promised to the priests who receive the people's tithes (Num. 18:21) or the pronouncements of blessing uttered by the priests at the time of the sacrifices (Num. 6:24–27), which then become a curse.

Lit. "I will rebuke your seed" (text note). This could mean a curse on the priest's offspring or a literal curse on their agricultural seed (cf. Lev. 26:16; Deut. 28:38). Or, both could be in view. spread dung on your faces. Refers to the animal intestines and their excretory contents, which are a byproduct of the sacrificial process.
This covenant includes Levi's descendants, entitling them to a hereditary priesthood (cf. Ex. 32:29; Num. 25:11–13; Jer. 33:20, 21).

The central thrust of Deuteronomy is to show the connection between covenant obedience and life. Commitment to God leads to a full life. Some see in "covenant \... of \... peace" an allusion to the covenant with Phinehas mentioned in Num. 25:10–13.

See Ezra 7:10; Hos. 4:6. The connection between the true knowledge of the Lord and priestly instruction in the law is set forth vividly in 2 Chr. 15:3: "For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law." Providing this instruction is the first task of the priesthood (Deut. 33:10). messenger of the LORD of hosts. The Hb. word translated "messenger" is the same one elsewhere translated "angel," underlining the authority with which the priests speak.

See Neh. 13:29. The priests' attitudes and actions set a bad example for the people. They have abandoned their true calling, both to teach and practice the truth. Instead of turning people from iniquity (v. 7), they actually are actually leading the people off the true path.

The basis for this censure is the character of God. God "is not partial and takes no bribe" (Deut. 10:17; cf. Lev. 19:15). Possibly the priests are favoring society's rich and powerful people at the expense of the poor and powerless.

Lack of faithfulness toward God leads to breakdowns in human relationships. Malachi addresses two problems: marriage to idolatrous wives (vv. 10–12) and the divorcing of Israelite wives (vv. 13–16). 2:10 one Father. Some interpret this as referring to Abraham (Is. 51:2). More likely it refers to God (1:6; Ex. 4:22, 23; Deut. 32:6; Is. 63:16; 64:8; Jer. 3:4, 19; 31:9). As a good Father, He will discipline the disobedient (Heb. 12:5–11).

This verb is used five times in vv. 10–16. In Jer. 3:20, it refers to marital unfaithfulness; more generally, it applies to any breach of covenant obligations. abomination. The Hb. word here, prominently employed in Deuteronomy, refers to idolatrous religious practices (Deut. 7:25, 26; 12:31; 13:14; 18:12). It can also refer to sexual transgression (Lev. 18:22, 26, 29, 30; Deut. 24:4). profaned the sanctuary of the LORD. The Hb. word translated "sanctuary" can also be understood as referring to the people themselves ("holy seed"; Is. 6:13; cf. Ezra 9:2). The people, who are loved by God, defile themselves by disobedience in their marriage practices. married the daughter of a foreign god. This phrase refers to marrying a woman still committed to a foreign god — an idolater outside the covenant (cf. Gen. 24:3, 4; Ex. 34:12–16; Deut. 7:3, 4; Josh. 23:12; 1 Kin. 11:1–10). The prohibition against marrying unbelievers continues in the NT (1 Cor. 7:39; 2 Cor. 6:14).

's altar with tears.]{.rsb-studynote-bold} These are not the marks of true repentance here; the people's actions demonstrate them to be an empty gesture, more in line with pagan rituals than with the true worship of God.

See v. 15; Prov. 5:18. The motivation for abandoning these marriages may be romantic or to pursue politically advantageous relationships with the surrounding ethnic groups, who hold a great deal of power. your companion. A related form of this unique word is used to describe a seam or a joint in a building, or the process of cementing something together. your wife by covenant. God's covenant faithfulness is to be mirrored in the marriage relationships of His people (Prov. 2:17; Eph. 5:22–33).
See Gen. 2:24. portion of the Spirit. The marriage union is not merely physical but spiritual as well, and has as its goal godly offspring for God Himself.

See Is. 50:1; Deut. 24:1–4; theological note "Marriage" above, and "Divorce" on p. 1755. As in 1:3, "hate" is a covenantal word that describes the rejection of relationship. garment. Entering into marriage and obtaining a wife is sometimes portrayed as covering with a garment (Ruth 3:9 text note; Ezek. 16:8). Abusing and divorcing a wife metaphorically stains a person's garment, making him unfit to enter God's presence.

Religious cynics charge the Lord with injustice. God responds with the promise that He will send a messenger to prepare the way before Him before returning to His temple. His presence among a wicked people requires judgment and gracious refinement (3:2, 3). He will change the Levites' hearts and they will offer sacrifices in righteousness once again. The judgment will be exacting (3:5). The Lord Himself will be the chief witness for the prosecution of His people. 2:17 wearied the LORD. See Is. 43:24. In Malachi, the offenses revolve around the cynical rejection of God's moral government and the attendant insolent spirit that constantly puts God on trial. Everyone who does evil is good. This is an explicit rejection of the Lord's statement in Deut. 18:12. They stumble over the same issues that caused the psalmist difficulties in Ps. 73.

This section rebuts two cynical statements from ch. 2. First, the allegation in 2:17 that God does not differentiate between good and evil is answered in 3:2 by referring to the refining and purifying ministry of the messenger of the covenant. The second statement, "Where is the God of justice?" (2:17), is answered in v. 5. The Jews in Malachi's day are looking for the Lord to judge the nations, but instead the Lord will come near to them for judgment (v. 5). 3:1 my messenger. See 4:5; also Is. 40:3 (where "prepare the way" also occurs). It was the practice in the ancient Near East to send messengers in advance of a visiting king to announce his coming and to remove all hindrances or obstacles. This prophetic messenger (Matt. 11:10) will be the last of his kind to appear before the coming of the Lord, who is "the messenger of the covenant." suddenly. This word is almost always associated in Scripture with an unhappy and calamitous circumstance (Num. 12:4; Is. 47:11; cf. 2 Pet. 3:10). the messenger of the covenant. A person distinct from "my messenger," He will purify the sacrifices, the priests, and the nation (vv. 2–5). This "messenger of the covenant" is the Messiah, and this prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus, who alone has performed the perfect sacrifice on behalf of His people.
Ancient launderers used harsh chemicals extracted from plants to remove stubborn stains from clothing

The priests have been instrumental in leading the people astray. The work of purification will begin with them, and it will spread from them to the whole of the nation. The Levites are the pattern for the nation, which is to be "a kingdom of priests" (Ex. 19:6). Silver is harder to purify than gold. offerings in righteousness. See "a pure offering" in 1:11. Because of the work of the messenger of the covenant, proper worship will again be offered, since the hearts and lives of the worshipers will be purified (Ps. 4:5; Zeph. 3:9).

This section began with the religious cynics' accusing the Lord of injustice. It ends with a covenant lawsuit in which the Lord brings charges against His people. The seven specific sins mentioned in v. 5 are a broad cross section of offenses clearly forbidden in the law of God. The root cause of these sins is that they "do not fear me."

The people are not only bringing defective offerings but also are withholding the tithe, apparently due to the crops' meager returns. But withholding the tithe is stealing from the Lord. As a consequence, the righteous Lord withholds blessing. Their sin also evidences a lack of trust in the Lord to provide for their needs if they keep His commands. So, the Lord urges them to put Him to the test. If they do so, the consequent provision will be so great that the nations will see the difference and pronounce Israel blessed. 3:6 I \... do not change. The immutability, or unchangeable character, of God is seen in His purpose to bless His elect people. Thus, in spite of their numerous sins, they are not destroyed (Ex. 34:6, 7; Jer. 30:11). This verse closes the previous section and begins the next one.

The command to repent is connected with a promise (cf. Zech. 1:3; James 4:8). Sin separates people from God and causes God to hide His face (Is. 59:2). How shall we return. This is not a genuine question; there is plenty of information on how to return to the Lord in the Scriptures that they already possessed.

Lit. "a tenth." The practice of tithing is mentioned in the accounts of Abraham (Gen. 14:20) and Jacob (Gen. 28:22), and is codified in the law of Moses as an annual requirement to bring in one-tenth of the agricultural produce as a mark of the Lord's ownership of the Promised Land (Lev. 27:30; Num. 18:26; Deut. 14:22–29). contributions. Portions of the animal sacrifices to which the priests are entitled (Ex. 29:27, 28; Lev. 9:22).

Refers to a room in the temple designated for the storage of gifts so that they can be distributed to the priests and the Levites, as well as to the poor of the community (2 Chr. 31:11; Neh. 10:38, 39; 12:44; 13:12). put me to the test. This is a reversal of the ordinary biblical pattern, in which God typically tests human beings (Pss. 11:5; 26:2; 66:10; Prov. 17:3; Jer. 11:20; 12:3; 17:10). Only in a few instances are humans invited to test God (i.e., to prove His claims and justify His commands; Is. 7:11, 12; 1 Kin. 18:22–46). Because the tithe is a covenantal obligation under the Sinai covenant, specific blessings and curses were attached to it. Under the new covenant, Paul calls us to excel in the grace of giving (2 Cor. 8:7). This suggests that love should move us to greater generosity than the law ever could, and that the old covenant tithe is really just the minimum that people should give to God's work. windows of heaven. See Gen. 7:11. Rain in its appropriate time is a blessing from the Lord and is crucial to the agricultural well-being of the community.

In addition to providing the all-important rain, the Lord also promises to protect the crops against destructive pests, which are themselves a sign of covenant curse under the Mosaic covenant (see Deut. 28:38–42). The result of these blessings will be fruitful harvests.

The last section returns to the prophecy in 3:1–5 concerning the forerunner (Matt. 11:10) and the coming of God. In various ways, the beginning of the section is reminiscent of a psalm of lament. The complaints, however, are interpreted as hard words against the Lord. Yet there are those who sense the same injustices without concluding that it is futile to serve the Lord. The first group speaks hard words and invites the Lord's response; the latter fears the Lord and so He writes words of remembrance concerning them. He promises that they will be His special possession in the great day of the Lord. A reference to "the day" (v. 17) again introduces the last day of judgment, a day of destruction for the wicked but healing for the righteous. The final verses return to the promised forerunner and exhort the people to keep the law of Moses. 3:13Your words have been hard. This aptly describes the people's responses to the Lord throughout the book of Malachi, which have revealed the corresponding hardness of their hearts. Instead of repenting, the people consistently have contested the validity of each of the Lord's charges against them.

Lit. "empty" or "useless." The hardness of the people's hearts is revealed by their response to the prosperity of the wicked. They have concluded that serving the Lord is worthless. profit. The Hb. term usually refers to unjust gain. Greed is inconsistent with a desire for God's truth (Ps. 119:36).

Typically an expression of blatant unbelief (Num. 14:22; Deut. 6:16; Ps. 95:9; Matt. 4:7). Rarely, the Lord actually invites people to put Him to the test, in which case to decline is a sign of unbelief (3:10 note).

The conversation and conduct of those who fear God is occasioned by the preceding words of murmuring and is placed in contrast to them. Instead of speaking hard words against God, this group esteems the Lord's name. book of remembrance. This exact phrase is found only here, but references to a special book are found elsewhere (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 7:10). This provides the answer to those who earlier asked, "Where is the God of justice?" (2:17). The Lord is aware of what is happening and watching over those who truly belong to Him.

Refers to the remnant described in v. 16. my treasured possession. In the early stage of OT revelation, the nation of Israel is called God's "treasured possession" (Ex. 19:5; Deut. 7:6; 14:2). On the day when the Lord constitutes this precious remnant, it will become clear to all that serving the Lord has not, in fact, been in vain (3:14). his son who serves him. See 1:6.

Two images of fire are used in Malachi to describe the Lord: a refining fire (3:2) and a destroying fire (4:1). Evildoers do not actually put the Lord to the test and escape (see 3:15). root nor branch. The wicked are compared to a tree (Amos 2:9) that will be totally destroyed, consumed from the topmost branch down to the roots.

An expression unique to Malachi (cf. Ps. 84:12). The Davidic king will reign in righteousness (Is. 32:1) and will be called "a righteous Branch" (Jer. 23:5, 6). The rising sun reveals the truth about the Lord and His people, vindicating those who are faithful and condemning those who remain rebellious. healing in its wings. The Bible considers physical sickness and spiritual sickness or sin to be analogous. Salvation is often compared to bodily healing (Ex. 15:26; 2 Chr. 7:14; Ps. 103:3; Is. 53:5; Jer. 17:14). The sun was often depicted in antiquity as a winged disk. calves from the stall. Calves that have been specially fattened and are full of vigor.
Patience is required until the day when God acts to demonstrate the decisive difference between the fate of the righteous and the wicked.

Together, Moses and Elijah (v. 5) represent the Law and the Prophets. Moses communicated God's law with its statutes and rules, which the priests have been failing to teach the people (2:6). However, the righteous remnant will remember them.

The task of the prophets is to convict those who have failed to heed the law of Moses and to call them to repentance for their sin. The literary connection of this verse with 3:1 indicates that "Elijah" is the same person as "my messenger." Both verses begin with the word "Behold" and use the same form of the verb "to send." In both cases, the mission is to bring repentance in advance of the coming day of the Lord. The NT identifies this "Elijah" as John the Baptist, who epitomized the prophet's message of judgment and repentance (Matt. 11:14; 17:10; Mark 9:11–13; Luke 1:17).

Repentance and turning to God will be seen in the restoration of family relationships (Luke 1:17). Since God is our Father (1:6), repentance also means restoration in that relationship as well. lest I come and strike the land with a decree. Malachi began with the announcement of God's electing love, yet the book ends with the threat of a curse. Malachi's dual thrust of mercy and judgment is echoed by Paul's pronouncement, "Note then the kindness and the severity of God" (Rom. 11:22; cf. Deut. 30:19, 20). Strikingly, Luke 1:17 focuses on the positive side of Malachi's prophecy, for in His first coming Jesus came to seek and to save that which was lost. Yet those who refuse the salvation that Christ came to bring will face another coming in which Jesus rides out to bring destruction on the unrepentant (Rev. 19:11–21).

Matthew.note: The same phrase is used at Gen. 2:4; 5:1 in the Septuagint. Here it may refer not only to the genealogy immediately following but also to the account of Jesus' birth or the Gospel as a whole. The Gk. word translated "genealogy" here is rendered "birth" in 1:18. See Introduction: Title. Christ. This title comes from the Gk. word christos, meaning "anointed." It is the Gk. translation of the Hb. "Messiah"; see note on 1 Sam. 2:10. In the OT, prophets, priests, and kings were anointed with oil (cf. Ex. 29:7; 1 Sam. 16:13; 1 Kin. 19:16). Anointing dramatized the bestowal of wisdom and power from the Holy Spirit, granting an officer the ability to fulfill his calling. The OT promised the coming of the righteous servant of the Lord (Is. 42:1–9), who would be a prophet like Moses (Deut. 18:18, 19), a priest like Melchizedek (Ps. 110:4), and a king like David, the Lord's anointed (Is. 55:3–5; Jer. 30:9; Ezek. 34:24; Hos. 3:5; Zech. 12:8). Matthew reveals that Jesus is the Christ, the promised king and deliverer.
The specifics of this genealogy differ from the one found in Luke; see note on Luke 3:23–38.

Women are not usually named in ancient Near Eastern genealogies, but they are intrinsic to God's purpose in sending Christ. The five women named in Jesus' genealogy all remind us that God often does the unexpected and chooses the unlikely. Tamar (v. 3) reminds us of Judah's failures (Gen. 38:6–30); Rahab (v. 5) was a harlot (Josh. 2); Ruth was a Moabite (Ruth 1:4) and thus subject to a special curse (Deut. 23:3–5); Uriah's wife, Bathsheba (v. 6), was David's downfall (2 Sam. 11). Mary fulfills Is. 7:14 (v. 23) and the even more important promise of Gen. 3:15 (Gal. 4:4). At least three of the five (Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba) have Gentile associations, an important theme in this gospel (2:1–12; 28:18–20).

Matthew organizes the genealogy into three groups of fourteen to show that God has a purpose in history. The early history leading to David, the monarchy leading to the exile in Babylon, and the history of Israel after the exile all lead up to and point to Christ. Jechoniah (Jehoiachin) is included in both the second and third groups of fourteen, whereas three kings (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah) are omitted from the second group (2 Kin. 8:25–14:22; 2 Chr. 21:4–26:13). Biblical genealogies are selective in order to reinforce theological motifs or to aid readers in memorizing the genealogical data.
In Joseph's day, engagement is nearly as binding as marriage, and infidelity during betrothal makes divorce virtually obligatory.

God imparted special revelation through dreams to Joseph (also 2:13, 19, 22), the magi (2:12), and the wife of Pontius Pilate (27:19), as He had to OT figures such as Joseph, son of Jacob (Gen. 37:5–11; 40:5–19; 41:1–36).
The Gk. equivalent of "Joshua," meaning "Yahweh is salvation," or "Yahweh saves." Often in names, a shortened form of God's name is used (e.g., in Elijah, Isaiah, Joshua).

See note on Is. 7:14. Jesus' conception by a virgin is miraculous, announcing that God is present with His people and will soon redeem them. This quotation is the first of many OT references Matthew uses to show that Jesus fulfills the OT (2:6, 15, 18, 23 and notes). In the entire gospel there are twelve such fulfillment formulas, and more than fifty OT quotations. See theological note "The Virgin Birth" on p. 1782. Immanuel \... God with us. The second line of the quotation in Matthew appears to say the opposite of the second line of Mic. 5:2 ("too little"), but Matthew is giving the sense of the prophetic text, namely, that though Bethlehem appears to be insignificant, it is in truth important. Hos. 11:1 refers to God's calling His son Israel out of Egypt in the exodus (see Ex. 4:22, 23). Matthew means that the history of God's redemption of Israel points forward to Jesus, the true Son of God. When Israel left Egypt, its fidelity as God's son was tested forty years in a wilderness, and the record of this testing is largely one of failure (Deut. 8:2–5). Jesus is later tested in the wilderness forty days. He sustains His test and shows that He is indeed the faithful Son of God (Matt. 4:1–11).

Matthew is quoting from Jer. 31:15, a prophecy about the exile. Jeremiah uses the imagery of Rachel weeping for her sons Joseph and Benjamin to describe the sorrow of Israel at the time of the exile. In the next section of Jeremiah's prophecy, he foresees the return from exile, a new exodus. Matthew's use of this prophecy appears to portray Jesus as a new Moses (the one who led Joseph's descendants out of Egypt) who fulfills the prophecy of a second exodus. Like Moses, Jesus escapes slaughter as an infant. Like Moses, He is sent to rescue God's chosen ones.

Jesus' identification with His people includes His baptism and death, His anointing with the Spirit, and His victory over temptation. See theological note "The Baptism of Christ" on p. 1733.

Those who lack God's righteousness but hunger and thirst for it will be filled (5:6; 6:33). Jesus calls those burdened with the load of self-righteousness to find their rest in Him (11:28–12:8).

Although God Himself tempts no one (James 1:13), our temptations are included in His sovereign plan for our good. If we overcome, we are strengthened; if we succumb, we recognize more clearly our need for further sanctification and grace. The temptation of Jesus (vv. 1–11) parallels the testing of Israel in the wilderness. The forty days correspond to the forty years of wandering (cf. Num. 14:34). His temptation recalls Deut. 8:1–5, which He quoted in response to one of the temptations. The experience of Israel in the wilderness was the type or shadow of Jesus' temptation in the wilderness after His baptism. The temptations appeal to common motivations: physical drives, pride, and the desire for possessions (1 John 2:16). But each is pointed specially at the Messiah. Satan challenges Jesus to prove the truth of the Father's words at His baptism: "If you are the Son of God" (vv. 3, 6; cf. 27:40). The third temptation offers Jesus a path to kingship that avoids the cross. Jesus was tempted in every way just as we are (Heb. 4:15), but He did not sin. He represents us before God as a "merciful and faithful high priest" (Heb. 2:17), one who knows through His human nature what it is to endure temptation. The Sermon on the Mount is the first of five great blocks of Jesus' teaching in Matthew (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). It is the classic statement of the ethics of the kingdom of God. The early church favored a literal interpretation but fully applied the sermon only to special classes of Christians, especially monastics. Others, such as the Anabaptists, have attempted to apply it literally to every Christian, or even to society and the state. Still others have viewed it as a heightening of the law of Moses with the aim of inducing repentance (Luther). Some consider its demands too risky to implement in the present age and expect them to become applicable in a future millennium, when Jesus reigns. Finally, some have argued that the demands of the sermon are not to be understood literally but that Jesus is concerned with inward disposition rather than outward conduct, or that the severity of the sermon is intended to compel a decision by the hearers either for or against God's demands on their lives. We must recognize that the sermon is directed to the disciples and through them to the whole church today. The sermon addresses both inward motives and outward conduct (5:21, 22, 27, 28), calling the adopted sons of God (5:9) to reflect the character of their heavenly Father (5:16, 48; 6:1, 6, 9, 32, 33). These legitimate demands set the bar so high (5:48) that no one except Jesus, the king Himself, fulfills them flawlessly. We are therefore driven to the grace and mercy of God both for forgiveness in our failure (6:12) and for the Spirit's strength when our faith and faithfulness are tried (6:13). 5:1 went up on the mountain. Since Jesus reveals the depth of the commands given through Moses, His ascent of a mountain is reminiscent of Mount Sinai. The primary value of salt is not as a flavoring but as a preservative. Disciples are to hinder the world's corruption. Jesus does not criticize the Pharisees for their strict observance of the law but for their emphasis on outward conformity to it without a proper inner attitude. By focusing on externals, they avoid the real intent of the law and so obscure its real demands (23:23–28). The Dead Sea Scrolls refer to the Pharisees as "seekers after smooth things" because they accommodated and compromised the law to fit the realities of life. Such accommodation removed awareness of the need for grace and dependence on God. In the following verses, Jesus restores the true nature of God's law as demanding total and radical holiness. Jesus demands a deeper obedience, not disregard of God's commands.

Gehenna, the "valley of Hinnom," was a trash dump outside Jerusalem where fires burned constantly. It was notorious as the location of human sacrifices by fire during the reigns of Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Chr. 28:3; 33:6). Jeremiah called it the "Valley of Slaughter," an appropriate symbol of God's fearful judgment (Jer. 7:32). See theological note "Hell" on p. 1753. Jesus uses this site as a metaphor for perpetual physical and spiritual torment awaiting the wicked.

Some have understood Jesus' prohibition of oaths to be universal, but Jesus Himself submitted to an oath (26:63) and Paul invoked God as his witness in Rom. 1:9. God Himself takes an oath so that we might be encouraged (Heb. 6:17). Jesus is addressing a narrow and misleading legalism that requires a specific oath to make spoken promises binding, implying that trustworthiness in speaking is optional when unaccompanied by a solemn oath. Jesus demands an integrity in speaking such that everything is spoken as though it is under oath. He also prohibits the implicit idolatry of swearing by anything less than God. Jesus contradicted those who saw in this principle grounds for personal vengeance.

The order of the miracles and events in these chapters differs from that found in Mark and Luke. Matthew probably arranges them by topic rather than chronology.

A variety of skin diseases are referred to by the Gk. word used here, not just leprosy (Hansen's disease). Touching a leper makes one ceremonially unclean (cf. Lev. 15:7), but in this case, rather than Jesus' becoming unclean, the leper is healed and becomes clean.

The command to the leper to be silent is to prevent miracle seekers from hindering Jesus' main mission, which is to proclaim God's kingdom, bringing comprehensive — spiritual as well as physical — cleansing (Mark 1:38, 45). By showing himself to the priest, the leper will fulfill the requirements of the law and be able to rejoin Jewish society (Lev. 14:1–32).

A Roman military officer in charge of approximately one hundred men. This centurion has an appreciation for Jesus' authority that surpasses anything in Israel, an awareness of his own unworthiness, and faith that Jesus can overcome the difficulty of his unworthiness. Matthew, who often prefers a condensed style, does not mention the intermediaries who appear in the parallel account in Luke 7:1–10.

The faith of the Gentile centurion provides the occasion for the prediction that Israel will be hardened and the gospel will be extended to the Gentiles. The Great Commission (28:18–20) closes the gospel with Jesus' charge to make disciples of all nations.

A reference to the messianic banquet theme of Is. 25:6–9. Gentiles now appear in place of the natural sons. This theme recurs in the parable of the wicked tenants (21:33–44, esp. v. 43) and the banquet parable (22:1–14). Jesus' prediction is an early example of the principle developed by Paul in Rom. 9:30–32: Israel tries to pursue righteousness by works and does not obtain it, but Gentiles who know they deserve only condemnation seek God's mercy and obtain it.
These figures of speech represent the grief and despair of those who are everlastingly excluded from the kingdom.

Is. 53:4 mentions "griefs" and "sorrows" (rendered "illnesses" and "diseases" in Matthew) as resulting from sin, for which they are the curse (Is. 53:5). Jesus came to bear the curse as well as the guilt of sin on the cross, and in His ministry He demonstrated the power of His coming death and resurrection to reverse all the effects of Adam's fall (including physical effects) for those who trust Him. Yet He has not promised to remove sickness from the world or the church before the second coming (Rom. 8:20–23; 1 Cor. 15:26), when our lowly bodies will be conformed to His glorious body through resurrection (Phil. 3:20, 21).

These two events show the radical commitment Jesus demands of disciples. Those who identify with Jesus will be "sojourners and exiles" in the world (1 Pet. 2:11). Honoring one's parents by providing a proper burial was a strict obligation in Jewish society, a fitting application of the fifth commandment (Ex. 20:12), which Jesus affirmed as God's Word (Matt. 15:4–6). But Jesus demands a greater allegiance to Himself.

This title occurs only three times in the NT outside the Gospels (Acts 7:56; Rev. 1:13; 14:14). All of the many occurrences in the Gospels involve assertions made by Jesus about Himself and may be classified into three categories. (1) "Son of Man" can mean "a human being," especially in statements about what is typical of humanity generally. This use is similar to God's calling Ezekiel "son of man" (Ezek. 2:1 note) or to Paul's reference to the human race as "the sons of men" (Eph. 3:5). (2) The title is used by Jesus when He predicts the suffering, death, and resurrection He would accomplish for humanity (17:22, 23 note). (3) It can refer to the apocalyptic "Son of Man" who appears at the judgment at the end times (24:30; 26:64 note). This usage stems from Dan. 7:13, 14, where "one like a son of man" appears before the Ancient of Days and receives world dominion and worship. Jesus may have used "Son of Man" and avoided using "Messiah" because of popular conceptions that the Messiah would be a political and military leader. Yet in Dan. 7, the Ancient of Days confers on the one like a son of man "dominion \... that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him" — a prophecy now being fulfilled as the ascended Son of Man expands His reign through the global preaching of the gospel (Matt. 28:18–20).

Jesus' sleeping may well be an allusion to David's sleeping in Pss. 3 and 4. There, David's sleeping indicates his trust as a king in God to deliver him from impending danger. David's trust expressed in sleep points to Jesus, the greater Davidic king, who now is portrayed as the perfectly trusting king.

The psalmists answer the disciples' astonished question, "What sort of man is this?" Only God can still turbulent and threatening seas as Lord of the storm (Pss. 29:3, 4; 65:5–7; 89:9; 107:23–30, the latter of which is likely alluded to here). Jesus is not only the perfect king who perfectly trusts in God but also God Himself incarnate.

two demon-possessed men. Perhaps only one of these two demoniacs is exceedingly violent, so Mark and Luke mention only that one. Matthew may mention both to suggest that two witnesses attest this victory of Jesus over demons (Deut. 19:15; see Matt. 18:16; 20:30).

See note on 16:16. the time. The demons complain that it is not yet "the time," the day of judgment. But Jesus is present and God's kingdom is near, so the powers of darkness cannot resist the king's liberating light (12:28).

The Gk. word translated "demons" is a broad term for "divinities" (Acts 17:18), that is, supernatural beings. "Unclean spirits" (10:1) cause havoc with men, sometimes by possession. They are in league with Satan, the prince of demons (9:34; 12:24–28).

The demons ask permission to enter a herd of pigs, apparently imagining that this will prolong their influence on earth. But their defiling presence drives the disturbed swine into the sea, hastening the spirits' consignment to the abyss (Luke 8:31). Subsequent events demonstrate the perverse values of the people, who prefer their pigs to the rescue of two human beings.
Forgiveness is the prerogative of the one who has been offended, so for Jesus to forgive sins is to claim divine authority (Is. 43:25), as the scribes rightly discern.

Ultimately, forgiving sins is more difficult than performing a miracle, as the scribes understand, since they recognize that only God can forgive sins. But the forgiveness of sins cannot be seen by observers. Jesus performs the lesser deed to prove the greater, showing that He has authority as Son of Man to render a justifying verdict not only in heaven after His exaltation (Dan. 7:13, 14) but also presently on earth.

Just as Jesus is not defiled by contact with lepers, so He is not defiled by contact with sinners such as Matthew and his colleagues who collaborate with Rome's occupying forces. He is the physician who heals spiritual as well as physical sickness. Those who think they are well are puzzled by Jesus' activities and found Him offensive.

Although Luke notes that Pharisees ask about fasting, Mark includes both John's disciples and Pharisees among those who raise the question. John's summons to sorrow over sin in view of the coming kingdom make the self-denial of fasting an appropriate practice for his disciples (Lev. 16:29–31; Ps. 35:13).

John characterized Jesus as the bridegroom to whom the bride belongs (John 3:29, 30), evoking OT imagery of Israel as the Lord's bride (Jer. 2:2, 3; Hos. 2:2–20). The arrival of the groom brings the joy of the wedding feast, at which fasting is not fitting. then they will fast. Jesus recognizes a future time when the bridegroom will not be with them. This points out that from the earliest stages of His ministry, Jesus has anticipated a time between His initial coming in redemption and His final coming to consummate both judgment and salvation.

New wine continues to ferment and builds up pressure that will burst a used wineskin. Old patterns of piety are inappropriate while the king is present, although Jesus assumes that His followers may resume fasting after His ascension if they do so out of proper motives (6:16–18).

As usual, Matthew has a more condensed form of this story than Mark and Luke. The stories of the ruler's daughter and of the woman with a hemorrhage, whom Jesus calls "daughter," illustrate the relation between the work of Jesus and the role of faith in the kingdom. The same point appears in the following accounts of the blind man and the mute demoniac. These works (raising the dead, healing the sick, etc.) are in response to faith.
Her faith has made her well because the blessings of the kingdom come to those who look to Jesus for the solution to their problems, not because of any power of faith in itself.
Professional mourners and others who help the bereaved express their grief.
Jesus is prophesying that He will raise her from death (John 11:11–14; 1 Thess. 4:13–18). In the presence of the Lord of life, death is no more final or irreversible than slumber.

This healing of two blind men is similar to the account in 20:29–34, which seems to be parallel to the healing of Bartimaeus in Mark 10:46–52 (cf. Luke 18:35–43). Both Bartimaeus and the blind men in Matt. 9 and 20 express their faith by calling Jesus "Son of David," a messianic title. The similarities have suggested to some that both accounts in Matthew are based on the healing of Bartimaeus, but differences between the two accounts in Matthew suggest separate incidents.

This paragraph summarizes the activity of Jesus in chs. 5–9 (teaching, preaching, healing; cf. 4:23) and introduces the mission discourse of ch. 10. The background is Ezek. 34:5, 6. Jesus is the true Shepherd, who is concerned for His sheep (John 10), and He is identified with the "Lord God" of Ezek. 34:11–16.

Often a metaphor for the end-time activity of God. That the harvest is plentiful indicates that the harvest is not the harvest time (as in John 4:35) but the crop (as in Luke 10:2). The emphasis here is on the proclamation of the gospel, the eschatological announcement that precedes judgment and urges people to repent and believe God's promises. The "laborers" are not the angels sent to gather for judgment (13:49) but disciples who imitate Jesus by proclaiming the coming of the kingdom (10:7). Jesus first commands His disciples to pray to God to send workers, and then He immediately sends these same men out to announce the near approach of God's kingdom and to exert its power over evil.

The Gk. word apostolos designates an authorized representative or emissary whose word has the authority of the sender (cf. 2 Cor. 8:23, where it is translated "messengers," and 2 Cor. 1:1 note). Here the Twelve receive authority to do exactly what Jesus has been doing (vv. 7, 8).

A member of a revolutionary movement ("Simon \... called the Zealot," Luke 6:15). According to Josephus, the Zealots were a political party whose religious enthusiasm led them to advocate armed rebellion against Rome. Simon's presence among the Twelve, along with Matthew, a tax collector who collaborated with Roman functionaries, shows the reconciling power of Christ. Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. Well before the turning point where Jesus speaks explicitly of His coming suffering (16:21), the cross casts its shadow over His inner circle. As He sends these apostles out, He now prepares them for persecution, even to the extreme of the cross, (10:38) like the one awaiting their master (10:24, 25).

This section contains several lines of teaching regarding the Christian mission that are found elsewhere in the other Gospels. This does not mean Matthew invented the occasion for the teaching, but in this, the second of the five major discourses, he may include relevant materi­al taught by Jesus on other occasions. Particularly 10:17–22, which envisions a world mission and being "dragged before governors and kings" (v. 18), seems to go beyond v. 5, which restricts the mission to Israel. Nevertheless, the future mission of the disciples to the whole world (28:18–20) is linked to this early experience of preaching to Israel, and Matthew's grouping of the material is appropriate. 10:5 Go nowhere among the Gentiles. Although Jesus has already commended a Gentile's faith as greater than that found in Israel (8:10), the focus of this first mission of the disciples, like that of Jesus generally before His passion and resurrection (15:24), is to the biological descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Israel's "lost sheep" (Ezek. 34:16). Faithful to His promises to the patriarchs, God has sent His Messiah to bring salvation "to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" (Rom. 1:16).
The same signs of the kingdom that Jesus performed in chs. 8; 9 will be done by His disciples.

That is, the dust on one's garment kicked up by the feet. Jews sometimes shook the dust off their clothing when returning from Gentile lands as a sign of contempt; Jesus uses it here as a sign of judgment. A town that does not receive Jesus' representatives does not receive Jesus and becomes spiritually defiled and is subject to judgment as Sodom and Gomorrah (Acts 13:51).

These verses anticipate a later, more extensive mission than the immediate occasion of v. 5 (10:5–11:1 note). Persecution will occur at the hands of both Jewish (v. 17) and Gentile (v. 18) authorities. But disciples are not to respond to this as pagans do, by hiring professional orators to defend them in court. The Holy Spirit will provide their defense (Acts 4:8).
Every kind of people. The allusion is to Mic. 7:6, which Jesus later quotes (v. 35).

There are several interpretations of this coming of the Son of Man: (1) The coming is the second coming of Christ to judge the earth. This view fits most of the other occurrences of the phrase (24:30; 25:31; 26:64; but see 16:28). The chief difficulty is that the note of urgency in v. 23 seems incompatible with a delay until the last judgment. (2) The coming is the resurrection and ascension of Jesus or the sending of the Spirit at Pentecost. However, there is no evidence that the disciples were persecuted with the intensity assumed in vv. 17–22 before Jesus' resurrection or Pentecost. (3) The phrase "before the Son of Man comes" is a way of saying, "before I rejoin you." But again, the persecution described in vv. 17–22 does not occur during this time, and the purpose for the coming of the Son of Man elsewhere (to bring judgment) makes this meaning unlikely. (4) The coming refers to the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 as an act of judgment against the nation of Israel. Although the NT writers do not typically use this word for the destruction of Jerusalem, this understanding retains the note of urgency and fits the experience of the church before A.D. 70. It may be the traumatic time that Jesus foretells when He says that the Jewish leaders will "see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power" (which begins at His ascension) "and coming on the clouds of heaven" in providential judgment through Rome's legions (Matt. 26:64). Other references to the coming of the Son of Man present it as a terrible display of God's judgment. Although these cannot be limited to the destruction of Jerusalem, that event was terrible in intensity and fell on what had been the central visible symbol of God's presence, the temple.

Gk. beelzeboul, a transliteration of a Hb. or Aramaic name for the prince of demons, through whose cooperation Jesus allegedly exorcises unclean spirits according to His critics among the Pharisees (12:24–27). The name probably means "lord of heaven" and appears in the OT in the intentionally distorted form Baal-zebub ("lord of the flies") as a name for the god of Ekron (2 Kin. 1:2).

This injunction to fear God and not people is perhaps a development of Is. 8:12, 13 (cf. 1 Pet. 3:14, 15). It is supported by four arguments: (1) the acts of the wicked will be exposed for what they are; (2) although people can kill the body, God can punish soul and body; (3) God orders everything, down to the fall of a sparrow and the number of hairs on the head; and (4) those who deny Jesus when threatened by humans will be denied by Jesus in the presence of His heavenly Father. The Bible consistently teaches that fear and reverence are appropriate responses to God.
See note on 5:22.

Mic. 7:6 addresses the rebelliousness and strife characteristic of Israel during the time of Ahaz. Just as Israel's history foreshadows Jesus' history (2:15 note), its turmoil and strife foreshadow the strife that results from the coming of the Messiah (Luke 2:34, 35), even to the division of families. Although coming to Christ brings peace to the heart (11:29) and even reconciliation between generations (Luke 1:17), embracing the gospel also makes life more difficult in some respects, for Jesus demands allegiance that takes priority over the natural ties of life (Matt. 10:37–39).
This is to obey and identify with Jesus even unto death, not simply to bear some particular burden imposed by the Lord.
This verse emphasizes the principle that receiving those who are emissaries of another is equivalent to receiving the person who sent them (v. 40).

While not excluding children, this phrase refers to all Jesus' disciples, who are like little children, vulnerable and unable to repay kindnesses shown them by others (18:1–6, 10, 14). Jesus so identifies Himself with these "little ones" that mercy shown to them will be rewarded as mercy shown to the King Himself (25:31–46).

John the Baptist predicted that the coming one would bring judgment, chopping down the trees of wickedness (3:10, 12). Presumably John heard reports of Jesus' exorcisms and miraculous healings, which show that He is the Messiah. But Jesus allows His forerunner to be imprisoned by the wicked Herod, evoking John's question whether He is indeed the royal executor of divine justice for which God's suffering people have been longing.

Jesus invites John's disciples to witness His miracles, which directly fulfill Is. 35:5, 6. Jesus the Messiah will one day inflict on the wicked the judgment they deserve, but in His first coming His purpose is to bring blessing by bearing God's judgment on others' behalf.

John the Baptist is the immediate forerunner of the One to whom all the prophets pointed, and hence he points to Christ more clearly than they did. As such, he himself is the object of prophecy, the one predicted in Mal. 3:1, the fulfillment of the Elijah prophecy of Mal. 4:5, 6 (Matt. 11:14), the herald of the Lord's arrival (3:3; cf. Is. 40:3).

The least in the kingdom are more privileged than John because they stand after the cross and resurrection and thus, having received the fullness of the Spirit and the revelation of Christ's full ministry in the new age, they participate in what the prophets only saw from a distance (1 Pet. 1:10–12). Thus, the "least in the kingdom of heaven" is greater than John because they have received more revelation than any OT prophet, including John, the greatest prophet of the old age.

The kingdom is pressing ahead with force, although violent men such as Herod are trying to overcome it by force. It is not the strong and forceful who obtain the kingdom but the weak and helpless who depend on God (vv. 28–30; cf. Luke 16:16 note).

Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who Malachi predicted would come as the forerunner of the Messiah (Mal. 4:5). Believing this identification requires the eyes of faith ("if you are willing to accept it"). There may have been some misunderstanding in the first century that Elijah himself would return to earth, but John denied that he was Elijah in that sense (John 1:21). The angel Gabriel's announcement was that John would come "in the spirit and power" of Elijah (Luke 1:17).

People who resist God's Word can always find an excuse by critiquing God's messengers. Like children stubbornly complaining that others do not dance to their tune, "this generation" critiques John for his austerity and conscience-indicting call to repentance and then turns around and complains that Jesus' style is too celebratory and welcoming of unseemly, undeserving companions.

See note on 8:20. wisdom is justified by her deeds. Despite the contrast in the tones of their ministries, both John and Jesus bring God's wisdom, as is demonstrated by the redemptive outcome of their deeds.

King Ahab's alliance by marriage with Sidon led to the rampant spread of Baal worship in Israel (1 Kin. 16:31–33), and both Tyre and Sidon were condemned by God's prophets (Is. 23; Ezek. 27; 28). God's destruction of Sodom by fire for its perversion and injustice (Gen. 19) turned the city into a byword exemplifying the ruinous results of sin. The Galilean towns that have witnessed Jesus' miracles may not have sunk to the same depth of degradation, but exposure to the fuller revelation of the Messiah makes them more culpable than those pagan cities. See Luke 12:48.
God is sovereign in choosing those to whom He will reveal His truth. No one can know God by worldly wisdom and learning (1 Cor. 1:26–31).

Jesus makes extraordinary claims. He claims that God's sovereign disposition of all things has been committed to Him. As in Dan. 7, the Son of Man has received all power and dominion (anticipating Matt. 28:18). He alone knows the Father and can reveal the Father to others (John 14:6). The Father alone knows Him, so Peter's later confession that Jesus is the Christ can only be through the Father's revelation of the Son (Matt. 16:16, 17). Jesus' knowledge is equal to the Father's, and His sonship is unique.

Echoing personified wisdom in Prov. 9:1–5 and intertestamental wisdom literature, Jesus invites the weary to find rest and refreshment in Him. He does not extend His invitation to those who are naturally intelligent but to little children (v. 25), not to the strong but to the weary and heavy-laden. Both Jesus and John convey God's wisdom (v. 19 note), but Jesus transcends His forerunner, for He Himself is the incarnate wisdom of God.

The yoke, placed on the shoulders of beasts and humans who pull plows and wagons, symbolizes submission and slavery (Gen. 27:40; Is. 10:27; Hos. 11:4). Jewish sources spoke of the yoke of the law and of wisdom. Though the law was God's good gift to His people, the scribes' oral traditions and the spiritual disability of sinful humanity turned the law into an unbearable burden (12:2 note; 15:2; 23:2–4; Acts 15:10). When the law was understood as a way of meriting salvation, it became a "yoke of slavery" (Gal. 5:1). By contrast, the yoke of Jesus, while demanding, is "easy" because it is from one who is "gentle and lowly in heart" (Matt. 11:29, 30). He has fulfilled the law's righteous demand perfectly for His people (Matt. 3:15; Gal. 4:4, 5; 2 Cor. 5:21), and His Spirit empowers their grateful obedience (Rom. 8:2–4). Therefore, He alone can provide true rest for the soul.

God's law requires farmers to leave grain at the edge of fields to be gleaned by those in need (Lev. 19:9, 10; Deut. 23:24, 25), and it does not prohibit plucking grain on the Sabbath in order to satisfy hunger — after all, the disciples are not farmers laboring in the harvest. The Pharisees' objections are based on an oral tradition that both obscures and counters the law's true purpose. Sabbath. The Sabbath is a symbol of God's sovereignty over the whole created universe (Ex. 20:8). It is a reminder of His redemption of His people (Deut. 5:12), and it is a representation of the hope of eternal rest at the consummation (Heb. 4:9). As Lord of the Sabbath, Jesus fulfills all aspects of the meaning of the Sabbath (Col. 2:16, 17), and He defines how His followers should observe the Sabbath. Regulations that contravene the Sabbath's life-sustaining and life-restoring purposes are at cross-purposes with God's design for the day (Matt. 12:9–13).

In His reply to the accusations of the Pharisees, Jesus uses two arguments from the lesser to the greater, both focusing on His own person and authority. In an hour of need, David, God's anointed, transgressed a ceremonial law concerning the bread of the presence in the tabernacle. Now one with much greater authority is present. Similarly, the demands of temple worship require priests to labor on the Sabbath, and now "something greater than the temple" is here (v. 6).

The one in whom God dwells personally is greater than God's dwelling place in Israel that foreshadowed the incarnate Son. Jesus, Immanuel ("God with us"), is the true temple to whom the symbol pointed (John 1:14; 2:21). The disciples, being in the presence of Jesus, have a far greater service than the priests who served in the Jerusalem temple. Jesus is greater not only than the temple (associated with priests) but also than ancient prophets such as Jonah (Matt. 12:41) and the great sage-king Solomon (12:42).

Again quoting Hos. 6:6 (cf. 9:13), Jesus condemns the Pharisees' perversion of the Sabbath, multiplying regulatory restrictions and minimizing God's merciful purpose for granting His people rest (Matt. 11:29; cf. Mark 2:27).

The Son of Man has received dominion over creation (8:20 note) and redemption (20:28). So also He has dominion over the Sabbath, the sign of God's sovereignty in creation and redemption (v. 2 note). The claims Jesus makes here (as well as His disregard of rabbinic tradition in His practice) undoubtedly shock the Pharisees, furthering their resolve to kill Him (v. 14).

Another example of Christ's lordship over the Sabbath. Again, no OT text prohibits healing on the Sabbath, and Jesus' critics' practice of rescuing an at-risk sheep in an emergency reinforces Jesus' logic that the Sabbath is a fitting day to heal human beings, who bear God's image and exceed sheep in value. Jesus does not teach that the Sabbath is abolished by the coming of the kingdom. He has come not to destroy the law but to fulfill it (5:17 note). The problem is not that the Pharisees observe the Sabbath but that they misinterpret it and turn what should be a delight into a burden.

Is. 42:1–4 is cited as an explanation of why Jesus commands people not to reveal to others who He is. He has come to proclaim and establish justice, but not by a showy display of power and not by leading a political or military movement (11:4–6 note). The Messiah, who is gentle and lowly in heart (11:29), will enter Jerusalem in humility (21:5) and defeat His and our great enemy through humbly enduring crucifixion (1 Cor. 1:18; Col. 2:14, 15).
See note on 10:25.
Jesus' deity is manifest in His knowledge of people's thoughts, regardless of whether they articulate them aloud or in His hearing (9:4; John 2:24, 25).

By His victory over Satan in the wilderness (3:16, 4:1; 4:10 note) and exorcism of demons, Jesus demonstrates that He has bound the "strong man" and that Satan is powerless to prevent the coming of the kingdom. The binding of Satan is a symbol of the messianic age in Jewish apocalyptic literature (see also Rev. 20:2).

To call the work of God's Spirit the work of Satan involves an explicit, willful, and decisive rejection of the very divine person who alone can bring about repentance. The notion of the "unforgivable sin" has caused needless anxiety. Anyone who has been convicted of sin by the Spirit (John 16:8) and now believes the truth cannot possibly have committed it. See theological note "The Unforgivable Sin" on p. 1739. One result of the divine Son's humility in His incarnation is that ignorant slander against Him can be forgiven when the Spirit grants repentance (1 Tim. 1:13–16).
Through the metaphors of trees and treasures, Jesus teaches that the words one speaks reveal the condition of one's heart, whether good and healthy or bad and diseased (see 15:10–20).

Words, even carelessly spoken words, are eternally important. Scripture condemns verbal sins such as lies, gossip, or insults as severely as it condemns adultery and murder (5:22, 37; 2 Cor. 12:20; 1 Tim. 1:10; James 3:6; Rev. 21:8).

That they should ask for a sign is incredible in the light of what they have already seen, which provoked their conspiracy against Jesus (12:14). Jesus does not do miracles on demand. Yet God will give one climactic sign, the resurrection of His Son from the dead, and that sign will expose the adamant rebellion of that unbelieving generation.

Jonah was swept away from the land of the living in the sea and the great fish but then restored to life again to proclaim God's word to Nineveh. The Son of Man's rising from the dead (v. 40) is the greatest sign of all that the kingdom has come. The repentance of the notorious Gentiles of Nineveh shames Israel's hardness of heart when confronted with one greater than Jonah.
An emphatic way of saying "three days."
The lengths traveled by a Gentile queen to hear Solomon's wisdom again indicts those who doubt and resist Christ, who is wisdom incarnate.

The dispute over Jesus' power to exorcise demons (12:22–32) leads Him to use exorcism as an illustration to show that ridding oneself of evil influences only creates a dangerous spiritual vacuum. Unless God's Spirit takes up residence (Rom. 8:9), a person purged by self-denial becomes vulnerable to reinfestation by graver evils such as pride, hypocrisy, and contempt for others.
This collection of parables on the nature of the kingdom of heaven is the third great discourse in Matthew (Introduction: Literary Features).

The term "parable," like the OT term translated "proverb," refers broadly to a comparison of some sort. Jesus' parables are His distinctive teaching through brief comparisons or longer narratives. They usually have one central point, although some have multiple points of correspondence between elements in the story and the realities they symbolize; e.g., four soils referring to four types of hearers (13:18–23) or two sons symbolizing flagrant sinners and the judgmental self-righteous (Luke 15:1, 2, 11–32; cf. Matt. 21:28–32). Most of Jesus' parables are clear, but they also contain a depth of meaning that only one with a right relationship to Jesus can comprehend. It is only to the disciples that Jesus gives the interpretation of the parable of the sower (vv. 18–23) and the parable of the weeds (vv. 36–43). The ungodly miss this deeper meaning because their lack of a proper relationship with God has darkened their thoughts and hearts (Rom. 1:21). A sower. Contrary to expectations that the inbreaking of God's kingdom would be a harvest season, when the righteous are gathered and the wicked destroyed (Ps. 1:3–5), Jesus' first coming is a season of sowing, in which the word that He disseminates, like vulnerable seed, meets both resistant and receptive responses.

The ability to understand God's message, let alone respond to it, is the gift of God, distributed according to His sovereign choice. 13:11 To you \... to them. "Secrets" may be better translated "mysteries," as an allusion to Dan. 2:28–30, 47, where God reveals to the unbelieving Babylonian king a parabolic prophetic vision, which must be interpreted for him by Daniel. The focus of the vision is on God's future defeat of the kingdoms of evil and the establishment of His kingdom on earth. Jesus sees this as beginning to be fulfilled in His ministry, albeit mysteriously. The "mystery" is that Daniel's kingdom is beginning to be fulfilled but in an unexpected way. The following parables reveal that it starts small and will only slowly and invisibly reach great size. The kingdom is present, but there is no final judgment or reward, and both the wicked and righteous still exist together. These are unexpected features of the kingdom from the Jewish perspective, which anticipates a great kingdom that will come suddenly in full form and where the wicked will be judged and the righteous rewarded. See theological note "The Illumination of the Holy Spirit" on p. 2018.

To those who have a relationship with Jesus, parables deepen understanding and foster that relationship, but to those who do not, parables increase their confusion and ignorance. Thus the function of parables is both to enlighten and to conceal.

Mark 4:12 (cf. Luke 8:10) phrases this statement even more strongly, with "so that" rather than "because." For Mark, Jesus' purpose in telling parables is to prevent understanding and to cause unbelief (Mark 4:11 note); in Matthew, Jesus' parables are in response to people's unbelief and inability to understand. Though some see Matthew as softening the divine sovereignty emphasized in Mark, the word "lest" in v. 15 indicates that God's sovereign choice lies behind the hardening of hearts, deafening of ears, and blinding of eyes. While Matthew highlights the culpability of those who reject Christ, his citation of Is. 6:9, 10 illustrates the compatibility of God's sovereignty and human responsibility. The parables serve as an instrument of judgment by hardening the impenitent.

Jesus' disciples and NT believers are doubly blessed. God's grace has made their hearts, ears, and eyes receptive to the revelation of His kingdom; and they live in the era of the fulfillment of God's promises, for which OT believers earnestly hoped.
See theological note "The Kingdom of God" on p. 1823.

Two soils represent initially positive responses to the word that prove fruitless in the end. Rocky soil symbolizes an immediate interest — "with joy" — that proves shallow and withers in the face of persecution. Thorny soil shows the danger of distraction by means of the worries and pleasures of everyday life. Again, what seems at first to be a positive response to the word yields no final harvest.
Wealth is a blessing from God if He is honored, but it is a dangerous snare if it captivates the heart (Eccl. 5:19; 1 Tim. 6:9).

Only hearing and understanding the word (a faith that finds expression in obedience is implied) results in fruit. Some temporarily receive the word but fall away to avoid opposition or to pursue earthly wealth (v. 22). Likewise there are differing levels of bearing fruit. There are ultimately only two kinds of ground, that which "holds fast" the word and bears fruit "with patience" (Luke 8:15), and that which does not.

Again, Jesus Himself provides the interpretation (vv. 36–43). The field is the whole world, not just Israel or the church. God withholds immediate judgment for the sake of the elect who are in the world. The righteous have had to live in the midst of the unrighteous from the beginning.

The mustard shrub can grow to a height of ten feet (3 m). The inbreaking of God's kingdom seems insignificant, almost imperceptible, like a tiny seed or like yeast hidden in bread dough, yet its influence will eventually spread throughout the nations. Certainly in the first century, the kingdom of heaven appears to be nothing in comparison with Rome, yet it will prove to be much greater.
The picture of a tree with birds nesting in the branches recalls Ezek. 17:23, where the birds represent the Gentile nations taking refuge in the Messiah and enjoying the blessings of the covenant.
Although leaven or yeast is often a symbol of evil (16:11), here the analogy makes a positive point: the kingdom's quiet presence will fill and change the world.

As the apex of Israel's wisdom tradition, Jesus fulfills Ps. 78:2, where the "parables" or "dark sayings" are events in the history of God's redemption of His people, climaxing in the choice of David as king. The redemptive events themselves are not "hidden," but their meaning becomes clear only as the psalmist reveals their meaning. The psalm contains repeated patterns of Israel's unbelief in the OT, which foreshadow the unbelieving patterns being recapitulated by Israel in not responding in faith to Jesus' ministry.
See note on 8:20.

The final judgment will be a separation not only of the ungodly from the godly but also of ungodliness from the godly. Note that the Son of Man will send His angels — Jesus clearly asserts divine authority.
See theological note "Hell" on p. 1753.
An allusion to the promise of the future resurrection (Dan. 12:3).

Jesus' parables display the heretofore hidden kingdom of heaven (v. 35), but its worth remains hidden from most people. Those who discover its priceless value, however, like a man who finds treasure in a field or the trader in pearls, gladly sacrifice anything and everything to obtain it (Phil. 3:8).

As in the parable of the weeds, in this parable Jesus teaches that the separation of those who belong to the kingdom of heaven and those destined for destruction awaits the close of the age. Until that time, believers and unbelievers coexist as God's reign advances quietly and invincibly.

Many scribes in Judaism are castigated by Jesus, not because of their positions as teachers but because, in their hypocrisy, their actions contradict their instruction. Yet the Gospels show us scribes who become Jesus' disciples, such as Nicodemus (John 3:1, 10; 19:38–40), or who at least draw near to the kingdom (Mark 12:34). trained for the kingdom. The Gk. phrase could be rendered "has become a disciple of the kingdom." Since this saying immediately follows Jesus' asking the disciples if they understand, the implication is that the disciples will become teachers and will, like a hospitable host, bring from their treasury to share with others the gifts they have received — an understanding both of Israel's ancient redemptive history that anticipated Christ and of His fulfillment in new redemptive acts, which signal the presence of the kingdom.

As when Jesus read Is. 61 and declared it fulfilled in the synagogue of Nazareth (Luke 4:16–30), the neighbors among whom Jesus grew up found His teaching authority both amazing and offensive. Superficial acquaintance with God's humble Messiah blinds His lifelong neighbors to His true identity (cf. John 4:44).
The Gk. word translated "carpenter" is also a general term for any craftsman or worker. Joseph could have worked with wood or stone.
Jesus' refusal to do many miracles in Nazareth is not because He depended on the faith of people to empower Him but because those without faith will not grasp the miracle's message (cf. 1 Cor. 13:2).

See notes on Mark 6:14, 17. Herod Antipas governed Galilee and Perea, roughly one-quarter of the realm once ruled by his late father, Herod the Great. Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, would send Jesus (a Galilean) to Herod Antipas for a ruling on the Sanhedrin's accusations. When Jesus would not perform to suit Herod's curiosity, however, Herod returned Him without a verdict to Pilate (Luke 23:6–12).

A daughter by an earlier marriage to Herod Philip. According to the Jewish historian Josephus, the daughter's name was Salome, and she later married another son of Herod the Great, Philip the tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis (Luke 3:1).

John's disciples thus honor the prophet who brought God's word to them; and Joseph of Arimathea will similarly express a disciple's devotion by claiming Jesus' body and arranging His burial after the apostles themselves abandon Him in fear (27:57–60).

According to v. 2, enough time has elapsed after the death of John the Baptist for reports of Jesus' miracles to come back to Herod, leading the tetrarch to fear that God has raised his prophetic accuser from the dead. Jesus hears about Herod's renewed inquiries and crosses the Sea of Galilee to its northeastern shore, far from Tiberias, Herod's capital.

The feeding of the five thousand is one of the few miracles, besides Jesus' resurrection, that is recorded in all four Gospels (Mark 6:32–44; Luke 9:10–17; John 6:1–15). As God provided manna for Israel in the wilderness in the days of Moses, so Jesus provides bread for the people in a remote place. Matthew reports the details concisely, whereas John elaborates at length the significance of the miracle as a sign that Jesus is the bread of life, given from heaven.

Jesus challenges the disciples to provide for the crowd. Then, when they confess how inadequate their resources are, He blesses His heavenly Father, multiplies the small loaves and fish, and enlists His disciples to be ministers of His provision.
