Jesus is conscious of His unique relationship to the Father as the eternal Son, yet with respect to His true human nature there is a limitation of His knowledge. According to Jesus' humanity, what the Father has not revealed to Him about the future He does not know.

Unlike the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, the end of the age at Jesus' bodily second coming will not be predictable by clearly observable signs (Acts 1:7). Also, Mark 13:1–30 repeatedly speaks of "those days" or merely the "days" relating to circumstances concerning the fall of Jerusalem that the disciples can know about, whereas v. 32 refers to that "day or that hour" (singular) that "no one knows," likely referring to the very end of history at Christ's final coming. The certainty of Christ's return and uncertainty as to its timing provide the strongest motivation to stay awake and be found faithful at His arrival.

That is, Passover would be "on the second (or next) day;" cf. 8:31. Mark places the plotting of the chief priests and scribes on Wednesday of Passion Week. the Passover. The Passover is one of the most important of the Jewish feasts, since it celebrates the deliverance from Egypt when the angel of death "passed over" the homes of the people of Israel (Ex. 12:1–30). At the time of Jesus, the Passover was celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month of the Jewish calendar (Nisan,which corresponds to the end of March and beginning of April). It was observed the last day before the first full moon after the spring equinox. On that day when the paschal lambs were killed and eaten, all leaven (symbolizing sin) was to be removed from the house, and only unleavened bread was to be eaten for the seven days after the Passover. The entire eight-day observance, beginning with Passover evening, was inclusively called the "Feast of Unleavened Bread" (14:12; Ex. 12:15–20). chief priests. See note on 8:31. scribes. See note on 7:1.

Being one of the Jewish pilgrimage feasts, the Passover drew enormous numbers of people to Jerusalem. Josephus estimated that the population of 50,000 increased to 3,000,000. Though his figures are generally considered greatly exaggerated (250,000 is more likely), the authorities' fears are not groundless. See 11:8–10, 31, 32; 12:12, 37.

See note on 11:1. Simon the leper. No doubt no longer a leper, he may have been cleansed by Jesus. He is clearly an important member of the wider circle of disciples, since Jesus chooses to visit his house at this time. reclining. For formal dinners in first-century Judea, people reclined rather than sat at the table (Luke 22:14 note; John 13:23). a woman. According to John 12:3, this woman is Mary, the sister of Lazarus and Martha. John also indicates that the meal occurs "six days before the Passover" (John 12:1), before Jesus entered Jerusalem. Mark may have placed the account here to associate this pre-anointing for burial (v. 8 note) more closely with the plot to kill Jesus (v. 1). Matthew agrees with Mark's order (Matt. 26:3–13). alabaster flask. Alabaster is a type of gypsum, in its pure form white or translucent, found in limestone deposits in caves and at the exits of springs. It was often used for making ointment jars and was considered a luxury item. pure nard. A rare and costly perfume imported from India and made from the root of a plant grown in the Himalayas. Its value of "three hundred denarii" (v. 5) is roughly equivalent to a year's wages in the first century. broke the flask. To prevent loss, amounts suitable for a single application were sealed into flasks that were then broken at the neck at the time of use. According to John 12:3, Mary's flask contains twelve ounces of perfume.

Jesus commends ongoing generosity to the poor, but devotion to Him, while He is still among His disciples, takes precedence (v. 7). John notes that Judas Iscariot is among the objectors to the "waste" of this precious ointment, and that his motive is not compassion for the poor but personal greed (John 12:4–6).

Jesus approves of what others see as a waste, for by this gesture she shows the inestimable worth of Jesus, of His death (v. 8), and of the profound communion that His sacrifice on the cross will establish. This gesture recalls the precious ointment poured over Aaron the high priest, which the psalmist compares to the priceless blessing of the fellowship of believers (Ps. 133).

Jesus alludes to the anointing of dead bodies with spices and perfume, a common first-century practice in Palestine. His resurrection from the dead will prevent other women from performing this act of devoted love after his burial (16:1).

Judas stands in stark contrast to the unnamed woman (in Mark) who has lavished costly love on Jesus. Judas will receive thirty silver coins (not even half the value of the perfume) for his betrayal of Jesus (v. 11).

This feast symbolizes the removal of sin in the lives of Israelite believers (Ex. 12:14–20). The Passover meal falls on the first day of this feast (v. 1 note; Ex. 12:14, 15), the fourteenth day after the beginning of the Jewish year (Ex. 12:6). sacrificed the Passover lamb. Jesus died at Passover, the feast that celebrates how the blood of a lamb protected the Israelites in Egypt from God's wrath. Jesus' death shows the profound continuity in the divine plan of redemption (see 1 Cor. 5:7). In the order of these feasts, the priority of God's act of salvation (Passover and redemption) is shown to precede our response of holy living (Feast of Unleavened Bread and the believer's putting away of sin).

Women usually carried water jars in Jesus' day. For Jesus' knowledge of future and distant events, see 11:1, 2 and John 1:48. As the incarnate God-man in whose one person His fully divine nature and fully human nature are united, Jesus can and does exercise on earth divine powers of knowledge (13:32 note). It is possible, however, that Jesus has simply made prior arrangements with this man.

The Gospels record that those present at this high point in the ministry of Jesus are the twelve disciples He chose at the beginning (see 3:14). According to Luke 22:30, at this time Jesus announces their future ministry as judges of the new people of God. They are witnesses at the inauguration of the new covenant.

Jesus' prediction of the betrayal comes from His intimate knowledge of Judas and also from His understanding of the Scriptures (v. 21; Ps. 41:9; see Acts 1:15–20). dipping bread into the dish with me. Bread or meat was dipped into a central bowl of sauce. The detail emphasizes the deep personal betrayal, since table fellowship is a token of genuine friendship (see 2:16).

See note on 8:31. woe to that man. Although Judas's betrayal is part of God's plan and predicted in Scripture, his motives and treachery are not thereby excused. His subsequent suicide is symptomatic of the eternal condemnation he incurs.

The sacramental meal of the new covenant is intrinsically related to and grows out of that of the old (cf. Ex. 24:9–11). Jesus takes two elements of the Passover meal, unleavened bread and wine, to express His new work of redemption. See "The Lord's Supper" at 1 Cor. 11:23.

In the original Passover the blood of the lamb protected the Israelites from death (Ex. 12:23, 30). The phrase "blood of the covenant" comes from Ex. 24:8 and recalls that biblical covenants are sealed in blood, which symbolizes the lethal consequences of violating the covenant commitment (Gen. 15:9–21; 17:9–14; Ex. 24:4–8; Heb. 9:15). As in Moses's day, divine judgment will pass over those who are covered by the blood of the final Passover lamb, Jesus Christ. poured out for many. Jesus is alluding to Is. 53:12, where the servant of the Lord "poured out His soul to death" and "bore the sin of many."

Jesus is hereby predicting the imminence of His death. drink it new. Jesus expresses His faith in God, who will not abandon Him in death. the kingdom of God. The eschatological reign of God, foretold by the OT prophets and announced as "at hand" by John the Baptist and Jesus (1:15; Matt. 3:1, 2), was inaugurated in Jesus' ministry and is about to reach a greater stage in Jesus' sacrifice and resurrection (Acts 2:30–36).
This mention of singing may refer to the Passover liturgy. If so, Jesus and His disciples sing Pss. 115–118, the Hallel of Egypt, which is the traditional close of the meal.
Not only Jesus' suffering but also the fact that His disciples will abandon Him is predicted in ancient Scripture (Zech. 13:7).
The angel at the empty tomb will recall this promise and allude to Peter's denial (16:7).
For other examples of Jesus' knowledge of future events, see note on v. 13. The seemingly specific reference could also be a poetic way of saying "before dawn."

Jesus' followers must carry the cross, an instrument of death, and be willing to lose their lives for His sake, unashamed to identify with Him (8:34). Peter believes that he has such strong faith, but he is mistaken (vv. 66–72).

As in the display of His glory at the transfiguration, so now in the depth of His struggle with the prospect of the suffering that awaits in His Father's will, Jesus seeks the company of these three closest disciples. See note on 5:37. troubled. This verb expresses deep emotional distress (Phil. 2:26).

A colloquial Aramaic word for "father," which expresses Jesus' close relationship with God the Father. Mark records the Semitic word used by Jesus along with its Gk. equivalent for his readers' comprehension, as he does elsewhere (5:41; 7:34; 11:9; 14:45; 15:22, 34). Perhaps alluding to the tradition of Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, Paul declares that by the Spirit believers may address God as "Abba Father" (Gal. 4:6; Rom. 8:15). cup. As in OT imagery, the cup symbolizes God's wrath and the destruction it inflicts (Is. 51:17–22). See note on 10:38. not what I will, but what you will. Appropriately, the preference of Jesus' innocent human soul is to avoid the torment of being forsaken by His Father as He bears the guilt of others' sin on the cross. Yet the eternal Son has assumed humanity in order to do God's will, which centers on His offering His body (Heb. 10:5–10). Confronted now with the full cost of His obedient resolve, He completes His utter submission to God's will in the covenant of redemption.
In spite of noble intentions (14:29, 31), Peter, like James and John, is incapable of one hour of true discipleship.

This exhortation recalls the warning of 13:32–37 to watch and not fall asleep before the coming of the Son of Man. Temptation is the trap of Satan to cause God's people (in this case the Twelve) to fall and, if possible, to bring to nothing the plan of redemption.
Probably a force sent by the Sanhedrin, since the three categories of members of that body are mentioned (v. 53; 8:31 note).
A sign of respect that disciples showed to teachers in that day. After eating from the same dish (v. 20 note), Judas now feigns submission and respect.

The Greek can mean either "robber" or "insurrectionist," but in view of the charges brought against Jesus at His trial (Luke 23:2), "insurrectionist" is better. The same term describes those crucified with Jesus (Mark 15:27), and they (as well as Barabbas, who was released instead of Jesus, 15:7) were probably also condemned as terrorist insurgents.
See note on 8:31. In view of v. 50, the passage Jesus has in mind may be Zech. 13:7 (see v. 27).

Some interpreters have suggested that in this cryptic detail, as in the mention of the linen garment (a sign of wealth), there might be a veiled reference to Mark himself, since he was from a well-to-do family in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12). At least he identified himself closely enough with Jesus' group that the authorities tried to seize him. Yet he, like the Eleven, escaped, leaving Jesus in the custody of enemies.

This section of the narrative concerns Jesus' trials before the Jews and the Romans, which were full of errors and irregularities, with the principles of justice subordinated to expediency and politics. The Jewish trial had three parts: a hearing before Annas (reported only in John 18:12–14, 19–23); a trial before the Sanhedrin, led by Caiaphas in his house (14:53–65); and an early morning session of the Sanhedrin (15:1). The Roman trial was likewise in three parts: before Pilate (15:2–5); before Herod Antipas (reported only in Luke 23:6–12); and before Pilate again (15:6–15).

Normally in Jesus' day, the Sanhedrin would hold its sessions in the marketplace near the temple. This trial takes place in the high priest's residence. The trial is irregular in time (at night) and place and in its unusual haste.

Deut. 19:15–21 requires that for guilt to be established, there must be two or three corroborating witnesses. False witnesses are to receive the same punishment as the accused. These regulations are not followed in the trial of Jesus.

The first three (Synoptic) gospels do not record Jesus saying anything resembling this. However, in John's account of the temple cleansing, Jesus says that His enemies (not He) will destroy "this temple" (His body) and that He will raise it up in three days (John 2:19). This supports the probability that Christ cleansed the temple twice, since the lapse of three years would explain the false witnesses' garbled version. See note on Matt. 26:59–61 for why these witnesses are "false" in their testimony against Jesus.

As the submissive and suffering Servant of the Lord, Jesus maintains silence, refusing to defend Himself and to repay insult with insult (Is. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23). Christ. From the Gk. word meaning "anointed one." "Messiah" is the Hb. word of the same meaning (1 Sam. 2:10 note). Son of the Blessed. "The Blessed" is an indirect substitute for "God," used by the Jews to avoid the risk of taking God's name in vain. The whole title means "Son of God" and in the context indicates royal messiahship rather than absolute divinity.

Asked point-blank about His messianic identity, Jesus answers frankly. See notes on 6:50; 13:6. Son of Man. See note on 2:10. Jesus modifies the title "Messiah" in terms of the divine figure of Dan. 7. clouds of heaven. The fact that the high priest will see evidence of the Son of Man's enthronement supports the view that Jesus' prophecy of the Son of Man's coming in 13:24–27 refers to the destruction of Jerusalem and the growth of the church among the Gentiles.

A symbolic gesture expressing shock, sorrow, or horror (Gen. 37:29; 2 Kin. 18:37; 19:1; Ezra 9:3; Jer. 36:24; Joel 2:13). What further witnesses. The high priest makes the whole Sanhedrin witness to what he considers Jesus' blasphemy.

Jesus is condemned not for insurrection but for His claim to deity, the essence of His message. The prescribed punishment for blasphemy (insulting the honor of God's name) according to Jewish law is death by stoning (Lev. 24:16), but in Jesus' day only Roman courts can order capital punishment. Thus, Jesus will die by crucifixion, a Roman punishment (John 18:31, 32 and notes).

In their agreement with the accusation of the high priest, all the members of the Sanhedrin condemn Him (v. 64), and some express their hostility with physical violence and personal insult. Spitting in the face indicates exclusion from the group (Num. 12:14, 15), as if by ritual defilement. As the Lord's Servant, Jesus does not hide His face from disgrace and spitting (Is. 50:6). At this point, the Sanhedrin breaks decisively with the Messiah. Prophesy. Since Jesus has been acclaimed as a prophet (6:15; 8:28; Luke 7:16), His tormentors challenge Him to exercise that gift by naming those who strike Him, though His head is covered.
In the first century, Nazareth was dismissed as a backwater town from which no one of significance would come (John 1:46). See note on 1:24.

The Jews of Judea hold the Galilean Jews in contempt as culturally and religiously inferior (John 7:52). Peter's manner and accent give him away, especially in the courtyard of a Sadducean aristocrat.

Cowed twice by a servant girl and now by a bystander, Peter invokes God's wrath to strengthen his repudiation of Jesus: "I do not know this man." Immediately a second rooster crow reminds Peter of Jesus' sober prediction (v. 30), which has been fulfilled precisely. Shocked at his cowardice and overwhelmed with shame, he weeps.

Probably at dawn. The purpose of the new meeting is apparently to draw up a political charge that will lead the Roman authorities to condemn and execute Jesus (see Luke 23:2). Pilate. The Apostles' Creed mentions Pilate as the representative of Rome who faces Jesus in this trial. Pilate was Roman governor of Judea from A.D. 26 to 36. As magistrate, only he had the legal right to pronounce capital sentences (14:64 note).

Pilate's question implies that the Sanhedrin's charge is that Jesus' claim to kingship subverts Rome's authority over its subjects in Judea, Galilee, and elsewhere. The title itself is ambiguous. In a political sense, the Herods are kings and Jesus is not. Nevertheless, Jesus is King of the Jews, offered to them as the fulfillment of their messianic hopes. You have said so. Though indirect, Jesus' reply will naturally be interpreted as affirming the identification implied in Pilate's question.

Pilate apparently wants to make Jesus realize that, before the law, silence means consent to all the charges being lodged against him by the Sanhedrin's representatives. Again the Servant of the Lord maintains silence in the face of His enemies (cf. 14:61; Is. 53:7).

Apparently he is an insurrectionist who has sought the military overthrow of Rome. Matt. 27:16 (in some manuscripts) gives his first name as "Jesus" (Hb. "Joshua"), a common name of the period. The choice Pilate proposes to the crowd (v. 9) is unwittingly ironic: Jesus Barabbas, the would-be political savior of Israel, or Jesus of Nazareth, the true Savior of the world.

Of Persian origin and adopted by the Romans, this cruel and shameful form of capital punishment was used mainly against rebellious slaves and insurrectionists. Metal spikes were driven through the wrists or hands (John 20:25) and heels of the victim, who suffered terrible pain. Death usually resulted over the course of days from the effects of the injuries, hunger, dehydration, muscle fatigue, and exposure. Breaking the condemned's legs (John 19:33) caused rapid death by asphyxiation, since the legs could no longer lift the body to help the person breathe. As Paul notes, the crucifixion of Jesus identified the form of His execution with being "hanged on a tree," identified in the law of Moses as a sign of death under the curse of God (Gal. 3:13; see Deut. 21:23).
In Roman custom crucifixion was preceded by the act of flogging with a leather whip that had sharp pieces of bone and metal at the end of its lashes.

Originally the word for a military headquarters or barracks generally. In the Gospels it refers to an official residence (see Acts 23:35). whole battalion. Lit. "cohort," the tenth part of a Roman legion, consisting of approximately six hundred men.

In Jesus' day, purple is expensive and hard to produce, and for this reason is a mark of high rank (Esth. 1:6; Prov. 31:22; Luke 16:19; Rev. 17:4), especially of royalty (2 Chr. 2:7, 14; 3:14; Song 3:10). The cruel troops spare no expense to mock Jesus' acknowledgment that He is King of the Jews. crown of thorns. Jesus bears the divine curse (v. 13 note) on the ground, which has produced thorns since Adam's fall (Gen. 3:17, 18). The soldiers use the crown to ridicule the idea that Jesus was a king.
This salutation and the homage paid (v. 19) are mockeries of the respect due to royalty.

Cyrene was an important city in what is today Libya. There was a large Jewish settlement in Cyrene going back several hundred years (Acts 6:9). Alexander and Rufus. Since Matthew and Luke also name Simon but only Mark mentions his sons, they may have been members of the Christian community to which Mark wrote, probably at Rome (see Rom. 16:13). carry his cross. Usually the condemned man carries the crossbeam, weighing thirty to forty pounds. Simon, in taking up Jesus' cross, becomes a visual image of the true discipleship that Jesus demands (8:34).
An ominous name, possibly referring to the shape of the hill where executions are carried out but also reinforcing its association with death.

A primitive form of painkiller. Jesus' refusal of this mild anesthetic mixture signals His resolve to endure the horrors of the cross fully conscious of the pain. Later in the afternoon, to fulfill Scripture, He will accept a sip of bitter wine (John 19:28, 29; Ps. 69:21). Myrrh was an expensive spice used as a cosmetic in the first century. It was offered to Jesus at His birth as a gift for a king (Matt. 2:11) and used in His burial by Nicodemus (John 19:39, 40).

These are the spoils reserved for the execution squad. This seemingly unimportant detail is a fulfillment of Ps. 22:18, which describes the agony of a violent and undeserved death, suffered by one forsaken by God (Ps. 22:1, 16).
About nine a.m.

Called the titulus in Latin, this was a sign carried before the prisoner on the way to execution and affixed to the cross over his head. The King of the Jews. The charge is true, though not in the sense that the executioners understand it.

Though the Gk. word often means "robber," it can also mean "insurrectionist" (14:48 note) or more generally "criminal." Since robbery was not punishable by crucifixion under Roman law (v. 13 note), one of the latter two meanings is more probable here. 15:28 This verse is lacking in the most ancient manuscripts, although it is present in the majority of existing manuscripts. Since Jesus was obviously "numbered with the transgressors" as He hung on a cross between two brigands or terrorists, it is possible that early copyists inserted the citation of Is. 53:12, based on the parallel passage of Luke 22:37.
Observers pick up the garbled report that false witnesses presented during the Sanhedrin's nighttime hearing, using it to taunt Jesus. See note on 14:58.

This is both an insult and a diabolical temptation similar to those proposed to Jesus at the beginning of His ministry (Matt. 4:2–6). The devil is still seeking to subvert the work of redemption at the very moment of its accomplishment, when Jesus is at His greatest physical weakness (14:38).

Oblivious to the irony of their words, the chief priests and scribes speak truly: because the Son of Man has come to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10), He has no other course but to lay down His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

Noon. darkness. This recalls the darkness in Egypt, which lasted three days before the death of the firstborn sons (Ex. 10:22). See also the prophecy of Amos 8:9, 10, where the Lord promises to "darken the earth in broad daylight" in a time "like the mourning for an only son"; and Joel 2:30, 31, part of a larger prophecy to be fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21). ninth hour. About three p.m.

Aramaic of the first verse of Ps. 22. Even near death, Jesus' life is determined by what is written in Scripture. Again Mark preserves the Semitic wording of the tradition and then translates it for his Gentile readers.

Some mistake the word Eloi for "Elijah," perhaps because in some circles during that day it is believed that Elijah would return (6:15; 8:28; 9:11–13). This belief is based on an overly literal reading of Mal. 4:5, 6, a prediction fulfilled in John the Baptist's ministry (cf. Matt. 17:9–13).

A cheap wine that has almost become vinegar. Unlike the offer of wine and myrrh (v. 23), there is no humanitarian desire to relieve the suffering here but rather a cruel intention to prolong it by reviving Jesus in order to see if "Elijah" would come at His call.

From the parallel order in John's account, it appears that the loud cry is, "It is finished" (John 19:30). Jesus has been hanging on the cross for six hours (vv. 25, 34). Crucifixion might last two or three days (v. 13 note), but He voluntarily lays down His life. He gives up His life at the moment He chooses; no one can take it from Him (John 10:17, 18).

The downward direction of the tear shows that it is God's act. It is likely that Mark is referring to the veil separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, which may have been as much as eighty feet (24 m) tall. The death of Jesus is the final and definitive sacrifice for sin (Heb. 7:27). The old covenant administration of the covenant of grace is brought to a decisive end. No longer will the high priest need to enter into the Most Holy Place behind the veil to atone for the sins of the people (Ex. 26:31–33; cf. Heb. 9:1–10). Jesus is the new and eternal High Priest (Heb. 8:1), and also the perfect sacrificial victim (Heb. 9:14) who obtains for His people "eternal redemption" (Heb. 9:12). By means of His sacrificed body, believers of all tribes and races may now pass through the veil into God's presence in prayer and worship (Heb. 10:19–22).

A Roman officer responsible for one hundred men. This centurion is apparently responsible for the detachment that puts Jesus to death. He is well placed to observe the death of Jesus. Son of God. The Greek can be translated "a son of God." A Roman would not typically see in this term the OT Messiah nor the eternal Son of the Trinity but rather the Hellenistic idea of a human being favored by the gods. Nevertheless, the confession stands as the goal and climax of Mark's gospel, filled with the content of the Christian message, now confessed by a Gentile (see 1:1), who has been witness to Jesus' suffering, crucifixion, and death.

That is, from Magdala on the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus earlier cast seven demons out of Mary (Luke 8:2). Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses. Known only from this incident (cf. 16:1; Matt. 27:56). Salome. Mother of James and John (Matt. 27:56; cf. Matt. 20:20, 21).

All the men have fled except for the beloved disciple (John 19:26, 35). These women will come to the tomb two days later, intending to anoint Jesus' corpse, only to be told that He has risen from the dead (cf. 16:1, 9; John 20:11–18).

The day before the Sabbath (Friday; John 19:14 note). Food is prepared before sunset, when the Sabbath begins. Joseph must buy the linen, make arrangements for Jesus' burial, and ready the tomb (vv. 43–46) in the three hours remaining between Jesus' death and sunset.

Perhaps from Ramah in Judea, twenty miles (32 km) northwest of Jerusalem, the city of the prophet Samuel (1 Sam. 1:1). See note on Luke 23:50, 51. council. Joseph did not concur with the Sanhedrin's (8:31 note) verdict to condemn Jesus (Luke 23:50, 51). looking for the kingdom of God. Like Simeon and Anna and others, Joseph's longing for the arrival of God's reign met its fulfillment in Jesus (Luke 2:25, 38). See note on 1:15. Joseph is no doubt a pious Pharisee but also a secret follower of Jesus (John 19:38). took courage. This is apparently Joseph's first act of faith, but it comes at a time when all Jesus' disciples have fled. Joseph puts himself in conflict with the decision of the Sanhedrin and jeopardizes his entire future.
Pilate's surprise at how quickly Jesus dies provides more confirmation of the unusual character of Jesus' death as a voluntary sacrifice (v. 37 note).

According to Matt. 27:60, the tomb belongs to Joseph and his family. Such a family burial site would consist of an ornately painted vestibule from which a passageway leads to individual benches or shelves cut into the rock where the bodies are laid. The tomb is sealed by a heavy stone that is rolled along a groove cut into the rock at the entrance.
At sunset (six p.m.) on Saturday evening, a time appropriate for buying spices but not for visiting tombs. anoint. Anointing is a way of showing respectful affection in that day (14:8 note).
They saw the "very large" (v. 4) stone put in its place (15:46 note) and now wonder how it will be moved in order for them to do their work.

They enter the vestibule of the burial chamber, at the far end of which is the individual niche (a bench or shelf) where Jesus' body was laid (15:46 note). young man. Matt. 28:2 says the women met an angel at the tomb.

If this gospel reaches its climax in the confession that Jesus is the Son of God (15:39 note), a second climax is reached with the declaration of His resurrection, which attests that His many predictions of His suffering and resurrection are true (8:31; 9:31; 10:34; 14:25, 28) and that God's kingdom has come in power.

These two words make all the difference in the enormous role that Peter plays in the subsequent history of redemption. By them Mark indicates, as he brings his gospel to an end (16:9–20 note), that Jesus' work of preparation of the Twelve has not been in vain. Other gospels also attest Jesus' special care to restore the apostle who denied Him three times (Luke 24:34; John 21:15–23). he is going before you to Galilee. See note on 14:28. Since this rendezvous is predicted twice, first by Jesus and now by the angel at His empty tomb, it is striking that neither the widely attested "longer ending" of Mark (vv. 9–20) nor the later "shorter ending" records an appearance of Jesus to His disciples in Galilee. (Other gospels locate the appearances mentioned in vv. 9–20 in Jerusalem and its environs.)

If vv. 9–20 are not original (see introduction and note on 16:9–20), the gospel of Mark ends with this sentence. This is a surprising conclusion for a document that purports to be a "gospel," a proclamation of "good news." An opposing consideration is that the word translated "afraid" also means "reverential fear," and the same state of mind is produced in the disciples at the sight of Jesus' transfiguration (9:6), a type of the future resurrection.

Scholars differ regarding whether these verses were originally part of this gospel. Some important early Gk. manuscripts and ancient versions lack these verses, but many more manuscripts and versions include vv. 9–20 (known as the "longer ending"). One Latin manuscript has a "shorter ending" (roughly one verse long), which records the women's reporting to Peter and others and then sums up Jesus' sending His apostles from east to west to preach the gospel. A few Gk. manuscripts from the seventh through ninth centuries A.D. include both the shorter ending and the longer ending. Because of these differences among manuscripts and stylistic variance between vv. 9–20 and the rest of the gospel, many scholars believe that vv. 9–20 were not written by Mark but added by a later copyist. On the other hand, these verses are cited by writers from the late second century and are found in the majority of existing Gk. manuscripts of Mark's gospel. This abundance of external evidence (presence in so many early copies and translations) has persuaded some scholars that vv. 9–20 are authentic. Moreover, some find it hard to believe that Mark intended to end his gospel on the note of the women's fear and silence, without recounting an appearance of the risen Lord Jesus. When all of the evidence is taken into consideration, however, it appears most likely that the gospel of Mark originally concluded at v. 8. If so, then the addition of vv. 9–20 was a copyist's well-intentioned attempt to make sure Mark tells the complete story of what happened after Jesus' resurrection. Such additions should not trouble us, for they are easily discerned through the practice of NT textual criticism because God has preserved for us the original text written by the apostles in a variety of manuscripts. See topical article "New Testament Textual Criticism" on p. 2369. 16:9 Mary Magdalene. See John 20:11–18 and note on Mark 15:40. cast out seven demons. If vv. 9–20 are original, we would expect this detail, apparently drawn from Luke 8:2, to have appeared in an earlier mention of Mary (15:40 or 16:1).
Cf. Matt. 28:19. the whole creation. Cf. Col. 1:23.
Cf. Acts 2:38, 39. See theological note "Infant Baptism" on p. 37.

All the things predicted here (except drinking deadly poison) are recorded in the NT, especially in Acts: cast out demons (Acts 5:16; 8:7; 16:18; 19:12); new tongues (2:1–11; 10:44–46; 19:6); serpents (28:3–5); lay hands on the sick(9:12; 28:8). Jesus is tempted for forty days in the wilderness, and Israel wandered for forty years in the wilderness (Num. 14:34). Whereas Israel failed the test of obedience in the Promised Land, Jesus, the true Israel, is fully obedient to the Father in His forty-day task in the wilderness of the land.

In response to each temptation, Jesus cites Scripture, and all three passages are drawn from a section of Deuteronomy (6:13; 6:16; 8:3) in which Moses reminds the Israelites of lessons they should have learned in the wilderness. In so doing, Jesus demonstrates the way Israel should have responded but did not, revealing again that He sums up true Israel in Himself.

Jesus calls His followers to order their priorities correctly by focusing their hearts on the kingdom (vv. 31, 34).

As Simeon (2:34, 35) and John the Baptist (3:16, 17) anticipated, Jesus' coming precipitates a winnowing of believers from unbelievers in Israel, and the division often cuts across family ties, as the gospel continues to do in each generation.
The people can discern that a west wind (from the Mediterranean) means rain and a south wind (from the desert) means heat. But they do not discern what God is doing in their midst.

In legal matters, anyone with a weak defense does well to secure an out-of-court settlement before the case comes to trial. Sinners should be reconciled to God now; they will perish if they wait until judgment day.

To kill people in the act of worship is a grave offense. This incident, not recorded elsewhere, and similar acts of violence recorded by other first-century historians contributed to Pilate's reputation for cruelty.

Disaster is commonly held to be the result of extraordinary wickedness (John 9:1, 2; cf. Job 4:7–9; Ps. 73:2–14), but Jesus denies that one may deduce from this disastrous event that these Galileans were more sinful than others.

All are sinners, so Jesus calls on His hearers to repent — otherwise they will perish. See theological note "Repentance" on p. 1964.
This incident is unknown to us apart from this passage. The tower was probably on Jerusalem's southern wall, near the pool of Siloam (John 9:7).

In the OT prophets, both the fig tree and the vineyard are symbols of Israel (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13; 24:1–10; Is. 5:1–7). A vineyard was fertile soil for a fig tree, and "three years" points to an established tree. It is unlikely that it would ever bear fruit, but its owner gives it one more chance. In His later parable of the wicked tenants, Jesus implies that He, the "beloved son," has come as God's final messenger to claim the fruit of the Lord's vineyard from those who have mistreated servants (prophets) sent previously (Luke 20:9–18). That God does not punish sinners immediately does not mean that He approves of their sin. Rather, His patience shows that He is merciful, and that they should repent while there is time.
The right use of the Sabbath is a continuing dispute between Jesus and His enemies (6:1–11; 14:1–6).

The woman does not ask for healing. Jesus takes the initiative. 13:11 a disabling spirit \... She was bent over. As her contorted physical posture has visibly displayed her spiritual bondage for eighteen years, Jesus now releases her from "this bond" (v. 16).
The natural response from those who have experienced or witnessed Jesus' miracles (5:26; 7:16; cf. 4:15). The people will join her joyful praise (v. 17).

See note on 8:41. Come on those days and be healed. Jesus, however, contends that release from bondage is especially fitting on the Sabbath (vv. 15, 16).
The Jews released and watered their animals on the Sabbath as on other days, but this ruler of the synagogue objects to Jesus' act of compassion for this woman.

This woman alone is identified by this title in the Bible (cf. 19:9). Jesus stresses her privilege as a member of God's covenant community (Gal. 3:26–29), perhaps alluding to God's promise to Abraham that his descendants would be freed after centuries of bondage (Gen. 15:12–14). loosed from this bond. Jesus' exposure of His critics' double standard and His reasoning from the true significance of the Sabbath are unanswerable (14:6).

The brief parables of the mustard seed and the leaven, which illustrate the imperceptible but irrepressible growth of God's kingdom, are gathered by Matthew (ch. 13) and Mark (ch. 4) with other parables. Their placement here in Luke's gospel underscores the urgency of entering the kingdom immediately through the "narrow door" of repentant faith (vv. 22–30), though many (such as the synagogue ruler; v. 14) will not notice the signs that the kingdom has come.
A large amount; in Greek, three sata (Hb. seah), equivalent to about three-fifths of a bushel (22 liters). Alsothe amount used by Sarah (Gen. 18:6).
See note on 9:51. Luke presents Jesus as making unhurried progress toward Jerusalem where the climax will be reached. On the way He continues to serve the people.

The Jews in Jesus' day generally agree that all Israel (except for a few especially sinful people) would be in the number of the saved. This questioner senses that Jesus is drawing distinctions among the descendants of Abraham and Israel (2:34, 35; 3:17; 9:23–27) and that entrance into God's kingdom will entail a personal commitment to Jesus that many will find too costly.

This does not mean that salvation is by works; it is a strong way of saying that people must be in earnest about salvation because the opportunity to receive it will not last indefinitely. narrow door. Jesus does not say what the narrow door is, but clearly He is speaking of the way to salvation.

To have social fellowship with Jesus and to hear His teaching are not enough. In fact, to witness His miracles and hear His words without responding in faith actually compounds people's guilt (10:13–15).

There will be weeping in grief and gnashing of teeth in anger as they see the patriarchs and prophets, with whom Israelites had always identified, blissfully enjoying God's kingdom blessings while they themselves are thrown out.

As many who pride themselves on their covenant status as Abraham's children will be excluded through unbelief, Gentiles from all nations will be included at God's banqueting table through faith, fulfilling the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 12:1–3). Jesus will soon tell a parable in which guests invited to a banquet make excuses when the feast is ready, while outcasts from city streets and the countryside are welcomed to God's table (Luke 14:15–24; cf. 16:19–31). recline. This imagery of the messianic banquet describes the great joy there will be in the kingdom (14:15; Rev. 19:9). There will be a complete reversal of many ideas strongly held among humankind (v. 30).

Jesus may be in Perea where Herod is ruling. The Pharisees prefer to see Him in Judea where they have more influence, but Jesus will not succumb to fear or let threats from human rulers divert Him from the agenda assigned by the Father.

The Jews used the metaphor of a fox to mean worthless and sly. Jesus is unmoved by Herod's threats and says He will continue with His ministry. There is a limit to the remaining time of His ministry on earth, as the reference to the third day shows.
There is a compelling divine necessity to what Jesus is doing (9:22; 24:26, 44–49). Notice also the further reference to the certainty that Jerusalem is the place where He will die (cf. 9:31).

This lament over the city is probably uttered as Jesus reaches the city (Matt. 23:37, 38) and is included here by Luke because of its relevance to what Jesus has just said. 13:34 How often. Evidently to detect any violation of Sabbath observance.

Although the lawyers and Pharisees (perhaps including His host) are watching and not speaking, Jesus reads their minds and hearts and again takes the initiative to challenge their restrictive view of the Sabbath (6:6–11; cf. 5:22). Is it lawful. The law of Moses does not forbid healing on the Sabbath, but the "traditions of the elders" (Mark 2:16 note) prohibit medical treatment unless the condition was life threatening.

The Jews will pull a child or an animal out of a well on the Sabbath, though technically this is work. Their acts in an emergency show that deeds of mercy are lawful on the Sabbath and that Jesus has performed a deed of mercy.

Jesus is not offering a self-serving strategy for achieving recognition by feigning self-deprecation. He is advocating genuine humility that waits for eschatological vindication in dependence on God's gracious gift, as v. 11 shows (cf. 18:14; Matt. 23:12).

As guests must renounce self-interest in selecting seating at the banquet table, so the host must renounce self-interest by welcoming outcasts whose presence will not bring him social or financial benefit. Ancient biblical wisdom assured those who loaned to the poor that God Himself would repay their investment (Prov. 19:17). In the banqueting parable that follows, Jesus portrays God Himself as welcoming "the poor and crippled and blind and lame" to dine at His kingdom banquet (Luke 14:21).

This pious and conventional utterance, perhaps meant to change the subject, is evoked by Jesus' mention of "the resurrection of the just" (v. 14) and expresses the sentiment that the kingdom of God belongs to a comfortably distant future. Jesus' parable of the great banquet dramatizes the reality that God's invitation into His kingdom celebration is going out in the present, and no pretext for declining His urgent summons is an acceptable excuse.

everything is now ready. Evidently those invited accepted the invitation; none is said to have declined. A second invitation on the banquet day itself, when the food is ready, is customary (cf. Esth. 5:8; 6:14).

The excuses are transparently dishonest. No one buys a field or oxen without prior inspection, and if anyone did, there is no hurry — the field and the oxen will be there tomorrow. The man who had married might cite Deut. 24:5, but that freed a man from military service, not social contacts. Even within Israel, which received God's first invitation through the OT Scriptures, those who value commerce or family more than Jesus' call to commune with Him (vv. 25–33) will be displaced by those who know their need and heed His summons.

This parable is a prophecy of the extension of the gospel to those the Pharisees thought unworthy. The "poor and crippled and blind and lame" (v. 21; cf. v. 13) represent the despised Jews who are not able to observe the traditional laws of ritual purity (sometimes called "the people of the land"), while those outside the city along the "highways and hedges" (v. 23) represent the Gentiles. The parable concludes with a warning to the elite of Israel who reject the Messiah that they will not be given a second chance.

In contrast to rabbinic tradition, which permits hatred of one's enemies (particularly Gentiles outside the covenant), Jesus calls His followers to love their enemies (Matt. 5:43–46). Clearly, then, He is not demanding that we hate our family members in the conventional sense of hatred. Rather, through this shocking hyperbole, He teaches that being His disciple means loving Him so unreservedly that all other loves seem to be hatred by comparison.
The implement of violent death, representing utter renunciation of one's rights and life itself in the cause of God's kingdom (v. 33). See note on 9:23–25.
Calculating the cost is important before undertaking any serious project. The "tower" could be a watchtower or a farm building. That one must "sit down" points to a careful and unhurried process.

A flavoring agent and a preservative. The salt in use at this time is far from pure, and it is possible for the sodium chloride to leach out of it, leaving a residue that is useless. Just as salt devoid of its distinctive taste is worthless, so a would-be disciple who evades Jesus' demand of utter self-renunciation — the distinctive hallmark of allegiance to Him (v. 33) — is of no use in His kingdom.

See note on 3:12. Jesus regularly associates with tax collectors and other noteworthy violators of God's law, seeing such outreach as intrinsic to His mission from the Father (5:27–32; 7:29, 34; 19:2–10) and offering them God's forgiveness (18:9–14; cf. 7:28, 29). sinners. The immoral or those who followed occupations that the scribes held to be incompatible with keeping God's law. A rabbinic opinion stated that "one must not associate with an ungodly man," and the rabbis would not even teach such a person. Notice that ch. 14 ends with "let him hear," and ch. 15 begins with these "sinners" gathering around to hear Jesus.

Although Jesus tells three stories of lost things (sheep, coin, son/brother), Luke introduces them with the singular "parable." It is implied that the first two establish a general principle (when the lost is found, joyful celebration ensues) as backdrop to the third, in which the older brother (like the Pharisees and scribes) refuses to enter into the joy befitting the recovery of what has been lost. The rabbis taught that God would welcome a penitent sinner, but the first two parables teach that through Jesus, God is seeking out sinners. 15:3–7 Through Ezekiel, the Lord promised to come and fulfill the shepherding responsibilities that Israel's shepherds (both the kings and priests in Ezekiel's day and the scribes now criticizing Jesus) had neglected: "I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed" (Ezek. 34:16). In a different setting, Jesus uses the same parable to call leaders of His church to be proactive in protecting and retrieving members who go astray (Matt. 18:10–14).

The Gk. drachma (occurs only here in the NT) is equivalent to the Roman denarius, about a day's wage for a laborer. The ten coins may have been the woman's life savings, or they may have been strung together as a headdress. light a lamp. Houses had no windows or perhaps small ones, so a lamp was needed even in the daytime.

The parable of the prodigal son could be called the "parable of the welcoming father." While the repentance of the son is important to the parable, the father's willingness to forgive, and his unexpected actions (v. 20 note, vv. 22, 23) are a striking illustration of the fatherly love of God for wayward human beings. Unlike His illustrations of the lost sheep and lost coin, Jesus extends this parable to include the older brother's self-righteous refusal to celebrate the finding of the lost, just as the Pharisees and scribes resent Jesus' mission from His Father to seek sinners and bring them into God's family. 15:11, 12 According to the Mosaic law, the firstborn son is entitled to two-thirds of his father's property (Deut. 21:17). Sometimes the father gives the rights to the property (which means that he could not dispose of it himself, though the son can sell it) and retains the income (if the son were to sell the property, the buyer would be unable to take possession until the father's death). But to give a portion of the property to one of the sons before the father's death would be unusual, and for a son to request it would be highly insulting to the father.

Swine are unclean (Lev. 11:7). Since no conscientious Jew would take this job willingly, the son's willingness to do such work represents his indifference to God's holiness, his utter desperation, or both.
The father is apparently watching intently for his son's return. It is undignified for an older man to lift up his robes and run.

The father's actions indicate complete forgiveness and restoration of relationship. In his joy, he apparently interrupts the son's rehearsed apology (vv. 18, 19, 21). The "best robe" is a mark of distinction, and the ring signifies authority (Gen. 41:42; Esth. 3:10; 8:2). Because slaves do not wear shoes, the shoes point to the status of a free man. The fattened calf is reserved for special occasions.
The older son's attitude illustrates the judgmental spirit of the Pharisees who are offended at Jesus' welcome of "sinners" (vv. 1–3).

The older brother's refusal to participate in the father's joyful feast, no less than the younger brother's demand for his inheritance and departure to a distant country and dissolute life, insults the father's honor and reputation. As with the younger son (v. 20), the father again takes the initiative in restoring the relationship, leaving his house a second time to heal the alienation that had distanced the older, obedient (as he saw himself) son from the father's celebration. The parable as a whole points to the sovereign love of God, who actively seeks out unworthy sinners who do not seek Him (19:10).

The older brother views his relationship with the father as that of a slave who deserves reward for meritorious behavior. As the father's loving response to the undeserving younger son shows, salvation is not a reward for good works but entirely the gracious gift of God (Eph. 2:8, 9).

Within the framework of the parable, the property settlement remains unchanged. The attitude of the older son (v. 29 note) has caused him to lose sight of the relationship he does have with his father. Jesus is not implying, however, that those who share the older brother's resentment over divine grace to the unworthy can nonetheless be reassured that they are God's heirs. Such resentment puts one in danger of becoming like those in Jesus' day who cannot recognize the grace of the Lord.

The motif of fitting celebration when the lost is found ties the three stories together (vv. 6, 7, 9, 10, 23, 24). Jesus ends the parable without revealing the old brother's response to his father's appeal, confronting his critics with how they will respond to God's lavish grace toward the undeserving.
The man who runs the estate, freeing the owner from being involved in every detail (cf. Gen. 39:5, 6). Because he is not closely supervised, he can easily be careless, lazy, or dishonest.

The manager may have shrewdly deprived his master of funds legally owed him by debtors as he prepared the financial records for a final audit. But Jews are forbidden to take usury, and one way around the regulation is to overcharge. The first debtor might have borrowed four hundred gallons of oil and had the bill made out for eight hundred, the extra being the equivalent of a high rate of interest. By reducing the amount of interest the debtor owed, the manager would have obliged the debtor to assist him personally (v. 4) without diminishing the principal owed to his own master.

With the original bills destroyed, the owner is in an awkward position. He cannot establish his claim to the full amount, which includes the interest. He praises the shrewdness of his manager, acknowledging that he has been outwitted. Jesus uses the parable to illustrate that worldly people often use what they have to further worldly ends more strategically than people of the light do to further the quite different aims of God's kingdom.

Jesus' disciples are to use what wealth they have not for selfish purposes but to "make friends." Generosity to the poor is probably in view here, since God Himself will repay those who relieve the needy (14:13, 14; Prov. 19:17). receive you. The text does not explicitly specify who is doing the receiving. Possibilities include the poor who have been helped in this life, or, more likely, God Himself. In either case, salvation by works is not being taught (15:29 note). The loving help given to others in this life is a fruit of faith and a sign of genuine discipleship and salvation already enjoyed rather than a meritorious ground of salvation.

Financial resources exchanged in the commerce of this age are not intrinsically "unrighteous" (v. 9) or "dishonest" (reflecting the same Gk. word in vv. 8, 10). But "wealth" or "money" (mammon in vv. 11, 13) may compete with God for our trust and allegiance. Even when it does not, its value is "little" (v. 10) and short-lived when contrasted to eternal, true riches. true riches. Heavenly treasures, also described as "eternal dwellings" (v. 9).

If "that which is your own" refers to the "true riches" mentioned in v. 11, then Jesus is saying that faithfulness as a manager in this life determines one's reward in the heavenly kingdom (Matt. 25:34).
A slave is bound both to obey his master and to depend on the master's protection and provision. Either the living God or money may claim one's mastery, but not both (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

A reference to the entire OT. were until John. A tiny projection on some Hb. letters; it is the smallest part of a letter. The entire law comes from God, and it is as sure as its author (Matt. 5:17, 18 notes).

Jewish men at this time can divorce their wives easily and for slight cause. It is noteworthy that when Jesus actually raises a man named Lazarus, it does not bring His opponents to repentance (John 11:46–53; 12:9–11).
The Gk. word originally designated the bait stick of a trap; it came to mean anything that trips or traps people (text note).
Children or humble believers (cf. 10:21), who are helpless apart from God's aid.
The obligation to forgive even when a brother sins repeatedly is based in the reality that God has forgiven us a massive debt that we could never repay (Matt. 18:21–35).

Apparently, the apostles think great faith is needed to be so forgiving. Jesus points to what even small faith can bring about. More important than the quantity of faith is the object of faith — a great and powerful God.

In ordinary life, masters do not, and are not obligated to, relieve slaves of household duties merely because they have put in a hard day of outdoor labor. Yet Jesus has predicted such a reversal of roles in His kingdom (12:37, 38) and will enact it at the Last Supper (John 13:3–17; cf. Luke 22:24–27).

As God's servants we can never exceed, or even meet, our obligation to Him. This general principle is applicable here to the duty of forgiving a brother repeatedly (vv. 3, 4) which, in view of the grace we have received, neither demands extraordinary faith (vv. 5, 6) nor deserves extraordinary recognition.

People with leprosy (a term applied to various rashes and skin diseases) are ceremonially defiled with respect to Israel's worship in God's sanctuary and are therefore required by the law to keep away from people who are ritually clean (Lev. 13:46). These lepers come as close as they dare and call out loudly to Jesus.

Lev. 14:1–32 authorizes the Levitical priests to certify that a person formerly excluded from the community has been cleansed from his pollution. See note on 5:14. as they went. Gratitude brings back one man, who praises God for what had happened. That he is a Samaritan makes this all the more surprising, for he is not expected to show much gratitude to a Jewish healer. The antipathy between Samaritans and Jews is seen in a Samaritan village's refusal of hospitality to Jesus' entourage and in the readiness of Zebedee's sons to retaliate (9:52–55; cf. John 4:9; 8:48). But in a parable, Jesus makes a Samaritan the sole individual who loved his neighbor as himself (Luke 10:30–37; cf. Acts 8:4–25).

Jesus' answer to questions regarding the coming of the kingdom of God points to the mysterious and dynamic character of that kingdom. In this passage, Jesus presents the kingdom both as a reality that is present (v. 21) and as a reality that has yet to be fully revealed (vv. 22–37). Jesus often presents the kingdom as a hidden and growing reality (Matt. 13:31–33), which is both present and future. In the earthly ministry of Jesus, the kingdom is already present (11:20), but the full reality of the kingdom is yet to be manifested (cf. 19:11). Christians are to pray for the full realization of God's kingdom (11:2). See note on Matt. 13:11, 12 and the theological note "The Kingdom of God."

Cf. text note. The translation "in the midst of you" accurately points to the presence of the kingdom in the person of Jesus. Jesus' point is not that the kingdom indwells each of the Pharisees who have asked the question but that it is among them because He, the king, is present.

A probable reference to the full manifestation of the kingdom at the second coming of Christ (vv. 26, 30). Christians long for the coming of Christ and for the peace and justice that the second coming will bring.

Though some will seek after false messiahs (21:8, 9), and reports may circulate that "the day of the Lord has come" (2 Thess. 2:1–8), the final coming of Christ will be so public that everyone will know.
The word "must" indicates that Christ's suffering is mandated by the sovereign purpose of God (24:25–27, 44–49; Acts 4:27, 28).

People in the times of Noah and Lot carried on with the normal life of this world (Jesus does not speak of their sins) and neglected their opportunity to turn to God in repentance. Noah and Lot were sinners, but they heeded God's warnings and were saved.
His return will be not only unmistakably visible to all (v. 24) but also sudden and unexpected to many, offering no window of time for last-minute repentance.
Lot's wife came close to deliverance, but her backward look in disobedience to God's command doomed her (Gen. 19:26).
Jesus repeats the teaching of 9:24 that the selfish, self-affirming life means spiritual death.

Jesus apparently uses a popular proverb to teach that just as dead bodies attract vultures, so the spiritually dead invite judgment.

The preceding verses (17:22–37) and the reference to the second coming in v. 8 indicate that persistence in prayer for the coming of Christ and His final triumph over evil, even when that coming is seemingly delayed, is particularly in view (vv. 7, 8; 1 Cor. 16:22; Rev. 22:20). On the general principle that continued prayer is important in all matters, see 11:5–8 and notes.

Neither a sense of accountability to God, the supreme judge, nor concern for others' opinions will move this unrighteous judge (v. 6) to render a particular verdict. Only bribery or another appeal to his self-interest can sway the judge's decisions, and the widow has no resources to win his support.

As a woman without a husband or other male relative to press her case, the widow has no legal leverage and has nothing but right on her side. She seeks justice, not revenge, against a legal adversary who is exploiting her social vulnerability (Is. 1:17, 23).

Although the judge may mean that the woman will ruin his reputation, his indifference to public opinion (v. 2) makes this unlikely. Rather, he is graphically portraying the annoying discomfort caused by her stubborn persistence.

If even an "unrighteous" and reluctant judge (v. 6) will do what is right, how much more will God, who is eager to vindicate those whom He has chosen in His love? delay long. God will not keep putting them off like the judge in this parable; any delay will have a good reason in His infinite wisdom. In general, what seems like delay to us is the outworking of God's patience to gather all His elect through the preaching of the gospel (2 Pet. 3:9). We can be confident that He is working all things together for our good in every circumstance (Rom. 8:28).

This is in God's time (2 Pet. 3:8), not ours. will he find faith. This does not mean that there will be no believers but that unbelief and rebellion will be predominant in the "little while" that Satan is released after ages of gospel advance among the nations (Rev. 20:1–10; 2 Thess. 2:3–12).

If the preceding parable taught the necessity of persistence in prayer, this parable teaches that prayer is not automatically acceptable to God. The shocking outcome of this parable — a tax collector justified and a law-observant Pharisee left unforgiven — is Jesus' sharp corrective to those whose confidence in their own righteousness leads them to despise others whose keeping of the law falls short.
Personal prayers can be offered in the temple at any time of day, not only in formal services (2:37).
A common posture for prayer.

The only fast prescribed in the law of Moses is on the Day of Atonement (Lev. 16:29–31; 23:27), though voluntary fasting can accompany prayer (Ps. 35:13), penitence (1 Kin. 21:27), and mourning (2 Sam. 1:12). By the time of Christ, Jewish oral tradition has increased the number of fasts expected of the pious. Fasting can be a useful religious exercise (5:33–35; Acts 13:2, 3), but Jesus roundly condemns the practice when it is seen as a way of meriting God's favor or when it is publicized through ostentatious display (Matt. 6:16–18; cf. Is. 58:1–6). tithes of all that I get. The law required that crops be tithed by farmers (Lev. 27:30–33; Deut. 14:22–29), not the consumers who purchased those crops for food. This Pharisee boasts again of exceeding the demands of God's law.

Looking upward is typical while praying, but this man is too conscious of unworthiness to do this. He simply asks for mercy as he acknowledges his sin. be merciful to me. Not the customary term for showing mercy, but one descriptive of God's turning away His wrath through atoning sacrifice. A related noun is rendered "propitiation" in 1 John 2:2.

The Pharisee relies on his own merits, not having discovered that no human righteousness is sufficient before a God who demands perfection (Matt. 5:48; Ps. 143:2; Rom. 3:20). The tax collector relies on God's mercy and finds it.

As the Pharisee in the parable despises the guilty tax collector, so Jesus' disciples devalue infants and seek to keep them from interrupting Jesus' ministry to important, useful people (see 9:46–48). To receive the kingdom as a child is not to be innocent but to be utterly dependent on God, who shows mercy.

A general term meaning someone from the upper classes. Good Teacher. This is not a usual form of address in Judaism; it is mere flattery. The man assumes that his deeds will bring him to eternal life. He exemplifies "some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous" (v. 9).

Jesus is not denying His goodness but is challenging the ruler's flattery by reminding him that true goodness is an attribute of God alone. The ruler's estimation of goodness is too shallow, and his perception of Jesus is much too low. The insincerity of his flattery is shown by his failure to do what the "Good Teacher" teaches him (v. 23).

Instead of quibbling over the ruler's claim to have kept God's commands from youth, Jesus puts His finger on the idolatry at the core of the man's being. This challenge reveals that the young man has not really understood any of the commandments. When he faces the choice, it becomes clear that his possessions come before God, a direct violation of the first and tenth commandments (which, strategically, Jesus did not cite).

See note on Mark 10:25. The wealthy are tempted to rely on earthly things, together with those whose wealth is achievement in intellectual, artistic, or other fields. Great achievers often find it difficult to rely wholly and humbly on the mercy of God.
Jesus dramatizes with deliberate hyperbole how impossible it is for a rich man to enter God's kingdom, presenting an absurd image to the mind's eye. See note on Mark 10:25.

The hearers make the common mistake of assuming that wealth is a sign of God's favor (Job 1:1–5; 42:10–17). Thus, what they are essentially asking is this: "If the rich with all their advantages cannot easily be saved, who can be?" Salvation, for rich or poor, is always impossible for humans to attain on their own, so it will always be the gift of God (1:37).
Jesus' answer to Peter means that God's gifts surpass anything we can give up for Him. It does not mean that we should make sacrifices merely as a means of getting a better reward.
In His predictions of the Passion (cf. 5:35; 9:22, 43–45; 12:50; 13:32, 33; 17:25), this is the first time Jesus speaks of being handed over to the Gentiles.

Luke implies that Jesus is entering Jericho, whereas Matthew and Mark say the incident occurred as they "went out" of Jericho (Matt. 20:30; Mark 10:46). There seem to have been two "Jerichos" about a mile (1.6 km) apart in the first century: the ruins of the OT city conquered by Joshua (Josh. 6), and a city built by Herod the Great. The encounter may occur as Jesus is leaving the old city and entering the new. a blind man. Matthew mentions two blind men (cf. Matt. 9:27 and note). Luke and Mark mention only one; he may have been the spokesman for the two.

A messianic title, implied in Gabriel's promise to Mary (1:32) and grounded in God's promise to David (2 Sam. 7:12–16; see Ps. 89:19–37). David himself is not associated with miraculous healing, but this blind man expects the Messiah to exceed his ancestor (Is. 42:6, 7).

Faith is the means by which the gift is received. has made you well. This might be translated "has saved you," which would fit in with his following Jesus and glorifying God — a typical and appropriate response to Jesus' miracles (5:25, 26; 7:16, 13:13; 17:15).
The term is found nowhere else, but clearly it means the head of the local taxing agents. Jericho is near a major trade route. There is much to tax, and Zacchaeus is accordingly quite rich.
A tree frequently planted by the roadside; it is easy to climb.
Jesus takes the initiative, since His mission is to seek and save the lost (v. 10).
Jesus is again criticized for associating and eating with sinners (7:34; 15:1, 2; cf. Acts 11:2, 3).

The verb is in the present tense for vividness and emphasis. fourfold. The law requires restoration of the amount wrongfully taken, plus a fifth as a penalty (Lev. 6:5; Num. 5:7). In his joy over Jesus' gracious initiative (v. 6), Zacchaeus goes far beyond what the law demands.

Jesus has said it is hard for a rich person to be saved (18:24, 25), but the salvation of Zacchaeus shows it is not impossible for God to rescue even the affluent from enslavement to their wealth (18:27). a son of Abraham. Zacchaeus is one of the lost sheep of Israel, to whom Jesus' mission is specifically directed during His earthly ministry (cf. 13:16; Matt. 10:6; 15:24).
The recurring theme of the parables of the lost (15:3–7, 8–10, 24, 32).

Jesus' journey to Jerusalem is nearing its end, and some believe He will soon expel Rome's occupation forces and restore Israel's political independence and military dominance (cf. Acts 1:6, 7). They misunderstand both the timing of God's plan and the character of Christ's kingdom (John 18:33–37).

The parable of the talents (Matt. 25:14–29) resembles this one, but there the amounts are larger (one talent = 60 minas) and vary in quantity (five, two, one), testing the servants for their fitness for larger tasks. Here the amounts are small and the same for all (v. 13). The parable teaches that everyone has one basic task — to serve God faithfully. a far country. After the death of Herod the Great, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome hoping to be appointed king by Caesar Augustus. See note on v. 14.
Each servant receives one mina, the equivalent of one hundred drachmas (15:8 note), or one-sixtieth of a Gk. talent, representing several months' wages.

A delegation of Jewish leaders protested Archelaus's appointment as king to succeed his father, Herod, so Augustus gave him only the title "ethnarch." Jesus may be weaving that incident into this parable as a subplot, with the twist that His own departure (to His Father's right hand in heaven) opens an era in which His servants must invest His gifts, and His enemies may still, for a time, resist His rule.

Two servants do well and are rewarded with further opportunities of service in proportion to their success. Notice their modesty ("your mina has made") and the much greater responsibility allotted to them.

Fear keeps the third man from doing anything, though he knows his master expects much. Nothing is said about the other seven. The parable is concerned with two classes: those who dare to invest what the master has entrusted to them and those who do not.

The punishment for not using what one has is to lose it, a principle of wide application. Those who use their spiritual opportunities find more, while those who do nothing about them lose what opportunity they do have.
Lit. "on the table" — that is, of the money-exchange service at the temple, where a relatively risk-free and short-term investment yields a modest return as interest.
Luke reminds readers that Jesus' destination is Jerusalem, where He will suffer rejection and death, leading to His resurrection (13:22, 33, 34; 17:11; 18:31; 19:11). See note on 9:51.
A village about two miles (3.2 km) from Jerusalem. Bethphage must be nearby; it is regarded as the outer limit of Jerusalem.
This can refer to a horse or a donkey; the other gospels make clear that it is a donkey. It has never been used and is therefore fit for a sacred purpose (Num. 19:2; 1 Sam. 6:7).
The clothing evidently serves as a saddle. The clothes on the road form a triumphal carpet.

This entry into Jerusalem fulfills prophecy (Zech. 9:9) and is a public claim to messiahship, but of a distinctive kind: the donkey is the animal of a man of peace and is associated with humility in Zechariah's prophecy. A conquering king would ride a horse.

A quotation from Ps. 118:26 but with an explicit reference to the king. Luke alone has the words "peace" and "glory." Thus the themes of this crowd's welcoming praises echo the song sung by heaven's hosts to shepherds at Jesus' birth (2:14). Luke does not have "Hosanna" (representing the Hb. petition "Save!" but used as an expression of praise), which his Gentile readers might not understand.

The Pharisees do not want anything to disturb the peace and bring trouble from the Romans (John 11:45–52). Jesus' widespread popularity in the days leading up to the Passover, the feast commemorating Israel's liberation from Gentile (Egyptian) oppression, threatens to launch a revolutionary movement that will provoke brutal suppression by Rome.

Only Luke records Jesus' lament as He draws near the city (cf. 13:34, 35). Jesus knows that the excitement of the crowds does not correspond to genuine spiritual perception of His messianic mission. Although the crowds speak of "peace" (v. 38), they fail to grasp the reconciliation with God that was their deepest need and Jesus' central task. In a few days, the crowds will repudiate Him, and the ultimate result will be war, not peace, as God will use the Romans in A.D. 70 to judge the city that defied His Son.
A description of a typical siege of a city (Is. 29:1–4; 37:33). The embankment is erected as a protection for the invaders and a base from which to launch attacks.

The city will be completely destroyed and the temple razed by Roman forces under Titus in A.D. 70. The people must live with the consequences of their rejection of God's Messiah. your visitation. God's personal intervention to rescue His people in the person of the Messiah, Jesus (Gen. 50:24, 25; Ex. 4:31).

All four Gospels speak of Jesus' driving traders out of the temple precincts, but the Synoptics (Matt. 21:12–16; Mark 11:15–18) place it at the end of Jesus' ministry while John (John 2:12–22) places it at the beginning. The Gospel writers, therefore, are probably describing two cleansings (Mark 11:15 note). The merchants in the temple courts are money-changers and sellers of sacrificial animals, although Luke mentions only the latter. Both serve worshipers who have traveled from a distance, providing blemish-free animals for offering and coins from Tyre, the only currency acceptable for the payment of tithes. It is convenient to have them close to the temple, but their presence in the temple courts themselves makes true worship difficult. The traders are in the court of the Gentiles, the only place Gentiles can go in the first century to pray to the only true God. 19:45 entered the temple. Malachi prophesied, "The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple," purifying Israel's worship like a refiner's fire (Mal. 3:1–4).
The temple is a normal place for teaching. Jesus' opposition now includes a new group — "the principal men of the people." Evidently, prominent laypeople have now joined the priests and the scribes.
Jesus is bringing God's good news at the very time His enemies are plotting against Him. chief priests \... scribes \... elders. This may be a delegation from the Sanhedrin.

By driving the merchants out of the temple, Jesus directly insults the authority of the Sadducean chief priests who supervise the temple's operations. Thus His actions imply a claim of authority superior to theirs, and the Sanhedrin's representatives demand that He identify the source of His authority.
Jesus is not avoiding their question. John has testified that Jesus is the Messiah. If they answer Jesus' question, they will have the answer to their own.
They are not concerned with the truth but with the consequences of their possible answers and the reaction of public opinion (19:48).

Jesus will not overtly identify the source of His authority to men who evade an important religious question, the answer to which they already know. Yet the parable that He immediately tells contains His answer: "I will send my beloved son" (v. 13).
The tenants are a vivid picture of Israel and its leaders, who have rejected persistently the prophets whom God sent to call them to repentance (2 Chr. 36:15, 16; Is. 3:13–15).

Normally, a landowner confronted with persistent refusal to pay and with abuse of his messengers would take strong measures. But just as this landowner keeps giving the tenants the opportunity for repentance, so God repeatedly reaches out to His rebellious people. As did Jesus' earlier parable of the fig tree (13:6–9), this parable speaks of the last opportunity for Israel to bear for its owner the fruit that is His before judgment ensues.

Within the plot of the parable, apparently the tenants infer that the son's arrival means that the owner has died. They apparently reasoned that with the heir out of the way, they can establish their own title to the land. Jesus is making the point that the nation has behaved outrageously toward God, and the leaders' current plot to destroy Him (19:47) will lead only to their own destruction.

Jesus quotes Ps. 118:22, which uses architectural imagery to speak of the Lord's exalting one whom Israel's leaders ("builders") have scorned and rejected. The psalm identifies the "cornerstone" as the keystone to the temple, so that the application to Jesus identifies Him with the new form of the end-time temple. The psalm goes on to identify this marvelously exalted "stone" as the blessed one "who comes in the name of the Lord" (118:26), in the words echoed by the crowds at Jesus' triumphal entry a few days earlier (Luke 19:38). Peter later applies these words from the psalm to the Sanhedrin's repudiation of Jesus (Acts 4:11; cf. 1 Pet. 2:4, 7). cornerstone. Lit. "the head of the corner." It is likely a large stone in the foundation of the temple, laid at the corner and determining the position of two walls. Or it may be the stone at the top of the corner binding the building together.

See note on Matt. 21:44 regarding temple language from Dan. 2. 20:19 The religious teachers are hostile to Jesus but can find no way to do away with Him without arousing the rage of the people, who are "hanging on his words" (19:47, 48).
Clearly the "spies" hope to lure Jesus into saying something that will suggest insurrection against Rome, forcing the governor to arrest and punish Him.
The flattering approach is doubtless meant to put Jesus off guard, though the words themselves accurately describe Jesus' complete integrity (see John 3:2).

The question is whether paying taxes to Rome is in accordance with God's law (it is required by Roman law). From the questioners' point of view, the answer has to put Jesus at odds with either the Romans, who would view the refusal to pay taxes as a criminal act, or the Jews, who resent the taxes because they represent the subjugation of God's covenant people to a pagan Gentile empire.

Jesus asks for the silver coin that is the proper coinage for paying the tax, roughly equivalent to a day's wage (15:8 note). It bears an image of the emperor with his titles of honor, including "Lord" and "Savior." Whose likeness and inscription. There is only one answer to Jesus' question, and it opens the way for His unexpected reply. Jesus cannot be accused of disloyalty to either the Jews or the Romans. He makes it clear that there are duties owed to God but also duties to the state.

Since Caesar's image identifies the denarius as his property, Jesus may be alluding to Gen. 1:26, 27 to imply that human beings (including his deceitful interrogators) who bear God's image must recognize that they are God's property and thus render themselves to God in repentance and faith.

Luke mentions the Sadducees only here in his gospel but speaks of their beliefs and influence over the temple operations in Acts (4:1; 5:17; 23:6–9). None of their writings survive, so we know them only as their opponents saw them. They were conservative and aristocratic, and they counted the high priests among their ranks. They rejected the oral tradition of the Pharisees and found no basis for a doctrine of resurrection in the books of Moses, the portion of the OT that they valued most highly.

When a Jew died childless, his brother was required to marry the widow, and the first son would become the heir of the deceased (Deut. 25:5–10). The Sadducees clearly think that their story of a woman married in succession to seven brothers, in keeping with the law, makes nonsense of the doctrine of resurrection.

The Sadducees assume that if there is an afterlife, particularly a return to embodied existence through resurrection, it will simply replicate the conditions of this life. Jesus denies this. Marriage is an essential part of life in this age but not of life in the age to come. Therefore, the conundrum they pose is invalid.

At the resurrection, there will be a change in our physical nature, and believers will have resurrection bodies like that of Christ (1 Cor. 15:35–58 and notes). Jesus' point is not that human beings will be exactly like angels, but that the mode of existence of angels, and in particular their immortality, provides a clue to the post-resurrection existence of believers, who will also be immortal (1 Cor. 15:42, 52–55). Marriage and procreation will no longer be necessary or appropriate. See theological note "The Last Resurrection" on p. 2040.

Before the addition of chapter and verse divisions, passages in Scripture were referred to by their content. Jesus draws an interesting proof from a well-known text in the second book of Moses (Ex. 3) that people continue to live after they have died (Mark 12:26 note).

Jesus implies that when God appeared to Moses, centuries after the death of the patriarchs, He still sustained a faithful and vital relationship with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God's covenant commitment to His people means that physical death cannot ultimately overcome and eliminate them. Rather, death will be reversed in the end by the God who gives life.

Earlier generations were regarded in the first century as wiser than the present generation, and this opens the way for Jesus to pose a question of His own. Generally, sons are to be subordinate to their fathers (Ex. 20:12; Prov. 1:8), and in popular estimation David is greater than any of his descendants. How, then, can David call the Messiah his "Lord" (Ps. 110:1)? Jesus shows that the psalm implies that the Messiah is not simply the son of David; He is the Son of God and so David's Lord.
