Jesus' messiahship may be understood in part from His title "Son of David," but His identity encompasses more than His descent from the royal lineage of David.

On the scribes' love of popular acclaim, see Matt. 6:1–18. On their readiness to exploit the piety of needy widows, see note on Mark 12:40. Jesus' critique of such religious hypocrites highlights the contrast between them and the widow whom He is about to recognize for her costly generosity (21:1–4).
In the court of the women, there were thirteen trumpet-shaped collection boxes with inscriptions showing the use to which donations would be put.

An unusual word (used only here in the NT) meaning "very poor." Her total livelihood (v. 4) is two copper coins of the lowest value (text note). What makes her gift more valuable than those of the rich is not its amount but the strength of faith and devotion it expresses.
This is fulfilled during the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70.
False teachers will claim to be the Christ.

Although the "wars and tumults" accompanying the siege and destruction of Jerusalem by Roman forces under the general Titus will be traumatic, those events do not signal that the consummation of history is imminent. International conflict and natural disasters will continue (vv. 10, 11), along with persecution of Jesus' followers. the end. The end of all things. Some sections of this discourse refer to the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 and others to Jesus' coming at the end of the age (Mark 13:4 note).
Synagogues are centers for discipline as well as places of worship.
Persecution for the church also means opportunity to bear witness, as the book of Acts illustrates (Acts 4:8–12; 5:29–32; 13:44–48; 22:1–21).

This passage is a strong affirmation of God's overriding control and sovereign care of His people. For some of His followers, there will be a martyr's death; for others, deliverance. Either way, God is bringing His purposes to pass.
Although some will be put to death (v. 16), not even death itself can separate believers from God's love in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:35–39).
This section refers to the destruction of the city, not the end time (v. 9 note).
People would normally flee to a walled city for shelter from an invading army, but Jerusalem is doomed. People must run away from it, not try to enter it.
Not meaningless suffering, but the divine penalty.
The siege of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 will bring extreme suffering. The devastation awaiting the city's residents for repudiating God's Messiah evokes Jesus' earlier laments (13:34, 35; 19:41–44).

This may mean the time when the Gentiles will have their triumph over Israel, or the time when the gospel is preached to the Gentiles (Rom. 11:11, 12, 25–32), or both. fulfilled. A divine purpose will be worked out (cf. Rom. 11:1–32).

In biblical prophecy, scenes of cosmic dissolution sometimes symbolize major shifts in covenantal epochs (Acts 2:19, 20), but here it seems that Jesus shifts the subject to the second coming of Christ (v. 9 note), which will precipitate the destruction of the present heaven and earth and the introduction of a new heaven and earth (Rev. 20:11; 21:1). The Son of Man's glorious return will be preceded by signs that will puzzle many.

Forty days after His resurrection, Jesus ascends in a cloud to heaven, fulfilling the vision in which Daniel saw "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven to receive His universal dominion from the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7:13, 14; Acts 1:9–11). At the end of the age, Jesus' return as the Son of Man will be a coming in splendor to judge and to consummate His reign. Alternatively, this verse may refer to His coming in A.D. 70 to judge Jerusalem. See note on Matt. 24:29–31.

This word means "deliverance on payment of a price." Jesus pays the price at Calvary, and He here looks forward to the final fulfillment of what that deliverance means, which includes the bodily resurrection of believers (Rom. 8:23; Phil. 3:20, 21).

After these sentences in Mark 13:28–31, Jesus draws a contrast between the signs that forecast Jerusalem's impending destruction and the unpredictable timing of His second coming at the end of the age (Mark 13:32). This contrast, along with His statement that "this generation will not pass away until all this has taken place" (Luke 21:32), may suggest that Jesus is switching the topic back to the traumas of A.D. 70.

The appearance of leaves on the trees announces that summer is at hand. So the signs tell us that the kingdom is near, apparently in the transition from the old covenant to the new, signified by Jerusalem's fall and the spread of the gospel among the Gentiles.

The Gk. word usually means all the people alive at a given time, but it can also mean all of a certain kind of people (e.g., wicked or righteous) or a particular racial or ethnic group. In Luke, "this generation" typically refers to those who resist God's will (7:31; 11:29–32, 50, 51; 17:25), so Jesus seems to be predicting that human opposition to God's kingdom will continue right to the consummation.

Since "that day" will come upon all the earth's residents, Jesus has returned to the theme of His second coming and the end of time, which will spring "suddenly like a trap" not only on the ungodly but also on "you," His disciples.

Watchfulness and prayer are Christian duties to the end of time (cf. 12:35–48). to escape all these things. Although believers are not promised immunity from the woes of life in this fallen world and are assured that they will be persecuted for their faith (John 16:33; 2 Tim. 3:12), Jesus' blood and righteousness will shield them from God's wrath, which will come on the wicked at the end of history (3:7; 1 Thess. 1:10). to stand before the Son of Man. This signifies salvation at the last day.

Jesus' last days are spent teaching in Jerusalem, while at night He stays on the Mount of Olives nearby. The people's eagerness to hear Him continues to thwart the desire of their leaders to destroy Him (22:2; cf. 19:47, 48; 20:6, 19, 26).

Strictly speaking, Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are different but immediately successive festivals (Num. 28:16–25), although leaven is to be removed from Israel's dwellings before the evening on which the Passover is observed (Ex. 12:14–20). In NT times, the names are used interchangeably. The feast commemorates the great deliverance of Israel from Egypt (Ex. 12:17; Mark 14:1 note).
The chief priests have the political power among the Jews, and they, not the Pharisees, lead the final opposition to Jesus. feared the people. See note on 21:38.
Satan takes control of Judas (John 13:2), and it is Judas who seeks the chief priests, not they who seek him. The "officers" of the temple guard are mostly Levites.

The Gk. term means "hand over." It is also used to speak of the Father's "giving up" His own Son as our sacrifice (Rom. 8:32) and of Christ "giving up" Himself for us (Eph. 5:2). But in the Gospels, where it refers to Judas's treachery, "betray" is the fitting translation.
According to Ex. 12:5, the animal can be a lamb or a young goat. It is killed at twilight (Ex. 12:6).
Jesus is ready to die but at the time of His own choosing. This may be the reason for the way Jesus makes arrangements for the feast. None of the disciples know where they will eat it.

A man carrying a pitcher of water will stand out because in Jesus' day pitchers are used by women; men carry water in skins. As with the colt on which Jesus entered Jerusalem a few days earlier (19:29–34), the way that He directs His disciples to the room for their Passover observance may be intended to teach Jesus' omniscience.
The normal posture at such a meal. The diners lean on their left elbows, facing the table with their feet away from it, and eat with the right hand.

Aware that His suffering and death are imminent (12:50; 20:13–15; Mark 14:8; John 13:1), Jesus has an intense desire for fellowship with His disciples at the Passover. until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. Jesus' abstinence from the Passover and its wine "until the kingdom of God comes" (v. 18) looks far ahead to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:6–9). In preliminary forms, God's kingdom is present in Jesus' earthly ministry (17:20, 21) and will arrive in escalated form with His enthronement in heaven and bestowal of the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:3, 6–8; 2:32–36). The kingdom's consummate expression awaits the return of the king, Jesus.
At the Passover meal, each person drinks four cups of red wine. The wine is diluted, usually three parts of water to one of wine.
This future anticipation is an important aspect of the Lord's Supper as a sacrament; it points forward to the second coming of Christ (1 Cor. 11:26).

There has been much discussion of these words (Matt. 26:26 note). The verb "is" in this instance does not mean "is identical with" or "is transformed into" but rather "represents," "signifies," or perhaps "conveys." See theological note "The Lord's Supper" on p. 2032. in remembrance of me. The one thing Jesus has commanded His followers to do as a remembrance of Him refers to His death, underlining the centrality of the cross for the Christian faith.

By His death, Jesus offers the sacrifice that ratifies the new covenant of Jer. 31:31, which exceeds and replaces the cov­enant ratified in sacrificial blood at Sinai (Ex. 24:3–8; cf. Matt. 26:28; Mark 14:24).

Jesus immediately speaks of betrayal by one of those at the table. That Judas is enjoying table fellowship with Jesus makes his crime all the worse. Jesus will fulfill prophecy and go as it has been decreed (v. 37; 24:26, 27; Acts 1:16–20), but this does not lessen the guilt of the one who betrays Him. See Gen. 50:20.

Although Mark (10:35–45) and Matthew (20:20–28) record an earlier argument over greatness engendered by James's and John's request for preeminent places in Christ's kingdom, only Luke reports the shameful revival of this dispute as Jesus' thoughts are dominated by His suffering and sacrificial death in the hours to come. Their rivalry shows how far even the Twelve are from understanding the servant's mission that Jesus came to fulfill.
A number of kings in antiquity took the title "benefactor," often with little justification.

The disciples must serve, as Jesus does. At this meal He displays His readiness to perform the lowliest of service by washing their feet, the humiliating task of a slave that none of the disciples condescends to do (John 13:3–16).

That the disciples should serve rather than seek greatness does not mean they will go unnoticed. Jesus makes clear that He knows how they have stood with Him and that there will be a place for them in the kingdom. They are promised a wonderful future that includes judging the tribes of Israel (v. 30). In fact, because all believers are united by God's grace to Christ the king, they will rule with Him (Rev. 5:9, 10) and judge angels (1 Cor. 6:3).

The repetition conveys solemnity and emphasis, tinged with sadness and rebuke (10:41; 13:34). demanded to have you. The word "you" is plural. Satan has asked permission to trouble all the disciples. Notice that Satan has no power to act outside the area God allows him (cf. Job 1:6–12; 2:1–7).

Here the word "you" is singular. when you have turned again. Despite Peter's protestation of loyalty and courage, he will deny Jesus three times that very night. Yet Jesus' prayer is effective: despite his cowardice, Peter's faith will not utterly fail, and his turning again is a certainty, not a mere possibility. strengthen your brothers. When Peter has come through the trial, he is to strengthen others. The complete forgiveness and restoration that Jesus will grant after Peter's denials will be shown in the renewed assignment to feed and tend his Savior's sheep (John 21:15–17).

In their earlier missions, the Twelve and the seventy-two traveled light and received God's extraordinary provision through the hospitality of those who received them (9:3; 10:4). In the new era of gospel advance precipitated by Jesus' death, resurrection, and ascension, however, heralds of the kingdom should not expect extraordinary providential provision. They should expect ordinary providence and plan accordingly for their daily needs.
Jesus Himself faces the necessary fulfillment of Is. 53:12, and His followers will surely experience resistance and persecution.
The disciples take the words about the sword literally, but Jesus' reply means, "Enough of that sort of talk" (cf. v. 51).

Gethsemane (Mark 14:32), meaning "olive press," is the name of a grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron brook from Jerusalem's eastern wall (John 18:1). Pray. Unlike those of Mark and Matthew, Luke's account does not mention Peter, James, and John (who sleep while Jesus prays). Luke's emphasis is on Jesus' prayer, not the disciples' failings.
In Jesus' day people generally pray standing (18:11, 13), but at this solemn time Jesus kneels (cf. Eph. 3:14).

A symbol of suffering and divine anger (Is. 51:17; Ezek. 23:33). Earlier that evening, Jesus identified the cup of the new covenant, which He offered to His disciples, with His blood (v. 20). not my will. As one who has taken upon Himself a complete human nature, it is natural for Jesus to shrink from the horror of the cross, a horror magnified by His knowledge that in dying He will be forsaken by God and experience the weight of divine anger on sin, though He is Himself utterly innocent and righteous. Nevertheless, Jesus is determined to follow the will of His Father for the redemption of His people (John 6:38, 39; Heb. 10:5–10).

Luke alone tells of the angel who strengthens Jesus and of the sweat "like great drops of blood." These verses are absent in many early manuscripts (text note), so they may not have been written by Luke. As with all places in Scripture where the text is in question, the inclusion or omission of these verses does not affect any Christian doctrine. See topical article "New Testament Textual Criticism" on p. 2369.
The kiss is a common greeting (1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14), and to use it in this way is a horrible form of betrayal (2 Sam. 20:9, 10).

Still misunderstanding Jesus' earlier word about obtaining a sword in preparation for future hostility (vv. 36–38), the apostles momentarily stand ready to defend Jesus with violence. One wounds the high priest's servant before Jesus issues a sharp rebuke to His would-be defenders, as He did to James and John outside a Samaritan town (9:52–55). All four Gospels record this incident, and John gives the name of the swordsman (Simon Peter) and his victim (Malchus; John 18:10). Luke alone records that Jesus heals His enemy's severed ear.
A furtive arrest at night suits this effort of the forces of spiritual darkness (cf. Eph. 6:12; Col. 1:13).

Jesus is taken first to the high priest who ordered His arrest. All four Gospels give more space to the trial than to the crucifixion. They are answering questions about why the Jews condemned Jesus and why the Romans executed Him and are also bringing out His identity as the Son of God and king of the Jews. Peter was following at a distance. John 18:15, 16 indicates that "another disciple" (perhaps John) obtains access for Peter into the high priest's courtyard, but in all four Gospels the spotlight is on Peter, who confidently claimed before His denial that his loyalty toward Jesus overshadowed everyone else's. The distance that Peter keeps anticipates the denials by which he will disavow association with Jesus.

All four Gospels say that the first challenge comes from a servant girl, but the second variously from the same girl (Mark 14:69), a different girl (Matt. 26:71), or a man (Luke 22:58). Servants were around a fire in a courtyard; a challenge from any of them would be taken up by the others, and there would have been several voices challenging Peter. The threefold denial fulfills the prediction of v. 34.
Jesus is evidently left to a guard of soldiers who physically and psychologically torment Him.

Jesus was earlier acclaimed as a prophet of God (7:16, 39) and performed miracles reminiscent of those associated with Elijah and Elisha (7:11–17; 9:12–17). Now His captors mockingly demand that He prove His prophetic gift by identifying those who struck Him, without seeing them. Their mocking echoes Satan's taunt, "If you are the Son of God" (4:3).

No single gospel gives a complete account of Jesus' trial. It is clear that there were two main stages: the Jews tried Him before the Sanhedrin and obtained a verdict that He was a blasphemer and deserved to die. However, only the Romans had the right to execute Him, and they would not execute a man for blasphemy against the God of Israel. There had to be a further trial before the Romans to try to establish some violation of Roman law that would deserve capital punishment. 22:66 day. Jewish trials had to be held in the daytime. Mark indicates, however, that an unofficial hearing in the chief priest's home took place during the night (Mark 14:53–65, 72) and preceded the public meeting of the Sanhedrin (Mark 15:1), which Luke reports here.

Luke does not speak of a formal accusation or of a trial according to proper procedure. The Sanhedrin simply requires Jesus to incriminate Himself according to their understanding of the Messiah. This He declines to do, as they will not believe Him.

Jesus does say that a change is coming "from now on," when as the Son of Man He will be in the place of highest honor in heaven, fulfilling Dan. 7:14 and Ps. 110:1. His pouring out of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost constitutes a public display on earth of His enthronement at God's right hand in heaven (Acts 2:33).

Jesus' conflation of OT texts brings together the glorious "one like a son of man" who will rule all peoples with the priest king whom David calls his "Lord" (20:41–44). The Sanhedrin rightly infers that He is claiming to be Son of God in a uniquely exalted sense (1:31–35; 3:22; 9:35).

Jesus has conceded to the Sanhedrin's charge that He claimed to be the Son of God, and as far as they are concerned He is guilty of blasphemy (cf. Matt. 26:65; John 10:30–33). Persuading the Romans to act will require a different charge, but for the Sanhedrin the matter is over. Jesus is guilty in their eyes, and it remains only to secure His execution.
Not all of the members of the Sanhedrin are needed, but their united front will impress Pilate with their seriousness.

A curiously imprecise charge. Certainly, Jesus has taken issue with rabbinic tradition, but that will be of no concern to the Roman authorities. Aware of Jesus' popularity with ordinary Jews (19:48; 21:38), the Sanhedrin's spokesmen will go on to charge that His teaching "stirs up the people," hinting that He is inciting armed insurrection against the empire — a danger that the governor cannot ignore. forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar. Jesus did the opposite, commanding that what is Caesar's be rendered to Caesar (20:25). saying that he \... is Christ, a king. Jesus specifically refuses to use the title, although He does acknowledge that He is the Son of God (22:67–69). The Sanhedrin deliberately places a political-military connotation on these titles to give Pilate the impression that Jesus threatens Rome's occupation of Judea. In the senses that the Sanhedrin intends to convey, all the charges are false.

In one sense, Jesus is king of the Jews, but not in the sense in which Pilate understands the title. His answer is therefore ambiguous (cf. John 18:33–38). Without denying the title, Jesus distances Himself from its political and militant associations. From this reply, Pilate concludes that Jesus is no revolutionary (v. 4).

In the Roman Empire, a trial was usually held in the province where the offense was committed, but it could be transferred to the province from which the accused came. Pilate seizes on this to send Jesus to Herod Antipas, apparently trying to evade pressure from the Sanhedrin to execute Jesus, who is clearly not guilty of a capital offense under Roman law (vv. 4, 14–16). Only Luke mentions this temporary change of venue to Herod's legal authority as tetrarch of Galilee.

Herod Antipas earlier ordered the execution of John the Baptist (3:19, 20; 9:7–9; cf. 13:31). His interest in Jesus' case has nothing to do with justice but is driven by curiosity to see a miracle like those that have been reported to him. Therefore, Herod is the only person to whom Jesus refuses to speak.
Herod mocks Jesus by dressing Him royally, ridiculing the charge that He is Israel's anointed king.
These political leaders' complicity in the conspiracy "against the Lord and his Anointed" fulfills Ps. 2:1, 2, as the early Christians recognized (Acts 4:25–28).

Under Roman law, a person could be beaten and warned to be more careful in the future. Pilate is evidently hoping that this will placate the Jews and enable him to release one he knows to be innocent. 23:17 The custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover is not attested outside the Gospels, but this sort of thing was widely done at this time, and there is nothing improbable about it. This sentence may not occur in Luke's original (text note), but the custom and expectation that it describes appear in Mark 15:6, and it may be that an earlier copyist, who knew Mark's gospel well, inadvertently entered it into Luke's recounting of the Passion.
The crowds clamor for Barabbas, a man otherwise unknown. His name means "son of the father" in Aramaic.

Ironically, Barabbas is guilty of the defiant, disruptive crimes against the empire of which the Sanhedrin falsely accuse Jesus. Luke repeats Barabbas's crimes in v. 25, in connection with Pilate's release of that terrorist "for whom they asked."

Crucifixion is Rome's cruelest form of execution, reserved for slaves and the most violent of criminals. It involves a slow death by asphyxiation as the victim is suspended by his arms and supported by his feet until fatigue prevents his drawing breath into his lungs. The public exposure adds shame to the physical torment.
The hostile forcefulness of the Jewish leaders and the feeble acquiescence of the Roman governor, who knows that Jesus is innocent (v. 14), are repeatedly emphasized.

It is customary for the condemned to carry the horizontal crossbeam to the site of the crucifixion. Jesus starts to carry His cross (John 19:17), but He is weakened by the heavy scourging that Roman soldiers have already inflicted (Mark 15:15), which lacerated flesh and drew blood. The soldiers conscript a passerby named Simon, from Cyrene in North Africa. His sons apparently were known in the early church (Mark 15:21 note).

Only Luke records this lament of the people, especially women, over Jesus' suffering. Other gospels report that the fickle crowds who had welcomed Jesus' entrance into Jerusalem a few days earlier joined their leaders' demands for His execution (Mark 15:8–15; Matt. 27:20–23). But Luke notes that among the many common folk who have listened eagerly to Jesus' teaching that week (19: 48; 20:6, 19, 26; 21:38; 22:2), there are still many who are shocked and saddened by the unjust verdict against Him.

These are local people, not pilgrims from Galilee. Jesus is concerned for them, not for Himself, and turns their attention to the terrible troubles that will come upon the land and its capital city (21:20–24).

Since childlessness was an occasion of shame typically associated with God's displeasure (1:7, 24, 25), only the direst disaster could make barrenness a blessing. Worse than inability to bear children is seeing one's children slaughtered, as will occur when Jerusalem falls in A.D. 70 (21:23, 24).
Israel's prophets predicted that when God's righteous wrath is unleashed, people will seek shelter from it, even at the cost of being crushed by mountains (Hos. 10:8; Is. 2:19; cf. Rev. 6:16, 17).
Evidently a proverbial saying, possibly meaning that if Jesus (who is innocent) is crucified, what will happen to the Jewish leaders and populace (who unjustly demanded His death)?

From the Aramaic golgotha,(Gk. kranion,Latin calvaria), meaning "a skull." All four Gospels say that Jesus is crucified between two criminals; in His death, He "is numbered with the transgressors," as He foretold (22:37; Is. 53:12).

Both Jews and Romans. The mercy expressed in Jesus' request to His Father will reappear in the dying prayer of Stephen, the first recorded martyr after Pentecost (Acts 7:60). they know not what they do. The ignorance of the Jewish and Gentile conspirators against the Lord and His Messiah (Acts 4:25–28) does not excuse them, but it leaves the door to repentance open (1 Tim. 1:13–15; cf. 1 Cor. 2:8). This verse is absent in many early manuscripts (text note). See note on 22:43, 44. his garments. The clothing of a crucified person was normally given to those who carried out the execution. In this way, Ps. 22:18 (cited in John 19:24) is fulfilled.

The rulers, not the people, are sneering. They speak of "the Christ" and the "Chosen One." Although Jesus seems not to have used either title often, He implicitly granted the correctness of Peter's confession that He is the Christ of God (9:20–22) and did not disavow the title when interrogated by the Sanhedrin (22:67–70). The Father's voice at the transfiguration identified Jesus as the Father's "Chosen One" (9:35). save himself. The suffering Messiah's tormenters in Ps. 22:7, 8 taunt Him that God will rescue Him — if He actually enjoys God's favor.

Formally, "King of the Jews" states the crime for which execution was imposed. In God's providence, it also correctly identifies Jesus and implies the character of His kingship as He enters His dominion through suffering.
At first, both criminals crucified with Jesus echo the insulting taunts of the Jewish leaders and Roman soldiers (Mark 15:32), but Jesus' response persuades one that He is innocent.
This request indicates some measure of trust. The man believes that Jesus is not about to be annihilated in death but is going to a heavenly kingdom.

If the repentant criminal envisions bodily resurrection in a distant future kingdom, he is not wrong; but Jesus promises more immediate communion with Himself even in the interim between physical death and Christ's return and the final resurrection. See theological note "The Intermediate State" on p. 2109. Paradise. A Persian word for "garden," which came to mean "the place of the righteous dead" (2 Cor. 12:3; Rev. 2:7).

From about noon until three P.M., reckoning the hours of the day from dawn. darkness. This is a supernatural darkness, perhaps a fulfillment of Joel 2:30, 31, to be cited by Peter on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:19, 20).

Although the temple has several curtains, this is probably the curtain separating the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place, the outer chamber of the sanctuary structure. Mark 15:38 notes that the curtain is torn "from top to bottom," indicating a divine act (the curtain was approximately thirty feet \[9 m\] high). Jesus' death opens the way into the presence of God (Heb. 10:19–22), thereby making the temple obsolete as the place of atonement for sins. At this point, well before the temple's destruction in A.D. 70 (Luke 21:20–24), God inaugurates a new temple composed of living "stones" (i.e., believers) built on Jesus, the foundation (1 Pet. 2:4, 5; Eph. 2:20–22; Acts 2:3 note).

Matthew and Mark emphasize how terrible Jesus' death is. Luke does not deny this but records Jesus' words, quoting Ps. 31:6, thereby showing that His death is in accordance with the will of the Father. breathed his last. This is not the usual way of referring to death. None of the Gospels employs standard terminology for Jesus' death.

The way He died showed Him to be "innocent" (Gk. "righteous"). Matthew and Mark have "Son of God"; in this context, the two terms may have had similar meaning in the centurion's mind, although Matthew and Mark would expect their readers to grasp a fuller sense than the centurion himself perceived (Mark 15:39 note).
A sign of grief. The crowd came to be entertained, but Jesus' death disturbs them.

Luke does not say what effect the death has on the disciples who "stood at a distance" to witness it. Their aloofness may allude to the bleakest lament psalm (Ps. 88:18) and contrasts with the readiness of Joseph of Arimathea to risk his reputation and more by arranging Jesus' burial (23:50–53).

Joseph of Arimathea is mentioned in all four Gospels as taking the leading role in Jesus' burial. The location of Arimathea is uncertain (Mark 15:43 note). Joseph is a member of the Sanhedrin and must have been absent when the vote to execute Jesus was taken, for "all" agreed to it (Mark 14:64). That he is "looking for the kingdom of God" (v. 51) means that he is a disciple of Jesus, as Matthew states (Matt. 27:57).
The linen cloth is a shroud (placed over the linen strips mentioned in John 19:40). a tomb cut in stone. A rock tomb generally holds several bodies (Mark 15:46 note), but this one is empty.
Friday, the day on which people prepare for the Sabbath, which begins at sundown (John 19:14 note).

There is not time on Friday to do all that Jesus' followers would have liked for His burial. The women take note of where the body is laid, evidently to know where to come when the Sabbath is over to complete the burial process. Joseph and Nicodemus place a considerable quantity of myrrh and aloes with the body as they lay it in the tomb (John 19:38, 39), but the women want to make their own contribution. On the Sabbath they rested. Even in their heart-wrenching sorrow, the women observe God's command to rest on the seventh day (Ex. 20:10, 11).

Each gospel deals with the resurrection in its own way, though none describes how it happened. Some things are clear in all four: the empty tomb, the slowness of the disciples to believe that the resurrection had happened, and the prominence of women in the first appearances. But each gospel also has something that does not appear in the others. Luke includes the account of the walk to Emmaus and related events. 24:1 the first day of the week. This begins at sunset on Saturday, so the women have had the hours of darkness to complete their preparations before setting out for the tomb at daybreak.

In the first century, a stone tomb was closed by rolling a stone in front of the opening (Mark 15:46 note). Matthew notes that a seal was placed on the stone, signifying that Roman imperial authority would punish anyone who disturbed it (Matt. 27:66).
Spirit messengers (angels; v. 23) sent by God appear to be men, but their dazzling clothing shows that they are not human beings (Acts 1:10).

As the angels remind the women, Jesus told His followers repeatedly that He "must" suffer, die, and be raised on the third day (9:22, 44; 17:25; 18:32, 33; 22:37). This was God's sovereign plan announced in the OT (24:25, 26, 44–47; Acts 17:2, 3).

There is a large group of Jesus' followers in Jerusalem, in addition to the eleven apostles. Many are Galileans who traveled to Jerusalem for the Passover, including those who accompanied His triumphal entry (19:37).

Mary Magdalene is the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:10–18). She is mentioned in all four Gospels in connection with the crucifixion and the resurrection; but otherwise we hear of her only in 8:2, where we learn that Jesus had exorcised seven demons from her.

In general, the testimony of women was not highly regarded by first-century Jews, and some rabbinic tradition deemed their testimony inadmissible in a court of law. This mindset lies behind the misgivings later expressed by two disciples en route to Emmaus (vv. 22–24).

This detail exposes the mistake of the rumor later circulated by the Sanhedrin, that Jesus' body was stolen (Matt. 28:11–15). Peter's marveling is ambiguous, indicating astonishment or confusion, but not necessarily faith.
The exact site is not known, although Luke gives its distance ("about seven miles" \[11 km\]) from Jerusalem.

This appears to mean that God has prevented them from recognizing Jesus at this time. When they have been persuaded from Moses and the prophets to expect the Messiah's suffering and resurrection, they will be ready to recognize Him (see 16:29–31).
Cleopas is not mentioned elsewhere, nor is his companion identified.
Stephen will describe Moses in similar terms (Acts 7:22). Luke will summarize the contents of this gospel, his "first book," as "all that Jesus began to do and teach" (Acts 1:1).
The disciples place the principal responsibility for Jesus' death on their own people, not on the Romans.
The word means to set free by paying a price. Clearly, the two are thinking of the political deliverance of their nation.
The women's report of the empty tomb (confirmed by men) and the vision of angels amazes these men but does nothing to alleviate their sadness (v. 17) or dashed hopes (v. 21).
Their failure to embrace the Scriptures' predictions of the Messiah's suffering and subsequent glory is attributable not to the Bible's obscurity but to their spiritual blindness.
See vv. 44–47. Peter gives a similar outline of the message of the OT in 1 Pet. 1:10, 11.

The first two sections of the Hebrew OT canon are the books of Moses (Genesis–Deuteronomy) and the "Prophets," which in the Jewish reckoning include historical books such as Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings as well as prophetical writings such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Minor Prophets. Throughout these portions of God's Word, Jesus shows them promises and foreshadowings of Himself and His mission. See note on 24:44.
These were actions a host performs at a meal, but they are also reminiscent of Jesus' institution of the Lord's Supper a few evenings earlier (22:19; cf. 9:16).
This is by divine action (cf. v. 16).
Even before they recognize Jesus, His opening of the Scriptures to show them His suffering and subsequent glory replaces their despair with faith and joy.
They had not believed the women (v. 11), but an appearance to Simon Peter is more convincing.

The sudden appearance of Jesus among them, although the doors were locked (John 20:19), indicates that Jesus' resurrection body is not subject to the same limitations that our present mortal and "lowly bodies" are (Phil. 3:21; 1 Cor. 15:42–57).

Despite the testimony of Simon and the two who returned from Emmaus, confusion and doubt persist (cf. Matt. 28:17). Consequently, Jesus provides "many proofs" (Acts 1:3) that He has risen bodily, overwhelming their unbelief and qualifying them to bear eyewitness testimony to His resurrection (Acts 1:21, 22; 2:32; Luke 1:2).
That is, to see the nail marks. His risen body, though gloriously transformed, still bears the scars of His suffering (John 20:24–29).
The risen Christ eats and drinks, proving that He is not merely a visionary appearance (see Acts 1:3).

The word "must" indicates that the Messiah's suffering and resurrection, together with the blessings that flow from those events to all nations, are central to the purposes of God revealed in the OT. Therefore, God's sovereign will mandates that those Scriptures be fulfilled. the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms. The threefold division of the Hebrew Bible. As the first book in the third section of the Hebrew canon, "Psalms" stands for all the books in that section (called "the Writings"). Jesus is saying that every part of Scripture bears witness to Him.

Jesus shows them the way to understand the Bible, but He also removes the spiritual blindness and slowness of heart that has hindered their understanding and acceptance of its message. Christ's death and resurrection were foretold in the OT (v. 26 note). In addition, the calling of people to repentance and remission of sin were foretold, as was the fact that this message of salvation would go out from Jerusalem to all nations (v. 47; cf. Acts 1:8). These blessings are all based on Christ's atoning death and glorious resurrection.

The apostles (and preachers, who are their fallible successors) are not to produce some novel concepts of their own but to bear witness to what God has done. The apostles, uniquely, are Jesus' witnesses (Acts 1:8) to testify to His resurrection (Acts 1:21, 22; 2:32; 3:15; 5:32; 10:39, 41; 13:31). Only their words are inspired, and the task of church leaders is to remain faithful to the apostolic testimony of the Scriptures and not to claim the same authority for themselves. With the death of the last apostle at the end of the first century, special revelation ceased, though the Holy Spirit continues to bless His people with the understanding of His Word.

The risen Jesus will send what His Father has promised, the gift of the Holy Spirit (Joel 2:28–32; Acts 2:1–4; cf. Is. 44:3, 8). stay in the city. As Acts 1:5 shows, this command implies that the promised descent of the Spirit from the Father will occur "not many days from now." It also means that they will need the Spirit's power "from on high" (Is. 32:15) to fulfill their mission as witnesses.

Luke gives no time indication here, but elsewhere he states that the ascension takes place forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1:3). Bethany. A village on the Mount of Olives about two miles (3 km) east of Jerusalem (John 11:18).

Luke's account of the ascension is a brief but fitting conclusion to his gospel, which is an account of "all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up" (Acts 1:1, 2). Luke provides a more detailed ascension account at the beginning of his second book (Acts 1:9–11). The ascension marks the end of the work Jesus came to do on earth and the beginning of what He continues to do in and through the church. See theological note "The Ascension of Christ."

Whatever their view of Jesus in earlier days, they now recognize His divinity and worship Him. The separation does not bring sadness but "great joy," as the angel of the Lord promised at Jesus' birth (2:10, 11).
The gospel ends as it began, in Jerusalem with the worship of God.

John.note: This "prologue" to the gospel is a preface to the narrative beginning at v. 19. It introduces the gospel's central character (the divine Creator who "became flesh") and many of its themes (life, light vs. darkness, witness, rejection vs. reception, birth from God, truth). 1:1 In the beginning. John links his gospel to the original creation by echoing the opening words of the first book of Moses (and of the Bible; Gen. 1:1). Matthew's reference to "book of the genealogy" (Greek: "generation") likewise echoes Genesis (2:4), signaling that Christ's appearance in history initiates a new creation. the Word. The term "Word" (Greek: logos) designates God the Son with respect to His deity; "Jesus" and "Christ" refer to His incarnation and saving work. During the first three centuries, doctrines of the person of Christ focused intensely on His identity as the Logos. In Greek philosophy, the Logos was "reason" or "logic" as an abstract force that brought order and harmony to the universe. But in John's writings, such qualities of the Logos are gathered in the person of Christ. In Neo-platonic philosophy and the Gnostic heresy (second and third centuries A.D.), the Logos was seen as one of many intermediate powers between God and the world. Such notions are far removed from the simplicity of John's gospel. In this verse, the Word is expressly affirmed to be God. The Word existed already "in the beginning," which is a way of denoting the eternity that is unique to God. John states clearly, "the Word was God." Some have observed that the word translated "God" here has no definite article, and have argued on this basis that it means "a god" rather than "God." This is a misunderstanding; the article is omitted because of the word order in the Gk. sentence (the predicate "God" has been placed first for emphasis). The NT never endorses the idea of "a god," an expression that implies polytheism and is in sharp conflict with the consistent monotheism of the Bible (10:34–38 note). Depending on the requirements of Greek grammar, the Gk. word for "God" occurs often in the NT without the definite article when it obviously designates the only true God (e.g., vv. 6, 12, 13, 18; 3:2, 21). That "the Word was with God," indicates a distinction of persons within the unity of the Godhead. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not successive forms of appearance of one person, but are eternal persons present from "the beginning" (v. 2). "With" suggests a relationship of close personal intimacy. See theological note "The Triunity of God" on p. 1204.
This verse also emphasizes the deity of the Word, since creation belongs to God alone. See also v. 10; Col. 1:16, 17; Heb. 1:2.
Another affirmation of deity: the Son as well as the Father has "life in himself" (5:26).

It is characteristic of the style of this gospel to emphasize contrasting concepts (see Introduction). The plot of this gospel could be seen in terms of a struggle between the forces of faith and unbelief, light and darkness. The motif of "darkness overcoming" reappears at 12:35, 36, where Jesus identifies Himself as the source of the light that dispels darkness (see 3:19; 8:12; 12:35–36a).
The universal relevance of the gospel is asserted (v. 7) as well as the enlightening activity of God's common grace (v. 9). God's saving activity is not restricted to any particular people.

John testified that he was not the Messiah, but a "voice" sent ahead of the Lord to prepare His way (vv. 19–27). 1:9 The true light. In this gospel, "truth" and "true" are often employed to signify what is everlasting or heavenly, as opposed to the merely temporal or earthly. See notes on 4:24; 6:32.

Jesus' public ministry was one of rejection by "his own people" (text notes), so the gospel's first main section (1:19–12:50) closes with quotations from Is. 53:1 and 6:10 that sum up the blind unbelief of the covenant people as a whole (12:37–43).

Jesus' private instruction to those given to Him by the Father dominates the gospel's second main section (ch. 13–17), followed by His suffering, resurrection, and subsequent appearances to His followers (ch. 18–21). become children of God. Fallen human beings are not children of God by nature; this is the privilege only of those who have faith, a faith generated in them by the sovereign action of God (v. 13).

Early Latin versions understood this to describe the virgin birth of Christ. However, the plural verb "were born" shows that this verse is about the new birth of Christian believers (cf. 3:3, 5, 7, 8). This new birth takes place by the action of the Spirit giving life to those who were "dead in \... trespasses and sins" (Eph. 2:1). The new birth, often called "regeneration," is explained more fully in 3:1–21. It imparts the spiritual life by which we can believe in Christ (1:12) and see and enter God's kingdom (3:3–5). Paul typically uses the metaphor of resurrection from being dead in sin (Rom. 6:4–6; Eph. 2:5, 6; Col. 2:13; 3:1; cf. John 5:24), but he also invokes the imagery of new birth by God's Spirit (Gal. 4:22–29; Titus 3:5). God's work of salvation is wholly sovereign and gracious, but the reality of the human response in believing and receiving is never cancelled. See theological note "Predestination and Reprobation" on p. 1997.

This is the climactic assertion of the prologue. To some of John's contemporaries, spirit and the divine were utterly opposed to matter and flesh. Others believed that the gods visited the earth disguised as human beings (Acts 14:11). But here a chasm is bridged: the eternal Word of God did not merely appear to be a human being, but actually became flesh. He took to Himself a complete and genuine human nature. See theological note "The Deity of Christ" on p. 1851. dwelt among us. "Dwelt" means "pitched His tent." This not only indicates the temporary nature of Jesus' earthly sojourn, but it also does so with a term that recalls ancient Israel's tabernacle, where God resided in the midst of His people (Ex. 40:34, 35). we have seen his glory. His "glory" is beheld, even as God's was in the wilderness (Ex. 16:1–10; 33:18–23), in the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34, 35), and later in the temple (1 Kin. 8:1–11). There may also be a reference to the transfiguration, since John, along with Peter and James, witnessed it (Matt. 17:1–5). Moses had asked to behold the Lord's glory but could only glimpse His back (Ex. 33:18–23). "Glory" applies supremely to God, the Creator and Ruler of the universe, the One before whom all knees must bow. The Son has the divine glory by right (17:5). The Reformers declared their faith with the motto soli Deo gloria (to God alone the glory). the only Son. This phrase translates a single Gk. word. Some scholars argue that the Gk. word means "unique" or "one of a kind." See Heb. 11:17, which refers to Isaac as Abraham's "only-begotten" or "unique" son. Abraham had other sons (Ishmael and Keturah), so Isaac is a "unique" son, i.e., the son of promise, who was different in this sense from Abraham's other sons. The term explicitly points to the eternal generation of the Son in the Trinity (see 3:16; and "the only \[begotten\] God" in 1:18). full of grace and truth. These words correspond to OT terms describing God's covenant mercy that are often translated "steadfast love and faithfulness" (Gen. 24:27; Pss. 25:10; 26:3; Prov. 16:6). When Moses saw God's glory on Sinai, he heard the Lord proclaim His own name as the merciful God who is "abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Ex. 34:6), a divine self-description that is repeated in later Scripture (Neh. 9:17; Pss. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jon. 4:2). The Word made flesh fully manifests the gracious covenant-making and covenant-keeping character of God.
John the Baptist's ministry preceded the public ministry of Jesus (Matt. 3), yet the Word, being eternal, existed before John (cf. 8:58).

This word, frequent in Paul's epistles, appears in John's writings only in this passage and as a customary greeting in Rev. 1:4; 22:21. It emphasizes that salvation is a gift. The Reformation expressed this with the motto sola gratia (by grace alone). If v. 17 elaborates on this concise phrase, the sense is that the law imparted through Moses was a gift of God's grace that was succeeded by the fuller grace revealed in Jesus.
There is both contrast and comparison. Grace and truth truly existed in Moses' day, but they were fully revealed in the coming of Christ. grace and truth. See note v. 14.

It is fundamental that God is invisible and without form (1 Tim. 6:16). Moreover, if God were to manifest His glory in a form that we could see, His divine purity would destroy sinful humans (Ex. 33:20; Gen. 32:30; Is. 6:1–5). Yet Christ reveals God. He brings the invisible and the visible together in a way that has no parallel or analogy.
John the Baptist's testimony to those who question him reveals that his role is to prepare the world for Christ.

Mal. 4:5 promises the coming of Elijah before the day of the Lord. In Matt. 11:14, Jesus tells the crowd that John is the fulfillment of this prophecy as "Elijah who is to come." John comes in the "spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17), but the Baptist here affirms that his questioners are mistaken to expect a physical return of the ancient prophet who was caught up into heaven in a whirlwind and chariot of fire (2 Kin. 2:11). John is not Elijah himself. Symbolic imagery, not merely wooden literalism, should guide our interpretation of prophecies and their fulfillment. In this case, symbolism appears to be used. But neither only symbolic imagery nor mere wooden literalism should guide our interpretation of prophecies and their fulfillment. Ultimately, the modern interpreter should seek the original intention of the OT author and the NT author citing the OT. Here John is not the literal person of Elijah from the OT, but Elijah typologically foreshadowed John's coming, so that there is a sense in which John is identified with Elijah (as Jesus so identifies him; see Matt. 11:14; 17:12; Mark 9:13). In fact, John is so closely identified with Elijah that, as noted above, his father was told by an angel that John would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah," in fulfilling the prophecy about Elijah from Mal. 4:5, 6 (cf. Luke 1:17). the Prophet. There were different expectations among first-century Jews concerning the "prophet like me" that Moses announced in Deut. 18:15. Here the priests and Levites want to know whether John considers himself to be this Prophet.
In quoting Is. 40:3, John applies to Christ what is said of Yahweh in that passage. The same truth appears even more clearly in Mark 1:1–3 (see Luke 1:16, 17, 76).

Compare v. 36. Whether "the Lamb" is the Passover lamb or the servant lamb of Is. 53:7 cannot be easily determined. There is some evidence that the two figures were combined very early in Christian thought, no doubt under the influence of Isaiah's sacrificial imagery. Such imagery portrayed the servant's substitutionary suffering to redeem others and to render them righteous (Is. 53:4–6, 10–12). who takes away the sin of the world. The "world" designates humanity in its hostility to God, as elsewhere in this gospel. Although not all persons without exception will be saved, the sacrifice is the only atonement for human sin that God has provided, and its effectiveness is not limited by time or place (3:16 note).

John the Baptist may have had previous personal contact with Jesus, since their mothers were related (cf. Luke 1:39–45). But he did not know who Jesus was (the Lamb and Son of God) until the Spirit identified Him (v. 32; Luke 3:21, 22; Acts 10:38). See theological note "The Baptism of Jesus" on p. 1733.

The OT anticipated the time of redemption as the time when the Spirit would be poured out on God's people (Is. 44:3–5; Ezek. 37:1–10; Joel 2:28–32). Paul refers to Jesus as the second Adam who became "a life-giving spirit" (1 Cor. 15:45 note; cf. Mark 1:7, 8). It is after Jesus returns to heaven that He sends this heavenly helper to dwell with His people on earth (14:26; 16:7; Acts 2:32, 33). The baptism of the Holy Spirit occurs with the new birth that constitutes helpless sinners as sons and daughters of God (vv. 12, 13; 1 Cor. 12:13). This baptism also empowers all believers for Christian service (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8; 2:1–4).

This is John's way of reporting the heavenly voice that accompanied the heaven-sent Spirit, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3:17). While "son of God" was used variously by ancient Jews (2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 2:7) and Gentiles (Mark 15:39 note), the Baptist's witness, that of the last of the prophets of the old order (Matt. 11:11–14) is clear. Jesus is the Son of God, the "only \[begotten\] Son from of the Father" (v. 14). The purpose of the fourth gospel is to draw readers to this conviction (20:31).

Jesus calls His first disciples. Since the apostles had unique authority from Christ to bear witness, the witness on which the church is established (Eph. 2:20), it was necessary that they be identified as selected by Christ Himself (cf. 15:16; Acts 1:2).

Traditionally, the students of a Jewish rabbi walked behind him. Jesus' disciples follow Him physically, but more is in view. Following Jesus takes on deeper levels of meaning throughout this gospel (13:36–38; cf. 21:15–22).

Unlike his brother Simon Peter, Andrew does not become a member of Jesus' "inner three," along with the sons of Zebedee. Yet references to him in this gospel portray him as introducing people to Jesus: his brother Simon, a boy with a small lunch (6:8), and a group of Greeks who had approached Philip asking to meet Jesus (12:20–22).

When God assigns a new name, He is redefining the person and his or her destiny (Gen. 17:5, 15; 32:28). Jesus later reaffirms the name that spoke to His transforming Simon into a "rock" (despite Simon's remaining flaws) after Simon rightly confesses that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:17, 18).

Philip, whom Jesus will call to be one of the Twelve (Mark 3:18), will not only introduce Nathanael to Jesus but also bring certain Greeks who seek to meet Him, foreshadowing the gathering of the nations as a result of Jesus' glorification in His death (12:21–24). At other points, Philip's words will reflect the confusion that he shared with other disciples (6:5–6; 14:8, 9). Nathanael, who reappears by name in 21:2, may be another name for Bartholomew, who is linked with Philip in the lists of the twelve apostles (Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14). of whom Moses \... the prophets wrote. Philip recognizes that all the OT, both Law and Prophets, anticipated a great redemptive work of God to be accomplished by a special anointed one. The OT anticipation of Christ and His work is affirmed by Christ Himself (Luke 24:25–27, 44–47) and is central in the preaching of the apostles (Acts 2:29–32; 3:18, 21, 24; 7:52, 53; 8:30–35; 26:22, 23; 28:23). the son of Joseph. This does not imply a denial of the virgin birth, of which Philip may not in any case be aware at this point; it is simply a reference identifying Jesus by His town and family (Matt. 1:24; cf. Luke 2:46–48 note; 3:23).

Nathanael apparently expresses contemporary skepticism that a prophet could arise from Galilee (7:52). Nazareth is an insignificant village, not mentioned in the OT or other Jewish literature of the time.

The phrase is probably meant to call to mind Israel as the people of God, to whom the Messiah was promised. This phrase also alludes to vv. 50, 51, where Nathanael is promised an experience similar to that of Jacob, later renamed Israel (Gen. 28:12; 32:28), whose character God transformed from deceit to faithfulness.

Nathanael's confession may seem like an overreaction to Jesus' supernatural knowledge. But Philip has already indicated to Nathanael that Jesus is the one anticipated by the Law and the Prophets (v. 45). Nathanael comes to Jesus looking for reasons to believe or disbelieve, and he finds Jesus' knowledge convincing. King of Israel. This is a title for the Messiah, used in shouts of praise at the triumphal entry (12:13), similar to the announcement of the wise men (Matt. 2:2) and to the inscription on the cross (19:19).

Jesus' earthly miracles are signs of His redemptive power and work. The miracles are to be appreciated not merely for themselves, but for the redemptive realities they promise. Greater than such works is the salvation Christ brings (v. 51).

This verse alludes to Jacob's vision of a ladder or stairway stretching from earth to heaven, on which angels ascended to worship God and descended to do His bidding on earth. As Jacob slept, his resting place became a temple, a "house of God" (Bethel; Gen. 28:12). Jesus Himself is the reality to which the stairway pointed. In a dream, Jacob saw the reunion of heaven and earth; in reality, Christ is the end-time sanctuary in which God communes with His people (1:14; 2:19–22). Son of Man. Jesus uses this name often for Himself. It not only emphasizes His human nature, which enabled Him to die for His people, but also refers to the heavenly, messianic figure known from Daniel's vision who is invested with universal authority on behalf of God's saints — a second and last Adam (Dan. 7:13, 14; Matt. 8:20 note). Accordingly, Christ has begun to fulfill the Dan. 7:13, 14 prophecy that the Son of Man would come and reign over the earth.

Jesus' first sign: turning water into wine at Cana. Several signs, arguably seven in number, are recorded in chs. 2–12, and the reference to "many other signs" immediately after accounts of Jesus' post-resurrection appearances implies that the resurrection is the climactic sign that must draw us to believe that He is the Christ, the Son of God (20:30, 31). This miracle signifies the transformation of the old order associated with Moses (symbolized by the stone water jars used for ceremonial washing, v. 6) into the new (the wine standing for eternal life in God's kingdom) through Jesus Christ (1:16, 17; cf. 2 Cor. 5:17). See Is. 25:6–9 for the background image of eschatological salvation as a banquet of abundant food and fine wine. The abundant fruitfulness of vines and wine was to be characteristic of the coming new creation of the latter days (e.g., Hos. 2:22; Joel 2:19, 24; 3:18; Amos 9:13, 14; Zech 9:17). Those at the wedding celebration who knew that the wine came from Jesus and who had eyes to see would have realized that the end-time new creation was breaking in through Him.

This is a respectful way of addressing a woman within that culture and is the way Jesus normally addresses women (4:21; 8:10). what does this have to do with me. Jesus answers Mary's request, not because she is His mother, but as part of His work as the Messiah. This indicates that Mary's special relationship as Jesus' mother gives her no authority to intervene in Christ's messianic career — a strong argument against offering prayer to Mary. My hour. Usually Jesus' "hour" refers to the time of His suffering and death (7:30; 8:20; 12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1). Jesus is asserting that His Father, not Mary, must determine the timetable of His earthly ministry.
Accepting Jesus' clarification of their relationship, His mother understands His response to imply that He is willing nonetheless to meet the immediate need.

First-century wedding celebrations could last several days, so poor wine was reserved for later, when guests' tastes had been somewhat dulled. The compliment paid to the bridegroom for superior wine, the origin of which only the servants know, speaks more deeply of the greater grace now conveyed through Jesus Christ, superseding that made known in the law that came through Moses (1:17).

The theme of Christ's glory had already been introduced (1:14 note). In the OT, God manifested His glory in a variety of miraculous events, and John's comment indicates that he wants his readers to recognize Jesus' deity. And his disciples believed in him. See also v. 23 and 20:31, where John states that his purpose in writing is to evoke faith in Jesus.
See Mark 6:3 on sons and daughters born later to Joseph and Mary, after Jesus' birth from the virgin.

Jesus is the final and full expression of what was only a shadow in the OT (Heb. 10:1). Here He indicates that God is present in Him in a way that was only foreshadowed in the temple that stood on Mount Zion. The temple in Jerusalem could be destroyed, but not the temple that Jesus would rebuild in three days, His own body that was to be raised from the dead. John's record of the temple cleansing immediately after the miracle at Cana (vv. 1–11 note) offers an important key to the whole of Jesus' ministry. In these events are signaled replacement of the old order (water of ceremonial cleansing, Herod's temple) with the new (the wine of salvation, Is. 25:6–9; the risen Lamb as the new temple, Rev. 21:22). Matthew, Mark, and Luke report a cleansing of the temple in the week of Jesus' crucifixion. In spite of some similarities, these are best viewed as different incidents (Mark 11:15 note). It is noteworthy that Jesus' statement about destroying a temple, which John alone records (v. 19), probably was the basis for the accusation by false witnesses who misconstrued His meaning (Matt. 26:61; Mark 14:58), and again for the taunting comment of some spectators at the crucifixion (Matt. 27:40; Mark 15:29). The first three gospels confirm the historical character of John's narrative. An echo of the same thought is found in the accusation against Stephen (Acts 6:14).

Animals for sacrifice and coins appropriate for the payment of God's tithes (in exchange for Roman coinage, which bore idolatrous imagery and wording) were offered as a convenience to pilgrims who had traveled from a distance to worship at the temple. But this profitable commerce rendered the temple, "my Father's house," an unfit venue for worship, especially (as the Synoptic accounts of the later temple cleansing show) for Gentiles, who were restricted to the outer "court of the Gentiles," where the animal merchants and moneychangers conducted their business.
Jesus fulfills the prophecy of Mal. 3:1–4. He comes suddenly to the temple and purifies the sons of Levi, as a demonstration of His zeal for God and for keeping God's ordinances holy.

Observers demand a sign to show that Jesus has authority to purge the temple courts of businesses that operate under the permission of the high priest and his colleagues in the Sanhedrin. Jesus has just performed a sign that elicited faith in Cana of Galilee to the north, as John's readers know (2:11). Even after being miraculously fed in the wilderness, a crowd will demand a sign from Jesus to warrant their faith in Him (6:30).

Contrary to the garbled accusation of false witnesses at His trial, Jesus predicts that His opponents — not He — will destroy the temple. As His disciples realize after His resurrection, He is referring not to Herod's temple but to His own body as the location of God's dwelling with His people (vv. 21, 22).

-six years. The sentence itself does not indicate whether the temple was finished or was still under construction after these years of building. The first-century Jewish historian Josephus (Antiquities, 15.380) says that the temple was begun in the eighteenth year of Herod the Great (around 19 B.C.) and was not completed until the reign of Herod Agrippa (A.D. 63), indicating that construction was still continuing in Jesus' time. will you raise it up in three days. The Jews (and the disciples, v. 22) misunderstand Jesus' ambiguous statement. Such initial misunderstanding is common in John's gospel (e.g., 3:4; 6:52). Those who "receive" Jesus (1:12) are led on to full understanding, but those who reject Him remain at the level of complete misunderstanding (1:5).

During His final instruction of the disciples before His arrest, Jesus promises that what He has taught them will be brought to their remembrance by the Holy Spirit (14:25, 26). The ability to predict events otherwise unknowable is evidence of divine authority. This applies to the prophecies of the OT and to the predictions made by Jesus, especially about His resurrection.

In biblical times, the "name" summed up a person's character, activity, and place in God's purpose. The faith of those mentioned here remains superficial, however, because they come to it only because they have seen "the signs" (Introduction: Theology of John). For that reason, Jesus does "not entrust himself to them" (v. 24). saw the signs. Since the gospel has described only the transformation of water to wine at Cana so far, its record of Jesus' signs is obviously extremely selective, as is stated explicitly in 20:30, 31; 21:25.

During His humiliation, which Heb. 5:7 calls "the days of His flesh," Jesus sometimes exhibited limited knowledge befitting His true human nature, rather than His divine omniscience (11:34; Mark 13:32). Yet He also displayed supernatural knowledge, important for His redemptive work, that confirmed His deity and the Father's endorsement of His claims and mission (1:48; Matt. 9:4; 17:27; Mark 11:2–4; 14:13–16).

This is the first of many teaching discourses recorded by John. Typically, on being asked a question, Jesus answers in a way that steers the discussion into a deeper realm, often through misunderstandings that are corrected for those becoming true disciples. The new understanding reveals Jesus more fully.

This might betray a fear of being seen, or it might be a sign of deference to Jesus, a rabbi who should not be distracted during the day. Understood symbolically, Nicodemus is a person living in the darkness of this world, who now encounters the light (8:12; cf. 9:4; 11:10; 13:30). a teacher \... from God. Nicodemus understands that God authenticates His messengers through giving them power to perform miracles, but this understanding falls far short of Jesus' true identity. Nicodemus is a Pharisee who enjoys respect as "the teacher of Israel" (v. 10), and he may be approaching Jesus as a delegate of the Sanhedrin, since he says, "We know" (v. 2) and Jesus responds to him with the plural "you" in v. 11 (see text note). Yet his openness to Jesus' claims sets him apart from many Jewish leaders, as subsequent events in the gospel reveal (7:45–52; 19:39).

See text note. The translation "born from above" accords well with the discussion of "earthly" and "heavenly" things in v. 12, and the discussion of ascending and descending in v. 13. This is the meaning of the Gk. adverb in other places in this gospel (19:11, 23). Nicodemus apparently understands it to mean "a second time," since he speaks of reentering his mother's womb. It is possible that both meanings are intended — a new birth that is a birth from above. See theological note "Rebirth."

Some suggest that the "water" is the release of fluid that accompanies physical birth, but linguistic considerations point to understanding "water" and "Spirit" as referring to a single spiritual birth. Many interpreters understand "water" here as the water of baptism, but such a reference, before Christian baptism was instituted, would have been meaningless to Nicodemus. Others find a reference to John's baptism, but Jesus nowhere makes John's baptism a requirement for salvation. Probably the statement refers to OT passages in which the terms "water" and "Spirit" are linked to express the pouring out of God's Spirit in the end times, and the purification and new life that flow from His arrival (Is. 32:15; 44:3; Ezek. 36:25–27). The presence of such rich OT imagery accounts for Jesus' reproof of Nicodemus (v. 10): as a "teacher of Israel," he should have understood these things.

This passage emphasizes the priority and sovereignty of God in the work of salvation. It does not exclude the reality and necessity of human response in repentance and faith, but it shows that this response is the fruit of the Spirit's work and not the means by which we are regeneration. Regeneration precedes faith.

Jesus speaks on behalf of His people, since He has begun to gather disciples, but He particularly identifies His testimony with that of John the Baptist, whose mission was to be a witness (1:7, 19, 31–34; see 3:27–30). I say to you \... you do not receive our testimony. The first "you" is singular (Nicodemus) and the second "you" is plural (you and those whom you represent, Pharisees and other members of the Sanhedrin).

It could be said that in His divine nature Christ continued to dwell "in heaven" even during His life on earth, but Jesus' point is that in His incarnation He came to earth from the presence of His heavenly Father (8:38). Thus He has authority to speak of heavenly things, delivering the words given Him by the Father (15:15; 17:8). Later in the gospel, Jesus' origin "from heaven" becomes a chief matter of dispute (6:41, 42). For a similar but distinct perspective on Jesus' descent and ascent between heaven and earth, see Eph. 4:8–10. the Son of Man. Jesus' preferred self-designation has its roots especially in the vision of Dan. 7:8–14, wherein "one like a son of man" enters heaven and receives from God universal and eternal authority to rule. See 5:27; 6:62 and the note at Matt. 8:20.

Num. 21:4–9 records the story of the rebellious Israelites, who murmured and complained. God sent fiery serpents into their midst to punish them. Then God told Moses to put a bronze serpent on a pole, with the promise that whoever looked at it would live. Jesus' comparison implies that His impending crucifixion under God's curse will likewise impart salvation to those who look to Him in faith. must \... be lifted up. The phrase "lifted up" is an important one in this gospel (8:28; 12:32, 34), and carries the double meaning of crucifixion and exaltation. Christ's death on the cross, His resurrection, and His glorification together reveal the glory of God. The word "must" points to God's sovereign purpose. The crucifixion was the keystone of God's eternal plan to save His people (Acts 4:27, 28).

Some have insisted that God sent Jesus to die in order to make salvation possible for everyone without exception. However, Jesus makes clear that the salvation of those whom the Father gives Him is not a mere possibility but an absolute certainty. All of those whom God has chosen will come to Christ, who has laid down His life only for His sheep and not for those who have not been chosen from the foundation of the world (6:37–40; 10:14–18; 17:9). The point made by "the world" is that Christ's saving work is not limited to one time or place or people (the Jews), but applies to the elect from all over the world no matter the era in which they live or their ethnicity. Moreover, in John, "the world" often opposes God (1:10; 7:7; 14:17; 15:18, 19), so the wonder of God's love is displayed in the unworthiness of its object. Those who do not receive the remedy God has provided in Christ will perish. It remains true that anyone who believes in Christ will not die (be separated from God) but live in God's presence forever. See theological note "The Goodness of God" on p. 991.

Jesus elsewhere says that judgment does attend His coming into the world (9:39; 12:31). His point is not that He will not judge, but that the time has not yet come. The world was already under threat of judgment before He came, but with His coming, salvation becomes a reality offered to a hostile world (12:47; Matt. 23:37; Rom. 5:8).

Unbelief is not the only basis for condemnation, but it constitutes the climax of rebellion by resisting even God's gracious offer of salvation in Christ. Jesus comes into a world that is already condemned because of its rejection of God's self-revelation (Rom. 1:18–32); and apart from the faith that unites one to Christ, individuals remain under condemnation for their sins (John 3:36).

Jesus gives the reason for the world's rejection of Him: He is the light who exposes whether a person is righteous or not, and the world, loving wickedness, not only hates this exposure, but also hates the One who is light itself.
Jesus speaks of "doing" the truth. This indicates that "truth" is a matter of both thought and practice. Living by the truth is contrasted with doing what is wicked (v. 20).

There are three sections here. In vv. 22–24. the scene is set as Jesus and His disciples travel into Judea, where John is ministering, and both groups baptize those who are repenting. In vv. 25–30, the Baptist silences the competitive attitude of his own disciples by affirming once more that his entire role is to prepare for Christ. Verses 31–36 appear to be a continuation of the Baptist's words, or possibly a comment by the gospel writer.
Unlike the Synoptics (Matt. 14:3–12; Mark 6:17–29; Luke 3:19; 9:7–9), this gospel does not report the occasion or outcome of John's imprisonment, though it notes its occurrence.

John's baptism symbolized the forgiveness of sins that the coming Messiah would grant to those who repent (Mark 1:4; John 1:29), and previewed the Messiah's bestowal of the Spirit (1:32–34). Presumably, the baptism administered by Jesus' disciples at this point in their ministry has the same significance. See theological note "Baptism" on p. 1988.
God is the author of all that we receive (1 Cor. 4:7), so John is content to see Jesus receiving the greater honor that the Father was bestowing on Him (1:15, 20–27).

The friend of the bridegroom, like the best man in weddings today, does not resent but rejoices in the fact that the bride belongs to her groom. John's parable evokes OT imagery in which the Lord is husband and Israel is His bride (Is. 62:5; Jer. 2:2, 3; Ezek. 16; Hos. 2).
Jesus is distinguished from all other humans who are "of the earth" (v. 13 note).

John repeats the idea that neither Christ's own nation nor the world at large is ready to receive Him (cf. 1:10, 11). The barrier is the sin and blindness that God alone can penetrate (v. 3; cf. 1:5).

The world in general has refused the light, but John immediately mentions those who are coming to the light, especially himself as the first exponent of the truth. John's preaching is the culmination of the OT and the beginning of the New (1:15; cf. Matt. 11:11).

These words probably apply to the Spirit-empowered earthly ministry of Jesus (Luke 3:22; 4:1). But it is also possible that they refer to the fullness of the Spirit that Jesus gives to those who serve Him, and some ancient and modern commentators have understood the text this way. After His ascension, Jesus is the agent who sends the Spirit (1:33; 15:26; Acts 2:1–4, 33).
The "all things" that the Father has entrusted to the Son whom He loves (5:20) include the power to give life (5:21, 25, 26) and to judge (5:22, 27–29).

Believing in the Son is more than intellectual assent. Trust in Christ's person will inevitably motivate obedience to His words, so disobedience reveals a lack of saving faith (see Heb. 3:18, 19; James 2:14–26).

The background of this incident is the profound contempt that the Jews and the Samaritans felt for each other (v. 9; 8:48). Samaritan religion mingled reverence for Israel's God with the pagan practices of non-Israelite peoples who had been resettled into the territory of the northern kingdom by the conquering Assyrians (2 Kin. 17:24–41). Samaritan compromises with pagan idolatry under the Seleucid occupation intensified the Jews' hostility toward them. Not surprisingly, the Samaritans responded with enmity toward the Jews (Luke 9:52, 53). When traveling between Galilee and Judea, many Jews would cross the Jordan twice rather than pass through Samaria. Jesus did not follow this practice.
As a true human being, Jesus experienced fatigue and even exhaustion (Matt. 8:24). See theological note "The Humanity of Christ" on p. 2279. the sixth hour. Noon, in the heat of the day.

This phrase can also be translated, "Jews use nothing in common with Samaritans," referring to the legislation that forbade a Jew to eat or drink with Samaritans, who were more lax in their understanding of ritual cleanness. The surprise is not so much that Jesus would speak with a Samaritan, but that He would drink from a Samaritan vessel.

This expression emphasizes that salvation is not earned but given (Eph. 2:8). Jesus Himself is the gift of God (3:16; Gal. 2:20; Eph. 5:25). living water. At one level, "living" water referred to flowing water in springs and streams, and this sense occasions the woman's misunderstanding. In the OT, however, living or running water is employed figuratively as a reference to divine activity (Jer. 2:13; Zech. 14:8). Cf. v. 14; 7:37–39.
Like the Jews and Nicodemus before her, the Samaritan woman misunderstands the key terms Jesus uses (v. 15; 2:19–21; 3:3–10).
Jesus contrasts temporary with eternal satisfaction, teaching that all earthly pleasures, even if legitimate, are fading.
"I will give" expresses the divine origin of the blessing: "welling up" is its great abundance; "eternal life" is its endless duration.

Jesus' knowledge of the Samaritan woman's previous life is like His knowledge of Nathanael (1:48). Her serial relationships with men, whatever their causes, are symptomatic of a heart thirst that well water cannot quench.

At the division of the kingdom into Israel (north) and Judah (south), Jeroboam established shrines in the north, at Bethel and Dan, to discourage his subjects from traveling to Jerusalem for the three annual feasts (1 Kin. 12:25–33). After the northern kingdom fell to Assyria (721 B.C.), the split widened between the Jews in Jerusalem and the Israelites living in Samaria, who built a temple on Mount Gerizim, which was destroyed around 130 B.C. Samaritans have continued to worship on Mount Gerizim even into modern times.

While not making explicit pronouncement regarding the difference of opinion between Jews and Samaritans over worship sites, Jesus affirms the Scriptures that announce that the Messiah comes through the royal line of David, to which the southern kingdom of Judah remained loyal (2 Sam. 7:12–16; 1 Kin. 11:29–39; Is. 9:6, 7; 11:1–5; Jer. 23:5, 6; Ezek. 34:23).

The time is soon coming when divisions between Jews and Samaritans will be removed (v. 21), and temple worship will be superseded. The time "is now here" because Jesus is present and has begun the work leading to the presence of the Holy Spirit in the church (7:39; 20:22).

This is the one occasion before His trial when Jesus is recorded designating Himself as the Messiah. Perhaps the political overtones associated with this title make it unwise for Jesus to use it often (cf. 6:14, 15). The Greek reads, "I am, \[that is\] the one speaking to you." "I am" is a theologically significant construction in this gospel, often implying a claim to deity (6:35; 8:12, 24, 58, 59; 10:7, 11:25; 14:6; 15:1; 18:5, 6; cf. Mark 6:50).

The disciples' attitude reflects both the contempt of the Jews for the Samaritans and male chauvinism that regards giving instruction to a woman as a waste of time. During the first century, it was also a breach of propriety for a man to speak with a woman unrelated to him in public.
The witness of the woman is more effective than the visit of the twelve apostles.
The "nourishment" that sustains Jesus is His fulfillment of the Father's saving purpose for His incarnation (5:30; 6:38, 39; 7:16, 28; 8:29).

Ordinarily the planting of crops and the harvest are separated by months of patient waiting and uncertainty (Ps. 126:5, 6), but the presence of Christ accelerates the growth toward maturation, to the joy of the laborers.
Jesus makes it clear that His disciples have a responsibility distinct from His own. They will harvest what Jesus has sowed. The saying may deliberately anticipate 12:23, 24.
Jesus planted His Word into the heart of the Samaritan woman, and she in turn bore witness to the townsfolk, prompting them to come out to meet Him and believe (vv. 28–30, 39–42).
They recognize that Jesus is more than a prophet (vv. 19, 29, 39); He is the Savior (1 John 4:14).

In other gospels, the "hometown" that dishonors Jesus is Nazareth in Galilee (Matt. 13:53–58; Mark 6:1–6; Luke 4:24), and John likewise acknowledges Jesus' identification with Galilee (1:46; 2:1; 7:42, 52). Yet the Galileans "welcomed him" (v. 45), so here it may be that "his own hometown" is Judea (cf. v. 3), from where His ancestor David came, rather than Galilee. Or the point is that the Galileans' welcome of Jesus is superficial and ephemeral (7:2–5), based on their need to "see signs and wonders" in order to believe (v. 48; see Introduction: Theology of John).

An officer in the service of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee (cf. Matt. 14:1–12; Luke 23:7), since the term refers to one who serves a king. Although the location (Capernaum) and some details of this healing (e.g., gravity of the illness, Jesus' healing by a word spoken at a distance) resemble those of the cure of a centurion's servant (Matt. 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10), the differences (official vs. centurion, son vs. servant, etc.) indicate that the incidents are distinct miracles.
This is a word with power to heal, not merely a prophecy that he would recover.
Early afternoon, about 1 P.M.

While Jesus has performed many other signs (2:23), this is the second that takes place at Cana in Galilee (cf. 2:11). The repetition of "your son will live" (vv. 50, 53) shows the purpose of the sign is to reveal that Jesus has the power to give life (see 5:21), as will be seen climactically in the resurrection of Lazarus (ch. 11) and His own resurrection (10:18; 21:26–31). Corresponding to this repetition is the progression of the official's faith (vv. 48, 50, 53).
