Several priests serving their allotted week's temple service (Luke 1:8, 23) are near Solomon's Colonnade and can hear Peter's declarations about Jesus the Messiah, which now specifically mentions the involvement of Jewish rulers, who had charge of the temple, in pressuring Pilate to execute Jesus (3:13, 14, 17). Alarmed at this critique of Judaism's leaders, the priests probably alert the captain of the temple guard. This captain is the commander of the temple police force and a member of one of the important priestly families. The priests also alert the Sadducees, who hold prominent positions in the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council.

The Sadducees are annoyed because the apostles are teaching the people about the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:12–20). Unlike the other first-century Jewish sects such as the Pharisees, the Sadducees did not believe in the bodily resurrection even at the end of history (23:6–8; Luke 20:27–40).
This action is necessary because the temple sacrifices have concluded and the temple gates are closed; official actions by the Sanhedrin will have to be taken the next day.

Despite the persecution, the church has grown from three thousand on the day of Pentecost (2:41) to five thousand at the time Peter and John are arrested. The emphasis here is on men, probably as representative heads of households (Luke 9:14).

These groups constitute the Jewish religious council, the Sanhedrin. Luke 22:66 describes the body of chief priests and scribes as "their council." This body includes the high priest and members of his family (v. 6); other Sadducees; Pharisees (Matt. 27:62) such as Nicodemus (a "ruler of the Jews" and "teacher of Israel," John 3:1, 10) and Gamaliel (5:34; 22:3); and "elders" who, though neither priests nor scholars, are respected heads of Jerusalem's aristocratic families.

The men listed in this verse constitute what might be called the executive committee of the council. Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas the official high priest (John 18:13), is here called the high priest. However, since the Romans deposed Annas in A.D. 15, he is not officially the high priest at this time; rather, he is the power behind the office and probably still regarded as rightful high priest by many Jews, for the high priest is supposed to serve for life. John is possibly Jonathan son of Annas, who was appointed high priest in A.D. 36, or Jonathan ben Zaccai, who became president of the Great Synagogue after the fall of Jerusalem. Nothing is known of Alexander.

The answer is given in v. 10: "the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth." The power of the name of Jesus (which reveals His person) is the central and unifying theme in the healing of the lame man and its aftermath. Jesus' name or the name of the Lord is emphasized often throughout Acts (2:21, 38; 3:16; 4:10, 12, 17, 18, 30; 5:28, 40, 41; 8:16; 9:15, 28; 15:26; 16:18).

In Luke and Acts, this expression seems to refer to an intervention whereby the Spirit enables believers to speak God's message (2:4; 4:31; 9:17; 13:9–11a; Luke 1:15, 41, 67). The holy character that the Spirit's ongoing presence sustains in individuals distinguishes them as "full of the Holy Spirit" (6:3, 5; 7:55; 11:24; Luke 4:1; see Eph. 5:18).
In Acts, defense of the gospel often includes reference to the fulfillment of OT prophecy; here Ps. 118:22 is quoted (also cited in Matt. 21:42; 1 Pet. 2:7; cf. Rom. 9:33).

Just as the name of Jesus was the only hope for physical healing of the man crippled from birth, so also the name of Jesus is the only hope for the spiritual healing of mankind. This exclusive and total reliance upon Christ for salvation is the clear teaching of both Jesus and the apostles (John 14:6; 1 Tim. 2:5). See theological note "Salvation" on p. 2058.

The courage and ready witness of Peter and John is a fulfillment of Christ's promise to the disciples in Matt. 10:19, 20. The courage and knowledge of the unschooled Galilean fishermen astonishes the Sanhedrin. In taking note that these men "had been with Jesus," the council no doubt remembers how Jesus, though without formal training, likewise had surprised them with His teaching (Luke 2:46, 47; John 7:15).

Although God calls Christians to submit to authority structures that He has ordained for the family, the state, and the church (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–18), our obligation to God Himself has priority over the rights of the state or any human authority (Luke 14:26). The apostles affirm this principle even more strongly in Acts 5:29. See theological note "Civil Government" on p. 2004.

The whole church responds to the Sanhedrin's threats with prayer, the natural result of the apostles' training with Jesus and the habits they have formed (2:42). Sovereign Lord. A term used to express the total creative power and control of the Lord over all His physical creation and over the affairs of humanity (cf. vv. 25, 26; Jer. 10:12). made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. An echo of the description of the Lord in Ps. 146:5, 6, contrasting Him to princes, who cannot be trusted to save because their plans, like the princes themselves, are short-lived (vv. 3, 4).
A succinct summary of verbal inspiration (see 1:16; Heb. 10:15). Scripture's authors wrote under the guidance and control of the Spirit (2 Pet. 1:21).

At Jesus' baptism the Father's voice bound together His royal sonship as the Christ (anointed) (Ps. 2:7) with His identity as the well-pleasing and Suffering Servant (Is. 42:1; cf. Luke 3:22). So the church now recognizes Jesus as both anointed King and holy Servant. Herod and Pontius Pilate \... Gentiles \... peoples of Israel. The believers properly understand that both Jews and Gentiles, with their rulers, are responsible for the crucifixion of Jesus, and recognize that Psalm 2 foreshadowed this multiethnic conspiracy against the Lord's Anointed One, Jesus. The rulers were Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great and tetrarch (i.e., subordinate ruler under Rome) of Galilee and Perea (Luke 3:1; 23:6, 7), and Pontius Pilate, who was the Roman prefect (governor) of Palestine from A.D. 26 to 36 (Luke 3:1; 23:1–24).

Nothing, not even the wrongful death of God's Son, happens apart from God's sovereign will and control (see 2:23). The certainty of God's plan for the world is established by His sovereign "plan" and ensured by His almighty "hand." The early chapters of Acts teach the compatibility of divine sovereignty and human responsibility. While the murderers of Jesus acted in accord with what God had determined, they were morally responsible agents and accountable for their wickedness (3:15). Cf. Gen. 50:20.

This prayer illustrates the way in which the church should be emboldened and encouraged by God's sovereignty. In the face of the threat of violence, the church affirms God's control of the situation (v. 28) and, instead of requesting physical safety, they petition for greater boldness to testify to God's gospel. Lord. The word for "Lord" is kyrios, used in the Septuagint to translate the divine name Yahweh. It is used in the NT to refer both to God and also to Christ specifically (2:36; 7:31).
See 2:4 and 4:8 note.

Because the believers are "of one heart" (v. 32), they are conscious of the needy in the church. Consequently, they help the poor among them by selling land and entrusting the proceeds to the apostles to distribute for those needs. This giving is proportional to real need. It is voluntary, not compulsory (5:4).

The crowning proof of the salvation accomplished in Jesus Christ was His resurrection from the dead. The apostles, as chief witnesses, were especially appointed and authorized to bear eyewitness testimony about this redemptive event (1:2, 3, 8, 22; 2:32; 3:15; 4:19, 20; Luke 1:2). grace. Grace in bold witnessing and generous living.
The ancient promise of covenant blessing, when Israel obeys God's commands and cares for the poor (Deut. 15:4), is being fulfilled in the spontaneous generosity of Jesus' followers.

In the OT, the Levites did not have inherited land, as the other tribes had, although the Levites were allotted towns (Josh. 21). However, by the time of the NT, a Levite such as Joseph Barnabas may well have been able to own land. This would have been particularly true in a country outside of Palestine, such as Cyprus, in which Joseph had grown up among the Jewish dispersion. On the other hand, the land may have belonged to his wife. son of encouragement. Luke's interpretation may be a paraphrase of the Aramaic components of the nickname that the apostles gave to Joseph, "son of a prophet" — one who speaks words of courage from God. The introduction of Barnabas here lays the foundation for further reference to the significant influence of this outstanding first-century believer in the life of the Jewish and Gentile churches and in the life of Paul. Barnabas also interceded for Saul (9:27), encouraged the church at Antioch in Syria (11:22), led in missionary work abroad (13:2, 3), and continued in missionary work despite a disagreement with Paul (15:37–39).
Joseph Barnabas presents a good example of a Christian who gives to the needs of others (contrasted with the selfish and hypocritical example of Ananias and Sapphira, 5:1–11).

Ananias's actions mimic those of Barnabas (4:36, 37) with this exception: Ananias withholds part of the sale price while claiming to contribute it all. Ananias and his wife have the right to keep all of the proceeds from their land, since the land and the money is theirs (v. 4). Their sin is in their deception (vv. 3, 4) about how much they are bringing, as Peter's question to Sapphira implies (v. 8). The verb rendered "kept back," which is rare in Scripture, describes the deceptive theft of Achan at Jericho (Josh. 7:1, 19–26). Here, as there, the testimony of the whole church is at risk because of the sins of a few (cf. Lev. 10:1, 2; Num. 16:23–35; 2 Sam. 6:1–7).

Another example of Satan's influence is seen in the life of Peter (Mark 8:33). Later, Peter warns Christians against Satan's potential influence over them (1 Pet. 5:8). lie to the Holy Spirit. In v. 4 Peter tells Ananias that he has lied to God. Peter's words indicate that the Holy Spirit is God, and that He is a divine person whose patience may be provoked, not an impersonal force (v. 9).

The instantaneous, divinely inflicted deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not typical of the miracles recorded in the NT. See the death of Herod Agrippa (12:20–23) and the temporary blinding of Saul (9:8–18) and Elymas (13:11). Some at Corinth suffered illness and even death for abusing the Lord's Supper (1 Cor. 11:29, 30); but more typically, Christ maintains the purity of His community through the orderly process of church discipline, leading, if necessary, to excommunication (Matt. 18:15–20; 1 Cor. 5:1–5).

The Holy Spirit's presence in the Christian community brings great joy to the humble and repentant (13:52), but He is dangerous to those who prefer falsehood over transparency and truth (Heb. 12:28, 29). the whole church. This is the first of more than twenty occurrences in Acts of the Greek word ekklēsia, usually translated "church." Stephen uses this word for the OT "congregation" of Israel (7:38). In the Septuagint, the worshiping assembly of God's people is often designated with this word, and Jesus' two uses of the term (Matt. 16:18; 18:17) imply that His community stands in continuity with and fulfillment of Israel's calling as the Lord's assembly. In ancient Greece, the ekklēsia was the political "assembly" of citizens (19:32). The NT uses the word to refer to organized bodies of believers in one city (8:1; 13:1; 14:27), to a regional body of believers who meet in local congregations (9:31), and to the universal body of believers (Eph. 1:22, 23; 5:23, 24).

In the wake of God's judgment on Ananias and Sapphira, no insincere, superficial followers dare to identify with the church. All recognize that Christ's Spirit imposes high standards of integrity on the holy community that He indwells.

Despite the Spirit's dangerous holiness, new believers still came forward and join the church. Luke mentions women often in his gospel (Luke 7:28; 8:2, 3; 17:35; 23:27, 29, 49, 55) and in Acts (1:14; 8:3, 12; 9:2, 36; 13:50; 16:1, 13, 14; 17:4, 12, 34; 18:2; 21:5).

As when Jesus' healing power flowed from His garment at the touch of the woman who had been subject to bleeding (Mark 5:27, 28), here God allows the shadow of Peter to effect a cure, as He did also through cloths and aprons that Paul had used (19:11, 12).
The exalted Lord Jesus' exorcisms of demons and His healing acts, now through His apostles (see 1:1 note), replicate those that He performed while on earth (Luke 6:17–19).

The same Greek term describes commendable "zeal" (John 2:17), but here the Sadducean leaders of the temple are reacting from envy of the growing popular admiration (v. 13) and influence of the Christian community and the apostles (see also 13:44, 45).
See 12:6–19. Here the apostles' release is for the sake of their ongoing, public witness in the very temple that the high priest and his colleagues control.
This aptly characterizes the gospel, since Jesus alone has the words of eternal life (John 6:68), and eternal life consists in knowing God through Him (John 17:3).

The great Jewish religious council at Jerusalem, the Sanhedrin, composed of about seventy men. It included Sadducees, Pharisees, and their associates. Under the Romans, the Sanhedrin had broad authority in Palestine. According to ancient Jewish tradition, the members sat in a semicircle with two clerks and three rows of students at the front.

It is doubly ironic that the angel of the Lord should thwart and confuse a Sanhedrin dominated by Sadducees who deny the existence of angels (23:8), and that the apostles who could not be found in the locked temple prison are preaching openly in the temple courts.
The apostles' popular approval, like that of their master (Luke 19:47, 48; 20:6, 19, 26; 22:2), prevents the temple authorities from harshly arresting them in public.

In 2:23; 3:15, 16; and 4:10, 11, Peter and his associates blame the members of the Sanhedrin for the death of Jesus. The people have heard this accusation. Moreover, Jesus Himself earlier exposed the leaders' plot to destroy Him (Luke 20:9–17); and those leaders instigated the crowds to shout, "His blood be on us and on our children" (Matt. 27:20, 25).

The cruelest Roman mode of execution, crucifixion coincides with the symbolism of divine curse for the corpses of those who were executed under God's law through Moses (Deut. 21:22, 23). Since Jesus' resurrection demonstrates His righteousness, clearly He bore God's curse for others' sins, not His own (Gal. 3:13).
This declaration is understood by the Sanhedrin as a reference to the resurrection. Such an exaltation by God makes this resurrected Jesus equal with God (cf. John 5:18; 10:33).

Along with the apostles' unique, eyewitness testimony to Jesus' resurrection is the testimony that God's Spirit bears to and through all who obey the call to repent and believe (Is. 59:21). Thus at Pentecost, some 120 believers, men and women, young and old, declared God's deeds (2:4, 11, 17, 18); and soon, scattered believers (except apostles) carry the gospel outside Jerusalem, into Judea and Samaria (8:1, 4).

One of the most famous rabbis of his time, Gamaliel was Paul's teacher (22:3) and probably a grandson of Rabbi Hillel, the leader of one of the two great schools of Jewish legal interpretation. In contrast to the school of Shammai, Gamaliel and the school of Hillel were known for their lenient interpretation of the law (Matt. 19:3 and note).

The Jewish historian Josephus (Jewish War 20.118) speaks of a certain Galilean who stirred up a revolt because he resisted subservience and paying taxes to the Romans. The revolt failed, but it may have laid the groundwork for the party of the Zealots. The apostle Simon the Zealot (1:13; Matt. 10:4 and note) may have been a member of this group before becoming a disciple of Jesus. days of the census. Not the census of Luke 2:1, which was ordered by the Emperor Augustus in about 8 B.C. (but was delayed until 6 or 5 B.C.), but the census fourteen years later in A.D. 6, in the time of the Procurator Coponius.
The respected Gamaliel's counsel is far more cautious and restrained than the behavior of his disciple, Saul of Tarsus (7:58, 60; 8:3; 9:12; Gal. 1:14; Phil. 3:6; 1 Tim. 1:13).
The apostles likely receive the traditional "forty lashes less one" (2 Cor. 11:24; Deut. 25:3).
When one's identification with Jesus' name is the cause of ill treatment by others, such dishonor becomes, surprisingly, a privilege that imparts joy (1 Pet. 4:13–16).

The OT required care of the poor and needy (Ps. 9:18 note). This concern is seen in the social action set forth in 2:44, 45; 4:34–37. Possibly the widows among the Hellenists, that is, Greek-speaking Jews (text note), were being overlooked in the food distribution due to cultural discrimination: having resettled in Judea from the dispersion, they were considered outsiders by native-born Hebrew- or Aramaic-speaking Jews. Or, since the Jerusalem church at this point numbered in the thousands and likely worshiped in home gatherings in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek), the widows' needs taxed the distribution network beyond the capacity of the apostles to oversee it directly.

The twelve apostles including Matthias (1:26). This is a shift from "the eleven" (1:26; 2:14; Luke 24:9, 33). disciples. The first of a number of times the believers are called "disciples" in Acts (e.g., v. 7; 9:1; 11:26; 13:52). Paul does not use this term to identify Christians. It is not right. The high qualifications that the apostles specify (v. 3) for the men who will "serve tables" show that neither this ministry nor its recipients (Greek-speaking widows) are of minor value. The church must call others to serve these widows because the apostles' energies cannot be deflected from their primary calling from Christ — to preach His Word. the word of God. In this initial organization of the NT church, two important ministries are listed: the ministry of the Word and prayer (v. 4); and the ministry of meeting believers' physical needs, such as serving at table. The Greek verb applied to both is diakoneō ("serve"), from which the English word deacon is derived. In 6:1, the related noun is translated "distribution," and in v. 4, "the ministry." The office of deacon, which probably had its beginning here, is described in 1 Tim. 3:8–13.

The members of the church elect the seven, and the apostles set them apart (ordained) by prayer and the laying on of hands (v. 6). of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom. The two requirements for the ministry of service in all ages are dependence on and sensitivity to the Spirit and action guided by wisdom. Such qualities are discerned by others in the covenant community, who bear witness (the Greek verb martyreõ, "to bear witness," lies behind "good repute") on behalf of such leaders (Deut. 1:15; 1 Tim. 3:6, 7).

All seven men have Greek names, which may point to their being Jews from the Greek-speaking dispersion, although many first-century Palestinian Jews also had Greek names. Attributes are listed for the first and last of the seven: for Stephen ("full of faith and of the Holy Spirit") who appears in 6:8–7:60, and for Nicolaus, "a proselyte of Antioch." His identity as a proselyte indicates that he was born a Gentile, and subsequently converted to Judaism, presumably before coming to faith in Jesus. Antioch in Syria, third largest city of the empire (after Rome and Alexandria), will become the site of a church that welcomes Gentiles (11:19–21) and a center of missionary activity (13:1–3). Philip's later ministry to Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch is described in ch. 8.

Because God's Word is the source of the church's life, Luke sums up church growth as the growth of the Word (12:24; 13:49; 19:20). a great many of the priests. Priests and Levites in ancient Israel administered the distribution of resources from the tithes for the relief of widows and others in need (Deut. 14:28, 29; 26:1–4). Luke may be suggesting that as priests observed the followers of Jesus giving attention to this need, their hearts were opened to the gospel.
Philip, another of the seven, will also perform miracles later on, like the apostles who ordained him (8:6).

Composed of Jews freed from slavery, who in this case are from Cyrene and Alexandria, well-known cities of North Africa. Such a synagogue composed of Jews from the dispersion probably conducts its meetings in Greek. Cilicia. A Roman province in the southeast part of Asia Minor, with Paul's hometown of Tarsus (9:11, 30; 11:25) as one of its chief cities. Paul (called by his Hebrew name, Saul) first appears in Acts as one who supports Stephen's opponents (7:58, 60; 8:3). It is likely that he hears the disputations in which they cannot answer Stephen's wisdom and the Holy Spirit (6:10). Asia. The Roman province in the western part of modern-day Turkey.

These "false witnesses" (v. 13) imitate those who perjured themselves to accuse Jesus (Matt. 26:60, 61). blasphemous words against Moses and God. Jesus reinforced the validity of the law that Moses had received from God and made penetrating application of its precepts, but He challenged many accretions added to the law over centuries of rabbinic tradition (Matt. 5:17–48; Mark 2:23–3:6). He also predicted the destruction of the temple (Luke 21:6). Possibly Stephen's repetition of these teachings of his Master are deliberately misconstrued by his accusers as an assault on Moses, the lawgiver, and on God, whose presence is identified with the temple.

In his defense speech, Stephen does not speak directly against the temple, but only declares that God is not confined to an earthly temple since heaven is His home and throne (7:48–50). Stephen actually supports the Mosaic law and the true meaning of its teaching, which point forward to Christ (7:37, 38).

If, in his disputation with Hellenistic Jews (vv. 9, 10), Stephen had mentioned Jesus' statements in John 2:19 or Luke 21:6, the false witnesses misconstrued his words, since Jesus had said the Jews, not He, would destroy the temple, and He identified the temple with Himself, not a physical building (cf. Matt. 26:59–61; John 2:19–22). Stephen follows Jesus' own views of the temple in this respect.

If it is visibly radiant, that does not deter Stephen's opponents from violently taking his life (7:57–60). At the least, he displays an extraordinary calm, rooted in his deep confidence in Jesus (7:55, 56).

This title recalls the divine glory God showed His people in the time of Moses: the pillar of cloud (Ex. 14:19; 16:10; Ps. 105:39), the pillar of fire (Ex. 14:24), the glory of the Lord on the mountain (Ex. 24:15–18; 2 Cor. 3:7), and the glory on the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34, 35; cf. John 1:14). appeared to our father Abraham \... in Mesopotamia. Stephen's survey of OT history highlights God's presence with His people in locales outside the temple, Jerusalem, and the Promised Land (vv. 9, 30–34, 38, 44, 46–50).
Babylonia, in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq).
Ex. 12:40 has "430," but Stephen is speaking in round numbers, and may be following the text of Gen. 15:13, which has "four hundred years."

God established this covenant with Abraham. He was the father of all Israel but lived centuries before Moses came. This covenant has been fulfilled in Christ, so Gentiles need not be circumcised in order to be declared righteous before God (Rom. 4).

Whereas Stephen has been accused of blaspheming Moses, history shows repeatedly that the Israelites resisted the rescuers and rulers whom God gave them: Joseph, then Moses (vv. 24–29, 35–41), the prophets (v. 52), and finally the Righteous One promised by the prophets — Jesus Himself, in whose murder Stephen's audience is complicit (v. 52).

The Hebrew text of Ex. 1:5 has "seventy." But the Septuagint, which this sermon is basically following, and the fragments of Exodus found among the Dead Sea Scrolls read "seventy-five." The explanation of the "seventy-five" is to be found in the five additional descendants of Joseph included in the Septuagint's translation of Gen. 46:20, where two sons of Manasseh, two sons of Ephraim, and one grandson of Ephraim are included.

Stephen has condensed the events regarding the patriarchs' burial purchases. Jacob was buried in the cave of Machpelah at Hebron (Gen. 50:13), and according to Josephus (Antiquities 2.199), Joseph's brothers were buried in Hebron. Joseph's bones, however, were placed in the land Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor (Gen. 33:19; 50:25; Ex. 13:19; Josh. 24:32). Stephen's audience knew that Jacob and his sons were buried in two different places (Hebron and Shechem). The narrative here is highly condensed.

Ex. 2:10 states that when the child Moses grew older, the nurse (Moses's mother) took him to Pharaoh's daughter and "he became her son," with the assumption that in the royal household he would be given a full Egyptian education. Two first-century Jewish scholars, the historian Josephus and the philosopher Philo, tell of the extensive learning of Moses. mighty in his words and deeds. Compare the description of Jesus in Luke 24:19.

Without condoning Moses's motive and action in killing the abusive Egyptian (since Moses himself implies his cowardice in trying to evade discovery, Ex.2:11–15), Stephen directs attention to the Israelites' defiant refusal to receive him as the means of their deliverance (vv. 26–29, 35–41).
God's presence in the burning bush made that place in the Sinai desert holy, so to suggest that the Jerusalem temple has become obsolete (if Stephen did so) is not to blaspheme God.

Stephen does not explicitly identify Jesus as this prophet, foretold by Moses in Deut. 18:15, but Peter has made that identification (3:22) and it was implied by God's voice at the transfiguration (Luke 9:35 note).

"Congregation" translates the Greek word ekklēsia, which is used in the Septuagint to describe the assembly of Israel, gathered in God's presence, and throughout the NT to designate the "church." See note on 5:11. the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai. Although Moses received the law from God on Mount Sinai (Ex. 20:1, 21), angels had a role in its delivery (v. 53; Deut. 33:2; Gal. 3:19; Heb. 2:2). On the angel of the Lord, see notes on Gen. 16:7 and Judg. 2:1. living oracles. God gave His law to Moses on Sinai, though the Israelites rejected both the messenger and the words that he had received through the instrumentality of angels, just as Stephen's contemporaries are doing (v. 53).

Stephen cites Amos 5:25–27, showing that Israel's sin with the golden calf presaged further idolatry after they entered the Promised Land. Stephen replaces Amos's "Damascus" with "Babylon," since the northern kingdom's Assyrian captivity beyond Damascus was followed by Judah's later exile in Babylon.

The OT tabernacle contained the ark of the covenant and the tablets of the Ten Commandments, which are called "the testimony." Further symbolizing God's presence and life-giving power were the table of the consecrated bread (Ex. 37:10–16; Heb. 9:2), the seven-branched lampstand (Ex. 37:17–23; cf. John 8:12; Rev. 1:12–18), and the altar of incense (Ex. 37:25–29), pointing to the prayers of God's people rising up to the ever-present God (Ps. 141:2; Rev. 8:3, 4).

Solomon, who built the first temple, acknowledged that the "house" he constructed, majestic as it was, could not contain the Lord (1 Kin. 8:27). Solomon's prayer and Isaiah's prophecy (vv. 49, 50, citing Is. 66:1, 2) show that God's presence cannot be confined in any physical structure, even the Jerusalem temple.

They will not listen from their hearts, nor obey the Lord and the Scriptures Stephen has cited. These metaphors are OT figures meaning spiritually stubborn and unregenerate (Ex. 32:9; 33:3, 5; Deut. 9:6; 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4; 6:10).

A title used for the Lord Almighty (Is. 24:16), for the Suffering Servant (Is. 53:11), and for Jesus Christ (3:14; 22:14; 1 John 2:1). you have now betrayed and murdered. The murder of the Righteous One, for which Stephen's hearers bear partial responsibility (2:23; 3:13–15; 4:10; 5:28), brought to a climax Israel's rejection of God's messengers (vv. 9, 27, 28, 35–39).

The brilliance of God's presence (cf. Rev. 15:8; 21:11, 23). standing at the right hand of God. Usually Jesus is said to be sitting at the right hand of God because His work of atonement is finished (Rom. 8:34; Col. 3:1; Heb. 10:12), but here He is standing to receive Stephen or to defend him. In this scene, the Son of Man is both Judge and Advocate.

Stephen's vision of the Son of Man in heaven must vividly remind the Sanhedrin that when they asked Jesus, "Are you the Christ?" He replied, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:61, 62). Stephen sees the same Jesus standing in heaven at God's right hand, proving the truth of what he was saying and condemning the Sanhedrin. Here Jesus is seen in heaven, having received the kingdom authority prophesied of the Son of Man in Dan. 7:13.

Saul, later called by his Roman name, Paul (13:9), is a Pharisee and associated with the Sanhedrin (Phil. 3:5). He may be a witness or participant in the Hellenists' argument with Stephen and an instigator of Stephen's trial (6:9–12; 8:3; 9:1, 2). Saul, whose sermons along with those of Peter will dominate this book, thus enters the narrative as an adamant, violent opponent of the gospel of Jesus the Christ.
As Jesus committed His spirit to his divine Father in His death (Luke 23:46; see Ps. 31:5; 1 Pet. 2:23), so Stephen commits his spirit to his divine Savior, the glorified Son.
Compare the statement of Jesus in Luke 23:34 (see Luke 6:27, 28; Rom. 12:14, 17–21). The following narrative will show Stephen's dying prayer answered in a remarkable way in the case of Saul.

For OT Israel and Judah, scattering (or dispersion) was a covenant curse resulting from their unfaithfulness to the Lord (Deut. 28:64–68; Ezek. 36:19–21), but now Stephen's faithfulness unto death provokes the scattering of believers that spreads the good news more widely. Persecution drives the second phase and expansion of the church's witness-bearing mission, which Jesus foretold (Acts 1:8).
The Greek verb is strong; not just harassment, but an attempt to destroy the church is meant. He arrested and imprisoned women as well as men (9:2).

Since the apostles have remained in Jerusalem (v. 1), those who now herald the good news (the Greek verb behind "preaching" here) are other believers, not Jesus' specially designated witnesses to His resurrection (1:22). Philip, whose office focuses on mercy ministry to widows (6:2–6), is one example. Through persecution the message is spread farther and more rapidly (11:19). As the church father Tertullian said, "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church."

Samaritans, thought to be descended from intermarriage between Israel's northern tribes and pagan peoples relocated by Assyria, revered the five books of Moses but not the rest of the OT Scriptures, and they combined devotion to idols with formalistic service to the Lord (2 Kin. 17:24–41). Relationships between Jews and Samaritans were strained at best and hostile at worst (John 4:9). Jesus reached out to Samaritans in grace, even as He categorized them as outside the covenant people (4:22; Luke 17:16, 17). By preaching Jesus as the Christ to Samaritans, Philip carries the gospel not only across geographical boundaries but also across a vast religious and racial divide.

Simon Magus the sorcerer is frequently mentioned in ancient writings outside the Bible as an archenemy of the church and one of the leaders of the Gnostic heresy. Gnosticism (named from the Greek word gnōsis, meaning "knowledge") taught that a person gained salvation not by the merit of Christ's death for sinners, but by special knowledge about God. Justin Martyr (d. A.D. 165) says that almost all the Samaritans considered Simon the highest god (the "power of God that is called Great," v. 10, resembling the title of a later Gnostic text). Irenaeus (d. A.D. 180), who wrote extensively against the Gnostics, regarded Simon as one of the sources of their heresies. Although the Simon of v. 9 could be another Simon, the church fathers equate the two, and the context of 8:9–11 (his character and the Samaritans' attitude about him) permits but does not require the identification of the two as the same person.

Since Peter later states that Simon's "heart is not right before God" and that he remains "in the bond of iniquity" (vv. 21, 23), it becomes clear that Simon's profession of faith prior to baptism was not sincere. Luke describes Simon's response as it first appeared to Philip and his fellow Samaritans, allowing the unfolding story to disclose the true condition of the magician's heart.

The believing Samaritans to this point have not received observable evidence of the Holy Spirit's gifts for ministry (v. 16), although as believers the Holy Spirit is living in them (Rom. 8:9; 1:8 note; 2:38 note). It appears that the Spirit waits to impart His extraordinary gifts so that apostles can observe and testify to the truth of the report that "Samaria had received the word of God" (v. 14), which is the second geographical area to which Acts 1:8 says the witness of the Spirit will extend (cf.10:44–46; 11:1, 12–15). This is a repeated Pentecost experience. We are not told what evidence the Holy Spirit gives of His empowering of Samaritan believers, but He manifested His arrival in some way that Simon can see and/or hear (v. 18).
Despite his profession of faith, Simon still views supernatural power as a commodity to be purchased and controlled, and is blind to the utter graciousness of God's gift (v. 20).

By his words and actions, Simon proves that he does not believe in Christ (v. 13 note). He is still poisoned by "bitterness" (cf. Deut. 29:18; Heb. 12:15) and "in the bond of iniquity" (see Rom. 6:16; 8:8). A profession of faith without repentance is invalid.

Luke does not clarify whether Simon's plea for Peter's intercession is a symptom of real repentance at last (as Peter commanded, v. 22) or merely an expression of terror in the face of power superior to his own. Peter has instructed Simon to pray to the Lord for forgiveness, but Luke does not record whether Simon ever does so.

OT Ashdod (1 Sam. 5:1), one of the five Philistine cities, about twenty miles (32 km) north of Gaza and sixty miles (97 km) south of Caes­area on the coast. Philip preaches the gospel in all the towns along the coast until he reaches Caesarea, a large city that Herod the Great rebuilt (near Strato's Tower). It had an excellent harbor that Herod expanded for important sea traffic (21:8), and it served as headquarters for the Roman procurators such as Pilate, Felix (23:33–24:4), and Festus (25:6). Philip must have settled in Caesarea, because years later he still resides there (21:8). His ministry along the coastal cities will blaze the trail for Peter (9:32–43).

The repetition underscores the importance of this event, which is Christ's calling of the apostle to the Gentiles.

It is difficult for strict Jews who have not seen Peter's vision to realize that God does not show favoritism in His offer of salvation. even on the Gentiles. Anticipated in the conversion of the Samaritans (8:12–17) and the Ethiopian eunuch (8:26–39), the inclusion of uncircumcised Gentiles by the Spirit through faith in Jesus marks a new phase in the expansion of God's church to embrace all the nations. It occurs through the preaching of Peter, one of Jesus' "inner three" (with James and John) among the Twelve, and with "believers from among the circumcised" present as witnesses (11:12).

Together with v. 45 ("the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles"), this shows that the prophecy of Joel 2:28–32 — a prophecy about Israel's blessing that began to be fulfilled at Pentecost in believing Jews — is also being fulfilled in Gentiles. Thus, they also are becoming true end-time Israel in fulfilling this prophecy about Israel. This is why some Jewish bystanders are "amazed": they see a prophecy intended for Israel being fulfilled among Gentiles. Of course, the reason for this, noted in Acts 2:17–21, is that Jesus as true Israel was the first Israelite to fulfill the Joel prophecy, and all who identify with Him become Israel, and thus fulfill the prophecy. This is still part of the second geographical area to which Acts 1:8 says the witness of the Spirit would extend (Acts 8:15–17 note). This is a repeated Pentecost experience.

This Antioch was about a hundred miles (160 km) north of Perga and 3,600 feet (1,100 m) above sea level. It was in Phrygia but near Pisidia, and it was popularly called "Antioch in Pisidia" to distinguish it from another Antioch in Phrygia.
