About four hundred years plus the forty years in the wilderness and the period of Joshua's conquest (7:6 note).

Paul and Barnabas bring the same good news (v. 32) to their hearers in the dispersion that the original apostles are proclaiming in Judea, but the latter have a distinctive role as witnesses, since they accompanied Jesus during His ministry and saw Him repeatedly between His resurrection and ascension (1:3–8, 22; 2:32; 5:32).
That is, "Today in raising You from the dead, I am declaring that You are My Son and I am Your Father" (Heb. 1:5 note).

That is, never to die again, unlike David himself (vv. 36, 37), who did not personally receive "the holy and sure blessings" promised to him (citing Is. 55:3) but predicted their arrival in his messianic descendant, Jesus.

The law points the sinner to Christ (Gal. 3:24), for "a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ" (Gal. 2:16). To be justified is to be declared righteous by God (Rom. 3:21, 22), and therefore granted forgiveness of sins (Eph. 1:7). See theological note "Justification by Faith" on p. 2078.

Many, both ethnic Jews and Gentile proselytes, heed the missionaries' promise of forgiveness (vv. 38, 39) and their sober warning against scoffing unbelief from Hab. 1:5 (v. 41). On the next Sabbath, the hostile reaction of unbelieving Jews reveals how apt the warning was (v. 45).

Jews who have rejected the message about Jesus resent its popularity among the city's Gentiles (and other Jews), as jealousy has moved the high priest and other Sadducees to oppose the apostles in Jerusalem (5:17).

Since Jesus the Messiah came through the Jews (Gen. 12:3), Paul is consistent in applying the principle "to the Jew first and also to the Greek" (Rom. 1:16). He recognizes that God's plan also includes the Gentiles (Is. 49:6), a fact resisted by these Jews of Pisidian Antioch.

God's word to His servant, cited here from Is. 49:6, applies first of all to Jesus, as the aged prophet Simeon recognized (Luke 2:30–32). Yet Jesus, who is the light to the Gentiles and of the world (John 8:12) also commissions His followers to reflect His light to others as "the light of the world" (Matt. 5:14). Christ alluded to this prophecy in His promise that they would be His witnesses "to the ends of the earth" (Acts 1:8). Paul and his colleagues thus also fulfill the Is. 49:6 prophecy, first fulfilled by Jesus (Luke 2:32; Acts 26:23), because they are identified with Him by corporate solidarity. They are "apostles" in Christ and, therefore, participate in His commission given in Is. 49:6.

God chose these people beforehand (in eternity past), and now through giving them repentance (11:18; 2 Tim. 2:25) has brought them to faith in Christ (Eph. 2:8). Luke uses the passive voice ("were appointed"), indicating that God is the agent. Only God grants eternal life (Matt. 25:46; John 10:28; 17:2). See theological note "Predestination and Reprobation" on p. 1997.
A Jewish sign of repudiation and disassociation (Matt. 10:14).
Joy is the Spirit's fruit in believers' lives (8:39; Gal. 5:22; Rom. 14:17; 15:13; 1 Thess. 1:6).

Paul and Barnabas have traveled eighty miles (129 km) southeast from Antioch in Pisidia to Iconium, an ancient Phrygian town. The Greeks made it a city-state, and under Augustus it became a city in the province of Galatia.

For the first time in Acts, the term has a broader reference that includes men such as Barnabas in addition to the apostles chosen by Jesus (1:24–26; cf. Matt. 10:1–4; 2 Cor. 1:1 note). The term "apostle" means "one sent," with the connotation of bearing authority, so it is applied elsewhere in the NT to other individuals (2 Cor. 8:23) besides the Twelve and Paul, whom Jesus appointed apostle to the Gentiles on the Damascus Road (Rom. 11:13; Gal. 1:1).
Stoning was the way ancient Jews executed the death penalty for blasphemy against God (7:58, 59; cf. Lev. 24:13–16).

These two cities along with Iconium belonged strictly to the Roman province of Galatia, although they were part of the subdistrict called Lycaonia. From A.D. 37–72 Iconium was linguistically and politically on the Phrygian side of the border.

In 6 B.C., Augustus fortified this settlement and made it into a Roman colony of the province of Galatia. He also settled the colony with Roman army veterans. Returning to Lystra on a second journey, Paul would recruit a young believer named Timothy to join his missionary team (16:1–3). Perhaps it was during this first visit of Paul and Barnabas that Timothy and his Jewish mother and grandmother came to believe in Jesus as the Messiah promised in the OT (2 Tim. 1:5; 3:10, 11, 14, 15).

This healing, like that in the Jerusalem temple through Peter and John (3:1–4:22), enables a man crippled from birth to both walk and leap. Both miracles attracted the crowds' attention to the apostles, who hasten to direct glory away from themselves to God. See theological note "Miracles" on p. 532.

An ancient legend circulated in Lystra that the Greek gods Zeus and Hermes disguised themselves as men and came to the Phrygian hill country, seeking hospitality. Only one couple welcomed them, and in return their cottage was changed into a temple with a golden roof and marble columns. The houses of those who refused the gods were destroyed. The Lystrans may have been thinking of this legend when they welcomed Barnabas and Paul and prepared to sacrifice oxen, mistaking them for those gods, revisiting the region incognito.
A conventional sign of grief or distress (Mark 14:63).

The content of Paul's sermon is similar to his later sermon at Athens (17:22–31). Both sermons are addressed to pagan crowds who would not understand quotations from and explanations of OT Scriptures. Paul stresses that God's creative and providential power extends everywhere. See Rom. 1:18–23. See theological note "Divine Revelation" on p. 850.
When addressing the philosophers in Athens, Paul calls the era before Christ's coming "the times of ignorance" (17:30).
A Lycaonian border town in southeastern Galatia, sixty-five miles (105 km) southeast of Lystra.

As Jesus called those who would follow Him to count the cost and expect persecution (Matt. 5:10–12; Luke 9:23–26; John 15:20), so the apostles bluntly prepare believers to expect suffering along the path that leads to glory (Phil. 3:10, 11; 2 Tim. 2:11, 12; 3:12; 1 Pet. 4:10–19).

Elders governed ancient Israel's tribes (Num. 11:16–30; Deut. 1:9–18) and had a similar role in first-century Judaism (Luke 7:3; 22:66). So also, each of the congregations in the apostolic church was led by elders, men recognized for wisdom and mature character (11:30; Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9; 1 Pet. 5:1–4).

The reports of Paul's and Barnabas' direct contact with the Gentiles on the first missionary journey may have reached Judea and Jerusalem through John Mark after he returned home (13:13). Also, others from Syrian Antioch may have brought the news during Paul and Barnabas' extended stay there. This seems to have caused some Jewish Christians to fear that their Jewish heritage was threatened; they thought that the converted Gentiles must be brought into Judaism through circumcision, and that full compliance with the law of Moses was required in order to merit salvation (vv. 1, 5). Paul recognized that forcing Gentiles to be circumcised might make them think that salvation must be earned through keeping God's law (cf. Gal. 2:15, 16). He knew that the Judaizers had to be opposed lest their teaching obscure the freedom of God's grace and the sufficiency of Christ's cross and righteousness (Gal. 2:20, 21; Phil. 3:9), and thereby hinder the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles (1 Thess. 2:14–16).

Because the issue has great significance for the clarity of the gospel and the unity of the church, when it could not be resolved in Antioch, it is referred to a wider circle of leaders, the apostles and elders of the "mother church" in Jerusalem.
The church leaders take the lead in the discussion, but v. 12 indicates that the whole assembly is present.

Peter recounts the events surrounding Cornelius, noting specifically that God gave that centurion and his Gentile associates the Holy Spirit without their receiving circumcision, thereby demonstrating that He had "cleansed their hearts by faith" (v. 9) and saved them "through the grace of the Lord Jesus" (v. 11), just as Jewish believers had been saved.

The rabbis spoke of a person's commitment to submit to God's law using the imagery of a yoke, the farm implement by which oxen were bound to pull a plow. Peter reminds his fellow Jews that they themselves have been unable to fulfill the law with the perfection required if their obedience were the condition of God's acceptance (Gal. 5:1). They have been "saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus," which means they have been "freed from" the unbearable burden of the law by Jesus' death and resurrection (Acts 13:39).

James is the half-brother of Jesus (12:17; Matt. 13:55; Gal. 2:9; 1 Cor. 15:7; Introduction to James: Author). He seems by now to be a prominent leader of the Jerusalem church (21:18). James adds a third testimony that Gentile believers should not be burdened with keeping the details of the Jewish ceremonial law; his speech places the reports of Peter, Barnabas, and Paul in the context of the Scriptures, showing how the OT foretold that God would take the Gentiles as "a people for his name" (v. 14), in fulfillment of Amos 9:11, 12 (v. 17).
The resurrection of Jesus, David's messianic descendant, and His enthronement in heaven fulfilled God's promise to establish David's dynasty eternally (2:25–36; 13:22, 23).

James finds support in the Scriptures and in the testimonies of Simon Peter, Barnabas, and Paul that God wants the Gentiles to be free from the ceremonial law and the demands of the Judaizers. He proposes that both Jews and Gentiles practice moderation. The Jewish Christians are to recognize that Gentiles are not to be bound by Jewish ceremonial law. The Gentile believers must consider the scruples of Jewish Christians and not offend them by eating food sacrificed to idols, the meat of strangled animals, or blood (Lev. 17:10–14; 19:26). The inclusion of "sexual immorality" (a moral, not ceremonial, requirement) along with these dietary restrictions may indicate that all four practices from which Gentile Christians are to abstain relate to idolatrous pagan worship practices. However, the witness of the NT as a whole indicates that sexually immoral behavior is still off limits for Christians even in cases where it is not associated overtly with pagan worship (Matt. 5:27–30; 1 Cor. 5; 6:9).
Judas and Silas, who are prophets (v. 32), are sent by the council of apostles and elders to reinforce and clarify in person the meaning and implications of the council's written letter.

The Jewish Christians use this expression to set the Gentile Christians at ease, as does the letter's commendation of "our beloved Barnabas and Paul" (vv. 25–26), who have defended the Gentiles' freedom from the imposition of circumcision and the many ceremonial regulations of the law of Moses.
They are filled with the Spirit (2:1–41; 4:8; 6:5; 9:17; 13:4) and recognize the Spirit's role in their debate and decision.

Clearly, the Gentile Christians in Antioch do not interpret the restraint urged by the letter, following James's counsel (vv. 20, 28, 29), as an imposition of legal demands that compromise the graciousness of the gospel in any way.
Bringing encouragement and strength to believers was a primary function of the NT prophet (a spokesman for God).

Although they have stood together in defense of the gospel and the Gentiles' freedom, Paul and Barnabas sharply differ either over the seriousness of John Mark's defection in Pamphylia (13:13) or on whether Mark, having repented, has matured enough to be trusted as an aide for their next journey. True to his character throughout Acts, Barnabas believes that Mark is "salvageable" for gospel service, and so he is ready to risk enlisting Mark again. Though the remainder of Acts contains no further record of Paul's working with Barnabas, Paul mentions Barnabas in a positive light in 1 Cor. 9:6. Paul's later high regard for Mark — in part the fruit of Bar­nabas' mentoring — is evident in Col. 4:10; Philem. 24; 2 Tim. 4:11; cf. 1 Pet. 5:13. Barnabas took Mark \... Cyprus. Barnabas takes his cousin Mark (Col. 4:10) on a missionary journey to the island of Cyprus, Barnabas' home. This will also provide an opportunity for Barnabas to encourage (4:36) the younger man.

Paul's new colleague is one of the prophets sent by the council in Jerusalem to explain its letter and encourage the Gentile believers in Syrian Antioch. They set off over land to the north and west, traveling through Syria and Cilicia, Paul's home province (v. 41), en route to the interior cities of Galatia (16:1), in which Paul and Barnabas planted churches on their first trip to the region.

In the small Jewish community of Lystra, Paul finds this young man, part Jew and part Greek. Like his father, Timothy has been reared as a Greek, and so has not been circumcised. His mother is Jewish.

Although Paul adamantly resists the imposition of circumcision on Gentiles such as Titus (Gal. 2:3), Timothy's status as the offspring of a covenantally mixed marriage (v. 1) would be questionable in the eyes of the Jewish community. Rather than risking a hindrance to Timothy's ministry among those who might regard him as an uncircumcised Jew, Paul removes that obstacle (see 1 Cor. 9:19–23; 10:32, 33).

The unity of the visible church is evident in the fact that a decision reached by a council in Jerusalem, in response to an issue in Syrian Antioch, is now communicated as binding on churches in other cities and regions.

This was the southern part of the larger Roman province of Galatia. It included the Phrygian district, Antioch of Pisidia, and the surrounding area. Holy Spirit \... Asia. The Roman province of Asia, located in the western sector of Asia Minor, included the famous city of Ephesus where God wanted Paul to go at a later date (ch. 19). The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Jesus (v. 7), and He is God (v. 10; 5:3, 4; cf. 2 Cor. 3:17 note). These verses point to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity (cf. 2 Cor. 13:14).

Paul and Silas have come from Derbe and Lystra northwest to Mysia, a region to the south of the Hellespont, but the Spirit who forbade them from moving west into Asia also forbids traveling north into Bithynia. Instead, they go west to Troas, a seaport on the Aegean Sea.

Compare the visions by which the Lord brought Ananias to minister to the blinded Saul (9:10, 12) and Peter to preach to the centurion Cornelius (10:3, 17, 19; 11:5). Macedonia. Macedonia was across the Aegean Sea from Troas.

The first of several passages (16:10–17; 20:5–15; 21:1–18; 27:1–28:16) using the plural pronoun "we" starts here, indicating that the author of Acts is traveling with Paul and Silas at this point in their ministry.
A prominent island in the north Aegean where vessels regularly stopped.

Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, had established a large Greek colony here and named it Philippi. a Roman colony. This status, bestowed on Philippi by Octavian (to become Caesar Augustus) and Marc Antony, meant that Philippi's citizens had Roman citizenship and its privileges, including due process in Roman courts and exemption from taxation.

According to later Jewish practice, at least ten men were required to form a synagogue. Failing that, a place of prayer could be established outdoors, preferably near water. Although various local and imported pagan religions flourished in Philippi, the city likely had no Jewish synagogue for instruction in Israel's Scriptures and prayer to the true and living God. women who had come together. They are meeting to read and study the Scriptures, and they welcome the assistance of any Jewish teacher who happens to visit there.

Southeast of Pergamum and about forty miles (64 km) inland, Thyatira was in Asia Minor, across the Aegean Sea from Athens. Thyatira was known for wool and dyeing. Purple was an expensive dye. Lydia apparently has the means to maintain a home large enough to accommodate Paul's team, which includes at least Silas, Timothy, and Luke, and perhaps the church's gatherings (v. 40). Her "household" probably includes servants (v. 15). a worshiper of God. A Gentile who embraced Israel's monotheistic faith and the law's moral norms but did not fully convert to Judaism with respect to dietary and other ceremonial rules. See 10:2. The Lord opened her heart. Divine illumination and persuasion is necessary for the heart blinded by sin to respond to the gospel (Jer. 13:23; John 6:44, 65; Rom. 9:16; 1 Cor. 2:14). This effectual call of God ensures that all who have been chosen by God will believe (11:18; 13:48; 14:27; 2 Thess. 2:13, 14; 2 Tim. 1:9, 10).

Throughout redemptive history, God's dealings often include entire households, acknowledging family solidarity (2:38, 39; 11:14; 16:31; cf. Gen. 17:7–14). The household baptisms of Acts are striking examples of this (10:47, 48; 16:31–33; cf. 1 Cor. 1:16). Such household baptisms were apparently standard practice in the apostolic era. Assuming that these households included infants, the baptism of entire households is indirect evidence for the practice of infant baptism.

Lit. "a python spirit." The term originally referred to a mythical serpent believed to guard the temple and oracle of the Greek god Apollo at Delphi. Later the phrase meant a demon-possessed person or even a ventriloquist. The people at Philippi must have thought of her as having a demon that could tell fortunes.
A Jew would understand this to be Yahweh; a Gentile would apply it to Zeus.

As Jesus silenced demons rather that accepting their "endorsement" (Mark 1:34), so Paul is "annoyed" by the publicity that the evil spirit is offering through the girl. Following the common understanding of the expression "the Most High God," everyone would realize that Paul means to convey the thought that Jesus, as deity, expelled the demon. A subsequent incident in Ephesus shows that Paul has authority to invoke Jesus' name because he actually trusts in Jesus (19:13–17).

Like the silversmiths of Ephesus (19:23–28), the girls' owners are driven by greed but conceal their true motive behind a veneer of civic pride, invoking their Roman citizenship (v. 21). seized Paul and Silas. Because both Paul and Silas are Jews and the leaders of the missionary team, they are seized. Their companions are Gentiles (Luke, a Gentile from Syrian Antioch, and Timothy, a half-Gentile from Lystra) and are not charged.

The charge is that Paul and Silas are propagating an illegal religion and disturbing the peace. Because of Philippi's status as a colony, its citizens are Romans who enjoy legal status beyond those of other Macedonian cities. The charge is inflamed by cultural and religious prejudice ("these men are Jews"). Ironically, it will come to light that Paul and Silas themselves are Roman citizens whose civic rights are being violated (vv. 37, 38).
Paul and Silas are Roman citizens (v. 37) and should be exempt from such treatment. But in the mob atmosphere, the question of their citizenship status and legal rights is ignored.
They are treated like criminals.
Paul will later remind the Philippians of this suffering and his joyful response (Phil. 1:18, 29, 30).
Earthquakes accompanied Jesus' death and resurrection (Matt. 27:54; 28:2), as well as the outpouring of the Spirit on believers on one occasion (Acts 4:31).

On earlier occasions, God's angel led His messengers out of prisons (5:19; 12:10); but here not only Paul and Silas but also their fellow prisoners, who have heard their prayer and praises (v. 25), remained in their cells (v. 28). about to kill himself. Under Roman law, the jailer is liable to punishment if his prisoners escape (12:19; 27:42).

Throughout Acts (and the whole NT) the message is consistent: Salvation comes through faith in Jesus Christ alone (2:38; 3:16; 10:43; 13:39; 15:9–11). you and your household. For other instances of household salvation, see note on v. 15 note; cf. 2:38, 39; 10:24, 48; 1 Cor. 1:16. Because the head of the household has come to faith in Christ, the whole family is baptized (vv. 33, 34).

As Lydia's faith led her to insist on providing hospitality to the missionaries (v. 15), so the jailor's faith and repentance bear immediate fruit in his deeds of compassion for prisoners whom he previously handled with indifference at best. See theological note "Baptism" on p. 1988.

Roman citizens were exempted from scourging and torture, and had the right to due process in a trial before any punishment was inflicted. If Roman citizens were tried in a Roman court, they had the right to appeal their case to Caesar (25:11; 26:32).

Paul's insistence on a public apology from the magistrates (v. 37) is motivated not by a sense of personal insult but by a desire to rehabilitate the gospel's reputation in Philippi, refuting the slander that it advocates practices unfit for Romans (v. 21).

Early Christians often met in private homes (Philem. 2), and the mention of "the brothers" here suggests that Lydia was hostess to the gatherings of this young congregation. seen the brothers. "Brothers" would include all the believers — Lydia, her household, the jailer, perhaps other women at the river bank, and the others who responded to Paul's and Silas's preaching.

Amphipolis was thirty miles (48 km) southwest of Philippi and Apollonia twenty-five miles (40 km) farther on the highway to Thessalonica. Paul and his companions were eager to get to Thessalonica, forty miles (64 km) beyond Apollonia. Thessalonica had a population of two hundred thousand and was the provincial capital of Macedonia.

The Pauline Epistles suggest that Paul stayed in Thessalonica longer than three or four weeks (including the workdays before, between, and following three successive Sabbaths). According to Phil. 4:16, the church at Philippi sent him aid at least twice, and the Thessalonian epistles indicate that Paul had been able to give extensive doctrinal instruction to the Christians there. Acts does not state that the uproar surrounding Jason, the missionaries' host (v. 5), occurred immediately after Paul's third Sabbath of teaching in the synagogue. The conversions listed in v. 4 may have occurred over subsequent weeks, leading eventually to the hardening of Jewish opposition and the mob violence against Jason and other brothers.

Neither Jesus' disciples nor their Jewish hearers readily accepted the divine necessity of the Messiah's suffering (Luke 9:43–45; 18:31–34; 24:25, 26; 1 Cor. 1:18–25). When Paul establishes this point from the Scriptures and identifies Jesus as this suffering and triumphant Messiah, some of those who attend the synagogue, both Jews and Gentile God-fearers, as well as some of "the leading women," come to believe in Jesus (v. 4).

Paul proclaims Jesus as the anointed King who has inaugurated the spiritual kingdom of God (14:22; 19:8; 20:25; 28:23, 31), but his opponents distort Paul's message, alleging that the apostle advocates political insurrection against Rome. About this time, Claudius Caesar (A.D. 49–50) expelled the Jews from Rome (18:2) because of riots allegedly instigated by "Chrestus," a probable reference to disputes within the capital's Jewish community over the identity of the Christ.
Modern Verria, fifty miles (80 km) southwest of Thessalonica, in the foothills of the Olympian Mountains.
The Bereans give Paul's teaching an open hearing and compare it with God's written Word. Because of their integrity and discernment, many of them come to faith in Jesus the Christ.

The leading city of Greece, served by the port of Piraeus on the Aegean Sea. Athens reached its zenith in the fifth century B.C. under Pericles (495–429 B.C.), when the Parthenon and other magnificent structures were built. The classical poets Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes flourished at that time. Although conquered by the Romans in 146 B.C., Athens continued to be a great intellectual and cultural center. full of idols. There were statues of gods or goddesses in the Parthenon and other temples on the Acropolis, as well as in the public, commercial, and temple buildings below.

Epicurus (342–270 B.C.) taught that the purpose of life was pleasure and freedom from pain, passions, and fears. On the other hand, the Cypriot Zeno (340–265 B.C.), founder of Stoicism, stressed living in harmony with nature and depending on reason and other self-sufficient powers. Both schools stressed the quest for peace of mind. Zeno viewed God pantheistically as the "world-soul." babbler. A derogatory term meaning a scrap collector or peddler of assorted ideas. foreign divinities. The Greek word for "resurrection" (anastasia) is feminine in gender, and Athenian polytheists would be familiar with the personification of abstract qualities as though divine. Perhaps Paul's hearers confuse his declaration of an event (Jesus' resurrection from the dead) with a female deity. That these "divinities" originate outside Athens and Achaia would devalue them in the opinion of Athens's intellectual elite.

The name means "Mars Hill." This is a hill near the Acropolis where in ancient times a council had met. The council became the city council of Athens, and in Roman times it was the court supervising morals, education, and religion. In Paul's time, the court meets in the Royal Portico, in the marketplace below the Acropolis. Probably the purpose of Paul's hearing before the council is not only to satisfy its members' curiosity (v. 21) but also to evaluate the strange ideas that he is propagating.

The term is ambiguous, in some contexts having a negative connotation ("superstitious," as in KJV) and in others referring more neutrally to pious devotion to deities. Without endorsing the city-wide idolatry that has so distressed him, the apostle opens his discourse by acknowledging the abundant evidence of the Athenians' deep desire to honor those superhuman powers that, they believe, influence their destinies.

Possibly a reference to the Altar of the Twelve Gods at Athens, erected to ensure that no god is left out of their worship. Paul uses this point of contact to begin his discourse about the God who made the world, who is not carved out of stone or confined to any temple, and who controls the times and places where people live.

Epicureans conceived of the gods as remote, uninvolved in human affairs. Stoics conceived of the divine as a principle of reason that permeates the cosmos. Paul proclaims the God who is distinct from and transcendent over the universe (unlike Stoicism), but also (unlike Epicureanism) deeply engaged with His creatures, giving "to all mankind life and breath and everything" (v. 25) and assigning each nationality's time and place (v. 26; see Deut. 32:8, 9).

The whole human race descends from Adam, its original covenant representative, whose decision affects all his naturally conceived descendants (Rom. 5:12–21; 1 Cor. 15:21, 22). See theological note "Original Sin" on p. 17.

Elsewhere, Paul (echoing Ps. 14:1–3) bluntly diagnoses the innate rebellion of the whole human race apart from God's renewing grace: "No one seeks for God. All have turned aside" (Rom. 3:11, 12). To the Athenian philosophers, Paul's point is that God's general revelation makes the Gentiles' worship of false gods inexcusable. God's gift to all mankind of "life and breath and everything" (v. 25) should lead the whole human race to long to know their Creator. They cannot excuse their idolatries by alleging that His revelation in the created universe is insufficient, since "he is actually not far from each one of us" in that general revelation, as even pagan poets have recognized (v. 28).

Citing a seventh-century B.C. poet (see text note), Paul says that God brought all people into being and they only exist by His providence. In the ancient world, the three great mysteries of philosophy and science were the questions of life, motion, and being. See theological note "Divine Revelation" on p. 850. some of your own poets. Knowing that the Athenians do not know or respect the OT, Paul quotes from three of their own poets. Although their words originally referred to Zeus, the head of the Greek pantheon, whom Stoics reinterpreted as a personification of reason, Paul applies the quotations to the true and living God of heaven. The poets are Epimenides (c. 600 B.C.), Cleanthes (c. 331–233 B.C.), and Aratus (c. 315–240 B.C.).

Epicureans and Stoics would agree, at least implicitly, with Paul's critique of crass popular idolatry that equates "the divine being" with material images, though they themselves have formed misconceptions of the Creator by the "imagination of man." See theological note "The Self-Existence of God" on p. 938.

Until the coming of Jesus Christ, God's special, redemptive revelation was addressed almost exclusively to Israel, leaving the pagan nations largely in ignorance (except for the general revelation throughout the cosmos that left them without excuse; Rom. 1:18–25). God did not impose on the Gentiles the judgment they deserved, and now He has sent Paul to proclaim His truth to all people everywhere, calling them to repentance.

The final day of judgment (Rev. 20:12–15) would be an alien idea both to Epicureans, who believe that the gods could not be bothered by earthly events, and to Stoics, who view history as running in endless cycles. Yet the Athenians' rejection of the Man whom God appointed will result in Jesus' finally and justly rejecting them on that day of judgment. Paul stresses that God's call to repentance and faith is not merely an invitation but a command.

Some Greek philosophical schools viewed embodied life as undesirable, so they would consider absurd Paul's claim that the One who would judge everyone was designated by God through resurrection from the dead. Others perhaps dismiss Paul's focus on concrete historical events — resurrection and last judgment — from other philosophical or personal motives. Nonetheless, Paul's witness to the philosophers bears fruit in the lives of some, two of whom are named: Dionysus and Damaris (v. 34).

Since 27 B.C., this city had been the capital of the Roman province of Achaia. It was fifty miles (80 km) southwest of Athens, near the isthmus that joins Attica and the Peloponnesus. Corinth was large and prosperous in the eighth to sixth centuries B.C., but it declined and was captured in 338 B.C. by Philip II of Macedon. In 196 B.C., it was taken by the Romans. They sacked it in 146 B.C. as punishment for a revolt, but it was restored by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 B.C. In NT times, Corinth had more than two hundred thousand inhabitants, including Greeks, freedmen from Italy, Roman army veterans, businessmen, government officials, people from the Near East, a large number of Jews, and many slaves. Corinth was thoroughly pagan and immoral. The city was filled with pagan temples and on the south there was a high acropolis with a temple of Aphrodite. From the fifth century B.C., the expression "to Corinthianize" meant to engage in sexual immorality.

Pontus was on the north coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Priscilla is frequently listed before her husband (vv. 18, 19, 26; Rom. 16:3; 2 Tim. 4:19). She may have had higher social status or have been more prominent in their tent–making business. This Jewish-Christian couple is noteworthy for their hospitality, opening their homes in Corinth, Ephesus, and Rome (to which they eventually returned) to the church's meetings and leaders (Acts 18:24–26; Rom. 16:3–5; 1 Cor. 16:19). Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. See note on 17:7.

Like Aquila and Priscilla, Paul was a tentmaker by trade. His frequent practice was to support himself and his team through this work rather than expecting financial compensation from those whom he was evangelizing (20:33–35; 1 Cor. 4:12; 1 Thess. 2:9; 2 Thess. 3:7–9), although he gratefully received donations from established churches for the sake of further outreach. See note on 18:5.

Apparently, Paul's colleagues have brought a contribution from one or more Macedonian churches, allowing him to reduce his hours making tents and devote weekdays as well as Sabbaths to proclaiming Christ's Word (2 Cor. 11:7–9; Phil. 4:10–20).
They are responsible for their own sins. See 20:26; Ezek. 3:16–21.

The first home of the Corinthian church. Titius Justus is a Gentile adherent to the faith at the synagogue, and a Roman citizen. He may belong to one of the families Julius Caesar sent to colonize Corinth. It is also possible that he is the Gaius of Rom. 16:23, who was baptized by Paul (1 Cor. 1:14); Gaius could be a third name standing before Titius Justus.

As synagogue ruler, Crispus is in charge of the physical arrangements for the synagogue services. It is this Crispus (and presumably his household) whom Paul baptizes (1 Cor. 1:14). his entire household. See 16:15 and note; 16:31–33.

Jesus promises that Paul's labors in Corinth will be fruitful because many people whom God has appointed to eternal life (13:48) and given to the Son (John 17:6) live in that city. Even though the elect Corinthians have not yet believed the gospel, they nevertheless are known to God.

Luke's identification of the administrative head of this senatorial province as a proconsul is confirmed by an inscription found at Delphi, Greece, which identifies Gallio as the proconsul in A.D. 52.

The Jewish accusation is ambiguous. Roman law at the time forbids the practice of religions not legally recognized by Rome. Judaism is legally recognized in the first-century Roman Empire (Latin: religio licita), so perhaps the opponents claim that the faith that Paul is preaching is not an offshoot of Judaism and has no claim to legitimacy before the Empire. Gallio, however, views the issue as a dispute among Jews over "your own law" (v. 15) — the law of Moses — and refuses to get involved in an intramural religious argument among the Jewish people.

Though this phrase could apply to Aquila, it is probably Paul who is in view. The Nazirite vow requires rigorous ceremonial purity that are impractical in Gentile lands (Num. 6:1–21), so this vow is more likely a private one undertaken by Paul as a religious exercise. The hair is allowed to grow during the period of the vow, and cutting it marks the conclusion of the vow and is perhaps an expression of gratitude to God (21:23, 24). Paul's vow shows that, despite the accusations that jealous Jewish leaders have brought to the proconsul, he exercises his Christian freedom by occasionally observing Mosaic ceremonial ordinances even as he brings God's good news to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 9:19–23).

Although previously prevented by the Holy Spirit from evangelizing this major city in the province of Asia, Paul now preaches Christ in the synagogue, anticipating a longer ministry to come "if God wills" (v. 21). See ch. 19, 20.

Paul is in Antioch for several months, from about autumn of A.D. 52 to spring of A.D. 53. Galatia and Phrygia. Paul starts his third missionary journey in the Phrygian part of Galatia in central Asia Minor, near the Pisidian towns in which he and Barnabas planted churches on their first trip several years before.
Apollos's speaking ability and proficiency in the OT make him a strong encourager of fellow believers (v. 27) because he is a formidable gospel advocate in the Jewish community of Ephesus (v. 28).
The description of Apollos's ministry suggests that he is fervent in the (Holy) Spirit, unlike disciples of John the Baptist whom Paul will meet at Ephesus (19:1–7).

After finishing his ministry in Phrygian Galatia (18:23), Paul continues westward by land through the region of Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis (Col. 4:13) in the Lycus Valley, and finally arrives at Ephesus. Here he ministers for about three years (vv. 8, 10), from about A.D. 53 to 56. Ephesus. The capital of the Roman province of Asia, Ephesus was founded in about the twelfth century B.C. by Ionians from Athens. It became a great commercial power, but its economic prosperity declined, mainly because erosion into the river had silted and clogged the harbor. The city derived wealth and prestige from its temple of Artemis, built in honor of the goddess of fertility. The Ephesus of Paul's day has passed its zenith but is still an important commercial and religious center. some disciples. According to v. 7, "about twelve."

As followers of John the Baptist, these believers probably know that John foretold One who would baptize with the Spirit (Luke 3:16) but have not learned that John's prophecy was fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit on the Day of Pentecost. As in John 7:39 (where the ESV rightly renders a Greek clause that literally reads, "the Spirit was not yet," as "the Spirit had not been given"), probably these disciples' response does not mean that they do not know of the Holy Spirit's existence but that they do not know that He arrived in history and human experience at Pentecost, as promised through John and previous prophets such as Isaiah and Joel. Note that throughout Acts, all categories of people receive the baptism of the Holy Spirit: Jews, Samaritans, God-fearing Greeks, and other Gentiles.
John's baptism of repentance (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3) was directed toward repentance of sins and looked forward to the redeeming work of Jesus.

The experience the Ephesian Gentiles have when receiving the Holy Spirit parallels that of the Jews (2:4, 11), Samaritans (8:14–17), and God-fearing Gentiles (10:44–46). This episode is an extension of the Pentecost experience to yet another group of people (v. 2 note), which indicates that Christ's promise of the Spirit has now been extended to "the end of the earth," as the third and last geographical territory to which the apostolic witness was to extend (as stated in Acts 1:8). "Prophesying" in this passage may be equivalent to "telling \... the mighty works of God" (2:11) or speaking so as to extol God (10:46).

Nothing further is known about Tyrannus. Some manuscripts add "from the fifth to the tenth hour" (11 A.M. to 4 P.M.). Tyrannus may use the room in the cool morning hours, giving it to Paul for the rest of the day.
The Roman province in the western part of Asia Minor. As a result of this teaching, groups of believers are formed in numerous places (Col. 4:13, 16; Rev. 2; 3).

That is, sweat cloths or work aprons that Paul uses as he works at making tents or awnings (18:3). As a touch of faith on the hem of Jesus' garment brought healing to a woman (Luke 8:44, 48) and Peter's shadow was apparently instrumental in healing others (Acts 5:15, 16), so now in a pagan city God attests the truth of His gospel and the authority of His messenger with "extraordinary miracles" (19:11). to the sick. This is not Paul's doing; because of their pagan religious background, the Ephesians are used to employing superstitious means (v. 19). God accommodates His gracious work to their ignorance.

In ancient times, it was common practice to use magical names to drive out evil spirits. Jews in Ephesus presume "to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus" over those possessed, trying to imitate what Paul does (v. 12; 16:18). As the site of the famous temple of Artemis (v. 24 note), Ephesus attracted religious (pagan) pilgrims from throughout the empire. Papyri containing lists of divine names to be invoked in exorcisms, traced to Ephesus, have been found across the Mediterranean world.

The evil spirit perceives that Sceva's sons lack faith in Jesus and therefore have no authority to invoke His name. The saving power of Jesus' name is conveyed not by reciting its syllables but by trusting the person who bears the name (3:16).

These are scrolls with the names and incantations used in their magic. fifty thousand pieces of silver. Probably a reference to the Attic drachma. Divergent opinions concerning ancient-to-modern exchange rates and comparative standards of living make it difficult to estimate equivalent values in today's currencies, but Luke obviously preserves this figure to illustrate the depth of the conversion experienced by many who had practiced the dark arts but who now, freed through Christ, gladly destroy their extremely valuable occult libraries.

This summary of the Word's growth echoes and elaborates earlier summary statements (6:7; 12:24; 13:49). 19:20 the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. This summary of the growth of the word of the Lord echoes and elaborates earlier summary statements (6:7; 12:24; 13:49) to indicate the linear journey of the gospel (in Judea, then Samaria, and finally in the rest of the world, according to the outline of Acts 1:8). This coalesces with the repetition of the Pentecost experience earlier in the chapter (19:2–6), which also indicated that the witness of the Spirit was to travel to the three geographical areas of Jerusalem–Judea, Samaria, and the "end of the earth." Recall that this is an allusion to Ex. 1:7, 12, 20, "multiplied and grew strong" (on which see 6:7 and which occurs also in 12:24). Hence, throughout Acts a new exodus is happening to new Israel through belief in Jesus, the Lord of the new exodus. Recall also that "the word of God" is an allusion to God's Word prophesied to accomplish restoration in Isaiah (especially Is. 2:3, and its developments in Is. 45:22–24 and 55:10, 11). Here that prophecy of restoration is viewed as continuing to be fulfilled through belief in Jesus.

Presumably, Paul sends these helpers to Macedonia to motivate and organize the Gentile churches' offering for needy believers in Jerusalem and Judea, as he sent Titus and another trusted brother to Corinth in Achaia for this purpose (2 Cor. 8:1–6, 16–24).
See note on 9:2.

An important guild of silversmiths developed at Ephesus on account of the large numbers of religious pilgrims. The pilgrims came to worship the goddess Diana (Artemis in Greek) who was portrayed by a famous statue at Ephesus as a fertility goddess. Her "image" that had fallen "from the sky" (v. 35) was probably a meteorite that the people had begun to worship. The temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Not only was it the destination of religious pilgrimage, but it was a banking depository as well. Making silver shrines and images of the goddess was a trade important to the city's economic well-being.

The archaic Ionic temple of Artemis measured 220 feet (67 m) by 425 feet (136 m), with 127 marble columns each 62 feet (19 m) high. The lowest drums of the thirty-six western columns were carved with reliefs. The statue of the goddess was displayed in an inner room of the temple. Demetrius and other silversmiths are alarmed by Paul's persuasive words against idolatry not only because it threatens "this trade of ours" but also because it challenges the reputation of the goddess, her world-famous temple, and the city of Ephesus.
The Greek word ekklēsia is used here and in vv. 39 and 41 to denote a secular civic assembly of people, where legal decisions are made concerning the management of the city (5:11 note).

According to the first-century Jewish historian Josephus, these were common charges of Gentiles against Jews and Jewish Christians. If "sacrilegious" is construed literally as "temple robbers," the town clerk is correct to claim that Paul and his team cannot be charged with this crime. On the other hand, in view of Paul's remarks about idols in Athens (17:24, 25, 29), he may well have said things about Artemis and her glorious temple that her devotees would consider blasphemous. Luke records the official's placating words without endorsing their accuracy, showing that the gospel's opponents, not its advocates, have been responsible for the civil disruptions, the violations of Roman law and order, that have accompanied the gospel's dissemination (cf. 16:19–24, 36–39; 18:12–17).

Paul goes up the coast of Asia Minor from Ephesus, either by road or by ship, probably as far as Troas and then by ship to Macedonia (cf. 16:8–10) and Philippi (cf. 16:11–40), visiting groups of believers on the way. While in Macedonia, Paul may extend his ministry as far as Illyricum (modern Albania; Rom. 15:19). His decision to visit the churches of Macedonia first, before moving south to those in Achaia, is a change of intentions that he previously communicated to the church at Corinth. Some in Corinth will accuse him of vacillation, a charge that he answers forthrightly in terms of his pastoral sensitivity to the Corinthians' spiritual need (2 Cor. 1:15–24; 2:12, 13; 7:5–9).

Paul arrives at Corinth, where he spends the winter of A.D. 56–57. During this time he writes his epistle to the Romans, announcing his plan to deliver an offering from Gentile churches to believers in Judea before setting off for Rome, a journey which he has long desired to make (Rom. 1:11–15; 15:23, 24, 26).

Paul's traveling companions are listed by name. They may be official church representatives appointed to travel with Paul to deliver money collected for relief of the Jerusalem church (1 Cor. 16:1–4; 2 Cor. 9:1–5). Sopater may be the "Sosipater" mentioned in Rom. 16:21. Aristarchus faithfully accompanied Paul during the third missionary journey (19:29), and he later accompanies the apostle to Rome (27:2) where he shares Paul's imprisonment (Col. 4:10). Secundus is not mentioned elsewhere in the NT. Gaius is from Derbe in Lycaonia (central Asia Minor), a different man from the Macedonian Gaius mentioned in 19:29. On Timothy, see 16:1–3 and Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion. Tychicus is later Paul's representative to various churches during the apostle's imprisonments (Eph. 6:21; Col. 4:7–9; 2 Tim. 4:12). Trophimus accompanies Paul to Jerusalem, where his presence in the city (though not in a forbidden section of the temple, as opponents allege) leads to Paul's arrest (21:29). He apparently later accompanies Paul after the apostle's release from his first Roman imprisonment (2 Tim. 4:20).
Luke again uses the first person plural pronoun, indicating that he traveled with Paul to Jerusalem.

Sunday, which was sanctified by Jesus' resurrection and first appearances to His followers (John 20:19, 26) and apparently became the regular day for the churches' assemblies for worship (1 Cor. 16:2). to break bread. Since they are gathered together for worship on the first day of the week, the Lord's Day (Rev. 1:10), this celebration includes communion (2:42) — which on this occasion is observed well after midnight (20:11) — and is not just a fellowship meal (2:46). Paul talked. This is a Sunday evening preaching-teaching service that also includes, as a central element, the breaking of bread in remembrance of Jesus' sacrificial death.

Luke records that Eutychus was "taken up dead," the likely result of such a fall. Paul's restoration of the young man to life is one of two such raisings of the dead by apostles recorded in Acts (9:40; cf. Luke 7:11–17; 8:49–56; John 11:1–44).
Paul goes by road the twenty miles (32 km) from Troas to Assos, while Luke travels with the ship.
They sail down the coast to Miletus, about thirty miles (48 km) south of Ephesus.
These are the ordained representatives of the Ephesian congregation, called to be overseers and shepherds of the church of God (v. 28; cf. 1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9).

Paul's teaching during his three-year stay (v. 31) in Ephesus was extensive, including public lectures at the synagogue and the lecture hall of Tyrannus (19:8–10), as well as more private instruction in homes.
See note on 3:19. Both Jews and Gentiles must come to God in the same way — in repentance for sin (26:20; cf. Luke 24:47) and faith in Jesus Christ.

This probably refers to the direction of the Holy Spirit (19:21). Such explicit guidance by the Holy Spirit has often occurred during Paul's ministry (16:6–10). The Spirit also reveals that suffering awaits Paul in Jerusalem (v. 23), a prediction that other Christians understand as a reason for Paul to avoid Jerusalem (21:11, 12), despite the Holy Spirit's insistence that he must go there.

Paul's statement is based on his own judgment of the situation rather than on divine revelation. Because of continued plots against his life by the Jews (v. 3), the divine revelation that "imprisonment and afflictions" await him (v. 23), and his own intention to focus his future ministry on the western Mediterranean (Rom. 15:23–29), Paul considers it likely that he is seeing the Ephesian elders for the last time. However, it appears that Paul is later able to return to Ephesus after his release from prison in Rome (1 Tim. 1:3).

As a watchman on a city wall must sound the alarm of impending attack, so God's spokesmen are responsible to warn their hearers of divine judgment to come on those who do not repent. Paul has delivered the message entrusted to him, so he bears no blame for those who refuse it (Ezek. 3:16–21; 33:1–9).

The revelation of God culminating in His Son, Jesus Christ. Paul, in his ministry to the Ephesians, did not suppress any truths of the gospel, "anything that was profitable" to his hearers (v. 20), but preached the full gospel to Jew and Gentile. Throughout his ministry, he always uses tact and discretion but never compromises the good news.

Many ancient manuscripts have a different word order, reading "the blood of His own," that is, of Christ. On either reading, the elders' duty to protect God's church is shown by the infinite price He paid to purchase it for Himself (John 10:11, 14, 15). The phrasing is remarkable in the way it acknowledges that the blood of Christ is the blood of God. This points to the hypostatic union, the union of a complete human nature and the complete divine nature in the one person of Christ. Because of this union, the attributes of one nature — in this case blood, an attribute of His human nature — can be attributed to the one person of Christ, who as the second person of the Trinity, is very God of very God. The divine nature and human nature are united in the one person of Christ "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the distinction of natures being in no way annulled by the union, but rather the characteristics of each nature being preserved" (Definition of the Council of Chalcedon). In other words, the human nature does not take on uniquely divine attributes such as omnipresence and omniscience, and the divine nature does not take on uniquely creaturely attributes such as the possibility of change and various limitations in knowledge and power. Because the two natures are united in the one person of Christ, we may distinguish but not separate them. For example, when the Bible speaks of Christ sleeping (Mark 4:38), that is a manifestation of His humanity. The person of Christ in that case experienced tiredness according to His human nature, not His divine nature, for the divine nature has no need of sleep (Ps. 121:3, 4).

Paul's prophetic warning in this verse was fulfilled as the Ephesian church was soon to be plagued by false teachers, some of whom apparently were leaders of the church (1 Tim. 1:3, 7, 19, 20; 6:3–5; Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues).

Like Israel's prophet-judge Samuel (1 Sam. 12:3–5), Paul does not serve God's people for the sake of material gain, nor should the elders who will shepherd the church in the future (1 Pet. 5:2; 1 Tim. 3:3).
The saying cited by Paul is not preserved in any of the Gospels, but must have been circulated orally by the apostles. For Jesus' expressions of the thought, see Matt. 10:8; Luke 6:30, 31; 14:12–14.
The ancient Christian practice of the kiss of greeting (Luke 7:45; 1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14) is still practiced by Christians in some cultures today.

They sail on a direct course through the islands off the coast of Asia Minor to the port of Patara. The small island of Cos was a free state in the province of Asia. Rhodes, the capital on the north end of the island of Rhodes, was famous and prosperous in the earlier Greek period. Patara, a port on the southwest coast of Asia Minor, was an important harbor for ancient ships sailing the eastern Mediterranean, thus bringing Syria, Palestine, and Egypt into contact with Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Achaia.
Syria controlled Phoenicia in the Roman period.
This port, famous in OT times and conquered by Alexander the Great, was about four hundred miles (644 km) southeast of Patara, a sea journey of about five days.

Paul is not disobedient to the Spirit; the Holy Spirit is compelling him to go to Jerusalem (20:22 note), while also giving prophecies that hardship awaits him there (20:23). In response to such predictions, Paul's friends, assuming that he should avoid such suffering if possible, tried to persuade Paul "not to go on to Jerusalem" (cf. vv. 11, 12).

En route to Jerusalem (20:16), Paul's team enjoys a week of fellowship with "the disciples" in Tyre, a sizable congregation of believing families that was planted through the testimony of scattered Christians after Stephen's martyrdom (11:19).
A port twenty-five miles (40 km) south of Tyre, where the ship unloads its cargo.

This seaport, built by Herod the Great, was the provincial capital of Judea and located thirty-two miles (51 km) south of Ptolemais (10:1 note). Cornelius and the troops he commanded had been stationed there (10:1), and Paul is later held there for several years in Roman custody (23:23–26:32). Philip the evangelist \... one of the seven. One of the seven chosen to handle the food distribution (6:1–6). He has preached to the Samaritans, the Ethiopian eunuch, and the people along the Palestinian coast (ch. 8). Although originally ordained to perform mercy ministry within the church, his gospel witness to Samaria, the Ethiopian, and the coastal towns warrants the title evangelist, an office mentioned rarely in the NT (Eph. 4:11; 2 Tim. 4:5).
The same Agabus who fifteen years earlier prophesied the severe famine in Judea and the surrounding area (11:27, 28).

In the first-century context of the apostles, Agabus, as a prophet, is led directly by the Spirit to give God's inspired message. the Jews in Jerusalem will bind. As events unfold, Roman troops will take Paul into protective custody to prevent his being harmed by a mob of Jews (22:22–29). Yet the result is Paul's captivity by the Romans, initiated by his Jewish countrymen and prolonged by their leaders (24:1–9), as Paul himself sums up the situation in 28:17. Paul is thus to follow the same pattern of suffering that happened with Jesus. Agabus's prophetic act with Paul's belt and his abbreviated explanation accurately forecast events that will transpire when Paul reaches Jerusalem.
Like those who were apostles before his call, Paul considers it an honor to suffer disgrace for Jesus' name (5:41).

Pentecost, the fiftieth day after Passover, is fast approaching (they have spent at least thirty-six days traveling from Philippi to Caesarea, and they have spent several days at Caesarea), and Paul wants to be at Jerusalem for this feast (20:16).

Jesus' half-brother (Gal. 1:19) articulated the conclusion of the council of apostles and elders that secured Gentile believers' freedom from the imposition of the entire law of Moses. He was also respected even by the Jewish community outside the church for his prayer life and his scrupulous observance of the law's stipulations.

Thousands of Jewish Christians in Jerusalem strictly observe the Mosaic law. While many of these no doubt resent the fact that Gentile Christians are not required to observe the ceremonial law of Moses (v. 25; 15:1–31), the charge here is that Paul has been encouraging Jews to forsake the law as well (v. 21). Such a charge may have been prompted by reports that Paul himself does not follow the Jewish ceremonial law when in Gentile company. Though Paul has no objection to Jews' following their ancestral customs and does so when ministering to Jews (16:3; 18:18; see 1 Cor. 9:20), he opposes any attempt to impose the observance of Mosaic ceremonial laws on Gentiles, or to make such observance in some way necessary for salvation (Rom. 14:1–8; Gal. 2:3; 5:2–6). Always careful to avoid giving unnecessary offense, Paul's flexibility in such matters shows that the interests of the gospel are always foremost in his mind (1 Cor. 9:19–23). He even counsels Jewish believers in Corinth against a misguided attempt to reverse their circumcision (1 Cor. 7:18, 19).

This is the Nazirite vow (Num. 6:1–21), during which the devotee let his hair grow. When the period of the vow was over, he shaved off his hair, dedicated it to the Lord, and burned it together with the sacrifice for the fellowship offering (Num. 6:18). Paul pays the expenses for four Nazirites, goes to the priest with them for the sacrifices, and participates in the purification rites. In this way, Paul publicly demonstrates the falsehood of the rumor circulating about him in Jerusalem (18:18 note).

Placards on the low wall separating the courtyard of the Gentiles from that of the (Israelite) women sharply warned uncircumcised males not to proceed beyond that point to enter the areas nearer to the temple building itself. Paul's accusers, Jews from Asia, assume and allege without proof that he has brought an Ephesian Gentile colleague into a forbidden area of the temple precincts.
The tribune is surprised to hear Paul speak Greek; he has thought him to be an insurrectionist Jew from Egypt who three years before had appeared there claiming to be a prophet.
Lit. "dagger men," militant Jewish nationalists.

Probably the stairs leading from the temple area to the Antonia Fortress (rebuilt by Herod the Great and named after Mark Antony) on the north edge of the temple platform. Hebrew language. Perhaps Aramaic, as commonly spoken by Jews in Palestine, although the priests and Levites would also have known Hebrew, and some archaeological evidence suggests that Hebrew was still in everyday use by some Palestinian Jews. In the setting of the temple and in answer to accusations of disloyalty toward Judaism, a well-trained Pharisee may well have addressed the crowd in Hebrew (22:2). Greek was the common language of the Roman and Mediterranean world.

An important city, located in Cilicia on the eastern Mediterranean coast north of Cyprus. It was a noted intellectual center. 22:3 educated at the feet of Gamaliel. Gamaliel was a respected scholar (5:33–39) and leader of the school of Hillel, one of the two influential rabbinical movements in first-century Judaism.

This frequent identification of the Christian movement (19:9, 23; 24:14, 22; see 18:26) may have been derived from Jesus' self-description (John 14:6) or from an OT metaphor (Gen. 18:19; Deut. 8:6; Ps. 18:21). However, most likely it was a name that had its source in Is. 40:3 ("In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD"), part of a restoration and second exodus prophecy about Israel's deliverance, so that the very name of the Christian movement was understood to express the idea that Christians were the fulfillment of the prophecies of Israel's restoration (see the Introduction: Acts in the Larger Story of the Bible).

The second account of Christ's appearance on the road to Damascus, now from Paul's own mouth, reinforces the details of the earlier narrative (9:1–9), affirming that Paul's companions perceived extraordinary phenomena of sound (9:7) and light (22:9) but did not understand the divine speaker's words (22:9) or perceive His form (9:7). The revelation was not merely subjective, but its content was conveyed to Paul alone.

An appropriate person to meet Saul, who was a zealous Pharisee, "a Hebrew of Hebrews" (Phil. 3:5, 6). Being known to Ananias would recommend Paul to other Jews in the city who would otherwise be suspicious of him (9:10–19).
Saul heard Stephen apply this title of the Suffering Servant to Jesus (7:52; Is. 53:11) in the moments before Stephen's martyrdom.

As the original Eleven and Judas's replacement were witnesses who had seen the Lord and could testify that He had risen from the dead (1:8, 21, 22), so Saul too, though "one untimely born" (1 Cor. 15:8) would henceforth testify as an apostle that he had seen the risen Jesus (1 Cor. 9:1).
Baptism in the NT is an outward sign of an inward cleansing. As such, it parallels circumcision in the OT (Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Ezek. 44:7).

Echoing Is. 57:19 (Eph. 2:17), Paul's vision in the very temple that he is now charged with defiling revealed that his own people would reject his message but the Gentiles would welcome it, as Paul has seen in his travels (13:45–49).

The Roman scourge was a whip of leather thongs loaded with bits of metal or bone; it could maim for life or kill. Jesus was scourged with such a whip (John 19:1). Thus far, Paul has been beaten (Acts 16:22, 23; 2 Cor. 11:24, 25) but has never endured this severe punishment, which would not be inflicted on a Roman citizen without legal due process.
The soldiers either stretch Paul's arms around a pole to expose his back or tie his hands and hoist him from the ground to administer the whipping.

Paul appeals again to his Roman citizenship, knowing that he is going to be punished without trial (16:37). Roman citizenship was highly prized, usually given only to those of high position or those who had performed some valuable service to the state. It was then passed on to one's family, as in Paul's case, since he is "a citizen by birth" (v. 28).
Son of Nebedaeus, a brutal and violent man who ruled as high priest from A.D. 48–59. This is not the earlier Annas of John 18:13. Ananias was assassinated early in the war with Rome (A.D. 66–70).

Tombs were often whitewashed to make them more visible (Matt. 23:27, 28), so Paul's metaphor may mean that Ananias's splendid outward appearance only conceals the decay of death within. He may also be alluding to the imagery of Ezek. 13:8–16, in which whitewash on a wall enhances its appearance but does not add to its strength. Paul aptly characterizes a corrupt ruler whose abuse of authority demeans his priestly office. contrary to the law. According to Jewish law, Paul must be tried and found guilty before being punished.

Paul's response to the bystanders' rebuke implies that, however deserving Ananias is of divine retribution, respect for the high priest's office would have restrained the apostle's retort, had he recognized that the council member who ordered that Paul be assaulted was, in fact, the high priest. God's law (Ex. 22:28) obligates Paul to respect the people's leader even when a ruler is not behaving respectably, just as David honored Saul, the Lord's anointed, although the king sought to kill David (1 Sam. 24:3–15).

These two groups emerged during the historical period between the events described in the OT and the events recorded in the NT. They had different political and religious views. Paul seizes the opportunity to emphasize their religious differences by identifying himself as a Pharisee and a believer in the resurrection of the dead, against the Sadducees, who denied a future bodily resurrection and the existence of angels and spirits (v. 8; cf. 4:1, 2; Matt. 22:23–32).
These are teachers, expert interpreters of Jewish law. Paul's appeal to a tenet that sets their party apart from the Sadducees inclines them to come to his defense.

This encouragement given by special revelation from the Lord assures Paul of his survival to bring the gospel to the imperial capital, as Christ granted him a similarly encouraging vision in Corinth (18:9, 10). A host of obstacles — assassination conspiracies, legal delays, storm, shipwreck, and snakebite — will arise to threaten this promise, but none can prevent its fulfillment (27:23–26)
Evidently some members of Paul's family are in Jerusalem. told Paul. Prisoners received their necessary supplies from relatives and friends who regularly visited them.
Heavily equipped infantry and cavalry delivers Paul safely to Felix, the procurator of the imperial province of Judea. The official provincial headquarters is at Caesarea.

Felix was a former slave, and as a freedman had ascended to an influential position in the Roman government. In A.D. 52, the Emperor Claudius sent him as governor to Caesarea. Felix was addressed as "most excellent Felix" (24:2) during his eight-year administration. The Roman historian Tacitus said that Felix "occupied the office of a king while having the mind of a slave, saturated with cruelty and lust."
The tribune prudently omits the detail that he had ordered Paul's flogging before he learned of his Roman citizenship.

A town built by Herod the Great in honor of his father, Antipater, about thirty miles (48 km) northwest of Jerusalem. The official residence built by Herod the Great. It became a Roman praetorium or official residence and included prisoners' cells (John 18:28; Phil. 1:13).
As an orator, Tertullus is a kind of lawyer, possibly a Jew (he refers to Jewish law as "our" law; v. 6 text note).

Tertullus's flattery to curry the governor's favor is contradicted by records that show that Felix's tenure as governor was marred by brutal repression and violent acts against the populace of the province, both Jews and Samaritans.

Tertullus charges that Paul is a chronic troublemaker, the leader of a disreputable religious sect, and a person who has threatened to profane the temple (see 21:27–29). Paul replies to these accusations in his defense before Felix (vv. 10–21). 24:5 the Nazarenes. Christians at this time were identified as followers of Jesus of Nazareth. "Nazareth" may have been a term of contempt (John 1:46).

Paul assures Felix that as a Jew he follows a religion protected by Rome. As a follower of "the Way," Paul worships the "God of our fathers"; believes the faith revealed in Israel's Scriptures, the Law and the Prophets; and even shares his accusers' hope in the resurrection of the dead (Ps. 16:9, 10; Dan. 12:1, 2; Acts 13:34–37; 1 Thess. 4:13–18; 2 Thess. 1:8).

Conveniently absent are those who incited the mob in the temple by alleging (without ground) that Paul had brought an uncircumcised Ephesian believer into a forbidden courtyard of the temple (21:27–29). So, there are no witnesses present to testify to the original occasion that brought Paul into Roman custody.

Before the Sanhedrin, Paul's only controversial statement has nothing to do with Roman political interests, but concerns an issue internal to Judaism, a longstanding doctrinal disagreement between two established parties, the Sadducees and the Pharisees (23:6–10).

Felix knows enough to realize that the charges against Paul and the Christian movement are baseless, and even sends for Paul subsequently and repeatedly to learn more about faith in Jesus the Messiah (vv. 24, 26). His guilty conscience is struck with fear when Paul speaks of the coming judgment (v. 25); but he lacks the integrity to resist the hope of a bribe from Paul (v. 26) and the pressure of the Jewish leadership (v. 27).
As a Roman citizen whose case is still pending, Paul is given some freedom (28:16).

Daughter of Herod Agrippa I (12:1–23) and sister of Herod Agrippa II (25:13; 26:3 note) and Bernice (25:13 note). Drusilla left Azizus, king of Emesa in Syria, to marry Felix. She probably died along with her son Agrippa in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius at Pompeii, A.D. 79.
Festus is from a noble family in Rome. Though Felix was greedy and evil, Festus is wise and honorable.

Since Felix has kept Paul in custody in Caesarea for two years (24:27), presumably the assassins who earlier vowed to fast until they killed Paul (23:14) have violated their vow. Yet the plot to ambush and slay the apostle still simmers among the leadership of the Sanhedrin.

Festus must protect Paul while he was in Roman custody. Probably having reviewed the letter from the tribune Claudius Lysias (23:26–30) that explains Paul's relocation to custody in the provincial capital, Caesarea, Festus refuses the request of the Jews, saving Paul from their plot.
Although generally more just and judicious than his predecessors, Festus's political pragmatism replicates the craven expedience of Felix (24:27) and Pontius Pilate (Luke 23:4, 5, 13–24).

Fearing that Festus is going to grant the Jews their request, Paul exercises his right as a Roman citizen to be tried before Caesar (Nero) in Rome. At this time, Nero has not yet shown his hostility to Christianity. Paul could hope to be acquitted by Nero, particularly since his opponents have presented to the provincial governors no evidence whatsoever that he has violated imperial law (25:18, 19, 25–27; see 26:31, 32).

This is Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I (who martyred James the son of Zebedee and would have done the same to Peter if he could have; 12:1–19) and great-grandson of Herod the Great (26:3 note). Agrippa II was favored by Nero with an expansion of his domain in northern Palestine, so his expert opinion on Paul's case will carry weight with the Emperor. Bernice. The oldest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, Bernice was twice widowed before entering into what was alleged to be an incestuous relationship with her brother, Herod Agrippa II. Despite the scandal of this relationship, she was frequently presented as Herod's queen on official occasions (e.g., vv. 13, 23).

Like Gallio in Corinth, Festus concludes that the controversy between Paul and his opponents concerns matters internal to Judaism and involve no violation of Roman law (18:12–17). Unlike Gallio, who could dismiss the Jewish minority in Achaia without political fallout, Festus does not risk angering the community leaders in Judaea by daring to release Paul from custody.

To refer a Roman citizen's case to the emperor, rather than resolving it locally, entails some political jeopardy for a provincial governor, particularly if he cannot articulate alleged crimes against the empire that warrant further legal process rather than the prisoner's exoneration and release.

As the great-grandson of Herod the Great and son of Herod Agrippa I, who had persecuted the church (12:1–23), Herod Agrippa II (A.D. 27–c. 100) has an intimate knowledge of Jewish matters. Although influential in Jewish religious affairs because he had political authority to appoint the high priest, Agrippa II was unpopular with the Jews because of his incestuous relationship with his sister Bernice (25:13 note).

Knowing the background of Agrippa, Paul stresses his dependence on the God of his fathers (cf. 24:14) and his link to the Pharisees (Phil. 3:5, 6) in order to show that he continues to identify himself as a Jew.
Paul argues that God has promised the resurrection of the body. Although this is the belief of Jews in general and the Pharisees in particular, it is being used as the basis of charges against him.

Paul's experience on the road to Damascus (9:1–19) is so important to him that he recounts it twice, once before the Jewish crowd in the temple courtyard (22:6–16), and again before a Roman governor and a minor monarch whose family has ruled the Jewish people on Rome's behalf for several generations.

The record of Acts has borne witness to Christ's rescue of Paul from death at the hands of his Jewish kinsmen (9:29, 30; 13:50; 17:5–9; 18:12–17; 21:27–36; 23:12–35; 25:1–12) and of the Gentiles (14:19, 20; 16:19–39; 19:23–41), to whom he was commissioned (22:21; cf. Rom. 11:13).

Jesus and His apostles taught this doctrine from the Scriptures (17:2, 3; Luke 24:27; 1 Cor. 15:3, 4), yet unbelieving Jews rejected it, arrested Paul, and sought to kill him.

Agrippa faces a dilemma: if he says no, he will anger the Jews; if he says yes, he will lose face because Paul will urge him to acknowledge Jesus as the Messiah, in response to the testimony of the prophetic Scriptures.
The king uses a delaying tactic, arguing that a brief speech is insufficient time to become a Christian. In the first century, "Christian" (cf. 11:26) was probably a term of contempt (1 Pet. 4:16).

The consensus reached by Festus and Agrippa is that Paul is not guilty of any grave violation of Roman law, a conclusion reached earlier by other imperial officials (16:39; 18:14, 15; 25:18–20, 25). Agrippa, who understands Jewish issues well (26:3), concludes that Paul could be released if he had not invoked his right as a Roman citizen to appeal his case to the emperor. Festus still has no statement of charges to send with the prisoner to the imperial court.

Paul's ministry in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia concluded with a citation from Isaiah (13:47, citing Is. 49:6) and an announcement that the gospel that had been rejected by unbelieving Jews would be proclaimed to the Gentiles. Likewise, Acts concludes the account of Paul's ministry in Rome with a quotation from Isaiah concerning Israel's dull hearts, deaf ears and blind eyes (Is. 6:9, 10), and the declaration that God is sending his salvation to Gentiles, who will heed His word. These Jews continue to fulfill the prophecy of Israel's hardening that began even in Isaiah's own time and continued up until the time of Christ (e.g., see Matt. 13:14's "fulfilled" that introduces the same Is. 6:9, 10 text) and even up until Paul's own day.

From A.D. 60 to 62, Paul was under house arrest preaching and teaching to anyone who wanted to hear. His subject is summarized as the kingdom of God and Jesus Christ. At the end of Acts, Paul has not yet been tried before Nero, as the Lord said was going to happen (27:24). It appears that Paul expected to be acquitted and released (Phil. 1:25; 2:24; Philem. 22). This must have occurred before A.D. 64, when Nero set fire to Rome and accused Christians of that crime. When released, Paul seems to have taken up his ministry again, going as far as Greece (Nicopolis, Titus 3:12; Thessalonica, 2 Tim. 4:10), Crete (Titus 1:5), and Asia Minor (Ephesus, 2 Tim. 1:18; 4:12; Troas, 2 Tim. 4:13; Miletus, 2 Tim. 4:20). Possibly he went as far west as Spain (Rom. 15:23, 24, 28), as the first-century writing 1 Clement may indicate. In about A.D. 67, Paul was imprisoned again by Nero and executed. In 2 Tim. 4:6–8, Paul anticipates the end of his life.

Paul stresses the reality and universality of divine revelation, which is perpetual ("since the creation," v. 20) and perspicuous ("clearly perceived," v. 20). Divine invisibility, eternity, and power are all expressed in and through the created order (see theological note "Divine Revelation" on p. 850). The invisible God is revealed through the visible medium of creation and providence. This revelation is manifest; it is not obscured but is clearly seen.

Here Paul stresses that humanity not only has the opportunity to know God through general revelation, but that the revelation yields real knowledge. Human beings' ungodliness is their refusal to acknowledge, approve of, or delight in what they cognitively know to be true. Although at a deep level they cannot avoid awareness of their personal Creator, people refuse to honor Him as God or give thanks to Him. The consequence of rejecting God is that their minds and hearts have grown dark. A refusal to honor God leads all intellectual pursuits to frustration.

Intellectual arrogance before God displays a reversed sense of values; the worship of God is exchanged for devotion to man-made and man-reflecting idols. The indelible, God-given instinct to worship is perverted by being centered on the wrong object (v. 25).
Judgment involves the removal of divine restraints on both sinful actions and on their consequences (vv. 26, 28).

Exchanging God's truth for the lie that blurs the absolute distinction between the Creator, who alone deserves worship, and every product of His creative power and wisdom — whether individual creatures or the universe as a whole — is the source of all deluded thought and depraved practice that obscure and defy the distinctions by which He has ordered His creatures' natures and relationships (vv. 26, 27).

God judges fallen man's perversion of the divinely ingrained instinct to worship by giving sinful human beings over to the perversion of other instincts from their proper functions. Scripture views all homosexual actions in this light (Lev. 18:22; 21:13). The consequence is degradation of the body (v. 24), domination by lust, the disintegration of what is truly "natural" (i.e., in accordance with human nature as created by God; v. 26), and bondage to uncontrollable passions (v. 27).

Sin brings a disdain for God and what is pleasing to Him. It puts one in jeopardy of abandonment by God to a debased mind and a spirit of licentiousness (vv. 29–31). In Greek, "did not see fit" and "debased" have the same root: they did not "approve" acknowledging God, so He consigned them to a mindset that He did not "approve."

Paul sees as evidence of the guilt and bondage of sin that the knowledge of divine judgment no longer acts as a restraint, but it becomes a spur to further rebellion in the form of encouraging others to sin. This text confirms that God's revelation in nature communicates His moral character and a sense of moral duty in humanity.

In what follows, Paul turns to an imaginary representative of a real and identifiable group of people. Although he specifically mentions Jews only at v. 17, he probably has them in mind already. They agree with his statement about God's wrath against ungodly and unrighteous people, but assume that they stand outside of that wrath-deserving circle (hence his stern warning in v. 5). But the nature of this presumption, if not its specific form, is not limited to Jews but applies to God's people in every age. In this context, Paul sets forth the principles of the divine judgment all must face. It is based on truth (v. 2) and marked by righteousness (v. 5). It is according to works (v. 6), impartial in nature (v. 11), and executed through Christ (v. 16). Such judgment will bring agonizing ruin to all sinners (vv. 8, 9). 2:1 no excuse.
