Second, v. 25 suggests that an end to the partial hardening of Israel is in view. Third, "Israel" in v. 26 is not naturally interpreted as signifying a different entity from the Israel in view in vv. 1–24 and vv. 28–31, where national Israel (not spiritual Israel) is in view. Fourth, "mystery" — a matter known only through divine revelation — in v. 25 would seem inappropriate and exaggerated if Paul's teaching were simply that all elect Jews will be saved. Finally, this view accords well with the quotations in vv. 26, 27 from Is. 59:20, 21; 27:9; Jer. 31:33, 34, which appear to speak of a comprehensive banishment of that sin that has been the cause of Israel's alienation from God. 11:25 mystery. In Paul, and in Jewish thought generally, a divine secret that has now been revealed (16:25, 26; Eph. 3:3–9). Some interpreters conclude that what immediately follows constitutes the mystery (probably the widespread conversion of the Jews). Others hold that the mystery is the pattern of God's working in the Jew-Gentile interrelationship referred to in v. 11. The mystery may simply be the fact that, though it was evident that only a remnant of Israel would be saved in the latter days, it was not as clear according to OT prophecy that a majority of those saved would be Gentiles in comparison to only a remnant of saved Jews. fullness. The term may be taken to have a specifically numerical connotation. The ESV translates the same Gk. word as "full inclusion" in 11:12. has come in. An expression used infrequently by Paul, but commonly found in the Gospels to describe entrance into life or the kingdom of God (e.g., Mark 9:47).

A critical expression at this point in Paul's argument, and one whose meaning is much debated. It could mean "all (spiritual) Israel," that is, all elect persons, both Jew and Gentile. Alternately, it may mean "all" Israel in the sense of a remnant of "all Jews destined to be saved throughout history." Or, as also noted above, it may point to a time when a mass conversion of ethnic Jews to Christ will occur. The use of the term "Israel" to refer to the biological descendants of the patriarchs throughout Paul's discussion favors one of the last two interpretations. See note on 11:25–32, points (a), (b), and (c). The exegesis of "all Israel" will depend on the interpretation and weighing of other factors in the passage. The Deliverer will come from Zion. The quotation is from Ps. 14:7; Is. 27:9; 59:20, 21. Possibly Paul quotes this text in reference to the return of Christ from the heavenly Zion at the end of the age. Alternatively, it may refer to Christ's first coming, when "ungodliness" was banished by Jesus from those Jews who believed in Him, at which time Christ executed the new "covenant" (likely referred to at the end of v. 27, "when I \[God\] take away their sins"). The latter view accords most with the book of Hebrews, which sees Jesus' first coming to be the decisive time when He established the new covenant (e.g., Heb. 8:6–13; 10:1–16).

The presence of a believing remnant in Paul's day (including Paul himself) and the promise of God's ingathering of many more Jews to faith in Jesus the Messiah show that God has not revoked His calling and gifts to His ancient covenant people (9:6; 11:1, 2).

Paul's argument concludes in a manner parallel to 3:19–21, stressing that Jew and Gentile are united in two things: the disobedience of sin, and the offer to them of the mercy of God. The wisdom and sovereignty of God's grace are demonstrated in the way in which His purposes are fulfilled: the disobedience of the Jew leads to the Gentiles' receiving God's mercy; the mercy of God to the Gentiles leads to the reception of mercy by the Jews. There is no difference — all (Jew and Gentile alike) have sinned (3:23), and God has mercy on both (1:16).

Having drawn together the various strands of his argument, Paul now responds in lyrical fashion with a song of praise that reaches heights that correspond to the depth of concern he sounded in 9:2, 3. God's dealings with Jew and Gentile display a cross-section of His majesty in which His sovereign will ("from him"), His sovereign activity ("through him") and His sovereign glory ("to him") are richly displayed (v. 36).

The doxology at the end of ch. 11 and the nature of the opening verses of ch. 12 signal a new stage in Paul's exposition. Paul's "appeal" or exhortation, founded ("therefore") on God's mercies, turns the corner from his exposition of God's saving work to the response that God's grace should elicit from believers. From now until the conclusion of the letter, he focuses on applying his teaching to Christians' behavior and relationships. mercies of God. Paul can summarize the teaching of Rom. 3–11 in terms of God's undeserved favor to needy sinners. The biblical doctrine of grace leads to a life motivated by gratitude. present your bodies as a living sacrifice. Jew and Gentile now belong together as the people of God for whom the final blood sacrifice has been made (3:25). The sacrifice that remains is that of thankful response (cf. 6:17). "Bodies" means whole persons as embodied individuals (6:12, 13, 19; 8:13). Paul will use this sacrificial imagery in 15:16 to portray his "priestly" ministry as an apostle, bringing believing Gentiles as offerings in worship of his Lord (see Phil. 2:17). spiritual worship. The worship that is appropriate for redeemed creatures to offer (see text note, giving the alternative "rational service"). The Gk. term rendered "spiritual" here does not allude to God's Spirit (unlike, for instance, 1 Cor. 12:1), but distinguishes Christians' worship from the animal sacrifices of OT worship. Nevertheless, our worship is now undertaken by the power of the Holy Spirit (15:16).

Formerly, Christians were "futile in their thinking" (1:21). But now, the Christian's mindset is to be determined and reshaped by knowledge of the gospel, by the power of the Spirit, and by the concerns of the age to come (8:5–9; 13:11–14), rather than by the passing fashion of this age (2 Cor. 4:18; 1 John 2:17). Only by such sanctifying renewal is the Christian made sufficiently sensitive to "discern" the behavior that God's revealed will requires in each situation.

Paul's ministry exists only because of grace (1:5), as do spiritual gifts (Gk. charismata, v. 6). Realistic assessment of one's gift ("think with sober judgment") is essential, and involves a recognition of one's "measure of faith," that is, knowing to what extent one has the faith suited for exercising particular gifts (v. 6). The faith by which we are justified is a separate question.

As in 1 Cor. 12, Paul makes use of the analogy of the body and its various parts to illustrate the nature of the church. He stresses its unity (v. 5), its diversity (v. 6), and the need to recognize one's gift and to use it eagerly and appropriately in service to others (vv. 6–8).

To prophesy is, at its root, to speak the Word of God via the inspiration and calling of the Holy Spirit. In this sense, NT prophecy is identical to OT prophecy. Prophecy is distinguished here and elsewhere from teaching (v. 7; cf. Acts 13:1; 1 Cor. 12:29; Eph. 4:11) because it is a revelatory gift (Acts 13:1–3; 21:10, 11). in proportion to our faith. Some \`interpreters see "faith" as the prophet's own faith (cf. vv. 3, 6). Less plausibly, others understand "faith" to mean the truth content of the gospel as the standard and measure of each prophetic utterance (referred to in theology as "the analogy of faith"), a vital criterion for testing whether the utterance conforms to "the pattern of the sound words" (2 Tim. 1:13).

Paul recognizes the wide variety and practicality of these gifts (Gk. charismata) and the intertwining of natural endowments with them. Throughout this passage, it is clear that the blessing of those who are ministered to is the paramount consideration in using the gifts.

As in 1 Cor. 12; 13, when discussing the church as the body of Christ, Paul stresses the importance of love. His series of rapid exhortations carries echoes of Jesus' teaching and is expressed in vivid language. 12:9 be genuine. In classical Greek drama, the hypokrit?s (actor) wore a face-mask. The Christian's loving behavior should not be playing a part or wearing a mask, but an authentic expression of goodwill.
An unusual linguistic combination of brotherly love with the love of natural affection. The church is a family, the "household of God" (1 Tim. 3:15; cf. 1 Tim. 5:1, 2).

There must be no hesitation or sloth in Christian living. The Christian should be "fervent," living for Christ with enthusiasm and energy. The text note here and in Acts 18:25, where the same expression occurs, is probably correct to suggest that God's Spirit evokes and empowers believers' fervent eagerness to serve the Lord and His people.

Generosity toward believers in need distinguished the early believers' fellowship (Acts 2:42, 44–46; 4:32–37; Heb. 6:10; 13:16). hospitality. Hospitality for visiting Christians was another important part of early Christian life (Heb. 13:2; 3 John 5–8).
See Luke 6:27, 28.
See Luke 6:31. The genuine unity of the body of Christ is especially evident in the empathy of its members in moments of high joy or deep sorrow.

Paul's language gives the idea of Christians' sharing the same thoughts with respect to one another, another indication of the strategic role of the mind in sanctification (vv. 1, 2). One manifestation of this will be an absence of conceit and pride in worldly position (Phil. 2:1–8). Christians should be distinguished by their readiness to "associate with the lowly." Never be wise in your own sight. See Prov. 3:7. A further focus on the thought-world. How we think determines how we live.
The unifying theme in vv. 17–21 is the way the Christian reacts to the non-Christian environment.

The Christian is a peacemaker by obligation and aim. Harmony is not always possible, since truth divides as well as unites. Paul's double qualification ("If \... so far as") recognizes this, but the obligation to strive for peace in personal relations with others remains.

The Christian must be free from the desire to "get even." Such release from the instinct for revenge is possible because the believer knows that God will right all wrongs in His own perfect judgment (Deut. 32:35). Moreover, Scripture urges us to show grace to the wrongdoer because God is patient with him (Prov. 25:21, 22).
Doing good to an enemy may lead to his conscience's being pricked, and thus to his conversion, or it could at least lead to such a sense of shame that evil behavior is modified.

Christians have a distinct rationale for appropriate submission to the governing authorities: the recognition that God Himself is the source of government in society (Prov. 8:15, 16; Dan. 2:21). See theological note "Civil Government" on next page.
Rebellion against civil authority implies rebellion against God's ordinance (Ex. 22:28).

The state's authority is for the benefit of the governed, the defense of the innocent, and the restraint of evil behavior. These are its normal and divinely ordained functions, and Paul assumes that they may be realized in practical terms even when governments are professedly non-Christian. The NT also demonstrates, realistically, that human governments are quite capable of abusing justice (Rev. 13). the sword. The exercise of force by the civil magistrate (cf. 1 Pet. 2:13, 14). This power is given by God and must be used according to God's will. The civil magistrate may lawfully engage in defensive wars against aggression (cf. Deut. 20; 1 Chr. 5:22; Eccl. 3:8). The civil magistrate may also lawfully carry out capital punishment under specific conditions (cf. Gen. 9:6; Deut. 17:6, 7). Elsewhere Paul accepts the principle of such punishment where appropriate (Acts 25:11). wrath. What the individual must not do out of a motive of revenge (12:19), the state, as God's servant with a distinctive calling, may legitimately do in the pursuit of justice.

Christian submission is a response of the conscience as it is instructed by divine revelation. Because the task of government is divinely ordained and requires financial support, the Christian must pay taxes with a distinctive motive and understanding, as an element of obedience and devotion to God (Matt. 17:24–27; 22:15–21).

See Matt. 22:21. Paul is evidently familiar with Jesus' statement to "render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's," and here indicates how it is applied. On "honor," see 1 Pet. 2:17; Acts 23:2–5.

Paul now further applies his basic principle of Christian consecration. The connecting link between vv. 7 and 8 is found in the exhortation of v. 7 that the Christian has a financial obligation to the state. This is an application of a general principle now stated, that all obligations must be met. One obligation is permanent — to love others. 13:8 has fulfilled the law. See theological note "Antinomianism" on p. 2272. Since the law of God is the law of love (Matt. 22:38–40) and love of God and love of neighbor summarize our moral obligation, then truly loving one's neighbor (vv. 8, 9), or keeping the second table of the law, "fulfills" God's requirements (v. 10). Those who do not rely on their own law-keeping but on God's work in Christ are now empowered by His Spirit to progressively fulfill the law's righteous requirement (8:1–4).

See Lev. 19:18; theological note "Love" on p. 2036. This is not an encouragement to self-love, but rather a summons to extend to others the concern that we so naturally express in protecting and providing for ourselves (Luke 6:31).

Spiritual discernment is rooted in the apprehension of divine revelation. Paul's stress on the role of the mind is again evident. Paul wants the believer to live in the light of the return of Christ. salvation. Here in the sense of future, final redemption (5:9, 10; 8:23; 1 Thess. 5:9).

Paul speaks here of the "night" of this present age. The "light of the world" has come (John 8:12), and we must prepare for the second advent of Christ and the consummation of the age to come. let us cast off \... put on. The use of the metaphor "armor of light" stresses that developing positive spiritual graces, not merely rejecting vices, is essential to spiritual defense. Elsewhere, Paul lists pieces of this "armor" in contexts that similarly contrast daylight to night's darkness (1 Thess. 5:4–8; Eph. 6:10–20).

This passage played a crucial role in the conversion of Augustine of Hippo. Augustine wrote in his Confessions that upon reading these verses, "It was as though the light of confidence flooded my heart and all the darkness of doubt was dispelled." 13:13 Let us walk properly. Paul's warning against a sinful lifestyle strikingly includes not only the traditional sins of the body ("orgies and drunkenness \... sexual immorality and sensuality") but also insidious vices or practices that can be harbored in the heart or even paraded in the church ("quarreling and jealousy").

Paul now turns to address a specific application of the law of love to the Roman Christians. The Christian's basic attitude toward a fellow Christian is one of welcome and acceptance based on God's attitude to us in Christ (v. 3; 15:7). There must be charity toward the "weak" person whose conscience is still bound by scruples from which the gospel normally sets us free (v. 2). But those whose consciences still require them to abstain from meat (which is not in itself sinful) must refrain from condemning those who can consume it with a clear conscience (v. 3). Both "weak" and "strong" with respect to diet or calendar (vv. 5, 6) must welcome the other in deference to their common Lord, to whom each ultimately answers. quarrel over opinions. In this instance, questions of food, drink, and the religious observation of days. While Paul does not regard these controversies as insoluble, he regards the unity of the church's fellowship as more important than resolving them to everyone's satisfaction (cf. 12:5, 10, 16). The issues in view here do not belong to the gospel, but to the relative strength or weakness of the individual's faith in the gospel. Where essentials of the gospel are at stake, Paul's response is very different (e.g., Gal. 1:6, 7; 3:1–5; Phil. 3:2, 18, 19).

Vegetarianism is not required by the OT, though it appears there (e.g., Dan. 1:12). Possibly some in Rome have embraced a vegetarian diet to circumvent the issues of conscience surrounding the association of meat with pagan temple rituals (1 Cor. 8–10).

The tendency of those who better understand the gospel is to be impatient with the inhibitions of the "weak" as legalistic bondage. The temptation of the "weak" is to condemn the "strong" for behavior that seems to be lawless license. These mistaken responses should yield to the light of God's gracious acceptance of both "weak" and "strong." Furthermore, a fellow believer is God's servant, not ours, and is answerable to Him, not to us. It must be understood that the issues in such possible disputes are not matters of real morality, but of morally indifferent things.

A pattern of holy days characterizes the Jewish year, and it is to these days that Paul refers, and not the weekly Sabbath. If the Sabbath were in view it would have been more natural to say, "One man considers the Sabbath above the other days." Each one should be fully convinced. See 4:21 for another instance of this term. It is spiritually perilous to act contrary to one's conscience even if the conscience is weak and forbids what God Himself permits (vv. 14, 15; 1 Cor. 8:9–13).

An appeal to what is shared by both groups (v. 3), namely, the desire to honor the same Lord. That both belong to Him puts minor divisions into perspective. See theological note "The Kingdom of God" on p. 1823.

Christ alone is the Lord (v. 8) and Judge of His people. The cost to Him of this privilege was immense and exposes the inappropriateness of believers' judging or despising their brothers. We must give an account of our own lives to the Lord, as those being judged, not as those who judge.

While Paul's own conscience has been liberated by the teaching of Christ (v. 14; cf. Mark 7:18, 19) he recognizes that not all believers have come to enjoy such freedom. Consideration for such brethren ("walking in love," v. 15) means avoiding behavior that might distress them. Two specific injunctions to this effect follow in vv. 15, 16.

While Paul counsels stronger believers to be sensitive to the consciences of weaker believers, this statement, which the entire church will read, indirectly calls the weak believers to mature in the faith and understand that they are free in Christ to partake of His good gifts. Because nothing is unclean in itself, they may not exercise the "tyranny of the weaker brother" and impose their personal scruples regarding indifferent matters on other believers.

In the context of Jewish faith, "destroy" means to cut off from the covenant community (Deut. 28:21, 45, 48, 51, 61, 63). To encourage behavior that weak believers' consciences forbid is to encourage them to go against their conscience, a serious and dangerous act.

The strong are urged to weigh the importance of exercising their freedom against two considerations: (a) the use of their freedom may bring division and disrepute on the church; (b) God's kingdom (and therefore our freedom) is not a matter of food and drink, but of the blessings of grace (5:1, 2). Since freedom does not consist in these things, it cannot be lost by our refraining from them.
See v. 16. While God alone is our Judge (v. 12), the impact of our actions on others plays a vital role in fellowship and evangelism.

The believer's responsibility is now stated positively: avoiding the destruction of others is complemented by promoting "peace" and the things that "upbuild" (v. 19). For the "strong" (15:1), this includes both maintaining fellowship with the "weak" and also encouraging them to understand the liberty that is theirs in Christ. When such aims are in view, freedom to eat and drink will be made subordinate; the well-being of the brother will take precedence over the enjoyment of meat and wine.
Paul further urges the "strong" (15:1) to enjoy the fact of their liberty of conscience in God's presence (while refraining from publicly exercising it).

Paul considers himself one of the "strong." He sees the misinformed conscience of the "weak" as real weakness, yet he emphasizes the responsibility of the "strong" to be patient with the "weak." He does not encourage feelings of pride, or flaunting one's freedom in matters offensive to the weak.

. Paul will never modify the gospel for the sake of pleasing people (Gal. 1:10), but he is ready to forgo exercise of his liberty in Christ in order to serve and spiritually safeguard others. See 14:19; cf. 1 Cor. 8:1; 10:23, 24, 32, 33.

Paul quotes from Ps. 69, one of the most frequently quoted psalms in the NT (see 11:9–10; John 2:17; Acts 1:20). The willingness of the Messiah to deny Himself and suffer for the benefit of others should serve as an example to the Christians in Rome.
It is basic NT teaching that the OT Scriptures were written by divine inspiration for the benefit of Christians (1 Cor. 10:11; 2 Tim. 3:15–17; 1 Pet. 1:10–12).

See 10:9, 10. Unity in the church is essential if God is to be glorified. Paul has demonstrated that humanity has fallen short of God's glory but is restored to it in Christ's reconciling work (1:21, 23; 3:23; 5:2, 11; 8:17, 30).

The mutual acceptance of believers is rooted in Christ's humility (Mark 10:45). The ministry of Jesus the Messiah first of all to the lost sheep of Israel (Matt. 15:24) — "to the Jew first" (1:16) — confirms God's truthfulness in His fidelity to His promises, as Paul demonstrated at length in chs. 9–11. 15:9 the Gentiles. God's faithfulness in drawing a remnant of Israelites to faith in Christ gives Gentile believers reason to rely on His faithful Word, while the Gentiles' inclusion shows Jewish and Gentile believers alike that God keeps His promises not because He is indebted to His creatures but because of His mercy and faithfulness (see 11:30–32).

A series of quotations from three sections of the Hebrew Scriptures — the Law (v. 10, Deut. 32:43 LXX), the Prophets (v. 12, Is. 11:10), and the Writings (vv. 9, 11, Pss. 18:49; 117:1) — represents the unanimous testimony of the entire OT to God's intention to include the Gentiles with His people Israel in His worship and under His reign.

See theological note "Hope" on p. 2206. What was described as the effect of Scripture in v. 4 (having hope) and promised in the citation from Is. 11:10 (v. 12) is now attributed to the work of the Holy Spirit. Paul here follows a pattern evident throughout the NT: God's saving acts are attributed to God's Word as well as to the work of the Holy Spirit (e.g., regeneration, 1 Pet. 1:23; sanctification, John 17:17; salvation, Rom. 1:16; searching the heart, Heb. 4:12).

Paul now begins to draw his letter to a close by returning to the theme of its introduction — his own ministry and his vision for the expansion of the influence of the gospel. 15:14 my brothers. A further indication of deeply felt emotion (1:13; 7:1, 4; 11:25; 12:1). Paul graciously assures the Romans that his lengthy exposition of the gospel is not intended to raise doubts about their spiritual understanding. Their knowledge of the gospel and ability to apply it practically in mutual admonition ("able to instruct one another"; cf. Col. 3:16) is not in question.

Although Paul has not yet reached Rome, the largely Gentile composition of the congregations in the imperial capital brings these believers under his distinctive sphere of authority as apostle to the Gentiles (11:13; Gal. 2:7–9). priestly service of the gospel of God. Paul sees the preaching of the gospel as the means by which the Gentiles will be brought to God as a sacrificial thank offering (12:1). For similar uses of priestly sacrificial imagery, see Phil. 2:17; 4:18; Heb. 13:15, 16.
Paul describes his ministry very naturally in Trinitarian terms (God the Father, vv. 17, 18; God the Son, vv. 17–20; God the Holy Spirit, v. 19; cf. v. 16).

See Ex. 7:3; Deut. 4:34; 6:22; 7:19; Is. 8:18; Dan. 6:27. A phrase rooted in the authentication of Moses' ministry at the time of the exodus. God periodically gave such miracles at critical junctures of redemptive history, such as the exodus, the prophetic ministries of Elijah and Elisha, the preserving of His people in the time of Daniel, and the ministry of Christ and the apostles. These events are unusual rather than normal and point to the successive stages of redemptive history and the new revelation that accompanied them. As signs and wonders expressed God's endorsement of Jesus' ministry and claims (Acts 2:22–24; John 5:36), so Paul can invoke such signs as authenticating his own apostolic authority (2 Cor. 12:12; cf. Heb. 2:3, 4). from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum. Paul's journeys, according to Acts, stretched from the eastern Mediterranean as far west as Macedonia. There is no biblical record of his personally entering Illyricum (northwest of Macedonia). While he may have done so, it seems more likely that he means he went as far as Macedonia. He established centers of mission, rather than preaching personally in every village. From such centers, even Illyricum may have been reached with the gospel.
Paul's call is to focus on laying the foundation of the knowledge of Christ in communities where the gospel is unknown (1 Cor. 3:10, 11).

Two things now make the visit to Rome possible: (a) the present phase of Paul's commission has been fulfilled (he has "no \... room" to preach in the eastern Mediterranean because Christ's name has reached those region's urban centers, v. 20); (b) the new phase involving outreach to Spain is imminent, and Paul seeks their partnership in it.

Paul now discloses his immediate plans to visit Jerusalem with the gifts the Gentile churches raised for the Christians there (see 2 Cor. 8; 9). In this era, Jerusalem is an impoverished city in general; but additionally, the Christians there are suffering particular hardship as a suspect minority. But Paul sees a significance deeper than charity in the gift. It is a duty (v. 27), a solemn obligation of the Gentiles in view of the privilege they have received in being grafted into God's olive tree (11:17), coming to share in Israel's covenant relation to God through the gospel with its spiritual blessings. This reciprocity conforms to the general principle that those who receive spiritual blessings should share their own material blessings (1 Cor. 9:3–14; Gal. 6:6).

A striking comment in view of the manner in which Paul's aspirations are ultimately fulfilled, namely, in imperial custody (Acts 28:11–16) and facing unspecified charges that can, in principle, lead to execution (Phil. 1:19–21).

Paul's concern is twofold: (a) that he will be protected from the hostility of the unbelieving Jews that has pursued him for so much of the whole of his ministry (see Acts 21:27–22:39; 23:12–35); (b) that Jewish Christians in Jerusalem will respond favorably to the Gentile gift, and therefore to the apostle's ministry (v. 32; see Acts 21:17–20).
One of Paul's favorite designations for God (16:20; 2 Cor. 13:11; Phil. 4:9; 1 Thess. 5:23; 2 Thess. 3:16), but particularly appropriate here in regard to his present struggle (v. 30).

Paul's letters typically end with personal news and greetings. The closing chapter of Romans is remarkable for the large number of fellow believers mentioned. These verses give an insight into the warmth of the apostle's personal relationships as well as the fellowship of the early Christians. These greetings are especially noteworthy when we consider that Paul has not personally visited the church at Rome. He names so many among the believers at Rome to demonstrate his many personal ties with the congregations that make up this church in the imperial capital. 16:1 Phoebe. Probably the bearer of Paul's letter. The name is common in Greek mythology and indicates a Gentile background. a servant. Paul's word (Gk. diakonos) is variously translated as "servant" (1 Tim. 4:6), or "deacon" (Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:8). It is unlikely Paul uses the term to refer to the specific church office of deacon; he is instead describing Phoebe as a servant of the church in a more general sense. Cenchreae. The port of Corinth on the Saronic Gulf, indicating Paul's location when Romans was sent.

The couple were tentmakers like Paul (Acts 18:3). He was with them in Corinth. They had left Rome after the decree of Claudius and accompanied Paul to Ephesus (Acts 18:18). They taught Apollos (Acts 18:24–26) and later returned to Rome.
Evidently the first of a harvest of converts in the Roman province of Asia.
Paul recognizes the devoted service of women (v. 12).

Early commentators understood these to be a husband and wife. They were fellow Jews, and had been converted ("in Christ") before Paul himself. They had apparently been in prison at some time with Paul (cf. 2 Cor. 11:23) and had served with distinction. well known to the apostles. Some translate this as "outstanding among the apostles" (e.g., NIV) and use these words to justify women's ordination, though the ESV's rendering is the better translation. Either way, it must be recalled that the word "apostle" is used not only in a technical sense for the Twelve and Paul, but in a nontechnical sense as well, referring to church envoys (text note; 2 Cor. 1:1 note). Paul is elsewhere clear that only men may be ordained to the office of "overseer," i.e., elder. (1 Tim. 3:1–7)
Probably a slave, whose name appears on a tomb in the Catacomb of Domitilla, niece of the Emperor Domitian.
Common slave names, the former Roman, the latter Greek.

A common Greek name. It is likely that Paul declares him "approved in Christ" because he had distinguished himself through trial and remained faithful. Aristobulus. This may be the grandson of Herod the Great and friend of the Emperor Claudius.

Perhaps a freedman of the household of Herod, since freedmen took the name of their patron. Narcissus. Perhaps to be identified with Narcissus, the aide of Claudius, who was forced to commit suicide by Agrippina after Nero's accession.
Two women with names from a common root ("gentle," "delicate") and who were therefore possibly sisters. Persis. Another woman, recognized for her diligent work for the Lord.

One of the most intriguing of the names listed in view of Mark 15:21, a gospel possibly written from Rome. "Chosen" may reflect the unique circumstances that brought his family into contact with Christ. Simeon of Cyrene, whom soldiers compelled to carry Jesus' crossbeam to the place of execution, had two sons, Alexander and Rufus, who were presumably known to Mark's readers. The Rufus whom the apostle mentions here may be the same Rufus who was the son of Simon. Paul's allusion to the mother as "his mother \... to me as well" suggests deep affection for the family.

The kiss remains a common token of greeting in the East even to this day. Here and elsewhere, Paul urges the believers to sanctify their greetings as symbols of Christian fellowship (1 Cor. 16:20; 2 Cor. 13:12; 1 Thess. 5:26), and the practice was also enjoined by Peter for the churches of Asia Minor (1 Pet. 5:14).

Reflection on his knowledge of these believers, their problems in Rome (ch. 14), and the divisive activity of Satan (v. 20) evokes an urgent summons for Christians to guard their unity (Eph. 4:3). They are to avoid those "who cause divisions \... contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught." Bluntly, he indicates that their divisive spirit is sinful, a mark of life in the flesh, and a form of self-indulgence (Gal. 5:19, 20). Christians must learn not to be deceived by "smooth talk and flattery" (v. 18).

Not surprisingly, the faith of Jesus' followers living in the capital of the vast Roman Empire (1:8) and the obedience that flowed from that faith have become well known throughout the Greco-Roman world. innocent. The Romans need spiritual wisdom and hearts without any taint of evil.

Prior to the closing greetings and doxology, Paul includes a promise of a prophetic nature, rooted in the first biblical deliverance promise in Gen. 3:15 (see Ps. 91:13; Luke 10:18, 19). Satan stands behind what is "evil" (v. 19; cf. Gen. 3:12; see also theological note "Satan" on p. 760). "The God of peace" (wholeness and integrity as well as tranquility) will act as the divine warrior to overcome him. This will take place "soon." Paul is speaking here about the last things, which by faith are always seen as near at hand. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. A characteristically Pauline ending (Gal. 6:18; 1 Thess. 5:28).

Along with Silas, Timothy was Paul's closest coworker after the disagreement with Barnabas (Acts 15:36–40) and is mentioned in ten of Paul's letters. Lucius (whom some identify with Luke), Jason (possibly Paul's host in Thessalonica, Acts 17:5–9), and Sosipater (Acts 20:4) were possibly church delegates accompanying Paul to deliver the collection in Jerusalem.
Paul regularly used a secretary, identifying his letters as his own by a brief greeting written in his own handwriting (1 Cor. 16:21; Gal. 6:11; Col. 4:18; 2 Thess. 3:17).

Paul may have been residing with Gaius at the time of writing. He is presumably to be identified with the Gaius of 1 Cor. 1:14, and may be the (Gaius?) Titius Justus of Acts 18:7. An Erastus is mentioned in Acts 19:22 and 2 Tim. 4:20. We do not know whether this is the same man. Of greater interest is that a Christian held a post of such responsibility in the local government of Corinth, a fact that illustrates that the earliest Christians could and did render faithful service in governmental positions (see 13:1–7). Of Quartus nothing is known.

The authenticity of this closing doxology is questioned by some on the grounds of its length, its emphasis on mystery, and its textual history (it is found at different points in the letter, or even omitted altogether in various ancient manuscripts). There is, however, a certain appropriateness about its length, coming at the end of a letter like Romans. Its themes draw to a fitting conclusion much that has already been said. In particular, Paul draws attention to his own teaching of the gospel (2:16; cf. 1 Thess. 1:5; 2 Tim. 2:8) and its power to edify (1:11), to the revelation of God's mystery (11:25; cf. Eph. 3:2–6), to faith and obedience among the nations (1:5), and to the wisdom of God in redemption (11:33; cf. Eph. 3:10–12).

Paul's "now" might suggest that he is referring to the NT Scriptures, but his emphasis is that it is only now that the message already enshrined in the OT and "now" "disclosed" in the light of Christ's coming is spread to the nations, as he noted earlier in 1:2 and 3:21.

1 Corinthians.note: Someone commissioned directly by Christ as His authoritative messenger (2 Cor. 1:1 note). Paul explains the significance of this office elsewhere (ch. 9; 15:1–11; 2 Cor. 10–12; Gal. 1). Some of the problems in the Corinthian church that Paul addresses involve challenges to his authority. Sosthenes. Perhaps the same person mentioned in Acts 18:17, ruler of the synagogue in Corinth at the time of Paul's first visit to the city.

The word "saints" (lit. "holy ones") calls attention to the distinctive status of God's people as those set apart by God for Himself. Paul often uses it to identify the Christians to whom he writes (e.g., Rom. 1:7). The description "sanctified" underlines this reality of the Christian life. The Corinthians were plagued by ethical problems and this letter touches repeatedly on the subject of holiness. Significantly, however, Paul encourages them here in a pastoral way by reminding them that by God's grace they have already made a definitive break with sin and now serve the Lord Jesus Christ (6:11). The goal of progressive holiness is realistic because God has already changed their hearts (Rom. 6:1–14; Gal. 5:24, 25).

The Corinthians were tempted to become puffed up by their gifts of "knowledge" and of speaking "in tongues" (8:1; 14:23). Paul needs to rebuke them for their self-centered and loveless misuse of those gifts (12:14–26; 13:1–3, 9–13; 14:4–5), but he does not deny or minimize the spiritual gifts they have received (v. 7).

Paul encourages his readers by assuring them that God, who began a work of grace in them, can be trusted to complete it. Indeed, they will be presented "guiltless" at the time of Christ's return. Note the similarities between vv. 8, 9 and Phil. 1:6, 10 (cf. Eph. 5:26, 27; 1 Thess. 5:23, 24).

This exhortation begins the body of the letter and announces Paul's primary concern. He has heard (vv. 11, 12) that the unity of the Corinthian church has broken down. Many of the problems addressed in this letter (parties, lawsuits, tensions between "strong" and "weak," indifference to the poor at the Lord's Supper, boasting about spiritual gifts) reflect the spirit of dissension that was in the community.
Chloe must have been an influential Christian, perhaps a member of the Corinthian church, although she is not mentioned elsewhere.

An effective preacher from Alexandria who had ministered in Ephesus and Corinth (Acts 18:24–19:1). Paul will stress that he and Apollos have distinct and complementary ministries as servants privileged to co-labor with God (3:5–15). Paul's later report that he had urged Apollos to return to Corinth (16:12) shows their respective parties that he and Apollos did not view each other as rivals, but enjoyed mutual respect and unity. Cephas. The Aramaic name (meaning "rock," as does the Gk. petros) given by Jesus to Simon Peter (John 1:42). Paul acknowledged that Peter was regarded as among the "pillars" of the church (Gal. 2:8–9). Peter's prominence in the dissemination of the gospel is evident in the book of Acts. He was obviously popular among some groups in Corinth (perhaps the Jewish Christians), but it is unclear whether he had actually visited the church.

With this question, Paul anticipates one of his fundamental teachings about the church. Just as a physical body, though made up of many members, is one, so also the church, which is the body of Christ, cannot be divided (10:16, 17; 12:12 note).

The facts that Paul did not invoke his own name in baptizing but that of Christ (v. 13; Acts 2:38) and that he personally baptized few in Corinth (see v. 16) show that the apostle had no interest in enlisting a group of devotees for himself. Crispus. The synagogue ruler whose conversion is recorded in Acts 18:8. Gaius. A common name. Perhaps this is the Gaius described in Acts 19:29.

Paul's first converts in Corinth, respected for their dedication. Stephanas himself was one of the representatives who brought a communication from the Corinthians to Paul (16:15–17). See theological note "Infant Baptism" on p. 41.

The Corinthian church had an unhealthy regard for rhetorical display. Paul will focus attention on what true wisdom is (1:18–2:16; 3:18–23). In this verse, he reminds the Corinthians that the power of his own preaching in Corinth did not depend on such skills (2:1–5). cross of Christ. In the opinion of those who are wise according to this world, proclaiming the crucified Lord is foolishness. Paul therefore treats "wisdom" and "the cross" as opposites (v. 23 note).

According to the Bible, there will be two types of response to the gospel arising from God's elective purpose (Is. 6:9, 10; Luke 2:34; Rom. 9:10–13; 2 Cor. 2:15, 16; 1 Pet. 2:6–8). This truth does not make God responsible for the perishing of unbelievers; they perish because of their own sin and stubborn impenitence. Those who believe and are saved, on the other hand, are "those who are called" (v. 24; cf. Rom. 9:16).

It is not clear whether Paul intends a sharp distinction between these three categories. Possibly the first is general in character, while the other two are specifically Jewish scribes and Greek teachers. this age \... the world. Much of Paul's theology is built on the basic opposition between "the present evil age" (Gal. 1:4), or world, which is characterized by "the flesh" (human nature under the adverse effects of the fall), and the coming age of life and blessing, which has already dawned for those who have received the Spirit (10:11; Gal. 5:16, 17; Eph. 1:13, 14; 2:6; Phil. 3:20).

This passage is filled with intense irony. Those who are wise according to the standards of the world think the gospel is foolish, since it identifies one who has suffered shameful crucifixion as the unique and only remedy to the plight of humanity. But even the most "foolish" thing about God is wiser than human wisdom (vv. 25, 27). God can use the simplicity and seeming shamefulness of the gospel's central event, the cross, to demonstrate that real foolishness belongs to those who oppose Him (v. 27). The arrogance of human wisdom blinds unbelievers to the truth. Jesus thanked the Father for His good pleasure in hiding these things from the wise and learned but revealing them to little children (Matt. 11:25, 26).

Paul identifies precisely what the world finds offensive about the gospel (cf. v. 17; 2:2). Possibly these words also reflect the reason for Paul's opposition to the gospel before his conversion. The thought that the Messiah (God's anointed) had been hanged on a tree and thereby came under the divine curse (Gal. 3:13; Deut. 21:23) was intolerable to many Jews.
God's wisdom and power are not abstract forces but personal qualities that manifest themselves fully in the life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ (v. 30; Rom. 1:4, 16; Col. 2:1–3).

Salvation, by its very nature, does not depend on human values or achievement. Even those in the Corinthian church who might have been justly admired could not have claimed that they were chosen because of any good in them. Rather, God has mercy on all who acknowledge their sinfulness (Mark 2:17; John 9:39–41). See theological note "Effectual Calling" on p. 2146. not many were wise \... powerful \... of noble birth. God's election is not contingent or conditioned on qualities that He discerns in those whom He chooses. Moses reminded the Israelites that God had chosen them despite the fact that as a people they were both few (Deut. 7:6–8) and rebellious (Deut. 9:4–6). Likewise, most of the believers in Corinth lacked the wisdom prized by Greeks, the power admired by Romans (and Jews), and the pedigree admired by Greeks, Romans, and Jews. They had also been lacking in ethical purity until God's grace washed and sanctified them in Christ (6:9–11).

This principle, which Paul underscores in v. 31 by quoting Jer. 9:24, provides the foundation for the biblical doctrine of salvation: it is a gracious gift from God that rules out human boasting (Eph. 2:8, 9).

See note on v. 24. Paul explains how Jesus is "wisdom" to the believer. He is "our righteousness," by which we are justified (Rom. 3:21–26); He is "our sanctification" — the one by whose grace we are set apart to God (1:2) and progressively renewed (Rom. 6:1–23); He is "our redemption" — the one whose death and resurrection ensures that we, soul and body will be fully redeemed from sin's guilt (Eph. 1:7) and its penalty, death (Rom. 8:23).

Paul must be referring to his first visit to Corinth, recorded in Acts 18:1–17 (Introduction: Date and Occasion). with lofty speech or wisdom. Influenced by Greek culture, some of the Christians in Corinth may have been critical of Paul for not using the rhetorical techniques of their contemporaries (2 Cor. 11:5, 6). See notes on 4:1, 8–13; 9:3, 19; 10:30; 16:3.
See note on 1:23. Paul here identifies the substance of his preaching (Gal. 3:1; 1 Cor. 15:1ff.).

Taken by themselves, these verses might suggest that Paul was timid, uneducated, and unable to speak with force and eloquence. Both the book of Acts (e.g., 19:8) and Paul's own letters (ch. 13) prove otherwise. Yet some found Paul's oral delivery to fall short of the standards of Greek rhetoric (2 Cor. 10:10) and his personal appearance to be unattractive (2 Cor. 10:10; cf. Gal. 4:12–15). "Self-confidence," if it rests on arrogance concerning one's own strength, reflects a desire to be independent from God. Paul had learned that God can use human weakness to show forth His own glory (2 Cor. 12:7–10). Because he knew that men and women will be convinced by the gospel only "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power," Paul used his talents and training with a full and proper confidence in God, rather than relying on his own skills.

Lit. "perfect." The apostle does not have in mind a special category of elite Christians, an idea that may have been present among the Corinthians. Paul may be taking a term in use by the Corinthians and assigning it its proper meaning (see Phil. 3:15). Paul's expression here is no doubt equivalent to "spiritual" (vv. 13, 15; 3:1), referring to the influence of the Holy Spirit. The mature or spiritual person is the person in whom the Holy Spirit dwells and whose life the Holy Spirit directs (cf. v. 14). Since every true believer has received the Spirit, every believer is spiritual and can understand God's wisdom, the gospel of Jesus Christ. we do impart wisdom. The gospel, the proclamation of Christ crucified. Throughout this section (vv. 6–16), the "we" for whom Paul speaks are primarily the apostles, who receive revelation by the Spirit (v. 10) and speak it in Spirit-taught words (v. 13). Yet every believer has received God's Spirit and has thereby been enlightened to receive the apostolic message, which has been set into writing in the New Testament so that the church may have it in the post-apostolic age.

This passage should not be interpreted as a reference to mysteries accessible only to superior Christians. The riches of the gospel, though "hidden" during the OT period, have now been revealed by the Spirit (v. 10). Eph. 3:2–6 makes plain that the word "mystery" has a strong temporal meaning. The "mystery" is a truth that "was not made known \... in other generations" (Eph. 3:5); it was "kept secret for long ages" (Rom. 16:25). But now the truth has been clearly revealed to all those who have the Spirit, who live in "the end of the ages" (10:11). The "mystery" (mysterion) is something partially hidden in the OT that is now revealed in the NT as an end-time reality. (The word "mystery" occurs in the Septuagint only in Daniel 2 \[e.g., 2:28–29\] as a latter-day idea associated with the establishment of God's kingdom on earth.) At least part of the mystery here is that the Messiah suffers as "the Lord of glory," but the NT more clearly reveals that the Messiah is the glorious Lord God in the midst of suffering, reigning at the same time that He seems to be defeated by Satan on the cross and while He is bearing the divine curse on sin ("Lord" is the translation of the covenant name Yahweh in the OT, which is now applied to Jesus). It is this that "the rulers of this age" did not "understand." decreed. The word is used also in Rom. 8:29, 30 and Eph. 1:5 to express the certainty of God's goodwill for His people.

Unbelievers are still part of the old age and so have not received God's wisdom (v. 14). Paul emphasizes this point by focusing on the most influential members of society (1:20). The rulers' ignorance of God's mysterious plan did not excuse their crime (cf. Luke 23:34). crucified the Lord of glory. Although the incarnate Son of God suffered crucifixion with respect to His human nature, the unity of His two natures, divine and human, in one person makes it fitting for Paul to associate Christ's divine title "Lord of glory" with His human vulnerability to the anguish of death. See note on Acts 20:28.

In contrast to the wise of this world (who cannot even conceive of the greatness of divine salvation), those who love God both perceive and experience His blessings. The quotation is based on Is. 64:4, but it includes other ideas found in the OT.

See theological note "The Illumination of the Holy Spirit." searches everything. The idea of divine searching (cf. Ps. 139:1; Rom. 8:27) emphasizes God's omniscience, particularly His power to see what is invisible to humans (John 2:25). It does not imply that the Holy Spirit needs to seek knowledge of the Father that He otherwise lacks. The Spirit probes the depths of divine knowledge for our benefit.

This verse intends to make a common-sense observation, not to give an analysis of human personality. "Spirit" refers generally to the immaterial part of a human being, especially human mental faculties (v. 16 note).

The precise meaning of this clause is disputed. As the text note suggests, Paul may be restating and combining the points of vv. 10 and 13: as an apostle, Paul speaks the content revealed by the Spirit in the words given to him by the Spirit (2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:20–21). Probably Paul had been criticized in Corinth for not using human eloquence and wisdom (v. 1 note). In reply, he says that the truths revealed by the Spirit must be explained in a way that is harmonious with the Spirit.

The "natural" person, who still belongs to the old age, is contrasted with the one who is "spiritual," that is, one who is united to Christ, indwelt by His Spirit, and therefore belongs to the age to come. Note Nicodemus' confusion when Jesus speaks of being born from above by the Spirit (John 3:1–12).
The apostle may be responding to individuals who opposed him and passed negative judgments on him (v. 1 note).

Through the Spirit of the Lord, Paul has the mind of Christ, and therefore the mind of the Lord. Those opponents who do not see that the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of the Lord are one and the same have no warrant to instruct or examine him. By implication, those who accept Paul's teaching have the blessing of the Spirit and understand the things of God. Paul probably alludes to Is. 40:13, which associates the infinity of God's Spirit with His boundless wisdom and knowledge (cf. Rom. 11:34).

That is, belonging to the Holy Spirit (2:6 note). people of the flesh. "Flesh" is Paul's main word for describing the present evil age. Since the Corin­thians had received the Holy Spirit, they were spiritual in the most fundamental sense, but their behavior was so inconsistent with that truth that Paul had to treat them as people who had little understanding of what it means to think and live as those who belong to the new age.
See note on 1:10. These behaviors characterize life in the flesh, or this present evil age (cf. the works of the flesh in contrast to the fruit of the Spirit in Gal. 5:19–23).
Paul's aim was to preach the gospel in places where the message of Christ had not been heard (Rom. 15:20). Apollos. See note on 1:12.

Paul may mean either that Christian workers are co-laborers with God or that Christians who are co-laborers with one another belong to God. Paul's point is clear from the context: God alone is responsible for the success of Christian ministry (v. 7). For this reason, it is folly to boast in human ministers.

A clear allusion to the previous discussion of true wisdom (1:17; 2:9, 10 notes). The biblical concept of wisdom is broad enough to include artisans' skills useful in construction (Ex. 31:2–6; 2 Chr. 2:13, 14), the metaphor for gospel ministry that Paul employs here. foundation. As one called to proclaim the gospel where it was not known (v. 6 note), Paul had resolved to preach nothing but Christ crucified (v. 11; 2:2; cf. 1 Pet. 2:4–6).

These verses address the evaluation of Christian ministry. Some ministers who were seeking to build God's building in Corinth, but who depended on human wisdom, were using perishable materials ("wood, hay, straw") that would not survive the judgment of God's fire, while the builders themselves would barely escape destruction. Without pressing Paul's imagery too far, the perishable materials may be interpreted as either unsound teaching or the superficial and ephemeral "converts" that such teaching attracts for a time. Paul warns the church that they, like Solomon's temple (1 Chr. 22:14–16), should be built up with what is lasting.

God signaled His presence in the temple by filling it with the cloud of His glory (1 Kin. 8:10, 11). Now He lives in His people by the Holy Spirit. Paul's focus here is on God's people as a corporate whole; in 6:19, the emphasis shifts to the individual Christian's body.
Paul leaves open the possibility that some of the Christian builders in Corinth are not only using perishable material but are actively destroying God's work. They will not be spared at the judgment.

Here the apostle returns more directly to the contrast between human and divine wisdom (v. 10 note), between the wisdom characteristic of this age — the flesh — and that of the age to come — the Spirit.

See note on 1:29. all things are yours. This principle demonstrates the pettiness and absurdity of the Corinthians' quarreling. If we belong to Christ, then because of Him all things belong to us (Rom. 8:17, 38, 39; Heb. 1:2), including each of the teachers around whom the cliques in Corinth gathered. Since every true gospel minister — whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas — is Christ's gift to His whole church, rivalry and jealousy are needless and unfitting. How little the Corinthians appreciated their Christian privileges is pointed out again in 6:2. Paul will develop this point further in his treatment of spiritual gifts (1 Cor. 12–14).

Lest his reminder of the believers' privilege tempt them to pride, Paul hastens to repeat that though he and Apollos are their servants (v. 5), their owner is Christ, who in turn belongs to God the Father, whose purpose and plan He came to accomplish (John 6:38).

These verses show that Paul was being judged and attacked by at least some of the Corinthians (2:1 note). stewards. The steward was the preeminent servant in a Greco-Roman household, managing his master's finances, property, and other slaves. Owning virtually nothing but controlling virtually everything, the steward wielded vast delegated authority, but always with accountability to the master to "be found faithful" (cf. Luke 12:42–48; 16:1–13, where the same Gk. word is rendered "manager"). mysteries. See note on 2:7.
Though Paul's conscience is clear (v. 5), ultimately only God determines whether one has proved faithful.

Not an absolute command (5:2; 6:2), but a warning not to usurp Christ's role as judge in pronouncing final judgment. Paul speaks here to illegitimate criticisms raised against him. bring to light the things now hidden. At the judgment, nothing will escape God's searching light (Matt. 10:26 and parallels).

In this powerful passage, the apostle makes use of biting irony to show the Corinthians how trivial are their concerns and how unfair their criticisms. The sufferings of Paul are comparable to the pain and public humiliation of captives condemned to die (2 Cor. 11:23–30). In contrast, some of the Corinthians think of themselves as notably successful, but only because they do not understand what it means to be "fools for Christ's sake" (v. 10) — not to behave nonsensically, but to identify with Christ's cross, which seems foolish to the perishing but is God's true wisdom (1:18–25). The deprivation, contempt, and manual labor experienced by the apostles disqualify and devalue their mission in the eyes of the world and of many in the church as well (2 Cor. 11:12 — 12:11).
Paul's pastoral heart is revealed in these words. The harsh language of the previous passage was not intended to make them feel inferior but to raise their sensitivity to the truth.

The Corinthians boasted of their allegiance to Apollos, Peter, and others, with the implication that they had no need for Paul. The apostle reminds them that his fatherly relationship to them is unique and they have no good reason to attack him.
As the believers' spiritual father, Paul consciously sets an example of selfless suffering to be followed by his children in Christ Jesus (11:1; Phil. 3:15–17).
Timothy had left prior to the writing of this letter (16:10 note). As Paul's spiritual child, Timothy will show in his character and conduct what imitating Paul looks like (see Phil. 2:19–22).

Some in Corinth argued that Paul was bold only when absent and that he was afraid to meet them face to face (2 Cor. 10:1, 2). He sent Timothy to them (v. 17), apparently to avoid an ugly confrontation, but he will not hesitate to come in person. It is up to them what will happen when that visit takes place (v. 21; 2 Cor. 13:1–10).

The man's father may have died, or the woman may have been a stepmother (more likely, since she is not called the man's "mother"). In any case, the sexual relationship in view is the incestuous union explicitly condemned in Lev. 18:8. Though the Greco-Roman culture of Paul's day tolerated a wide array of immoral activities, even Gentiles censured this kind of incest.

This verse is the key to Paul's real concern. The underlying problem here was not the sin of one individual, but the failure of the Corinthian church to deal with the sin — indeed, their sense of pride in tolerating it (v. 6). Possibly, the Corinthians had developed a theology that could accommodate such immorality under the guise of celebrating their liberty in Christ from the restrictions of God's law, articulated in their slogan, "all things are lawful for me" (6:12; 10:23). They needed to grasp their responsibility to exercise discipline and defend Christ's reputation by excommunicating the offender ("removed from among you").

A very difficult passage. Though Paul is physically absent from the Corinthian community, he claims to pass authoritative judgment in their midst. The apostle is commanding the church to expel the offender from their fellowship ("deliver this man to Satan"). The purpose of this judgment is the reclamation of the offender, but that can be achieved only if his sinful tendencies are overcome ("the destruction of the flesh"). According to one interpretation of 2 Cor. 2:5–11, this man did repent of his sin. See theological note "Excommunication" on p. 1703.

See notes on v. 2; 1:29. leaven. Leaven is a common biblical metaphor for a corrupting influence (Matt. 16:11–12; Gal. 5:9). During the annual Feast of Passover, the Israelites removed all leaven from their houses (Ex. 12:15). So another purpose for church discipline, besides reclaiming the sinner (v. 5) and upholding Christ's reputation for purity (v. 1; see 1 Pet. 2:11–12), is to protect other believers from being influenced toward evil by the offender's example and the church's condoning complacency.

Paul makes this important qualification to encourage the Corinthians; in a fundamental sense, they are already purified (1:2 note). He calls the Corinthians to embrace a lifestyle in keeping with their identity in Christ. Christ, our Passover. The apostle develops the imagery by suggesting that the death of the Passover lamb instead of Israel's firstborn (Ex. 12–13), as a shadow of better things to come (Heb. 10:1), pointed forward to the death of Christ.

The final, and especially beautiful, step in Paul's argument is to draw a parallel between the Feast of Unleavened Bread and the life of purity that Christians should lead. This parallel helps us to understand the spiritual realities to which the OT ceremonies point (cf. Col. 2:16).

Prior to the writing of 1 Corinthians, Paul had sent a letter (no longer in existence) instructing the Corinthians to separate themselves from believers who practiced immorality. The Corinthians either misunderstood Paul, as if he were commanding complete separation from the world, or they tried to sidestep the issue by arguing that his request was unreasonable. The apostle explains that he had in mind anyone thought to be a Christian whose life openly contradicted the faith. The injunction to expel offenders ("not even to eat with such a one") has primary reference to community life within the church and probably does not mean that all personal contact must be avoided ( "warn him as a brother"; 2 Thess. 3:15).

By quoting the frequent command in Deuteronomy (e.g., Deut. 17:7) to purge or expel the wicked from Israel, Paul draws an important parallel between the OT covenant community and the Christian church (10:1–11), while also implying a difference. Ancient Israel was to maintain its communal purity through banishment and execution, whereas in the new covenant the church's disciplinary means are spiritual rather than physical. The church has authority to exercise discipline within its own fellowship, not to regulate the behavior of non-Christians. Paul assumes that believers can discern the boundary between those who are members of the church and under its spiritual supervision and those who are "outside" (Matt. 18:15–17).

With this verse, Paul appears to change the topic from the evils of immorality to the problem of lawsuits among Christians. It is important, however, to notice the connection. In the first place, the topic of immorality has not been abandoned, but will recur in v. 9 and vv. 12–20. Second, the failings of the Corin­thians with regard to lawsuits are an expression of the problem already discussed in ch. 5, namely, a weak doctrine of the church. Just as Christians are not responsible to regulate the lives of non-Christians, so non-Christians have no power to discipline in the church. If the Corinthians understood the relation between the Israelite community and the Christian fellowship (5:12, 13 note), they would realize it was absurd for believers to go outside the church to solve their disputes. Who could imagine a pagan Gentile settling disputes among Israelites in the wilderness? This text does not, however, negate the legitimate role of civil authorities to judge matters that God has put under them. See theological note "Civil Government" on p. 2004.

The absurdity of the situation in Corinth becomes clearer when one recognizes that, in the consummation of history (but not before; 5:12, 13), Christians will participate with Christ in judging not only unbelievers but also wicked angels. Even the least qualified among the Corinthians, since he has received God's Spirit and wisdom (2:14–16), is in a better position than an unbeliever to arbitrate disputes in the church.

This remarkable question makes obvious how critical is the principle of community for the apostle. The point is not that Christians should be encouraged to acquiesce passively to abuse from others. After all, cheating and injustice should not even exist within the Christian community. That such injustices do exist, and are indeed performed by Christians against one another, demonstrates how far the Corinthians have fallen. Nevertheless, if the Corinthians understood the serious implications of all the improprieties in their church, and if they appreciated the qualities that should characterize believers (cf. 13:4–7), they would much sooner bear injustice than bring disgrace upon the Christian community by publicly exposing their conflicts in the civil courts.

See theological note "Antinomianism" on p. 2272. That the things of this world are incompatible with the kingdom of God is a recurring principle in Scripture (15:50; Gal. 5:21). The question arises whether anyone at all can be saved, since none is sinless. Paul's answer is twofold: on the one hand, God delights in justifying the wicked (Rom. 4:5); on the other hand, those whom God justifies (declares righteous because of Christ's death) He also sanctifies (leads into a holy way of life; Rom. 6:1–4). Paul charitably regards the Corinthians in terms of their profession as believers, justified and sanctified (v. 11 note), and therefore considers their present misbehavior as an anomaly that can be corrected. But it must be corrected. Persistence in wickedness would be an indication that their possession of faith is false and that they have no true place in the kingdom.

See notes on 1:2; 5:7; theological note "The Holy Spirit as Sanctifier" on p. 2023. The saving work of God's Spirit through Jesus' name includes not only legal vindication ("justified") but also subjective purification and transformation ("sanctified").

Paul may be quoting sayings, probably common in Corinth, that were used to excuse immoral behavior (note the repetition, again with qualifying corrections, at 10:23). The apostle's corrective rejoinders suggest that, even if there is an element of truth in these slogans, the Corinthians have perverted it. Indeed, his qualifications have the effect of denying the very point of the sayings, and he ends by emphasizing the noble purpose for which God has given us bodies. Freedom in Christ is deployed in what is "helpful" to others, and does not lead us into being "dominated" by sinful desires, a senseless return to enslavement. Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food. Another Corinthian slogan, this may assume a parallel between hunger for food and the sexual drive as a pretext for justifying any form of sexual indulgence as natural and irresistible. Paul will not permit such trivializing of sexuality, nor of the physical body itself. Its appointed end, for Christians, is not destruction in the grave but resurrection by God's power to enjoy eternal blessing in the new heaven and earth (15:20–23, 35–58; Rev. 21:1–8). Those who die before the return of Christ and the final resurrection enjoy a spiritual existence with Christ in heaven (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:21–23), and their spirits will be reunited with their bodies at the resurrection.

This reference to the resurrection is unexpected here, and probably reflects the connection between inadequate doctrine and deficient life. Many of the Corinthians appear to have mistakenly denied the future bodily resurrection, believing that Christians have been fully been brought out of this age and fully brought into the age to come (ch. 15; 15:35 note). This was an erroneous understanding of eschatology (the last things), in which the only resurrection that is to take place is a spiritual resurrection, which had already occurred. But just as Christ was physically raised from the dead, so will all believers be physically raised at the very end of time. With such a false doctrine, some of the Corinthians may have regarded sexual relationships as unnecessary because sexual relations belong to this present age (7:1–5). The same doctrine could yield the opposite view: since what is done with the physical body has no spiritual significance, even promiscuous sexual behavior is not wrong.

The doctrine of the believer's union with Christ is one of the most fundamental teachings of the apostle. What is significant about this verse is that it represents that union as involving the whole person, including the physical body (Rom. 12:1). The Corinthians were wrong in thinking that sexual union with a prostitute, just because it was physical, did not affect their relationship with Christ.

Paul assumes the truth of Gen. 2:24 (see Eph. 5:31), that sexual intercourse effects a profound interpersonal union that is more than merely physical. The contrast is not that union with Christ is spiritual while union with a prostitute is physical; Paul has emphasized in v. 15 that union with Christ involves the body, a point developed in vv. 18–20. "One spirit" probably refers to the Holy Spirit (15:45 note). Through the Holy Spirit we (spirit and body) have become one with Christ, and this sublime union forbids our giving our bodies to prostitutes. If what Paul condemns here has to do with the prostitutes who served at the temple of the goddess Aphrodite, the religious implications of the Corinthians' immorality are even more obvious (10:20).

The meaning of this passage is disputed. There seem to be many sins that are against the body. Nevertheless, in Paul's teaching, the physical union involved in sexual immorality has special consequences because it interferes with our Christian identity as people who have been united with Christ through the Holy Spirit. It is perhaps significant that Paul's prohibition in this verse ("Flee from sexual immorality") is expressed in the same way as the command against idolatry (10:14).

Here Paul applies to the individual the concept of the church as the new temple where God dwells (3:16 note). While we must give due weight to this personal character of the Holy Spirit's indwelling of individuals, the emphasis in Scripture is on the corporate identity of God's people as a holy temple and a spiritual house (Eph. 2:19–22; 1 Pet. 2:4, 5).

See Introduction: Date and Occasion. It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman. Very possibly this saying was used by an ascetic group among the Corinthian Christians who not only condemned sexual promiscuity (rightly) but also argued (wrongly) that Christians should avoid marriage and abstain from sexual relations even in marriage. The apostle had to be careful lest his teaching be distorted in one direction or another. Paul does not simply dismiss the slogan; he too opposes sexual immorality, and he recognizes a certain value in remaining unmarried (vv. 7, 8). He can give specific and valid reasons why a Christian may decide to stay single (vv. 29–35). But he must correct those who demand celibacy. In different contexts, Paul speaks of marriage in only positive terms (e.g., Eph. 5:22–33; 1 Tim. 3:2), and he condemns those who forbid marriage (1 Tim. 4:3).

These are remarkable verses in that they reveal viewpoints that appear to be far ahead of their time: a healthy perception of the woman's sexuality, and an understanding of the complete equality that exists between a man and a woman in the most intimate area of their relationship. The Scripture gives no support whatever to the notion that sexual relations are solely at the direction and for the enjoyment of the husband. The apostle allows for temporary abstention from sex (in a way similar to fasting; v. 5), but he does not allow protracted abstinence. Sexual union is an expected part of marriage, not only a delight but also a debt owed to one's wife or husband.

The "concession" probably refers to the brief periods of abstinence in v. 5: spouses may — but need not — deprive each other for a short period and for a specific reason. It may, however, refer to the marital state in general, which is not demanded of all believers but permitted to those with that calling. On the other hand, remaining unmarried has certain advantages for the work of the kingdom and the advance of the gospel, as Paul had been called to do. Nevertheless, the apostle realizes that a celibate life is not possible for everyone and that singleness would lead many Christians into sexual temptation.

In v. 12, Paul says, "I, not the Lord," but Paul is not suggesting that there is an opposition between what he says and what the Lord says. With regard to the problem treated in vv. 10, 11, there was a well-known instruction given by Jesus during His earthly ministry (Mark 10:1–12). In vv. 12–16, however, Paul discusses a difficult situation that had not been expressly addressed by the Lord while He walked the earth. His apostolic commands, however, come by inspiration and have divine authority, as 14:37 makes clear (and is implied in Paul's surprising understatement in 7:40).

In spite of the Lord's command, it appears that some of the wives in Corinth, influenced by an ascetic viewpoint (v. 1), had in fact left their husbands. Because spouses are committed to each other until death (v. 39), even if they depart they may not remarry. Jesus had stated that a spouse's sexual infidelity provides grounds that allow for (but do not require) divorce (Matt. 19:2–9); but Paul here deals with separation for other reasons that do not breach the marital covenant itself.

See note on v. 10. Jesus' previous teaching on divorce presupposed that both husband and wife belonged to the covenant community. As the gospel invaded pagan cultures and communities, a new situation arose in which one spouse might come to trust Christ while the other would not (see 1 Pet. 3:1–7). who is an unbeliever. This is the special circumstance about which Jesus had left no direct instructions. If one spouse has been converted and the other not, should the marriage therefore be dissolved, especially if the unbelieving spouse separates?

A striking affirmation of the special character of the home in which at least one parent is a believer (1:2 note). In OT language, the whole family is regarded as being in covenant with God. Even the spouse who refuses to believe comes under the influence of God's work (v. 16) — much more so the children who are not old enough to profess their faith. Accordingly, Reformed theology has viewed this verse as providing part of the rationale for the baptism of the children of at least one professing believer. Because children of at least one believing parent are set apart, it is right to apply to these children the visible sign and seal of their separation from the world and incorporation into the covenant community. See notes on Acts 2:39; 16:15.

The thrust of this passage is that a Christian is not obligated to insist that the marriage remain intact. Such an insistence would prevent them from living in "peace." If the unbelieving spouse deserts the marriage, the believing partner may accept or seek a divorce, and subsequently remarry.

Paul may be returning to the thought of v. 14 and giving a reason why Christians should not leave their unbelieving spouses: since they are in some sense "sanctified," they are in a sphere within which they may be saved. Alternatively, v. 16 may explain v. 15: let the unbeliever go, because you have no assurance that he or she will be saved by being forced to stay married.

The following verses make clear that the phrase "God has called him" speaks to the circumstances within which God places a believer in order to serve Him. Note that vv. 17–24 set forth a principle that gives coherence to the whole chapter: becoming a believer does not require a change in status, whether marital, ethnic, or social (vv. 8, 20, 26). This verse has sometimes been misused as evidence that Christians should not attempt to improve their social or economic standing. On the contrary, Paul encourages slaves to obtain their freedom if the opportunity arises (v. 21), while assuring believers that they can live to God's glory and "with God" (v. 24) even when their living situations cannot be changed.

The first part of this verse is paralleled in Gal. 5:6 and 6:15. It would seem that the second part ("keeping the commandments of God") is another way of saying, "faith working through love" (Gal. 5:6), and that faith that bears the fruit of love is what characterizes the "new creation" (Gal. 6:15).

The desire to attain a better condition is not wrong, as the rest of the verse makes clear. However, Paul does not want Christians troubling themselves about a situation that cannot be changed. Dissatisfaction and complaint can be fatal spiritually (10:10): they reflect lack of confidence in God.

This statement supports v. 22. Here and in its previous appearance (6:20) it reminds believers of Christ's death and its inevitable result, that we are not our own but belong, body and soul, to the divine Redeemer who gave Himself for us. If we truly understood whose we are, we would realize that even slavery cannot damage our privileged position in Christ. Conversely, even the greatest human master is only a humble servant before Christ. Therefore, Christians need not, and must not, "become slaves of men."

A new, but related topic that the Corinthians had raised in their letter to Paul (Introduction: Date and Occasion). I have no command from the Lord. See note on v. 10. I give my judgment. This language suggests that the comments Paul are about to make are not absolute commandments for all circumstances, but recommendations for a particular situation. This interpretation is confirmed by the statement in v. 28 and by the concluding words in v. 38.

Lit. "the present necessity." Some believe that Paul is referring to a specific and unusual problem in Corinth. However, the language of v. 28 ("will have worldly troubles") suggests a more general idea: the predicament that faces all Christians as they seek to serve Christ in the present evil age (Gal. 1:4). We must consider this factor when making a decision about marriage, though other considerations should also be kept in mind (vv. 6–9 note).

The Christian life must be lived in the realization that this present age will pass away at Christ's return, when the age to come will be brought to consummation. Since Christians must always be ready for the coming of the Lord, there is no time to waste (Rom. 13:11, 12), as this age is already in process of "passing away."

Despite first appearances, Paul is not exalting the single, celibate life as spiritually superior to the call to marriage, which necessarily entails anxiety "about worldly things" and pleasing one's spouse. He offers realistic pastoral counsel, noting that those with the calling to singleness (which includes the gift of celibacy, v. 7) are spared the divided interests that require husbands and wives to attend to their spouses' desires and needs. Elsewhere (notably Eph. 5:22–33), Paul stresses that a married person's sacrificial and submissive love toward his or her spouse, far from competing with "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Cor. 7:35), beautifully expresses that devotion.

There are two different ways of understanding this passage. We simply do not know for certain whether Paul is addressing men who have deferred marriage to their fiancée ("betrothed") or fathers who have not permitted their daughters to marry. However, the main idea is clear: both being married and being unmarried are good options, even though Paul sees a particular benefit in remaining unmarried.

Marriage is a lifelong commitment. free to be married. A widow, no less than the others treated in this chapter, has the choice to remain unmarried or to marry. The only consideration is that if she marries again, the new spouse must be a Christian.

The Corinthians had raised the issue of idolatry dealt with in chs. 8–10, but the precise nature of their question is difficult to determine. According to some interpreters, the issues discussed in ch. 8 and in 10:25–30 are one and the same. Others, on the basis of 8:10, argue that ch. 8 deals with the serious problem that some Christians were attending pagan feasts and eating the food served there, while 10:25–30 concerns the lesser problem of meat purchased in the market and served in homes. all of us possess knowledge. Paul addresses the sin of arrogance as an introduction to the subject of idolatry (vv. 1–3). These comments reveal that behind the behavior of the Corinthians (or at least an important group among them) lay a serious problem of attitude. Their conduct was not guided by love (cf. ch. 13) but by pride, an overconfidence in what they thought was a full and complete spiritual knowledge.

The Corinthians should be less concerned about what they know than about who knows them (cf. 13:12). God's "knowing" people entails His personal, sovereign choice and love toward them (Gal. 4:9; Rom. 8:29; Amos 3:2), not merely acquaintance with information about them. Such sovereign grace should lead the Corinthians to the humility that they lack.
