Apparently some of the Corinthians used the doctrine of monotheism as an argument supporting their practice: If there is only one God, who teaches us to mock idols (Is. 46:6, 7), why should we worry about eating food offered to them? Paul acknowledges this truth and affirms it (vv. 4–6), but goes on to point out an error in the Corinthians' use of this doctrine.

Believers who have weak consciences are unable to dissociate various elements in pagan rituals from idolatry itself. When they eat food offered to idols, their consciences become "defiled." Such strong language (cf. "destroyed" in v. 11) suggests that these weak Christians are sinning not merely because they think they are doing something wrong, but because they have fallen back into their idolatrous ways.
See note on v. 1 (cf. 10:18–22).

What was a source of pride for some of the Corinthians became the instrument that harmed others (v. 1 note). destroyed. Paul underscores the seriousness of this matter — this professing believer may so fall from his profession of Christianity as to be "destroyed."

Although the conscience is not infallible, it is a serious matter to violate it or tempt others to do so. Addressing similar dietary issues among the Christians at Rome, Paul taught that any action that does not proceed from faith — that violates one's sense of what pleases God — is sin (Rom. 14:23).

This concluding comment is intended to set forth the basic principle of love: seeking the good of others above one's own good (10:24, 33; 13:5; Phil. 2:4). Paul is about to discuss his willingness to forgo his legitimate rights and freedoms as an apostle to reinforce this point through his own example (9:1–23).

Paul's willingness to forgo some of his rights is an illustration of the principle he states in 8:9. The questions in v. 1 may indicate that some in Corinth were questioning Paul's authority and criticizing his behavior (v. 3). Or they simply highlight the noncontroversial evidence of his apostolic authority (as v. 2 affirms; cf. 2 Cor. 3:1–3) to show that he has demonstrated the mindset that he is requiring of the Corinthians, the readiness to forfeit personal rights for others' well-being.

This statement makes explicit that Paul had indeed been criticized, though scholars debate the specific nature of the complaint (2:1 note). The next ten verses contain more than a dozen rhetorical questions that reflect Paul's deep emotion and provide clues about the historical situation. Paul defends his right to be supported by the churches, only to emphasize his choice not to receive support (vv. 15–18). Perhaps some of the Corinthians were upset because Paul refused their patronage, and concluded from this that he was not a legitimate apostle (2 Cor. 11:7–12). If he is not, why should they listen to his instruction?

The Corinthians themselves may have raised this issue, as though the lack of a wife discredited Paul and Barnabas, or it may be Paul's choice of an illustration to indicate the distinction between having a right and exercising it. Both Paul and Barnabas were unmarried at the time of their missionary work, but others labored as apostles while married. Paul takes for granted that if he were to be married, it would be with a believer, a "sister" in the Lord (see text note).

In spite of the strain that his secular work added to the heavy demands of his apostolic ministry, Paul was determined not to become a burden to the churches (1 Thess. 2:6–9) even though being supported by them was his "right" (9:8–14). It appears from 2 Cor. 11:7–12 that the Corinthians misinterpreted Paul's motives. For reasons that are unclear, the apostle did make an exception in the case of the Philippian church in Macedonia (Phil. 4:15, 16). Perhaps he permitted established churches to be his financial partners while refusing "compensation" from those to whom he was first introducing the good news, freely offering God's free grace, so that his ministry practice matched his message (v. 18).
This principle is reflected not only in the OT priesthood (v. 13) but also in several NT passages (e.g., Luke 10:7; Gal. 6:6; 1 Tim. 5:17, 18).

As the rest of the passage makes clear, Paul considers that he could hardly boast about preaching since he is compelled by God's will to preach. So his ground for boasting (his "reward") is that he preaches free of charge (v. 18), and he will not allow anyone to take this away from him.

Paul returns to the first question of v. 1. It appears that Paul must defend himself from the charge of inconsistency: he exercised freedom in his own behavior and therefore should not deprive others from doing the same. The apostle will return to this theme again in 10:23–33.

When ministering to Jews, Paul conforms to the OT ceremonial regulations even though he knows that these matters were not essential (Acts 16:1–3; 18:18; 21:20–26). See theological note "The Threefold Use of the Law" on p. 273.

When ministering to Gentiles, Paul is willing to live like them (for example, with respect to the Mosaic dietary laws), while recognizing that he is never free to disobey God's moral law, or the "law of Christ."

A restatement of the point made in 8:13. all things to all people. This generalization and that in 10:33 ("I try to please everyone in everything") must be read in light of the apostle's insistence that he seeks always to be within God's law and under Christ's law (v. 21 note). In any matter that was morally indifferent from the standpoint of God's revealed will, Paul will gladly set aside his personal preferences to further the gospel's reception by others and the gospel's work in them.
Paul elsewhere uses the illustration of a race and its prize to emphasize the need for single-mindedness, determination, and perseverance (Phil. 3:12–14; 2 Tim. 4:7, 8).

He continues the athletic metaphor by reminding his readers that fighters must discipline their bodies if they expect to win. Similarly, Christians must be willing to set aside their selfish interests for the sake of their primary goal (cf. 1 Tim. 4:7–8; 2 Tim. 2:5). lest \... I myself should be disqualified. This statement has often been used as evidence that Christians can lose their salvation. The witness of the NT and of Paul in particular is that those whom God has brought to Himself are His forever (Rom. 8:28–30) because the life they have been given in Christ is eternal in character (John 5:24; cf. Heb. 7:16). What God has begun He will bring to completion (Phil. 1:6). However, it would be wrong to dismiss or minimize Paul's concern (cf. 15:2; Phil. 3:11; Col. 1:23) by suggesting that it is merely hypothetical or relates only to rewards and not salvation. Paul was confident that absolutely nothing would be able to separate him from God's love (Rom. 8:38–39), but he never presumed that he was saved regardless of what he did. No Christian can afford to take lightly the warnings of Scripture (10:12), because these warnings are the God-appointed means by which true believers persevere to the end. Those of faith heed these warnings, as the Spirit works through them to make them will and work "for his good pleasure" (Phil. 2:12–13).

Christian baptism signifies the union of the believer with Christ, and Paul uses the language of baptism in comparing the Israelites and the Corinthians (5:12, 13 note). All the Israelites went through the ordeal and deliverance of the exodus by virtue of their identification with their leader, Moses. Note the repetition of "all" in vv. 1–3 (also 12:13). "All" the members of the Corinthian church have been baptized into Christ, and in that respect have been identified with God's deliverance in Christ, but baptism does not guarantee that God is pleased with each baptized individual without exception. This passage illustrates and explains the warning in 9:24–27. Heb. 3:7–4:13 (especially 3:16–4:2) draws the same cautionary lesson from the privileges and the judgment experienced by Israel's wilderness generation. Apart from saving faith, the external rite of baptism accomplishes nothing.

Following the analogy with baptism, Paul warns the Corinthians not to find false comfort in their participation in the Lord's Supper (vv. 14–22). The Israelites also experienced divinely given food and drink. Here "spiritual" does not mean "immaterial," but that it was supplied miraculously by God's power. Paul probably has in mind the activity of the Holy Spirit (2:6, 14; 3:1; 15:44–46; and notes). The Israelites had received a supernatural provision associated with the work of the Spirit. the Rock was Christ. In the OT, God is often compared with a rock, and Israel (called "Jeshurun") is described as having forsaken God, the "Rock of his salvation" (Deut. 32:15). The Lord identified Himself in a special way with the rock that gave forth water at Massah and Meribah, for He stood "before" Moses on the rock as it was struck (Ex. 17:5–6). The analogy between the Israelites and the Corinthians is not an arbitrary illustration; there is a theological connection, so Paul identifies the rock as a "type" of Christ (vv. 6, 11 notes). Without minimizing the privileges enjoyed by Christians (v. 11 note), Paul reminds us that the Deliverer of the Israelites was none other than our crucified and risen Savior.

These verses narrate Israel's sin of idol worship in the wilderness, after the Israelites left Egypt. The clearest OT reference to Israel's sin of idolatry in 10:5–11 is a quotation from Ex. 32:6 in v. 7: "And do not be idolaters, as some of them were; as it is written, 'The people sat down to eat and drink, and stood up to play.'" This was a description of the Israelites in their raucous worship of the calf idol. This quotation forms a central part of vv. 5–11, which is then the basis for the exhortations in vv. 12–14.

The Gk. word (typos) is related to the English term "type" (so also in v. 11). The use of this word likely further indicates that the events of the wilderness have a divinely intended correspondence with the experiences of the Christian church. Israel, in the wilderness of her pilgrimage, serves as a formative example for the church in her pilgrimage, now that redemptive history has reached fulfillment in the coming of Christ (v. 11 note).

This statement reflects Paul's conviction that the coming of Christ inaugurated the "last days" (Heb. 1:2), the time when the great promises of the OT come to pass (cf. 1:20 note). By pointing out this theme, Paul helps the Corinthians to realize that the OT events narrated here about Israel's idolatry in vv. 5–11 looked forward and applied to them. Israel's idolatry foreshadowed the idolatry of some in Corinth and stands also as a warning to what will happen to those in Corinth who commit idolatry (see 10:14, 20–22) as Israel did (note in this respect vv. 12, 14). Moreover, these facts suggest that given their privileged position, the Corinthians ought to recognize their greater responsibility (cf. Heb. 11:39, 40).
See note on 9:27. Receiving the benefits described in 10:1–4 did not inoculate idolatrous Israelites against God's judgment (10:5–11). The same principle applies in the church today.

This well-known verse has provided great encouragement to Christians facing temptations. At the same time, Paul's words contain an implicit rebuke. If God keeps us from temptations greater than we can withstand, we cannot plead our temptations as an excuse for sinning. Sin is never a necessity for a believer. the way of escape \... you may be able to endure it. Paul's carefully chosen words imply that at times "escape" from temptation will not entail a change of circumstances, but the Holy Spirit's power to withstand and endure (2 Cor. 12:2–10).

This command is related to Paul's previous remarks about eating food offered to idols (8:1 note; 8:10). Specifically, Paul is grieved that some of the Corinthians were participating in pagan meals that had an inseparable element of idolatry (see Rev. 2:14, 20).

These statements about the Lord's Supper demonstrate the significance of taking part in a distinctively religious meal. Just as it would be impossible to take the Lord's Supper and claim that it had no religious significance, so it is naive for the Corinthians to think they can participate in temple feasts without being involved in idolatry. Another point is that the unity "in the body of Christ" symbolized by taking the bread and wine excludes union with idols. See theological note "The Sacraments" on p. 1726.

. Later Paul will show the implications of the unity of the church in the body of Christ, symbolized by the bread, both for believers' relationships as they observe the Supper (11:23–34) and for their exercise of spiritual gifts to build each other up in unity (12:12–31).
Although idols are nothing (v. 19), behind pagan rituals is the reality of Satan's work, and Christians should have nothing to do with that.

See note 6:12, 13. Again the apostle qualifies and corrects the Corinthians' slogan of liberty, calling them to use their freedom to help and build up others, seeking "the good of his neighbor" (v. 24), rather than for self-indulgence.

In spite of his strong words against taking part in idolatrous feasts, Paul does not want the Corinthians to be overly scrupulous. The fact that food is offered to an idol does not change what the food is; it is still part of God's creation, as the citation from Ps. 24:1 (v. 26) shows. Therefore, the Corinthian believers do not have to ask whether food in the market was brought from the temple, nor do they need to raise the question when invited to a meal (v. 27). They may freely eat what God has provided.

A different problem arises if someone announces that the meat comes from a pagan sacrifice. Presumably, such a comment indicates that the speaker is a Christian who has problems of conscience about it, or even a pagan ("offered in sacrifice" reflects a Gk. term, "sacrificed to a holy thing," which differs from the term "offered to idols" elsewhere in this passage \[8:1, 4, 7, 10; 10:19; see Acts 15:29; Rev. 2:14, 20\]). In that case, it is right to abstain "for the sake of the one who informed you," lest he mistake your consumption for worship of an idol.

To voluntarily refrain from a practice that Christ's law permits for the sake of avoiding misperception by one who is weaker in faith (8:7) is not to forfeit one's true freedom of conscience in Christ.
This question suggests that Paul had been accused of eating meat offered to idols, with the suggestion that he has no right to forbid the Corinthians to do the same (9:19 note).

Paul brings his argument in chs. 8–10 to its climax — the Christian's every decision is to be governed and determined by what will promote the manifested excellence of God through the drawing of Jews and Greeks to faith and the strengthening of the church of God (v. 32).

See note on 9:22. When the purity of the gospel was at stake, Paul had no interest at all in pleasing people (Gal. 1:8–10). But where his personal preferences were concerned, he gladly subjected them to God's greater purpose, the salvation of His elect from all nations. not seeking my own advantage, but that of many. In conjunction with the desire to do everything for God's glory (v. 31), this principle provided Paul with his criterion of behavior. The submission of one's own advantage to what will promote the salvation of others is the principle of Christian love, which "does not insist on its own way" (13:5).
The apostle does not set himself up as an absolute example; he is to be imitated to the extent that he imitates Christ.

Paul transitions to address a new cluster of topics pertaining to the church's worship (vv. 2–34). He opens with a commendation for the Corinthians' fidelity to apostolic tradition entrusted to them by Paul. One such tradition is the wording in which Jesus instituted the Lord's Supper (v. 23). He finds it necessary, however, to mingle commendation with correction both with respect to women's roles in worship and with respect to the Corinthians' observance of the Supper (see v. 17).

The significance of this metaphor has long been debated by scholars — it may indicate leadership and authority, or source and origin. The two ideas should probably not be regarded as excluding each other. In two other contexts where Paul speaks of Christ as head (Eph. 4:15; Col. 2:19), the notion of "source" may be present (cf. v. 8). Elsewhere, Paul uses the metaphor with explicit reference to authority or submission (Eph. 1:22; 5:23, 24; Col. 1:18; 2:10). Here the stress probably falls on authority rather than source (cf. v. 10).

The evidence of Greco-Roman statuary seems to indicate that Roman men typically pulled their togas over their heads when offering pagan sacrifices, whereas in the first-century Jewish men left their heads uncovered while worshiping. The Jewish custom of men covering their heads at prayer probably does not go back to the NT period. dishonors his head. Probably a reference to Christ as the head (v. 7). Neither the Bible nor other documents explain why such a practice would dishonor Christ (cf. v. 10 note). Perhaps Paul's point is that the Roman practice tended to obscure the visible distinction between men and women and thus blurred the complementary relationships of leadership and submission that, ultimately, reflect the submission to God the Father that Christ displays in His redemptive mission (v. 3).

Given the contrast with the previous verse, this comment suggests that Jewish women in the first century normally worshiped with a head covering. Some scholars think that Paul refers to a particular hairstyle (in Num. 5:18, loosening a woman's hair is part of the test for an unfaithful wife). the same as if her head were shaven. In v. 6, shaving a woman's head is compared to having the hair cut short, presumably like a man's. But this would "shame" the very man she is called to honor or glorify (v. 7). It appears then that Paul is opposing a practice that tended to obliterate the visual distinction between the sexes. Possibly, the controversy reflects the idea of some Corinthians that they had achieved spiritual perfection and were no longer subject to normal rules (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

See theological note "Human Beings Created in the Image of God" on p. 13. Paul is not saying that woman is man's inferior (vv. 11–12), nor denying that God has made women after His image (Gen. 1:27). Rather, Paul stresses that each wife uniquely expresses the excellence of her husband.

Without devaluing woman's and man's equality as God's image-bearers (v. 7 note), Paul sees in the order of their creation (Gen. 2:7, 22) a sign of the man's functional leadership vis-à-vis the woman (1 Tim. 2:11–14). A counterbalancing reality, that henceforth every man is born of woman (vv. 11, 12), demands humility and an appreciation of our profound interdependence.

Many interpretations of this phrase have been suggested, but they are all speculative. Paul may be saying that it is particularly inappropriate to rebel against God's created order in the presence of these glorious, holy creatures.

These verses appear to be a qualification of the previous comments, offering a balancing perspective that furthers our humility and unity. Not only are men in general dependent on women, their mothers, for biological birth, but also with specific reference to our relationship "in the Lord," men and women are mutually dependent, since we are one in Him (Gal. 3:28).

Interpreters differ about the meaning of this term. Some believe it refers to the created order. Others argue that the apostle is here appealing to the common practices of his day. The fact that Paul has already referred to the created order (v. 8) seems to make it more likely that Paul is referring to the created order.
Some argue that the hair is "in place of" a covering. But Paul may mean that since the woman's long hair serves as a covering, it is equally appropriate for her to wear a veil.

Paul does not use exactly this kind of argument elsewhere in any of his letters. Such a conclusion to a difficult passage may give some support to the view that the apostle was not prescribing permanent forms of worship. However, the apostle's appeal to the created order (vv. 8, 14) must be taken into account as suggesting that Paul's instruction transcends the specific circumstances of the Corinthian church. In any case, even if Paul is dealing with questions of cultural appropriateness, such questions have theological implications (v. 5 note). Without a doubt, there is an underlying theological principle to Paul's teaching on head coverings that remains constant in every age — the concreated roles and relationships between husband and wife. The husband is to lead his wife in godliness, and his wife is to submit to his leadership as he does so (cf. Eph. 5:22–33).
The contrast between these words and v. 2 indicates the seriousness of the problem that Paul now addresses, which concerns abuses of the Lord's Supper.

Paul recognizes that nothing occurs outside the divine will and that God may use human sin to further His own purposes. Or, more probably, Paul may be using irony, trying to make the Corinthians see that their infighting has the unworthy motive of seeing who can argue the best.
Their mishandling of this observance has turned it into something quite different from what it should be.

Paul's concern here is not only with drunkenness but also with the humiliation of the poor. The Lord's Supper symbolizes, among other things, the unity of God's people (10:17). Those Corinthians who were well-off apparently did not share with the less fortunate among them at the feasts where the Lord's Supper was celebrated. This selfish behavior openly contradicted the meaning of the ceremony.

Paul's account of the institution of the Lord's Supper is in all essentials the same as what the Gospels record, and the words of institution correspond most closely with those preserved in Luke (cf. Matt. 26:26–29; Mark 14:22–25; Luke 22:17–20). These verses clarify what it means to partake of the elements of the Supper in a worthy manner (v. 27) and with discernment (v. 29). They therefore guide the believer in the kind of self-examination that should properly precede his participation in the sacrament (v. 28). See theological note "The Lord's Supper."

Note the connection between preaching the gospel and celebrating the Lord's Supper. The Supper sets forth God's Word through visible rather than verbal means. Note also that celebrating the Supper gives expression to our sure hope of the Lord's return.

It is important to take this whole section together as a unit, and vv. 33, 34 make plain that Paul still has in mind the abuses mentioned in vv. 21, 22. Phrases such as "in an unworthy manner" (v. 27) and "Let a person examine himself" (v. 28) can be extended and applied to many circumstances, but we should be careful not to wrench them from their context. In particular, it would be a misreading of v. 30 to think that God routinely brings illness and death to Christians who, in spite of their spiritual failings, partake of the Supper. Because some of the believers in Corinth were celebrating the Supper in a way that both profaned the spiritual significance of the atoning death of Christ, of which the elements are sign and seal, and destroyed the unity the Supper represents, God had brought judgment upon the community. God's purpose in judging these believers, however, was to prevent them from being "condemned along with the world" (v. 32).

This may refer to a failure to recognize that the bread of the Supper signifies Christ's sacrificed body (vv. 24, 27) and, implicitly, this would include a failure to see the cup as a sign and seal of Christ's shed blood. The fact that only the failure to "discern the body" is mentioned leads some scholars, however, to see the sin indicted here as conduct that disrupts the unity of the church as Christ's body (10:17; 12:12 note) by indifferent neglect of the hungry poor in the congregation (v. 21).

As an introduction to the subject of spiritual gifts in Corinth, Paul reminds his readers of the contrast between their pagan and Christian experience. It is not clear whether anyone was actually uttering curses against Jesus (the statement may be only an illustration), but the focus of v. 3 is on the content of religious speech. Paul invokes the ancient and widespread criterion for evaluating new prophetic utterances, namely, their consistency with previous divine revelation (Deut. 13:1–5; 1 John 4:1–3). In view of 14:6–19, we may infer that the apostle is anticipating his argument for understandable speech. Pagans may likewise have experienced miraculous speech, but what really matters is what is said.

Apparently, the Corinthians exaggerated the importance of the gift of tongues, so Paul must remind them that one and the same Spirit distributes a variety of gifts to His people. The added references to "the same Lord" (v. 5) and "the same God" (v. 6) reflect the importance of the doctrine of the Trinity for Paul; they also support his concern for unity within diversity.

We completely misunderstand the purpose of the Spirit's gifts (here called a "manifestation") if we use them for selfish reasons. Because there are different needs in the Christian community, different gifts are required. Furthermore, the Spirit gives gifts not for one's personal aggrandizement, but for the edification of the body of Christ.

This list of gifts is not intended as a complete catalog (others are included in v. 28); possibly, it reflects gifts that were especially evident in Corinth. We need not assume that all of the gifts were manifested in every church. The list in Rom. 12:6–8, for example, includes only two of the gifts mentioned here (prophesying and faith) and omits those that might be thought of as miraculous, such as healing and tongues. In determining the character of some of the gifts listed here, we are hindered by the absence of descriptions of them anywhere in the NT. "The utterance of wisdom" may have been an ability to resolve difficult spiritual problems and "the utterance of knowledge" a special revelation of some sort, but we cannot be certain. Similarly, it is not clear why Paul lists separately the gifts of "faith," "healing," and "working of miracles." The reference to "the ability to distinguish between spirits" perhaps should be understood in the light of 1 John 4:1–3. Our inability to determine the precise function of some of these gifts is not an obstacle to understanding the thrust of this passage, which aims not at giving detailed instruction about them but rather at emphasizing the variety of God's endowments to His church (v. 11).

Although the word translated "tongue" is the normal Gk. word for "language" (glossa), the proper description of this gift has generated much debate. According to one view, it refers to some kind of ecstatic speech, possibly related to "the tongues \... of angels" mentioned in 13:1. According to another view, it refers to foreign languages. There is no reason to conclude that the "tongues" of 1 Corinthians differ from the "tongues" of Acts 2. The phenomenon of "tongues" described in Acts 2 was clearly foreign languages (Acts 2:6), and here Paul uses the same Gk. wordto describe this gift.

This brief clause sets the preceding list of gifts in the proper perspective. Whether an individual or a church possesses a particular gift is not for us to decide. It is the Spirit who sovereignly provides for the people of God. That factor may explain why no NT passage gives a complete catalog of gifts or a precise definition of them, since they may vary significantly according to God's plans in changing situations. A church may appropriately pray for God to grant gifts to meet its needs, but such prayers must be offered in submission to His sovereign will and perfect wisdom.

See theological note "The Church" on p. 2094. The description of Christ's church as a body is one of the most distinctive and significant teachings of Paul (1:13 note). Indeed, the apostle explains that he was given a special revelation concerning this "mystery," which was hidden for many ages; namely, that God's people, both Jews and Gentiles, are now constituted as one body, on equal terms, by virtue of Christ's exaltation (Eph. 1:22, 23; 3:2–6). Both the existence and the growth of the church presuppose this unity established by Christ through the Spirit (Eph. 4:3–6, 11–16; Col. 2:19; 3:14, 15).

The emphasis on the word "all" and the allusion to the sacraments recalls the similar description of the Israelites in 10:2–4 (cf. notes). One of the truths signified and sealed by water baptism is the baptism of the Holy Spirit that incorporates believers into the one body of Christ. Baptism replaces circumcision as the sign of admission into God's covenant (Col. 2:11–14). Similarly, partaking of the Lord's Supper signifies our continued communion with Christ and His church (10:17; 11:29 note).

Having established the unity of Christ's church, Paul sets forth its diversity. Some scholars have commented that the Corinthians' most fundamental problem was not their rejection of the church's unity, but rather their failure to acknowledge its diversity. Paul corrects this error through a comparison with the human body. He appeals to the sovereign will of God, who has "arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose" (v. 18; cf. v. 11). If the Corinthians denied the validity of certain gifts, they were really questioning God's authority to distribute the gifts. Paul stresses unity, but not a uniformity that squelches valid forms of diversity in believers' service to others.

This comparison manifests the problem that has occupied Paul throughout most of the letter, namely, a sense of spiritual superiority among some of the Corinthians and their consequent disdain for those who appear to be "weaker" and "less honorable." Their devaluing of certain gifts (possibly in favor of the gift of tongues) is Paul's concern here.

The items in this verse are different from those in vv. 8–10, providing that Paul is not interested in giving a complete list of spiritual gifts and offices. Here Paul begins with "apostles" and "prophets," whom he considers the foundation (Eph. 2:20), and adds as a third category "teachers," so that this listing is similar to that in Eph. 4:11. Though the Gk. words for "helping" and "administrating" do not occur elsewhere in the NT, Paul probably has in mind the gifts of one who "does acts of mercy" and the one who "leads," respectively (Rom. 12:8).

These rhetorical questions bring to a climax Paul's argument that we should not expect everyone to have the same gifts, since God apportions them as He wills (vv. 11, 18). See theological note "The Apostles" on p. 1912.

The meaning of this sentence is disputed. Some believe it refers to the more important gifts in v. 28 (especially prophecy, 14:1); others argue that it introduces the discussion of love in ch. 13. Most likely, Paul is anticipating what he will say later about gifts for "building up the church" (14:12), i.e., speaking "words with my mind in order to instruct others" (14:19). more excellent way. Before explaining what the "higher gifts" are, as he will in ch. 14, Paul must point out what is the essential condition for the proper exercise of any gift — love.

Using intentional exaggeration, Paul emphasizes the uselessness of gifts exercised without love. The expression "tongues of men" probably refers to the gift of speaking in foreign languages (Acts 2:4–11), while the addition "and of angels" may be a deliberate exaggeration (similarly with "understand all mysteries" and "remove mountains"). Whether the Corinthians claimed to use angelic speech is impossible to determine (12:10 note). The expression "deliver up my body to be burned" may also be a dramatic overstatement.

Paul personifies love as a person who acts in the ways Christians should imitate. The total picture suggests a description of Christ Himself. Considering the kinds of problems this epistle addresses, these verses are a rebuke to the Corinthians, who were failing to conduct themselves with love (boastful and arrogant, 8:1; 12:21; insisting on one's own way, 6:1–8; etc.).
Paul may mean that those who love do not devise evil against others. More likely, he means that those who love do not focus their attention on the wrongs that others do to them.
Paul uses this word four times for rhetorical effect as he brings his description of love to a climax.

One could view this statement as a summary of the previous verse, especially in the light of the comment that love "bears all things." At the same time, the statement allows Paul to build a contrast between love, which always remains (v. 13), and the spiritual gifts, which will cease when their purpose, to promote the growth of the church, is completed (Eph. 4:11–13). prophecies \... tongues \... knowledge. It is likely that Paul mentions these three items because they were the spiritual gifts, of which the Corinthians were most proud. Some believe that these three gifts have a temporary, earthly function until the end of the age and will not continue at the consummation of the age to come. Others suggest that Paul mentions these three in particular because they have a revelatory function that came to an end with the completion of the NT canon (v. 10 note). This latter view is supported by Eph. 2:19, 20, where "apostles and \[NT\] prophets" are part of the "foundation" of the church temple, along with Christ as the "cornerstone." Thus, like Christ, the revelatory function of the apostles and prophets, who gave us our NT canon, was a foundation-laying activity like Christ's ministry, death, and resurrection. Thus, as with Christ, when the foundation-laying activity is accomplished, the activity is so unique that it ceases.

The context (especially v. 12) suggests strongly that Paul is here referring to the second coming of Christ as the final event in God's plan of redemption and revelation. In comparison with what we will receive then, the present blessings are only partial and thus imperfect. It is therefore a sign of immaturity for the Corinthians to treat the temporary, incomplete gifts of the Spirit as having ultimate significance. According to another view, Paul may be referring to the "complete" revelation of the NT Scriptures, revelation that makes prophecy and other revelatory gifts obsolete.

Perhaps because the Corinthians liked to boast of their knowledge (8:1 note), Paul concludes by stressing the partial character of all present knowledge. The shift from the active ("know") to the passive ("have been known") is found elsewhere in the apostle's letters and serves to emphasize dependence on God's grace (8:3; Gal. 4:9). Here the focus is on the intimacy and accuracy of God's knowing, which we will share someday (though the infinity of His knowledge — His omniscience — will always set Him apart from even His glorified creatures).
See theological note "Love."

Having set the discussion within the proper framework of love, Paul now encourages the Corinthians to recognize the value of the spiritual gifts. Because the Corinthians have exaggerated the importance of the gift of tongues, however, the emphasis of ch. 14 is on the understandable gifts (v. 19) — primarily prophecy, but also the interpretation of tongues (vv. 27, 28), which are the functional equivalent of prophecy. The superiority of prophecy to tongues lies in its power to communicate with hearers without the need of "interpretation," thus furthering "their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation" (v. 3).

This verse (cf. v. 14) describes the gift of tongues in a way that seems inconsistent with the gift of speaking in foreign languages mentioned in Acts 2:4–11 (although some believe that the miracle on Pentecost was a miracle of hearing). Accordingly, many argue that Paul is dealing with something different — a kind of ecstatic speech used for intimate prayer (Rom. 8:26). However, the word translated "tongue" is the normal Gk. term for "language." Second, Paul uses the term "mysteries" to indicate a divine truth not yet disclosed. The word does not have the meaning of the English word "mysterious" (2:7 note). Third, vv. 10, 11, as well as v. 21, support the idea that even here Paul is speaking of human languages (12:8–10 note). in the Spirit. The "tongues" in view here are revelatory. What is spoken are matters divinely revealed by the Holy Spirit. As Peter's quotation from Joel 2 implied, the "tongues" in which God's mighty deeds were declared at Pentecost were a subcategory of prophecy, similar to God's uttering His word through Joel and other OT prophets (Acts 2:16–18).

Those speaking in an uninterpreted language are encouraged and comforted. Unless the meaning of the message spoken in a "tongue" can be conveyed to others, however, the Holy Spirit's purpose for His gifts — to build up the church — is not achieved (vv. 5, 12). Prophecy delivered in a language known to the speaker and the hearers is superior to tongues, needing no interpretation to accomplish its aim, the edification of others.
This principle of benefiting others by edifying them becomes the central point of the passage. Paul is applying the teaching of 12:7 that God has granted a variety of gifts "for the common good."
These verses illustrate the principle mentioned in v. 6. Musical instruments convey nothing to those who listen unless they are played with intelligent purpose.

Without minimizing the significance of the gift of tongues, Paul encourages the Corinthians to use it in a way that makes it valuable for the congregation. At Pentecost, listeners who spoke various languages recognized their native dialects in the believers' proclamation (Acts 2:8–11), but the Holy Spirit also bestowed on some Christians a supernatural gift to be able to interpret messages delivered in unknown languages (12:10, 28–30).

Whatever spiritual benefit he might receive from the experience, the exercise of this gift does not bear "fruit," i.e., others are not built up. In the next verse, Paul emphasizes that he would rather have both benefits. Throughout this discussion, "my spirit" or "the spirits of the prophets" (vv. 14, 15, 16, 32) probably refers not to an aspect of the human personality distinguishable from one's mind, but rather to "my manifestation of the (Holy) Spirit" (so v. 12), or simply, "my spiritual gift."

The members of the congregation, if they are to participate in public worship, must be able to agree with the message of the hymns being sung and the prayers being offered. The custom of expressing their approval with an audible "Amen" ("So it is!") cannot be followed if no one understands what has been said.

It may be that some of the Corinthians justified their emphasis on the gift of tongues by arguing that Paul himself exercised this gift. Without denying the fact, the apostle puts the gift in proper perspective by pointing out how much more valuable it is to do something "in order to instruct others."

Up to this point, Paul has been discussing the use of tongues among believers. But what about unbelievers who hear the tongues? In their concern for tongues, the Corinthians have ignored unbelievers, and Paul admonishes the church for this display of spiritual immaturity. He appeals to "the Law," (the OT) to show that God uses unintelligible speech as a sign of His judgment. Is. 28:11 explains how God judged the Israelites through the Assyrians' speaking a foreign language. If non-Christians come to public worship and hear an unintelligible language, they will be repelled (v. 23) and reject the gospel. In this situation, uninterpreted tongues are a sign of judgment "for unbelievers" (v. 22). But the Corinthians should aim at bringing unbelievers to repentance and to the recognition that God is present (v. 25). Because God uses the understandable words of prophecy to accomplish this purpose, prophecy is a sign "for believers"; it is evidence of God's goodness to them (v. 22).

Rather than being attracted, unbelievers will find unintelligible speech offensive and dismiss a message that makes no sense to them, as Palestinian Jews in the crowd at Pentecost accused the believers of drunkenness, while those from other nations recognized that the Christians were speaking their languages and understood the Christians' message (Acts 2:12–13).

Paul alludes to the prophetic promise that foreigners will come, bow down, and acknowledge the Lord's presence in Israel's midst (Is. 45:14). This is one more indication that the church is now the true congregation of Israel that reveals God's truth to Gentile unbelievers (note the use of "church" \[ekklēsia\] in v. 23, a word that in the Septuagint often refers to the congregation of Israel).
See note on v. 6.

This concern for understanding has informed the whole discussion (v. 1 note). Paul's instructions in this verse and the following demonstrate that those who spoke in tongues controlled their utterance, although others may not have understood it.

Having given instructions for the proper exercise of the gift of tongues, Paul moves on to other directives that also affect the order of public worship. Since he had emphasized the importance of prophecy, he points out that even this gift should be exercised in an orderly fashion — "Let two or three prophets speak" (during the course of, or perhaps at various points in, the service) — while "the others" should explicate the message for the congregation. Apparently the Corinthians were speaking in tongues and prophesying without regard for each other or for the content of the message (12:2, 3 note). Their disorder was a threat to the unity of the body and was incompatible with the God "of peace" (v. 33).

These verses have created debate among Christians, at least partly because it is not known what problem exactly Paul was seeking to correct. It has even been proposed that these verses were not part of Paul's original letter. In view of 11:5 and other NT passages, it is certain that Paul is not absolutely forbidding women to speak in every church situation. Paul may have been addressing a particular problem in Corinth, such as women creating disorder during the worship service. He likely has in mind a specific function, such as the evaluation of prophecy (vv. 29, 32), in which women should not participate because this is the role of church elders in their function of the doctrinal guardianship of the church (on which cf. 1 Tim. 2:11–14). Another view, supported by Paul's direction that women should satisfy their "desire to learn" by asking their husbands at home, is that the Corinthian women were disruptively interrupting prophets or other teachers with their questions. This command is also related to Paul's later prohibition against women teaching at 1 Tim. 2:12, although the latter concerns the official teaching authority exercised by overseers (elders; cf. 1 Tim. 3:1–7), though that passage might also concern the relationship of husbands to wives. Wives are to "subject themselves as the Law also says." The "Law" here refers most likely to the OT, since all of Paul's other uses of "Law" in 1 Corinthians have this meaning (see 1 Cor. 9:8, 9; 20 21; 14:21; 15:56); thus it does not refer to a law of nature or some kind of Greco-Roman law. Though there is debate about what particular text from the "Law" is in mind, the submissive behavior of women under the old covenant in Israel continues to be the same under the new covenant in the eschatological Israel, i.e., "in the churches." Most likely, the particular reference is to Genesis 1–2, where the order of creation shows that Adam is the firstborn son of God (cf. Gen. 5:1–3) and high priest, which carries along with it authority over all creation, including authority over Eve. This is just what Paul argues in 1 Tim. 2:11–14 (cf. note). This is consistent with the emphasis on maintaining order "in all the churches of the saints" (v. 33).

These sarcastic questions show that Paul is addressing serious problems arising out of the Corin­thians' boastful arrogance. Since Corinth is not unique in receiving God's Word, this church should abide by the practices "in all the churches of the saints" (v. 33).

See note on 13:12 for the contrast between knowing and being known. This verse may be a warning that those who are stubborn will be disciplined by Paul or by the church (2 Thess. 3:14), but the language suggests that they will come under direct divine judgment.

These verses are a concise summary of ch. 14. The decency and orderliness of the church's worship furthers the aim of mutual edification (vv. 3, 5, 6, 12, 14, 17, 19, 24–26, 31) and displays that our God "is not a God of confusion but of peace" (v. 33).
With this verse, Paul shifts to a new topic of great concern to him — the integrity of the gospel message as it focuses on the doctrine of the resurrection.
See note on 9:27. believed in vain. Denying the resurrection of Christ makes our profession of faith useless (v. 14).

These verses give the essence not only of Paul's preaching but of the early church's teaching as a whole ("what I also received"): Christ's vicarious death and His resurrection as the fulfillment of the OT message (Luke 24:25–27, 45–46; 1 Pet. 1:10–11; cf. Rom. 4:23–25).

The fourfold repetition of "he appeared" indicates Paul's emphasis in this passage — the eyewitness proof that Christ was raised from the dead (cf. Luke 1:2; 24:48; Acts 1:1–3, 21–22). Most of those who witnessed the resurrection appearances were still living at the time Paul wrote this letter, so it was possible for anyone to check the facts. Particularly significant is the reference to "more than five hundred brothers at one time," for it shows that the appearances cannot be explained away as mere personal hallucinations.
This is not John's brother, the apostle executed by Herod Agrippa (Acts 12:2), but the half-brother of Jesus (John 7:5; Acts 12:17; 15:13; Gal. 1:19).

This self-deprecating remark may be an ironic criticism of the Corinthians who held Paul in low esteem (2:1 note). The Gk. word rendered "one untimely born" typically refers to a miscarriage or infant born prematurely, so Paul may allude to the fact that, unlike the Twelve (including Matthias, Judas' successor), he did not experience an extended "gestation period" of association with Jesus during His earthly ministry (cf. Acts 1:21–22). What the apostle means is suggested by the phrase "last of all." The appearances of the risen Lord had ceased with His ascension, and Paul was a persecutor of the church when he received his calling to be an apostle (Gal. 1:13, 23; Phil. 3:6; 1 Tim. 1:13–16). Although Paul had not been with Jesus during His earthly ministry, he was granted the privilege of seeing Jesus risen from the dead, and was commissioned as the last apostle, with a special ministry to the Gentiles (Acts 9:3–5, 15; Gal. 1:15, 16). Paul strongly suggests that the apostolic office was a unique, foundational gift to the church, not one expected to continue in later generations (Eph. 2:20).

Having freely admitted the abnormal and undeserving character of his experience, Paul moves on to stress that his past life is no reason to reject his message. Where sin abounds, God's effectual grace abounds all the more (Rom. 5:20); where we are weak, God's grace is strong (2 Cor. 12:9, 10). Divine grace did not make Paul lazy, but caused him to labor "harder" than anyone else.

Paul finally addresses the problem that needs correction. Some of the Corinthians, perhaps without denying that Jesus had been raised, were questioning the doctrine of the resurrection because of their unbiblical understanding of the significance of the human body, or of the principles of continuity and transformation that relate our present moral body to the coming resurrection body (v. 35 note). Neo-Platonic philosophy and proto-Gnostic religious movements devalued material reality generally, including the body, and the Corinthian Christians may have been influenced by such Greco-Roman ideologies. Paul needed to show them that the resurrection of Jesus cannot be separated from the resurrection of those who are His (vv. 20–23). If their resurrection is not true, neither is His. But to deny, even by implication, that Jesus' body was raised from the tomb destroys the message of the gospel.

Cf. v. 17. The truth of the Christian message is tied to the historical reality of Christ's death and exaltation. The apostle cannot conceive of his message as having any spiritual value if its historical foundation does not exist.

Though Paul would not deny that Christians in fact enjoy a better present life than non-Christians in many respects, this verse emphasizes that if Christ had not been raised from the dead then we ought to be pitied for our false hope. If we were still in our sins and lost (vv. 17, 18), we would have experienced the greatest and cruelest of all deceptions (vv. 31, 32). Moreover, if our hope in future resurrection is groundless, to forfeit present pleasure and endure persecution for Christ's sake is the height of folly (vv. 30–32).

At harvest time the Israelites were required to bring an offering from the first part of the crop (Lev. 23:10). This offering was a token of the whole harvest that belonged in its entirety to God. Jesus is the "firstfruits" because His resurrection and the resurrection of believers are closely related events. Jesus was "the first to rise from the dead" incorruptible (Acts 26:23), rising as our representative. His resurrection caused us to be raised with Him by the Holy Spirit (Rom. 6:4; Eph. 2:6), and at the same time guarantees that we will be raised bodily. Another use of the metaphor is found in Rom. 8:23 (cf. also 2 Cor. 1:22; 5:5; Eph. 1:14).

This passage succinctly states one of Paul's most profound teachings — our twofold solidarity with the first man, Adam, and with the last man, Christ. Outside of Christ, all people are by nature and by divine appointment united with Adam in sin and death; by grace and through faith, believers are united with Christ in in righteousness and in the life to come (vv. 45–49; Rom. 5:17–19). See theological note "The Last Resurrection."
See theological note "Original Sin" on p. 17. Adam's one sin, imputed to his posterity, results in their condemnation and death (Rom. 5:12, 15–19).

Although Paul's argument in this section is difficult in its details, its thrust is clear and powerful. The Corinthians must understand that the resurrection is not an isolated event with limited repercussions. It is rather an integrating and culminating event in God's sovereign rule over history. Verse 27 ("God has put all things in subjection under His feet") is a quotation of Ps. 8:6, which speaks of an end-time ideal Adam and which has begun to find its complete realization in Christ. Redemption is not complete "until he has put all his enemies under his feet" (v. 25, a clear reference to Ps. 110:1), and since death is "the last enemy" (v. 26), Christ's work in subduing every enemy is not complete until death is destroyed (Rev. 20:14). This final destruction of death coincides with Christ's coming, which effects the resurrection of those who belong to Him (v. 23; see vv. 53–55). Paul's statement that the Son "will also be subjected" to the Father (v. 28) does not mean that the Son is inferior in dignity and being. Rather, in His messianic work, the Son subjects Himself to the will of the Father "when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father" (v. 24). The climax of Christ's submissive, messianic work is this total conquest over His enemies, "that God may be all in all," when His absolute rule is universally acknowledged.

There are several interpretations of what this phrase means. Possibly, some in Corinth were being baptized on behalf of others who had already died, or, less probably, receiving baptism for the sake of reunion with believers who had died. This practice is not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible or in other ancient writings. Numerous explanations of the practice have been proposed, all of them speculative and none persuasive. Some believe that Paul mentions the rite only to show the logical inconsistency of his opponents' position. But the problem with this view is that Paul mentions "being baptized on behalf of the dead" positively, since it is based on "the dead being raised," a point he has been making since v. 4. A positive understanding of "being baptized on behalf of the dead" might take the reference to the "dead" as referring figuratively to Paul himself, since he says in v. 31, "I die every day," as a reference to the suffering that his ministry entails. Paul's suffering is mentioned immediately in vv. 30–32, and must be connected in some way with v. 29. If this interpretation is correct, then being "baptized on behalf of the dead" would mean "being baptized on behalf of Paul." This would mean they were "being baptized because of \[a viable meaning of the Gk. preposition hyper, which the ESV renders "on behalf of"\] the suffering ministry of Paul," through which they had heard the gospel and believed and were, consequently baptized. Paul perseveres in this ministry propelled by the belief that the believing dead will be raised (cf. v. 32).

Probably a reference to Paul's enemies in Ephesus (where this letter was written) who wanted to condemn him (cf. "the lion's mouth," 2 Tim. 4:17 note). One instance of potentially violent opposition against Paul was the riot stirred by the Ephesian silversmiths, although Paul's high-placed friends, the Asiarchs, kept him from harm in that instance (Acts 19:23–41). The hope of resurrection strengthens Paul to endure severe trials and persecutions (v. 19 note).

Derived from a comedy written by the popular Greek author Menander (342–292 B.C.), this proverb was common in the ancient world (note the comparable Jewish saying in 5:6). Those Christians in Corinth with a defective view of the resurrection not only had been influenced by the bad company they kept (v. 12 note), but in their turn they were corrupting others in the congregation.
Probably a reference to members of the church who boasted of their knowledge (8:1 note) but whose denial of the resurrection showed deep ignorance regarding the things of God.

In this verse, Paul considers what was apparently the primary objection raised by some of the Corinthians against the future resurrection. They may have been influenced by dualism, a pagan philosophy that contrasted the immaterial with the physical and argued that the immaterial was good but the material was evil (v. 12 note). Or these Corinthians had underestimated the degree to which Christians have not yet experienced the full benefits of our redemption, including the resurrection body. Paul proceeds to argue that our present body is not the resurrection body that Christians one day will possess.

Because God created the world, the processes of nature reflect in various ways how He works. Nature provides useful metaphors and analogies of the divine work of salvation (Is. 55:10, 11). Jesus uses a seed ("if it dies, it bears much fruit") as an illustration of the life-multiplying effect of His impending death (John 12:24). Here, Paul uses the same picture to illustrate the striking difference between what is planted and what eventually grows from the seed (v. 37). The same sort of analogy can be found in Plato's dialogue Symposium. In any case, Paul's analogy underscores the radical difference between our present bodies and our resurrection bodies, vv. 42–43.
At this point, Paul shifts the illustration to emphasize the variations among different plants. He goes on to apply the idea to living creatures (v. 39) and heavenly bodies (vv. 40, 41).

Finally, the illustration is applied to the human body that dies and is buried, and is transformed in its resurrection. Paul does not suggest that the resurrection body is a different body altogether. Just as a plant arises directly from its seed, so the resurrection body is in essence the same as the body that "is sown." But the apostle's emphasis is on the astounding change that will take place: from "perishable," "dishonor," and "weakness," to "imperishable," "glory," and "power."

This last contrast is difficult to understand but is of great importance. Paul does not have in mind a contrast between physical and nonphysical, material and immaterial. The resurrection body is a physical body, not an intangible ghost. The apostle has already used the words "natural" and "spiritual" to distinguish the individual who does not have the Holy Spirit from the one who does (2:6, 14 notes). The natural person belongs to the present age (1:20), while the spiritual person is a citizen of heaven (Phil. 3:20). Christians have received the Holy Spirit and are on that account "spiritual." They have not yet received the spiritual "body," the physical body that will be fully conformed to the life given by the Spirit. See Rom. 8:22–25 and note.

Paul clarifies his meaning by continuing the contrast between the first and the last Adam (vv. 21, 22 note). The Gk. word translated "being" (psychē) is related to the word translated "natural" in v. 44 (psychikos), while the word "spirit" (pneuma) corresponds to "spiritual" (pneumatikos). The words "life-giving spirit" are most probably a reference to the Holy Spirit. Jesus and the Holy Spirit share the same divine essence but are not the same divine person, but Christ and the Spirit are identified in terms of their presence and activity in the church. This identity, known to us because Jesus, too, is life-giving, is the fulfillment of Jesus' role as Messiah and commenced with His resurrection and ascension. To be in Christ is to be in the Spirit also (6:11, 15, 19; 12:11). The association of Christ, the Holy Spirit, and life is apparent in Rom. 8:9–11 and 2 Cor. 3:6, 17, 18. By citing and supplementing Gen. 2:7, Paul shows that Adam, even at his creation and before sin, did not possess and could not have conferred on his descendants the Spirit-empowered life of the age to come. Only the last Adam, Christ, can give others eternal life through His Spirit. The physically life-giving breath that the first Adam received foreshadowed typologically the "life-giving Spirit" that Christ, "the last Adam," would give to His people, as a result of His own resurrection. The apparent point is that the first human was created to reach the goal of such a glorious, imperishable body, if he had obeyed God and been faithful in reflecting God's image. In contrast to the first Adam, who failed because of faithless disobedience, Christ has subdued and obeyed in the way His progenitor should have. Consequently, Christ has inherited that for which humanity was originally destined but failed to reach. Jesus' body was not only a renewed physical body, but it had become "heavenly," "spiritual," and "imperishable."

Here is a final contrast, suggesting that vv. 42–44 refer to the distinction between earthly and heavenly human bodies. In this context, however, the distinction is not one of substance but of time; the present evil age is contrasted with the coming perfect age. Believers already enjoy some of the blessings of the coming age (10:11 note) but still await its consummation. God's work of redemption will not be complete until the bodily resurrection. We have borne the image of the first Adam, and since we belong to Christ, we are destined to bear the image of the last Adam, namely, Christ Himself (v. 49).

This phrase alludes to the weakness of earthly, human existence and is an equivalent to "perishable." Paul is warning the Co­rinthians that without new "imperishable" bodies, we "cannot inherit the kingdom of God." How, then, can some deny the doctrine of the resurrection?

See note on 2:7. For Paul, "mystery" is not an impenetrable paradox but a truth once partially hidden by God and now revealed in the gospel of Christ (Rom. 16:25–26; Eph. 3:3–9). The fuller truth revealed here in vv. 51–55 is about what will happen to living believers (those who do not "sleep," v. 51) when the resurrection of the dead occurs. Nowhere in the OT was it made clear that at this time living believers will be transformed along with dead ones, so that all will be changed into imperishable and immortal resurrection bodies. We shall not all sleep. Paul recognizes that many Christians will not die but will be alive at the time of Christ's return. Though these Christians will not be raised from death, they will also be transformed and receive imperishable and immortal bodies (1 Thess. 4:13–18 and notes).

This is one of the most eloquent and powerful passages in Scripture. With paraphrases of Isaiah and Hosea (based on the Septuagint), Paul alludes to his earlier argument in vv. 24–28 and vigorously assures us of the finality of death's destruction on the day of resurrection. This day will also mark the destruction of "sin" and "the law" as the instrument of sin. In the letter to the Romans, Paul explains in detail how sin is the venom bringing death to all (Rom. 5:12) and how the law, though itself holy, becomes an instrument through which sin can deceive (Rom. 7:7–12).

In the face of false teaching and various temptations, the hope of the resurrection should encourage the Corinthians to persevere in their faith. The exhortation to be "immovable," however, does not imply inactivity. On the contrary, the Corinthians must be fully active in "the work of the Lord." We can become easily discouraged by thinking that our labor may come to nothing (Gal. 2:2; Phil. 2:16; 1 Thess. 3:5), but we can remember the promise that when God creates the new heavens and new earth, His people will enjoy the fruits of their toil, and see that their efforts were never "in vain" (Is. 65:17–25).

From Rom. 15:25–27 and 2 Cor. 8:1–15, it appears that one of the purposes of Paul's third missionary journey was to raise an offering from the Gentiles for Jewish Christians in Judea who were in need, possibly as a result of persecution. Apparently, Paul had already told the Corinthians about this project in an earlier letter, in which he also addressed other issues (5:9). They had asked for more information, and Paul proceeds to give directions about taking up the collection (Introduction: Date and Occasion). for the saints. See note on 1:2. As in 2 Cor. 8:4; 9:1, here Paul has in view specifically the followers of Jesus residing in Judea, from whom the gospel went out to the Gentiles (Rom. 15:26–27).

The reference is to Sunday, the day on which the resurrected Lord met with His disciples (John 20:19, 26; cf. also "the Lord's day" in Rev. 1:10). Acts 20:7 indicates that the early Christians met on Sunday "to break bread" (part of their worship), and it would have been appropriate also to designate that day for collecting the offering in worship.

This comment possibly reflects doubts on the part of some as to whether Paul should be given sole responsibility for the money (2:1 note). In 2 Cor. 8:16–24, Paul emphasizes the full trustworthiness of Titus and one or more other brothers appointed by the churches themselves to administer the reception and transmission of this offering, to enlist the Corinthians' confidence that their gift will reach its intended destination (see Acts 20:4).

These verses make clear that Paul wrote the letter from Ephesus and intended to visit Corinth by way of the northern land route around the Aegean Sea. Both Acts 20:1, 2 and 2 Cor. 2:12, 13 indicate that he carried out this plan. What Paul did not foresee at this time was the prior need to make a short and unpleasant visit to Corinth soon after writing 1 Corinthians (2 Cor. 1:23; 2:1; 13:2; cf. Introduction to 2 Corinthians: Date and Occasion).
Paul's resolve to prolong his ministry in Ephesus until Pentecost was determined by the opportunity for fruitful gospel labor in the city, despite the many opponents arrayed against him (15:32).

Earlier (4:17), Paul mentioned that Timothy was coming as his representative (Acts 19:22). Paul wants them to treat his younger coworker with respect and kindness — in contrast to the criticism that some in the Corinthian church lodged against Paul himself.

Apparently, the Corinthians in their letter had asked for Apollos to return to them (Introduction: Date and Occasion; Acts 18:27–19:1). In spite of the improper attitude of the Corinthians (4:6; 4:15 note), Paul honored their request. It was not Apollos's "will" to go at this time, but he would come later. Thus, this brief report reinforces Paul's earlier affirmation that he and Apollos are not competitors but co-laborers with mutual respect for each other's distinctive ministries (3:4–11).

This passage commends "Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus," who probably had carried the letter from the church in Corinth. Paul's emphasis (especially in the words "I urge you, brothers \... be subject") suggests that these men, Stephanas in particular, were appointed leaders but did not enjoy proper respect from the congregation (cf. 1:16). The phrase "for your absence" does not necessarily imply a criticism (the Greek at the end of Phil. 2:30 is almost identical), but here it may suggest that the church as a whole failed to refresh his spirit.

Ephesus, where 1 Corinthians was written, was the most important city in the Roman province of Asia, the southwestern part of the Anatolian peninsula, which is today part of modern Turkey (Acts 19:10). Aquila and Prisca. This couple played an important role during Paul's initial visit to Corinth (Acts 18:1–3), so the congregation knew them well. They accompanied Paul from Corinth as far as Ephesus (Acts 18:18–19, 26), and thus were reunited with the apostle when he returned to that Asian metropolis (19:1). By the time he wrote to the church at Rome from Corinth, Prisca and Aquila had returned to Rome, from which an imperial edict had previously expelled them and other Jews, and were hosting a church in their home (Rom. 16:3–5) as they had done in Ephesus and probably elsewhere.

A normal greeting in the early church. Though this practice was not uncommon in Judaism and Roman culture, the word "holy" indicates the added significance such a greeting had among the saints, since it represented the special relationship of brothers and sisters in Christ (Rom. 16:16 note; 2 Cor. 13:12; 1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14).

Like some of Paul's other epistles, the letter up to this point would have been written by a trained scribe (Rom. 16:22), but Paul's custom was to add a few words himself as a personal signature (see Gal. 6:11; 2 Thess. 3:17).

These strong words, written in Paul's own hand, assert the apostolic authority behind the whole letter. This is not a curse on unbelievers in general but on those who reject the authority of the letter (14:37; Gal. 1:8, 9; 2 Thess. 3:14, 15). Our Lord, come. Paul gives a transliteration of the Aramaic words Marana tha (or Maran atha, "Our Lord has come"), reflecting the worship of the early church in Palestine. The phrase reflects the universal Christian desire for the Lord Jesus Christ to return in glory and to complete the work of salvation now begun in believers (Rev. 22:20).
After a long letter consisting primarily of severe rebukes, these affectionate words may come as a surprise. Paul has not forgotten the pastoral needs of his congregation (1:2 note).

2 Corinthians.note: Paul describes himself as "apostle," but not his associate (also 1 Cor.1:1; Col. 1:1). A man who held the office of apostle was an eyewitness of the resurrection (Acts 1:22; 1 Cor. 15:8) who had been personally appointed by Christ ("of Jesus Christ," see Matt. 10:1–7; Acts 1:24–26; Gal. 1:1) to govern the early church (1 Thess. 4:8; 2 Thess. 3:6, 14), and to teach or write with authority (1 Cor. 14:37; 1 Thess. 2:13; 4:15; 2 Pet. 3:15, 16) as one who had received special revelation from God (Eph. 2:20; 3:5). The term is used as a title of the twelve disciples and Paul in a distinctive sense. It is also used in a broader sense (Rom. 16:7), while in general or nontechnical use it means a "messenger" or "representative" (8:23; Phil. 2:25). When used in this way, it does not refer to a specific ordained office. by the will of God. It is God's sovereign choice that ultimately places people in church offices and ministries. The apostolic office was extraordinary and temporary, and it passed away once the last surviving eyewitness of the resurrection died and the NT was completed. The ordinary church offices continue to be necessary and are filled by elders (Acts 20:28) and others whose gifts equip them for ministries (1 Cor. 12:7, 11, 28). An individual's calling to one of the ordinary church offices is confirmed by the people of God as the church discerns who has the gifts and qualifications for the work (Eph. 4:11). Two ordinary church offices, elder and deacon, receive special attention in Scripture (Acts 6:1–6; 1 Tim. 3:1–13; Titus 1:5–9), but other callings are mentioned as well, including evangelist, shepherd (pastor), and teacher. Those callings, enumerated in Ephesians 4:11, are sometimes considered ordinary church offices as well, but it is possible that they are just callings and not ordained offices. Ephesians 4:11 also mentions the office of prophet, but as that was an extraordinary office given to establish the foundation of the church, it likewise passed away once the apostles had laid the church's foundation in their preaching and teaching (cf.Eph. 2:19–21). saints. Lit. "holy ones." Paul commonly uses the term to refer to all Christians (Rom. 15:25; Phil. 1:1). in the whole of Achaia. Though the letter was intended primarily for the church at Corinth, Paul apparently realized that it would be read by neighboring churches in the region of Achaia, the southern part of modern Greece. On Corinth, see note on Acts 18:1.

Grace is God's undeserved favor — not just in initial forgiveness of sins, but in the ordinary events of everyday life as well. peace. The outward blessing of social order and the inward blessing of a good relationship with God (Rom. 5:1; 1 Tim. 2:2). God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. It is evidence of the deity of Christ that He with the Father should be mentioned equally as the origin of grace and peace for the Corinthian church.

The three persons of the Trinity are equally divine, yet they are one God, not three. Paul may be appealing directly to the Corinthians to "be reconciled to God," since he later summons each member of the congregation to "examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith" (13:5). For Christians, reconciliation to God is in one sense renewed each day through repentance and faith (Matt. 6:12; 1 John 1:9). When Paul was at Corinth he supported himself (Acts 18:3) and accepted help from other churches as well (v. 8). Some of the Corinthians seem to have been offended by Paul's refusal to accept their gift, probably offered to him in response to his preaching of the gospel to them. In ancient times, giving and receiving gifts was often used to establish and maintain friendships among social equals, as well as to signal dependents' subordination to patrons. In this system, Paul's refusal of a gift might be taken as an insult, a proud refusal to be involved with inferiors. But the apostle views his relationship with the Corinthians, not from the standpoint of worldly social convention (5:16), but from the standpoint of the new creation (5:17) in which he has been called to be an apostle and spiritual father. As a father, he may rightly give to his children without receiving anything in return (12:14, 15). Moreover, as Paul previously explained to the Corinthians, he considered it aprivilege to "present the gospel free of charge" (1 Cor. 9:19) so that, when he first came to a new city, the mode of his communication illustrated the grace of his message.

Although he speaks indirectly and even seems to distinguish between the recipient of the vision and himself (v. 5), Paul clearly means himself, as becomes clear in v. 7. Through this transparent pretense of distancing himself from an anonymous individual so privileged to receive a visionary revelation, Paul's example signals his strong disapproval of self-promotion (10:18). third heaven. According to a common enumeration, the first heaven is the atmosphere of the birds and clouds, the second is the sky in which we see the stars, and the third is heaven, the invisible dwelling place of God. For fourteen years, Paul had not made this experience a focus of his teaching, as some would have done. His focus was the message of Christ: "What we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord" (4:5).

That is, the "third heaven" of v. 2. The Gk. word for "paradise" (derived from a term meaning "garden") is used with various meanings outside the NT, but in the NT, all three occurrences (v. 3; also Luke 23:43; Rev. 2:7) refer to heaven, the place where the saints dwell with God.
Paul wanted people to evaluate him on the basis of their firsthand knowledge of him.

Many possibilities have been suggested for this "thorn," such as a physical ailment of some sort ("in the flesh"; cf. Gal. 4:13–15), a harassing demon ("a messenger of Satan"), or the constant harassment of Jewish persecutors. Throughout the history of the church, no agreement has been reached among hundreds of commentators. As it stands, the "thorn" of Paul's experiences is readily applied to a variety of trials faced in this life. Few of God's servants have been free from at least some kind of hindrance, weakness, or opposition.

Paul's usual expression to refer to Christ, not to God the Father. Although prayers in the NT are most often directed to God the Father, this is an example of prayer directed to Christ (cf. Acts 1:24; 7:59; 1 Cor. 16:22; Rev. 22:20). It is striking that in his "boasting," Paul testifies about a request that God did not fulfill.

God will accomplish His purposes without taking from His servant the thorn that seems to hinder him. Despite human weaknesses, God's grace accomplishes His purposes in a fallen world. This promise from God no doubt gave Paul strength and encouragement in subsequent sufferings. Paul shortly ties the general principle to its source — the cross of Christ (13:4). Paul's whole response to attacks on his apostolic authority has been patterned consciously on Christ and Him crucified, and not on the so-called "Jesus" and the different "gospel" that his opponents foisted upon the erring Corinthians (11:4 note).
Paul's spiritual view is so clear that he can see his sufferings as reasons for rejoicing, for he knows that in them all of Christ's power is at work.

Paul has to "boast" about his apostolic weakness because the Corinthians, who know him well, have not defended him against the false apostles, but instead have been seduced (11:1–3) by inflated self-claims and untrue criticism of Paul.

Paul identifies the "signs of a true apostle" with miracles, "wonders and mighty works." Throughout this epistle, Paul also points to other marks that distinguish him from the false apostles: the changed lives of the Corinthians (3:2, 3), the blameless character of his ministry (6:3–10; 7:2; 8:20, 21), his genuine love for his churches (6:11, 12; 7:3; 11:7–11), and his sacrificial endurance of suffering (6:3–10; 11:23–33). In addition to these marks, Paul is ready to mention miraculous signs as divinely authenticating his apostolic ministry. See 1 Cor. 13:2; theological note "The Apostles" on p. 1912.

See Introduction: Date and Occasion. The first visit was on Paul's second missionary journey (Acts 18:1–18). The second visit (2:1) is not recorded in Acts but occurred sometime during Paul's extended stay at Ephesus (Acts 19:1–41). I seek not what is yours but you. Unlike those preachers whose goal is their own financial reward.
Perhaps Paul's opponents were saying that his apparent selflessness was a trick to deceive them. Paul answers that he never exploited them through others (v. 17).
Titus was coming ahead of Paul (8:6, 16, 17).

Paul again emphasizes that he has not been speaking for his own reputation or glory but for the good of the church and for the glory of God. Again he reveals a strong awareness that everything he writes and does is "in the sight of God." See note on 2:10.

Paul's fatherly ties with the Corinthian church are strong, and he knows that if he returns to find some of them (his "children," v. 14) still unruly, it will be humiliating for him, just as parents are humiliated by the misbehavior of their children. many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented. False apostles were not the only problem in Corinth. There were some people still engaging in sin, and Paul warns them (see 1 Cor. 5:1, 2; 6:9–20).

See note on 12:14. Paul quotes Deut. 17:6 and 19:15. The "two or three witnesses" likely does not mean Paul's two or three visits to Corinth (for Paul is still only one witness), but is rather a reminder that when he comes, all charges will be considered fairly and dealt with in a just way. On the other hand, in view of his apostolic authority from Christ, he may be implying that each of the warnings he previously delivered both in person and by letter constitutes a distinct testimony or evidence to establish a "case" against those who resist God's truth.
A strong statement of Paul's apostolic authority. Christ Himself was speaking through Paul, and Christ's words through Paul would powerfully silence any offenders.

Paul's life (as that of all Christians) was united with Christ in His death and resurrection, and he continued to share in the resurrection power of Christ as long as he lived (see 4:10–12; Phil. 3:10, 11).

See 1 Cor. 11:28; Gal. 6:4. Paul's words help clarify the doctrine of assurance of faith. Paul asks the Corinthians to examine their own lives for evidence of salvation. Such evidence would include trust in Christ (Heb. 3:6), obedience to God (Matt. 7:21), growth in holiness (Heb. 12:14; 1 John 3:3), the fruit of the Spirit (Gal. 5:22, 23), love for other Christians (1 John 3:14), positive influence on others (Matt. 5:16), adhering to the apostolic teaching (1 John 4:2), and the testimony of the Holy Spirit within them (Rom. 8:15, 16).
Christians in the church from which Paul was writing (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

A Trinitarian benediction, corresponding to the threefold placing of the Lord's name upon Israel in the benediction pronounced by OT priests (Num. 6:23–27). See theological note "The Triunity of God" on p. 1204.

Galatians.note: We know from fifteen references in Acts 7–13 that Paul was also called "Saul," the Hb. name borne by Israel's first king, who had belonged to the tribe of Benjamin (1 Sam. 9:1, 2), as did the apostle (Phil. 3:5). In his letters, however, he always calls himself "Paul," a common Roman name, probably connected with his Roman citizenship (Acts 16:37, 38; 22:25–28). Before entering Galatia, Paul had evangelized the proconsul of Cyprus, who bore the same name (Sergius Paulus; Acts 13:9 note). apostle. The word means "messenger." Paul could on occasion use it to refer to an envoy sent by a church such as Epaphroditus (Phil. 2:25), but he uses it often in Galatians to denote emissaries uniquely sent by the risen Christ and bearing His delegated authority, including the original apostles at Jerusalem (1:17, 19; 1 Cor. 15:9). Paul here identifies himself as an apostle along these latter lines. Paul claims the authority of an apostle to lay the foundation of the church (1 Cor. 3:10; 9:1; 14:37, 38; Eph. 2:20; 3:3–5).
