As outlined in the following verses, the "fullness" of God, which the false teachers pretended to offer, actually resides in Christ, and it does so "bodily" through His incarnation, which occurred for the sake of His reconciling death (1:20, 22). This fullness is therefore obtained only through Him (1:19, 20). See theological note "The Deity of Christ" on p. 1851.

It is often thought that Paul mentions circumcision at this point because the false teachers in Colossae were commending it, just as the Judaizers in Galatia were. The heresy threatening the Colossian believers does seem to reflect Jewish influences (2:16, 17; see Introduction: Special Issues). However, in this letter, there is no direct argument made against circumcision, as there is in Galatians. It is better to think of Paul as introducing the topic to show that something of what the false teachers have promised the Colossians — power over the flesh (v. 23) — is already theirs in their relationship with Christ. As the initiating rite of the old covenant, circumcision signified cutting away sin, undergoing a change of heart, and being included in the household of faith (Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4; 9:25, 26; Ezek. 44:7, 9). Dramatically, Paul says that in their baptism into Christ and into His body, these Gentiles have already been circumcised. Baptism is "the circumcision of Christ," and it signifies the washing away of sin, personal renewal by the Spirit of God, and membership in the body of Christ (cf. v. 13; Acts 2:38; Rom. 6:4; 1 Cor. 12:13; Titus 3:5; 1 Pet. 3:21). The passage makes an important point about the unity of the covenant of grace in both the OT and NT era: Gentile believers are not expected to follow the old covenant mode of identification with God and His people (Acts 15). But their faith in Christ has nevertheless made them as much children of Abraham as if they were ethnic Jewish believers (Rom. 2:28, 29; Gal. 3:26–29; Phil. 3:3). Baptism is not identical to circumcision, but it corresponds to it in essence (Rom. 4:11), pointing to the same spiritual benefits, and has replaced it as the sign of the covenant. Given the association between circumcision and baptism, 2:11 is important evidence for the practice of infant baptism. If infant children of old covenant believers were circumcised, and if baptism replaces circumcision under the new covenant, then there is a strong argument that infant children of new covenant believers should be baptized. They should receive the sign of covenant initiation just as children who lived before the coming of Christ did. Moreover, as was true of circumcision, baptism avails nothing for its recipient apart from the recipient's faith in the promises of God (Rom. 2:25–29; 1 Pet. 3:18–25). See theological notes "Infant Baptism" on p. 41 and "Baptism" on p. 1988.

It is characteristic of Paul to speak of justification rather than forgiveness, and of sin in the singular rather than of sins in the plural (Rom. 5:12–21). His purpose here may be to emphasize that God has put away the guilt that stems from particular sinful acts. See theological note "Rebirth" on p. 1857.

The law is compared to a certificate of indebtedness written in the debtor's own hand. Jesus was born "under the law," subject to its demands and curses (Gal. 4:4). On the cross, He was "made \... to be sin" (2 Cor. 5:21) and endured the law's curse against unrighteousness (Gal. 3:13). In the execution of the death sentence on Jesus when He was nailed to the cross, Paul sees the cancellation of the death warrant that stood against transgressors of the law. Paul also sees here the fulfillment of their obligation to keep perfectly the law's demands in order to enter into life. The believer is no longer subject to the threat of the law's condemnation.

The image is of a conquering Roman general parading his vanquished and humiliated enemies behind his chariot. An invisible cosmic struggle took place at the cross, and the prince of this age was "cast out" (John 12:31), "thrown down to the earth" (Rev. 12:9), and "bound" (Rev. 20:2; see also Matt. 12:29; Luke 10:18). Through Jesus' death for sinners, Satan was robbed of his power to intimidate and control people through the threat of death and eternal separation from God (Ezek. 18; Rom. 5:12; 6:23; Heb. 2:14, 15). The struggle with Satan and his legions will not see its conclusion until the Lord's return in glory (2 Cor. 4:4; Eph. 6:10–18; 1 Pet. 5:8), but the devil's power is broken. As Luther sang, "Lo, his doom is sure." With the ground of their constant accusations taken away, the hostile powers of Satan have lost their advantage forever. See theological note "Demons" on p. 299.

In Colossae, observance of the Jewish Sabbath feast days (the monthly "new moon" and annual feasts) was apparently being advocated in order to placate supernatural powers or angels thought to direct the course of the stars, regulate the calendar, and determine human destiny. This, Paul says, is a form of bondage from which Christ came to liberate men and women. Paul is not speaking here of the observance of a weekly day of rest and worship, which is grounded in creation and integral to the abiding moral law (Ex. 20:8–11). See Introduction: Special Issues.

This has been taken by some scholars as a reference to practices found among some Jewish mystics, whose goal was to participate in angelic worship before the throne of God and to attain to ecstatic prayer through asceticism and strict observance of the Torah. In this case, "worship of angels" would mean "worship along with angels." This line of interpretation assumes that the false teachers actually practiced a relatively orthodox Judaism and wanted to worship God. But the appearance given by Colossians is that the church was being tempted to worship not God but spirits intermediate between God and humans (see Introduction: Special Issues).

To seek the favor of angelic beings is to fail to honor Christ for what He is as the fullness of deity (v. 9; 1:19) and to not enjoy the totality of the redemption that has been won in His death and resurrection (vv. 10–15; 1:20–22). Head \... body. This language looks back at 1:18 and ahead to the way Paul develops the idea of the Christian life under Christ's headship in the context of membership in the church in 3:1–4:6.

Believers' union with Christ in His death (Rom. 6:3–7) has freed them from worldly rules that enslave the consciences of others. Paul will next argue (3:1–5) that believers' union with Christ in His resurrection and ascension entails their responsibility to have their minds (perspectives, affections, values) defined by heaven and the Christ "who is your life," who lives and reigns there. elemental spirits of the world. Or "elements of the world." See Introduction: Special Issues.

God only accepts worship offered according to His will revealed in Scripture, not religious exercises done at the dictate of presumptuous human whim (Matt. 15:9). The idea that God must be worshiped only in the way He has instituted has had a profound influence in Reformed churches, which identifies the idea as the "Regulative Principle of Worship." of no value. The Greek of this verse is very difficult. It may mean that the ascetic disciplines Paul is opposing are not only worthless but actively harmful, exciting their own sort of "indulgence of the flesh." For Paul, "the flesh" is manifested not only in bodily sensuality but also in attitudes of the heart such as pride, jealousy, and rivalry (Gal. 5:19–21). This is precisely what the Reformers — preeminently Luther — saw themselves as opposing in the extrabiblical rituals that had emerged in the medieval church.

The route to maturity is not the path of secret revelations, or of self-punishing disciplines. It consists in understanding and living on the basis of the believer's death (2:20; 3:5), resurrection, and heavenly enthronement "with Christ" (3:1). The Colossians have a false notion of heavenly reality, which ironically leads them to fruitless efforts on the earthly plane. Fruitful living on earth begins, rather, with a right understanding of heavenly reality. 3:1 If then you have been raised with Christ. Note the parallel statements of fact in this section: believers have died with Christ (v. 3; 2:11, 12, 20); they have been raised with Him (v. 1; 2:12, 13); they are with Christ in heaven (v. 3; Eph. 2:6); they will be with Him at His return (v. 4); they have "put off the old self" (literally, "old man," v. 9); and they have "put on the new self" (lit. "new man," v. 10). Paul's instructions for behavior come only after his description of the redemption God has richly bestowed on His people (2:6, 7 note). Obedience is a response of gratitude to God's favor already bestowed and not a means of gaining it. seated at the right hand of God. A pivotal, exultant theme in the NT, based on the prophetic promise of Ps. 110:1 (Acts 2:33–35; 5:31; 7:55, 56; Rom. 8:34; Eph. 1:20; Heb. 1:3, 13; 8:1; 10:12; 12:2; 1 Pet. 3:22; Rev. 3:21). The phrase refers to the very authority of Jesus over the world about which Paul wrote in Col. 1. The Christian life must be lived with an abiding confidence in and submission to the lordship of Christ.

Some understand this to mean that the new life of the Christian is not obvious to others and is "hidden" or concealed in that sense. However, comparison with 2:3 indicates that more is in view. The believer is inseparably united to Christ (John 6:51–58 note; cf. Gal. 2:20). The full reality of the new life is not yet fully revealed, but to be "hidden with Christ in God" means that this new life is secure in Christ. What God has freely given, neither man nor angel can take away (John 10:29).
The hope of Christ's return is central to the ethics of this section (vv. 5–11).

The first of a series of behavioral imperatives that continue through 4:6. Although Paul rejects legalistic asceticism, he calls upon believers to become in practice what they are in principle: dead to sin and alive to God (Rom. 6:1–14). There is a way of living that is incompatible with life in Christ, and Paul calls for a rigorous and radical departure from that old life. In v. 5, he lists five vices, four of which have to do with sex, with the fifth being covetousness; in v. 8, he lists five more vices, all having to do with anger and abusive speech.
That is, before they were brought "to the kingdom of his beloved Son" (1:13).
Believers' "change of clothing" is from their fallen identity in Adam ("old self" is "old man," per the text note) to their new identity in Christ, the "new man." See Eph. 2:15; 4:22–24).

This verse was probably written with an eye to the exclusiveness of the Colossian false teachers. However, the cross-cultural unity of all those who belong to Christ is an idea that comes readily enough to Paul's mind (Gal. 3:28; 1 Cor. 7:17–24). barbarian. Refers to non-Greek speakers, who were considered uncivilized by Greeks (see Rom. 1:14). Scythian. By reputation, an uncultured slave class drawn from tribes around the Black Sea. Scythians were lampooned in Greek comedy because of their uncouth ways and speech, and the first-century Jewish historian Josephus called them "little better than wild beasts." slave, free. Distinctions of social position are irrelevant to one's spiritual standing in Christ (1 Cor. 7:17–24). Simultaneously, as Paul's separate instructions to slaves and slaveholders in 3:22–4:1 make clear, unity in Christ does not mandate or imply a uniformity of function or capacity. But it is important to recognize that "Christ is all, and in all." In the Pauline churches, diverse social positions continued to exist and were not subject to a uniform leveling process. Rather, they become opportunities for expressing Christ's love across traditional social boundaries.

These verses outline the obligations all Christians have toward one another; 3:18–4:2 will focus on opportunities for service within specified relationships. 3:12 Put on. Paul envisions believers' taking on the character of the Lord Himself. The "new self" of v. 10 is not something believers must construct by their own power. Their new identities, already bestowed by God's grace through faith, take shape as they come to know Christ better, since He is the image of the invisible God and the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (1:15; 2:3). as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved. In contrast to the Colossians' fear of cosmic powers, believers are entitled to a clear sense that God guarantees their relationship with Him (John 6:37, 44, 65; 15:16; Eph. 1:4, 5; Phil. 1:6). They can know that they have been declared righteous on the basis of a righteousness that is not their own (Rom. 3:21–26; 1 Cor. 1:2, 30), and that God genuinely, even passionately, loves them (John 3:16; Rom. 8:32; Gal. 2:20; Titus 3:4; 1 John 4:9, 10). compassionate hearts. An emotional, caring relationship with those whose lives are hurt and broken (Matt. 9:36; 14:14; Rom. 12:1). kindness. Readiness to do good, even when it may be undeserved (Rom. 2:4; Titus 3:4). humility. A posture of lowliness and servanthood (Mark 10:45; Phil. 2:1–11). meekness. Or, "gentleness" in offering help, a non-coercive approach to encouraging change in others' lives (Matt. 11:29; 2 Cor. 10:1; Gal. 6:1; 2 Tim. 2:25). patience. Willingness to take the long view in the face of human frailty (Rom. 2:4; 1 Tim. 1:16).
See Eph. 4:32–5:2, where Paul grounds Christian forbearance, forgiveness, and love explicitly in the example provided by the redemptive pattern of Christ's work.

In its practice of love, forgiveness, and graciousness, the Christian community is to be a showcase of the reconciliation Christ has brought to the universe (1:20–22; 2:14, 15), and to individual sinners (vv. 11, 13; see Eph. 2:14–18).

Because believers are united to Christ (3:3 note), not only the "word of Christ" but Christ Himself lives in their hearts (Gal. 2:20; Eph. 3:17; cf. Rom. 8:9). With God's wisdom present in this way (3:3; cf. 1 Cor. 1:30), the ethical demands of Christian love can be lived out in every part of life, including the everyday responsibilities that are reviewed in 3:18–4:6. teaching and admonishing. The first half of this verse is strongly reminiscent of 1:28. In the Colossians' ministry to one another, the word of Christ will be as effective as the presence of the apostle himself. psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. In the Septuagint, the three nouns used in this phrase are often synonymous. It is unlikely that in Colossians they designate three separate types of song (Eph. 5:19). See topical article "Worship" on p. 2383.
See note on Eph. 5:22–32.
See notes on Eph. 6:1–3, 4.

This treatment of slave and free in Colossians may be related to the subject matter of the letter to Philemon. Onesimus was a runaway slave whom Paul was returning with a letter to his owner, Philemon. Onesimus was accompanying Tych­icus with the letter to the Colossians (4:7–9), and they were probably carrying the letter to Philemon as well (see Introduction to Philemon).

Two other ways in which believers can set their "minds on things that are above" (3:2) are praying (Eph. 6:18–20 note) and telling their faith wisely and persuasively to outsiders so that they may be drawn to the fullness of life in Christ.

Or "bound," the verb related to "chains," which Paul asks the Colossians to remember in his personally handwritten closing (v. 18). His captivity tested his resolve to seize opportunities for speaking the mystery of Christ boldly and clearly, so he needed the support of other believers' prayers.

In the ancient world, salt was used as a preservative for meat, helping to retard spoilage. Christians' speech, like their lives (Matt. 5:13), must promote purity rather than fostering spiritual, ethical, or relational corruption (Eph. 4:29; 5:3, 4).

The letter ends with a brief look at the complex and fluid network of leaders that tied Paul's churches together. Some of the same names occur in Philem. 23, 24. 4:7 Tychicus. The primary carrier of the letters to the Colossians, Philemon, and the Ephesians (Eph. 6:21, 22). First mentioned as part of Paul's entourage in Acts 20:4, Tychicus was from the Roman province of Asia (in modern-day Turkey), and appears to have been one of Paul's more trusted emissaries toward the end of his ministry (2 Tim. 4:12; Titus 3:12).
See Introduction to Philemon.

This Jew from Thessalonica had been publicly associated with Paul's tumultuous ministry in Ephesus (Acts 19:29). He had traveled with Paul's company through Greece (Acts 20:4) and on to Jerusalem and Rome (Acts 27:2), where he shared the apostle's imprisonment. Mark. The rift that had emerged more than a decade earlier between Paul and the cousins Barnabas and John Mark (author of the gospel of Mark, Acts 13:13; 15:37–40) was finally healed (2 Tim. 4:11; Philem. 24). Paul's special mention of Mark testifies to the power of the reconciling work of Christ (1:20–22) and to the peace that is to rule within Christ's body (3:15).
Otherwise unknown.
The resident of Colossae who had brought the gospel to his hometown (1:7) and reported to Paul the church's vitality in faith, love, and hope (1:3–5, 8). See Introduction: Date and Occasion.
See Introduction: Date and Occasion.

This traveling companion of Paul in Acts was also with Paul on what may have been the eve of his death (2 Tim. 4:11). As author of the gospel of Luke and Acts, he was also Paul's chronicler. Though his writing shows him to be exceptionally literate, the mention of his occupation does not necessarily mark him as a man of high social standing, since physicians were often slaves. Demas. Demas abandoned Paul during his second imprisonment in Rome (2 Tim. 4:10). He is mentioned one other time (Philem. 24).

Some manuscripts identify this person, who hosted a Laodicean house church, as a woman ("her house"). There are several references to women (whose marital status is not mentioned) as patrons or hosts of churches, or as workers in ministry (Acts 12:12; 16:13–15; Rom. 16:1, 2, 6, 7, 12, 13; Phil. 4:2, 3; possibly 2 John 1, 5; cf. Introduction to 2 John: Characteristics and Primary Themes). The standard of relationships between men and women, particularly husbands and wives, set out in 3:18 and parallels (1 Cor. 14:33–35; Eph. 5:22–33; 1 Tim. 2:11–15), was not inconsistent with the partnership in some forms of Christian ministry that existed between men and women in the early church. church in her house. There is no evidence of churches owning separate property for worship until the middle of the third century. Until then, it was the norm for churches to meet in private dwellings. Those who exercised a ministry of hospitality by having churches in their homes were important benefactors of the early church (Acts 12:12; Rom. 16:5; 1 Cor. 16:19; Philem. 2). On hospitality, see Rom. 12:13; 1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:8; Heb. 13:2; 1 Pet. 4:9.

Some suggest that Paul is referring to the letter to the Ephesians, which in some ancient manuscripts lacks a destination, and which may have gone out as a circular letter (see Introduction to Ephesians: Date and Occasion). Since Tychicus is the bearer of Ephesians as well (Eph. 6:21, 22), the conclusion that the Ephesian and Laodicean letters were one and the same would imply that Colossians and Ephesians were written at about the same time, and that Tychicus traveled first to Laodicea and then to Colossae. However, it may be more natural to assume, on the basis of the more reflective style of Ephesians, that it was written some time after Colossians, and that Tychicus brought the Ephesian letter around to the churches on a subsequent trip (if, indeed, it was a circular letter). The best proposal for the identity of the letter from Laodicea is that it was a separate letter that has not survived.
If Philemon was the host of the church in Colossae, which had seen the Onesimus incident, this verse may suggest that Archippus was its spiritual leader ("our fellow soldier"; Philem. 2).

Paul's general practice was to dictate his letters, but to write the closing sentences himself. These concluding sections would vary, depending on the circumstances. Sometimes they include personal greetings to strengthen the bond between himself, his workers, and his churches (vv. 7–17; cf. Rom. 16); sometimes they include a summary of the contents of the letter (e.g., Gal. 6:11–17); and sometimes they have a signature that guaranteed the authenticity of the letter (1 Cor. 16:21; 2 Thess. 3:17; Philem. 19). Remember my chains. See note on v. 3.

1 Thessalonians.note: The Latin name of Silas, a prophet of the Jerusalem church delegated to accompany Paul and Barnabas to Antioch to deliver the decision of the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:22, 27, 32, 40). Silas was chosen by Paul to be his associate on his second missionary journey, during which the church in the Macedonian city of Thessalonica was planted (Acts 17:1–9). He, or another "faithful brother" of the same name, was also associated with Peter's ministry (1 Pet. 5:12). Timothy. The son of a Greek father and a devout Jewish mother, he was at the time of writing a relative newcomer to the Christian mission. Paul and Silas had drafted this young but highly regarded disciple to join in their ministry roughly a year earlier in Lystra (Acts 16:1). in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. This statement points to the unique intimacy between the Father and the Son, for the church is said to be "in" both (see Introduction: Characteristics and Themes).

In this epistle, Paul speaks consistently on behalf of the team, named in v. 1, that planted the Thessalonian church — Silas, Timothy, and himself. He uses plural first-person pronouns nearly eighty times, while referring to himself individually only four times (2:18; 3:5; 5:27). Paul does not give any degree of thanks to the Thessalonians but gives all thanks to God, since God is completely the cause of their salvation and good works (which v. 4 also bears out).

The faith of the Thessalonians, obviously a chief concern for Paul, is referred to again in v. 8; 3:2, 5–7, 10; 5:8. True, saving faith necessarily bears fruit in obedience to the Lord. labor of love. Their love was shown especially in the welcome they gave to the travelers (v. 9). Paul commends their love again in 4:9, 10, where he says they are "taught by God" in their love for one another. steadfastness of hope. Their eschatological hope is their assurance that the Lord Jesus will return to deliver them from their present troubles and from God's coming wrath. For the triad of "faith," "hope," and "love," see 5:8; Rom. 5:2–5; 1 Cor. 13:13; Gal. 5:5, 6; Col. 1:4, 5; Heb. 6:10–12; 10:22–24; 1 Pet. 1:3–8, 21, 22.

Divine election is a theme of both Thessalonian epistles (5:9; 2 Thess. 2:13). Paul is not afraid to assure this young, predominantly Gentile congregation that they were elected by God. Paul sees in them the fruit of God's electing grace, manifested in their response to the preaching of the gospel and their early progress in sanctification (2 Thess. 2:13 note).

Paul repeatedly urged believers to follow his example as he followed that of Christ (1 Cor. 4:16; 11:1; 2 Thess. 3:7–9; Phil. 3:15–17). the joy of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit plays an especially prominent role in sustaining the believer who undergoes persecution for Christ (Matt. 10:19, 20; 1 Pet. 4:12–14).

Paul writes from Achaia, having traversed Macedonia and come through Athens to Corinth. Along the way, he has found that the Christians already know of his work in Thessalonica and have learned of the faith of the Thessalonians. The Thessalonian Christians, beginners in Christ though they are, are examples to others of faith, love, and hope.

These verses parallel the preaching of Paul at Athens (Acts 17:22–31). In preaching to the Jews, Paul could presuppose that his hearers acknowledged the true God and the authority of the OT Scriptures, and then go on to proclaim the advent of God's promised Messiah. To those uninstructed in the faith of Israel, Paul stressed two things: first, the need to acknowledge the true and living God and forsake dead idols; second, God's coming universal judgment to be executed by Jesus Christ, the God-man, who died and rose from the dead (4:6; Acts 17:29–31). 1:10 from heaven. See 4:16; 2 Thess. 1:7; cf. Acts 1:11; Phil. 3:20. Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come. Jesus' death turned away God's wrath long ago, but the full import of this saving work will not be displayed until judgment day. Then, through Christ's intervention, believers will be spared the condemnation and punishment their sins would otherwise deserve (Rom. 5:9). This is a key verse for explaining what exactly we are saved from. We are saved by God from the wrath of God in order that we will live for God.

Paul seems to respond to certain doubts or criticisms of his ministry. The tumultuous circumstances and precipitous nature of his team's departure from Thessalonica (though the latter was at the initiative of local believers; Acts 17:5–10), apparently raised misgivings in some minds about Paul's commitment to the Thessalonian church and his willingness to risk a second visit to their city (vv. 17–19). He implicitly defends his ministry of the gospel, and at the same time, by recalling the work he and his companions have done, he gives the Thessalonians a pattern of loving service to follow.

Despite being called by God to enter Macedonia (Acts 16:9, 10), Paul and Silas had been severely beaten and chained in a Macedonian prison (at Philippi). The missionaries had to be courageous and selflessly devoted to God's purpose. the gospel of God. Paul stresses the pure, and indeed divine, source of his message and ministry. Note the repetition of the phrase in vv. 8 and 9. The gospel is always carried as a trust from God Himself.

Paul's constant awareness that he served as a steward of God's mysteries in the very presence of God "who tests our hearts" (v. 4) restrained him from modifying his message through "flattery" and protected his heart from the motive of "greed," unlike others who vied for believers' allegiance (1 Cor. 4:1–5; 2 Cor. 2:17; 4:2; 11:4, 5, 13–15; 1 Tim. 6:3–5).

Paul consistently defended his apostolic authority, delegated to him by the risen Lord Jesus, but at times he refrained from exercising it for the sake of serving others' needs and setting an example of selflessness (1 Cor. 9:1–18; Philem. 8).

Apparent throughout this section (vv. 17–20; 3:6–12) is Paul's deep affection for his spiritual children, who only months before were complete strangers to him, alienated by race, culture, and religion. His treatment of these believers reflects both a mother's gentleness (v. 7) and a father's loving encouragement to mature conduct (vv. 11, 12).

This verse summarizes Paul's exhortation and charge during his initial visit in Thessalonica. In contrast to the idols the Thessalonians had forsaken (1:9), the true and living God has a "kingdom and glory," and in His fathomless mercy He chooses to share this kingdom with those who worship Him through Jesus Christ. Called to enter this kingdom, believers know in part its power and enjoy a measure of its life here and now (Rom. 14:17; 1 Cor. 4:20; Col. 1:13, 14) while they long for the day when they will experience its its fullness.
The Word of God, though it comes through human agency, is a divine message that works in believers through the Holy Spirit (Is. 55:11; Acts 20:32; 2 Tim. 2:15–17; Heb. 4:12).
The power of God's Word in them was proved as they faced fierce persecution from their kinsmen and, like the churches in Judea, endured it with faith and joy (Acts 17:5–9, cf. v. 6).

Just as Jesus noted the continuity of those who persecuted the prophets with those who persecuted Him (Matt. 23:29–32) and His followers (Matt. 5:10–12), so Paul (also Stephen; Acts 7:52) sees the same continuity extending to those Jews (with whom he formerly worked) who persecute Christ by opposing the gospel (Acts 9:4). Paul's fullest elaboration of his approach to this problem of Jewish opposition to the gospel is found in Rom. 9–11.

See text note. These last two words may also be translated "the end" (Matt. 10:22; 1 Cor. 1:8; 15:24). This may be a prophecy of the catastrophe that overtook Jerusalem with the destruction of the temple in A.D. 70, within twenty years of Paul's writing, or it may refer to the sequence of calamities that had already begun and were to reach their culmination in that momentous disaster. Or, it may refer to the punitive hardening of a large segment of Israel in their culpable rejection of Christ, a hardening that Jesus saw as the fulfillment of Isaiah's dire prophecy (Is. 6:9, 10; Matt. 13:14, 15). Compare a similar outworking of God's wrath upon Gentiles outlined in Rom. 1:18–32. As Paul would later write (Rom. 11:25), a "partial hardening" has befallen Israel that will remain until the full number of Gentiles is brought in (i.e., until the end). The part of Israel not subject to hardening is the remnant (Is. 6:13) that in the gospel era continues as the object of God's mercy, finding salvation in Jesus the Messiah.

The Gk. word means "orphaned," a word used for parents as well as children who have been separated. Paul continues to use the family imagery of vv. 7, 11 in depicting his relationship with the Thessalonian congregation. As suggested in the note on vv. 1–12, the sudden departure of Paul's team from Thessalonica may have occasioned misgivings in some hearts about his paternal care for and commitment to the believers whom he left behind.

Paul used the same terms of endearment with respect to another Macedonian church, that in Philippi (Phil. 4:1). These churches, which suffered both poverty (2 Cor. 8:1–5) and persecution, seem to have had a special place in the apostle's heart (vv. 17, 18; 3:1–3, 6–8; Phil. 1:7, 8) at his coming. The Gk. word parousia ("coming") is used for the second coming of Christ six times in the Thessalonian epistles (see also 3:13; 4:15; 5:23; 2 Thess. 2:1, 8). Paul's only other use of the term in this sense is in 1 Cor. 15:23. Christ's coming is presented as the time when the outcome of believers' works done in faith will be disclosed. Paul's joy and crown at that day will be his beloved spiritual children, those who converted and matured under his ministry (2 Cor. 1:14; Phil. 2:16).

Paul did not promise the followers of Jesus a life of ease or public approval, nor did Jesus (Mark 8:34; John 15:18–21). Rather, Paul's consistent message of encouragement to newly planted churches was that "through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22).

Paul's anxiety (2 Cor. 11:28) over the stability of the church amid its persecutions had been so intense that Timothy's report of the Thessalonians' solid faith brought the apostle a comfort and joy akin to a foretaste of resurrection from the dead.

Paul addresses God the Father and the Lord Jesus jointly in prayer, indicating their equality and showing that Christ is very God of very God (see Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). The answer to this prayer for reunion came several years later (Acts 20:1).

The example of Paul's team (2:10) as well as their instruction (4:1–3) emphasized the call for the Thessalonians' faith in the Lord Jesus to be expressed in holy living, particularly with respect to sexual purity and marital faithfulness (4:3–8). Blameless holiness will be central to his closing benediction to these believers (5:23). at the coming of our Lord Jesus. The work of sanctification already begun in believers is incomplete and will be brought to glorious completion at the second coming of the Lord (5:23; cf. 1 Cor. 1:8; Phil. 1:6; 2 Thess. 3:3; Jude 24). his saints. Lit. "holy ones." Either the angels who will accompany Christ at His return (2 Thess. 1:7; cf. Matt. 13:39, 48, 49; 16:27), human saints (2 Thess. 1:10; Rev. 19:14), or both.

Paul praises the Thessalonians for their progress in learning how to please God, but he also challenges them to excel further. Paul recognized the constant need for growth and for "straining forward" (Phil. 3:13). Spiritual complacency contradicts a believer's confession.
Again Paul stresses that the authority for his instructions is not his own and not of human origin, but from the risen Lord (2:13).

Scripture generally speaks of the will of God in one of two senses. Sometimes, as in Eph. 1:11, what is meant is the eternal purpose of God that determines history. We cannot know the content of this will that determines history except by observing the outworking of history or through a special revelation (prophecy). Theologians often refer to this history-determining will as the "decretive," "hidden," or "secret" will of God. The second sense in which Scripture speaks of God's will, found in texts such as 4:3 and 5:18, is the duty God has announced through revelation. This is the "preceptive" or "revealed" will of God, which tells us those things that the Lord finds pleasing in His sight (cf. Deut. 29:29). your sanctification. Sanctification is the process by which God's Holy Spirit transforms believers' thoughts, motives, and behavior to conform to the holiness — purity, separation from sin's defilement — of Christ Himself. Paul links love to holiness in 3:12, 13, and reaffirms that God's call is to holiness, not (sexual) impurity, in v. 7.

Pagan society in Paul's day provided little inducement to sexual purity. Marital infidelity, at least for men, was the norm, and some of the pagan religions from which the Thessalonians had been freed approved of gross sexual misconduct in their rituals. The Christian gospel brings a moral awakening and a fresh revelation of God's righteous standards.

Illicit sexual involvement affects not only the consenting parties. Spouses are wronged and families, friends, and fellow Christians shamed. Ultimately, these sins, like all others, are sins against God.

Paul claims divine authority, not merely for his spoken proclamation, but for his written instructions as well (see also 5:27). gives his Holy Spirit. Paul pointedly reminds the Thessalonians of their renewed capacity for holiness resulting from God's continual endowment of the Holy Spirit who dwells within them (1 Cor. 6:19; Gal. 3:5). Here, the construction in Greek emphasizes the word "Holy," which is especially fitting in this context (vv. 3, 7; 3:13 note).

The Gk. word for this term often denoted the attempt to garner civic honor and recognition through outward displays of generosity by the wealthy. Paul's use of the term turns that concept on its head: the Thessalonians should be zealous for the honor that comes not through self-assertion or an ostentatious show of personal greatness, but through humble, industrious, and unimpeachable behavior. This exhortation, pertinent to all Christians, had a particular urgency in Thessalonica, where the Christians had already been falsely accused of sedition (Acts 17:6–9). By living lives that were respectable and unpretentious, the Christians in Thessalonica were to allay any lingering suspicions. This remains the call for all believers.

This was a standard metaphor for death among pagans as well as Jews and Christians. The term has no particular reference to the state of the soul or consciousness of the deceased, since it is used freely by groups with widely diverging beliefs on this subject. For the NT understanding of a conscious and blessed existence between death and the resurrection, see Luke 16:19–31; 23:42, 43; John 14:1–3; 2 Cor. 5:6–8; Phil. 1:23; Rev. 6:9–11; 7:9–17; 20:4–6. See theological note "The Intermediate State" on p. 2109. grieve. Christ's resurrection affords Christians a deeply seated hope and assurance of never-ending fellowship with Him. Therefore, their genuine grief over departed brethren is softened, and they are upheld in hope.

Probably this is to be understood as a "bringing" into God's presence (3:13) and kingdom by resurrection (1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14), though some believe it signifies a bringing of the saints to earth when Christ returns.

According to 2 Esdras, a Jewish work of the second century A.D., those who survive until the coming of the glorious Messiah are more blessed than those who have died before (2 Esdras 13:14–24). Some of the Thessalonians may have caught wind of a similar misconception. Paul assures the Thessalonians that, to the contrary, both groups will be on equal footing (1 Cor. 15:52); both will enter the fullness of the kingdom together.

For Paul, those "in Christ" constitute a subcategory of those "in Adam" (the whole human race), and comprise all who participate in the salvation of Christ (1 Cor. 15:22, 23), including those old covenant believers who lived before His incarnation and, of course, all who have trusted in Him since the incarnation. Therefore, this rising of the "dead in Christ" at the time of His return is a resurrection of all the righteous (believing) dead, and not merely of NT believers (as in 1 Cor. 15:23; cf. John 5:28, 29). The resurrection of the unrighteous is mentioned explicitly by Paul only in Acts 24:15 (cf. John 5:28, 29; Rev. 20:11–15), though he also presupposes it in his warnings of a universal judgment of individuals at the time of Christ's return (Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:5–16).

This verse is prominent in dispensationalist theology's affirmation of the so-called "rapture of the church," which in the most common form of dispensationalism refers to the catching up of believers into the air just prior to a seven-year period of final tribulation before the second coming of Christ. Although the word "rapture" is most commonly used by dispensationalists with this specific meaning, the word itself can rightly be used without any dispensational connotations to refer to the catching-up into the air that Paul says will occur at the return of Christ. This description of the catching-up or "rapture" of the church is not presented so as to satisfy all our cravings for detailed knowledge of end-time chronology. For instance, we are not told whether the assembled company will descend to earth or return to heaven. The presentation is pastoral, to comfort those grieved and confused by the death of beloved Christians. The burden of the passage is the assurance that all the righteous without distinction will be united at the coming of Christ and will live with the Lord forever (v. 18). The "cry," "voice," and "trumpet" of v. 16 give the distinct impression that the rapture will be public and not secret (Luke 17:24; 21:35; Rev. 1:7). Paul speaks elsewhere of "the last trumpet," which will announce Christ's second coming, and the consequent destruction of death, "the last enemy," in the resurrection of those who are in Christ (1 Cor. 15:26, 51–55). See note on 5:1–11.

The Thessalonians are told to prepare for the same thing that will come unexpectedly upon the ungodly — the day of the Lord (vv. 2, 4). Paul assumes that Christians and non-Christians alike will be alive and present when that day arrives. In other words, the rapture of Christians spoken of in 4:17 (see note at 4:17) will not occur before the arrival of the day of the Lord that will also bring sudden and inescapable destruction to the wicked (2 Thess. 2:1, 2 notes).

A prominent designation of the day on which Christ returns. It is well known from the OT (e.g., Joel 2:1, 31; Amos 5:18; Zeph. 1:7, 14; Mal. 4:5), where it is used of God's drawing near in judgment. The NT can also speak of the day of the Lord as having begun in the pouring out of saving blessings through the risen Christ (cf. Acts 2:14–36). The prominent OT association of the day of the Lord with judgment is continued in the NT, where the last judgment and final rewards and punishments are in view (Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:5, 16; 2 Cor. 1:14; 2 Pet. 3:10–13). Christ has already passed through the judgment of the day of the Lord for believers, so they need not fear His return (Heb. 9:27, 28). Unbelievers, however, will feel the wrath of God when the day of the Lord is consummated at the second coming of Christ. like a thief in the night. See Matt. 24:43, 44; 2 Pet. 3:10; Rev. 3:3; 16:15. Paul seems to be familiar with at least some of Jesus' Olivet Discourse (Matt. 24:3–25:46; Mark 13:3–37; Luke 21:5–36).

Sober alertness befits soldiers who belong to the day (Eph. 5:11–17). breastplate of faith \... helmet the hope of salvation. As in other texts concerning spiritual warfare (Rom. 15:12–14; Eph. 6:10–17), Paul echoes an OT passage that describes armor that God Himself wears in waging war against His people's enemies (Is. 59:17).

The "wrath" in this context is evidently the condemnation and punishment that the impenitent will receive on "the day of wrath" (Rom. 2:5; Eph. 5:6; Col. 3:6; Rev. 6:16, 17; 11:18). God has appointed His people to obtain salvation and glory in Jesus Christ, not wrath (1:10; 2 Thess. 2:14). Yet the Thessalonians and many other Christians have been appointed by God also to undergo and withstand tribulation of every kind (3:2–4; 2 Thess. 1:4; James 1:2–4; 1 Pet. 4:12–14; Rev. 1:9). Christians should not interpret their own suffering as God's wrath against their sins, for believers are not destined for wrath. Instead, they should view suffering as part of God's plan to lovingly discipline them and to conform them to the image of His Son.

Even at this early stage in the life of the congregation, there were leaders who had spiritual care and oversight. Paul endorses a proper esteem for church workers and leaders, exhorting believers to love and respect them. Some Thessalonians named elsewhere who may have been in Paul's mind here are Jason (Acts 17:6–9), Aristarchus (Acts 20:4; 27:2; Col. 4:10; Philem. 24), Secundus (Acts 20:4), and possibly Gaius (Acts 19:29).

This address (also v. 12) indicates that the exhortations that follow assign the responsibility for ministry to the entire congregation, not just to its acknowledged leaders. the idle. The context here and in 2 Thess. 3:6, 7, 11 show that the form of idleness in view is an irresponsible refusal to work for a living (text note). See also 4:11, 12.

A Christian must treat others justly and work for their genuine good (Is. 56:1; 58:6–8). It is a remarkable part of Christian morality that the Christian, following the example of Christ (1 Pet. 2:21–23), should refuse to seek personal retaliation (Matt. 5:38–42; Rom. 12:17–21; 1 Cor. 6:7; 1 Pet. 3:9).

Paul admonishes the Thessalonians not to despise legitimate prophecy, which at the time Paul was writing remained an ongoing gift of the Spirit. Both Silas and Paul were "prophets" (Acts 13:1; 15:32). Nevertheless, claims to divine prophecy must be tested and not accepted uncritically (2 Thess. 2:2; cf. 1 Cor. 14:29). Since prophets were appointed to lay the foundation of the church, the gift of prophecy has since passed away (cf. Eph. 2:19–21).

The complete mending of all human imperfection is not only possible — it is certain. God is faithful and will accomplish it (v. 24). This confident hope sustains believers' present pursuit of holiness, despite ongoing struggles with temptation (4:3, 7; see 1 John 3:1–3). The time element must be remembered. Ultimate perfection, to include a glorified physical body as well, will be accomplished at the second coming of Jesus Christ (3:13; Phil. 1:6; 3:20, 21). See theological note "The Holy Spirit as Sanctifier" on p. 2023. your whole spirit and soul and body. Three words are used to emphasize the wholeness of the perfection. "Spirit" and "soul" are used as virtual synonyms in the Bible for the spiritual component of a person. When the terms occur together (as here and in Heb. 4:12), it is difficult to find any significant difference in meaning. Compare the fourfold representation of "heart," "soul," "mind," and "strength" in Mark 12:30.

The Gk. verb is unusually strong. Paul is laying a solemn weight upon the whole congregation to learn the contents of this epistle, so important did he consider his apostolic teaching for their spiritual good (2:13; 4:2 notes).

2 Thessalonians.note: See note on 1 Thess. 1:1.

One instance of persecution is recounted in Acts 17:5–9, and the Thessalonian epistles reveal that the Christians in Thessalonica were still facing antagonism at the time Paul wrote (1 Thess. 1:6; 2:14; 3:3).

A life worthy of God (1 Thess. 2:12), of God's calling (1:11; Eph. 4:1), of the Lord (Col. 1:10), of the gospel (Phil. 1:27, 28), or of the kingdom (v. 5) is a life of patient, joyful discipleship even in the face of life-threatening abuse from those hostile to the faith (Matt. 5:10–12; Acts 5:41). Such lives are sure evidence that God's judgment is right. for which you are also suffering. Even while enjoying the benefits of citizenship in the heavenly kingdom (1 Thess. 2:12 note), Christians still must suffer for its sake (Acts 14:22), since the kingdom will inevitably confront diabolical opposition.

In Rom. 2:9, the same Gk. word for "tribulation" (trouble) is used for the woe brought upon evildoers at the last judgment. Paul appears to be speaking of the same judgment here, as the next verses are concerned with ultimate bliss and woe.
The gospel must be accepted, believed, and obeyed (1 Pet. 4:17). Its divine command is for absolute surrender to God through the peace made by Jesus Christ.

The fearful doctrine of eternal punishment (Is. 66:24; Matt. 25:42, 46; Mark 9:43, 48), staggering as it is, assured the hounded Thessalonian Christians of final and perfect justice. They were to refrain from taking personal revenge (1 Thess. 5:15; cf. Rom. 12:17–21) for the atrocities they suffered (v. 4), entrusting themselves instead to the God "who judges justly" (1 Pet. 2:23; cf. Jer. 17:10; Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:6, 11, 16; Rev. 22:12).

The "day of the Lord" (1 Thess. 5:2). The impression given is that the final judgment of the ungodly closely accompanies the coming of Christ for His saints. As in 1 Thess. 3:13, "saints" here may refer either to God's holy angels (v. 7) or to His completely sanctified people, although the parallel expression in v. 12, "glorified in you," favors the latter interpretation.
Such "calling" should be related to 1 Thess. 2:12, where God is the one who calls. What God calls us to is His own kingdom and glory (2:14).

As it stands, the Greek can also be translated "our God and Lord, Jesus Christ." This would be a distinct use of the term "God" in reference to Jesus Christ. Arguing against such a translation is the infrequent application of this term to Christ in the NT (Rom. 9:5; Titus 2:13; 2 Pet. 1:1). On the other hand, Paul often brings Christ and God the Father together into close unity in other phrases in these letters (e.g., vv. 1, 2; 2:16; cf. 1 Thess. 1:1; 3:11), and he clearly ascribes attributes of deity to Christ. Paul and the rest of the New Testament clearly attribute the same dignity and deity to the Father and the Son (cf. John 1:1–18).

This is the rapture of the saints spoken of in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 (note). Paul appears to equate the time of Christ's coming and the rapture with the "day of the Lord" (1 Thess. 5:2; cf. 1 Cor. 1:7, 8; Phil. 2:16). In this scene, all believers are gathered before the Lord "at his coming" (1 Thess. 2:19) and "on the day of our Lord Jesus" (2 Cor. 1:14). The "rebellion" must come and the "man of lawlessness" (v. 3) must be revealed before the day of the Lord arrives; therefore, this rebellion and revelation must also occur before the rapture of the saints. If the false teachers were saying that the day of the Lord had arrived (v. 2) and were anticipating the rapture at any moment, they could be proved wrong by the absence of these prior signs.

This reference does not prove there was a forged letter bearing Paul's name already in existence, but only that Paul saw this as a possibility. Word may have reached him that the new teaching was circulating with some pretense of having his authority. Paul's injunction is meant to ensure that no vehicle of instruction — even one supposed to have come from him — should be heeded if it asserts that the day of the Lord has already come (cf. Gal. 1:8). He calls special attention to his personal handwriting in the closing greeting (3:17), emphasizing that his signature certifies the epistle's authenticity.

Lit. "falling away" or "apostasy."This might refer to a falling away of many within the church (1 Tim. 4:1; 2 Tim. 3:1–9; Jude 17–19), to an apostasy of the Jewish people, or to a worldwide rebellion against God. man of lawlessness. This is an individual embodiment of wickedness, whose arrogant blasphemies Paul lists (cf. 1 John 2:22). He will draw away by deception those already inclined against the true God (v. 10) and will ultimately commit the sacrilege of thrusting himself upon humanity as its object of worship (v. 4). He comes by the power of Satan, as Christ came by the power of God, and he works fraudulent wonders as Christ worked true ones (v. 9; cf. Acts 2:22). Paul depicts this imposter as a parody or antithesis of the true Christ. Paul himself does not use the term "antichrist" (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3), but it is a fitting designation of this individual. In any case, his fate is sealed; he will be destroyed by the coming of Christ.

This description of the man of lawlessness echoes that of Daniel's little "horn" (Dan. 7:8, 20, 21; 8:9–12; cf. 11:31, 36) and foreshadows John's description of the beast from the sea (Rev. 13:1–8). takes his seat in the temple of God. Some conclude from this verse that the temple in Jerusalem, which was still standing when Paul wrote this letter but was destroyed in A.D. 70, must be rebuilt for the future use of "the man of lawlessness." Others understand "temple" according to one of its other NT meanings, such as the church (Eph. 2:19–22; 1 Pet. 2:5). Still others see this prophecy as having been fulfilled around A.D. 70, when the Romans invaded and desecrated the temple and proclaimed themselves the true rulers of the Jewish people. The reference may simply be an intentionally exaggerated way of talking about the imposter's aspirations to heavenly power. Just as another prototype of sin, the king of Babylon, wanted to set his throne in heaven (Is. 14:12–14; cf. the prince of Tyre in Ezek. 28:1–10), so the man of lawlessness will boast of himself as the possessor of God's heavenly sanctuary (Rev. 13:6).

Although it seems that the original audience of 2 Thessalonians knew the identity of that which restrains the man of lawlessness (vv. 6, 7; cf. Rev. 20:1–3), this identity is not self-evident to later readers of the epistle. Interpreters have proposed numerous possibilities. The restraining power seems to be both impersonal (v. 6, "what is restraining") and personal (v. 7, "he who now restrains"). Hence it may be an institution that can also be represented by a single person, such as the Roman state with its emperor, the Jewish state with its leader, or the universal ministry of the gospel with Paul as its chief minister. Whatever the precise reference, it is clear that behind the restraining power is the will of God.

Though the man of lawlessness has not yet appeared, Paul will not allow his readers to let down their guard. The same satanic power that will ultimately spawn this unholy deceiver was already at work in Paul's day (1 John 2:18) and is at work in ours. Because it is now restrained, the church has a strong encouragement to carry out its mission.

The description is from Is. 11:4. It reappears in Rev. 19:15, 21, where the beast and his false prophet meet their final end. The phrase captures how effortlessly Christ will overwhelm His enemies at the last day, when He appears "in flaming fire" and "the glory of his might" (1:8, 9).
The second coming of Christ will be preceded by the "coming of the lawless one."

Paul's logic here anticipates his argument in the later epistle to the Romans that sinful humanity's eagerness to embrace the lie will be judged by God through His handing them over to a corrupt and deceived mind. Their punishment is God's fulfillment of their desire to evade His truth (v. 12; cf. Rom. 1:21–28).

There is a wealth of instruction in these two verses. Major elements in the biblical doctrine of salvation — election, calling, faith, sanctification, and glorification — are presented in their mutual relations. There is a harmonious working of all three persons of the Trinity: God the Father in choosing and calling, God the Son in sharing His glory with His people, and God the Holy Spirit in imparting His sanctifying grace (cf. 1 Pet. 1:2). 2:13 But. With this word, Paul begins to assure his readers that he does not include them with those he has just mentioned in vv. 11 and 12, individuals who refuse to love the truth and will fall prey to deception. God chose you. See note on 1 Thess. 1:4. From the beginning (Eph. 1:4), God chose them "through" sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, not "because of" these actions. Thus, God's pre-temporal election to salvation is carried out by His Spirit's setting apart (a literal rendering of "sanctification") the hearts of people from the old world to the new world. This gracious act on God's part results in their "belief in the truth" and works itself out in their lives. According to Paul, the elect will not continue to live in a godless fashion after they are converted (cf. Rom. 8:1–4). firstfruits. Believers in Philippi and then in Thessalonica were the beginning of the gospel harvest after Paul and his team crossed the Aegean Sea into Macedonia and then proceeded south to Achaia (cf. Rom. 16:5).
Paul passed on authoritative practical and doctrinal traditions, by word and by letter (Rom. 6:17; 1 Cor. 11:2, 23; 15:3; 2 Tim. 1:13). letter. Probably 1 Thessalonians.

Paul requests prayer for the success of the gospel and for the protection of those who bring it. Paul faced almost constant physical danger during his years of ministry. This text, along with Rom. 15:30, 31; 2 Cor. 1:11; Phil. 1:19, shows how much he relied on the prayers of God's people for the continuation of his ministry, if not for his own survival.
Contrasting with the faithlessness mentioned in the previous verse is the steadfast faithfulness of our unchanging God (Mal. 3:6; 1 Cor. 1:9; 10:13; 2 Cor. 1:18; James 1:17).
This verse reiterates the essential idea of v. 3. Our hearts, by the grace of God, should continually return to and reflect on the truths of God's grace in the gospel.

See Introduction: Characteristics and Themes. Paul takes firm measures against an ongoing problem of idleness and its consequences (v. 10; cf. 1 Thess. 4:11). Paul obviously regards the offense as serious, but he treats the offenders as fellow believers. 3:6 keep away. Paul may have had in mind Jesus' instructions on church discipline recorded in Matt. 18:15–17. He gives similar charges in vv. 14, 15; Rom. 16:17; 1 Cor. 5:9–13; 2 Tim. 3:1–5; Titus 3:10, 11.

Paul consistently teaches that those who labor in the gospel deserve their wages (1 Cor. 9:6–18; Gal. 6:6). Paul sometimes accepted support for his ministry, at least from already established churches (2 Cor. 11:7–11; Phil. 4:10–20). But when he was preaching in a new city in which he wanted to exemplify the freeness of the gift offered in the gospel, or when he feared his motives would be called into question, or when (as in Thessalonica) a strong example was needed for those who refused to work, Paul forsook his rights and would not accept compensation from the church.
Apparently, the problem of idleness had surfaced before Paul and his companions left the city. Even then, they had felt it necessary to urge the "idle" to work (vv. 6, 11).
Without any business of their own, these idlers attended to the business of others (see 1 Tim. 5:11–15).

By such responsible and peaceable living, believers adorn the gospel in the eyes of outsiders (1 Thess. 4:11, 12; 1 Tim. 2:2).Paul's "command" is "in the Lord Jesus Christ," underscoring that the command is ultimately from Christ, not merely from Paul. This further reinforces the command of v. 6, where Paul says, "we command you \... in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ."

See note on vv. 6–15. See theological note "Excommunication" on p. 1703. be ashamed. This is not retribution, but an attempt to elicit repentance and, ultimately, restoration to fellowship in the church.

Since such an offender is still to be regarded as a brother, this seems to be a "step" of church discipline that stops short of final excommunication, which officially removes an impenitent person from the community of the church and calls on congregants to view and treat said individual "as a Gentile and a tax collector," (Matt. 18:17; 1 Cor. 5:4, 5, 13).

Though Paul had the help of secretaries in writing his letters, he customarily penned the final greeting or benediction in his own hand. He calls attention to this practice as a mark of the letter's authenticity here and in 1 Cor. 16:21; Col. 4:18. From Gal. 6:11 and Philem. 19, it appears that Paul wrote more than just the concluding phrases of his letter to the Galatians and his letter to Philemon, respectively.

1 Timothy.note: One sent out as an official representative of Christ, exercising authority that He has delegated and receiving new revelation from the risen Lord (Eph. 3:5). See note on 2 Cor. 1:1. This phrase is commonly used by Paul as a self-designation in the openings of his letters. God our Savior. As author of the covenant of grace, God is Savior (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4). Christ Jesus our hope. Jesus is the basis for Christian hope because He is the mediator of the covenant of grace (2:5; 4:10; 5:5; 6:17). See theological note "Hope" on p. 2206.

Cf. Titus 1:4. Paul views Timothy as his spiritual son, who can be trusted to reflect the apostle's character and perspective, as a son reflects his father's, in his dealings with churches (v. 18; 1 Cor. 4:17; Phil. 2:22; 2 Tim. 1:2; 2:1; Introduction: Date and Occasion). Grace, mercy, and peace. Paul commonly substitutes "grace" for the more standard salutation "greetings" (literally, "rejoice"; e.g., James 1:1). He typically adds the Jewish greeting "peace," referring to the peace with God that Christ has secured for His people. Here and in 2 Tim. 1:2, he also adds "mercy."

Paul moves into the body of the letter, bypassing the expression of thanksgiving or praise to God that is customary in his epistles to churches (except Galatians) and proceeding immediately to Timothy's pastoral assignment in Ephesus (cf. Titus 1:5). His intention is to instruct Timothy in how to act as Paul's representative in establishing good order in the church at Ephesus (3:14, 15) and in responding to specific spiritual threats to the believers there (see Introduction: Date and Occasion). Assuming that the entire church will hear the epistle (6:21; see Introduction: Literary Features), Paul intends his directives to substantiate Timothy's authority to implement Paul's instructions in the eyes of the congregation. He begins with the problem of false teaching at Ephesus (see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues). 1:3 teach any different doctrine. The conflict in Ephesus centers on proper teaching (v. 10; 4:1, 2; 6:3; 2 Tim. 2:2, 18).

See 4:7; 2 Tim. 4:4. In Titus 1:14, Paul speaks of "Jewish myths," perhaps referring to the kinds of legends about OT figures that are found in many of the apocryphal Jewish writings. endless genealogies. Perhaps a reference to an early form of the detailed speculations (often combined with Jewish myths) that developed in Gnosticism concerning the origins of the world and the innumerable spiritual beings supposedly involved in creation (cf. Titus 3:9). stewardship from God. Ministers of the gospel, like the slave who is steward of his master's estate, are accountable to the Lord for their conduct in leadership and preservation of the message of Christ (v. 11; 6:20; 2 Tim. 1:13, 14; 2:1, 2). Above all, the steward must be faithful (1 Cor. 4:1, 2).
Paul's command highlights the close and necessary connection between true Christian belief and practice (cf. Gal. 5:6).
The law of Moses.
Paul's comments about the false teachers lead him into a digression on the purpose of the law. 1:8 the law is good. See Rom. 7:7–12; Gal. 3:19–25.

The law's commandments prohibit and indict the sorts of sins that Paul goes on to list — violent defiance of parents, murder, sexual immorality, etc. (evils that also contradict the sound doctrine of the gospel; vv. 10, 11). If people's hearts were intrinsically upright, the law's stipulations would not be necessary. As it is, however, the law exposes the heart's sinful proclivity (Rom. 3:20; 7:7, 8). The law also acts an external restraint on sin, holding people back from doing the worst that they can externally even while those whom the law restrains seize on the commandments and break the commandments with abandon internally in their hearts, souls, and minds.

Or "sound teaching," a theme running throughout the Pastoral Epistles (3:9; 4:6; 6:3; 2 Tim. 1:13, 14; 2:2; 4:3; Titus 1:9, 13; 2:1, 2). The word "sound" implies that true doctrine preserves and promotes spiritual health, unlike false doctrine, which destroys spiritual vitality and spreads infection "like gangrene" (2 Tim. 2:17).
The good news of what God has done in Christ is the standard by which doctrine, as well as one's understanding and use of the law, is judged to be sound.

From his comments about the law and the misuse of the law by false teachers, Paul turns to his call by Christ and provides an exposition of the gospel as the grace that God pours out upon sinners in Jesus Christ.

Before his conversion, Paul persecuted the church (Acts 8:3; 9:1–5; 22:4, 5; 26:9, 11; Gal. 1:13). At that time, he saw it as his obligation in his zeal for God's glory (Phil. 3:6); but now, having received grace through Jesus the Christ, he views his history as a persecutor as constituting him "the least of the apostles" (1 Cor. 15:8–10); "the least of all the saints" (Eph. 3:8), and the "foremost" of sinners (vv. 15, 16). because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief. God did not grant Paul what he deserved, but what he needed (cf. Acts 3:17–20). Paul did nothing to merit or qualify for God's mercy in Christ. The apostle is not saying that ignorance can excuse sin, for even those who sin when they do not know the will of the Master receive punishment if they do not repent (Luke 12:35–48).

This expression calls attention to an important point. In the NT it is found only in the Pastoral Epistles (3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim. 2:11; Titus 3:8). to save sinners. This concise and comprehensive statement of Christ's mission in His incarnation, focused on the redemptive purposes of His death and resurrection, merits comparison with similar NT statements, including John 3:16; Gal. 4:4, 5; and Heb. 10:5–10. I am the foremost. Lit. "I am the first." This is not a characterization only of his record as a blasphemous and violent persecutor prior to his conversion. Rather, as Paul has grown in Christ, even as the Holy Spirit has been conforming him to his Savior's purity and love, he has also become increasingly aware of his own sinfulness.
God grants to all who believe in Christ not just "eternal" life, but life in all its fullness (cf. 4:8; 6:12, 19; 2 Tim. 1:1, 10; Titus 1:2; 3:7).
Jonathan Edwards recalls this text in the account of his conversion. As he read these words, "he had a sense of the glory of the divine being," and "prayed to God that I might enjoy him."

Paul returns to the theme of vv. 3–7, focusing less on Timothy's potential for success as Paul's representative than on Timothy's continued faithfulness to Christ, especially in contrast to two members (perhaps leaders) of the church at Ephesus who "made shipwreck of their faith" (v. 19). 1:18 prophecies previously made about you. This refers to an event, mentioned also in 4:14 and in 2 Tim. 1:6 (cf. 2 Tim. 2:2), in which a group of elders, along with Paul, laid hands on Timothy (when Timothy was set apart for ministry). At that time, Timothy received a spiritual gift, along with a word of prophecy appointing him for service (cf. Acts 13:1–3). wage the good warfare. In this conflict, victory is perseverance in faith and integrity (v. 19; 2 Tim. 4:7).

Singling out these two individuals raises the question as to whether they were leaders in the church. Hymenaeus is mentioned again in 2 Tim. 2:17, 18 as one who has "swerved from the truth." It is unclear whether the name "Alexander" here and in Acts 19:33, 34 and 2 Tim. 4:14, 15 all refer to the same person. I have handed over to Satan. This is probably a reference to putting these two individuals outside the fellowship of the church and, hence, back into the world — the domain of Satan (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11; 2 Cor. 4:4; Eph. 2:2). Paul uses a similar expression in 1 Cor. 5:5 (cf. Matt. 18:17). may learn not to blaspheme. The purpose of this excommunication, like that in 1 Cor. 5:5, is not punitive but, by the Spirit's convicting grace, restorative — that the two would recognize their errors and repent (2 Tim. 2:25, 26; Titus 3:10).

Paul moves to a series of instructions on prayer and worship, perhaps in response to abuses caused by the false teachers (see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues). After the instructions for worship, he moves on to the qualifications of church officers (3:1–13), summing up the entire section as directives "how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God" (3:15). 2:1 all people. As can be seen from the next expression ("for kings and all who are in high positions"), this does not mean "every human being"; rather, it refers to "all types of people," whatever their station in life.

Civil government, though led by flawed human beings and vulnerable to corruption and exploitation, is ordained by God to maintain justice (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). a peaceful and quiet life. Christ's name is honored when Christians live peaceably and responsibly among their neighbors (3:7; 1 Thess. 4:11, 12; 2 Thess. 3:12).

This does not mean that God sovereignly wills every human being to be saved (i.e., that God saves or wishes to save everyone, since Rom. 9:18–24 says otherwise, and speaks of God's "desire" in expressing His election and reprobation). It may refer to God's general benevolence in taking no delight in the death of the wicked (Ezek. 33:11) or to God's desire that all types of people (v. 1 note) be saved (i.e., God does not choose His elect from any single nationality, class, or other group).

This is the fundamental affirmation of both OT and NT religion (Deut. 6:4; cf. Rom. 3:30; 1 Cor. 8:6; Gal. 3:20; Eph. 4:6). one mediator between God and men. There is only one who arbitrates between God and humanity and reconciles them. See theological note "Jesus Christ as Mediator." the man Christ Jesus. In speaking of Christ as mediator, Paul's focus is on Christ's humanity. This may be because the false teachers in Ephesus denied that Christ was truly human. The full humanity of Christ is essential to His serving as mediator of the covenant of grace (Heb. 2:17; 4:14–5:10; 9:13–15).

By His death on the cross, Christ paid the price necessary to free His people from their sins (Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19). This is a centerpiece of His work as the "one mediator" (v. 5). all. In keeping with vv. 1 and 4, this is probably a reference to all types of people (i.e., from every tongue, tribe, and nation; cf. Rev. 7:9). Alternatively, it expresses Paul's conviction that although Christ's death was sufficient to ransom all humanity if that had been God's intent in offering up His Son for sinners, God has never intended to save all people and the purpose of the atonement was to pay only for the sins of the elect. See theological note "Definite Atonement" on p. 1875.
An odd statement to make to a close friend, but Paul intended for the letter to be read to the whole church (6:21 note). Presumably, the false teachers had questioned Paul's call and mission.

Paul moves to specific admonitions for men and women in the context of worship (vv. 1–15 note). 2:8 every place. The principles governing corporate worship are not limited to a single congregation but are applicable to churches everywhere, although local issues sometimes influence how the principles should be applied. See 1 Cor. 14:33–36. men. Paul assumes in 1 Cor. 11:5 that women, too, will pray when the church meets for worship. Here he may be addressing specific problems at Ephesus, such as conflict among men, and indiscreet clothing and preoccupation with appearance among women. lifting holy hands. On this posture in prayer, see Ps. 63:4; 141:2. without anger or quarreling. Paul is not concerned to mandate a particular posture, but to encourage a proper attitude (1:5).
Paul is not concerned with clothing and jewelry as such, but with the attitude of the one wearing them (1 Pet. 3:3, 4). Greco-Roman society was characterized by extravagance in dress.

As 1 Cor. 11:5 indicates, Paul does not forbid all vocal participation by women in the worship service. Rather, Paul enjoins silence of a particular sort — a silence that respects the authoritative teaching and governing role assigned to the male leaders of the church (v. 12). all submissiveness. Submission does not mean that one is inferior in being to another. Elsewhere, Paul applies the concept to wives (Eph. 5:22; Col. 3:18; Titus 2:5; cf. 1 Cor. 14:34), husbands and wives (Eph. 5:21), children (3:4), slaves (Titus 2:9), prophets (1 Cor. 14:32), Christians (Rom. 13:1, 5; 1 Cor. 16:16; Titus 3:1), the church (Eph. 5:24), and even Christ Himself (1 Cor. 15:28).

Here Paul exercises his apostolic authority in restricting women from exercising a specific kind of authority and teaching, namely that which is associated with the ecclesiastical office of overseer, or elder (3:1–7). This verse indicates that women should not be ordained to the office of elder. to exercise authority over. This Gk. word appears only here in the NT and is used by Paul to refer to some level of judicial or governing authority. Under the influence of the false teachers, certain women have apparently moved into positions of governing authority within the church, which Paul prohibited (1 Cor. 14:34). quiet. See note on v. 11.

Paul appeals to the creation order instituted by God Himself (Gen. 2:7, 21, 22; he uses a similar argument, though with some qualification, in 1 Cor. 11:8–12). As "firstborn," Adam had the rights of primogeniture, which, according to passages about firstborn sons in the OT, entailed not only inheritance rights but authority over the household. The fact that the apostle appeals to the created order is strong evidence against seeing this teaching about the role of women in the church as limited only to the particular circumstances in Ephesus. From the beginning, as Paul teaches in Eph. 5:22–30. God designed husbands to lovingly lead their wives and for wives to submit themselves to their husbands' authority, for by this believers illustrate the relationship of Christ, our husband, and the church, His bride (Eph. 5:22–30 and notes). In the church, this relationship is illustrated by the intelligent submission of both women and non-ordained men to those men who have been appointed to the office of elder. Elders are to exercise their authority in a loving manner and not abuse the believers under their care, just as husbands are to love their wives enough to die for them (1 Pet. 5:1–4 and notes).

Again Paul alludes to Genesis, this time to the account of the fall (Gen. 3:1–6). The argument might seem unfair, since both Adam and Eve sinned. But Paul's point is correct: Eve was the one who was "deceived" by the serpent. Paul's argument here, with its emphasis on who was deceived, may reflect the relative success that the false teachers at Ephesus were having in leading women astray (5:11–15; 2 Tim. 3:6, 7). Elsewhere, Paul has no qualms about assigning responsibility for the fall to Adam (Rom. 5:12–19; 1 Cor. 15:21, 22).

This probably refers to any woman, not simply to Eve. will be saved. Unlikely to mean "brought safely" (physically preserved through the process of childbirth), as some hold. Paul uses his normal word meaning "redemption from sin," thereby contrasting being deceived into sin (v. 14) with being saved from it. Alternately, the term "saved" may indicate the reception of some important, though unspecified, benefit from God. through childbearing. The interpretation "through the birth of the Child" (Jesus), however attractive it might be theologically, is doubtful. Paul intends another allusion to Genesis, this time to God's statement to Eve after the fall concerning her role in childbearing (Gen. 3:16). if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control. This qualification shows that Paul is not suggesting that childbearing is an act that merits salvation, which would contradict his doctrine of justification by faith. Rather, his point is that those women at Ephesus who have been deceived by the false teachers, and Christian women generally, need to focus on their proper God-assigned role, and especially on embracing their calling with Christlike attitudes befitting women of faith (vv. 8–10; 1:5, 19). Given his use of Genesis 2; 3 in his argument and the false teachers' disparagement of marriage (4:3), Paul finds "childbearing" (1 Tim. 5:14) and "bringing up children" (1 Tim. 5:10) to be important symbols for that role (5:14). Ultimately, Paul wants women to understand that they do not have to reject their homes and families in order to have worth in God's sight or to enjoy all the benefits of redemption; rather, they work out their salvation in fear and trembling (Phil. 2:13, 14) as they fulfill their calling in the home.

Paul now turns to the subject of leadership in the church, continuing his instructions for behavior befitting the church as God's household (v. 15). He first discusses overseers (vv. 1–7; v. 1 text note) and then discusses deacons (vv. 8–10, 12, 13, with a digression on women in v. 11). Paul focuses more on the personal qualities of those who are qualified to serve in these positions than on their duties. This emphasis indicates his concern to install the right people, perhaps because some of the false teachers in Ephesus had come from, or were selfishly seeking, positions of leadership. 3:1 The saying is trustworthy. See note on 1:15. The use of this expression here reflects the importance Paul attaches to the task of the overseer, or elder. overseer. One of a group of individuals charged with the general care of the church (v. 5; cf. Phil. 1:1). The word is used interchangeably with "elder" and describes the elder's role in providing spiritual oversight in the church (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). The Gk. term (episkopos) is the origin of the En­glish words "bishop" and "episcopal," but NT usage (unlike later church practice) shows that each congregation had a plurality of elders who held each other accountable with shared authority (Acts 20:28–30).

A general heading to the qualifications for overseer or elder. This expression does not mean "without sin," which would disqualify everyone except Jesus, but "above scandalous reproach." Paul's overriding concern is that overseers (elders) have a good standing among both Christians and non-Christians (v. 7). On the qualifications for overseers (elders), see also Titus 1:6–9. the husband of one wife. This difficult expression (v. 12; Titus 1:6; cf. 5:9) has been variously understood to prohibit polygamy, remarriage after a divorce, or marital infidelity. Given the widespread immorality in the Greco-Roman world and a similar use of the phrase at 1 Tim. 5:9, the last seems to fit Paul's focus best. Paul is not banning single men from the office of elder, since both he and Barnabas were apparently unmarried during their ministry (1 Cor. 9:5); rather, his emphasis is that the elder's sexual conduct must be exemplary in purity whether he is married or not. able to teach. To mention the teaching competency of the overseer (elder) is important given the problem at Ephesus (5:17). Titus 1:9 indicates that elders' firm grasp of God's Word will enable them both to teach it and to refute errors that contradict it. Since this ability is not repeated in the qualifications for deacons, it seems that teaching the Word is one function that sets the overseer's task apart from the deacon's. For the general distinction between ministry of the Word and ministry of deeds in service, see Acts 6:2–4; 1 Pet. 4:10, 11.

Again, men who do not have children are not excluded from the eldership (v. 2 note); but for those who do, the attitudes of their children reflect the fruit of their spiritual management of his home and thus forecast the effect of his leadership in the church.
A general statement of the overseer's (elder's) responsibility.

For a Christian to move too quickly into this position could be an occasion for pride. fall into the condemnation of the devil. Paul does not view lightly the fall of those holding this office, perhaps because some overseers in Ephesus had become involved in the false teaching (v. 1).

Deacons are officers in the church alongside overseers/elders (cf. Phil. 1:1). The precise tasks of the deacon are not spelled out in this passage. The church has usually viewed the ministry in terms of the role of the seven chosen to help the apostles in Acts 6:1–6 (specifically by tending to widows' material needs). Although the noun "deacon" is not used in regard to the seven in that passage, a related term in that passage describes both the apostles' "ministry of the word" and the "ministry of tables" conducted by the seven.

A term used elsewhere by Paul to refer to the revealed truth of the gospel (v. 16; Rom. 16:25, 26; 1 Cor. 2:7; 4:1; Eph. 1:9; 3:3–9; 6:19; Col. 1:26, 27; 2:2; 4:3). Perhaps some of the deacons at Ephesus had been taken in by the false teaching.

This is probably not a reference to a specific testing period, but rather a careful examination of their conduct and their commitment to sound teaching. prove themselves blameless. Paul uses the same Gk. word in regard to overseers in Titus 1:6, 7; his requirement that overseers be "above reproach" in v. 2 (note) uses a Gk. synonym.

Lit. "women." This verse abruptly interrupts the section on deacons. Its meaning is contested. The "women" are probably either the wives of the deacons or female assistants to the deacons; however, they may also be female deacons on par with the male deacons. The absence of a similar set of qualifications for the wives of elders (vv. 1–7) suggests that the women in view here, whether deacons' wives or others, actively participate in the ministry of mercy led by the deacons (whereas elders' wives would not share their husbands' oversight authority). The abruptness of the insertion may reflect Paul's concern that women, in particular, have not fared well at the hands of the false teachers (2:14; 5:15).
See note on v. 2.

Although deacons' supportive ministries may often be unnoticed and unrecognized in the church, the apostle injects a special promise to encourage them in their faithful service. See Mark 10:43–45, where "servant" and "serve" represent Gk. terms for "deacon."

Having provided Timothy with specific instructions on prayer, worship, and church offices, Paul now states his reason for writing the letter (see Introduction: Date and Occasion). He discusses the nature of the church and offers a poetic meditation on the work of Christ.
