. Both terms connote the church's foundational role in publicly presenting or displaying the truth before the world. Paul's intent is to emphasize, over against the false teachers, that the truth of the gospel is found in and held out to the world by God's church (2 Tim. 2:19). He is not imputing infallibility to the church or stating that the authority of later church leaders is equivalent to the authority of the apostles or their testimony, which now makes up the New Testament.

See note on v. 9. What follows may be a fragment of an early Christian hymn or creedal confession, composed of three balanced couplets. It certainly reflects Paul's understanding of the person and work of Christ as the center or core of the Christian gospel (cf. 1 Cor. 15:1ff.). He was manifested in the flesh. A reference to the incarnation, with a hint at Christ's preexistence. vindicated by the Spirit. A reference to Christ's resurrection (Rom. 1:4). The point is that Christ's resurrection "vindicated" Him (the Gk. word is the one Paul uses for "justified") by overturning the guilty verdict of the ungodly world's court. The world's court judged Him to be in the wrong and a liar and false teacher, but the resurrection proved that He lived a life of perfect righteousness. Elsewhere, believers are identified with Christ's resurrection (see Rom. 4:25) and are thus identified with His perfect righteousness as well. seen by angels. A reference to the ascension (Acts 1:10, 11) and the audience that witnessed Christ's victory in the heavenly sphere. proclaimed among the nations. In the power of the Spirit who descended at Pentecost, the apostles proclaimed Christ's glory to an international audience in the earthly sphere (Matt. 28:18–20). believed on in the world. The effect of gospel proclamation in the earthly sphere is the Gentiles' coming to faith and salvation in Christ. taken up in glory. A reference to Christ's exaltation to the right hand of God (Acts 7:56) and His present reign as Lord over all (heavenly sphere).

Returning to the purpose for which he left Timothy in Ephesus (1:3–20), Paul continues his attack on the false teachers and their teachings. 4:1 the Spirit expressly says. Presumably a specific revelation the Holy Spirit granted to someone, perhaps Paul himself (Acts 20:22–31; cf. 21:11). in later times. This is not a future period just before the second coming of Christ. Rather, in keeping with the overall NT perspective, it is the era inaugurated by Christ's first advent and consummated at His return (Acts 2:17; Heb. 1:2; 1 Pet. 1:20; 1 John 2:18; cf. 2 Tim. 3:1). The end-time tribulation has begun (2 Thess. 2:7; 1 John 2:18) and will get worse as the very end draws near (2 Thess. 2:3, 4). some will \... demons. A reference to the false teachers, who have arisen within the church. The particular aspect of the latter-day tribulation in mind here is that of false teaching and deception.

The false teachers promoted a rigorous lifestyle (cf. Col. 2:20–23). Some argued that since the material world was evil, the spiritual individual should avoid it. Others inferred from the same negative view of material reality that indulging one's sensual desires has no effect on one's spiritual standing and identity (1 Cor. 6:14 note). It is just as demonic to repudiate the thankful and holy enjoyment of God's material gifts as it is to abuse those gifts in ways contrary to His Word. foods that God created. The following argument focuses on foods. Paul has already affirmed marriage in 3:2, 12.
Contrary to the false teachers, the Christian affirms the essential goodness of God's creation (Gen. 1) and therefore uses created things in the way that God commands us to use them.

Having exposed the false teachers for what they are, Paul continues with a series of personal admonitions to Timothy regarding his ministry. 4:6 trained. The "good servant" must be continually nourished by true doctrine in order to nourish others in that same truth.

See note on 1:4. train yourself for godliness. Throughout this section, Paul intertwines spiritual discipline with official duties, invoking athletic metaphors that he uses elsewhere (2 Tim. 2:5; 4:7; 1 Cor. 9:24–27; Gal. 2:2; 5:7; Phil. 2:16).
See note on 1:15.

The general call to repentance and salvation is extended to all people (Matt. 11:28), for we do not know whom God has chosen to save but we do know that He has elected people from every tribe and tongue (Rev. 7:9–17). See theological note "Definite Atonement" on p. 1875. especially of those who believe. Salvation is God's gift, in particular to those who trust in His provision in Christ (Matt. 22:14; Rom. 8:30). The Gk. word translated "especially" may also be translated "that is to say," as can be elsewhere in Paul's letters. In this case, Paul clarifies that, by "all people," he means those who come to believe in Christ. But sometimes the Gk. word may mean "especially" or "particularly," thus referring to a smaller group that is a part of the general group previously mentioned. In this case, Paul may be using "Savior" in a broader sense as "benefactor," as it was applied to Roman emperors: in His common grace, God lavishes generous provision on "all people" or "on the just and the unjust" (Matt. 5:45); but He focuses special, redemptive grace on "those who believe."

The negative commands here and in v. 14 may indicate that Timothy had a tendency towards shyness or timidity (2 Tim. 1:6–8). Furthermore, some in the church at Ephesus may not have accepted his authority (Introduction: Date and Occasion). Timothy was probably in his thirties, and therefore younger than many of the Christians (and elders) at Ephesus. example \... in purity. Timothy is to establish his authority not by flaunting it or insisting upon it but by setting an example of godly living (Titus 2:7).

See 3:14, 15 and Introduction: Date and Occasion. devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture \... to teaching. These are positive methods for exposing the false teaching and neutralizing its impact (cf. 1:3, 4). Not only the exposition and application of God's Word in exhortation and teaching, but also the public reading of Scripture is a means of grace.
See note on 1:18; 2 Tim. 1:6.

A reference to the advancement of Timothy's spiritual life, his ministry, or perhaps both. Noteworthy is the fact that it is "progress," not arrival. Although Christians must not perform good works for the sake of gathering others' attention and admiration (Matt. 6:1), Christ's reputation and believers' spiritual growth are enhanced when growing maturity can be seen in the church's leaders and members (3:7; Col. 4:5; 1 Thess. 4:12; Titus 2:5, 7, 8, 10).

That Paul summarizes his instructions to Timothy in this manner is an indication of where the false teachers have gone astray, and, hence, where both ministers and Christians in general can go astray, both in character and in convictions. you will save. God alone grants salvation (v. 10; 1:1; 2:3), but He is pleased to use His people as instruments in bringing salvation to others. Salvation is not completed in our experience when we come to saving faith. To be sure, faith brings justification and the assurance of salvation, and having been justified, there is no doubt that we will be glorified and freed from the presence of sin, which is the consummation of our salvation (Rom. 8:28–30). Faith also begins the lifelong process of sanctification by which we are conformed to Christ that continues until the Christian's final glorification in heaven. In other words, everyone who has been justified will certainly be sanctified and glorified, but whereas our justification is complete the moment we believe, our sanctification is an ongoing process that is not completed until we die. Even then, we do not receive our full and final glorification until the resurrection of our bodies, although in heaven we will be free of sin as we await the final resurrection (Rom. 8:1–30). Theologically speaking, salvation refers to the entire work of God's redemption that encompasses predestination, regeneration, justification, sanctification, and glorification, although the biblical writers sometimes use the terms "salvation" and "saved" as synonyms for one of the aforementioned aspects of what the Lord does in redeeming us. For example, when Paul says that "by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast," he is using the term "saved" as a synonym for "justified." By grace we have been justified by faith, which is not our own doing but the gift of God and not the result of our works. yourself. Sanctification is a work of God that includes the cooperative activity of the Christian. However, God's work in His people guarantees that they will cooperate (Phil. 2:12, 13). The Lord never fails to sanctify those whom He justifies. Having changed our hearts in regeneration, our natural and inevitable response is to walk by the Spirit and put sin to death.

A command that balances the exhortation Paul gave Timothy in 4:12. Timothy is not to abuse the authority he possesses, nor to overstep the boundaries of respect that are appropriate for those of advanced age, even when they need correction. encourage. The good minister appeals to other believers with the respect owed to members of one's family.

The final phrase almost certainly focuses on the pastor's relationship to young women, in which increased temptations to impurity may arise. Elsewhere, Paul advises Titus to instruct older men, older women, and younger men directly; but he indicates that older women are to train the young women in godly living (Titus 2:1–8).

Paul now turns his attention to three groups in which problems had apparently arisen in the church at Ephesus: widows, elders, and slaves. 5:3–16 Paul's concern to identify needy widows and to provide for their proper care forms the backdrop for a discussion of the problems of younger widows, some of whom have apparently been influenced by the false teaching at Ephesus (see Introduction: Date and Occasion). 5:3 Honor. That is, care for as well as respect. See Mark 7:9–13. who are truly widows. The care of widows, who frequently had great material needs, is a major theme in the OT (Deut. 24:19–21; Is. 1:17; Jer. 22:3; Zech. 7:9, 10; Mal. 3:5) and was a special concern of the early church (v. 16; Acts 6:1; James 1:27). Paul's designation ("truly widows") means that not every window is eligible for the church's material benevolences. Women whose husbands had died but who had children or other family members to provide for them were not "truly widows" by Paul's criteria here (vv. 4, 8, 16), but only those "left all alone" (v. 5). Also younger widows (under sixty years) who can remarry and so fulfill their callings as wives and mothers should do so, rather than being financially supported by the church (vv. 9–15).
The truly needy widow had no family from which to receive support (vv. 8, 16).

Genuine poverty often drove widows to exemplary lives of prayer and faithful dependence upon God. For such widows, the church is to be the visible hand of God in providing for needs. Note the example of Anna (Luke 2:36–38).
Spiritually dead.
Perhaps a reference not to the whole church, but specifically to the widows.

Some have seen here an official order of widows with duties to perform (vv. 5, 10); others have seen an agreement whereby some widows provide certain services for the church in exchange for material support. More likely the list is simply of widows who are to receive support from the church (v. 16), and whose entire pattern of living has been characterized by the good works that are evidence of living faith in Christ (v. 10). This list probably consists of the larger group of widows dealt with in vv. 3–5. less than sixty years of age. A round number reflecting the expectation in that culture of the age under which remarriage would still be possible (cf. vv. 11–14). the wife of one husband. See note on 3:2.

The verbs in this verse are in the past tense. Paul's concern is not with what the widow might still do for the church but with the pattern of "faith working through love" (Gal. 5:6) that has been seen throughout her life. washed the feet of the saints. A conventional expression of hospitality and self-negating service in a culture where people wore sandals and walked dusty roads (cf. John 13:4, 5). Jesus commanded His disciples to wash each other's feet (John 13:14, 15).

Lit. "when they live sensually." they desire to marry. Such a desire in younger widows is not wrong in itself, nor would remarriage necessarily "draw them away from Christ." In fact, Paul recommends this course (v. 14). It is possible that enrollment on the list of widows is what makes subsequent remarriage a grievous offense that incurs condemnation (v. 12), so such enrollment seems to have entailed a vow of lifelong celibacy in singleness.

This may refer to a vow or pledge of celibacy that was entailed in being enrolled as a widow who would receive ongoing support from the church. Others believe that Paul is referring to younger widows' marriage to non-Christian husbands (1 Cor. 7:39), compromising or even renouncing their basic commitment to Christ (vv. 11, 15). However, 1 Tim. 5 does not overtly address the issue of marriage to unbelievers.
Lit. "those who talk nonsense." This is probably a reference to the false teachings (v. 15; 1:3; 4:7).
See note on 2:15.
Paul gives much attention to widows because some of the younger widows had come under the influence of the false teachers (2 Tim. 3:6, 7).

As with widows, Paul addresses the twin issues of proper honor for elders and how to deal with those who sin. 5:17 elders. See note on 3:1. double honor. The honor befitting the position of leadership as well as financial remuneration. The Gk. term "honor," like the English "honorarium," can refer to a monetary amount (Acts 4:34; 19:19; 1 Cor. 6:20; 7:23). The Scriptures cited in v. 18 enjoin the financial support of the officers who teach the Word and shepherd the flock (see 1 Cor. 9:9–14; Gal. 6:6). especially \... teaching. This seems to refer to two kinds of elders: those who govern the church and those who, in addition, carry out the more specialized ministry of preaching and teaching. Some elders can and should be recognized as ruling well, even though the focus of their ministry is not public exposition of Scripture. This verse is the basis of the distinction between teaching elders and ruling elders. Teaching elders, also known as ordained pastors or ministers, have the primary responsibility of teaching and preaching in their congregations. Ruling elders, on the other hand, are able to teach but spend less time teaching and preaching than teaching elders do even as ruling elders share in the responsibility of governing the church, as well as praying for and caring for the people under their watch.

That Paul cites both Deut. 25:4 (also cited in 1 Cor. 9:9) and a saying of Jesus recorded in Luke 10:7 as "Scripture" is an indication of how Christian writings that were written by the apostles or their closest associates under their authority were early understood to be on the same level of authority as the OT (2 Pet. 3:15, 16).

Throughout Scripture, an accusation of misconduct against any member of God's community must be substantiated by testimony from multiple witnesses (Deut. 19:15; Matt. 18:16; 2 Cor. 13:1; Heb. 10:28). This standard of reliable evidence is all the more essential when charges are brought against an elder, whose office deserves special respect and whose maturity the church has (presumably) verified (3:1–7; 5:22, 24, 25).

Elders who sin (some had apparently become involved in the false teaching, although the application is wider, including character and conduct as well as the content of instruction; 4:16). rebuke them in the presence of all. The influence of an elder's example sometimes requires public rebuke to safeguard others (see Gal. 2:11–14).

Those who will presumably serve as witnesses at the judgment (cf. Matt. 25:31; Rev. 14:10). without prejudging. Elders are not to be condemned on insufficient evidence; nor are they to be exempted from discipline because of their office and authority if their sin is demonstrated.
To participate in the ordination of an elder known to be unqualified is to approve of his sins and to risk sharing the guilt for them. keep yourself pure. See 4:12, 16.

The practice of abstaining from wine as a matter of principle perhaps reflects the influence of the false teachers' concept of purity (4:3). use a little wine \... ailments. Paul recognizes a medicinal value of wine. Believers are free to make use of ordinary means in caring for themselves. It is no mark of faith to reject the advice of doctors or to forego medical treatment.

Although Timothy, other elders, and church members cannot see into others' hearts, the spiritual state of the heart eventually comes to light, for ill or for good. Therefore, the church should call its officers on the basis of their observed behavior, and those officers should hold each other accountable based on what they seen in the actions of one another. The sins of some people \... judgment. Another reference to the importance of care in screening candidates for ordination.
Paul addresses the problem of slaves who have not been showing proper respect for their Christian masters.

Paul returns one last time to the problem of the false teachers, noting especially their divisiveness and their greed. This leads him to reflect upon the proper perspective one should have on material possessions.
Contentiousness was one of the prominent characteristics of the false teachers (1:4; 2 Tim. 2:14, 23; Titus 3:9).
Perhaps some of the false teachers were seeking the position of elder out of greed (v. 10; Titus 1:11).

Christians can be content because their needs are met by Christ (2 Cor. 12:9, 10; Phil. 4:11, 13). great gain. The gain that godliness brings is not financial, since such profit is short-lived and cannot be taken along when we leave this world at death (v. 7). As Timothy is to show those who are financially wealthy, being "rich in good works" means treasuring up "a good foundation" for an eternal future (vv. 17–19).
Paul may allude to Job's expression of submission to God's hard providence when wealth and family were stripped away from him.
The desire for wealth, like the quest for prominence (3:6, 7) and stubborn resistance to truth (2 Tim. 2:25, 26), poses a trap, disguising lethal danger behind appealing appearances.
See note on v. 5.
As he has done previously, Paul follows his comments about the false teachers with personal exhortations to Timothy, concluding with a marvelous doxology.

A metaphor for the Christian life viewed in terms of faithfulness to Christ (2 Tim. 4:7). Take hold of the eternal life. That is, do not become complacent. While faith in Christ begins new life (4:8), the goal of the Christian life is always future (v. 19; 1:16 note; Phil. 3:12; 2 Tim. 4:8). to which you were called. Eternal life is not something we naturally choose, but something to which God supernaturally calls us (Rom. 8:30). good confession in the presence of many witnesses. This probably refers to Timothy's baptism. The "good confession" that one has come to faith in Christ leads naturally into the "good fight" of seeking to live in faithfulness to Him.
This may refer to Jesus' trial before Pilate (Matt. 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3; John 18:33–37; 19:8–11), but it may be an allusion to His calm and voluntary death as well.
Probably a reference to all that Paul has charged concerning Timothy's personal discipline and official duties. the appearing. The second coming of Christ (2 Tim. 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13).
This expression is applied to Christ in Rev. 19:16; cf. 17:14.

As spirit, God is "invisible" to our physical eyes (1:17). Yet God condescends to make His glory visible to sinful human beings while at the same time shielding them from the full manifestation of His divine being, lest they be destroyed by His consuming holiness (Gen. 32:30; Ex. 24:10, 11; 33:18–23; Num. 12:6–8; Is. 6:1–5). Paul refers here to the overpowering radiance of God's divine being in Himself, which we His sinful creatures cannot perceive apart from the mediation of Christ the divine Son (John 1:18; Rev. 22:3–5). In glory, however, once all sin has been removed from us, we will see the Lord as He is and view Him face to face (1 Cor. 13:12; 1 John 3:2).

Having condemned the love of money and affirmed the future orientation of Christian hope, Paul provides an exhortation for those who do find themselves rich in this world (presumably not from greed). 6:17 to enjoy. Christ does not demand that every believer embrace abject poverty and ascetic self-denial. See note on 4:4.

The financial wealth of prosperous Christians is not merely for their personal consumption, but provides resources for them to amass eternal "riches" through generous sharing with others. God blesses His people so that they may be a blessing to others.

See Matt. 6:20. take hold of that which is truly life. See note on v. 12. Generous distribution of one's wealth to meet others' needs does not earn eternal life, but it demonstrates that one's hope has been transferred from "the uncertainty of riches" and placed instead on God, the lavish giver (v. 17).

Paul brings the letter to a close with one final charge to Timothy, once again set within the context of dealing with the false teachers. 6:20 the deposit entrusted to you. That is, the sound doctrine of the gospel (1:10, 11). Timothy is a trustee of God's invaluable treasure, charged to maintain it undamaged and to entrust it unmodified into the custody of future generations of faithful stewards (2 Tim. 1:14; 2:2). what is falsely called "knowledge." The false teachers emphasize "knowledge" (Gk. gnōsis, from which the word Gnosticism is derived; see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues). Paul began his letter by addressing false teaching (1:3–7), and here in vv. 20 and 21 he concludes the epistle by once more addressing false teaching. Thus, the letter is bounded by the conceptual bookends of false teaching, which shows that false teaching is the main occasion that inspired Paul to write this letter. Accordingly, much of what is said in this letter is, in one way or another, related to aspects of the false teaching (on which, see especially the comment on 4:3–4).

2 Timothy.note: One sent out as an eyewitness of the resurrected Christ and as His official representative (2 Cor. 1:1 note). by the will of God. Paul identifies the one who commissioned him, stressing that his apostleship is not due to human appointment or self-appointment (1 Cor. 1:1; 2 Cor. 1:1; Eph. 1:1; Col. 1:1). according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus. The role of the apostle is to proclaim the life that is found in Christ alone (1 Tim. 1:16 note).
See Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion; 1 Cor. 4:17 (cf. note 1 Tim. 1:2). Grace \... our Lord. See note 1 Tim. 1:2.

As in most of his letters (the exceptions are Galatians, 1 Timothy, and Titus), Paul follows his salutation with a section giving thanks to God for the recipients of the letter. Here he focuses on his relationship with Timothy and his confidence in Timothy's faith.
Probably the tears Timothy shed the last time Paul left him. I long to see you. Paul anticipates his request in 4:9, 21.

These women are named only here in the NT. They were Jewish, unlike Timothy's father, a Greek, who apparently had not allowed Eunice to have their son circumcised in infancy (Acts 16:1–3). Nonetheless, Timothy had been taught the sacred Scriptures "from childhood" (3:15), and the seed of God's Word had flourished in Timothy's heart as Paul brought the news of Jesus the Messiah to Lystra. See Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion.

Paul moves into the body of the letter. As he exhorts Timothy to boldness and faithfulness, Paul discusses the gospel and his own role in proclaiming it. 1:6 fan into flame the gift of God. This strong expression suggests that Timothy was being less forceful than he should have been in using the spiritual gift God had given him (1 Tim. 4:14). laying on of my hands. See note 1 Tim. 1:18; 4:14; 5:22.
Or, "cowardice." This strong expression was necessary, given Timothy's natural timidity and the gravity of his situation.
Paul is in prison in Rome (2:9; cf. Introduction: Date and Occasion).

The goal of God's election and calling is the sanctification of His people (Eph. 1:4). not \... grace. This is a marvelous affirmation that salvation is by grace, not by human merit (Eph. 2:8, 9; see Titus 3:4–6). because of his own purpose. God's decree and work of redemption is based solely on His own purpose and good pleasure. Elsewhere, this divine purpose is identified in terms of mercy (Titus 3:5) and love (Eph. 1:4, 5). before the ages began. An affirmation that the divine decree of redemption through Christ is from eternity (Eph. 1:4; Titus 1:2; 1 Pet. 1:20; Rev. 13:8). In this way, Paul underscores this point that our redemption is entirely of grace and not at all in response to or grounded upon our efforts.

Elsewhere Paul consistently applies this term to Jesus' second coming at the end of history (4:1, 8; 1 Tim. 6:14; Titus 2:13), but here it refers to His incarnation in His first coming. our Savior Christ Jesus. Christ is the Mediator of the covenant of grace (Titus 1:4; 2:13; 3:6). who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. That is, through His death and resurrection (Heb. 2:14, 15; Rev. 1:18).
See 1 Tim. 2:7.

Paul is in prison (v. 8; 2:9). Paul's entire ministry has been characterized by suffering for Christ (Acts 9:16; 2 Cor. 11:23–33). I am not ashamed. Having exhorted Timothy not to be ashamed to speak out for Christ (v. 8), Paul presents himself as a model of boldness in the face of suffering (2:8–10; 3:10, 11). The gospel is folly to a perishing world, but God's servants are not ashamed of the gospel because it is the very wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:18–2:5; Rom. 1:16, 17). He had asked for the churches' prayers, that he might not be ashamed of Christ and His gospel but present it boldly in the highest court of the empire (Phil. 1:19, 20; Eph. 6:19, 20). Now, in his second imprisonment at Rome, their prayers are still being answered. that Day. Judgment Day (v. 18; 4:8). what has been entrusted to me. This relative clause reflects the concise Gk. expression, "my deposit," as a reference to the gospel of which Paul has been a steward and trustee. As he completes his own race, Paul knows that God will guard His own word from loss or distortion. Since God will do so by means of His messengers, Paul also charges Timothy, using the same term, to "guard the good deposit entrusted to you" (v. 14).

This theme runs throughout the Pastoral Letters (1 Tim. 1:10 note; 6:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1), although only here does Paul indicate that these health-imparting words are arranged in a "pattern" — a system of interlocking and related truths.
See v. 12 and note on 1 Tim. 6:20.

Paul's concern that Timothy be faithful leads him to set forth specific examples of unfaithfulness and faithfulness. 1:15 all. Paul is probably writing with intentional exaggeration to make sure his readers see the extent of the disloyalty. At the same time, he later expresses his distress over being virtually alone, through a combination of desertion (Demas, 4:10; others, 4:16) and the deployment of faithful colleagues to other places (Crescens, Titus, Tychicus, 4:10, 12). Asia. A Roman province across the Aegean Sea from Greece and today part of western Turkey. Ephesus, where Timothy was serving as Paul's representative, was the leading city of this province. Phygelus and Hermogenes. Not mentioned elsewhere in the NT. Probably Paul mentions them because he had counted on their support.

A member of the church at Ephesus who distinguished himself through his loyalty to Paul (v. 18; cf. 4:19). His proactive readiness, upon arriving at Rome, to find and serve Paul without shame, despite the apostle's chains, is a salutary example for Paul's beloved child Timothy (see v. 8).
Onesiphorus may have come to Rome specifically to aid Paul, as Epaphroditus had earlier traveled there on behalf of the Philippian church (Phil. 2:25–30; 4:18).
The day of judgment (v. 12; 4:8).
Paul again exhorts Timothy to be faithful, beginning with three analogies from everyday life that emphasize wholehearted devotion to a task. 2:1 my child. See note on 1:2.

This statement may therefore refer to Timothy's ordination through the laying on of hands by Paul and a gathering of elders (1:6; 1 Tim. 1:18; 4:14). faithful men who will be able to teach others. Presumably bishops (overseers), that is, elders (1 Tim. 3:1 note; 5:17; cf. Titus 1:7 note).

–7 Paul draws analogies to Timothy's ministry to Christ from three spheres of vocation: military life (vv. 3, 4), athletics (v. 5), and farming (v. 6). Then he summons Timothy to meditate on the implications of these illustrations (v. 7). 2:3, 4 A good soldier of Christ Jesus. Readiness to suffer, loyalty, and a single-minded commitment to please one's commander are demanded of Christ's soldiers. For Paul's other uses of military metaphors for the Christian life, see 4:7; Rom. 13:12, 14; 1 Cor. 9:7; 2 Cor. 6:7; 10:4; Eph. 6:10–20; Phil. 1:27; 2:25; 4:3; 1 Tim. 1:18; 6:12; Philem. 2.
These athletic and farming analogies add a promise of future reward, which is the consummation of our salvation in our glorification (vv. 10–12).

The resurrection of Christ is at the center of Paul's theology (Rom. 4:25; Rom. 6:4–10; 1 Cor. 15:12–22). It is the basis for the hope expressed in vv. 11, 12. the offspring of David. Jesus fulfills God's promise to grant to one of David's descendants an eternal kingship (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Matt. 1:1; Mark 12:35; Luke 1:32, 33; John 7:42; Acts 2:30–36; 13:22, 23; Rev. 5:5). For the association of Christ's resurrection and His descent from David, see Rom. 1:3, 4.

See note on 1:8. the word of God is not bound. In his prior imprisonment, Paul saw his chains actually advance the gospel of Christ (Phil. 1:12–14). Though under house arrest, he spoke the Word "without hindrance" to all who visited him (Acts 28:31).

Those whom God has chosen from before the foundation of the world to be saved (Titus 1:1). the salvation that is in Christ Jesus. The salvation that comes through faith in Christ (3:15). See theological note "Salvation" on p. 2058. eternal glory. This glory is the final, complete salvation of the elect in the new order of God. The saints will have resurrection bodies and transformed human natures (1 Cor. 15:42–49). They will experience fully the triumph of Christ over sin and death, and know fullness of joy in a life secured for them by Christ's death, resurrection, and ascension (v. 11; Matt. 13:43; 1 Tim. 1:16 note; cf. Ps. 16:11).
See note on 1 Tim. 1:15. What follows may be part of an early Christian hymn. If we have died with him. A reference to the believer's union with Christ in His death on the cross (Rom. 6:3–11).

This refers to perseverance in the face of hardship (v. 10). we will also reign with him. A NT image for the eternal glory that Christians receive through Christ (Matt. 19:28; Rom. 5:17; Rev. 3:21; 5:10; 20:4, 6; 22:5). if we deny him, he also will deny us. A sober warning against apostasy, grounded in the words of Jesus Himself (Matt. 10:33).

This is a wonderful affirmation of assurance that although we are called to endure and be faithful, salvation does not rest ultimately on our faithfulness, but upon the perfect faithfulness of Christ (v. 19). he cannot deny himself. Christian hope is rooted firmly in the unchanging character of God (Num. 23:19; Titus 1:2) and His unchangeable redemptive purpose for His elect (Heb. 6:13–20).
One of the characteristics of the false teachers (v. 23; 1 Tim. 1:4; 6:4; Titus 3:9). False teaching "only ruins the hearers," but sound doctrine alone can save and restore its hearers.
The whole counsel of God, with emphasis upon the gospel (2:8, 9; 4:2).
Mentioned also in 1 Tim. 1:19, 20 as one who has made "shipwreck" of his faith. Philetus. Mentioned nowhere else in the NT.

This false belief denied the future bodily resurrection of Christians and affirmed instead that a spiritual resurrection at conversion was the sum total of the Christian's resurrection. Thus, this false belief resulted in an overemphasis on present experience (1 Cor. 15:12–14). Furthermore, to deny a final bodily resurrection is to deny that there is a final reversal of Adam's sin, which not only introduced spiritual death but also physical death. Thus, it is to deny a final salvation of the whole person in an eternal new creation. Consequently, such a teaching is heresy. They are upsetting the faith of some. The doctrines of the false teachers are at odds with the gospel. Timothy must warn the church about them (v. 14).

This statement is a reference to God's elect (cf. 2:10; Titus 1:1). stands. In contrast to those who wander away (v. 18). seal. An expression of ownership and security. The Lord knows those who are his. A quotation of Num. 16:5 (according to the Septuagint). In the OT context, Korah and other rebels insisted that they had the right to demand access to God's presence, but the Lord reasserted His sovereign right to choose Aaron as His high priest to draw near in His most holy place. Inscribed on the people of God is His eternal decree of election (v. 11), which ensures the security of the body of Christ (John 10:29). Let everyone \... depart. Perhaps also inscribed on the membership of God's people is His call to holiness (v. 21), including the repudiation of false teaching. Paul may be paraphrasing, from the same OT context, God's summons to the Israelites to keep their distance from Korah and his comrades (Num. 16:26). In accordance with the Num. 16:26 allusion, the idea is that the false teachers are being exhorted to "depart" from their false teaching (perhaps in line with and developed in 2:25, 26).
These verses provide an example from everyday life of the importance of holiness — being set apart for a noble (godly) task.
See note on 2:14; 1 Tim. 1:3, 4, 6, 7.

This title evokes the image of the servant of the Lord in Isaiah, who treats the bruised reed and smoldering wick with gentleness (Is. 42:1–3, applied to Jesus in Matt. 12:15–21). See also Matt. 11:28–30. Jesus' patience and kindness in response to obstinate opponents project the pattern for those who teach His church.

The Christian must never assume that those who are ensnared by the devil's false teaching are irretrievably lost. The gospel must be proclaimed to all. Notice Paul's concern for the manner in which Timothy is to engage his opponents — with kindness, patience, gentleness, and the other fruit of the Holy Spirit (cf. Gal. 5:22).

Paul continues on the theme of false teaching by turning to an attack on the false teachers themselves, noting their impact upon the church at Ephesus, but concluding with the affirmation that they will not succeed in the end. 3:1 the last days. The era inaugurated by Christ's first advent and completed by His second (1 Tim. 4:1 note).
What makes the false teachers so dangerous is that they appear to be Christians (Matt. 7:15, 21–23).

Paul's point is not that all women are this way, but that some have been especially vulnerable to deception. The false teachers at Ephesus had been especially successful in deceiving women (1 Tim. 2:14; 5:13–15).

According to Jewish tradition, these are the names of two of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses before Pharaoh (Ex. 7; 8). Paul's inclusion of these names in his second letter to Timothy indicates that this Jewish tradition reflects actual history.

With the problem of the false teachers fully in view, Paul once more turns to exhorting Timothy to faithfulness, first in terms of the example that Paul has set (and implicitly that of Timothy's mother and grandmother), and then in terms of confidence in and obedience to Scripture. 3:10, 11 Once again, Paul appeals to his own life, both his faithfulness and his sufferings, as an example for Timothy (1:11–13; 2:8–10).

The NT teaches that Christians should expect persecution and should not be surprised when it comes upon them as they pursue godliness (Matt. 10:17, 18; John 15:20; 1 Pet. 4:12; 5:9). This was the apostles' consistent message when encouraging newly converted believers in newly planted churches (Acts 14:22).
A reference to Timothy's mother and grandmother (1:5), as well as to Paul himself.

According to custom, the Jewish parent was to begin instructing a child in the law when the child reached five years old. you have been acquainted with the sacred writings. The false teachers have been misinterpreting the OT (1 Tim. 1:7; Titus 3:9). Timothy needs to remember the proper instruction he received at the hands of his mother and grandmother. The "sacred writings" here are the books of the OT. The NT did not yet exist as a complete collection. Indeed, some of the NT books had not yet been written. salvation \... in Christ Jesus. The OT, interpreted properly, leads one to understand the central role of Jesus Christ in God's overall plan for His creation (Luke 24:25–27, 44–49; John 5:45–47). This fact confirms both the error and danger of the false teachers' mishandling of the OT law.

The OT (v. 15 note). breathed out by God. This is one of the most important expressions in the NT of the doctrine of the divine inspiration of Scripture. The Bible has been breathed out by the Spirit of God (2 Pet. 1:21). God is the source and ultimate author of Scripture. Though written by human authors, Scripture nevertheless has the full weight of His authority. The Bible, from start to finish and down to its very words, is the inerrant Word of God. The great American Reformed theologian, B.B. Warfield, who taught at Princeton Theological Seminary from 1887–1921, demonstrated that the Gk. term translated "breathed out by God" (theopneustos) refers to all of Scripture and not just portions of it. In other words, the entirety of the canon of Scripture, down to the individual words themselves, were given by God and therefore entirely true. The Bible affirms no errors and is the only infallible source of Christian doctrine.

Paul brings to a conclusion the appeal to Timothy begun in 1:6. 4:1 in the presence of God. Paul mentions witnesses to impress on Timothy the utmost seriousness of the charge, just as elsewhere he invokes God as a witness to emphasize the truth of his assertions (Rom 1:9; 9:1; 2 Cor. 1:23; Phil. 1:8; 1 Thess. 2:5). Christ Jesus, who is to judge. For Christ as the Judge of all, see v. 8; Matt. 25:31–46; John 5:22, 27; Acts 10:42. his appearing. Christ's second coming (cf. v. 8; 1 Tim. 6:14; Titus 2:13).
The whole Word of God, with emphasis upon the gospel (cf. 2:15). in season and out of season. In every situation, whether good or bad, the Word is to be proclaimed.

See note on 1:13. itching ears. Some people have an endless fascination with everything but the truth. They look for and attract false teachers to themselves. they. Presumably a reference to some who are associated with the church.
See note on 1 Tim. 1:4.

A final exhortation to faithfulness, even though others may be turning away. the work of an evangelist. One who announces good news (the evangel, or gospel), particularly to those not yet converted. In Eph. 4:11, evangelists are listed alongside apostles, prophets, shepherds, and teachers as those who bring God's Word. Philip, first ordained to care for widows' material needs, was later sent out to proclaim the gospel in Samaria, to an Ethiopian, and in coastal towns; thus, he is also called an evangelist (Acts 21:8).

Paul's impending death provides the reason for his extended appeal to Timothy (Introduction: Date and Occasion). 4:6 already. Paul accepts the inevitability of his death, even if it may still be several months away. His sense of completion in this second imprisonment differs markedly from his expectation of release to carry on further ministry when he wrote Philippians (Phil. 1:24–26; 2:24). poured out as a drink offering. This metaphor for death (cf. Phil. 2:17) is taken from the language of the OT sacrificial system. A drink offering of wine was poured out in the sanctuary as an offering to God (Num. 15:5, 7, 10; 28:7). Paul understands his impending death as an offering to Christ. my departure. Another metaphor for death (Phil. 1:23). Paul held steadfastly to the hope and assurance of a destination beyond the grave (v. 18; cf. Phil. 2:21–23).

With these three metaphors, Paul signifies the end of his ministry. His concern is not that he has been a success, but rather that he has been faithful to his Lord. He has exhorted Timothy through similar metaphors to be faithful (1 Tim. 6:12; 2 Tim. 2:4).

Perhaps the crown awarded for the faithful life of one who has received the righteousness of Christ through faith (Rom. 3:22). More likely, this is the crown consisting of perfect righteousness — eternal life that is given to the believer as the climax of the process of sanctification (2:10; James 1:12; 1 Pet. 5:4; Rev. 2:10). the righteous judge. Christ in His role as the divine Judge who brings to completion the work He has begun in His elect. that Day. Judgment day (1:12, 18). his appearing. Christ's second coming (v. 1).

Paul now turns to his primary reason for writing the letter: he wants to see Timothy one last time. Paul gives Timothy various instructions regarding his journey to Rome, informs Timothy of his present status, and concludes with a profound expression of trust in his Lord. 4:9 Do your best to come to me. Paul hinted at his desire to see Timothy in 1:4. soon. See note on v. 21.

A coworker present with Paul during his first Roman imprisonment (Col. 4:14; Philem. 24). Thessalonica. A city in the Roman province of Macedonia where Paul had established a church on his second missionary journey (Acts 17:1–10). Crescens. Mentioned nowhere else in the NT, he was apparently another of Paul's coworkers. Galatia. Either a Roman province Paul visited on his first missionary journey (3:11 note), or a region in Asia Minor that Paul visited on his second missionary journey (Acts 16: 6). Titus. Another of Paul's coworkers. See Introduction to Titus: Date and Occasion. Dalmatia. Another name for the Roman province of Illyricum, the westernmost province reached by Paul on his first three missionary journeys (Rom. 15:19).

The "beloved physician," mentioned in Col. 4:14 and Philem. 24, who traveled with Paul throughout much of his second and third missionary journeys (Introduction to Luke: Author). Get Mark and bring him with you. A beautiful example of Christian forgiveness and restoration. John Mark's desertion of Paul and Barnabas during their first missionary journey (Acts 13:13) had occasioned the dissolution of the partnership between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39). Later, Mark regained Paul's favor (Col. 4:10; Philem. 24). Now, at the end of his life, Paul wants to see him, "for he is very useful."

The coworker of Paul, mentioned in Acts 20:4 and Titus 3:12, who carried Paul's epistles to the churches in Ephesus and Colossae during Paul's first Roman imprisonment (Eph. 6:21; Col. 4:7). to Ephesus. Tychicus is to take this letter to Timothy and serve as his replacement.

A heavy woolen garment used for protection against dampness and cold. Paul is anticipating the arrival of winter (v. 21). Carpus. Mentioned nowhere else in the NT. Troas. A port linking the Roman province of Asia with Macedonia across the Aegean Sea (Acts 16:7, 8 note). Paul had traveled through Troas on his second and third missionary journeys (Acts 16:8, 11; 20:5, 6). When Paul was in Troas on this fourth and final journey is not clear. This may have been the place where Paul was arrested and from where he was transported to Rome. books. Likely materials for writing to the churches and/or copies of Paul's writings that he had already sent to his coworkers and the churches under his care. parchments. Parchment is a writing material made from the skins of animals, especially sheep or goats. It is significantly more durable than papyrus. Probably Paul was asking for parts of the OT.

See note on 1 Tim. 1:20. did me great harm. This incident is mentioned nowhere else in the NT. the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. That is, on the day of final judgment (Matt. 16:27; Rom. 2:6; Rev. 22:12).

A preliminary hearing before Paul's actual trial, which he now awaits (Introduction: Date and Occasion). May it not be charged against them. An expression of forgiveness in the face of death reminiscent of Christ (Luke 23:34) and of Stephen (Acts 7:60), whose death Paul had witnessed and approved of in his years of unbelief (Acts 7:58; 8:1).

Paul had learned long ago that he could always depend upon the one who had commissioned him (2 Cor. 12:9, 10; Phil. 4:11–13). the message might be fully proclaimed. This probably refers to Paul's proclamation of the gospel at his preliminary hearing. all the Gentiles might hear. Paul had preached the gospel in a public forum at the center of the Roman Empire. rescued from the lion's mouth. A metaphor for a narrow escape from death, perhaps alluding to Daniel's deliverance from actual lions (Dan. 6). Paul's preliminary hearing resulted in a temporary reprieve. See note on 1 Cor. 15:32.

Paul does not believe that Christ will prevent his physical death (v. 6), but is expressing his absolute trust in Christ (2:13) as the one who purposes to overrule evil for His glory and for the good of His servants. bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. This is the ultimate hope of all who trust in Christ. Death, far from keeping Paul from Christ's kingdom, is the very means of his entrance into the fullness of the blessings of Christ's spiritual kingdom.

As is his custom, Paul closes the letter with personal greetings and a benediction. 4:19 Prisca and Aquila. "Prisca" is a shortened form of "Priscilla," as it is spelled elsewhere in Acts and Paul's letters. She and her husband, Aquila, had been friends of Paul from the time he first visited Corinth on his second missionary journey. They were Jews, and like Paul were tentmakers (Acts 18:2, 3). They had come to Corinth from Rome. Later, they accompanied Paul to Ephesus (Acts 18:18, 19) and hosted a church in their home there for several years before returning to Rome (Rom. 16:3, 4; 1 Cor. 16:19). They had now apparently returned to Ephesus where Timothy was (1 Tim. 1:3). the household of Onesiphorus. See note on 1:16. This greeting indicates that Timothy was still in Ephesus (1:18).

Presumably the same person as Corinth's treasurer mentioned in Rom. 16:23. Corinth. The provincial capital of the Roman province of Achaia. It was visited by Paul on his second and third missionary journeys. Corinth is fifty miles (80 km) west of Athens. Trophimus. A member of the church at Ephesus who accompanied Paul to Jerusalem at the close of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4; 21:29). Miletus. A seaport just south of Ephesus, which Paul visited at the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:15, 17). When Paul visited Miletus on his fourth and final journey is not clear.

Winter weather would prevent travel by ship (see Acts 27:9–12; 28:11). Paul may have felt that if Timothy waited too long, he would not arrive before Paul's execution (v. 9). In any event, he needed his cloak before winter (v. 13). Eubulus \... Pudens and Linus and Claudia. These were Christians in Rome, although none is mentioned elsewhere in the NT.
The Gk. word for "you" is plural (text note). Presumably, Paul intended the letter to be read to the entire church (1 Tim. 6:21 note; Titus 3:15).

Titus.note: Or "slave of God," one who is owned by and who serves God (Rom. 1:1; Phil. 1:1). apostle of Jesus Christ. One sent out as an eyewitness of the resurrected Christ and as His official representative (2 Cor. 1:1 note; 1 Tim. 1:1 note). for the sake of the faith \... godliness. The goal of Paul's apostleship is faith in Christ, which is grounded in knowledge and leads to godly living on the part of God's elect (see Rom. 1:5). Paul does not simply desire to convey information, but to see God's people grow in godliness through a believing reception of the truth he proclaims. Paul will note that the appearing of God's grace in Christ trains believers to renounce evil passions and live godly lives (2:11, 12), devoted to good works (3:4–8). God's elect. Those whom God has chosen to believe in Christ (cf. John 15:16; 1 Cor. 1:26–31; 2 Tim. 2:10).

The blessings secured by Christ that believers experience in part presently, and in full at Christ's return (1 Tim. 1:1, 16 note; 2 Tim. 1:1). who never lies. An affirmation of the complete trustworthiness of God (Num. 23:19). His Word (v. 3) is therefore entirely trustworthy. promised before the ages began. Affirmation of the eternal nature of the divine decree of redemption through Christ (2 Tim. 1:9).
As author of the covenant of grace, God is Savior (2:10; 3:4; 1 Tim. 1:1; 2:3; 4:10).

Titus was a Gentile believer (Gal. 2:1–3). If the epistle to the Galatians was written before the council recorded in Acts 15 (see Introduction to Galatians: Date and Occasion), his conversion was the fruit of Barnabas's and Paul's early ministry in Antioch of Syria (Acts 11:19–30). While ministering in Ephesus, Paul sent Titus on a delicate mission to Corinth, bearing a letter of rebuke that Paul had composed in tears to seek reconciliation with that church (2 Cor. 2:1–4, 13; 7:6–9). Paul trusted Titus to coordinate the collection from Gentile churches for relief of believers in Judea (2 Cor. 8:6, 16, 23; 12:18). Although Paul addresses this letter specifically to Titus, he intends for it to be read to the whole church (3:15 note). true child. Lit. "legitimate son" (1 Tim. 1:2). This probably indicates that Titus was one of Paul's converts. Grace and peace. See note on 1 Tim. 1:2. For Paul, these two blessings summarize the blessings that Christ has secured for His people. Christ Jesus our Savior. As mediator of the covenant of grace, Christ is Savior (2:13; 3:6; 2 Tim. 1:10). Paul uses the title "Savior" interchangeably for both God and Christ throughout this letter (v. 3 note), reflecting the apostle's belief in the deity of Christ (2:13).

Paul moves into the body of the letter. His intention is to instruct Titus regarding how to act as Paul's representative on Crete (Introduction: Date and Occasion). He begins by discussing church organization. 1:5 I left you in Crete. An island in the eastern Mediterranean, south of the Aegean Sea. The ship on which Paul was transported to Rome (in response to his appeal to the emperor) put in briefly at a small harbor on Crete's southern coast, Fair Havens (Acts 27:7–12). It is unlikely, however, that this brief stopover is the background of this epistle, for two reasons: (1) The tasks before Titus after Paul's departure presuppose and follow up on the apostle's evangelistic ministry on Crete. (2) As he writes, Paul is free to travel and expects to winter in Nicopolis, a city on the west coast of Greece (3:12). Paul's and Titus's ministry in Crete probably took place after his release from his first imprisonment in Rome (See Introduction: Date and Occasion). put what remained into order. As the rest of the verse makes clear, what was left unfinished were details pertaining to the organization of the newly formed churches. elders. A group of individuals charged with the spiritual oversight and leadership of a local church (Acts 14:23; 20:17; 1 Tim. 5:17). As v. 7 makes clear, Paul used the term interchangeably with "overseer." Paul discusses the qualifications for overseers in similar terms, yet with some differences, in 1 Tim. 3:2–7. Paul intends neither list to be complete, but simply to indicate the kind of character that those who are qualified to serve as church leaders must possess.
Probably a reference to marital fidelity (1 Tim. 3:2 note).

Paul's casual shift from "elder" to "overseer" shows that he understands the two terms as referring to the same office: "elder" suggesting one's character (spiritually mature) and "overseer" suggesting one's task (Acts 20:17, 28). God's steward. Stewards were slaves (see v. 1) entrusted with authority to manage their masters' estates, and therefore accountable to their masters for the preservation and expansion of their properties (Luke 16:1–13). Paul here extends the metaphor that he applied earlier to his own apostolic ministry (1 Cor. 4:1, 2) to the responsibility of all elders (see Acts 20:28 for the same charge via the shepherding metaphor). greedy for gain. A greedy desire to gain great wealth should not be the motive that drives a man into church leaders (v. 11; cf. 1 Tim. 6:5, 10). However, that does not mean church leaders are required to live in poverty, for Paul calls for remunerating certain church leaders (1 Tim. 5:17).
Or, sensible and sober-minded. The call for self-control is a major emphasis of this letter (2:2, 4–6, 12).

As in his letters to Timothy, Paul is concerned with the transmission of and commitment to sound doctrine in accordance with the gospel (1 Tim. 1:10 note). rebuke those who contradict. Two tasks of the elder that are especially relevant in view of the false teachers on Crete are teaching sound doctrine (1 Tim. 3:2) and refuting that which is false (Acts 20:29, 30).

Paul's mention of the necessity to refute false teaching leads him into a discussion of the false teachers and how Titus is to deal with them. 1:10 those of the circumcision. This is not a reference to Jewish Christians per se, but to those Jewish Christians who understood circumcision to be necessary for the Christian's salvation (Acts 15:1, 5; Gal. 6:12, 13).

This may refer to the false teachers' activity in churches meeting in private homes, thus the necessity for better organization (v. 5). shameful gain. See note on v. 7. what they ought not to teach. Their teaching was not in accord with "sound doctrine" (v. 9).

Paul quotes Epimenides, a sixth-century B.C. poet and religious reformer from the city of Knossos on Crete, who was known for his predictions and wisdom. Paul is not placing Epimenides on the same level as the OT prophets; he is simply appealing to the esteem in which Epimenides was held in the ancient world and confirming the accuracy of Epimenides's observations concerning the ethical defects that were characteristic of his countrymen.
He means the false teachers (2 Tim. 2:25, 26), and probably also their followers.

Perhaps a reference to the kinds of legends about OT figures that are found in many non-canonical Jewish writings (1 Tim. 1:4; 4:7; 2 Tim. 4:4). commands. These are probably related to the false teachers' distinctive and erroneous interpretations of the Jewish law (3:9; 1 Tim. 1:7; 4:3).
The false teachers apparently prohibited the use of certain things that God permits His people to use (1 Tim. 4:3 note). For Paul's response, see 1 Tim. 4:3–5.

The NT teaches that lacking actions consistent with a changed life renders one's faith in Christ suspect (Matt. 7:16–20; James 2:14–16; 1 John 3:17). by their works. Paul condemns not only the doctrine of the false teachers, but also their actions (2 Tim. 3:2–5). Both sound doctrine and actions in accordance with a changed life are necessary for Christians (see 1:1, 2).

Paul now turns to the kinds of things that Titus, in contrast with the false teachers, ought to teach and concludes with a meditation on the grace of God. 2:1 sound doctrine. The term "sound" implies that true doctrine preserves and promotes spiritual health (see 1:9). See note on 1 Tim. 1:10.

As in 1 Tim. 5:1, 2, Paul prescribes instructions to be given to various groups (older men, older women, young women, young men, and slaves) regarding the virtues and behavior that make up the fitting response for each group to the grace of the gospel. 2:2 sober-minded. The quality of sober-mind­ed­ness dominates Paul's advice in this section (vv. 4–6, 12; 1:8 and note).

Older women are to exhibit the spiritual maturity appropriate to their teaching role and are also to exemplify to young women their roles as Christian wives and mothers. teach what is good. Probably, as the next verse suggests, in the sense of their manner in the home.

That is, "bring them to their senses." This is a verbal form of the adjective translated "sober-minded" (v. 2) and "self-controlled" (v. 5) throughout this section. Paul probably has in mind the kinds of problems that some of the younger widows encountered at Ephesus (1 Tim. 5:11–13).

Lit. "sober-minded" (vv. 2, 4, 6, 12; 1:8 note). working at home. Or, "busy at home." This does not forbid their employment elsewhere. Paul is concerned to prevent these women from idleness and being busybodies. Contrast the behavior of some of the younger widows at Ephesus (1 Tim. 5:13). submissive. Part of being "sober-minded" is embracing the order that God has given for the home. See note on 1 Tim. 2:11. that the word of God may not be reviled. Paul's overriding concern throughout this section is that the behavior of Christians reflect positively on the gospel (vv. 8, 10; see 1 Pet. 3:1–6).

Paul gives similar counsel to Timothy (1 Tim. 4:12 note). good works. One of Paul's main themes in this letter from here on (v. 14; 3:1, 8, 14). It is primarily by the doing of good works that believers commend the gospel to non-Christians.

Paul gives instructions to slaves in Eph. 6:5–8; Col. 3:22–25; and 1 Tim. 6:1, 2. Paul does not affirm slavery as a positive good. Instead, he calls slaves and masters to live in God-honoring ways toward one another.

See notes on vv. 5, 7. Whereas Paul's concern in vv. 5 and 8 was to forestall occasions of justifiable criticism from those outside the faith, here he motivates slaves by the positive prospect that their faithful service will display the beauty of the gospel.

These verses provide the theological basis for the practical instructions given in vv. 2–10, showing that the saving grace of God and the redemptive suffering of Jesus Christ are directed toward the purpose of the godly living and good works of God's redeemed people. 2:11 the grace of God. The unmerited favor or compassion of God. has appeared. That is, in the person and work of Jesus Christ (3:4, 6; cf. 2 Tim. 1:10). bringing salvation. God's purpose in extending grace to sinners is their salvation (3:4–7; cf. 2 Tim. 1:9). all people. All types of people, regardless of gender, age, or social class are in view (vv. 2–10; 1 Tim. 2:1–6). See notes on 1 Tim. 2:1, 6; theological note "Definite Atonement" on p. 1875.

The second coming of Christ (1 Tim. 6:14; 2 Tim. 4:1, 8). See theological note "Hope" on p. 2206. our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. In the Greek, this construction identifies the "Savior Jesus Christ" with "our great God." Here Paul explicitly affirms the deity of Christ (cf. Rom. 9:5; John 1:1; 20:28).

That is, on the cross. Paul follows with two purposes of the work of Christ on the cross. redeem us from all lawlessness. Paul's first point focuses on the individual: Christ paid the price necessary to free people from their sins (Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; 1 Tim. 2:6; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19). purify for himself a people for his own possession. Paul's second point focuses on the church: Christ purifies individuals from their sins (Heb. 9:14; 1 John 1:7, 9) so that together they might constitute a people special to Him (Ex. 19:5; Ezek. 37:23; 1 Pet. 2:9). On Christ's purifying the church, see Eph. 5:25–27. zealous for good works. See note on v. 7. Far from fostering complacency, Christ's redeeming grace even more strongly motivates believers' grateful love, expressed in obedience (Luke 7:41–47; 1 Cor. 15:8–10; Phil. 3:7–14).

An appropriate summation of the two dimensions of Paul's charge to Titus in vv. 2–10 and 1:10–16. with all authority. That is, as Paul's representative, and as an elder in Christ's church. Let no one disregard you. See v. 8; 1 Tim. 4:12.

Having provided instructions for specific groups, Paul now gives Titus general counsel, centered around another meditation on the grace of God, on encouraging the people to do "every good work" (v. 1). 3:1 rulers and authorities. On Christian submission to governing authorities, see Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17; cf. 1 Tim. 2:2. every good work. The theme for this section is doing good (v. 8; 2:7 note).
This verse presents a graphic description of human depravity apart from Christ (Eph. 2:1–3; Rom. 1:28–32).
Paul ties our salvation (v. 5) to the work accomplished by Christ at His first advent. The terms "goodness" and "loving kindness" emphasize that our salvation is by grace alone.

Paul's words in v. 3 show that from which believers have been saved. not because of works \... but according to his own mercy. Salvation is by the grace of God, not by believers' own works (v. 6; Eph. 2:8, 9; 2 Tim. 1:9). washing. Spiritual cleansing, of which baptism is the sign and seal (1 Cor. 6:11; Eph. 5:26). of regeneration and renewal. Both words characterize the "washing." "Regeneration" is the new life that begins when a person comes to faith in Christ (John 3:3, 5; 1 Pet. 1:3, 23). In the outworking of salvation, regeneration actually precedes faith. We cannot see, let alone enter the kingdom of God unless He first changes our hearts (John 3:3, 5). Renewal is closely related to rebirth; it signifies the complete transformation of a person's life that begins when one is regenerated (Rom. 12:2; 2 Cor. 5:17). See theological note "Rebirth" on p. 1857. of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit applies to individuals the grace of God that is extended in Christ (John 3:5, 6). Note the Trinitarianism of vv. 4–6. God (the Father) saves us by the regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, who is poured out on us through Christ.

Declared righteous before God (Rom. 4; 5; Gal. 3; 4). by his grace. Left to ourselves (vv. 3, 4), we could never stand righteous before God. The point of vv. 3–7 is that righteousness comes through God's grace alone, and we receive it by faith alone in Christ alone (Rom. 3:21–26). heirs. God's purpose in extending His grace to sinners is not only to save them from eternal judgment, but to make them part of His family through adoption and thus heirs of His promises (Rom. 8:17; Gal. 3:29; 4:7).

See note on 1 Tim. 1:15. The expression points back to vv. 4–7. good works. See note on v. 1. Once again, Paul underscores the necessary connection between professing faith in Christ and devoting one's life to His service in obedience to His commands.

By way of contrast with the instructions he has just given, Paul returns one last time to the problem of the false teachers. Only the gospel — not false teaching — is capable of bringing the blessings and renewal of which Paul spoke in 3:1–8. 3:9 controversies, genealogies. A prominent characteristic of the false teachers was their contentiousness (1 Tim. 1:4; 6:4). Controversy need not be sinful, but "foolish controversies" always are. Biblical genealogies have a vital purpose, demonstrating God's faithfulness in keeping His covenant and His promises throughout the generations, but according to the books of 1 Timothy and Titus, false teachers found ways to distort and misuse these portions of Scripture (3:9; cf. 1 Tim. 1:4). about the law. The law of Moses (1:10 note; cf. 1 Tim. 1:7). unprofitable. To be contrasted with doing what is good, which is "profitable" (v. 8).

Church discipline involves a series of warnings designed to call the sinning brother to repentance (Matt. 18:15–17). For certain types of sins, it is appropriate to withdraw oneself from close fellowship with the recalcitrant person while issuing a loving warning and treating the offender as a brother in Christ (2 Thess. 3:14, 15). However, for those who threaten a congregation's unity, the process of warning leading to excommunication must be considered seriously and carefully. Nevertheless, the purpose of excommunication is ultimately restorative, as seen in 1 Cor. 5:4, 5. The hope is that the person might finally confess their sin and return to the fellowship of the church. division. The false teachers had caused division in the churches (1 Tim. 6:4, 5).

Paul closes the letter with personal instructions to Titus, final greetings, and a benediction. 3:12 Artemas. Mentioned nowhere else in the NT, he was apparently one of Paul's coworkers. Tychicus. A coworker of Paul mentioned in Acts 20:4; Eph. 6:21; Col. 4:7; 2 Tim. 4:12. come to me. Titus's ministry on Crete was nearing its end when Paul wrote his letter to Titus (Introduction: Date and Occasion). Nicopolis. A city on the west coast of the Roman province of Epirus (west of Achaia, in modern-day Albania), on the Adriatic Sea. I have decided to \... winter there. Paul may be in Macedonia, planning to travel southwest to the milder climate of a seaside city.

Probably the bearers of this letter. Zenas is mentioned nowhere else in the NT; he is apparently one of Paul's coworkers. Apollos was a native of Alexandria and noted for his eloquence (Acts 18:24–26). He is best known for his ministry at Corinth (Acts 18:27–19:1; 1 Cor. 1:12; 3:4–22; 16:12).
See note on 2:7. Given Paul's emphasis upon good works as the necessary fruit of the gospel in the lives of the redeemed, this exhortation provides a fitting conclusion to the letter.
Paul apparently intended the letter to be read to the entire church, given that the "you" is plural in Greek and that Paul adds the term "all" (cf. plural "you" in 1 Tim. 6:21; 2 Tim. 4:22).

Philemon.note: Paul knows that he belongs to Christ, and if he is in prison, it is by Christ's permission (Phil. 1:7).

These are probably members of Philemon's household, since they are mentioned in addition to the church. Since Paul calls Archippus "our fellow soldier" (see Phil. 2:25) and instructs the Colossian church to encourage him to fulfill his ministry (Col. 4:17), it appears that Archippus had leadership responsibilities in the congregation hosted in Philemon's home. Apphia may have been Philemon's wife, who bore significant hospitality responsibilities, as did Nympha for a house church in Laodicea (Col. 4:15). in your house. The early Christians met in believers' homes (1 Cor. 16:19; Col. 4:15).
Paul is going to suggest a good work that will call on Philemon's generosity in an important and visible way.

The Gk. word translated "hearts" is used also in vv. 12 and 20 (cf. 2 Cor. 7:15; Phil. 1:8, where the same word is translated into English as "affection"). It emphasizes the emotions more than the usual Gk. word for "heart."

Paul has apostolic authority to command and was instrumental in Philemon's salvation through his preaching of the gospel (v. 19), but he declines to exert coercive pressure. Instead, he prefers to offer persuasion that will lead Philemon to a free decision to extend undeserved mercy to a runaway slave who had wronged him. an old man. Paul appeals for mercy by describing himself as old and in prison. He does this "for love's sake," not for his own sake.
Onesimus is Paul's spiritual son because he was converted through Paul's ministry.

Paul makes a play on words — Onesimus's name means "useful" or "beneficial" (text note). The pun softens the effect on Philemon of having to hear about someone who had injured him. Onesimus had run away and perhaps had stolen something from Philemon (v. 18).

The same term, expressing deep affection that Paul used in v. 7 and will use again in v. 20. Onesimus himself has become so dear to Paul, a spiritual child born to the apostle in his chains (v. 10), that returning Onesimus to Philemon in Colossae will feel to Paul like parting from the very core of his emotional life.
In his letters, Paul appeals more than once to the principle that a voluntary action is of more value than one that is constrained externally (1 Cor. 9:16, 17; 2 Cor. 9:7).

Paul is not necessarily making an overt and direct call Philemon to emancipate Onesimus from slavery, though this may be implicit. The phrase rendered in the ESV as "but more than a slave" may be translated also as "but beyond a slave," the "beyond" referring to Onesimus's being "a beloved brother," whom Philemon could "have back forever" (v. 15). His point is that Onesimus will be to Philemon not only a slave ("in the flesh"), but also a brother in Christ ("in the Lord"), and being such a Christian brother is a higher status than being a slave. The status of "slave" is clearly only temporary, since it does not last "forever," as the status of "beloved brother" does. The gospel transforms and ennobles the entirety of a person's life (even if that person is a lowly slave). So, for example, when a slave becomes a Christian, especially being a slave of a Christian master, that slave is transformed into a Christian brother and is to be treated accordingly. See Introduction: History of Interpretation and Introduction: Special Issues.

Paul is willing to throw his friendship with Philemon into the balance to make sure that Philemon will not refuse his request for Onesimus. As Christ, the sinless one, was made "sin" for Paul, that Paul might be welcomed as righteous by the Father (2 Cor. 5:21), so Paul asks Philemon to impute to the undeserving Onesimus the welcome that is rightly Paul's, while imputing to Paul whatever debt Onesimus owes to Philemon. Paul's offer to pay Onesimus's debts (v. 18) is real but secondary in comparison to the apostle's appeal for reconciliation between the master and the slave, both of whom are now brothers in Christ.
This means that Philemon, like Onesimus, owed his Christian faith to the ministry of Paul.

Philemon had offered such emotional refreshment to many brothers and to Paul previously (v. 7). Now that Paul has identified Onesimus with "my heart" (v. 12), this appeal implicitly includes a request that Philemon extend to his slave the refreshment that he would gladly offer to the apostle.
Paul anticipates being released, which apparently happened (see Phil. 1:22–26; 2:19–24 notes). Whether he ever reached Colossae is not known.
A native of Colossae who had evangelized the city (Col. 1:6–8) and was no doubt well known to Philemon and the congregation he hosted.
Paul's fellow workers in his imprisonment, from whom he brought greetings at the close of the epistle to the Colossians. See Col. 4:10, 14 notes.

Hebrews.note: The prologue introduces the two time periods in God's speaking to His people: "Long ago" (v. 1) and "these last days" (v. 2). The Son's coming marks our time period as the "latter days" of salvation promised through the prophets (Jer. 23:20; Hos. 3:5; Mic. 4:1; cf. 1 Cor. 10:11). 1:1 at many times. The piecemeal character of prophetic revelation showed its incompleteness, just as the repetition of animal sacrifices showed that they could not remove guilt (10:1). in many ways. These ways included visions, dreams, and prophetic sayings (Num. 12:6–8, alluded to in 3:5). God spoke. An important theme in Hebrews (2:2, 3; 4:12; 6:5; 11:3; 12:25).

This revelation is qualitatively superior to that given through the prophets. Moses, the greatest prophet, was only a servant in God's house; Christ is "over God's house as a son" (3:6). The Son speaks, as the prophets did, but speaks as the Son whose revelation is final. heir of all things. The Son's supremacy will be displayed at the end of history, for "all things were created \... for him" (Col. 1:16). He is the firstborn (v. 6), the preeminent heir, whose enemies will be put under His feet (v. 13, citing Ps. 110:1). The "last days" have been inaugurated by Jesus, beginning the fulfillment of the Ps. 2 prophecy that God's "Son" would inherit the "nations" and the "earth" (Ps. 2:7, 8). As God's adopted sons through Christ Jesus, we are likewise heirs (v. 14; 6:12, 17; cf. Gal. 4:6, 7; Rom. 8:14–17). through whom \... he created the world. The Son's supremacy was displayed at the dawn of history, for "by him all things were created" (Col. 1:16; cf. John 1:3). The Gk. word rendered "world" is lit. "ages" (also "universe" in 11:3), highlighting the successive periods of history in the created order. Verses 10–12 quote Ps. 102:25–27 as testimony to the Son's role in creation and His eternal permanence, in contrast to the created universe.

The Gk. word rendered "radiance" describes divine wisdom personified in the Jewish intertestamental book Wisdom of Solomon (7:25–28). But Hebrews speaks not merely of a personified divine attribute, but of a divine person — the Son of God — who entered history to purify sinners. exact imprint of his nature. This verse expresses both the Son's oneness with the Father and the distinction of divine persons. As One whose being corresponds exactly to the Father, the Son accurately reveals the Father. Christ is "the image of the invisible God" (Col. 1:15), through whom we see the Father (John 14:9; 2 Cor. 4:4–6). upholds the universe by the word of his power. The Son's command holds the created order in existence (Col. 1:17; 2 Pet. 3:4–7), preserving it from destruction until that day when His voice will remove all but the unshakable kingdom of God and its heirs (12:26–28). purification for sins. A change of verb tense focuses attention on the Son's atoning death in history, the priestly act that cleanses us to worship in God's presence (9:14). sat down at the right hand \... on high. The Son's enthronement at God's "right hand" in heaven, promised in Ps. 110:1 (1:13), reveals His superiority in two ways. At the "right hand" of the Majesty, Christ is ministering in the true, heavenly sanctuary and not an earthly copy (8:1, 2, 5). Second, He "sat down" because His sacrificial work (unlike that of Levitical priests) was finished once for all (10:11, 12).

This is proved by the series of OT quotations that follow (vv. 5–14). inherited \... more excellent. The eternal Son took on a human nature to rescue us from sin and death (2:14, 15). Having for a time voluntarily taken a position "lower than the angels" (2:7), He is now in His resurrection and ascension "declared to be the Son of God in power" (Rom. 1:4) to save His people (v. 5 note). Christ's exaltation thus inaugurates a new phase of His messianic and redemptive Sonship, and gives Him a dignity far above that of angels.

The series of quotations begins with examples from the Psalms (v. 5, from Ps. 2:7, which further develops the Ps. 2 allusion from v. 2), the Prophets (v. 5, from 2 Sam. 7:14; in the Hebrew Bible the books of Samuel are counted with the Prophets), and the Law (v. 6, from Deut. 32:43). Verse 6 is probably from the Septuagint of Deut. 32:43, though it also recalls Ps. 97:7. 1:5 You are my Son. The Father's decree declaring the Messiah to be His Son is identified with Christ's exaltation (v. 4 note; 5:5; cf. Acts 13:32–35; Rom. 1:4). Though Jesus is the eternal and divine Son of God (Mark 1:11; John 3:16), the declaration of redemptive Sonship prophesied in Ps. 2:7 was conferred on Him in time, when He completed His messianic work. Believers cannot become divine and share in Christ's eternal divine Sonship, but their adoption as sons of God means that they participate in Christ's redemptive Sonship through union with the "founder of their salvation" (2:10; 3:14 note; cf. Rom. 8:29).

The storm clouds of Ps. 104 adorn the Lord's heavenly court. "Winds" and "flame" associate angels with the created world's mutability in contrast to the Son's eternal permanence (vv. 10–12). ministers. In contrast to the Son's royal enthronement (vv. 8, 9), the angels are merely "ministers," or "servants."

From Ps. 45:6, 7. The one who addresses the Son with the words "O God" is Himself "God, your God." In the Psalm, the address is to the human Davidic king, who derives authority from God and is associated with God Himself because he exercises God's authority (much like Moses in Ex. 7:1, of whom God said, "I make you God to Pharaoh," highlighting that Moses was speaking God's authoritative word to the Egyptian king). However, Christ is greater than David; He not only has authority from God, but He Himself is God, so that the Davidic kings who reigned before the incarnation point to Him as greater than they. The Son is God, and yet distinct from the Father (John 1:1).
On the Son as Creator, see v. 2 and note.
The Son's unchanging eternity as God is essential to His high priesthood (7:3, 23, 24). Through Him, the inheritance of believers is secure forever (10:34; 12:27, 28; 13:14).
This verse makes virtually the same point as v. 11, except the emphasis is upon Christ's unchanging nature in contrast to the changeable creation.

The Son's position of heavenly authority (v. 3; 8:1) is contrasted to the angels' role as servants to "those who are to inherit salvation" (that is, who share as co-heirs in the Son's rights as heir; vv. 2, 5; 2:10; 6:12; cf. Rom. 8:17, 29). The angels are servants to Christ, but also to His people, who inherit salvation through union with Him. In this, His people are favored above the angels (2:16; cf. 1 Cor. 6:3).
Cf. similar exhortations in 3:12–14; 4:1, 11; 6:11, 12; 10:22–25; 12:1–13; and especially 12:25–29, another reminder of Sinai.

The argument is from the lesser to the greater, as in 1:8, 9. If what the angels said was "reliable," then what comes from One superior to angels must be more so. The Gk. word for "reliable" is legal terminology, as is "witness" in v. 4. 2:2 declared by angels. The role of the angels in the giving of the law is suggested in Deut. 33:2 and became a standard element of both Jewish and Christian descriptions of the events that happened at Sinai (Acts 7:53; Gal. 3:19). just retribution. Illustrated in 10:28, 29 (cf. 6:6). Violators of the Lord's covenant were purged from the covenant community through death.

These terms are used in the NT for the special miracles that God used to demonstrate the authority of the Savior (Acts 2:22), as well as to certify the ministries of the apostles and Stephen (Acts 6:8; 14:3; Rom. 15:19; 2 Cor. 12:12).

The author uses the contrast between angels and human beings in v. 5 to point to the way that the Son, in assuming a full and complete humanity (vv. 14, 17), restores man's dignity and divinely intended place in creation.

Such vagueness in scriptural references is characteristic of the author of Hebrews, who stresses the divine authorship of Scripture more than he does the human authors (e.g., 1:5, 7, 8; 2:12; 3:7; 4:3; 5:5, 6). This way of citing a well-known OT proof text (Ps. 8:4–6) about man in creation is evidence for the Jewish background of the recipients (though Gentile God-fearers associated with the synagogue would have been similarly familiar with the OT).
Ps. 8 describes the glorious status of man as the head of all creation. But it is obvious that man is far from enjoying any such status, and some explanation is required.

Jesus has the crown of glory and honor. It must now be shown that He received it as a man, and so can satisfy the words of the psalm quoted. This psalm about the ideal eschatological (last, final) Adam has found its complete realization in Jesus, in His earthly ministry, death, and resurrection. made lower. The expression can refer to status or to time (i.e., "a little later," Luke 22:58; Acts 5:34). If it connotes status, it alludes to Jesus' choosing not exercise all of His prerogatives as the preincarnate divine Son and then assuming human flesh (cf.
